# The OpenAI Board Ousts Sam Altman, November 2023

As reported on November 18, 2023, the OpenAI board had ejected billionaire and AI evangelist Sam Altman from his CEO role after an apparent vote of no confidence. The board's exact wording in a release issued that afternoon: Altman's "departure follows a deliberative review process by the board, which concluded that he was not consistently candid in his communications with the board, hindering its ability to exercise its responsibilities."

What followed was a whirlwind four days for OpenAI, the generative AI poster child behind the smash hit ChatGPT. The board ousted CEO and co-founder Altman and demoted president and co-founder Greg Brockman, who subsequently resigned, paving the way for what looked like a mutiny by staff insisting the founders be reinstated post-haste. By the time TechCrunch wrote again on November 21, 2023, Microsoft had already hired Altman and Brockman to head up a new internal AI unit — though, as things transpired, nothing had actually been signed yet, with rumors suggesting the ousted leaders might actually return to OpenAI after all, in some capacity at least.

TechCrunch cautioned on November 18 that the full truth would not be known for a long time, as the characters in the drama are likely to be NDA'ed up. Per various whispers and leaks, an all-hands meeting about the situation that afternoon did not produce any revelations beyond banal reassurances that the company is fine and they will get a fresh CEO soon.



---


# The OpenAI Board's Firing Of Sam Altman

ChatGPT-maker OpenAI said on Friday, 2023-11-17, that it had pushed out its co-founder and CEO Sam Altman after a review found he was "not consistently candid in his communications" with the board of directors. "The board no longer has confidence in his ability to continue leading OpenAI," the artificial intelligence company said in a statement. Mira Murati, OpenAI's chief technology officer, would take over as interim CEO effective immediately while the company searched for a permanent replacement.

OpenAI declined to answer questions on what Altman's alleged lack of candor was about; the statement said only that his behavior was hindering the board's ability to exercise its responsibilities. Altman posted on X that Friday: "i loved my time at openai. it was transformative for me personally, and hopefully the world a little bit. most of all i loved working with such talented people. will have more to say about what's next later."



---


# Sam Altman's Rise As The Face Of Generative AI

In the year since Altman catapulted ChatGPT to global fame, he became Silicon Valley's sought-after voice on the promise and potential dangers of artificial intelligence, and his sudden and mostly unexplained exit brought uncertainty to the industry's future. He helped start OpenAI as a nonprofit research laboratory in 2015, but it was ChatGPT's explosion into public consciousness that thrust him into the spotlight as a face of generative AI — technology that can produce novel imagery, passages of text and other media. On a world tour in 2023 he was mobbed by a crowd of adoring fans at an event in London.

He has sat with multiple heads of state to discuss AI's potential and perils. On Thursday, 2023-11-16, he took part in a CEO summit at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation conference in San Francisco, where OpenAI is based. At OpenAI's first developer conference the week before, Altman was the main speaker, showcasing a vision for a future of AI agents that could help people with a variety of tasks; days later he announced the company would have to pause new subscriptions to its premium version of ChatGPT because it had exceeded capacity.



---


# Altman's Argument On AI's Promise And Existential Risk

Sam Altman predicted that AI will prove to be "the greatest leap forward of any of the big technological revolutions we've had so far."

He paired that claim with its counterweight rather than leaving it alone: he also acknowledged the need for guardrails, calling attention to the existential dangers future AI could pose.



---


# Greg Brockman Departure From OpenAI

OpenAI's longtime president and co-founder Greg Brockman was first removed as chairman of the board and then resigned from the company outright, citing "today's news" — the firing of Sam Altman on Friday, November 17, 2023.

By Brockman's own account, he got a text from OpenAI chief scientist and co-founder Ilya Sutskever shortly after noon on the Friday asking for a quick call. After Brockman sent a Google Meet link, he was told that he was being removed from the board as chairman "but was vital to the company and would retain his role" as president, and that Altman had been fired. Brockman then announced his resignation from OpenAI, sending a memo internally and publishing the text on X: "After learning today's news, this is the message I sent to the OpenAI team." He also posted jointly with Altman that "Sam and I are shocked and saddened by what the board did today," thanking the people they had worked with at OpenAI, their customers and their investors, and saying they were "still trying to figure out exactly" what had happened.

Brockman's account also places events the day before, on November 16: according to his post on X, Sutskever texted Altman on the Thursday evening about scheduling a Friday noon call, and Brockman alleges that Mira Murati, OpenAI's CTO and now interim CEO, was informed on Thursday night that Altman would be fired. Three senior OpenAI researchers resigned after Brockman, including director of research Jakub Pachocki and head of preparedness Aleksander Madry.



---


# OpenAI Employee Revolt And Sutskever's Reversal

Nearly 500 of OpenAI's roughly 770 employees signed a letter saying they might quit unless the startup's board resigned and reappointed the ousted Sam Altman — a number that climbed to over 650 later that Monday — and, remarkably, the signatories included Ilya Sutskever, the chief scientist who had taken part in the removal.

Sutskever publicly reversed himself, publishing a post on X suggesting that he regretted his decision to remove Altman and that he would do everything in his power to reinstate Altman as CEO: "I deeply regret my participation in the board's actions. I never intended to harm OpenAI. I love everything we've built together and I will do everything I can to reunite the company." This was a reversal of the position he had taken days earlier. At an OpenAI all-hands meeting on the Friday afternoon, Sutskever had defended Altman's ouster, dismissing suggestions that pushing Altman out amounted to a "hostile takeover" and claiming that it was necessary to protect OpenAI's mission of "making AI beneficial to humanity."



---


# OpenAI Board Composition And The Helen Toner Dispute

At the time of Sam Altman's ouster in November 2023, OpenAI's board of directors consisted of OpenAI chief scientist Ilya Sutskever, Quora CEO Adam D'Angelo, tech entrepreneur Tasha McCauley, and Helen Toner, the director of strategy at Georgetown University's Center for Security and Emerging Technology — and a clash between Altman and Toner is reported to have contributed to the crisis.

The New York Times reported that, before his ousting, Altman made a move to push out board member Helen Toner because he thought a paper she had co-written was overly critical of OpenAI. That, among other issues, led to OpenAI's predicament. The Times also indicated that negotiations to hire Altman back were continuing, but that one major sticking point remaining was "guardrails" intended to improve Altman's communication with the board.



---


# Sam Altman's Side Ventures: Helion, Retro And Worldcoin

Altman has a number of possible next steps after leaving OpenAI, because even while running the company he placed large bets on several other ambitious projects.

Among them are Helion Energy, for developing fusion reactors that could produce prodigious amounts of energy from the hydrogen in seawater, and Retro Biosciences, which aims to add 10 years to the human lifespan using biotechnology. Altman also co-founded Worldcoin, a biometric and cryptocurrency project that has been scanning people's eyeballs with the goal of creating a vast digital identity and financial network.



---


# Analyst Assessment Of Altman's Departure Impact

Gartner analyst Arun Chandrasekaran argued that Altman's exit "is indeed shocking as he has been the face of" generative AI technology — the ground for the shock being his public role rather than any operational gap.

Chandrasekaran qualified the consequence for the company itself: OpenAI still has a "deep bench of technical leaders," but its next executives will have to steer it through the challenges of scaling the business and meeting the expectations of regulators and society.

qid: Are the U.S.-headquartered venture capitalists mentioned in the TechCrunch article investing more in Chinese companies compared to the previous year, or are Investors, as reported by the Financial Times, showing a decreased interest in Japan for similar reasons?
context:
# Capital Rotation from China into Japanese Assets

One of the most significant changes, according to asset managers quoted by the Financial Times on 1 October 2023, is a fundamental shift in the way global funds now look at China — and the mechanism runs directly to Japan's benefit. The geopolitics of US-China tensions, chip wars, decoupling and "friendshoring" seem in particular to be working significantly in Japan's favour: Asia-focused global investment is rotating out of China and into Tokyo stocks, real estate and other assets, just as large parts of corporate Japan are engaging more actively with shareholders than at any time in the past.

The push side of the model is China's loss of sheen after years of stunning growth and investor attention. Its economy is growing more slowly and the expected post-pandemic rebound is proving elusive. On top of that, Beijing's policymaking — with sudden crackdowns on entire industries such as video games and private tutoring — has generated a series of nasty surprises and the unshakeable fear that others could occur at any time.

"You are seeing more interest in Japan from investors, who were primarily invested in China, as China has slowed and some of its economic policies have been confusing and opaque," says Kirk Neureiter, president of Fidelity Management & Research Japan. "Deployment of capital to China has been a bit more risky in terms of eventual outcome of investment decisions, given that lack of clarity." He qualifies the model's range: interest in Japan has not only come about because of the push away from China.



---


# Renewed Global Investor Interest in Japanese Equities

Global investors' interest in Japan was sharply heightened in late 2023, but many funds found themselves short of the expertise to act on it. Tokyo conference guests were told by various experts that the stars do appear aligned in Japan's favour, both on its own merits and in comparison with what is happening around it — yet because so many global funds have diverted expertise away from Japan in recent years, they are concerned that they need to know more, as a matter of urgency.

"There is heightened interest in Japan after what has been, for many, a long period of not being focused on that country," says Paul Hitchens, head of the Japan research department at Jefferies, which hosted a major investor conference in Hong Kong. He names distinctive catalysts: a recent push by the Tokyo Stock Exchange for companies to improve their capital efficiency, and Warren Buffett's high-profile decision to invest heavily in five of Japan's largest trading houses. "Is there some healthy scepticism? Yes. However, global investment firms know that they need to invest and build their offerings in Japan to meet the growing appetite, and that they need to pay attention to an equity market at a 33-year high."

The market backdrop reinforced the urgency: Topix, Japan's main stock index, had risen more than 25 per cent in 2023 to the date of this Financial Times report, outperforming almost all the world's developed market indices and, as some conference attendees admit, creating a "fear of missing out" on a rally that may have significantly further to go.



---


# The Decline In US VC Investment In China: The Data

China's USD investors continue to deploy capital in industries that are not in the crosshairs of U.S.-China competition, but overall their activity has dwindled significantly due to the changing regulatory and geopolitical currents, coupled with a slowing economy.

The year 2022 saw just $14.5 billion invested in Chinese companies by U.S.-headquartered VCs, compared to $45.4 billion the year before, according to a report from research firm PitchBook. The number of deals nearly halved to 595, and the share of deals with U.S. investor participation dropped to 18.2% in 2022 after hovering above 30% for half a decade.

The scaleback is most notable in prolific investors like Sequoia Capital China, which recently changed its name to HongShan after splitting off its China operation; despite its proactive move to decouple, Sequoia still faces scrutiny from the U.S. government over its decades of activity in China. For the first three quarters of 2023, HongShan completed just 47 deals, compared to 99 deals in the same period of 2022, according to Crunchbase data.



---


# Kishida's Pitch to Global Investors 2023

Japanese prime minister Fumio Kishida was preparing, in the week of 1 October 2023, to make his strongest ever push for a bet on Asia's biggest advanced economy, as BlackRock founder Larry Fink and other heads of global funds gathered in Tokyo for a series of events to attract investment. "I would urge you to evaluate what we are doing in my country, look at the underlying strength of our economy and our plans for the future and then invest in Japan," Kishida said in a recent speech at the Economic Club of New York.

The pitch followed a month of conferences on the same question. Throughout September, in Tokyo, New York, Hong Kong and London, the world's biggest investment banks hosted a series of conferences for the world's biggest investors, all gravitating around the theme of whether Japan is really back. The events were run by JPMorgan, Goldman Sachs, Bank of America, Mizuho, BNP Paribas and Jefferies, and according to both attendees and hosts the answer is now clearer than it has been in a very long time: Japan is back, but global investors may take a little more persuasion that it is truly back for the duration.



---


# The USD Fund Copycat Playbook In China

USD-denominated funds in China have long operated on a benchmark model: draw inspiration from Silicon Valley startups and use them as templates for investment targets back home. They would seek out the equivalents of Facebook, Amazon and Uber on the other side of the Pacific Ocean and hope they become winners in the country's largely untapped internet market.

The range over which that model worked was two decades. Since their entry into China in the late 1990s, American venture capital firms — led by powerhouses like Sequoia Capital, IDG Capital and GGV — have played a major role in funding high-risk, high-reward startups in the country's consumer internet sector.

The relationship now hangs in the balance as changes at home and abroad diminish the pool of investment opportunities for outside financiers. This dealmaking strategy of American funds in China has become less effective in the face of shifting global and domestic landscapes; driven by a confluence of factors, from China's crackdown on the tech industry to escalating U.S.-China tensions, some of these investors are now turning their gaze to opportunities abroad, tracing the footsteps of a new generation of Chinese-founded startups that are expanding overseas.



---


# The Outlook For US-China VC Dealmaking

There are no signs that USD funds' dealmaking in China will bounce back to its heights in the foreseeable future. The PitchBook report predicts that VC activity with U.S. participation in China during 2023 will hit a nine-year low, followed by a decade low in 2024.

Many Chinese general partners have already been sourcing capital from the Middle East, which might eventually limit the impact of U.S. investors' pullback. But the open question is whether Chinese tech firms, now under a new stringent regulatory regime, can deliver the same level of strong growth and returns they experienced in the previous laissez-faire era.

If the U.S. market turns out to be too challenging to penetrate due to competitive and geopolitical factors, there are still other markets to explore. Japan, known for its openness to new technologies, has been particularly popular among China's SaaS startups venturing abroad; sniffing opportunity, China's USD fund managers, still anchored in the Middle Kingdom, will likely follow them to the neighboring country or any other market that will help hedge against uncertainties presented at home and abroad.



---


# Why USD Funds Follow Chinese Founders Abroad

The claim is that the diaspora financing gap is the natural hunting ground for USD fund managers looking beyond China. "It's just a lot easier to raise their first round from China's USD funds," said a former investor at one of China's top VC firms. "In some sense, the entrepreneurs are taking these investors on an international expedition."

The grounds for why they cannot simply compete for American deals instead are twofold. Besides the low-hanging fruit of the diaspora community, Chinese VCs flying in from Beijing and Shanghai have limited avenues to source deals in the U.S.: American startups are courted by a plethora of local investors, let alone the geopolitical risks of accepting Chinese-managed money. These parachuting investors also run into competition from local investors already tailored to U.S.-China cross-border opportunities, most famously UpHonest Capital.

The warrant is a claim about what venture investing actually depends on: "VCs thrive on information arbitrage. In the U.S., we don't really have that same extensive network as at home," said an investor from the China arm of a global VC firm who now spends a third of their time abroad. Lacking that network locally, the diaspora is where their information advantage still holds.



---


# Faction Driverless Funding Round

Faction, the driverless tech developer, raised an undisclosed amount in a round led by TDK Ventures, TechCrunch reported on 2023-10-30. Ducera Partners, Trucks Venture Capital and Fifty Years also joined the round.

# Betting The Other Majors And Team Golf Events

The US Open, PGA Championship and British Open — often referred to as The Open Championship — are among the four major championships in professional golf alongside the Masters, and each has unique course challenges and attributes that create many betting opportunities. The most popular markets for these events are to win; top 5, 10, 20 and so on; head-to-head matchups; nationality; first round leader; hole-in-one props; and top amateur.

Team golf events such as the Ryder Cup and the Presidents Cup offer a thrilling twist to tournament viewing. Bettors can choose from betting on the winning team, on outcomes of individual matches, or on prop bets such as which team scores highest in a round, who makes more birdies, or even the best-dressed team captain.

When placing bets on these events, evaluating each team's strengths and weaknesses is vital, and the factors to consider include recent player form, their history on the event's course, and any potential impacts such as injuries.



---


# The Bet Types Available In Golf Betting

Golf bets are typically placed on professional tournaments, including PGA and DP World Tour events, and the popular options are a distinct set of market types. Bet to Win means picking a specific golfer to win the entire tournament. Betting Against the Field means wagering on a golfer to outperform the rest of the players. Head-to-Head Bets involve choosing between two golfers on which will finish with a superior score. Each-Way Bets are dual bets where one part is on the golfer to win outright and the other on them finishing within a set range of places, often top 5 or top 10. First-Round Leader bets on who will lead after the first round.

The remaining markets extend the same logic. Top 10/Top 20 Bets wager on a golfer to finish within the top 10 or 20 players. Win/Place Bets are similar to each-way bets but might cover more places. Matchup Bets pick which golfer from a specific pair will have the better tournament performance, while Group Matchups bet on which golfer from a pre-selected group will fare best. Nationality Bets wager on a winning golfer hailing from a certain country. Prop Bets are special bets such as predicting whether a golfer will score a hole-in-one.

Golf betting has surged in popularity, especially live golf betting, which allows fans to bet on every shot and hole for PGA Tour events, The Match, the Ryder Cup and more; sports betting apps and live streaming have made it easier and more exciting, letting you bet on golfers live as the round unfolds with just a few taps.



---


# Moneyline Outcomes: Win, Loss, Draw And Push

A moneyline wager can end in several ways: the most straightforward outcomes are a win or a loss, determined by whether the team or individual you backed was victorious or defeated, and there is also the possibility of a draw if the event ends in a tie. Winning is simply a matter of picking the eventual winner — bet on Boxer B in a bout between Boxer A and Boxer B, and if Boxer B wins you are paid based on the odds at the time you placed the wager. A loss means the side you backed did not win: bet $100 on Team A in an NBA game and, if Team B wins, the bet on Team A loses.

Some sports price the draw as its own selection. In soccer especially, games can end in a draw and bettors can wager on that outcome, so a moneyline typically shows three sets of odds — one for each team to win and one for the draw. For a match between Team A and Team B, the odds might read Team A +150, Draw +220, Team B +180; a $100 wager on "Draw" that lands returns $220 in profit on top of the $100 stake, totaling $320, while a win by either team loses the $100.

A tie handled as a "push" is a different case, and the scope condition matters. When a push occurs bettors are refunded their original wager, with no money won or lost; but sports that typically allow a tie, like soccer, often offer the draw as a bet instead, and if the game ends in a draw and you did not bet that option, you lose. It is therefore essential to understand the specific rules of the sportsbook and the sport to know how ties are handled. Finally, in most sports and with most sportsbooks — including new betting sites — overtime or any extra time or tiebreakers do count toward a moneyline bet, though you should always check your sportsbook's specific rules.



---


# Why Moneyline Odds Change

Lines at sports betting apps change quickly for two primary reasons — public betting and new information — and sportsbooks adjust moneyline odds to stay profitable, balance their book and reflect the most current information about an event. Before setting odds oddsmakers gather extensive data, then release the finalized odds to the public; from that point a bettor can bet immediately or wait for shifts, though predicting those shifts is challenging.

The time dimension shows how an opening price drifts. Odds for the next Super Bowl champion released shortly after the previous Super Bowl are based mostly on the recently concluded season; as the new season approaches and teams make changes, the odds adjust to perceived championship chances, and as games progress the lines keep evolving with team performances.

The mechanism has five named drivers. Public betting patterns move a line because, when a significant amount of money lands on one team or participant, sportsbooks adjust the odds to balance their liability — making the price less favorable for the heavily-bet side and more favorable for the less-bet side to encourage even betting and reduce financial risk. New information matters because changes in player injuries, player substitutions or weather conditions alter the perceived outcome, and books adjust once such information becomes public. Professional bettors move lines because large wagers from sharp bettors often reflect insights or information that can influence the odds. Initial miscalculation is a fourth driver: sometimes the opening odds are perceived as offering value, and heavy betting on one side signals that the initial price was potentially "off," prompting an adjustment. Event dynamics is the fifth, applying to live betting placed while the event is in progress, where the evolving dynamics of the match lead to frequent changes.



---


# Moneyline Odds Examples By Sport

Typical moneyline prices look the same across sports — a minus number on the favorite, a plus number on the underdog — but the shape of the market varies with the sport, most obviously where draws or large fields exist. In an NFL game between the Dallas Cowboys (-130) and the New York Giants (+110), the Cowboys are the favorites: a $130 bet on Dallas returns $100 profit if they win, while a $100 wager on the Giants earns $110 profit on an upset. An NBA game between the Los Angeles Lakers (-150) and the Miami Heat (+130) works the same way, with $150 on the Lakers profiting $100 and $100 on the Heat profiting $130.

Baseball and hockey illustrate slight favorites and even money. For an MLB game with the New York Yankees at -120 and the Boston Red Sox at +100, the Yankees are slight favorites — a $120 bet returns $100 profit — while the Red Sox are at even odds, so a $100 bet also returns $100 profit. For an NHL game with the Toronto Maple Leafs at -140 and the Chicago Blackhawks at +120, $140 on Toronto profits $100 and $100 on Chicago profits $120.

Soccer adds a third selection. In an MLS match between the Seattle Sounders (+110), the Draw (+230) and Atlanta United (+140), neither team is a clear favorite though the Sounders have slightly better odds: $100 on Seattle profits $110, $100 on the draw profits $230 if the match ends tied, and $100 on Atlanta profits $140. In soccer, the possibility of a draw is a common outcome to bet on, which is different from many other major sports.

Combat sports, tennis and golf round out the pattern. A UFC fight between Conor McGregor (-200) and Dustin Poirier (+170) pays $100 profit on a $200 bet on McGregor and $170 profit on a $100 bet on Poirier. A tennis match between Serena Williams (-150) and Maria Sharapova (+130) makes Williams the favorite, with $150 on her profiting $100 and $100 on Sharapova profiting $130. PGA Tour odds price individual golfers to win a tournament — Tiger Woods +500, Rory McIlroy +600 — so a $100 bet profits $500 or $600 respectively; in golf, with usually many players in the field, the odds can be much higher than in head-to-head matchups.



---


# Live In-Play Golf Betting

Live betting offers the opportunity to bet on golf tournaments as they unfold, with the main options covering the overall tournament victor, winners of individual rounds, and direct head-to-head matchups. Using a sportsbook app streamlines the process and gives immediate access to fluctuating, real-time odds.

The most lucrative live bets in golf often revolve around backing players who have had a slow start but have the talent to stage a comeback.

The live odds set by sportsbooks for golf events are determined by continually evaluating player performance alongside considerations such as course dynamics, prevailing weather, and player stamina.

# Honorable Mentions on Polygon's Best Movies of 2023 List

Polygon published an honorable-mentions section alongside its best-movies-of-2023 list, defined as movies that received votes but did not crack the top 50.

The listed titles were: The Pope's Exorcist, Bottoms, Rye Lane, No Hard Feelings, Hundreds of Beavers, Evil Dead Rise, Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 3, Nimona, The Starling Girl, Thanksgiving, Guy Ritchie's The Covenant, The Eight Mountains, The Roundup: No Way Out, The Royal Hotel, Red, White & Royal Blue, Blue Jean, The Venture Bros.: Radiant Is the Blood of the Baboon Heart, Quiz Lady, Air, Elemental, Extraction 2, Fair Play, Metalocalypse: Army of the Doomstar, A Haunting in Venice, Fast X, You Hurt My Feelings, The Super Mario Bros. # The Exorcist III

The Exorcist III, written and directed by William Peter Blatty — the original screenwriter of The Exorcist and author of the novel it was based on — is, in Polygon's judgment, the sequel that came closest to capturing the same lightning in a bottle as William Friedkin's original, which nearly 50 years after its theatrical release has withstood the test of time as one of the most terrifying and influential horror films in American cinema. It was the Oct. 31 pick in Polygon's 2023-10-10 Halloween Countdown, listed on Prime Video and the Criterion Channel.

When a series of gruesome murders matching the modus operandi of an infamous serial killer begins to terrorize the city of Georgetown, Lt. William F. Kinderman, played by George C. Scott, investigates the psych ward of a local hospital in search of leads. Confronted with a suspect whose appearance matches that of his late friend Father Damien Karras, Kinderman is thrust into a battle for his very soul as he confronts an evil beyond his comprehension.

Polygon's Toussaint Egan calls the production history a tangled mess of false starts, studio interference, and thwarted artistic ambitions: it was originally conceived with Friedkin in mind to return as director, but he left over creative differences with Blatty; John Carpenter was at one time tapped to direct before he too stepped aside to let Blatty take the reins; and financier Morgan Creek Productions demanded Blatty reshoot the final act, which originally ended without an exorcism. Even so, Egan calls it a fascinating and terrifying film in its own right, with a hodgepodge of fascinating creative choices and literary dialogue that makes it feel like a sister piece to Blatty's The Ninth Configuration — maybe not the Exorcist sequel audiences at the time wanted, but still a damn fine picture.



---


# In The Mouth Of Madness: Carpenter's Apocalypse Trilogy Closer

In the Mouth of Madness is among the wildest movies John Carpenter has ever made — and Polygon notes that is saying something. Starring Sam Neill, Julie Carmen and Jurgen Prochnow, and watchable on YouTube, it follows insurance investigator John Trent (Neill), who is hired to find a missing famous horror novelist; things become increasingly unhinged as the plots of the author's books and the various monsters seem to invade the real world.

Neill, a staple of this list, is absolutely fantastic responding to the horrors of hell, slowly becoming exactly as off-kilter as they are: by the third act the door to hell is halfway open and Trent is ready to dive headfirst into the void, which the reviewer says is honestly how every movie's third act should go. Its place in Carpenter's work is specific — this is the third film in his apocalypse trilogy, which also includes two other stone-cold classics, The Thing and Prince of Darkness, which are not on the list but which the reviewer recommends anyway.



---


# The Roland Doe Case and The Exorcist

Perhaps the most famous instance of purported demonic possession connected to Ouija board usage was the case of "Roland Doe", a young teenage boy from Maryland, who underwent numerous major exorcisms in 1949, said Fr. Dan Reehil.

Doe's story was adapted into the 1971 book "The Exorcist" by William Peter Blatty, which was then made into the 1973 movie starring Ellen Burstyn and Linda Blair.



---


# Overlord (2018 Nazi Zombie Film)

Overlord is a slept-on genre-mashing gem that places a cast of excellent actors about to do bigger things — Jovan Adepo, Wyatt Russell, John Magaro, Pilou Asbæk, and more — and up-and-coming director Julius Avery, of The Pope's Exorcist, behind Nazi lines during World War II, where the Nazis are up to more than usual: there be zombies in these labs. It was the Oct. 24 pick in Polygon's 2023-10-10 Halloween Countdown, listed on Paramount Plus and Pluto TV.

On the eve of D-Day, a group of Allied paratroopers are sent into Germany on a covert mission. Things go wrong instantly when their plane crashes, and they soon discover twisted Nazi experiments after connecting with the residents. Things get bloody fast, with great action from second unit director Shaun O'Dell, of The Woman King and Brotherhood of the Wolf, and stunt coordinator Jo McLaren of Heart of Stone.

Polygon's Pete Volk calls it a gleeful, intentionally ridiculous Nazi-zombie-bashing time with tight direction and a fantastic group of actors, recommended for anyone who loves the Wolfenstein games, Call of Duty's Zombies mode, or B-movies with A-movie production.



---


# Polygon's Selection Process for the Best Movies of 2023

Polygon builds its best-movies-of-the-year list by having each of the staff's film fans create an individual ballot of their top movies every year, with an option to rank the entries numerically or simply weight them; those ballots are then used to generate a collective list, weighted by strength of opinion so that a much-seen mainstream movie does not gain too much advantage over a terrific but underseen indie. The result is then published, with the top 10 picks on each staffer's list listed in the comments.

The eligibility rule is that any movie released in the US during that calendar year qualifies. A stated limitation follows from the publication timing: because the list is published in early December, some December releases are underrepresented.

Polygon frames the exercise as inherently difficult, likening a collaborative best-movies list to forming a committee to definitively rank apples and oranges — how to account for personal tastes, or for access when a given movie is only available in certain markets at certain times, or for the fact that the entries are so qualitatively different they have little in common. The weighted-ballot procedure exists to accommodate that spread: the staff describes its collective tastes as eclectic, with some hungriest for action, horror, epic fantasy, or challenging science fiction, some preferring complicated drama or dark neo-noir, and others drawn to musicals, comedy, animated adventures, and other lighter fare. The best-of-the-year list is meant to reflect that range.



---


# Hellraiser: Clive Barker's Lament Configuration And The Cenobites

Hellraiser is Clive Barker's 1987 directorial debut, adapting his own 1986 novella The Hellbound Heart, starring Andrew Robinson, Clare Higgins and Ashley Laurence, and available on Prime Video, AMC+, Shudder, Tubi, Pluto and Hoopla. Polygon calls it easily the best and most enduring of the Hellraiser movie series and a must-watch for horror fans.

The core narrative concerns Larry and Julia Cotton, a married couple who move into the home of Larry's recently deceased brother Frank, with whom Julia had a previous affair. After Frank is inadvertently resurrected by a drop of blood spilled by Larry on the floor of the house's attic, he seduces Julia into luring new men to the house so he can drain their life force and fully regain his mortal form.

Surrounding that story is the Lament Configuration, a puzzle box Frank acquired before his untimely death: when solved, it conjures hellish beings known as Cenobites to the mortal plane of existence, which indulge in hellish exercises of sadomasochistic mutilation.



---


# A Haunting In Venice

A Haunting in Venice became available to stream on Hulu in early November 2023. The horror mystery runs 1 hour 43 minutes, is directed by Kenneth Branagh, and stars Branagh alongside Michelle Yeoh and Jamie Dornan.

Polygon's assessment places it within Branagh's Poirot cycle: his adaptations have generally been a fun time even when they have problems — Death on the Nile is singled out — and A Haunting in Venice is his best yet, as his confidence as director and performer in this mode continues to grow. The verdict: it is perfect fall viewing.

qid: Which company is facing allegations of anticompetitive practices in both the app distribution and payment processing markets for Android, as well as accusations of unfairly affecting news publishers' bottom lines and potentially engaging in foul play according to reports by TechCrunch and The Age?

# Hypocrisy On Both Sides Of The Courtroom

Each side's central talking point is undercut by its own conduct, so neither party's framing should be taken at face value. Epic says it is not in this for the money, only suing to end Google's monopoly — but Epic would surely profit if it does not have to pay Google's cut. Epic also looks set to argue that you are locked into Android after buying an Android phone, though switching back and forth between the platforms is easier than ever.

Google's talking points have the same problem. Google will say that every Samsung Galaxy phone has "a competing app store right there on the homescreen," even though Google apparently tried to quash that store too, fearing it could cost the company billions. Google was caught trying to play the China card in a pre-briefing with press, reminding journalists that Epic is 40 percent owned by Chinese company Tencent — even though Google itself allegedly considered teaming up with Tencent to eliminate the Epic threat. The parties cannot argue that in court, but Google can attempt to play the China card subtly: "Google may ask a witness once about Tencent's domicile," reads one of Judge Donato's orders.

In the same press briefing, Google suggested to journalists that Epic should have joined the company's "User Choice Billing" program if it wanted an alternative payment system, instead of suing — but that program did not exist until 2022, long after the lawsuit, and it only knocks 4 percentage points off Google's fee.



---


# Google's Defense: Android Competes With iOS

Google's defense denies the premise that Android app stores are a market of their own: "You cannot separate the quality of a phone from the quality of the apps in its app store, and that means Google and Apple compete against each other," began Google lead attorney Glenn Pomerantz. If Google can convince the jury of that, it could be a winning argument, because obviously Google does not have a monopoly on app stores or phones in general.

Pomerantz's commonsense line was that Google cannot possibly have a monopoly on Android app stores when "every single Samsung phone comes with two app stores right on the homescreen," and that the download charts reflect user preference rather than exclusion: "When they show these charts that show all these downloads from Play and not from the Galaxy Store, that's what the Samsung phone users are choosing. They're touching Play. Nothing's keeping them from touching the Galaxy Store; it's just what works for them."

Google's second plank is openness relative to Apple. Epic promised to "show that Google has closed off each and every other option" to the Play Store during this trial, but Google points to the simple fact that it allows alternate app channels at all — something Android rival iOS does not. Pomerantz boasted that over a billion people have gone through the process Epic portrays as needlessly onerous to get apps outside the Play Store; Google told The Verge over email that this refers to how many users have enabled the Android sideloading flow, not necessarily followed through with an install. "A billion people have done it after getting notified of the potential risks," Pomerantz said. "That's because Android users have a real choice."

Google also argues about consequences: if Epic wins, according to Google, it could make Android phones less safe by dismantling basic protections against sideloaded apps, and damage Android's ability to compete with the iPhone because it arguably cannot run a competitive app store by giving it away for free. Google's execution was uneven, though — it wound up spending much of its opening statement attempting to explain away its seemingly bad behavior as normal business practices and did not always succeed out of the gate.



---


# Epic's Antitrust Claims Against Google Play

Epic's claim is that the Android operating system's Google Play Store constitutes an unlawful monopoly, and that Google is separately tying its Google Play payments platform to that store, keeping other potential app payment mechanisms from competing.

The grounds Epic offers are the frictions it says Google creates: Google makes it so difficult for developers and users to get around its Android app store, and that app store's standard fees, that it has created an illegal monopoly which unjustly enriches Google while artificially driving up app prices because other stores cannot compete. The warrant joining that to the legal claim is the competitive-harm chain — no viable rival stores means no fee discipline, which means the "Google Tax" is paid either by developers or passed along to consumers. Epic wants to break up Google's alleged monopoly on Android app stores and payment methods so developers are not stuck paying that tax.

Google's answer contests the warrant rather than the fees: it says Epic's demands would damage Android's ability to offer a secure user experience and to compete with Apple's iOS. Both sides agree the future of Google's app store could depend on this trial. Epic sued in 2020 after a fight over in-app purchase fees.



---


# Epic Games v. Google Goes To Trial On November 6, 2023

Epic Games, the maker of Fortnite, went to trial with Google on November 6, 2023, hoping to convince a jury that Google engages in anticompetitive behavior with regard to its Android app store, Google Play, and its commission structure. Match had settled its own antitrust lawsuit with Google the week before, but Epic's case proceeded.

This case differs slightly from Epic's battle with Apple on the same topic, because this time Epic cannot allege there is no other way to load apps onto Android devices, as it could with Apple: Android does allow for sideloading apps. Epic will suggest Google makes that process cumbersome, but the bulk of its arguments will center on what it believes are anticompetitive agreements between Google and device manufacturers and developers.

The precedent Epic's case relies on is a Microsoft case in which courts found Microsoft to have a monopoly over the operating system and to be abusing it, making it hard for users to download alternative browsers, like Netscape, on Windows devices. To make its case, Epic plans to bring claims under Sections 1 and 2 of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act, as well as California's anticompetitive laws, the Cartwright Act and the Unfair Competition Law. It will attempt to argue that Google restrains competition within two separate markets: the distribution of apps to Android users, and the market for payment processing solutions for content inside Android apps.



---


# Google's Parallel Antitrust Proceedings In Late 2023

As of mid-November 2023, Google was fighting antitrust on more than one front at once. The Epic Games case was not its only antitrust case in trial: Google had settled a separate antitrust lawsuit with dating site Match Group the week before November 13, and on November 6 it went to trial with Fortnite maker Epic Games, which hoped to prove that Google engages in anticompetitive behavior with regard to its Android app store, Google Play, and its commission structure. Separately, Google was involved in an antitrust lawsuit with the Department of Justice over its alleged search monopoly.

The Epic case had shed co-plaintiffs on its way to trial. Epic's lawsuit originally involved Match and several U.S. attorneys general, but Google reached a settlement with the attorneys general in October 2023 and with Match the week before November 6, so Epic fought the antitrust battle on its own. The lawsuit, held in the U.S. District Court in California's Northern District, would include testimony from a number of Google and Android execs, including CEO Sundar Pichai, and Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, as well as from Apple, Netflix and other Android developers. Epic, meanwhile, had lost its antitrust battle with Apple and was asking the Supreme Court to weigh in.



---


# Google's Defense: Android Openness And Sideloading

Google plans to push back at Epic's claim that it does not have competition in the app store business — the premise on which Epic's monopoly theory rests. It will point out that not only does the Play Store compete with Apple's App Store, which the Ninth Circuit ruling in the Apple case agreed upon too, but Android also supports competitive app stores like Samsung's Galaxy Store and Amazon's Appstore.

Google will also attack the foreclosure premise directly. It will note that, unlike Apple, it allows apps to be sideloaded on Android devices — something Epic takes advantage of today — and that this process is streamlined and helps keep users safe. Epic will claim in response that the process is made to be overly difficult for end users, with multiple steps involved and "scare screens" that warn users of the security risks involved with sideloading.

On discovery, Epic will suggest that Google hid items by allowing execs and employees to have "off the record" chats; Google will counter this as well, saying it has provided the court with thousands of chat logs and millions of documents. Google will ultimately push the notion that this case is not about competition but about money — that is, that Epic Games wants to reach the Play Store's 2.5 billion users without having to pay. As a Google blog post by Wilson White, VP, Government Affairs & Public Policy, put it: "Android's choice and flexibility work well for consumers and developers of all sizes. We look forward to making our case in court as we fight to keep our users safe from harm, partner with developers to grow their businesses, and keep the Android ecosystem thriving and healthy for everyone."

# Class Action

## Definition

A class action, as it appears across this corpus, is a single lawsuit pursued on behalf of a group of similarly affected people rather than filed by each person individually.

The corpus documents several such suits from 2023: FTX customers against crypto promoters including Paradigm, a news publisher against Google, consumers against PayPal, and the Authors Guild against OpenAI.

It also shows the mechanism can be blocked by contract, as with Uber's terms of use barring class actions in sexual-assault cases.

## Context

The corpus shows the mechanism used across very different disputes: FTX customers brought a class-action lawsuit accusing crypto investment firm Paradigm and other promoters of defrauding customers by promoting the exchange, publisher Helena World Chronicle filed a class action antitrust suit against Google and Alphabet under the Sherman Act alleging AI tools like Search Generative Experience and Bard siphon off publishers' content and ad revenue, and consumers represented by law firm Hagens Berman filed a class action against PayPal over anti-steering rules that allegedly stifle competition from cheaper platforms like Stripe and Shopify.

The Authors Guild of America, representing Stephen King, John Grisham and 134 other authors, likewise filed its own class-action suit against OpenAI over unauthorized use of copyrighted books in training data, run in parallel to (but distinct from) comedian Sarah Silverman's separate, non-class suit.

Apple's earlier MacBook Pro keyboard class-action settlement is cited in the corpus as a business driver — the corpus notes the settlement cost probably factored into Apple's decision to redesign the keyboard, a change introduced alongside separate updates like a new camera and the removal of the Touch Bar.

## Key Characteristics

- **Collective standing** — a class action lets one or a few plaintiffs (e.g., Helena World Chronicle, the Authors Guild, unnamed FTX customers) litigate on behalf of an entire group with the same underlying grievance, rather than requiring each affected person to sue separately.
- **Can be contractually blocked** — the corpus shows companies can preempt this mechanism: under Uber's terms of use, class action lawsuits cannot be filed against the company in sexual assault cases, forcing survivors to litigate individually and preventing them from advocating for themselves collectively.
- **Used across dispute types** — the corpus applies the same mechanism to fraud (FTX), antitrust (Helena World Chronicle v. Google, PayPal anti-steering), and copyright (Authors Guild v. OpenAI) claims, showing it is a general procedural tool rather than one tied to a single area of law.
- **Settlement exposure shapes corporate behavior** — Apple's keyboard class-action settlement is presented in the corpus as a concrete cost that influenced a subsequent product redesign decision.
- **Defendants, not just plaintiffs, can be named as a group** — the FTX-related suit accuses Paradigm "and others" collectively of defrauding customers, showing the mechanism can target a class of co-defendants as well as aggregate a class of claimants.

## Background (external)

Cornell Law School's Legal Information Institute (Wex) defines a class action generically as "a procedural device that permits one or more plaintiffs to file and prosecute a lawsuit on behalf of a larger group, or 'class'" (Cornell Law School, Legal Information Institute, Wex: "class action," accessed 2026-09-02, https://www.law.cornell.edu/wex/class_action).

# Helena World Chronicle's Class Action Antitrust Suit Against Google

A class action lawsuit filed in the week of 15 December 2023 in the U.S. District Court in D.C. accuses Google and parent company Alphabet of anticompetitive behavior in violation of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act and others, on behalf of news publishers. The case was filed by Arkansas-based publisher Helena World Chronicle, which argues that Google "siphons off" news publishers' content, their readers and their ad revenue through anticompetitive means, and it specifically cites new AI technologies such as Google's Search Generative Experience (SGE) and the Bard AI chatbot as worsening the problem.

Helena World Chronicle owns and publishes two weekly newspapers in Arkansas. In the complaint it argues that Google is "starving the free press" by sharing publishers' content on Google, losing them "billions of dollars."

Beyond damages, the suit asks for an injunction that would require Google to obtain consent from publishers before using their website data to train its general artificial intelligence products, including Google's own and those of rivals. It also asks that publishers who opt out of SGE still be allowed to show up in Google search results, among other things.

The law firm handling the case is Hausfeld, whose announcement states that "the anticompetitive effects of Google's scheme cause profound harm to competition, to consumers, to labor, and to a democratic free press," and that "Plaintiff Helena World Chronicle, LLC invokes the Sherman Act and Clayton Act to seek class-wide monetary and injunctive relief to restore and ensure competition for digital news and reference publishing and set up guardrails to preserve a free marketplace of ideas in the new era of artificial intelligence."

# Google's Parallel Antitrust Proceedings In Late 2023

As of mid-November 2023, Google was fighting antitrust on more than one front at once. The Epic Games case was not its only antitrust case in trial: Google had settled a separate antitrust lawsuit with dating site Match Group the week before November 13, and on November 6 it went to trial with Fortnite maker Epic Games, which hoped to prove that Google engages in anticompetitive behavior with regard to its Android app store, Google Play, and its commission structure. Separately, Google was involved in an antitrust lawsuit with the Department of Justice over its alleged search monopoly.

The Epic case had shed co-plaintiffs on its way to trial. Epic's lawsuit originally involved Match and several U.S. attorneys general, but Google reached a settlement with the attorneys general in October 2023 and with Match the week before November 6, so Epic fought the antitrust battle on its own. The lawsuit, held in the U.S. District Court in California's Northern District, would include testimony from a number of Google and Android execs, including CEO Sundar Pichai, and Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, as well as from Apple, Netflix and other Android developers. Epic, meanwhile, had lost its antitrust battle with Apple and was asking the Supreme Court to weigh in.



---


# What A Ruling Against Google Would Mean For Big Tech

A ruling against Google would not stop at Google: the remedy would likely resemble the Microsoft settlement and the outcome would ripple through the other pending Big Tech cases, because enforcers are using this trial to demonstrate that antitrust law can still take on the largest and most powerful companies in the world.

The grounds for the first half of that claim are the available remedies. If the judge rules against Google, the outcome could look a lot like the Microsoft deal, in which the computer company was required to change its behavior and share its APIs with third-party developers, and was also banned from making anticompetitive and exclusive deals with computer manufacturers. Google might likewise end up having to turn over all or most of the data it has collected to other search engines so they can improve their products and attract more users — a remedy scaled to the disparity the DOJ has cited, that Google gets 16 times more data than Bing does everyday.

The grounds for the ripple effect are the cases already queued behind this one. The FTC sued Amazon in September for using anticompetitive and unfair strategies to illegally maintain its monopoly power. The DOJ has been investigating Apple for years over the company's policy for third-party apps on its devices and whether it unfairly favors its own products. And there is an ongoing case between the FTC and Facebook, in which the agency calls on Facebook to sell Instagram and WhatsApp.

The warrant joining grounds to claim is enforcers' own stake in the result: they will want to show that antitrust law is still relevant and can successfully take on the biggest, most powerful companies in the world, so a win here sets the template the neighbouring cases are argued against. The scope condition is that nothing was settled as of this report — the case is expected to continue for several weeks, bringing to a head one of the biggest fights in tech antitrust since the U.S. took Microsoft to trial in the 1990s.



---


# Rogers Communications' Rebuttal On Information Access

Rogers Communications denied the sisters' premise that they were improperly cut off from information, saying the company took "reasonable steps" to protect company information from a competitor. Spokesperson Sarah Schmidt added that Melinda Rogers-Hixon and Martha Rogers could have resolved the matter by choosing a different lawyer, "and they chose not to do so" — putting the cause of their exclusion on their own choice rather than on any vendetta.

The company also disputed that the courtroom was the right venue and that the dispute was harming the business. "This matter should be resolved privately," Schmidt said by email. "We've demonstrated that we will not be distracted by these actions — we have significant momentum in the market, our merger is tracking ahead of plan, and we remain squarely focused on doing what's right for our customers and stakeholders."

Erling Haaland scored 50 goals in the 2023 calendar year for Manchester City and Norway, placing him fourth on TalkSport's list of the year's top scorers. No player in Premier League history has made more of an impact following their arrival than Haaland, who broke the goal record for a single season with 36 strikes the previous term.

He has already been firing in many top-flight goals this term, as well as being the joint-leading scorer from the Champions League group stages, and he is the leading goalscorer in the Premier League this season. With two games left for City in 2023, Haaland had time to become the overall top scorer, though it remained to be seen whether Pep Guardiola would play him against Everton and Sheffield United. Haaland had missed City's last five games with a foot injury, but it was believed he could be in contention to return to action.

# The 2023 Calendar-Year Top Goalscorer Race

Al Nassr striker Cristiano Ronaldo looked set to be the top scorer in the 2023 calendar year after his Boxing Day double against Al Ittihad. He was not the only star in great form, with players across Europe banging them in for fun.

The Portugal international had been battling with Kylian Mbappe, Erling Haaland and Harry Kane for the title of the best goalscorer of 2023.

# Manchester United's Striker Scoring Problem, 2023

Manchester City forward Erling Haaland had scored more Premier League goals in the 2023-24 season (9) than Manchester United's five forwards had managed in all competitions combined (8), and United's top scorer was actually defensive midfielder Casemiro with four strikes, Sky Sports reported on 28 October 2023 ahead of the derby.

Erik ten Hag declined to place the blame on the forwards alone. Asked if they were at fault for the frontline problem, he replied: "Fault? It's co-operation. It has to click. We have shown in some games, we have so many in overload positions to the opponents goal and we don't net or don't even hit the target. We should be doing this better."

Marcus Rashford's start to the season had been sobering, with one goal so far that term, but Ten Hag said he had full faith the England forward, who scored 30 goals last season, can find his scoring boots again. "If you give him the trust and I play him every game, most games also he finishes the game. I have strong belief he will return to scoring a lot of goals," said Ten Hag. "It also has to do with the co-operation, with the movement around and the distribution to him. We have to work on that and that's my focus point."

# Haaland's Major Tournament Prospects With Norway

Norway failed to qualify directly from their Euro 2024 qualification group, with Spain and Scotland already securing the top two spots, despite the presence of Erling Haaland and Arsenal captain Martin Odegaard, as reported by The New York Times on 17 November 2023.

The remaining route is narrow. They are at least likely to qualify for the play-offs, and therefore will have two must-win games in March to secure their first major tournament appearance since 2000 — the summer when Haaland was born — but there's been little in recent performances to think Norway will breeze through those play-offs.

The article closes the comparison with the record holder: Juve's individual record will soon be surpassed, but captaining his side to a bronze medal at the Olympics may stand as his nation's greatest achievement for much longer.

# Manchester United 2-1 Chelsea, December 2023

Manchester United got themselves back to winning ways with a 2-1 victory over Chelsea thanks to a superb Scott McTominay brace, per Sporting News on Dec. 6, 2023. The final score was Man United 2 (McTominay 19', 70'), Chelsea 1 (Palmer 45').

The victory remarkably put United within three points of rivals Manchester City, after the reigning champions were defeated by Aston Villa, and kept them in reach of the top four places.

# Scott McTominay's Advanced Role And Goal Threat

Under Ten Hag, Scott McTominay functions as a marauding midfield engine and late-running goal threat with a licence to create overloads wherever he finds them — the job United once paid Paul Pogba to do.

The structure of the role differs from his previous, more conventional midfield positions. Against low blocks and structured defences — and, the piece notes, nobody is remotely accusing Chelsea of possessing one of those — he provides the extra body in a tightly marked penalty area; but he also pops up in the channels and on the wing, either supporting the man in possession or offering himself for the quick switch of play. The relation between that role and his output shows in the numbers: against Chelsea he scored his fifth and sixth goals of the season, having previously never got more than seven. The piece attributes this partly to opponents still not quite cottoning on to his goal threat — those late runs to the far post, the blur on the edge of the 18-yard box you do not spot until it is too late — and partly to how Ten Hag is using him. The range over which the relation holds is the current team: for all the undoubted leadership qualities of Bruno Fernandes and Harry Maguire, tactically it is McTominay running the show right now, a development with numerous interesting consequences. The Pogba comparison is drawn with the caveat that McTominay is a different kind of player with a different kind of skillset; Pogba's United career never quite worked out, largely — if you believe his most vehement critics — on account of his hair.

# Haaland's Chase Of Norway's International Goalscoring Record

Erling Haaland was just six goals away from Norway's international goalscoring record, making it surely inevitable that he will soon be his nation's most prolific striker ever, as reported by The New York Times on 17 November 2023.

The report notes the two ways of reading the timing: on one hand it will have happened remarkably quickly, since Haaland only scored his first goals for Norway in 2020; on the other, this has been an incredibly long time coming. At this point Norway appear to have the most prolific striker in Europe, and it's not unreasonable to consider where Haaland might end up in the all-time international goalscoring charts worldwide, never mind just among his compatriots.

His rate is the striking figure, with a caveat attached. Haaland is averaging nearly a goal a game for his country, which will inevitably be difficult for the 23-year-old to sustain over his career, but is impressive even at this early stage: excluding countries who have never qualified for a World Cup, only Jorgen Juve, Gigi Riva, Ferenc Puskas and Poul Nielsen, plus Japan's Kunishige Kamamoto, hold their nation's international goalscoring records while also boasting a rate of 0.75 goals per game or more. qid: Which company is at the center of claims involving the manipulation of search results to maximize ad revenue according to 'The Age', the lack of a valid alternative for search engine services as stated by 'The Verge', and the anticompetitive siphoning off of content, readers, and ad revenue from news publishers as reported by 'TechCrunch'?
