# OpenAI Developer Platform And API Releases

OpenAI progressively opened its models to developers through paid APIs and fine-tuning programmes, beginning with a paid API for ChatGPT — a move toward monetization whose initial customers included Instacart, Snap (Snapchat's parent company) and Quizlet.

Model access followed. OpenAI announced the general availability of GPT-4: starting July 6, all existing OpenAI developers "with a history of successful payments" could access GPT-4, with access planned for new developers by the end of July. OpenAI said it would in future allow developers to fine-tune GPT-4 and GPT-3.5 Turbo — one of the original models powering ChatGPT — with their own data, as had long been possible with several of OpenAI's other text-generating models, and that the capability should arrive later that year. It then brought fine-tuning to GPT-3.5 Turbo: companies using the model through the API can make it better follow specific instructions, such as always responding in a given language, improve its ability to consistently format responses, and hone the "feel" of its output, such as tone, so it better fits a brand or voice; most notably, fine-tuning lets customers shorten text prompts to speed up API calls and cut costs. OpenAI partnered with Scale AI to allow companies to fine-tune GPT-3.5, though it was unclear whether OpenAI was developing an in-house tuning tool to complement platforms like Scale AI or to serve a different purpose. Fine-tuning costs were $0.008 per 1K tokens for training, $0.012 per 1K tokens for usage input and $0.016 per 1K tokens for usage output. A GPT-4 fine-tuning programme followed, but unlike the GPT-3.5 programme it involves more oversight and guidance from OpenAI teams, largely because of technical hurdles.

OpenAI also extended the platform beyond text. DALL-E 3, its text-to-image model, became available via an API after first coming to ChatGPT-4 and Bing Chat, and OpenAI released a text-to-speech API, the Audio API, offering six preset voices and two generative AI model variants.



---


# OpenAI DevDay 2023 Announcements

On November 6, 2023 — prior to the leadership chaos — OpenAI held its first developer conference, OpenAI DevDay, and announced a slew of updates to GPT, including GPT-4 Turbo, a multimodal API, and a GPT store where users can create and monetize their own custom versions of GPT.

GPT-4 Turbo, unveiled at the conference, is a super-charged version of GPT-4, OpenAI's latest language-writing model, and comes in two versions: one that is strictly text-analyzing and another that understands the context of both text and images. The GPT Store was announced alongside it: users and developers would soon be able to make their own GPT with no coding experience required, list it on OpenAI's marketplace, and monetize it in the future. OpenAI also announced the Assistants API to help developers build "agent-like experiences" within their apps, with use cases ranging from a natural language-based data analysis app to a coding assistant or even an AI-powered vacation planner.

The GPT store slipped. According to a memo seen by Axios, OpenAI planned to delay the launch of its highly anticipated GPT store to early 2024; custom GPTs and the accompanying store had been a major DevDay announcement, with the store expected to open the previous month.



---


# GPTs: OpenAI's Custom Chatbots And The Dev Day Announcements

GPTs are OpenAI's tool for building custom conversational, action-taking AI systems powered by OpenAI's models, including the models underpinning ChatGPT. They were announced at OpenAI's first-ever developer conference, held Monday, November 6, 2023, where the Microsoft-backed AI startup announced a host of new products — the more notable being tools to create custom "GPTs" (that is, domain-specific chatbots), new text-to-speech models, an API for the text-to-image model DALL-E 3, and an improved version of OpenAI's flagship model GPT-4, called GPT-4 Turbo.

What distinguishes a GPT from a prompt is that the knowledge is built in. With GPTs, a user can train a model on a cookbook collection, for example, so that it can answer questions about ingredients for a specific recipe; or they can give a model their company's proprietary codebases so that developers can check their style or generate code in line with best practices. Some of the initial GPTs, all created by OpenAI, include a Gen Z meme translator, a coloring book and sticker creator, a data visualizer, a board game explainer and a creative writing coach. ChatGPT can accomplish these tasks given carefully engineered prompts and foreknowledge, but purpose-built GPTs drastically simplify things — and might just kill the cottage industry that emerged around creating and editing prompts to feed to ChatGPT.

The consequence TechCrunch draws for ChatGPT itself is a change of role: with GPTs, ChatGPT could become more a gateway to a broader ecosystem of AI-powered chatbots than the end-all-be-all. GPTs introduce a level of personalization far beyond that ChatGPT offers today, and — once OpenAI sorts out its capacity issues — TechCrunch expects an explosion of creativity there. Will ChatGPT be as visible as it once was after GPTs flood the marketplace? Perhaps not; but it will not go away, it will simply adapt and evolve, no doubt in ways not even its creators can anticipate.



---


# GPT Model Releases From GPT-3.5 To GPT-4

ChatGPT first launched to the public as OpenAI quietly released GPT-3.5: the model broke cover with ChatGPT, a fine-tuned version of GPT-3.5 that is essentially a general-purpose chatbot able to engage with a range of topics including programming, TV scripts and scientific concepts.

Writers everywhere rolled their eyes at the new technology, much as artists did with OpenAI's DALL-E model, but the chat-style iteration seemingly broadened its appeal and audience. GPT-4 followed on March 14: a powerful image- and text-understanding AI model, released to paying ChatGPT Plus users and through a public API, with developers able to sign up on a waitlist to access the API.



---


# ChatGPT FAQ: Basics And Definitions

ChatGPT is a general-purpose chatbot developed by tech startup OpenAI that uses artificial intelligence to generate text after a user enters a prompt; it runs on GPT-4, a large language model that uses deep learning to produce human-like text. GPT stands for Generative Pre-Trained Transformer.

The boundary against the wider category matters: a chatbot can be any software or system that holds dialogue with a person and does not necessarily have to be AI-powered — there are rules-based chatbots that give canned responses to questions — whereas ChatGPT is AI-powered and uses LLM technology to generate text after a prompt. ChatGPT was released for public use on November 30, 2022. Both the free version of ChatGPT and the paid ChatGPT Plus are regularly updated with new GPT models, and the most recent model is GPT-4; the free version requires only a sign-in. There is a free ChatGPT app, at launch limited to U.S. iOS users, with OpenAI saying an Android version is "coming soon," and there is an API, released March 1, 2023.

Anyone can use ChatGPT, and more and more tech companies and search engines are using the chatbot to automate text or quickly answer user questions and concerns. Multiple enterprises use it, although others limit use of the tool. Microsoft announced at its 2023 Build conference that it is integrating its ChatGPT-based Bing experience into Windows 11; the Brooklyn-based 3D display startup Looking Glass uses ChatGPT to produce holograms you can communicate with; and the nonprofit organization Solana integrated the chatbot into its network with a ChatGPT plug-in geared toward end users to help onboard into the web3 space.



---


# ChatGPT Plus And The Plugin Platform

March saw more of the same, with OpenAI announcing a new subscription-based service — ChatGPT Plus — which offers users the chance to skip to the head of the queue during peak usage hours and adds features not found in the free version. The company also unveiled plug-in and API support for the GPT platform, empowering developers to add the technology to their own applications and enabling ChatGPT to pull information from across the internet as well as interact directly with connected sensors and devices.

ChatGPT also notched 100 million users per day in March, 30 times higher than two months prior, and companies from Slack and Discord to GM announced plans to incorporate GPT and generative AI technologies into their products.

qid: After the report by Fortune on September 26, 2023, claiming Donald Trump inflated the value of his Trump Tower apartment, did The Age report on November 7, 2023, maintain consistency regarding the allegations of Donald Trump's financial misrepresentations?
context:
# Trump Net Worth Valuation Dispute at Trial

Thousands of pages of exhibits detailing the performance of Donald Trump's assets, made available during the New York fraud trial, have provided a deeper look into his fortune. His 2021 statement of financial condition, filed as part of the lawsuit, pegged his net worth at $US4.5 billion. Bloomberg's calculation has consistently been below Trump's figures; at the same time, Bloomberg measured the value of some Trump properties higher than what New York state claims.

Trump took the stand and testified that the properties whose values he is accused of inflating were actually undervalued, based on the premium his "brand" adds. He also said that banks did not rely on his statements of financial condition when weighing loans: "They just weren't a very important element in banks' decision-making process," Trump told the court. "And we'll explain that as this trial goes along."

The Age's 7 November 2023 report set out New York state's valuation of four high-profile Trump properties where the prosecution alleges fraud occurred, alongside Bloomberg's own approach to assessing the assets.



---


# Trump Tower Fifth Avenue Penthouse Valuation Dispute

Among the allegations in the New York case was that Trump claimed his Trump Tower apartment in Manhattan — a three-storey penthouse replete with gold-plated fixtures — was nearly three times its actual size, and valued the property at $327 million; no apartment in New York City has ever sold for close to that amount, Attorney General Letitia James said. The Age's comparison in November 2023 listed Trump's 2021 valuation at $US131.3 million and Bloomberg's 2023 valuation at $US40 million, with no current New York estimate available.

The size inflation is documented over a specific window: between 2011 and 2016, Trump valued the apartment on the basis of it being 30,000 square feet (2,787 square metres), almost triple its actual measurement of 10,996 square feet, and because of this New York State arrived at a valuation about a third of Trump's in those years. Space inflation was not the only issue: between 2014 and 2015 Trump increased the apartment's value to $US327 million from $US200 million, which the prosecution argues was to mask a drop in the value of another of his properties. "A discrepancy of this order of magnitude, by a real estate developer sizing up his own living space of decades, can only be considered fraud," Judge Arthur Engoron wrote in his September ruling.

Bloomberg values the property using recent Trump Tower sales and those of comparable Manhattan penthouses. While some splashy residences in much newer Billionaires Row buildings have listed for well in excess of $US100 million, they typically boast higher ceilings, more up-to-date finishes, contemporary layouts, outdoor space and better views. A better comparison, the report says, would be a 9,450-square-foot penthouse in Olympic Tower, five blocks south on Fifth Avenue, on and off the market for $US35 million since 2016; or Carl Icahn's 14,000-square-foot penthouse at Museum Tower on West 53rd Street, listed for $US35 million in 2019 before he attempted to split and sell it as two apartments, both eventually delisted.



---


# Engoron Summary Judgment That Trump Committed Fraud

A judge ruled on Tuesday 26 September 2023 that Donald Trump committed fraud for years while building the real estate empire that catapulted him to fame and the White House. Judge Arthur Engoron, ruling in a civil lawsuit brought by New York's attorney general, found that the former president and his company deceived banks, insurers and others by massively overvaluing his assets and exaggerating his net worth on paperwork used in making deals and securing financing.

As punishment, Engoron ordered that some of Trump's business licences be rescinded, and said he would continue to have an independent monitor oversee the Trump Organization's operations. A Trump spokesperson did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the ruling, and Trump has long insisted he did nothing wrong.

Fortune described the decision, which came days before the start of a non-jury trial in Attorney General Letitia James' lawsuit, as the strongest repudiation yet of Trump's carefully coiffed image as a wealthy and shrewd real estate mogul turned political powerhouse.



---


# Letitia James Asset Inflation Allegations

Letitia James, a Democrat, sued Trump and the Trump Organization a year before this September 2023 ruling, alleging a pattern of duplicity that she dubbed "the art of the steal" — a twist on the title of Trump's 1987 business memoir "The Art of the Deal."

The lawsuit accused Trump and his company of routinely inflating the value of assets like skyscrapers, golf courses and his Mar-a-Lago estate in Florida, padding his bottom line by billions.



---


# Trump Park Avenue Rent-Stabilised Unit Valuations

Trump Park Avenue, the residential condo tower on Manhattan's Upper East Side formerly known as the Hotel Delmonico, is not one of Trump's best-known buildings, but according to the prosecution it has been the source of some significant asset inflations. Trump's 2021 valuation was $US90.9 million, Bloomberg's 2023 valuation $US86.4 million, and New York's 2021 valuation $US80 million.

The dispute centres on rent-stabilised units. The building's value to Trump mostly stems from unsold condo units owned by the Trump Organisation and rented out, a varying number of which have been rent-stabilised, meaning tenants pay below market rates; such apartments are typically valued at a discount because tenants can stay indefinitely, sometimes even passing them on to children. In 2010, 12 rent-stabilised apartments owned by Trump were valued at an average of $US62,500 each in an appraisal provided by a real estate company; the following year Trump valued them at $US4.1 million each, more than 65 times greater, and has continued to value stabilised apartments in the building at market rates, including in his 2021 statement of financial condition. Rent-stabilised units "with a positive cash flow are often valued at 15-25 cents a dollar of the open market value, versus single digits for negative cash flow," said Jonathan Miller, president of appraiser Miller Samuel.

Trump's optimism was shown to be at least partially justified: by 2021, only five of the 12 apartments remained rent stabilised. The prosecution also claims two additional non-stabilised apartments in the building were overvalued because Trump ignored an option his daughter, Ivanka Trump, had to buy them at a price lower than the market value he used. The Age also records an assessment of the brand effect on price generally: "There would be a Trump premium because the person that would want that property is likely to be a Trump supporter," Eli Beracha said, though it is also likely that the association with Trump would turn off some buyers.



---


# Trump's Other Criminal and Civil Cases 2023

Letitia James' lawsuit is one of several legal headaches for Trump as he campaigns for a return to the White House in 2024. He has been indicted four times in the six months to September 2023 — accused in Georgia and Washington, D.C., of plotting to overturn his 2020 election loss; in Florida of hoarding classified documents; and in Manhattan of falsifying business records related to hush money paid on his behalf.

Separately, the Trump Organization was convicted of tax fraud in 2022 in an unrelated criminal case for helping executives dodge taxes on extravagant perks such as Manhattan apartments and luxury cars, and the company was fined $1.6 million. One of the executives, Trump's longtime finance chief Allen Weisselberg, pleaded guilty and served five months in jail; he is a defendant in James' lawsuit and gave sworn deposition testimony for the case in May.



---


# Engoron's "Fantasy World" Finding on Trump Financial Statements

Judge Arthur Engoron's finding is that Trump's conduct went beyond boasting into legal violation: beyond mere bragging about his riches, Trump, his company and key executives repeatedly lied about them on his annual financial statements, reaping rewards such as favourable loan terms and lower insurance premiums.

Those tactics crossed a line and violated the law, the judge said, rejecting Trump's contention that a disclaimer on the financial statements absolved him of any wrongdoing.

The warrant he offers is that the defence position requires an internally incoherent picture of valuation and responsibility. "In defendants' world: rent regulated apartments are worth the same as unregulated apartments; restricted land is worth the same as unrestricted land; restrictions can evaporate into thin air; a disclaimer by one party casting responsibility on another party exonerates the other party's lies," Engoron wrote in his 35-page ruling. "That is a fantasy world, not the real world."



---


# Letitia James' History of Investigating Trump

Letitia James, who campaigned for office as a Trump critic and watchdog, started scrutinising his business practices in March 2019, after his former personal lawyer Michael Cohen testified to Congress that Trump exaggerated his wealth on financial statements provided to Deutsche Bank while trying to obtain financing to buy the NFL's Buffalo Bills.

Her office had previously sued Trump for misusing his own charitable foundation to further his political and business interests. Trump was ordered to pay $2 million to an array of charities as a fine, and the charity, the Trump Foundation, was shut down.

qid: Has the 'Sporting News' maintained consistency in its explanation of sports betting terms, specifically regarding 'Bettors who wager on the "over"' before November 6, 2023, as compared to its earlier report on November 1, 2023?
context:
# ESPN Bet's Vermont Application And The Offers It Runs Elsewhere

ESPN Bet Sportsbook had also applied to operate an online sportsbook in Vermont, so it could soon be among the new online wagering options for Vermont bettors, Sporting News reported on 2023-09-26. ESPN Bet brings a very familiar brand to sports fans but a relatively new one when it comes to online sports betting: after acquiring the old Barstool Sportsbook earlier in the year, ESPN Bet Sportsbook launched the rebranded site in 17 different states in Nov. 2023, and had already begun taking advantage of various tie-ins with the renowned sports programming network, which helped establish the site in the overall marketplace.

In other states, the ESPN Bet welcome offer has included a 100% deposit match bonus worth up to $1,000, with a 20x wagering requirement. ESPN Bet has also run a welcome promo that invites new sign-ups to place a wager of any amount and receive $200 in Bonus Bets, split into four $50 Bonus Bets. The article notes it will keep an eye out for any news regarding ESPN Bet Sportsbook VT.



---


# Totals Bet Outcomes: Push And Overtime

An over/under wager has three potential outcomes: if the combined score exceeds the set total, the "over" bet wins; if the score is below the set total, the "under" bet wins; and if the combined score of the game matches the total exactly, the bet is typically considered a "push" and the wager is refunded.

A push therefore occurs when the combined score of a game matches the set total established by the bookmaker, meaning bettors neither win nor lose and their original wager is returned. To avoid this outcome, most sportsbooks employ half-points in their totals: by setting a total at 200.5 instead of 200, sports betting sites ensure that a game's combined score cannot possibly match the set total exactly.

Overtime is a separate boundary case. In most sports and with the majority of sportsbooks, overtime does count toward a totals wager; Sporting News advises always checking the specific rules of the sportsbook you are betting with to confirm, but says overtime is generally included in totals wagers.



---


# Totals Bet Worked Examples: Win And Loss

Settling a totals bet means adding the two teams' scores and comparing the sum against the posted line. Sporting News works this through twice for the NBA — once where the bet wins and once where it loses.

In the winning case, the NBA over/under odds for a game between the Los Angeles Lakers and the Boston Celtics are 220.5 points. A bettor who believes the game will be high-scoring and that the teams' combined score will exceed this mark places an "over" bet. The game unfolds with the Lakers scoring 115 points and the Celtics 110, a combined score of 225. Since 225 exceeds the set total of 220.5, the bettor who wagered the "over" wins.

In the losing case, a top sports betting app sets a total of 200.5 points for an NBA game between the New York Knicks and the Chicago Bulls. A bettor who believes the game will be defensive and low-scoring places an "under" bet, predicting a combined score of 200 points or less. The game turns out offensively charged: the Knicks score 105 and the Bulls 100, a combined 205. Since 205 exceeds the set total of 200.5, the bettor who wagered the "under" loses.



---


# The 2023 NFL Best Bets Season Record

Through eight weeks of the 2023 NFL season, Sporting News' best bets stood at 65-46-1 — a winning percentage of over .590, a number the column noted many professional bettors wish they were maintaining during a rollercoaster season. That was despite falling three bets under .500 over the previous two weeks, going 5-6 in Week 7 and 6-8 in Week 8, after starting the first six weeks with a best bets winning percentage well over .700.

The column publishes every Friday afternoon, unveiling favorite moneyline, spread, over/under and player prop wagers for the upcoming weekend after handpicking the best value opportunities on Caesars and SuperDraft and explaining how and why to attack the books.

The breakdown of the previous week was mixed rather than uniformly bad: the against-the-spread picks went 1-3 and player props a pitiful 0-3, but the moneyline and over/under picks went 5-2 — so, as the Nov. 3, 2023 column put it, like the Chiefs after a pathetic loss to the Broncos (one of the incorrect picks), it was moving on to Week 9 with its head held high.



---


# Over/Under Totals Bet Definition

A totals bet, commonly known as an over/under bet, is a wager on the combined score of both teams in a game: bookmakers set a predicted total score, and bettors choose whether the actual combined score will surpass it ("over") or fall short of it ("under"). Rather than picking the winner or the winning margin, totals betting asks only about the game's combined score, and it sits alongside point spreads and moneylines as a favorite option in sports betting.

The discriminating feature is that the bettor's only concern is whether the final combined score falls over or under the line set by oddsmakers — the identity of the winner is irrelevant. Sporting News illustrates with an NBA game whose total is set at 210.5 points: those who bet the "over" win if the combined score of the two teams is 211 or more, while those who bet the "under" win if the score totals 210 or less. The 0.5 ensures no chance of a tie, since teams cannot score in half-points.

The category is broader than points. Over/under bets involve wagering on whether a particular number will be over or under the figure the bookmaker set, and that number can be combined points scored in a game, total rounds in a fight, or total games in a tennis match.



---


# Sports Betting Terminology Glossary

CBS Sports set out the top Kentucky betting terms for new bettors on 13 October 2023, defining each bet type by what the bettor is actually wagering on and, in several cases, by a worked Kentucky example.

Against the spread means that instead of betting on an exact winner, the widely popular spread bet levels the playing field by letting you wager on how many points a team will win by: in basketball, if Kentucky is the 7.5-point favorite against Louisville then Kentucky covers by winning by 8 or more, while Louisville as the 7.5-point underdog covers by winning outright or losing by 7 or fewer. Money line is an elevated outright bet with odds adjusted to reflect a favored team and an underdog: if Kentucky is a -200 favorite against Florida you'd need to bet $200 to return $100, while Florida at +200 would return $200 on a $100 bet. An outright bet is the easiest wager to place and is perfect for horse racing, one of Kentucky's biggest sporting events — bettors choose one athlete, or thoroughbred, to win an entire event. An Over/Under has the sportsbook post an estimated total of both teams' final scores, with the bettor wagering on whether the actual final will be higher or lower: if the Over/Under for a Kentucky-Louisville basketball game is 125.5, you wager on the final total being Over 126 or Under 125. A player prop projects a player's stat at the end of a game and asks you to wager over or under that projection, with popular examples being how many touchdown passes a quarterback throws or how many three-pointers a basketball player hits; Kentucky is one of the 18 states that allows prop bets on collegiate athletes.

The remaining terms describe the market's participants and mechanics. The underdog is the team deemed less likely to win based on the odds, and a bet on one typically yields a larger return than a bet on the favorite; the favorite is deemed more likely to win, and bettors often pay a premium for backing one though they more often win outright. Consensus odds are generally defined as an average of all available betting markets, since different sportsbooks may price markets variably based on the action they've taken or their own interpretation of information. Futures markets encompass almost anything outside single-game bets — total regular-season wins, championship odds, MVP odds and more. A parlay requires two or more bets within a single wager, all of which must win: wagering $100 on a three-leg parlay at 6 to 1 odds could win $600 if all three legs win. Juice, also known as the vig or vigorish, is effectively the tax oddsmakers charge for handling a wager — if a book judges a game a virtual coinflip it may price both options at -110 to give itself a 10% rake on all the action. A push is a bet where neither the bettor nor the sportsbook wins: if an over/under for total points is set at 44 and both teams combine for exactly 44, the result is a push and the principal is returned. Live or in-game betting allows bets on several different markets in real time — in basketball, on the outcome of a quarter, individual statistics and live-updated spreads and totals.

# Matt Huang And Paradigm's FTX Investment

Matt Huang, co-founder and managing partner of Paradigm, a crypto venture capital firm that invested over $275 million in FTX — a stake that was wiped out — was the third witness to take the stand, and testified about his firm's due diligence.

Huang told the court that Bankman-Fried assured him funds would be used for FTX and not Alameda, and that he was promised Alameda had no preferential treatment on the FTX platform, even though the hedge fund was one of its top traders. Huang said he was concerned about FTX's lack of a board of directors but eventually invested anyway. During cross-examination he said Paradigm pressed Bankman-Fried on the board issue and was told he did not want investors as directors but did plan on having a board with experts.



---


# Testimony At The SBF Trial

Across the first three weeks of the trial, a run of former colleagues, an outside investor and a forensic accounting expert testified that FTX customer money flowed into Alameda Research and out again to other uses, and that FTX's investors were never told about the two firms' special relationship. TechCrunch's running coverage, published 2023-10-06, summarises each week.

In week one, FTX's co-founder and CTO Gary Wang testified Thursday on the extent to which Alameda Research was used for whatever purposes he and SBF saw fit: according to Wang, the crypto trading firm pulled funding directly from FTX customers, whose transactions would be funneled toward Alameda and then directed elsewhere. Thursday also brought testimony from Matt Huang, co-founder and managing partner at crypto investment firm Paradigm, which invested $278 million in FTX across 2021 and 2022 and is part of a class-action lawsuit accusing it and others of defrauding customers by promoting FTX. His testimony centered around being left uninformed about FTX's utilization of customer money to keep Alameda Research afloat — a practice Huang says would have halted his involvement — and covered his relationship with FTX stretching back to 2019.

Week two's standout testimony came from Alameda Research's former CEO Caroline Ellison, who claimed she took $14 billion from customers to repay debts to lenders, using them as a line of credit under the instruction of SBF. Ellison also went into detail about how a $2 billion venture fund, FTX Ventures, was funded by money that had previously been allocated to Alameda from third-party lenders. And though there are no charges of bribery in the case, she also testified to paying Chinese officials $150 million to restore access to $1 billion in frozen trading accounts.

The third week featured a couple of noteworthy moments for the prosecution. FTX's former general counsel Can Sun, like many of SBF's former colleagues, opted to cooperate with authorities and testified that SBF asked him to create a theoretical "legal justification" for the use of billions in consumer funds just days before FTX filed for bankruptcy. Robert Boroujerdi, managing director of the hedge fund Third Point, testified about his experience working with SBF and FTX in a partnership that ultimately resulted in a $60 million investment and a lack of awareness about the special relationship between Alameda Research and FTX; had he known of such a relationship, he testified, Third Point would not have invested in FTX in the first place. And earlier in the week, Peter Easton — a University of Notre Dame professor who helped the government prosecution of Enron and WorldCom — testified about what he uncovered after tracing the flow of billions of dollars between Alameda Research and FTX: much of that funding came from customers, and Easton testified that he found user deposits were used by both FTX and Alameda to purchase real estate, make investments or direct funding toward political causes and charities.



---


# Alameda's Special Privileges Written Into FTX's Code

Gary Wang told the court that Alameda received advantages through code baked into FTX's software granting it special access to the exchange — "We gave special privileges on FTX that gave unlimited withdrawals on the platform to Alameda" — privileges that ultimately resulted in Alameda owing FTX $8 billion worth of customer deposits.

The structure had several linked parts. Alameda was allowed to withdraw and transfer funds and had a $65 billion line of credit. "When customers deposited USD, it went to Alameda," Wang said. "It existed in the computer code. Alameda could have negative balances and unlimited withdrawals." That "bug" in the code was written by Nishad Singh, FTX's director of engineering, and reviewed by Wang, with Bankman-Fried calling the shots. Wang also told the court about a $1 million personal loan he received and a $200 million to $300 million loan in his name from Alameda that was never deposited into his account but was used to make investments into other companies on behalf of FTX — all done by Bankman-Fried, he testified. The escalation was visible over time: in early 2020 Wang discovered for the first time that Alameda's negative balance exceeded FTX's revenue, an indication that Alameda was taking customer funds, and he brought this to Bankman-Fried's attention several times; in late 2021 he discovered Alameda had withdrawn $3 billion from its $65 billion line of credit. The ownership and authority around it: Wang owned 10% of Alameda while his boss owned the other 90%, his compensation was a base salary of $200,000 per year plus stock, and he owned roughly 17% of FTX — and even though they were co-founders, "ultimately it was Sam's decision to make" when there were disagreements. Born in China, Wang moved to the U.S. at age 7 and grew up in Minnesota before going to MIT to study math and computer science, worked at Google after college, and first met Bankman-Fried during high school at a summer camp.



---


# FTX Ventures Was Funded By Alameda

Caroline Ellison testified that the money behind FTX Ventures came from Alameda Research, even though Bankman-Fried announced the fund publicly without naming its source: on January 14th, 2022 he tweeted, "We're launching a $2b venture fund: FTX Ventures!" She said he did not want to go public with where the funds came from, telling her he thought Alameda's brand was less good and that he did not want his name associated with it.

The Verge reported the episode on October 10th, 2023 as part of Ellison's testimony, framing it as FTX keeping cozy private ties with Alameda while publicly holding it at arm's length — an echo, the reporter wrote, of Bankman-Fried and Ellison's romantic relationship. The same distancing appears in another transaction: Alameda bought Robinhood shares for Bankman-Fried, who moved them to a vehicle called "Emergent Fidelity Technologies" to avoid association with Alameda.



---


# FTX's Final Days And The Alameda Shortfall, As Wang Described Them

Much of Gary Wang's Friday testimony focused on the final days at FTX before the operation imploded: after media reports detailing Alameda's business practices and its troubling ties to FTX, an emergency meeting was called between Bankman-Fried, Wang and Singh to discuss shutting down Alameda, and they decided against it because he and Bankman-Fried knew Alameda had no way to repay the roughly $14 billion hole in its books.

Wang, 30, was technology chief for FTX, which spiralled into bankruptcy in November; he spoke so fast that U.S. District Judge Lewis Kaplan and the prosecutor both stopped him at points to ask that he slow his pace. Prosecutors took the jury through a series of tweets beginning on Nov. 7 — posts from the company blaming bank hours for slow withdrawals, while Bankman-Fried tweeted from his personal account assuring customers that all was fine. "FTX was not fine and assets were not fine," Wang testified. On Nov. 12, after FTX declared bankruptcy, Bankman-Fried asked Wang to drive with him to the Bahamas Securities Commission for a meeting; on the drive, Bankman-Fried told Wang to transfer assets to Bahamian liquidators because he believed they would allow him to maintain control of the company. Wang said he was not in the meeting with the securities authority, though Bankman-Fried's dad was present.



---


# Alameda Research As The Alleged Conduit For FTX Customer Funds

In the prosecution's account offered by Thane Rehn, the key to Sam Bankman-Fried's alleged scheme was Alameda Research, a crypto hedge fund that Bankman-Fried also owned. The structure the government described works as follows: Caroline Ellison — Bankman-Fried's on-again off-again girlfriend and the CEO of Alameda — served as a front for the fund, and through that arrangement Bankman-Fried had "secret access" to customer money, both cash and crypto.

Two further relations complete the alleged mechanism. Bankman-Fried is said to have directed employees to conceal the flow of money into FTX's coffers, and to have forged financial documents distributed to lenders and investors. "The defendant lied to the world," Rehn alleged. These are the government's allegations as presented in its opening statement, not established findings.

# Day Two Of The Bankman-Fried Trial: Jury Selection And The Courtroom Audience

On the second day of Sam Bankman-Fried's fraud trial, the jury was selected on Wednesday morning, after which lawyers for the government and then for Bankman-Fried delivered opening statements that told two very different stories of the former FTX CEO's sudden rise and almost instantaneous fall. The central question framed by the proceedings was who Bankman-Fried, the former CEO of crypto exchange FTX, really is: a liar and a fraud, or someone who acted in good faith and, like many a startup founder, flew too close to the sun. That answer, the account notes, ultimately lies with the jury.

The day featured pointed allegations, a friend from MIT, and an audience replete with big names, including Bankman-Fried's professorial parents and Damian Williams, the U.S. attorney for the Southern District of New York. Bankman-Fried himself spent most of the day in court staring into a laptop while seated between his two attorneys. The prosecution's account of his alleged crimes was described as featuring a study in contrasts.



---


# Sam Bankman-Fried

Sam Bankman-Fried is the former CEO of the bankrupt crypto exchange FTX, whose highly anticipated criminal trial started on the Tuesday before TechCrunch's 2023-10-01 report, to determine whether he is guilty of seven counts of fraud and conspiracy. As one former federal prosecutor put it: "The odds seem to be stacked against him at this point."

He was 31 years old and co-founded FTX in 2019; within a few years the once third-largest crypto exchange's valuation hit $32 billion at its peak, and the company is now trying to claw back any funds to distribute to creditors. Before the fall he was even compared to Warren Buffet, and many called him the white horse of crypto — a description TechCrunch notes it never applied to him.

Bankman-Fried, however, maintained his innocence. At The New York Times' DealBook Summit he appeared virtually from the Bahamas and said, "I didn't ever try to commit fraud on anyone; I was shocked by what happened this month"; in a published DM exchange with a Vox reporter he said he regretted filing for bankruptcy and thought that "regulators make everything worse." In January he pleaded not guilty to all counts, which include wire fraud, conspiracy to commit money laundering and conspiracy to misuse customer funds. He could face up to 115 years in jail if convicted on all charges.

TechCrunch's 2023-10-02 summary of his standing on the eve of trial: SBF has been denied bail; his name is mud (or much worse) among those who have lost money in Alameda or FTX; and those who might not have had positions in these still blame him for other crypto woes, because he set off a ripple effect.



---


# The Prosecution's Opening Statement Against Bankman-Fried

Thane Rehn, a prosecutor for the government, opened the case against Sam Bankman-Fried with the line "One year ago, it looked like the defendant was on the top of the world," and then argued that this appearance was false: "all of that, all of it, was built on lies," he declared to the jury, adding "Behind the curtains, he was not what he appeared to be." Rehn described a defendant who, as former CEO of FTX, oversaw a supposedly thriving crypto exchange, jetted between international locales, hobnobbed with celebrities like Tom Brady and Larry David, and repeatedly emphasized to customers that their money was safe and secure.

What followed was a roughly 30-minute story that repeatedly emphasized how Bankman-Fried allegedly stole customer funds to facilitate his jet-setting lifestyle, donate millions to political candidates, and finance risky bets. Rehn also directly contested the media framing of the defendant: he was not a crypto "boy" genius, as so many in the media — Fortune included — have written, but a "man" who "stole billions of dollars from thousands of victims." Rehn closed the characterization with a promise to the jury: "You will see the full picture."



---


# FTX Fraud Charges And The SEC's Allegation

Sam Bankman-Fried, the founder of the failed cryptocurrency exchange FTX, faced seven counts of wire fraud and conspiracy — specifically, two counts of wire fraud and five conspiracy charges — and the Securities and Exchange Commission alleged that FTX was a fraud "from the start," with a "multi-billion-dollar deficiency caused by his own misappropriation of customer funds." The Verge repeated this framing at the head of each of its trial dispatches through October 2023, and in its October 28th, 2023 write-up reported that Bankman-Fried had been found guilty on seven counts including charges of wire fraud.

The boundary of the concept is the mix of charge types: the indictment paired substantive wire fraud counts with conspiracy counts rather than resting on a single offence, and the SEC's civil allegation about the exchange's origins ran alongside the criminal case rather than being part of it. The Verge's reporter, writing as the prosecution's case neared its end on October 26th, 2023, added an impression of the people the charges swept in: all the co-conspirators seemed oddly younger than their years, as though they had got stuck in the "math camp forever" environment Bankman-Fried created for them and simply failed to grow up.



---


# The SBF Trial Proceedings

Sam Bankman-Fried is in court for alleged fraud and money laundering while leading crypto exchange FTX and sister company Alameda. TechCrunch's 2023-10-02 preview placed the case in the Manhattan Federal Court, describing the disgraced cryptocurrency entrepreneur as accused of orchestrating "one of the biggest financial frauds in American history": the multibillion-dollar collapse of FTX, the crypto exchange he founded and led. SBF, as he is known, has pleaded not guilty to some seven charges of fraud and conspiracy.

The trial kicked off with jury selection October 3. By TechCrunch's 2023-10-06 update the case was entering its next chapter, with proceedings resuming Thursday: as confirmed during a teleconference Wednesday, SBF would be taking the stand along with a handful of other witnesses, as the onus shifted toward the defense after the prosecution brought its case to its conclusion.

Access to the proceedings is limited: no devices are allowed, so reports are being physically put together within the courtroom, or sent to overflow rooms. The jury's composition ranges from a train conductor to a retired investment banker who attended Stanford University, and TechCrunch pointed readers to a special joint episode of its Equity and Chain Reaction podcasts for a better sense of the vibe between the jurors and the rest of the court.

A second account of the same events was arriving in parallel: "Going Infinite," a book by Michael Lewis chronicling the rise and fall of SBF, was set to debut on the first day of the trial.



---


# FTX's Bankruptcy And Leadership

The man who represented FTX before Congress after its failure told lawmakers the exchange had effectively no internal governance at all, and the prosecutor bringing the case called Bankman-Fried's alleged crimes one of the biggest financial frauds in American history. TechCrunch reported both on 2023-10-01.

Ray represented the company during a House Financial Services Committee hearing regarding FTX. Asked whether the firm had significant risk management systems, Ray said at the time that "there were virtually no internal controls and no separateness whatsoever," and added that he did not "trust a single piece of paper" in the exchange's organization. Separately, in a press conference, U.S. Attorney Damian Williams called Bankman-Fried's alleged crimes "one of the biggest financial frauds in American history."



---


# The FTX Trial's Stakes For The Wider Crypto Industry

The Verge argued that the trial of Sam Bankman-Fried is likely to be more consequential than just whether the man himself is found guilty: depending on what evidence is introduced, it could be rough for the entire crypto industry.

The grounds are the unpredictability of what a trial surfaces, voiced by Yesha Yadav, a law professor at Vanderbilt University: "How much damage can this trial do to the already beaten-down reputation of the industry at this point? This trial is going to be an excruciating moment for the industry because no one knows what kind of evidence might come out." The warrant joining that uncertainty to industry-wide stakes is that the industry's reputation is already beaten down, so evidence introduced against one exchange's founder lands on the whole sector rather than on him alone.



---


# Sam Bankman-Fried's Federal Fraud Trial

Sam Bankman-Fried, the founder of bankrupt cryptocurrency exchange FTX, is charged with seven counts of fraud and money laundering following the collapse of his cryptocurrency empire the previous year, and was on trial in New York in October 2023.

Two fixed points anchor the proceeding as CNBC described it on 2023-10-06. A U.S. judge revoked Bankman-Fried's bail at a hearing in a New York courthouse on August 11, 2023. And on Thursday, Oct. 5, 2023, Matt Huang, co-founder of Paradigm Operations LP, arrived at the New York court to appear in the case.

# Thesis That Music Labels Are Headed for Irrelevance

The argument, common among music business observers from the world of tech, is that record labels could in the long term be headed for irrelevance. Its grounds are the arrival of digital platforms, including open ones like YouTube and SoundCloud, together with the proliferation of indie music distribution platforms such as DistroKid and TikTok's SoundOn.

The warrant joining grounds to claim is a claim about what labels are for: in a world where anyone can record music using a desktop audio workstation (DAW) and upload it directly to YouTube, or to Spotify via a distribution platform, labels have little left to do. Recording and distribution — the functions the label historically supplied — are available to any artist directly, so on this reasoning the label's remaining role shrinks toward nothing. Music Business Worldwide presented this as the speculation that tech-world observers "like to" make, and as the position Warner Music Group CEO Robert Kyncl was answering at the Code Conference in September 2023.



---


# Kyncl Prediction: Music Is the First Industry to Feel AI's Impact

Robert Kyncl's proposition, put at the Code Conference in September 2023, is that the music business will be out ahead of other industries in exploiting the potential of AI, and — out of necessity — also ahead on the question of how to regulate and monetise the use of AI by non-rights-holders. He attached a date to it: asked when that sea change would occur, he said "I would say within the next year you will see lots of evolution around AI… What you will likely see is increasing quality at a very fast pace."

His reasoning is structural rather than accidental. "Music – because it's so broadly distributed and it's so well aligned with the internet, because it's short format, it lends itself to recommendations, it's on all platforms – is generally first in most transformations and most innovations. So it digitizes first." He generalises from the previous cycle: "Whatever happened to the music industry 20 years ago is starting to happen in the movies and TV shows now. In the meantime, music emerged out of [digitization] better and stronger and more resilient. So, I would imagine the same will happen here, which is we'll likely be first."

The hypothesis is falsifiable on two fronts as stated. It fails if other industries, rather than music, lead on both exploiting and regulating AI; and it fails on its own timetable if the year following September 2023 does not bring the predicted rapid evolution and fast-rising quality in AI. Because the argument rests on music's broad distribution, short format and recommendation-friendliness, an AI transformation that arrives first in a long-format medium would also count against the mechanism he proposes.



---


# AI Day Of Action Campaign

In the week of 2023-10-06, digital rights organization Fight for the Future partnered with music industry labor group United Musicians and Allied Workers to launch #AIdayofaction, a campaign that calls on Congress to block corporations from obtaining copyrights on music and other art made with AI.

The mechanism the campaign is betting on is indirect. The idea is that by preventing industry behemoths like major record labels, for example, from copyrighting music made with the assistance of AI, those companies will be forced to keep looping humans into the creative process. Those same concerns — and the same potential strategies for pushing back against the onslaught of AI — exist across creative industries, which is why the launch was pitched beyond music.

The launch landed in a moment when creative industries were grappling with AI's explosion into every artistic medium at once, and separate calls from artists warning the world to take action before it's too late were starting to converge. From fake Drake songs to stylized Instagram profile pictures, art conjured with newly sophisticated AI tools was suddenly ubiquitous — and so were conversations about how to rein in the technology before it does irrevocable harm to creative communities.

By the following week, on 2023-10-13, TechCrunch characterized the effort as a campaign that targets potential corporate abuse of AI technology while remaining realistic about the ways that musicians and some other creatives could benefit on an individual level from automating parts of their work. The stated goal is that AI tools "become ways for individual humans to make more money, work less, and compete with the corporations that exploit them."



---


# Sony Music's Pipeline Of AI Startup Partnerships

Kooker said Sony Music has "roughly 200 active conversations taking place with startups and established players" right now about building new AI-related products and tools, and that some of these conversations "also include potential equity investments which would accelerate the development of these companies."

He framed this as the optimistic counterweight to the harms: despite the negative impacts of AI, including unauthorized clones and low-quality AI music, there are still "many positive and optimistic developments to highlight," and he highlighted legitimate AI startups and established firms "with music ideas that want to partner with the industry." The products under discussion range from tools for "creative or marketing assistance," to tools that "potentially give us the ability to better protect artist content or find it when used in an unauthorized fashion," as well as "brand new products that have never been launched before."



---


# Robert Kyncl, Warner Music Group CEO

Robert Kyncl is the CEO of Warner Music Group, and the defining feature of his profile in the music business is that he came to it from 'Big Tech' — specifically from YouTube, where he was Chief Business Officer. That background is why, in the months before September 2023, he had been keeping a close eye on AI in the music industry.

His current role explains a second position associated with him: he has been pushing for price hikes at music streaming services. Both themes — AI in music, and streaming pricing — came up during Kyncl's Q&A session at the Code Conference in Laguna Niguel, California, on Tuesday 26 September 2023, as reported by Music Business Worldwide two days later.



---


# Capitol Music Group's Turnaround Results In 2023

Two years into Michelle Jubelirer's tenure, CMG had returned to calmer waters with US market share year-to-date in the high-5% region, alongside glittering successes and a promising array of new talent being primed. Jubelirer said that year-over-year market share is up by 25 per cent and that the company has moved up a notch in the label rankings, while noting she is not one to rattle off a lot of statistics. On TikTok's 2023 wrap-up lists, Capitol was the top-performing label across both the global and US lists.

Asked what she is most proud of in the past 12 months, she called it an incredible year and said that calling it the biggest, the best or the strongest would all be accurate. Her summary claim, made in the interview published 7 December 2023, is that she does not think any label group has been able to turn things around as quickly as she and her team have done in less than two years.



---


# Music Catalog Acquisition Market Slowdown 2023

Robert Kyncl's assessment in September 2023 was that the hot music rights acquisitions space is "likely slowing down a bit" — and that this is fine for a buyer like Warner Music Group, because it makes acquisition multiples come down.

The backdrop given is that the second half of 2022 saw a notable slowdown in music rights acquisitions, which some blamed on higher interest rates and the reduced liquidity that came with them. There had been something of a rebound in 2023, but in Kyncl's view the slowdown persisted. He explained the earlier boom as a one-off shift in seller behaviour: "I think what happened was there was an opening where artists and songwriters were suddenly open to selling catalogs, which they were not open to before. And they just created this incredible tidal wave. And these things happen in waves, ebb and flow. So I think it likely is slowing down a little bit, but that's okay. Because it makes the multiples come down a little bit more."

Asked whether that means Warner Music can buy more if multiples are low enough, Kyncl said: "Of course. We are in the business of buying catalogs, obviously. We have the publishing catalog of David Bowie, for instance, which we bought a few years ago. So yeah, we are in that business. We are in the business of administering [rights], which means collecting revenue from thousands of platforms around the world; very complicated matters. But we're also in the business of ownership."



---


# Music Streaming Price Hikes and Emerging Market Growth

Robert Kyncl told the Code Conference in September 2023 that the opportunity ahead of the music business is twofold: "One, the continued growth in emerging markets, and also the GDPs of those countries will be rising at the same time. So there's lots of growth there. And then there is the price elasticity optimization in mature markets."

Music Business Worldwide read that last point as a reference to the price hikes seen among all the major music streaming services over the past year or so, and to the growing belief within the music industry that streaming price hikes will be sustained — evidenced recently, at the time of writing in September 2023, by Deezer's second price hike within a year.

Speculation that Travis Kelce and Taylor Swift were dating began in July 2023, when Kelce confessed that he had tried and failed to give Swift a friendship bracelet bearing his phone number at one of her Eras Tour concerts; he later invited her on his podcast to one of his games at Arrowhead Stadium, an invitation she famously accepted on 24 September 2023, and she had attended three more of his games by 25 November 2023.

# How Taylor Swift And Travis Kelce's Relationship Began

Taylor Swift, 33, revealed in her December 2023 Time interview — her first time publicly speaking about Travis Kelce — that the relationship began in July 2023, after he confessed on his podcast that he had tried and failed to give her a friendship bracelet with his phone number on it during one of her Eras Tour shows. # Travis Kelce's First Contact Attempt And The Eras Tour Bracelet

The first link between Taylor Swift and Travis Kelce was established in 2016 when Kelce played "Kiss, Marry, Kill" on AfterBuzz TV and said he would kiss Swift, and the first real contact attempt came in July 2023, when he tried and failed to give her a friendship bracelet with his number on it at her Eras Tour concert in Kansas City, The Age reported on 26 September 2023.

That was about six years earlier, but it more recently set tongues wagging as fans wondered how long the plan for them to meet had been in the works.

The bracelet never made it to her wrist, nor his digits to her phone. "I was disappointed that she doesn't talk before or after her shows because she has to save her voice for the 44 songs she sings," he said. "She doesn't meet anybody, or at least she didn't want to meet me, so I took it personal[sic]." At that point any attraction seemed one-sided, but Kelce, exhibiting the tenacity typical of a professional sportsman, remained determined to get her attention — and the Kelce brothers could not stop talking about Swift on the podcast, her name popping up everywhere, including during conversations about facial hair.

# Taylor Swift And Joe Alwyn's Relationship And Breakup

# Holiday Season Stress And The Question Of Partner Introductions

The holiday season is often perceived as the most wonderful time of year, but survey data says otherwise for a large minority: in a recent poll by the American Psychological Association, cited by The Independent in December 2023, 41 per cent of US adults said their stress levels increased from November to January compared with other months of the year, and nearly 50 per cent of Americans described their stress level during the season as "moderate."

That backdrop is what makes introducing a new partner to your family over the holidays a genuine question rather than an obvious opportunity. People approaching Christmas, Hanukkah or New Year carry different concerns — from family drama at the dinner table to small spats with a mother about decorations — which raises the question of whether you really want to bring a partner into the mix. The Independent's framing is that while it is important to introduce your loved ones to your significant other eventually, relationship experts believe there are discussions to have beforehand, especially during the holidays.

# Govee LED Strip Light M1 Matter Deal

Govee's Matter-ready LED Strip Light M1 went on sale for an all-time low of $44.99 at Amazon — $15 off, down from $60, a 25 percent discount — when buyers clipped the on-page coupon, and could also be bought for $3 more, at $48, direct from Govee through October 31st, which The Verge called still one of its better prices to date. The customizable 6.56-foot (2m) strip can display millions of colors and shades of white and can create light patterns that sync with music.

The Verge framed the timing on October 28th, 2023 around the calendar: Halloween is not the only holiday on the horizon as October draws to a close, since once the clock strikes midnight on October 31st, Mariah Carey will defrost, peppermint mochas will inevitably return, and the 2023 holiday season will have officially begun. While handy throughout the year, the light strip is particularly convenient during Halloween and other holidays — the bright, tunable LEDs can flash and blink to the beat of your music and act as festive decor that adds a pop of color to holiday parties. What is particularly great about this strip, the writer noted, is that it supports the newer Matter protocol, which allows you to control the lights with a wide array of smart home platforms.



---


# Preparing Both Partner And Family Before A Holiday Introduction

Relationship experts told The Independent that the preparation for introducing a partner to your family at the holidays happens in a set order, and before anyone travels. The precondition is clarity between the couple: Saba Lurie, a licensed marriage and family therapist at Take Root Therapy in California, says there is no right or wrong time for the introduction, but the intentions behind it must be clear — you should already have discussed where the relationship is headed. Step one is then to brief your partner on the purpose: "I think you should tell the person why you're bringing them home for the holidays, so you're on the same page about the intentions and what's motivating the decision to include," Lurie said. Step two is to brief them on the family they are walking into: "Sometimes it can be helpful for them to know about the dynamics that they're stepping into and how they can best support you. Frankly, they should be aware if there is tension or if there is stress within your family."

Step three runs the other way. Rachel Zar, a licensed marriage and family therapist at Spark Chicago Therapy, says the family needs advance notice too: "If there's something about your partner that could be surprising to your family, or that's a notable difference from who someone you've brought home before, tell your relatives that. Let's set your family and partner up for success." Step four is to say how you want your family to include your partner — for example by incorporating your partner's family traditions into your own celebration. The limit on the procedure is oversharing: Zar advises against telling too much before Christmas, since you still want your family and partner to connect in person rather than hearing about each other through the grapevine. Zar also sets the context for why the preparation matters — every family is different, but problems arise mainly because we put too much pressure on having a joyful holiday: "I think anytime that emotions are heightened, with the holidays certainly being one of those times, our expectations are really high. We're expecting it to be this joyful, happy, perfect occasion. So, we sometimes forget that the holidays come with a lot of stress."

# The Verge Staff Favorites Black Friday Roundup

With federal student loan payments just resuming, it's going to add another often very significant line item into holiday budgets."



---


# The White Company's Christmas Range: Overview

The organising claim of the collection, as presented in The Independent's festive guide, is that the products not only make good presents but can also help place your home at the centre of the celebrations. The brand is described as known for carefully crafted products and an attention to detail that make it one of Britain's most cherished lifestyle brands, and the article picks out a few favourite products from an extensive range.

# Holiday 2023 Shipping Deadline Planning

The Verge's December 18, 2023 guide collects the upcoming domestic shipping deadlines for various retailers and shipment carriers, so readers sending gifts via traditional mail can ensure packages arrive before Christmas, Kwanzaa, or whatever holiday they celebrate this time of year.

Its framing is the annual pattern the deadlines are meant to defuse: the same thing happens year after year, as things get busy with work, school, and life in general until you're suddenly up against the clock racing your gifts to the local post office, FedEx store, or UPS location. The stated purpose is to help with planning your next move as you begin sending out holiday packages and, hopefully, to avoid some holiday stress.



---


# Logistics And Check-Ins During A Holiday Family Visit

Beyond the initial conversations, relationship experts told The Independent that two practical steps remain when bringing a partner home for the holidays. The first is settling logistics in advance: if you are travelling, you may need to decide on sleeping arrangements — potentially staying somewhere other than a parent's house — in order to minimise family stress. "It would be really helpful to have conversations beforehand, so it's clear what you are agreeing or not agreeing to," said Saba Lurie. "For example, if your family isn't comfortable with you bringing someone home and sleeping in the same bedroom, then you and your partner may stay elsewhere. But those would be conversations that you all need to have together. It really depends on your relationship with your family and with your partner."

The second is checking in with your partner during the visit itself, including some quality time together, so that any family drama that arises does not damage the relationship. "I'd recommend pulling your partner aside and saying: 'How are we doing?' Like a temperature check," Lurie added. "Those are points where the two of you can come and remind each other: 'We are a team in this.' Or, the two of you could go on a walk and separate from the family, just for a little bit of time to reset within the relationship."

qid: Who is the individual associated with OpenAI, recognized for both his vision of AI's future and his philanthropic nature, who also invested in a teen's startup and was subject to controversy involving the board as reported by Fortune and multiple TechCrunch articles?
context:
# OpenAI's Founding And Its 2023 Board Crisis

The Rosewood hotel dinner led to the creation of a startup called OpenAI later that year; backed by hundreds of millions of dollars from Elon Musk and other funders, the lab promised to protect the world from Larry Page's vision. Thanks to its ChatGPT chatbot, OpenAI has fundamentally changed the technology industry and introduced the world to the risks and potential of artificial intelligence, and it is valued at more than $US80 billion, about $A123 billion, according to two people familiar with the company's latest funding round. Musk and Sam Altman's partnership did not survive, and the two have since stopped speaking. Altman's own gloss on such splits: "There is disagreement, mistrust, egos. The closer people are to being pointed in the same direction, the more contentious the disagreements are. You see this in sects and religious orders. There are bitter fights between the closest people."

The month before the 9 December 2023 article, that infighting came to OpenAI's boardroom: rebel board members tried to force out Altman because they believed they could no longer trust him to build AI that would benefit humanity, and over five chaotic days OpenAI looked as if it were going to fall apart until the board, pressured by giant investors and by employees who threatened to follow Altman out the door, backed down. The drama gave the world its first glimpse of the bitter feuds among those who will determine the future of AI, but years before the near meltdown there was a little-publicised but ferocious competition in Silicon Valley for control of the technology now quickly reshaping the world, from how children are taught to how wars are fought. That earlier story begins with DeepMind: five years before the Napa Valley party and two before the cat breakthrough on YouTube, Demis Hassabis, a 34-year-old neuroscientist, walked into a cocktail party at Peter Thiel's San Francisco town house and realised he had hit pay dirt, because there in Thiel's living room, overlooking the city's Palace of Fine Arts and a swan pond, was a chessboard; Hassabis had once been the second-best player in the world in the under-14 category, and said "I was preparing for that meeting for a year. I thought that would be my unique hook in: I knew that he loved chess."



---


# OpenAI's Nonprofit Governance And Capped-Profit Structure

OpenAI's for-profit subsidiary, OpenAI Global, LLC, is fully controlled by OpenAI's nonprofit: the subsidiary is permitted to commercialize its technology, but it is subject to the nonprofit's mission of attaining artificial general intelligence (AGI), which OpenAI defines as AI that can "outperform humans at most economically valuable work."

The discriminating feature of this structure is where the power over AGI sits. The nonprofit OpenAI's board has the power both to determine when the company has achieved AGI and to exclude that AGI from IP licenses and other commercial terms — including terms with Microsoft, one of OpenAI's biggest investors and a steadfast integrator of OpenAI's technologies. OpenAI was founded as a nonprofit in 2015 but restructured in 2019 as a "capped-profit" company in order to raise capital, an acknowledgement of the huge costs associated with training cutting-edge AI systems. Altman underlined the point in an interview with the Financial Times in the week of his firing, saying he "hoped" Microsoft would increase its investment to help pay for "huge" imminent model training costs.



---


# The OpenAI Board Ousts Sam Altman, November 2023

As reported on November 18, 2023, the OpenAI board had ejected billionaire and AI evangelist Sam Altman from his CEO role after an apparent vote of no confidence. The board's exact wording in a release issued that afternoon: Altman's "departure follows a deliberative review process by the board, which concluded that he was not consistently candid in his communications with the board, hindering its ability to exercise its responsibilities."

What followed was a whirlwind four days for OpenAI, the generative AI poster child behind the smash hit ChatGPT. The board ousted CEO and co-founder Altman and demoted president and co-founder Greg Brockman, who subsequently resigned, paving the way for what looked like a mutiny by staff insisting the founders be reinstated post-haste. By the time TechCrunch wrote again on November 21, 2023, Microsoft had already hired Altman and Brockman to head up a new internal AI unit — though, as things transpired, nothing had actually been signed yet, with rumors suggesting the ousted leaders might actually return to OpenAI after all, in some capacity at least.

TechCrunch cautioned on November 18 that the full truth would not be known for a long time, as the characters in the drama are likely to be NDA'ed up. Per various whispers and leaks, an all-hands meeting about the situation that afternoon did not produce any revelations beyond banal reassurances that the company is fine and they will get a fresh CEO soon.



---


# Musk's Founding Of OpenAI And His Departure

Convinced that Larry Page's optimistic view of AI was dead wrong, and angry at his loss of DeepMind, Musk built his own lab: OpenAI was founded in late 2015, just a few months after he met with Sam Altman at the Rosewood hotel in Silicon Valley. Musk pumped money into the lab and his former PayPal buddies, Reid Hoffman and Peter Thiel, came along for the ride; the three men and others pledged to put $US1 billion into the project, which Altman, then 30, would help run, and to get started they poached Ilya Sutskever from Google, one of the graduate students Google had "bought" in Hinton's auction. Initially Musk wanted to operate OpenAI as a nonprofit, free from the economic incentives driving Google and other corporations, but by the time Google wowed the tech community with its Go stunt he was changing his mind about how it should be run: he desperately wanted OpenAI to invent something that would capture the world's imagination and close the gap with Google, and it wasn't getting the job done as a nonprofit.

In late 2017 Musk hatched a plan to wrest control of the lab from Altman and the other founders and transform it into a commercial operation that would join forces with Tesla and rely on supercomputers the car company was developing, according to four people familiar with the matter; when Altman and others pushed back, Musk quit and said he would focus on his own AI work at Tesla. In February 2018 he announced his departure to OpenAI's staff on the top floor of the startup's offices in a converted truck factory, three people who attended said; when he said OpenAI needed to move faster, one researcher retorted that Musk was being reckless, and Musk called the researcher a "jackass" and stormed out, taking his deep pockets with him. OpenAI suddenly needed new financing in a hurry: Altman flew to Sun Valley for a conference and ran into Satya Nadella, Microsoft's CEO, and a tie-up seemed natural, since Altman knew Microsoft's chief technology officer Kevin Scott and Microsoft had bought LinkedIn from Hoffman, an OpenAI board member; Nadella told Scott to get it done. The deal closed in 2019, leaving Altman and OpenAI with a for-profit company formed under the original nonprofit, $US1 billion in fresh capital, and Microsoft with a new way to build AI into its vast cloud computing service. Not everyone inside OpenAI was happy.



---


# OpenAI's Nonprofit-To-For-Profit Structure

OpenAI started out as a nonprofit when it launched with financial backing from Tesla CEO Elon Musk and others, with stated aims to "advance digital intelligence in the way that is most likely to benefit humanity as a whole, unconstrained by a need to generate financial return." That changed in 2018, when it incorporated a for-profit business, OpenAI LP, and shifted nearly all its staff into that business, not long after releasing its first generation of the GPT large language model for mimicking human writing.

Around the same time, Musk — who had co-chaired its board with Altman — resigned from the board, in a move OpenAI said would eliminate a "potential future conflict for Elon" due to Tesla's work on building self-driving systems. The resulting arrangement is a split one: OpenAI's board has preserved its nonprofit governance structure, while the startup it oversees has increasingly sought to capitalize on its technology by tailoring its popular chatbot to business customers.



---


# OpenAI's Partnerships With Microsoft And The Associated Press

OpenAI's key business partner is Microsoft, which has invested billions of dollars into the startup and helped provide the computing power to run its AI systems. Microsoft said the leadership transition would not affect its relationship: "We have a long-term partnership with OpenAI and Microsoft remains committed to Mira and their team as we bring this next era of AI to our customers," an emailed Microsoft statement said.

A second, narrower arrangement is with a news organization: The Associated Press and OpenAI have a licensing and technology agreement allowing OpenAI access to part of the AP's text archives.

# The Taylor Swift And Travis Kelce Romance Overview

Rumours that singer Taylor Swift and Chiefs tight end Travis Kelce were dating ran for weeks and only intensified as Swift attended five Chiefs games during the season, according to CBS Sports' timeline of the rumoured romance published 12 October 2023.

The report gives the pattern of appearances. The week before publication she was in attendance to watch the Chiefs defeat the Denver Broncos in Week 6 on "Thursday Night Football." # The Swifties' Second Video: Operating A CD Player

qid: Does the Engadget article suggest that the Wonder Flowers in Nintendo's Super Mario Bros. Wonder introduce variability in game mechanics and enemies, while the Globes English | Israel Business Arena article implies that the State of Israel's reliance on technology creates a vulnerability to enemy challenges?
context:
# Super Mario Bros. Wonder: The Verdict

The review's verdict is that Super Mario Bros. Wonder is a marvelous game: its art and animations have a level of polish practically unmatched by rival titles, and the addition of Wonder Seeds subverts your expectations and keeps this 40-year franchise feeling new and innovative.

The grounds are a three-part answer to the problem the review poses — Mario has been stomping Goombas, smashing blocks and running from left to right for damn near 40 years, so how is Nintendo supposed to keep its classic side scroller feeling fresh? First, you shift the location to a brand new kingdom; next, you introduce a bunch of new enemies and power-ups; but what really pushes things over the top is the introduction of a new mechanic that turns everything you think you know about Mario games on its head. What you get is a game that dazzles and delights while living up to its name in a variety of ways.

The warrant is comparative: in a lot of ways Wonder reminds the reviewer of his favorite 2D Mario game, Super Mario World. The one reservation is about the wait — he wishes it had not taken more than 10 years for Nintendo to create a proper sequel to its last mainline platformer — but as he concludes, if that is what it takes to get a game like this, he is happy to sit and wonder what is next for Mario.



---


# Super Mario Bros. Wonder

Super Mario Bros. Wonder, developed by Nintendo EPD for Nintendo Switch, is ranked 4 on Polygon's best video games of 2023 list of 2023-10-31 — the first side-scrolling 2D platformer in the Super Mario Bros. line since New Super Mario Bros. U in 2012, and both a faithful rendition of the classic format and a complete reinvention of the series' irresistible formula.

When you activate the game's delightful whimsy via the aptly named Wonder Flower, it becomes more than a 2D platformer: a musical, a quiz show, a race, or a hidden object game, where pipes become inchworms, Piranha Plants burst into song, and Yoshi becomes a dragon. Critic N. Carpenter writes that each and every level finds some new way to delight and surprise, constantly introducing new ideas, enemies, and wrinkles only to pull back on them just when it is on the verge of becoming rote — like everything else in the Flower Kingdom, a few enemies shift and change in bizarre ways when the Wonder Flower is activated, such as Hoppo, the bouncy, round hippo equivalent that grows in size to create chaos. All of this weirdness, combined with Nintendo's platforming expertise, makes it an entrancing romp alone, with friends, or with strangers online, and the freshest Mario has felt in decades.

Polygon's 2023-10-20 couch co-op roundup adds the local multiplayer detail: Wonder brings together platforming shenanigans, silly power-ups, and lots of map secrets, and the best part is that four people can play local multiplayer, picking from classic characters including Mario, Luigi, Princess Peach, Princess Daisy, Toad, and Toadette.



---


# Super Mario Bros. Wonder's Art And Overworld Map

This might be the best Mario and friends have ever looked, and that includes recent 3D titles like Odyssey: there is just so much detail packed into every level and character, from the determined face Mario makes when he runs around to the little flames that sprout from your feet every time you jump.

Wonder's map is also surprisingly engaging. In the beginning the reviewer was not sure the ability to freely roam around added all that much, but as he progressed he found a number of secret nooks and crannies that would not have fit if the game were locked to a handful of paths. And with Wonder Flowers giving Nintendo the freedom to mix and match mechanics and enemies, there is just so much to see.



---


# Badges And Level Variety In Super Mario Bros. Wonder

Badges are Wonder's customization mechanic: they are earned by completing specific levels, and some may even be required to find secrets or reveal alternate exits. Some allow you to jump farther or float, while others make extra coins appear, and there are protective badges too — like the one that automatically saves you if you fall into lava or poison.
