It is a mechanic that feels inspired by recent roguelikes such as Hades, and it does a great job of adding customizability and replayability.

The level design is similarly varied. Wonder features six main worlds, each with a distinctive theme, but within those you will still run into reimagined haunted houses, pirate ships, underwater stages and more, along with a number of familiar baddies and some new foes across an incredible range of environments.

Even without the aid of a Wonder Flower, the sheer variety of level types is impressive. Alongside classic stages capped off by grabbing a flag, there are races, badge challenges, puzzle levels and more. KO Arenas let you pick your power-up of choice — Fire Flower, Elephant Suit, Bubble Mushroom or the Drill Hat — before taking down waves of enemies, while Break Time levels provide quick 30-second bursts of excitement. You will never be bored, even if you want a change from standard platform jumping.



---


# Minor Criticisms Of Super Mario Bros. Wonder

The reviewer's reservations are explicitly minor and do not disturb the overall verdict. Mummy enemies draw a complaint — pulling their wraps feels a bit tedious — and he fears the Elephant Suit might be a bit overpowered in comparison to the Drill Hat.

The other two are complaints about scarcity rather than quality: the 5-star levels and rhythm stages are so good he wishes there were more of them, and he is slightly disappointed the adorable penguins from the movie did not make an appearance somewhere in Wonder's ice levels.



---


# Wonder As A Return To 2D Mario Experimentation

Polygon argues that Super Mario Bros. Wonder shares the inventiveness of the earliest 2D Mario games and their disregard for what should and shouldn't be in a Mario game — making it, for middle-aged fans, a candidate for the first "true new Mario game" since Super Mario World in 1990. The grounds lie in a history the reviewer sets out: with each Super Mario Bros. on the NES and SNES, Nintendo's designers learned from the previous entry, cut what didn't work, made audacious additions (there was a time when adding a dinosaur named Yoshi felt like a gimmick), and gradually accumulated the pieces and tropes that would recur for the next thirty-plus years. Then, with Super Mario 64, 3D Mario games became the de facto labs for Nintendo's greatest experimentation — magical hats, water guns, galactic travel — while 2D Mario defaulted to a vessel for nostalgia, including the cheekily named New Super Mario Bros. series.

The warrant is that Wonder revives the old spirit specifically by letting the designers break their own machine. The traditional layer is intact — every level can be enjoyed as a loyal continuation of the plumber's work in the 2D platformer genre, which has kept a healthy cadence since the series debuted in 1985: dash from left to right, jump over pits, concuss enemies, collect the occasional power-up, and leap onto the flagpole that ends one level and unlocks the next. But the wonder of playing Super Mario Bros. in 1985 came from discovery, with Nintendo anticipating that players would climb outside the confines of the level and placing shortcuts in hidden crevices to reward the most rule-breaking players; badges now build on that freedom with skills that let you soar over towering enemies or use the Piranha Plant grappling hook to climb above the stage. "This is the most significant difference between 1985 and 2023," the reviewer writes: "Mario's creators have joined in the fun of breaking the machine." He imagines the game's origin as a notebook in which, since the '90s, every Nintendo developer wrote down each idea that "didn't fit the tone" or "wasn't Mario enough," until someone had the gall to say: "Let's turn this stuffed notebook of chaos into a game. Because why shouldn't Mario be an elephant? Why shouldn't Wigglers wear roller skates? And why shouldn't Luigi skydive?"



---


# The Wonder Flower Transformation Mechanic

The Wonder Flowers are the biggest twist in the game: in addition to the one Bowser stole, there is one hidden in almost every stage, and touching them transports you to an alternate dimension where the rules of the Marioverse have been completely rewritten.

The defining feature is unpredictability rather than a fixed effect. In one level Super Stars rain down from the sky; in another you might be transformed into a giant slime. You may also run into Wonder Flowers that convert the game from a side scroller into a top-down 2D maze, or suddenly find yourself the target in a shooting gallery. Almost every flower is different and the possibilities are seemingly endless.

The scale of the design work behind that is documented: in a recent volume of Nintendo's Ask the Developer, the reviewer learned the team had a wall of sticky notes with over 2,000 ideas — and after playing Wonder, he believes it. Wonder Flowers feel like they add an extra half a level to every stage; they are a delicious dessert on top of an already bountiful meal.

qid: After the TechCrunch report on Google's antitrust case published on October 31, 2023, and the subsequent TechCrunch report on Epic Games' antitrust battle with Google that started on November 6, 2023, was there consistency in the portrayal of Google's alleged anticompetitive behavior?
context:
# Google's Parallel Antitrust Proceedings In Late 2023

As of mid-November 2023, Google was fighting antitrust on more than one front at once. The Epic Games case was not its only antitrust case in trial: Google had settled a separate antitrust lawsuit with dating site Match Group the week before November 13, and on November 6 it went to trial with Fortnite maker Epic Games, which hoped to prove that Google engages in anticompetitive behavior with regard to its Android app store, Google Play, and its commission structure. Separately, Google was involved in an antitrust lawsuit with the Department of Justice over its alleged search monopoly.

The Epic case had shed co-plaintiffs on its way to trial. Epic's lawsuit originally involved Match and several U.S. attorneys general, but Google reached a settlement with the attorneys general in October 2023 and with Match the week before November 6, so Epic fought the antitrust battle on its own. The lawsuit, held in the U.S. District Court in California's Northern District, would include testimony from a number of Google and Android execs, including CEO Sundar Pichai, and Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, as well as from Apple, Netflix and other Android developers. Epic, meanwhile, had lost its antitrust battle with Apple and was asking the Supreme Court to weigh in.



---


# Epic v. Google: What The Trial Is

Epic v. Google is the antitrust case in which Fortnite publisher Epic Games drags a tech giant into court alleging that its mobile app store is an illegal monopoly — and although Epic's parallel claims against Apple already got their day in court, the similar lawsuit against Google never did, which is why the case goes to trial on November 6th, a mere 1,180 days after Epic originally sued.

The déjà vu is the point of confusion the piece sets out to clear up: Epic already went to trial with Apple, resulting in a ruling where Apple mostly won, and its Llamacorn legal gambit failed to #FreeFortnite years ago. The distinction is that the Apple claims were heard and the Google ones were not.

An update dated December 15th, 2023 notes that the case is basically over by then.



---


# What A Ruling Against Google Would Mean For Big Tech

A ruling against Google would not stop at Google: the remedy would likely resemble the Microsoft settlement and the outcome would ripple through the other pending Big Tech cases, because enforcers are using this trial to demonstrate that antitrust law can still take on the largest and most powerful companies in the world.

The grounds for the first half of that claim are the available remedies. If the judge rules against Google, the outcome could look a lot like the Microsoft deal, in which the computer company was required to change its behavior and share its APIs with third-party developers, and was also banned from making anticompetitive and exclusive deals with computer manufacturers. Google might likewise end up having to turn over all or most of the data it has collected to other search engines so they can improve their products and attract more users — a remedy scaled to the disparity the DOJ has cited, that Google gets 16 times more data than Bing does everyday.

The grounds for the ripple effect are the cases already queued behind this one. The FTC sued Amazon in September for using anticompetitive and unfair strategies to illegally maintain its monopoly power. The DOJ has been investigating Apple for years over the company's policy for third-party apps on its devices and whether it unfairly favors its own products. And there is an ongoing case between the FTC and Facebook, in which the agency calls on Facebook to sell Instagram and WhatsApp.

The warrant joining grounds to claim is enforcers' own stake in the result: they will want to show that antitrust law is still relevant and can successfully take on the biggest, most powerful companies in the world, so a win here sets the template the neighbouring cases are argued against. The scope condition is that nothing was settled as of this report — the case is expected to continue for several weeks, bringing to a head one of the biggest fights in tech antitrust since the U.S. took Microsoft to trial in the 1990s.



---


# The Google Antitrust Case

The Google antitrust case is the U.S. government's trial over Google's dominance in the online search market, stemming from a 2020 antitrust claim, in which the government argues that Google uses its platforms and its deals with partners to block out competition in search or advertising and thereby to hinder competitors from accessing the data they would need to improve their products.

Its defining features are the conduct at issue and the defence offered against it. Google CEO Sundar Pichai testified Monday in the trial, defending Google's business tactics, including its deal with Apple and other partners to make Google the default search engine. Google's answer is that it is just doing business: everybody wants Google as the default engine because it is the best, and that, the company says, does not make its actions illegal.

The important boundary case is which Google antitrust matter this is. The 2020 search claim is separate from the one filed in January by the Department of Justice, along with eight states including New York, California and Colorado, which aims to "halt Google's anticompetitive scheme, unwind Google's monopolistic grip on the market and restore competition to digital advertising." The search case and the digital-advertising case are distinct proceedings and should not be conflated.

The trial is the venue in which the underlying numbers surface. Monday's hearing revealed plenty of juicy tidbits, including the $26.3 billion Google spent making itself the default search engine across platforms in 2021, and how Google tried to take it further and have Chrome preinstalled on iPhones.



---


# The Settlements That Left Epic Standing Alone

Other plaintiffs brought app store antitrust claims against Google and then all settled: all 50 state attorneys general and a number of consumers have tentatively settled, though it is not clear what the deal might include, and Match Group — the company behind Tinder, Match.com, OkCupid and other dating apps — just reached a surprise last-minute settlement too, one that makes it sound like Match effectively gave up. Epic stands alone.

Epic seems to have no interest in settling as long as the "Google tax" exists, and the company has repeatedly said it is not interested in cash. So far it has been willing to push these cases all the way through multiple appeals, cost be damned. It is not clear what Google could proactively offer that would satisfy Epic, since CEO Tim Sweeney has also publicly suggested that Google would simply circumvent any settlement it offers. If you want to see a vision of a future Epic would accept, look to the letter it sent to state attorneys general, laying out a settlement that would basically prohibit Google from doing the anticompetitive things Epic claims it did. Google would not tell The Verge whether it has offered Epic any kind of settlement.



---


# Helena World Chronicle's Class Action Antitrust Suit Against Google

A class action lawsuit filed in the week of 15 December 2023 in the U.S. District Court in D.C. accuses Google and parent company Alphabet of anticompetitive behavior in violation of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act and others, on behalf of news publishers. The case was filed by Arkansas-based publisher Helena World Chronicle, which argues that Google "siphons off" news publishers' content, their readers and their ad revenue through anticompetitive means, and it specifically cites new AI technologies such as Google's Search Generative Experience (SGE) and the Bard AI chatbot as worsening the problem.

Helena World Chronicle owns and publishes two weekly newspapers in Arkansas. In the complaint it argues that Google is "starving the free press" by sharing publishers' content on Google, losing them "billions of dollars."

Beyond damages, the suit asks for an injunction that would require Google to obtain consent from publishers before using their website data to train its general artificial intelligence products, including Google's own and those of rivals. It also asks that publishers who opt out of SGE still be allowed to show up in Google search results, among other things.

The law firm handling the case is Hausfeld, whose announcement states that "the anticompetitive effects of Google's scheme cause profound harm to competition, to consumers, to labor, and to a democratic free press," and that "Plaintiff Helena World Chronicle, LLC invokes the Sherman Act and Clayton Act to seek class-wide monetary and injunctive relief to restore and ensure competition for digital news and reference publishing and set up guardrails to preserve a free marketplace of ideas in the new era of artificial intelligence."



---


# The U.S. Justice Department's Parallel Antitrust Suits Against Google

The Helena World Chronicle class action arrives alongside the filing of the U.S. Justice Department's lawsuit against Google for monopolizing digital ad technologies, and the complaint also references the Justice Department's 2020 civil antitrust suit over search and search advertising.

The two government cases concern different markets: search and search advertising in the 2020 suit are distinct from the digital ad technologies at issue in the more recent one.

qid: Does 'The Roar | Sports Writers Blog' suggest that 'The All Blacks' motivation for playing is the same as the Springboks' as per the first article, while also indicating that 'The All Blacks' handling was compromised by external factors in the second article, and does it confirm 'The All Blacks' losses to Argentina as stated in the third article?
context:
# The All Blacks' Final Moments In The 2023 World Cup Final

New Zealand's last chance in the 2023 Rugby World Cup final died in the 80th minute when Ardie Savea forced a ball out wide just as the men in black saw space and looked to open up the Springboks — a killer blow, in The Roar's phrase.

The wider failing was handling. The All Blacks had their chances, but their usual safe handling — a feature throughout the World Cup after their first-up loss to France — evaded them against the Springboks' blitz defence in the wet conditions, and all night their timing was off.

The end came at a set piece. Wayne Barnes, who was booed relentlessly, called a scrum reset as the seconds ticked by; moments later New Zealand hearts sank as the Springboks won the scrum and then hung onto the ball.



---


# The Ireland Series Loss Backlash As All Blacks Motivation

The Roar argued on Oct. 26, 2023 that where the Springboks play for their country, the All Blacks were playing for themselves as much as anyone — and for the generation of players and leaders who would call time on their international careers at week's end — which is why the World Cup final was personal for the men in black.

The framing question is how New Zealand could withstand and overcome the hitherto unshakable wave of momentum and spirit the Springboks play with under Rassie Erasmus in that weekend's final. The grounds offered for the All Blacks' personal motivation are the backlash and toxicity that followed their historic home series loss to Ireland, described as a humbling and public reminder of the expectation of being an All Black — All Blacks social media managers were forced to delete a thousand comments an hour following the humbling series loss in Wellington.

The warrant is that the hurt persisted and became fuel: the pain of the days and weeks after that dark July, as well as the bumps and bruises along the way — including as recently as August when they suffered their biggest defeat to the Boks to lose the inaugural and prestigious Qatar Cup — still ran deep.



---


# The All Blacks' Generational Change After The 2023 World Cup

The 2023 World Cup final marked the end of an All Blacks era on and off the field: Ian Foster's tenure as coach came to an end with Scott Robertson taking over, and multiple generational players — Dane Coles, Sam Whitelock, Brodie Retallick and Aaron Smith — were to call time on their international careers, with others including Ardie Savea, Richie Mo'unga, Beauden Barrett and Shannon Frizell heading to Japan.

Writing before the final on Oct. 26, The Roar reported that the All Blacks would experience a changing of the guard the next season, and noted that the team's own social media channels described the World Cup final selection as the "Last Dance". Dane Coles, a 2015 World Cup winner, would call time on his career, while his tight-five teammates Retallick and Whitelock — the latter bidding to become the first player to win the Webb Ellis Cup for a third time — would head overseas, and fellow World Cup winners Aaron Smith and Beauden Barrett would also head to Japan.

Coles, labelled by Samisoni Taukei'aho as a "Grandad" type figure in the All Blacks, was even denied the chance of a farewell send-off after missing selection for the final. Foster called the conversation with the 36-year-old the hardest of his coaching life: "Yeah, tough. We don't want to talk too much about post-game stuff, but that was a tough one, probably the toughest I have had as a coach. He took it the way I expected him to. He's a champion." After the final, The Roar added that Robertson would have an almighty task on his hands given the scale of the departures.



---


# Pieter-Steph Du Toit And The Springboks' Rush Defence In The Final

Pieter-Steph du Toit, the 2019 World Rugby player of the year, played his best match in four years in the 2023 World Cup final, spearheading the Springboks' physical onslaught with 28 tackles, each as bone-crunching as the next.

The collective effect was the Springboks' rush defence, which caused the All Blacks problems all evening, with Damian de Allende and Jesse Kriel forcing their opponents into errors.

Its most visible victim was one of New Zealand's most dangerous attackers: Will Jordan, the impressive young outside back who scored eight tries in the tournament, had a difficult night and was replaced midway through the second half.



---


# Springboks Beat All Blacks 12-11 To Win A Record Fourth World Cup

South Africa beat New Zealand 12-11 at the Stade de France on Oct. 28, 2023 to claim a record fourth Rugby World Cup, moving into uncharted territory by leapfrogging the All Blacks — and doing it, as The Roar noted, twenty-eight years after the famous Ellis Park win at which Nelson Mandela handed the William Webb Ellis Cup to Francois Pienaar.

The conditions and the setting could not have been more different from 1995: instead of the blue skies over Johannesburg and the Boeing 747 that sent shivers down spines in attendance, rain and dampness poured down on the Stade de France, though nothing dampened an evening into which 80,065 fans poured. It was, the report says, that kind of evening, where the margins were tiny and the outcomes almighty.

The margin itself came down to one kick. A missed Richie Mo'unga conversion following Beauden Barrett's 58th-minute try — the only five-pointer of the match — ultimately proved the difference, as Handre Pollard's four three-pointers led the Springboks to World Cup glory. The win was South Africa's third one-point knockout victory in a row, and the second straight tournament they had won in France, having beaten England at the same venue in 2007.



---


# The Springboks' Selection Philosophy: Playing For South Africa

Jacques Nienaber argued before the 2023 World Cup final that Springbok selection is not about individuals at all but about the country — "We explain to the whole squad why we are going a certain route. It is not about individual selection… It is for South Africa" — speaking shortly after announcing two changes to his starting side and five in total, having gone in with a forwards-heavy 7-1 bench split.

The warrant is that shared explanation removes ego from the equation and lets players accept decisions they might otherwise contest: "As selectors we know there will be pressure on us if we don't deliver a result but at the back of our minds we know this selection is for South Africa. The players take it like that. It is not about person or ego, not that they have egos, but you can't think of that. You have to think about South Africa and the Springboks."

The Roar's reading is that the Springboks are seemingly playing for more than themselves — they are playing for their country — and calls it a powerful force, one that saw them progress through the knockout stages to reach the final after consecutive one-point victories. Pressure, on this account, is relative: the South African laughs at the notion of what pressure is compared to the inequality and challenges the Rainbow Nation continues to experience.



---


# Erasmus' 2019 Final Speech: Country Over Ego

Rassie Erasmus argued before the 2019 World Cup final that worrying about your own mistakes is a symptom of ego, and that a Springbok's job on the day is to represent South Africa rather than himself — one of the great rugby speeches, delivered before the Springboks sealed a stunning 32-12 victory over England to claim their third William Webb Ellis Cup.

The claim and its warrant are in his own words: "You don't have the right today to worry about your mistakes. If you worry about your mistakes today, you've got ego problems." The grounds are what the players are actually playing for: "You are not representing yourself today. You are fighting for the things that happen in South Africa. You are tackling for the boy who didn't get the same opportunities that you got eventually."

Writing four years later on Oct. 26, 2023, The Roar observed that the "ego" Erasmus spoke about is what is driving the standards and expectations around the Springboks' bid to go back-to-back.



---


# Joe Schmidt's Wallabies Candidacy And The Rival Candidates

The Roar reported on 11 December 2023 that Joe Schmidt — the 2018 World Rugby coach of the year, former Ireland coach and All Blacks assistant — is interested in the vacant Wallabies coaching job, with Dan McKellar, Stephen Larkham, Andy Friend and Ian Foster also remaining interested in the role.

The link the report draws is personal. Peter Horne's close relationship with Schmidt could be one of the keys to landing him: after leaving his Irish post following the 2019 World Cup, ending six years in the job, Schmidt worked alongside Horne at World Rugby, and it is believed the duo have a strong working relationship.

qid: Which company, reported by both The Verge and TechCrunch, uses relevance, distance, and prominence to rank local search results, has spent billions to be the default search engine on multiple platforms, and has been accused of anticompetitive practices affecting news publishers' revenues?
context:
# Google Local Search Ranking Factors

Google's public documentation says it uses three categories to rank results that are local to a searcher: relevance, distance, and prominence. To improve local ranking, Google encourages businesses to provide a trove of information on their profile — basics like updated hours of operation and accurate location details, but also responding to reviews, adding photos, and even posting individual items in stock to their Google page. The prominence measure in Maps includes data from the web: links to the business, how the business ranks in traditional search, and press coverage, for example. In this way SEO affects how a business appears in local search results, and news articles and links are one way Google tries to determine the relevance of a page — which is why reporters' inboxes are overrun with spammy requests to buy "guest posts" on their sites from marketers.

The model bounds what a keyword-matched business name can do. Asked whether naming a business after a search term works, Danny Sullivan, Google's public liaison for Search, said, "I doubt it": owners doing this might find success, but Google pulls in other data to serve results to users, like location, reviews, or ratings — a "hodgepodge of different things that we have that are out there." Sullivan added, "I've seen these kinds of things over the years, and they kind of make me laugh and have a bit of a chuckle. But I don't think they're really great marketing campaigns," and said Google's advice has always been that businesses should make decisions that serve their customers, not the platform.

The behaviour the names target is real even if the leverage is limited. The term "Thai food near me" is searched, on average, nearly a million times a month in the US, according to Semrush, a company that provides keyword research and other popular SEO tools; Semrush notes you will need referring domains and optimized content to compete for the term and grades it as "difficult" to rank for — competitive, but not even the hardest category. Adding "near me" to a search term is both a learned behavior and encouraged by Google, since "___ near me" is a top autofilled search suggestion on both Search and Maps and has become synonymous with Google, which is why the joke works. One anomaly showed the distance factor being outweighed: a search The Verge's reporter did in Google Maps for "Thai food near me" from Wisconsin surfaced the Manhattan restaurant as a suggestion above any local businesses, making it easier to find from the Midwest than from Brooklyn. Sullivan said this could be due to Google recognizing there is a business with an exact-match name that has some degree of notoriety that people are searching for in different areas, and that while it could encourage others to name businesses this way, he does not see it as an issue that needs addressing.



---


# Why Traditional E-Commerce Search Has Degraded

Deft co-founder Zach Hudson told TechCrunch that there are a few plaguing problems with the traditional search experience that prevent users from finding a suitable item — that is, the claim is that search has gotten worse, not that users have gotten worse at searching.

He offers three grounds, each a different actor degrading the result set: "You have companies like Google and Amazon that continue to push the most relevant listings down so they can make more advertising dollars. Some easy searches are now hard because marketers have learned how to game these search engines. Plus, now you have AI content that is putting the burden on users to separate fact from fiction," he said.

The warrant tying them together is that each mechanism moves cost onto the user: platform ad incentives bury relevance, SEO gaming inflates the noise, and AI-generated content shifts verification work to the person searching.



---


# Google Paid $26.3 Billion In 2021 For Default Search Placement

Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to multiple browsers, phones and platforms — from companies including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla — to be everyone's default search engine. The figure was revealed by Google's search head Prabhakar Raghavan when he testified in court on October 28, according to The Verge.

About $18 billion of that total went directly to Apple, according to a New York Times report published earlier in October 2023, and Google has had its deal with Apple in place since 2003 — so the payment is the current year of a two-decade arrangement, not a one-off. Questioned on the amount of money Google spends to get first pick of search engines, Pichai said the decision was made with the consumer in mind: Google pays big bucks to be everywhere so that it can take in all the data and be the best search engine across different companies' devices, he said, according to The Verge.

The trial also produced evidence that Google understood the value of defaults very early on. U.S. Justice Department lawyer Meagan Bellshaw showed Pichai a 2007 email from a Google product strategy meeting containing data showing that when people changed their browser homepage to Google, they did 15% more Google searches, and that when they switched away, their Google searches dropped 27%. The email summarizing that meeting, sent to Pichai as well as other Google leaders, read: "Nitin argues that focusing on homepage market share is one of the most effective things we can do to make gains in search market share," according to The Verge.



---


# US v. Google: Two Months Into The Search Antitrust Trial

As of TechCrunch's November 13, 2023 roundup, the Justice Department's landmark antitrust case against Google was nearly two months old, and the trial record was still producing fresh revelations. TechCrunch framed it as one of the biggest fights in tech antitrust since the U.S. took Microsoft to trial in the 1990s.

An earlier roundup had already surfaced that Google spent $26.3 billion in 2021 making itself the default search engine across platforms, and that Google tried to have Chrome preinstalled on iPhones. Over the couple of weeks preceding this roundup, more of Google's inner workings came to light, including some of the search engine's most lucrative search queries, the shape of the revenue-share agreements between Google and Android OEMs, and why Expedia has a bone to pick with Google.



---


# Google's Link-Based Ranking And The Market It Created

Google revolutionized search by evaluating websites based on links from other websites, seeing each link as a vote of relevance and trustworthiness — a structure that made the ranking of any page a function of what other pages pointed to it. The founders pledged to be a neutral navigation system with no ads: just a clean white screen with a search box that would bring people off the Google landing page and out to a helpful website as seamlessly as possible. Users quickly decided this link-based sorting methodology was superior to the existing search engines, and by the end of 1999 Google was handling the majority of online queries.

The model arrived in response to a documented problem. In 1997 an Italian professor published a journal article about what he called Search Engines Persuasion: "Finding the right information on the World Wide Web is becoming a fundamental problem," he wrote, and "a vast number of new companies was born just to make customer Web pages as visible as possible," which "has led to a bad performance degradation of search engines."

The relation between votes and rank held only as long as links were scarce and organic, and it did not. Mapstead, like many early practitioners of SEO, figured out how to adapt: almost as soon as Google took over, a secondary market emerged for links. For a few hundred bucks, a firm in India or the Philippines could provide thousands of links from blog networks built entirely for that purpose. It was easy — buy links that led to your site and watch your ranking in Google's results rise.



---


# The Google Antitrust Case

The Google antitrust case is the U.S. government's trial over Google's dominance in the online search market, stemming from a 2020 antitrust claim, in which the government argues that Google uses its platforms and its deals with partners to block out competition in search or advertising and thereby to hinder competitors from accessing the data they would need to improve their products.

Its defining features are the conduct at issue and the defence offered against it. Google CEO Sundar Pichai testified Monday in the trial, defending Google's business tactics, including its deal with Apple and other partners to make Google the default search engine. Google's answer is that it is just doing business: everybody wants Google as the default engine because it is the best, and that, the company says, does not make its actions illegal.

The important boundary case is which Google antitrust matter this is. The 2020 search claim is separate from the one filed in January by the Department of Justice, along with eight states including New York, California and Colorado, which aims to "halt Google's anticompetitive scheme, unwind Google's monopolistic grip on the market and restore competition to digital advertising." The search case and the digital-advertising case are distinct proceedings and should not be conflated.

The trial is the venue in which the underlying numbers surface. Monday's hearing revealed plenty of juicy tidbits, including the $26.3 billion Google spent making itself the default search engine across platforms in 2021, and how Google tried to take it further and have Chrome preinstalled on iPhones.

qid: Does the 'Business World' article suggest that the 'Finance department of the Philippines' is ignoring the need to reduce debt, while the 'Globes English | Israel Business Arena' article indicates that the 'high-tech industry' is experiencing a reduction in spending?
context:
# Philippine 2024 Budget Deficit and Debt Trajectory

The Philippine national budget for 2024 is P5.768 trillion, 9.5% higher than the 2023 budget of P5.268 trillion — an increase of P499.6 billion — and observers note that this first budget fully prepared by the current administration accounts for 21.7% of gross domestic product. Supported mainly by P3.5 trillion in tax revenues, based on 2023 tax revenue projections, it implies a budget deficit of some P2.268 trillion to be funded by additional borrowings, which could increase government debt from P14.24 trillion as of July to P16+ trillion by the end of 2024.

At the Congressional budget hearing, Finance Secretary Benjamin Diokno optimistically provided updates on the government's fiscal and revenue collection performances and presented sources of funding for the national budget. He told the Philippine News Agency on 10 August that tax revenue is projected to increase from P3.5 trillion in 2023 to P6.5 trillion in 2028, while non-tax revenues are expected to decline from P191 billion in 2023 to P184 billion in 2028. Diokno said the Finance department aims to gradually reduce net financing, or new debt, from P1.42 trillion in 2022 to P1.22 trillion in 2024, which will help bring the country's debt-to-GDP ratio to almost below 60% by 2025.

Against that optimism, President Ferdinand Marcos, Jr. told members of the US-ASEAN Business Council who visited Malacañang, in remarks reported by ABS-CBN on 9 August 2023: "We worry about our debt-to-GDP ratio in the Philippines, as it stands at about 63% and that's a little high for us and it is not ideal."



---


# Fiscal Cost Channels of the Israel-Gaza War

Leo Leiderman set out the war's cost to the Israeli budget as a set of direct and indirect channels: "As with any war, the current war has and will have direct and indirect impacts."

On the spending side, the war will substantially raise defence spending in the coming years for procurement of equipment, ammunition and advanced systems in accordance with the new needs. A second direct expense is payment for the reserve duty days of those mobilised. A third channel runs through financing costs: given current interest rate levels around the world, the cost of servicing public debt as a proportion of GDP will rise.

On the revenue side, he expects a decline in state revenues from taxation. The combined result of these channels is a rise in the fiscal deficit.



---


# Philippine Development Plan 2023-2028 Targets

The Philippine Development Plan 2023-2028 aims for a deep economic and social transformation to reinvigorate job creation and accelerate poverty reduction by steering the economy back to a high-growth path, and two main performance indicators are identified and will be monitored by the National Government.

The first is for the country to graduate into upper middle-income class status within the term of the current administration, for which the economy must grow its per capita income above the threshold set by the World Bank, a gross national income per capita of at least $4,466; in 2022 the Philippines achieved a GNI per capita of $3,950. The second is to lower the poverty level from 18.1% in 2021 to single digits by 2028, the end of the term of the current administration. Both indicators require high growth rates, and for the next year through 2028 the government pencils the growth rate between 6.5% and 8%.



---


# DBM Case for a Surplus Budget Policy

The Department of Budget and Management argues that a surplus budget is preferable to a deficit because less government borrowing frees resources for the private sector and reduces the state's own debt burden. Business World quoted the budget managers word for word, saying their exhortations must be quoted in full to educate non-economists and questioning common people about why a surplus budget is necessary.

The first ground is crowding-out. "The less the government borrow from the public, the lesser the pressure on interest and inflation rates and the more funds are made available in the financial market. Such funds may be used by businessmen to build factories, hire workers, buy equipment and open more employment opportunities. By keeping more funds in the hands of the private sector rather than competing for credit, the government helps make financing available for families who want to own homes, buy cars, or support their children's education."

The second ground is debt reduction, with a stated scope condition. "The government also needs to generate a budget surplus to repay the huge debt it has accumulated over the years. The reduction of the national budget debt will correspondingly lessen government's requirements for interest and principal payments. This becomes important particularly during periods of rising interest rates and unstable exchange rates."



---


# Philippine Inflation and Deficit Vicious Cycle

The cycle described is mutual reinforcement between deficits and inflation: some economists say that deficit budgets and their remedies — monetary, through borrowings that increase money supply, and fiscal, such as raising taxes — increase inflation, and stubborn inflation further entrenches structural deficits in the system. Business World calls this a vicious cycle, and prefaces it by noting that whomever one believes, inflation "independently says it as it is."

The measurement anchor given is the Philippine target arithmetic at the time. While inflation in the Philippines had been on a downward trend since January, the country needed to achieve a 3.7% average inflation rate for the next five months to hit the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas forecast of 5.5% inflation for 2023, Assistant National Statistician Rachel Lacsa said.



---


# Philippine Debt And The Case For Fiscal Consolidation

The argument for fiscal consolidation is that although the current 61% debt-to-GDP ratio may be manageable for an emerging economy like the Philippines for some time, the country may not have the fiscal space to respond to another potential domestic or external shock. The grounds are historical: the National Government's debt was less than 40% before the pandemic struck, and it expended much of its fiscal space combatting the pandemic, incurring debt and large budget deficits. The warrant is a crowding-out mechanism: if the debt continues to rise more than the economy, risks will increase and the government may crowd out private investment as it competes with the private sector for funds to service its debt.

The planned consolidation entails harmonizing revenue needs with the promotion of investment through the structure and administration of the reformed incentive system. The National Government plans to raise more revenue to finance the country's socio-economic needs, largely through a progressive and simplified tax system and more efficient and effective tax collection measures through digitalization, and to some extent from policy measures such as value-added tax on digital service providers and excise tax on sweetened beverages and junk food. The conclusion is stated as a conditional pair: achieving fiscal stability presupposes the sustainability of fiscal policy, and fiscal stability helps crowd in private investment.



---


# Philippine National Government Budget Definition

The Department of Budget and Management (DBM) defines the government budget as "the financial plan of the government…which shows what its resources are, and how they will be generated and used over the fiscal period. It refers to the income, expenditures and sources of borrowings of the National Government (NG) that are used to achieve national objectives, strategies and programs."

Its constitutional basis is Section 22, Article VII: "The President shall submit to the Congress within 30 days from the opening of every regular session, as the basis of the general appropriation bill, a budget of expenditures and sources of financing including receipts from existing and proposed revenue measures."

The National Government budget is the totality of the budgets of all government entities: the National Government itself, the non-financial government-owned and -controlled corporations (usually only the 14 major GOCCs), government financial institutions, local government units, the social security institutions (GSIS, SSS, military pensions, PhilHealth and others), the Oil Price Stabilization Fund, the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas, and the Central Bank-Board of Liquidators. It is allocated for the implementation of government programmes and projects, the operation of government offices, payment of salaries of government employees and payment of public debts, with expenditures classified by expense class, sector and implementing unit of government.

Appropriations come from two sources: new general appropriations legislated by Congress for every budget year under the General Appropriations Act, and existing appropriations previously authorised by Congress. Under Article VI, Section 29 of the Constitution, no money can be withdrawn from the Treasury except in pursuance of an appropriation made by law.



---


# Private Sector Volunteers In Terror Finance Tracking

The network blocking terror financing funds includes many entities, including private citizens: IMPA has been approached by many experts from the private sector — people with intelligence experience because they have worked in these organizations, or with high-tech experience — who "have mobilized like crazy."

"The world's financial intelligence authorities are now at the heart of this struggle, and we're working together to thwart the financing channels that we've located," Ostrovitch-Levi said. "Israeli entrepreneurs in Silicon Valley have contacted us; they write code, search for information, and give us lots of information. We aggregate and examine everything."

qid: Between the TechCrunch report on Sam Bankman-Fried's trial published on October 1, 2023, and the TechCrunch report on the allegations against Sam Bankman-Fried published on October 7, 2023, was there consistency in the portrayal of the accusations against Sam Bankman-Fried?
context:
# Day Two Of The Bankman-Fried Trial: Jury Selection And The Courtroom Audience

On the second day of Sam Bankman-Fried's fraud trial, the jury was selected on Wednesday morning, after which lawyers for the government and then for Bankman-Fried delivered opening statements that told two very different stories of the former FTX CEO's sudden rise and almost instantaneous fall. The central question framed by the proceedings was who Bankman-Fried, the former CEO of crypto exchange FTX, really is: a liar and a fraud, or someone who acted in good faith and, like many a startup founder, flew too close to the sun. That answer, the account notes, ultimately lies with the jury.

The day featured pointed allegations, a friend from MIT, and an audience replete with big names, including Bankman-Fried's professorial parents and Damian Williams, the U.S. attorney for the Southern District of New York. Bankman-Fried himself spent most of the day in court staring into a laptop while seated between his two attorneys. The prosecution's account of his alleged crimes was described as featuring a study in contrasts.



---


# Going Infinite: Michael Lewis's Account Of SBF's Political Dealings

Michael Lewis's book "Going Infinite" debuted on the first day of Sam Bankman-Fried's trial, and details about Bankman-Fried's political dealings emerging from it include his alleged attempt to buy off Donald Trump to get him not to run again for president.

TechCrunch's team was focused on the Manhattan Federal Court for the trial of Bankman-Fried, the disgraced entrepreneur accused of orchestrating the collapse of the cryptocurrency exchange FTX; the Lewis book is the second channel through which the week's revelations arrived. The reporting is framed as allegation rather than established fact, and it comes from the book rather than from courtroom testimony. The item appeared in TechCrunch's Week in Review of October 7, 2023.



---


# The FTX Trial's Stakes For The Wider Crypto Industry

The Verge argued that the trial of Sam Bankman-Fried is likely to be more consequential than just whether the man himself is found guilty: depending on what evidence is introduced, it could be rough for the entire crypto industry.

The grounds are the unpredictability of what a trial surfaces, voiced by Yesha Yadav, a law professor at Vanderbilt University: "How much damage can this trial do to the already beaten-down reputation of the industry at this point? This trial is going to be an excruciating moment for the industry because no one knows what kind of evidence might come out." The warrant joining that uncertainty to industry-wide stakes is that the industry's reputation is already beaten down, so evidence introduced against one exchange's founder lands on the whole sector rather than on him alone.



---


# Sam Bankman-Fried

Sam Bankman-Fried is the former CEO of the bankrupt crypto exchange FTX, whose highly anticipated criminal trial started on the Tuesday before TechCrunch's 2023-10-01 report, to determine whether he is guilty of seven counts of fraud and conspiracy. As one former federal prosecutor put it: "The odds seem to be stacked against him at this point."

He was 31 years old and co-founded FTX in 2019; within a few years the once third-largest crypto exchange's valuation hit $32 billion at its peak, and the company is now trying to claw back any funds to distribute to creditors. Before the fall he was even compared to Warren Buffet, and many called him the white horse of crypto — a description TechCrunch notes it never applied to him.

Bankman-Fried, however, maintained his innocence. At The New York Times' DealBook Summit he appeared virtually from the Bahamas and said, "I didn't ever try to commit fraud on anyone; I was shocked by what happened this month"; in a published DM exchange with a Vox reporter he said he regretted filing for bankruptcy and thought that "regulators make everything worse." In January he pleaded not guilty to all counts, which include wire fraud, conspiracy to commit money laundering and conspiracy to misuse customer funds. He could face up to 115 years in jail if convicted on all charges.

TechCrunch's 2023-10-02 summary of his standing on the eve of trial: SBF has been denied bail; his name is mud (or much worse) among those who have lost money in Alameda or FTX; and those who might not have had positions in these still blame him for other crypto woes, because he set off a ripple effect.



---


# Sam Bankman-Fried's Federal Fraud Trial

Sam Bankman-Fried, the founder of bankrupt cryptocurrency exchange FTX, is charged with seven counts of fraud and money laundering following the collapse of his cryptocurrency empire the previous year, and was on trial in New York in October 2023.

Two fixed points anchor the proceeding as CNBC described it on 2023-10-06. A U.S. judge revoked Bankman-Fried's bail at a hearing in a New York courthouse on August 11, 2023. And on Thursday, Oct. 5, 2023, Matt Huang, co-founder of Paradigm Operations LP, arrived at the New York court to appear in the case.



---


# The SBF Trial Proceedings

Sam Bankman-Fried is in court for alleged fraud and money laundering while leading crypto exchange FTX and sister company Alameda. TechCrunch's 2023-10-02 preview placed the case in the Manhattan Federal Court, describing the disgraced cryptocurrency entrepreneur as accused of orchestrating "one of the biggest financial frauds in American history": the multibillion-dollar collapse of FTX, the crypto exchange he founded and led. SBF, as he is known, has pleaded not guilty to some seven charges of fraud and conspiracy.

The trial kicked off with jury selection October 3. By TechCrunch's 2023-10-06 update the case was entering its next chapter, with proceedings resuming Thursday: as confirmed during a teleconference Wednesday, SBF would be taking the stand along with a handful of other witnesses, as the onus shifted toward the defense after the prosecution brought its case to its conclusion.

Access to the proceedings is limited: no devices are allowed, so reports are being physically put together within the courtroom, or sent to overflow rooms. The jury's composition ranges from a train conductor to a retired investment banker who attended Stanford University, and TechCrunch pointed readers to a special joint episode of its Equity and Chain Reaction podcasts for a better sense of the vibe between the jurors and the rest of the court.

A second account of the same events was arriving in parallel: "Going Infinite," a book by Michael Lewis chronicling the rise and fall of SBF, was set to debut on the first day of the trial.



---


# FTX Fraud Charges And The SEC's Allegation

Sam Bankman-Fried, the founder of the failed cryptocurrency exchange FTX, faced seven counts of wire fraud and conspiracy — specifically, two counts of wire fraud and five conspiracy charges — and the Securities and Exchange Commission alleged that FTX was a fraud "from the start," with a "multi-billion-dollar deficiency caused by his own misappropriation of customer funds." The Verge repeated this framing at the head of each of its trial dispatches through October 2023, and in its October 28th, 2023 write-up reported that Bankman-Fried had been found guilty on seven counts including charges of wire fraud.

The boundary of the concept is the mix of charge types: the indictment paired substantive wire fraud counts with conspiracy counts rather than resting on a single offence, and the SEC's civil allegation about the exchange's origins ran alongside the criminal case rather than being part of it. The Verge's reporter, writing as the prosecution's case neared its end on October 26th, 2023, added an impression of the people the charges swept in: all the co-conspirators seemed oddly younger than their years, as though they had got stuck in the "math camp forever" environment Bankman-Fried created for them and simply failed to grow up.



---


# Going Infinite: Michael Lewis On Sam Bankman-Fried

Michael Lewis's October 2023 book is an account of Sam Bankman-Fried, published by Allen Lane at $55 on 3 October, The Sydney Morning Herald listed on 1 October 2023.

Its subject is defined by the arc: Bankman-Fried set up his cryptocurrency exchange, FTX, in 2019 and three years later was rolling in money, but when the crypto world went pear-shaped his business hit an irreversible tailspin, and he now faces multiple charges and was due in court on 3 October.

The reviewer's warrant for reading it is the author: "If anyone can be relied on to tell this story of a financial Icarus with verve and narrative flair, it's Michael Lewis, author of Liar's Poker, Moneyball, and The Big Short." A caveat is attached — "No doubt the updated edition will have the verdict on SBF."

qid: Does 'The Guardian' describe Shai Hope's performance against legspin bowling in the first T20 international differently from how 'The Guardian' describes his role in the fifth T20 international?
context:
# West Indies Win The 2023 T20I Series 3-2

West Indies beat England by four wickets in the fifth and deciding T20 international on Dec. 21, 2023, taking the series 3-2 when Shai Hope pinged Chris Woakes over extra cover for six at 19.2 overs, with West Indies 133-6.

It was the 120th six of the series, and Hope played a gem of an innings, calmly anchoring West Indies in an increasingly nervous chase with a run-a-ball 43; England fought admirably to defend a below-par total and, but for Hope, would probably have done it. Cricket on TNT Sports posted that the win claimed the series 3-2 and a white-ball clean sweep. The Guardian's report framed the finish as the sequel to a very different match: Tuesday's ludicrous, record-smashing, high-scoring entertainment had been followed on the same surface by thrilling low-scoring entertainment and a different result claimed in very different style, eventually won with four balls to spare and in the most unfitting of ways — with a massive six — by Hope, again proving himself the right man for a run chase. A series marked by stunning power hitting, roaring run rates and an unexpected midway transformation in England's performances and prospects concluded with a 3-2 triumph for West Indies, who extended their supremacy over England at home to four series in three formats across nearly five years.



---


# Andre Russell's Comeback In The First T20I

Andre Russell was named Player of the Match in the first T20I against England, taking 3-29 and smashing 29 not out off just 14 deliveries in his first T20I in over two years.

He seemed very pleased to be back in maroon, saying: "Life is so funny. Since when I got selected for the West Indies two weeks ago I've been dreaming of being man of the match." His bowling figures at the end of England's innings were 3-19, which the live blog described as balancing the attack perfectly on his comeback. As Tim Wigmore put it, Russell at his best adds so much to the West Indies side — with him at seven, and Holder, Shepherd and Hosein to follow, West Indies bat incredibly deep.



---


# Shai Hope's Anchor Innings In The T20 Decider

Shai Hope's 43 off 43 balls steered West Indies to their target in the deciding T20I, an exemplary anchoring innings that the live blog identified as the wicket England really needed.

At 16 overs West Indies were 112-4 with Hope on 29, and he opened the face to steer Rehan Ahmed for his first boundary; Rehan had struggled as the series progressed, and later in the over Powell muscled him over long-on for six, leaving West Indies 21 runs from a hat-trick of T20 series wins that year — South Africa away, India and England at home. In the 17th over, with West Indies 114-5, Hope was quietly guiding his side towards the finish line. The Guardian's report noted West Indies were 62 for three halfway through their innings, and if England had had 15 more runs at the same point they had also made a complete hash of the rest of it — a trap West Indies avoided thanks to Hope's 43-ball 43 as he again steered his side to their target. The batting display may have lacked their usual flamboyance, but until the final ball it was entirely appropriate for the occasion.



---


# Adil Rashid's T20I Milestones And Series Form

Adil Rashid reached his 100th T20I wicket in the first match of the December 2023 series against West Indies — on his 100th T20I appearance — and finished the series with eight wickets at 15 and an economy rate of 6.26.

In the first T20I in Barbados he had Kyle Mayers caught by Brook in the deep for 35 at 79-3, his 99th T20I wicket, off what was in truth a bit of a drag down but delivered from the front of the hand so it skidded on; England needed that badly. He then bowled Hetmyer's dismissal for 1 at 101-4, caught by Duckett on the midwicket sponge after Hetmyer danced out of his crease and got a good piece of the length ball — the 100th wicket, and a crucial one in the context of the game as England looked to ramp up the pressure. In the deciding fifth T20I he finished with figures of 4-0-21-2, and the live blog noted he had had a great series with those eight wickets at 15 and an absurd economy rate of 6.26, but was going to end on the losing side. The Guardian's report added that amid the wider theme of transformation Rashid's excellence remained constant: the 35-year-old, who had risen to the top of the T20 bowling rankings for the first time that Wednesday, took two wickets and conceded just 21 in the decider, while Topley was even better, also claiming a pair of victims but conceding only 17 — England took plenty of positives from the series, but the result was not one.



---


# Rehan Ahmed And Adil Rashid Through The Middle Overs

England's spinners were taken apart and then struck back through the middle of West Indies' chase in the first T20I, with Rehan Ahmed conceding nineteen in his first over before removing Nicholas Pooran.

In the seventh over Rehan bowled to Kyle Mayers, whose first ball was dragged down and launched over the midwicket boundary for six, followed by a supreme lofted drive down the ground for six more; Rehan came back with two sharply turning leg breaks before Shai Hope smeared a length ball over mid-on for the third six of the over, leaving West Indies 78-1. In the ninth over Tymal Mills replaced Rehan and started with another wide before a series of slower balls and back-of-the-hand trickery restricted Pooran and Hope, with the final ball top-edged over Buttler's head for a one-bounce four — 87-2, and West Indies needing 85 from 66 balls. In the tenth Adil Rashid was given another over after an excellent first: Pooran spotted the googly and drove it down the ground for six, singles were exchanged, and a short ball was panned into the deep for a couple, leaving West Indies 99-2 and needing 73 from 60. In the eleventh Rehan returned and had Pooran caught and bowled for 13, taking a nifty tumbling catch to his left at 100-3; Shimron Hetmyer opened his account with a single and Rehan got out of the over with three dots. In the twelfth just a single and a wicket came from the over as Hope could not break the legspin shackles, with West Indies captain Rovman Powell the new man and Buttler cranking the pressure by inserting a slip.



---


# West Indies' Death Overs Win In The First T20I

West Indies won the first T20I by four wickets when Andre Russell smashed the winning runs off Sam Curran — a length ball spanked over point for a one-bounce four — to go 1-0 up in the series.

The closing overs swung twice. In the thirteenth Rehan Ahmed had two balls left, the first flayed for four by Powell behind point and the last a dot, leaving West Indies needing 60 from 42. In the fourteenth Liam Livingstone came on instead of Rashid and kept it to singles as England tried to take the game as deep as possible and hope West Indies fluffed their lines at the death, with 55 needed from 36. Rehan then struck twice: Shai Hope, who had just hit him for six, holed out to Brook for 36 at 123-5, and Shepherd poked a leg break to Curran at slip first ball for 0 at 123-6, putting Rehan on a hat-trick. Russell faced the hat-trick ball and patted a decent delivery on the stumps back, then worked a couple; Ahmed finished with 3-39 from his four overs, leaving 47 needed from 30. In the sixteenth Livingstone conceded four singles before Rovman Powell crunched consecutive sixes down the ground for sixteen off the over — 31 needed from 24. In the seventeenth Tymal Mills conceded sixteen, including a mighty top-edged six from Powell and a short, wide ball sent to the fence, leaving 15 needed from 18. In the eighteenth Rashid was recalled and Russell smashed his googly clean out of the ground for six, then drove a four, eleven off the over leaving West Indies needing four.

qid: Does the Fortune article suggest that Alameda Research's business practices with FTX were legal, in contrast to the TechCrunch article's focus on the valuation of Alameda Research's assets in FTT tokens?
context:
# Alameda Research

Alameda Research is the crypto-trading firm Sam Bankman-Fried co-founded in 2017, before FTX existed. FTX came two years later, in 2019, and Bankman-Fried co-founded it as a complement to Alameda — to help bring in revenue and liquidity for the trading arm. The founding order is the discriminating fact: the exchange was created to serve the trading firm, not the other way round.

The feature that later set Alameda's balance sheet apart was how much of it consisted of the affiliated exchange's own token. A report showed that Alameda's largest asset was $3.66 billion of "unlocked FTT," alongside $2.16 billion of "FTT collateral." FTT was the token behind FTX. So the trading firm's single biggest asset was the token issued by the exchange founded to support it.



---


# The Mechanism Of FTX's Collapse

FTX came apart in early November 2022 through a chain with four links: a leaked balance sheet revealed that Alameda's largest holding was FTX's own token in a quantity larger than the token's whole market, the disclosure destroyed confidence, the world's largest rival exchange pulled its holdings out, and the resulting bank run forced FTX and Alameda into Chapter 11 within days. TechCrunch's 2023-10-01 account sets out the sequence: in early November 2022, that all changed.

Concerns surrounding FTX's liquidity grew after CoinDesk published a copy of Alameda's balance sheet, showing the firm held $14.6 billion in assets and $8 billion in liabilities as of June 30, 2022. The balance sheet showed that the $5.82 billion in FTT tokens that Alameda owned was 193% higher than the total FTT market cap, which was about $3 billion at the time — meaning Alameda purported to have more FTT tokens on its balance sheet than what existed in the world. Around the same time it was exposed, the world's largest crypto exchange, Binance, started pulling out its remaining $2.1 billion equivalent of cash in BUSD and FTT; Binance had held an equity position in FTX from 2019 to 2021. That withdrawal essentially triggered a bank run on FTX. FTX and Alameda filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in the U.S. mid-November 2022, Bankman-Fried resigned, and John J. Ray III, the Enron turnaround veteran, was appointed the new CEO.

The condition the whole mechanism rests on is the fragility of the underlying valuations. As TechCrunch put it on 2023-10-02, all of that activity came to a crashing end because the value of cryptocurrencies on FTX was not banked to much more than speculation and the promise of higher value — so when those valuations fell, they fell very, very hard. The chain therefore only runs as described where an asset is priced on expectation, held in size by a related party, and exposed to a counterparty large enough that its exit alone starts the run.



---


# The FTT Token And The "Sam Coins"

FTT was a token created by Bankman-Fried and Wang and issued by FTX, and it was one of several "Sam coins" — a nickname for tokens Bankman-Fried was heavily involved in and owned a lot of, either personally or through Alameda. Wang described FTT as being "sort of equity" in FTX, a characterisation The Verge's reporter suspected some crypto lawyers would dispute but that would probably please the SEC.

The distribution was lopsided from the start. Alameda got its war chest — 60 percent to 70 percent of the initial supply — for free, while seed investors got FTT at 10 cents a coin and FTT first listed at $1 a coin. Ellison testified that Bankman-Fried felt $1 per coin was psychologically important and directed her to buy up FTT using Alameda if the price fell below a dollar.

The discriminating feature of the Sam coins was that their book value was not realisable: they were almost certainly worth less than the value displayed on the balance sheet, because trying to sell them all at once would crater the prices. Bankman-Fried nonetheless directed Ellison to put those coins on the balance sheets Alameda showed to lenders, even though she felt doing so was "somewhat misleading." FTT also figures in the origin story of Alameda's negative-balance privilege: Wang said Bankman-Fried at first told him the code change letting an account go negative was to pay for expenses for the FTT token, but once implemented the ability to go negative was used for other things, including trading and unlimited withdrawals of FTX's trading fees and customer money.

## Corpus References

Corpus notes whose source text references this term (evidence-backed, from `term_links.json`):

- [The Mechanism Of FTX's Collapse](ftx_collapse_mechanism.md)
- [Bankman-Fried And Ellison: Relationship And Alameda Leadership](sbf_and_ellison_relationship_and_alameda_leadership.md)



---


# FTX Ventures Was Funded By Alameda

Caroline Ellison testified that the money behind FTX Ventures came from Alameda Research, even though Bankman-Fried announced the fund publicly without naming its source: on January 14th, 2022 he tweeted, "We're launching a $2b venture fund: FTX Ventures!" She said he did not want to go public with where the funds came from, telling her he thought Alameda's brand was less good and that he did not want his name associated with it.

The Verge reported the episode on October 10th, 2023 as part of Ellison's testimony, framing it as FTX keeping cozy private ties with Alameda while publicly holding it at arm's length — an echo, the reporter wrote, of Bankman-Fried and Ellison's romantic relationship. The same distancing appears in another transaction: Alameda bought Robinhood shares for Bankman-Fried, who moved them to a vehicle called "Emergent Fidelity Technologies" to avoid association with Alameda.



---


# The Escalation Of Alameda's Negative Balance

Alameda Research first ran a negative balance on FTX in late 2019, and the amount it was allowed to go negative crept upward in steps, each one justified after the fact — the model of the fraud that Gary Wang's and Caroline Ellison's testimony described was escalation rather than a single decision. As The Verge's reporter summarised Wang's testimony: first it was okay to dip into FTX's profits, then it was okay to take more, then even more; first it was a little line of credit just to provide liquidity, then a bigger one, then an effectively limitless one.

The steps ran as follows. Because Alameda and FTX shared an open-plan office, Wang heard a trader ask Bankman-Fried whether it was okay to keep withdrawing money from the negative account, and Bankman-Fried said it was okay as long as the amount stayed lower than FTX's total trading revenue; he was CEO of both companies at the time. Around 2019 or 2020, Wang checked the database and found Alameda was negative by about $200 million, more than the $150 million FTX had made in revenue — which had to mean Alameda was taking customer money. Wang was surprised and discussed it with Bankman-Fried, who told him he just needed to take into account the value of FTT, the token the two of them had launched; Wang trusted his judgment and did not pursue it. Later Alameda's balance was more negative than FTT and the trading revenue combined, and Wang had further conversations with Bankman-Fried about it. Wang testified he knew at the time that Alameda was using FTX customers' funds and that he knew it was wrong.

The same gradual accommodation shows in Ellison's account. Choking back tears, she testified: "When I started working at Alameda, I don't think I would have believed you if you told me I would be sending false balance sheets to our lenders or taking customer money, but over time, it was something I became more comfortable with."



---


# Alameda Research As The Alleged Conduit For FTX Customer Funds

In the prosecution's account offered by Thane Rehn, the key to Sam Bankman-Fried's alleged scheme was Alameda Research, a crypto hedge fund that Bankman-Fried also owned. The structure the government described works as follows: Caroline Ellison — Bankman-Fried's on-again off-again girlfriend and the CEO of Alameda — served as a front for the fund, and through that arrangement Bankman-Fried had "secret access" to customer money, both cash and crypto.

Two further relations complete the alleged mechanism. Bankman-Fried is said to have directed employees to conceal the flow of money into FTX's coffers, and to have forged financial documents distributed to lenders and investors. "The defendant lied to the world," Rehn alleged. These are the government's allegations as presented in its opening statement, not established findings.



---


# Shield AI's 2023 Funding Round

Shield AI, a startup specializing in autonomous flying systems for the U.S. military, has raised $200 million in a new funding round.

The round takes the company to a valuation of $2.7 billion.

qid: Does the TechCrunch article suggest that users are turning to Snapchat for information on a specific topic due to distrust in other platforms, while The Guardian article discusses legal actions against Snapchat for a completely different reason related to the platform's use?
context:
# Palestinian Content Moderation Distrust On Meta's Platforms

Users are also turning to Snapchat for information about Gaza as accusations of shadowbanning Palestinian content fuel distrust in platforms like Instagram and Facebook.

The policies themselves are not what separates the platforms: Meta's policies are not dissimilar to Snap's Community Guidelines, which prohibit pornographic content, content that advocates or advances terrorism, and content that portrays gratuitous or graphic violence.

What differs is the volume of complaint and the resulting user behavior. Allegations of censorship against Snapchat are not as frequent as they are against Meta's platforms, but many users are still urging others to screen record Stories posted from Gaza in case they are taken down.



---


# Snapchat Design Features Alleged To Enable Drug Sales

The lawsuit against Snap claims that Snapchat's features facilitate practices like drug sales by connecting dealers to young customers while promising them safety from legal repercussions through anonymity.

Chief among those designs, according to Matthew Bergman, the lead attorney on the case, is the promise that a message will disappear not only for fellow users but also on the software's back end. That is the ground that turns a product feature into an enabler of crime: it prevents law enforcement officials from seeing the activity of a dealer even after the dealer has been identified.

The complaint names other features as problematic too: notifying individuals when another person screenshots their post, the ability to geolocate fellow users, and algorithms that suggest new connections based on demographics.



---


# Section 230

## Definition

Section 230 (of the Communications Decency Act) is a US law that shields online platforms from legal responsibility for the illegal actions of their users, and separately protects the platforms' own content moderation decisions.

## Context

In the corpus the statute surfaces in two distinct disputes. In the Snapchat fentanyl-death lawsuits, Snap's motion to dismiss cites Section 230 as its liability shield against claims that its platform facilitated illegal drug sales between users. In the Supreme Court case over the Texas and Florida content-moderation laws, Oregon Senator Ron Wyden — described as Section 230's co-author — invokes the statute's other function, protecting the moderation decisions platforms make about what content to host, arguing that the state laws would gut what Section 230 lets platforms do.

## Key Characteristics

- **Dual shield** — the corpus shows it protecting platforms on two separate fronts: liability for users' illegal conduct on the service (the drug-sale claims against Snap) and liability for how a platform moderates content (the basis of Wyden's objection to the Texas/Florida laws).
- **Conditional, not absolute, immunity** — per the Snap case, the statute "only offers immunity to companies that have acted responsibly and taken precautions to prevent illegal activity from taking place on their platforms," a condition the plaintiffs' attorney argues Snap failed to meet.
- **Legislative authorship tied to the moderation function** — Senator Ron Wyden is named in the corpus as a co-author of Section 230, invoked specifically to defend its role in enabling platforms to remove harmful content without losing legal protection.



---


# The Section 230 Defense In The Snap Fentanyl Lawsuit

Snapchat's answer to the parents' complaint attacks its legal foundation rather than its facts: the company filed a motion to dismiss citing Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act, which protects online platforms from being held responsible for the illegal actions of their users. A hearing on that motion was scheduled for 18 October.

The plaintiffs' rebuttal concedes the statute but disputes that Snap qualifies for its shelter. Section 230 only offers immunity to companies that have acted responsibly and taken precautions to prevent illegal activity from taking place on their platforms — something lead attorney Matthew Bergman says Snap has not done.

"It's the world's largest open-air drug market," Bergman said. "It was clearly designed with the intention of allowing and encouraging nefarious activity with a lack of record."



---


# Shadowbanning

## Definition

Shadowbanning, as TechCrunch describes it, is when a platform "shadowbans, or limits the visibility of" a user's content without the platform notifying the user that anything has been restricted, so the user only discovers it by noticing a drop in views or reach.

## Context

In the corpus the term names the central accusation in the October 2023 controversy over Meta's handling of Palestine-related content: Instagram users accused Meta of shadowbanning their Stories about Palestine, and TechCrunch frames the belief that Meta "shadowbans, or limits the visibility of," such content as longstanding rather than new to that month.
The same allegation is cited beyond Meta's own platforms as a driver of platform choice: users turned to Snapchat's Snap Map for firsthand Gaza content specifically because accusations of shadowbanning Palestinian content on Instagram and Facebook had eroded their trust in those platforms.
Meta's official response did not deny that reach had dropped; it denied the mechanism, attributing the reduced Story reach specifically to a global, content-neutral bug in Stories that re-shared Reels or Feed posts, and separately attributed a different global bug — one that had prevented some users from going live — to technical error rather than deliberate suppression tied to subject matter.

## Key Characteristics

- **Covert, not disclosed** — the defining feature reporters and users pointed to is that visibility drops silently, with no notification to the affected account; Bella Hadid described being "immediately shadowbanned" and her Story views dropping by "almost 1 million" with no explanation from the platform.
- **Detected by comparison, not confirmation** — users inferred shadowbanning by comparing engagement across their own posts (e.g., a user whose Stories fell from "100s of views to zero or a handful" and rebounded only after posting unrelated content like a cat photo), since the platform provided no direct evidence of restriction.
- **Contested mechanism** — Meta disputed that the effect was shadowbanning-by-design, attributing the reduced Story reach to a bug that "affected accounts equally around the globe" and "had nothing to do with the subject matter of the content," rather than confirming intentional visibility limits.
- **Trust-eroding beyond the platform itself** — the accusation pushed users toward alternative platforms (Snap Map) even though the accused conduct occurred on Instagram and Facebook, showing shadowbanning claims can shift audience behavior across platforms, not just within one.



---


# Snap's Moderation Response To Drug Dealer Accounts

Snap's defence against the charge that it does nothing about dealers is that it moderates: after the Guardian's story published, a spokesperson said Snap works to "block search results for drug-related terms" and redirects at-risk users to resources on the dangers of fentanyl. "We have great empathy for families who have suffered unimaginable losses. At Snap, we are working hard to stop dealers from abusing our platform," the spokesperson said. Snap did not respond to the Guardian's request for comment prior to the story's release.

Parents in the suit contest that claim on the record of what actually happened when they reported dealers. Perla Mendoza, whose son Daniel (Elijah) Figueroa died after buying fentanyl-laced pills from a dealer on Snapchat, found that Snap did little to prevent illegal drug sales in the weeks and months after his death: even after she created her own account and found her son's dealer posting images with hundreds of pills, her reports to the help center went unanswered, and it took eight months for them to flag his account. "It was really disheartening," she said.

Hanh Badger's objection goes further, attacking the sufficiency of account removal as a remedy at all. "They'll just create another," she said, emphasising the need for structural reforms that clearly warn young users of dealers' predatory practices, or that make it so drugs cannot be peddled to kids on the platform in the first place. "Snapchat perpetuated this crisis," she said.



---


# The Social Media Victims Law Center's Lawsuit Against Snap

In April 2023, the relatives of more than 65 victims, represented by the Social Media Victims Law Center, filed lawsuits against Snap, the parent company of Snapchat — an app known for its disappearing messages features, and the platform used by the vast majority of the suit's victims.

The suits are one expression of a wider response by bereaved parents. In their grief, victims' parents are motivated to end this crisis to prevent another family's suffering while also giving meaning to their loss, and many have launched awareness campaigns, founded educational programs and advocated for legislative change.

What is new is the venue: some parents are now taking to the civil courts, targeting the tech giants whose platforms facilitated their children's purchases of the pills that killed them.
