---


# Snap's Decision To Keep The Gaza Heat Map Live

Snap decided to keep Snap Map live in Gaza, a choice that stands against its own precedent. The company is not indifferent to geopolitical conflict: in 2022 Snap disabled its heat map in Ukraine as a "safety precaution," The Verge said, to prevent Russia from tracking civilian evacuations, and instead displayed a "curated feed" of public Stories.

A spokesperson for Snap told TechCrunch that Snap Map will stay live to allow users to continue sharing their experiences during the crisis, and that the company is monitoring hot spots for content that may spread misinformation or incite violence. Snap will "closely assess" if it needs to take additional action.

The spokesperson also acknowledged that Snap Map is a crucial resource for "authentic user-generated content" from perspectives that may not be reflected by traditional news outlets.

qid: After Sporting News reported on Johnny Cardoso's inclusion in the USMNT squad post-injury on October 4, 2023, and CBSSports.com announced De'Von Achane's move to Injured Reserve on October 12, 2023, which player's status changed between the two reports, Johnny Cardoso or De'Von Achane?
context:
# NFL Week 11 2023: Achane, Walker And Foreman All Exit With Injuries

CBS Sports' Week 11 injury roundup, dated 2023-11-19, records three running backs leaving their games. De'Von Achane of the Dolphins returned from injured reserve and a four-game absence but limped to the sidelines after his second touch of the first quarter against the Raiders. Miami ruled him questionable to return with a knee injury, and while he later returned to the sidelines from a locker-room visit, he was replaced on the field indefinitely by Raheem Mostert. Head coach Mike McDaniel told reporters on the Monday that Achane is day-to-day; he had not been ruled out of Friday's matchup with the Jets but had not been given the green light either, so his status was worth monitoring.

Kenneth Walker III of the Seahawks took four carries against the Rams before leaving with an oblique injury. He was seen walking on the sidelines shortly afterward but was ruled doubtful to return, and rookie Zach Charbonnet — who entered Week 11 with just over 200 rushing yards on the year — replaced Walker as Seattle's top ball carrier. After the game, Seahawks head coach Pete Carroll told reporters Walker suffered an "oblique strain that was legit" and could miss time. D'Onta Foreman of the Bears remained a headliner of Chicago's backfield against the Lions even with Khalil Herbert back from injured reserve, but managed just 14 yards on the ground before suffering an ankle injury; he walked off with a limp and attempted to run on the sidelines but did not return to the field after the Bears ruled him questionable.



---


# Who The USMNT Was Missing Through Injury In October 2023

Gregg Berhalter largely had his entire first-choice player pool available for the October 2023 friendlies, with only a few injuries to work around. Goalkeepers Zack Steffen and Sean Johnson remained out of action injured; Josh Sargent was sidelined with a long-term ankle injury; Daryl Dike was out after tearing his Achilles; and Antonee Robinson was missing with what Berhalter described as a sports hernia — Robinson had played through it in the previous camp and recently for his club, but it was affecting him, so rest was judged the best option.

Two midfield situations went the other way. Johnny Cardoso, who had pulled out of the September camp with an ankle injury, had returned to action with Brazilian club Internacional, indicating a return to fitness, and was included in the squad. And with Tyler Adams injured, social media noise calling for Heidenheim midfielder Lennard Maloney to be brought in was answered with a call-up: the 23-year-old was born in Berlin to an American father, had appeared for the U.S. at U-20 level and had stated his desire to reach the USMNT senior squad.



---


# The USMNT's 23-Man Roster For The October 2023 Friendlies

Gregg Berhalter called in 23 players for the October 2023 friendlies against Germany and Ghana — one fewer than the squad brought in for the previous month's friendlies against Uzbekistan and Oman. The squad was announced on Thursday, October 5. PSV midfielder Malik Tillman was forced to withdraw due to injury, with Alex Zendejas of Club America named to the roster in his place.

The official 23-man roster, by position with club, caps and goals, was: goalkeepers Ethan Horvath (Nottingham Forest, 9 caps, 0 goals) and Matt Turner (Nottingham Forest, 33, 0); defenders Cameron Carter-Vickers (Celtic, 12, 0), Sergino Dest (PSV Eindhoven, 28, 2), DeJuan Jones (New England Revolution, 7, 0), Kristoffer Lund (Palermo, 2, 0), Kevin Paredes (Wolfsburg, 1, 0), Tim Ream (Fulham, 52, 1), Chris Richards (Crystal Palace, 12, 1), Miles Robinson (Atlanta United, 27, 3) and Joe Scally (Gladbach, 6, 0); midfielders Johnny Cardoso (Internacional, 7, 0), Luca de la Torre (Celta Vigo, 17, 0), Lennard Maloney (Heidenheim, 0, 0), Weston McKennie (Juventus, 46, 11), Yunus Musah (AC Milan, 29, 0), Gio Reyna (Borussia Dortmund, 20, 4) and Malik Tillman (PSV Eindhoven, 6, 0); and forwards Brenden Aaronson (Union Berlin, 34, 8), Folarin Balogun (Arsenal, 4, 2), Ricardo Pepi (PSV Eindhoven, 18, 9), Christian Pulisic (AC Milan, 62, 26), Tim Weah (Juventus, 33, 5) and Alex Zendejas (Club America, 7, 1).



---


# USMNT Substitute Ratings Against Germany, October 2023

The Sporting News rated the United States' six substitutes against Germany on Oct. 14, 2023 as Luca de la Torre 5, Cameron Carter-Vickers 7, Brenden Aaronson 7, Ricardo Pepi 5, Johnny Cardoso 6 and Kevin Paredes 5.

De la Torre, brought on to replace Gio Reyna at halftime, was unable to stem the German tide despite being a more defensive-minded option than Reyna in what should have been a swap to shore up the midfield. Carter-Vickers, on at the 65th minute, remains a top-tier centre-back in the U.S. player pool and a clear starter when healthy, with Tim Ream and even Chris Richards struggling at various stages; he came off the bench due to recent hamstring troubles but was stout in his 25 minutes, recording 22 touches, giving away possession just twice, completing two dribbles and making two clearances, and was not targeted by Germany nearly as much as the other three defenders on the pitch — a strong nod to his abilities. Aaronson, also on at 65 minutes, was probably the U.S. substitute to make the biggest impact, bright in attack, dazzling with his dribbling and helping usher the U.S. forward amid a second-half onslaught — a good showing from the Union Berlin winger who needs confidence at the moment.

Pepi entered at the same time in a far from ideal situation, coming on with the U.S. shell-shocked from the quickfire Germany double; he provided very little up front with just eight touches in 24 minutes, featured his usual pressing and came close to scoring once on a messy chance that Germany just barely cleared, but otherwise did not cause the opposing back line problems to open spaces for teammates. Cardoso, on at 75 minutes, had only 15 minutes to showcase his abilities, losing possession just once in his 10 touches and completing a tackle while also being dribbled past a few times — which begged the question why he or Lennard Maloney weren't introduced at halftime instead of de la Torre. Paredes, also on at 75 minutes, had 10 touches in 15 minutes at the end of a mucked-up game of numerous substitutions, losing possession four times and completing four passes; the Sporting News found his time tough to evaluate but concluded he didn't stand out.



---


# USMNT 1-3 Germany, Hartford, October 2023

The United States lost 3-1 to Germany at Rentschler Field in Hartford on Oct. 14, 2023, having appeared well positioned to fight with a European power through 45 minutes before the house of cards came crashing down after the break.

The U.S. entered the interval level, as a Christian Pulisic stunner was cancelled out by Ilkay Gundogan's poaching. After halftime, as Gio Reyna was withdrawn from his first start back under Gregg Berhalter to build his fitness, the U.S. midfield was overrun and the defense committed a multitude of errors, allowing the Germans to gain full control of proceedings. Goalkeeper Matt Turner summed it up afterwards: "It's frustrating because it's just little moments. Little moments made a big difference at the World Cup, and it's kinda the same story here."

The U.S. started in a 4-3-3, right to left: 1. Turner in goal; 19. Scally, 4. Richards (replaced by Carter-Vickers, 66'), 13. Ream and 2. Dest across the back; 7. Reyna (de la Torre, 46'), 6. Musah and 8. McKennie (Cardoso, 75') in midfield; and 21. Weah (Aaronson, 66'), 20. Balogun (Pepi, 66') and 10. Pulisic (Paredes, 75') in attack.

qid: Did "The Independent - Life and Style" article on "Jada Pinkett Smith and Will Smith's marriage" disagree with the same publication's report on "Jada and Will Smith's marital status" regarding the year they began their separation?
context:
# How Will Smith And Jada Pinkett Smith Met And Married In 1997

Will Smith and Jada Pinkett Smith met when she auditioned for the role of his girlfriend on The Fresh Prince of Bel-Air; she did not get the part, but the two hit it off — even though Smith was married to Sheree Zampino at the time, with whom he shares son Trey. Smith later described the moment of recognition on Pinkett Smith's Red Table Talk in 2018: "I had a realisation I wasn't with the person I was supposed to be with. I was sitting in a [bathroom] stall and I was crying and laughing uncontrollably, and I knew [Jada] was the woman I was supposed to be with."

The pair only began seriously dating in 1995, after Smith finalised his divorce from Zampino. He proposed in November 1997 and they married just one month later, in Baltimore. Pinkett Smith was not initially enthusiastic about marrying at all: she told People in 2019, "I never wanted to get married. But my mother was like: 'You have to get married' — she's so old-school — and Will wanted a family. So I said: 'All right, maybe it's something I should do.'"



---


# Why Will Smith And Jada Pinkett Smith Never Signed A Prenup

Jada Pinkett Smith revealed in an interview with Parade, published 13 October 2023 and given while promoting her memoir Worthy, that she and Will Smith deliberately did not sign a prenuptial agreement before their 1997 wedding, because they had already decided divorce was not in the cards for them. The Independent presents the missing prenup as of a piece with their promise not to divorce: the absence of a legal fallback was itself the commitment.

She described the decision as an unromantic, deliberate conversation rather than a wedding-day gesture: "Listen, weddings are beautiful, but they can be very romanticised. I feel that was a very real moment for the two of us to look each other in the eyes, recognise that there would be tough times in this journey and to say to each other: 'No matter what, we're going to figure it out and that's why we don't need a prenup, because I'm making a promise that divorce won't be necessary, that we will figure this out.'" She added that the promise was made "without all of the bridal wedding beauty; it was just sitting on a log in his mother's backyard, and going: 'Hey' — having to really look at the possibility of us not being together."



---


# Jada Pinkett Smith's "Entanglement" With August Alsina

Jada Pinkett Smith confirmed in 2020 that she had had a relationship with the singer August Alsina during a period when she and Will Smith were separated, describing it on her Facebook Watch series Red Table Talk as an "entanglement." Alsina and Pinkett Smith were introduced in 2015, but it was only in 2020 that he claimed publicly that the two had dated while she was married and that the Smiths' marriage was open at the time. Alsina said Will Smith had given the pair his "blessing," explaining: "I actually sat down with Will and had a conversation due to the transformation from their marriage to life partnership that they've spoken on several times and it not involving romanticism." He added that he "totally gave myself to that relationship for years of my life and I truly and really, really deeply loved and have a ton of love for her."

Pinkett Smith's representatives called the claims "absolutely not true" on the day they surfaced. Less than two weeks later, she and Will Smith appeared together on Red Table Talk, where she confirmed the relationship but placed it inside an amicable separation that had not been disclosed to the press at the time: "We decided that we were going to separate for a period of time and you go figure out how to make yourself happy and I'll figure out how to make myself happy. From there, as time went on, I got into a different kind of entanglement with August... Yes, it was a relationship absolutely." Prompted by her husband, she confirmed it "was a relationship, absolutely." She also rejected Alsina's framing of permission, saying Will had not given it because the only person who could give her permission was herself. The episode is one of the grey areas in the couple's account of the terms of their separation.



---


# The Smiths' Denials Of Open-Marriage, Divorce And Infidelity Rumours

Will Smith and Jada Pinkett Smith have each publicly rejected the recurring claims made about their marriage — that it was an open relationship, that they were divorcing, and that either had been unfaithful. Pinkett Smith attacked the open-relationship premise directly on Facebook, after a quiet decade and a half spent making films and raising their children: "Here is how I will change my statement... Will and I BOTH can do WHATEVER we want, because we TRUST each other to do so. This does NOT mean we have an open relationship... this means we have a GROWN one." Her counter is that mutual freedom follows from trust, not from an open-marriage arrangement, so the inference from one to the other does not hold.

Will Smith answered the separation-and-divorce rumours in a mocking Facebook post: "Under normal circumstances, I don't usually respond to foolishness. But, so many people have extended [to] me their 'deepest condolences' that I figured — 'What the hell… I can be foolish, too!' So, in the interest of redundant, repetitious, over and over-again-ness… Jada and I are… NOT GETTING A DIVORCE!!!!!!!!!!!!!" In an interview on CBS Sunday Morning in October 2023 he also denied the infidelity premise outright: "Never. There's never been infidelity in our marriage... And we have never surprised one another with anything ever." He added that he had decided public chatter about his life "can be of a benefit to people," since "chatter is the first stage to having a real conversation and being able to truly explore if some of the things in your heart are loving, or poisonous."



---


# The Smiths' 2021 Public Accounts Of Marital Strain

In late 2021 both Will Smith and Jada Pinkett Smith described the difficulty of their marriage in public, first on her show and then in his memoir. In an October 2021 episode of Red Table Talk, Pinkett Smith said it "takes work" to maintain a spark in the bedroom: "It's hard... the thing Will and I talk about a lot is the journey. We started in this [relationship] at a very young age, 22 years old... I think you expect your partner to know — especially when it comes to sex. It's like: 'Well, if you love me, you should know. If you love me, you should read my mind.' That's a huge pitfall."

The following month Will Smith's memoir was released, detailing several problems the couple had had over the years. He wrote that they were "suffering the brutal death of our romantic fantasies, the burning away of the idealistic illusion of the perfect marriage and the perfect family. Neither of us wanted a divorce; we knew we loved each other, and some aspects of our union were magical. But the structure of the life that we had established was strangling both of us."



---


# Will And Jada As A New, Unconventional Marriage Model

Relationship expert Susan Winter argues that the Smiths' seven-year separation is not a stalled marriage waiting to be repaired but a fluid arrangement outside the traditional marriage design — an evolving model that could come to serve other couples. Her starting point is a limit on what outsiders can know: the public will never fully learn what "heavy-duty work" Will Smith and Jada Pinkett Smith are doing in their relationship, and, she says, it is not necessarily anyone's business.

The grounds are that a couple who have already built something different have no reason to revert to the conventional form. "They're in the rough with a machete, carving a new path for themselves," Winter said. "Why would they say: 'Hey, let's go back to the house and just relax?' They're really exploring something vastly different. It doesn't end up that you go back into that little box of 'this is a marriage, we're living together'. It just doesn't do that." The Independent frames the same point as a question: if the Smiths have spent seven years apart as a married couple, why would they decide to return to a shared household?



---


# Britney Spears And Justin Timberlake's Relationship

Britney Spears' first highly public relationship was with Justin Timberlake, her co-star from the Mickey Mouse Club. The pair made many appearances together while dating, including the moment — described by The Independent as iconic — when they wore matching all-denim outfits to the American Music Awards in 2001.

They broke up in 2002, shortly after Timberlake and his boy band NSYNC released their hit "Cry Me a River." The song's music video, which featured a woman with blonde hair, sparked rumours that the couple had split because Spears had allegedly cheated on him.

qid: Who is the individual accused of using Caroline Ellison as a front at Alameda Research, presented as a trustworthy figure in the crypto industry before a major platform's collapse, and is alleged to have persuaded a former Jane Street colleague to join his ventures, with the prosecution claiming this was part of a scheme to fraudulently obtain wealth, power, and influence, according to reports by Fortune, The Verge, and TechCrunch?
context:
# Testimony At The SBF Trial

Across the first three weeks of the trial, a run of former colleagues, an outside investor and a forensic accounting expert testified that FTX customer money flowed into Alameda Research and out again to other uses, and that FTX's investors were never told about the two firms' special relationship. TechCrunch's running coverage, published 2023-10-06, summarises each week.

In week one, FTX's co-founder and CTO Gary Wang testified Thursday on the extent to which Alameda Research was used for whatever purposes he and SBF saw fit: according to Wang, the crypto trading firm pulled funding directly from FTX customers, whose transactions would be funneled toward Alameda and then directed elsewhere. Thursday also brought testimony from Matt Huang, co-founder and managing partner at crypto investment firm Paradigm, which invested $278 million in FTX across 2021 and 2022 and is part of a class-action lawsuit accusing it and others of defrauding customers by promoting FTX. His testimony centered around being left uninformed about FTX's utilization of customer money to keep Alameda Research afloat — a practice Huang says would have halted his involvement — and covered his relationship with FTX stretching back to 2019.

Week two's standout testimony came from Alameda Research's former CEO Caroline Ellison, who claimed she took $14 billion from customers to repay debts to lenders, using them as a line of credit under the instruction of SBF. Ellison also went into detail about how a $2 billion venture fund, FTX Ventures, was funded by money that had previously been allocated to Alameda from third-party lenders. And though there are no charges of bribery in the case, she also testified to paying Chinese officials $150 million to restore access to $1 billion in frozen trading accounts.

The third week featured a couple of noteworthy moments for the prosecution. FTX's former general counsel Can Sun, like many of SBF's former colleagues, opted to cooperate with authorities and testified that SBF asked him to create a theoretical "legal justification" for the use of billions in consumer funds just days before FTX filed for bankruptcy. Bankman-Fried was arrested in December 2022 in the Bahamas, where FTX was based, and was then extradited to the U.S. to face a number of criminal charges. Prosecutor Danielle Sassoon's brief redirect of Caroline Ellison on October 12th, 2023 set a trap that opened the door to the jury hearing a secret recording of an Alameda all-hands meeting in which Ellison confessed to stealing billions of FTX customers' money at Bankman-Fried's direction. # Sam Bankman-Fried

Sam Bankman-Fried is the former CEO of the bankrupt crypto exchange FTX, whose highly anticipated criminal trial started on the Tuesday before TechCrunch's 2023-10-01 report, to determine whether he is guilty of seven counts of fraud and conspiracy. As one former federal prosecutor put it: "The odds seem to be stacked against him at this point."

He was 31 years old and co-founded FTX in 2019; within a few years the once third-largest crypto exchange's valuation hit $32 billion at its peak, and the company is now trying to claw back any funds to distribute to creditors. Before the fall he was even compared to Warren Buffet, and many called him the white horse of crypto — a description TechCrunch notes it never applied to him.

# FTX's Fabricated Backstop Insurance Fund

Gary Wang testified on October 6th, 2023 that FTX lied about how much money was in its backstop fund, and the court was shown the code that generated the fake number published on FTX's website: it took the daily trading volume on FTX, multiplied it by a random number, divided it by a billion, and added the result to the number already displayed on the site. That figure had nothing to do with the actual amount of money in the insurance fund.

The fund mattered because of what FTX advertised. In many crypto networks, if someone lost enough money the exchanges could stick other traders with the losses too; FTX touted its automated liquidation as the way to avoid this, so that one customer going bankrupt would not affect the others. In the process of liquidating, FTX would try to sell the collateral on the open market, and if it could not finish, backstop liquidity providers would step in — market makers, including Alameda, which could be compensated for the losses they took from the backstop fund. Wang also testified that when there was not enough money in the fund, money was moved there from Alameda's accounts in order to pay the insurance out.

The prosecution's framing was that this was not merely a matter of Alameda holding special, secret privileges: it claimed those privileges were used to obfuscate basic elements of FTX's operations, exposing the exchange's supposed selling points as a lie.

FTX came apart in early November 2022 through a chain with four links: a leaked balance sheet revealed that Alameda's largest holding was FTX's own token in a quantity larger than the token's whole market, the disclosure destroyed confidence, the world's largest rival exchange pulled its holdings out, and the resulting bank run forced FTX and Alameda into Chapter 11 within days. TechCrunch's 2023-10-01 account sets out the sequence: in early November 2022, that all changed.

Concerns surrounding FTX's liquidity grew after CoinDesk published a copy of Alameda's balance sheet, showing the firm held $14.6 billion in assets and $8 billion in liabilities as of June 30, 2022. The balance sheet showed that the $5.82 billion in FTT tokens that Alameda owned was 193% higher than the total FTT market cap, which was about $3 billion at the time — meaning Alameda purported to have more FTT tokens on its balance sheet than what existed in the world. Around the same time it was exposed, the world's largest crypto exchange, Binance, started pulling out its remaining $2.1 billion equivalent of cash in BUSD and FTT; Binance had held an equity position in FTX from 2019 to 2021. That withdrawal essentially triggered a bank run on FTX. FTX and Alameda filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in the U.S. mid-November 2022, Bankman-Fried resigned, and John J. Ray III, the Enron turnaround veteran, was appointed the new CEO.

The condition the whole mechanism rests on is the fragility of the underlying valuations. As TechCrunch put it on 2023-10-02, all of that activity came to a crashing end because the value of cryptocurrencies on FTX was not banked to much more than speculation and the promise of higher value — so when those valuations fell, they fell very, very hard. Sporting News' framing is that just four minutes after Destiny Udogie's escape, another Tottenham defender again got away with only a booking despite a VAR review for a possible red card; Romero, often criticised for his reckless nature, had a kick-out at Colwill that went unpunished. Social media clips circulated at the time noting that Romero intentionally kicked Colwill but VAR had not checked it.

# Romero's Red Card And Palmer's Penalty Equaliser

The defining moment of Tottenham vs. Chelsea on Nov. 6, 2023 came in the 31st minute, when a wild passage of play ended with Moises Caicedo's goal ruled out, Cristian Romero sent off on VAR review, and Cole Palmer converting the resulting penalty to level the scoreline at 1-1.

The sequence began with the ball pinging around the Tottenham penalty area, Spurs unable to clear after blocking multiple efforts, until Caicedo finally buried a long-distance effort with a low finish inside the left post. Despite initially appearing to count, the offside flag was raised extremely late, with the assistant referee determining, after a moment to think, that Nicolas Jackson was interfering with play from an offside position.

That was only the beginning of the saga. With the goal disallowed, a VAR review began for a penalty, as Romero had swung wildly into the shins of Raheem Sterling: while he got the ball with his tackle, he followed through with extreme force straight onto both of Sterling's legs, and referee Michael Oliver was sent to the monitor. # USC vs. Notre Dame 2023: Broadcast And Venue Details

The Week 7 2023 USC-Notre Dame game was played at Notre Dame Stadium in South Bend, Ind. on Saturday, Oct. 14 at 7:30 p.m. ET, televised on NBC and streamed on Peacock or Fubo.

The defining features of the listing are its four fields: date (Saturday, Oct. 14), time (7:30 p.m. ET), location (Notre Dame Stadium, South Bend, Ind.) and TV channel (NBC), with live stream options listed separately. The Sporting News framed the fixture as the latest edition of the rivalry between USC and Notre Dame, carried on NBC.

For viewers without the NBC broadcast there were several streaming options: the game could be found on Peacock or on Fubo, the latter of which offers a free trial. The boundary of this note is scheduling and distribution only — it says nothing about the result, which is covered by the game's play-by-play notes.

# The VAR Intervention Window Before Play Restarts

VAR can only intervene in an incident before play restarts; once the game has resumed, the official cannot act on it. Sporting News invoked this window on Nov. 6, 2023 to explain why one passage of play in Tottenham vs. Chelsea was not reviewed at all.

It was unclear exactly why the incident went unreviewed, but the assumption offered was that the VAR official was likely not aware of it until play had already restarted, at which point he cannot intervene. The boundary condition Sporting News stresses is practical rather than legal: such incidents have to be caught before play restarts, which is extremely difficult to do as the game continues to flow.

# PGMOL: The Body That Apologises For Refereeing And VAR Mistakes

The Professional Game Match Officials Limited (PGMOL) is the body responsible for referees in English football, and it has apologised on multiple occasions for mistakes made during matches, Sporting News explained on 2023-09-30. # Tottenham-Chelsea First Half VAR Chaos

The opening 45 minutes of Tottenham vs. Chelsea on Monday, Nov. 6, 2023 produced one red card, four yellow cards, four Chelsea goals ruled out and 12 minutes of stoppage time, ending level at 1-1 with Tottenham down to 10 men — what Sporting News called one of the greatest train wrecks in the history of the English top flight.

Sporting News noted that while many of the decisions were widely analysed as correct, the lengthy review processes were criticised just as much as the eventual results, and Premier League fans had plenty to talk about with friends, fans and coworkers afterwards.

# Nicolas Jackson's Goal Disallowed For Offside

Chelsea saw a third goal of the first half disallowed at Tottenham on Nov. 6, 2023 when Nicolas Jackson put the ball in the net on 37 minutes but Raheem Sterling was offside in the buildup, just past the midfield stripe.

# Reece James' Elbow On Udogie: No Red Card

Reece James avoided a red card just before halftime at Tottenham on Nov. 6, 2023 despite catching Destiny Udogie in the face with a trailing elbow while challenging for a bouncing ball in the air, escaping with only a yellow.

# The Attacking Handball Automatic Foul Rule

By rule, any contact by the ball with the arm or hand of an attacking player is an automatic foul, regardless of arm position, intent, or any other factor. Sporting News cited this on Nov. 6, 2023 as the reason a Chelsea goal at Tottenham was disallowed.

The rule's discriminating feature is that it removes the usual mitigating considerations — where the arm was, whether the player meant it, or anything else — for an attacking player. Once contact with the arm or hand is established, the foul follows and the goal is ruled out.

# Kulusevski's Opener And Son's Disallowed Goal

Dejan Kulusevski opened the scoring for Spurs against Chelsea on Nov. 6, 2023, benefitting from a large deflection off Chelsea defender Levi Colwill that left Roberto Sanchez with no chance to make a save, and the match got out of hand quickly with both sides flying forward with electric attacking intent.

qid: Does the article from The Verge suggest that Sam Bankman-Fried was aware of the financial discrepancies at FTX, while the TechCrunch article alleges that he knowingly committed fraud, or do both articles imply a level of awareness and intent by Sam Bankman-Fried regarding the financial issues at FTX?
context:
# Sam Bankman-Fried

Sam Bankman-Fried is the former CEO of the bankrupt crypto exchange FTX, whose highly anticipated criminal trial started on the Tuesday before TechCrunch's 2023-10-01 report, to determine whether he is guilty of seven counts of fraud and conspiracy. As one former federal prosecutor put it: "The odds seem to be stacked against him at this point."

He was 31 years old and co-founded FTX in 2019; within a few years the once third-largest crypto exchange's valuation hit $32 billion at its peak, and the company is now trying to claw back any funds to distribute to creditors. Before the fall he was even compared to Warren Buffet, and many called him the white horse of crypto — a description TechCrunch notes it never applied to him.

Bankman-Fried, however, maintained his innocence. At The New York Times' DealBook Summit he appeared virtually from the Bahamas and said, "I didn't ever try to commit fraud on anyone; I was shocked by what happened this month"; in a published DM exchange with a Vox reporter he said he regretted filing for bankruptcy and thought that "regulators make everything worse." In January he pleaded not guilty to all counts, which include wire fraud, conspiracy to commit money laundering and conspiracy to misuse customer funds. He could face up to 115 years in jail if convicted on all charges.

TechCrunch's 2023-10-02 summary of his standing on the eve of trial: SBF has been denied bail; his name is mud (or much worse) among those who have lost money in Alameda or FTX; and those who might not have had positions in these still blame him for other crypto woes, because he set off a ripple effect.



---


# FTX's Bankruptcy And Leadership

The man who represented FTX before Congress after its failure told lawmakers the exchange had effectively no internal governance at all, and the prosecutor bringing the case called Bankman-Fried's alleged crimes one of the biggest financial frauds in American history. TechCrunch reported both on 2023-10-01.

Ray represented the company during a House Financial Services Committee hearing regarding FTX. Asked whether the firm had significant risk management systems, Ray said at the time that "there were virtually no internal controls and no separateness whatsoever," and added that he did not "trust a single piece of paper" in the exchange's organization. Separately, in a press conference, U.S. Attorney Damian Williams called Bankman-Fried's alleged crimes "one of the biggest financial frauds in American history."



---


# Gary Wang's Testimony At The FTX Fraud Trial

Gary Wang, the lesser-known co-founder of FTX, told a Manhattan courtroom on Thursday that he had committed financial crimes while working at FTX — including wire and commodities fraud — carried out with the help of Sam Bankman-Fried, FTX ex-engineering head Nishad Singh, and Caroline Ellison, who ran sister hedge fund Alameda Research and had been Bankman-Fried's girlfriend.

Asked by Assistant U.S. Attorney Nicolas Roos, "Did you commit financial crimes while working at FTX?" Wang responded, "Yes." Asked whether he saw any of the people he committed those crimes with in the courtroom, Wang — dressed in an oversized and wrinkled suit with a red tie and glasses — awkwardly stood up, looked around, and answered, "Yes"; asked who, he said, "Sam Bankman-Fried." He was one of two former friends of Bankman-Fried's from MIT who also worked at FTX while living with the founder in the Bahamas and who took the stand that week to testify against their former classmate, confidant and boss, a man who allegedly ran a crypto empire that defrauded thousands of customers out of billions of dollars. The trial, set to last six weeks, was to resume on Tuesday with key testimony expected from Ellison, considered the prosecution's star witness, who had already pleaded guilty to multiple charges. Bankman-Fried faces seven federal charges, including wire fraud, securities fraud and money laundering, that could put him in prison for the rest of his life. Thus far Bankman-Fried, 31, has remained mostly quiet in court, intently listening to witnesses and at times writing notes to his attorneys — but as Wang testified against him, he looked visibly upset, shifting his gaze from his former friend to the ground and at one point putting his head in his hands.



---


# FTX Fraud Charges And The SEC's Allegation

Sam Bankman-Fried, the founder of the failed cryptocurrency exchange FTX, faced seven counts of wire fraud and conspiracy — specifically, two counts of wire fraud and five conspiracy charges — and the Securities and Exchange Commission alleged that FTX was a fraud "from the start," with a "multi-billion-dollar deficiency caused by his own misappropriation of customer funds." The Verge repeated this framing at the head of each of its trial dispatches through October 2023, and in its October 28th, 2023 write-up reported that Bankman-Fried had been found guilty on seven counts including charges of wire fraud.

The boundary of the concept is the mix of charge types: the indictment paired substantive wire fraud counts with conspiracy counts rather than resting on a single offence, and the SEC's civil allegation about the exchange's origins ran alongside the criminal case rather than being part of it. The Verge's reporter, writing as the prosecution's case neared its end on October 26th, 2023, added an impression of the people the charges swept in: all the co-conspirators seemed oddly younger than their years, as though they had got stuck in the "math camp forever" environment Bankman-Fried created for them and simply failed to grow up.



---


# Prosecution And Defense Arguments On Day Two Of The SBF Trial

On the second day of the trial of Sam Bankman-Fried and FTX, the prosecution argued that Bankman-Fried knowingly committed fraud, and it grounded that claim in motive: he did so, prosecutors said, to achieve great wealth, power and influence.

The defense countered with the opposite reading of the same conduct. Its claim was that the FTX founder acted in good faith, never meant to commit fraud or to steal, and basically got in over his head — an argument whose warrant is that inexperience and overreach, rather than intent, explain what happened. The two sides therefore contest intent rather than the underlying events, and the reporting on this exchange comes from Rebecca and Jacquelyn in TechCrunch's Week in Review of October 7, 2023, covering day two of the trial only.



---


# Sam Bankman-Fried's Charges And The Collapse Of FTX

Sam Bankman-Fried, the founder of FTX and Alameda Research, is facing seven counts of criminal charges: two counts of wire fraud and five counts of conspiracy charges.

FTX was a failed cryptocurrency exchange founded in 2019. According to a now-deleted profile from FTX investors Sequoia Capital, FTX was founded because of Bankman-Fried's frustration with other exchanges while he was running Alameda Research, his crypto trading firm. According to the SEC, FTX was a fraud "from the start," diverting customers' funds to Alameda, with a "multi-billion-dollar deficiency caused by his own misappropriation of customer funds."



---


# Bankman-Fried's Pre-Collapse Public Image Strategy

Before his fall, Bankman-Fried made himself out to be the Good Boy of crypto — the trustworthy face of a sometimes-shady industry — and he was very interested in publicity, sitting for many interviews both before and after the collapse of FTX.

The Verge attributes FTX's quick rise as an industry force at least in part to that appetite for attention: Bankman-Fried gave interviews freely and quickly rose to public prominence, positioning himself as an important, boyish face for crypto even though FTX hadn't been in the business as long as competing exchanges such as Coinbase, Kraken, or Gemini. At one point he told a colleague at FTX that "I honestly think it's negative EV" — possibly "expected value," as in poker — "for me to cut my hair. I think it's important for people to think I look crazy." Because he was so successful at this kind of public relations, his fall from grace became another mark against an industry already roiled by bankruptcies and scandals; The Verge adds that more trouble for the industry is likely to come from one crucial element of the fraud trial, the part where the government must prove intent.



---


# The FTX Trial's Stakes For The Wider Crypto Industry

The Verge argued that the trial of Sam Bankman-Fried is likely to be more consequential than just whether the man himself is found guilty: depending on what evidence is introduced, it could be rough for the entire crypto industry.

The grounds are the unpredictability of what a trial surfaces, voiced by Yesha Yadav, a law professor at Vanderbilt University: "How much damage can this trial do to the already beaten-down reputation of the industry at this point? This trial is going to be an excruciating moment for the industry because no one knows what kind of evidence might come out." The warrant joining that uncertainty to industry-wide stakes is that the industry's reputation is already beaten down, so evidence introduced against one exchange's founder lands on the whole sector rather than on him alone.

qid: Does the 'Business World' article claim that the same individuals will serve on the Board of Trustees for the Philippine Education Development Fund (PhilEd) as the current Board of Trustees of the Fund, in contrast to the 'Music Business Worldwide' article where Andrew Wilkinson is reported to be retiring from the Hipgnosis Songs Fund board?
context:
# Folding FAPE And PEAC Into PhilEd

The authors propose that the FAPE/PEAC structure and organization be moved to PhilEd, which operationally means folding into PhilEd the roles and responsibilities of FAPE and PEAC as well as their financial resources. The asset transfer step covers FAPE's funds of P277 million as of 31 May 2022, plus the assets and liabilities of PEAC amounting to P567 million as of the same date.

The programs step moves the DepEd programs presently managed by PEAC and lodged in the DepEd budget into PhilEd: Educational Service Contracting at P9.3 billion in School Year 2021-2022, the Senior High School Voucher Program at P20.3 billion in School Year 2021-2022, and the Teachers' Salaries Subsidy at P793 million in School Year 2021-2022. The governance step keeps the existing people in place: the present Board of Trustees of the Fund, consisting of the Secretary of Education as Chairman with the Director-General of the National Economic and Development Authority and the three Presidents of the Association of Christian Schools, Colleges and Universities, the Catholic Educational Association of the Philippines, and the Philippine Association of Colleges and Universities, shall also constitute the proposed Board of Trustees of PhilEd, and the management team of PEAC will be the incoming management team of PhilEd.



---


# Hipgnosis Songs Fund Board Changes September 2023

On 28 September 2023, Hipgnosis Songs Fund confirmed that Andrew Sutch, 73, the Chair of its board since 2018, is stepping down both as HSF board Chair and as a director of the company.

HSF said it had begun a process to recruit a new Chair, and that Sutch will leave his post as and when that person is hired, or in any case before HSF's AGM the following year, in Q4 2024. In addition, Andrew Wilkinson, 72, informed the HSF board of his intention to retire as a board director, a departure that will reduce the company's board to five directors.



---


# Hipgnosis Board Defence of Portfolio Value

In its note to shareholders on 28 September 2023, the Hipgnosis Songs Fund board argued that the fund's share price understates the worth of what it owns. It reiterated its belief — and Hipgnosis Song Management's belief — that HSF owns "a unique portfolio of iconic, culturally significant songs that will deliver strong long-term value as they benefit from the structural tailwinds in the music industry".

The board's second ground is the adviser's method rather than the assets alone: "the [HSF] Board believes that the Investment Adviser's approach to Song Management should enable the Company to outperform the wider music market." Its evidence for that claim is the $440 million transaction — "This has been evidenced by the 44% total return, including right to income, transaction fees and expected taxes, realised since acquisition on the [$440 million] Transaction."

The warrant joining evidence to conclusion is a commitment rather than a further fact: "the Board and the Investment Adviser are committed to ensuring that this value is achieved for shareholders by a re-rating of the share price and are determined to deliver on the ongoing opportunity of the Company." The argument is therefore that quality of assets plus adviser performance, demonstrated by a realised 44% total return, justifies expecting the market to close the gap.



---


# PhilHealth's Earmarked Revenue Model As A Template For PhilEd

PhilHealth's financing model combines member premiums and local government subsidies for enrolled indigents with earmarked national revenues. It receives a share of the "sin taxes" collected from tobacco and sugar-sweetened beverages, justified on the ground that tobacco smokers and sugar-sweetened beverage drinkers impose an additional burden on the healthcare system and so must contribute to health services; in Fiscal Year 2022 this amounted to P74 billion. Under the Universal Health Care Law, PhilHealth also receives 50% of the government share from the income of the Philippine Amusement Gaming Corp. and 40% of the Charity Fund of the Philippine Charity Sweepstakes Office, which in 2022 amounted to P188 billion.

The proposal transposes that structure to education. In addition to the school vouchers funded under the Expanded Government Assistance to Students and Teachers in Private Education Act, the authors suggest PhilEd be allocated a share of the taxes imposed on extractive industries, on the argument that the depletion of natural resources can only be justified if the taxes collected enhance human resources. Like PhilHealth, PhilEd could also be mandated to receive a percentage from the collection of documentary stamps, which have recently been raised, and PhilEd can be given access to the Special Education Funds of the local school boards of the Local Government. The legislative parallel closes the analogy: Congress enacted Republic Act 7875, "The National Health Insurance Act of 1995", which created PhilHealth, and the authors hope some members of Congress would file a Universal Education Financing Law to create PhilEd.



---


# Hipgnosis Songs Fund Continuation Vote

A 'continuation vote' at Hipgnosis Songs Fund (HSF), the UK-listed music rights fund, is a vote of the firm's shareholders on whether to keep the entity going as a closed-ended investment entity — that is, as a publicly-traded bundle of music rights. It takes place at HSF's Annual General Meeting, and the 2023 vote looked likely to be held on Thursday 26 October, according to an announcement from the firm on 28 September 2023.

The 2023 vote was only "likely" rather than definite because it might still get bumped into November, and its outcome was unknown at the time of reporting, with a looming $440 million transaction that could potentially influence it. The vote itself was not a new event: it had been scheduled ever since HSF went public in 2018, five years after the float.

The changes HSF announced on 28 September invited the question of whether they amounted to concessions designed to keep investors happy and confident in long-term prospects — and voting to keep going. One such measure directly extends the mechanism: if shareholders vote at the next AGM to remain a publicly-traded fund, another continuation vote will be put to HSF shareholders at an Extraordinary General Meeting in January 2026, roughly two years later.



---


# The PhilEd Education Development Fund Proposal

PhilEd, the proposed Philippine Education Development Fund, is defined by its purpose: its role would be to fund the education dreams of all Filipinos, especially the neediest and most deserving.

The definition is drawn by analogy to a corporate finance role. When Isidro Consunji, President of DMCI Holdings, Inc., was asked by his officers what the role of his Chief Financial Officer would be, he gave a three-word answer: "Fund my dreams." PhilEd is cast in the same terms for the country's education ambitions.



---


# The Board Appoints And Oversees Its Own Valuer

The oddest thing about the board's complaint, MBW argues, is that Citrin Cooperman's valuation of Hipgnosis Songs Fund is, according to HSF's own company documentation, appointed and overseen by the HSF board itself. This attacks the implicit premise that the disputed valuation is something imposed on the board from outside, and therefore something whose failings can be laid at another party's door.

The documentary grounds are two recurring lines in HSF filings. Every annual and interim report from HSF so far states: "Portfolio Independent Valuer… Citrin Cooperman Advisors LLC, formerly Massarsky Consulting, Inc., [is] appointed by the Board to independently value the Company's Catalogues within the Portfolio." Various HSF company reports to date also state: "The [HSF] Board is ultimately and solely responsible for overseeing the valuation of the Company's investments in music catalogues and has appointed [Citrin Cooperman] to perform this specialist work."



---


# The HSF Board Versus Hipgnosis Song Management

As part of its 19 December 2023 announcement, the HSF board took something of a swipe at its investment adviser, Merck Mercuriadis' Hipgnosis Song Management. HSF said that after seeing Citrin Cooperman's latest valuation and believing it to be too high, it "sought advice from Hipgnosis Song Management… which is majority owned by funds managed and/or advised by Blackstone, on their opinion on the independent valuer's valuation", and added that HSM "eventually provided an opinion, which was heavily caveated, such that the Board has concerns as to the valuation of the Company's assets in its interim results".

Hipgnosis Song Management issued its own statement the same day, saying it "has fulfilled its duties to [HSF] with respect to both the independent valuation and preparation of the interim results in a timely and efficient manner", and that "notwithstanding the Board's decision to delay publication of the interim financial statements, [we] will continue to work in a constructive manner to support the interests of the Company and its shareholders".



---


# Autobrains Hires Uri Yacovy As COO

Autobrains hired Uri Yacovy, a former SVP at Mobileye, as its chief operating officer, TechCrunch reported on 2023-10-22.

qid: Did Sporting News fail to indicate a similar issue with Williams and Rice's attempt at a deep shot in the USC vs. Notre Dame game on October 14th after CBSSports.com reported on the Dallas Cowboys' offensive strategy involving deeper passes on October 12th?
context:
# Notre Dame's First Quarter Against USC, Oct. 14 2023

Notre Dame led USC 7-3 after the first quarter of their Oct. 14, 2023 game, scoring first on a four-yard Sam Hartman touchdown pass to Gi'Bran Payne set up by Xavier Watts' interception, with USC answering through a Denis Lynch field goal.

Coverage picked up at 7:29 p.m. with the stadium dark as fans welcomed the Fighting Irish to the field. USC started with the ball at its own 25; MarShawn Lloyd ran up the middle for a yard on the first offensive play, and Caleb Williams scrambled for no gain on the next. At 7:37 p.m. Williams found Brendan Rice for an 11-yard gain and a first down, then over-shot Lake McRee and was picked off by Watts, who returned the ball all the way to the USC 12. Two Audric Estime runs picked up eight yards to set up third-and-2, and at 7:39 p.m. Hartman dropped back and threw to a leaping Payne, who back-pedalled into the end zone for the four-yard touchdown: Notre Dame 7, USC 0.

USC's response drive began with Zachariah Branch returning the kickoff to the USC 19. Austin Jones gained five on first down, and a defensive holding call on Notre Dame's Benjamin Morris on a second-down pass gave USC a first down at the 34. A Williams rush for four was followed by a snap infraction creating second-and-11, then a three-yard Jones run; Williams connected with Tahj Washington but the receiver was stopped three yards short of the marker, bringing out the punting unit, and Notre Dame fair caught at its own 14. Estime opened Notre Dame's next drive with an 11-yard run past the marker and caught a pass for four to set up second-and-6, but at 7:53 p.m. the Fighting Irish punted after Estime gained only a yard and Hartman's pass to Rico Flores Jr. fell incomplete.

USC began its next drive at its own 33 with 6:38 left in the quarter. Williams was flushed from the pocket and scrambled 11 yards, with a Notre Dame defensive holding penalty adding to the gain and moving USC to the Notre Dame 46. Williams then hit Dorian Singer up the middle to the Notre Dame 35 after a one-yard Jones run, and Jones added three on the ground before Williams dumped a pass to Branch for seven yards and another first down. Singer made a 13-yard catch but was flagged for offensive pass interference for pushing off Morrison, backing USC to the Notre Dame 39 for first-and-25; Michael Jackson then caught a pass for 12 yards and a personal foul on Morrison moved USC to the Notre Dame 13 with an automatic first down. Three short plays stalled the offense at the Notre Dame 8, and on fourth-and-5 Lynch drilled a 25-yard field goal at 8:04 p.m.: Notre Dame 7, USC 3. Devyn Ford returned the ensuing kickoff 28 yards so Notre Dame began at its own 36, and the quarter closed with Jeremiyah Love losing a yard before Hartman completed a seven-yard pass to Jordan Faison, leaving the Irish to open the second quarter on third-and-4.



---


# Notre Dame's Third Quarter Against USC, Oct. 14 2023

Both teams scored a touchdown in the third quarter of Notre Dame's Oct. 14, 2023 game against USC — a 31-yard MarShawn Lloyd run for the Trojans and a Sam Hartman deep ball to Chris Tyree for the Irish — leaving Notre Dame ahead 31-13 with Audric Estime finishing the quarter on a 14-yard run.

The half opened at 9:25 p.m. with Notre Dame starting at its own 22 after a 17-yard Devyn Ford return. Hartman's play-action deep shot to Mitchell Evans was broken up by Christian Roland-Wallace, the second time he had defended a pass to Evans; Evans was injured on the play and, though able to walk off, had to go to the blue tent. Hartman then threw short to Holden Staes for three and missed on third down, forcing a punt after a three-and-out. Branch boomed a 50-yard punt and hopped back on it so USC retained possession, starting at its own 30, but the Trojans went three-and-out quickly — an incompletion, a pass for a loss of four and another incompletion — with the Sporting News noting the Trojans still looked lost on offense. Tyree returned the punt two yards to the Notre Dame 25, where a short Faison gain and a four-yard Love run set up third-and-5 at the Notre Dame 30; another short Hartman pass was met by a great open-field tackle from Calen Bullock after just a yard, Notre Dame punted, and Branch returned it 21 yards to the USC 43.

USC then moved into scoring position through a stretch of trading penalties. Mario Williams was flagged for USC's second offensive pass interference of the night after a 10-yard Washington catch, creating first-and-25, and Notre Dame's Benjamin Morrison was then called for pass interference — his third penalty of the night — on a deep shot to Rice, moving USC back to its own 43. Branch got back to the line of scrimmage after a reverse, Williams found Singer down the right sideline for 11 before a sack for a loss of 10 gave the yardage back, and Williams then bailed USC out of second-and-long with a 21-yard completion to McRee on the run. At 9:45 p.m. USC scored its first touchdown of the evening: after a four-yard Williams rush, Lloyd took a pitch from Williams, carved through the left side and broke loose for a 31-yard score, making it Notre Dame 24, USC 13.

Notre Dame responded on the next drive. Ford's return gave the Irish the ball at their own 32, Estime ran for seven, four and three yards, Evans returned from injury to catch a short pass and fight for eight yards to the USC 46, and at 9:53 p.m. Hartman uncorked a deep ball down the middle to the speedy Tyree, who ran the remaining 15 yards into the end zone to push the lead back to 18: Notre Dame 31, USC 13. USC started its reply at its own 25, with Williams hitting Washington for 13 on the sideline; a batted pass and a four-yard Lloyd run brought up third-and-6 from the USC 32 and Notre Dame used its first timeout of the half. Williams found Jackson over the middle for 10 and a first down, but Marist Liufau sacked him for a loss of eight back to the USC 44, and then Rylie Mills and Nana Osafo-Mensah brought him down for another eight-yard loss, leaving third-and-28. Notre Dame conceded a 10-yard wide receiver screen to Jackson, and a false start preceded Eddie Czaplicki's punt, which went out of bounds at the Notre Dame 7 with eight seconds left in the quarter. Estime then ended the third quarter with a run to the left, hitting the hole and being brought down at the Notre Dame 21 by Zion Branch after a gain of 14.



---


# Turnovers, Not Yardage, Decided Notre Dame's Win Over USC

Notre Dame beat USC on Oct. 14, 2023 despite being out-gained and out-performed on third down, because a 5-0 turnover margin is difficult for any team to overcome — the claim the Sporting News advances is that field position bought by turnovers, plus pressure in the trenches, outweighed USC's statistical edges.

The grounds are the box score. In a season in which much had been made of USC's defensive woes holding back the offense, on this night it was the other way around: USC's defense held Notre Dame to just 251 total yards of offense, 51 fewer than the Trojans gained on offense, and Notre Dame converted only three of 10 third downs against USC's six of 13. The warrant joining those grounds to the conclusion is field position: the 5-0 turnover margin frequently left Notre Dame with only a short field to work with, so that the Fighting Irish started drives on average at their own 47 while the Trojans began on average at their own 28.

A second strand of the argument is that Watts made the headline-grabbing plays but a massive part of Notre Dame's defensive success came in the trenches.
