qid: Does the article from Fortune suggest that Sam Bankman-Fried's persuasive abilities were a factor in Adam Yedidia joining Alameda and FTX, while The Verge article indicates that Sam Bankman-Fried's management capabilities were challenged by the growth of FTX and Alameda Research?
context:
# Sam Bankman-Fried's Charges And The Collapse Of FTX

Sam Bankman-Fried, the founder of FTX and Alameda Research, is facing seven counts of criminal charges: two counts of wire fraud and five counts of conspiracy charges.

FTX was a failed cryptocurrency exchange founded in 2019. According to a now-deleted profile from FTX investors Sequoia Capital, FTX was founded because of Bankman-Fried's frustration with other exchanges while he was running Alameda Research, his crypto trading firm. According to the SEC, FTX was a fraud "from the start," diverting customers' funds to Alameda, with a "multi-billion-dollar deficiency caused by his own misappropriation of customer funds."



---


# Alameda Research As The Alleged Conduit For FTX Customer Funds

In the prosecution's account offered by Thane Rehn, the key to Sam Bankman-Fried's alleged scheme was Alameda Research, a crypto hedge fund that Bankman-Fried also owned. The structure the government described works as follows: Caroline Ellison — Bankman-Fried's on-again off-again girlfriend and the CEO of Alameda — served as a front for the fund, and through that arrangement Bankman-Fried had "secret access" to customer money, both cash and crypto.

Two further relations complete the alleged mechanism. Bankman-Fried is said to have directed employees to conceal the flow of money into FTX's coffers, and to have forged financial documents distributed to lenders and investors. "The defendant lied to the world," Rehn alleged. These are the government's allegations as presented in its opening statement, not established findings.



---


# Adam Yedidia's First Testimony And His Immunity Deal

Late in the afternoon of the second day of Sam Bankman-Fried's trial, the government called Adam Yedidia to the stand, and lead prosecutor Danielle Sassoon disclosed that this college friend of Bankman-Fried had legal immunity during his testimony. Asked why he had made such a deal with the government, Yedidia answered: "I was concerned that I had unwittingly written code that contributed to a crime."

Yedidia, described as a fast-talking graduate of MIT, testified that he and Bankman-Fried were close friends in college. After Bankman-Fried left Jane Street — the high-frequency trading firm where the former billionaire got his start in finance after MIT — he persuaded Yedidia to join him, first as a trader at Alameda and then as a developer at FTX.

The testimony was cut short when the clock neared 4:30 p.m. and court adjourned for the day. Yedidia was scheduled to continue his testimony on Thursday, to be followed by Matt Huang, a former partner at the venture capital firm Sequoia Capital, and then by Gary Wang, a key Bankman-Fried lieutenant and one of the government's star witnesses.



---


# Bankman-Fried's Claimed Ignorance Of Alameda's Finances

Testifying on October 28th, 2023, Bankman-Fried attacked the prosecution's premise that he knew about the hole in FTX by claiming he did not learn of the $8 billion liability associated with Alameda until October 2022, that he found it all by himself by looking at a computer database, and that when he found it he was "very surprised." The Verge's reporter recorded the claim with heavy scepticism.

The counter-argument extended to reinterpreting each earlier warning as something innocuous. On why Alameda served as FTX's "payment provider" for bank transfers, he said FTX could not get bank accounts right away and he anticipated it would take a year or two, so rather than wait he used Alameda: "My understanding at the time was that there were teams managing the process. At the time, I wasn't entirely sure what was happening." On Adam Yedidia's testimony about an August 2022 conversation regarding the enormous amount Alameda owed FTX, Bankman-Fried remembered it differently — Yedidia was just asking about Alameda's risk profile and he was not talking about insolvency at all. On the dramatic balcony conversation with Nishad Singh at their penthouse, he said Singh thought Alameda's liabilities had gotten too high and that FTX was spending too much on marketing, while Bankman-Fried still thought Alameda had more assets than liabilities so it was all fine, and besides, if Singh thought he would be better at marketing he could take it over — it did not have anything to do with the money Alameda owed FTX at all.



---


# Adam Yedidia's Testimony And The $8 Billion Bug

Adam Yedidia, the prosecution's second witness, testified that in June 2022 he submitted a report to Bankman-Fried on Signal showing that $8 billion in customer money held in an internal database tracking cash wired to an Alameda account called "fiat at ftx.com" was missing.

Yedidia met Bankman-Fried in college at MIT and the pair remained close friends; assuming a robotic posture on the stand, he said he worked out of FTX's Hong Kong office from January to October of 2021 and then in the Bahamas until the collapse. He referred to a group Signal thread called "People of the House," referring to Bankman-Fried's $35 million penthouse where many employees lived; on who was paying the rent, Yedidia recalled Bankman-Fried saying he "assumed it's just Alameda paying for it in the end." Yedidia said Bankman-Fried had told him, before he began working in the Bahamas in 2019, that he and Ellison had had sex, and asked whether it was a good idea for them to date — Yedidia said no, and Bankman-Fried responded that he was expecting that answer. One of Yedidia's responsibilities was fixing the bug in the code that gave Alameda preferential treatment. He said he and Bankman-Fried spoke about the missing $8 billion at the pickleball court at the resort in Nassau, Bahamas, where he asked his boss if things were OK because it "seemed like a lot of money" from FTX customers was at risk. "Sam said, we were bulletproof last year. We aren't bulletproof this year," Yedidia testified; asked when they would be bulletproof again, Bankman-Fried said he was not sure, but it might be six months to three years. Yedidia said Bankman-Fried appeared "worried or nervous," which was atypical, but that he still trusted Bankman-Fried and Ellison to "handle the situation." On cross-examination, Christian Everdell, Bankman-Fried's attorney, focused on how Yedidia was the one responsible for developing and reviewing the code.



---


# Alameda's Special Privileges Written Into FTX's Code

Gary Wang told the court that Alameda received advantages through code baked into FTX's software granting it special access to the exchange — "We gave special privileges on FTX that gave unlimited withdrawals on the platform to Alameda" — privileges that ultimately resulted in Alameda owing FTX $8 billion worth of customer deposits.

The structure had several linked parts. Alameda was allowed to withdraw and transfer funds and had a $65 billion line of credit. "When customers deposited USD, it went to Alameda," Wang said. "It existed in the computer code. Alameda could have negative balances and unlimited withdrawals." That "bug" in the code was written by Nishad Singh, FTX's director of engineering, and reviewed by Wang, with Bankman-Fried calling the shots. Wang also told the court about a $1 million personal loan he received and a $200 million to $300 million loan in his name from Alameda that was never deposited into his account but was used to make investments into other companies on behalf of FTX — all done by Bankman-Fried, he testified. The escalation was visible over time: in early 2020 Wang discovered for the first time that Alameda's negative balance exceeded FTX's revenue, an indication that Alameda was taking customer funds, and he brought this to Bankman-Fried's attention several times; in late 2021 he discovered Alameda had withdrawn $3 billion from its $65 billion line of credit. The ownership and authority around it: Wang owned 10% of Alameda while his boss owned the other 90%, his compensation was a base salary of $200,000 per year plus stock, and he owned roughly 17% of FTX — and even though they were co-founders, "ultimately it was Sam's decision to make" when there were disagreements. Born in China, Wang moved to the U.S. at age 7 and grew up in Minnesota before going to MIT to study math and computer science, worked at Google after college, and first met Bankman-Fried during high school at a summer camp.

qid: Who is the Silicon Valley prodigy recognized for his early influence in generative AI technology, who was also involved in a situation where he was accused of not being fully truthful with the board, but did not face an attempt of removal by co-founders of a related AI firm, as reported by Fortune, The Age, and TechCrunch?
context:
# Sam Altman's Career Before OpenAI

Sam Altman, 38 as of November 2023, is not trained as an AI engineer, yet has been seen as a Silicon Valley wunderkind since his early 20s. The defining credential of that earlier phase is that he was recruited in 2014 to take the lead of the startup incubator YCombinator.

The reputation attached to him at the time is captured in YCombinator co-founder Paul Graham's 2014 announcement that Altman would become its president: "Sam is one of the smartest people I know, and understands startups better than perhaps anyone I know, including myself." Graham said then that Altman was "one of those rare people who manage to be both fearsomely effective and yet fundamentally benevolent."



---


# DeepMind's Sale To Google And Facebook's AI Lab

Google offered $US650 million for DeepMind. Mark Zuckerberg of Facebook offered a bigger payout to DeepMind's founders but would not agree to the conditions the founders had set, and DeepMind sold to Google.

Zuckerberg was determined to build an AI lab of his own and hired Yann LeCun, a French computer scientist who had also done pioneering AI research, to run it. A year after Hinton's auction, Zuckerberg and LeCun flew to Lake Tahoe for the same AI conference, and while padding around a suite at the Harrah's casino in his socks Zuckerberg personally interviewed top researchers, who were soon offered millions of dollars in salary and stock. AI was once laughed off; now the richest men in Silicon Valley were shelling out billions to keep from being left behind.



---


# Sam Altman's Rise As The Face Of Generative AI

In the year since Altman catapulted ChatGPT to global fame, he became Silicon Valley's sought-after voice on the promise and potential dangers of artificial intelligence, and his sudden and mostly unexplained exit brought uncertainty to the industry's future. He helped start OpenAI as a nonprofit research laboratory in 2015, but it was ChatGPT's explosion into public consciousness that thrust him into the spotlight as a face of generative AI — technology that can produce novel imagery, passages of text and other media. On a world tour in 2023 he was mobbed by a crowd of adoring fans at an event in London.

He has sat with multiple heads of state to discuss AI's potential and perils. On Thursday, 2023-11-16, he took part in a CEO summit at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation conference in San Francisco, where OpenAI is based. At OpenAI's first developer conference the week before, Altman was the main speaker, showcasing a vision for a future of AI agents that could help people with a variety of tasks; days later he announced the company would have to pause new subscriptions to its premium version of ChatGPT because it had exceeded capacity.



---


# The AI Risk Paradox Among Tech Billionaires

At the heart of the competition to build artificial intelligence is a brain-stretching paradox: the people who say they are most worried about AI are among the most determined to create it and enjoy its riches, and they have justified their ambition with their strong belief that they alone can keep AI from endangering Earth. The grounds are the shape of the debate itself. Eight years after an argument between Elon Musk and Larry Page, that argument seems prescient, because the question of whether AI will elevate the world or destroy it, or at least inflict grave damage, has framed an ongoing debate among Silicon Valley founders, chatbot users, academics, legislators and regulators about whether the technology should be controlled or set free.

That debate has pitted some of the world's richest men against one another: Musk, Page, Mark Zuckerberg of Meta, tech investor Peter Thiel, Satya Nadella of Microsoft and Sam Altman of OpenAI, all of whom have fought for a piece of a business that one day could be worth trillions of dollars, and for the power to shape it. The narrative anchor is that Musk and Page stopped speaking soon after the party that summer, and that a few weeks later Musk dined with Altman, who was then running a tech incubator, and several researchers in a private room at the Rosewood hotel in Menlo Park, California, a favoured deal-making spot close to the venture capital offices of Sand Hill Road.



---


# Neural Networks And DeepMind's Atari Demonstration

A neural network is a complex algorithm created in the image of the human brain, essentially a giant mathematical system that spends days, weeks or even months identifying patterns in large amounts of digital data. First developed in the 1950s, these systems could learn to handle tasks on their own: after analysing names and addresses scribbled on hundreds of envelopes, for instance, they could read handwritten text. Flush with cash, DeepMind hired researchers who specialised in them.

DeepMind took the concept further, building a system that could learn to play classic Atari games such as Space Invaders, Pong and Breakout to illustrate what was possible. This got the attention of another Silicon Valley powerhouse, Google, and specifically Larry Page, who saw a demonstration of DeepMind's machine playing Atari games and wanted in. The boundary of what the field could then show was pushed again in the spring of 2012, when Geoffrey Hinton, a 64-year-old professor at the University of Toronto, and two graduate students published a research paper that showed the world what AI could do by training a neural network to recognise common objects such as flowers, dogs and cars.



---


# Gaza As A Tech Outsourcing Hub

Gaza, despite being one of the most economically challenged regions in the world, has ironically always been a tech hub — not only for Palestine and Palestinians, but also for the world, with international companies having for many years sought out a presence there to collaborate with talented tech freelancers and the startups that gradually emerged from the region. According to sources who helped build those bridges, Nvidia, famed for its role in the new AI boom, has been working with at least 100 engineers from the region for years; tragically, the initiative to employ Palestinians in this outsourcing was that of Mellanox founder Eyal Waldman, whose daughter was brutally murdered in the attacks by Hamas.

The hub's scale marks its boundary. Since at least 2008, TechCrunch has been covering technology companies out of Palestine, some serving their direct audience and some serving the tech world internationally, and Silicon Valley had taken an increasing interest in Palestine as a tech hub — but like the ecosystem itself, that interest is nascent: to date, those working in the region estimate that as much as $10 million has been invested in the Palestinian tech ecosystem. Notably, in 2017, Salesforce founder and CEO Marc Benioff joined Silicon Valley luminaries in backing the first-ever coding academy to be created in Gaza.



---


# The OpenAI Board Ousts Sam Altman, November 2023

As reported on November 18, 2023, the OpenAI board had ejected billionaire and AI evangelist Sam Altman from his CEO role after an apparent vote of no confidence. The board's exact wording in a release issued that afternoon: Altman's "departure follows a deliberative review process by the board, which concluded that he was not consistently candid in his communications with the board, hindering its ability to exercise its responsibilities."

What followed was a whirlwind four days for OpenAI, the generative AI poster child behind the smash hit ChatGPT. The board ousted CEO and co-founder Altman and demoted president and co-founder Greg Brockman, who subsequently resigned, paving the way for what looked like a mutiny by staff insisting the founders be reinstated post-haste. By the time TechCrunch wrote again on November 21, 2023, Microsoft had already hired Altman and Brockman to head up a new internal AI unit — though, as things transpired, nothing had actually been signed yet, with rumors suggesting the ousted leaders might actually return to OpenAI after all, in some capacity at least.

TechCrunch cautioned on November 18 that the full truth would not be known for a long time, as the characters in the drama are likely to be NDA'ed up. Per various whispers and leaks, an all-hands meeting about the situation that afternoon did not produce any revelations beyond banal reassurances that the company is fine and they will get a fresh CEO soon.



---


# Private Sector Volunteers In Terror Finance Tracking

The network blocking terror financing funds includes many entities, including private citizens: IMPA has been approached by many experts from the private sector — people with intelligence experience because they have worked in these organizations, or with high-tech experience — who "have mobilized like crazy."

"The world's financial intelligence authorities are now at the heart of this struggle, and we're working together to thwart the financing channels that we've located," Ostrovitch-Levi said. "Israeli entrepreneurs in Silicon Valley have contacted us; they write code, search for information, and give us lots of information. We aggregate and examine everything."

qid: Which company, according to allegations discussed in articles from 'The Age' and 'TechCrunch', has both manipulated its search service to increase ad revenue and spent billions to secure its position as the default search engine, while also facing legal scrutiny for potentially anticompetitive practices that could affect its legal standing as outlined by 'The Verge'?
context:
# Wired's Retracted Claim That Google Manipulates Search Queries

In October 2023, Wired posted an opinion article by lawyer and privacy advocate Megan Gray alleging that Google had accidentally revealed during the trial that it manipulates people's search queries for maximum ad revenue — the example given being the replacement of a search for "children's clothing" with "NIKOLAI-brand kidswear" — and Wired subsequently removed the article for not meeting its standards.

Google rejected the claim in very strong terms, saying the piece was misleading and inaccurate and denying that it ever altered search terms. The Age drew a lesson from the episode's reach: the degree to which the article was shared on social media and boosted in write-ups at other outlets shows just how willing people are to accept foul play on Google's part, and a suspicion of privacy invasion and inappropriate data handling follows the company at all times. The article placed the episode in the wider context of the US case — which, having to prove Google somehow broke the law to achieve the status quo, could be an uphill battle for the government, but which offers everyone else a rare opportunity for insight into what the tech giant does with its enormous market share, and whether it is still focused on being the best or uses its ubiquity to squeeze users for money at the expense of product quality.



---


# Google Paid $26.3 Billion In 2021 For Default Search Placement

Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to multiple browsers, phones and platforms — from companies including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla — to be everyone's default search engine. The figure was revealed by Google's search head Prabhakar Raghavan when he testified in court on October 28, according to The Verge.

About $18 billion of that total went directly to Apple, according to a New York Times report published earlier in October 2023, and Google has had its deal with Apple in place since 2003 — so the payment is the current year of a two-decade arrangement, not a one-off. Questioned on the amount of money Google spends to get first pick of search engines, Pichai said the decision was made with the consumer in mind: Google pays big bucks to be everywhere so that it can take in all the data and be the best search engine across different companies' devices, he said, according to The Verge.

The trial also produced evidence that Google understood the value of defaults very early on. U.S. Justice Department lawyer Meagan Bellshaw showed Pichai a 2007 email from a Google product strategy meeting containing data showing that when people changed their browser homepage to Google, they did 15% more Google searches, and that when they switched away, their Google searches dropped 27%. The email summarizing that meeting, sent to Pichai as well as other Google leaders, read: "Nitin argues that focusing on homepage market share is one of the most effective things we can do to make gains in search market share," according to The Verge.



---


# The Google Antitrust Case

The Google antitrust case is the U.S. government's trial over Google's dominance in the online search market, stemming from a 2020 antitrust claim, in which the government argues that Google uses its platforms and its deals with partners to block out competition in search or advertising and thereby to hinder competitors from accessing the data they would need to improve their products.

Its defining features are the conduct at issue and the defence offered against it. Google CEO Sundar Pichai testified Monday in the trial, defending Google's business tactics, including its deal with Apple and other partners to make Google the default search engine. Google's answer is that it is just doing business: everybody wants Google as the default engine because it is the best, and that, the company says, does not make its actions illegal.

The important boundary case is which Google antitrust matter this is. The 2020 search claim is separate from the one filed in January by the Department of Justice, along with eight states including New York, California and Colorado, which aims to "halt Google's anticompetitive scheme, unwind Google's monopolistic grip on the market and restore competition to digital advertising." The search case and the digital-advertising case are distinct proceedings and should not be conflated.

The trial is the venue in which the underlying numbers surface. Monday's hearing revealed plenty of juicy tidbits, including the $26.3 billion Google spent making itself the default search engine across platforms in 2021, and how Google tried to take it further and have Chrome preinstalled on iPhones.



---


# US v. Google: Two Months Into The Search Antitrust Trial

As of TechCrunch's November 13, 2023 roundup, the Justice Department's landmark antitrust case against Google was nearly two months old, and the trial record was still producing fresh revelations. TechCrunch framed it as one of the biggest fights in tech antitrust since the U.S. took Microsoft to trial in the 1990s.

An earlier roundup had already surfaced that Google spent $26.3 billion in 2021 making itself the default search engine across platforms, and that Google tried to have Chrome preinstalled on iPhones. Over the couple of weeks preceding this roundup, more of Google's inner workings came to light, including some of the search engine's most lucrative search queries, the shape of the revenue-share agreements between Google and Android OEMs, and why Expedia has a bone to pick with Google.



---


# The Hypocrisy Argument: Google Became The Monopoly It Denounced

The DOJ's argument, pressed in cross-examination by Bellshaw, is that Google has become the monopoly it denounced years ago — that the company objected to a rival's search default when it was the one being shut out, and now defends the same arrangement when it is the beneficiary.

The grounds are Google's own 2005 letter. Cast your memories back to 2005, when Microsoft's Internet Explorer became the default search engine: Google's legal chief David Drummond sent Microsoft an angry letter saying that making Internet Explorer the search default was anticompetitive. After establishing that Google understands the inherent value of defaults, Bellshaw brought up Drummond's letter precisely to establish the hypocrisy of Google today. The letter declared that problems with a default setting are made worse by how changes to defaults are handled, and that most end users "do not change defaults."

The warrant is that the letter's reasoning has not changed hands with the market position. These are exactly the arguments that other search engine companies, like DuckDuckGo, Brave or Microsoft's Bing, make when they accuse Google of being anticompetitive by making deals with Apple and others — so if Drummond's reasoning was sound in 2005, it convicts Google now. The DOJ doubled down on this in the trial.

The same cross-examination pressed a second consistency question, on the litigation hold. Pichai said that he took action against the history-off default for chat in February to comply with the DOJ's litigation hold, according to CNBC. Bellshaw then pulled up a message exchange in 2021 where Pichai asked for history to be turned off in a group chat. Pichai responded that he wanted to discuss a personnel matter and that the subject had nothing to do with the litigation hold, which he said he takes great care to comply with.



---


# Consumer Search Startups And Switching Barriers

The premise attacked is that a better search product wins users. The cautionary case is Neeva, founded by former Google execs, which tried to convince people to switch to paid and private search with additional features; earlier in 2023 the startup shut down its consumer efforts and eventually got acquired by Snowflake.

Adii Pienaar, an investor in Deft, said that Deft has to give compelling reasons to users to switch to its service. His grounds are behavioral rather than technical: "Users' natural behavior for search is to follow the path of least resistance, i.e. most people just pick up their phone and just use the default search engine."

The conclusion he draws sets the bar Deft must clear: "For Deft to change that behavior, they will need to create a high-value proposition."



---


# Search Quality Complaints Explained By Data Volume Growth

The Age argued that the common online complaint that "Google Search was a lot better 10 years ago" could absolutely be true, but that it would be a stretch to blame the company's monetisation practices when there is a much simpler explanation: the sheer growth in the data Google has to index.

The grounds are the volumes. In 2013, people were creating around 9 ZB of data every year — nine zettabytes, or nine trillion gigabytes — which Google had to index constantly, whereas in 2023 it is more like 120 ZB. The warrant is a change in kind as well as quantity: not a whole lot of that is static websites as it was a decade ago; it is live information that may be nested within various services and apps, which is harder to index well. The article then turned to what actually happens when we search, noting that Google has published extensive information about its Search procedures, so it is not difficult to get the company's own take on what happens in the background when you send off a query.

qid: After Polygon reported on October 18th that 'Wonder Seeds cause the levels in Super Mario Bros. Wonder to collapse and contort, breaking the traditional rules of Mario games,' did Engadget's review on October 20th agree or disagree on the significant change in gameplay experience introduced by the new mechanic in Super Mario Bros. Wonder?
context:
# Wonder As A Return To 2D Mario Experimentation

Polygon argues that Super Mario Bros. Wonder shares the inventiveness of the earliest 2D Mario games and their disregard for what should and shouldn't be in a Mario game — making it, for middle-aged fans, a candidate for the first "true new Mario game" since Super Mario World in 1990. The grounds lie in a history the reviewer sets out: with each Super Mario Bros. on the NES and SNES, Nintendo's designers learned from the previous entry, cut what didn't work, made audacious additions (there was a time when adding a dinosaur named Yoshi felt like a gimmick), and gradually accumulated the pieces and tropes that would recur for the next thirty-plus years. Then, with Super Mario 64, 3D Mario games became the de facto labs for Nintendo's greatest experimentation — magical hats, water guns, galactic travel — while 2D Mario defaulted to a vessel for nostalgia, including the cheekily named New Super Mario Bros. series.

The warrant is that Wonder revives the old spirit specifically by letting the designers break their own machine. The traditional layer is intact — every level can be enjoyed as a loyal continuation of the plumber's work in the 2D platformer genre, which has kept a healthy cadence since the series debuted in 1985: dash from left to right, jump over pits, concuss enemies, collect the occasional power-up, and leap onto the flagpole that ends one level and unlocks the next. But the wonder of playing Super Mario Bros. in 1985 came from discovery, with Nintendo anticipating that players would climb outside the confines of the level and placing shortcuts in hidden crevices to reward the most rule-breaking players; badges now build on that freedom with skills that let you soar over towering enemies or use the Piranha Plant grappling hook to climb above the stage. "This is the most significant difference between 1985 and 2023," the reviewer writes: "Mario's creators have joined in the fun of breaking the machine." He imagines the game's origin as a notebook in which, since the '90s, every Nintendo developer wrote down each idea that "didn't fit the tone" or "wasn't Mario enough," until someone had the gall to say: "Let's turn this stuffed notebook of chaos into a game. Because why shouldn't Mario be an elephant? Why shouldn't Wigglers wear roller skates? And why shouldn't Luigi skydive?"



---


# Wonder Seeds And The Transformations They Trigger

A Wonder Seed is the object that gives Super Mario Bros. Wonder its name: a Mario-sized ball of botany hidden inside each Wonder stage that, when found, morphs the environment into something quite wonderful. Choosing to seek it out — being "not too precious about video game tradition," as Polygon puts it — floods the atmosphere with lava-lamp plasma, sends gravity into convulsions, or transforms the hero into any variety of creatures or even inanimate objects, so that for a moment Mario gets to be the background. The second level of the game illustrates the range: it can become a musical, depending on whether you pursue the "Super Mario Bros." of the title or the "Wonder."

The defining property, in the reviewer's reading, is that the choice is one of "and," not "or" — the traditional and the topsy-turvy coexist. Across six worlds the creators offer a menu of familiar stages that can, if you like, be prepared with extra spice, or paired with the family-friendly equivalent of ayahuasca; the drug comparison is not flippant, since at one point Toad licks a Wonder Seed and is suddenly riding a dragon. Sometimes the effects go further and the levels themselves collapse and contort, disobeying laws established by decades of Mario games: giant, sudsy, rainbow-tinted bubbles fill a stage and burst through the ceiling, and a colossal snowball knocks down a flagpole, extending the stage beyond its official conclusion.



---


# Super Mario Bros. Wonder: The Verdict

The review's verdict is that Super Mario Bros. Wonder is a marvelous game: its art and animations have a level of polish practically unmatched by rival titles, and the addition of Wonder Seeds subverts your expectations and keeps this 40-year franchise feeling new and innovative.

The grounds are a three-part answer to the problem the review poses — Mario has been stomping Goombas, smashing blocks and running from left to right for damn near 40 years, so how is Nintendo supposed to keep its classic side scroller feeling fresh? First, you shift the location to a brand new kingdom; next, you introduce a bunch of new enemies and power-ups; but what really pushes things over the top is the introduction of a new mechanic that turns everything you think you know about Mario games on its head. What you get is a game that dazzles and delights while living up to its name in a variety of ways.

The warrant is comparative: in a lot of ways Wonder reminds the reviewer of his favorite 2D Mario game, Super Mario World. The one reservation is about the wait — he wishes it had not taken more than 10 years for Nintendo to create a proper sequel to its last mainline platformer — but as he concludes, if that is what it takes to get a game like this, he is happy to sit and wonder what is next for Mario.



---


# Super Mario Bros. Wonder As A Send-Off For The Switch

Polygon argues that Super Mario Bros. Wonder would be a fitting last big release for the Nintendo Switch, on the grounds that the game embodies the same combination that defined the console. With rumours that the Switch's successor could arrive early the following year, the reviewer says he would be fine if Wonder were the console's final major title. The historical grounds: to survive after the Wii U, Nintendo had to bring its console and handheld designers together and create something unlike anything on the market without sacrificing what had got the company to that point — and as the sun sets on the Switch, after an unprecedented run of success and arguably the best entries in many of Nintendo's biggest franchises, Wonder arrives. "Like the Switch itself, Wonder is a collision between the traditional and the new. A game that's the same as it ever was and nothing like Mario has ever been."

The reviewer sets aside the fan question of whether Wonder is the unofficial Super Mario Bros. 5 that "dorks like me have long wanted," leaving that to the forums, and rests his praise on the experience instead: "What a joy it is to play a Mario game and not already know how to read it, to not have my muscle memory do more work than my brain." The scope conditions of the review are stated: Super Mario Bros. Wonder was released on 20 October 2023 on Nintendo Switch, and was reviewed on that console using a pre-release download code provided by Nintendo. Polygon notes that Vox Media has affiliate partnerships which do not influence editorial content, though it may earn commissions on products purchased via affiliate links.



---


# Minor Criticisms Of Super Mario Bros. Wonder

The reviewer's reservations are explicitly minor and do not disturb the overall verdict. Mummy enemies draw a complaint — pulling their wraps feels a bit tedious — and he fears the Elephant Suit might be a bit overpowered in comparison to the Drill Hat.

The other two are complaints about scarcity rather than quality: the 5-star levels and rhythm stages are so good he wishes there were more of them, and he is slightly disappointed the adorable penguins from the movie did not make an appearance somewhere in Wonder's ice levels.



---


# The Badge System In Super Mario Bros. Wonder

The badge system is Super Mario Bros. Wonder's mechanism for optional special abilities: each unlockable upgrade or special move is assigned to a badge that can be found or purchased, and one collected badge can be selected before each stage. The abilities range from helpful (a high, floating leap) to playful (a Piranha Plant grappling hook) to silly (a triple jump tied to a musical rhythm), and Polygon's reviewer describes rotating them by need — opting for the Safety Bounce badge once later stages added instant-death bottomless pits, so that plunging into an abyss has the darkness spit you back up "like a piece of hamburger caught in its throat." The badges are worn by Prince Florian, a little royal bug who joins the journey and provides most of the conversation on the road trip, alongside very talkative flowers sprouting across every corner of the Flower Kingdom, eager to offer a tip for a metatextual wink.

Badges sit inside a wider design of considerate rather than patronising assistance: Wonder Seeds can add a splash of difficulty, but help is perpetually available — time limits are gone and extra lives can be purchased cheaply with the game's abundant purple currency. The balance question the system raises is answered by escalation: the reviewer expects many players to brag that their favourite badge is "the overpowered one," which is sort of always true, since whichever you use you will feel you have an unfair advantage as you float over chunks of the stage or vacuum coins through walls — so the designers layered on new challenges to keep Wonder inside the Goldilocks window, not too hard and not too easy.

qid: Which company, recently discussed in articles from The Verge and TechCrunch, is at the center of issues involving Android app distribution and in-app payment systems, has provided extensive evidence to counter claims in an antitrust battle, and is accused of harming news publishers' revenue through anticompetitive practices?
context:
# Epic's Antitrust Claims Against Google Play

Epic's claim is that the Android operating system's Google Play Store constitutes an unlawful monopoly, and that Google is separately tying its Google Play payments platform to that store, keeping other potential app payment mechanisms from competing.

The grounds Epic offers are the frictions it says Google creates: Google makes it so difficult for developers and users to get around its Android app store, and that app store's standard fees, that it has created an illegal monopoly which unjustly enriches Google while artificially driving up app prices because other stores cannot compete. The warrant joining that to the legal claim is the competitive-harm chain — no viable rival stores means no fee discipline, which means the "Google Tax" is paid either by developers or passed along to consumers. Epic wants to break up Google's alleged monopoly on Android app stores and payment methods so developers are not stuck paying that tax.

Google's answer contests the warrant rather than the fees: it says Epic's demands would damage Android's ability to offer a secure user experience and to compete with Apple's iOS. Both sides agree the future of Google's app store could depend on this trial. Epic sued in 2020 after a fight over in-app purchase fees.



---


# Epic's Opening Statement: Bribes And Blocks

Epic lead attorney Gary Bornstein's case that Android functions as an unlawful monopoly rested on characterising Google as a bully and a cheat that "bribes" or "blocks" any attempt to compete with Android's Google Play store — with the resulting status quo being that the vast, vast majority of Android app installs come from Google Play, and only a tiny sliver is attributable to the Galaxy Store that comes preinstalled on every Samsung phone.

The grounds were money and conduct. Bornstein showed jurors charts of Google's fat app profit margins — 70 percent on $12 billion in revenue a year, says Epic — and pointed out several ugly-seeming ways Google has allegedly attempted to keep anyone from taking that money away, like paying game developers not to build their own app stores or standalone app launchers as Epic did with Fortnite. "Google pays actual and potential competitors not to compete. Literally gives them money and other things of value," said Bornstein. "It's like Google saying, 'Here's $360 million' — that's an actual number you'll hear about — why don't you sit this one out and let me win?"

The warrant linking payments to consumer harm was left mostly implicit on day one. The upshot for consumers, Epic's earlier legal filings have suggested, is that we pay higher prices for apps than we would if there were more competition and/or lower app store and payment processing fees; but while that will probably come up later in the trial, Epic chose to focus more on simply painting Google as the bad guy on day one.



---


# Google's Defense: Android Openness And Sideloading

Google plans to push back at Epic's claim that it does not have competition in the app store business — the premise on which Epic's monopoly theory rests. It will point out that not only does the Play Store compete with Apple's App Store, which the Ninth Circuit ruling in the Apple case agreed upon too, but Android also supports competitive app stores like Samsung's Galaxy Store and Amazon's Appstore.

Google will also attack the foreclosure premise directly. It will note that, unlike Apple, it allows apps to be sideloaded on Android devices — something Epic takes advantage of today — and that this process is streamlined and helps keep users safe. Epic will claim in response that the process is made to be overly difficult for end users, with multiple steps involved and "scare screens" that warn users of the security risks involved with sideloading.

On discovery, Epic will suggest that Google hid items by allowing execs and employees to have "off the record" chats; Google will counter this as well, saying it has provided the court with thousands of chat logs and millions of documents. Google will ultimately push the notion that this case is not about competition but about money — that is, that Epic Games wants to reach the Play Store's 2.5 billion users without having to pay. As a Google blog post by Wilson White, VP, Government Affairs & Public Policy, put it: "Android's choice and flexibility work well for consumers and developers of all sizes. We look forward to making our case in court as we fight to keep our users safe from harm, partner with developers to grow their businesses, and keep the Android ecosystem thriving and healthy for everyone."



---


# Epic's Jury Verdict Against Google, December 2023

On Monday, a federal jury sided with Fortnite maker Epic Games in its fight to break Google's control over Android apps, surprising the world. The nine-person jury decided that Google has an illegal monopoly over Android app distribution and in-app payment systems, and that Google illegally tied its Google Play billing system to its app store.

The outcome was striking because "walled garden" rival Apple almost entirely won a similar case two years earlier. For Tim Sweeney, this was, at last, a win.



---


# The $360 Million Activision Payment And Its Evidentiary Weakness

The counter to Epic's headline number attacks the factual premise beneath it: the $360 million refers to an alleged payment that kept Activision from opening an app store that could compete with Google Play, but Activision told The Verge in 2022 that it "never entered into an agreement that Activision would not open its own app store" — and Google says it is now armed with the evidence to prove it.

Epic itself conceded a related point. On Monday Epic's attorney admitted Google "was too clever" to draw up contracts that specifically forced developers not to compete with the Play Store, so it is not clear how much of Epic's evidence will hold up on closer examination.

The narrative advantage may nonetheless survive the evidentiary weakness. The overall story Epic tells is compelling, and it is not clear Google's opening statement countered it: Google spent its 45 minutes attempting to explain that its dominance over the Android app market is not anything nefarious but simply the natural outcome of Google fiercely competing with the iPhone and its iOS App Store, where Google would like the court to believe the competition truly lies.



---


# Epic Games v. Google Goes To Trial On November 6, 2023

Epic Games, the maker of Fortnite, went to trial with Google on November 6, 2023, hoping to convince a jury that Google engages in anticompetitive behavior with regard to its Android app store, Google Play, and its commission structure. Match had settled its own antitrust lawsuit with Google the week before, but Epic's case proceeded.

This case differs slightly from Epic's battle with Apple on the same topic, because this time Epic cannot allege there is no other way to load apps onto Android devices, as it could with Apple: Android does allow for sideloading apps. Epic will suggest Google makes that process cumbersome, but the bulk of its arguments will center on what it believes are anticompetitive agreements between Google and device manufacturers and developers.

The precedent Epic's case relies on is a Microsoft case in which courts found Microsoft to have a monopoly over the operating system and to be abusing it, making it hard for users to download alternative browsers, like Netscape, on Windows devices. To make its case, Epic plans to bring claims under Sections 1 and 2 of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act, as well as California's anticompetitive laws, the Cartwright Act and the Unfair Competition Law. It will attempt to argue that Google restrains competition within two separate markets: the distribution of apps to Android users, and the market for payment processing solutions for content inside Android apps.



---


# Hypocrisy On Both Sides Of The Courtroom

Each side's central talking point is undercut by its own conduct, so neither party's framing should be taken at face value. Epic says it is not in this for the money, only suing to end Google's monopoly — but Epic would surely profit if it does not have to pay Google's cut. Epic also looks set to argue that you are locked into Android after buying an Android phone, though switching back and forth between the platforms is easier than ever.

Google's talking points have the same problem. Google will say that every Samsung Galaxy phone has "a competing app store right there on the homescreen," even though Google apparently tried to quash that store too, fearing it could cost the company billions. Google was caught trying to play the China card in a pre-briefing with press, reminding journalists that Epic is 40 percent owned by Chinese company Tencent — even though Google itself allegedly considered teaming up with Tencent to eliminate the Epic threat. The parties cannot argue that in court, but Google can attempt to play the China card subtly: "Google may ask a witness once about Tencent's domicile," reads one of Judge Donato's orders.

In the same press briefing, Google suggested to journalists that Epic should have joined the company's "User Choice Billing" program if it wanted an alternative payment system, instead of suing — but that program did not exist until 2022, long after the lawsuit, and it only knocks 4 percentage points off Google's fee.

qid: Considering the reported details from 'The Independent - Life and Style' regarding Jada Pinkett Smith's memoir, the undisclosed efforts in their relationship, the timeframe of their separation mentioned at the 2022 Academy Awards, and Jada's pre-marital views on divorce, what longstanding Hollywood couple's union embodies these aspects and has faced public scrutiny despite a commitment made before their marriage to remain under the same roof?
context:
# Jada Pinkett Smith's 2023 Disclosure Of A Seven-Year Separation

Jada Pinkett Smith revealed in October 2023 that she and her husband Will Smith had been separated for the previous seven years — that is, since 2016 — while remaining married. The disclosure came in an interview with People given while she was promoting her memoir Worthy; The Independent's timeline piece dates the publication to 11 October, while its other reports on the same interview date it 10 October. Pinkett Smith, 52, said of her 26-year marriage to the 55-year-old actor that the couple are "still figuring it out": "We've been doing some really heavy-duty work together. We just got deep love for each other and we are going to figure out what that looks like for us."

She anchored the timeline to the 2022 Academy Awards, when Will Smith slapped Chris Rock after the comedian made a joke about her appearance: at that moment, she said, the pair had already been separated for six years. The revelation was treated as major news — "sent shockwaves around the world," in The Independent's phrasing — because both Smiths had previously doubled down on their stance against divorce, so a lengthy separation raised a new question: when should a couple simply get a divorce?



---


# The Smiths' 2021 Public Accounts Of Marital Strain

In late 2021 both Will Smith and Jada Pinkett Smith described the difficulty of their marriage in public, first on her show and then in his memoir. In an October 2021 episode of Red Table Talk, Pinkett Smith said it "takes work" to maintain a spark in the bedroom: "It's hard... the thing Will and I talk about a lot is the journey. We started in this [relationship] at a very young age, 22 years old... I think you expect your partner to know — especially when it comes to sex. It's like: 'Well, if you love me, you should know. If you love me, you should read my mind.' That's a huge pitfall."

The following month Will Smith's memoir was released, detailing several problems the couple had had over the years. He wrote that they were "suffering the brutal death of our romantic fantasies, the burning away of the idealistic illusion of the perfect marriage and the perfect family. Neither of us wanted a divorce; we knew we loved each other, and some aspects of our union were magical. But the structure of the life that we had established was strangling both of us."



---


# Jada Pinkett Smith's "Entanglement" With August Alsina

Jada Pinkett Smith confirmed in 2020 that she had had a relationship with the singer August Alsina during a period when she and Will Smith were separated, describing it on her Facebook Watch series Red Table Talk as an "entanglement." Alsina and Pinkett Smith were introduced in 2015, but it was only in 2020 that he claimed publicly that the two had dated while she was married and that the Smiths' marriage was open at the time. Alsina said Will Smith had given the pair his "blessing," explaining: "I actually sat down with Will and had a conversation due to the transformation from their marriage to life partnership that they've spoken on several times and it not involving romanticism." He added that he "totally gave myself to that relationship for years of my life and I truly and really, really deeply loved and have a ton of love for her."

Pinkett Smith's representatives called the claims "absolutely not true" on the day they surfaced. Less than two weeks later, she and Will Smith appeared together on Red Table Talk, where she confirmed the relationship but placed it inside an amicable separation that had not been disclosed to the press at the time: "We decided that we were going to separate for a period of time and you go figure out how to make yourself happy and I'll figure out how to make myself happy. From there, as time went on, I got into a different kind of entanglement with August... Yes, it was a relationship absolutely." Prompted by her husband, she confirmed it "was a relationship, absolutely." She also rejected Alsina's framing of permission, saying Will had not given it because the only person who could give her permission was herself. The episode is one of the grey areas in the couple's account of the terms of their separation.



---


# Why Will Smith And Jada Pinkett Smith Never Signed A Prenup

Jada Pinkett Smith revealed in an interview with Parade, published 13 October 2023 and given while promoting her memoir Worthy, that she and Will Smith deliberately did not sign a prenuptial agreement before their 1997 wedding, because they had already decided divorce was not in the cards for them. The Independent presents the missing prenup as of a piece with their promise not to divorce: the absence of a legal fallback was itself the commitment.

She described the decision as an unromantic, deliberate conversation rather than a wedding-day gesture: "Listen, weddings are beautiful, but they can be very romanticised. I feel that was a very real moment for the two of us to look each other in the eyes, recognise that there would be tough times in this journey and to say to each other: 'No matter what, we're going to figure it out and that's why we don't need a prenup, because I'm making a promise that divorce won't be necessary, that we will figure this out.'" She added that the promise was made "without all of the bridal wedding beauty; it was just sitting on a log in his mother's backyard, and going: 'Hey' — having to really look at the possibility of us not being together."



---


# The Smiths' Denials Of Open-Marriage, Divorce And Infidelity Rumours

Will Smith and Jada Pinkett Smith have each publicly rejected the recurring claims made about their marriage — that it was an open relationship, that they were divorcing, and that either had been unfaithful. Pinkett Smith attacked the open-relationship premise directly on Facebook, after a quiet decade and a half spent making films and raising their children: "Here is how I will change my statement... Will and I BOTH can do WHATEVER we want, because we TRUST each other to do so. This does NOT mean we have an open relationship... this means we have a GROWN one." Her counter is that mutual freedom follows from trust, not from an open-marriage arrangement, so the inference from one to the other does not hold.

Will Smith answered the separation-and-divorce rumours in a mocking Facebook post: "Under normal circumstances, I don't usually respond to foolishness. But, so many people have extended [to] me their 'deepest condolences' that I figured — 'What the hell… I can be foolish, too!' So, in the interest of redundant, repetitious, over and over-again-ness… Jada and I are… NOT GETTING A DIVORCE!!!!!!!!!!!!!" In an interview on CBS Sunday Morning in October 2023 he also denied the infidelity premise outright: "Never. There's never been infidelity in our marriage... And we have never surprised one another with anything ever." He added that he had decided public chatter about his life "can be of a benefit to people," since "chatter is the first stage to having a real conversation and being able to truly explore if some of the things in your heart are loving, or poisonous."



---


# Will Smith's Response To Jada Pinkett Smith's Memoir Worthy

Will Smith broke his silence on his wife's memoir Worthy on 16 October 2023 in an interview with The New York Times, saying the book "kind of woke him up" and that he had come to realise she is more "resilient, clever and compassionate than he'd understood." He added: "When you've been with someone for more than half of your life, a sort of emotional blindness sets in, and you can all too easily lose your sensitivity to their hidden nuances and subtle beauties." The statement was framed as support for his partner and her success.

Before giving that statement he had appeared to mock the publicity storm surrounding the couple in a video titled "Official statement" posted on Instagram. "So, here's the thing. My opinion is... uh…" he said, before sneezing into the crook of his arm; as he sneezed, the video comically zoomed out to show several different landscapes including lakes and mountains.



---


# Britney Spears And Justin Timberlake's Relationship

Britney Spears' first highly public relationship was with Justin Timberlake, her co-star from the Mickey Mouse Club. The pair made many appearances together while dating, including the moment — described by The Independent as iconic — when they wore matching all-denim outfits to the American Music Awards in 2001.

They broke up in 2002, shortly after Timberlake and his boy band NSYNC released their hit "Cry Me a River." The song's music video, which featured a woman with blonde hair, sparked rumours that the couple had split because Spears had allegedly cheated on him.

# Google's Defense: Android Competes With iOS

Google's defense denies the premise that Android app stores are a market of their own: "You cannot separate the quality of a phone from the quality of the apps in its app store, and that means Google and Apple compete against each other," began Google lead attorney Glenn Pomerantz. If Google can convince the jury of that, it could be a winning argument, because obviously Google does not have a monopoly on app stores or phones in general.

Pomerantz's commonsense line was that Google cannot possibly have a monopoly on Android app stores when "every single Samsung phone comes with two app stores right on the homescreen," and that the download charts reflect user preference rather than exclusion: "When they show these charts that show all these downloads from Play and not from the Galaxy Store, that's what the Samsung phone users are choosing. They're touching Play. Nothing's keeping them from touching the Galaxy Store; it's just what works for them."

Google's second plank is openness relative to Apple. Epic promised to "show that Google has closed off each and every other option" to the Play Store during this trial, but Google points to the simple fact that it allows alternate app channels at all — something Android rival iOS does not. Pomerantz boasted that over a billion people have gone through the process Epic portrays as needlessly onerous to get apps outside the Play Store; Google told The Verge over email that this refers to how many users have enabled the Android sideloading flow, not necessarily followed through with an install. "A billion people have done it after getting notified of the potential risks," Pomerantz said. "That's because Android users have a real choice."

Google also argues about consequences: if Epic wins, according to Google, it could make Android phones less safe by dismantling basic protections against sideloaded apps, and damage Android's ability to compete with the iPhone because it arguably cannot run a competitive app store by giving it away for free. This case differs slightly from Epic's battle with Apple on the same topic, because this time Epic cannot allege there is no other way to load apps onto Android devices, as it could with Apple: Android does allow for sideloading apps. Epic will suggest Google makes that process cumbersome, but the bulk of its arguments will center on what it believes are anticompetitive agreements between Google and device manufacturers and developers.

The precedent Epic's case relies on is a Microsoft case in which courts found Microsoft to have a monopoly over the operating system and to be abusing it, making it hard for users to download alternative browsers, like Netscape, on Windows devices. To make its case, Epic plans to bring claims under Sections 1 and 2 of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act, as well as California's anticompetitive laws, the Cartwright Act and the Unfair Competition Law. It will attempt to argue that Google restrains competition within two separate markets: the distribution of apps to Android users, and the market for payment processing solutions for content inside Android apps.



---


# Apple Versus Google: A Contrast In Antitrust Conduct

Asked to compare the Apple and Google cases, Tim Sweeney summed up the difference as "Apple was ice and Google was fire" — arguing that Apple keeps all of its antitrust trickery internal to the company while Google had to go outside itself, and that the paper trail this produced is why the Google case played out differently.

His grounds are the mechanics of each scheme. Apple uses its own store and its own payments, and forces developers, OEMs and carriers to all have the same terms. Google, to achieve things with Android, went around paying off dozens of game developers not to compete and dozens of carriers and OEMs not to compete — and when many different companies do deals together, lots of people put things in writing, so it is right there for everybody to read. The warrant is evidentiary rather than moral: Sweeney said the Apple case would be no less interesting if Apple's internal thoughts and deliberations could be seen, but Apple was not putting it in writing whereas Google was, and he observed that because Google distributes Android as open source it had to put these deals more out in the open, even though it still wanted to keep them secret. He was careful not to let Apple off: he called Apple's restrictions on competition absolute — "thou shalt not have a competing store on iOS and thou shalt not use a competing payment method" — and said Apple should receive at least as harsh antitrust scrutiny as Google, adding that documents from both companies show them similarly self-serving in their deals.



---


# Google Play Billing And The User Choice Billing Alternative

Google Play's billing arrangement, as of November 2023, has two tiers. The baseline requires apps to use Google's own first-party billing system and charges app developers a 15% to 30% commission on the sales it processes. The alternative is User Choice Billing, a program still in pilot testing, open to all developers who sell apps in the 35 markets where it is then available, including the U.S., which reduces the standard commission by 4% for companies who choose to use their own payment processing solution. Spotify and Bumble were the initial testers for the new system, first introduced in November 2022, and Match, as part of its settlement agreement, will also now take advantage of this option. Epic has declined to use it.

Google's defense of the commission rests on what it says the commission buys. It will argue that its commissions are not just tied to payment processing, but help it develop other features and controls to keep Android users safe and guide them to discovering new applications, as well as helping fund the tools and services developers need to build and grow their apps. Google also helps developers reach a broader audience beyond the mobile phone, with support for Android across platforms ranging from tablets to TVs to autos and more. And it notes that 99% of its developers qualify for a commission of 15% or less, based on their revenues — so the headline 30% is the boundary case, not the typical one.

# The OpenAI Board Ousts Sam Altman, November 2023

As reported on November 18, 2023, the OpenAI board had ejected billionaire and AI evangelist Sam Altman from his CEO role after an apparent vote of no confidence. The board's exact wording in a release issued that afternoon: Altman's "departure follows a deliberative review process by the board, which concluded that he was not consistently candid in his communications with the board, hindering its ability to exercise its responsibilities."

What followed was a whirlwind four days for OpenAI, the generative AI poster child behind the smash hit ChatGPT. The board ousted CEO and co-founder Altman and demoted president and co-founder Greg Brockman, who subsequently resigned, paving the way for what looked like a mutiny by staff insisting the founders be reinstated post-haste. By the time TechCrunch wrote again on November 21, 2023, Microsoft had already hired Altman and Brockman to head up a new internal AI unit — though, as things transpired, nothing had actually been signed yet, with rumors suggesting the ousted leaders might actually return to OpenAI after all, in some capacity at least.

TechCrunch cautioned on November 18 that the full truth would not be known for a long time, as the characters in the drama are likely to be NDA'ed up. Per various whispers and leaks, an all-hands meeting about the situation that afternoon did not produce any revelations beyond banal reassurances that the company is fine and they will get a fresh CEO soon.



---


# Sam Altman's Next Move After The OpenAI Firing

In the days after his firing, Sam Altman's destination was genuinely unsettled: on November 20, 2023 he and Greg Brockman announced they would join Microsoft to lead a new AI research team, yet on the same day both were reported to be still open to returning to OpenAI, and Altman was separately telling investors he planned to launch a new venture.

On November 20 Altman, Brockman and colleagues announced they would join Microsoft to lead a new AI research team, with Satya Nadella leaving the door open to other OpenAI staffers and saying they would be given the resources they needed should they choose to join. As reported by The Verge, however, Altman's move to Microsoft was not a done deal — both Altman and Brockman remained open to returning to OpenAI if the remaining board members who initially fired him stepped aside. At the same time, according to The Information, Altman had been telling investors he was planning to launch a new venture, with Brockman expected to join the effort in whatever form it took — possibly an AI chip startup. Altman also posted on X on November 18: "i love you all. today was a weird experience in many ways. but one unexpected one is that it has been sorta like reading your own eulogy while you're still alive. the outpouring of love is awesome. one takeaway: go tell your friends how great you think they are."

Nadella himself hedged. In a series of interviews he stepped back from earlier reporting that Altman and Brockman were headed to Microsoft, telling CNBC: "Obviously, we want Sam and Greg to have a fantastic home if they're not going to be in OpenAI," and saying he was "open" to them settling at Microsoft or returning to OpenAI should the board and employees support the move.



---


# OpenAI Board Composition And The Helen Toner Dispute

At the time of Sam Altman's ouster in November 2023, OpenAI's board of directors consisted of OpenAI chief scientist Ilya Sutskever, Quora CEO Adam D'Angelo, tech entrepreneur Tasha McCauley, and Helen Toner, the director of strategy at Georgetown University's Center for Security and Emerging Technology — and a clash between Altman and Toner is reported to have contributed to the crisis.

The New York Times reported that, before his ousting, Altman made a move to push out board member Helen Toner because he thought a paper she had co-written was overly critical of OpenAI. That, among other issues, led to OpenAI's predicament. The Times also indicated that negotiations to hire Altman back were continuing, but that one major sticking point remaining was "guardrails" intended to improve Altman's communication with the board.



---


# Dismissed Theories: A Murati Coup And A Personal Matter

TechCrunch pushes back on two explanations circulating for Altman's removal. The first is that interim CEO Mira Murati engineered the ouster: probably not — she seems cool, and anyway what CTO wants to be CEO?

The second is that the trigger was personal or legal rather than professional. When someone is kicked out in a hurry, it is not uncommon that there was some kind of unprofessional behavior in the workplace; some CEOs get a pass on things like having kids with direct reports, but not all. Altman also has three siblings, and his younger sister Annie has publicly accused him of abuse — allegations TechCrunch says it has no way of evaluating, and which involve private matters.

The premise both theories rest on is that the board's action had a personal or legal cause. TechCrunch's read on the board's language in dismissing Altman is that it was not a legal or personal problem that provoked the action, but a professional or business one.



---


# Sam Altman's Career And Public Profile

Sam Altman has a long history steering OpenAI: he co-founded the company alongside Peter Thiel, LinkedIn co-founder Reid Hoffman and others, and initially served as a co-chair of OpenAI alongside Elon Musk, who left in 2018 to avoid a conflict of interest with Tesla.

Altman formerly headed the startup accelerator Y Combinator and also holds a seat on the board at Worldcoin, the ambitious cryptocurrency project. In the several months before his firing he played an active role in attempting to shape regulators' responses to AI, appearing at U.S. congressional hearings and meeting personally with world leaders including President Joe Biden, German Chancellor Olaf Scholz and French President Emmanuel Macron, among others, on an international policy tour.

His standing in the industry was reflected in the reaction to his ouster. Eric Schmidt posted on X: "Sam Altman is a hero of mine. He built a company from nothing to $90 Billion in value, and changed our collective world forever. I can't wait to see what he does next. I, and billions of people, will benefit from his future work- it's going to be simply incredible." His brother Jack Altman wrote: "More important than being one of the most brilliant and impactful people our industry has ever had Sam is one of the most generous and caring people I know. I've never met someone who has supported and lifted up more people around them than him. Couldn't be a prouder brother."



---


# Sam Altman Fired As OpenAI CEO In November 2023

Sam Altman was fired as CEO of OpenAI late on Friday, November 17, 2023, by the board of directors of OpenAI, Inc. — the 501(c)(3) nonprofit that acts as the governing body for OpenAI, the startup behind ChatGPT, GPT-4 and DALL-E 3. He both left the company's board of directors and stepped down as CEO, with chief technology officer Mira Murati stepping in as interim CEO.

OpenAI announced the shake-up in a post on its official blog; the company's management team was made aware shortly after. The blog post said Altman's departure followed a "deliberative review process by the board" which concluded that Altman "wasn't consistently candid in his communications" with other board members, "hindering its ability to exercise its responsibilities," and that the board "no longer has confidence in [Altman's] ability to continue leading OpenAI." In a joint statement the board wrote that "OpenAI was deliberately structured to advance our mission: to ensure that artificial general intelligence benefits all humanity," said it remained "fully committed to serving this mission," thanked Altman for "his many contributions to the founding and growth of OpenAI," and said that "we believe new leadership is necessary as we move forward" and that Mira, "as the leader of the company's research, product, and safety functions," was "exceptionally qualified" as interim CEO. OpenAI said it would begin a formal search for a permanent CEO immediately.

Altman responded on X: "i loved my time at openai. it was transformative for me personally, and hopefully the world a little bit. most of all i loved working with such talented people. will have more to say about what's next later." The removal came unexpectedly. OpenAI had just hosted its first developer conference, OpenAI DevDay, the week before with Altman emceeing; Altman had spoken at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation conference and at an Oakland, California event on the Thursday. According to The Verge and The New York Times, citing multiple internal sources, OpenAI employees learned of Altman's firing when it was announced publicly. The same change also saw co-founder Greg Brockman step down as chairman of the board while remaining OpenAI's president, reporting to Murati.

# Jordan Love As A Week 5 2023 Start Against The Raiders

CBS Sports listed Jordan Love under "Start Him" for Week 5 of the 2023 season against Las Vegas: the claim is that Love has upside to get back to the 25-plus fantasy points he posted in Weeks 1-3, and the warrant is that the Raiders' track record against quarterbacks plus the return of Green Bay's injured personnel restore the conditions under which Love produced.

The grounds are personnel and opponent behaviour. Aaron Jones and Christian Watson return without snap limits, and guard Elgton Jenkins is back too. The Raiders deserve credit for trying — over the previous two weeks they led the NFL in pass-rush pressure rate and ranked 10th in blitz rate — but playing the weaker offensive lines of Pittsburgh and the Los Angeles Chargers helped boost those numbers, and quarterbacks still found success at 13.9 yards per catch and 7.07 yards after catch per reception over those two games, both bottom-three in the league. Both quarterbacks Las Vegas faced in Weeks 3 and 4 posted at least 22 fantasy points: Kenny Pickett, and Justin Herbert without his second-best receiver and without his top running back. The column's hunch is that the Raiders will keep blitzing and play a lot of gutsy man coverage behind it, having leaned man in two of their past three games and moved to heavy zone only against Denver in Week 1.
