# Gio Reyna's Return Under Berhalter, And His 45 Minutes Against Germany

Gio Reyna was called into the USMNT for the first time under Gregg Berhalter since their falling out at the 2022 World Cup, having recovered from a leg fracture suffered in summer Nations League duty under an interim head coach. The 20-year-old Borussia Dortmund playmaker's return was announced alongside that of defender Cameron Carter-Vickers, who had only just made his Celtic debut that season after a hamstring injury.

The working relationship had been a major talking point since the 2022 fallout: Reyna's lack of playing time at that World Cup was exacerbated by his parents' actions in the following weeks, which sparked a domestic violence investigation of Berhalter before his eventual re-hire as national team head coach. Berhalter had been forthcoming, admitting on his re-hire that the two had a "lot of work to do" while insisting time was needed to broach the situation, and later confirming they had broken the ice by phone. After the October roster release he confirmed they had spoken "weeks ago" on Zoom, said he appreciated Reyna's willingness to move forward, and — because Reyna had not yet played for his club that season — set the goal of getting him minutes so he could build fitness and return to Dortmund in the best position to begin his club campaign. Berhalter said they saw Reyna able to play three positions: central midfielder, attacking midfielder and winger, clarifying that his skill set fit a "between the lines" style of wide play rather than one glued to the touchline.

In the Oct. 14 friendly against Germany, Reyna looked sharp in the starting lineup in all the ways a young man can: unyielding energy, a surprising eagerness to cover the whole of the midfield, periodic flashes of skill, and bleach-blond hair that let viewers spot him instantly. He was exceptional throughout the first half — less influential than he might have been with greater access to the ball, but showing a welcome taste for covering ground to help on defense or retrieve the ball and launch an attack — while Weston McKennie was his typical self, particularly connecting with Christian Pulisic down the left. Playing 45 minutes was a victory of sorts after only 27 minutes in his one club appearance that season for Dortmund, having been injured in June with the U.S. and missed all of preseason and nearly two months of the Bundesliga. The one substantial element missing was being able to endure from starting to finishing. "The goal is to send him back to Dortmund in a really good spot," Berhalter said. "I think he played a good game, showed his quality. I think everyone in the first half played well. So it was good to see him, good to have him on the field." Many national team fans had sided with Reyna during the World Cup controversy; in this game they got what they argued for, but not what they wished.



---


# Germany's Decline And The Appointment Of Julian Nagelsmann

Germany entered their October 2023 friendly against the United States in a transitional phase, with Julian Nagelsmann having taken over as new head coach after Hansi Flick was unable to steer the team to safer waters in Qatar.

Germany are considered one of the preeminent national team programs in the world, but recent years have humbled Die Mannschaft. They had been eliminated in the group stage of two straight World Cup tournaments — an unthinkable slip in stature given they had never been bounced from any World Cup that early in history prior to 2018.

The Sporting News set that decline alongside the United States' own position: with the U.S. set to test themselves against one of Europe's most powerful sides, the opponents were entering a transitional phase as well.



---


# Manchester United's Injury List Before The Fulham Match

Manchester United were yet to recover from their large number of long-term injuries ahead of the November 2023 Fulham fixture, and had been fighting a battle to line up their best XI as players fell victim to one injury after another. Casemiro, who got injured during the international break, got back on the field against Newcastle United in the EFL Cup match, but was taken off at half-time with a new hamstring issue and would probably remain sidelined for weeks.

Other than Casemiro, Tyrell Malacia and Amad Diallo were suffering from knee issues, Lisandro Martinez was nursing a foot injury, Jadon Sancho was out due to disciplinary issues, and Luke Shaw was yet to recover from a muscle problem. Adding to that, Victor Lindelof was suffering from a bug that could see him miss the weekend's match.

On the other hand, Raphael Varane, who missed the previous match due to an illness of his own, could be back. Aaron Wan-Bissaka was also able to participate in the last match, coming on as a substitute, so he should be able to make a comeback. Marcus Rashford, Rasmus Hojlund and Bruno Fernandes could all see themselves in the starting lineup.



---


# Man United Vs Fulham, 4 November 2023: The Fixture

Fulham hosted Manchester United on 4 November 2023 at 6:00 PM IST, in what was United's 11th Premier League match of the season. Manchester United travelled to Greater London for the fixture, with Fulham hoping to finally beat them for the first time since 2019.

It did not seem Fulham would get a better chance, considering Manchester United's horrible run of form. However, the Red Devils had come away as winners in both of their last games on the road, so the job would not be easy for Fulham.

qid: Does the article from Fortune suggest that Generation Z experiences distress primarily due to high employment rates, while the article from Eos: Earth And Space Science News calls for a deeper understanding of sea surface temperature patterns as a significant climate driver?
context:
# Open Questions on SST Patterns and Earth's Radiation Budget

The article argues that pressing, fundamental questions for climate dynamics concern how surface temperature patterns come about, how Earth's radiation budget depends on the details of those patterns, and the extent to which the two depend on each other.

Three tasks follow from that claim. First, understanding must improve of the drivers of sea surface temperature patterns — decadal coupled variability; the pace and spatial structure of ocean heat uptake; and forcing by aerosols, greenhouse gases, and volcanoes — as well as the relative timing of these drivers, with the goal of explaining historical patterns quantitatively and predicting their likely future evolution. Second, the dependence of local and remote top-of-the-atmosphere radiative fluxes on the magnitude, spatial scale, and sign (positive or negative) of surface temperature changes must be quantified. Third, it must be explained how ocean heat uptake and radiative feedback are connected on various timescales, both globally and regionally.



---


# Coupled Models Fail to Reproduce Observed Warming Patterns

Coupled climate models seem unable to simulate observed surface warming patterns across some key regions in which surface sensitivity modulates clouds: most importantly, models do not re-create observed cooling in the equatorial and subtropical eastern Pacific and Southern Ocean, and it is concerning that all models have the same sign of error in the trend patterns (Wills et al., 2022).

Coupled climate models simulate a freely evolving ocean surface and hence have their own expression of internal variability — one would not expect a coupled model to simulate El Niño events at the same time as they happened in nature, except by chance — which complicates comparisons between models and observations, especially on decadal timescales and beyond, for which little is known about the spectrum of internal variability in the real world. Even accounting for internal variability, the pattern failure persists, and models strongly disagree about the timescales over which future warming may occur in these regions. Limited knowledge of the drivers of surface warming pattern biases hampers the ability to evaluate them: it is not known whether the models' inability to reproduce observed trends is due to biases in how they represent the spectrum of internal variability, aerosol forcing, ocean-atmosphere interactions, deep and shallow atmospheric convection, Southern Ocean cloud-radiative properties, ocean thermocline depth, and ocean circulation, or something else entirely.



---


# Emerging Tools for Quantifying the Pattern Effect

Promising new tools and observations are beginning to emerge for quantifying the pattern effect: targeted model experiments and intercomparisons, extended global satellite observations of clouds and radiation, Argo floats sampling deep-ocean heat uptake, estimates of radiative imbalances before the year 2000, and new observational constraints on clouds' sensitivity to environmental controlling factors.

These developments encourage an optimistic outlook on the ability to quantify the pattern effect and its implications over the next couple of years. Working to solve these problems at the intersection of different disciplines and with input from different research communities will likely benefit related research into, for example, the sensitivity of tropical cyclones and future rainfall changes in the southwestern United States or in South America to surface warming patterns.



---


# Gen Z Mental Health And Climate Anxiety

Gen Z has the worst reported mental health of any generation: 45% of young people report having "excellent" or "very good" mental health, according to a 2018 report by the American Psychological Association. One of the major sources of that distress is climate change — nearly seven in 10 Gen Zers say they experience anxiety when viewing climate change content on social media, according to a 2021 Pew Research report.

They are not only reading about the effects of human-caused global warming but living through the consequences. The summer of 2023 reached record-breaking temperatures, with July the hottest month the planet has seen in over 100,000 years; Arizona experienced a monthlong heat wave with temperatures at or above 110 degrees every day; deadly fires broke out across the Mediterranean; suffocating smoke from Canadian wildfires blanketed New York City and the Northeast for days; and ice melt in the Arctic accelerated. Extreme heat is likely here to stay — and get worse — unless countries can rapidly reduce their carbon emissions, which is why Gen Z is more concerned with sustainability than any generation before them.

Greta Thunberg is the emblem the article offers: the 20-year-old has become one of the best-known environmental activists, famously speaking at the United Nations in 2019 with scathing words for world leaders. "You have stolen my dreams and my childhood with your empty words. And yet I'm one of the lucky ones," Thunberg said. "People are suffering. People are dying. Entire ecosystems are collapsing. We are in the beginning of a mass extinction, and all you can talk about is money and fairy tales of eternal economic growth. How dare you!"



---


# Gen Z News Distress Impairing Work Performance

Forty-six percent of young workers ages 18 to 26 say that they are regularly so distraught over what is happening in the news that they are unable to function at work, according to a 2023 Edelman report. The generational gradient is steep: by comparison, 38% of millennials, 24% of Gen Xers, and 19% of baby boomers and older generations say the same.

The article reads this as of a piece with the rest of the cohort's behavior — everything about their behavior communicates that Gen Z is just not okay with it, ranging from their widespread, hell-bent determination to find purpose in work and pushing their employers to have a social conscience, to a sense of despair over their own and the world's future finances. They have largely given up on saving money and instead dish out for little "treats" as a way to cope with the larger absurdity of 21st-century life.



---


# The US CLIVAR Pattern Effect Workshop, 2022

To foster work on the pattern effect across research communities, 140 scientists from around the world and from different disciplines gathered for a US CLIVAR (U.S. Climate Variability and Predictability Program) workshop in May 2022 in Boulder, Colorado.

The Eos article presents the current consensus that emerged during that workshop and raises questions that its authors say require urgent attention from scientists.



---


# "No Place Is Safe": Climate Impacts on Kalmus's Life

Kalmus concluded that "no place was safe" after a 2020 heat wave — considered nearly impossible if not for the influence of climate change — seared the Pacific Northwest for three days, killing hundreds of people, buckling roadways and sending overheated baby birds jumping from their nests to their deaths, in the very region where he had dreamed of making a life he thought might be buffered from the worst of climate change.

"It feels like it's worse than I thought it would be in 2023," Kalmus said, pointing to record-low Antarctic sea ice and record-high sea surface and land temperatures as signs that Earth systems could be shifting more quickly than the scientific community can grasp. In recent years climate change has begun to sting his personal life: in summer 2020 he sickened himself hiking in a California heat wave, then watched a wildfire burn a few miles from his California home, spewing smoke that left his voice raspy and his head aching, while the searing temperatures killed a dogwood tree in his front yard and his productivity slowed so that he could not focus on science. His family relocated to North Carolina for his wife Sharon's work, but the Pacific Northwest experience planted a seed: if he could not stop climate change and could not avoid it, could he at least find a better way to survive it? He knew what would not work — "I very quickly eliminated the idea of being a prepper — you know, hoarding beans and ammunition," he said — but he found himself daydreaming of a simpler life where he could keep bees, grow vegetables and press cider to drink on a Friday night, living closer to the land.



---


# Why Communicating Deep-Sea Science Matters

Jon Copley argues that communicating deep sea science matters because the deep sea is not somewhere people think about every day: we can go out at night and look at the sky and wonder what is going on up there, but you cannot glance into the deep sea in the same way, so it has become a realm of myth and darkness.

Even the names of the deepest parts — the abyssal plains and the hadal zone — evoke that kind of underworld, he says. The conclusion he draws is that it is nice to be able to shine a light on that for people and to highlight how our lives are connected to it.



---


# Gen Z Workplace Purpose And ESG Priorities

By 2030 Gen Z will account for nearly one-third of the U.S. workforce, but they are already radically redefining the meaning of work. Wanting a sense of purpose, they prioritize environmental, social, and governance (ESG) considerations in the workplace — which for them encompasses their companies taking accountability for their sustainability and environmental impacts, providing education and awareness for social issues, and ensuring diverse and inclusive boards and teams.

The behavioral evidence matches the stated priority: roughly two-thirds of Gen Zers say they frequently speak about important societal issues while at work, according to the Edelman report. They are also influencing their older coworkers when it comes to areas like work-life balance, fair pay, and employers' involvement on social issues.

qid: Does 'The New York Times' article attribute the failure of the Buffalo Bills' defense to the contributions of Jordan Poyer, while the 'Sporting News' article suggests that the Baltimore Ravens' defense needs to improve before their game against the Cincinnati Bengals?
context:
# The Baltimore Ravens' Pass-Oriented Offense Shift

The New York Times questioned on 16 October 2023 whether Baltimore's shift toward a more conventional pass offense will make the Ravens tougher to defend, noting they have never scored fewer points or amassed less offensive EPA through the first six games of a season with Lamar Jackson in the lineup.

The grounds are Jackson's changed rushing profile. He has one rush longer than 20 yards, where he had four or five by that point in previous seasons, and he is gaining at least eight yards on 15 percent of carries, half his previous rate. The schedule and injuries have played roles in the scoring decline, but the open question is whether the explosive quarterback runs are mostly in the past — and the writer is not expecting a consistent precision passing game to suddenly materialise.

An executive pressed the argument further, holding that the change subtracts more than it adds: "The defense keeps them in it, but I don't necessarily think this offensive change is going to make them any better when it counts. Lamar Jackson does not appear as dynamic as a runner, but in this offense, he does not need to be. He is regulated to pass from the pocket, but you are taking away the biggest weapon the offense had when you do that. Odell (Beckham) is not that guy anymore. Who are you truly afraid of on that offense? Nobody but Lamar, and if you are not using Lamar in a certain capacity, he becomes just like the rest of these quarterbacks around the league — hit or miss."



---


# Buffalo Bills Defensive Injuries And The 2023 Outlook

The New York Times argued on 16 October 2023 that this can still be Buffalo's season despite defensive injuries, because the rest of the AFC is the key variable and no other team has taken the conference over.

The grounds are comparative rather than absolute. The Bills are diminished and have imperfections, but Buffalo had already defeated the Dolphins, and the other AFC teams aren't exactly peaking: Kansas City and Cincinnati appear easier to defend that season than in the recent past, and it remains to be seen how well the Dolphins hold up. The warrant is that a contender only needs to be better than the available competition, not to match its own earlier form.

An executive agreed on both halves of the point: "Matt Milano and Tre'Davious White, those are huge injuries for that football team. The Bills are not as dominant as they felt going into it with so many injuries on defense. But the division they are in, they will still be able to slug it out and get to where they need to go. Nobody has really emerged in the AFC to unseat these teams at the top."



---


# The Detroit Lions' Defensive Improvement, 2023

The New York Times argued on 16 October 2023 that the Lions' defensive improvement is real but not yet testable: Detroit is 11.3 EPA per game better on defense than the previous season, the second-largest gain for any team, yet the true measure will have to wait for the postseason.

The qualifications are built into the grounds. The schedule has something to do with the gain, and the 2022 defense was so bad that it couldn't stop Carolina, so the baseline was low. Looking forward, the remaining schedule features so many weak offenses — including Chicago twice, Green Bay, Denver and Las Vegas — that the improvement cannot be properly assessed before January. The writer nonetheless expects Detroit to win the NFC North and return to the playoffs, which will make the season successful no matter what happens from there.

An executive endorsed the team on the grounds of self-knowledge rather than personnel: "Yes, I do buy them. This is a league full of teams who do not really know who they are week to week. Detroit knows who they are, and they play to their identity. Anytime you know who you are and play to that style, you have a chance to be dangerous."



---


# The Dallas Cowboys' 2023 Contender Credentials

The New York Times argued on 16 October 2023 that it does not see where Dallas is better or going to get considerably better, especially on offense, though it conceded this was a tough time to evaluate the Cowboys fairly because they were so bad against San Francisco on a big stage in their most recent game.

The additional ground offered is cultural rather than statistical: every time the Cowboys enjoy success, they seem to enjoy it a little too much, which the writer treats as a reflection of their owner.

An executive located the problem in identity and consistency: "Run defense and consistency on defense, and then offensively, what is their identity? They just are not very good. Their best games are when they play great defense and get turnovers, but that is not going to happen enough, especially against the good teams." The warrant on both sides is that a contender needs a repeatable formula, and Dallas's best path — great defense plus turnovers — is not repeatable often enough against strong opposition.



---


# Jordan Poyer's Versatile Safety Role With The Buffalo Bills

The Buffalo Bills have what The New York Times described on 15 December 2023 as a new safety: Jordan Poyer, the same player who had been with the team the previous six seasons, but changed by ayahuasca and deployed in a far wider range of roles.

He sometimes plays close to the line of scrimmage, even lining up in the gaps and banging helmets with interior linemen. The Bills use him as a hybrid linebacker in a three-safety dime package, and he has played free safety, strong safety, outside cornerback, inside cornerback, left linebacker and right linebacker — and more. Physically and mentally he is being challenged, but he is grateful, content and all in.

His record establishes the standing behind the role: he is the only player in the NFL to have 500 or more tackles, 20 or more interceptions and 10 or more sacks over that six-season time frame, a Bills captain for the fourth time, an Ed Block Courage Award winner in 2017, a Pro Bowl safety the previous year and an All-Pro the year before that.



---


# Cincinnati Bengals: Joe Burrow's Durability And The Line

The New York Times argued on 16 October 2023 that Joe Burrow is looking healthier over the past two weeks, but worried he will wear down against the defenses on Cincinnati's remaining schedule.

The grounds are the calendar. The bye week comes at a great time for Burrow to get even healthier, but on the other side of it are San Francisco, Buffalo, Houston, Baltimore, Pittsburgh and Jacksonville, and Cincy still has a second game with the Steelers plus games against Kansas City and Cleveland. The warrant is that a quarterback recovering from injury faces cumulative rather than one-off risk across a run of strong defenses.

An executive located the underlying problem in protection rather than health: "You cannot always expect Joe Burrow to create magic with a bottom-half offensive line. The line is my concern all the way."



---


# Jordan Poyer's Football Performance After Ayahuasca

Jordan Poyer hoped ayahuasca would elevate his football performances as Aaron Rodgers believes it did his, but it hasn't worked that way for him, The New York Times reported on 15 December 2023: he is the Bills' second-leading tackler but hasn't made as many big plays as he would like for a defense plagued by injuries.

The immediate physical aftermath was weight loss. Two days before OTAs began last April, Poyer returned to the Bills' headquarters and stepped on the scale, and the needle settled at 179 pounds, about 20 pounds below his playing weight; after resuming his regular routine, the weight came back quickly. He discussed his experience with curious teammates, coaches and the team psychologist.

What he has done, according to former Bills defensive coordinator Les Frazier, now an analyst for NFL Network, is enable his defense to be the best it can by lifting others through versatility, sacrifice, toughness and communication — Poyer wears his "C" well. Poyer's own assessment, given during the Bills' bye week on the patio of his Florida home: "I feel like I'm playing OK this year. I'm not playing the best that I've played in my career. There are probably two plays I really want back. But I'm doing a lot. And in a very deep sense, I absolutely love that I'm entrusted with doing as much as I'm doing on this defense."



---


# Anthony Richardson's Season-Ending Shoulder Surgery

News that Indianapolis Colts rookie quarterback Anthony Richardson might undergo season-ending shoulder surgery could carry a silver lining, The New York Times reported on 16 October 2023.

The reasoning is that Richardson got to play enough for the Colts to evaluate where he stands, so if he shuts it down for the season, neither he nor the team would have to suffer through a full season of growing pains.

The counter-evidence is Gardner Minshew's three-pick game against Jacksonville that Sunday, which works against the idea that Indy is better positioned to compete with the journeyman in the lineup — though most coaches and execs the writer had spoken with believed that to be the case in the short term.

qid: Which football club, discussed on both TalkSport and Sporting News, has both set an unwanted record by conceding 14 goals in the Champions League group stages and has been eliminated from European competitions following a defeat at their home ground, known as Old Trafford?
context:
# Manchester United's European Decline Since Ferguson

The Independent argued on 12 December 2023 that Manchester United's 1-0 defeat to Bayern Munich should have been a landmark low but instead felt grimly routine, because group-stage elimination has become the club's normal European outcome in the post-Ferguson era rather than an aberration.

The grounds are frequency and pattern. Manchester United, one of the grandest and richest names in this competition, have again gone out of the Champions League at the group stage; it is the third time it has happened since Sir Alex Ferguson, meaning it is their most common round of exit in that period. The night is presented as one more entry in a decade of disappointment in a competition in which this club rose to its most emotional heights — a low, but just part of that longer run.

The warrant is the gap between the occasion and the performance. These are not the sounds we are used to hearing after that Champions League theme; something does stir when the anthem is played at Old Trafford amid the lights — well, for most, that is, except the players. United should not be performing like this on what is supposed to be the classic European night at Old Trafford, and the display was a reminder that all they are going to have for some time are their memories. Having been involved in so many ludicrously chaotic matches, the biggest of all ended up being a non-event: this game never threatened to stir anything, and United never threatened at all. That, the argument runs, can now be talked about definitively, since it has been decisively ended.



---


# Manchester United's 2023/24 Champions League Elimination

Manchester United were out of Europe altogether after a limp display against Bayern at Old Trafford, where Kingsley Coman sealed a 1-0 win for Thomas Tuchel's side on the final day of Champions League group-stage play, per Sporting News on Dec. 12 and Dec. 13, 2023.

The Red Devils finished bottom of their four-team group, leaving them eliminated from Europe in their worst performance in the competition since 2005. On top of that, they set the record for most goals against in a Champions League group stage by an English club, with 15 conceded in their six games.

Their defensive record had collapsed as the season went on: from a Premier League standpoint they sat eighth in the English top flight, but their -5 goal differential was the worst of any club in the top 10.



---


# Manchester United's 2023-24 Champions League Group-Stage Record

Manchester United finished bottom of their 2023-24 Champions League group with four points, in fourth place, eliminated from European competition altogether rather than dropping into the Europa League, The Independent reported on 12 December 2023.

The decisive results came from outside the Bayern fixture. It was not Bayern who eliminated them: it was Galatasaray, who won at Old Trafford and scored six goals over 180 minutes against United, and FC Copenhagen, who qualified instead of them — Rasmus Hojlund's former club will be in the last 16 while his current one will not, making Copenhagen the anomalies in the draw, the outsiders with the spot that had seemed reserved for United. The second place United aimed for went instead to Copenhagen, a club with a fraction of United's budget, and that is where the damage was done. On the final night the Danish side's victory over Galatasaray ensured any United win would be irrelevant, leaving only a slim hope beforehand.

The campaign produced records of the wrong kind. When Coman scored, United became the first Premier League side to concede 15 goals in a Champions League group stage. United won a lone game in the competition, and even that required a penalty save to deny FC Copenhagen a draw. Two months earlier Raphael Varane had said United could win the Champions League; the quadruple Champions League winner may need a rethink. There was no hint of a repeat of their most famous comeback against Bayern, nor even the sense of heroic failure that accompanied their 2010 quarter-final exit to the same club — just crushing failure. When Maguire hobbled off holding his groin and Evans came on, United had a man who played in their 2007-08 Champions League-winning campaign dragooned into service 16 years later.



---


# Manchester United's Defensive Imbalance: Ferdinand's Critique

Rio Ferdinand argued that Manchester United's European problems stem from a lack of balance in the team — they can score at will but make defensive mistakes that undo the game plan — and that the fix has to be applied over a period of games, not one or two, talkSPORT reported on 29 November 2023.

The grounds are the numbers and the pattern of the concessions. Eight points have been dropped from winning positions, and no other team has suffered a worse fate that term. United had conceded 14 goals in the Champions League group stages, a new and unwanted record for the club that could get worse when they faced Bayern in the final match, while their 12 goals scored was the fifth-highest tally of any club — so the downfall was defensive. "I think they've got to look at themselves," said Ferdinand, a 2007/08 Champions League winner with United. "You can't go into a Champions League campaign and score nine goals in three away games and have one point at the end of it. I think that shows you that there's a lack of balance in the team at the moment. Yes they can get goals and yes they are attacking at will and creating chances, many of them coming through Bruno. But I think defensively, they just made mistakes, I think the goalkeeper today has to hold his hands up and say, 'Yep, I was at fault for a couple of goals. He should do better."

The warrant is that the tactical work was sound and the errors, not the plan, cost the points — and that repeated collapses leave a psychological residue. "I think the manager will be scratching his head and thinking, 'The game plan first-half worked perfectly,' and then all of a sudden they score a goal, it changes the dynamic of the game. They were 2-0 up, 2-1, and you're thinking, 'Wow, I set the team up perfectly well, they execute it but then a mistake cost us,' and at 3-1, the same again. So I think there's a lot of question marks in the performances and the way they're going about things at the moment but balance for me is one of the key aspects that they've got to really find." He continued: "We mentioned in commentary, scars from throwing away leads, those are hard to get away, you've got to really manage games and he mentioned that himself Bruno, you've got to go out managing games correctly. They've got to do that not over one or two or three games, they've got to do that over a period of games now so they can erase those scars that they've created and they'e grown through bad results and throwing away leads, especially in Europe."



---


# Preview Of Chelsea's December 2023 Visit To Old Trafford

Manchester United would love a repeat of the previous season's 4-1 home win over Chelsea when the Blues visited Old Trafford that Wednesday, per Sporting News on Dec. 5, 2023.

The pressure on United had grown again following their lacklustre 1-0 defeat at Newcastle on the Saturday, and another setback against a Chelsea side — who beat Brighton & Hove Albion 3-2 the following day — would worsen the misery around Old Trafford.

Sporting News framed the meeting as one between two heavyweights of world football: United and Chelsea are two of only seven teams to have won the modern Premier League, and are only behind Liverpool when it comes to English success with European trophies. Chelsea's recent record against United was poor, but they had won the Premier League twice since United last did so in the 2012/13 season and could exploit the poor form of Ten Hag's side. The article set out to look at a rivalry that stretches back decades and had been sharply in focus over recent years.



---


# Manchester United Recent Champions League Failures

Thirty years on from Istanbul, United headed to Turkey knowing they had rarely been convincing in the Champions League in recent years, The Guardian reported on Nov. 27, 2023: a 3-1 away win against Paris Saint-Germain in the 2018-19 round of 16, after losing the home leg 2-0, was the last time they won a crunch match.

In 2020-21 they lost their final two group games and were eliminated, while back in 2015-16 Wolfsburg won the deciding group match to knock them out. United had done little learning in recent times, repeating the same failures in Europe's elite competition. It would not be a disgrace to lose against a good Galatasaray team, especially given Erik ten Hag was missing key players, but if the worst happened, everyone would need to come out of the experience stronger — regardless of the result, it should be a night of education about the demands of the Champions League.



---


# Everton Case Implications For Manchester City And Chelsea

Sean Dyche declined to comment on the implications of Everton's punishment for Manchester City and Chelsea, The Guardian reported on Nov. 24, 2023.

Manchester City had been charged with 115 financial breaches by the Premier League and deny any wrongdoing; Chelsea were also under investigation by the football authorities.

qid: Considering the information provided by TechCrunch regarding Meta's alleged GDPR non-compliance, its proposal to shift teen app oversight to parents, the accusation of neglecting children's online privacy, and the reported suppression of Palestinian voices, which company is implicated in multiple controversies related to user privacy, content moderation, and the responsibility of safeguarding young users' online activities?
context:
# Critique Of Meta's App Store Parental Approval Proposal

The critique attacks the premise that moving approval to the app stores is a protection measure at all rather than a reallocation of blame. Meta's proposed "better way" of requiring parents to manage a teen's app downloads pushes the burden back to the app stores and to parents, who often today do not monitor or manage their teens' smartphone use.

TechCrunch grants the factual half of Meta's warrant and rejects the inference: while it is true that the app stores and smartphone makers would know the ages of their users, requiring parents to approve apps is the equivalent of overriding parental discretion and choice. Other entertainment ratings — like those for TV, movies or video games — are meant to be guidelines for parents, not laws, so Meta's position that apps are somehow different is a fairly extreme position to take.

Sacha Haworth, executive director of the Tech Oversight Project, a nonprofit devoted to reigning in Big Tech, attacked the proposal's motive: "Instead of designing its products with kids' safety and privacy in mind, Meta would rather push blame onto parents and other companies to obscure the damage they've already done to young people. No one disputes that Google and Apple need to do more to protect children on their platforms, apps and devices. That fact does not absolve Mark Zuckerberg or Meta for years of willful negligence, and this announcement shows that the company's outright hostility toward protecting kids is sewn into the fabric of its profit model." Apple and Google did not return requests for comment.



---


# The 42-State Lawsuit Against Meta Over Harms To Young Users

A coalition of 42 states and D.C. is suing Meta over its harms to teens and young users, in part referencing findings from Meta whistleblower Frances Haugen. The former employee had provided to news outlets a treasure trove of documents that appeared to indicate Meta understood the harms it was causing — including things like body image issues among teens — but did not take action. Instagram head Adam Mosseri was later hauled before Congress in December 2021 to defend the app's teen safety record, but as of November 15, 2023 legislators had not come to any decision about how to regulate teen usage of these platforms.

The suit was filed in October 2023, and a newly unredacted version reported on November 27, 2023 alleges a troubling pattern of deception and minimization in how the company handles kids under 13 on its platforms, with internal documents that appear to show the company's approach to this ostensibly forbidden demographic is far more laissez-faire than it has publicly claimed. The lawsuit alleges a wide spread of damaging practices at the company relating to the health and well-being of younger people using it: from body image to bullying, privacy invasion to engagement maximization, all the purported evils of social media are laid at Meta's door — perhaps rightly, TechCrunch notes, but it also gives the appearance of a lack of focus.

In one respect at least the documentation obtained by the attorneys general of 42 states is quite specific, "and it is damning," as AG Rob Bonta of California put it. That is in paragraphs 642 through 835, which mostly document violations of the Children's Online Privacy Protection Act, or COPPA — a law that created very specific restrictions around young folks online, limiting data collection and requiring things like parental consent for various actions, but which a lot of tech companies seem to consider more suggestion than requirement.



---


# Meta Researchers Avoided Documenting Under-13 Users

A potential smoking gun in the lawsuit is a series of anecdotes from Meta researchers delicately avoiding the possibility of inadvertently confirming an under-13 cohort in their work.

One wrote in 2018: "We just want to make sure to be sensitive about a couple of Instagram-specific items. For example, will the survey go to under 13 year olds? Since everyone needs to be at least 13 years old before they create an account, we want to be careful about sharing findings that come back and point to under 13 year olds being bullied on the platform." In 2021, another, studying "child-adult sexual-related content/behavior/interactions," said she was "not includ[ing] younger kids (10-12 yos) in this research" even though there "are definitely kids this age on IG," because she was "concerned about risks of disclosure since they aren't supposed to be on IG at all." Also in 2021, Meta instructed a third-party research company conducting a survey of preteens to remove any information indicating a survey subject was on Instagram, so the "company won't be made aware of under 13." Later that year, external researchers provided Meta with information that "of children ages 9-12, 45% used Facebook and 40% used Instagram daily."

During an internal 2021 study on youth in social media described in the suit, researchers first asked parents if their kids were on Meta platforms and removed them from the study if so. But one researcher asked, "What happens to kids who slip through the screener and then say they are on IG during the interviews?" Instagram Head of Public Policy Karina Newton responded, "we're not collecting user names right?" — in other words, TechCrunch notes, what happens is nothing. As the lawsuit puts it: "Even when Meta learns of specific children on Instagram through interviews with the children, Meta takes the position that it still lacks actual knowledge of that it is collecting personal information from an under-13 user because it does not collect user names while conducting these interviews. In this way, Meta goes through great lengths to avoid meaningfully complying with COPPA, looking for loopholes to excuse its knowledge of users under the age of 13 and maintain their presence on the Platform."



---


# Meta Moderation Bias

TechCrunch's claim, published 19 October 2023, is that Meta has a moderation bias problem rather than a "bug": the suppression of Palestinian voices is the latest in a lengthy history of incidents on Meta platforms that reflect an inherent bias against Palestinian users in its processes, documented by years of complaints from both inside and outside the company. The argument's careful qualifier is that intent is not asserted — the company may not intentionally suppress specific communities, but its moderation practices often disproportionately affect Palestinian users.

The first ground is Meta's own commissioned evidence. During the last violent outbreak between Hamas and Israel in 2021, a report commissioned by Meta and conducted by a third party concluded that the company's actions had an "adverse human rights impact" on Palestinian users' right to freedom of expression and political participation.

The second ground is the pattern of disproportionate scrutiny during that outbreak. Amid the violence following the May 2021 court ruling to evict Palestinian families from Sheikh Jarrah, a neighborhood in occupied East Jerusalem, users across Facebook and Instagram accused Meta of taking down posts and suspending accounts that voiced support for Palestinians. The digital rights nonprofit Electronic Frontier Foundation described Meta's actions in 2021 as "systemic censorship of Palestinian voices," and in its 2022 report on Palestinian digital rights, 7amleh said Meta is "still the most restricting company" compared with other social media giants in the extent of its moderation of the Palestinian digital space.

The third ground is internal. That same month, a group of Facebook employees filed internal complaints accusing the company of bias against Arab and Muslim users; in internal posts obtained by BuzzFeed News, an employee attributed the bias to "years and years of implementing policies that just don't scale globally."

The fourth ground is the measured asymmetry between languages. At the recommendation of its Oversight Board, Meta conducted a third-party due diligence report about the platform's moderation during the May 2021 conflict. The report found that Arabic content was flagged as potentially violating at significantly higher rates than Hebrew content was, and was more likely to be erroneously removed. It noted that Meta's moderation system may not be as precise for Arabic content as for Hebrew, because the latter is a "more standardized language," and suggested that reviewers may lack the linguistic and cultural competence to understand less common Arabic dialects like Palestinian Arabic.

The warrant joining grounds to claim is duration and convergence. Because the disparity is recurrent across separate escalations, is corroborated from inside the company as well as by outside nonprofits and by Meta's own commissioned reviewers, and is traceable to standing properties of the moderation system rather than to a one-off failure, it is better described as bias inherent in the processes than as an isolated technical error.



---


# Meta's Under-13 Policy Versus Its Internal Growth Goals

An internal presentation called "2017 Teens Strategic Focus" appears to specifically target kids under 13, noting that children use tablets as early as 3 or 4, and that "Social identity is an Unmet need Ages 5-11." One stated goal, according to the lawsuit, was specifically to "grow [Monthly Active People], [Daily Active People] and time spent among U13 kids" — a growth objective aimed at the age group Meta's own account rules exclude.

TechCrunch flags an important boundary on what this does and does not show. While Meta does not permit accounts to be run by people under 13, there are plenty of ways it can lawfully and safely engage with that demographic: some kids just want to watch videos from SpongeBob Official, and that is fine. What the law requires is that Meta must verify parental consent, and the ways it can collect and use their data are limited. So targeting under-13s as an audience is not by itself unlawful; the legal question is consent and data use.

qid: Do the articles from The Verge and TechCrunch both suggest that interactive activities, such as dressing up for parents of children interested in Pokémon and conversing with Alexa, are methods to engage with children, or do they propose different engagement strategies?
context:
# Explore With Alexa

"Explore with Alexa" is a feature on Amazon's Echo devices that lets kids have interactive conversations with an AI-powered Alexa. It was first announced in September and, as reported by TechCrunch on 25 October 2023, launched as an addition to the Amazon Kids+ content subscription, allowing children to have kid-friendly conversations with Alexa, powered by generative AI, but in a protected fashion designed to ensure the experience remains safe and appropriate.

The discriminating feature is the combination of generative AI, conversation, and an audience of children under 13. Some AI experiences already cater to younger users — the AI chatbots from Character.ai and other companies, including Meta — but Amazon is among the first to specifically look to generative AI to develop a conversational experience for kids under the age of 13. The two qualifiers that bound the concept are the subscription it lives inside (Amazon Kids+) and the protective framing: this is not an unbounded chatbot but a conversational experience deliberately constructed to stay safe and age-appropriate.



---


# Pokémon As A Lifestyle: The Reinvention Thesis

The claim is that Pokémon is no longer a series for children but a franchise that promises something for everyone, and that this reinvention is what has kept it growing.

The grounds are commercial and cultural at once. In recent years The Pokémon Company has recorded record profits and revenue, while the games, anime, and TCG are more popular than ever, with both new mainline Switch entries selling over 20 million copies. The phenomenon of growing out of Pokémon is no longer a concern: even if young kids stop playing the video games as they grow, that does not mean they will not still engage with this world via other means, nor that they will not introduce their own children to the series in the future.

The warrant is that PokéTsume is only possible because of that reinvention, and so serves as its proof. In reality it is a mostly light, inoffensive promotional tool to sell games — it is no coincidence the second episode has a scene of a young kid playing the latest entries on his Nintendo Switch — but it represents everything the franchise has aimed to be in recent years. New adults seeking direction in life might find a fellow directionless 20-something employee more relatable than a kid wanting to be a Pokémon Champion; frankly, it is a way to see they are not alone, no different from how your party of pokémon kept you company through the deepest caverns of Mt. Moon.



---


# The Two-Way Interaction Design Of Explore With Alexa

The interaction model behind "Explore with Alexa" runs in both directions: unlike more traditional conversations with Alexa, it is not just kids asking Alexa a question and receiving a response — Alexa is now asking kids questions too. As Venkataswamy put it, "One of the things we think is really cool about this paradigm is kids aren't just asking Alexa questions and getting the answers — Alexa is now asking kids questions," giving as an example a trivia question like "What's the fastest animal on Earth?"

Kids reach the experience through three paths. The first is an explicit trigger: uttering a particular phrase that kicks off "Explore with Alexa," such as "Alexa, let's explore animals" or "Alexa, tell me an animal fact." The second, described as the more interesting way to use the feature, is organic conversation — a kid asking something like "What does a lion's roar sound like?" or "How fast can a cheetah run?" also drops them into the more conversational Q&A experience. The third path is Alexa-initiated: over the few months following the launch, Alexa will also prompt kids on some occasions, asking if they want to hear something interesting about animals.

The warrant for making Alexa the questioner is pedagogical rather than technical: as any teacher will tell you, by having kids try to think of the answer first, the answer will stick in their minds better when they hear the response. Underneath, the AI's job is content transformation at scale — "What our AI is doing is taking trusted content and then figuring out what's fun, looking at what's fun, turning them into a trivia question — so it is doing useful things for us at scale that we wouldn't have been able to do without this tooling…but we feel really good about the safety guardrails that are in place right now in terms of content," says Venkataswamy.

The model holds over a deliberately narrow range as of this description. "Right now it's, it's narrow. Alexa is asking kids trivia questions," Venkataswamy continues. "But we want to continue expanding on that and making it more interactive." Two-way interaction, in other words, currently means trivia prompts and nothing wider, with expansion stated as an intent rather than a shipped capability.



---


# Digital Engagement Protects The Ageing Brain

The Guardian's 10 October 2023 piece sets out a model in which grappling with technology — not being rescued from it — protects the ageing brain, because novel and difficult tasks force the brain to work in new ways.

The structure has three linked parts. First, the difficulty itself is the active ingredient: a recent study from the University of Texas involving more than 200 elderly adults found that those who engaged with technology had better cognition and memory than their non-engaging peers, and the study authors concluded that digital engagement — whatever the device — protects the brain; even the stress experienced while battling with a computer can be helpful, sharpening mental acuity. These findings reflect earlier studies that found older people who made active use of technology were less likely to get dementia. The implication is that the well-meaning helpfulness of children who "delight in parenting" their parents on all things digital "might not be as beneficial as we think".

Second, novelty generalises beyond devices. Dr Eamon Laird, researcher in health and ageing at Limerick university, agrees that older parents should be encouraged to try new things, and the further out of their comfort zone they feel, the better: "It's always good to keep the mind active and fresh. New challenges can help build and maintain new brain connections and can be good for brain and overall health." Third, sociability compounds the effect: if older people use technology to keep in touch with extended family and friends, "that's a double whammy" — when the author's 84-year-old mother recently joined Instagram she both expanded her grey matter and found an effective means of staying in touch with her grandchildren. Being social, says Laird, is as important as trying new things: "Research shows that those who are more social are also more resilient to chronic conditions and often have a stronger immune system."



---


# Kelley Coleman on Child-Centred Disability Disclosure

Kelley Coleman — Los Angeles-based author of the upcoming book "Everything No One Tells You About Parenting a Disabled Child", and the mother of an autistic son — argues that Halloween should "always be about your child", and that the decision to use a blue bucket must be made with the child rather than for the benefit of onlookers.

Her grounds are the three considerations she asks parents to weigh: safety, comfort and privacy. "Especially for children trick-or-treating without parents directly at their side — is it the safest option to have your child carrying a bright indicator of their disability?" she asked. "For children who prefer privacy, would they want that information broadcasted? For children who prefer to share their neurodivergence, perhaps this is something they are proud to display." The conversation should be between child and parent, Coleman stressed, regardless of communication level, and should "center their experience and preferences."

She grants that the bucket does educational work, but subordinates it: "The blue bucket can be a teaching tool for others; however, it should never be about others — it should always be about your child." The warrant is that the burden of educating the public should not fall on the family: "In an ideal world, all adults would understand that not everyone communicates the same way, and that one's ability to communicate does not indicate one's interest in candy," she said. "But, the reality is that not all adults know this. It's exhausting teaching others to be inclusive. So, yes, the blue bucket can be a teaching tool for others; however, it should never be about others — it should always be about your child."



---


# The Social And Developmental Costs Of Heavy Phone Use

Licensed clinical social worker Jennifer Kelman argues that heavy phone use costs children the capacities that only in-person life builds: face-to-face connection, problem-solving skills, and confidence.

Kelman, who is based in Boca Raton, Florida, provides expert advice on the Justanswer platform and was not involved in the study. "They lose the ability to have face-to-face interactions, and to converse and connect with others," she said in an interview with Fox News Digital. "The phones and all the apps aren't real-life interactions, and there is beauty in connecting with others face-to-face that is lost," Kelman went on.

Kids also lose out on developing problem-solving skills, since they aren't typically tasked with negotiating "tough spaces" or navigating human challenges, the expert added. "The more apps we use, the more likely it is that we lose parts of ourselves, our confidence and self-esteem," said Kelman.

Her warrant is that the substitute does not deliver what the original does: "People feel good and are enhanced by interactions with others, and those feelings cannot be replicated by connecting through a phone."

qid: Who is the individual associated with FTX that expressed intentions to form a board with experts, acknowledged challenges in managing the significant growth of both FTX and Alameda Research, and is alleged by the prosecution to have committed fraud for personal gain, as reported by Cnbc | World Business News Leader, The Verge, and TechCrunch?
context:
# Matt Huang And Paradigm's FTX Investment

Matt Huang, co-founder and managing partner of Paradigm, a crypto venture capital firm that invested over $275 million in FTX — a stake that was wiped out — was the third witness to take the stand, and testified about his firm's due diligence.

Huang told the court that Bankman-Fried assured him funds would be used for FTX and not Alameda, and that he was promised Alameda had no preferential treatment on the FTX platform, even though the hedge fund was one of its top traders. Huang said he was concerned about FTX's lack of a board of directors but eventually invested anyway. During cross-examination he said Paradigm pressed Bankman-Fried on the board issue and was told he did not want investors as directors but did plan on having a board with experts.



---


# FTX's Inner Circle: Family And Friends Implicated

The Verge's October 26th, 2023 account of the trial catalogued how everyone who loved Bankman-Fried most in the world was caught up in the case. Adam Yedidia, his college roommate, testified with immunity because he was concerned he may have unknowingly worked on code that contributed to the fraud; "I love you Sam," he had texted at one point, "I'm not going anywhere" — that was before he realized FTX had stolen customer funds, at which point he resigned. Nishad Singh, a longtime family friend, copped to what sounded an awful lot like classic embezzlement, saying he had backdated transactions on FTX to help create doctored balance sheets to show to investors, and pleaded guilty to six charges including wire fraud, money laundering, and conspiracy counts around his political donations. Caroline Ellison, Bankman-Fried's ex-girlfriend, told the court about the seven phony balance sheets she had created and was clear that Alameda took customer funds, that Bankman-Fried knew about it, and that he even invested them against her advice.

His family was drawn in too. Joe Bankman, his father, is among the people included in the "small group chat," the Signal group where the FTX inner circle strategized during the exchange's last days. Barbara Fried's political action committee, Mind the Gap, is among the entities that received FTX customer money as political donations; Fried and Bankman lived together in a Bahamas house purchased for them using FTX investor funds, according to a financial expert called by the prosecution, and in a lawsuit filed by FTX's bankruptcy estate the two are alleged to have been given $10 million of FTX customer funds. Gabe Bankman-Fried's nonprofit, Guarding Against Pandemics, got millions from FTX; he was also in a Signal group chat, Donations Processing, that Singh says was used to coordinate the transfer of FTX and Alameda money to various political causes, and in that chat he can be seen recommending that some donations be made "in the dark" to avoid public relations headaches. Singh also said Gabe had an assistant fly to the Bahamas with a stack of blank checks for Singh to sign.

The consequences outlast the trial. Wang, Singh, and Ellison are now felons; even if they never do time — and they may very well be imprisoned or subjected to house arrest — their lives are irrevocably changed, not least by whatever restitution requirements they face, they are barred from taking certain kinds of jobs, and there is the publicity. Bankman, Fried, and Gabe Bankman-Fried's reputations are tarnished, and in the political arenas where they once operated they are suddenly undesirable. Beyond the courtroom, everyone who had money trapped on the exchange when it collapsed — as a result of Alameda purloining customers' funds — had their lives altered: even if they are made whole by the bankruptcy proceedings, that is still money they should have had access to at any time, which may mean houses that were not purchased, medical procedures left undone, and life savings lost. The reporter's summary: it is a Greek tragedy, precipitated by one man's character flaw, the arrogance of Sam Bankman-Fried.



---


# FTX's Bankruptcy And Leadership

The man who represented FTX before Congress after its failure told lawmakers the exchange had effectively no internal governance at all, and the prosecutor bringing the case called Bankman-Fried's alleged crimes one of the biggest financial frauds in American history. TechCrunch reported both on 2023-10-01.

Ray represented the company during a House Financial Services Committee hearing regarding FTX. Asked whether the firm had significant risk management systems, Ray said at the time that "there were virtually no internal controls and no separateness whatsoever," and added that he did not "trust a single piece of paper" in the exchange's organization. Separately, in a press conference, U.S. Attorney Damian Williams called Bankman-Fried's alleged crimes "one of the biggest financial frauds in American history."



---


# FTX Ventures Was Funded By Alameda

Caroline Ellison testified that the money behind FTX Ventures came from Alameda Research, even though Bankman-Fried announced the fund publicly without naming its source: on January 14th, 2022 he tweeted, "We're launching a $2b venture fund: FTX Ventures!" She said he did not want to go public with where the funds came from, telling her he thought Alameda's brand was less good and that he did not want his name associated with it.

The Verge reported the episode on October 10th, 2023 as part of Ellison's testimony, framing it as FTX keeping cozy private ties with Alameda while publicly holding it at arm's length — an echo, the reporter wrote, of Bankman-Fried and Ellison's romantic relationship. The same distancing appears in another transaction: Alameda bought Robinhood shares for Bankman-Fried, who moved them to a vehicle called "Emergent Fidelity Technologies" to avoid association with Alameda.



---


# Alameda Research As The Alleged Conduit For FTX Customer Funds

In the prosecution's account offered by Thane Rehn, the key to Sam Bankman-Fried's alleged scheme was Alameda Research, a crypto hedge fund that Bankman-Fried also owned. The structure the government described works as follows: Caroline Ellison — Bankman-Fried's on-again off-again girlfriend and the CEO of Alameda — served as a front for the fund, and through that arrangement Bankman-Fried had "secret access" to customer money, both cash and crypto.

Two further relations complete the alleged mechanism. Bankman-Fried is said to have directed employees to conceal the flow of money into FTX's coffers, and to have forged financial documents distributed to lenders and investors. "The defendant lied to the world," Rehn alleged. These are the government's allegations as presented in its opening statement, not established findings.



---


# Gary Wang's Testimony At The FTX Fraud Trial

Gary Wang, the lesser-known co-founder of FTX, told a Manhattan courtroom on Thursday that he had committed financial crimes while working at FTX — including wire and commodities fraud — carried out with the help of Sam Bankman-Fried, FTX ex-engineering head Nishad Singh, and Caroline Ellison, who ran sister hedge fund Alameda Research and had been Bankman-Fried's girlfriend.

Asked by Assistant U.S. Attorney Nicolas Roos, "Did you commit financial crimes while working at FTX?" Wang responded, "Yes." Asked whether he saw any of the people he committed those crimes with in the courtroom, Wang — dressed in an oversized and wrinkled suit with a red tie and glasses — awkwardly stood up, looked around, and answered, "Yes"; asked who, he said, "Sam Bankman-Fried." He was one of two former friends of Bankman-Fried's from MIT who also worked at FTX while living with the founder in the Bahamas and who took the stand that week to testify against their former classmate, confidant and boss, a man who allegedly ran a crypto empire that defrauded thousands of customers out of billions of dollars. The trial, set to last six weeks, was to resume on Tuesday with key testimony expected from Ellison, considered the prosecution's star witness, who had already pleaded guilty to multiple charges. Bankman-Fried faces seven federal charges, including wire fraud, securities fraud and money laundering, that could put him in prison for the rest of his life. Thus far Bankman-Fried, 31, has remained mostly quiet in court, intently listening to witnesses and at times writing notes to his attorneys — but as Wang testified against him, he looked visibly upset, shifting his gaze from his former friend to the ground and at one point putting his head in his hands.



---


# FTX's Cooperating Witnesses

FTX co-founder and former CTO Gary Wang and Alameda Research's former CEO Caroline Ellison both pleaded guilty in December 2022 to federal criminal charges in relation to the FTX collapse, and both planned to cooperate with prosecutors. TechCrunch reported on 2023-10-01 that they would be major witnesses in the trial, given their close ties to Bankman-Fried, FTX and Alameda.

The criminal charges were not their only exposure. Alongside them, Wang and Ellison face civil penalties from the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC).

qid: Does 'The Guardian' article suggest that Scott McTominay is the tactical leader for Manchester United, while 'Essentially Sports' claims that Kevin Durant has been criticized for his lack of leadership, indicating a difference in their respective leadership roles?
context:
# Scott McTominay's Advanced Role And Goal Threat

Under Ten Hag, Scott McTominay functions as a marauding midfield engine and late-running goal threat with a licence to create overloads wherever he finds them — the job United once paid Paul Pogba to do.

The structure of the role differs from his previous, more conventional midfield positions. Against low blocks and structured defences — and, the piece notes, nobody is remotely accusing Chelsea of possessing one of those — he provides the extra body in a tightly marked penalty area; but he also pops up in the channels and on the wing, either supporting the man in possession or offering himself for the quick switch of play. The relation between that role and his output shows in the numbers: against Chelsea he scored his fifth and sixth goals of the season, having previously never got more than seven. The piece attributes this partly to opponents still not quite cottoning on to his goal threat — those late runs to the far post, the blur on the edge of the 18-yard box you do not spot until it is too late — and partly to how Ten Hag is using him. The range over which the relation holds is the current team: for all the undoubted leadership qualities of Bruno Fernandes and Harry Maguire, tactically it is McTominay running the show right now, a development with numerous interesting consequences. The Pogba comparison is drawn with the caveat that McTominay is a different kind of player with a different kind of skillset; Pogba's United career never quite worked out, largely — if you believe his most vehement critics — on account of his hair.



---


# The Three Concurrent Roles Of A Manchester United Manager

Barney Ronay models the Manchester United job as three concurrent roles — managing the past, managing the dysfunction of the present, and managing the everyday metrics on which the manager is judged.

First you must manage the past, which is constantly in the room and which skews every act, achievement and expectation. Second you must manage the dysfunction of the present, which expresses itself in every detail from a leaking stadium roof to the deep ills of a playing squad peopled with squatters and long-term missteps. Finally you get to manage the everyday metrics — team, results, style, energy, messaging: win things, improve players, create a coherent and happy internal culture, but do it during an unceasing takeover circus while star players sulk and brief against you, and while the ghost of Hamlet's father still skulks in the eaves. The three hold together only under those conditions; as of the December 2023 Champions League exit, Ronay judged, this felt like the end of one thing, perhaps even the beginning of the end of something else.



---


# Kevin Durant Sensitivity And Burner Account Criticism

Against the case that Durant is simply disrespected, Essentially Sports set out on Dec. 1, 2023 the counter-case that his own conduct and post-Warriors record explain much of the criticism — attacking the premise that the disregard is unearned.

His vulnerability to criticism and thin-skinned nature has on several occasions got the better of him: NBA legend Charles Barkley called Durant "sensitive" in an interview with 60 Minutes, saying "He's very sensitive. Great player. He's part of that generation who thinks he can't be criticized." That susceptibility became glaringly evident when he used a burner account in 2017 to defend himself on Twitter, and was exposed after inadvertently failing to switch accounts and posting a tweet through his verified account. Fans also criticize him for a lack of leadership and a lack of titles since leaving the Warriors: since his 2019 departure Durant has not secured an NBA title, and despite forming a formidable trio with Kyrie Irving and James Harden in Brooklyn, their best result was a second-round exit in the 2021 playoffs at the hands of the Milwaukee Bucks. Fans and media also strongly disapprove of his inclination to switch teams repeatedly even when he receives substantial support from the organizations — after the Brooklyn experiment did not work he requested a trade, and at the previous year's trade deadline the Nets traded him to the Suns, where despite teammates like Devin Booker and Chris Paul he again fell short of a title. His inability to clinch an NBA title without Curry and the Warriors has heightened the narrative questioning his status as an icon of the game.



---


# Kevin Durant Most Disrespected Superstar Claim

Essentially Sports argued on Dec. 1, 2023 that Kevin Durant stands as perhaps the most disrespected icon of the sport, on the grounds that his acknowledged talent and accolades are out of proportion to how he is regarded.

The grounds start with where he sits in the league's history. The NBA is home to the world's best basketball players and teams, and throughout its history iconic figures like Magic Johnson, Larry Bird, Kareem Abdul-Jabbar and Michael Jordan have left an indelible mark; but for the better part of the past two decades, players like Stephen Curry, LeBron James and Kevin Durant have dominated the NBA landscape. While LeBron James and Stephen Curry may have accumulated more championships and accolades, Durant is universally acknowledged as the best pure talent of his generation. The dispute the argument answers is that Durant divides opinions: some view him as the most skilled basketball player of his generation, others as a diva who rode the coattails of Stephen Curry to secure his two NBA championships. The warrant is that a careful consideration of Durant's game-changing impact and his multitude of accolades reveals a glaring gap between what he has done and how he is treated.



---


# Kevin Durant 2016 Move To Warriors Legacy

In the 2016 Western Conference finals, the Kevin Durant and Russell Westbrook-led OKC Thunder faced the 73-9 Warriors and, after swiftly securing a 3-1 series lead, seemed poised for an NBA Finals appearance — but the Warriors orchestrated a remarkable comeback to win the series in seven games, meaning Durant would go trophy-less for another season, Essentially Sports recounted on Dec. 1, 2023.

In the 2016 offseason, Durant made the pivotal decision to join the very team that had defeated him. The move had profound consequences, leading to a shift in public opinion, with many labeling him a "snake" and "spineless." While Durant achieved the success he craved in the Bay Area, his decision to join the Warriors has permanently cast a shadow on his legacy.



---


# The Manchester United Crisis News Cycle Under Ten Hag

The Guardian's argument is that results at Manchester United no longer settle anything, because the club's crisis news cycle consumes wins as quickly as defeats: a stirring recovery against Chelsea bought Erik ten Hag only a few days' grace.

The grounds are the pattern of the week itself — rancour, rumour and recrimination, barbs in the press and barbs at the press, defeat at Newcastle followed by the Chelsea win and the startling realisation that United were three points behind Manchester City, all before Thursday. The warrant is a claim about the institution rather than the team: such is the way of things at football's most reliable content provider, and this beast must always eat, so the warm flume of goodwill would last only as long as it took for Dominic Solanke to run through on goal for Bournemouth on the Saturday afternoon, returning United to the grip of crisis and the now-familiar lexicon of surly unsourced stories about dressing room discontent. A second, related argument is that assessing any United manager requires filters: Ten Hag would of course take the blame for the early Champions League exit, and plenty of mistakes had been made, not least in the players the manager had been allowed to sign — but to be United manager is to undertake three concurrent roles.



---


# Kevin Durant Career Accolades And Scoring Ranks

Kevin Durant, as Essentially Sports characterized him on Dec. 1, 2023, stands as one of the most exceptionally skilled players in NBA history — a transcendent superstar across an illustrious 17-year career whose stellar performances have endeared him to millions of fans, yet who regularly faces disregard from both the media and fans, making him one of the most polarizing figures in basketball.

The discriminating feature is his physical and technical profile at entry: Durant rose to prominence in 2007, when the Seattle SuperSonics drafted him with the No. 2 pick, and the NBA had never witnessed a player possessing his unique skill set — a 6'11" forward renowned for his exceptional jump shot and lethal three-point accuracy, epitomizing the concept of a "Unicorn" in its truest sense. The record makes the disrespect more perplexing still: Durant has amassed 27,393 points in the regular season, ranking 11th in NBA history, and has contributed an additional 4,878 points in the playoffs, placing him 7th on the all-time list. He is a surefire future first-ballot Hall of Famer with a resume few can match — two NBA titles, two NBA Finals MVP awards, four scoring titles, and multiple selections to the All-Star and All-NBA teams.



---


# Mr. Irrelevant: The NFL Draft's Final Pick

"Mr. Irrelevant" is the nickname given to the final pick of the NFL Draft. What distinguishes the title is purely positional: it attaches to whoever is selected last, regardless of the player or the team.
