context:
# The Woman In Me: Publication Details Of Britney Spears' Memoir

*The Woman in Me* is Britney Spears' memoir, published by Simon & Schuster on 25 October 2023 at $49.99 and reportedly written for a $US15 million ($23.3 million) advance; its defining subject is the conservatorship under which her father and others held almost complete control of her life for 13 years.

The Sydney Morning Herald's 1 October 2023 books preview describes the book as a candid account of a life in which the "huge-selling American singer has negotiated the slings and arrows of outrageous fortune in her 41 years", with the controversial conservatorship at its heart — an arrangement that nonetheless "still failed to stop it going off the rails many times" — and predicts it is sure to be a bestseller and exactly what her fans want.

The Guardian, reviewing the memoir on 24 October 2023, observes that it "feels fitting" the book is released a week before Halloween: however much was already known about the 13 years Spears lived under the conservatorship, her recounting of its imposition, life under it and her inability to escape it "is nothing short of a horror story", appalling "like something out of a Victorian novel, not the very real experiences of a thirtysomething in the last decade".



---


# Justin Timberlake's Apology And Support For Britney Spears

Justin Timberlake publicly apologised to Britney Spears on Instagram in 2021 after the documentary Framing Britney, which addressed the public scrutiny Spears faced during the 2000s, prompted criticism of how he had behaved following their breakup. Neither had ever acknowledged the rumours about why they split. His apology read: "I've seen the messages, tags, comments, and concerns and I want to respond. I am deeply sorry for the times in my life where my actions contributed to the problem, where I spoke out of turn, or did not speak up for what was right. I understand that I fell short in these moments and in many others and benefited from a system that condones misogyny and racism."

In June 2021 he also backed Spears after she testified publicly in a bid to end the conservatorship controlled by her father, Jamie Spears. At the Los Angeles court hearing, Spears alleged she had been forced to take lithium against her will and claimed the team managing her conservatorship had prevented her from having another baby by refusing to remove her IUD. Timberlake wrote on X, formerly known as Twitter: "After what we saw today, we should all be supporting Britney at this time. Regardless of our past, good and bad, and no matter how long ago it was. What's happening to her is just not right. No woman should ever be restricted from making decisions about her own body."



---


# Britney Spears On Body Scrutiny And Diet Control

The Guardian's 24 October 2023 account of *The Woman in Me* reports that Spears' body was treated as public property "from day one" and that, once she was under the conservatorship, her father policed her weight and every calorie she ate was recorded.

Between the videos for her debut single Baby, One More Time and Sometimes, the media noted her changing physique and concluded that the 16-year-old must have had breast implants rather than simply going through puberty. She noticed that talkshow hosts asked her about her chest while her boyfriend Justin Timberlake was asked serious questions about his music. Writing about shaving her head in a salon in 2007, she frames it as a "fuck you" to impossible beauty standards: "I'd smiled politely while TV show hosts leered at my breasts, while American parents said I was destroying their children by wearing a crop top."

That brief moment of freedom did not last: a year later she was ambushed into the conservatorship, which also exercised jurisdiction over her body. "No matter how much I dieted and exercised, my father was always telling me I was fat," she writes; punishing gym routines left her feeling "out of my mind", and her diet was monitored along with every other detail of her life while she went through the motions of her Las Vegas residency. "My body was strong enough to carry two children and agile enough to execute every choreographed move perfectly onstage. And now here I was, having every calorie recorded so people could continue to get rich off my body." On the other side of the conservatorship, she writes, freedom looks like being able to gain weight without anyone "shouting at me", eating chocolate again, and posting selfies — nude or clothed — on Instagram; people who do not understand the last of these, she suggests, have not been "photographed by other people thousands of times, prodded and posed for other people's approval".



---


# Britney Spears' Memoir On Early Fame And The Loss Of Freedom

In *The Woman in Me*, as summarised by The Guardian on 24 October 2023, Britney Spears describes how fame converted her childhood escape into confinement: by the age of 16 she was "public property", unable to go outside without being mobbed, and her love of singing and dancing had become a lucrative resource for other people.

Spears writes that as a child she escaped a difficult home life — her alcoholic father often rowing with her mother — into the outdoors, which "gave me a sense of aliveness and danger", and that performing made her feel invincible. By the time of her second album she wanted for so little; skinny-dipping with her dancers after playing Rock in Rio in January 2001 is one of her happiest memories, "a taste of rebellion and freedom, but I was just having fun and being a 19-year-old". After her split from Justin Timberlake she dreamed about quitting pop and opening a shop, and writes with hindsight that she "hadn't given myself enough time to heal from the breakup" — yet her requests for a break were not only turned down but interpreted as a potential sign of sedition to be quashed and interrogated.

In that restrictive environment small kindnesses took on outsized significance, such as Paris Hilton encouraging her "to have fun for the first time in a long time", which led to infamous nights out with the heiress and Lindsay Lohan; once again Britney was seen as stepping out of bounds and potentially damaging her earning potential. One night, after her mother babysat her sons, she returned home tipsy and Lynne Spears screamed at her: "The shame I felt killed my heart. I stood there, reeling, and thought, OK, I guess it's forbidden for me to party." As the restrictions tightened she acted out, and ended up legally denied her freedom for 13 years under a conservatorship controlled by her father.



---


# Britney Spears On Motherhood And Postpartum Depression

Spears writes in *The Woman in Me*, per The Guardian's 24 October 2023 account, that she suffered severe postpartum depression after her sons were born — depression she only recognised later — and that it left her suicidal: "I'll admit it, I felt that I couldn't live if things didn't get better."

When she became pregnant with her first son she initially thought it might protect her — "I wanted everyone to stay away: stand back! There's a baby here!" — but the paparazzi became more aggressive, particularly once she had her children in quick succession, becoming pregnant a second time three months after giving birth to her first. She felt hopeless about her ability to protect her sons: "I got a little depressed once I was no longer keeping them safe inside my body … I wanted them back inside me so the world couldn't get at them."

She has a keen sense of injustice about a contract with the public and the press that she never signed: "They just kept acting like I owed it to them to let the men who kept trying to catch me looking fat take photos of my infant sons." Her postpartum body and shots of her without makeup were treated as "some kind of a sin – as if gaining weight was something unkind I'd done to them personally, a betrayal. At what point did I promise to stay 17 for the rest of my life?" What she knows now, she writes, "is that every part of normal life had been stripped from me – going out in public without becoming a headline, making normal mistakes as a new mother of two babies, feeling like I could trust the people around me. I had no freedom and yet also no security."



---


# The Fan Movement And The 2021 End Of Britney Spears' Conservatorship

According to The Guardian's 24 October 2023 account of *The Woman in Me*, Spears first learned of the blossoming fan movement questioning her conservatorship from a nurse, called 911 in June 2021 to report her father for conservatorship abuse days before a probate court hearing, and was granted her freedom in November 2021.

A nurse showed her the fan movement that was spreading awareness of its suspicions that all was not right with the arrangement. Of speaking publicly at that point she writes: "My voice had been used for me and against me so many times that I was afraid nobody would recognise it now if I spoke freely."

When freedom came in November 2021, she says she felt shock, relief, elation, sadness and joy.

qid: Between the TechCrunch report on Epic Games' antitrust battle with Google published on November 6, 2023, and the TechCrunch report on the class action antitrust suit against Google published on December 15, 2023, was there consistency in reporting Google's engagement in anticompetitive behavior?
context:
# Google's Parallel Antitrust Proceedings In Late 2023

As of mid-November 2023, Google was fighting antitrust on more than one front at once. The Epic Games case was not its only antitrust case in trial: Google had settled a separate antitrust lawsuit with dating site Match Group the week before November 13, and on November 6 it went to trial with Fortnite maker Epic Games, which hoped to prove that Google engages in anticompetitive behavior with regard to its Android app store, Google Play, and its commission structure. Separately, Google was involved in an antitrust lawsuit with the Department of Justice over its alleged search monopoly.

The Epic case had shed co-plaintiffs on its way to trial. Epic's lawsuit originally involved Match and several U.S. attorneys general, but Google reached a settlement with the attorneys general in October 2023 and with Match the week before November 6, so Epic fought the antitrust battle on its own. The lawsuit, held in the U.S. District Court in California's Northern District, would include testimony from a number of Google and Android execs, including CEO Sundar Pichai, and Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, as well as from Apple, Netflix and other Android developers. Epic, meanwhile, had lost its antitrust battle with Apple and was asking the Supreme Court to weigh in.



---


# The Settlements That Left Epic Standing Alone

Other plaintiffs brought app store antitrust claims against Google and then all settled: all 50 state attorneys general and a number of consumers have tentatively settled, though it is not clear what the deal might include, and Match Group — the company behind Tinder, Match.com, OkCupid and other dating apps — just reached a surprise last-minute settlement too, one that makes it sound like Match effectively gave up. Epic stands alone.

Epic seems to have no interest in settling as long as the "Google tax" exists, and the company has repeatedly said it is not interested in cash. So far it has been willing to push these cases all the way through multiple appeals, cost be damned. It is not clear what Google could proactively offer that would satisfy Epic, since CEO Tim Sweeney has also publicly suggested that Google would simply circumvent any settlement it offers. If you want to see a vision of a future Epic would accept, look to the letter it sent to state attorneys general, laying out a settlement that would basically prohibit Google from doing the anticompetitive things Epic claims it did. Google would not tell The Verge whether it has offered Epic any kind of settlement.



---


# Helena World Chronicle's Class Action Antitrust Suit Against Google

A class action lawsuit filed in the week of 15 December 2023 in the U.S. District Court in D.C. accuses Google and parent company Alphabet of anticompetitive behavior in violation of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act and others, on behalf of news publishers. The case was filed by Arkansas-based publisher Helena World Chronicle, which argues that Google "siphons off" news publishers' content, their readers and their ad revenue through anticompetitive means, and it specifically cites new AI technologies such as Google's Search Generative Experience (SGE) and the Bard AI chatbot as worsening the problem.

Helena World Chronicle owns and publishes two weekly newspapers in Arkansas. In the complaint it argues that Google is "starving the free press" by sharing publishers' content on Google, losing them "billions of dollars."

Beyond damages, the suit asks for an injunction that would require Google to obtain consent from publishers before using their website data to train its general artificial intelligence products, including Google's own and those of rivals. It also asks that publishers who opt out of SGE still be allowed to show up in Google search results, among other things.

The law firm handling the case is Hausfeld, whose announcement states that "the anticompetitive effects of Google's scheme cause profound harm to competition, to consumers, to labor, and to a democratic free press," and that "Plaintiff Helena World Chronicle, LLC invokes the Sherman Act and Clayton Act to seek class-wide monetary and injunctive relief to restore and ensure competition for digital news and reference publishing and set up guardrails to preserve a free marketplace of ideas in the new era of artificial intelligence."



---


# The U.S. Justice Department's Parallel Antitrust Suits Against Google

The Helena World Chronicle class action arrives alongside the filing of the U.S. Justice Department's lawsuit against Google for monopolizing digital ad technologies, and the complaint also references the Justice Department's 2020 civil antitrust suit over search and search advertising.

The two government cases concern different markets: search and search advertising in the 2020 suit are distinct from the digital ad technologies at issue in the more recent one.



---


# Sweeney And Pichai's Settlement Talks

Asked about his settlement talks with Google CEO Sundar Pichai, Tim Sweeney said he could not discuss their content, but that the two met for an hour and had a professional discussion in which they did not reach a settlement — they were, in his words, "rather far apart."

He explained the gap in terms of what Epic was asking for: free and fair competition for everybody, removal of the payments tie, and removal of the anticompetitive measures, which he said obviously leads to far better deals for consumers and developers. What Epic does not want is a special deal just for itself. Sweeney characterised Google's strategy so far, as visible from all these deals, as taking out potential competitors one at a time while they are still weak and small, before they build up or unite into a formidable force — and said Epic is not going to go along with something like that.



---


# Epic v. Google: What The Trial Is

Epic v. Google is the antitrust case in which Fortnite publisher Epic Games drags a tech giant into court alleging that its mobile app store is an illegal monopoly — and although Epic's parallel claims against Apple already got their day in court, the similar lawsuit against Google never did, which is why the case goes to trial on November 6th, a mere 1,180 days after Epic originally sued.

The déjà vu is the point of confusion the piece sets out to clear up: Epic already went to trial with Apple, resulting in a ruling where Apple mostly won, and its Llamacorn legal gambit failed to #FreeFortnite years ago. The distinction is that the Apple claims were heard and the Google ones were not.

An update dated December 15th, 2023 notes that the case is basically over by then.



---


# What A Ruling Against Google Would Mean For Big Tech

A ruling against Google would not stop at Google: the remedy would likely resemble the Microsoft settlement and the outcome would ripple through the other pending Big Tech cases, because enforcers are using this trial to demonstrate that antitrust law can still take on the largest and most powerful companies in the world.

The grounds for the first half of that claim are the available remedies. If the judge rules against Google, the outcome could look a lot like the Microsoft deal, in which the computer company was required to change its behavior and share its APIs with third-party developers, and was also banned from making anticompetitive and exclusive deals with computer manufacturers. Google might likewise end up having to turn over all or most of the data it has collected to other search engines so they can improve their products and attract more users — a remedy scaled to the disparity the DOJ has cited, that Google gets 16 times more data than Bing does everyday.

The grounds for the ripple effect are the cases already queued behind this one. The FTC sued Amazon in September for using anticompetitive and unfair strategies to illegally maintain its monopoly power. The DOJ has been investigating Apple for years over the company's policy for third-party apps on its devices and whether it unfairly favors its own products. And there is an ongoing case between the FTC and Facebook, in which the agency calls on Facebook to sell Instagram and WhatsApp.

The warrant joining grounds to claim is enforcers' own stake in the result: they will want to show that antitrust law is still relevant and can successfully take on the biggest, most powerful companies in the world, so a win here sets the template the neighbouring cases are argued against. The scope condition is that nothing was settled as of this report — the case is expected to continue for several weeks, bringing to a head one of the biggest fights in tech antitrust since the U.S. took Microsoft to trial in the 1990s.



---


# Google's Rebuttal To The Publisher Antitrust Suit

Google rejects the premise that it deprives publishers of readers and traffic. A Google spokesperson called the Helena World Chronicle lawsuit "meritless," and attacked the claim of foreclosure directly: "People have many ways to access information and news content today – through publishers' websites, dedicated apps, social media platforms, print papers and more. Google links people to publishers' websites more than 24 billion times each month – at no cost to them."

The rebuttal therefore contests two of the suit's premises at once: that Google is a bottleneck between readers and publishers, and that publishers are uncompensated, by pointing to the volume of free referrals Google sends.

# Belgium-England: The Second Half And Wullaert's Penalty

Belgium won the game on 31 October 2023 through Tessa Wullaert's 85th-minute penalty, awarded by referee Esther Staubli after Georgia Stanway handballed Yana Daniels' 83rd-minute effort; Wullaert fired it into the bottom-left corner despite Mary Earps diving the correct way, Sport Grill reported.

England had the better of the half without converting. On the restart Fran Kirby quickly drew a foul from Kassandra Missipo, but Alessia Russo fumbled control from Chloe Kelly's free-kick and her shot was blocked; Nicky Evrard then saved Kirby's shot from Lucy Bronze's pullback pass in the 52nd minute as England continued to test the Red Flames' defence. Just past the hour mark England were given an almighty scare as Wullaert pounced on a through ball and side-stepped both Jess Carter and Millie Bright, only for Earps to block her shot with a stunning save.

Belgium were forced to defend for much of the last half-hour as Russo and Stanway saw shots denied, while substitute Rachel Daly nodded wide in the 80th minute from Keira Walsh's deep corner towards the left post. Sarina Wiegman's Lionesses were eventually made to pay for their wasted chances.



---


# Belgium 3-2 England: The Women's Nations League Result, October 2023

Tessa Wullaert's brace fired Belgium to a dramatic 3-2 home win over England in League A1 of the 2023-24 UEFA Women's Nations League, reported by Sport Grill on 31 October 2023.

Wullaert equalised for Belgium in first-half injury time before taking advantage of Georgia Stanway's handball to fire in an 85th-minute winning penalty.

The result put Belgium second in the group, one point ahead of England and two points behind group leaders the Netherlands, with those two rivals set to meet on 1 December in a blockbuster showdown.

# Belgium-England: First-Half Goals And Incidents

The first half in Leuven on 31 October 2023 finished 2-2: Laura De Neve curled Belgium ahead in the ninth minute, Lucy Bronze and Fran Kirby put England in front late in the half, and Tessa Wullaert levelled in first-half injury time, Sport Grill reported.

Having battled to a narrow home win the previous Friday, 27 October, England began on the front foot with a fourth-minute free-kick cleared by Belgium's Nicky Evrard. Belgium drew first blood in this Halloween encounter after Chloe Kelly was penalised for handball just outside the box, allowing De Neve to curl her ninth-minute free-kick straight into the near-top right corner beyond the reach of an outstretched Mary Earps. England struggled to mount a response as Belgium continued to soak up their pressure and hit them on the counter attack, until Alex Greenwood and Jassina Blom banged heads in the 18th minute as they tried to meet an aerial pass, halting play.

That lengthy delay reignited England's intensity, which paid off as Bronze drew a 36th-minute foul from Marie Detruyer and headed in from Kelly's subsequent free-kick two minutes later to restore parity. Kelly then fired wide in the 41st minute as Belgium were forced to substitute De Neve due to injury, which unsettled their defence; while Belgium's defence adjusted, Bronze's header a minute later from Keira Walsh's cross was fired wide on the rebound by Alessia Russo. England continued to press and got their reward in the 44th minute as Lauren Hemp was unleashed up the left flank by Walsh and found Kirby on the pullback to rifle in beyond Evrard and turn the tie around. England's lead lasted only seven minutes into 14 minutes of first-half injury time, as Wullaert was played through on the counter-attack by Janice Cayman to slot into the far left corner and pull Belgium level at the break.

# Harry Kane's 2023 Goal Tally And Bayern Munich Scoring Records

Harry Kane scored 52 goals in the 2023 calendar year for Bayern Munich, Tottenham and England, tied for second on TalkSport's list of the year's top scorers. A stunning 2022/23 season saw Bayern splash out over £100m to sign the Spurs legend in August, and Kane repaid the Bundesliga club's faith by breaking a number of records with his 25 goals in all competitions so far in the season.

The leading scorer in the German top flight with 22 goals, the Three Lions skipper set a new Bundesliga record the previous month by finding the back of the net 17 times in his opening 11 outings. Kane, who scored nine goals for England in 2023, is also the first player to register a hat-trick in their first outing against Borussia Dortmund. He is on course to score the most goals in a debut Bundesliga campaign as he hunts down Uwe Seeler's record of 30 for Hamburg in the 1963/64 season, and is on track to break Robert Lewandowski's record of 41 goals in a single season. He is adding assists too, as evidenced by his "filthy" effort against Man United in the Champions League. Like Mbappe, Kane could not overtake Ronaldo's calendar-year tally because of the German winter break.

Earlier in the season, in Bayern's 2-2 draw at RB Leipzig, Bayern earned a 57th-minute penalty against the run of play for a handball and Kane cut the deficit with his eighth league goal. Only Manchester City's Erling Haaland, when he played for Borussia Dortmund, had scored more often in his first six Bundesliga games, with nine goals.

# England's Olympic Qualification Heartbreak

Scoring six goals against Scotland on Dec. 5, 2023 was not enough to close the goal difference gap on the Netherlands, because the Dutch scored a fourth against Belgium deep in added time to secure top spot in the Nations League group ahead of England.

No one could question the effort, the heart or the drive of Sarina Wiegman's Lionesses in the game, but qualification hinged on a back and forth of goals in the final round of fixtures — England's against Scotland and the Netherlands' in their win over Belgium — a showdown that ended in an anxious wait and then complete heartbreak. An added-time save by Mary Earps at full stretch from a header by substitute Martha Thomas kept England in it. With the Netherlands having scored in the 91st minute, Bronze's powering header put England back in for two minutes, until the Dutch scored in the 95th to crush the Lionesses while they stood in a huddle waiting for news of the other game's result, the pain sweeping across their faces as it came through.



---


# Alex Greenwood's Head Injury Versus Belgium

Alex Greenwood was stretchered off after a clash of heads with Belgium's Jassina Blom on 31 October 2023, an incident that forced a 13-minute delay for medical treatment, Sport Grill reported.

The impact resulted in both players falling to the ground. Blom was eventually able to continue after concussion checks, while Greenwood was taken from the field on a stretcher.

England tweeted at half-time that Greenwood was conscious and talking to medical staff under observation: "Alex Greenwood is conscious and talking, and is being monitored by our medical staff," the Lionesses posted on October 31, 2023.



---


# Cole Palmer Stoppage-Time Penalty Vs Manchester City

Cole Palmer, who left Manchester City for Chelsea in a deal worth around $A82 million in September, showed supreme composure to fire past Ederson in the dying stages of the 4-4 draw at Stamford Bridge, scoring from the spot in the 95th minute, The Roar reported on Nov. 12, 2023.

In his post-match interview he said of penalties: "I'm not going to say I work on them, because I don't. I just trust in my natural abilities."



---


# Cole Palmer's Goal Against Manchester City In The 4-4 Draw

Cole Palmer marked his goal against Manchester City with a shrug rather than a celebration, out of respect for the club where he spent 15 years. "I spent 15 years at the club," he noted. "I can't really go and celebrate how I would celebrate if I have scored a 95th-minute equaliser because it would have been disrespectful." Perhaps it summed up Palmer's inability to feel intimidated by anything; there was no getting carried away.

The alternative explanation is that Palmer has scored so many major goals in the last few months that this was merely another. He struck in the Community Shield and the European Super Cup for City, and against Arsenal and Tottenham for Chelsea. That big-match temperament may equip him for tournament football in an England shirt — and so, too, may his nerveless penalty-taking.

# The College Football Week 6 2023 Ranked Matchup Slate

Four AP Top 25 matchups were on deck in Week 6 of the 2023 college football season, headlined by the annual Red River Rivalry between No. 3 Texas and No. 12 Oklahoma at the Cotton Bowl Stadium in Dallas, as previewed by CBS Sports on 1 October 2023.

The four games are described in turn. The Red River Rivalry would be the first time the two rivals had matched up undefeated since 2011, both sitting at 5-0. Saturday would also mark the first time top-ranked Georgia had squared off against a ranked opponent that season, as the Bulldogs welcomed No. 20 Kentucky in a matchup of 5-0 squads — one of two ranked SEC matchups. The fourth and final AP Top 25 matchup was in ACC territory, where No. 25 Louisville, 5-0 in its first season under coach Jeff Brohm, hosted No. 10 Notre Dame; the Fighting Irish were looking to secure a second ranked victory in as many weeks and remain in the playoff hunt after a comeback win at Duke in Week 5.

The framing is the season stage: an eventful first month was in the rearview mirror, and October should provide even more separation between pretenders and contenders in the ongoing College Football Playoff race. Betting lines for those battles and other key Week 6 matchups were released on the Sunday.

# LSU At Missouri: The 2023 Week 6 Betting Line

No. 23 LSU was favoured by 6.5 points at No. 21 Missouri, according to CBS Sports' Week 6 lines published 1 October 2023.

The two teams' trajectories are set in contrast. LSU had already gone from a trendy College Football Playoff pick to a two-loss team, while Missouri was looking to improve on an impressive start that already included a Week 3 win against defending Big 12 champion and longtime former conference-mate Kansas State.

The matchup's pivot is LSU's defense against Missouri's quarterback. # Will Alabama Make The 2023 College Football Playoff?

Sporting News concluded on Dec. 1, 2023 that Alabama's path was real but not clean: Oregon had lost, and seeing at least one of Texas or Florida State lose would be helpful for the Crimson Tide.

The supporting grounds are institutional rather than purely statistical. There is the power of the SEC at work, and the emotional response by the committee to seeing Alabama beat Georgia might be enough on its own; the SEC is the only conference that has put a team in the CFP every single year.

The counterweight is the head-to-head and unbeaten logic. If Alabama beat Georgia, the arguments around those other conferences would get heated — yet Florida State as an unbeaten team would still theoretically have the drop on the Crimson Tide, and so would Texas based on the head-to-head victory. # Alabama's Preferred Championship Weekend Scenarios

Sporting News argued on Dec. 1, 2023 that Alabama had options with a victory against Georgia, but that a specific set of results in the other four championship games would be the preferred scenario for the Crimson Tide.

The framing premise is the size of the field: the Crimson Tide were one of eight Power 5 teams with one loss or less heading into conference championship weekend, and no two-loss team had ever made the four-team College Football Playoff. Each preferred result therefore works by pushing a rival into the two-loss pile or freeing a spot.

Washington beating Oregon in the Pac-12 championship: Alabama got this piece in their favor, since Washington beat Oregon on Friday, which knocked the Ducks into the two-loss pileup and out of the CFP picture. Oklahoma State beating Texas in the Big 12 championship: this would make life easier in a lot of ways for Alabama, because Texas had a 34-24 head-to-head non-conference victory against the Crimson Tide — the Longhorns would have two losses at that point, so there would be nothing to discuss. Iowa beating Michigan in the Big Ten championship: while this was the most unlikely result, it could knock the Big Ten out of the CFP; Alabama was ranked behind No. 6 Ohio State, a one-loss team, but the Crimson Tide would leap-frog them with a victory against Georgia, and the committee would also take an SEC champion over a one-loss Michigan team. # Alabama's CFP Situation Ahead Of The 2023 SEC Championship Game

No. 8 Alabama (11-1) had to beat No. 1 Georgia in the SEC championship at 4 p.m. on Saturday on CBS to keep its College Football Playoff hopes alive, with the question being whether the Crimson Tide would endure a three-year drought in the CFP, per Sporting News on Dec. 1, 2023.

# Notre Dame At Louisville: The 2023 Week 6 Betting Line

No. 10 Notre Dame was favoured by 6.5 points at No. 25 Louisville, according to CBS Sports' Week 6 lines published 1 October 2023.

Notre Dame arrived off two consecutive dogfights: the Fighting Irish had their hearts broken by Ohio State in Week 4 before playing the role of heartbreaker at Duke in Week 5. Louisville remained unbeaten a month into the Jeff Brohm era.

# The Oklahoma-Texas Red River Rivalry 2023 Betting Line

CBS Sports listed Terry McLaurin under "Start Him" in Week 5 of the 2023 season and then under "Sit Him" in Week 6, and the reversal turns on two things changing: the Commanders' targets diffused among three receivers, and the opponent shifted from a depleted Bears secondary to an ascending Falcons one in a low-total game.

Terrell there isn't a matchup that's great for McLaurin. qid: Who is the individual associated with the crypto exchange FTX, whose purported success was questioned in a Fortune article, who admitted to being informed of financial discrepancies as reported by The Verge, and is alleged by the prosecution to have committed fraud for personal gain according to TechCrunch?
context:
# Sam Bankman-Fried

Sam Bankman-Fried is the former CEO of the bankrupt crypto exchange FTX, whose highly anticipated criminal trial started on the Tuesday before TechCrunch's 2023-10-01 report, to determine whether he is guilty of seven counts of fraud and conspiracy. As one former federal prosecutor put it: "The odds seem to be stacked against him at this point."

He was 31 years old and co-founded FTX in 2019; within a few years the once third-largest crypto exchange's valuation hit $32 billion at its peak, and the company is now trying to claw back any funds to distribute to creditors. Before the fall he was even compared to Warren Buffet, and many called him the white horse of crypto — a description TechCrunch notes it never applied to him.

Bankman-Fried, however, maintained his innocence. At The New York Times' DealBook Summit he appeared virtually from the Bahamas and said, "I didn't ever try to commit fraud on anyone; I was shocked by what happened this month"; in a published DM exchange with a Vox reporter he said he regretted filing for bankruptcy and thought that "regulators make everything worse." In January he pleaded not guilty to all counts, which include wire fraud, conspiracy to commit money laundering and conspiracy to misuse customer funds. He could face up to 115 years in jail if convicted on all charges.

TechCrunch's 2023-10-02 summary of his standing on the eve of trial: SBF has been denied bail; his name is mud (or much worse) among those who have lost money in Alameda or FTX; and those who might not have had positions in these still blame him for other crypto woes, because he set off a ripple effect.



---


# Marc-Antoine Julliard's Testimony As FTX's First Witness-Victim

The prosecution's first witness at Sam Bankman-Fried's trial was not a blockbuster name or a former lieutenant-turned-cooperator like Caroline Ellison but a victim: Marc-Antoine Julliard, a Paris-born cocoa trader who lives in London and whose money got stuck on FTX. Julliard testified that on Nov. 8, 2022, in the crypto exchange's final few days, he tried to pull out almost $100,000 in cash and crypto, and that he was never able to. The withdrawal screenshots shown in court were of attempts to move $20,000 USD and about 4 Bitcoin, worth about $20,000 at the time — roughly $100,000 in total, inaccessible.

Julliard explained why he had chosen FTX in 2021 when he decided to invest in crypto, trading currencies like Bitcoin and Dogecoin there. He trusted FTX because Bankman-Fried came across as a leading figure of the industry; because the sheer volume of users mattered to him, and FTX was at the time among the top three biggest exchanges; and because major VC firms had invested. "They don't commit hundreds of millions without doing due diligence, checking the books, the accountancy of the firm, going through several compliance process[es], so that was a vote of confidence for me," he said. He also noted FTX's glossy ads — featuring Gisele Bündchen, for instance — which suggested a very high budget, and reasoned that it wouldn't make sense to spend that much money unless FTX had very strong financials. He opened an account, transferred in both regular money and cryptocurrency, and used the exchange to execute his plan of buying Bitcoin to sell back in five to ten years at higher prices.

In November 2022 things went bad. Julliard followed Bankman-Fried on Twitter and read aloud in court the "FTX is fine. Assets are fine" tweets, along with "FTX has enough to cover all client holdings. We don't invest client assets" and a few others, which gave him the impression that his money was there and that any problem might be technical — anti-spam measures — or regulatory. By the time he tried to get his money out on November 8th, it was too late. Cross-examining a customer whose money is gone is described as a thankless task, but Mark Cohen tried anyway, noting that Julliard was a licensed commodities broker who was trading in crypto because he didn't have to disclose it, that he knew crypto was new and risky, and that he didn't review the terms of service agreement he had assented to when making his FTX account. The next witness called was Bankman-Fried's former college and FTX roommate, Adam Yedidia.



---


# FTX's Bankruptcy And Leadership

The man who represented FTX before Congress after its failure told lawmakers the exchange had effectively no internal governance at all, and the prosecutor bringing the case called Bankman-Fried's alleged crimes one of the biggest financial frauds in American history. TechCrunch reported both on 2023-10-01.

Ray represented the company during a House Financial Services Committee hearing regarding FTX. Asked whether the firm had significant risk management systems, Ray said at the time that "there were virtually no internal controls and no separateness whatsoever," and added that he did not "trust a single piece of paper" in the exchange's organization. Separately, in a press conference, U.S. Attorney Damian Williams called Bankman-Fried's alleged crimes "one of the biggest financial frauds in American history."



---


# FTX Fraud Charges And The SEC's Allegation

Sam Bankman-Fried, the founder of the failed cryptocurrency exchange FTX, faced seven counts of wire fraud and conspiracy — specifically, two counts of wire fraud and five conspiracy charges — and the Securities and Exchange Commission alleged that FTX was a fraud "from the start," with a "multi-billion-dollar deficiency caused by his own misappropriation of customer funds." The Verge repeated this framing at the head of each of its trial dispatches through October 2023, and in its October 28th, 2023 write-up reported that Bankman-Fried had been found guilty on seven counts including charges of wire fraud.

The boundary of the concept is the mix of charge types: the indictment paired substantive wire fraud counts with conspiracy counts rather than resting on a single offence, and the SEC's civil allegation about the exchange's origins ran alongside the criminal case rather than being part of it. The Verge's reporter, writing as the prosecution's case neared its end on October 26th, 2023, added an impression of the people the charges swept in: all the co-conspirators seemed oddly younger than their years, as though they had got stuck in the "math camp forever" environment Bankman-Fried created for them and simply failed to grow up.



---


# Day Two Of The Bankman-Fried Trial: Jury Selection And The Courtroom Audience

On the second day of Sam Bankman-Fried's fraud trial, the jury was selected on Wednesday morning, after which lawyers for the government and then for Bankman-Fried delivered opening statements that told two very different stories of the former FTX CEO's sudden rise and almost instantaneous fall. The central question framed by the proceedings was who Bankman-Fried, the former CEO of crypto exchange FTX, really is: a liar and a fraud, or someone who acted in good faith and, like many a startup founder, flew too close to the sun. That answer, the account notes, ultimately lies with the jury.

The day featured pointed allegations, a friend from MIT, and an audience replete with big names, including Bankman-Fried's professorial parents and Damian Williams, the U.S. attorney for the Southern District of New York. Bankman-Fried himself spent most of the day in court staring into a laptop while seated between his two attorneys. The prosecution's account of his alleged crimes was described as featuring a study in contrasts.



---


# The Prosecution's Opening Statement Against Bankman-Fried

Thane Rehn, a prosecutor for the government, opened the case against Sam Bankman-Fried with the line "One year ago, it looked like the defendant was on the top of the world," and then argued that this appearance was false: "all of that, all of it, was built on lies," he declared to the jury, adding "Behind the curtains, he was not what he appeared to be." Rehn described a defendant who, as former CEO of FTX, oversaw a supposedly thriving crypto exchange, jetted between international locales, hobnobbed with celebrities like Tom Brady and Larry David, and repeatedly emphasized to customers that their money was safe and secure.

What followed was a roughly 30-minute story that repeatedly emphasized how Bankman-Fried allegedly stole customer funds to facilitate his jet-setting lifestyle, donate millions to political candidates, and finance risky bets. Rehn also directly contested the media framing of the defendant: he was not a crypto "boy" genius, as so many in the media — Fortune included — have written, but a "man" who "stole billions of dollars from thousands of victims." Rehn closed the characterization with a promise to the jury: "You will see the full picture."
