# The Artificial Intelligence Advancement Act Of 2023

Tuesday's Senate AI forum followed the recent introduction of new AI legislation dubbed the Artificial Intelligence Advancement Act of 2023 (S. 3050), co-sponsored by Senators Martin Heinrich (D-NM), Mike Rounds (R-SD), Charles Schumer (D-NY) and Todd Young (R-IN).

The bill proposes AI bug bounty programs and would require a vulnerability analysis study for AI-enabled military applications. Its passage into law would also launch a report into AI regulation in the financial services industry, as well as a second report on data sharing and coordination.

The financial-services provision lands on a problem the SEC's own chairman has been lamenting. "It's frankly a hard challenge," SEC Chairman Gary Gensler told The Financial Times recently, speaking on the challenges the financial industry faces in AI adoption and regulation. "It's a hard financial stability issue to address because most of our regulation is about individual institutions, individual banks, individual money market funds, individual brokers; it's just in the nature of what we do."



---


# The Biden AI Executive Order Of October 2023

The Biden Administration unveiled its next steps in addressing and regulating artificial intelligence development on Monday: an expansive executive order (EO) that seeks to establish further protections for the public as well as improve best practices for federal agencies and their contractors.

The order is framed as a whole-of-government instrument. "The President several months ago directed his team to pull every lever," a senior administration official told reporters on a recent press call. "That's what this order does, bringing the power of the federal government to bear in a wide range of areas to manage AI's risk and harness its benefits ... It stands up for consumers and workers, promotes innovation and competition, advances American leadership around the world and like all executive orders, this one has the force of law."

Its provisions are phased rather than immediate. The actions will be introduced over the next year, with smaller safety and security changes happening in around 90 days and more involved reporting and data transparency schemes requiring nine to 12 months to fully deploy. To keep that schedule, the administration is also creating an "AI council," chaired by White House Deputy Chief of Staff Bruce Reed, who will meet with federal agency heads to ensure the actions are being executed on time.



---


# Critical Infrastructure And CBRN Provisions Of The AI Executive Order

The executive order encourages the Departments of Energy and Homeland Security to address AI threats "to critical infrastructure, as well as chemical, biological, radiological, nuclear, and cybersecurity risks," and it attaches those standards to money: "Agencies that fund life-science projects will establish these standards as a condition of federal funding, creating powerful incentives to ensure appropriate screening and manage risks potentially made worse by AI." In short, any developers found in violation of the EO can likely expect a prompt and unpleasant visit from the DoE, FDA, EPA or other applicable regulatory agency, regardless of their AI model's age or processing speed.

The order also looks to use AI defensively. In an effort to proactively address the decrepit state of America's digital infrastructure, it seeks to establish a cybersecurity program, based loosely on the administration's existing AI Cyber Challenge, to develop AI tools that can autonomously root out and shore up security vulnerabilities in critical software infrastructure. It remains to be seen whether those systems will be able to address the concerns of misbehaving models that SEC head Gary Gensler recently raised.



---


# Foundation Model Reporting And Red-Team Disclosure Under The EO

The executive order sets out a reporting procedure for the most capable AI systems: a company developing any foundation model that poses a serious risk to national security, national economic security, or national public health and safety must notify the federal government when training the model, and must share the results of all red-team safety tests — and that information must be shared prior to the model being made available to the public, which could help reduce the rate at which companies unleash half-baked and potentially deadly machine learning products. The legal instrument used to compel this is the Defense Production Act.

Alongside red-team results, the EO also requires disclosure of the system's training runs — essentially its iterative development history. The purpose officials gave for the sequencing is verification: "What that does is that creates a space prior to the release… to verify that the system is safe and secure." The EO more broadly directs the establishment of new standards for AI safety and security, including reporting requirements for developers whose foundation models might impact national or economic security, and those requirements also apply in developing AI tools to autonomously implement security fixes on critical software infrastructure.

The procedure has a deliberately narrow scope. Administration officials were quick to point out that the reporting requirement will not affect any AI models currently available on the market, nor independent or small- to medium-size AI companies going forward, because the threshold for enforcement is quite high. It is geared specifically at the next generation of systems that the likes of Google, Meta and OpenAI are already working on, with enforcement on models starting at 10^26 petaflops — a capacity currently beyond the limits of existing AI models. "This is not going to catch AI systems trained by graduate students, or even professors," the administration official said.

The order was cast as a step past voluntary measures. "In response to the President's leadership on the subject, 15 major American technology companies have begun their voluntary commitments to ensure that AI technology is safe, secure and trustworthy before releasing it to the public," the senior administration official said. "That is not enough."



---


# The CPPA's Risk-Based Approach Versus The EU AI Act

The CPPA's approach to regulating ADMT is risk-based, per Soltani. That echoes another piece of in-train EU legislation, the AI Act — a dedicated risk-based framework for regulating applications of artificial intelligence which has been on the table in draft form since 2021 but is now at a delicate stage of co-legislation, with the bloc's lawmakers clashing over the not-so-tiny detail of how, or even whether, to regulate Big AI, among several other policy disputes on the file.

The relation TechCrunch draws between the two is one of comparative advantage under discord: given the disagreement around the EU's AI Act, as well as the ongoing failure of US lawmakers to pass a comprehensive federal privacy law — since there is only so much presidential Executive Orders can do — there is a plausible prospect of California ending up as one of the top global rulemakers on AI.

That relation holds only over a limited range. The impact of California's AI rules is likely to remain local, given its focus on affording protections and controls to state residents. In-scope companies might choose to go further, such as offering the same package of privacy protections to residents of other US states, but that is up to them; the bottom line is that the CPPA's reach and enforcement is tied to the California border.



---


# The EU AI Office And Its Scientific Advisory Panel

The AI Act will be implemented through a new AI Office set up within the EU's executive, which will coordinate with the Member State oversight bodies that will need to enforce the rules on AI firms and will oversee the most advanced AI models, including by contributing to fostering standards and testing practices — with a scientific panel of independent experts appointed to advise it about GPAI models.

Per internal market commissioner Thierry Breton, work to implement the agreement starts immediately with the set up of the AI Office. "We will welcome new colleagues… a lot of them," said Breton. "We will work — starting tomorrow — to get ready." The AI Office will play a key role in setting risk classification thresholds for GPAIs, but the Commission confirmed there is no budget nor headcount defined for the expert body as yet. Asked about resourcing, a Commission official said it will be decided in the future by the EU's executive taking "an appropriate and official decision," adding: "The idea is that we can create a dedicated budget line for the Office and that we will be able also to recruit the national experts from Member States if we wish to on top of contractual agents and on top of permanent staff. And some of these staff will also be deployed within the European Commission."

The scientific advisory panel, which the law will also establish, is meant to help the Office better understand the capabilities of advanced AI models for the purpose of regulating systemic risk. "We have identified an important role for a scientific panel to be set up where the scientific panel can effectively help the Artificial Intelligence Office in understanding whether there are new risks that have not been yet identified," the official noted. "And, for example, also flag some alerts about the models that are not captured by the FLOP threshold that for certain reasons could actually give rise to important risks that governments should should look at."



---


# EU AI Act Scope Exclusions For National Security And Research

The AI Act does not apply to areas outside the scope of EU law, and the Council's press release on the deal emphasizes that the provisional agreement "clarifies that the regulation does not apply to areas outside the scope of EU law and should not, in any case, affect member states' competences in national security or any entity entrusted with tasks in this area."

The Council also confirmed that the AI Act will not apply to systems exclusively for military or defence purposes. A further exclusion covers early-stage and non-commercial use: "Similarly, the agreement provides that the regulation would not apply to AI systems used for the sole purpose of research and innovation, or for people using AI for non-professional reasons," the Council added.

qid: After TechCrunch reported on November 6, 2023, that Google provided extensive evidence to counter Epic Games' claims in their antitrust battle, did the consistency of Google's stance on antitrust issues remain unchanged according to a later report by TechCrunch on December 15, 2023, regarding a class action lawsuit filed by a news publisher against Google?
context:
# Google's Parallel Antitrust Proceedings In Late 2023

As of mid-November 2023, Google was fighting antitrust on more than one front at once. The Epic Games case was not its only antitrust case in trial: Google had settled a separate antitrust lawsuit with dating site Match Group the week before November 13, and on November 6 it went to trial with Fortnite maker Epic Games, which hoped to prove that Google engages in anticompetitive behavior with regard to its Android app store, Google Play, and its commission structure. Separately, Google was involved in an antitrust lawsuit with the Department of Justice over its alleged search monopoly.

The Epic case had shed co-plaintiffs on its way to trial. Epic's lawsuit originally involved Match and several U.S. attorneys general, but Google reached a settlement with the attorneys general in October 2023 and with Match the week before November 6, so Epic fought the antitrust battle on its own. The lawsuit, held in the U.S. District Court in California's Northern District, would include testimony from a number of Google and Android execs, including CEO Sundar Pichai, and Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, as well as from Apple, Netflix and other Android developers. Epic, meanwhile, had lost its antitrust battle with Apple and was asking the Supreme Court to weigh in.



---


# Epic v. Google: What The Trial Is

Epic v. Google is the antitrust case in which Fortnite publisher Epic Games drags a tech giant into court alleging that its mobile app store is an illegal monopoly — and although Epic's parallel claims against Apple already got their day in court, the similar lawsuit against Google never did, which is why the case goes to trial on November 6th, a mere 1,180 days after Epic originally sued.

The déjà vu is the point of confusion the piece sets out to clear up: Epic already went to trial with Apple, resulting in a ruling where Apple mostly won, and its Llamacorn legal gambit failed to #FreeFortnite years ago. The distinction is that the Apple claims were heard and the Google ones were not.

An update dated December 15th, 2023 notes that the case is basically over by then.



---


# Epic Games v. Google Goes To Trial On November 6, 2023

Epic Games, the maker of Fortnite, went to trial with Google on November 6, 2023, hoping to convince a jury that Google engages in anticompetitive behavior with regard to its Android app store, Google Play, and its commission structure. Match had settled its own antitrust lawsuit with Google the week before, but Epic's case proceeded.

This case differs slightly from Epic's battle with Apple on the same topic, because this time Epic cannot allege there is no other way to load apps onto Android devices, as it could with Apple: Android does allow for sideloading apps. Epic will suggest Google makes that process cumbersome, but the bulk of its arguments will center on what it believes are anticompetitive agreements between Google and device manufacturers and developers.

The precedent Epic's case relies on is a Microsoft case in which courts found Microsoft to have a monopoly over the operating system and to be abusing it, making it hard for users to download alternative browsers, like Netscape, on Windows devices. To make its case, Epic plans to bring claims under Sections 1 and 2 of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act, as well as California's anticompetitive laws, the Cartwright Act and the Unfair Competition Law. It will attempt to argue that Google restrains competition within two separate markets: the distribution of apps to Android users, and the market for payment processing solutions for content inside Android apps.



---


# The Settlements That Left Epic Standing Alone

Other plaintiffs brought app store antitrust claims against Google and then all settled: all 50 state attorneys general and a number of consumers have tentatively settled, though it is not clear what the deal might include, and Match Group — the company behind Tinder, Match.com, OkCupid and other dating apps — just reached a surprise last-minute settlement too, one that makes it sound like Match effectively gave up. Epic stands alone.

Epic seems to have no interest in settling as long as the "Google tax" exists, and the company has repeatedly said it is not interested in cash. So far it has been willing to push these cases all the way through multiple appeals, cost be damned. It is not clear what Google could proactively offer that would satisfy Epic, since CEO Tim Sweeney has also publicly suggested that Google would simply circumvent any settlement it offers. If you want to see a vision of a future Epic would accept, look to the letter it sent to state attorneys general, laying out a settlement that would basically prohibit Google from doing the anticompetitive things Epic claims it did. Google would not tell The Verge whether it has offered Epic any kind of settlement.



---


# The U.S. Justice Department's Parallel Antitrust Suits Against Google

The Helena World Chronicle class action arrives alongside the filing of the U.S. Justice Department's lawsuit against Google for monopolizing digital ad technologies, and the complaint also references the Justice Department's 2020 civil antitrust suit over search and search advertising.

The two government cases concern different markets: search and search advertising in the 2020 suit are distinct from the digital ad technologies at issue in the more recent one.



---


# Helena World Chronicle's Class Action Antitrust Suit Against Google

A class action lawsuit filed in the week of 15 December 2023 in the U.S. District Court in D.C. accuses Google and parent company Alphabet of anticompetitive behavior in violation of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act and others, on behalf of news publishers. The case was filed by Arkansas-based publisher Helena World Chronicle, which argues that Google "siphons off" news publishers' content, their readers and their ad revenue through anticompetitive means, and it specifically cites new AI technologies such as Google's Search Generative Experience (SGE) and the Bard AI chatbot as worsening the problem.

Helena World Chronicle owns and publishes two weekly newspapers in Arkansas. In the complaint it argues that Google is "starving the free press" by sharing publishers' content on Google, losing them "billions of dollars."

Beyond damages, the suit asks for an injunction that would require Google to obtain consent from publishers before using their website data to train its general artificial intelligence products, including Google's own and those of rivals. It also asks that publishers who opt out of SGE still be allowed to show up in Google search results, among other things.

The law firm handling the case is Hausfeld, whose announcement states that "the anticompetitive effects of Google's scheme cause profound harm to competition, to consumers, to labor, and to a democratic free press," and that "Plaintiff Helena World Chronicle, LLC invokes the Sherman Act and Clayton Act to seek class-wide monetary and injunctive relief to restore and ensure competition for digital news and reference publishing and set up guardrails to preserve a free marketplace of ideas in the new era of artificial intelligence."



---


# The Epic v. Apple Ruling And Its Limited Weight Here

In the Apple case both sides lost, but Epic arguably lost more: even though Apple has incredible power over the iPhone, Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers ruled the company did not have an unfair monopoly in that case, partly because she decided the relevant market for Fortnite was "digital mobile gaming transactions" rather than, say, iPhone apps. She also decided that Epic violated its developer agreement with Apple and would have to pay.

Epic did win something. Rogers barred Apple from keeping iPhone users in the dark about alternate ways they can pay for apps, and may have even allowed developers to add their own payment mechanisms.

The precedent's reach into the Google trial is limited in two specific ways. First, that was a different case — and it is not over until the Supreme Court weighs in or declines to take a look. Second, Google cannot tell jurors that Apple won its case, or that other plaintiffs settled; the judge in this case says so. Epic declined to answer on the record when asked about the Apple outcome.



---


# Epic v. Google Is A Jury Trial

Epic and Google have to convince a jury, not the judge, which is totally different from how the Apple case played out — that one was a "bench trial."

The consequence is that persuasion cuts both ways and is hard to predict. All the evidence of tricky deals inside Google might sway a jury against the company; alternatively, Google scaremongering that sideloaded apps equal gaping security holes might sway a jury against Epic. Who knows.

The jury is also sealed off from coverage: Judge Donato explicitly told jurors they are in a "news-free bubble" through mid-December.



---


# The Epic v. Google Witness Lineup

A whole cast of intriguing people were set to be called as witnesses during the trial, going straight to the top of the org chart: Google CEO Sundar Pichai and Epic CEO Tim Sweeney are absolutely expected to attend.

Beyond the two chief executives, Android co-founder Andy Rubin might be deposed, and Google says the court will hear from current Android — and Chrome, and Chrome OS — boss Hiroshi Lockheimer. Google also says representatives from Apple, Netflix, Motorola, and AT&T should testify.

qid: Between the Sporting News report on the Minnesota Vikings' offensive performance published on November 13, 2023, and the Sporting News report on the Minnesota Vikings' performance against the Chicago Bears published on November 27, 2023, was there a change in the effectiveness of the Vikings' gameplay as reported by the same news source?
context:
# Playoff And Roster Stakes In Bears-Vikings On Monday Night

Heading into Week 13 on Nov. 27, 2023, the game was the difference between the No. 6 and No. 7 seed for the Vikings, with larger ramifications: a loss would leave the Packers, Rams and Saints trailing Minnesota by only a half-game in the wild-card race, while a win would keep the Vikings well within striking distance in the NFC North. After the 12-10 loss Minnesota (6-6) dropped to the No. 7 seed in the NFC with those three teams a half-game back; a win would have put the Vikings in position to compete for the division crown down the stretch, but merely holding a playoff spot would now be a battle for Kevin O'Connell's squad. Chicago's own hopes remained extraordinarily distant at 4-8.

The individual stakes centred on Justin Fields. Sporting News called the final six games critically important for a quarterback fighting to prove he is the Bears' franchise passer, and noted Chicago had a strong chance of landing the No. 1 overall pick in April's draft thanks to the Panthers' ugly season. On the night Fields flashed the good and the bad — excellent on Chicago's opening drive, though it ended without points, then undone by missed throws and costly turnovers that let the Vikings hang around — but when it mattered most he was poised and sealed the Bears' first win over an NFC North opponent since 2021. The Bears entered the night holding the No. 1 and No. 4 picks in the 2024 NFL Draft and would remain in those slots with or without a loss, thanks to the strength-of-schedule tiebreaker.

Availability shaped both sides. The Vikings were officially without Justin Jefferson, holding out their star receiver until they returned from their bye in Week 14, as Adam Schefter reported that day; D'Onta Foreman remained out for the Bears along with cornerback Tyrique Stevenson. Dobbs came in having shown good command of the Vikings' offense in three games since a trade out of Arizona, with an especially strong connection with T.J. Hockenson. Conditions were 15 degrees in Minnesota with a feels-like of 2, making the roof at U.S. Bank Stadium useful, and Vikings legend Adrian Peterson was in the building to watch his former team.



---


# Bears-Vikings Monday Night Broadcast Details

Chicago Bears vs. Minnesota Vikings kicked off at 8:15 p.m. ET (7:15 p.m. local time) on Monday, Nov. 27, 2023 from U.S. Bank Stadium in Minneapolis, Minn., televised on ESPN, which has long held the broadcast rights to Monday Night Football. Joe Buck led the broadcast as play-by-play announcer with Troy Aikman as color analyst and Lisa Salters providing updates from the sidelines.

Streaming was available via ESPN+ or Fubo, which offers a free trial, with viewers in Canada able to stream every NFL game via DAZN.

The series history favored the home side: the Bears had not beaten the Vikings since 2020, with Minnesota 6-1 against Chicago over the previous four seasons, and the Vikings were 8-3 at home in the fixture since 2012.



---


# Bears 12, Vikings 10 On Monday Night Football

Chicago beat Minnesota 12-10 on Monday Night Football on Nov. 27, 2023, by quarters of Bears 0-3-3-6 and Vikings 0-3-0-7, ending what Sporting News called the honeymoon period for Joshua Dobbs in Minnesota. The folk-hero quarterback threw four interceptions, leading a sluggish offense that did not find its footing until the fourth quarter in a game Minnesota would not have needed many points to win.

The Bears' defense swarmed Dobbs all night, sacking him only twice but generating a great deal of pressure as the defensive backs made plays. Despite the barrage of turnovers, Chicago largely failed to capitalize, scoring only three points off the four Dobbs interceptions.

Chicago's own first turnover — a deflating fumble by Justin Fields when the Bears had a chance to extend their lead to two possessions — was quickly turned into a Vikings touchdown. That score looked like it might be the difference, particularly after Fields fumbled away the ball again on the next possession, but the Bears' defense put the ball back in his hands in the final minutes and Fields delivered. Facing 3rd & 10 outside field goal range, he hit an open D.J. Moore for a 36-yard gain; from there Chicago only had to kneel and let Cairo Santos, who drilled the 30-yard attempt with 10 seconds remaining, seal it.



---


# The Third Quarter Of Bears 12, Vikings 10

Chicago led 6-3 at the end of the third quarter on Nov. 27, 2023, having added a field goal while Minnesota gave the ball away again. Alexander Mattison, who had drawn the ire of Vikings fans all season, started the second half with a booming 21-yard run, but the Bears answered immediately by sacking Dobbs with Montez Sweat and Jaquan Brisker taking him down. Kevin O'Connell then went for it on 4th & 7 and Hockenson gained only six; the play looked good but the Bears' defense looked better, and Chicago took over with favorable field position.

The Bears converted that into points, though not efficiently. Roschon Johnson, impressive in spurts, picked up a first down to keep the drive alive, Fields ran up the middle for another, and then a questionable third-down call had Fields throw behind the line of scrimmage to D.J. Moore for nothing — leaving Cairo Santos to extend the lead with a field goal at 9:58 p.m. for Bears 6, Vikings 3.

Minnesota's running game worked and its passing game did not: Mattison had 19 yards three plays into the next drive. A hold by Jaylon Johnson gifted the Vikings a first down, but they still could not capitalize, with Ty Chandler unable to make T.J. Edwards miss on third down, sending Minnesota to a fourth-down attempt. At 10:08 p.m. Dobbs threw his third interception of the night, deflected by Jaylon Johnson and caught by Edwards — leaving the Bears, interestingly, with less favorable field position than an incompletion would have given them. Chicago then started to look respectable on third down again, completing to Moore to move deeper into Vikings territory, though it might still need another first down to give Santos a fair shot.



---


# Prisco's Week 12 Sunday Night And Monday Night Picks

Pete Prisco's Week 12 prime-time picks, published by CBS Sports on 2023-11-23, cover two games. For the Sunday 8:20 p.m. ET game on NBC and fubo, he argued the Chargers are having major issues right now and face one of the best teams in the league; the Ravens offense will miss tight end Mark Andrews, but the Chargers defense is perfect for any team throwing the football, so the Ravens will win it with a big game from Lamar Jackson. Pick: Ravens 30, Chargers 23.

For the Monday 8:15 p.m. ET game on ABC/ESPN and fubo, he noted both teams were coming off tough losses, with the Bears blowing a huge lead late — though it was more damning for the Vikings, a team that had been surging. His warrant: Minnesota's defense will be the difference as they get the best of Justin Fields. Pick: Vikings 24, Bears 14.



---


# Alexander Mattison Vikings Hot Seat

Yardbarker's Nov. 30, 2023 NFC hot-seat roundup named running back Alexander Mattison as the Minnesota Vikings' hottest seat: he had floundered in his first season as the starter.

The grounds are production and volume together — zero rushing touchdowns on a career-best 13.2 attempts a game, and a rank of 22nd among qualified backs in yards per carry at 3.8. He was still getting more snaps than second-year RB Ty Chandler, but the Vikings would likely look for a replacement that offseason if Mattison did not show more. The warrant is that career-high usage without production leaves nothing to point to in defense of the job. The entry was written by Mike Santa Barbara.



---


# Vikings-Broncos Sunday Night Pregame And Broadcast

Before kickoff on Nov. 19, 2023, Vikings starting running back Alexander Mattison was confirmed active for Sunday Night Football after going through concussion protocol that week, as Adam Schefter reported. Broncos legend Peyton Manning showed some love to Vikings star receiver Justin Jefferson ahead of the game; Jefferson remained out with a hamstring injury.

The broadcast aired on NBC nationally, with viewers also able to stream the game on Fubo, which offers a free trial, in the U.S., and on DAZN, which carries NFL Game Pass, in Canada. Mike Tirico called play-by-play, with Cris Collinsworth as analyst and Melissa Stark reporting.

qid: Does the article from 'The Age' about Tyler Mitchell suggest that his career has been successful due to his early photography experiences, while the article from 'The Roar | Sports Writers Blog' about Graham Arnold indicates that his career choices involved staying with the Australian national team despite offers from Europe?
context:
# Graham Arnold Socceroos Coaching Appearance Record

Graham Arnold would prowl the technical area for a 59th time on the Thursday, taking him clear of Frank Farina as the Socceroos' record-holder for matches coached, in a match against Bangladesh as 2026 World Cup qualifying started, The Roar reported on Nov. 13, 2023.

On the Tuesday, Football Australia CEO James Johnson, who had held firm on Arnold 20 months earlier, congratulated the coach on the impending record-breaking match. In a remarkable few weeks the previous year Arnold had gone from on the nose to a man revived; since then he had been linked to club jobs in Europe but opted to stick with the national team. Arnold, in his second stint as national team manager, also represented the Socceroos 56 times as a player and has been involved in national team coaching ranks since 2000, first as an assistant to Farina and then Guus Hiddink, before a brief period as caretaker coach in 2006. "It's certainly a proud moment and an achievement that I'll reflect on when the time is right," Arnold said. "I look at some of the names on that list – Farina, Arok, Thompson, Rasic – guys I played under or assisted in the early part of my coaching career, and it gives you some perspective on what a journey it's been so far."



---


# Tyler Mitchell On His Career Trajectory And Artistic Outlook

Interviewed by The Age ahead of the NGV Triennial and published on 27 November 2023, Mitchell says early success does not unsettle him — "The idea of the road ahead only excites me" — and that he deliberately allows himself space for quiet periods and for work that does not come off.

He traces his choice of medium to impatience: "I was impatient when I got started and just wanted to make visual things now, and I didn't want to wait for permission, or didn't want to wait on equipment, or didn't want to lug large amounts of equipment up flights of stairs. I just wanted to make something that I felt compelled by, immediately." His career has only blossomed in the years since the trip that started him in photography, and where some artists might feel trepidation at so much success so early, he is clear-eyed about the rhythm of a long career: there will be "very quiet, sleepy periods, and frenetic periods, or hyperactive periods", and it is "always refreshing as a young person to see how the career of a much older, more senior artist has really gone" — senior artists we know and love today "had decades where they were out of style, out of fashion, people thought their work was done, their best work was behind them, and yet, often had resurgences".

Crafting a career, he says, means "allowing space for bad and good, allowing space for artists to make and work through complicated and sometimes not-so-favourable ideas. And I try to give myself that same space. It's only about giving yourself grace and space and thinking one day at a time." Asked about a dream project or collaborator, he says there are too many; with one monograph behind him — 2020's I Can Make You Feel Good — he is hungry to make more.



---


# Graham Arnold Reflections On Coaching Development

Reflecting on his milestone, Graham Arnold said his 2006 caretaker period taught him a great deal about coaching and that, on reflection, he probably was not ready for it — as quoted by The Roar on Nov. 13, 2023.

"I think back to that caretaker period and how much I learnt about coaching; it was a challenging experience and one that on reflection I probably wasn't ready for. I'm grateful for the opportunity I was given and what it was able to teach me ahead of my pathway into club coaching," he said. "I was able to put lessons from that time into practice, develop and eventually return to the Socceroos much more prepared for the role. It's been a privilege to be part of the national team again with the benefit of that experience, and I'm immensely proud of what this group has been able to achieve in the last four years. In my opinion, there's no greater honour than representing your nation on the international stage. I look at the young players coming through the Socceroos system now full of pride in the work they've put in to get where they are, and the journey that's ahead of them. I've always loved being a part of the Socceroos culture and my desire to see Australia fulfil its footballing potential is still driving me to take this group to further success."



---


# James Johnson Tribute To Graham Arnold

Football Australia CEO James Johnson paid tribute to Graham Arnold in a statement marking the coach's milestone, calling him one of the greatest contributors to the Socceroos, as reported by The Roar on Nov. 13, 2023.

"Graham is one of the greatest contributors to the Socceroos," Johnson said. "He's been a constant in the Australian football landscape for more than 30 years as both a player and coach, being a part of some of the Socceroos most memorable moments. Anyone who knows Arnie will tell you he bleeds green and gold. His love for the Socceroos and football in Australia is both infectious and inspiring. That energy and passion is a huge element to the way he's able to lead and inspire our nation's best male footballers in some of our sport's most challenging arenas. On behalf of Football Australia, I'd like to congratulate Arnie on everything he's achieved in reaching this milestone and we look forward to him continuing to build on what is already an exceptional legacy."



---


# Graham Arnold 2022 World Cup Qualification Crisis

In March 2022 Graham Arnold seemed a dead man walking — the Socceroos' World Cup qualification campaign was lurching towards failure and the manager was being battered from all sides, The Roar recounted on Nov. 13, 2023.

Arnold's team had finished seven points off automatic qualification for Qatar after a shocking run of one win in seven games, leaving them facing an Asian playoff against the United Arab Emirates and then another against Peru to make the finals. While rumours swirled and ex-players and fans bayed for his blood, Football Australia took the pragmatic course and stuck by Arnold — a decision that likely had more to do with the lateness of the hour and financial considerations than any overwhelming faith in Arnie to turn around the fortunes. But he did just that, with qualification and an excellent run at the finals, bowing out to eventual champions Argentina after nearly taking them to extra time. He also got to answer critics like Mark Bosnich and Craig Foster, bluntly rejecting their negativity with a dismissive "who cares?" — which would have tasted sweet.



---


# Tyler Mitchell's Vogue Covers And NGV Triennial Works

Tyler Mitchell was just 23 when he became the first Black photographer to shoot the cover of American Vogue, photographing Beyoncé, and in November 2023 three of his works were on show in the NGV's Triennial exhibition, The Age reported on 27 November 2023.

His dreamy, delicately hued Beyoncé portraits spoke of a precocious visual talent, and in the five years since he has exhibited around the world, become an Instagram darling with more than 500,000 followers, and shot what became the most controversial vice-presidential portrait in living memory. When his portrait of Kamala Harris dressed in sneakers and casual clothing was chosen for the cover of Vogue for February 2021, the social media backlash was swift: critics questioned why his alternative image — in which Harris looked more vice-presidential — had not been used instead, and the magazine, bowing to outrage over the perceived lack of respect shown to the first woman to reach such high office, later issued a limited edition using the more formal shot. The controversy did little to dent the New York-based photographer's reputation as a rising star of the medium.

Of the three Triennial works, Picnic depicts a family gathering — young men throwing a football, a child lifted on shoulders, wicker baskets and a thermos, and in the background a darkened wood that perhaps hints at the fragility of a moment so peaceful and pure. In the others his figures are arranged across a sandy expanse in idealised depictions of Black American leisure: in Albany, Georgia a football flies through the air, a father in dress shirt and tails twirls a child, and a young boy rides a toy truck; Vastness focuses on a teenage boy standing patiently as his younger siblings stretch his wildly elongated sleeves out beside him, with a dog nearby sitting listening to a violinist. These carefully staged set-ups are evidence of Mitchell's desire to establish a new visual narrative for Black Americans.



---


# Jordan Morgan's Senior Day At Arizona Stadium

Fifth-year senior captain Jordan Morgan, who had missed his opportunity to play in Senior Day the previous season due to injury, said that being able to compete and win in his final game at Arizona Stadium "means so much." The Tucson native was playing at home for the last time in his career.

"I finally got to finish off with a bang like this at home for the last time in my career, so really enjoyed it," Morgan said.

qid: Did the TechCrunch article on the Google antitrust case report a different amount of money spent by Google in 2021 to maintain its default search engine status across various platforms than the amount cited in another TechCrunch article discussing payments for default search engine status?
context:
# Google Paid $26.3 Billion In 2021 For Default Search Placement

Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to multiple browsers, phones and platforms — from companies including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla — to be everyone's default search engine. The figure was revealed by Google's search head Prabhakar Raghavan when he testified in court on October 28, according to The Verge.

About $18 billion of that total went directly to Apple, according to a New York Times report published earlier in October 2023, and Google has had its deal with Apple in place since 2003 — so the payment is the current year of a two-decade arrangement, not a one-off. Questioned on the amount of money Google spends to get first pick of search engines, Pichai said the decision was made with the consumer in mind: Google pays big bucks to be everywhere so that it can take in all the data and be the best search engine across different companies' devices, he said, according to The Verge.

The trial also produced evidence that Google understood the value of defaults very early on. U.S. Justice Department lawyer Meagan Bellshaw showed Pichai a 2007 email from a Google product strategy meeting containing data showing that when people changed their browser homepage to Google, they did 15% more Google searches, and that when they switched away, their Google searches dropped 27%. The email summarizing that meeting, sent to Pichai as well as other Google leaders, read: "Nitin argues that focusing on homepage market share is one of the most effective things we can do to make gains in search market share," according to The Verge.



---


# Default Search Engine

## Definition

The default search engine is the search provider a device, browser, or platform is pre-configured to use unless a user actively changes the setting — the search box that runs when a person types a query without first choosing an alternative, such as Google on the iPhone's Safari address bar or Firefox's search bar.

## Context

The term is central to *US v. Google*, the DOJ's antitrust case, because default status is the mechanism through which Google secures the overwhelming share of search queries: the Information Services Agreement (ISA) between Apple and Google, in place since 2002/2003, makes Google the default on all Apple devices, and Google separately pays Samsung, Mozilla, and other partners for the same status.
Apple executive Eddy Cue testified that Apple's iPhone setup flow deliberately omits any search-engine choice screen, arguing that presenting users with unfamiliar alternatives would harm the setup experience, while conceding the ISA does not permit Apple to offer such a choice.
Google spent $26.3 billion in 2021 on default-placement deals across browsers, phones, and platforms — about $18 billion of that to Apple alone — a scale that the DOJ used to argue Google understands the mechanism's value: internal 2007 data showed users who set Google as their homepage searched 15% more, while switching away dropped searches 27%.
The Mozilla/Yahoo episode shows the same mechanism working in reverse: when Firefox switched its default from Google to Yahoo under a 2014 deal, Mozilla's CEO testified that user retention declined, illustrating how disruptive changing the default can be even when a paying competitor is involved.
Outside the antitrust trial, the term also frames ordinary consumer behavior: an investor in e-commerce search startup Deft described users' "natural behavior" as following the path of least resistance and just using the default search engine, meaning challenger search products must offer a high-value proposition to displace that inertia.

## Key Characteristics

- **Set by agreement, not by user choice** — default status on major platforms (Apple's Safari/iOS, Android OEMs, Firefox) is typically established through commercial deals (e.g., the Apple-Google ISA, Yahoo-Mozilla's $375M/year deal) rather than user selection at setup.
- **Backed by large recurring payments** — Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 across partners to hold default placement, with roughly $18 billion of that going to Apple.
- **Technically reversible but rarely changed** — Apple and Google both argued switching is easy, but DuckDuckGo's CEO countered that it takes "too many steps" to switch, and Google's own 2005 complaint about Internet Explorer's defaults argued that "most end users do not change defaults," so default status functions as durable market power.
- **Distinct from pre-installation** — Google's separate push to get Chrome and Search merely pre-installed (not necessarily defaulted) on Android and iPhones shows default status is a stronger, more contested tier than simple presence on a device.
- **Drives user behavior even outside browsers** — the concept extends to any search product; consumers default to "the path of least resistance," which challenger search startups must specifically overcome.

# US v. Google: Two Months Into The Search Antitrust Trial

As of TechCrunch's November 13, 2023 roundup, the Justice Department's landmark antitrust case against Google was nearly two months old, and the trial record was still producing fresh revelations. TechCrunch framed it as one of the biggest fights in tech antitrust since the U.S. took Microsoft to trial in the 1990s.

An earlier roundup had already surfaced that Google spent $26.3 billion in 2021 making itself the default search engine across platforms, and that Google tried to have Chrome preinstalled on iPhones. Over the couple of weeks preceding this roundup, more of Google's inner workings came to light, including some of the search engine's most lucrative search queries, the shape of the revenue-share agreements between Google and Android OEMs, and why Expedia has a bone to pick with Google.

# The Google Antitrust Case

The Google antitrust case is the U.S. government's trial over Google's dominance in the online search market, stemming from a 2020 antitrust claim, in which the government argues that Google uses its platforms and its deals with partners to block out competition in search or advertising and thereby to hinder competitors from accessing the data they would need to improve their products.

Its defining features are the conduct at issue and the defence offered against it. Google CEO Sundar Pichai testified Monday in the trial, defending Google's business tactics, including its deal with Apple and other partners to make Google the default search engine. Google's answer is that it is just doing business: everybody wants Google as the default engine because it is the best, and that, the company says, does not make its actions illegal.

The important boundary case is which Google antitrust matter this is. The 2020 search claim is separate from the one filed in January by the Department of Justice, along with eight states including New York, California and Colorado, which aims to "halt Google's anticompetitive scheme, unwind Google's monopolistic grip on the market and restore competition to digital advertising." The search case and the digital-advertising case are distinct proceedings and should not be conflated.

The trial is the venue in which the underlying numbers surface. Monday's hearing revealed plenty of juicy tidbits, including the $26.3 billion Google spent making itself the default search engine across platforms in 2021, and how Google tried to take it further and have Chrome preinstalled on iPhones.



---


# Google's Agreement Not To Promote Chrome To Safari Users

As part of its search deal with Apple, Google agreed not to promote Chrome to Safari users, according to Bloomberg — a restraint that mattered because Google would otherwise have been able to do this with banners, pop-ups and other annoying means in its other Google apps. The same agreement also meant that Apple never switched to a Google competitor, and never allowed users to choose their browser when setting up their iPhones.

The observation surfaced in the antitrust trial, where the amount Google spent on homepage market share has been a fixing point. Earlier in October 2023, the CEOs of Microsoft and DuckDuckGo testified that their search engines would have been far more successful, even competitive with Google, had they been able to make similar deals with Apple. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella even said he was willing to spend $15 billion per year to get Bing into Apple's default search, per The Information — a stated willingness to pay, not a deal that happened.

A second, related admission came from Google's side: Pichai admitted to attempting to get Tim Cook to preinstall Google on every iOS device back in 2018, according to The Verge. His aim, as reported, was to make Google's and Apple's services so connected as to be inseparable.

# The U.S. Justice Department's Parallel Antitrust Suits Against Google

The Helena World Chronicle class action arrives alongside the filing of the U.S. Justice Department's lawsuit against Google for monopolizing digital ad technologies, and the complaint also references the Justice Department's 2020 civil antitrust suit over search and search advertising.

The two government cases concern different markets: search and search advertising in the 2020 suit are distinct from the digital ad technologies at issue in the more recent one.

Spotify reported an operating profit for the first time in a year, sending the stock up nearly 10 percent, with the revenue bump largely due to the streamer's $1 price increase earlier in 2023 — but executives also pointed to the downsizing of the podcast operation, which included hundreds of layoffs and the dissolution of Gimlet and Parcast, as a contributing factor. # OpenAI's Nonprofit Governance And Capped-Profit Structure

OpenAI's for-profit subsidiary, OpenAI Global, LLC, is fully controlled by OpenAI's nonprofit: the subsidiary is permitted to commercialize its technology, but it is subject to the nonprofit's mission of attaining artificial general intelligence (AGI), which OpenAI defines as AI that can "outperform humans at most economically valuable work."

The discriminating feature of this structure is where the power over AGI sits. The nonprofit OpenAI's board has the power both to determine when the company has achieved AGI and to exclude that AGI from IP licenses and other commercial terms — including terms with Microsoft, one of OpenAI's biggest investors and a steadfast integrator of OpenAI's technologies. The gap between vendor hype and buyer behaviour is the context. To hear the hype from vendors, you would think enterprise buyers are all in on generative AI, but like any newer technology, large companies tend to move cautiously; throughout the year, as vendors feverishly announced new generative AI-fueled products, CIOs took note. Some companies have actually been looking to cut back on spending, or at least stay even, rather than looking for new ways to spend money, with the big exception being when technology enables companies to operate more efficiently and do more with less.

Generative AI certainly has the potential to do that, but it also carries its own costs — whether a higher cost for these features in a SaaS product or the price of hitting a large language model API when building software internally — so it is important for the people implementing the technology to understand whether they are getting a return on their investment.
