# Critical Infrastructure And CBRN Provisions Of The AI Executive Order

The executive order encourages the Departments of Energy and Homeland Security to address AI threats "to critical infrastructure, as well as chemical, biological, radiological, nuclear, and cybersecurity risks," and it attaches those standards to money: "Agencies that fund life-science projects will establish these standards as a condition of federal funding, creating powerful incentives to ensure appropriate screening and manage risks potentially made worse by AI." In short, any developers found in violation of the EO can likely expect a prompt and unpleasant visit from the DoE, FDA, EPA or other applicable regulatory agency, regardless of their AI model's age or processing speed.

The order also looks to use AI defensively. In an effort to proactively address the decrepit state of America's digital infrastructure, it seeks to establish a cybersecurity program, based loosely on the administration's existing AI Cyber Challenge, to develop AI tools that can autonomously root out and shore up security vulnerabilities in critical software infrastructure. It remains to be seen whether those systems will be able to address the concerns of misbehaving models that SEC head Gary Gensler recently raised.



---


# Foundation Model Reporting And Red-Team Disclosure Under The EO

The executive order sets out a reporting procedure for the most capable AI systems: a company developing any foundation model that poses a serious risk to national security, national economic security, or national public health and safety must notify the federal government when training the model, and must share the results of all red-team safety tests — and that information must be shared prior to the model being made available to the public, which could help reduce the rate at which companies unleash half-baked and potentially deadly machine learning products. The legal instrument used to compel this is the Defense Production Act.

Alongside red-team results, the EO also requires disclosure of the system's training runs — essentially its iterative development history. The purpose officials gave for the sequencing is verification: "What that does is that creates a space prior to the release… to verify that the system is safe and secure." The EO more broadly directs the establishment of new standards for AI safety and security, including reporting requirements for developers whose foundation models might impact national or economic security, and those requirements also apply in developing AI tools to autonomously implement security fixes on critical software infrastructure.

The procedure has a deliberately narrow scope. Administration officials were quick to point out that the reporting requirement will not affect any AI models currently available on the market, nor independent or small- to medium-size AI companies going forward, because the threshold for enforcement is quite high. It is geared specifically at the next generation of systems that the likes of Google, Meta and OpenAI are already working on, with enforcement on models starting at 10^26 petaflops — a capacity currently beyond the limits of existing AI models. "This is not going to catch AI systems trained by graduate students, or even professors," the administration official said.

The order was cast as a step past voluntary measures. "In response to the President's leadership on the subject, 15 major American technology companies have begun their voluntary commitments to ensure that AI technology is safe, secure and trustworthy before releasing it to the public," the senior administration official said. "That is not enough."

That statement frames HIPAA as the first, foundational layer of a security stack described in the same quote — ahead of encryption in transit and at rest, multi-factor authentication, and security audits and penetration testing, before the statement closes on ongoing staff training and a strict privacy policy. A separate paragraph attributes further remarks to Wilkins naming an additional external-review layer (Coalition Cybersecurity and Stendard) on top of that stack, distinct from the quoted statement itself. The regulation is invoked specifically because Keep Labs provides real-time and de-identified aggregate patient-adherence data to enterprise healthcare partners such as the McKesson Digital Health Network in Canada, which is the kind of health data flow that data-protection regulation like HIPAA is meant to govern.

## Key Characteristics

- **Named as a compliance baseline, not explained** — the corpus cites HIPAA as a regulation a health-data company adheres to but does not state what obligations it imposes.
- **Paired with a Canadian counterpart** — Keep Labs names HIPAA (U.S.) and PIPEDA (Canada) together as the two jurisdictions' data-protection regimes it follows, reflecting its cross-border footprint (U.S. consumers, Canadian enterprise partnership).

The corpus names HIPAA without defining it, so this section fills the gap from the web, quarantined from the scored sections above. "It's another game where we've dominated a game of football but we haven't taken advantage," Postecoglou said. "I thought we were poor in both areas with our finishing and also both goals we conceded were terrible."

He then refused the consolations available to him and named the only remedy he would accept: "There's no point in feeling sorry for ourselves, looking for a cuddle anywhere. There's only one way to change our circumstances and that is to come here on Sunday and put in a performance, not just play good football but go out there and show some conviction about ourselves as a team." He tied that to a standard he says he set on arrival: "Sometimes we can disguise how we're going by playing some nice stuff but like I said from day one, that's not what I'm about. I want to win and that's why I came to this football club and that's the message. We've still got a long way to go, I've said that from the start, we're still right at the beginning what we need to create and days like today just give me further evidence and fuel of how much we need to do."

# Ten Hag's Defence Of Manchester United's Performance

Erik ten Hag tried to put a positive spin on the defeat to West Ham on 23 December 2023 by claiming to the BBC that his side were the better team before the first goal: the claim is that the loss came from a single lapse rather than a systemic failure, and the warrant is that United created the better chances and had recently matched the top of the league.

His grounds for the first part are the shape of the match: "I think it was a decent 72 minutes where we didn't take our chances. We should've gone in the lead but we didn't and then it was one moment of switching off."

# Jaguars Survive Late Saints Rally To Win 31-24 On Thursday Night Football

Jacksonville beat New Orleans 31-24 in the Week 7 "Thursday Night Football" game on Thursday, Oct. 19, 2023, surviving a late scare at the Caesars Superdome. Doug Pederson's crew improved to 5-2 and extended its winning streak to four games, while the loss dropped the Saints to 3-4.

The Jaguars controlled most of the game, building an early first-half lead and entering the fourth quarter up 24-9, at which point the Saints offense was completely out of sync — Derek Carr had just thrown a pick-six to Foye Oluokun and was struggling to connect with any key weapon other than running back Alvin Kamara. But Trevor Lawrence and the Jaguars failed to put the game away, and New Orleans scored two fourth-quarter touchdowns to tie the game with less than six minutes to go, with the momentum fully shifted to the home side. Christian Kirk then broke loose for a 44-yard touchdown after an exchange of punts, retaking the lead for Jacksonville with 3:08 remaining. New Orleans nearly tied it in the final seconds: tight end Foster Moreau had a touchdown in his fingertips on third-and-goal but could not hold the catch, and a fourth-down pass to Chris Olave was broken up. The quarter-by-quarter line was Jaguars 7-10-7-7 for 31 and Saints 3-3-3-15 for 24.

Kickoff was 8:15 p.m. ET (7:15 p.m. CT), the normal start time for all of Amazon's "TNF" games in 2023; because the game was in New Orleans, in the Central time zone, local viewers saw it at 7:15 p.m. Historically the Saints had the Jaguars' number: in seven meetings between the franchises New Orleans held a 5-2 record and a four-game winning streak, and the previous meeting, in 2019, was a 13-9 Saints win in a defensive battle.

# Howe On Newcastle's Inconsistency And Injury Load

Eddie Howe accepted after the 3-0 defeat at Everton on 7 December 2023 that Newcastle have to do better, while attributing the inconsistency to an inability to rotate: the claim is that there are reasons behind every performance, and the warrant is that the quality of players unavailable makes it harder the longer the run goes on.

The Roar frames the pattern Howe was answering for: his side are proving one of the most inconsistent in the league, albeit with a lengthy injury list. In the previous month they had defeated Manchester United, Arsenal and Chelsea, and drawn at French heavyweights PSG in the Champions League, but had now lost comfortably to two cellar dwellers in Everton and Bournemouth.

"We have to do better," Howe said. "There are reasons behind every performance and we have struggled to change players. That is a big miss with the quality of players out. The longer you do it, the harder it gets. I am disappointed, a missed opportunity, we did not grab it." He also located the turning point within the match itself: "The game was there for us to win in the second half. The first half was even and we had them penned in in the second half. We conceded the first goal and it changed the momentum of the match. Frustrating and a chance missed."

qid: Does the article from FOX News - Entertainment suggest that Arnold Schwarzenegger and Reese Witherspoon advocate for a similar parenting style, as opposed to the article from The Independent - Life and Style which discusses the issue of parental controls with Roblox?
context:
# Celebrity Tough-Love Parenting In Hollywood

"Tough-love parenting" is FOX News Entertainment's 10 October 2023 label for the harsher styles some celebrities have described in interviews, prompted by the fact that Hollywood is a tough place to raise kids.

The category has two discriminating strands. The first is disciplinary severity: stars like Arnold Schwarzenegger, who admitted to being like a "drill instructor" when his kids were young, and Reese Witherspoon, who said she wants kids to deal with failure more directly.

The second is a wealth-and-gratitude strand: others, like Ashton Kutcher and Mila Kunis and Kristen Bell and Dax Shepard, are focused on keeping their kids grateful for growing up in famous families with wealth and privilege at their fingertips.



---


# Schwarzenegger's Warning On "A Generation Of Wimps"

Arnold Schwarzenegger warned on "The Howard Stern Show" that if young people are over-pampered, the nation may be "creating a generation of wimps and weak people", FOX News Entertainment reported on 10 October 2023.

His grounds are a claim about how character forms: "You can only strengthen your character and become a really strong person inside if you have resistance, if you fail, if you get up again and if you work hard."

The warrant joining the two is that pampering removes exactly the resistance, failure and effort he identifies as the mechanism of strength — so protecting children from hardship produces weakness rather than preventing it. The former California governor issued the warning recently, in the context of his own disciplinarian parenting.



---


# Roblox's Response On Its Parental Safety Tools

Roblox rejected the premise of Sarah Michelle Gellar's complaint that it lacks parental help, telling The Independent that such tools already exist and that the company was investigating her case. "We are looking into this case and we reached out directly to the user to help. We are committed to ensuring that our users have a positive experience on the platform," a spokesperson said.

The substance of the rebuttal is the provision the company says is already in place: "In partnership with safety groups, we've developed tools and resources like our Parent & Caregiver Guide and other helpful resources for parents to have conversations with their kids and teens about staying safe, spending controls and protecting their account. Our support team works with parents and users directly 24/7 and can be contacted with questions here," the spokesperson added, including a link to the company's support page.



---


# Arnold Schwarzenegger's "Drill Instructor" Discipline

Arnold Schwarzenegger recently admitted he had a "drill instructor" approach to parenting when his children were young, telling People while promoting his new book that he once burned his daughter Katherine's shoes in front of her, FOX News Entertainment reported on 10 October 2023.

Schwarzenegger, who shares four children with ex-wife Maria Shriver and also shares a son with Mildred Baena, the family's former housekeeper, recalled a moment when Katherine brought over her 3-year-old daughter Lyla and he saw the lesson passed down: "Katherine comes over with Lyla, and she says, 'Lyla, I told you already not to put the shoes there. Keep your shoes on, or you put them away, but you don't leave them there by the stand in front of the fireplace because you know what Daddy did? When I left my shoes there twice? The third time, he burned them in front of me and I cried,'" he said. Schwarzenegger said the story was "absolutely" true and took pride in knowing that Katherine uses the same methods, "which she cried over, and she complained about", with Lyla as well as her other daughter Eloise, both of whom she shares with husband Chris Pratt.

The 76-year-old described similar approaches with his eldest son Patrick. When Patrick was 9 and had not made his bed, Schwarzenegger threw his mattress off the balcony: "I opened up the door to the balcony, picked up the mattress and threw it down with the bedsheets, the pillows, everything. I said, 'Don't ever make someone come in and clean your room, clean your shower or make your bed… Because I taught you how to make the bed.'" He also battled over shower time with Patrick, feeling he was taking too long, and installed a timer similar to ones he had used in Munich: "And so when he got the shower on, and he was whistling and singing in there and thinking Daddy's not around, all the sudden the ice-cold shower came on. And all of a sudden, we heard downstairs the scream."



---


# The Social Media Reaction To Gellar's Roblox Feud

Many users on X, formerly known as Twitter, were surprised by Sarah Michelle Gellar's unexpected feud with the online gaming platform. Responding to her Instagram Story, one person said: "This is the most important beef of 2023." Another joked: "Buffy vs Roblox is where all this Millennial vs Gen Z discourse has been heading."

Reactions were not uniformly sympathetic. While one user agreed that "being hacked on Roblox is life ruining," another questioned why Gellar's 11-year-old son had access to his mother's credit card in the first place: "Oh please. # Gellar And Prinze's Strict Household Rules

Freddie Prinze Jr. said he and Sarah Michelle Gellar "are strict as hell" with their two children, and that Gellar has "100 rules" the kids know they cannot break, in a 2021 Us Weekly interview reported by FOX News Entertainment on 10 October 2023.

# Sarah Michelle Gellar's Complaint After Her Son's Roblox Account Was Hacked

Sarah Michelle Gellar, 46, publicly criticised Roblox on 4 December 2023 after her son's account on the platform was allegedly hacked, forcing her to cancel her credit card. The Buffy the Vampire Slayer star — who shares son Rocky, 11, and daughter Charlotte Grace, 14, with husband Freddie Prinze Jr — posted to her Instagram Story a screenshot from her iPhone showing a notification that her iCloud account "has been disabled" in the App Store and iTunes.

Candace Cameron Bure described her parenting style to L.A. Parent as strict but loving — "We set firm boundaries, but there is always love and grace" — and said her goal is not to make her kids happy but to guide them into responsible adults, FOX News Entertainment reported on 10 October 2023.

The "Full House" star is a mom of three with husband Valeri Bure — Natasha, Lev and Maksim, all now in their early 20s — and spoke to the outlet when they were teenagers. "I hope my kids would say that I'm a loving mom," she said. "They would also describe me as strict." She continued: "I'm the mom that needs to meet the parents before my kids can go to a new friend's house. I want to know who they're with, where they're going. Even now that they're driving, I want them to text me when they arrive and when they're heading home."

My goal as a parent is not to make my kids happy but to guide them to be respectful, curious, responsible, resilient, kind, giving and thoughtful adults."

qid: Was there inconsistency in the portrayal of Sam Bankman-Fried's involvement in the FTX collapse between the TechCrunch report published on October 6, 2023, and the TechCrunch report published on October 7, 2023?
context:
# Sam Bankman-Fried

Sam Bankman-Fried is the former CEO of the bankrupt crypto exchange FTX, whose highly anticipated criminal trial started on the Tuesday before TechCrunch's 2023-10-01 report, to determine whether he is guilty of seven counts of fraud and conspiracy. As one former federal prosecutor put it: "The odds seem to be stacked against him at this point."

He was 31 years old and co-founded FTX in 2019; within a few years the once third-largest crypto exchange's valuation hit $32 billion at its peak, and the company is now trying to claw back any funds to distribute to creditors. Before the fall he was even compared to Warren Buffet, and many called him the white horse of crypto — a description TechCrunch notes it never applied to him.

Bankman-Fried, however, maintained his innocence. At The New York Times' DealBook Summit he appeared virtually from the Bahamas and said, "I didn't ever try to commit fraud on anyone; I was shocked by what happened this month"; in a published DM exchange with a Vox reporter he said he regretted filing for bankruptcy and thought that "regulators make everything worse." In January he pleaded not guilty to all counts, which include wire fraud, conspiracy to commit money laundering and conspiracy to misuse customer funds. He could face up to 115 years in jail if convicted on all charges.

TechCrunch's 2023-10-02 summary of his standing on the eve of trial: SBF has been denied bail; his name is mud (or much worse) among those who have lost money in Alameda or FTX; and those who might not have had positions in these still blame him for other crypto woes, because he set off a ripple effect.



---


# FTX's Bankruptcy And Leadership

The man who represented FTX before Congress after its failure told lawmakers the exchange had effectively no internal governance at all, and the prosecutor bringing the case called Bankman-Fried's alleged crimes one of the biggest financial frauds in American history. TechCrunch reported both on 2023-10-01.

Ray represented the company during a House Financial Services Committee hearing regarding FTX. Asked whether the firm had significant risk management systems, Ray said at the time that "there were virtually no internal controls and no separateness whatsoever," and added that he did not "trust a single piece of paper" in the exchange's organization. Separately, in a press conference, U.S. Attorney Damian Williams called Bankman-Fried's alleged crimes "one of the biggest financial frauds in American history."



---


# Going Infinite: Michael Lewis's Account Of SBF's Political Dealings

Michael Lewis's book "Going Infinite" debuted on the first day of Sam Bankman-Fried's trial, and details about Bankman-Fried's political dealings emerging from it include his alleged attempt to buy off Donald Trump to get him not to run again for president.

TechCrunch's team was focused on the Manhattan Federal Court for the trial of Bankman-Fried, the disgraced entrepreneur accused of orchestrating the collapse of the cryptocurrency exchange FTX; the Lewis book is the second channel through which the week's revelations arrived. The reporting is framed as allegation rather than established fact, and it comes from the book rather than from courtroom testimony. The item appeared in TechCrunch's Week in Review of October 7, 2023.



---


# Sam Bankman-Fried's Charges And The Collapse Of FTX

Sam Bankman-Fried, the founder of FTX and Alameda Research, is facing seven counts of criminal charges: two counts of wire fraud and five counts of conspiracy charges.

FTX was a failed cryptocurrency exchange founded in 2019. According to a now-deleted profile from FTX investors Sequoia Capital, FTX was founded because of Bankman-Fried's frustration with other exchanges while he was running Alameda Research, his crypto trading firm. According to the SEC, FTX was a fraud "from the start," diverting customers' funds to Alameda, with a "multi-billion-dollar deficiency caused by his own misappropriation of customer funds."



---


# Reaction To Lewis's Portrayal Of SBF

The backlash to Michael Lewis's 60 Minutes appearance attacks one specific premise of his account — that FTX was a sound business brought down only by an unwarranted loss of confidence — and, behind it, the inference that SBF's story is therefore a tragic fall rather than a fraud. The episode has fired up a lot of people, indignant at what they feel was too-easy treatment for someone who many believe brought down the whole crypto house. TechCrunch collected the reaction on 2023-10-02.

The premise is attacked head-on by Dan Held, who on October 2, 2023 quoted Lewis — "They had a great real business. If no one had cast aspersions on the business, if there hadn't been a run on customers deposits, they'd still be making tons of money" — and answered: "That's not true. They are not a bank, they're…", prefacing it with "Shameful that Michael Lewis is defending SBF." Ryan Selkis attacked the framing instead of the balance sheet, writing the same day that "The Michael Lewis interview is infuriating. SBF was a scumbag, and now we need to hear about his 'tragic fall' in the MSM because Sam told them he was an 'effective altruist' and people like Michael Lewis were so far up his ass they couldn't tell truth from fiction." Tobi Lutke attacked the coverage itself: "60 Minutes got rightly community noted here. How is it that SBF is still getting super positive media coverage when the media has nothing good to say about the founders that have actually created things and brought value into the world?"

Two qualifications sit against the backlash. Noff is defensive: she believes crypto is no worse than the stock market, which can also be manipulated and mishandled, adding that "Even when you identify corruption, I don't think that means we don't believe in the system in question." And TechCrunch's own reading is that the thing being attacked may not be quite what the critics take it for — Lewis's picture is a little less stark from the looks of the 60 Minutes episode, and it is not that clear at all whether SBF is getting a kicking or a coat of polish in the interview, given Lewis's celebration of SBF's self-proclaimed (yet not quite proven) idealism and the "Bankman-Fried-shaped hold in the world" that exists. The writer's closing point is that this confused message is very apt for cryptocurrency, where the process by which it works is forever murky and often misrepresented, at least to most people.



---


# FTX's Collapse And Bankruptcy, November 2022

FTX went bankrupt on November 11th, 2022, days after Gary Wang and Bankman-Fried had determined that about $8 billion in customer money was gone. On November 7th, Bankman-Fried tweeted "FTX is fine. Assets are fine," and another tweet in the thread said "FTX has enough to cover all client holdings." Wang testified flatly: "FTX was not fine and assets were not fine because FTX did not have enough assets for customer withdrawals."

Prosecutor Thane Rehn placed the trigger in the same month: when CoinDesk published its article in November 2022, people realized FTX was a house of cards, while Bankman-Fried was tweeting "FTX is fine. Assets are fine" and "We don't invest customer assets even in treasuries."

The day after the bankruptcy, on November 12th, Bankman-Fried directed Wang to send customer funds to Bahamian regulators. Customers could not take their funds off the exchange at that point because FTX had run out of money and its servers had been shut down. Bankman-Fried and his father met with lawyers while Wang waited outside with liquidators; the US lawyers wanted the remaining FTX assets transferred to the US, but Wang testified that Bankman-Fried told him to stall the US lawyers and transfer the funds to the Bahamian regulators instead, who were more likely to let him stay in control of the company. The collapse also propagated outward: the government put Zac Prince, the founder and former CEO of crypto lender BlockFi, on the stand just long enough to blame FTX's bankruptcy for BlockFi's subsequent bankruptcy.



---


# The FTX Trial's Stakes For The Wider Crypto Industry

The Verge argued that the trial of Sam Bankman-Fried is likely to be more consequential than just whether the man himself is found guilty: depending on what evidence is introduced, it could be rough for the entire crypto industry.

The grounds are the unpredictability of what a trial surfaces, voiced by Yesha Yadav, a law professor at Vanderbilt University: "How much damage can this trial do to the already beaten-down reputation of the industry at this point? This trial is going to be an excruciating moment for the industry because no one knows what kind of evidence might come out." The warrant joining that uncertainty to industry-wide stakes is that the industry's reputation is already beaten down, so evidence introduced against one exchange's founder lands on the whole sector rather than on him alone.

qid: Do 'The Age' and 'FOX News - Lifestyle' suggest that the actions of parents can lead to negative outcomes for their children, or do their claims point to different consequences of parental behavior?
context:
# "Grinchy Griping" and Child Egocentric Thinking

Hannah Keeley's model of why parents should not vent about holiday stress in front of their children has two components that process the same event differently. The "mom brain" is wired to process problems rapidly and move on to solutions. The "child brain", however, is wired to process a problem internally and take on the responsibility.

The relation between the two produces the mismatch: children up to the age of 9 process information egocentrically, which means that if there is a problem, they see themselves as the cause. So the same episode that a parent experiences as temporary venting is received by the child as attribution of blame: "Knowing this, make sure you don't do any 'grinchy griping' out loud to the children. You may see it as temporary venting, but they see it as, 'Mom is upset and I'm probably the reason.'"

The scope condition matters — the egocentric processing Keeley describes holds for children up to the age of 9. Within that range, the prescription is that parents should avoid "processing their frustration around the holidays audibly around the children", and should instead stay calm, find a reason to be grateful and vocalise it, even when frustrations accumulate.



---


# Michele Borba on Labelling a Child

Parenting expert and child psychologist Dr. Michele Borba, commenting on the blue bucket controversy, told Fox News Digital that it is "always advisable not to label a child — unless it's for a positive reason."

Her ground is the effect of labels on the child: "Negative labels can impact a child's self-confidence," said the California-based psychologist. But she attaches an immediate limiting clause that keeps the judgment with the family: "But no one knows a child better than a parent."

The decision rule she proposes is therefore comparative rather than categorical: parents should consider whether the label hurts or helps their child interact with others. "For instance, is the child speech delayed? Does he have difficulty interacting with others or expressing his needs? Are others (including his peers) aware of the child's challenges?" she questioned. And the criterion that settles it is the child's own experience, not onlookers': "The ultimate goal is for the child to have a fun Halloween. The parents should never be concerned about others' responses; only do what is best for [the] child."



---


# Online Predation And Sextortion Risk For Children

Kelman argues that children are structurally unable to protect themselves online, because their brains are not fully developed -- "so they aren't able to sniff out who is safe on the other end of the chat or the game."

Kelman stressed that kids "can't unsee what they have already seen," and that many adult apps may put kids "in harm's way."

The harm she names is coercive and self-perpetuating: "Kids are coerced into sending photos of themselves, often finding themselves victims of sextortion after they share the photos," the expert warned. "This leads to shame, despair and fear of telling their parents."



---


# Hannah Keeley's Five Christmas Parenting Mistakes

"The biggest mistakes parents make at Christmastime" is a set of five holiday blunders identified by parenting expert Hannah Keeley, the Virginia-based expert who set them out in an email to Fox News Digital published on 9 December 2023.

The organising premise is that pressures are high for parents and caregivers around the holidays, which means there is room for error. Keeley identified the top five holiday blunders that parents often make, and presented them as things parents should try to avoid rather than as a diagnosis of any particular family.



---


# Meta Researchers Avoided Documenting Under-13 Users

A potential smoking gun in the lawsuit is a series of anecdotes from Meta researchers delicately avoiding the possibility of inadvertently confirming an under-13 cohort in their work.

One wrote in 2018: "We just want to make sure to be sensitive about a couple of Instagram-specific items. For example, will the survey go to under 13 year olds? Since everyone needs to be at least 13 years old before they create an account, we want to be careful about sharing findings that come back and point to under 13 year olds being bullied on the platform." In 2021, another, studying "child-adult sexual-related content/behavior/interactions," said she was "not includ[ing] younger kids (10-12 yos) in this research" even though there "are definitely kids this age on IG," because she was "concerned about risks of disclosure since they aren't supposed to be on IG at all." Also in 2021, Meta instructed a third-party research company conducting a survey of preteens to remove any information indicating a survey subject was on Instagram, so the "company won't be made aware of under 13." Later that year, external researchers provided Meta with information that "of children ages 9-12, 45% used Facebook and 40% used Instagram daily."

During an internal 2021 study on youth in social media described in the suit, researchers first asked parents if their kids were on Meta platforms and removed them from the study if so. But one researcher asked, "What happens to kids who slip through the screener and then say they are on IG during the interviews?" Instagram Head of Public Policy Karina Newton responded, "we're not collecting user names right?" — in other words, TechCrunch notes, what happens is nothing. As the lawsuit puts it: "Even when Meta learns of specific children on Instagram through interviews with the children, Meta takes the position that it still lacks actual knowledge of that it is collecting personal information from an under-13 user because it does not collect user names while conducting these interviews. In this way, Meta goes through great lengths to avoid meaningfully complying with COPPA, looking for loopholes to excuse its knowledge of users under the age of 13 and maintain their presence on the Platform."



---


# Bonta: The Numbers Are For Impact, The Violation Is The Point

AG Rob Bonta's claim is that the scale of Meta's under-13 user base is rhetorical, not legal: any child at all makes the conduct illegal. It is difficult to extrapolate from the 2015 and 2020 numbers to today's, which as the evidence presented shows will almost certainly not be the whole story, but Bonta noted that the large figures are presented for impact, not as legal justification. "The basic premise remains that their social media platforms are used by millions of children under 13. Whether it's 30 percent, or 20 or 10 percent… any child, it's illegal," he said. "If they were doing it at any time, it violated the law at that time. And we are not confident that they have changed their ways."

Bonta also distinguishes the strength of the counts. The other complaints in the lengthy lawsuit have softer edges, such as the argument that use of the platforms contributes to poor body image and that Meta has failed to take appropriate measures, which is arguably not as actionable; the COPPA material is far more cut and dry. His evidence that notice was given: "We have evidence that parents are sending notes to them about their kids being on their platform, and they're not getting any action. I mean, what more should you need? It shouldn't even have to get to that point."

The warrant is a claim about design as choice: "These social media platforms can do anything they want. They can be operated by a different algorithm, they can have plastic surgery filters or not have them, they can give you alerts in the middle of the night or during school, or not. They choose to do things that maximize the frequency of use of that platform by children, and the duration of that use. They could end all this today if they wanted, they could easily keep those under 13 from accessing their platform. But they're not."



---


# Gellar And Prinze's Strict Household Rules

Freddie Prinze Jr. said he and Sarah Michelle Gellar "are strict as hell" with their two children, and that Gellar has "100 rules" the kids know they cannot break, in a 2021 Us Weekly interview reported by FOX News Entertainment on 10 October 2023.

The "Buffy the Vampire Slayer" star and her husband have been married for more than 20 years and share two kids, aged 13 and 11 at the time of the 2021 interview. "Look, I don't believe in whooping kids. I've never whooped mine. My mom whooped me. They were, like, preventative whooping, so I know how to be strict," the "I Know What You Did Last Summer" star told the outlet. Of the rules he added: "They know they can't break [those rules]. Friendships come and go. I tell my kids all the time that family is forever. So, we have rules, and they've got to follow [them]."

Gellar told Us Weekly in 2020 that as parents their "expectations are a little higher than most": "I think [our children] know what the rules are. We have [family dinner] as many nights as we can. We have no phones at the table. We sit, we all have dinner together."

qid: Did the TechCrunch report on October 7, 2023, concerning Dave Clark's comments on Flexport, and the subsequent TechCrunch article on September 30, 2023, regarding Ryan Petersen's actions at Flexport, result in a change in the nature of the events reported?
context:
# Flexport Leadership Change And Layoffs

Logistics company Flexport is laying off 20% of workers, or about 600 people, topping off a spate of staff upheavals at the company, TechCrunch reported on 2023-10-22.

The following week TechCrunch supplied the leadership context: Flexport founder Ryan Petersen had just taken back the CEO title after his hand-picked successor was pushed out. Petersen's big message has been getting the company's financial house back in order, and he has criticized former CEO Dave Clark of overspending, specifically around hiring and expanding too quickly. Petersen has spent the past month cutting costs, including laying off about 20% of its workers, or about 600 people.



---


# Flexport And Convoy Technology Acquisition Talks

Flexport is in talks to acquire the technology of Convoy, the once buzzy digital freight startup that abruptly shuttered after failing to find a buyer, TechCrunch reported on 2023-10-30. The possible deal was reported by WSJ and came without other details, but still made TechCrunch's writer raise an eyebrow.

If Flexport acquires the technology, the company plans to restore Convoy's trucking services for as many customers and partners as possible, according to WSJ's source — which, TechCrunch notes, is going to cost money, prompting the question of whether Petersen's reign of financial frugality is already over.



---


# Flexport Leadership Turmoil

Dave Clark, the former Amazon executive who was ousted as CEO of Flexport just a year into the job, fired back at the company's founder and board, calling recent reporting on the logistics company "deeply concerning."

Clark made the comments on Monday of the week covered by TechCrunch's October 7, 2023 Week in Review, in a lengthy post on the social media site X. The post followed a CNBC report that had provided new information about his last days at Flexport. Flexport is described as a freight forwarding and customs brokerage startup valued at $8 billion.



---


# Dave Clark's Hiring And Flexport's IPO Plan

Clark arrived at Flexport in 2022 as the apparently perfect hire for a tech startup trying to disrupt the age-old logistics industry — he had built Amazon's logistics unit into a juggernaut that rivalled carriers like UPS and FedEx — and among his goals was to help Petersen prepare Flexport for an IPO, something the company had discussed doing within a two- to three-year window.

Since 2021 Petersen had been seeking a successor for then-operating chief Sanne Manders, in part to address what several ex-employees described as lingering issues with the company's troubled billing processes; fixing that was Clark's job. Petersen and Clark worked together as co-CEOs for the first six months, and in March Petersen transitioned to executive chairman — an arrangement meant to free Petersen up to do what he loved, "getting beers with customers," in the words of two former Flexport employees, while Clark, a self-described "builder at heart," was at the wheel. "There's a perfect complement of skill sets," Petersen told Forbes in June 2022. "Mine are much more creative, zero-to-one founder time, and Dave is the supreme executor and a legend in the supply chain world." Buying Deliverr was meant to be the first step in turning Flexport into a more full-scale logistics service. Shopify had acquired Deliverr in May 2022 for $2.1 billion, but the e-commerce software company was being hammered by Wall Street as its Covid pandemic pop faded, and by January 2023 CEO Tobias Lutke knew he needed to get rid of it; around that time Lutke first approached Petersen to float a deal, and Petersen told Clark he should engage with Shopify's team. Initial talks fell apart but resumed when Flexport executives learned Shopify was about to execute deep cost cuts and was eager to sell. Clark and Petersen flew to Miami to meet Shopify's leadership, and as a transaction neared, Clark — who had a reputation as a deft negotiator — got Shopify, already an investor in Flexport, to sweeten it with $40 million in cash and the framework for a $260 million convertible note that could help Flexport on its path to an IPO, according to an internal document analyzing the deal. The sale would be announced alongside Shopify's first-quarter earnings report on May 4. "We did not change the terms of a deal or rush it just to have it line up with an earnings call," Shopify said in a statement, adding that with Flexport "we are tightly mission-aligned to ensure the success of our merchants, which is why we chose to deepen our partnership with them earlier this year." The night before the announcement, Petersen appeared at a "Tech Talk" at Flexport's Bellevue, Washington office to pitch the "Flexport vision" to hundreds of people; asked whether Flexport would ever get into last-mile logistics, he paused, glanced at his watch, and said to keep an eye on the morning news, according to an employee who witnessed the exchange and a person told independently. The comment alarmed Clark and Flexport executives, who were concerned Petersen had disclosed material nonpublic information about a publicly traded company. Petersen did not respond to calls or messages from CNBC, the company declined to make him available for an interview, and a Flexport spokesperson did not respond to CNBC's question about whether Petersen was aware of concerns about his statement.



---


# Dave Clark's Ouster From Flexport

On Sept. 13, 2023, Flexport founder Ryan Petersen took the stage at North America's premier supply chain conference in Phoenix — exactly a week after he had forced out his hand-picked successor as CEO, ex-Amazon executive Dave Clark, so Petersen could once again run the show — and Clark, whom he had ousted just a year into the job, was sitting in the first few rows.

Petersen was surprised that Clark showed up, according to people with knowledge of the matter. Days earlier Petersen had excoriated Clark, alleging he had secretly expanded the company's headcount and taken on unnecessary leases without Petersen's or the board's knowledge, and posting on X, formerly Twitter, "Strategic Plan, Day 1: Make better decisions!" With Clark a few feet away, Petersen struck a different tone: "I think we're going to look back and go, 'Wow I'd probably do that all over again because of the progress that we've made,'" he said on stage, and personally commended Clark for orchestrating the $1.3 billion purchase of Deliverr from Shopify, announced in May, which picked up supply chain technology for last-mile deliveries. "I'm very, very lucky because I wouldn't have had the courage to go and do that acquisition, but I give all the credit in the world to Dave Clark," Petersen said. "There's no one probably in the world who would be better at running that last-mile e-com fulfillment network." The mixed messaging from the 43-year-old founder underscores the dysfunction surrounding the sudden firing of Clark, who previously spent 23 years at Amazon and built its mammoth logistics network on the way to becoming one of Jeff Bezos' top deputies. It is also indicative of a bigger challenge facing Flexport, whose software is designed to simplify transporting goods: valued at $8 billion by private investors in early 2022, just as the economy was turning and the 10-year tech bull market was ending, the company has been trying to operate in Silicon Valley startup growth mode while restraining expenses to reflect new economic realities and cope with supply chain bottlenecks. CNBC's account is based on conversations with people close to Clark and Petersen who requested anonymity, corroborated by internal documents and communications. Petersen has publicly said Clark overspent, overhired and overpromised, burned through cash and kept Petersen in the dark about key financials and an ambitious expansion into end-to-end supply chain tools for small and medium-sized businesses — something his allies echoed to CNBC. But documents viewed by CNBC and sources close to Clark undermine those claims, showing that Clark, who arrived when the company was struggling to bill customers and track containers, worked closely with the board and Petersen to implement decisions Flexport now suggests were ill-advised; evidence to support the claims of financial mismanagement is lacking, raising questions about whether that narrative was put forward to justify Clark's exit. A Flexport spokesperson rejected that characterization: "Ryan Petersen returned as CEO in order to restore Flexport's culture of customer engagement, and drive the growth and cost discipline required to return the company to profitability."



---


# Flexport's Board Composition

Flexport's board was made up largely of investors who were betting on the founder — a composition that matters because Clark's first quarterly board meeting as sole CEO was June 1 and his second was Aug. 31, days before he was forced out.

The board included Founders Fund's Trae Stephens, who had helped start defense-tech firm Anduril Industries, and Michael Ronen, who left SoftBank in 2020. Andreessen Horowitz was represented by Bob Swan, an operating partner at the firm and former CEO of Intel.



---


# Faction Driverless Funding Round

Faction, the driverless tech developer, raised an undisclosed amount in a round led by TDK Ventures, TechCrunch reported on 2023-10-30. Ducera Partners, Trucks Venture Capital and Fifty Years also joined the round.

qid: Does the TechCrunch article on Meta's advertising practices involve the European Commission in a similar capacity to how the European Commission is involved in Amazon's iRobot purchase and Elon Musk's X company's DSA probe, as reported by TechCrunch in both cases?
context:
# Amazon's Response To The EU's iRobot Objections

Amazon's response attacks the premise that iRobot's rivals could be foreclosed at all, by asserting that the competitive constraint on iRobot is already intense. Contacted for a response to the EU's statement of objections, a company spokesperson claimed iRobot faces "intense competition" from other RVC suppliers.

The full statement: "We continue to work through the process with the European Commission and are focused on addressing its questions and any identified concerns at this stage. iRobot, which faces intense competition from other vacuum cleaner suppliers, offers practical and inventive products. We believe Amazon can offer a company like iRobot the resources to accelerate innovation and invest in critical features while lowering prices for consumers."

The second half of the statement targets the Commission's predicted effect rather than its premise: where the EU foresees higher prices, lower quality and less innovation, Amazon asserts the merger would accelerate innovation and lower prices.



---


# Microtargeting

## Definition

In the corpus, microtargeting refers to using a platform's ad-targeting tools to aim political or advertising messaging at narrow, algorithmically selected audience segments — including by deliberately excluding groups defined by their interests or political views — rather than at a general audience.

## Context

In the corpus, microtargeting appears in two related EU controversies over data-driven ad targeting on major platforms.
Meta's "pay or consent" model is accused of forcing users to accept being "tracked and profiled" so the company can keep "profiting from microtargeting them," with nearly 20 consumer groups arguing this breaches EU consumer protection law.
Separately, the European Commission itself ran a microtargeted political ad campaign on X to build support for its CSAM-scanning proposal, which became the subject of a DSA-compliance investigation and a European Parliament committee hearing.
Both cases involve platforms designated Very Large Online Platforms (VLOPs) under the DSA — Facebook and Instagram in the Meta case, X in the Commission's campaign — though only the Commission's campaign was exposed using X's DSA-mandated ad-transparency tools, while the Meta case instead centers on a coordinated consumer-protection complaint.

## Key Characteristics

- **Exclusion-based mechanics** — technologist Danny Mekić's analysis of X's Transparency Report showed the Commission's campaign was configured to exclude specific interest groups (people interested in Julian Assange, in "nexit"/"brexit"/"spanexit," in figures like Viktor Orbán or Nigel Farage, and people interested in Christianity), after which the platform's algorithm found remaining users receptive to the message.
- **Echo-chamber effect** — Mekić described the resulting audience, once critical political and religious groups were filtered out, as "an uncritical echo chamber."
- **Regulatory exposure under the DSA** — the DSA prohibits using sensitive personal data, such as political opinions, to target ads; Mekić argued the Commission's campaign violated X's own advertising policy, the DSA, and the GDPR.
- **Basis for consumer-protection complaints** — separately, Meta's monetization of tracked-and-profiled user data for microtargeted advertising was central to BEUC's complaint that its pay-or-consent model is "unfair" and "illegal" under EU consumer law.
- **Exposed via VLOP transparency obligations** — the Commission's microtargeted campaign became visible only because Mekić used the public ad-transparency tools the DSA requires X, as a VLOP, to provide; Meta's microtargeting practice, by contrast, was already publicly known and became the basis of a separate consumer-protection complaint rather than something uncovered through ad-transparency tools.

## Background (external)

Outside the corpus, microtargeting is generally defined as the use of online data to tailor advertising or political messaging to individuals or small groups based on their personal characteristics or vulnerabilities, rather than addressing a broad, undifferentiated audience (Wikipedia, "Microtargeting," accessed 2026-09-02, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microtargeting).



---


# DSA And DMA Oversight Of Meta's Ad Tracking

Meta's subscription plan faces three overlapping regimes, not one. As well as needing to comply with the GDPR, which delineates the qualities necessary for consent to be legal — such as that it is specific, informed and freely given — Meta is now also subject to the pan-EU Digital Services Act (DSA), which also sets conditions on larger platforms when it comes to tracking and profiling people for ads; so it won't just be data protection authorities making a call on whether Meta's subscription-or-tracking offer flies, since the European Commission is responsible for oversight of very large online platforms' DSA compliance.

Meta has also been designated as a so-called gatekeeper under the DSA's sister regulation, the Digital Markets Act (DMA), which also puts some limits on use of people's data for ads, and the Commission is the sole enforcer of the DMA. Meta is already in the Commission's sights over its approach to the DSA — the EU's executive has in recent days requested more information from the tech giant about its approach to content threats flowing from the Israel-Hamas war and about election security issues — but it remains to be seen whether the EU will apply the same close scrutiny to Meta's ad tracking offer.



---


# The Commission's Microtargeted Ad Campaign For CSAM Scanning

The European Commission's advertising campaign for its CSAM-scanning proposal was microtargeted so that the ads did not reach privacy-minded, eurosceptic or Christian audiences, and EU home affairs commissioner Ylva Johansson admitted to MEPs that the EU's executive is investigating the matter — after she had earlier claimed the campaign was "100%" legal. TechCrunch reported the admission on 25 October 2023, from an exchange of views with the European Parliament's civil rights, justice and home affairs (LIBE) committee that afternoon.

The targeting detail comes from Mekić, who wrote that X's Transparency Report shows the European Commission used "microtargeting" to ensure that the ads did not appear to people who care about privacy (people interested in Julian Assange) and eurosceptics (people interested in "nexit", "brexit" and "spanexit" or in Victor Orbán, Nigel Farage, or the German political party AfD). For unclear reasons, people interested in Christianity were also excluded.

Mekić's account of the mechanism is that after excluding critical political and religious groups, X's algorithm was set to find people in the remaining population who were indeed interested in the ad message, resulting in what he called "an uncritical echo chamber". On that basis he argued the microtargeting on political and religious beliefs violates X's advertising policy, the Digital Services Act — which the Commission itself has to oversee — and the General Data Protection Regulation.

Johansson's position moved between two dates. In a tweet earlier that month, on 13 October 2023, she had sought to dismiss criticism over the legality of the microtargeting, writing that as her services had been directly accused of illegal acts she thought it important she step in, and setting out three points: that @EUHomeAffairs "have followed the guidelines & the law 100%"; that "the promotion of our proposal is standard normal practice"; and that "this proposal is about protecting children from sexual abuse".

Asked by the LIBE committee about the discrepancy between that tweet and the existence of an investigation, Johansson said she had been given "new information" related to DSA compliance that merited looking into. "When I made a tweet on the 100% legal [point] that was based on the information I had. But I have to be very open; then I got other information that there could be question marks on the compliance with the DSA — and I take this very seriously," she told the committee. "If that is the case then of course there has to be consequences on that. So that's why it's important that we have to look into [it]. Of course we always have to comply with the regulation. There's no question about that."



---


# The EU's First Formal DSA Proceeding, Against X

On 18 December 2023 the European Commission announced the opening of a "formal proceeding" against Elon Musk's X, making it the first confirmed investigation opened by the European Union under its rebooted digital rulebook, the Digital Services Act (DSA). The investigation will look at whether the social networking platform may have breached rules linked to risk management, content moderation, dark patterns, advertising transparency and data access for researchers.

The Commission set out the evidentiary basis for the step: "On the basis of the preliminary investigation conducted so far, including on the basis of an analysis of the risk assessment report submitted by X in September, X's Transparency report published on 3 November, and X's replies to a formal request for information, which, among others, concerned the dissemination of illegal content in the context of Hamas' terrorist attacks against Israel, the Commission has decided to open formal infringement proceedings against X under the Digital Services Act."

The EU added that "if proven, these failures would constitute infringements of Articles 34(1), 34(2) and 35(1), 16(5) and 16(6), 25(1), 39 and 40(12) of the DSA," and said it will now carry out an in-depth investigation "as a matter of priority." Internal market commissioner Thierry Breton announced the same day that the proceedings covered a suspected breach of obligations to counter illegal content and disinformation, a suspected breach of transparency obligations, and suspected deceptive design of the user interface.

qid: Does the FOX News - Health article linking Influenza to minor health issues disagree with the FOX News - Health article on GLP-1 agonist medications concerning the potential for rare but serious health complications from medical conditions or treatments?
context:
# Allison Miller's Influenza, Sepsis And Leg Amputation

Allison Miller, a Virginia-based communications director who was a healthy 33-year-old at the time, lost her left leg above the knee after a case of influenza escalated into bilateral bacterial pneumonia, sepsis and septic shock; a decade later she described the sequence to Fox News Digital for an article published on October 18, 2023, which noted that this year marked ten years since those complications caused her life-changing loss.

The illness began with a sore throat and headache. When her symptoms got worse she went into urgent care for a chest X-ray, but it showed nothing alarming. "It looked like it was just some sort of run-of-the-mill stuff -- they gave me some prescription cough syrup and said to let them know if it got worse," she said. Back at home that night she started feeling worse and began having intense back pain. "Thinking it was the flu or something I could get over, I kept waiting to turn the corner -- like, this is the worst of it. It'll get better. And clearly that wasn't the case," she said. The next morning, when the back pain was causing her to have periodic blackouts, she managed to call a friend, who came over and called an ambulance. That is where her memory stops: "I remember being loaded into the ambulance -- and then I really don't remember a whole lot after that for about three weeks to a month thereafter. It just escalated very quickly."

As Miller would later learn, her influenza had caused bilateral bacterial pneumonia, which affects both lungs and is more severe than viral pneumonia. That led to sepsis, which quickly turned to septic shock. "All of my organs were shutting down," she said. "Within a short amount of time, I was in the ICU and they were doing everything they could. But ultimately, my last best chance was to be put on life support."

After five days on life support she experienced a rare complication. "A known complication of that form of life support is amputation," she said. "Some patients lose blood circulation, and that's what happened to me." Doctors ultimately had to amputate her left leg above the knee while she was still in a medically induced coma. "By the time I came out of it, it had been three weeks. I awoke in a very hazy position -- and I didn't have a left leg," she recalled. She spent another two months in the hospital and then had to do weeks of inpatient rehabilitation.



---


# CDC's 2021-2022 Flu Burden Estimate And Vaccination Recommendation

During the 2021-2022 influenza season, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention estimates that there were nine million illnesses, four million medical visits, 10,000 hospitalizations and 5,000 deaths related to the flu.

On the strength of that burden, the CDC recommends that everyone 6 months and older get a flu vaccine every season, with rare exceptions.



---


# The Case For Adding Gastroparesis To GLP-1 Warning Labels

The UBC researchers recommend that regulatory agencies and drugmakers consider updating the warning labels for their products, which currently do not include the risk of gastroparesis.

Their grounds are the mismatch between a rare event and an enormous exposed population. Although these complications were rare, the researchers found them concerning, given that millions of people are using these medications worldwide. Accessibility compounds the problem: "These drugs are becoming increasingly accessible, and it is concerning that, in some cases, people can simply go online and order these kinds of medications when they may not have a full understanding of what could potentially happen," said first author Mohit Sodhi, a graduate of UBC's experimental medicine program, in the release.

The warrant joining rarity to a labeling change is that patients cannot weigh or act on a risk they have never been told about. "Given the wide use of these drugs, these adverse events, although rare, must be considered by patients thinking about using them for weight loss," the researchers said. "This is critical information for patients to know so they can seek timely medical attention and avoid serious consequences," said Sodhi.



---


# Limitations Of The UBC GLP-1 Claims Analysis

The study's own authors qualify how far its findings can be pushed: the claims analysis could not establish subjects' full medical histories, could not separate the risk of individual GLP-1 drugs, and did not identify which groups are most susceptible.

"We did not have access to medical charts to ascertain all subjects' medical histories," said Etminan. "Also, we could not look at risk with individual GLP-1 drugs, but this is probably a class effect of these drugs." That concession undercuts any inference from the results to a particular product, while leaving the class-level signal intact.

The researchers also did not determine whether certain groups were at higher risk of this adverse side effect, but Etminan said he suspects that those with preexisting GI conditions might be more susceptible -- a suspicion, not a finding.



---


# Recognizing A Severe Flu And Seeking Early Care

When flu symptoms are severe or start to change dramatically, the rule both Miller and Sylvester give is to seek medical attention immediately rather than spend time deliberating about whether it is warranted.

Miller thinks most people do not understand how severe the flu can be, so they do not recognize the signs that they need immediate medical attention. The window can be very short: "In my case, it was very quick -- it was within 24 to 48 hours that it went from just coming on, to me being in the hot seat."

Her instruction is to treat the flu as a serious illness and to act on the body's signals. "Don't dismiss the flu as just the flu. It's so much more than that. And it can be life-altering," she urged. She continued, "If you're sick and the symptoms are severe, don't waste time wondering if you should seek medical attention. Listen to your body -- it's better to go in proactively, rather than regret it later."

Sylvester agreed, stressing the need for people to be their own patient advocates. "It's important to seek care early, especially if symptoms start to change dramatically," he said.



---


# Novo Nordisk's Response To The GLP-1 Gastroparesis Findings

Novo Nordisk's rebuttal attacks two premises at once: that the gastrointestinal risks are unlabeled and unknown, and that the study's window supports conclusions about its current weight-management products.

In a statement at the time, a spokesperson for Novo Nordisk told FOX Business that gastrointestinal events "are well-known side effects of the GLP-1 class" and "are mild to moderate in severity and of short duration." The company provided a further statement to Fox News Digital on Friday, Oct. 6.

On labeling, the company said: "At Novo Nordisk, patient safety is a top priority. We work closely with the U.S. Food and Drug Administration to continuously monitor the safety profile of our medicines. The FDA-approved product labeling for Novo Nordisk's GLP-1RA medicines indicated for use in weight management (Saxenda and Wegovy) includes information about their potential side effects, including pancreatitis, acute gallbladder disease, ileus and delayed gastric emptying." It went on: "Similar information is included in the product labeling for our GLP-1RA medicines indicated for the treatment of type 2 diabetes (Ozempic, Rybelsus and Victoza)." The company added that it "stands behind the safety and efficacy of all of our GLP-1RA medicines when used consistent with the product labeling and approved indications."

On the study itself, Novo Nordisk said, "With respect to the study, as the authors acknowledge, the study has limitations, including potential confounding by indication and by other factors." The company added a timing objection: "It is also important to note that the study analyzed data collected during the period between 2006 and 2020. During this time, Wegovy was not on the market; Saxenda was first approved in December 2014. In addition, Victoza was FDA-approved in January 2010 and Ozempic was FDA-approved in December 2017."



---


# How Influenza Sets Up A Secondary Bacterial Infection

Influenza can lead to a more serious illness later because the virus triggers inflammation of the respiratory tract, which causes the tract to become irritated and can allow secondary or bacteria to enter -- the mechanism described by Dr. Gregg Sylvester, chief health officer at CSL Seqirus, a New Jersey biopharmaceutical company.

The range over which this matters is narrow but not negligible. For most of the millions of people who get the flu each year in the U.S., the virus brings a few days of fever, body aches and weakness before it goes away. But for some, the influenza virus can lead to severe illness, hospitalization -- even death. Sylvester noted that while Miller's experience is not typical of most women in her age range, "it probably occurs more often than we know."

Sylvester draws the practical consequence directly from the mechanism: "A viral illness like influenza can set you up for something more serious further on," he warned. "That's why it's so important to get a vaccine."

qid: Was there inconsistency in the portrayal of Sam Bankman-Fried's actions related to the allegations of fraud between the report from Fortune published on October 4, 2023, and the report from TechCrunch?

# Day Two Of The Bankman-Fried Trial: Jury Selection And The Courtroom Audience

On the second day of Sam Bankman-Fried's fraud trial, the jury was selected on Wednesday morning, after which lawyers for the government and then for Bankman-Fried delivered opening statements that told two very different stories of the former FTX CEO's sudden rise and almost instantaneous fall. The central question framed by the proceedings was who Bankman-Fried, the former CEO of crypto exchange FTX, really is: a liar and a fraud, or someone who acted in good faith and, like many a startup founder, flew too close to the sun. That answer, the account notes, ultimately lies with the jury.

The day featured pointed allegations, a friend from MIT, and an audience replete with big names, including Bankman-Fried's professorial parents and Damian Williams, the U.S. attorney for the Southern District of New York. Bankman-Fried himself spent most of the day in court staring into a laptop while seated between his two attorneys. The prosecution's account of his alleged crimes was described as featuring a study in contrasts.



---


# Sam Bankman-Fried

Sam Bankman-Fried is the former CEO of the bankrupt crypto exchange FTX, whose highly anticipated criminal trial started on the Tuesday before TechCrunch's 2023-10-01 report, to determine whether he is guilty of seven counts of fraud and conspiracy. As one former federal prosecutor put it: "The odds seem to be stacked against him at this point."

He was 31 years old and co-founded FTX in 2019; within a few years the once third-largest crypto exchange's valuation hit $32 billion at its peak, and the company is now trying to claw back any funds to distribute to creditors. Before the fall he was even compared to Warren Buffet, and many called him the white horse of crypto — a description TechCrunch notes it never applied to him.

Bankman-Fried, however, maintained his innocence. At The New York Times' DealBook Summit he appeared virtually from the Bahamas and said, "I didn't ever try to commit fraud on anyone; I was shocked by what happened this month"; in a published DM exchange with a Vox reporter he said he regretted filing for bankruptcy and thought that "regulators make everything worse." In January he pleaded not guilty to all counts, which include wire fraud, conspiracy to commit money laundering and conspiracy to misuse customer funds. He could face up to 115 years in jail if convicted on all charges.

TechCrunch's 2023-10-02 summary of his standing on the eve of trial: SBF has been denied bail; his name is mud (or much worse) among those who have lost money in Alameda or FTX; and those who might not have had positions in these still blame him for other crypto woes, because he set off a ripple effect.



---


# Sam Bankman-Fried's Federal Fraud Trial

Sam Bankman-Fried, the founder of bankrupt cryptocurrency exchange FTX, is charged with seven counts of fraud and money laundering following the collapse of his cryptocurrency empire the previous year, and was on trial in New York in October 2023.

Two fixed points anchor the proceeding as CNBC described it on 2023-10-06. A U.S. judge revoked Bankman-Fried's bail at a hearing in a New York courthouse on August 11, 2023. And on Thursday, Oct. 5, 2023, Matt Huang, co-founder of Paradigm Operations LP, arrived at the New York court to appear in the case.



---


# FTX's Bankruptcy And Leadership

The man who represented FTX before Congress after its failure told lawmakers the exchange had effectively no internal governance at all, and the prosecutor bringing the case called Bankman-Fried's alleged crimes one of the biggest financial frauds in American history. TechCrunch reported both on 2023-10-01.

Ray represented the company during a House Financial Services Committee hearing regarding FTX. Asked whether the firm had significant risk management systems, Ray said at the time that "there were virtually no internal controls and no separateness whatsoever," and added that he did not "trust a single piece of paper" in the exchange's organization. Separately, in a press conference, U.S. Attorney Damian Williams called Bankman-Fried's alleged crimes "one of the biggest financial frauds in American history."



---


# The Prosecution's Opening Statement Against Bankman-Fried

Thane Rehn, a prosecutor for the government, opened the case against Sam Bankman-Fried with the line "One year ago, it looked like the defendant was on the top of the world," and then argued that this appearance was false: "all of that, all of it, was built on lies," he declared to the jury, adding "Behind the curtains, he was not what he appeared to be." Rehn described a defendant who, as former CEO of FTX, oversaw a supposedly thriving crypto exchange, jetted between international locales, hobnobbed with celebrities like Tom Brady and Larry David, and repeatedly emphasized to customers that their money was safe and secure.

What followed was a roughly 30-minute story that repeatedly emphasized how Bankman-Fried allegedly stole customer funds to facilitate his jet-setting lifestyle, donate millions to political candidates, and finance risky bets. Rehn also directly contested the media framing of the defendant: he was not a crypto "boy" genius, as so many in the media — Fortune included — have written, but a "man" who "stole billions of dollars from thousands of victims." Rehn closed the characterization with a promise to the jury: "You will see the full picture."



---


# FTX Fraud Charges And The SEC's Allegation

Sam Bankman-Fried, the founder of the failed cryptocurrency exchange FTX, faced seven counts of wire fraud and conspiracy — specifically, two counts of wire fraud and five conspiracy charges — and the Securities and Exchange Commission alleged that FTX was a fraud "from the start," with a "multi-billion-dollar deficiency caused by his own misappropriation of customer funds." The Verge repeated this framing at the head of each of its trial dispatches through October 2023, and in its October 28th, 2023 write-up reported that Bankman-Fried had been found guilty on seven counts including charges of wire fraud.

The boundary of the concept is the mix of charge types: the indictment paired substantive wire fraud counts with conspiracy counts rather than resting on a single offence, and the SEC's civil allegation about the exchange's origins ran alongside the criminal case rather than being part of it. The Verge's reporter, writing as the prosecution's case neared its end on October 26th, 2023, added an impression of the people the charges swept in: all the co-conspirators seemed oddly younger than their years, as though they had got stuck in the "math camp forever" environment Bankman-Fried created for them and simply failed to grow up.



---


# Prosecution And Defense Arguments On Day Two Of The SBF Trial

On the second day of the trial of Sam Bankman-Fried and FTX, the prosecution argued that Bankman-Fried knowingly committed fraud, and it grounded that claim in motive: he did so, prosecutors said, to achieve great wealth, power and influence.

The defense countered with the opposite reading of the same conduct. Its claim was that the FTX founder acted in good faith, never meant to commit fraud or to steal, and basically got in over his head — an argument whose warrant is that inexperience and overreach, rather than intent, explain what happened. The two sides therefore contest intent rather than the underlying events, and the reporting on this exchange comes from Rebecca and Jacquelyn in TechCrunch's Week in Review of October 7, 2023, covering day two of the trial only.



---


# The SBF Trial Proceedings

Sam Bankman-Fried is in court for alleged fraud and money laundering while leading crypto exchange FTX and sister company Alameda. TechCrunch's 2023-10-02 preview placed the case in the Manhattan Federal Court, describing the disgraced cryptocurrency entrepreneur as accused of orchestrating "one of the biggest financial frauds in American history": the multibillion-dollar collapse of FTX, the crypto exchange he founded and led. SBF, as he is known, has pleaded not guilty to some seven charges of fraud and conspiracy.

The trial kicked off with jury selection October 3. By TechCrunch's 2023-10-06 update the case was entering its next chapter, with proceedings resuming Thursday: as confirmed during a teleconference Wednesday, SBF would be taking the stand along with a handful of other witnesses, as the onus shifted toward the defense after the prosecution brought its case to its conclusion.

Access to the proceedings is limited: no devices are allowed, so reports are being physically put together within the courtroom, or sent to overflow rooms. The jury's composition ranges from a train conductor to a retired investment banker who attended Stanford University, and TechCrunch pointed readers to a special joint episode of its Equity and Chain Reaction podcasts for a better sense of the vibe between the jurors and the rest of the court.

A second account of the same events was arriving in parallel: "Going Infinite," a book by Michael Lewis chronicling the rise and fall of SBF, was set to debut on the first day of the trial.
