# T.J. Hockenson's Week 10 Injury Status

T.J. Hockenson (ribs) was officially ACTIVE for the Vikings' Week 10 game against New Orleans, with NFL Network's Ian Rapoport reporting Sunday morning that he was expected to play. He had been listed as "questionable" but had already said he planned to play, and although he dealt with his share of injury woes that season he had yet to miss a game; after three limited practices, Sporting News trusted he was ready, especially since he had continued playing through the ailment in Week 9 as a big part of the offense with Josh Dobbs under center.

The fantasy verdict was unequivocal. As long as Hockenson is playing he is not being benched in any fantasy format: he projected as a top option at the position and remained the Vikings' leader in targets with 80 on the season, while Dobbs had enjoyed targeting tight ends in Arizona and continued that trend in his Minnesota debut — making Hockenson's floor, as the piece put it, equivalent to that of a rooftop bar.



---


# Week 14's Top Fantasy Tight End Starts

Travis Kelce topped Sporting News' Week 14 2023 tight end rankings, with T.J. Hockenson, Sam LaPorta, David Njoku and Dalton Kincaid not far behind.

Kelce (vs. Bills) held the top spot as usual. LaPorta (at Bears) and Njoku (vs. Jaguars) both had great matchups against defenses that entered the previous week in the top 10 in fantasy points per game allowed to tight ends, and the column noted we know what Kelce, Hockenson (at Raiders) and Kincaid (at Chiefs) do every week in PPR formats. George Kittle (vs. Seahawks) did not have a great matchup — especially remembering he had just three catches for 19 yards against Seattle in Week 12 — but remained a must-start given his high ceiling in any matchup.



---


# Tyler Lockett Week 13: A Flex Starter Facing Another Lean Night

CBS Sports' Week 13 verdict on Tyler Lockett is Flex Starter — playable as a WR3 but likely to be quiet. The grounds: Lockett has seven-plus targets in four of his past five games, but he still does not have as many as Metcalf has gotten in those games, and he does not see nearly as many deep throws — literally two targets in his past two games traveled 15 or more Air Yards. The article grants the upside case, that he always has potential to pop off for a big game like he did against a tough Browns defense five weeks ago, then sets against it that recent matchups against the Niners, Rams and Ravens were not kind to Lockett, and were even less kind to Geno Smith, with this week not expected to be much different. Added to that is the tough assignment of Stephon Gilmore in coverage — with the stated caveat, unless the Cowboys use shadow coverage for the first time this year — leaving Lockett in for another lean night.

The resulting ranking: the author does not mind him as a WR3 over Drake London, DeAndre Hopkins and Diontae Johnson, but would start Rashee Rice and Adam Thielen over Lockett. Scope: Lockett is a Seattle wide receiver, #16, age 31 with 9 years of experience; the weekly breakdown lists the matchup at Dallas with Dallas favored by 9 and an over/under of 47.5, the opponent 10th versus wide receivers, projected points of 10.6 and a WR rank of 31st; year-to-date he has 54 receptions on 79 targets for 575 receiving yards, 4 touchdowns and 12.5 Fantasy points per game, with projections powered by SportsLine.



---


# NFL Week 13 Injuries Bengals At Jaguars

In the Week 13 final injury reports published by CBSSports.com on Dec. 1, 2023, for the Monday game with the Jaguars listed at -8.5, Cincinnati ruled out CB Cam Taylor-Britt (quad/ankle), D'Ante Smith (knee) and Jay Tufele (illness), while Jacksonville listed CB Tyson Campbell (hamstring), RB Travis Etienne (ribs), TE Brenton Strange (foot) and TE Luke Farrell (toe) as questionable.

The Bengals got good news on the injury front ahead of Monday's game: wide receiver Tee Higgins (hamstring/ankle) and linebacker Logan Wilson (ankle/foot) were set to play, according to head coach Zac Taylor, and both were full participants in practice. Cornerback Cam Taylor-Britt hurt his foot in practice and was out. For the Jaguars, Travis Etienne (ribs) was also expected to play, Doug Pederson told reporters, despite the running back being limited in practice all week; Strange was a late addition to the injury report, not practicing Saturday.



---


# Justin Jefferson's Week 10 Injury Status

Justin Jefferson (hamstring) was officially ruled OUT for the Vikings' Week 10 game against the Saints, with NFL Network's Tom Pelissero reporting that Minnesota would not activate him before Sunday. He had been listed as "questionable" ahead of the 1 p.m. ET kickoff, and fantasy owners did not have to wait long for clarity, because to be eligible to play he needed to be activated by 4 p.m. ET on Saturday.

The expectation had been cautious. Earlier in the week head coach Kevin O'Connell said it would be "a little aggressive" for Jefferson to get back on the field, though three straight limited practices were enough for the team to at least weigh the decision.

The fantasy read came with a caveat about the quarterback. Jefferson's outlook is always through the roof, but it was an open question whether that changed with Josh Dobbs under center instead of Kirk Cousins. K.J. Osborn (concussion) was also listed as "questionable," with his status steadily improving from DNP on Wednesday to full practice on Friday. If Jefferson were back he would be a must-start; with him out and Osborn returning, both Osborn and Jordan Addison were worth using.



---


# K.J. Osborn As A Week 6 2023 Sit At Chicago

CBS Sports listed K.J. Osborn under "Sit Him" for Week 6 of the 2023 season at Chicago: the claim is that there is some potential here but several hunches keep the author from falling for Osborn this week, and the warrant is that with Justin Jefferson out the Vikings should lean on the run and on more explosive weapons, while Chicago's heavy zone coverage is the scheme in which Osborn does least.

Three grounds are given in order. First, the Vikings will try to get their run game going since they don't have Justin Jefferson. Second, Jordan Addison is far more explosive and T.J. Hockenson has been a much more relied-upon weapon, so both should see more targets than Osborn. Third, the expected zone coverage Chicago will play further limits him unless he sees more targets than expected — the Bears play zone at the fourth-highest rate of any defense this season, 79.2%, and because Kirk Cousins is much more explosive against man coverage, Chicago is expected to keep it up. Osborn's own splits make that a problem: he has a 50% catch rate on the year against both zone and man, but sees more targets per route run against man and averages more yards per catch and more yards after catch against man, and over his career targets have come more frequently against man coverage, where he has been more explosive with them.

The recent usage and film support the caution, with one countervailing precedent. Over 19 snaps without Jefferson the previous week, Osborn ran 18 routes and caught both of his two targets for 30 total yards — a delightful receiving average but a saddening small-sample target share of 12.5%; the odd part is that his target share was much higher with Jefferson playing, 23.3%, while his receiving average tanked to 6.3. On film he didn't beat coverage with speed and his burst and agility were just OK: his 22-yard catch came on a Kirk Cousins scramble where he waited in a spot and then ran inside instead of outside where he might have scored, and he ducked under an end-zone target instead of leaping for it — though a 36-yard crosser against the Chargers flies in the face of that, as he separated from man coverage with speed and technique, turned upfield, ran outside and raced past a defender to dive for the pylon. The historical upside is real: in 20 career games with at least five targets, Osborn has scored at least 12 PPR points in 13 of them, 11 of those involving a touchdown catch, and one of his two career 100-yard games came last January at Chicago. The breakdown lists Minnesota at Chicago, the Vikings favoured by 2.5, an over/under of 44.5, an opponent ranked 20th versus wide receivers, 10.7 projected points, a 33rd receiver ranking, and year-to-date totals of 13 receptions on 26 targets for 166 yards, two touchdowns and 8.3 fantasy points per game. The verdict gives him more upside than Jerry Jeudy, Jahan Dotson and Tutu Atwell, while preferring a shot on Drake London, Terry McLaurin or Chris Godwin.

qid: Who is the Silicon Valley figure associated with the rise of artificial intelligence and generative AI technology, who was recently in the news for being removed from OpenAI's leadership amidst allegations of dishonesty with the board, as reported by both Fortune and TechCrunch?
context:
# Sam Altman's Rise As The Face Of Generative AI

In the year since Altman catapulted ChatGPT to global fame, he became Silicon Valley's sought-after voice on the promise and potential dangers of artificial intelligence, and his sudden and mostly unexplained exit brought uncertainty to the industry's future. He helped start OpenAI as a nonprofit research laboratory in 2015, but it was ChatGPT's explosion into public consciousness that thrust him into the spotlight as a face of generative AI — technology that can produce novel imagery, passages of text and other media. On a world tour in 2023 he was mobbed by a crowd of adoring fans at an event in London.

He has sat with multiple heads of state to discuss AI's potential and perils. On Thursday, 2023-11-16, he took part in a CEO summit at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation conference in San Francisco, where OpenAI is based. At OpenAI's first developer conference the week before, Altman was the main speaker, showcasing a vision for a future of AI agents that could help people with a variety of tasks; days later he announced the company would have to pause new subscriptions to its premium version of ChatGPT because it had exceeded capacity.



---


# Sam Altman's Career Before OpenAI

Sam Altman, 38 as of November 2023, is not trained as an AI engineer, yet has been seen as a Silicon Valley wunderkind since his early 20s. The defining credential of that earlier phase is that he was recruited in 2014 to take the lead of the startup incubator YCombinator.

The reputation attached to him at the time is captured in YCombinator co-founder Paul Graham's 2014 announcement that Altman would become its president: "Sam is one of the smartest people I know, and understands startups better than perhaps anyone I know, including myself." Graham said then that Altman was "one of those rare people who manage to be both fearsomely effective and yet fundamentally benevolent."



---


# Second Senate AI Insight Forum, October 2023

Senator Charles Schumer (D-NY) hosted Silicon Valley's AI leaders on Tuesday as the US Senate reconvened its AI Insight Forum for a second time, and on leaving the meeting Schumer told the assembled press that "it is clear that American leadership on AI can't be done on the cheap," reporting that almost all of the experts in the forum called for robust, sustained federal investment in the private and public sectors to achieve American-led transformative and sustainable innovation in AI.

The guest list for this second session included manifesto enthusiast Marc Andreessen and venture capitalist John Doerr, along with Max Tegmark of the Future of Life Institute and NAACP CEO Derrick Johnson. According to a release from Schumer's office, the agenda covered "the transformational innovation that pushes the boundaries of medicine, energy, and science, and the sustainable innovation necessary to drive advancements in security, accountability, and transparency in AI."

On cost, National Security AI Commission estimates put the required federal investment at around $32 billion a year. Schumer believes those funding challenges can be addressed by "leveraging the private sector by employing new and innovative funding mechanisms — like the Grand Challenges prize idea." He framed the goal as a balance: "We must prioritize transformational innovation, to help create new vistas, unlock new cures, improve education, reinforce national security, protect the global food supply, and more," but in doing so "we must act sustainably in order to minimize harms to workers, civil society and the environment." As he put it, "We need to strike a balance between transformational and sustainable innovation. Finding this balance will be key to our success."

Schumer closed by saying the participants would leave "with a deeper understanding of how to approach American-led AI innovation," and that the conversation would continue "in weeks and months to come — in more forums like this and committee hearings in Congress — as we work to develop comprehensive, bipartisan AI legislation."



---


# The AI Risk Paradox Among Tech Billionaires

At the heart of the competition to build artificial intelligence is a brain-stretching paradox: the people who say they are most worried about AI are among the most determined to create it and enjoy its riches, and they have justified their ambition with their strong belief that they alone can keep AI from endangering Earth. The grounds are the shape of the debate itself. Eight years after an argument between Elon Musk and Larry Page, that argument seems prescient, because the question of whether AI will elevate the world or destroy it, or at least inflict grave damage, has framed an ongoing debate among Silicon Valley founders, chatbot users, academics, legislators and regulators about whether the technology should be controlled or set free.

That debate has pitted some of the world's richest men against one another: Musk, Page, Mark Zuckerberg of Meta, tech investor Peter Thiel, Satya Nadella of Microsoft and Sam Altman of OpenAI, all of whom have fought for a piece of a business that one day could be worth trillions of dollars, and for the power to shape it. The narrative anchor is that Musk and Page stopped speaking soon after the party that summer, and that a few weeks later Musk dined with Altman, who was then running a tech incubator, and several researchers in a private room at the Rosewood hotel in Menlo Park, California, a favoured deal-making spot close to the venture capital offices of Sand Hill Road.



---


# The OpenAI Board's Firing Of Sam Altman

ChatGPT-maker OpenAI said on Friday, 2023-11-17, that it had pushed out its co-founder and CEO Sam Altman after a review found he was "not consistently candid in his communications" with the board of directors. "The board no longer has confidence in his ability to continue leading OpenAI," the artificial intelligence company said in a statement. Mira Murati, OpenAI's chief technology officer, would take over as interim CEO effective immediately while the company searched for a permanent replacement.

OpenAI declined to answer questions on what Altman's alleged lack of candor was about; the statement said only that his behavior was hindering the board's ability to exercise its responsibilities. Altman posted on X that Friday: "i loved my time at openai. it was transformative for me personally, and hopefully the world a little bit. most of all i loved working with such talented people. will have more to say about what's next later."



---


# Musk's Founding Of OpenAI And His Departure

Convinced that Larry Page's optimistic view of AI was dead wrong, and angry at his loss of DeepMind, Musk built his own lab: OpenAI was founded in late 2015, just a few months after he met with Sam Altman at the Rosewood hotel in Silicon Valley. Musk pumped money into the lab and his former PayPal buddies, Reid Hoffman and Peter Thiel, came along for the ride; the three men and others pledged to put $US1 billion into the project, which Altman, then 30, would help run, and to get started they poached Ilya Sutskever from Google, one of the graduate students Google had "bought" in Hinton's auction. Initially Musk wanted to operate OpenAI as a nonprofit, free from the economic incentives driving Google and other corporations, but by the time Google wowed the tech community with its Go stunt he was changing his mind about how it should be run: he desperately wanted OpenAI to invent something that would capture the world's imagination and close the gap with Google, and it wasn't getting the job done as a nonprofit.

In late 2017 Musk hatched a plan to wrest control of the lab from Altman and the other founders and transform it into a commercial operation that would join forces with Tesla and rely on supercomputers the car company was developing, according to four people familiar with the matter; when Altman and others pushed back, Musk quit and said he would focus on his own AI work at Tesla. In February 2018 he announced his departure to OpenAI's staff on the top floor of the startup's offices in a converted truck factory, three people who attended said; when he said OpenAI needed to move faster, one researcher retorted that Musk was being reckless, and Musk called the researcher a "jackass" and stormed out, taking his deep pockets with him. OpenAI suddenly needed new financing in a hurry: Altman flew to Sun Valley for a conference and ran into Satya Nadella, Microsoft's CEO, and a tie-up seemed natural, since Altman knew Microsoft's chief technology officer Kevin Scott and Microsoft had bought LinkedIn from Hoffman, an OpenAI board member; Nadella told Scott to get it done. The deal closed in 2019, leaving Altman and OpenAI with a for-profit company formed under the original nonprofit, $US1 billion in fresh capital, and Microsoft with a new way to build AI into its vast cloud computing service. Not everyone inside OpenAI was happy.



---


# OpenAI's Board Composition In November 2023

The OpenAI board that fired Sam Altman consisted, the company said, of OpenAI's chief scientist Ilya Sutskever plus three non-employees.

Those three were Quora CEO Adam D'Angelo, tech entrepreneur Tasha McCauley, and Helen Toner of the Georgetown Center for Security and Emerging Technology.

qid: Does the TechCrunch article suggest that Google's actions towards news publishers are anticompetitive, while The Age article implies that users are accepting of potential misconduct by Google, and another TechCrunch article reports on Google's hardware event, indicating different contexts of Google's activities in each source?
context:
# Helena World Chronicle's Class Action Antitrust Suit Against Google

A class action lawsuit filed in the week of 15 December 2023 in the U.S. District Court in D.C. accuses Google and parent company Alphabet of anticompetitive behavior in violation of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act and others, on behalf of news publishers. The case was filed by Arkansas-based publisher Helena World Chronicle, which argues that Google "siphons off" news publishers' content, their readers and their ad revenue through anticompetitive means, and it specifically cites new AI technologies such as Google's Search Generative Experience (SGE) and the Bard AI chatbot as worsening the problem.

Helena World Chronicle owns and publishes two weekly newspapers in Arkansas. In the complaint it argues that Google is "starving the free press" by sharing publishers' content on Google, losing them "billions of dollars."

Beyond damages, the suit asks for an injunction that would require Google to obtain consent from publishers before using their website data to train its general artificial intelligence products, including Google's own and those of rivals. It also asks that publishers who opt out of SGE still be allowed to show up in Google search results, among other things.

The law firm handling the case is Hausfeld, whose announcement states that "the anticompetitive effects of Google's scheme cause profound harm to competition, to consumers, to labor, and to a democratic free press," and that "Plaintiff Helena World Chronicle, LLC invokes the Sherman Act and Clayton Act to seek class-wide monetary and injunctive relief to restore and ensure competition for digital news and reference publishing and set up guardrails to preserve a free marketplace of ideas in the new era of artificial intelligence."



---


# The Claim That SGE And Bard Appropriate Publisher Content

The Helena World Chronicle lawsuit claims that Google's recent advances in AI-based search were implemented with "the goal of discouraging end-users from visiting the websites of Class members who are part of the digital news and publishing line of commerce." The grounds are that Google's AI products both retain users and consume publisher content without permission.

On the Search Generative Experience, the suit argues that SGE offers web searchers a way to seek information in a conversational mode but ultimately keeps users in Google's "walled garden" as it "plagiarizes" their content. The warrant that turns this into a harm publishers cannot escape is that publishers also cannot block SGE, because it uses the same web crawler as Google's general search service, GoogleBot — so opting out of the AI experience would mean opting out of search itself.

On Bard, the suit says Google's Bard AI was trained on a dataset that included "news, magazine and digital publications," citing both a 2023 report from the News Media Alliance and a Washington Post article about AI training data. The Post, which worked with researchers at the Allen Institute for AI, had found that News and Media sites were the third largest category of AI training data.

The case points to other concerns too, such as changing AdSense rates and evidence of improper spoliation of evidence on Google's part through its destruction of chat messages — an issue raised in the recent Epic Games lawsuit against Google over app store antitrust issues, which Epic won.



---


# Wired's Retracted Claim That Google Manipulates Search Queries

In October 2023, Wired posted an opinion article by lawyer and privacy advocate Megan Gray alleging that Google had accidentally revealed during the trial that it manipulates people's search queries for maximum ad revenue — the example given being the replacement of a search for "children's clothing" with "NIKOLAI-brand kidswear" — and Wired subsequently removed the article for not meeting its standards.

Google rejected the claim in very strong terms, saying the piece was misleading and inaccurate and denying that it ever altered search terms. The Age drew a lesson from the episode's reach: the degree to which the article was shared on social media and boosted in write-ups at other outlets shows just how willing people are to accept foul play on Google's part, and a suspicion of privacy invasion and inappropriate data handling follows the company at all times. The article placed the episode in the wider context of the US case — which, having to prove Google somehow broke the law to achieve the status quo, could be an uphill battle for the government, but which offers everyone else a rare opportunity for insight into what the tech giant does with its enormous market share, and whether it is still focused on being the best or uses its ubiquity to squeeze users for money at the expense of product quality.



---


# The Google Antitrust Case

The Google antitrust case is the U.S. government's trial over Google's dominance in the online search market, stemming from a 2020 antitrust claim, in which the government argues that Google uses its platforms and its deals with partners to block out competition in search or advertising and thereby to hinder competitors from accessing the data they would need to improve their products.

Its defining features are the conduct at issue and the defence offered against it. Google CEO Sundar Pichai testified Monday in the trial, defending Google's business tactics, including its deal with Apple and other partners to make Google the default search engine. Google's answer is that it is just doing business: everybody wants Google as the default engine because it is the best, and that, the company says, does not make its actions illegal.

The important boundary case is which Google antitrust matter this is. The 2020 search claim is separate from the one filed in January by the Department of Justice, along with eight states including New York, California and Colorado, which aims to "halt Google's anticompetitive scheme, unwind Google's monopolistic grip on the market and restore competition to digital advertising." The search case and the digital-advertising case are distinct proceedings and should not be conflated.

The trial is the venue in which the underlying numbers surface. Monday's hearing revealed plenty of juicy tidbits, including the $26.3 billion Google spent making itself the default search engine across platforms in 2021, and how Google tried to take it further and have Chrome preinstalled on iPhones.



---


# What A Ruling Against Google Would Mean For Big Tech

A ruling against Google would not stop at Google: the remedy would likely resemble the Microsoft settlement and the outcome would ripple through the other pending Big Tech cases, because enforcers are using this trial to demonstrate that antitrust law can still take on the largest and most powerful companies in the world.

The grounds for the first half of that claim are the available remedies. If the judge rules against Google, the outcome could look a lot like the Microsoft deal, in which the computer company was required to change its behavior and share its APIs with third-party developers, and was also banned from making anticompetitive and exclusive deals with computer manufacturers. Google might likewise end up having to turn over all or most of the data it has collected to other search engines so they can improve their products and attract more users — a remedy scaled to the disparity the DOJ has cited, that Google gets 16 times more data than Bing does everyday.

The grounds for the ripple effect are the cases already queued behind this one. The FTC sued Amazon in September for using anticompetitive and unfair strategies to illegally maintain its monopoly power. The DOJ has been investigating Apple for years over the company's policy for third-party apps on its devices and whether it unfairly favors its own products. And there is an ongoing case between the FTC and Facebook, in which the agency calls on Facebook to sell Instagram and WhatsApp.

The warrant joining grounds to claim is enforcers' own stake in the result: they will want to show that antitrust law is still relevant and can successfully take on the biggest, most powerful companies in the world, so a win here sets the template the neighbouring cases are argued against. The scope condition is that nothing was settled as of this report — the case is expected to continue for several weeks, bringing to a head one of the biggest fights in tech antitrust since the U.S. took Microsoft to trial in the 1990s.



---


# Gemini Pro's News Summarization Refusals And Stale Answers

Asked to summarise topical news in early December 2023, Gemini Pro often would not do it, despite having Google Search and Google News at its disposal. It seemed loath to comment on potentially controversial news topics, instead telling users to Google it themselves.

The TechCrunch reporter tried the same prompt and got a very similar response. ChatGPT, by contrast, gave a bullet-list summary with citations to news articles.

There was one partial exception, and it exposed a second problem: Gemini Pro did provide a summary of updates on the war in Ukraine when the reporter asked for one, but the information was over a month out of date.



---


# Google's Rebuttal To The Publisher Antitrust Suit

Google rejects the premise that it deprives publishers of readers and traffic. A Google spokesperson called the Helena World Chronicle lawsuit "meritless," and attacked the claim of foreclosure directly: "People have many ways to access information and news content today – through publishers' websites, dedicated apps, social media platforms, print papers and more. Google links people to publishers' websites more than 24 billion times each month – at no cost to them."

The rebuttal therefore contests two of the suit's premises at once: that Google is a bottleneck between readers and publishers, and that publishers are uncompensated, by pointing to the volume of free referrals Google sends.

qid: Does the Sporting News article suggest that bettors earn a fixed profit when betting on the Red Sox, while the CBSSports.com article indicates that Spread betting involves wagering on the margin of victory rather than a fixed outcome?
context:
# Point Spread Variants By Team Sport

Spread betting is popular across sports but takes slightly different forms in each: football and basketball use a point spread, baseball calls it the "run line," hockey the "puck line," and soccer the "goal line." In every case the mechanism is the same — the favorite must win by more than the posted margin, and the underdog wins the bet by winning outright or losing by less than it.

In a hypothetical NFL spread with the Patriots as -5.5 favorites over the Steelers, a bet on the Patriots needs them to win by 6 or more points, while a bet on the Steelers wins if they win outright or lose by 5 or fewer. In a hypothetical NBA spread with the Warriors as -9 favorites over the Raptors, a Warriors bet needs a win by 10 or more points and a Raptors bet wins on an outright win or a loss by 8 or fewer; at Warriors 110, Raptors 104, Raptors bets win because they lost by only 6, whereas a 115-104 Warriors win covers the spread by 11 points.

In a hypothetical MLB matchup between the Yankees and Red Sox with the Yankees at -1.5 on the run line — baseball's point spread — a Yankees bet requires a win by 2 or more runs, and Red Sox bets win on a victory or a 1-run loss; Yankees 5, Red Sox 4 means Red Sox bets win, while a 6-3 Yankees win covers the run line with a 3-run margin. At NHL betting sites the "puck line" is akin to the point spread: with the Canadiens as -1.5 favorites over the Blackhawks, the Canadiens need to win by 2 or more goals, and Blackhawks bets win on an outright win or a one-goal loss; Canadiens 3, Blackhawks 2 means Blackhawks bets win because the one-goal victory does not cover 1.5, while a 4-1 Canadiens win covers by a 3-goal margin. In a hypothetical MLS game between LA Galaxy and Atlanta United with LA Galaxy at -1 on the goal line, the Galaxy need to win by 2 or more goals and Atlanta bets win on an outright win or a single-goal loss; LA Galaxy 2, Atlanta United 1 means Atlanta bets win, while a 3-1 Galaxy win covers with a 2-goal margin.



---


# Point Spread Odds And Line Movement

Alongside a point spread, sportsbooks attach odds indicating the potential payout relative to the amount wagered, and those odds sit close to even because the spread itself is designed to level the playing field between the two teams. The same payout can be expressed in several formats: American (for example -110 or +110), Decimal (for example 1.91), and Fractional (for example 10/11), each a different way of stating the same potential return.

Point spread odds are not fixed once set; the shifts are commonly called "line movement." Lines move when the point spread or the odds attached to a particular bet change after sportsbooks have initially set them, and Sporting News identifies several drivers. The most common cause is an imbalance in the money being wagered on one side: if a significant majority of bettors back one team to cover, the top sports betting apps adjust the spread to make the other side more appealing and thereby balance the betting action. A second driver is unexpected events — injuries to key players, changes in team strategy, or significant weather events that might affect a game's outcome; for instance, if a star quarterback is announced as injured days before a big game, the spread might shift in favor of the opposing team. A third driver is information and public perception: when a piece of news or a prevailing sentiment about a team's increased chances of winning gains traction, it influences how people bet and leads sportsbooks to adjust their lines accordingly.



---


# Sports Betting Terminology Glossary

CBS Sports set out the top Kentucky betting terms for new bettors on 13 October 2023, defining each bet type by what the bettor is actually wagering on and, in several cases, by a worked Kentucky example.

Against the spread means that instead of betting on an exact winner, the widely popular spread bet levels the playing field by letting you wager on how many points a team will win by: in basketball, if Kentucky is the 7.5-point favorite against Louisville then Kentucky covers by winning by 8 or more, while Louisville as the 7.5-point underdog covers by winning outright or losing by 7 or fewer. Money line is an elevated outright bet with odds adjusted to reflect a favored team and an underdog: if Kentucky is a -200 favorite against Florida you'd need to bet $200 to return $100, while Florida at +200 would return $200 on a $100 bet. An outright bet is the easiest wager to place and is perfect for horse racing, one of Kentucky's biggest sporting events — bettors choose one athlete, or thoroughbred, to win an entire event. An Over/Under has the sportsbook post an estimated total of both teams' final scores, with the bettor wagering on whether the actual final will be higher or lower: if the Over/Under for a Kentucky-Louisville basketball game is 125.5, you wager on the final total being Over 126 or Under 125. A player prop projects a player's stat at the end of a game and asks you to wager over or under that projection, with popular examples being how many touchdown passes a quarterback throws or how many three-pointers a basketball player hits; Kentucky is one of the 18 states that allows prop bets on collegiate athletes.

The remaining terms describe the market's participants and mechanics. The underdog is the team deemed less likely to win based on the odds, and a bet on one typically yields a larger return than a bet on the favorite; the favorite is deemed more likely to win, and bettors often pay a premium for backing one though they more often win outright. Consensus odds are generally defined as an average of all available betting markets, since different sportsbooks may price markets variably based on the action they've taken or their own interpretation of information. Futures markets encompass almost anything outside single-game bets — total regular-season wins, championship odds, MVP odds and more. A parlay requires two or more bets within a single wager, all of which must win: wagering $100 on a three-leg parlay at 6 to 1 odds could win $600 if all three legs win. Juice, also known as the vig or vigorish, is effectively the tax oddsmakers charge for handling a wager — if a book judges a game a virtual coinflip it may price both options at -110 to give itself a 10% rake on all the action. A push is a bet where neither the bettor nor the sportsbook wins: if an over/under for total points is set at 44 and both teams combine for exactly 44, the result is a push and the principal is returned. Live or in-game betting allows bets on several different markets in real time — in basketball, on the outcome of a quarter, individual statistics and live-updated spreads and totals.



---


# Determining A Point Spread Bet Outcome

To settle a point spread wager, compare the final margin of victory against the spread: the favorite covers by winning by a margin greater than the specified point spread, while the underdog covers by either winning the game outright or losing by fewer points than the spread. Those are the potential outcomes of a point spread wager as Sporting News sets them out.

Applied to a favorite that covers, suppose an NBA betting site has set the point spread for a Los Angeles Lakers-New York Knicks game at Lakers -7. This means the Lakers are the favorites and are expected to win by 7 points, so a spread wager on the Lakers requires them to win by more than 7. If the final score is Lakers 110, Knicks 100, the Lakers won by a margin of 10 points; since that is more than the 7-point spread, a bet on the Lakers wins.

Applied to a favorite that fails to cover, suppose an NFL betting site has set the point spread for a Chicago Bears-Miami Dolphins game at Bears -4, indicating the Bears are the favorites and are expected to win by 4 points; betting the Bears means betting they will win by more than 4. If the final score is Chicago Bears 24, Miami Dolphins 23, the Bears have won by only a 1-point margin. Since that is less than the 4-point spread, a bet on the Bears loses — despite winning the game, they failed to "cover" the 4-point spread, so those who wagered on them lost.



---


# Sports Betting As An Investment Mindset

Sporting News' best bets column argues that sports betting is not a gamble: with the right mindset, strategies and preparedness it is an investment, and the column said on Nov. 3, 2023 that it was loving its return on investment through seven weeks. On that view the activity is not a hobby but "a second job that allows us to punch in while we're sitting on our couch."

The grounds are the work that goes into it. Because the reader's goal is to boost their bankroll, the column's top priority is to help achieve that by putting in a ton of statistical research, attacking all the angles, uncovering betting trends and pinpointing value across all the sports betting sites each week — which is how it arrives at its best moneyline, spread, over/under and SuperDraft player prop bets for a slate it describes as featuring a plethora of lucrative opportunities.

qid: Did The Age report on November 7, 2023, contradict the allegations of Donald Trump's financial misrepresentations after the report by Fortune on September 26, 2023, claiming Donald Trump inflated the value of his Trump Tower apartment?
context:
# Trump Tower Fifth Avenue Penthouse Valuation Dispute

Among the allegations in the New York case was that Trump claimed his Trump Tower apartment in Manhattan — a three-storey penthouse replete with gold-plated fixtures — was nearly three times its actual size, and valued the property at $327 million; no apartment in New York City has ever sold for close to that amount, Attorney General Letitia James said. The Age's comparison in November 2023 listed Trump's 2021 valuation at $US131.3 million and Bloomberg's 2023 valuation at $US40 million, with no current New York estimate available.

The size inflation is documented over a specific window: between 2011 and 2016, Trump valued the apartment on the basis of it being 30,000 square feet (2,787 square metres), almost triple its actual measurement of 10,996 square feet, and because of this New York State arrived at a valuation about a third of Trump's in those years. Space inflation was not the only issue: between 2014 and 2015 Trump increased the apartment's value to $US327 million from $US200 million, which the prosecution argues was to mask a drop in the value of another of his properties. "A discrepancy of this order of magnitude, by a real estate developer sizing up his own living space of decades, can only be considered fraud," Judge Arthur Engoron wrote in his September ruling.

Bloomberg values the property using recent Trump Tower sales and those of comparable Manhattan penthouses. While some splashy residences in much newer Billionaires Row buildings have listed for well in excess of $US100 million, they typically boast higher ceilings, more up-to-date finishes, contemporary layouts, outdoor space and better views. A better comparison, the report says, would be a 9,450-square-foot penthouse in Olympic Tower, five blocks south on Fifth Avenue, on and off the market for $US35 million since 2016; or Carl Icahn's 14,000-square-foot penthouse at Museum Tower on West 53rd Street, listed for $US35 million in 2019 before he attempted to split and sell it as two apartments, both eventually delisted.



---


# Trump Net Worth Valuation Dispute at Trial

Thousands of pages of exhibits detailing the performance of Donald Trump's assets, made available during the New York fraud trial, have provided a deeper look into his fortune. His 2021 statement of financial condition, filed as part of the lawsuit, pegged his net worth at $US4.5 billion. Bloomberg's calculation has consistently been below Trump's figures; at the same time, Bloomberg measured the value of some Trump properties higher than what New York state claims.

Trump took the stand and testified that the properties whose values he is accused of inflating were actually undervalued, based on the premium his "brand" adds. He also said that banks did not rely on his statements of financial condition when weighing loans: "They just weren't a very important element in banks' decision-making process," Trump told the court. "And we'll explain that as this trial goes along."

The Age's 7 November 2023 report set out New York state's valuation of four high-profile Trump properties where the prosecution alleges fraud occurred, alongside Bloomberg's own approach to assessing the assets.



---


# Engoron Summary Judgment That Trump Committed Fraud

A judge ruled on Tuesday 26 September 2023 that Donald Trump committed fraud for years while building the real estate empire that catapulted him to fame and the White House. Judge Arthur Engoron, ruling in a civil lawsuit brought by New York's attorney general, found that the former president and his company deceived banks, insurers and others by massively overvaluing his assets and exaggerating his net worth on paperwork used in making deals and securing financing.

As punishment, Engoron ordered that some of Trump's business licences be rescinded, and said he would continue to have an independent monitor oversee the Trump Organization's operations. A Trump spokesperson did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the ruling, and Trump has long insisted he did nothing wrong.

Fortune described the decision, which came days before the start of a non-jury trial in Attorney General Letitia James' lawsuit, as the strongest repudiation yet of Trump's carefully coiffed image as a wealthy and shrewd real estate mogul turned political powerhouse.



---


# Letitia James Asset Inflation Allegations

Letitia James, a Democrat, sued Trump and the Trump Organization a year before this September 2023 ruling, alleging a pattern of duplicity that she dubbed "the art of the steal" — a twist on the title of Trump's 1987 business memoir "The Art of the Deal."

The lawsuit accused Trump and his company of routinely inflating the value of assets like skyscrapers, golf courses and his Mar-a-Lago estate in Florida, padding his bottom line by billions.



---


# Trump Park Avenue Rent-Stabilised Unit Valuations

Trump Park Avenue, the residential condo tower on Manhattan's Upper East Side formerly known as the Hotel Delmonico, is not one of Trump's best-known buildings, but according to the prosecution it has been the source of some significant asset inflations. Trump's 2021 valuation was $US90.9 million, Bloomberg's 2023 valuation $US86.4 million, and New York's 2021 valuation $US80 million.

The dispute centres on rent-stabilised units. The building's value to Trump mostly stems from unsold condo units owned by the Trump Organisation and rented out, a varying number of which have been rent-stabilised, meaning tenants pay below market rates; such apartments are typically valued at a discount because tenants can stay indefinitely, sometimes even passing them on to children. In 2010, 12 rent-stabilised apartments owned by Trump were valued at an average of $US62,500 each in an appraisal provided by a real estate company; the following year Trump valued them at $US4.1 million each, more than 65 times greater, and has continued to value stabilised apartments in the building at market rates, including in his 2021 statement of financial condition. Rent-stabilised units "with a positive cash flow are often valued at 15-25 cents a dollar of the open market value, versus single digits for negative cash flow," said Jonathan Miller, president of appraiser Miller Samuel.

Trump's optimism was shown to be at least partially justified: by 2021, only five of the 12 apartments remained rent stabilised. The prosecution also claims two additional non-stabilised apartments in the building were overvalued because Trump ignored an option his daughter, Ivanka Trump, had to buy them at a price lower than the market value he used. The Age also records an assessment of the brand effect on price generally: "There would be a Trump premium because the person that would want that property is likely to be a Trump supporter," Eli Beracha said, though it is also likely that the association with Trump would turn off some buyers.



---


# Trump's Other Criminal and Civil Cases 2023

Letitia James' lawsuit is one of several legal headaches for Trump as he campaigns for a return to the White House in 2024. He has been indicted four times in the six months to September 2023 — accused in Georgia and Washington, D.C., of plotting to overturn his 2020 election loss; in Florida of hoarding classified documents; and in Manhattan of falsifying business records related to hush money paid on his behalf.

Separately, the Trump Organization was convicted of tax fraud in 2022 in an unrelated criminal case for helping executives dodge taxes on extravagant perks such as Manhattan apartments and luxury cars, and the company was fined $1.6 million. One of the executives, Trump's longtime finance chief Allen Weisselberg, pleaded guilty and served five months in jail; he is a defendant in James' lawsuit and gave sworn deposition testimony for the case in May.



---


# Engoron's "Fantasy World" Finding on Trump Financial Statements

Judge Arthur Engoron's finding is that Trump's conduct went beyond boasting into legal violation: beyond mere bragging about his riches, Trump, his company and key executives repeatedly lied about them on his annual financial statements, reaping rewards such as favourable loan terms and lower insurance premiums.

Those tactics crossed a line and violated the law, the judge said, rejecting Trump's contention that a disclaimer on the financial statements absolved him of any wrongdoing.

The warrant he offers is that the defence position requires an internally incoherent picture of valuation and responsibility. "In defendants' world: rent regulated apartments are worth the same as unregulated apartments; restricted land is worth the same as unrestricted land; restrictions can evaporate into thin air; a disclaimer by one party casting responsibility on another party exonerates the other party's lies," Engoron wrote in his 35-page ruling. "That is a fantasy world, not the real world."



---


# Letitia James' History of Investigating Trump

Letitia James, who campaigned for office as a Trump critic and watchdog, started scrutinising his business practices in March 2019, after his former personal lawyer Michael Cohen testified to Congress that Trump exaggerated his wealth on financial statements provided to Deutsche Bank while trying to obtain financing to buy the NFL's Buffalo Bills.

Her office had previously sued Trump for misusing his own charitable foundation to further his political and business interests. Trump was ordered to pay $2 million to an array of charities as a fine, and the charity, the Trump Foundation, was shut down.

qid: What type of establishments, as reported by Sporting News, would alter betting lines due to news about team performance, suspend bets for weather-related game suspensions, modify odds in response to roster changes, and update NBA Rookie of the Year betting lines based on collected data?
context:
# Totals Line Movement Drivers

The totals line can move, and Sporting News attributes that movement to four kinds of input: betting activity, injury updates, weather conditions, and other news and updates.

Betting activity is one of the most common reasons for line movement — a significant amount of money wagered on one side, either the over or the under, leads bookmakers to adjust the line to balance the action and protect themselves from potential losses. Injury updates work through the expected score: if a key player is injured or unable to play, that can influence the expected total score, leading bookmakers to adjust the line accordingly. Weather conditions matter in outdoor sports; heavy rain or snow in a football game might create expectations of a lower-scoring game, causing the line to move down. Finally, any other news that might affect team performance — changes in team strategy or recent performances — can influence totals lines.



---


# Why Moneyline Odds Change

Lines at sports betting apps change quickly for two primary reasons — public betting and new information — and sportsbooks adjust moneyline odds to stay profitable, balance their book and reflect the most current information about an event. Before setting odds oddsmakers gather extensive data, then release the finalized odds to the public; from that point a bettor can bet immediately or wait for shifts, though predicting those shifts is challenging.

The time dimension shows how an opening price drifts. Odds for the next Super Bowl champion released shortly after the previous Super Bowl are based mostly on the recently concluded season; as the new season approaches and teams make changes, the odds adjust to perceived championship chances, and as games progress the lines keep evolving with team performances.

The mechanism has five named drivers. Public betting patterns move a line because, when a significant amount of money lands on one team or participant, sportsbooks adjust the odds to balance their liability — making the price less favorable for the heavily-bet side and more favorable for the less-bet side to encourage even betting and reduce financial risk. New information matters because changes in player injuries, player substitutions or weather conditions alter the perceived outcome, and books adjust once such information becomes public. Professional bettors move lines because large wagers from sharp bettors often reflect insights or information that can influence the odds. Initial miscalculation is a fourth driver: sometimes the opening odds are perceived as offering value, and heavy betting on one side signals that the initial price was potentially "off," prompting an adjustment. Event dynamics is the fifth, applying to live betting placed while the event is in progress, where the evolving dynamics of the match lead to frequent changes.



---


# Point Spread Odds And Line Movement

Alongside a point spread, sportsbooks attach odds indicating the potential payout relative to the amount wagered, and those odds sit close to even because the spread itself is designed to level the playing field between the two teams. The same payout can be expressed in several formats: American (for example -110 or +110), Decimal (for example 1.91), and Fractional (for example 10/11), each a different way of stating the same potential return.

Point spread odds are not fixed once set; the shifts are commonly called "line movement." Lines move when the point spread or the odds attached to a particular bet change after sportsbooks have initially set them, and Sporting News identifies several drivers. The most common cause is an imbalance in the money being wagered on one side: if a significant majority of bettors back one team to cover, the top sports betting apps adjust the spread to make the other side more appealing and thereby balance the betting action. A second driver is unexpected events — injuries to key players, changes in team strategy, or significant weather events that might affect a game's outcome; for instance, if a star quarterback is announced as injured days before a big game, the spread might shift in favor of the opposing team. A third driver is information and public perception: when a piece of news or a prevailing sentiment about a team's increased chances of winning gains traction, it influences how people bet and leads sportsbooks to adjust their lines accordingly.



---


# Line Movement As A Signal Of Betting Value

Sporting News argues that bettors should monitor line movement before a game starts, because line moves reveal where the value in a bet lies. The claim is stated for both markets it covers: point spread odds can and do change based on a combination of actual betting patterns, unexpected events, and shifts in public perception, and savvy bettors keep a close eye on these line moves, as they can offer insights into where the value lies in a particular bet.

The grounds are how the lines are made and remade. Sportsbooks set game totals considering factors like recent performances, weather, and player status, and as new data emerges and betting trends develop, this line can shift — if many bettors choose the "over," the sportsbook might raise the total to balance the bets. The warrant joining grounds to claim is that line movements often reflect public betting sentiments and therefore offer insights to informed bettors: because a move encodes information the book has absorbed about data and about where the public money is, watching it tells the bettor something they did not otherwise have. Hence bettors must monitor any line changes before the game starts and strategize accordingly to optimize their betting success.

# How Sportsbooks Set And Move Betting Lines

The oddsmakers and services use computer models and algorithms that consider analytics, statistics, injury and roster news, performance, matchup data and more to develop the lines and odds. Those lines are then subject to change based on the betting public's reaction and any additional information that emerges before the game, and a book will move the line or change the odds if the public bets heavily on one side.

The governing objective is balance rather than prediction. Every sportsbook's goal is to even out the betting on both sides of every bet, because that lets the book earn the small profit built into the odds and lines without worrying about which side wins. Sportsbooks want even betting so much that they will move a line or change the odds specifically to draw more bets to the other side.

The relation that matters to a bettor is that books do not all move together. The betting is rarely the same at every sportsbook: one book may be forced to move a line or change the odds because of the money it has taken while another is not, and the lines and odds may even differ right from the jump. That divergence is what creates the chance to book a bet at improved odds or a more favorable line.

The range over which this holds is narrow and specific. When a line moves for a legitimate reason such as an injury or roster move, every sportsbook jumps on board, and it is difficult to find value; when a line moves because of betting patterns, only the sportsbook that saw that betting makes the change, and that is the opportunity. # Helena World Chronicle's Class Action Antitrust Suit Against Google

A class action lawsuit filed in the week of 15 December 2023 in the U.S. District Court in D.C. accuses Google and parent company Alphabet of anticompetitive behavior in violation of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act and others, on behalf of news publishers. The case was filed by Arkansas-based publisher Helena World Chronicle, which argues that Google "siphons off" news publishers' content, their readers and their ad revenue through anticompetitive means, and it specifically cites new AI technologies such as Google's Search Generative Experience (SGE) and the Bard AI chatbot as worsening the problem.

Helena World Chronicle owns and publishes two weekly newspapers in Arkansas. In the complaint it argues that Google is "starving the free press" by sharing publishers' content on Google, losing them "billions of dollars."

Beyond damages, the suit asks for an injunction that would require Google to obtain consent from publishers before using their website data to train its general artificial intelligence products, including Google's own and those of rivals. It also asks that publishers who opt out of SGE still be allowed to show up in Google search results, among other things.

The law firm handling the case is Hausfeld, whose announcement states that "the anticompetitive effects of Google's scheme cause profound harm to competition, to consumers, to labor, and to a democratic free press," and that "Plaintiff Helena World Chronicle, LLC invokes the Sherman Act and Clayton Act to seek class-wide monetary and injunctive relief to restore and ensure competition for digital news and reference publishing and set up guardrails to preserve a free marketplace of ideas in the new era of artificial intelligence."



---


# Google Paid $26.3 Billion In 2021 For Default Search Placement

Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to multiple browsers, phones and platforms — from companies including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla — to be everyone's default search engine. The figure was revealed by Google's search head Prabhakar Raghavan when he testified in court on October 28, according to The Verge.

About $18 billion of that total went directly to Apple, according to a New York Times report published earlier in October 2023, and Google has had its deal with Apple in place since 2003 — so the payment is the current year of a two-decade arrangement, not a one-off. Questioned on the amount of money Google spends to get first pick of search engines, Pichai said the decision was made with the consumer in mind: Google pays big bucks to be everywhere so that it can take in all the data and be the best search engine across different companies' devices, he said, according to The Verge.

The trial also produced evidence that Google understood the value of defaults very early on. U.S. Justice Department lawyer Meagan Bellshaw showed Pichai a 2007 email from a Google product strategy meeting containing data showing that when people changed their browser homepage to Google, they did 15% more Google searches, and that when they switched away, their Google searches dropped 27%. The email summarizing that meeting, sent to Pichai as well as other Google leaders, read: "Nitin argues that focusing on homepage market share is one of the most effective things we can do to make gains in search market share," according to The Verge.



---


# US v. Google: Two Months Into The Search Antitrust Trial

As of TechCrunch's November 13, 2023 roundup, the Justice Department's landmark antitrust case against Google was nearly two months old, and the trial record was still producing fresh revelations. TechCrunch framed it as one of the biggest fights in tech antitrust since the U.S. took Microsoft to trial in the 1990s.

An earlier roundup had already surfaced that Google spent $26.3 billion in 2021 making itself the default search engine across platforms, and that Google tried to have Chrome preinstalled on iPhones. Over the couple of weeks preceding this roundup, more of Google's inner workings came to light, including some of the search engine's most lucrative search queries, the shape of the revenue-share agreements between Google and Android OEMs, and why Expedia has a bone to pick with Google.



---


# The Google Antitrust Case

The Google antitrust case is the U.S. government's trial over Google's dominance in the online search market, stemming from a 2020 antitrust claim, in which the government argues that Google uses its platforms and its deals with partners to block out competition in search or advertising and thereby to hinder competitors from accessing the data they would need to improve their products.

Its defining features are the conduct at issue and the defence offered against it. Google CEO Sundar Pichai testified Monday in the trial, defending Google's business tactics, including its deal with Apple and other partners to make Google the default search engine. Google's answer is that it is just doing business: everybody wants Google as the default engine because it is the best, and that, the company says, does not make its actions illegal.

The important boundary case is which Google antitrust matter this is. The 2020 search claim is separate from the one filed in January by the Department of Justice, along with eight states including New York, California and Colorado, which aims to "halt Google's anticompetitive scheme, unwind Google's monopolistic grip on the market and restore competition to digital advertising." The search case and the digital-advertising case are distinct proceedings and should not be conflated.

The trial is the venue in which the underlying numbers surface. Monday's hearing revealed plenty of juicy tidbits, including the $26.3 billion Google spent making itself the default search engine across platforms in 2021, and how Google tried to take it further and have Chrome preinstalled on iPhones.



---


# The U.S. Justice Department's Parallel Antitrust Suits Against Google

The Helena World Chronicle class action arrives alongside the filing of the U.S. Justice Department's lawsuit against Google for monopolizing digital ad technologies, and the complaint also references the Justice Department's 2020 civil antitrust suit over search and search advertising.

The two government cases concern different markets: search and search advertising in the 2020 suit are distinct from the digital ad technologies at issue in the more recent one.



---


# The Claim That SGE And Bard Appropriate Publisher Content

The Helena World Chronicle lawsuit claims that Google's recent advances in AI-based search were implemented with "the goal of discouraging end-users from visiting the websites of Class members who are part of the digital news and publishing line of commerce." The grounds are that Google's AI products both retain users and consume publisher content without permission.

On the Search Generative Experience, the suit argues that SGE offers web searchers a way to seek information in a conversational mode but ultimately keeps users in Google's "walled garden" as it "plagiarizes" their content. The warrant that turns this into a harm publishers cannot escape is that publishers also cannot block SGE, because it uses the same web crawler as Google's general search service, GoogleBot — so opting out of the AI experience would mean opting out of search itself.

On Bard, the suit says Google's Bard AI was trained on a dataset that included "news, magazine and digital publications," citing both a 2023 report from the News Media Alliance and a Washington Post article about AI training data. The Post, which worked with researchers at the Allen Institute for AI, had found that News and Media sites were the third largest category of AI training data.

The case points to other concerns too, such as changing AdSense rates and evidence of improper spoliation of evidence on Google's part through its destruction of chat messages — an issue raised in the recent Epic Games lawsuit against Google over app store antitrust issues, which Epic won.



---


# Google's Rebuttal To The Publisher Antitrust Suit

Google rejects the premise that it deprives publishers of readers and traffic. A Google spokesperson called the Helena World Chronicle lawsuit "meritless," and attacked the claim of foreclosure directly: "People have many ways to access information and news content today – through publishers' websites, dedicated apps, social media platforms, print papers and more. Google links people to publishers' websites more than 24 billion times each month – at no cost to them."

The rebuttal therefore contests two of the suit's premises at once: that Google is a bottleneck between readers and publishers, and that publishers are uncompensated, by pointing to the volume of free referrals Google sends.



---


# Deft's Competitive Landscape: Search Incumbents

Given that it is building a search solution for e-commerce, Deft already faces challenges from Amazon and Google, both of which have shipped comparable features.

In September 2023, Amazon updated its visual search feature that lets users snap a photo of a product and search for similar items on the platform. Google released its multi-search feature in 2022, letting users fuse images and text — the same combination Deft offers.

Separately, Deft will also face competition from other startups like Objective, a Matrix Partners-backed startup building an API platform for multimodal search.

# Sam Bankman-Fried

Sam Bankman-Fried is the former CEO of the bankrupt crypto exchange FTX, whose highly anticipated criminal trial started on the Tuesday before TechCrunch's 2023-10-01 report, to determine whether he is guilty of seven counts of fraud and conspiracy. As one former federal prosecutor put it: "The odds seem to be stacked against him at this point."

He was 31 years old and co-founded FTX in 2019; within a few years the once third-largest crypto exchange's valuation hit $32 billion at its peak, and the company is now trying to claw back any funds to distribute to creditors. Before the fall he was even compared to Warren Buffet, and many called him the white horse of crypto — a description TechCrunch notes it never applied to him.

Bankman-Fried, however, maintained his innocence. At The New York Times' DealBook Summit he appeared virtually from the Bahamas and said, "I didn't ever try to commit fraud on anyone; I was shocked by what happened this month"; in a published DM exchange with a Vox reporter he said he regretted filing for bankruptcy and thought that "regulators make everything worse." In January he pleaded not guilty to all counts, which include wire fraud, conspiracy to commit money laundering and conspiracy to misuse customer funds. He could face up to 115 years in jail if convicted on all charges.

TechCrunch's 2023-10-02 summary of his standing on the eve of trial: SBF has been denied bail; his name is mud (or much worse) among those who have lost money in Alameda or FTX; and those who might not have had positions in these still blame him for other crypto woes, because he set off a ripple effect.

# Day Two Of The Bankman-Fried Trial: Jury Selection And The Courtroom Audience

On the second day of Sam Bankman-Fried's fraud trial, the jury was selected on Wednesday morning, after which lawyers for the government and then for Bankman-Fried delivered opening statements that told two very different stories of the former FTX CEO's sudden rise and almost instantaneous fall. The central question framed by the proceedings was who Bankman-Fried, the former CEO of crypto exchange FTX, really is: a liar and a fraud, or someone who acted in good faith and, like many a startup founder, flew too close to the sun. That answer, the account notes, ultimately lies with the jury.

The day featured pointed allegations, a friend from MIT, and an audience replete with big names, including Bankman-Fried's professorial parents and Damian Williams, the U.S. attorney for the Southern District of New York. Bankman-Fried himself spent most of the day in court staring into a laptop while seated between his two attorneys. The prosecution's account of his alleged crimes was described as featuring a study in contrasts.

# Going Infinite: Michael Lewis On Sam Bankman-Fried

Michael Lewis's October 2023 book is an account of Sam Bankman-Fried, published by Allen Lane at $55 on 3 October, The Sydney Morning Herald listed on 1 October 2023.

Its subject is defined by the arc: Bankman-Fried set up his cryptocurrency exchange, FTX, in 2019 and three years later was rolling in money, but when the crypto world went pear-shaped his business hit an irreversible tailspin, and he now faces multiple charges and was due in court on 3 October.

A caveat is attached — "No doubt the updated edition will have the verdict on SBF."

# Sam Bankman-Fried's Federal Fraud Trial

Sam Bankman-Fried, the founder of bankrupt cryptocurrency exchange FTX, is charged with seven counts of fraud and money laundering following the collapse of his cryptocurrency empire the previous year, and was on trial in New York in October 2023.

Two fixed points anchor the proceeding as CNBC described it on 2023-10-06. A U.S. judge revoked Bankman-Fried's bail at a hearing in a New York courthouse on August 11, 2023. And on Thursday, Oct. 5, 2023, Matt Huang, co-founder of Paradigm Operations LP, arrived at the New York court to appear in the case.

# The FTX Trial's Stakes For The Wider Crypto Industry

The Verge argued that the trial of Sam Bankman-Fried is likely to be more consequential than just whether the man himself is found guilty: depending on what evidence is introduced, it could be rough for the entire crypto industry.

The grounds are the unpredictability of what a trial surfaces, voiced by Yesha Yadav, a law professor at Vanderbilt University: "How much damage can this trial do to the already beaten-down reputation of the industry at this point? # FTX Fraud Charges And The SEC's Allegation

Sam Bankman-Fried, the founder of the failed cryptocurrency exchange FTX, faced seven counts of wire fraud and conspiracy — specifically, two counts of wire fraud and five conspiracy charges — and the Securities and Exchange Commission alleged that FTX was a fraud "from the start," with a "multi-billion-dollar deficiency caused by his own misappropriation of customer funds." The Verge repeated this framing at the head of each of its trial dispatches through October 2023, and in its October 28th, 2023 write-up reported that Bankman-Fried had been found guilty on seven counts including charges of wire fraud.

The boundary of the concept is the mix of charge types: the indictment paired substantive wire fraud counts with conspiracy counts rather than resting on a single offence, and the SEC's civil allegation about the exchange's origins ran alongside the criminal case rather than being part of it. The Verge's reporter, writing as the prosecution's case neared its end on October 26th, 2023, added an impression of the people the charges swept in: all the co-conspirators seemed oddly younger than their years, as though they had got stuck in the "math camp forever" environment Bankman-Fried created for them and simply failed to grow up.

Sam Bankman-Fried is in court for alleged fraud and money laundering while leading crypto exchange FTX and sister company Alameda. TechCrunch's 2023-10-02 preview placed the case in the Manhattan Federal Court, describing the disgraced cryptocurrency entrepreneur as accused of orchestrating "one of the biggest financial frauds in American history": the multibillion-dollar collapse of FTX, the crypto exchange he founded and led. SBF, as he is known, has pleaded not guilty to some seven charges of fraud and conspiracy.

The trial kicked off with jury selection October 3. By TechCrunch's 2023-10-06 update the case was entering its next chapter, with proceedings resuming Thursday: as confirmed during a teleconference Wednesday, SBF would be taking the stand along with a handful of other witnesses, as the onus shifted toward the defense after the prosecution brought its case to its conclusion.

Access to the proceedings is limited: no devices are allowed, so reports are being physically put together within the courtroom, or sent to overflow rooms.
