# Engoron Summary Judgment That Trump Committed Fraud

A judge ruled on Tuesday 26 September 2023 that Donald Trump committed fraud for years while building the real estate empire that catapulted him to fame and the White House. Judge Arthur Engoron, ruling in a civil lawsuit brought by New York's attorney general, found that the former president and his company deceived banks, insurers and others by massively overvaluing his assets and exaggerating his net worth on paperwork used in making deals and securing financing.

As punishment, Engoron ordered that some of Trump's business licences be rescinded, and said he would continue to have an independent monitor oversee the Trump Organization's operations. A Trump spokesperson did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the ruling, and Trump has long insisted he did nothing wrong.

Fortune described the decision, which came days before the start of a non-jury trial in Attorney General Letitia James' lawsuit, as the strongest repudiation yet of Trump's carefully coiffed image as a wealthy and shrewd real estate mogul turned political powerhouse.

# FTX Fraud Charges And The SEC's Allegation

Sam Bankman-Fried, the founder of the failed cryptocurrency exchange FTX, faced seven counts of wire fraud and conspiracy — specifically, two counts of wire fraud and five conspiracy charges — and the Securities and Exchange Commission alleged that FTX was a fraud "from the start," with a "multi-billion-dollar deficiency caused by his own misappropriation of customer funds." The Verge repeated this framing at the head of each of its trial dispatches through October 2023, and in its October 28th, 2023 write-up reported that Bankman-Fried had been found guilty on seven counts including charges of wire fraud.

The boundary of the concept is the mix of charge types: the indictment paired substantive wire fraud counts with conspiracy counts rather than resting on a single offence, and the SEC's civil allegation about the exchange's origins ran alongside the criminal case rather than being part of it. The Verge's reporter, writing as the prosecution's case neared its end on October 26th, 2023, added an impression of the people the charges swept in: all the co-conspirators seemed oddly younger than their years, as though they had got stuck in the "math camp forever" environment Bankman-Fried created for them and simply failed to grow up.

# ASX November 2023 Session and RBA Rate Expectations

In the Australian session reported by The Sydney Morning Herald on 5 November 2023, energy companies were the main drag on the index, down one per cent, with Woodside off 0.8 per cent, Santos down 0.4 per cent and Ampol down 1.2 per cent, alongside coal miners Yancoal (down 1.7 per cent) and Whitehaven (down 2 per cent). Lynas Rare Earths was the biggest large-cap decliner at down 3.1 per cent, while industrials fell 0.2 per cent, including Computershare (down 2.9 per cent), Seven West Holdings (down 1.9 per cent) and Worley (down 1.3 per cent).

TMS Capital portfolio manager Ben Clark said the big news for markets on the Monday was Westpac's trading update, which he said led a resurgence in the banking sector's performance. "Westpac's results were better than expected, especially because it's been a bit of a perennial underperformer in the past few years," he said, adding that it set the tone for results from NAB and ANZ due to report in the following week. Clark also described a reversal of the interest-rate trade of recent weeks: "Long-term bond yields came off quite significantly in the last few days following weaker than expected employment data on Friday, which has seen some investors swivel back into growth stocks." On his account the market had switched from pricing in an 80 per cent chance of a rate rise on the Tuesday to 50-50.

Other commentary framed the risk of a further increase. "Our view is that in the high likelihood there is another cash rate increase on Tuesday, that is going to be the nail in the coffin for consumer confidence," said CreditorWatch chief economist Anneke Thompson, amid warnings from some economists that another rate rise would dampen spending intentions just in time for Christmas. The same wrap noted that the men who built pubs and liquor juggernaut Endeavour Group into the world's largest poker machine operator had triggered a public spat over the future of a business they say has lost its way.



---


# How Treasury Yields And "Higher For Longer" Transmit To Equities

Treasury bonds are seen as some of the safest investments possible, and when they pay higher yields, investors are less likely to pay high prices for stocks and other riskier investments — which is a big reason why the S&P 500 dropped 4.9 per cent in September 2023, dragging what had been a big gain for the year down to 11.7 per cent.

The chain running into those yields is the Federal Reserve's stance. Treasury yields have been climbing sharply as Wall Street accepts a new normal in which the Fed is likely to keep interest rates high for longer; the Fed is trying to push still-high inflation down to its target, and its main tool of high interest rates does that by trying to slow the economy and hurting prices for investments. The Fed's main interest rate is at its highest level since 2001, and the central bank indicated the previous week that it may cut interest rates next year by less than it earlier expected. The data cuts both ways within this model. Friday's economic data showed that not only was inflation a touch cooler than expected in August, so was growth in spending by US consumers, which can be a positive for inflation because it means not as many dollars are pouring into purchases and that in turn could give companies less encouragement to raise prices further — but it may also dent what has been a big driver keeping the US economy out of a recession.

# ASX Outlook And RBA Rate Expectations At End-September 2023

The Australian sharemarket was set to retreat with futures pointing to a fall of 38 points, or 0.5 per cent, at the open, after Wall Street closed out its worst month and quarter of the year with more losses on Friday.

Most sectors traded lower, but interest-rate sensitive sectors including healthcare and consumer companies were among the weakest amid expectations that the RBA would keep rates on hold in October; the National Australia Bank has forecast another rate hike to 4.35 per cent in November. On Wall Street the S&P 500 slipped 0.3 per cent with the majority of stocks within the index sinking, the Dow Jones fell 0.5 per cent and the Nasdaq composite edged 0.1 per cent higher. # Renewed Global Investor Interest in Japanese Equities

Global investors' interest in Japan was sharply heightened in late 2023, but many funds found themselves short of the expertise to act on it. Tokyo conference guests were told by various experts that the stars do appear aligned in Japan's favour, both on its own merits and in comparison with what is happening around it — yet because so many global funds have diverted expertise away from Japan in recent years, they are concerned that they need to know more, as a matter of urgency.

"There is heightened interest in Japan after what has been, for many, a long period of not being focused on that country," says Paul Hitchens, head of the Japan research department at Jefferies, which hosted a major investor conference in Hong Kong. He names distinctive catalysts: a recent push by the Tokyo Stock Exchange for companies to improve their capital efficiency, and Warren Buffett's high-profile decision to invest heavily in five of Japan's largest trading houses. The market backdrop reinforced the urgency: Topix, Japan's main stock index, had risen more than 25 per cent in 2023 to the date of this Financial Times report, outperforming almost all the world's developed market indices and, as some conference attendees admit, creating a "fear of missing out" on a rally that may have significantly further to go.

Real estate investment trusts (down 2 per cent) dropped further following the latest inflation data, with Mirvac (down 3.7 per cent) and Dexus (down 3.3 per cent) sliding lower, as the Australian sharemarket shook off a positive lead from Wall Street after hotter-than-expected inflation data raised the prospect of another interest rate rise at the Reserve Bank's next meeting.

Infratil (down 3.6 per cent), Meridian Energy (down 2.7 per cent) and Resmed (down 2 per cent) were among the biggest large-cap decliners.

# Kishida's Pitch to Global Investors 2023

Japanese prime minister Fumio Kishida was preparing, in the week of 1 October 2023, to make his strongest ever push for a bet on Asia's biggest advanced economy, as BlackRock founder Larry Fink and other heads of global funds gathered in Tokyo for a series of events to attract investment. "I would urge you to evaluate what we are doing in my country, look at the underlying strength of our economy and our plans for the future and then invest in Japan," Kishida said in a recent speech at the Economic Club of New York.

The pitch followed a month of conferences on the same question. Throughout September, in Tokyo, New York, Hong Kong and London, the world's biggest investment banks hosted a series of conferences for the world's biggest investors, all gravitating around the theme of whether Japan is really back. The events were run by JPMorgan, Goldman Sachs, Bank of America, Mizuho, BNP Paribas and Jefferies, and according to both attendees and hosts the answer is now clearer than it has been in a very long time: Japan is back, but global investors may take a little more persuasion that it is truly back for the duration.

qid: Who is the individual associated with the crypto exchange FTX, who has been accused of using customer funds for a buyout and is facing multiple charges of fraud and conspiracy, as reported by sources like Fortune, The Verge, and TechCrunch?
context:
# Sam Bankman-Fried

Sam Bankman-Fried is the former CEO of the bankrupt crypto exchange FTX, whose highly anticipated criminal trial started on the Tuesday before TechCrunch's 2023-10-01 report, to determine whether he is guilty of seven counts of fraud and conspiracy. As one former federal prosecutor put it: "The odds seem to be stacked against him at this point."

He was 31 years old and co-founded FTX in 2019; within a few years the once third-largest crypto exchange's valuation hit $32 billion at its peak, and the company is now trying to claw back any funds to distribute to creditors. Before the fall he was even compared to Warren Buffet, and many called him the white horse of crypto — a description TechCrunch notes it never applied to him.

Bankman-Fried, however, maintained his innocence. At The New York Times' DealBook Summit he appeared virtually from the Bahamas and said, "I didn't ever try to commit fraud on anyone; I was shocked by what happened this month"; in a published DM exchange with a Vox reporter he said he regretted filing for bankruptcy and thought that "regulators make everything worse." In January he pleaded not guilty to all counts, which include wire fraud, conspiracy to commit money laundering and conspiracy to misuse customer funds. He could face up to 115 years in jail if convicted on all charges.

TechCrunch's 2023-10-02 summary of his standing on the eve of trial: SBF has been denied bail; his name is mud (or much worse) among those who have lost money in Alameda or FTX; and those who might not have had positions in these still blame him for other crypto woes, because he set off a ripple effect.



---


# FTX Fraud Charges And The SEC's Allegation

Sam Bankman-Fried, the founder of the failed cryptocurrency exchange FTX, faced seven counts of wire fraud and conspiracy — specifically, two counts of wire fraud and five conspiracy charges — and the Securities and Exchange Commission alleged that FTX was a fraud "from the start," with a "multi-billion-dollar deficiency caused by his own misappropriation of customer funds." The Verge repeated this framing at the head of each of its trial dispatches through October 2023, and in its October 28th, 2023 write-up reported that Bankman-Fried had been found guilty on seven counts including charges of wire fraud.

The boundary of the concept is the mix of charge types: the indictment paired substantive wire fraud counts with conspiracy counts rather than resting on a single offence, and the SEC's civil allegation about the exchange's origins ran alongside the criminal case rather than being part of it. The Verge's reporter, writing as the prosecution's case neared its end on October 26th, 2023, added an impression of the people the charges swept in: all the co-conspirators seemed oddly younger than their years, as though they had got stuck in the "math camp forever" environment Bankman-Fried created for them and simply failed to grow up.



---


# Sam Bankman-Fried's Charges And The Collapse Of FTX

Sam Bankman-Fried, the founder of FTX and Alameda Research, is facing seven counts of criminal charges: two counts of wire fraud and five counts of conspiracy charges.

FTX was a failed cryptocurrency exchange founded in 2019. According to a now-deleted profile from FTX investors Sequoia Capital, FTX was founded because of Bankman-Fried's frustration with other exchanges while he was running Alameda Research, his crypto trading firm. According to the SEC, FTX was a fraud "from the start," diverting customers' funds to Alameda, with a "multi-billion-dollar deficiency caused by his own misappropriation of customer funds."



---


# The SBF Trial Proceedings

Sam Bankman-Fried is in court for alleged fraud and money laundering while leading crypto exchange FTX and sister company Alameda. TechCrunch's 2023-10-02 preview placed the case in the Manhattan Federal Court, describing the disgraced cryptocurrency entrepreneur as accused of orchestrating "one of the biggest financial frauds in American history": the multibillion-dollar collapse of FTX, the crypto exchange he founded and led. SBF, as he is known, has pleaded not guilty to some seven charges of fraud and conspiracy.

The trial kicked off with jury selection October 3. By TechCrunch's 2023-10-06 update the case was entering its next chapter, with proceedings resuming Thursday: as confirmed during a teleconference Wednesday, SBF would be taking the stand along with a handful of other witnesses, as the onus shifted toward the defense after the prosecution brought its case to its conclusion.

Access to the proceedings is limited: no devices are allowed, so reports are being physically put together within the courtroom, or sent to overflow rooms. The jury's composition ranges from a train conductor to a retired investment banker who attended Stanford University, and TechCrunch pointed readers to a special joint episode of its Equity and Chain Reaction podcasts for a better sense of the vibe between the jurors and the rest of the court.

A second account of the same events was arriving in parallel: "Going Infinite," a book by Michael Lewis chronicling the rise and fall of SBF, was set to debut on the first day of the trial.



---


# Marc-Antoine Julliard's Testimony As FTX's First Witness-Victim

The prosecution's first witness at Sam Bankman-Fried's trial was not a blockbuster name or a former lieutenant-turned-cooperator like Caroline Ellison but a victim: Marc-Antoine Julliard, a Paris-born cocoa trader who lives in London and whose money got stuck on FTX. Julliard testified that on Nov. 8, 2022, in the crypto exchange's final few days, he tried to pull out almost $100,000 in cash and crypto, and that he was never able to. The withdrawal screenshots shown in court were of attempts to move $20,000 USD and about 4 Bitcoin, worth about $20,000 at the time — roughly $100,000 in total, inaccessible.

Julliard explained why he had chosen FTX in 2021 when he decided to invest in crypto, trading currencies like Bitcoin and Dogecoin there. He trusted FTX because Bankman-Fried came across as a leading figure of the industry; because the sheer volume of users mattered to him, and FTX was at the time among the top three biggest exchanges; and because major VC firms had invested. "They don't commit hundreds of millions without doing due diligence, checking the books, the accountancy of the firm, going through several compliance process[es], so that was a vote of confidence for me," he said. He also noted FTX's glossy ads — featuring Gisele Bündchen, for instance — which suggested a very high budget, and reasoned that it wouldn't make sense to spend that much money unless FTX had very strong financials. He opened an account, transferred in both regular money and cryptocurrency, and used the exchange to execute his plan of buying Bitcoin to sell back in five to ten years at higher prices.

In November 2022 things went bad. Julliard followed Bankman-Fried on Twitter and read aloud in court the "FTX is fine. Assets are fine" tweets, along with "FTX has enough to cover all client holdings. We don't invest client assets" and a few others, which gave him the impression that his money was there and that any problem might be technical — anti-spam measures — or regulatory. By the time he tried to get his money out on November 8th, it was too late. Cross-examining a customer whose money is gone is described as a thankless task, but Mark Cohen tried anyway, noting that Julliard was a licensed commodities broker who was trading in crypto because he didn't have to disclose it, that he knew crypto was new and risky, and that he didn't review the terms of service agreement he had assented to when making his FTX account. The next witness called was Bankman-Fried's former college and FTX roommate, Adam Yedidia.



---


# Day Two Of The Bankman-Fried Trial: Jury Selection And The Courtroom Audience

On the second day of Sam Bankman-Fried's fraud trial, the jury was selected on Wednesday morning, after which lawyers for the government and then for Bankman-Fried delivered opening statements that told two very different stories of the former FTX CEO's sudden rise and almost instantaneous fall. The central question framed by the proceedings was who Bankman-Fried, the former CEO of crypto exchange FTX, really is: a liar and a fraud, or someone who acted in good faith and, like many a startup founder, flew too close to the sun. That answer, the account notes, ultimately lies with the jury.

The day featured pointed allegations, a friend from MIT, and an audience replete with big names, including Bankman-Fried's professorial parents and Damian Williams, the U.S. attorney for the Southern District of New York. Bankman-Fried himself spent most of the day in court staring into a laptop while seated between his two attorneys. The prosecution's account of his alleged crimes was described as featuring a study in contrasts.

qid: Does the 'Fortune' article claim that 'The Talking Heads' concert film "Stop Making Sense" had a theater re-release decades after its original showing, while the 'Polygon' article discusses a recent release of BTS's "Yet to Come" concert film, indicating a difference in the timing of the releases?

# BTS Yet To Come Concert Film

In February, K-pop septet BTS released a filmed version of their "Yet to Come" concert — a one-night-only performance for 50,000 fans in Busan, South Korea — and the concert film made more than $50 million worldwide.

The figure is notable because the show had already been given away once: it was previously streamed via the Korean platform Weverse, allowing a reported 49 million fans to watch at home. Polygon reports the theatrical release still cleared $50 million after that.



---


# Concert Film Versus Live Concert

Polygon's writer argues that seeing a concert film in a movie theater is not the same as attending a live concert but is not an inherently lesser experience either — a claim she grounds in having attended the BTS Yet to Come concert both in person and in cinemas.

Her case is that the concert film has value past its re-creation of a specific intersection of place, time, and performance: she went to theaters to relive a once-in-a-lifetime show, but the film version was also its own unique collective fan experience. The practical advantages she names are arriving at the theater just 20 minutes before showtime, being able to go with all her BTS fan friends this time, and watching in a theater full of fellow fans with BTS lightsticks in hand and a BT21 Tata headband on head, which gave the same sense of fandom camaraderie as the in-person concert. She concedes the losses: she missed some of the freedom of the in-person experience, such as choosing where to direct her attention across an expansive stage bedecked with intricate sets calling back to different eras in BTS history. But she argues the clarity and focus of detail in the film evened the score, giving a much closer view of the choreography and the members' interaction with a close-up camera intimacy she had not gotten in person, and letting her share those fandom moments not only with her cinema audience but with millions of other fans viewing the same film around the world. She adds that Yet to Come would stream on Amazon Prime Video starting November 9, further expanding the number of fans able to see it.



---


# Movie Theaters' Pivot To Alternative Content

The mechanism that turned the once declared-for-dead multiplex into the go-to place for stars previously at home on Netflix is a supply problem meeting a format opportunity. When studios began diverting some of their titles to streaming platforms, movie theaters began thinking harder about how they could fill their screens — a question exacerbated in autumn 2023 by an actors strike that led to the postponement of big releases like "Dune: Part Two." Movie theaters are increasingly not just a marquee of movie showtimes but a big-screen stage for a variety of visual media: BTS released a concert film earlier in 2023 with higher ticket prices and limited showtimes, and the Metropolitan Opera has for years done popular live broadcasts in theaters.

Concert films are not themselves new — just the month before, the Talking Heads classic "Stop Making Sense" returned to theaters for a decades-later encore — but "The Eras Tour" heralds something new and potentially game-changing in the movie industry. The scope condition is important: few acts can do what Swift and Beyoncé can, and their expected success is unlikely to be replicated. Still, "The Eras Tour" could be the start of an expansion of what a movie theater can be — think the Sphere, only much cheaper and in most towns.

Greg Marcus states the underlying business redefinition: "You could say we're in the movie business, but really we're in the getting-together-with-other-people business. The more we do of it, the more the customers will think about it and the more talent will go: This is something I could do."



---


# Concert Films Flatten The Fandom Hierarchy

Polygon argues that attending a concert in person does not make you a bigger fan, and that concert films are levelling the field by dropping some of the barriers of price, location, and accessibility — which is why they increasingly look like the future of pop music fandom.

The grounds start with what fans go for. The writer says she goes to a BTS concert to see BTS perform but also to be among other BTS fans who already understand why she cares so much about a Korean boy band: they trade freebies and photocards, help each other set up lightsticks, and share favorite songs or members. That sense of belonging is available whether in a stadium in Korea or a cinema at her local mall. The second ground is who actually gets in: fans able to attend the stadium and arena concerts of the biggest musical artists in the world are not necessarily more passionate — they just have a combination of luck and privilege that others lack — so using in-person attendance to enforce a fandom hierarchy misreads what it measures. She notes that BTS, Taylor Swift, and Beyoncé, whose concert film Renaissance: A Film by Beyoncé hits theaters in December, all have massive fandoms that are geographically scattered and often stigmatized by a mainstream culture that belittles female-driven fan culture, and that in a time when in-person community is harder to come by and can mean pushing people's financial or physical limits, a filmed concert can feel like a gift. The conclusion is qualified: concert films may not be the future of pop music for everyone, but they are increasingly the future of pop music fandom — and that is a good thing, because pop music fandom is a way to find collective joy and connection in art, and anyone who wants in should be able to join the party.



---


# Conditions At The BTS Busan Concert

Polygon's writer, who attended the Yet to Come show in Busan, reports that getting 50,000 people into a 20-year-old stadium was not simple: by the time BTS took the stage, most attendees had been in line for hours with limited access to bathrooms, water, or information about what was going on.

Once the concert started, conditions in the 3,000-strong standing areas got intense as fans pushed toward the stage, crowding people at the front and prompting BTS to alter plans to come down into the audience for their performance of their 2018 hit "IDOL." The writer notes this was not her first chaotic, stressful in-person stadium concert experience and doubts it will be her last, and states the scope condition plainly: she is able and willing to make that trade for the chance to see her favorite musical group perform, but not everyone is, even if they could get tickets.



---


# The AMC-Taylor Swift Direct Distribution Deal

Two of the biggest stars on the planet — Taylor Swift, and Beyoncé in December under a very similar arrangement — are heading into cinemas in first-of-their-kind deals made directly with AMC Theaters that circumvent Hollywood studios and which, for now, leave streamers waiting on the sidelines. The relation that defines the model is the revenue split and the window: ticket sales will be split 43% with theaters and 57% shared by Swift and AMC, with the lion's share of that going to Swift, and the film will play exclusively in theaters for at least 13 weeks — longer than many Hollywood releases do now.

AMC CEO Adam Aron has called the deal "a coup for AMC" on social media. Both AMC and representatives for Swift declined to discuss the film's release, so the terms above are the extent of what the parties have put on the record as of 2023-10-10.



---


# The Early December 2023 Box Office Slowdown

The first weekend of December 2023 was a slow one overall at the North American box office — films in the top 10 were expected to gross only $85 million in total — despite several new releases including "Godzilla Minus One," the Hindi-language "Animal," Angel Studios' sci-fi thriller "The Shift," and Lionsgate's John Woo-directed revenge picture "Silent Night."

It was in this traditional "lull" that AMC Theatres found a good opportunity for "Renaissance" to shine. "They chose a great weekend," said Paul Dergarabedian, the senior media analyst for Comscore. "There was competition but it was from very different kinds of movies." Things were expected to pick up in the final weeks of 2023, with films like "Wonka" and "The Color Purple" yet to come, and the industry was looking at a $9 billion year — still trailing the $11 billion pre-pandemic norm, but a marked improvement on the last few years. "We had a slow Thanksgiving and we're having a pretty slow weekend this weekend, but it's a great weekend to be a moviegoer in terms of the breadth and depth of the movies out there," Dergarabedian said, with the industry's awards season getting into full swing.



---


# Biggest Concert Films: The Box Office Records

"Taylor Swift: The Eras Tour" is poised to become the biggest concert film ever in about two days of release, as of 2023-10-10. Not accounting for inflation, the mark belongs to 2011's "Justin Bieber: Never Say Never," which took $73.1 million across its entire run.

Accounting for inflation, the comparison is much harder: it will be more difficult for "The Eras Tour" to catch "Woodstock," which grossed $50 million in 1970, a total that translates to nearly $400 million today.

qid: Who is the Silicon Valley figure associated with the rise of artificial intelligence, mentioned in articles by 'The Age', 'Fortune', and 'TechCrunch', who faced no removal efforts by Anthropic co-founders, has been described as generous and impactful, yet is also theorized to have had transparency issues with the board?
context:
# The AI Risk Paradox Among Tech Billionaires

At the heart of the competition to build artificial intelligence is a brain-stretching paradox: the people who say they are most worried about AI are among the most determined to create it and enjoy its riches, and they have justified their ambition with their strong belief that they alone can keep AI from endangering Earth. The grounds are the shape of the debate itself. Eight years after an argument between Elon Musk and Larry Page, that argument seems prescient, because the question of whether AI will elevate the world or destroy it, or at least inflict grave damage, has framed an ongoing debate among Silicon Valley founders, chatbot users, academics, legislators and regulators about whether the technology should be controlled or set free.

That debate has pitted some of the world's richest men against one another: Musk, Page, Mark Zuckerberg of Meta, tech investor Peter Thiel, Satya Nadella of Microsoft and Sam Altman of OpenAI, all of whom have fought for a piece of a business that one day could be worth trillions of dollars, and for the power to shape it. The narrative anchor is that Musk and Page stopped speaking soon after the party that summer, and that a few weeks later Musk dined with Altman, who was then running a tech incubator, and several researchers in a private room at the Rosewood hotel in Menlo Park, California, a favoured deal-making spot close to the venture capital offices of Sand Hill Road.



---


# Sam Altman's Career Before OpenAI

Sam Altman, 38 as of November 2023, is not trained as an AI engineer, yet has been seen as a Silicon Valley wunderkind since his early 20s. The defining credential of that earlier phase is that he was recruited in 2014 to take the lead of the startup incubator YCombinator.

The reputation attached to him at the time is captured in YCombinator co-founder Paul Graham's 2014 announcement that Altman would become its president: "Sam is one of the smartest people I know, and understands startups better than perhaps anyone I know, including myself." Graham said then that Altman was "one of those rare people who manage to be both fearsomely effective and yet fundamentally benevolent."



---


# DeepMind's Sale To Google And Facebook's AI Lab

Google offered $US650 million for DeepMind. Mark Zuckerberg of Facebook offered a bigger payout to DeepMind's founders but would not agree to the conditions the founders had set, and DeepMind sold to Google.

Zuckerberg was determined to build an AI lab of his own and hired Yann LeCun, a French computer scientist who had also done pioneering AI research, to run it. A year after Hinton's auction, Zuckerberg and LeCun flew to Lake Tahoe for the same AI conference, and while padding around a suite at the Harrah's casino in his socks Zuckerberg personally interviewed top researchers, who were soon offered millions of dollars in salary and stock. AI was once laughed off; now the richest men in Silicon Valley were shelling out billions to keep from being left behind.



---


# Private Sector Volunteers In Terror Finance Tracking

The network blocking terror financing funds includes many entities, including private citizens: IMPA has been approached by many experts from the private sector — people with intelligence experience because they have worked in these organizations, or with high-tech experience — who "have mobilized like crazy."

"The world's financial intelligence authorities are now at the heart of this struggle, and we're working together to thwart the financing channels that we've located," Ostrovitch-Levi said. "Israeli entrepreneurs in Silicon Valley have contacted us; they write code, search for information, and give us lots of information. We aggregate and examine everything."



---


# Second Senate AI Insight Forum, October 2023

Senator Charles Schumer (D-NY) hosted Silicon Valley's AI leaders on Tuesday as the US Senate reconvened its AI Insight Forum for a second time, and on leaving the meeting Schumer told the assembled press that "it is clear that American leadership on AI can't be done on the cheap," reporting that almost all of the experts in the forum called for robust, sustained federal investment in the private and public sectors to achieve American-led transformative and sustainable innovation in AI.

The guest list for this second session included manifesto enthusiast Marc Andreessen and venture capitalist John Doerr, along with Max Tegmark of the Future of Life Institute and NAACP CEO Derrick Johnson. According to a release from Schumer's office, the agenda covered "the transformational innovation that pushes the boundaries of medicine, energy, and science, and the sustainable innovation necessary to drive advancements in security, accountability, and transparency in AI."

On cost, National Security AI Commission estimates put the required federal investment at around $32 billion a year. Schumer believes those funding challenges can be addressed by "leveraging the private sector by employing new and innovative funding mechanisms — like the Grand Challenges prize idea." He framed the goal as a balance: "We must prioritize transformational innovation, to help create new vistas, unlock new cures, improve education, reinforce national security, protect the global food supply, and more," but in doing so "we must act sustainably in order to minimize harms to workers, civil society and the environment." As he put it, "We need to strike a balance between transformational and sustainable innovation. Finding this balance will be key to our success."

Schumer closed by saying the participants would leave "with a deeper understanding of how to approach American-led AI innovation," and that the conversation would continue "in weeks and months to come — in more forums like this and committee hearings in Congress — as we work to develop comprehensive, bipartisan AI legislation."



---


# Anthropic's Founding By Former OpenAI Researchers

Dario Amodei, a researcher with ties to the effective altruist community, had been on hand at the Rosewood hotel when OpenAI was born, and was leading the lab's efforts to build a neural network called a large language model that could learn from enormous amounts of digital text: by analysing countless Wikipedia articles, digital books and message boards it could generate text on its own, and it also had the unfortunate habit of making things up. It was called GPT-3 and was released in the summer of 2020, and researchers inside OpenAI, Google and other companies thought this rapidly improving technology could be a path to artificial general intelligence. Amodei was unhappy about the Microsoft deal because he thought it was taking OpenAI in a really commercial direction, and he and other researchers went to the board to try to push Altman out, according to five people familiar with the matter; after they failed, they left, worrying, like DeepMind's founders before them, that their new corporate overlords would favour commercial interests over safety.

In 2021 the group of about 15 engineers and scientists created a new lab called Anthropic, with the plan of building AI the way the effective altruists thought it should be done, with very tight controls. Anthropic disputes the account of the board approach: "There was no attempt to remove Sam Altman from OpenAI by the co-founders of Anthropic," said an Anthropic spokesperson, Sally Aldous. "The co-founders themselves came to the conclusion that they wished to depart OpenAI to start their own company, made this known to OpenAI's leadership, and over several weeks negotiated an exit on mutually agreeable terms." Anthropic accepted a $US4 billion investment from Amazon and another $US2 billion from Google two years later. After OpenAI received another $US2 billion from Microsoft, Altman and another senior executive, Greg Brockman, visited Bill Gates at his sprawling mansion on the shores of Lake Washington, outside Seattle; the Microsoft founder was no longer involved in the company day to day but kept in regular touch with its executives.



---


# Sam Altman's Rise As The Face Of Generative AI

In the year since Altman catapulted ChatGPT to global fame, he became Silicon Valley's sought-after voice on the promise and potential dangers of artificial intelligence, and his sudden and mostly unexplained exit brought uncertainty to the industry's future. He helped start OpenAI as a nonprofit research laboratory in 2015, but it was ChatGPT's explosion into public consciousness that thrust him into the spotlight as a face of generative AI — technology that can produce novel imagery, passages of text and other media. On a world tour in 2023 he was mobbed by a crowd of adoring fans at an event in London.

He has sat with multiple heads of state to discuss AI's potential and perils. On Thursday, 2023-11-16, he took part in a CEO summit at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation conference in San Francisco, where OpenAI is based. At OpenAI's first developer conference the week before, Altman was the main speaker, showcasing a vision for a future of AI agents that could help people with a variety of tasks; days later he announced the company would have to pause new subscriptions to its premium version of ChatGPT because it had exceeded capacity.



---


# OpenAI's AI Chip Ambitions

The company has suggested that it might be entering the AI chip market at some point in the future, in an effort to shore up the speed and performance of its API services.

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman had previously pointed to industry-wide GPU shortages for the service's spotty performance, and producing its own processors might mitigate those supply issues while potentially lowering the current four-cent-per-query cost of operating the chatbot to something more manageable.

The Seahawks and Cowboys met in Dallas on "Thursday Night Football" to open NFL Week 13 at 8:15 p.m. ET on Amazon Prime Video — a prime-time matchup featuring two potential playoff teams and plenty of key fantasy football start 'em, sit 'em question marks, as previewed by Sporting News on Nov. 30, 2023.

qid: Who is the individual, previously likened to Warren Buffet and dubbed the white horse of crypto by some, but not by TechCrunch, that is now facing allegations of committing fraud for personal gain, as reported by TechCrunch?
context:
# Sam Bankman-Fried

Sam Bankman-Fried is the former CEO of the bankrupt crypto exchange FTX, whose highly anticipated criminal trial started on the Tuesday before TechCrunch's 2023-10-01 report, to determine whether he is guilty of seven counts of fraud and conspiracy. As one former federal prosecutor put it: "The odds seem to be stacked against him at this point."

He was 31 years old and co-founded FTX in 2019; within a few years the once third-largest crypto exchange's valuation hit $32 billion at its peak, and the company is now trying to claw back any funds to distribute to creditors. Before the fall he was even compared to Warren Buffet, and many called him the white horse of crypto — a description TechCrunch notes it never applied to him.

Bankman-Fried, however, maintained his innocence. At The New York Times' DealBook Summit he appeared virtually from the Bahamas and said, "I didn't ever try to commit fraud on anyone; I was shocked by what happened this month"; in a published DM exchange with a Vox reporter he said he regretted filing for bankruptcy and thought that "regulators make everything worse." In January he pleaded not guilty to all counts, which include wire fraud, conspiracy to commit money laundering and conspiracy to misuse customer funds. He could face up to 115 years in jail if convicted on all charges.

TechCrunch's 2023-10-02 summary of his standing on the eve of trial: SBF has been denied bail; his name is mud (or much worse) among those who have lost money in Alameda or FTX; and those who might not have had positions in these still blame him for other crypto woes, because he set off a ripple effect.



---


# Engoron Summary Judgment That Trump Committed Fraud

A judge ruled on Tuesday 26 September 2023 that Donald Trump committed fraud for years while building the real estate empire that catapulted him to fame and the White House. Judge Arthur Engoron, ruling in a civil lawsuit brought by New York's attorney general, found that the former president and his company deceived banks, insurers and others by massively overvaluing his assets and exaggerating his net worth on paperwork used in making deals and securing financing.

As punishment, Engoron ordered that some of Trump's business licences be rescinded, and said he would continue to have an independent monitor oversee the Trump Organization's operations. A Trump spokesperson did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the ruling, and Trump has long insisted he did nothing wrong.

Fortune described the decision, which came days before the start of a non-jury trial in Attorney General Letitia James' lawsuit, as the strongest repudiation yet of Trump's carefully coiffed image as a wealthy and shrewd real estate mogul turned political powerhouse.



---


# The SBF Trial Proceedings

Sam Bankman-Fried is in court for alleged fraud and money laundering while leading crypto exchange FTX and sister company Alameda. TechCrunch's 2023-10-02 preview placed the case in the Manhattan Federal Court, describing the disgraced cryptocurrency entrepreneur as accused of orchestrating "one of the biggest financial frauds in American history": the multibillion-dollar collapse of FTX, the crypto exchange he founded and led. SBF, as he is known, has pleaded not guilty to some seven charges of fraud and conspiracy.

The trial kicked off with jury selection October 3. By TechCrunch's 2023-10-06 update the case was entering its next chapter, with proceedings resuming Thursday: as confirmed during a teleconference Wednesday, SBF would be taking the stand along with a handful of other witnesses, as the onus shifted toward the defense after the prosecution brought its case to its conclusion.

Access to the proceedings is limited: no devices are allowed, so reports are being physically put together within the courtroom, or sent to overflow rooms. The jury's composition ranges from a train conductor to a retired investment banker who attended Stanford University, and TechCrunch pointed readers to a special joint episode of its Equity and Chain Reaction podcasts for a better sense of the vibe between the jurors and the rest of the court.

A second account of the same events was arriving in parallel: "Going Infinite," a book by Michael Lewis chronicling the rise and fall of SBF, was set to debut on the first day of the trial.



---


# The Prosecution's Opening Statement Against Bankman-Fried

Thane Rehn, a prosecutor for the government, opened the case against Sam Bankman-Fried with the line "One year ago, it looked like the defendant was on the top of the world," and then argued that this appearance was false: "all of that, all of it, was built on lies," he declared to the jury, adding "Behind the curtains, he was not what he appeared to be." Rehn described a defendant who, as former CEO of FTX, oversaw a supposedly thriving crypto exchange, jetted between international locales, hobnobbed with celebrities like Tom Brady and Larry David, and repeatedly emphasized to customers that their money was safe and secure.

What followed was a roughly 30-minute story that repeatedly emphasized how Bankman-Fried allegedly stole customer funds to facilitate his jet-setting lifestyle, donate millions to political candidates, and finance risky bets. Rehn also directly contested the media framing of the defendant: he was not a crypto "boy" genius, as so many in the media — Fortune included — have written, but a "man" who "stole billions of dollars from thousands of victims." Rehn closed the characterization with a promise to the jury: "You will see the full picture."



---


# Prosecution And Defense Arguments On Day Two Of The SBF Trial

On the second day of the trial of Sam Bankman-Fried and FTX, the prosecution argued that Bankman-Fried knowingly committed fraud, and it grounded that claim in motive: he did so, prosecutors said, to achieve great wealth, power and influence.

The defense countered with the opposite reading of the same conduct. Its claim was that the FTX founder acted in good faith, never meant to commit fraud or to steal, and basically got in over his head — an argument whose warrant is that inexperience and overreach, rather than intent, explain what happened. The two sides therefore contest intent rather than the underlying events, and the reporting on this exchange comes from Rebecca and Jacquelyn in TechCrunch's Week in Review of October 7, 2023, covering day two of the trial only.



---


# Day Two Of The Bankman-Fried Trial: Jury Selection And The Courtroom Audience

On the second day of Sam Bankman-Fried's fraud trial, the jury was selected on Wednesday morning, after which lawyers for the government and then for Bankman-Fried delivered opening statements that told two very different stories of the former FTX CEO's sudden rise and almost instantaneous fall. The central question framed by the proceedings was who Bankman-Fried, the former CEO of crypto exchange FTX, really is: a liar and a fraud, or someone who acted in good faith and, like many a startup founder, flew too close to the sun. That answer, the account notes, ultimately lies with the jury.

The day featured pointed allegations, a friend from MIT, and an audience replete with big names, including Bankman-Fried's professorial parents and Damian Williams, the U.S. attorney for the Southern District of New York. Bankman-Fried himself spent most of the day in court staring into a laptop while seated between his two attorneys. The prosecution's account of his alleged crimes was described as featuring a study in contrasts.



---


# Bankman-Fried's Pre-Collapse Public Image Strategy

Before his fall, Bankman-Fried made himself out to be the Good Boy of crypto — the trustworthy face of a sometimes-shady industry — and he was very interested in publicity, sitting for many interviews both before and after the collapse of FTX.

The Verge attributes FTX's quick rise as an industry force at least in part to that appetite for attention: Bankman-Fried gave interviews freely and quickly rose to public prominence, positioning himself as an important, boyish face for crypto even though FTX hadn't been in the business as long as competing exchanges such as Coinbase, Kraken, or Gemini. At one point he told a colleague at FTX that "I honestly think it's negative EV" — possibly "expected value," as in poker — "for me to cut my hair. I think it's important for people to think I look crazy." Because he was so successful at this kind of public relations, his fall from grace became another mark against an industry already roiled by bankruptcies and scandals; The Verge adds that more trouble for the industry is likely to come from one crucial element of the fraud trial, the part where the government must prove intent.



---


# Letitia James Asset Inflation Allegations

Letitia James, a Democrat, sued Trump and the Trump Organization a year before this September 2023 ruling, alleging a pattern of duplicity that she dubbed "the art of the steal" — a twist on the title of Trump's 1987 business memoir "The Art of the Deal."

The lawsuit accused Trump and his company of routinely inflating the value of assets like skyscrapers, golf courses and his Mar-a-Lago estate in Florida, padding his bottom line by billions.

# Big Tech Declines And The Amazon FTC Antitrust Lawsuit

On Wall Street the vast majority of stocks fell under the pressure of high rates, including 90 per cent of those within the S&P 500. Big Tech stocks tend to be among the hardest hit by high rates, and they were the heaviest weights on the index: Apple fell 2.3 per cent and Microsoft lost 1.7 per cent. Amazon tumbled 4 per cent after the Federal Trade Commission and 17 state attorneys general filed an antitrust lawsuit against it, accusing the e-commerce behemoth of using its dominant position to inflate prices on other platforms, overcharge sellers and stifle competition.

Elsewhere, in China, concerns continued over heavily indebted real estate developer Evergrande, with the property market crisis there dragging on China's economic growth and raising worries about financial instability. France's CAC 40 fell 0.7 per cent, and Germany's DAX lost 1 per cent.



---


# The Rogers Governance Committee Investigation Of The 2021 Events

Rogers' corporate governance committee is conducting an investigation of the events that took place in 2021, documents show. The committee has asked for copies of "all correspondence" between Melinda Rogers-Hixon and former CEO Joe Natale, three other former executives, the five ousted directors, Martha Rogers, journalists and others, according to a letter to Rogers-Hixon included with the October 2023 court filing.

The stakes for her are explicit. "The investigation is intended to inform decisions that may be made about your status as a director of RCI," says the letter, signed by Robert Gemmell, a former Citigroup Inc. banker who is Rogers' lead director.



---


# Rogers Communications' Rebuttal On Information Access

Rogers Communications denied the sisters' premise that they were improperly cut off from information, saying the company took "reasonable steps" to protect company information from a competitor. Spokesperson Sarah Schmidt added that Melinda Rogers-Hixon and Martha Rogers could have resolved the matter by choosing a different lawyer, "and they chose not to do so" — putting the cause of their exclusion on their own choice rather than on any vendetta.

The company also disputed that the courtroom was the right venue and that the dispute was harming the business. "This matter should be resolved privately," Schmidt said by email. "We've demonstrated that we will not be distracted by these actions — we have significant momentum in the market, our merger is tracking ahead of plan, and we remain squarely focused on doing what's right for our customers and stakeholders."



---


# The Rogers Family Boardroom Battle Of 2021

The bad blood inside the Rogers family spilled into full view in October 2021, when Edward Rogers publicly battled his sisters and his mother for control of the board and won in court. The result was that five Rogers Communications directors were fired and replaced by five allies of Edward Rogers. Soon after, then-CEO Joe Natale was sacked and replaced by Tony Staffieri, the former chief financial officer; Melinda Rogers-Hixon and Martha Rogers had opposed the CEO change.

This was not an isolated episode. The children of late founder Ted Rogers have frequently fought one another — sometimes driving down Rogers' stock price as investors grew worried about the company's governance.



---


# The Rogers Family Truce During The Shaw Takeover

In early 2022, Rogers family members agreed to temporarily shelve their disagreements, according to the October 2023 court filing, to avoid negative publicity as the company sought regulators' approval for the takeover of Shaw Communications Inc. The C$20 billion transaction was the company's biggest deal ever and among the largest corporate transactions in Canadian history. As part of that truce, Melinda Rogers-Hixon and Martha Rogers agreed not to participate in board discussions about the Shaw deal or receive materials on it, because of an argument about Rogers-Hixon's personal lawyer, whose firm also does work for Telus Corp., a competitor to Rogers and Shaw.

The Shaw takeover finally closed on April 3, 2023, and the Rogers siblings then engaged in talks "intended to resolve all issues between us," Rogers-Hixon stated in an affidavit, adding "I was hopeful all issues could be resolved without negative publicity." Those negotiations collapsed in September 2023. It isn't clear from the court filings whether the discussions included the possibility that any Rogers family members would sell their stake in Rogers Communications, leave their roles at the company, or exit the family trust that controls almost all of the voting shares of the public company.



---


# Rogers Communications Company Profile

Rogers Communications is Canada's largest wireless provider and the owner of a cable television empire, the Toronto Blue Jays baseball team, and other media and sports assets. The Rogers family's controlling stake in the public company is worth close to C$8 billion ($5.9 billion), according to calculations based on company filings for its 2023 annual meeting.

The company is inseparable from the prominent Toronto family behind it, and the court documents of October 2023 show that the fractures inside that family have never healed.



---


# Seller Complaints About Amazon's Fees And Pricing Policies

Many sellers have zeroed in on Amazon's pricing policies and rising fees as rightful areas of concern in the FTC's lawsuit.

Molson Hart, whose company Viahart sells toys on Amazon, has been a longtime critic of Amazon's pricing policies: he complained about how Amazon's seller fees impact pricing in a 2019 Medium post and later that year testified about his experience before a House committee. Hart said Amazon sales comprise about 90% of his business, meaning any hit those sales take on Amazon has a considerable impact. He recalled "24 anxious hours" in September 2022 when a third-party seller of his popular construction toy Brain Flakes listed the toy for a lower price on Target than it was offered on Amazon.



---


# The FTC's Antitrust Lawsuit Against Amazon

The Federal Trade Commission's sweeping 172-page antitrust lawsuit, filed in late September 2023, accuses Amazon of wielding its monopoly power to squeeze merchants and thwart rivals, which the agency alleges has led to artificially inflated prices and a degraded shopping experience for consumers.

The mechanism the FTC describes is an "anti-discounting strategy" backed by a "massive web-crawling apparatus that constantly tracks online prices" to stifle competition: Amazon punishes third-party sellers who offer cheaper products elsewhere by threatening to disqualify them from appearing in the buy box if it detects a lower price, and losing the buy box is an "existential threat" to sellers' businesses, the complaint alleges. The end result, the FTC argues, is elevated prices across the web — the company steadily hikes the fees it charges sellers and prevents them from discounting on other sites, so sellers often inflate their prices off Amazon, creating an "artificial price floor everywhere." The FTC is seeking to hold Amazon liable for allegedly violating anti-monopoly law but has not yet outlined the specific remedies it believes would best resolve its concerns; in antitrust cases, remedies are often determined only after a court finds the defendant liable. Amazon general counsel David Zapolsky responded in a blog post that third-party sellers set their own prices on the marketplace and that the company invests in tools to help sellers offer "competitive prices": "Even with those tools, some of the businesses selling on Amazon might still choose to set prices that aren't competitive. Just like any store owner who wouldn't want to promote a bad deal to their customers, we don't highlight or promote offers that are not competitively priced." Zapolsky argued the lawsuit could force Amazon to stop highlighting low prices, "a perverse result that would be directly opposed to the goals of antitrust law."



---


# Alphabet's Q3 2023 Results And Cloud Miss

Shares in Alphabet fell 6 per cent after hours after the Google parent delivered a mixed result: revenue climbed 11 per cent to $US76.7 billion with net income of $US19.7 billion thanks to a recovery in digital advertising revenue, but its closely watched cloud division — which houses its data storage business and many of its AI efforts — missed Wall Street expectations.

"Investors were disappointed by the relatively weak performance at its Google cloud platform, which is at risk of falling further behind" competitors' offerings, Jesse Cohen, a senior analyst at Investing.com, wrote in an email. During trading hours the S&P 500 slipped off session highs, led by losses in energy shares as oil slid below $US84 a barrel, but once again the index found support above the key 4200 mark; Verizon Communications, 3M and General Electric climbed on bullish forecasts, while Facebook and Instagram owner Meta dropped after being sued by California and dozens of other US states over harmful youth marketing claims. Bitcoin briefly topped $US35,000, and Treasury 10-year yields edged lower following Monday's intense volatility. Investors looking to the earnings season for a dose of good news were hanging their hopes on big tech: the five biggest companies in the S&P 500 — Apple, Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon and AI chipmaker Nvidia — account for about a quarter of the benchmark's market capitalisation, and their earnings were projected to jump 34 per cent from a year earlier on average, according to analyst estimates compiled by Bloomberg Intelligence.
