qid: Has the perspective on managing dementia in 'The Guardian' articles shown a change from the time Susan Saunders was reported to be caring for her mother with dementia (published at '2023-10-10') to the more recent report on new Alzheimer’s drugs (published at '2023-12-17')?
context:
# Joining The Dementia Research Register For Trial Participation

Health coach Susan Saunders' advice, reported by The Guardian on 10 October 2023, is a two-step procedure for anyone with a parent in the early stages of dementia: investigate all the available research trials, and start by joining Dementia Research, a nationwide register that matches volunteers to research programmes.

The precondition is stated explicitly — the advice is for a parent in the early stages of dementia, not later ones — and Saunders speaks from experience, having found herself "parenting" her mother, who had dementia, while her own daughters were babies.

The scope of the advice as given is limited to finding and entering trials through that register; the source does not extend it to any other treatment step.



---


# The First Drugs to Treat the Cause of Alzheimer's

The arrival of the first drugs that treat the actual cause of Alzheimer's — rather than merely helping patients manage symptoms, which is all doctors have been able to prescribe until now — has been welcomed as a justifiable cause for excitement, although experts warn their use should be treated with some caution.

"The new drugs slow down the development of Alzheimer's by six months to a year and are useful only for those in the early stages of the condition, so they are certainly not miracle medicines," said David Thomas, head of policy at Alzheimer's Research UK. "However, after decades of research, they are the first to improve patients' lives directly, and that is a justifiable cause for excitement. If nothing else, they suggest we are probably on the right road to tackling Alzheimer's." The point was backed by neurologist Cath Mummery, of the Dementia Research Centre at University College London: "It has been a very long, hard road, but finally we have something positive to look at. That is very welcome."



---


# UK Dementia Burden and Projections

About a million people are living with dementia in the UK, and this is expected to rise to about 1.7 million by 2040; last year dementia took the lives of 66,000 people in England and Wales, and it is now the leading cause of death in Britain, with Alzheimer's accounting for two-thirds of cases.

The prospect of the new drugs has raised hopes that, after years of effort, scientists may be closing in on ways to directly tackle the UK's dementia crisis — a crisis whose projected growth the article describes as carrying potentially grim consequences.



---


# Delayed Alzheimer's Diagnosis: Patient Cases

Two families illustrate how long a dementia diagnosis can take: Mike Mackenzie-Smith waited over 10 years from the start of his symptoms, and Trina Armstrong waited six years from her first symptoms in 2006 before receiving the correct diagnosis.

Eleanor Mackenzie-Smith's father, Mike, has young-onset Alzheimer's, and his first symptoms were spotted 17 years ago, when Eleanor was 11. "However, it took over 10 years from the start of his symptoms and four separate tests between 2009 and 2017 to get my dad's final diagnosis, when he was 65. It was distressing not knowing what was happening. Too many families, like mine, have had to watch as dementia takes hold of our loved ones while we are left without a diagnosis and the support and access to treatments." Graeme Armstrong's wife, Trina, began having trouble recognising faces and reading telephone numbers in 2006 and was told, after a CT scan three years later, that she had probably had a stroke — although her symptoms did not suggest such a diagnosis. It took another three years before she was diagnosed with posterior cortical atrophy, a rare variant of Alzheimer's disease that affects the way the brain interprets information from the eyes. "Had we had an accurate diagnosis four years earlier, Trina could have been placed on the correct medication, which may have been more effective and helped her day to day," Armstrong said.



---


# The UK Dementia Diagnosis Bottleneck

The main problem facing doctors is the difficulty of pinpointing dementia not just in its early stages but even in its later phases: most cases are first presented to GPs, who then refer patients to memory clinics for a dementia test, but waiting times for appointments at these centres run up to two years on average.

Diagnosing Alzheimer's and other forms of dementia is usually based on pen-and-paper tests, followed by lumbar punctures and brain scans before a final diagnosis, and about 65% of cases are confirmed this way — meaning the remaining third of dementia cases are never diagnosed. Yet patients can only expect to receive treatments, including the new drugs, if their condition is identified.



---


# Robin Williams' Lewy Body Dementia And 2014 Death

Robin Williams was unaware in the years before his death that he was dealing with Lewy body dementia; he died by suicide on 11 August 2014 and was diagnosed with the neurological disorder posthumously after an autopsy, FOX News Entertainment reported on 19 October 2023.

Before he died he reportedly appeared tired while on set and did not seem to be his usual self. Lewy body dementia is the second most common type of dementia after Alzheimer's, and the disease affects brain regions involved in thinking, memory and movement, according to the Mayo Clinic. The autopsy found no illegal drugs or traces of alcohol in Williams' system.

Comedian and friend Steven Pearl described the change during the Vice documentary: "The last time I saw Robin Williams, I hadn't seen him for a few months, and he was thin, and he didn't recognize my wife. He hardly said a word. It took him a second to recognize me. I go, 'Whoa, something's wrong here.' I didn't know what. Nobody would really tell me. And then I never saw him again after that."



---


# Multivitamins And Cognition In Older Adults

A recent Columbia University study involving 2,200 adults aged 60 and over found that an inexpensive multivitamin formulated specifically for older people improved cognition, memory and focus, The Guardian reported on 10 October 2023.

The results were so marked that the researchers said the supplement could slow age-related memory decline by three years.

The article frames this as an option even where parents do not require intensive "parenting": a simple supplement could help.



---


# Blood Tests and Brain Health Clinics for Earlier Diagnosis

Doctors argue that diagnosis must move much earlier in the disease course — through blood tests that could pinpoint the disease quickly and effectively, and through new brain health clinics — because, as Cath Mummery puts it, "By the time you have dementia, you will have had Alzheimer's disease developing in your brain for at least 20 years."

Blood tests are not yet available: "These are under research, but we are several years away from having them in widespread use," said David Thomas. "Meanwhile, we have got to get the NHS to a state where it is much more focused and better organised in getting better and earlier dementia diagnoses. That will be crucial in our battle against the condition." Mummery agreed, continuing: "Dementia is the latest stage; we need to pick up signals much earlier. So we need to be thinking about how to diagnose people at the very earliest stages of disease, when they may only have very, very subtle symptoms. Our current service isn't good for doing that, and we need to develop brain health clinics where we can pinpoint the disease much earlier, then help to build resilience against dementia in a patient when it is only in a very early stage."



---


# The Blood-Brain Barrier and Active Drug Transport

A major challenge for dementia treatment is the blood-brain barrier, which controls the movement of ions and molecules from the body to the brain and makes it difficult to get drugs into the central nervous system to tackle problems such as amyloid plaques.

Researchers are developing active transport methods for getting drugs across that barrier, said Cath Mummery: "For example, we are now exploring ways of helping drugs get into the brain much more efficiently, and that could have a major impact." Scientists caution that such developments will take years to realise, and that a great deal needs to be done in the short term to deal with dementia. "It is clear we have taken a step in the right direction but there is much more to do before we can have successfully dealt with these processes that are happening to our brains," said David Thomas. "It is a challenge, and a very important one."



---


# UK Support Organisations For Older Adults

The Guardian's 10 October 2023 piece lists five organisations older adults and their families can turn to, each defined by a distinct function.

Age UK has a database of social activities and groups for older folk. The Walking Football Association keeps keen amateur footballers playing long into their 50s and 60s. Action for Elders offers social and exercise programmes.

The Centre for Ageing Better provides information on working and living as an older person, and u3a, a charity collective, provides local opportunities for people no longer in work to acquire new skills and knowledge.

qid: After the report by The Age on October 22, 2023, suggesting people suspect Google of foul play, did TechCrunch's reporting on October 31, 2023, and December 15, 2023, regarding Google's antitrust issues and the impact on news publishers show a consistent perspective on Google's market behavior?
context:
# Google Paid $26.3 Billion In 2021 For Default Search Placement

Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to multiple browsers, phones and platforms — from companies including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla — to be everyone's default search engine. The figure was revealed by Google's search head Prabhakar Raghavan when he testified in court on October 28, according to The Verge.

About $18 billion of that total went directly to Apple, according to a New York Times report published earlier in October 2023, and Google has had its deal with Apple in place since 2003 — so the payment is the current year of a two-decade arrangement, not a one-off. Questioned on the amount of money Google spends to get first pick of search engines, Pichai said the decision was made with the consumer in mind: Google pays big bucks to be everywhere so that it can take in all the data and be the best search engine across different companies' devices, he said, according to The Verge.

The trial also produced evidence that Google understood the value of defaults very early on. U.S. Justice Department lawyer Meagan Bellshaw showed Pichai a 2007 email from a Google product strategy meeting containing data showing that when people changed their browser homepage to Google, they did 15% more Google searches, and that when they switched away, their Google searches dropped 27%. The email summarizing that meeting, sent to Pichai as well as other Google leaders, read: "Nitin argues that focusing on homepage market share is one of the most effective things we can do to make gains in search market share," according to The Verge.



---


# Google's Parallel Antitrust Proceedings In Late 2023

As of mid-November 2023, Google was fighting antitrust on more than one front at once. The Epic Games case was not its only antitrust case in trial: Google had settled a separate antitrust lawsuit with dating site Match Group the week before November 13, and on November 6 it went to trial with Fortnite maker Epic Games, which hoped to prove that Google engages in anticompetitive behavior with regard to its Android app store, Google Play, and its commission structure. Separately, Google was involved in an antitrust lawsuit with the Department of Justice over its alleged search monopoly.

The Epic case had shed co-plaintiffs on its way to trial. Epic's lawsuit originally involved Match and several U.S. attorneys general, but Google reached a settlement with the attorneys general in October 2023 and with Match the week before November 6, so Epic fought the antitrust battle on its own. The lawsuit, held in the U.S. District Court in California's Northern District, would include testimony from a number of Google and Android execs, including CEO Sundar Pichai, and Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, as well as from Apple, Netflix and other Android developers. Epic, meanwhile, had lost its antitrust battle with Apple and was asking the Supreme Court to weigh in.



---


# Helena World Chronicle's Class Action Antitrust Suit Against Google

A class action lawsuit filed in the week of 15 December 2023 in the U.S. District Court in D.C. accuses Google and parent company Alphabet of anticompetitive behavior in violation of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act and others, on behalf of news publishers. The case was filed by Arkansas-based publisher Helena World Chronicle, which argues that Google "siphons off" news publishers' content, their readers and their ad revenue through anticompetitive means, and it specifically cites new AI technologies such as Google's Search Generative Experience (SGE) and the Bard AI chatbot as worsening the problem.

Helena World Chronicle owns and publishes two weekly newspapers in Arkansas. In the complaint it argues that Google is "starving the free press" by sharing publishers' content on Google, losing them "billions of dollars."

Beyond damages, the suit asks for an injunction that would require Google to obtain consent from publishers before using their website data to train its general artificial intelligence products, including Google's own and those of rivals. It also asks that publishers who opt out of SGE still be allowed to show up in Google search results, among other things.

The law firm handling the case is Hausfeld, whose announcement states that "the anticompetitive effects of Google's scheme cause profound harm to competition, to consumers, to labor, and to a democratic free press," and that "Plaintiff Helena World Chronicle, LLC invokes the Sherman Act and Clayton Act to seek class-wide monetary and injunctive relief to restore and ensure competition for digital news and reference publishing and set up guardrails to preserve a free marketplace of ideas in the new era of artificial intelligence."



---


# The Claim That SGE And Bard Appropriate Publisher Content

The Helena World Chronicle lawsuit claims that Google's recent advances in AI-based search were implemented with "the goal of discouraging end-users from visiting the websites of Class members who are part of the digital news and publishing line of commerce." The grounds are that Google's AI products both retain users and consume publisher content without permission.

On the Search Generative Experience, the suit argues that SGE offers web searchers a way to seek information in a conversational mode but ultimately keeps users in Google's "walled garden" as it "plagiarizes" their content. The warrant that turns this into a harm publishers cannot escape is that publishers also cannot block SGE, because it uses the same web crawler as Google's general search service, GoogleBot — so opting out of the AI experience would mean opting out of search itself.

On Bard, the suit says Google's Bard AI was trained on a dataset that included "news, magazine and digital publications," citing both a 2023 report from the News Media Alliance and a Washington Post article about AI training data. The Post, which worked with researchers at the Allen Institute for AI, had found that News and Media sites were the third largest category of AI training data.

The case points to other concerns too, such as changing AdSense rates and evidence of improper spoliation of evidence on Google's part through its destruction of chat messages — an issue raised in the recent Epic Games lawsuit against Google over app store antitrust issues, which Epic won.



---


# Projected Publisher Traffic Losses From AI Search

Publishers believe they will lose somewhere between 20% and 40% of their website traffic once Google's AI products fully roll out, according to a Wall Street Journal report noted by TechCrunch on 15 December 2023. That report also led with a modelling result from the online magazine The Atlantic: when The Atlantic modelled what would happen if Google integrated AI into search, it found that 75% of the time the AI would answer the user's query without requiring a click-through to its website, losing it traffic.

The stakes are set by how much publisher traffic Google currently supplies. According to data from Similarweb cited in the same coverage, Google today drives nearly 40% of publishers' traffic, so a shift to AI-answered queries could have a major impact on publishers' traffic going forward. The suit filed by Helena World Chronicle takes up precisely this question of how AI will impact publishers' businesses.

Some publishers are trying to get ahead of the problem: Axel Springer inked a deal with OpenAI in the same week to license its news for AI model training.



---


# Google's News Content Payment Deal With Canada

In November 2023, the month before the Helena World Chronicle suit was filed, Google reached an agreement with the Canadian government under which the search giant would pay Canadian media for use of their content. Under the terms of the deal, Google will provide $73.5 million (100 million Canadian dollars) every year to news organizations in the country, with funds distributed based on the news outlets' headcount.

Negotiations with Meta over the same Canadian law were still unresolved as of mid-December 2023. Meta had begun blocking news in Canada in August, in light of the pressure to pay for content under the new Canadian law.



---


# The U.S. Justice Department's Parallel Antitrust Suits Against Google

The Helena World Chronicle class action arrives alongside the filing of the U.S. Justice Department's lawsuit against Google for monopolizing digital ad technologies, and the complaint also references the Justice Department's 2020 civil antitrust suit over search and search advertising.

The two government cases concern different markets: search and search advertising in the 2020 suit are distinct from the digital ad technologies at issue in the more recent one.



---


# Epic v. Google: What The Trial Is

Epic v. Google is the antitrust case in which Fortnite publisher Epic Games drags a tech giant into court alleging that its mobile app store is an illegal monopoly — and although Epic's parallel claims against Apple already got their day in court, the similar lawsuit against Google never did, which is why the case goes to trial on November 6th, a mere 1,180 days after Epic originally sued.

The déjà vu is the point of confusion the piece sets out to clear up: Epic already went to trial with Apple, resulting in a ruling where Apple mostly won, and its Llamacorn legal gambit failed to #FreeFortnite years ago. The distinction is that the Apple claims were heard and the Google ones were not.

An update dated December 15th, 2023 notes that the case is basically over by then.

qid: Does the TechCrunch article that discusses Sam Bankman-Fried's backing of a teens' startup present a different allegation of misconduct against Sam Bankman-Fried compared to the TechCrunch article covering the FTX collapse's courtroom updates, with the former alleging fraud for personal gain and the latter discussing the misuse of customer funds?
context:
# Day Two Of The Bankman-Fried Trial: Jury Selection And The Courtroom Audience

On the second day of Sam Bankman-Fried's fraud trial, the jury was selected on Wednesday morning, after which lawyers for the government and then for Bankman-Fried delivered opening statements that told two very different stories of the former FTX CEO's sudden rise and almost instantaneous fall. The central question framed by the proceedings was who Bankman-Fried, the former CEO of crypto exchange FTX, really is: a liar and a fraud, or someone who acted in good faith and, like many a startup founder, flew too close to the sun. That answer, the account notes, ultimately lies with the jury.

The day featured pointed allegations, a friend from MIT, and an audience replete with big names, including Bankman-Fried's professorial parents and Damian Williams, the U.S. attorney for the Southern District of New York. Bankman-Fried himself spent most of the day in court staring into a laptop while seated between his two attorneys. The prosecution's account of his alleged crimes was described as featuring a study in contrasts.



---


# Sam Bankman-Fried

Sam Bankman-Fried is the former CEO of the bankrupt crypto exchange FTX, whose highly anticipated criminal trial started on the Tuesday before TechCrunch's 2023-10-01 report, to determine whether he is guilty of seven counts of fraud and conspiracy. As one former federal prosecutor put it: "The odds seem to be stacked against him at this point."

He was 31 years old and co-founded FTX in 2019; within a few years the once third-largest crypto exchange's valuation hit $32 billion at its peak, and the company is now trying to claw back any funds to distribute to creditors. Before the fall he was even compared to Warren Buffet, and many called him the white horse of crypto — a description TechCrunch notes it never applied to him.

Bankman-Fried, however, maintained his innocence. At The New York Times' DealBook Summit he appeared virtually from the Bahamas and said, "I didn't ever try to commit fraud on anyone; I was shocked by what happened this month"; in a published DM exchange with a Vox reporter he said he regretted filing for bankruptcy and thought that "regulators make everything worse." In January he pleaded not guilty to all counts, which include wire fraud, conspiracy to commit money laundering and conspiracy to misuse customer funds. He could face up to 115 years in jail if convicted on all charges.

TechCrunch's 2023-10-02 summary of his standing on the eve of trial: SBF has been denied bail; his name is mud (or much worse) among those who have lost money in Alameda or FTX; and those who might not have had positions in these still blame him for other crypto woes, because he set off a ripple effect.



---


# The Defense's Good-Faith Case For Bankman-Fried

Mark Cohen, one of Sam Bankman-Fried's lawyers, attacked the prosecution's central premise that his client was a liar who stole from customers, stating early in his opening statement that "Sam didn't defraud anyone." The defense's counter-picture is of a nerdy startup founder who acted in "good faith," not the prosecution's "cartoon of a villain"; Cohen repeatedly harped on Bankman-Fried's allegedly good-faith actions throughout his address to the jury. Bankman-Fried, whose cheekbones were more prominent after spending about seven weeks in a Brooklyn prison, appeared in court as this argument was made.

Cohen also disputed the specific claim that Alameda Research was a covert conduit. Alameda was not subterranean or shady, he said; it was a successful hedge fund. FTX was no Ponzi scheme but a "very innovative, successful company." The business practices between the two were reasonable, he argued, claiming that Alameda acted legally as an FTX customer, payment processor, and market maker — that is, a financial entity that acts as a trading partner for customers looking to buy and sell cryptocurrencies.

The defense's warrant for reading failure as something other than fraud was an analogy Cohen employed throughout: "working at a startup is like building a plane as you're flying it," and businesses sometimes fail. He specifically pointed the finger at Ellison, the former CEO of Alameda, who he said did not adequately protect her hedge fund from the inherent risk of the crypto markets. And when the walls came closing in and the aforementioned plane approached the "eye of the storm," Cohen argued, Bankman-Fried did not act like someone who was guilty — he was willing to give up his personal wealth to make customers whole. "In the end, Sam started and built two billion-dollar businesses," he concluded. "He didn't steal any money."



---


# Alameda Research As The Alleged Conduit For FTX Customer Funds

In the prosecution's account offered by Thane Rehn, the key to Sam Bankman-Fried's alleged scheme was Alameda Research, a crypto hedge fund that Bankman-Fried also owned. The structure the government described works as follows: Caroline Ellison — Bankman-Fried's on-again off-again girlfriend and the CEO of Alameda — served as a front for the fund, and through that arrangement Bankman-Fried had "secret access" to customer money, both cash and crypto.

Two further relations complete the alleged mechanism. Bankman-Fried is said to have directed employees to conceal the flow of money into FTX's coffers, and to have forged financial documents distributed to lenders and investors. "The defendant lied to the world," Rehn alleged. These are the government's allegations as presented in its opening statement, not established findings.



---


# The Prosecution's Opening Statement Against Bankman-Fried

Thane Rehn, a prosecutor for the government, opened the case against Sam Bankman-Fried with the line "One year ago, it looked like the defendant was on the top of the world," and then argued that this appearance was false: "all of that, all of it, was built on lies," he declared to the jury, adding "Behind the curtains, he was not what he appeared to be." Rehn described a defendant who, as former CEO of FTX, oversaw a supposedly thriving crypto exchange, jetted between international locales, hobnobbed with celebrities like Tom Brady and Larry David, and repeatedly emphasized to customers that their money was safe and secure.

What followed was a roughly 30-minute story that repeatedly emphasized how Bankman-Fried allegedly stole customer funds to facilitate his jet-setting lifestyle, donate millions to political candidates, and finance risky bets. Rehn also directly contested the media framing of the defendant: he was not a crypto "boy" genius, as so many in the media — Fortune included — have written, but a "man" who "stole billions of dollars from thousands of victims." Rehn closed the characterization with a promise to the jury: "You will see the full picture."



---


# Going Infinite: Michael Lewis's Account Of SBF's Political Dealings

Michael Lewis's book "Going Infinite" debuted on the first day of Sam Bankman-Fried's trial, and details about Bankman-Fried's political dealings emerging from it include his alleged attempt to buy off Donald Trump to get him not to run again for president.

TechCrunch's team was focused on the Manhattan Federal Court for the trial of Bankman-Fried, the disgraced entrepreneur accused of orchestrating the collapse of the cryptocurrency exchange FTX; the Lewis book is the second channel through which the week's revelations arrived. The reporting is framed as allegation rather than established fact, and it comes from the book rather than from courtroom testimony. The item appeared in TechCrunch's Week in Review of October 7, 2023.



---


# FTX Fraud Charges And The SEC's Allegation

Sam Bankman-Fried, the founder of the failed cryptocurrency exchange FTX, faced seven counts of wire fraud and conspiracy — specifically, two counts of wire fraud and five conspiracy charges — and the Securities and Exchange Commission alleged that FTX was a fraud "from the start," with a "multi-billion-dollar deficiency caused by his own misappropriation of customer funds." The Verge repeated this framing at the head of each of its trial dispatches through October 2023, and in its October 28th, 2023 write-up reported that Bankman-Fried had been found guilty on seven counts including charges of wire fraud.

The boundary of the concept is the mix of charge types: the indictment paired substantive wire fraud counts with conspiracy counts rather than resting on a single offence, and the SEC's civil allegation about the exchange's origins ran alongside the criminal case rather than being part of it. The Verge's reporter, writing as the prosecution's case neared its end on October 26th, 2023, added an impression of the people the charges swept in: all the co-conspirators seemed oddly younger than their years, as though they had got stuck in the "math camp forever" environment Bankman-Fried created for them and simply failed to grow up.

qid: Does the Engadget article suggest that Discord users will experience a new system for policy enforcement, while The Sydney Morning Herald article indicates that the aircraft safety reforms will include a warning system for identifying suspicious components?
context:
# Discord's Graduated Warning System And Account Standing

Discord is introducing a new warning system for people who violate its policies: outside of incidents involving the most "extreme" violations, the company is moving away from permanent bans, doing so under the belief that most users will choose to be better online citizens given the chance and proper guidance.

In practice the system notifies a person when they have violated one or more of Discord's policies and details the restrictions on their account. It also links out to the company's Terms of Service, Community Guidelines and appeal mechanism. A new "Account Standing" tab within the settings menu lets users see all their current and past policy violations.

Discord frames the design as a model for the industry. "We think we've built the most nuanced and proportionate reporting system," Badalich told Engadget, adding that the company hopes other platforms will look to what Discord has created for inspiration in their own enforcement efforts. "We believe people, especially teens, have the capacity to grow."



---


# Scrutiny Of Discord's CSAM Response After The NBC News Report

Teen Safety Assist arrived amid increased scrutiny of Discord's efforts to limit the spread of child sexual abuse material (CSAM) and protect young users from predatory adults, triggered by an NBC News investigation published in June that identified 35 cases over a period of six years where adults had allegedly used the platform to kidnap, groom or sexually assault minors. The outlet also found 165 cases where authorities were prosecuting adults for sharing CSAM over Discord or allegedly using the platform to extort young users into sending sexual images of themselves.

In the aftermath of that report, Discord banned teen dating servers and changed its safety policies to ban the sharing of AI-generated CSAM. It also announced new rules explicitly prohibiting any other kind of text or media content that sexualizes children, and at the same time introduced Family Center, a dashboard for parents and guardians to keep track of what their teens are doing on Discord.



---


# Discord Teen Safety Assist

Teen Safety Assist is a package of new safeguards Discord announced on Thursday to protect young users, consisting of two features — automated alerts and content filters — with the rollout happening in the coming weeks.

The alert feature works on unfamiliar contacts: when a user a teen has not chatted with before sends a direct message, Discord will display a safety alert if the platform's automated systems suspect the teen's safety could be at risk. The prompt nudges the young person to reconsider whether they want to respond, and points them to the app's block feature and related safety tips. The filter feature works on imagery: by default Discord will now automatically blur potentially sensitive images from a teen's friends. Young people can disable the feature through an option in Discord's settings menu, and adults can enable the filters for themselves if they want the additional protections.

The design principle Discord gives is agency rather than restriction. "Teens are still in the process of learning about themselves and what it means to be online, and our new safety features are rooted in providing them with agency on the platform, to give them ways to learn and grow in safe and age-appropriate online spaces," said Savannah Badalich, senior director of policy at Discord. "These newest features are part of an ongoing, multi-year effort to continually evolve and advance safety on Discord."

One boundary is worth recording. An update to the story on October 20, 2023 noted the features are rolling out in the coming weeks rather than that week, and removed a mention that Discord would automatically delete potentially sensitive content from strangers — that had been part of a briefing but was not included in the final release.



---


# Ofcom's First Guidelines Under The UK Online Safety Act

After the Online Safety Act's arduous multiyear passage through the UK's lawmaking process, regulator Ofcom published its first guidelines for how tech firms can comply with the mammoth legislation — a proposal, part of a multiphase publication process, outlining how social media platforms, search engines, online and mobile games, and pornography sites should deal with illegal content like child sexual abuse material (CSAM), terrorism content, and fraud.

The defining feature of the regime is a duty of care rather than a fixed rulebook. "What this does for the first time is to put a duty of care on tech firms to have a responsibility for the safety of their users," Ofcom's online safety lead, Gill Whitehead, told The Verge. "When they become aware that there is illegal content on their platform, they have got to get it down, and they also need to conduct risk assessments to understand the specific risks that those services might carry."

The guidelines' status is a discriminating detail. They are released as proposals so Ofcom can gather feedback before the UK Parliament approves them toward the end of next year, and even then the specifics will be voluntary: tech firms can guarantee they are obeying the law by following the guidelines to the letter, but they can take their own approach so long as they demonstrate compliance with the act's overarching rules — and, presumably, are prepared to fight their case with Ofcom.

The aim is to require that sites be proactive to stop the spread of illegal content and not just play whack-a-mole after the fact. It is meant to encourage a switch from a reactive to a more proactive approach, says lawyer Claire Wiseman, who specializes in tech, media, telecoms, and data.



---


# Technology Neutrality: How The Online Safety Act Covers AI Content

The Online Safety Act attempts to address online harms in a "technology neutral" way, Whitehead says, regardless of how they have been created — so although artificial intelligence is not emphasized in Ofcom's consultation, that does not mean AI-generated content falls outside the rules.

The discriminating test is the harm, not the tool. AI-generated CSAM would be in scope by virtue of it being CSAM, and a deepfake used to conduct fraud would be in scope by virtue of the fraud. As Whitehead puts it: "We're not regulating the technology, we're regulating the context."



---


# The Scope Of The EU's DSA Investigation Into X

Per the Commission, the EU's investigation of X covers four areas. The first is compliance with DSA obligations related to countering the dissemination of illegal content in the EU, notably in relation to the risk assessment and mitigation measures adopted by X, as well as the functioning of the notice and action mechanism for illegal content in the EU mandated by the DSA, including in light of X's content moderation resources.

The second is the effectiveness of measures taken by X to combat information manipulation, with a focus on the effectiveness of its "Community Notes" system of crowdsourcing fact-checking to aggregated views of users, who may vote to label disputed tweets with additional context. The EU said the probe will also look at the effectiveness of related policies mitigating risks to civic discourse and electoral processes.

The third is transparency requirements, with a focus on "suspected shortcomings" by X in giving researchers access to publicly accessible data as mandated by Article 40 of the DSA, and suspected shortcomings in its ads repository, the ads transparency library the regulation also mandates. The fourth is suspected deceptive design elements in X's user interface, notably in relation to checkmarks linked to certain subscription products, the so-called Blue checks.



---


# OpenAI's Three-Tier AI Safety Team Structure

OpenAI divides safety work across three teams distinguished by how far along a model is. In-production models are governed by a "safety systems" team, which handles, for example, systematic abuses of ChatGPT that can be mitigated with API restrictions or tuning. Frontier models in development get the "preparedness" team, which tries to identify and quantify risks before the model is released. Finally there is the "superalignment" team, which is working on theoretical guide rails for "superintelligent" models — which, as TechCrunch notes, we may or may not be anywhere near.

The discriminating feature between the tiers is thus the model's lifecycle stage: shipped, in development, or hypothetical future superintelligence.



---


# The Regulatory Gap Around Unapproved Aircraft Parts

Mary Schiavo's argument is that the regulatory perimeter stops in the wrong place: while plane and engine manufacturers, pilots and aviation companies are heavily regulated, distributors are not — and she pushed for tighter rules in the 1990s but was ignored.

Her grounds are her own casework and its stakes: "I've had cases where counterfeit parts have caused deaths. What's at stake is the safety of the lives of the flying public." The scope of the exposure, in her words, is total: "Literally, if it's on an aeroplane, it could be fake." Following her investigation various reforms came in, including a warning system to flag suspicious components — but not regulation of distributors. The current case is still running: the High Court case against AOG began on September 21 and is ongoing, and the UK's Civil Aviation Authority has said it is supporting the US Federal Aviation Administration and European Aviation Safety Agency in investigating the matter. A spokesman for CFM said: "We are working collaboratively with operators, so they can promptly remove the unauthorised parts from their engines in accordance with the recommendations issued by the regulatory agencies. We remain united with the aviation community in working to keep unapproved parts out of the global supply chain." B&H was approached for comment, and Zamora was approached for comment through friends and his barrister.

# War Duration and Scenarios Driving Israeli Growth Damage

Leo Leiderman's model of the war's economic damage has two drivers: duration and breadth. "First of all, the duration and character of the war will have a decisive impact on the depth of damage to the economy. Many studies, as well as past experience, indicate that the longer the war lasts, the broader will be the impact on the economy. It is also known that this connection between the length of the fighting and the economic damage might not be linear. And of course, the more the war widens to more fronts, the greater will be the economic damage."

He declined to quantify the effect. Asked on 12 October 2023 for a forecast of the consequences for growth, he said it was too early to make a quantitative estimate of the effects on the economy's growth in 2024 and 2025. Israel has a great deal of information about loss of growth and product in past episodes — the Yom Kippur War, the Lebanon War, two intifadas, various military operations, and the Covid pandemic — but in his view this is a completely different episode: "This is a new situation that has no precedent as far as the damage to the economy is concerned."

The range over which the model runs is therefore a spectrum of scenarios rather than a point estimate: "from a short war on the southern front only, to the nightmare scenario of a prolonged war with additional sectors involved." He noted the interview was taking place only on the fifth day of the war, and expressed the hope that the picture would start to become clearer.



---


# Azrieli Group's Office Portfolio In Q3 2023

Azrieli Group (TASE: AZRG) is one of the biggest companies in Israel's income-producing property sector, with 15 office buildings comprising 632,000 square meters of space and 97% occupancy.

In the week before 3 December 2023 Azrieli published its financial results for the third quarter of 2023, saying the company had not been impacted by the war. The company added a caveat: due to the uncertainty about the length of the war and its development, it could not assess the future impact of the war on business activities in Israel in general and on the company in particular.



---


# AI21 Labs' Tel Aviv Office Lease

Less than a month before the war, Globes reported a huge deal in which Amnon Shashua's unicorn AI21 Labs announced it was leasing 7,000 square meters for NIS 15 million annually in Tel Aviv's Da Vinci project.

Writing on 3 December 2023, Globes notes that it will now be interesting to see when the next such big office-space deal is signed in Tel Aviv following the impact of the Israel-Hamas war. Sources in the income-producing property sector in Israel say that over the past few weeks there has been some interest in the sector, although mainly for smaller deals involving hundreds of square meters each.



---


# Amot Investments' Portfolio And War Scenario Assessment

Amot Investments (TASE: AMOT), another of the biggest companies in the income-producing property sector, has 1.15 million square meters of office space for leasing with 93.5% occupancy and a further six projects in various stages of construction. Amot wrote that "in the third quarter several new contracts were signed including the exercising of options and the renewal of immaterial contracts for 14,000 square meters of space for an unchanged rent".

Amot raises concerns about the continuation of the war leading to damage to the economy, including to the company's tenants. Its report says the uncertainty that existed in the profitable real estate market in Israel even before the outbreak of the war, felt in the moderation in demand and the lengthening of negotiations to close agreements, has intensified following the war. Management's scenario assessment is explicit about its bounds: given that the war will focus only on the southern front and the duration of fighting at the current intensity will not exceed two to three months, the effect of the war is not material on the company's business, and in that situation, despite damage to revenue which cannot yet be accurately estimated, the effects will be reflected in the company's annual NOI and FFO within the forecast. In the company's assessment, the continuation of the fighting for a long time and/or a full conflict on the northern border front, or on other fronts, will result in significant and wider damage to the economy, including deepening the damage to private consumption and businesses including the company's tenants, and as a result will cause a decrease in payments and changes in other economic parameters.



---


# Israeli Economy in the First Week of the Gaza War

As the first week of fighting in the war in Israel's south drew to a close, the main index on the Tel Aviv Stock Exchange, the Tel Aviv 35, had fallen 6.4% over the week, with financial markets trying to gauge the damage the Israeli economy would sustain. Globes reported on 12 October 2023 that this was clearly a very significant event, but that the fog of war made it hard to estimate its full consequences.

The assessment came from Prof. Leo Leiderman, chief economic adviser at Bank Hapoalim and a professor of economics at Tel Aviv University, who set out for Globes his proposals for rehabilitating the economy and repairing the damage the war would cause. Asked what had been going through his mind in those first days, Leiderman said: "What most preoccupies me is not the economy but concern for the families of the soldiers, the wounded, and the captives, and solidarity with them. I have four relatives from Kibbutz Nir Oz who are still missing, and we have no information about them. I find it hard to understand how a war like this landed on us in a country as powerful as Israel. But we have no choice but to win."



---


# Egypt's Role In The Israel-Hamas War And The Leverage It Creates

The war between Israel and Hamas has turned the spotlight on Egypt's role as a regional powerbroker, potentially winning it Western support as it tries to escape a grinding economic crisis. The structure linking the two is that Egypt's two assets in this conflict — long-held ties to Israel and a border with Gaza — make its stance decisive for outcomes the West wants.

Specifically, Egypt's position is shaping up as key to the fate of any refugees and to a sustained flow of aid for the besieged territory's 2 million residents, after Israel cut off crucial supplies in response to Hamas's deadly Oct. 7 assault. That dependence is what converts Egypt's geography and relationships into potential leverage over Western backing for its economy, as of the reporting date of 2023-10-22.



---


# Egypt's Strategic Value To Europe: Gas And Security

The war "underscores the important role Egypt has always played vis-a-vis security in and around Gaza," said Robert Satloff, executive director at The Washington Institute for Near East Policy — a role that is not lost on European governments.

Those governments woke up to Egypt's importance as a regional gas producer after Vladimir Putin's invasion of Ukraine in 2022. European officials visited to assess Egypt's potential as a gas supplier — with Israel's help — to supplant at least some Russian supplies.



---


# Egypt's Refusal To Host Palestinian Refugees

President Abdel-Fattah El-Sisi has rejected any suggestion that Egypt host Gazan refugees, even as the same Western governments now court him for help in alleviating the pressure on Gaza, suggesting instead that Israel take in Palestinians in its Negev desert: "They can transport Palestinians there until Israel implements its announced plan to destroy Hamas," he said on Wednesday, 2023-10-18. The core political ground is that "there is little to no constituency for going against decades of policy on not allowing Palestinian displacement," said Mirette Mabrouk of the Middle East Institute, while the inducements offered "might wind up becoming a political liability, especially in an election year."

Three further grounds support the refusal. Egypt already hosts some 9 million refugees and other migrants from countries including Syria, Sudan, Yemen and Libya. Opening a route for Palestinians may also present a new security risk in the Sinai peninsula, where the army has only just managed to get a handle on its fight with Islamist militants. And Jordan has also refused to accept more Palestinians, making it unlikely Egypt would become a regional exception and take in refugees many suspect may never be let back into Gaza — which would risk being seen in the Arab world as facilitating another mass displacement and betraying the Palestinian cause all Arab countries vocally espouse.

The warrant tying these grounds to the policy is that the domestic political cost outranks the economic one. While Egypt could absorb a certain number of people, the domestic political consequences would be "huge," said the Washington Institute's Robert Satloff: "The political leadership considers this a red line not to be crossed and would prefer to face worsening financial distress than accept a significant number of refugees."



---


# Gaza Sky Geeks Accelerator

Gaza Sky Geeks is an Alphabet-backed initiative based in Gaza that provides pre-seed investments, training and technology resources to Palestine's Gazan population, and has been a beacon of entrepreneurship in the region.

It is the largest tech hub in Palestine, providing a wide range of tech training at scale: in 2022, 5,000 coders and developers from across the West Bank and Gaza graduated from the program.

# How Will Smith And Jada Pinkett Smith Met And Married In 1997

Will Smith and Jada Pinkett Smith met when she auditioned for the role of his girlfriend on The Fresh Prince of Bel-Air; she did not get the part, but the two hit it off — even though Smith was married to Sheree Zampino at the time, with whom he shares son Trey. Smith later described the moment of recognition on Pinkett Smith's Red Table Talk in 2018: "I had a realisation I wasn't with the person I was supposed to be with. I was sitting in a [bathroom] stall and I was crying and laughing uncontrollably, and I knew [Jada] was the woman I was supposed to be with."

The pair only began seriously dating in 1995, after Smith finalised his divorce from Zampino. He proposed in November 1997 and they married just one month later, in Baltimore. Pinkett Smith was not initially enthusiastic about marrying at all: she told People in 2019, "I never wanted to get married. But my mother was like: 'You have to get married' — she's so old-school — and Will wanted a family. So I said: 'All right, maybe it's something I should do.'"



---


# Jada Pinkett Smith's "Entanglement" With August Alsina

Jada Pinkett Smith confirmed in 2020 that she had had a relationship with the singer August Alsina during a period when she and Will Smith were separated, describing it on her Facebook Watch series Red Table Talk as an "entanglement." Alsina and Pinkett Smith were introduced in 2015, but it was only in 2020 that he claimed publicly that the two had dated while she was married and that the Smiths' marriage was open at the time. Alsina said Will Smith had given the pair his "blessing," explaining: "I actually sat down with Will and had a conversation due to the transformation from their marriage to life partnership that they've spoken on several times and it not involving romanticism." He added that he "totally gave myself to that relationship for years of my life and I truly and really, really deeply loved and have a ton of love for her."

Pinkett Smith's representatives called the claims "absolutely not true" on the day they surfaced. Less than two weeks later, she and Will Smith appeared together on Red Table Talk, where she confirmed the relationship but placed it inside an amicable separation that had not been disclosed to the press at the time: "We decided that we were going to separate for a period of time and you go figure out how to make yourself happy and I'll figure out how to make myself happy. From there, as time went on, I got into a different kind of entanglement with August... Yes, it was a relationship absolutely." Prompted by her husband, she confirmed it "was a relationship, absolutely." She also rejected Alsina's framing of permission, saying Will had not given it because the only person who could give her permission was herself. The episode is one of the grey areas in the couple's account of the terms of their separation.



---


# The Smiths' Denials Of Open-Marriage, Divorce And Infidelity Rumours

Will Smith and Jada Pinkett Smith have each publicly rejected the recurring claims made about their marriage — that it was an open relationship, that they were divorcing, and that either had been unfaithful. Pinkett Smith attacked the open-relationship premise directly on Facebook, after a quiet decade and a half spent making films and raising their children: "Here is how I will change my statement... Will and I BOTH can do WHATEVER we want, because we TRUST each other to do so. This does NOT mean we have an open relationship... this means we have a GROWN one." Her counter is that mutual freedom follows from trust, not from an open-marriage arrangement, so the inference from one to the other does not hold.

Will Smith answered the separation-and-divorce rumours in a mocking Facebook post: "Under normal circumstances, I don't usually respond to foolishness. But, so many people have extended [to] me their 'deepest condolences' that I figured — 'What the hell… I can be foolish, too!' So, in the interest of redundant, repetitious, over and over-again-ness… Jada and I are… NOT GETTING A DIVORCE!!!!!!!!!!!!!" In an interview on CBS Sunday Morning in October 2023 he also denied the infidelity premise outright: "Never. There's never been infidelity in our marriage... And we have never surprised one another with anything ever." He added that he had decided public chatter about his life "can be of a benefit to people," since "chatter is the first stage to having a real conversation and being able to truly explore if some of the things in your heart are loving, or poisonous."



---


# The Smiths' 2021 Public Accounts Of Marital Strain

In late 2021 both Will Smith and Jada Pinkett Smith described the difficulty of their marriage in public, first on her show and then in his memoir. In an October 2021 episode of Red Table Talk, Pinkett Smith said it "takes work" to maintain a spark in the bedroom: "It's hard... the thing Will and I talk about a lot is the journey. We started in this [relationship] at a very young age, 22 years old... I think you expect your partner to know — especially when it comes to sex. It's like: 'Well, if you love me, you should know. If you love me, you should read my mind.' That's a huge pitfall."

The following month Will Smith's memoir was released, detailing several problems the couple had had over the years. He wrote that they were "suffering the brutal death of our romantic fantasies, the burning away of the idealistic illusion of the perfect marriage and the perfect family. Neither of us wanted a divorce; we knew we loved each other, and some aspects of our union were magical. But the structure of the life that we had established was strangling both of us."



---


# "Life Partnership" As The Smiths' Own Term For Their Marriage

"Life partnership" is the term Will Smith and Jada Pinkett Smith use for their relationship in place of a conventional marriage description, and its defining feature is unconditionality rather than cohabitation or romance. Will Smith set out the definition on TIDAL's Rap Radar podcast: he and Jada "refer to ourselves as life partners, where you get into that space where you realise you are literally with somebody for the rest of your life. There's no deal breakers. There's nothing she could do — ever. Nothing that would break our relationship. She has my support till death and it feels so good to get to that space."

Pinkett Smith used the same term as the goal of the couple's repair work. On the Today show on 16 October 2023 she told Hoda Kotb that she and the Suicide Squad actor were "working hard" and "concentrating on healing": "There's no finding another great love, and I think that's the point. It's like we are in a place now that we are in a deep, healing space. And we are really concentrating on healing the relationship between us." She added: "There's no divorce on paper. We really have been working hard. That's the whole thing. We are working very hard at bringing our relationship together. Back to a life partnership." Speaking about the family — the couple's children Jaden, 25, and Willow, 22, plus Will's 30-year-old son Trey with ex-wife Sheree Zampino — she framed the term as what the relationship has become rather than a permanent verdict: "We love our family and we love each other. It's more of a life partnership. Now, 10 years from now, Hoda, who knows?"



---


# Will And Jada As A New, Unconventional Marriage Model

Relationship expert Susan Winter argues that the Smiths' seven-year separation is not a stalled marriage waiting to be repaired but a fluid arrangement outside the traditional marriage design — an evolving model that could come to serve other couples. Her starting point is a limit on what outsiders can know: the public will never fully learn what "heavy-duty work" Will Smith and Jada Pinkett Smith are doing in their relationship, and, she says, it is not necessarily anyone's business.

The grounds are that a couple who have already built something different have no reason to revert to the conventional form. "They're in the rough with a machete, carving a new path for themselves," Winter said. "Why would they say: 'Hey, let's go back to the house and just relax?' They're really exploring something vastly different. It doesn't end up that you go back into that little box of 'this is a marriage, we're living together'. It just doesn't do that." The Independent frames the same point as a question: if the Smiths have spent seven years apart as a married couple, why would they decide to return to a shared household?

# Default Search Engine

## Definition

The default search engine is the search provider a device, browser, or platform is pre-configured to use unless a user actively changes the setting — the search box that runs when a person types a query without first choosing an alternative, such as Google on the iPhone's Safari address bar or Firefox's search bar.

## Context

The term is central to *US v. Google*, the DOJ's antitrust case, because default status is the mechanism through which Google secures the overwhelming share of search queries: the Information Services Agreement (ISA) between Apple and Google, in place since 2002/2003, makes Google the default on all Apple devices, and Google separately pays Samsung, Mozilla, and other partners for the same status.
Apple executive Eddy Cue testified that Apple's iPhone setup flow deliberately omits any search-engine choice screen, arguing that presenting users with unfamiliar alternatives would harm the setup experience, while conceding the ISA does not permit Apple to offer such a choice.
Google spent $26.3 billion in 2021 on default-placement deals across browsers, phones, and platforms — about $18 billion of that to Apple alone — a scale that the DOJ used to argue Google understands the mechanism's value: internal 2007 data showed users who set Google as their homepage searched 15% more, while switching away dropped searches 27%.
The Mozilla/Yahoo episode shows the same mechanism working in reverse: when Firefox switched its default from Google to Yahoo under a 2014 deal, Mozilla's CEO testified that user retention declined, illustrating how disruptive changing the default can be even when a paying competitor is involved.
Outside the antitrust trial, the term also frames ordinary consumer behavior: an investor in e-commerce search startup Deft described users' "natural behavior" as following the path of least resistance and just using the default search engine, meaning challenger search products must offer a high-value proposition to displace that inertia.

## Key Characteristics

- **Set by agreement, not by user choice** — default status on major platforms (Apple's Safari/iOS, Android OEMs, Firefox) is typically established through commercial deals (e.g., the Apple-Google ISA, Yahoo-Mozilla's $375M/year deal) rather than user selection at setup.
- **Backed by large recurring payments** — Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 across partners to hold default placement, with roughly $18 billion of that going to Apple.
- **Technically reversible but rarely changed** — Apple and Google both argued switching is easy, but DuckDuckGo's CEO countered that it takes "too many steps" to switch, and Google's own 2005 complaint about Internet Explorer's defaults argued that "most end users do not change defaults," so default status functions as durable market power.
- **Distinct from pre-installation** — Google's separate push to get Chrome and Search merely pre-installed (not necessarily defaulted) on Android and iPhones shows default status is a stronger, more contested tier than simple presence on a device.
- **Drives user behavior even outside browsers** — the concept extends to any search product; consumers default to "the path of least resistance," which challenger search startups must specifically overcome.

## Corpus References

Corpus notes whose source text references this term (evidence-backed, from `term_links.json`):

- [The Google Antitrust Case](google_antitrust_case.md)
- [The Hypocrisy Argument: Google Became The Monopoly It Denounced](google_default_hypocrisy_argument.md)
- [US v. Google: Two Months Into The Search Antitrust Trial](us_v_google_search_antitrust_trial_overview.md)



---


# The Epic v. Apple Ruling And Its Limited Weight Here

In the Apple case both sides lost, but Epic arguably lost more: even though Apple has incredible power over the iPhone, Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers ruled the company did not have an unfair monopoly in that case, partly because she decided the relevant market for Fortnite was "digital mobile gaming transactions" rather than, say, iPhone apps. She also decided that Epic violated its developer agreement with Apple and would have to pay.

Epic did win something. Rogers barred Apple from keeping iPhone users in the dark about alternate ways they can pay for apps, and may have even allowed developers to add their own payment mechanisms.

The precedent's reach into the Google trial is limited in two specific ways. First, that was a different case — and it is not over until the Supreme Court weighs in or declines to take a look. Second, Google cannot tell jurors that Apple won its case, or that other plaintiffs settled; the judge in this case says so. Epic declined to answer on the record when asked about the Apple outcome.



---


# Epic Games v. Google Goes To Trial On November 6, 2023

Epic Games, the maker of Fortnite, went to trial with Google on November 6, 2023, hoping to convince a jury that Google engages in anticompetitive behavior with regard to its Android app store, Google Play, and its commission structure. Match had settled its own antitrust lawsuit with Google the week before, but Epic's case proceeded.

This case differs slightly from Epic's battle with Apple on the same topic, because this time Epic cannot allege there is no other way to load apps onto Android devices, as it could with Apple: Android does allow for sideloading apps. Epic will suggest Google makes that process cumbersome, but the bulk of its arguments will center on what it believes are anticompetitive agreements between Google and device manufacturers and developers.

The precedent Epic's case relies on is a Microsoft case in which courts found Microsoft to have a monopoly over the operating system and to be abusing it, making it hard for users to download alternative browsers, like Netscape, on Windows devices. To make its case, Epic plans to bring claims under Sections 1 and 2 of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act, as well as California's anticompetitive laws, the Cartwright Act and the Unfair Competition Law. It will attempt to argue that Google restrains competition within two separate markets: the distribution of apps to Android users, and the market for payment processing solutions for content inside Android apps.



---


# Google's Defense: Android Competes With iOS

Google's defense denies the premise that Android app stores are a market of their own: "You cannot separate the quality of a phone from the quality of the apps in its app store, and that means Google and Apple compete against each other," began Google lead attorney Glenn Pomerantz. If Google can convince the jury of that, it could be a winning argument, because obviously Google does not have a monopoly on app stores or phones in general.

Pomerantz's commonsense line was that Google cannot possibly have a monopoly on Android app stores when "every single Samsung phone comes with two app stores right on the homescreen," and that the download charts reflect user preference rather than exclusion: "When they show these charts that show all these downloads from Play and not from the Galaxy Store, that's what the Samsung phone users are choosing. They're touching Play. Nothing's keeping them from touching the Galaxy Store; it's just what works for them."

Google's second plank is openness relative to Apple. Epic promised to "show that Google has closed off each and every other option" to the Play Store during this trial, but Google points to the simple fact that it allows alternate app channels at all — something Android rival iOS does not. Pomerantz boasted that over a billion people have gone through the process Epic portrays as needlessly onerous to get apps outside the Play Store; Google told The Verge over email that this refers to how many users have enabled the Android sideloading flow, not necessarily followed through with an install. "A billion people have done it after getting notified of the potential risks," Pomerantz said. "That's because Android users have a real choice."

Google also argues about consequences: if Epic wins, according to Google, it could make Android phones less safe by dismantling basic protections against sideloaded apps, and damage Android's ability to compete with the iPhone because it arguably cannot run a competitive app store by giving it away for free. Google's execution was uneven, though — it wound up spending much of its opening statement attempting to explain away its seemingly bad behavior as normal business practices and did not always succeed out of the gate.



---


# Google's Agreement Not To Promote Chrome To Safari Users

As part of its search deal with Apple, Google agreed not to promote Chrome to Safari users, according to Bloomberg — a restraint that mattered because Google would otherwise have been able to do this with banners, pop-ups and other annoying means in its other Google apps. The same agreement also meant that Apple never switched to a Google competitor, and never allowed users to choose their browser when setting up their iPhones.

The observation surfaced in the antitrust trial, where the amount Google spent on homepage market share has been a fixing point. Earlier in October 2023, the CEOs of Microsoft and DuckDuckGo testified that their search engines would have been far more successful, even competitive with Google, had they been able to make similar deals with Apple. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella even said he was willing to spend $15 billion per year to get Bing into Apple's default search, per The Information — a stated willingness to pay, not a deal that happened.

A second, related admission came from Google's side: Pichai admitted to attempting to get Tim Cook to preinstall Google on every iOS device back in 2018, according to The Verge. His aim, as reported, was to make Google's and Apple's services so connected as to be inseparable.

# Walmart Cyber Monday 2023 Over-Ear Headphone Deals

WIRED's Walmart Cyber Monday roundup of 27 November 2023 recommended six discounted over-ear headphones: Sony's WH-1000XM5 and WH-1000XM4, Bose's QuietComfort Ultra, Sennheiser's HD 660S2, a cheaper pair of Sony noise cancellers and Soundcore's Life Q30.

As Sony's priciest wireless headphones, the WH-1000XM5 had a lot to live up to after the remarkably popular WH-1000XM4, but WIRED says they deliver with upgraded noise cancelling, a posh new design and a more refined sound signature — especially on sale. Bose's QuietComfort Ultra (9/10, WIRED Recommends) arrived in October 2023 with only one notable problem, their very high price; the discount makes it easier to get their class-leading noise cancelling, great sound and luxuriously comfy, feature-loaded design. Sony's older WH-1000XM4 (9/10, WIRED Recommends) have been a stalwart for years, offering excellent noise cancelling, warm and detailed sound and a ton of modern features in a comfy design that puts them among the best travel headphones you can buy.

WIRED's only complaints about Sennheiser's HD 660S2 (7/10, WIRED Review) — bass-enriched audiophile headphones — were the high price and stiff clamping force, and at this price it can live with the tighter fit given gloriously clear and richly detailed sound. Sony's "working-class" noise cancellers offer solid performance, clear sound and impressive battery life at a much more reasonable price than the brand's top offerings, and with this sale WIRED calls them some of the best value in their class from one of the top names in the business. Soundcore's Life Q30 are already impressive at full price thanks to noise cancelling that punches well above its class, so the deal makes them something of a steal, with accessible and adjustable sound quality, good features and great battery life.



---


# Sony WH-1000XM5 Black Friday Deal

The Sony WH-1000XM5 came down to $328 at Amazon, B&H and other retailers for Black Friday 2023 — a $72 drop from its $400 list price. Engadget's headphone roundup calls that a tie with the lowest price it has seen; the wider Black Friday roundup describes it as not an all-time low but about $70 off Sony's list price and $20 lower than the headphones' usual recurring sale price.

The XM5 is the top recommendation in Engadget's guide to the best wireless headphones and earned a review score of 95 last year. Its active noise cancellation is among the better options tested, its design is comfortable to wear over extended periods, its call quality is crisp and its battery lasts a solid 30 or so hours per charge. By default its sound goes heavy on the bass, which should please fans of hip-hop, EDM and pop, though the EQ curve can be customized through Sony's app, and like many Sony headphones it comes with useful bonus features such as "Speak-to-Chat," which automatically pauses your music when you start speaking.



---


# Bose QuietComfort 45 Headphones Deal Prices

The Bose QuietComfort 45 over-ear headphones fell to $229-$230 for October Prime Day 2023 and then to a record-low $199 in Amazon's Cyber Monday sale, according to Engadget and Mashable roundups across the season.

Mashable's Cyber Monday post of 27 November 2023 said there is "only one pair of Bose over-ear headphones you can grab for just under $200, and that's the QuietComfort 45s at a record-low price of $199", crediting the classic pair with top-of-the-line ANC, 20 hours of battery life and all-day comfort "for less than half of the AirPods Max's sale price". Engadget's 10 October 2023 Prime Day roundup put them at $230, about $80 cheaper than their usual selling price, and said they earned a spot in its best wireless headphone guide thanks to their comfortable if a little dated design, excellent ANC and balanced audio.

Engadget's headphone-specific Prime Day list, also 10 October 2023, listed them at $229 against a $329 list price (save $100), noting that $229 is $30 more than the lowest price it had tracked but still $80 below their average street price. That piece adds that this is another noise-cancelling set Bose recently replaced, but the differences between the QC 45 and the new QuietComfort Headphones appear small, so the older model is worth a look when discounted; Engadget gave the QC 45 a review score of 86 in 2021 and still likes its lightweight design, upper-tier ANC and easygoing sound. The caveats: you cannot manually adjust ANC intensity, unlike the newer model, and Sony's XM5 and XM4 provide longer battery life and a more versatile feature set for those willing to pay up.



---


# Beyerdynamic DT 900 Pro X Deal

qid: What company spends billions to maintain its default search engine status on various platforms, influences local search rankings with specific criteria, and is accused by news publishers of anticompetitive practices that harm their revenue, according to articles from The Verge and TechCrunch?
