qid: Do the articles from The Roar | Sports Writers Blog discussing The All Blacks' actions in the Rugby World Cup final and their previous encounters with Argentina both present The All Blacks as having effortlessly dominated in their gameplay, or do they portray different situations regarding The All Blacks' performance?
context:
# The All Blacks' Final Moments In The 2023 World Cup Final

New Zealand's last chance in the 2023 Rugby World Cup final died in the 80th minute when Ardie Savea forced a ball out wide just as the men in black saw space and looked to open up the Springboks — a killer blow, in The Roar's phrase.

The wider failing was handling. The All Blacks had their chances, but their usual safe handling — a feature throughout the World Cup after their first-up loss to France — evaded them against the Springboks' blitz defence in the wet conditions, and all night their timing was off.

The end came at a set piece. Wayne Barnes, who was booed relentlessly, called a scrum reset as the seconds ticked by; moments later New Zealand hearts sank as the Springboks won the scrum and then hung onto the ball.



---


# The All Blacks' Generational Change After The 2023 World Cup

The 2023 World Cup final marked the end of an All Blacks era on and off the field: Ian Foster's tenure as coach came to an end with Scott Robertson taking over, and multiple generational players — Dane Coles, Sam Whitelock, Brodie Retallick and Aaron Smith — were to call time on their international careers, with others including Ardie Savea, Richie Mo'unga, Beauden Barrett and Shannon Frizell heading to Japan.

Writing before the final on Oct. 26, The Roar reported that the All Blacks would experience a changing of the guard the next season, and noted that the team's own social media channels described the World Cup final selection as the "Last Dance". Dane Coles, a 2015 World Cup winner, would call time on his career, while his tight-five teammates Retallick and Whitelock — the latter bidding to become the first player to win the Webb Ellis Cup for a third time — would head overseas, and fellow World Cup winners Aaron Smith and Beauden Barrett would also head to Japan.

Coles, labelled by Samisoni Taukei'aho as a "Grandad" type figure in the All Blacks, was even denied the chance of a farewell send-off after missing selection for the final. Foster called the conversation with the 36-year-old the hardest of his coaching life: "Yeah, tough. We don't want to talk too much about post-game stuff, but that was a tough one, probably the toughest I have had as a coach. He took it the way I expected him to. He's a champion." After the final, The Roar added that Robertson would have an almighty task on his hands given the scale of the departures.



---


# Joe Schmidt's Coaching Record With Ireland And The All Blacks

Joe Schmidt took Ireland to the top of World Rugby's rankings while his Irish sides bombed out in successive World Cup quarter-finals under his leadership, and he later helped transform an All Blacks team that reached the 2023 World Cup final, as reported by The Roar on 11 December 2023.

His Ireland tenure is credited with more than results: Schmidt played an instrumental role in not just seeing them become one of the world's best teams but helped usher through transformational change off the field, as Ireland moved to a centralised system.

The New Zealander briefly exited the international coaching scene following the 2019 World Cup, citing a desire to move home to New Zealand to be closer to his family. After initially moving back into the coaching fray with the Blues in Super Rugby, he joined the All Blacks ahead of the previous year's Rugby Championship, as New Zealand Rugby shook up the All Blacks coaching team following their historic series loss to Andy Farrell's Irish. His expertise proved telling: he and Jason Ryan transformed the All Blacks and helped Ian Foster's side reach the final of that year's World Cup after stunning wins over Ireland and Argentina in the knockout stages.



---


# Foster Rejects The Favourites Label Against Argentina

Although the All Blacks were 18-point favourites for the opening 2023 World Cup semi-final, Ian Foster rejected the premise that his side sees itself that way: "Firstly, you've never heard us say we're favourites."

His grounds for rejecting the label are recent results and a limit on what the past predicts. Argentina had knocked over the All Blacks the previous year in Christchurch, as well as inflicting a maiden defeat in 2020 in Sydney, and New Zealand had themselves suffered a shock semi-final loss to Eddie Jones' England in 2019. Foster also argued that familiarity does not transfer to this stage: "The past sets us up beautifully for both teams. We do know each other but we don't know each other in terms of a Rugby World Cup, so at this stage in the tournament it's new territory for us and as we've seen World Cups are very different."

He then converted the rejection into a demand on his own team: "We have learnt to greatly respect Argentina. They have a rich history of overachieving at the World Cup and have done a fantastic job to get here at the same level we are, so it is going to be a heck of a game." And: "We know these games are do or die. We're going to have to improve our performance. The stage gets bigger at this time in the tournament and you've got to grow your game. That's our strong focus. The best team on the night wins – Argentina has done that to us."



---


# The Ireland Series Loss Backlash As All Blacks Motivation

The Roar argued on Oct. 26, 2023 that where the Springboks play for their country, the All Blacks were playing for themselves as much as anyone — and for the generation of players and leaders who would call time on their international careers at week's end — which is why the World Cup final was personal for the men in black.

The framing question is how New Zealand could withstand and overcome the hitherto unshakable wave of momentum and spirit the Springboks play with under Rassie Erasmus in that weekend's final. The grounds offered for the All Blacks' personal motivation are the backlash and toxicity that followed their historic home series loss to Ireland, described as a humbling and public reminder of the expectation of being an All Black — All Blacks social media managers were forced to delete a thousand comments an hour following the humbling series loss in Wellington.

The warrant is that the hurt persisted and became fuel: the pain of the days and weeks after that dark July, as well as the bumps and bruises along the way — including as recently as August when they suffered their biggest defeat to the Boks to lose the inaugural and prestigious Qatar Cup — still ran deep.



---


# Joe Schmidt's Wallabies Candidacy And The Rival Candidates

The Roar reported on 11 December 2023 that Joe Schmidt — the 2018 World Rugby coach of the year, former Ireland coach and All Blacks assistant — is interested in the vacant Wallabies coaching job, with Dan McKellar, Stephen Larkham, Andy Friend and Ian Foster also remaining interested in the role.

The link the report draws is personal. Peter Horne's close relationship with Schmidt could be one of the keys to landing him: after leaving his Irish post following the 2019 World Cup, ending six years in the job, Schmidt worked alongside Horne at World Rugby, and it is believed the duo have a strong working relationship.



---


# The Second Half Of The 2023 Rugby World Cup Final

New Zealand's only try of the 2023 Rugby World Cup final, scored by Beauden Barrett after a Mark Telea break, left them trailing by a single point when Richie Mo'unga missed the conversion — and that lone point proved the difference as the Springboks celebrated a remarkable victory.

The half turned on discipline and missed chances. Minutes into it Siya Kolisi was off after cannoning into Ardie Savea; he later returned, much to the anger of the New Zealanders in the crowd who were calling for justice. Sensing an opportunity to strike against 14 men, the All Blacks kicked for the corner on a couple of occasions out wide, and it came back to haunt them as their usually silky and composed skill sets failed them.

That pattern held when the TMO intervened after Aaron Smith thought he had a try in his final Test, only for an error at the lineout to cancel out the five-pointer. Eventually the All Blacks did have a try: Mark Telea, their best and biggest attacking threat all night, got on the outside and drew in two defenders before offloading to Beauden Barrett — but Mo'unga missed the conversion, leaving them a point behind.



---


# The Case For Schmidt Bringing Rugby Smarts To The Wallabies

Several sources told The Roar in December 2023 that Joe Schmidt is exactly the type of person the Wallabies need: the claim is that the highly detailed Schmidt would bring rugby smarts to the Australian program, and the warrant is that the Wallabies' detail and nous were clearly absent on the field over the previous year, which is precisely what his coaching supplies.

The evidence offered for that capability is what his Ireland teams demonstrably did: the manipulation and ability to play both sides of the ruck was clearly visible during his Irish tenure.

The argument also carries a political ground about acceptance within Australian rugby: should Rugby Australia move on him, Schmidt's backing would be largely supported by the Super Rugby franchises.

qid: Does the TechCrunch article claim that "Microsoft's investment in OpenAI" is unspecified, while The Age article focuses on the "founding of OpenAI" without specifying financial figures?
context:
# OpenAI's Nonprofit Governance And Capped-Profit Structure

OpenAI's for-profit subsidiary, OpenAI Global, LLC, is fully controlled by OpenAI's nonprofit: the subsidiary is permitted to commercialize its technology, but it is subject to the nonprofit's mission of attaining artificial general intelligence (AGI), which OpenAI defines as AI that can "outperform humans at most economically valuable work."

The discriminating feature of this structure is where the power over AGI sits. The nonprofit OpenAI's board has the power both to determine when the company has achieved AGI and to exclude that AGI from IP licenses and other commercial terms — including terms with Microsoft, one of OpenAI's biggest investors and a steadfast integrator of OpenAI's technologies. OpenAI was founded as a nonprofit in 2015 but restructured in 2019 as a "capped-profit" company in order to raise capital, an acknowledgement of the huge costs associated with training cutting-edge AI systems. Altman underlined the point in an interview with the Financial Times in the week of his firing, saying he "hoped" Microsoft would increase its investment to help pay for "huge" imminent model training costs.



---


# The Microsoft-OpenAI Partnership And Microsoft's Response To The Firing

Microsoft is OpenAI's largest corporate backer — it had poured $13 billion into OpenAI as of November 2023 and holds what amounts to a 49% stake — and its public response to Altman's firing was to reaffirm the partnership and to back interim CEO Mira Murati rather than to intervene.

The relationship has three visible features in this account: the scale of the investment, a long-term agreement giving Microsoft access to OpenAI's technology, and deep product integration. Frank Shaw, Microsoft's chief communications officer, said: "We have a long-term partnership with OpenAI and Microsoft remains committed to Mira and their team as we bring this next era of AI to our customers." CEO Satya Nadella then published a fuller statement: "As you saw at Microsoft Ignite this week, we're continuing to rapidly innovate for this era of AI, with over 100 announcements across the full tech stack from AI systems, models and tools in Azure, to Copilot. Most importantly, we're committed to delivering all of this to our customers while building for the future. We have a long-term agreement with OpenAI with full access to everything we need to deliver on our innovation agenda and an exciting product roadmap; and remain committed to our partnership, and to Mira and the team. Together, we will continue to deliver the meaningful benefits of this technology to the world."

The partnership's limits also showed. Microsoft's stock price fell more than 1% in the last 30 minutes of trading after Altman's departure was announced, and Axios reported that Microsoft was notified Altman would be leaving only "minutes" before the public announcement. OpenAI's press relations declined to comment beyond the official blog post.



---


# OpenAI's Partnerships With Microsoft And The Associated Press

OpenAI's key business partner is Microsoft, which has invested billions of dollars into the startup and helped provide the computing power to run its AI systems. Microsoft said the leadership transition would not affect its relationship: "We have a long-term partnership with OpenAI and Microsoft remains committed to Mira and their team as we bring this next era of AI to our customers," an emailed Microsoft statement said.

A second, narrower arrangement is with a news organization: The Associated Press and OpenAI have a licensing and technology agreement allowing OpenAI access to part of the AP's text archives.



---


# Microsoft's OpenAI Investment And Early Capability Tests

The first look at the disruptive potential that generative AI offers came when ChatGPT managed to pass a series of law school exams — albeit by the skin of its digital teeth, Engadget notes.

Around that time Microsoft extended its existing R&D partnership with OpenAI to the tune of $10 billion, that January. Engadget's aside on the figure: that number is impressively large and likely why Altman still has his job.



---


# Musk's Founding Of OpenAI And His Departure

Convinced that Larry Page's optimistic view of AI was dead wrong, and angry at his loss of DeepMind, Musk built his own lab: OpenAI was founded in late 2015, just a few months after he met with Sam Altman at the Rosewood hotel in Silicon Valley. Musk pumped money into the lab and his former PayPal buddies, Reid Hoffman and Peter Thiel, came along for the ride; the three men and others pledged to put $US1 billion into the project, which Altman, then 30, would help run, and to get started they poached Ilya Sutskever from Google, one of the graduate students Google had "bought" in Hinton's auction. Initially Musk wanted to operate OpenAI as a nonprofit, free from the economic incentives driving Google and other corporations, but by the time Google wowed the tech community with its Go stunt he was changing his mind about how it should be run: he desperately wanted OpenAI to invent something that would capture the world's imagination and close the gap with Google, and it wasn't getting the job done as a nonprofit.

In late 2017 Musk hatched a plan to wrest control of the lab from Altman and the other founders and transform it into a commercial operation that would join forces with Tesla and rely on supercomputers the car company was developing, according to four people familiar with the matter; when Altman and others pushed back, Musk quit and said he would focus on his own AI work at Tesla. In February 2018 he announced his departure to OpenAI's staff on the top floor of the startup's offices in a converted truck factory, three people who attended said; when he said OpenAI needed to move faster, one researcher retorted that Musk was being reckless, and Musk called the researcher a "jackass" and stormed out, taking his deep pockets with him. OpenAI suddenly needed new financing in a hurry: Altman flew to Sun Valley for a conference and ran into Satya Nadella, Microsoft's CEO, and a tie-up seemed natural, since Altman knew Microsoft's chief technology officer Kevin Scott and Microsoft had bought LinkedIn from Hoffman, an OpenAI board member; Nadella told Scott to get it done. The deal closed in 2019, leaving Altman and OpenAI with a for-profit company formed under the original nonprofit, $US1 billion in fresh capital, and Microsoft with a new way to build AI into its vast cloud computing service. Not everyone inside OpenAI was happy.



---


# OpenAI Corporate Deals And Business Moves

Alongside its product releases, OpenAI made a series of corporate moves in 2023: a news-content partnership with Axel Springer, an indemnity promise to business customers over copyright claims, its first acquisition, a $300 million share sale, and a stalled attempt to trademark "GPT."

OpenAI struck a deal with the Berlin-based news publisher Axel Springer, which owns Business Insider and Politico, to "help provide people with new ways to access quality, real-time news content through our AI tools"; under it OpenAI will train its generative AI models on the publisher's content and add recent Axel Springer-published articles to ChatGPT. Bowing to peer pressure, OpenAI also said it would pay legal costs incurred by customers who face lawsuits over IP claims against work generated by an OpenAI tool, though the protections seemingly do not extend to all OpenAI products, such as the free and Plus tiers of ChatGPT. In its first public acquisition in its seven-year history, OpenAI acquired Global Illumination, a New York-based startup leveraging AI to build creative tools, infrastructure and digital experiences; OpenAI wrote in a brief blog post, "We're very excited for the impact they'll have here at OpenAI. The entire team has joined OpenAI to work on our core products including ChatGPT."

On financing, OpenAI closed a $300 million share sale at a $27 billion to $29 billion valuation, with VC firms including Sequoia Capital, Andreessen Horowitz, Thrive and K2 Global picking up new shares according to documents seen by TechCrunch, and a source saying Founders Fund was also investing. That round was separate from a large Microsoft investment announced earlier in the year, which closed in January and is believed to be around $10 billion. On trademarks, OpenAI applied for a trademark for "GPT" — Generative Pre-trained Transformer — in December, and petitioned the USPTO to speed up the process, citing the "myriad infringements and counterfeit apps" beginning to spring into existence; the petition was dismissed because OpenAI's attorneys neglected to pay an associated fee and to provide "appropriate documentary evidence supporting the justification of special action," meaning a decision could take up to five more months.



---


# Sam Altman's Side Ventures: Helion, Retro And Worldcoin

Altman has a number of possible next steps after leaving OpenAI, because even while running the company he placed large bets on several other ambitious projects.

Among them are Helion Energy, for developing fusion reactors that could produce prodigious amounts of energy from the hydrogen in seawater, and Retro Biosciences, which aims to add 10 years to the human lifespan using biotechnology. Altman also co-founded Worldcoin, a biometric and cryptocurrency project that has been scanning people's eyeballs with the goal of creating a vast digital identity and financial network.

qid: Did TechCrunch report on DeepMind's expected release of a next-generation chatbot named Gemini before TechCrunch reported that Google released only a "lite" version of the Gemini model known as Gemini Pro?
context:
# Anecdotal Evidence Undercuts Google's Gemini Pro Claims

Against Google's promises for Gemini Pro, TechCrunch's rejoinder on 7 December 2023 was blunt: "the anecdotal evidence suggests otherwise." The counter-argument attacks the evidential basis of the launch claims rather than the model's architecture, setting user experience after release against what Google said the model would do.

The grounds are the reception of the rollout itself. A "lite" version of Gemini, Gemini Pro, began rolling out to Bard the day before the article, and it did not take long before users began voicing their frustrations with it on X, formerly Twitter.



---


# Google's Gemini Model Family And Its Capability Claims

Gemini is Google's new flagship generative AI model, unveiled in the first week of December 2023 and meant to power a range of products and services including Bard, Google's ChatGPT competitor. In blog posts and press materials, Google touted Gemini's superior architecture and capabilities, claiming that the model meets or exceeds the performance of other leading generative AI models such as OpenAI's GPT-4, and it emphasised Gemini's coding capabilities and multimodal prowess, claiming that the model can understand images, audio and videos just as well as text.

The family has tiers, and only the lower one shipped. Google did not release the full model, Gemini Ultra — which is set to launch sometime in 2024 in Bard and other products — but only a "lite" version called Gemini Pro. Gemini Pro is therefore not the most capable version of Gemini, and Google compared its performance to GPT-4's predecessor, GPT-3.5, a model that was around a year old. Google nevertheless promised improvements in reasoning, planning and understanding with Gemini Pro over the previous model powering Bard, claiming Gemini Pro was better at summarizing content, brainstorming and writing.

The shipped tier is also narrower than the multimodal claims suggest: Gemini Pro is strictly text-in, text-out, and has proven to be mistake-prone. In a worse look for Google, the company was caught faking a Gemini demo by tuning text prompts with still images off camera.



---


# The Competitive Response To ChatGPT Across The AI Industry

ChatGPT became priority number one at OpenAI — not simply a one-off product but a development platform to build upon — and, as often happens in a competition-driven marketplace, it shifted the focus at other AI firms and research labs too.

Google scrambled to launch a response to ChatGPT, eventually releasing Bard, a more or less comparable AI chatbot, in February 2023. Countless other ChatGPT rivals and derivatives have arrived to market since, most recently Amazon Q, a more business-oriented take on ChatGPT. And DeepMind, Google's premier AI research lab, is expected to debut a next-gen chatbot, Gemini, before the end of 2023.



---


# Gemini Pro's Coding Task Failures

Google emphasized Gemini's enhanced coding skills in a briefing in the first week of December 2023, and posts on X suggest it may genuinely have improved in some areas — but it also appears that Gemini Pro struggles with basic coding functions in Python. TechCrunch collected several user reports from 6 and 7 December 2023.

Filip Piekniewski reported that Gemini-based Bard still could not write the intersection of two polygons, calling it one of those rare, relatively simple to express functions that was never implemented in Python and has no Stack Overflow post, and noting that all these models fail on it. Mohsen Azimi found Gemini Pro "pretty disappointing" for his example: he asked it to make an analog clock using HTML like one ChatGPT made, and while it could cite some code from GitHub, it was off by a few milliseconds.

Two head-to-head comparisons went the same way. Edison Ade created a Tic Tac Toe game with both ChatGPT and Bard running on Gemini Pro, and reported that ChatGPT wrote the code on the first try while Bard took three tries, concluding GPT-4 was still greater than Gemini Pro. N Kiran Kumar tested Bard with the Gemini Pro update and got no bugless snake game on the first try; after reporting the bug and asking for a fix, the model could not fix it, whereas the free version of ChatGPT 3.5 returned correct, bug-free code on the first attempt.



---


# Gemini Pro's Translation And Multilingual Weakness

Translation did not appear to be Gemini Pro's strong suit in early December 2023 tests: it struggled to give a six-letter word in French. Benjamin Netter posted an example on X on 6 December 2023 with the verdict "FYI, Google Gemini is complete trash."

When the TechCrunch reporter ran the same prompt through Bard — "Can you give me a 6-letters word in French?" — Gemini Pro responded with a seven-letter word instead of a five-letter one, which he took as giving some credence to the reports about Gemini's poor multilingual performance.



---


# Gemini Pro's News Summarization Refusals And Stale Answers

Asked to summarise topical news in early December 2023, Gemini Pro often would not do it, despite having Google Search and Google News at its disposal. It seemed loath to comment on potentially controversial news topics, instead telling users to Google it themselves.

The TechCrunch reporter tried the same prompt and got a very similar response. ChatGPT, by contrast, gave a bullet-list summary with citations to news articles.

There was one partial exception, and it exposed a second problem: Gemini Pro did provide a summary of updates on the war in Ukraine when the reporter asked for one, but the information was over a month out of date.



---


# ChatGPT Competitors And Alternatives

There are multiple AI-powered chatbot competitors to ChatGPT — Together, Google's Bard and Anthropic's Claude among them — and developers are creating open source alternatives, though the latter are harder, if not impossible, to run today.

Bard is the closest comparison. Much like ChatGPT, Bard is a chatbot that answers questions in natural language; Google announced at its 2023 I/O event that it would soon add multimodal content to Bard, meaning it can deliver answers in more than just text, with rich visuals — pictures for now, and later possibly maps, charts and other items. The discriminating advantage claimed for ChatGPT is time in the field: its generative AI has had a longer lifespan and thus has been "learning" for a longer period than Bard.

Two further challengers were in development. The Google-owned research lab DeepMind claimed that its next LLM would rival, or even best, ChatGPT; DeepMind is using techniques from AlphaGo — its AI system that was the first to defeat a professional human player at the board game Go — to make a ChatGPT-rivaling chatbot called Gemini. Apple is developing AI tools to challenge OpenAI, Google and others, and has created a chatbot that some engineers internally refer to as "Apple GPT," although Apple has yet to determine a strategy for releasing the AI to consumers.



---


# Robust Intelligence's Jailbreak Of Gemini Pro

As with all generative AI models, Gemini Pro is not immune to "jailbreaks" — prompts that get around the safety filters in place to attempt to prevent it from discussing controversial topics. AI security researchers at Robust Intelligence, a startup selling model-auditing tools, demonstrated this in the week of 7 December 2023.

Their method was automated: they algorithmically changed the context of prompts until Gemini Pro's guardrails failed. With that approach they managed to get Gemini Pro to suggest ways to steal from a charity and to assassinate a high-profile individual — albeit with "nanobots," admittedly not the most realistic weapon of choice.



---


# ChatGPT's Mid-2023 Usage Decline

By June, a little bit of ChatGPT's shine had started to wear off: Congress reportedly limited Capitol Hill staffers from using the application over data handling concerns, and user numbers had declined nearly 10 percent month-over-month.

Even so, ChatGPT was already well on its way to ubiquity, and a March update enabling the AI to comprehend and generate Python code in response to natural language queries only increased its utility.



---


# GPT Model Releases From GPT-3.5 To GPT-4

ChatGPT first launched to the public as OpenAI quietly released GPT-3.5: the model broke cover with ChatGPT, a fine-tuned version of GPT-3.5 that is essentially a general-purpose chatbot able to engage with a range of topics including programming, TV scripts and scientific concepts.

Writers everywhere rolled their eyes at the new technology, much as artists did with OpenAI's DALL-E model, but the chat-style iteration seemingly broadened its appeal and audience. GPT-4 followed on March 14: a powerful image- and text-understanding AI model, released to paying ChatGPT Plus users and through a public API, with developers able to sign up on a waitlist to access the API.

qid: Between the TechCrunch report on Sam Bankman-Fried's trial published on October 1, 2023, and the TechCrunch report on the allegations against Sam Bankman-Fried published on October 7, 2023, was there consistency in the portrayal of Sam Bankman-Fried's actions related to the FTX collapse?
context:
# Sam Bankman-Fried

Sam Bankman-Fried is the former CEO of the bankrupt crypto exchange FTX, whose highly anticipated criminal trial started on the Tuesday before TechCrunch's 2023-10-01 report, to determine whether he is guilty of seven counts of fraud and conspiracy. As one former federal prosecutor put it: "The odds seem to be stacked against him at this point."

He was 31 years old and co-founded FTX in 2019; within a few years the once third-largest crypto exchange's valuation hit $32 billion at its peak, and the company is now trying to claw back any funds to distribute to creditors. Before the fall he was even compared to Warren Buffet, and many called him the white horse of crypto — a description TechCrunch notes it never applied to him.

Bankman-Fried, however, maintained his innocence. At The New York Times' DealBook Summit he appeared virtually from the Bahamas and said, "I didn't ever try to commit fraud on anyone; I was shocked by what happened this month"; in a published DM exchange with a Vox reporter he said he regretted filing for bankruptcy and thought that "regulators make everything worse." In January he pleaded not guilty to all counts, which include wire fraud, conspiracy to commit money laundering and conspiracy to misuse customer funds. He could face up to 115 years in jail if convicted on all charges.

TechCrunch's 2023-10-02 summary of his standing on the eve of trial: SBF has been denied bail; his name is mud (or much worse) among those who have lost money in Alameda or FTX; and those who might not have had positions in these still blame him for other crypto woes, because he set off a ripple effect.



---


# The FTX Trial's Stakes For The Wider Crypto Industry

The Verge argued that the trial of Sam Bankman-Fried is likely to be more consequential than just whether the man himself is found guilty: depending on what evidence is introduced, it could be rough for the entire crypto industry.

The grounds are the unpredictability of what a trial surfaces, voiced by Yesha Yadav, a law professor at Vanderbilt University: "How much damage can this trial do to the already beaten-down reputation of the industry at this point? This trial is going to be an excruciating moment for the industry because no one knows what kind of evidence might come out." The warrant joining that uncertainty to industry-wide stakes is that the industry's reputation is already beaten down, so evidence introduced against one exchange's founder lands on the whole sector rather than on him alone.



---


# Going Infinite: Michael Lewis's Account Of SBF's Political Dealings

Michael Lewis's book "Going Infinite" debuted on the first day of Sam Bankman-Fried's trial, and details about Bankman-Fried's political dealings emerging from it include his alleged attempt to buy off Donald Trump to get him not to run again for president.

TechCrunch's team was focused on the Manhattan Federal Court for the trial of Bankman-Fried, the disgraced entrepreneur accused of orchestrating the collapse of the cryptocurrency exchange FTX; the Lewis book is the second channel through which the week's revelations arrived. The reporting is framed as allegation rather than established fact, and it comes from the book rather than from courtroom testimony. The item appeared in TechCrunch's Week in Review of October 7, 2023.



---


# Day Two Of The Bankman-Fried Trial: Jury Selection And The Courtroom Audience

On the second day of Sam Bankman-Fried's fraud trial, the jury was selected on Wednesday morning, after which lawyers for the government and then for Bankman-Fried delivered opening statements that told two very different stories of the former FTX CEO's sudden rise and almost instantaneous fall. The central question framed by the proceedings was who Bankman-Fried, the former CEO of crypto exchange FTX, really is: a liar and a fraud, or someone who acted in good faith and, like many a startup founder, flew too close to the sun. That answer, the account notes, ultimately lies with the jury.

The day featured pointed allegations, a friend from MIT, and an audience replete with big names, including Bankman-Fried's professorial parents and Damian Williams, the U.S. attorney for the Southern District of New York. Bankman-Fried himself spent most of the day in court staring into a laptop while seated between his two attorneys. The prosecution's account of his alleged crimes was described as featuring a study in contrasts.



---


# FTX's Bankruptcy And Leadership

The man who represented FTX before Congress after its failure told lawmakers the exchange had effectively no internal governance at all, and the prosecutor bringing the case called Bankman-Fried's alleged crimes one of the biggest financial frauds in American history. TechCrunch reported both on 2023-10-01.

Ray represented the company during a House Financial Services Committee hearing regarding FTX. Asked whether the firm had significant risk management systems, Ray said at the time that "there were virtually no internal controls and no separateness whatsoever," and added that he did not "trust a single piece of paper" in the exchange's organization. Separately, in a press conference, U.S. Attorney Damian Williams called Bankman-Fried's alleged crimes "one of the biggest financial frauds in American history."



---


# The SBF Trial Proceedings

Sam Bankman-Fried is in court for alleged fraud and money laundering while leading crypto exchange FTX and sister company Alameda. TechCrunch's 2023-10-02 preview placed the case in the Manhattan Federal Court, describing the disgraced cryptocurrency entrepreneur as accused of orchestrating "one of the biggest financial frauds in American history": the multibillion-dollar collapse of FTX, the crypto exchange he founded and led. SBF, as he is known, has pleaded not guilty to some seven charges of fraud and conspiracy.

The trial kicked off with jury selection October 3. By TechCrunch's 2023-10-06 update the case was entering its next chapter, with proceedings resuming Thursday: as confirmed during a teleconference Wednesday, SBF would be taking the stand along with a handful of other witnesses, as the onus shifted toward the defense after the prosecution brought its case to its conclusion.

Access to the proceedings is limited: no devices are allowed, so reports are being physically put together within the courtroom, or sent to overflow rooms. The jury's composition ranges from a train conductor to a retired investment banker who attended Stanford University, and TechCrunch pointed readers to a special joint episode of its Equity and Chain Reaction podcasts for a better sense of the vibe between the jurors and the rest of the court.

A second account of the same events was arriving in parallel: "Going Infinite," a book by Michael Lewis chronicling the rise and fall of SBF, was set to debut on the first day of the trial.



---


# FTX Fraud Charges And The SEC's Allegation

Sam Bankman-Fried, the founder of the failed cryptocurrency exchange FTX, faced seven counts of wire fraud and conspiracy — specifically, two counts of wire fraud and five conspiracy charges — and the Securities and Exchange Commission alleged that FTX was a fraud "from the start," with a "multi-billion-dollar deficiency caused by his own misappropriation of customer funds." The Verge repeated this framing at the head of each of its trial dispatches through October 2023, and in its October 28th, 2023 write-up reported that Bankman-Fried had been found guilty on seven counts including charges of wire fraud.

The boundary of the concept is the mix of charge types: the indictment paired substantive wire fraud counts with conspiracy counts rather than resting on a single offence, and the SEC's civil allegation about the exchange's origins ran alongside the criminal case rather than being part of it. The Verge's reporter, writing as the prosecution's case neared its end on October 26th, 2023, added an impression of the people the charges swept in: all the co-conspirators seemed oddly younger than their years, as though they had got stuck in the "math camp forever" environment Bankman-Fried created for them and simply failed to grow up.



---


# Sam Bankman-Fried's Federal Fraud Trial

Sam Bankman-Fried, the founder of bankrupt cryptocurrency exchange FTX, is charged with seven counts of fraud and money laundering following the collapse of his cryptocurrency empire the previous year, and was on trial in New York in October 2023.

Two fixed points anchor the proceeding as CNBC described it on 2023-10-06. A U.S. judge revoked Bankman-Fried's bail at a hearing in a New York courthouse on August 11, 2023. And on Thursday, Oct. 5, 2023, Matt Huang, co-founder of Paradigm Operations LP, arrived at the New York court to appear in the case.



---


# Bankman-Fried's Post-Bankruptcy Media Tour

After FTX declared bankruptcy, Bankman-Fried went on an extensive media tour, doing interviews with The New York Times' Andrew Ross Sorkin and Good Morning America — and he kept giving interviews even under house arrest, including with The New Yorker.

The Verge's reading of his motive: Bankman-Fried seemed to think that if he just explained things, everyone would understand that what he did was a mistake, not a crime.

qid: Does the article from Sporting News involving Luciano Acosta mention the same type of game interruption as the article from The Roar | Sports Writers Blog involving Marcus Lee, with both discussing a foul resulting in a free-kick?
context:
# Luciano Acosta's 2023 Golden Boot Chase And MVP Case

FC Cincinnati forward Luciano Acosta was one goal behind Denis Bouanga for the MLS goal scoring lead with two matches left in the 2023 season, sitting on 16 for the year, and was an MVP candidate. With 13 assists alongside those goals, his 29 total goal contributions were the best in the league, above Thiago Almada's 27 and Hany Mukhtar's 25, and he ranked as the second-highest rated player by WhoScored across all of Major League Soccer that season.

He started against Inter Miami on Oct. 7, 2023 despite the match being meaningless for FC Cincinnati from a tangible standpoint — understandable given his Golden Boot chase — even though Sporting News wondered before the lineups whether he would be rested with the Supporters' Shield and the No. 1 seed locked up, since an injury in a meaningless game would be devastating. Acosta had been partially rested midweek, coming off the bench to score the team's only goal against the Red Bulls in 32 minutes; Alvaro Barreal, who led the team in minutes, was also rested midweek and logged just 32 minutes on the Wednesday. In the same lineup, Ian Murphy came in for Yerson Mosquera at the back and Aaron Boupendza was rotated out with Brandon Vazquez and Sergio Santos starting together up front.

FC Cincinnati goalkeeper Roman Celentano offered his own verdict: "Luciano Acosta's the MVP... He's been an unbelievable player for us this year."



---


# Inter Miami-FC Cincinnati Second Half: Messi Comes On, Barreal Wins It

Gerardo Martino kept Lionel Messi on the bench to start the second half of the Oct. 7, 2023 Inter Miami-FC Cincinnati match, and Alvaro Barreal's 78th-minute goal decided it 1-0. There were no Inter Miami changes at the restart, which Sporting News called a huge call with playoff hopes squarely on the line and one that could speak to how fit Messi truly was; FC Cincinnati made one change, Aaron Boupendza replacing Sergio Santos up front.

The visitors created the better early chances. Luciano Acosta won a free-kick on the edge of the attacking third in the 47th minute and Barreal's floated delivery was cleared after a nervy moment, while Messi began warming up on the touchline. In the 50th minute Drake Callender made a massive double save with FC Cincinnati right on the doorstep, Boupendza most aggrieved after being stymied by Callender's outstretched right foot from directly in front of goal. Jean Mota shot just wide from distance in the 57th. Messi's influence was immediate after he came on: in the 58th minute he earned a dangerous free-kick just outside the area from a Matt Miazga shirt pull — he appeared to be struggling for footing on the field — but put the effort way over the crossbar, looking a bit rusty.

FC Cincinnati kept threatening on the counter. In the 64th minute an Acosta switch across the top of the area found Barreal in space but his hit was blocked, and Pat Noonan made his second change, Yuya Kubo on for Junior Moreno. Brandon Vazquez headed a corner off the post in the 65th — the visitors' turn to strike the woodwork — and in the 67th Callender made another bonkers save when Boupendza crossed to Vazquez clean through on goal; the offside flag went up, but the replay looked incredibly close, so Callender's stop meant VAR had no chance to intervene. Inter Miami made two more changes in the 76th, Josef Martinez curiously withdrawn for Nick Stefanelli and Robert Taylor on for DeAndre Yedlin, with the hosts needing to win to stay alive.

The goal came in the 79th minute: Callender parried Yuya Kubo's effort but drove it right into Barreal's path, and Barreal buried the follow-up low into the far corner. Roman Celentano took a yellow card for time wasting over a goal kick in the 84th, to the home crowd's delight. In the 88th FC Cincinnati brought on Dominique Badji for Acosta — ending his night early despite trailing by a goal in the Golden Boot race — and Malik Pinto for Vazquez, with Acosta and Boupendza jawing at each other as the change was made, an alarming sign with the playoffs on the horizon. In the 89th Messi drew a very contentious foul from Kubo whose tackle from behind looked clean; his floated delivery was headed out by Miazga for a corner, the short set-piece came back to Messi, whose deep delivery was nervously tapped wide by Celentano, and a Messi foul ended the chance with Santiago Arias left rolling on the ground. With five minutes of added time shown, Messi drew another, more obvious foul just outside the area in a central position at 90+3 and clipped the very top of the crossbar — officially the fourth time the woodwork was struck, though less dramatically.



---


# Romero's Unchecked Kick-Out On Colwill

Cristian Romero kicked Levi Colwill in the calf in the 22nd minute of Tottenham vs. Chelsea on Nov. 6, 2023 — behind the play, while lying on the ground — and no action was taken at all.

Sporting News' framing is that just four minutes after Destiny Udogie's escape, another Tottenham defender again got away with only a booking despite a VAR review for a possible red card; Romero, often criticised for his reckless nature, had a kick-out at Colwill that went unpunished. Social media clips circulated at the time noting that Romero intentionally kicked Colwill but VAR had not checked it.



---


# The VAR Intervention Window Before Play Restarts

VAR can only intervene in an incident before play restarts; once the game has resumed, the official cannot act on it. Sporting News invoked this window on Nov. 6, 2023 to explain why one passage of play in Tottenham vs. Chelsea was not reviewed at all.

It was unclear exactly why the incident went unreviewed, but the assumption offered was that the VAR official was likely not aware of it until play had already restarted, at which point he cannot intervene. The boundary condition Sporting News stresses is practical rather than legal: such incidents have to be caught before play restarts, which is extremely difficult to do as the game continues to flow.



---


# Kulusevski's Opener And Son's Disallowed Goal

Dejan Kulusevski opened the scoring for Spurs against Chelsea on Nov. 6, 2023, benefitting from a large deflection off Chelsea defender Levi Colwill that left Roberto Sanchez with no chance to make a save, and the match got out of hand quickly with both sides flying forward with electric attacking intent.

The flood of VAR interventions then began on a relatively innocuous decision: Heung-Min Son seemingly put Tottenham 2-0 up in the 14th minute, but on review the play appeared extremely tight. Ultimately Son did look as if he was just an inch offside, and the goal was ruled out — a call circulated at the time alongside the official VAR image.



---


# Georgia's Third-Quarter Field Goal And Lovett's Gain

The third quarter of Georgia's win over Ole Miss on Nov. 11, 2023 ended Ole Miss 14, Georgia 38, with the Bulldogs' last points of the period coming on Peyton Woodring's 27-yard field goal at 9:32 p.m., his first attempt of the night.

The kick followed a 43-yard gain by Dominic Lovett at 9:29 p.m. that the live blog suggested might just seal the deal for Georgia: his catch, together with a personal foul against Ole Miss, set the Bulldogs up inside the Rebels' red zone with the score Ole Miss 14, Georgia 35.



---


# The Attacking Handball Automatic Foul Rule

By rule, any contact by the ball with the arm or hand of an attacking player is an automatic foul, regardless of arm position, intent, or any other factor. Sporting News cited this on Nov. 6, 2023 as the reason a Chelsea goal at Tottenham was disallowed.

The rule's discriminating feature is that it removes the usual mitigating considerations — where the arm was, whether the player meant it, or anything else — for an attacking player. Once contact with the arm or hand is established, the foul follows and the goal is ruled out.



---


# The NFL's International Games And Its Concussion Initiatives

Amid the media frenzy surrounding the two lovebirds, other issues get thrown out of the window, Essentially Sports observed on 2023-10-25 — Kaepernick, who? Deflategate, what? Two of those overlooked efforts are its international expansion and its player-safety work.

The NFL had scheduled 5 games abroad that season, organized outside American borders with a view to garnering international appeal. It was also addressing the concussion controversies, having recently added both new concussion rules and a new $100 million initiative called "Play Smart, Play Safe" to make the sport safer for players — and, the article concludes, all the effort is showing.

qid: Between the report by The Verge on Apple's defense of its Google Search deal published on September 26, 2023, and the TechCrunch report on the class action antitrust suit against Google published on December 15, 2023, was there no change in the portrayal of Google's business practices from a perspective of exclusivity to anticompetitive concerns?
context:
# The U.S. Justice Department's Parallel Antitrust Suits Against Google

The Helena World Chronicle class action arrives alongside the filing of the U.S. Justice Department's lawsuit against Google for monopolizing digital ad technologies, and the complaint also references the Justice Department's 2020 civil antitrust suit over search and search advertising.

The two government cases concern different markets: search and search advertising in the 2020 suit are distinct from the digital ad technologies at issue in the more recent one.



---


# What A Ruling Against Google Would Mean For Big Tech

A ruling against Google would not stop at Google: the remedy would likely resemble the Microsoft settlement and the outcome would ripple through the other pending Big Tech cases, because enforcers are using this trial to demonstrate that antitrust law can still take on the largest and most powerful companies in the world.

The grounds for the first half of that claim are the available remedies. If the judge rules against Google, the outcome could look a lot like the Microsoft deal, in which the computer company was required to change its behavior and share its APIs with third-party developers, and was also banned from making anticompetitive and exclusive deals with computer manufacturers. Google might likewise end up having to turn over all or most of the data it has collected to other search engines so they can improve their products and attract more users — a remedy scaled to the disparity the DOJ has cited, that Google gets 16 times more data than Bing does everyday.

The grounds for the ripple effect are the cases already queued behind this one. The FTC sued Amazon in September for using anticompetitive and unfair strategies to illegally maintain its monopoly power. The DOJ has been investigating Apple for years over the company's policy for third-party apps on its devices and whether it unfairly favors its own products. Google is that Google uses its platforms and its deals with partners to block out any competition in search or advertising, thereby hindering competitors from accessing the data they would need to improve their products. The grounds offered for this is a data asymmetry: the DOJ has said Google gets 16 times more data than Bing does every day, so exclusion from distribution compounds into a permanent quality gap for rivals.

The warrant joining the claim to the remedy is that if the deals are what starve rivals of data, then unwinding the deals and redistributing the data restores competition. # The Google Antitrust Case

The Google antitrust case is the U.S. government's trial over Google's dominance in the online search market, stemming from a 2020 antitrust claim, in which the government argues that Google uses its platforms and its deals with partners to block out competition in search or advertising and thereby to hinder competitors from accessing the data they would need to improve their products.

Its defining features are the conduct at issue and the defence offered against it. Google CEO Sundar Pichai testified Monday in the trial, defending Google's business tactics, including its deal with Apple and other partners to make Google the default search engine. Google's answer is that it is just doing business: everybody wants Google as the default engine because it is the best, and that, the company says, does not make its actions illegal.

The important boundary case is which Google antitrust matter this is. The 2020 search claim is separate from the one filed in January by the Department of Justice, along with eight states including New York, California and Colorado, which aims to "halt Google's anticompetitive scheme, unwind Google's monopolistic grip on the market and restore competition to digital advertising." The search case and the digital-advertising case are distinct proceedings and should not be conflated.

The trial is the venue in which the underlying numbers surface. # Google Paid $26.3 Billion In 2021 For Default Search Placement

Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to multiple browsers, phones and platforms — from companies including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla — to be everyone's default search engine. The figure was revealed by Google's search head Prabhakar Raghavan when he testified in court on October 28, according to The Verge.

About $18 billion of that total went directly to Apple, according to a New York Times report published earlier in October 2023, and Google has had its deal with Apple in place since 2003 — so the payment is the current year of a two-decade arrangement, not a one-off. Questioned on the amount of money Google spends to get first pick of search engines, Pichai said the decision was made with the consumer in mind: Google pays big bucks to be everywhere so that it can take in all the data and be the best search engine across different companies' devices, he said, according to The Verge.

The trial also produced evidence that Google understood the value of defaults very early on. U.S. Justice Department lawyer Meagan Bellshaw showed Pichai a 2007 email from a Google product strategy meeting containing data showing that when people changed their browser homepage to Google, they did 15% more Google searches, and that when they switched away, their Google searches dropped 27%. The email summarizing that meeting, sent to Pichai as well as other Google leaders, read: "Nitin argues that focusing on homepage market share is one of the most effective things we can do to make gains in search market share," according to The Verge.

# Prosecution And Defense Arguments On Day Two Of The SBF Trial

On the second day of the trial of Sam Bankman-Fried and FTX, the prosecution argued that Bankman-Fried knowingly committed fraud, and it grounded that claim in motive: he did so, prosecutors said, to achieve great wealth, power and influence.

The defense countered with the opposite reading of the same conduct. Its claim was that the FTX founder acted in good faith, never meant to commit fraud or to steal, and basically got in over his head — an argument whose warrant is that inexperience and overreach, rather than intent, explain what happened. The two sides therefore contest intent rather than the underlying events, and the reporting on this exchange comes from Rebecca and Jacquelyn in TechCrunch's Week in Review of October 7, 2023, covering day two of the trial only.



---


# FTX's Bankruptcy And Leadership

The man who represented FTX before Congress after its failure told lawmakers the exchange had effectively no internal governance at all, and the prosecutor bringing the case called Bankman-Fried's alleged crimes one of the biggest financial frauds in American history. TechCrunch reported both on 2023-10-01.

Ray represented the company during a House Financial Services Committee hearing regarding FTX. Asked whether the firm had significant risk management systems, Ray said at the time that "there were virtually no internal controls and no separateness whatsoever," and added that he did not "trust a single piece of paper" in the exchange's organization. Separately, in a press conference, U.S. Attorney Damian Williams called Bankman-Fried's alleged crimes "one of the biggest financial frauds in American history."



---


# The SBF Trial Proceedings

Sam Bankman-Fried is in court for alleged fraud and money laundering while leading crypto exchange FTX and sister company Alameda. TechCrunch's 2023-10-02 preview placed the case in the Manhattan Federal Court, describing the disgraced cryptocurrency entrepreneur as accused of orchestrating "one of the biggest financial frauds in American history": the multibillion-dollar collapse of FTX, the crypto exchange he founded and led. SBF, as he is known, has pleaded not guilty to some seven charges of fraud and conspiracy.

The trial kicked off with jury selection October 3. By TechCrunch's 2023-10-06 update the case was entering its next chapter, with proceedings resuming Thursday: as confirmed during a teleconference Wednesday, SBF would be taking the stand along with a handful of other witnesses, as the onus shifted toward the defense after the prosecution brought its case to its conclusion.

Access to the proceedings is limited: no devices are allowed, so reports are being physically put together within the courtroom, or sent to overflow rooms. The jury's composition ranges from a train conductor to a retired investment banker who attended Stanford University, and TechCrunch pointed readers to a special joint episode of its Equity and Chain Reaction podcasts for a better sense of the vibe between the jurors and the rest of the court.

A second account of the same events was arriving in parallel: "Going Infinite," a book by Michael Lewis chronicling the rise and fall of SBF, was set to debut on the first day of the trial.



---


# Trump Motions to Dismiss the Fraud Case Rejected

Trump's lawyers asked the judge to throw out the case, and he denied the request. Their arguments attacked the attorney general's standing and the timing of the claims: they contend that James was not legally allowed to file the lawsuit because there is no evidence that the public was harmed by Trump's actions, and they also argued that many of the allegations in the lawsuit were barred by the statute of limitations.

Engoron, noting that he had "emphatically rejected" those arguments earlier in the case, equated them to the "time-loop in the film 'Groundhog Day.'"



---


# FTX Fraud Charges And The SEC's Allegation

Sam Bankman-Fried, the founder of the failed cryptocurrency exchange FTX, faced seven counts of wire fraud and conspiracy — specifically, two counts of wire fraud and five conspiracy charges — and the Securities and Exchange Commission alleged that FTX was a fraud "from the start," with a "multi-billion-dollar deficiency caused by his own misappropriation of customer funds." The Verge repeated this framing at the head of each of its trial dispatches through October 2023, and in its October 28th, 2023 write-up reported that Bankman-Fried had been found guilty on seven counts including charges of wire fraud.

The boundary of the concept is the mix of charge types: the indictment paired substantive wire fraud counts with conspiracy counts rather than resting on a single offence, and the SEC's civil allegation about the exchange's origins ran alongside the criminal case rather than being part of it. The Verge's reporter, writing as the prosecution's case neared its end on October 26th, 2023, added an impression of the people the charges swept in: all the co-conspirators seemed oddly younger than their years, as though they had got stuck in the "math camp forever" environment Bankman-Fried created for them and simply failed to grow up.



---


# Caroline Ellison's Guilty Plea And First Day Of Testimony

Caroline Ellison, head of the hedge fund Alameda Research during its implosion along with FTX, took the stand on October 10th, 2023 having already pleaded guilty to criminal charges — fraud, conspiracy to commit fraud, and money laundering — and told the jury that Bankman-Fried "directed me to commit these crimes." She quantified the taking: "We ultimately took about $14 billion, some of which we were not able to pay back."

Her long-anticipated first day took the form of walking through a damning spreadsheet she had prepared for her ex and boss, now the defendant in a criminal fraud trial. She entered hunched in on herself, wearing a dusty rose dress with a gray blazer over it, looking less like an executive than like a girl who had borrowed her boyfriend's coat because she was cold. Asked by the prosecution to identify Bankman-Fried, she had trouble finding him and gazed around the courtroom for more than 20 seconds — apparently he was incognito with his new haircut — and when she did spot him she identified him as the one wearing a suit, which got chuckles from the rest of the defense table, also all in suits. She tilted her head down to answer questions and lifted it when she had finished each answer.

The defendant's own reaction registered the shift: Bankman-Fried had been vibrating slightly during Wang's testimony, and during Ellison's his bouncing became more noticeable. By the end of the day, The Verge's reporter wrote, the spreadsheet seemed like a sideshow.



---


# Engoron Summary Judgment That Trump Committed Fraud

A judge ruled on Tuesday 26 September 2023 that Donald Trump committed fraud for years while building the real estate empire that catapulted him to fame and the White House. Judge Arthur Engoron, ruling in a civil lawsuit brought by New York's attorney general, found that the former president and his company deceived banks, insurers and others by massively overvaluing his assets and exaggerating his net worth on paperwork used in making deals and securing financing.

As punishment, Engoron ordered that some of Trump's business licences be rescinded, and said he would continue to have an independent monitor oversee the Trump Organization's operations. A Trump spokesperson did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the ruling, and Trump has long insisted he did nothing wrong.

Fortune described the decision, which came days before the start of a non-jury trial in Attorney General Letitia James' lawsuit, as the strongest repudiation yet of Trump's carefully coiffed image as a wealthy and shrewd real estate mogul turned political powerhouse.



---


# Day Two Of The Bankman-Fried Trial: Jury Selection And The Courtroom Audience

On the second day of Sam Bankman-Fried's fraud trial, the jury was selected on Wednesday morning, after which lawyers for the government and then for Bankman-Fried delivered opening statements that told two very different stories of the former FTX CEO's sudden rise and almost instantaneous fall. The central question framed by the proceedings was who Bankman-Fried, the former CEO of crypto exchange FTX, really is: a liar and a fraud, or someone who acted in good faith and, like many a startup founder, flew too close to the sun. That answer, the account notes, ultimately lies with the jury.

The day featured pointed allegations, a friend from MIT, and an audience replete with big names, including Bankman-Fried's professorial parents and Damian Williams, the U.S. attorney for the Southern District of New York. Bankman-Fried himself spent most of the day in court staring into a laptop while seated between his two attorneys. The prosecution's account of his alleged crimes was described as featuring a study in contrasts.



---


# USVI Attorney General Authority Versus The Governor's Purse Strings

The structural tension in the US Virgin Islands arrangement is that legal authority and financial authority sit in different hands. Officially, Denise George, not the governor, was in charge of making the legal calls.

But Governor Bryan was still her boss and held the purse strings. It was a delicate balance, George said.

# Housing Affordability Is Worse Now Than At The 2006 Peak

Roger Ashworth, a managing director at Goldman Sachs, argued in a credit strategy research paper released in mid-October 2023 that although some economic factors are stronger today than during the Global Financial Crisis, housing affordability is undeniably worse: "While housing and more generally consumer fundamentals are in a much stronger position today, affordability for the incremental buyer is worse than it was at the peak in 2006 before the crash." The claim is deliberately narrow — it is about the incremental buyer's affordability, not about overall fundamentals, which he grants are stronger.

The proximate causes cited are the same constraints that have held all year. "As has been the case throughout this year, limited inventory and low housing affordability continue to hamper home sales," NAR chief economist Lawrence Yun said in a statement, adding a policy conclusion: "The Federal Reserve simply cannot keep raising interest rates in light of softening inflation and weakening job gains." The Fed had raised rates several times in 2023, with Chair Jerome Powell arming his "higher for longer" stance.



---


# US Home Prices Peaked In June 2022 And Returned To A Record High By July 2023

National U.S. home prices did not peak until June 2022 — even as mortgage rates soared and purchase applications plummeted amid the Federal Reserve's first interest rate hikes — and although prices fell more than 5% from that peak by January 2023, they returned to a record high in July 2023. This is the observation that has so far vindicated the majority of real estate veterans, who despite a widely bearish industry outlook avoided arguing that home prices would drop the way they did during the 2008 crash that kicked off the Global Financial Crisis.

The backdrop, as of the reporting date of 2023-10-06, is that housing market pessimists had been sounding the alarm for years about a pending crash in U.S. residential real estate. Even before the Fed began hiking interest rates to fight inflation in 2022 — pushing mortgage rates to a 23-year high in October 2023 — years of surging home prices had left some experts warning that the housing market was a massive bubble ready to pop.



---


# Bank Of America's Warning Of More Housing "Turbulence"

A Bank of America team led by U.S. economist Jeseo Park warned in the week of 2023-10-06 that there is more "turbulence" coming for the housing market because of high mortgage rates: "With rates likely staying higher for longer, we are cautious of potential turbulence ahead," the group wrote. The grounds are the persistence of high rates rather than a repeat of a past crash — the team said they were getting an eerie feeling of "déjà vu," but it was not 2008 that came to mind, it was the 1980s.

The forecast attached to this warning is qualified. Bank of America had previously forecast 0% home price growth and falling home sales for the full year 2023, but it did not offer a new prediction in its latest note. The warrant joining the rate outlook to the housing outlook runs the other way as well: eventually, as inflation fades and leads the Fed to cut interest rates, housing affordability will improve. "At that stage, we should see a more stable and healthy housing market," Park and her team wrote. "Until then, hang tight, it may be a bumpy ride."



---


# The US Housing Inventory Shortage Of 2023

Declining housing inventory levels contributed to the drop in housing transactions in 2023: inventory was down 8.1% from a year earlier, according to the National Association of Realtors. More recent inventory data makes the issue starker still — between September 2018 and September 2023 the average number of homes on the market dropped a whopping 60%, to fewer than 700,000 active listings, according to Realtor.com.

Set against this shortage, some real-estate experts and economists argue that housing affordability is even worse now than during 2008, when a damaging downturn in the U.S. housing market set off the dominoes that became the Great Financial Crisis — a crisis that defined a whole decade economically and, in some ways, shaped the current predicament.



---


# The Affordable Housing Supply Gap For Low-Income Renters

The United States has long had an affordable housing crisis, but it has been exacerbated as of late by a surge in mortgage interest rates and low inventory, and the problem is especially acute for lower-income families.

The argument, as put to TechCrunch in December 2023, is that the market is not producing housing for them from either direction. Most iBuyers are focused on buying, renovating and either selling or renting homes in middle to upper class neighborhoods. And most home builders are "out of touch and building homes that no one who needs affordable housing could ever afford," Simply Homes CEO Brian Bagdasarian told TechCrunch in an interview.



---


# Why 2023 Is Not A Repeat Of The 2008 Housing Crash

Against the premise that today's housing market is heading for a 2008-style crash, Bank of America's Jeseo Park and her team concluded flatly: "We reiterate that we do not expect another housing crash like 2008." The attacked premise is the assumed similarity of conditions — the 2008 crash was fueled by the collapse of subprime mortgages, and the real estate market of that era was very different from what Bank of America's experts see today.

The specific rebuttals are four. There are no "noticeable signs" of excess housing development today like there were back then. Households are not nearly as burdened by mortgage debt: household mortgage debt represented roughly 65% of U.S. consumers' disposable income in the second quarter, compared to 100% before the Global Financial Crisis. The ratio of Americans' mortgage debt to their real estate assets — loan-to-value — was just 27% in the second quarter, compared to over 40% in 2008 and roughly 50% in 2010, on Bank of America's data. And new legislation enacted since the GFC has helped prevent worst-case scenarios, most obviously by leaving far fewer risky adjustable-rate mortgages, which can lead to higher default rates when interest rates rise: they now represent less than 5% of total purchase and refinance loans, compared with over 35% at the peak of the pre-GFC housing cycle.



---


# The 1980s, Not 2008, Is The Better Analogy For Today's Housing Market

Bank of America economists argued in a Thursday note that "Looking back at previous housing recessions, we think the 1980s are a better analogy for today's market than the 2008 housing crash." The grounds they gave are structural: back in the early 1980s, just like today, home prices had boomed for years before Fed officials were ultimately forced to hike interest rates aggressively in an attempt to fight inflation.

First American chief economist Mark Fleming made the same case in a Tuesday report titled "1980s Déjà Vu for the Housing Market," arguing from the absence of the specific 2000s failure modes: "Today's housing market isn't anything like the housing market of the mid-2000s. The housing market today is not overbuilt, nor is it driven by loose lending standards, subprime mortgages, or homeowners who are highly leveraged." The claim is offered with a scope qualification — the housing market today isn't identical to that of the '80s, but it's pretty close — and with a demographic warrant: in a lot of ways, millennials are being forced to follow the housing journey of their boomer parents as they face a frozen, unaffordable market with rising interest rates, as noted by both BofA Research economist Jeseo Park and Fleming.



---


# US Existing-Home Sales Fell To A 13-Year Low In September 2023

Existing-home sales dropped a stunning 15% in September 2023 on a year-over-year basis, to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 3.96 million transactions, according to the National Association of Realtors — the lowest figure in 13 years, since 2010, when the world economy and particularly the U.S. housing market were struggling to pull out of the Great Financial Crisis. After a long, hot summer that saw mortgage rates creep ever higher, October brought an early winter for the housing market.

The contributing factors named for the continuous decline in home transactions are surging mortgage rates, which hit 8% in the week of 2023-10-20, a record in the 21st century; low inventory levels; and home prices that refuse to stop rising. In other words, there aren't enough homes to buy, money isn't cheap anymore, and the ones for sale are too rich for most homebuyers' blood. Existing-home sales prices topped $306,000, a 5% increase since the year began, according to the Case-Shiller U.S. National Home Price Index. With transactions at their lowest level in 13 years coupled with century-high mortgage rates of 8%, many real estate experts and economists aren't hopeful that affordability constraints will let up soon.
