The four-port charger has enough power to juice up two MacBook Pro models simultaneously and suits a desk full of devices, with a little stand to prop it up, a short cord to the outlet, and four USB-C ports outputting 100 watts each; this is the lowest price WIRED has tracked. Apple's dual USB-C port power adapter is called an essential accessory for people who forget to pack chargers: its two USB-C ports recharge a MacBook and iPhone simultaneously, and at 35 watts it is powerful enough to recharge an iPhone 15 Pro Max or iPad Pro. The folding charger packs two USB-C ports, one of which outputs 65 watts when used alone, dropping to 45 watts on the top port and 20 watts on the bottom when two devices are plugged in.

Satechi's four-port hub is, in WIRED's view, a little too large for the number of ports it offers, but for a reason: popping off the aluminium cover reveals a slot for an M.2 SATA solid-state drive, giving access to an external SSD alongside two USB-A jacks, one 100-watt USB-C pass-through charging port and a 4K HDMI at the same time. WIRED is explicit that it did not have an M.2 SATA drive to test, that a specific 1-terabyte card should work, and that the hub does not support NVME M.2 cards. The last pick is a tiny 30-watt Anker adapter for iPads: WIRED notes Apple has not nixed the charging adapter from its iPads yet but probably will before long, and this compact, fold-away plug can fast-charge the iPad Pro, making it a good spare or travel option.



---


# Prime Day 2023 iPhone Wireless Charger Deals

WIRED's charging picks include its favorite Apple 3-in-1 wireless charger, an orb-shaped charger with extra ports, Apple's dual USB-C port power adapter, the MagSafe Duo, iOttie's Velox Pro car mount, and Nomad's MagSafe wireless charger.

The 3-in-1 charger has a compact T-shaped design that won't take much space on a nightstand or desk, with a charging tree suspending two devices midair: it charges an iPhone at the fastest 15-watt speed Apple allows, fast-charges the Apple Watch Series 7/8/9/Ultra, and uses the base for AirPods Pro or AirPods with a wireless charging case, all from a single outlet; normally around $150, it was discounted to $100 in August, so Prime Day may not be the last chance to get it cheaper. The orb charger starts charging as soon as you stick an iPhone to it, and its back holds two USB-C ports, two USB-A ports, and three AC outlets — both cute and tidy, with a price that fluctuates often. Apple's dual USB-C port power adapter is essential if you tend to forget chargers on the go, recharging an iPhone and MacBook simultaneously and, at 35 watts, powerful enough for an iPad Pro or iPhone 15 Pro Max. The MagSafe Duo is an excellent travel companion for iPhone and Apple Watch owners, combining both chargers in a compact, foldable form factor that also charges AirPods with a wireless charging case and other Qi-certified devices. iOttie's Velox Pro Magnetic Wireless Cooling Charger suits dash or windshield mounting with an iPhone 12 or later: its suction cup attaches to a dashboard pad or windshield and proved secure in testing, and a telescopic arm with a ball joint delivers a wide range of movement, though charging maxes out at 7.5 watts — the USB-C cable can be removed once the phone is full — and a built-in fan helps keep temperature down when it's hot. Nomad's charger is one of WIRED's favorite MagSafe wireless chargers, delivering the maximum 15-watt speed but not meant to be held up while using the phone; it has no power adapter but includes a USB-C-to-USB-C cable, sits securely on a desk, and can charge an Apple Watch too.



---


# Prime Day 2023 Phone Charging And Gaming Accessory Deals

Three accessories feature in this section of WIRED's roundup: Ugreen's 145-watt power bank, the Backbone One mobile game controller, and a 20,000-mAh metal power bank for laptops and smaller gadgets.

Ugreen's charger is a 145-watt unit with a 25,000-mAh battery, surprisingly compact for the power it provides though definitely not ultralight at 1.1 pounds, with two USB-C ports and one USB-A port; what sets it apart is that you can actually draw the full 145 watts while charging — one USB-C port at 100W and the other at 45W — a feat very few other batteries WIRED has tested can manage. WIRED is a big fan of the Backbone One (8/10, WIRED recommends), which appears in its Best Mobile Game Controllers guide: it slides open to cradle your phone and is very responsive, with buttons and bumpers that feel nice and clicky, and the USB-C version on sale works with most Android phones and the new iPhone 15 range. The heavy metal brick packs 20,000 mAh and supports a wide variety of fast charging standards, with one USB-C PD port rated at 65 watts, two USB-A QC ports at 30 watts apiece, and a micro-USB input — though USB-C is best for recharging it — and WIRED hasn't seen it go on sale very often.



---


# Anker 321 Travel Power Strip

The Anker 321 Power Strip was $15, down from $26 — 42 percent off at Amazon. It is an all-in-one 20W USB-C power cube with three AC outlets, two USB-A ports, and one USB-C port, and it is deputy features editor Sarah Jeong's pick.

Her case for it starts from a specific failure. Nobody wants to carry a power strip or extension cord on vacation, and it is probably unnecessary in relatively modern buildings and definitely unnecessary while camping — but sometimes you stay in a charming historical hotel or a lovely cabin in the woods and discover at bedtime that the only electrical socket in the bedroom is in the corner farthest from the bed, with two lamps already plugged into it. Older buildings especially suffer from what she calls loose socket syndrome, where those convenient modern boxy socket extenders with five different USB and USB-C charging ports cannot stay in place and fall right out of the wall because they are too heavy. After one otherwise pleasant vacation spent charging her phone, watch, AirPods, and laptop in a weird corner of the room with the charging hub propped on a strategically balanced mountain of books and sham pillows, she bought this Anker combination extension cord and power strip.

It is not a full power strip — just a cube with a few sockets plus USB and USB-C charging ports at the end of a five-foot cable. It takes up extra space in her suitcase, but each trip has left her feeling vindicated about the purchase.

The design detail that matters is that the three prongs at the end of the cable are static rather than folding flat for easy packing, which is key because the loose sockets of older buildings reject the beautiful convenience of folding prongs. There are more than enough sockets for one person, and with some finagling — and maybe an extra charging brick — it can accommodate two people's devices. If you are traveling overseas, do not forget to buy a different plug type for the region or pack an adapter.



---


# Anker Nano Magnetic Power Bank Deal Listings

Both of WIRED's October 10, 2023 Prime Day roundups list the Anker Nano, a power bank that clicks right into the bottom of a phone via a built-in connector, with the 22.5-watt USB-C version for the iPhone 15 or Android phones at $22 ($10 off).

WIRED's general roundup calls it one of its favorite portable power banks, particularly for phones, available in fun colors, with the listed model carrying a 12-watt Lightning connector; both connectors fold away when not in use, and you'll likely be able to charge most phones fully once before recharging the bank itself via the included USB-C cable. The Apple roundup adds that it's great if you don't want to worry about carrying a cable, thanks to the built-in rotating USB-C or Lightning connector, which is MFi certified, and that it offers 5,000 mAh of energy with a USB-C port for recharging and a short cable included. Both versions carry the same caveat: it may not work if you use a particularly thick case.

# Four Sportsbooks For NBA MVP Futures Betting

The Sporting News names four favourite sportsbooks for placing MVP futures bets — DraftKings, FanDuel, BetMGM and Caesars — distinguished mainly by usability and the breadth of their markets.

The DraftKings app is one of the most prominent in the US, offering bets for just about any market including the NBA MVP award and known for its ease of use, with top features including live betting options and a diverse prop betting selection. FanDuel is touted as one of the industry's most user-friendly and best sports betting apps and has built a massive following; beyond a packed futures menu that includes NBA MVP, it has a noteworthy selection of player props and a same-game parlay feature.

BetMGM trades ease of use for depth: the app may take a little getting used to, but the sheer number of betting opportunities is fantastic, and popular features such as "edit my bet" and "easy parlay" have helped make it a leading sportsbook in many states where sports betting is legal. Caesars sits at the opposite end — the betting app may be basic, but the simplicity is part of the draw for customers, along with an outstanding selection of competitive odds, and Caesars also provides NBA betting promos and more sports betting bonuses and promotions for existing customers.

# Opening And Funding An Online Sportsbook Account

The first step to betting on NBA props or MVP futures is opening an account at an online sportsbook — a process the Sporting News describes as simple, free and quick, running in six ordered steps: choose your sportsbook, register, accept the terms and conditions, claim your bonus, make a deposit, and start betting.

Choose your sportsbook first. Any state with legal online sports betting has a variety of sportsbooks, and not all are created equal — some are easier to use than others and some offer more incentives — so research and read reviews to find which fit your needs, remembering you can have an account with more than one. Following a link from the review site takes you to the sportsbook homepage and qualifies you for the best new customer welcome bonus. Then register for an account: at the top of the homepage you will find a button that says "register" or "sign up", which opens a form asking for personal information such as your name, phone number, email address, and the last four digits of your Social Security number. Before finalizing your account information you must accept the sportsbook's terms and conditions, which the Sporting News recommends reading through to understand the rules your sportsbook will enforce regarding bets — especially for the sports you intend to wager on — and which remain available on the site to read at any point.

With the account set up and the terms accepted you can claim your welcome bonus as a new customer; if a bonus code is needed you input it during the registration process, and you should read through the bonus requirements before accepting anything so you are aware of any restrictions or other rules. Next, make a deposit to start funding your bankroll: most legal sportsbooks offer a variety of ways to add funds, such as through your bank or an e-wallet, and many deposit options will work for withdrawals as well. Finally, start betting — go to the basketball section of your sportsbook and select the NBA, where you can choose individual games and make bets like money lines, point spreads, totals, props, futures and more; NBA MVP futures sit under the basketball tab, and you click the bet you want to add it to your bet slip, adjust how much you're wagering, and finalize the bet.

# BetRivers Sportsbook: Alternate Lines, An Integrated Casino, And iRush Rewards

BetRivers is distinguished by its iRush Rewards loyalty program and by an app that integrates sports betting with online casino games under a single account. For Major League Baseball it presents bettors with a wealth of stats and insightful tips on upcoming games to aid decision-making, and alongside standard betting options offers a vast selection of alternate lines and prop bets tailored to baseball. Loyal MLB bettors accumulate iRush Rewards points as they place bets, redeemable for exclusive VIP gifts, MLB event tickets, BetRivers branded merchandise and a range of special offers; on the NBA side the same program lets users earn points as they bet on sports, with the added flexibility of spending accumulated points on BetRivers' online casino.

Dedicated promotions are a hallmark of the book, and its engagement with NBA fans is evident. A past promotion dubbed "NBA Wednesdays" allowed users to wager up to $25 on any NBA game scheduled on a Wednesday, with a 20% profit boost if the bet was successful.

New accounts typically can claim a second-chance bet that could reach up to $500, although the amount might differ based on the state.



---


# The Four Recommended Sportsbook Apps: DraftKings, FanDuel, BetMGM, Caesars

Sporting News recommends the same four sportsbook apps — DraftKings, FanDuel, BetMGM and Caesars — for both NBA Rookie of the Year futures and golf betting, describing what each offers.

For NBA Rookie of the Year betting: DraftKings, known as a daily fantasy sports operator before becoming a renowned sportsbook, offers a nice variety of futures bets including the ROTY award, with an intuitive online sportsbook and app and a competitive welcome bonus for new players. FanDuel, also known from the DFS market, has one of the largest followings in the country, offers competitive ROTY odds and one of the best betting apps, with a quality welcome bonus and attractive promotions for existing customers. BetMGM, one of the most recognizable names in the gambling industry, attracts and keeps customers with competitive odds for all bet types including futures and ROTY, many deposit and withdrawal options, 24/7 customer service and generous bonuses and promotions. Caesars offers favorable odds for almost every bet type including ROTY, a nice variety of deposit and withdrawal options, a competitive welcome bonus and NBA betting promos for existing players.

For golf betting: DraftKings offers markets and props for PGA Tour events and major championships including tournament winners, top 5, 10 and 20 finishes and matchup betting, and allows live betting on individual holes and shots during a tournament. FanDuel offers a wide range of markets and props including top-20 finishes, head-to-head matchups and first-round leaders, and covers international events such as the DP World Tour and the Ryder Cup. BetMGM provides event winners, top finishers and hole-in-one props, and like DraftKings and FanDuel offers live betting for golf. Caesars offers a user-friendly platform with a wide range of bets for the PGA Tour and other major events, such as winning margin, top finishes and live betting props, and is known for its strong selection of bets and live betting interface.



---


# Line Movement As A Signal Of Betting Value

Sporting News argues that bettors should monitor line movement before a game starts, because line moves reveal where the value in a bet lies. The claim is stated for both markets it covers: point spread odds can and do change based on a combination of actual betting patterns, unexpected events, and shifts in public perception, and savvy bettors keep a close eye on these line moves, as they can offer insights into where the value lies in a particular bet.

The grounds are how the lines are made and remade. Sportsbooks set game totals considering factors like recent performances, weather, and player status, and as new data emerges and betting trends develop, this line can shift — if many bettors choose the "over," the sportsbook might raise the total to balance the bets. The warrant joining grounds to claim is that line movements often reflect public betting sentiments and therefore offer insights to informed bettors: because a move encodes information the book has absorbed about data and about where the public money is, watching it tells the bettor something they did not otherwise have. Hence bettors must monitor any line changes before the game starts and strategize accordingly to optimize their betting success.

The argument stops short of endorsing either side of a totals bet in the abstract: neither wager holds a universal advantage, and success in over/under betting hinges on a thorough evaluation of both the set line and the competing teams.



---


# DraftKings Sportsbook: MLB And NBA Markets And Promotions

DraftKings is a premier sportsbook platform with an extensive array of Major League Baseball betting options for novice and seasoned bettors, and one of the most recognizable names in online sports betting for NBA wagering. Its MLB odds include intriguing player and game prop bets, such as predicting the First Inning Winner or First Team to Score, which allow bettors to engage with games beyond simple outcomes; for the bigger picture it provides futures bets, letting fans bet on potential division victors or predict the next World Series champion.

On the NBA side, DraftKings is noted for frequent promos to enhance NBA odds, a diverse range of prop bets tailored to the most prominent NBA players, and a seamless live NBA betting experience through its app.

Its new-customer offer requires no special code, with a total promotional value of up to $1,200. In the past DraftKings has run special promotions tailored to NBA enthusiasts — one allowed customers to earn $200 in bonus bets simply by placing a $5 bet on any NBA Finals game — which Sporting News reads as a commitment to delivering value to its betting community.

qid: Who is the Silicon Valley prodigy associated with the rise of generative AI technology, who faced no removal efforts by the co-founders of Anthropic, but was involved in a controversial departure from OpenAI, as discussed in articles by 'The Age', 'Fortune', and 'TechCrunch'?
context:
# Sam Altman's Rise As The Face Of Generative AI

In the year since Altman catapulted ChatGPT to global fame, he became Silicon Valley's sought-after voice on the promise and potential dangers of artificial intelligence, and his sudden and mostly unexplained exit brought uncertainty to the industry's future. He helped start OpenAI as a nonprofit research laboratory in 2015, but it was ChatGPT's explosion into public consciousness that thrust him into the spotlight as a face of generative AI — technology that can produce novel imagery, passages of text and other media. On a world tour in 2023 he was mobbed by a crowd of adoring fans at an event in London.

He has sat with multiple heads of state to discuss AI's potential and perils. On Thursday, 2023-11-16, he took part in a CEO summit at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation conference in San Francisco, where OpenAI is based. At OpenAI's first developer conference the week before, Altman was the main speaker, showcasing a vision for a future of AI agents that could help people with a variety of tasks; days later he announced the company would have to pause new subscriptions to its premium version of ChatGPT because it had exceeded capacity.



---


# Sam Altman's Career Before OpenAI

Sam Altman, 38 as of November 2023, is not trained as an AI engineer, yet has been seen as a Silicon Valley wunderkind since his early 20s. The defining credential of that earlier phase is that he was recruited in 2014 to take the lead of the startup incubator YCombinator.

The reputation attached to him at the time is captured in YCombinator co-founder Paul Graham's 2014 announcement that Altman would become its president: "Sam is one of the smartest people I know, and understands startups better than perhaps anyone I know, including myself." Graham said then that Altman was "one of those rare people who manage to be both fearsomely effective and yet fundamentally benevolent."



---


# Musk's Founding Of OpenAI And His Departure

Convinced that Larry Page's optimistic view of AI was dead wrong, and angry at his loss of DeepMind, Musk built his own lab: OpenAI was founded in late 2015, just a few months after he met with Sam Altman at the Rosewood hotel in Silicon Valley. Musk pumped money into the lab and his former PayPal buddies, Reid Hoffman and Peter Thiel, came along for the ride; the three men and others pledged to put $US1 billion into the project, which Altman, then 30, would help run, and to get started they poached Ilya Sutskever from Google, one of the graduate students Google had "bought" in Hinton's auction. Initially Musk wanted to operate OpenAI as a nonprofit, free from the economic incentives driving Google and other corporations, but by the time Google wowed the tech community with its Go stunt he was changing his mind about how it should be run: he desperately wanted OpenAI to invent something that would capture the world's imagination and close the gap with Google, and it wasn't getting the job done as a nonprofit.

In late 2017 Musk hatched a plan to wrest control of the lab from Altman and the other founders and transform it into a commercial operation that would join forces with Tesla and rely on supercomputers the car company was developing, according to four people familiar with the matter; when Altman and others pushed back, Musk quit and said he would focus on his own AI work at Tesla. In February 2018 he announced his departure to OpenAI's staff on the top floor of the startup's offices in a converted truck factory, three people who attended said; when he said OpenAI needed to move faster, one researcher retorted that Musk was being reckless, and Musk called the researcher a "jackass" and stormed out, taking his deep pockets with him. OpenAI suddenly needed new financing in a hurry: Altman flew to Sun Valley for a conference and ran into Satya Nadella, Microsoft's CEO, and a tie-up seemed natural, since Altman knew Microsoft's chief technology officer Kevin Scott and Microsoft had bought LinkedIn from Hoffman, an OpenAI board member; Nadella told Scott to get it done. The deal closed in 2019, leaving Altman and OpenAI with a for-profit company formed under the original nonprofit, $US1 billion in fresh capital, and Microsoft with a new way to build AI into its vast cloud computing service. Not everyone inside OpenAI was happy.



---


# Anthropic's Founding By Former OpenAI Researchers

Dario Amodei, a researcher with ties to the effective altruist community, had been on hand at the Rosewood hotel when OpenAI was born, and was leading the lab's efforts to build a neural network called a large language model that could learn from enormous amounts of digital text: by analysing countless Wikipedia articles, digital books and message boards it could generate text on its own, and it also had the unfortunate habit of making things up. It was called GPT-3 and was released in the summer of 2020, and researchers inside OpenAI, Google and other companies thought this rapidly improving technology could be a path to artificial general intelligence. Amodei was unhappy about the Microsoft deal because he thought it was taking OpenAI in a really commercial direction, and he and other researchers went to the board to try to push Altman out, according to five people familiar with the matter; after they failed, they left, worrying, like DeepMind's founders before them, that their new corporate overlords would favour commercial interests over safety.

In 2021 the group of about 15 engineers and scientists created a new lab called Anthropic, with the plan of building AI the way the effective altruists thought it should be done, with very tight controls. Anthropic disputes the account of the board approach: "There was no attempt to remove Sam Altman from OpenAI by the co-founders of Anthropic," said an Anthropic spokesperson, Sally Aldous. "The co-founders themselves came to the conclusion that they wished to depart OpenAI to start their own company, made this known to OpenAI's leadership, and over several weeks negotiated an exit on mutually agreeable terms." Anthropic accepted a $US4 billion investment from Amazon and another $US2 billion from Google two years later. After OpenAI received another $US2 billion from Microsoft, Altman and another senior executive, Greg Brockman, visited Bill Gates at his sprawling mansion on the shores of Lake Washington, outside Seattle; the Microsoft founder was no longer involved in the company day to day but kept in regular touch with its executives.



---


# The AI Risk Paradox Among Tech Billionaires

At the heart of the competition to build artificial intelligence is a brain-stretching paradox: the people who say they are most worried about AI are among the most determined to create it and enjoy its riches, and they have justified their ambition with their strong belief that they alone can keep AI from endangering Earth. The grounds are the shape of the debate itself. Eight years after an argument between Elon Musk and Larry Page, that argument seems prescient, because the question of whether AI will elevate the world or destroy it, or at least inflict grave damage, has framed an ongoing debate among Silicon Valley founders, chatbot users, academics, legislators and regulators about whether the technology should be controlled or set free.

That debate has pitted some of the world's richest men against one another: Musk, Page, Mark Zuckerberg of Meta, tech investor Peter Thiel, Satya Nadella of Microsoft and Sam Altman of OpenAI, all of whom have fought for a piece of a business that one day could be worth trillions of dollars, and for the power to shape it. The narrative anchor is that Musk and Page stopped speaking soon after the party that summer, and that a few weeks later Musk dined with Altman, who was then running a tech incubator, and several researchers in a private room at the Rosewood hotel in Menlo Park, California, a favoured deal-making spot close to the venture capital offices of Sand Hill Road.



---


# DeepMind's Sale To Google And Facebook's AI Lab

Google offered $US650 million for DeepMind. Mark Zuckerberg of Facebook offered a bigger payout to DeepMind's founders but would not agree to the conditions the founders had set, and DeepMind sold to Google.

Zuckerberg was determined to build an AI lab of his own and hired Yann LeCun, a French computer scientist who had also done pioneering AI research, to run it. A year after Hinton's auction, Zuckerberg and LeCun flew to Lake Tahoe for the same AI conference, and while padding around a suite at the Harrah's casino in his socks Zuckerberg personally interviewed top researchers, who were soon offered millions of dollars in salary and stock. AI was once laughed off; now the richest men in Silicon Valley were shelling out billions to keep from being left behind.



---


# OpenAI's AI Chip Ambitions

The company has suggested that it might be entering the AI chip market at some point in the future, in an effort to shore up the speed and performance of its API services.

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman had previously pointed to industry-wide GPU shortages for the service's spotty performance, and producing its own processors might mitigate those supply issues while potentially lowering the current four-cent-per-query cost of operating the chatbot to something more manageable.

qid: What institution, prominently featured in articles from 'The Sydney Morning Herald', is considered to have substantial influence over global financial markets and determines its interest rate policies based on US economic data?
context:
# Bank of Israel Interest Rate Policy During the War

Asked what the Bank of Israel should do at its interest rate decision on 23 October 2023, Leo Leiderman argued for holding: "As for cutting the interest rate, it's too early to consider that. The current interest rate is at the right level for the state of the economy, and together with the policy on exchange rates, it contributes to ensuring financial stability."

His first ground is that the inflation effect of the war is indeterminate. It was still too early to tell how the war would affect the rate of inflation in the short and medium term: just as there are new inflationary factors, such as the depreciation of the shekel, there will also be factors working in the opposite direction, given the expected decline in private consumption, tourism and other items.

His second ground extends his fiscal reasoning to monetary policy: as with fiscal policy, a country at war is allowed to deviate temporarily from the set inflation target. He judged that at the moment there was no surge in inflation expectations, and that the investment community is aware of the existence of index-linked assets and the exchange rate that can assist in hedging inflation risk. The warrant tying this to a hold rather than a cut is that financial stability, not inflation, is the binding objective while the shock is unresolved.



---


# Australian Market Resilience And The Range-Bound Reading

Novus Capital senior client adviser Gary Glover argued that the Australian sharemarket was surprisingly resilient following a negative lead from Wall Street and the latest inflation data, with markets starting to wake up to the fact that interest rates could stay higher for longer. His ground was the mismatch between the overseas move and the local one: "Considering the damage overnight in the US, Australian markets held on pretty well. I thought it would be a bigger down day across the board."

Glover characterised the market as volatile but quite range-bound, drawing an analogy to previous periods of high inflation in the 1940s and 1970s. The Wall Street lead he referred to was severe: Wall Street's ugly September got even worse on Tuesday as a sharp drop for stocks brought them back to where they were in June, with the S&P 500 tumbling 1.5 per cent for its fifth loss in the last six days, the Dow Jones dropping 1.1 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite losing 1.6 per cent.



---


# What Drove The ASX Rally On 10 October 2023

TMS Capital portfolio manager Ben Clark attributed the Australian sharemarket's strength to three things acting together: a calming bond market, a positive lead from Wall Street, and positive news out of China.

He set out how each fed through. "The bond market is retracing," he said. "There's also been strength in resource stocks amid rumours that the Chinese government might launch a substantial stimulus package." On the rates channel, Clark said interest-rate sensitive sectors climbed on increased probabilities of an easing in interest rates, because "Consumer discretionary and information technology companies are winners in lower-interest rate environments." Looking ahead, as more annual general meetings kicked off over the following weeks, Clark said he would be looking at trading updates, especially of companies that did not give solid guidance in their last update.



---


# Bank of Israel Thirty Billion Dollar FX Intervention

On the Monday of the week in which this 12 October 2023 interview was published, the Bank of Israel announced a dramatic plan to sell $30 billion of its foreign currency reserves to stabilise the shekel. By the time of the report the shekel had in fact recovered slightly and was trading at around NIS 3.96/$.

Leo Leiderman endorsed the move: "It's important to welcome the Bank of Israel's decision to intervene, as necessary, in the foreign exchange market, in order to ensure the market's regular operation." He also treated leadership continuity as stabilising, citing the decision to extend the term of Amir Yaron as governor at least for the duration of the war, and in his hope beyond it. He added that the banking system is stable with enough liquidity in the system, and that the behaviour of the investment community in Israel, including the financial institutions, indicates high confidence in the economy's resilience and financial strength — an "asset" he said a level-headed, correct economic policy must preserve.



---


# How Treasury Yields And "Higher For Longer" Transmit To Equities

Treasury bonds are seen as some of the safest investments possible, and when they pay higher yields, investors are less likely to pay high prices for stocks and other riskier investments — which is a big reason why the S&P 500 dropped 4.9 per cent in September 2023, dragging what had been a big gain for the year down to 11.7 per cent.

The chain running into those yields is the Federal Reserve's stance. Treasury yields have been climbing sharply as Wall Street accepts a new normal in which the Fed is likely to keep interest rates high for longer; the Fed is trying to push still-high inflation down to its target, and its main tool of high interest rates does that by trying to slow the economy and hurting prices for investments. The Fed's main interest rate is at its highest level since 2001, and the central bank indicated the previous week that it may cut interest rates next year by less than it earlier expected. The data cuts both ways within this model. Friday's economic data showed that not only was inflation a touch cooler than expected in August, so was growth in spending by US consumers, which can be a positive for inflation because it means not as many dollars are pouring into purchases and that in turn could give companies less encouragement to raise prices further — but it may also dent what has been a big driver keeping the US economy out of a recession.



---


# ASX November 2023 Session and RBA Rate Expectations

In the Australian session reported by The Sydney Morning Herald on 5 November 2023, energy companies were the main drag on the index, down one per cent, with Woodside off 0.8 per cent, Santos down 0.4 per cent and Ampol down 1.2 per cent, alongside coal miners Yancoal (down 1.7 per cent) and Whitehaven (down 2 per cent). Lynas Rare Earths was the biggest large-cap decliner at down 3.1 per cent, while industrials fell 0.2 per cent, including Computershare (down 2.9 per cent), Seven West Holdings (down 1.9 per cent) and Worley (down 1.3 per cent).

TMS Capital portfolio manager Ben Clark said the big news for markets on the Monday was Westpac's trading update, which he said led a resurgence in the banking sector's performance. "Westpac's results were better than expected, especially because it's been a bit of a perennial underperformer in the past few years," he said, adding that it set the tone for results from NAB and ANZ due to report in the following week. Clark also described a reversal of the interest-rate trade of recent weeks: "Long-term bond yields came off quite significantly in the last few days following weaker than expected employment data on Friday, which has seen some investors swivel back into growth stocks." On his account the market had switched from pricing in an 80 per cent chance of a rate rise on the Tuesday to 50-50.

Other commentary framed the risk of a further increase. "Our view is that in the high likelihood there is another cash rate increase on Tuesday, that is going to be the nail in the coffin for consumer confidence," said CreditorWatch chief economist Anneke Thompson, amid warnings from some economists that another rate rise would dampen spending intentions just in time for Christmas. The same wrap noted that the men who built pubs and liquor juggernaut Endeavour Group into the world's largest poker machine operator had triggered a public spat over the future of a business they say has lost its way.



---


# ASX Outlook And RBA Rate Expectations At End-September 2023

The Australian sharemarket was set to retreat with futures pointing to a fall of 38 points, or 0.5 per cent, at the open, after Wall Street closed out its worst month and quarter of the year with more losses on Friday.

# Total Addressable Market (TAM)

## Definition

Total addressable market (TAM) is the overall revenue opportunity a market represents — the size of the "pie" a company could theoretically capture — as distinct from market share, the slice of that pie a specific competitor has actually won.
The corpus uses "TAM" directly only once: in a TechCrunch roundup on AI startup strategy, after VC Edward Tsai of Alumni Ventures argued that startups "may want to temporarily reduce their focus on defensibility and increase their focus on products that deliver compelling value and focusing on speed to market," the article's author adds, as an editorial aside rather than part of Tsai's quote, "Presuming massive TAM, that could work!" — treating TAM as a measure of how much upside is still up for grabs regardless of who wins any single deal.
Far more often the corpus talks about the narrower, already-contested slice of a market — "market share" — across search, payments, betting, retail, crypto, autos, and music.

## Context

The corpus's clearest TAM reference sits inside a broader discussion of how AI startups should compete: Edward Tsai of Alumni Ventures told TechCrunch that startups might "temporarily reduce their focus on defensibility and increase their focus on products that deliver compelling value and focusing on speed to market," a view the article's author then glossed with "Presuming massive TAM, that could work!" and Rick Grinnell of Glasswing Ventures separately described the goal of "capturing market share or meeting a critical market need before competitors" — TAM as the size of the opportunity, market share as who is winning it.
The rest of the corpus's "market share" usage documents that same capture-and-defend dynamic in mature markets rather than emerging ones: Google's roughly 90% share of online search (and the $26.3 billion it paid in 2021 to secure default placement across Apple, Samsung, and Mozilla to protect that share); Chrome's climb from nearly 50% of desktop browser usage at the end of 2014 to nearly 65% by the end of 2017, the same year Google regained the default-search slot on Firefox; Binance's share of the crypto-exchange market falling from over 60% to under 50% after its DOJ settlement; Reliance Retail's roughly 3% share of India's retail market against Walmart's roughly 10% of the US market; Capitol Music Group's "high-5%" US label market share; Tesla losing EV market share to rivals amid price cuts; and fintech Rainforest explicitly trying to "take market share" from Stripe and legacy processors Fiserv and FIS.
Sportsbooks entering new states (Kentucky, Vermont) frame their promotional bonus wars in the same terms — "fighting for market share" in a market that is still being carved up as it launches.

## Key Characteristics

- **TAM is the whole opportunity; market share is the captured slice** — the corpus's one TAM mention treats it as license to chase growth over defensibility, while every market-share mention describes a company's already-won or already-lost portion of a market.
- **Market share is measured differently by market** — percentage of search queries (Google's ~90%), percentage of desktop browser usage (Chrome's ~65%), percentage of exchange volume/assets (Binance's 60%→50% decline), percentage of retail floor space or sales (Reliance Retail's ~3% vs. Walmart's ~10%), and record-label percentage of a national market (Capitol Music Group's "high-5%").
- **Share can be bought as well as earned** — Google's $26.3 billion in 2021 default-placement payments to Apple and other partners, and sportsbooks' signup bonuses in newly legalized states, are both framed as direct spend to acquire or defend market share rather than organic growth.
- **Share shifts are framed as zero-sum among incumbents** — Rainforest is described as taking share "from" Stripe, Fiserv, and FIS; EV rivals are described as taking share "from" Tesla; new entrants into Vermont and Kentucky sports betting are described as "fighting" each other for the same pool of bettors.
- **A large presumed TAM changes competitive strategy** — the corpus's TechCrunch commentary on VC Edward Tsai's view suggests that when the addressable opportunity is presumed to be very large, startups may rationally prioritize speed to market over building defensible moats, since there is enough unclaimed opportunity for multiple winners.

qid: Has the portrayal of Google's business practices in TechCrunch articles shown inconsistency after the report on Epic Games' antitrust battle with Google on November 6, 2023, compared to the subsequent class action antitrust suit reported on December 15, 2023?
context:
# Google's Parallel Antitrust Proceedings In Late 2023

As of mid-November 2023, Google was fighting antitrust on more than one front at once. The Epic Games case was not its only antitrust case in trial: Google had settled a separate antitrust lawsuit with dating site Match Group the week before November 13, and on November 6 it went to trial with Fortnite maker Epic Games, which hoped to prove that Google engages in anticompetitive behavior with regard to its Android app store, Google Play, and its commission structure. Separately, Google was involved in an antitrust lawsuit with the Department of Justice over its alleged search monopoly.

The Epic case had shed co-plaintiffs on its way to trial. Epic's lawsuit originally involved Match and several U.S. attorneys general, but Google reached a settlement with the attorneys general in October 2023 and with Match the week before November 6, so Epic fought the antitrust battle on its own. The lawsuit, held in the U.S. District Court in California's Northern District, would include testimony from a number of Google and Android execs, including CEO Sundar Pichai, and Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, as well as from Apple, Netflix and other Android developers. Epic, meanwhile, had lost its antitrust battle with Apple and was asking the Supreme Court to weigh in.



---


# The Settlements That Left Epic Standing Alone

Other plaintiffs brought app store antitrust claims against Google and then all settled: all 50 state attorneys general and a number of consumers have tentatively settled, though it is not clear what the deal might include, and Match Group — the company behind Tinder, Match.com, OkCupid and other dating apps — just reached a surprise last-minute settlement too, one that makes it sound like Match effectively gave up. Epic stands alone.

Epic seems to have no interest in settling as long as the "Google tax" exists, and the company has repeatedly said it is not interested in cash. So far it has been willing to push these cases all the way through multiple appeals, cost be damned. It is not clear what Google could proactively offer that would satisfy Epic, since CEO Tim Sweeney has also publicly suggested that Google would simply circumvent any settlement it offers. If you want to see a vision of a future Epic would accept, look to the letter it sent to state attorneys general, laying out a settlement that would basically prohibit Google from doing the anticompetitive things Epic claims it did. Google would not tell The Verge whether it has offered Epic any kind of settlement.



---


# Helena World Chronicle's Class Action Antitrust Suit Against Google

A class action lawsuit filed in the week of 15 December 2023 in the U.S. District Court in D.C. accuses Google and parent company Alphabet of anticompetitive behavior in violation of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act and others, on behalf of news publishers. The case was filed by Arkansas-based publisher Helena World Chronicle, which argues that Google "siphons off" news publishers' content, their readers and their ad revenue through anticompetitive means, and it specifically cites new AI technologies such as Google's Search Generative Experience (SGE) and the Bard AI chatbot as worsening the problem.

Helena World Chronicle owns and publishes two weekly newspapers in Arkansas. In the complaint it argues that Google is "starving the free press" by sharing publishers' content on Google, losing them "billions of dollars."

Beyond damages, the suit asks for an injunction that would require Google to obtain consent from publishers before using their website data to train its general artificial intelligence products, including Google's own and those of rivals. It also asks that publishers who opt out of SGE still be allowed to show up in Google search results, among other things.

The law firm handling the case is Hausfeld, whose announcement states that "the anticompetitive effects of Google's scheme cause profound harm to competition, to consumers, to labor, and to a democratic free press," and that "Plaintiff Helena World Chronicle, LLC invokes the Sherman Act and Clayton Act to seek class-wide monetary and injunctive relief to restore and ensure competition for digital news and reference publishing and set up guardrails to preserve a free marketplace of ideas in the new era of artificial intelligence."



---


# The U.S. Justice Department's Parallel Antitrust Suits Against Google

The Helena World Chronicle class action arrives alongside the filing of the U.S. Justice Department's lawsuit against Google for monopolizing digital ad technologies, and the complaint also references the Justice Department's 2020 civil antitrust suit over search and search advertising.

The two government cases concern different markets: search and search advertising in the 2020 suit are distinct from the digital ad technologies at issue in the more recent one.



---


# Epic v. Google: What The Trial Is

Epic v. Google is the antitrust case in which Fortnite publisher Epic Games drags a tech giant into court alleging that its mobile app store is an illegal monopoly — and although Epic's parallel claims against Apple already got their day in court, the similar lawsuit against Google never did, which is why the case goes to trial on November 6th, a mere 1,180 days after Epic originally sued.

The déjà vu is the point of confusion the piece sets out to clear up: Epic already went to trial with Apple, resulting in a ruling where Apple mostly won, and its Llamacorn legal gambit failed to #FreeFortnite years ago. The distinction is that the Apple claims were heard and the Google ones were not.

An update dated December 15th, 2023 notes that the case is basically over by then.



---


# Epic Games v. Google Goes To Trial On November 6, 2023

Epic Games, the maker of Fortnite, went to trial with Google on November 6, 2023, hoping to convince a jury that Google engages in anticompetitive behavior with regard to its Android app store, Google Play, and its commission structure. Match had settled its own antitrust lawsuit with Google the week before, but Epic's case proceeded.

This case differs slightly from Epic's battle with Apple on the same topic, because this time Epic cannot allege there is no other way to load apps onto Android devices, as it could with Apple: Android does allow for sideloading apps. Epic will suggest Google makes that process cumbersome, but the bulk of its arguments will center on what it believes are anticompetitive agreements between Google and device manufacturers and developers.

The precedent Epic's case relies on is a Microsoft case in which courts found Microsoft to have a monopoly over the operating system and to be abusing it, making it hard for users to download alternative browsers, like Netscape, on Windows devices. To make its case, Epic plans to bring claims under Sections 1 and 2 of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act, as well as California's anticompetitive laws, the Cartwright Act and the Unfair Competition Law. It will attempt to argue that Google restrains competition within two separate markets: the distribution of apps to Android users, and the market for payment processing solutions for content inside Android apps.



---


# Google's Secret OEM And Carrier Deals And Its Deleted Chats

Asked what surprised him in the courtroom, Tim Sweeney said the trial confirmed practices he had suspected since around 2018 — when some people called him a conspiracy theorist for saying so — including that Google leaked Epic's conversations to reporters to get negative stories written, paid other developers off to convince them not to launch their own stores, and went around paying carriers and OEMs secretly not to carry competing stores.

Sweeney gave a concrete instance from Epic's own experience: when Epic tried to bundle Fortnite with other smartphone manufacturers such as OnePlus and with carriers of all sorts, those partners told Epic they couldn't do a deal because Google had done a secret deal with them. He called it disconcerting to see the extent of bad-faith efforts inside a company of Google's size, saying you would expect a trillion-dollar company to have developed respectable processes and leadership structures providing checks and balances against wrongdoing. Instead, he said, Google employees were "rampantly destroying all their chats on these topics": long conversation threads would start to get into a spicy antitrust issue, somebody would point out that history was on, and the chat would go silent — history turned off so the documents would be destroyed. Sweeney said it was great to see all of that called out in detail at trial.



---


# Sweeney And Pichai's Settlement Talks

Asked about his settlement talks with Google CEO Sundar Pichai, Tim Sweeney said he could not discuss their content, but that the two met for an hour and had a professional discussion in which they did not reach a settlement — they were, in his words, "rather far apart."

He explained the gap in terms of what Epic was asking for: free and fair competition for everybody, removal of the payments tie, and removal of the anticompetitive measures, which he said obviously leads to far better deals for consumers and developers. What Epic does not want is a special deal just for itself. Sweeney characterised Google's strategy so far, as visible from all these deals, as taking out potential competitors one at a time while they are still weak and small, before they build up or unite into a formidable force — and said Epic is not going to go along with something like that.

qid: Who is the individual accused of using Caroline Ellison as a front to secretly access Alameda Research's customer funds and is also alleged by the prosecution to have committed fraud for wealth, power, and influence, as reported by both Fortune and TechCrunch?
context:
# Caroline Ellison's Guilty Plea And First Day Of Testimony

Caroline Ellison, head of the hedge fund Alameda Research during its implosion along with FTX, took the stand on October 10th, 2023 having already pleaded guilty to criminal charges — fraud, conspiracy to commit fraud, and money laundering — and told the jury that Bankman-Fried "directed me to commit these crimes." She quantified the taking: "We ultimately took about $14 billion, some of which we were not able to pay back."

Her long-anticipated first day took the form of walking through a damning spreadsheet she had prepared for her ex and boss, now the defendant in a criminal fraud trial. She entered hunched in on herself, wearing a dusty rose dress with a gray blazer over it, looking less like an executive than like a girl who had borrowed her boyfriend's coat because she was cold. Asked by the prosecution to identify Bankman-Fried, she had trouble finding him and gazed around the courtroom for more than 20 seconds — apparently he was incognito with his new haircut — and when she did spot him she identified him as the one wearing a suit, which got chuckles from the rest of the defense table, also all in suits. She tilted her head down to answer questions and lifted it when she had finished each answer.

The defendant's own reaction registered the shift: Bankman-Fried had been vibrating slightly during Wang's testimony, and during Ellison's his bouncing became more noticeable. By the end of the day, The Verge's reporter wrote, the spreadsheet seemed like a sideshow.



---


# Alameda Research As The Alleged Conduit For FTX Customer Funds

In the prosecution's account offered by Thane Rehn, the key to Sam Bankman-Fried's alleged scheme was Alameda Research, a crypto hedge fund that Bankman-Fried also owned. The structure the government described works as follows: Caroline Ellison — Bankman-Fried's on-again off-again girlfriend and the CEO of Alameda — served as a front for the fund, and through that arrangement Bankman-Fried had "secret access" to customer money, both cash and crypto.

Two further relations complete the alleged mechanism. Bankman-Fried is said to have directed employees to conceal the flow of money into FTX's coffers, and to have forged financial documents distributed to lenders and investors. "The defendant lied to the world," Rehn alleged. These are the government's allegations as presented in its opening statement, not established findings.



---


# Prosecution And Defense Arguments On Day Two Of The SBF Trial

On the second day of the trial of Sam Bankman-Fried and FTX, the prosecution argued that Bankman-Fried knowingly committed fraud, and it grounded that claim in motive: he did so, prosecutors said, to achieve great wealth, power and influence.

The defense countered with the opposite reading of the same conduct. Its claim was that the FTX founder acted in good faith, never meant to commit fraud or to steal, and basically got in over his head — an argument whose warrant is that inexperience and overreach, rather than intent, explain what happened. The two sides therefore contest intent rather than the underlying events, and the reporting on this exchange comes from Rebecca and Jacquelyn in TechCrunch's Week in Review of October 7, 2023, covering day two of the trial only.



---


# Sassoon's Redirect And The Alameda All-Hands Recording

Prosecutor Danielle Sassoon's brief redirect of Caroline Ellison on October 12th, 2023 set a trap that opened the door to the jury hearing a secret recording of an Alameda all-hands meeting in which Ellison confessed to stealing billions of FTX customers' money at Bankman-Fried's direction. On direct examination, near the end, Sassoon had asked about the all-hands meeting without bringing up many specifics; during the cross, Mark Cohen asked Ellison what topics were covered in the meeting while avoiding details — which let Sassoon work the confession in on redirect. The judge then ruled in favour of the jury hearing the recordings, and the court briefly recessed; that was when Bankman-Fried's mother approached the defense lawyers.

The tape was set up by a short afternoon witness. Christian Drappi, a former Alameda software engineer who looked like a handsome funeral director in a black suit and tie, testified that when Binance CEO Changpeng Zhao announced on Twitter that he intended to acquire FTX, Ellison confessed the theft of customer funds to him and a few other employees. The all-hands took place the following day and was secretly recorded by an employee who had joined Alameda three days before. In the recording Ellison did indeed confess to stealing customer funds with Bankman-Fried's approval. Drappi said he resigned less than 24 hours after the meeting; the recording was later sent to him, and he sent it to the government.

The reporter's assessment was that Sassoon demolished any points Cohen had attempted to make and that she did not fully appreciate the cleverness until after Ellison left the stand and the jurors left the room. In the family seats, Joseph Bankman, the defendant's father and a senior advisor to FTX's philanthropic arm, was not in the room for the recording, and Barbara Fried looked unhappy, rubbing her left temple as though she had a tremendous headache.



---


# SBF's Arrest And Bail

Bankman-Fried was arrested in December 2022 in the Bahamas, where FTX was based, and was then extradited to the U.S. to face a number of criminal charges. He was released on a $250 million bail bond and remained under house arrest at his parents' home in Palo Alto. TechCrunch set out the sequence on 2023-10-01.

That release did not hold. It was revoked in August, after he was accused of intimidating Alameda's former CEO, Caroline Ellison, by leaking her private diary.



---


# Cohen's Cross-Examination Of Caroline Ellison

Mark Cohen's cross-examination of Caroline Ellison on October 12th, 2023 aimed at the premise that her direct testimony was reliable — she had recounted many conversations held in person or on auto-deleting messaging platforms, and she had an incentive to flip on Bankman-Fried in the form of possible leniency at sentencing — but The Verge's reporter judged that the defense absolutely biffed it. In Cohen's disorganized cross-examination he mostly bored the jury; at one point two different jurors appeared to be asleep, and midway through the morning the reporter began wondering whether there was a mercy rule for cross-examinations.

The lines of attack were opened and dropped. Cohen established that Bankman-Fried had a much larger appetite for risk than Ellison, that the two reacted differently to stress, and that they took different approaches to media — Ellison avoided it while Bankman-Fried sought it out — without building on any of it. He drew out that Alameda had one accountant in 2021 and hired two more junior accountants in 2022, and had a problem retaining accountants, then dropped that too. He appeared to be trying to suggest the government had coerced Ellison's testimony by getting her to plead guilty to defrauding investors, conduct she could not have been involved in since she did not prepare materials for them; unfortunately she said she had had conversations with investors as part of their due diligence, and Alameda was in any case taking on losses from FTX to keep FTX's balance sheet pristine. Cohen also pressed the hedge he had blamed her for not taking out in his opening — hedging being long crypto by selling Nasdaq futures — which raised the question of whether the defense was that she should have taken more customer funds, or taken them sooner.

Small failures accumulated. Cohen asked Ellison to define what "buy on the way down" meant as though it were a term of art, which seemed to puzzle her, and at other times he seemed to forget what she had testified to and brought up things she had not said; like FTX employee Adam Yedidia before her, Ellison was fastidious about making sure a question was clear and her answer precise. She appeared at one point to be toying with him: having testified on direct about the token Luna, she noted when Cohen asked about Terra/Luna that she had only spoken about Luna, leaving him to fumble the relationship between the two. There were many sidebars, enough that several jurors looked entertained when one occurred, and in one the day before the prosecution complained that Bankman-Fried was visibly scoffing at Ellison's answers, per the court transcript. What Cohen was up against was strong direct evidence: fake balance sheets, one sent to crypto lender Genesis, after which a Genesis representative texted Ellison to say he had spoken to Bankman-Fried — strongly suggesting Bankman-Fried knew the contents of the fake balance sheet. Afterwards, the defendant's mother Barbara Fried engaged Christian Everdell in an animated conversation, gesticulating and clearly holding a strong opinion; Everdell walked off and Cohen talked to her for a bit.

qid: Who is the individual associated with the rise of artificial intelligence as discussed by 'The Age' and is also the subject of speculation regarding truthfulness with the board as per 'TechCrunch'?
context:
# The Artificial Intelligence Advancement Act Of 2023

Tuesday's Senate AI forum followed the recent introduction of new AI legislation dubbed the Artificial Intelligence Advancement Act of 2023 (S. 3050), co-sponsored by Senators Martin Heinrich (D-NM), Mike Rounds (R-SD), Charles Schumer (D-NY) and Todd Young (R-IN).

The bill proposes AI bug bounty programs and would require a vulnerability analysis study for AI-enabled military applications. Its passage into law would also launch a report into AI regulation in the financial services industry, as well as a second report on data sharing and coordination.

The financial-services provision lands on a problem the SEC's own chairman has been lamenting. "It's frankly a hard challenge," SEC Chairman Gary Gensler told The Financial Times recently, speaking on the challenges the financial industry faces in AI adoption and regulation. "It's a hard financial stability issue to address because most of our regulation is about individual institutions, individual banks, individual money market funds, individual brokers; it's just in the nature of what we do."



---


# The AI Risk Paradox Among Tech Billionaires

At the heart of the competition to build artificial intelligence is a brain-stretching paradox: the people who say they are most worried about AI are among the most determined to create it and enjoy its riches, and they have justified their ambition with their strong belief that they alone can keep AI from endangering Earth. The grounds are the shape of the debate itself. Eight years after an argument between Elon Musk and Larry Page, that argument seems prescient, because the question of whether AI will elevate the world or destroy it, or at least inflict grave damage, has framed an ongoing debate among Silicon Valley founders, chatbot users, academics, legislators and regulators about whether the technology should be controlled or set free.

That debate has pitted some of the world's richest men against one another: Musk, Page, Mark Zuckerberg of Meta, tech investor Peter Thiel, Satya Nadella of Microsoft and Sam Altman of OpenAI, all of whom have fought for a piece of a business that one day could be worth trillions of dollars, and for the power to shape it. The narrative anchor is that Musk and Page stopped speaking soon after the party that summer, and that a few weeks later Musk dined with Altman, who was then running a tech incubator, and several researchers in a private room at the Rosewood hotel in Menlo Park, California, a favoured deal-making spot close to the venture capital offices of Sand Hill Road.



---


# DeepMind's Founding And Thiel's Investment

In 2010 Demis Hassabis and two colleagues, all living in Britain, were looking for money to start building "artificial general intelligence", a machine that could do anything the brain could do, at a time when few people were interested in AI because after a half-century of research the field had failed to deliver anything remotely close to the human brain. Some scientists and thinkers had nonetheless become fixated on AI's downsides, and many, including the three young men, had a connection to Eliezer Yudkowsky, an internet philosopher and self-taught AI researcher who led a community calling themselves Rationalists or, later, effective altruists; they believed AI could find a cure for cancer or solve climate change but worried that AI bots might do things their creators had not intended, arguing that machines more intelligent than humans could turn on their creators. Peter Thiel, enormously wealthy through an early investment in Facebook and his work with Musk in the early days of PayPal, had developed a fascination with the singularity, the science-fiction trope describing the moment when intelligent technology can no longer be controlled by humanity, and with his funding Yudkowsky had expanded his AI lab and created an annual conference on the singularity; one of Hassabis' colleagues had met Yudkowsky years before and snagged them speaking spots at that conference, ensuring an invitation to Thiel's party, where Yudkowsky introduced Hassabis to Thiel. Assuming many guests would be trying to squeeze their host for money, Hassabis' strategy was to arrange another meeting: he told Thiel there was a deep tension between the bishop and the knight, pieces carrying the same value whose strengths the best players understood to be vastly different. Charmed, Thiel invited the group back the next day, gathering in the kitchen where their host, just finished with his morning workout and still sweating in a shiny tracksuit, was handed a Diet Coke by a butler; the three made their pitch and soon Thiel and his venture capital firm agreed to put £1.4 million, about $A2.7 million, into their startup, making him their first major investor.

They named the company DeepMind, a nod to "deep learning", a way for AI systems to learn skills by analysing large amounts of data, to neuroscience, and to the Deep Thought supercomputer from The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy, and by the spring of 2010 they were building their dream machine, wholeheartedly believing that because they understood the risks they were uniquely positioned to protect the world. Mustafa Suleyman, one of the three founders, said "I don't see this as a contradictory position. There are huge benefits to come from these technologies. The goal is not to eliminate them or pause their development. The goal is to mitigate the downsides." Having won over Thiel, Hassabis worked his way into Musk's orbit: about two years later they met at a conference organised by Thiel's investment fund, which had also put money into SpaceX, and Hassabis secured a tour of SpaceX headquarters, after which, with rocket hulls hanging from the ceiling, the two lunched in the cafeteria; Musk explained his plan to colonise Mars to escape overpopulation and other dangers on Earth, and Hassabis replied that the plan would work so long as superintelligent machines didn't follow and destroy humanity on Mars too. Musk was speechless, not having thought about that particular danger, and soon invested in DeepMind alongside Thiel so he could be closer to the creation of the technology.



---


# Anthropic's Founding By Former OpenAI Researchers

Dario Amodei, a researcher with ties to the effective altruist community, had been on hand at the Rosewood hotel when OpenAI was born, and was leading the lab's efforts to build a neural network called a large language model that could learn from enormous amounts of digital text: by analysing countless Wikipedia articles, digital books and message boards it could generate text on its own, and it also had the unfortunate habit of making things up. It was called GPT-3 and was released in the summer of 2020, and researchers inside OpenAI, Google and other companies thought this rapidly improving technology could be a path to artificial general intelligence. Amodei was unhappy about the Microsoft deal because he thought it was taking OpenAI in a really commercial direction, and he and other researchers went to the board to try to push Altman out, according to five people familiar with the matter; after they failed, they left, worrying, like DeepMind's founders before them, that their new corporate overlords would favour commercial interests over safety.

In 2021 the group of about 15 engineers and scientists created a new lab called Anthropic, with the plan of building AI the way the effective altruists thought it should be done, with very tight controls. Anthropic disputes the account of the board approach: "There was no attempt to remove Sam Altman from OpenAI by the co-founders of Anthropic," said an Anthropic spokesperson, Sally Aldous. "The co-founders themselves came to the conclusion that they wished to depart OpenAI to start their own company, made this known to OpenAI's leadership, and over several weeks negotiated an exit on mutually agreeable terms." Anthropic accepted a $US4 billion investment from Amazon and another $US2 billion from Google two years later. After OpenAI received another $US2 billion from Microsoft, Altman and another senior executive, Greg Brockman, visited Bill Gates at his sprawling mansion on the shores of Lake Washington, outside Seattle; the Microsoft founder was no longer involved in the company day to day but kept in regular touch with its executives.



---


# Theory: An AGI And Mission Rift Between Altman And The Board

The proposition is that Altman's zeal for AGI, even absent a secret project or agreement, led to a major rift between him and the board. Altman is a proud techno-optimist and often speaks fondly of the possibilities of AGI, or artificial general intelligence, a theoretical software system that achieves human-like intellect and versatility. The board's statement pointedly includes that "OpenAI was deliberately structured to advance our mission: to ensure that artificial general intelligence benefits all humanity" and that new leadership was necessary.

The supporting observation is a directional one: it has been obvious to all that Altman took the company in a much more corporate direction from its origins, changing its legal status and aggressively pursuing enterprise and consumer applications, which does not sound a lot like the "mission" the board wants to advance.

What counts against it is timing. This shift did not happen today, and it certainly does not seem like a plausible reason for abruptly firing the CEO and a few others on a beautiful fall Friday afternoon — a gradual drift does not explain an abrupt dismissal.

# Sam Altman's Career Before OpenAI

Sam Altman, 38 as of November 2023, is not trained as an AI engineer, yet has been seen as a Silicon Valley wunderkind since his early 20s. The defining credential of that earlier phase is that he was recruited in 2014 to take the lead of the startup incubator YCombinator.

# DeepMind's Sale To Google And Facebook's AI Lab

Google offered $US650 million for DeepMind. Mark Zuckerberg of Facebook offered a bigger payout to DeepMind's founders but would not agree to the conditions the founders had set, and DeepMind sold to Google.

Zuckerberg was determined to build an AI lab of his own and hired Yann LeCun, a French computer scientist who had also done pioneering AI research, to run it. A year after Hinton's auction, Zuckerberg and LeCun flew to Lake Tahoe for the same AI conference, and while padding around a suite at the Harrah's casino in his socks Zuckerberg personally interviewed top researchers, who were soon offered millions of dollars in salary and stock. # Gaza As A Tech Outsourcing Hub

Gaza, despite being one of the most economically challenged regions in the world, has ironically always been a tech hub — not only for Palestine and Palestinians, but also for the world, with international companies having for many years sought out a presence there to collaborate with talented tech freelancers and the startups that gradually emerged from the region. According to sources who helped build those bridges, Nvidia, famed for its role in the new AI boom, has been working with at least 100 engineers from the region for years; tragically, the initiative to employ Palestinians in this outsourcing was that of Mellanox founder Eyal Waldman, whose daughter was brutally murdered in the attacks by Hamas.

The hub's scale marks its boundary. Since at least 2008, TechCrunch has been covering technology companies out of Palestine, some serving their direct audience and some serving the tech world internationally, and Silicon Valley had taken an increasing interest in Palestine as a tech hub — but like the ecosystem itself, that interest is nascent: to date, those working in the region estimate that as much as $10 million has been invested in the Palestinian tech ecosystem. Notably, in 2017, Salesforce founder and CEO Marc Benioff joined Silicon Valley luminaries in backing the first-ever coding academy to be created in Gaza.



---


# The OpenAI Board Ousts Sam Altman, November 2023

As reported on November 18, 2023, the OpenAI board had ejected billionaire and AI evangelist Sam Altman from his CEO role after an apparent vote of no confidence. The board's exact wording in a release issued that afternoon: Altman's "departure follows a deliberative review process by the board, which concluded that he was not consistently candid in his communications with the board, hindering its ability to exercise its responsibilities."

What followed was a whirlwind four days for OpenAI, the generative AI poster child behind the smash hit ChatGPT. The board ousted CEO and co-founder Altman and demoted president and co-founder Greg Brockman, who subsequently resigned, paving the way for what looked like a mutiny by staff insisting the founders be reinstated post-haste. By the time TechCrunch wrote again on November 21, 2023, Microsoft had already hired Altman and Brockman to head up a new internal AI unit — though, as things transpired, nothing had actually been signed yet, with rumors suggesting the ousted leaders might actually return to OpenAI after all, in some capacity at least.

TechCrunch cautioned on November 18 that the full truth would not be known for a long time, as the characters in the drama are likely to be NDA'ed up. Per various whispers and leaks, an all-hands meeting about the situation that afternoon did not produce any revelations beyond banal reassurances that the company is fine and they will get a fresh CEO soon.



---


# The AI Risk Paradox Among Tech Billionaires

At the heart of the competition to build artificial intelligence is a brain-stretching paradox: the people who say they are most worried about AI are among the most determined to create it and enjoy its riches, and they have justified their ambition with their strong belief that they alone can keep AI from endangering Earth. The grounds are the shape of the debate itself. Eight years after an argument between Elon Musk and Larry Page, that argument seems prescient, because the question of whether AI will elevate the world or destroy it, or at least inflict grave damage, has framed an ongoing debate among Silicon Valley founders, chatbot users, academics, legislators and regulators about whether the technology should be controlled or set free.

That debate has pitted some of the world's richest men against one another: Musk, Page, Mark Zuckerberg of Meta, tech investor Peter Thiel, Satya Nadella of Microsoft and Sam Altman of OpenAI, all of whom have fought for a piece of a business that one day could be worth trillions of dollars, and for the power to shape it. The narrative anchor is that Musk and Page stopped speaking soon after the party that summer, and that a few weeks later Musk dined with Altman, who was then running a tech incubator, and several researchers in a private room at the Rosewood hotel in Menlo Park, California, a favoured deal-making spot close to the venture capital offices of Sand Hill Road.

# Private Sector Volunteers In Terror Finance Tracking

The network blocking terror financing funds includes many entities, including private citizens: IMPA has been approached by many experts from the private sector — people with intelligence experience because they have worked in these organizations, or with high-tech experience — who "have mobilized like crazy."

"The world's financial intelligence authorities are now at the heart of this struggle, and we're working together to thwart the financing channels that we've located," Ostrovitch-Levi said. "Israeli entrepreneurs in Silicon Valley have contacted us; they write code, search for information, and give us lots of information. We aggregate and examine everything."



---


# Musk's Founding Of OpenAI And His Departure

Convinced that Larry Page's optimistic view of AI was dead wrong, and angry at his loss of DeepMind, Musk built his own lab: OpenAI was founded in late 2015, just a few months after he met with Sam Altman at the Rosewood hotel in Silicon Valley. Musk pumped money into the lab and his former PayPal buddies, Reid Hoffman and Peter Thiel, came along for the ride; the three men and others pledged to put $US1 billion into the project, which Altman, then 30, would help run, and to get started they poached Ilya Sutskever from Google, one of the graduate students Google had "bought" in Hinton's auction. Initially Musk wanted to operate OpenAI as a nonprofit, free from the economic incentives driving Google and other corporations, but by the time Google wowed the tech community with its Go stunt he was changing his mind about how it should be run: he desperately wanted OpenAI to invent something that would capture the world's imagination and close the gap with Google, and it wasn't getting the job done as a nonprofit.

In late 2017 Musk hatched a plan to wrest control of the lab from Altman and the other founders and transform it into a commercial operation that would join forces with Tesla and rely on supercomputers the car company was developing, according to four people familiar with the matter; when Altman and others pushed back, Musk quit and said he would focus on his own AI work at Tesla. In February 2018 he announced his departure to OpenAI's staff on the top floor of the startup's offices in a converted truck factory, three people who attended said; when he said OpenAI needed to move faster, one researcher retorted that Musk was being reckless, and Musk called the researcher a "jackass" and stormed out, taking his deep pockets with him. OpenAI suddenly needed new financing in a hurry: Altman flew to Sun Valley for a conference and ran into Satya Nadella, Microsoft's CEO, and a tie-up seemed natural, since Altman knew Microsoft's chief technology officer Kevin Scott and Microsoft had bought LinkedIn from Hoffman, an OpenAI board member; Nadella told Scott to get it done. The deal closed in 2019, leaving Altman and OpenAI with a for-profit company formed under the original nonprofit, $US1 billion in fresh capital, and Microsoft with a new way to build AI into its vast cloud computing service. Not everyone inside OpenAI was happy.
