qid: Does the article from The Age suggest that 'People with an Aboriginal ancestor' have the same process to identify with their Aboriginal heritage compared to the stance of 'Indigenous people' on cultural identity as presented by The Guardian?
context:
# Lucashenko's Argument Against The Trope Of The Dying Race

Melissa Lucashenko's claim is that Aboriginal people have survived colonisation and that the "dying race" trope has finally begun to lose its grip. "That was really the impetus for this book, to say, 'This is what was, and we've survived it,'" she says of Edenglassie. Her grounds are about pressure and its recent easing: "There's a very strong economic and social and psychological drive in non-Aboriginal people to see us as, if not dead, then very diminished. Until probably 10 years ago, I would have said the trope of the dying race was, ironically, immortal. But now there's so much about us in the media all the time, and in the education system to an extent, most Australians have to recognise that Aboriginal people haven't died out."

Census data supports the point: the number of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people has risen from 548,368 in 2011 to 649,171 in 2016, then up 25 per cent to 812,728 in 2021 — an increase attributed in large part to people feeling more comfortable identifying as Indigenous, and also to the growing popularity of genealogical research. Lucashenko's own reading of Aboriginality is not primarily about descent or appearance: she says there is a "whole demographic of people who have an Aboriginal ancestor, who sometimes think they're Aboriginal, but actually, regardless of skin colour, they're white people and they have to go on a very long and different journey if they're going to become Aboriginal", and skin colour "is not irrelevant but it's almost irrelevant". What matters is "the lens you see the world through" — she illustrates it with the myna bird in a native fig tree in West End, which should be full of fig birds, magpies, butcher birds, cat birds and parrots, but where there have been no cat birds and parrots for a hundred years.

The warrant tying her novel to the claim is formal as well as thematic: "F---ing up the simple binaries of black and white is a lot of what I'm about", and the book's dual time-stamp structure is an attempt to render in words what she has called the "double-vision" of Aboriginal people, the layering of the structures of modernity on the ancient landscape of their ancestors. Survival was, she stresses, achieved against the best efforts of some colonists — one of the historical events that inspired the book was the public hanging of the Indigenous warrior Dundalli, the last person publicly executed in Queensland, who was labelled on his death "one of the most guiltiest and most incorrigible of the aboriginal natives of this quarter" by The Brisbane Courier, evaded capture for 14 years, and was convicted in 1854 of two murders whose charges may have been trumped up.



---


# Vincent Namatjira's Call For A Foster Care Apology

Vincent Namatjira told The Guardian on 16 October 2023 that the government should apologise for taking young Indigenous people into foster care: "To be honest, I would like the government to apologise [for] taking these young Indigenous people into foster care."

His grounds are cultural loss rather than individual harm alone: "In reality, we are losing much more of where we're originally from, and our background, and our history. We have lost a lot of things, our culture, languages and our tradition."

The warrant is a claim about voice and standing, made from the country he lives in: "And around here, this is the hard country, we work hard to be who we are today. Indigenous people, we want to be heard and to take a stand. To show our tradition and culture, and art – also to show the rest of the world that Indigenous people, we need to be heard."



---


# Albert Namatjira, Hermannsburg Watercolour Painter

Albert Namatjira (1902-59) was a western Arrernte artist and one of the most well-known Aboriginal figures in 20th-century Australia, defined by watercolour landscapes that blended western influences with a unique perspective on country, The Guardian noted on 16 October 2023.

The discriminating features of his practice are the medium and the fusion: watercolour landscape painting that carried western influence while holding a distinctly Aboriginal view of country. He did not work alone — the elder Namatjira and the Hermannsburg school of artists became a cultural phenomenon.

The boundary case that defines his legacy is the contradiction between that fame and his treatment: despite fame and success, Albert faced legal and health troubles that illustrated a gap in this country — the same gap between white and black Australia that would later shape his descendants.



---


# Edenglassie: A Dual-Timeline Novel Of Colonial And Contemporary Brisbane

Edenglassie is Melissa Lucashenko's new novel, published the week before this 6 October 2023 profile by University of Queensland Press, and named after Brisbane's early moniker. It is a historical epic depicting the period in Brisbane's history when the former penal colony was morphing into a settler town and Aboriginal people still outnumbered white colonists; in the book the two groups coexist uneasily at the Queensland frontier, their interactions defined by mutual curiosity and suspicion, economic co-dependence and outbreaks of violence.

The novel runs on two narrative threads. In the historical part, set in the 1850s, Lucashenko tells the story of Mulanyin, a heroic young fisherman from saltwater country in the south who works with Thomas Petrie as a young man; Mulanyin falls in love with Nita, who has lived with the Petries as a servant girl-cum-ward since she was small, and dreams of buying a boat and taking his beloved home to Yugambeh country, though evading the colonial system to live a traditional life is becoming harder and more dangerous. The book uses the impending calamity of colonialism to tragic effect — the reader knows what is going to happen but the characters do not, and some of them think the British might still go back home. The second thread is set in Brisbane in 2024, where the centenarian grandmother Eddie trips on a tree root and goes to hospital, an event that brings together her feisty granddaughter Winona and young doctor Johnny, who has just discovered his Aboriginal ancestry and is playing at being a blackfella, much to Winona's contempt.

Its origin lies in a single source text. "I'd wanted to write a novel of colonial Brisbane for a very long time, since I read Tom Petrie's Reminiscences of Early Queensland," Lucashenko says. She devoured Reminiscences — a 1904 classic recording the memories of the Scottish-born explorer, gold prospector, logger and grazier who lived in the Moreton Bay penal colony, subsequently Brisbane, from 1831 to 1910 — back in the 1990s, and it stayed in her consciousness for decades. She also felt she had to be in place to write it: "I just had this vague awareness that I should be living in Brisbane to write this book, because it's very different to write a book when you're walking the streets every day and looking at the river every week, than trying to do it at a distance." Lucashenko is the only person ever to have won both the Miles Franklin Literary Award and TV's Millionaire Hot Seat.



---


# Vincent Namatjira: Australia In Colour Survey Exhibition

Vincent Namatjira turned 40 in June 2023 and launched a monograph and major survey exhibition, Australia in Colour, in October as part of Tarnanthi festival, the Art Gallery of South Australia's annual celebration of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander art, The Guardian reported on 16 October 2023.

Collating this formative decade of his work, the exhibition's title alludes to "the blue skies, the red deserts, the green hills, the yellow fields, the blue oceans, the white sands, the creek beds" seen in the backdrop of his portraits, but it is also a more visceral reflection on a continent thrown into stark contrast. "Australia in Colour is gut-wrenching painting, and hard work," he says — in an interview that took place before Saturday's failed referendum vote.

Vincent Namatjira: Australia in Colour opens on 20 October at the Art Gallery of South Australia before touring nationally; Desert Songs is showing until 28 October at Yavuz Gallery in Surry Hills, Sydney; and the monograph Vincent Namatjira (Thames & Hudson) is out now.



---


# Killing for Country By David Marr

David Marr's October 2023 book is an investigation of the Native Police and his own family's connections to it through his great-great-grandfather, published by Black Inc. at $32.99 on 3 October, The Sydney Morning Herald listed on 1 October 2023.

The book's defining premise is a genealogical shock the reviewer poses to the reader: how would you feel if, while doing a bit of genealogical research, you discovered that you were descended from professional killers of Aboriginal people? For Marr, who has "been writing about the politics of race all my life. I know what side I'm on", it prompted this confronting investigation.

Marr describes the book as "an act of atonement, of penance by storytelling". The reviewer calls it a timely, vital story.

# Google Paid $26.3 Billion In 2021 For Default Search Placement

Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to multiple browsers, phones and platforms — from companies including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla — to be everyone's default search engine. The figure was revealed by Google's search head Prabhakar Raghavan when he testified in court on October 28, according to The Verge.

About $18 billion of that total went directly to Apple, according to a New York Times report published earlier in October 2023, and Google has had its deal with Apple in place since 2003 — so the payment is the current year of a two-decade arrangement, not a one-off. Questioned on the amount of money Google spends to get first pick of search engines, Pichai said the decision was made with the consumer in mind: Google pays big bucks to be everywhere so that it can take in all the data and be the best search engine across different companies' devices, he said, according to The Verge.

The trial also produced evidence that Google understood the value of defaults very early on. U.S. Justice Department lawyer Meagan Bellshaw showed Pichai a 2007 email from a Google product strategy meeting containing data showing that when people changed their browser homepage to Google, they did 15% more Google searches, and that when they switched away, their Google searches dropped 27%. The email summarizing that meeting, sent to Pichai as well as other Google leaders, read: "Nitin argues that focusing on homepage market share is one of the most effective things we can do to make gains in search market share," according to The Verge.



---


# Default Search Engine

## Definition

The default search engine is the search provider a device, browser, or platform is pre-configured to use unless a user actively changes the setting — the search box that runs when a person types a query without first choosing an alternative, such as Google on the iPhone's Safari address bar or Firefox's search bar.

## Context

The term is central to *US v. Google*, the DOJ's antitrust case, because default status is the mechanism through which Google secures the overwhelming share of search queries: the Information Services Agreement (ISA) between Apple and Google, in place since 2002/2003, makes Google the default on all Apple devices, and Google separately pays Samsung, Mozilla, and other partners for the same status.
Apple executive Eddy Cue testified that Apple's iPhone setup flow deliberately omits any search-engine choice screen, arguing that presenting users with unfamiliar alternatives would harm the setup experience, while conceding the ISA does not permit Apple to offer such a choice.
Google spent $26.3 billion in 2021 on default-placement deals across browsers, phones, and platforms — about $18 billion of that to Apple alone — a scale that the DOJ used to argue Google understands the mechanism's value: internal 2007 data showed users who set Google as their homepage searched 15% more, while switching away dropped searches 27%.
The Mozilla/Yahoo episode shows the same mechanism working in reverse: when Firefox switched its default from Google to Yahoo under a 2014 deal, Mozilla's CEO testified that user retention declined, illustrating how disruptive changing the default can be even when a paying competitor is involved.
Outside the antitrust trial, the term also frames ordinary consumer behavior: an investor in e-commerce search startup Deft described users' "natural behavior" as following the path of least resistance and just using the default search engine, meaning challenger search products must offer a high-value proposition to displace that inertia.

## Key Characteristics

- **Set by agreement, not by user choice** — default status on major platforms (Apple's Safari/iOS, Android OEMs, Firefox) is typically established through commercial deals (e.g., the Apple-Google ISA, Yahoo-Mozilla's $375M/year deal) rather than user selection at setup.
- **Backed by large recurring payments** — Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 across partners to hold default placement, with roughly $18 billion of that going to Apple.
- **Technically reversible but rarely changed** — Apple and Google both argued switching is easy, but DuckDuckGo's CEO countered that it takes "too many steps" to switch, and Google's own 2005 complaint about Internet Explorer's defaults argued that "most end users do not change defaults," so default status functions as durable market power.
- **Distinct from pre-installation** — Google's separate push to get Chrome and Search merely pre-installed (not necessarily defaulted) on Android and iPhones shows default status is a stronger, more contested tier than simple presence on a device.
- **Drives user behavior even outside browsers** — the concept extends to any search product; consumers default to "the path of least resistance," which challenger search startups must specifically overcome.

## Corpus References

Corpus notes whose source text references this term (evidence-backed, from `term_links.json`):

- [The Google Antitrust Case](google_antitrust_case.md)
- [The Hypocrisy Argument: Google Became The Monopoly It Denounced](google_default_hypocrisy_argument.md)
- [US v. Google: Two Months Into The Search Antitrust Trial](us_v_google_search_antitrust_trial_overview.md)



---


# The Google Antitrust Case

The Google antitrust case is the U.S. government's trial over Google's dominance in the online search market, stemming from a 2020 antitrust claim, in which the government argues that Google uses its platforms and its deals with partners to block out competition in search or advertising and thereby to hinder competitors from accessing the data they would need to improve their products.

Its defining features are the conduct at issue and the defence offered against it. Google CEO Sundar Pichai testified Monday in the trial, defending Google's business tactics, including its deal with Apple and other partners to make Google the default search engine. Google's answer is that it is just doing business: everybody wants Google as the default engine because it is the best, and that, the company says, does not make its actions illegal.

The important boundary case is which Google antitrust matter this is. The 2020 search claim is separate from the one filed in January by the Department of Justice, along with eight states including New York, California and Colorado, which aims to "halt Google's anticompetitive scheme, unwind Google's monopolistic grip on the market and restore competition to digital advertising." The search case and the digital-advertising case are distinct proceedings and should not be conflated.

The trial is the venue in which the underlying numbers surface. Monday's hearing revealed plenty of juicy tidbits, including the $26.3 billion Google spent making itself the default search engine across platforms in 2021, and how Google tried to take it further and have Chrome preinstalled on iPhones.



---


# The DOJ Theory That Google's Default Deals Foreclose Search Rivals

The Justice Department's case against Google is focused on the deals Google makes — with Apple, but also with Samsung and Mozilla and many others — to ensure it is the default search engine on practically every platform.

The grounds the DOJ pressed through Eddy Cue's testimony were framed as a single question: whether Apple picked Google because it is the most lucrative choice or the best product. That question was a key part of Cue's testimony and, in The Verge's account, a key part of the DOJ's entire case. The warrant is the inference joining the two: if the defaults are bought rather than earned, then the network of default agreements, not product quality, is what keeps Google in place across platforms.



---


# US v. Google: Two Months Into The Search Antitrust Trial

As of TechCrunch's November 13, 2023 roundup, the Justice Department's landmark antitrust case against Google was nearly two months old, and the trial record was still producing fresh revelations. TechCrunch framed it as one of the biggest fights in tech antitrust since the U.S. took Microsoft to trial in the 1990s.

An earlier roundup had already surfaced that Google spent $26.3 billion in 2021 making itself the default search engine across platforms, and that Google tried to have Chrome preinstalled on iPhones. Over the couple of weeks preceding this roundup, more of Google's inner workings came to light, including some of the search engine's most lucrative search queries, the shape of the revenue-share agreements between Google and Android OEMs, and why Expedia has a bone to pick with Google.



---


# The Apple-Google Information Services Agreement

The Information Services Agreement, or ISA, is the deal that makes Google's search engine the default on Apple's products — and it is the reason Apple was in court in US v. Google at all.

The ISA has been in place since 2002, but Eddy Cue was responsible for negotiating its current iteration with Google CEO Sundar Pichai in 2016. In testimony on the day The Verge reported, the Justice Department grilled Cue about the specifics of the deal.



---


# The U.S. Justice Department's Parallel Antitrust Suits Against Google

The Helena World Chronicle class action arrives alongside the filing of the U.S. Justice Department's lawsuit against Google for monopolizing digital ad technologies, and the complaint also references the Justice Department's 2020 civil antitrust suit over search and search advertising.

The two government cases concern different markets: search and search advertising in the 2020 suit are distinct from the digital ad technologies at issue in the more recent one.

qid: Who is the individual whose legal and financial actions, including using a colleague as a front for accessing customer funds at Alameda Research and deciding to use $1 billion of FTX customer funds to buy out Binance, are being scrutinized by a jury to ascertain the truth, as reported by Fortune, The Verge, and TechCrunch?

# Testimony At The SBF Trial

Across the first three weeks of the trial, a run of former colleagues, an outside investor and a forensic accounting expert testified that FTX customer money flowed into Alameda Research and out again to other uses, and that FTX's investors were never told about the two firms' special relationship. TechCrunch's running coverage, published 2023-10-06, summarises each week.

In week one, FTX's co-founder and CTO Gary Wang testified Thursday on the extent to which Alameda Research was used for whatever purposes he and SBF saw fit: according to Wang, the crypto trading firm pulled funding directly from FTX customers, whose transactions would be funneled toward Alameda and then directed elsewhere. Thursday also brought testimony from Matt Huang, co-founder and managing partner at crypto investment firm Paradigm, which invested $278 million in FTX across 2021 and 2022 and is part of a class-action lawsuit accusing it and others of defrauding customers by promoting FTX. His testimony centered around being left uninformed about FTX's utilization of customer money to keep Alameda Research afloat — a practice Huang says would have halted his involvement — and covered his relationship with FTX stretching back to 2019.

Week two's standout testimony came from Alameda Research's former CEO Caroline Ellison, who claimed she took $14 billion from customers to repay debts to lenders, using them as a line of credit under the instruction of SBF. Ellison also went into detail about how a $2 billion venture fund, FTX Ventures, was funded by money that had previously been allocated to Alameda from third-party lenders. And though there are no charges of bribery in the case, she also testified to paying Chinese officials $150 million to restore access to $1 billion in frozen trading accounts.

The third week featured a couple of noteworthy moments for the prosecution. FTX's former general counsel Can Sun, like many of SBF's former colleagues, opted to cooperate with authorities and testified that SBF asked him to create a theoretical "legal justification" for the use of billions in consumer funds just days before FTX filed for bankruptcy. Robert Boroujerdi, managing director of the hedge fund Third Point, testified about his experience working with SBF and FTX in a partnership that ultimately resulted in a $60 million investment and a lack of awareness about the special relationship between Alameda Research and FTX; had he known of such a relationship, he testified, Third Point would not have invested in FTX in the first place. And earlier in the week, Peter Easton — a University of Notre Dame professor who helped the government prosecution of Enron and WorldCom — testified about what he uncovered after tracing the flow of billions of dollars between Alameda Research and FTX: much of that funding came from customers, and Easton testified that he found user deposits were used by both FTX and Alameda to purchase real estate, make investments or direct funding toward political causes and charities.



---


# Alameda Research As The Alleged Conduit For FTX Customer Funds

In the prosecution's account offered by Thane Rehn, the key to Sam Bankman-Fried's alleged scheme was Alameda Research, a crypto hedge fund that Bankman-Fried also owned. The structure the government described works as follows: Caroline Ellison — Bankman-Fried's on-again off-again girlfriend and the CEO of Alameda — served as a front for the fund, and through that arrangement Bankman-Fried had "secret access" to customer money, both cash and crypto.

Two further relations complete the alleged mechanism. Bankman-Fried is said to have directed employees to conceal the flow of money into FTX's coffers, and to have forged financial documents distributed to lenders and investors. "The defendant lied to the world," Rehn alleged. These are the government's allegations as presented in its opening statement, not established findings.



---


# VC And Lender Testimony As Collateral Risk For Crypto

The Verge argued that calling lenders, venture capitalists and customers to testify — necessary to establish the basis for some charges — might create collateral damage for the crypto industry beyond Bankman-Fried himself.

The grounds are the shape of the indictment and who it drags in: prosecutors allege that Bankman-Fried lied to FTX investors, so some of those investors may be called on to testify, which is not the kind of thing VC big shots generally enjoy. The worked example is Sequoia Capital: if Sequoia did due diligence around its investment in FTX, whatever Bankman-Fried told its partners could be important — was FTX already sending Alameda customer funds at that point, did Bankman-Fried know, and did he tell the VCs at the time? If he told them it wasn't happening, that would establish intent. Hermine Wong, the former head of policy at Coinbase and a former SEC regulator, adds that Binance was also an early investor in FTX and that former executives may be called on to testify as well.



---


# FTX's Inner Circle: Family And Friends Implicated

The Verge's October 26th, 2023 account of the trial catalogued how everyone who loved Bankman-Fried most in the world was caught up in the case. Adam Yedidia, his college roommate, testified with immunity because he was concerned he may have unknowingly worked on code that contributed to the fraud; "I love you Sam," he had texted at one point, "I'm not going anywhere" — that was before he realized FTX had stolen customer funds, at which point he resigned. Nishad Singh, a longtime family friend, copped to what sounded an awful lot like classic embezzlement, saying he had backdated transactions on FTX to help create doctored balance sheets to show to investors, and pleaded guilty to six charges including wire fraud, money laundering, and conspiracy counts around his political donations. Caroline Ellison, Bankman-Fried's ex-girlfriend, told the court about the seven phony balance sheets she had created and was clear that Alameda took customer funds, that Bankman-Fried knew about it, and that he even invested them against her advice.

His family was drawn in too. Joe Bankman, his father, is among the people included in the "small group chat," the Signal group where the FTX inner circle strategized during the exchange's last days. Barbara Fried's political action committee, Mind the Gap, is among the entities that received FTX customer money as political donations; Fried and Bankman lived together in a Bahamas house purchased for them using FTX investor funds, according to a financial expert called by the prosecution, and in a lawsuit filed by FTX's bankruptcy estate the two are alleged to have been given $10 million of FTX customer funds. Gabe Bankman-Fried's nonprofit, Guarding Against Pandemics, got millions from FTX; he was also in a Signal group chat, Donations Processing, that Singh says was used to coordinate the transfer of FTX and Alameda money to various political causes, and in that chat he can be seen recommending that some donations be made "in the dark" to avoid public relations headaches. Singh also said Gabe had an assistant fly to the Bahamas with a stack of blank checks for Singh to sign.

The consequences outlast the trial. Wang, Singh, and Ellison are now felons; even if they never do time — and they may very well be imprisoned or subjected to house arrest — their lives are irrevocably changed, not least by whatever restitution requirements they face, they are barred from taking certain kinds of jobs, and there is the publicity. Bankman, Fried, and Gabe Bankman-Fried's reputations are tarnished, and in the political arenas where they once operated they are suddenly undesirable. Beyond the courtroom, everyone who had money trapped on the exchange when it collapsed — as a result of Alameda purloining customers' funds — had their lives altered: even if they are made whole by the bankruptcy proceedings, that is still money they should have had access to at any time, which may mean houses that were not purchased, medical procedures left undone, and life savings lost. The reporter's summary: it is a Greek tragedy, precipitated by one man's character flaw, the arrogance of Sam Bankman-Fried.



---


# Prosecution Allegations In The FTX Superseding Indictment

In a superseding indictment filed August 14th, prosecutors argued that Bankman-Fried lied about consumer protection: that his statements that FTX was "avoiding or managing conflicts of interest" and that "as a general principle FTX segregates customer assets from its own assets across our platforms" were lies.

The indictment also says there were special features in FTX's code that "permitted Alameda to spend and withdraw unlimited amounts of money from FTX," created at Bankman-Fried's direction, effectively exempting Alameda from the kinds of risk management other customers faced — while, the government alleges, "Bankman-Fried publicly and repeatedly asserted that Alameda did not have privileged access to FTX." Bankman-Fried is accused of using "billions of dollars in misappropriated FTX customer deposits" to help buy more than $200 million of real estate for himself, make billions of dollars of investments for his own interest, and repay Alameda's lenders. He allegedly used more than $100 million of customer funds to make political contributions; prosecutors can show evidence of those contributions in this trial even though they aren't part of the charges brought. A second trial is scheduled for March 2024, with additional charges.

qid: Do the articles from The Roar | Sports Writers Blog discussing The All Blacks' actions in the Rugby World Cup final and their previous encounters with Argentina both present The All Blacks as having faced challenges in their gameplay, or do they portray different situations regarding The All Blacks' performance?
context:
# The All Blacks' Final Moments In The 2023 World Cup Final

New Zealand's last chance in the 2023 Rugby World Cup final died in the 80th minute when Ardie Savea forced a ball out wide just as the men in black saw space and looked to open up the Springboks — a killer blow, in The Roar's phrase.

The wider failing was handling. The All Blacks had their chances, but their usual safe handling — a feature throughout the World Cup after their first-up loss to France — evaded them against the Springboks' blitz defence in the wet conditions, and all night their timing was off.

The end came at a set piece. Wayne Barnes, who was booed relentlessly, called a scrum reset as the seconds ticked by; moments later New Zealand hearts sank as the Springboks won the scrum and then hung onto the ball.



---


# The All Blacks' Generational Change After The 2023 World Cup

The 2023 World Cup final marked the end of an All Blacks era on and off the field: Ian Foster's tenure as coach came to an end with Scott Robertson taking over, and multiple generational players — Dane Coles, Sam Whitelock, Brodie Retallick and Aaron Smith — were to call time on their international careers, with others including Ardie Savea, Richie Mo'unga, Beauden Barrett and Shannon Frizell heading to Japan.

Writing before the final on Oct. 26, The Roar reported that the All Blacks would experience a changing of the guard the next season, and noted that the team's own social media channels described the World Cup final selection as the "Last Dance". Dane Coles, a 2015 World Cup winner, would call time on his career, while his tight-five teammates Retallick and Whitelock — the latter bidding to become the first player to win the Webb Ellis Cup for a third time — would head overseas, and fellow World Cup winners Aaron Smith and Beauden Barrett would also head to Japan.

Coles, labelled by Samisoni Taukei'aho as a "Grandad" type figure in the All Blacks, was even denied the chance of a farewell send-off after missing selection for the final. Foster called the conversation with the 36-year-old the hardest of his coaching life: "Yeah, tough. We don't want to talk too much about post-game stuff, but that was a tough one, probably the toughest I have had as a coach. He took it the way I expected him to. He's a champion." After the final, The Roar added that Robertson would have an almighty task on his hands given the scale of the departures.



---


# Foster Rejects The Favourites Label Against Argentina

Although the All Blacks were 18-point favourites for the opening 2023 World Cup semi-final, Ian Foster rejected the premise that his side sees itself that way: "Firstly, you've never heard us say we're favourites."

His grounds for rejecting the label are recent results and a limit on what the past predicts. Argentina had knocked over the All Blacks the previous year in Christchurch, as well as inflicting a maiden defeat in 2020 in Sydney, and New Zealand had themselves suffered a shock semi-final loss to Eddie Jones' England in 2019. Foster also argued that familiarity does not transfer to this stage: "The past sets us up beautifully for both teams. We do know each other but we don't know each other in terms of a Rugby World Cup, so at this stage in the tournament it's new territory for us and as we've seen World Cups are very different."

He then converted the rejection into a demand on his own team: "We have learnt to greatly respect Argentina. They have a rich history of overachieving at the World Cup and have done a fantastic job to get here at the same level we are, so it is going to be a heck of a game." And: "We know these games are do or die. We're going to have to improve our performance. The stage gets bigger at this time in the tournament and you've got to grow your game. That's our strong focus. The best team on the night wins – Argentina has done that to us."



---


# Joe Schmidt's Coaching Record With Ireland And The All Blacks

Joe Schmidt took Ireland to the top of World Rugby's rankings while his Irish sides bombed out in successive World Cup quarter-finals under his leadership, and he later helped transform an All Blacks team that reached the 2023 World Cup final, as reported by The Roar on 11 December 2023.

His Ireland tenure is credited with more than results: Schmidt played an instrumental role in not just seeing them become one of the world's best teams but helped usher through transformational change off the field, as Ireland moved to a centralised system.

The New Zealander briefly exited the international coaching scene following the 2019 World Cup, citing a desire to move home to New Zealand to be closer to his family. After initially moving back into the coaching fray with the Blues in Super Rugby, he joined the All Blacks ahead of the previous year's Rugby Championship, as New Zealand Rugby shook up the All Blacks coaching team following their historic series loss to Andy Farrell's Irish. His expertise proved telling: he and Jason Ryan transformed the All Blacks and helped Ian Foster's side reach the final of that year's World Cup after stunning wins over Ireland and Argentina in the knockout stages.



---


# The Second Half Of The 2023 Rugby World Cup Final

New Zealand's only try of the 2023 Rugby World Cup final, scored by Beauden Barrett after a Mark Telea break, left them trailing by a single point when Richie Mo'unga missed the conversion — and that lone point proved the difference as the Springboks celebrated a remarkable victory.

The half turned on discipline and missed chances. Minutes into it Siya Kolisi was off after cannoning into Ardie Savea; he later returned, much to the anger of the New Zealanders in the crowd who were calling for justice. Sensing an opportunity to strike against 14 men, the All Blacks kicked for the corner on a couple of occasions out wide, and it came back to haunt them as their usually silky and composed skill sets failed them.

That pattern held when the TMO intervened after Aaron Smith thought he had a try in his final Test, only for an error at the lineout to cancel out the five-pointer. Eventually the All Blacks did have a try: Mark Telea, their best and biggest attacking threat all night, got on the outside and drew in two defenders before offloading to Beauden Barrett — but Mo'unga missed the conversion, leaving them a point behind.



---


# The Ireland Series Loss Backlash As All Blacks Motivation

The Roar argued on Oct. 26, 2023 that where the Springboks play for their country, the All Blacks were playing for themselves as much as anyone — and for the generation of players and leaders who would call time on their international careers at week's end — which is why the World Cup final was personal for the men in black.

The framing question is how New Zealand could withstand and overcome the hitherto unshakable wave of momentum and spirit the Springboks play with under Rassie Erasmus in that weekend's final. The grounds offered for the All Blacks' personal motivation are the backlash and toxicity that followed their historic home series loss to Ireland, described as a humbling and public reminder of the expectation of being an All Black — All Blacks social media managers were forced to delete a thousand comments an hour following the humbling series loss in Wellington.

The warrant is that the hurt persisted and became fuel: the pain of the days and weeks after that dark July, as well as the bumps and bruises along the way — including as recently as August when they suffered their biggest defeat to the Boks to lose the inaugural and prestigious Qatar Cup — still ran deep.



---


# Joe Schmidt's Wallabies Candidacy And The Rival Candidates

The Roar reported on 11 December 2023 that Joe Schmidt — the 2018 World Rugby coach of the year, former Ireland coach and All Blacks assistant — is interested in the vacant Wallabies coaching job, with Dan McKellar, Stephen Larkham, Andy Friend and Ian Foster also remaining interested in the role.

The link the report draws is personal. Peter Horne's close relationship with Schmidt could be one of the keys to landing him: after leaving his Irish post following the 2019 World Cup, ending six years in the job, Schmidt worked alongside Horne at World Rugby, and it is believed the duo have a strong working relationship.



---


# The Case For Schmidt Bringing Rugby Smarts To The Wallabies

Several sources told The Roar in December 2023 that Joe Schmidt is exactly the type of person the Wallabies need: the claim is that the highly detailed Schmidt would bring rugby smarts to the Australian program, and the warrant is that the Wallabies' detail and nous were clearly absent on the field over the previous year, which is precisely what his coaching supplies.

The evidence offered for that capability is what his Ireland teams demonstrably did: the manipulation and ability to play both sides of the ruck was clearly visible during his Irish tenure.

The argument also carries a political ground about acceptance within Australian rugby: should Rugby Australia move on him, Schmidt's backing would be largely supported by the Super Rugby franchises.

# The EU's Urgent Warning Letter To X

The European Union fired a public warning at Elon Musk-owned X (formerly Twitter) for failing to tackle illegal content circulating on the platform in the wake of Saturday's deadly attacks on Israel by Hamas terrorists based in the Gaza Strip — an "urgent" letter from internal market commissioner Thierry Breton that TechCrunch described as a very swift test of the bloc's newly updated content moderation rulebook. Breton shared the letter publicly, tweeting on October 10, 2023: "Following the terrorist attacks by Hamas against 🇮🇱, we have indications of X/Twitter being used to disseminate illegal content & disinformation in the EU. Urgent letter to @elonmusk on #DSA obligations". TechCrunch's later account places the letter on the Wednesday.

The letter's substance was twofold. Breton said the bloc had seen "indications" from "qualified sources" that X was being used to disseminate illegal content and disinformation in the EU following Saturday's attacks, then reminded X of the DSA's "very precise obligations" on content moderation: "When you receive notices of illegal content in the EU, you must be timely, diligent and objective in taking action and removing the relevant content when warranted." Separately, the European Commission raised concerns about the spread of disinformation on X related to the terrorist attacks and their aftermath.

On the disinformation side Breton was specific about what had been reported and what he wanted done: "Public media and civil society organisations widely report instances of fake and manipulated images and facts circulating on your platform in the EU, such as repurposed old images of unrelated armed conflicts or military footage that actually originated from video games. This appears to be manifestly false or misleading information," he wrote. "I therefore invite you to urgently ensure that your systems are effective, and report on the crisis measures taken to my team."

TechCrunch's own characterisation of the platform at that moment was blunter than the letter's: rather than tackling the problem, it wrote, X "appears to be turning into an engine of disinformation" — one that had demonstrably enabled the very swift amplification of a smorgasbord of toxic fakes around the Israel-Hamas war, falsehoods that might be trying to manipulate opinion around the conflict, or otherwise exploit horrific events to drive engagement (clickbait) or for even more cynical and potentially harmful ends.



---


# EU Enforcement Steps Against X Over DSA Compliance

Between 10 and 13 October 2023 the European Union escalated against Elon Musk-owned X in two steps: a public warning letter on Wednesday from internal market commissioner Thierry Breton, and then, late on Thursday, a formal request for information sent by the Commission under the Digital Services Act. Crucially, no investigation had been opened at that point — EU officials confirmed to TechCrunch that an investigation had not been taken, and TechCrunch substantially revised its original report to make clear that a formal request for information, while it could prefigure a formal announcement of an investigation, is not yet that formal technical step.

The warning came first. In his "urgent" letter, shared on X by Breton himself, the bloc sent the strongest signal yet that it believed Musk's platform was in breach of the DSA — though this was by no means Musk's first warning. Breton wrote that the EU had "indications" that X was being used to disseminate illegal content and disinformation in the EU following Saturday's attacks, then reminded the company of the DSA's "very precise obligations" on content moderation: "When you receive notices of illegal content in the EU, you must be timely, diligent and objective in taking action and removing the relevant content when warranted," he warned, adding, "We have, from qualified sources, reports about potentially illegal content circulating on your service despite flags from relevant authorities." He also took issue with a change X had made the previous night to the public interest policy under which it judges newsworthiness — the test for whether posts that infringe its rules may nonetheless remain on the site — which Breton said had left "many European users uncertain" about how X applies its own rules. That matters under the DSA because the regulation requires platforms to be clear and transparent about their rules and how they apply them, "particularly relevant when it comes to violent and terrorist content that appears to circulate on your platform." Breton further said X should have "proportionate and effective mitigation measures" in place to tackle "the risks to public security and civic discourse stemming from disinformation." The EU asked Musk to make contact with relevant law enforcement authorities and Europol and to "ensure that you respond promptly to their requests", flagged unspecified additional DSA compliance issues his team would raise "shortly" — "with a specific request" — and gave Musk a deadline of 24 hours to respond, stipulating that his answer would be added to the bloc's assessment file on X's DSA compliance. The letter closed: "I remind you that following the opening of a potential investigation and a finding of non-compliance, penalties can be imposed."

The formal request for information followed. It came after the Wednesday warning about reports of illegal content and disinformation targeting the Israel-Hamas war circulating on the platform, and after Twitter's CEO sent a high-level, non-specific response to that warning. The Commission said it was looking at X's compliance with the DSA across a number of areas — its policies and practices regarding notices on illegal content; complaint handling; risk assessment; and measures to mitigate the risks identified. In its press release the EU wrote that "This request follows indications received by the Commission services of the alleged spreading of illegal content and disinformation, in particular the spreading of terrorist and violent content and hate speech," adding that the ask also addressed other aspects of DSA compliance.

The request carried explicit deadlines and consequences. X had until October 18 to provide information about "the activation and functioning of X's crisis response protocol", and until October 31 to respond to the other requests. "Based on the assessment of X replies, the Commission will assess next steps," the Commission wrote. "This could entail the formal opening of proceedings pursuant to Article 66 of the DSA." The regulation also includes powers to impose fines for "incorrect, incomplete or misleading information in response to a request for information", and the EU added that "In case of failure to reply by X, the Commission may decide to request the information by decision. In this case, failure to reply by the deadline could lead to the imposition of period penalties." TechCrunch noted that the pace at which regulators were moving was a strong indication of the bloc's direction of travel, and that its revised report also corrected an error in the original which had referred to Interpol rather than Europol.



---


# EU Warnings To Other Platforms

X was not the only platform the European Union warned over Israel-Hamas war content in October 2023: TikTok and Meta were warned too, but X drew markedly greater attention from the bloc. Both TechCrunch reports carrying these details are dated 13 October 2023, and the warnings they describe were issued "in recent days" and "earlier this week" relative to that date.

Meta, the subject of one of the two reports, is described as "not alone in being warned by the bloc over content concerns attached to the Israel-Hamas war." Elon Musk's X "has been singled out for even greater attention here" — the bloc issued an "urgent" warning earlier that week and then followed it with a formal request for information about X's compliance approach. TikTok also received a warning from the EU, framed in one report as being about DSA content risks related to the conflict and in the other as being about disinformation related to the war.

The EU's sharper focus on X has a documented antecedent in the same reporting: back in September, a study commissioned via the EU's Code of Practice suggested X is the worst of the major platforms when it comes to spreading disinformation.



---


# The EU's First Formal DSA Proceeding, Against X

On 18 December 2023 the European Commission announced the opening of a "formal proceeding" against Elon Musk's X, making it the first confirmed investigation opened by the European Union under its rebooted digital rulebook, the Digital Services Act (DSA). The investigation will look at whether the social networking platform may have breached rules linked to risk management, content moderation, dark patterns, advertising transparency and data access for researchers.

The Commission set out the evidentiary basis for the step: "On the basis of the preliminary investigation conducted so far, including on the basis of an analysis of the risk assessment report submitted by X in September, X's Transparency report published on 3 November, and X's replies to a formal request for information, which, among others, concerned the dissemination of illegal content in the context of Hamas' terrorist attacks against Israel, the Commission has decided to open formal infringement proceedings against X under the Digital Services Act."

The EU added that "if proven, these failures would constitute infringements of Articles 34(1), 34(2) and 35(1), 16(5) and 16(6), 25(1), 39 and 40(12) of the DSA," and said it will now carry out an in-depth investigation "as a matter of priority." Internal market commissioner Thierry Breton announced the same day that the proceedings covered a suspected breach of obligations to counter illegal content and disinformation, a suspected breach of transparency obligations, and suspected deceptive design of the user interface.

qid: Does the TechCrunch article claim that Google's anticompetitive behavior specifically harms news publishers' revenue, while The Age article suggests a general acceptance of foul play by Google without specifying the impact on revenue?
context:
# Helena World Chronicle's Class Action Antitrust Suit Against Google

A class action lawsuit filed in the week of 15 December 2023 in the U.S. District Court in D.C. accuses Google and parent company Alphabet of anticompetitive behavior in violation of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act and others, on behalf of news publishers. The case was filed by Arkansas-based publisher Helena World Chronicle, which argues that Google "siphons off" news publishers' content, their readers and their ad revenue through anticompetitive means, and it specifically cites new AI technologies such as Google's Search Generative Experience (SGE) and the Bard AI chatbot as worsening the problem.

Helena World Chronicle owns and publishes two weekly newspapers in Arkansas. In the complaint it argues that Google is "starving the free press" by sharing publishers' content on Google, losing them "billions of dollars."

Beyond damages, the suit asks for an injunction that would require Google to obtain consent from publishers before using their website data to train its general artificial intelligence products, including Google's own and those of rivals. It also asks that publishers who opt out of SGE still be allowed to show up in Google search results, among other things.

The law firm handling the case is Hausfeld, whose announcement states that "the anticompetitive effects of Google's scheme cause profound harm to competition, to consumers, to labor, and to a democratic free press," and that "Plaintiff Helena World Chronicle, LLC invokes the Sherman Act and Clayton Act to seek class-wide monetary and injunctive relief to restore and ensure competition for digital news and reference publishing and set up guardrails to preserve a free marketplace of ideas in the new era of artificial intelligence."



---


# The Claim That SGE And Bard Appropriate Publisher Content

The Helena World Chronicle lawsuit claims that Google's recent advances in AI-based search were implemented with "the goal of discouraging end-users from visiting the websites of Class members who are part of the digital news and publishing line of commerce." The grounds are that Google's AI products both retain users and consume publisher content without permission.

On the Search Generative Experience, the suit argues that SGE offers web searchers a way to seek information in a conversational mode but ultimately keeps users in Google's "walled garden" as it "plagiarizes" their content. The warrant that turns this into a harm publishers cannot escape is that publishers also cannot block SGE, because it uses the same web crawler as Google's general search service, GoogleBot — so opting out of the AI experience would mean opting out of search itself.

On Bard, the suit says Google's Bard AI was trained on a dataset that included "news, magazine and digital publications," citing both a 2023 report from the News Media Alliance and a Washington Post article about AI training data. The Post, which worked with researchers at the Allen Institute for AI, had found that News and Media sites were the third largest category of AI training data.

The case points to other concerns too, such as changing AdSense rates and evidence of improper spoliation of evidence on Google's part through its destruction of chat messages — an issue raised in the recent Epic Games lawsuit against Google over app store antitrust issues, which Epic won.



---


# Wired's Retracted Claim That Google Manipulates Search Queries

In October 2023, Wired posted an opinion article by lawyer and privacy advocate Megan Gray alleging that Google had accidentally revealed during the trial that it manipulates people's search queries for maximum ad revenue — the example given being the replacement of a search for "children's clothing" with "NIKOLAI-brand kidswear" — and Wired subsequently removed the article for not meeting its standards.

Google rejected the claim in very strong terms, saying the piece was misleading and inaccurate and denying that it ever altered search terms. The Age drew a lesson from the episode's reach: the degree to which the article was shared on social media and boosted in write-ups at other outlets shows just how willing people are to accept foul play on Google's part, and a suspicion of privacy invasion and inappropriate data handling follows the company at all times. The article placed the episode in the wider context of the US case — which, having to prove Google somehow broke the law to achieve the status quo, could be an uphill battle for the government, but which offers everyone else a rare opportunity for insight into what the tech giant does with its enormous market share, and whether it is still focused on being the best or uses its ubiquity to squeeze users for money at the expense of product quality.



---


# Epic's Opening Statement: Bribes And Blocks

Epic lead attorney Gary Bornstein's case that Android functions as an unlawful monopoly rested on characterising Google as a bully and a cheat that "bribes" or "blocks" any attempt to compete with Android's Google Play store — with the resulting status quo being that the vast, vast majority of Android app installs come from Google Play, and only a tiny sliver is attributable to the Galaxy Store that comes preinstalled on every Samsung phone.

The grounds were money and conduct. Bornstein showed jurors charts of Google's fat app profit margins — 70 percent on $12 billion in revenue a year, says Epic — and pointed out several ugly-seeming ways Google has allegedly attempted to keep anyone from taking that money away, like paying game developers not to build their own app stores or standalone app launchers as Epic did with Fortnite. "Google pays actual and potential competitors not to compete. Literally gives them money and other things of value," said Bornstein. "It's like Google saying, 'Here's $360 million' — that's an actual number you'll hear about — why don't you sit this one out and let me win?"

The warrant linking payments to consumer harm was left mostly implicit on day one. The upshot for consumers, Epic's earlier legal filings have suggested, is that we pay higher prices for apps than we would if there were more competition and/or lower app store and payment processing fees; but while that will probably come up later in the trial, Epic chose to focus more on simply painting Google as the bad guy on day one.



---


# What A Ruling Against Google Would Mean For Big Tech

A ruling against Google would not stop at Google: the remedy would likely resemble the Microsoft settlement and the outcome would ripple through the other pending Big Tech cases, because enforcers are using this trial to demonstrate that antitrust law can still take on the largest and most powerful companies in the world.

The grounds for the first half of that claim are the available remedies. If the judge rules against Google, the outcome could look a lot like the Microsoft deal, in which the computer company was required to change its behavior and share its APIs with third-party developers, and was also banned from making anticompetitive and exclusive deals with computer manufacturers. Google might likewise end up having to turn over all or most of the data it has collected to other search engines so they can improve their products and attract more users — a remedy scaled to the disparity the DOJ has cited, that Google gets 16 times more data than Bing does everyday.

The grounds for the ripple effect are the cases already queued behind this one. The FTC sued Amazon in September for using anticompetitive and unfair strategies to illegally maintain its monopoly power. The DOJ has been investigating Apple for years over the company's policy for third-party apps on its devices and whether it unfairly favors its own products. And there is an ongoing case between the FTC and Facebook, in which the agency calls on Facebook to sell Instagram and WhatsApp.

The warrant joining grounds to claim is enforcers' own stake in the result: they will want to show that antitrust law is still relevant and can successfully take on the biggest, most powerful companies in the world, so a win here sets the template the neighbouring cases are argued against. The scope condition is that nothing was settled as of this report — the case is expected to continue for several weeks, bringing to a head one of the biggest fights in tech antitrust since the U.S. took Microsoft to trial in the 1990s.



---


# Projected Publisher Traffic Losses From AI Search

Publishers believe they will lose somewhere between 20% and 40% of their website traffic once Google's AI products fully roll out, according to a Wall Street Journal report noted by TechCrunch on 15 December 2023. That report also led with a modelling result from the online magazine The Atlantic: when The Atlantic modelled what would happen if Google integrated AI into search, it found that 75% of the time the AI would answer the user's query without requiring a click-through to its website, losing it traffic.

The stakes are set by how much publisher traffic Google currently supplies. According to data from Similarweb cited in the same coverage, Google today drives nearly 40% of publishers' traffic, so a shift to AI-answered queries could have a major impact on publishers' traffic going forward. The suit filed by Helena World Chronicle takes up precisely this question of how AI will impact publishers' businesses.

Some publishers are trying to get ahead of the problem: Axel Springer inked a deal with OpenAI in the same week to license its news for AI model training.

qid: Who is the individual accused of using a colleague as a front for unauthorized access to customer funds, persuading a former coworker to join his trading and development ventures, and making an executive decision to use a substantial amount of customer money to settle with a competitor, all while facing allegations of committing fraud for personal gain, as reported by Fortune, The Verge, and TechCrunch?
context:
# The Prosecution's Opening Statement Against Bankman-Fried

Thane Rehn, a prosecutor for the government, opened the case against Sam Bankman-Fried with the line "One year ago, it looked like the defendant was on the top of the world," and then argued that this appearance was false: "all of that, all of it, was built on lies," he declared to the jury, adding "Behind the curtains, he was not what he appeared to be." Rehn described a defendant who, as former CEO of FTX, oversaw a supposedly thriving crypto exchange, jetted between international locales, hobnobbed with celebrities like Tom Brady and Larry David, and repeatedly emphasized to customers that their money was safe and secure.

What followed was a roughly 30-minute story that repeatedly emphasized how Bankman-Fried allegedly stole customer funds to facilitate his jet-setting lifestyle, donate millions to political candidates, and finance risky bets. Rehn also directly contested the media framing of the defendant: he was not a crypto "boy" genius, as so many in the media — Fortune included — have written, but a "man" who "stole billions of dollars from thousands of victims." Rehn closed the characterization with a promise to the jury: "You will see the full picture."



---


# Caroline Ellison's Guilty Plea And First Day Of Testimony

Caroline Ellison, head of the hedge fund Alameda Research during its implosion along with FTX, took the stand on October 10th, 2023 having already pleaded guilty to criminal charges — fraud, conspiracy to commit fraud, and money laundering — and told the jury that Bankman-Fried "directed me to commit these crimes." She quantified the taking: "We ultimately took about $14 billion, some of which we were not able to pay back."

Her long-anticipated first day took the form of walking through a damning spreadsheet she had prepared for her ex and boss, now the defendant in a criminal fraud trial. She entered hunched in on herself, wearing a dusty rose dress with a gray blazer over it, looking less like an executive than like a girl who had borrowed her boyfriend's coat because she was cold. Asked by the prosecution to identify Bankman-Fried, she had trouble finding him and gazed around the courtroom for more than 20 seconds — apparently he was incognito with his new haircut — and when she did spot him she identified him as the one wearing a suit, which got chuckles from the rest of the defense table, also all in suits. She tilted her head down to answer questions and lifted it when she had finished each answer.

The defendant's own reaction registered the shift: Bankman-Fried had been vibrating slightly during Wang's testimony, and during Ellison's his bouncing became more noticeable. By the end of the day, The Verge's reporter wrote, the spreadsheet seemed like a sideshow.



---


# FTX's Inner Circle: Family And Friends Implicated

The Verge's October 26th, 2023 account of the trial catalogued how everyone who loved Bankman-Fried most in the world was caught up in the case. Adam Yedidia, his college roommate, testified with immunity because he was concerned he may have unknowingly worked on code that contributed to the fraud; "I love you Sam," he had texted at one point, "I'm not going anywhere" — that was before he realized FTX had stolen customer funds, at which point he resigned. Nishad Singh, a longtime family friend, copped to what sounded an awful lot like classic embezzlement, saying he had backdated transactions on FTX to help create doctored balance sheets to show to investors, and pleaded guilty to six charges including wire fraud, money laundering, and conspiracy counts around his political donations. Caroline Ellison, Bankman-Fried's ex-girlfriend, told the court about the seven phony balance sheets she had created and was clear that Alameda took customer funds, that Bankman-Fried knew about it, and that he even invested them against her advice.

His family was drawn in too. Joe Bankman, his father, is among the people included in the "small group chat," the Signal group where the FTX inner circle strategized during the exchange's last days. Barbara Fried's political action committee, Mind the Gap, is among the entities that received FTX customer money as political donations; Fried and Bankman lived together in a Bahamas house purchased for them using FTX investor funds, according to a financial expert called by the prosecution, and in a lawsuit filed by FTX's bankruptcy estate the two are alleged to have been given $10 million of FTX customer funds. Gabe Bankman-Fried's nonprofit, Guarding Against Pandemics, got millions from FTX; he was also in a Signal group chat, Donations Processing, that Singh says was used to coordinate the transfer of FTX and Alameda money to various political causes, and in that chat he can be seen recommending that some donations be made "in the dark" to avoid public relations headaches. Singh also said Gabe had an assistant fly to the Bahamas with a stack of blank checks for Singh to sign.

The consequences outlast the trial. Wang, Singh, and Ellison are now felons; even if they never do time — and they may very well be imprisoned or subjected to house arrest — their lives are irrevocably changed, not least by whatever restitution requirements they face, they are barred from taking certain kinds of jobs, and there is the publicity. Bankman, Fried, and Gabe Bankman-Fried's reputations are tarnished, and in the political arenas where they once operated they are suddenly undesirable. Beyond the courtroom, everyone who had money trapped on the exchange when it collapsed — as a result of Alameda purloining customers' funds — had their lives altered: even if they are made whole by the bankruptcy proceedings, that is still money they should have had access to at any time, which may mean houses that were not purchased, medical procedures left undone, and life savings lost. The reporter's summary: it is a Greek tragedy, precipitated by one man's character flaw, the arrogance of Sam Bankman-Fried.



---


# Testimony At The SBF Trial

Across the first three weeks of the trial, a run of former colleagues, an outside investor and a forensic accounting expert testified that FTX customer money flowed into Alameda Research and out again to other uses, and that FTX's investors were never told about the two firms' special relationship. TechCrunch's running coverage, published 2023-10-06, summarises each week.

In week one, FTX's co-founder and CTO Gary Wang testified Thursday on the extent to which Alameda Research was used for whatever purposes he and SBF saw fit: according to Wang, the crypto trading firm pulled funding directly from FTX customers, whose transactions would be funneled toward Alameda and then directed elsewhere. Thursday also brought testimony from Matt Huang, co-founder and managing partner at crypto investment firm Paradigm, which invested $278 million in FTX across 2021 and 2022 and is part of a class-action lawsuit accusing it and others of defrauding customers by promoting FTX. His testimony centered around being left uninformed about FTX's utilization of customer money to keep Alameda Research afloat — a practice Huang says would have halted his involvement — and covered his relationship with FTX stretching back to 2019.

Week two's standout testimony came from Alameda Research's former CEO Caroline Ellison, who claimed she took $14 billion from customers to repay debts to lenders, using them as a line of credit under the instruction of SBF. Ellison also went into detail about how a $2 billion venture fund, FTX Ventures, was funded by money that had previously been allocated to Alameda from third-party lenders. And though there are no charges of bribery in the case, she also testified to paying Chinese officials $150 million to restore access to $1 billion in frozen trading accounts.

The third week featured a couple of noteworthy moments for the prosecution. FTX's former general counsel Can Sun, like many of SBF's former colleagues, opted to cooperate with authorities and testified that SBF asked him to create a theoretical "legal justification" for the use of billions in consumer funds just days before FTX filed for bankruptcy. Robert Boroujerdi, managing director of the hedge fund Third Point, testified about his experience working with SBF and FTX in a partnership that ultimately resulted in a $60 million investment and a lack of awareness about the special relationship between Alameda Research and FTX; had he known of such a relationship, he testified, Third Point would not have invested in FTX in the first place. And earlier in the week, Peter Easton — a University of Notre Dame professor who helped the government prosecution of Enron and WorldCom — testified about what he uncovered after tracing the flow of billions of dollars between Alameda Research and FTX: much of that funding came from customers, and Easton testified that he found user deposits were used by both FTX and Alameda to purchase real estate, make investments or direct funding toward political causes and charities.

qid: Was the policy on price matching for customers at HP inconsistent according to The Verge before Polygon reported on the ineligibility for price matching on purchases?
context:
# HP Price Match Policy

According to HP's website, the company will match the current pre-tax price for new comparable PCs and for identical HP printer, display, and accessory model numbers from nationally recognized online retailers such as Dell, Amazon, Newegg, and Best Buy. For computers the specs have to be the same, but the product model number does not need to be identical. The claim must be made at the time of purchase by calling 1-800-888-0229 — you cannot request a price match via email or chat.

The policy does not extend to items bought during promotional periods, and it does not apply to membership stores like Costco and Sam's Club.

There is a separate post-purchase route: if you find a comparable product at a lower price during the return period, you can email HP at myhpsales@hp.com. That applies only to branded HP products and not to products purchased during certain promotional events, including Green Monday and products on sale during the week of Thanksgiving and the week after. The Verge published this summary on October 25th, 2023, illustrating it with HP's Spectre x360 14.



---


# Lenovo Price Match And Guarantee Refund

Lenovo matches pricing on comparable PCs from Lenovo, HP, or Dell with the same key specs, as long as they are sold through a list of recognized retailers. The preconditions are that the comparable PC must be in stock and readily available from both Lenovo and the competing retailer, and you have to contact a Lenovo sales rep in order to facilitate the match. You cannot take advantage of coupons or special discounts while receiving a price match, the policy does not apply to membership stores like Costco, and it does not apply to "Marketplace" items where third parties fulfill the order — so double-check that you bought the product directly from the retailer.

Lenovo also offers a separate price guarantee refund for laptops and personal desktop computers bought from Lenovo.com within 30 days of purchase. To receive a refund you must contact Customer Care and show the lower price of the identical product offered on Lenovo.com. This policy does not apply to doorbuster or clearance products. The Verge published this summary on October 25th, 2023.



---


# B&H Photo And Costco Price Adjustment

B&H says it might be able to honor a current lower price or match the price of a competitor, but it does so on a case-by-case basis rather than under a fixed policy; to ask, you have to contact its Customer Service team using the on-site chat, email, or by calling 800-606-6969 / 212-444-6615.

Costco does not price-match with competitors. According to its website, however, it will issue a credit for the difference between the price a member paid and a promotional price if you bought the item online at Costco and requested the credit up to 30 days before the change in price. If you bought the product from a Costco warehouse location, visit the membership counter at the store where you made the purchase. The boundary The Verge flagged on October 25th, 2023: Costco does not price-match items bought from Costco warehouses against Costco.com purchases.



---


# Holiday Price Matching Policies, 2023

Some major retailers ensured price protection on purchases during the 2023 holiday season, but the terms differ sharply by retailer, so whether you get price matching depends on where and when you shop.

Amazon does not price match, which Polygon calls annoying but tolerable since it often has the lowest prices of all retailers anyway; Amazon only protects the price on pre-orders carrying its "Pre-order Price Guarantee," which ensures you pay the lowest amount a product sells for before it launches. Best Buy not only matches prices from "qualified competitors" but says on its site that most products bought between the article's publication and December 30 can be price-matched through January 13, 2024. Walmart's policy says it will not price match with competitors, nor does it price match for products purchased online that later decrease in price. Target says purchases made between October 22 and December 24 can be price-adjusted if the cost falls within that span and you show proof of purchase; eligibility exists, but the rules for submitting documentation vary depending on whether you shop online or in store.



---


# Retailer Price-Matching Overview

To avoid overpaying, check the price-matching policy of the retailer you bought from: many retailers promise to match a lower price you have found elsewhere in order to keep customers happy and prevent them from going elsewhere, which The Verge noted on October 25th, 2023 was information that could come in handy with Black Friday and Cyber Monday just around the corner. The frustration it addresses is buying a new pair of headphones, an OLED TV, or a backpack only to find out you could have got it for a lot cheaper somewhere else.

Three cautions apply before using any of these policies. First, all price-matching policies have a number of rules attached to them: The Verge summarised some of them but advised readers to follow the links it provided and read each policy carefully. Second, and logically enough, retailers that serve as marketplaces for other sellers, such as Costco, do not have price-matching policies. Third, there are always exceptions to the rules — if you are looking for a deal on a product and you know it is available for a lower price elsewhere, or was previously offered at the same retailer, it never hurts to call or chat with a customer service rep and ask if they will match the price.

The illustration The Verge used: if Best Buy offers a better discount than Target on the latest Kindle Paperwhite, Target will refund you the difference.



---


# GameStop And Google Store Price Matching

GameStop does not mention an official price-matching policy on its website. Last year, however, GameStop tweeted that the store will price-match items sold and shipped by Amazon as long as they are available online or in-store, and although the tweet mentioned only Amazon, others have reported the store will price-match items purchased from Target and elsewhere.

The Google Store's policy is explicit but narrow. Google will match online pricing from select retailers — specifically Amazon, Best Buy, Walmart, B&H Photo, and Target — if a request is made within the standard return period. It does not match preorder pricing from other retailers or carrier deals; the product must be identical, right down to the color and configuration, and must be in stock; and you need to provide a public link to the promo page or product listing to verify the rival's price. You may also get the difference if a product purchased from the Google Store drops in price within the standard return period. To get the price match or correction, contact Google. The Verge published this summary on October 25th, 2023.



---


# Walmart Price Match Policy

Walmart does not price-match the prices of its competitors. Its online store does offer price-matching on items purchased from Walmart stores, but only if the item is in stock at Walmart.com.

The boundaries of that narrow policy are geographic, temporal, and structural. It does not apply to shoppers who live in Alaska, Hawaii, or Puerto Rico; it does not apply to special event prices, like those seen during Black Friday; Walmart does not retroactively price-match items bought from Walmart.com that have dropped in price after the time of purchase; and it does not price-match items purchased from Walmart Marketplace retailers or third-party sellers. The Verge published this summary on October 25th, 2023.



---


# Amazon Price Matching And Return Policy

Amazon does not offer price matching — full stop. You can contact customer support, but even if you are an Amazon Prime customer they are not likely to help you out.

The workaround Amazon's own rules allow is its return policy, which The Verge described on October 25th, 2023 as pretty liberal: you can often return an item you purchased from Amazon if it becomes available for less elsewhere, or at Amazon itself, and then simply repurchase the product wherever it is cheapest.



---


# Home Depot And Lowe's Price Match Policies

The Home Depot will match the price of identical, in-stock products from other retailers, except for membership-based wholesalers. To claim it, bring the ad or listing with you in-store to the register. Two limits apply: the policy does not cover special events like Black Friday, and The Home Depot will only honor requests submitted by the original buyer — no friends or family allowed.

Lowe's will match the price of identical, in-stock products when you present an ad, product listing, or photo from a qualifying online or local retailer, including Amazon, Best Buy, Target, and Walmart. To request a match, head to the store, call 1-877-465-6937, or chat online. The product must have been purchased directly from the retailer and not a third-party seller; the policy does not apply to special sales like Black Friday and other holiday promotions; and Lowe's does not match prices from one Lowe's store to another. The Verge published these summaries on October 25th, 2023.



---
