qid: Which company spent $26.3 billion to ensure its position as the default search engine, while being accused of manipulating search results to maximize ad revenue and siphoning off content and ad revenue from news publishers, as reported by TechCrunch and The Age?
context:
# US v. Google: Two Months Into The Search Antitrust Trial

As of TechCrunch's November 13, 2023 roundup, the Justice Department's landmark antitrust case against Google was nearly two months old, and the trial record was still producing fresh revelations. TechCrunch framed it as one of the biggest fights in tech antitrust since the U.S. took Microsoft to trial in the 1990s.

An earlier roundup had already surfaced that Google spent $26.3 billion in 2021 making itself the default search engine across platforms, and that Google tried to have Chrome preinstalled on iPhones. Over the couple of weeks preceding this roundup, more of Google's inner workings came to light, including some of the search engine's most lucrative search queries, the shape of the revenue-share agreements between Google and Android OEMs, and why Expedia has a bone to pick with Google.



---


# Google Paid $26.3 Billion In 2021 For Default Search Placement

Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to multiple browsers, phones and platforms — from companies including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla — to be everyone's default search engine. The figure was revealed by Google's search head Prabhakar Raghavan when he testified in court on October 28, according to The Verge.

About $18 billion of that total went directly to Apple, according to a New York Times report published earlier in October 2023, and Google has had its deal with Apple in place since 2003 — so the payment is the current year of a two-decade arrangement, not a one-off. Questioned on the amount of money Google spends to get first pick of search engines, Pichai said the decision was made with the consumer in mind: Google pays big bucks to be everywhere so that it can take in all the data and be the best search engine across different companies' devices, he said, according to The Verge.

The trial also produced evidence that Google understood the value of defaults very early on. U.S. Justice Department lawyer Meagan Bellshaw showed Pichai a 2007 email from a Google product strategy meeting containing data showing that when people changed their browser homepage to Google, they did 15% more Google searches, and that when they switched away, their Google searches dropped 27%. The email summarizing that meeting, sent to Pichai as well as other Google leaders, read: "Nitin argues that focusing on homepage market share is one of the most effective things we can do to make gains in search market share," according to The Verge.



---


# Wired's Retracted Claim That Google Manipulates Search Queries

In October 2023, Wired posted an opinion article by lawyer and privacy advocate Megan Gray alleging that Google had accidentally revealed during the trial that it manipulates people's search queries for maximum ad revenue — the example given being the replacement of a search for "children's clothing" with "NIKOLAI-brand kidswear" — and Wired subsequently removed the article for not meeting its standards.

Google rejected the claim in very strong terms, saying the piece was misleading and inaccurate and denying that it ever altered search terms. The Age drew a lesson from the episode's reach: the degree to which the article was shared on social media and boosted in write-ups at other outlets shows just how willing people are to accept foul play on Google's part, and a suspicion of privacy invasion and inappropriate data handling follows the company at all times. The article placed the episode in the wider context of the US case — which, having to prove Google somehow broke the law to achieve the status quo, could be an uphill battle for the government, but which offers everyone else a rare opportunity for insight into what the tech giant does with its enormous market share, and whether it is still focused on being the best or uses its ubiquity to squeeze users for money at the expense of product quality.



---


# Default Search Engine

## Definition

The default search engine is the search provider a device, browser, or platform is pre-configured to use unless a user actively changes the setting — the search box that runs when a person types a query without first choosing an alternative, such as Google on the iPhone's Safari address bar or Firefox's search bar.

## Context

The term is central to *US v. Google*, the DOJ's antitrust case, because default status is the mechanism through which Google secures the overwhelming share of search queries: the Information Services Agreement (ISA) between Apple and Google, in place since 2002/2003, makes Google the default on all Apple devices, and Google separately pays Samsung, Mozilla, and other partners for the same status.
Apple executive Eddy Cue testified that Apple's iPhone setup flow deliberately omits any search-engine choice screen, arguing that presenting users with unfamiliar alternatives would harm the setup experience, while conceding the ISA does not permit Apple to offer such a choice.
Google spent $26.3 billion in 2021 on default-placement deals across browsers, phones, and platforms — about $18 billion of that to Apple alone — a scale that the DOJ used to argue Google understands the mechanism's value: internal 2007 data showed users who set Google as their homepage searched 15% more, while switching away dropped searches 27%.
The Mozilla/Yahoo episode shows the same mechanism working in reverse: when Firefox switched its default from Google to Yahoo under a 2014 deal, Mozilla's CEO testified that user retention declined, illustrating how disruptive changing the default can be even when a paying competitor is involved.
Outside the antitrust trial, the term also frames ordinary consumer behavior: an investor in e-commerce search startup Deft described users' "natural behavior" as following the path of least resistance and just using the default search engine, meaning challenger search products must offer a high-value proposition to displace that inertia.

## Key Characteristics

- **Set by agreement, not by user choice** — default status on major platforms (Apple's Safari/iOS, Android OEMs, Firefox) is typically established through commercial deals (e.g., the Apple-Google ISA, Yahoo-Mozilla's $375M/year deal) rather than user selection at setup.
- **Backed by large recurring payments** — Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 across partners to hold default placement, with roughly $18 billion of that going to Apple.
- **Technically reversible but rarely changed** — Apple and Google both argued switching is easy, but DuckDuckGo's CEO countered that it takes "too many steps" to switch, and Google's own 2005 complaint about Internet Explorer's defaults argued that "most end users do not change defaults," so default status functions as durable market power.
- **Distinct from pre-installation** — Google's separate push to get Chrome and Search merely pre-installed (not necessarily defaulted) on Android and iPhones shows default status is a stronger, more contested tier than simple presence on a device.
- **Drives user behavior even outside browsers** — the concept extends to any search product; consumers default to "the path of least resistance," which challenger search startups must specifically overcome.

## Corpus References

Corpus notes whose source text references this term (evidence-backed, from `term_links.json`):

- [The Google Antitrust Case](google_antitrust_case.md)
- [The Hypocrisy Argument: Google Became The Monopoly It Denounced](google_default_hypocrisy_argument.md)
- [US v. Google: Two Months Into The Search Antitrust Trial](us_v_google_search_antitrust_trial_overview.md)



---


# Consumer Search Startups And Switching Barriers

The premise attacked is that a better search product wins users. The cautionary case is Neeva, founded by former Google execs, which tried to convince people to switch to paid and private search with additional features; earlier in 2023 the startup shut down its consumer efforts and eventually got acquired by Snowflake.

Adii Pienaar, an investor in Deft, said that Deft has to give compelling reasons to users to switch to its service. His grounds are behavioral rather than technical: "Users' natural behavior for search is to follow the path of least resistance, i.e. most people just pick up their phone and just use the default search engine."

The conclusion he draws sets the bar Deft must clear: "For Deft to change that behavior, they will need to create a high-value proposition."



---


# Search Quality Complaints Explained By Data Volume Growth

The Age argued that the common online complaint that "Google Search was a lot better 10 years ago" could absolutely be true, but that it would be a stretch to blame the company's monetisation practices when there is a much simpler explanation: the sheer growth in the data Google has to index.

The grounds are the volumes. In 2013, people were creating around 9 ZB of data every year — nine zettabytes, or nine trillion gigabytes — which Google had to index constantly, whereas in 2023 it is more like 120 ZB. The warrant is a change in kind as well as quantity: not a whole lot of that is static websites as it was a decade ago; it is live information that may be nested within various services and apps, which is harder to index well. The article then turned to what actually happens when we search, noting that Google has published extensive information about its Search procedures, so it is not difficult to get the company's own take on what happens in the background when you send off a query.

# The U.S. Justice Department's Parallel Antitrust Suits Against Google

The Helena World Chronicle class action arrives alongside the filing of the U.S. Justice Department's lawsuit against Google for monopolizing digital ad technologies, and the complaint also references the Justice Department's 2020 civil antitrust suit over search and search advertising.

The two government cases concern different markets: search and search advertising in the 2020 suit are distinct from the digital ad technologies at issue in the more recent one.



---


# Remedies Sought Against Google And The Ripple Effect On Big Tech Cases

The government's argument in US v. Google is that Google uses its platforms and its deals with partners to block out any competition in search or advertising, thereby hindering competitors from accessing the data they would need to improve their products. The grounds offered for this is a data asymmetry: the DOJ has said Google gets 16 times more data than Bing does every day, so exclusion from distribution compounds into a permanent quality gap for rivals.

The warrant joining the claim to the remedy is that if the deals are what starve rivals of data, then unwinding the deals and redistributing the data restores competition. On that logic, if Judge Amit Mehta rules against Google, the search giant may have to change its behavior and share its APIs with third-party developers; it may also be banned from making anticompetitive and exclusive deals with smartphone and computer manufacturers and wireless carriers; and Google might end up having to turn over all or most of the data it has collected to other search engines so they can improve their products and attract more users. Enforcers want to show that antitrust law remains relevant and that even though Google is basically the God of the internet, it is still no match for U.S. law.

The Google outcome could also have a ripple effect on other Big Tech cases. The FTC sued Amazon in September for using anticompetitive and unfair strategies to illegally maintain its monopoly power. The DOJ has been investigating Apple for years over the company's policy for third-party apps on its devices and whether it unfairly favors its own products. And there is an ongoing case between the FTC and Facebook, in which the agency calls on Facebook to sell Instagram and WhatsApp.

A class action lawsuit filed in the week of 15 December 2023 in the U.S. District Court in D.C. accuses Google and parent company Alphabet of anticompetitive behavior in violation of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act and others, on behalf of news publishers. The case was filed by Arkansas-based publisher Helena World Chronicle, which argues that Google "siphons off" news publishers' content, their readers and their ad revenue through anticompetitive means, and it specifically cites new AI technologies such as Google's Search Generative Experience (SGE) and the Bard AI chatbot as worsening the problem.

Helena World Chronicle owns and publishes two weekly newspapers in Arkansas. In the complaint it argues that Google is "starving the free press" by sharing publishers' content on Google, losing them "billions of dollars."

Beyond damages, the suit asks for an injunction that would require Google to obtain consent from publishers before using their website data to train its general artificial intelligence products, including Google's own and those of rivals. It also asks that publishers who opt out of SGE still be allowed to show up in Google search results, among other things.

The law firm handling the case is Hausfeld, whose announcement states that "the anticompetitive effects of Google's scheme cause profound harm to competition, to consumers, to labor, and to a democratic free press," and that "Plaintiff Helena World Chronicle, LLC invokes the Sherman Act and Clayton Act to seek class-wide monetary and injunctive relief to restore and ensure competition for digital news and reference publishing and set up guardrails to preserve a free marketplace of ideas in the new era of artificial intelligence."

Google's answer is that it is just doing business: everybody wants Google as the default engine because it is the best, and that, the company says, does not make its actions illegal.

The important boundary case is which Google antitrust matter this is. The 2020 search claim is separate from the one filed in January by the Department of Justice, along with eight states including New York, California and Colorado, which aims to "halt Google's anticompetitive scheme, unwind Google's monopolistic grip on the market and restore competition to digital advertising." The search case and the digital-advertising case are distinct proceedings and should not be conflated.

The trial is the venue in which the underlying numbers surface. Monday's hearing revealed plenty of juicy tidbits, including the $26.3 billion Google spent making itself the default search engine across platforms in 2021, and how Google tried to take it further and have Chrome preinstalled on iPhones.

The email summarizing that meeting, sent to Pichai as well as other Google leaders, read: "Nitin argues that focusing on homepage market share is one of the most effective things we can do to make gains in search market share," according to The Verge.



---


# What A Ruling Against Google Would Mean For Big Tech

A ruling against Google would not stop at Google: the remedy would likely resemble the Microsoft settlement and the outcome would ripple through the other pending Big Tech cases, because enforcers are using this trial to demonstrate that antitrust law can still take on the largest and most powerful companies in the world.

The grounds for the first half of that claim are the available remedies. If the judge rules against Google, the outcome could look a lot like the Microsoft deal, in which the computer company was required to change its behavior and share its APIs with third-party developers, and was also banned from making anticompetitive and exclusive deals with computer manufacturers. The DOJ has been investigating Apple for years over the company's policy for third-party apps on its devices and whether it unfairly favors its own products. And there is an ongoing case between the FTC and Facebook, in which the agency calls on Facebook to sell Instagram and WhatsApp.

The warrant joining grounds to claim is enforcers' own stake in the result: they will want to show that antitrust law is still relevant and can successfully take on the biggest, most powerful companies in the world, so a win here sets the template the neighbouring cases are argued against. # Class Action

## Definition

A class action, as it appears across this corpus, is a single lawsuit pursued on behalf of a group of similarly affected people rather than filed by each person individually.

The corpus documents several such suits from 2023: FTX customers against crypto promoters including Paradigm, a news publisher against Google, consumers against PayPal, and the Authors Guild against OpenAI.

It also shows the mechanism can be blocked by contract, as with Uber's terms of use barring class actions in sexual-assault cases.

## Context

The corpus shows the mechanism used across very different disputes: FTX customers brought a class-action lawsuit accusing crypto investment firm Paradigm and other promoters of defrauding customers by promoting the exchange, publisher Helena World Chronicle filed a class action antitrust suit against Google and Alphabet under the Sherman Act alleging AI tools like Search Generative Experience and Bard siphon off publishers' content and ad revenue, and consumers represented by law firm Hagens Berman filed a class action against PayPal over anti-steering rules that allegedly stifle competition from cheaper platforms like Stripe and Shopify.

The Authors Guild of America, representing Stephen King, John Grisham and 134 other authors, likewise filed its own class-action suit against OpenAI over unauthorized use of copyrighted books in training data, run in parallel to (but distinct from) comedian Sarah Silverman's separate, non-class suit.

Apple's earlier MacBook Pro keyboard class-action settlement is cited in the corpus as a business driver — the corpus notes the settlement cost probably factored into Apple's decision to redesign the keyboard, a change introduced alongside separate updates like a new camera and the removal of the Touch Bar.

## Key Characteristics

- **Collective standing** — a class action lets one or a few plaintiffs (e.g., Helena World Chronicle, the Authors Guild, unnamed FTX customers) litigate on behalf of an entire group with the same underlying grievance, rather than requiring each affected person to sue separately.
- **Can be contractually blocked** — the corpus shows companies can preempt this mechanism: under Uber's terms of use, class action lawsuits cannot be filed against the company in sexual assault cases, forcing survivors to litigate individually and preventing them from advocating for themselves collectively.
- **Used across dispute types** — the corpus applies the same mechanism to fraud (FTX), antitrust (Helena World Chronicle v. Google, PayPal anti-steering), and copyright (Authors Guild v. OpenAI) claims, showing it is a general procedural tool rather than one tied to a single area of law.
- **Settlement exposure shapes corporate behavior** — Apple's keyboard class-action settlement is presented in the corpus as a concrete cost that influenced a subsequent product redesign decision.
- **Defendants, not just plaintiffs, can be named as a group** — the FTX-related suit accuses Paradigm "and others" collectively of defrauding customers, showing the mechanism can target a class of co-defendants as well as aggregate a class of claimants.

## Background (external)

Cornell Law School's Legal Information Institute (Wex) defines a class action generically as "a procedural device that permits one or more plaintiffs to file and prosecute a lawsuit on behalf of a larger group, or 'class'" (Cornell Law School, Legal Information Institute, Wex: "class action," accessed 2026-09-02, https://www.law.cornell.edu/wex/class_action).

## Corpus References

Corpus notes whose source text references this term (evidence-backed, from `term_links.json`):

- [The M3 MacBook Pro Lineup And Its Configurations](m3_macbook_pro_lineup_and_configurations.md)

# Helena World Chronicle's Class Action Antitrust Suit Against Google

A class action lawsuit filed in the week of 15 December 2023 in the U.S. District Court in D.C. accuses Google and parent company Alphabet of anticompetitive behavior in violation of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act and others, on behalf of news publishers. The case was filed by Arkansas-based publisher Helena World Chronicle, which argues that Google "siphons off" news publishers' content, their readers and their ad revenue through anticompetitive means, and it specifically cites new AI technologies such as Google's Search Generative Experience (SGE) and the Bard AI chatbot as worsening the problem.

Helena World Chronicle owns and publishes two weekly newspapers in Arkansas. In the complaint it argues that Google is "starving the free press" by sharing publishers' content on Google, losing them "billions of dollars."

Beyond damages, the suit asks for an injunction that would require Google to obtain consent from publishers before using their website data to train its general artificial intelligence products, including Google's own and those of rivals. It also asks that publishers who opt out of SGE still be allowed to show up in Google search results, among other things.

The law firm handling the case is Hausfeld, whose announcement states that "the anticompetitive effects of Google's scheme cause profound harm to competition, to consumers, to labor, and to a democratic free press," and that "Plaintiff Helena World Chronicle, LLC invokes the Sherman Act and Clayton Act to seek class-wide monetary and injunctive relief to restore and ensure competition for digital news and reference publishing and set up guardrails to preserve a free marketplace of ideas in the new era of artificial intelligence."



---


# The U.S. Justice Department's Parallel Antitrust Suits Against Google

The Helena World Chronicle class action arrives alongside the filing of the U.S. Justice Department's lawsuit against Google for monopolizing digital ad technologies, and the complaint also references the Justice Department's 2020 civil antitrust suit over search and search advertising.

The two government cases concern different markets: search and search advertising in the 2020 suit are distinct from the digital ad technologies at issue in the more recent one.



---


# Google's Parallel Antitrust Proceedings In Late 2023

As of mid-November 2023, Google was fighting antitrust on more than one front at once. The Epic Games case was not its only antitrust case in trial: Google had settled a separate antitrust lawsuit with dating site Match Group the week before November 13, and on November 6 it went to trial with Fortnite maker Epic Games, which hoped to prove that Google engages in anticompetitive behavior with regard to its Android app store, Google Play, and its commission structure. Separately, Google was involved in an antitrust lawsuit with the Department of Justice over its alleged search monopoly.

The Epic case had shed co-plaintiffs on its way to trial. Epic's lawsuit originally involved Match and several U.S. attorneys general, but Google reached a settlement with the attorneys general in October 2023 and with Match the week before November 6, so Epic fought the antitrust battle on its own. The lawsuit, held in the U.S. District Court in California's Northern District, would include testimony from a number of Google and Android execs, including CEO Sundar Pichai, and Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, as well as from Apple, Netflix and other Android developers. Epic, meanwhile, had lost its antitrust battle with Apple and was asking the Supreme Court to weigh in.



---


# PayPal's Anti-Steering Class Action

On October 5, TechCrunch's Mary Ann broke the news that PayPal had been hit with a class action lawsuit by consumers represented by law firm Hagens Berman, alleging that the fintech giant's anti-steering rules stifle competition against lower-cost payment platforms such as Stripe and Shopify. According to an investigation conducted by the firm's consumer rights attorneys, PayPal has subjected consumers to excess charges when purchasing from online merchants that accept PayPal or Venmo.

The suit was covered as one over allegedly "Draconian" payment policies. When someone commented on social media that they did not see the problem with what PayPal was doing, and questioned whether Visa and Mastercard do the same thing, TechCrunch went back to the attorneys who filed the lawsuit. They noted that anti-steering rules are not the first of their kind, and placed PayPal's rules in that lineage: "Visa and MasterCard once imposed similar anti-steering rules on merchants accepting their cards but, after the Justice Department sued the networks for antitrust violations, they agreed in 2010 to eliminate their anti-steering rules as part of the settlement. With payments transitioning into the digital realm, PayPal has simply ripped a page right from the Visa and MasterCard [sic] playbook."



---


# Google's Rebuttal To The Publisher Antitrust Suit

Google rejects the premise that it deprives publishers of readers and traffic. A Google spokesperson called the Helena World Chronicle lawsuit "meritless," and attacked the claim of foreclosure directly: "People have many ways to access information and news content today – through publishers' websites, dedicated apps, social media platforms, print papers and more. Google links people to publishers' websites more than 24 billion times each month – at no cost to them."

The rebuttal therefore contests two of the suit's premises at once: that Google is a bottleneck between readers and publishers, and that publishers are uncompensated, by pointing to the volume of free referrals Google sends.

# Streaming's Walls Are Crumbling: Exclusivity Gives Way To Rights Payments

The Sydney Morning Herald's claim, in its 30 November 2023 December guide, is that the corporate and creative philosophy behind streaming television is in a state of flux and cracks in the prevailing wisdom are starting to appear — specifically around the value of exclusivity. For the past five or so years entertainment companies have been focused on creating their own streaming platforms built around exclusive control of their original content, whether original new series or a sister studio's Hollywood movies. But now that income is desired most, some streamers are once again willing to sell non-exclusive rights to others.

The grounding case is Yellowjackets: in December, one of the best original shows on Paramount+, the compelling horror-laced drama, will become available on Netflix. The warrant is that both sides gain — Netflix gets a buzzy show the vast majority of its subscribers have never had access to, while Paramount+ earns a rights payment and broadens the audience for a show that has a third season commissioned. "Streaming's walls are crumbling." The scope condition matters, though: there are still plenty of promising new shows and movies, most of them exclusive to their services, debuting in December, whether you're after an awards season blockbuster (Netflix's Maestro) or an Australian comic-drama (Binge's Strife).

The month's top Netflix recommendation is Maestro (December 20). Not since Warren Beatty in the late 1970s has a Hollywood leading man so completely — perhaps obsessively — given themselves over to filmmaking as Bradley Cooper: the credit he banked from the Hangover comedies, Silver Linings Playbook and American Sniper let him co-write, direct and star in the 2018 hit A Star is Born, and he now fills the same three positions in another movie about a tormented musician, the superstar American conductor and composer Leonard Bernstein. Alex Casassovici, founder and CEO of Azarus — a company that works with online creators to enhance the streaming experience — told Polygon for its 2023-10-20 story that livestreaming sports and sports-related content on platforms like Twitch creates a more intimate experience for streamers and fans alike.

# Polygon's Guide To The Best Comedies On Streaming

Polygon argues that comedy is an ignored genre in modern moviemaking, and that the remedy for viewers is to look to streaming rather than to new studio releases. The grounds are a comparison across genres: horror was having a fantastic 2023, thrillers come out on a weekly basis, and even action movies had seen stellar recent releases, while Hollywood has been in a comedic rut with fewer and fewer notable releases from big studios.

The warrant joining the complaint to the recommendation is that the good comedies still exist, just not in cinemas — so the site compiled a list of the best comedy movies to watch at home, scraping streaming services including Netflix, Hulu, Prime Video and HBO Max, as well as free services, "to find the best of the best." The list deliberately spans registers, from romantic comedies that make your heart sing to gut-busting laugh-out-loud comedies. Polygon maintains a separate companion list for the best comedies on Netflix alone, and notes that its latest update added The Road to El Dorado as an editor's pick.



---


# Twitch's Scale and the Unsustainable Creator Economy

Twitch is the livestreaming platform where the games industry's disasters converge, home to over 30 million daily viewers, as Polygon described it on 2023-10-19. Many would say the writing is on the wall for Twitch after endless headlines about losing top talent, poor management, bad platform policies, and creator burnout — but Polygon argues the idea that Twitch has lost its way after an ostensible golden era is an easy narrative that misses something much starker: if Twitch is in trouble in 2023, it is not because things have gotten worse, but because everything visible is the natural progression of an unsustainable system whose prognosis has always been terminal, unrecognized because it has been profitable.

The origin conditions were specific to their moment. In 2011, when Twitch first launched, content creation was not fully a career and people still uploaded their photos to Facebook; normal, everyday teens were not yet decrying the hungry maw of the internet, and the generational shift toward work-life balance had not taken hold. Twitch happened at exactly the right time, benefiting from a cadre of optimistic young users who grew up on the internet and were happy to give away as much of themselves as they could — in many cases without realizing it was happening, and unable to imagine the unsustainable system it would create. People were just having fun.

Things have changed. Twitch has crowned millionaires, like Félix "xQc" Lengyel, who wear thick diamond chains around their necks while streaming. At the same time viewership is dropping after years of platform growth partially bolstered by the COVID-19 pandemic, while top creators are streaming less. The gaming industry, which likes to boast about how much money it makes compared with other forms of entertainment, is laying off workers nearly every week at top studios, and the overall gaming market is shrinking — the cracks in the system that produces and promotes big-budget games are getting hard to ignore.

# Polygon's Selection Process for the Best Movies of 2023

Polygon builds its best-movies-of-the-year list by having each of the staff's film fans create an individual ballot of their top movies every year, with an option to rank the entries numerically or simply weight them; those ballots are then used to generate a collective list, weighted by strength of opinion so that a much-seen mainstream movie does not gain too much advantage over a terrific but underseen indie. The result is then published, with the top 10 picks on each staffer's list listed in the comments.

The eligibility rule is that any movie released in the US during that calendar year qualifies. A stated limitation follows from the publication timing: because the list is published in early December, some December releases are underrepresented.

Polygon frames the exercise as inherently difficult, likening a collaborative best-movies list to forming a committee to definitively rank apples and oranges — how to account for personal tastes, or for access when a given movie is only available in certain markets at certain times, or for the fact that the entries are so qualitatively different they have little in common. The weighted-ballot procedure exists to accommodate that spread: the staff describes its collective tastes as eclectic, with some hungriest for action, horror, epic fantasy, or challenging science fiction, some preferring complicated drama or dark neo-noir, and others drawn to musicals, comedy, animated adventures, and other lighter fare. The best-of-the-year list is meant to reflect that range.



---


# Broadcast Rights Limits on Twitch Sports Streams

Livestreams of major league games are less common to find on Twitch because of broadcast rights, Polygon reported on 2023-10-20 — though some leagues, nationally and globally, have experimented with streaming games in recent years.

The NBA signed a deal with Twitch in 2017 to stream minor league games while giving fans the chance to interact with each other, and the two teamed up again in 2019 for a separate deal to exclusively stream USA Basketball games globally.

When Amazon began airing Thursday Night Football games the previous fall, Nielsen reported a total viewership figure of 13 million for its first exclusive game, a figure that included U.S. Prime Video subscribers who streamed on Twitch.



---


# Cocoon Wins Best Indie Game, 2023

Cocoon won Best Indie Game during the 2023 Game Awards, and Polygon reports it is a personal favorite among much of its staff.

The game is the latest title from a studio founded by Jeppe Carlsen, the person responsible for the unsettling narrative platformers Limbo and Inside, and Polygon describes it as a psychedelic odyssey.

Jeff and Eileen Shiffrin, both avid and passionate skiers from a tender age, introduced their children to the sport from early childhood, moving between Vail and New England as the family's skiing and careers required, as reported by Essentially Sports on 3 November 2023.

The chronology given is precise. In 1986, a year after they first met, the couple married. A year after moving they welcomed Taylor, Mikaela's brother, in 1992, and Mikaela arrived three years later in 1995. The family moved to Vail in 2009, but Mikaela went back to Burke, and her mother decided to move with her, home-schooling her while monitoring her training.

The results and the parenting are given together. Think first. Have fun," which Shiffrin has affixed to the back of her helmet. Taylor also made immense progress and went on to win two NCAA team titles with the University of Denver. # Why Canada Belongs On A Skier's Bucket List

Canada may be further afield than the Alps or the Dolomites, but The Independent argues a trip there makes it onto the bucket lists of ski lovers everywhere for good reason: from the world-famous Whistler Blackcomb and its attractive resort towns to the steep verticals of Revelstoke, there is enough choice — for every level of skier — to keep you coming back for years.

# Google's Gemini Model Family And Its Capability Claims

Gemini is Google's new flagship generative AI model, unveiled in the first week of December 2023 and meant to power a range of products and services including Bard, Google's ChatGPT competitor. In blog posts and press materials, Google touted Gemini's superior architecture and capabilities, claiming that the model meets or exceeds the performance of other leading generative AI models such as OpenAI's GPT-4, and it emphasised Gemini's coding capabilities and multimodal prowess, claiming that the model can understand images, audio and videos just as well as text.

The family has tiers, and only the lower one shipped. Google did not release the full model, Gemini Ultra — which is set to launch sometime in 2024 in Bard and other products — but only a "lite" version called Gemini Pro. Gemini Pro is therefore not the most capable version of Gemini, and Google compared its performance to GPT-4's predecessor, GPT-3.5, a model that was around a year old. Google nevertheless promised improvements in reasoning, planning and understanding with Gemini Pro over the previous model powering Bard, claiming Gemini Pro was better at summarizing content, brainstorming and writing.

The shipped tier is also narrower than the multimodal claims suggest: Gemini Pro is strictly text-in, text-out, and has proven to be mistake-prone. In a worse look for Google, the company was caught faking a Gemini demo by tuning text prompts with still images off camera.

Against Google's promises for Gemini Pro, TechCrunch's rejoinder on 7 December 2023 was blunt: "the anecdotal evidence suggests otherwise." The TechCrunch reporter tried the same prompt and got a very similar response. ChatGPT, by contrast, gave a bullet-list summary with citations to news articles.

# Helena World Chronicle's Class Action Antitrust Suit Against Google

A class action lawsuit filed in the week of 15 December 2023 in the U.S. District Court in D.C. accuses Google and parent company Alphabet of anticompetitive behavior in violation of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act and others, on behalf of news publishers. The case was filed by Arkansas-based publisher Helena World Chronicle, which argues that Google "siphons off" news publishers' content, their readers and their ad revenue through anticompetitive means, and it specifically cites new AI technologies such as Google's Search Generative Experience (SGE) and the Bard AI chatbot as worsening the problem.

Helena World Chronicle owns and publishes two weekly newspapers in Arkansas. In the complaint it argues that Google is "starving the free press" by sharing publishers' content on Google, losing them "billions of dollars."

Beyond damages, the suit asks for an injunction that would require Google to obtain consent from publishers before using their website data to train its general artificial intelligence products, including Google's own and those of rivals. It also asks that publishers who opt out of SGE still be allowed to show up in Google search results, among other things.

The law firm handling the case is Hausfeld, whose announcement states that "the anticompetitive effects of Google's scheme cause profound harm to competition, to consumers, to labor, and to a democratic free press," and that "Plaintiff Helena World Chronicle, LLC invokes the Sherman Act and Clayton Act to seek class-wide monetary and injunctive relief to restore and ensure competition for digital news and reference publishing and set up guardrails to preserve a free marketplace of ideas in the new era of artificial intelligence."



---


# The Claim That SGE And Bard Appropriate Publisher Content

The Helena World Chronicle lawsuit claims that Google's recent advances in AI-based search were implemented with "the goal of discouraging end-users from visiting the websites of Class members who are part of the digital news and publishing line of commerce." The grounds are that Google's AI products both retain users and consume publisher content without permission.

In October 2023, Wired posted an opinion article by lawyer and privacy advocate Megan Gray alleging that Google had accidentally revealed during the trial that it manipulates people's search queries for maximum ad revenue — the example given being the replacement of a search for "children's clothing" with "NIKOLAI-brand kidswear" — and Wired subsequently removed the article for not meeting its standards.

# Testimony At The SBF Trial

Across the first three weeks of the trial, a run of former colleagues, an outside investor and a forensic accounting expert testified that FTX customer money flowed into Alameda Research and out again to other uses, and that FTX's investors were never told about the two firms' special relationship. TechCrunch's running coverage, published 2023-10-06, summarises each week.

In week one, FTX's co-founder and CTO Gary Wang testified Thursday on the extent to which Alameda Research was used for whatever purposes he and SBF saw fit: according to Wang, the crypto trading firm pulled funding directly from FTX customers, whose transactions would be funneled toward Alameda and then directed elsewhere. Thursday also brought testimony from Matt Huang, co-founder and managing partner at crypto investment firm Paradigm, which invested $278 million in FTX across 2021 and 2022 and is part of a class-action lawsuit accusing it and others of defrauding customers by promoting FTX. His testimony centered around being left uninformed about FTX's utilization of customer money to keep Alameda Research afloat — a practice Huang says would have halted his involvement — and covered his relationship with FTX stretching back to 2019.

Week two's standout testimony came from Alameda Research's former CEO Caroline Ellison, who claimed she took $14 billion from customers to repay debts to lenders, using them as a line of credit under the instruction of SBF. Ellison also went into detail about how a $2 billion venture fund, FTX Ventures, was funded by money that had previously been allocated to Alameda from third-party lenders. And though there are no charges of bribery in the case, she also testified to paying Chinese officials $150 million to restore access to $1 billion in frozen trading accounts.

The third week featured a couple of noteworthy moments for the prosecution. FTX's former general counsel Can Sun, like many of SBF's former colleagues, opted to cooperate with authorities and testified that SBF asked him to create a theoretical "legal justification" for the use of billions in consumer funds just days before FTX filed for bankruptcy. Robert Boroujerdi, managing director of the hedge fund Third Point, testified about his experience working with SBF and FTX in a partnership that ultimately resulted in a $60 million investment and a lack of awareness about the special relationship between Alameda Research and FTX; had he known of such a relationship, he testified, Third Point would not have invested in FTX in the first place. And earlier in the week, Peter Easton — a University of Notre Dame professor who helped the government prosecution of Enron and WorldCom — testified about what he uncovered after tracing the flow of billions of dollars between Alameda Research and FTX: much of that funding came from customers, and Easton testified that he found user deposits were used by both FTX and Alameda to purchase real estate, make investments or direct funding toward political causes and charities.



---


# Alameda Absorbed FTX's Losses, Including MobileCoin

Alameda Research functioned as FTX's sin-eater: when FTX took a loss, the loss was moved onto Alameda's balance sheet so that FTX would not look bad. Gary Wang testified that in 2021 FTX was facing a "several hundred million dollar" loss from an exploit in MobileCoin — apparently in April 2021, though Wang did not give a month — and Bankman-Fried directed him to have Alameda take it on instead, because FTX's balance sheets were visible to investors and Alameda's were not.

The relation was general, not a one-off. Ellison testified that her tenure as CEO of Alameda Research was an exercise in optics: when FTX took a loss in the hundreds of millions of dollars because a trader had exploited its system, Wang moved that loss onto Alameda's balance sheet, and FTX's "insurance fund," meant to keep traders from getting stuck with other traders' losses, was totally made up, with Alameda simply picking up the tab. The concealment held all the way to investors: Paradigm Capital's Matt Huang showed the court the balance sheets he had received from Bankman-Fried, and they did not include the loss, which should have appeared in the second-quarter numbers he was given — those instead showed $63 million in trading expenses and $63 million in "other expenses" for the quarter, and an estimated profit of $732 million.

Bankman-Fried offered a benign reading of the same arrangement from the stand: he said the MobileCoin loss, the one Wang said Alameda took to keep off FTX's balance sheet, was a totally innocent matter in which he thought it appropriate that Alameda take the position as a backstop liquidity provider.



---


# Alameda Research

Alameda Research is the crypto-trading firm Sam Bankman-Fried co-founded in 2017, before FTX existed. FTX came two years later, in 2019, and Bankman-Fried co-founded it as a complement to Alameda — to help bring in revenue and liquidity for the trading arm. The founding order is the discriminating fact: the exchange was created to serve the trading firm, not the other way round.

The feature that later set Alameda's balance sheet apart was how much of it consisted of the affiliated exchange's own token. A report showed that Alameda's largest asset was $3.66 billion of "unlocked FTT," alongside $2.16 billion of "FTT collateral." FTT was the token behind FTX. So the trading firm's single biggest asset was the token issued by the exchange founded to support it.



---


# June 2022: Alameda's Reckoning And Lender Repayment

By 2022 Alameda's negative balance on FTX had become a cause for concern for Caroline Ellison, Nishad Singh, and Gary Wang, who built a spreadsheet to work out how negative Alameda actually was; the version shown in court ran to several pages of attempts to reconcile, and Wang figured Alameda owed FTX about $11 billion at a time when FTX's revenue was about $1.5 billion. Ellison, Singh, Wang, and Bankman-Fried then met in the Bahamas office, where Alameda's lenders wanted their money back and Bankman-Fried directed the group to pay the lenders back using FTX customer funds.

Bankman-Fried considered shutting Alameda down and even wrote a long memo about it, but Wang testified that in a now-deleted Signal discussion of that memo he told Bankman-Fried and Singh they could not shut Alameda down because they could not repay its debt. Another empty Signal chat, with its setting to delete messages after a week, was shown to the court; its members were Ellison, Singh, Wang, and Bankman-Fried.

Bankman-Fried's own account from the stand ran differently. He testified that in June 2022 he heard about the account called "fiat@ftx" tracking how much money Alameda owed to FTX, that he did not know what it was and did not bother to find out because he was busy, and that this was when he directed Ellison to repay Alameda's lenders because he thought Alameda was good for it. He also gave BlockFi and Voyager, two crypto lenders, some capital infusions for good measure.



---


# The Mechanism Of FTX's Collapse

FTX came apart in early November 2022 through a chain with four links: a leaked balance sheet revealed that Alameda's largest holding was FTX's own token in a quantity larger than the token's whole market, the disclosure destroyed confidence, the world's largest rival exchange pulled its holdings out, and the resulting bank run forced FTX and Alameda into Chapter 11 within days. TechCrunch's 2023-10-01 account sets out the sequence: in early November 2022, that all changed.

Concerns surrounding FTX's liquidity grew after CoinDesk published a copy of Alameda's balance sheet, showing the firm held $14.6 billion in assets and $8 billion in liabilities as of June 30, 2022. The balance sheet showed that the $5.82 billion in FTT tokens that Alameda owned was 193% higher than the total FTT market cap, which was about $3 billion at the time — meaning Alameda purported to have more FTT tokens on its balance sheet than what existed in the world. Around the same time it was exposed, the world's largest crypto exchange, Binance, started pulling out its remaining $2.1 billion equivalent of cash in BUSD and FTT; Binance had held an equity position in FTX from 2019 to 2021. That withdrawal essentially triggered a bank run on FTX. FTX and Alameda filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in the U.S. mid-November 2022, Bankman-Fried resigned, and John J. Ray III, the Enron turnaround veteran, was appointed the new CEO.

The condition the whole mechanism rests on is the fragility of the underlying valuations. As TechCrunch put it on 2023-10-02, all of that activity came to a crashing end because the value of cryptocurrencies on FTX was not banked to much more than speculation and the promise of higher value — so when those valuations fell, they fell very, very hard. The chain therefore only runs as described where an asset is priced on expectation, held in size by a related party, and exposed to a counterparty large enough that its exit alone starts the run.

He trusted FTX because Bankman-Fried came across as a leading figure of the industry; because the sheer volume of users mattered to him, and FTX was at the time among the top three biggest exchanges; and because major VC firms had invested. "They don't commit hundreds of millions without doing due diligence, checking the books, the accountancy of the firm, going through several compliance process[es], so that was a vote of confidence for me," he said. He also noted FTX's glossy ads — featuring Gisele Bündchen, for instance — which suggested a very high budget, and reasoned that it wouldn't make sense to spend that much money unless FTX had very strong financials. He opened an account, transferred in both regular money and cryptocurrency, and used the exchange to execute his plan of buying Bitcoin to sell back in five to ten years at higher prices.

In November 2022 things went bad. Julliard followed Bankman-Fried on Twitter and read aloud in court the "FTX is fine. Assets are fine" tweets, along with "FTX has enough to cover all client holdings. We don't invest client assets" and a few others, which gave him the impression that his money was there and that any problem might be technical — anti-spam measures — or regulatory. By the time he tried to get his money out on November 8th, it was too late. Cross-examining a customer whose money is gone is described as a thankless task, but Mark Cohen tried anyway, noting that Julliard was a licensed commodities broker who was trading in crypto because he didn't have to disclose it, that he knew crypto was new and risky, and that he didn't review the terms of service agreement he had assented to when making his FTX account. The next witness called was Bankman-Fried's former college and FTX roommate, Adam Yedidia.



---


# Testimony At The SBF Trial

Across the first three weeks of the trial, a run of former colleagues, an outside investor and a forensic accounting expert testified that FTX customer money flowed into Alameda Research and out again to other uses, and that FTX's investors were never told about the two firms' special relationship. TechCrunch's running coverage, published 2023-10-06, summarises each week.

In week one, FTX's co-founder and CTO Gary Wang testified Thursday on the extent to which Alameda Research was used for whatever purposes he and SBF saw fit: according to Wang, the crypto trading firm pulled funding directly from FTX customers, whose transactions would be funneled toward Alameda and then directed elsewhere. Thursday also brought testimony from Matt Huang, co-founder and managing partner at crypto investment firm Paradigm, which invested $278 million in FTX across 2021 and 2022 and is part of a class-action lawsuit accusing it and others of defrauding customers by promoting FTX. His testimony centered around being left uninformed about FTX's utilization of customer money to keep Alameda Research afloat — a practice Huang says would have halted his involvement — and covered his relationship with FTX stretching back to 2019.

Week two's standout testimony came from Alameda Research's former CEO Caroline Ellison, who claimed she took $14 billion from customers to repay debts to lenders, using them as a line of credit under the instruction of SBF. Ellison also went into detail about how a $2 billion venture fund, FTX Ventures, was funded by money that had previously been allocated to Alameda from third-party lenders. And though there are no charges of bribery in the case, she also testified to paying Chinese officials $150 million to restore access to $1 billion in frozen trading accounts.

The third week featured a couple of noteworthy moments for the prosecution. FTX's former general counsel Can Sun, like many of SBF's former colleagues, opted to cooperate with authorities and testified that SBF asked him to create a theoretical "legal justification" for the use of billions in consumer funds just days before FTX filed for bankruptcy. Robert Boroujerdi, managing director of the hedge fund Third Point, testified about his experience working with SBF and FTX in a partnership that ultimately resulted in a $60 million investment and a lack of awareness about the special relationship between Alameda Research and FTX; had he known of such a relationship, he testified, Third Point would not have invested in FTX in the first place. And earlier in the week, Peter Easton — a University of Notre Dame professor who helped the government prosecution of Enron and WorldCom — testified about what he uncovered after tracing the flow of billions of dollars between Alameda Research and FTX: much of that funding came from customers, and Easton testified that he found user deposits were used by both FTX and Alameda to purchase real estate, make investments or direct funding toward political causes and charities.



---


# The SBF Trial Proceedings

Sam Bankman-Fried is in court for alleged fraud and money laundering while leading crypto exchange FTX and sister company Alameda. TechCrunch's 2023-10-02 preview placed the case in the Manhattan Federal Court, describing the disgraced cryptocurrency entrepreneur as accused of orchestrating "one of the biggest financial frauds in American history": the multibillion-dollar collapse of FTX, the crypto exchange he founded and led. SBF, as he is known, has pleaded not guilty to some seven charges of fraud and conspiracy.

The trial kicked off with jury selection October 3. By TechCrunch's 2023-10-06 update the case was entering its next chapter, with proceedings resuming Thursday: as confirmed during a teleconference Wednesday, SBF would be taking the stand along with a handful of other witnesses, as the onus shifted toward the defense after the prosecution brought its case to its conclusion.

Access to the proceedings is limited: no devices are allowed, so reports are being physically put together within the courtroom, or sent to overflow rooms. The jury's composition ranges from a train conductor to a retired investment banker who attended Stanford University, and TechCrunch pointed readers to a special joint episode of its Equity and Chain Reaction podcasts for a better sense of the vibe between the jurors and the rest of the court.

A second account of the same events was arriving in parallel: "Going Infinite," a book by Michael Lewis chronicling the rise and fall of SBF, was set to debut on the first day of the trial.



---


# John J. Ray III Running The FTX Estate

What's left of FTX is now being led by John J. Ray III — the man who cleaned up Enron, and who has said FTX is worse than Enron.

Just before the trial began, the FTX lawyers filed suit against Bankman-Fried's parents, saying they should give back millions of dollars they got from their kid. Ray has also referred to Bankman-Fried's conduct as "really just old-fashioned embezzlement."

qid: Does the article from The Verge suggest that the Echo Frames require the Alexa app to be running for functionality, while the TechCrunch article discusses a new feature for Amazon's Echo devices that does not specify such a requirement?
context:
# Alexa's Limitations As An On-The-Go Assistant On Echo Frames

The feature meant to set the Echo Frames apart is that Alexa is built in — and that is exactly the premise The Verge's reviewer attacked: Alexa has never been and still isn't a particularly good voice assistant when you're on the go, being fine at answering odd queries, setting timers and telling you the weather, but much better at controlling your smart home than at replacing Siri or Assistant.

It isn't that the glasses can't do things: you can now make non-Alexa calls and, on an Android phone, reply to text messages, and directions are possible but clunky. Alexa told the reviewer they'd get a notification on their phone to start, which meant tweaking notification settings to a less preferred option; once working, it suggested going to Bowling Green in Kentucky instead of the Manhattan train station five minutes away. Most things remain easier and faster on the phone, so the reviewer had little reason to use Alexa on the glasses, a problem exacerbated by having sunglasses instead of regular glasses. The dependency on the phone cuts both ways: with a stable Bluetooth connection and phone signal, Alexa works reliably on the go, but there's little offline usability, and the Alexa app must always be open and running in the background. A further, cultural objection: it's just weird to say "Alexa" in public — the wake word can be changed to Echo, which didn't help the reviewer — and this applies to nearly every pair of smart glasses with a voice assistant, because earbuds are a visual and cultural signal we all implicitly understand. Talking to midair with AirPods in reads as being on a call; talking with no phone or AirPods in sight got odd looks from strangers and confused looks from friends.



---


# Echo Frames: Alexa At Home And Find My Frames

Testing Alexa commands on the Echo Frames at home, The Verge's reviewer was pleasantly surprised that issuing them didn't trip up any of their Echo speakers.

The frames also support a feature that lets you ask any Echo speaker you own to locate them. The reviewer called that nice but doubted most people will use it frequently: as a lifelong glasses wearer, theirs are always either in a case or on the nightstand, and they have a specific drawer for sunglasses. The feature also carries a precondition — it relies on the glasses having a decent charge.



---


# The Third-Gen Echo Frames Are Only An Incremental Improvement

The Verge's verdict on the third-gen Echo Frames is that Amazon isn't straying far from its existing formula and the changes are "a half-step in the right direction" rather than enough to turn the Echo Frames into a must-have gadget.

The grounds are the specific gains: the new frames are lighter, the battery lasts longer, the bass is more bassy, and they look a lot more stylish than previous iterations, and the reviewer singles out improving the range of available styles as a much-needed change. The warrant for the negative verdict is that each gain falls short of the comparison that matters: beefing up the audio is good, but it wasn't enough of a change to make these stand above the competition or serve as a compelling alternative to wireless earbuds — and, most crucially, the reviewer wasn't convinced to use Alexa more than they otherwise would have. The summary judgment: Amazon is getting there with form, but is not quite there with function.



---


# Alexa Kids Data Handling And The Echo Pop Kids Launch

Amazon says it is not training its LLM on kids' answers, and that "Explore with Alexa" and any future LLM-backed features will continue to follow the same data handling policies as "classic Alexa" — the non-AI Alexa. In practice that means the Alexa app will include a list of the questions asked by kids in the household, for those with a kids' profile, along with the response Alexa provided; that history can be stored or deleted either manually or automatically, depending on the account's settings. These statements were made by the company to TechCrunch and reported on 25 October 2023, alongside the launch of the feature.

The launch also brought hardware. The new Echo Pop Kids speakers became available for purchase at the same time, starting at $49.99 in the U.S., in two new designs — Marvel's Avengers and Disney Princess — that feature corresponding character themes, letting kids hear a greeting, fun fact or joke about an Avenger or Disney Princess in keeping with the theme. Both include six months of access to the Amazon Kids+ subscription service, which, beyond "Explore with Alexa," also offers a range of kid-friendly games, apps, books, videos and more, including custom Alexa themes. Buying a Kids device is not a precondition for the feature, however: "Explore with Alexa" works on any device set to kids mode, or any communal family device, if parents have set up their kids' voice ID.

Two scope limits attach to the launch as described. The experience is available in English only at first, with internationalization further down the road. And the offline arrangement is framed as a stage rather than an endpoint — Amazon eventually wants the generative AI experience integrated at runtime for both kids and adults, while knowing it needs to proceed carefully, especially with kids: "We do want to integrate an LLM in runtime in a more protected way than we would integrate it for adults…However, this approach lets us iterate and figure out the right ways to get both safe and delightful content outputted from the LLM for kids," says Venkataswamy. On the adult side, he says Amazon was preparing to launch an AI-powered "Let's Chat" Alexa experience later that same year.



---


# Smart Glasses Category Expectations And Echo Frames Positioning

The purpose of the Amazon Echo Frames is obvious — quick access to Alexa no matter where you are, because it's on your face — but The Verge argued that is not why anyone wants smart glasses, let alone a pair costing $389.99 like the Carrera Cruiser model the reviewer wore for a week.

The category expectation the Echo Frames sit against is cinematic: most people's vision of smart glasses is informed by Tony Stark, James Bond, and other iconic sci-fi and spy movie characters — sleek, discreet devices with some sort of hidden mixed reality display or the ability to capture the world around you. The original Google Glass cemented that image, while successors like the Snap Spectacles and the Ray-Ban Meta Smart Glasses have leaned heavily into content creation. The discriminating feature of the Echo Frames is that they have never been quite that ambitious: like the Bose Frames, Amazon's approach has primarily been a pair of open-ear headphones you can take calls on, listen to music with, and ask the occasional Alexa query. There is no camera, no screen, and nothing to clue anyone in that you're not just wearing ordinary glasses.



---


# Echo Frames Notification Control And The VIP Filter

The VIP Filter is the Echo Frames' notification-control feature: a list you curate so that only select apps and contacts will notify you.

Its defining behaviour is deliberately minimal. The glasses play a sound whenever you get a notification, and then you pull your phone out to check; they won't read your texts. The Verge's reviewer appreciated that restraint, citing the annoyance of Siri taking ten years to read out the URL of a funny link a friend sent. The trade-off implied by the design is that, because you only hear a ping, you have to be ruthless when setting up your VIP list.



---


# Explore With Alexa

"Explore with Alexa" is a feature on Amazon's Echo devices that lets kids have interactive conversations with an AI-powered Alexa. It was first announced in September and, as reported by TechCrunch on 25 October 2023, launched as an addition to the Amazon Kids+ content subscription, allowing children to have kid-friendly conversations with Alexa, powered by generative AI, but in a protected fashion designed to ensure the experience remains safe and appropriate.

The discriminating feature is the combination of generative AI, conversation, and an audience of children under 13. Some AI experiences already cater to younger users — the AI chatbots from Character.ai and other companies, including Meta — but Amazon is among the first to specifically look to generative AI to develop a conversational experience for kids under the age of 13. The two qualifiers that bound the concept are the subscription it lives inside (Amazon Kids+) and the protective framing: this is not an unbounded chatbot but a conversational experience deliberately constructed to stay safe and age-appropriate.



---


# The Verge's Score And Verdict For The Echo Frames Carrera Cruiser

The Verge gave the Amazon Echo Frames Carrera Cruiser a Verge Score of 6, listing the price as $314.99 and linking to it at $315 at Amazon.

Under The Good, the review credits the frames as more stylish and offering more options, with improved battery life and audio, and the ability to use them with multiple devices. Under The Bad: bass still isn't great and audio leaks; they do less or sound not as good as others in this category; Alexa still isn't the best assistant when you're on the go; and they are pricey for the category. The scorecard is accompanied by The Verge's standard "How we rate and review products" link.

qid: Does the Polygon article suggest that Valve has made multiple physical upgrades to the Steam Deck, while The Verge article indicates that Valve's focus is solely on games for their store, and does the Engadget article confirm that Valve will launch the Steam Deck OLED on a specific date with immediate availability, unlike the other two sources which do not mention a launch date?
context:
# Steam Deck OLED As A Mid-Cycle Refresh

The first thing to know about the Steam Deck OLED is that it's not the Steam Deck 2: it is a mid-cycle refresh from Valve, similar to the Switch OLED upgrade, but with a lot more going on internally. Its screen is better, its battery life is better, its thumbsticks are better, the haptics are better, and its chip and thermals are better. One thing that hasn't changed is its form factor — this is still one of the biggest babies on the handheld block.

Engadget's launch coverage on 2023-11-09 frames it the same way: it might not look like a big change from the outside, but the Steam Deck OLED is a thorough mid-cycle refresh of a machine that's not even two years old, and at the same time Valve is also adjusting the configuration of its entry-level model, making it a far more compelling option. At an event held for press prior to the device's launch, Greg Coomer, a product designer at Valve, called the new model "the definitive version of the Steam Deck," explaining that the device contains many things the company wanted to include at the LCD model's launch but wasn't able to, along with some additions based on community feedback.



---


# Steam Deck OLED Hardware Refinements

Beyond the screen, the Steam Deck OLED adds a gaggle of minor physical upgrades that Polygon argues matter as much as the headline change. Since the original Steam Deck launched Valve has been improving the hardware through updates — its team estimates around 300 to date — and that continues for both models, with the original getting a fresh BIOS update to align it with some of the OLED's upgrades, including some battery life improvement, though not the OLED model's 30-50% jump.

Some changes demand new hardware. The Steam Deck OLED includes a Wi-Fi 6E radio, useful if you have a modern router and connection to make use of it, and a dedicated Bluetooth module, which allows improved audio quality with wireless headphones, the option to wake the Steam Deck from a controller, and the capability to connect many Bluetooth controllers for multiplayer. The haptics are noticeably improved with a wider frequency range, and the touchscreen is markedly better — responsive to the point where the reviewer no longer feels the need to plug in a USB-C keyboard to type a few words. Valve also claims the device is more repairable, which the reviewer did not have occasion to test, with parts again sold through iFixit. He did enjoy the new power supply, with faster charging — 45 minutes gets you from 20% to 80% — and a 2.5-meter cable that stretches the length of his couch. One charming detail: the carrying case now has a tinier carrying case within it, with the bulky original recommended for the cautious and the slim case for tossing the Deck in a backpack for a day trip.



---


# Handheld PC Gaming Market Growth

The argument is that the Steam Deck's own success created the component supply that made the OLED model possible. According to the developers Engadget spoke with at Valve, this is the definitive version of the Steam Deck — the HDR OLED model is what they would have released the first time around, if the technology had existed before 2022.

The grounds are the market's pace: the handheld market has evolved quickly, and in just over a year the Steam Deck proved there's widespread demand for handheld PCs, with its success helping drive chip makers and display manufacturers to build hardware specifically for high-fidelity mobile play. The warrant is that this supply-side shift benefits the whole category, not only Valve: this is great news for Valve and the Steam Deck, and also the other handhelds coming out of companies like Ayaneo, ASUS, Ayn, Logitech, Retroid and Razer — and, joking, maybe even Playdate will get an HDR OLED display one day, though Playdate is literally perfect.



---


# Steam Deck OLED Battery Life

Valve says the Steam Deck OLED battery lasts 30 to 50 percent longer than the original's depending on how you play, with an official claim of "three to 12 hours," and Engadget's November 2023 testing measured gains at the top of or above that range.

The original Steam Deck's short battery life was one of its downsides, maxing out at eight hours and only under ideal conditions. The OLED pairs a more-efficient processor with a 25 percent larger battery — 50Whr capacity against the original's 40Whr — and charges faster, going from 20 percent to 80 percent in 45 minutes by Valve's claim. Engadget tested with Hades, its reviewer's most-played game on the original: although Hades does not support HDR it pops on the OLED, with animations looking more fluid than on the LCD version, and the OLED lasted four hours and 23 minutes before dying, against two hours and 42 minutes for the original at the same settings of 800p with a 60 fps cap and similar brightness — a 62 percent improvement that surpasses Valve's own estimates. Engadget flags the confound: batteries degrade, and its LCD Steam Deck dated from the device's launch in early 2022, an 18-month-old unit at review time, which explains why its gains were more pronounced. A harsher stress test playing Elden Ring with everything maxed out gave the OLED two hours and 20 minutes, about 40 percent longer than the original. Polygon separately resolved the obvious ambiguity in Valve's 30-50% figure by asking whether the comparison was against a Steam Deck running original firmware, which had poor battery life, or the latest firmware; Valve's answer was the latter, so existing owners should expect the big improvements over their current experience. Polygon's conclusion is that the OLED screen makes for a fancier Steam Deck, but it is the battery life — plus tweaks throughout the design to carve out more of it — that lets the handheld truly deliver on its promise of a portable gaming PC.



---


# Steam Deck OLED Review Verdict

Engadget's verdict, scoring the Valve Steam Deck OLED 89, is that this isn't the Steam Deck 2 some are waiting for — it's just a welcome improvement on an already good device, at $549 at Steam. The pros listed are improved battery life, bright and smooth visuals, better thermals, feeling less top-heavy, and a long charging cable; the cons are that it is still ridiculously large — "Seriously it's so big."

The grounds are the specific gains: the Steam Deck OLED is the facetuned, photoshopped, spit-shined version of Valve's handheld, and it features tangible, clever improvements, with the updated display as the highlight while things like faster charging, improved antennas and smoother haptics are welcome bonuses. The larger warrant is strategic: more importantly, this is Valve renewing its commitment to portable PC gaming, and that's a relief to see, since the Steam Deck is the granddaddy of handheld PCs and Valve has the resources to continue innovating in this space. For now, the OLED model is a half-step toward the Steam Deck 2, which may be the final version of the device — unless Valve finally learns how to count to three.



---


# Steam Deck OLED Pricing And Lineup

The Steam Deck OLED goes on sale on November 16th at 1pm ET, with Valve holding units ready to ship that same day, and it starts at $549, replacing all but the entry-level model in the range. Valve says the lineup moving forward is: 256GB Steam Deck LCD at $399, 512GB Steam Deck OLED at $549, and 1TB Steam Deck OLED at $649. There is also a limited edition 1TB OLED version — priced at $680 in the review and $679 in the launch coverage — that comes with a special carrying case, a translucent gray body and orange accents.

Valve has lowered the price of its LCD lineup and will sell through its backstock of 64GB and 512GB models until they're all gone: the 64GB LCD Steam Deck, previously sold at $399, drops to $349, and the 512GB LCD, previously $649, drops to $499, after which both lines will be discontinued — though Valve says it will continue to support all LCD models with software updates. So the long-term lineup starts at the same $399 price, which gets the old LCD Steam Deck but with 256GB of storage instead of 64GB; the new step-up model costs $20 more at $549 but comes with an OLED display, the hardware improvements and double the storage; and the range still tops out at $649, now with 1TB of storage instead of 512GB, an improved carry case that can pop out into a slimmer shell that's smaller and easier to fit in a bag, and the same anti-glare etched glass as the outgoing 512GB LCD model. The updated pricing on the existing LCD models is already in effect.



---


# Steam Deck Game Compatibility Labels

Valve's compatibility labels are markers on Steam games signifying how well they'll work on the handheld, with four levels: unknown, unsupported, playable and verified.

The discriminating line runs between the top two: playable games generally come with a small caveat, like having to deploy the on-screen keyboard, while verified games have been fully optimized for portable play. Currently, more than 10,000 titles on Steam fall under the playable or verified labels, with more added every day.
