# The 2023 NFL Best Bets Season Record

Through eight weeks of the 2023 NFL season, Sporting News' best bets stood at 65-46-1 — a winning percentage of over .590, a number the column noted many professional bettors wish they were maintaining during a rollercoaster season. That was despite falling three bets under .500 over the previous two weeks, going 5-6 in Week 7 and 6-8 in Week 8, after starting the first six weeks with a best bets winning percentage well over .700.

The column publishes every Friday afternoon, unveiling favorite moneyline, spread, over/under and player prop wagers for the upcoming weekend after handpicking the best value opportunities on Caesars and SuperDraft and explaining how and why to attack the books.

The breakdown of the previous week was mixed rather than uniformly bad: the against-the-spread picks went 1-3 and player props a pitiful 0-3, but the moneyline and over/under picks went 5-2 — so, as the Nov. 3, 2023 column put it, like the Chiefs after a pathetic loss to the Broncos (one of the incorrect picks), it was moving on to Week 9 with its head held high.



---


# Sports Betting As An Investment Mindset

Sporting News' best bets column argues that sports betting is not a gamble: with the right mindset, strategies and preparedness it is an investment, and the column said on Nov. 3, 2023 that it was loving its return on investment through seven weeks. On that view the activity is not a hobby but "a second job that allows us to punch in while we're sitting on our couch."

The grounds are the work that goes into it. Because the reader's goal is to boost their bankroll, the column's top priority is to help achieve that by putting in a ton of statistical research, attacking all the angles, uncovering betting trends and pinpointing value across all the sports betting sites each week — which is how it arrives at its best moneyline, spread, over/under and SuperDraft player prop bets for a slate it describes as featuring a plethora of lucrative opportunities.



---


# Prop Bet Examples By Sport

Every major sport with odds at the best sports betting apps will have prop bets, and the shape of those props follows each sport's statistics. The NBA offers a wide range, varying from player to team bets and leaning heavily on the statistical side of the game: how many points a player will score, the number of assists or three-pointers a player will have, which player will score the first basket. Team props are also available, such as whether a team will lead at the end of a certain quarter, or an over/under on the total number of points a team will score.

The NFL is the king of sports betting, and NFL betting sites have no qualms about showcasing every possible bet type. Bettors find many prop opportunities, especially for the Super Bowl; during the regular season one of the most popular options is the "anytime touchdown scorer" bet, where you wager on a player to score a touchdown at any point in the game, and other props focus on one team or both teams.

Baseball, hockey and soccer follow the same logic on their own stat lines. MLB props focus primarily on individual players and statistical achievements such as home runs, RBI and strikeouts — an over/under for a starting pitcher's strikeouts, or the number of bases a hitter will reach. NHL sites carry the props you would expect from a major North American league, such as player assists or a certain player scoring a goal, plus shots on goal, team goals in a game, and which team will score first. In Major League Soccer, where demand has increased as the sport's popularity grows nationwide, props often focus on individual accomplishments such as scoring a goal or collecting an assist, and also include how many cards the two teams will combine to draw or a team's total number of corner kicks.



---


# US Sports Betting Legality Since The 2018 Supreme Court Ruling

NBA betting is permitted in the US but its legality varies across the nation, because the significant turning point came in 2018 when the US Supreme Court overturned a longstanding federal law and allowed individual states the autonomy to determine their own sports betting regulations.

That groundbreaking decision sparked a wave of change: since the landmark ruling, over 30 states have embraced sports betting, including wagers on the NBA. For those residing in or visiting betting-friendly states, the experience promises fairness and security, because state-regulated online betting platforms are in place, ensuring bettors receive fair odds and adhering to strict standards for a safe and transparent betting environment.

The boundary case is offshore books. Bettors should ensure they are using only legal online sportsbooks for any type of betting: offshore sportsbooks advertise widely on the internet, but they are illegal and offer no protection against fraud and other criminal activities.



---


# NBA In-Game Betting: Wagering While The Game Unfolds

In-game betting, also known as live betting, allows you to bet on a game while it is unfolding, and it has exploded nationwide thanks to the increased popularity of online sports betting apps. The action is fast and the odds are constantly shifting, making for a new way to enjoy the flow of a game while staying engaged as a bettor.

Depending on the sportsbook there is usually a strong variety of live betting opportunities. These include game and player prop bets such as whether the next bucket will be worth one, two or three points; bets on the team leading at the end of the current quarter; bets on whether there will be a comeback victory; and wagers boiled down to the results of the next possession.

The most popular sportsbook apps — DraftKings, FanDuel and BetMGM — offer NBA in-game betting, though each has its own lines and betting opportunities.



---


# Betting The Masters: Markets And The Augusta National Factors

The Masters is one of the most prestigious golf tournaments globally and gets significant interest from sports bettors, with sportsbooks providing a wide array of odds ranging from standard outright winner bets to unique prop bets. Popular options include Top 10, 20 or 30 Finishes, betting on whether a golfer will finish within the specified range; Head-to-Head Matchups, picking one golfer to outperform another in the tournament; and Group Matchups, betting on which golfer in a predefined group will perform best. The best sports betting sites also offer odds boosts and free contests leading up to the Masters.

For successful Masters betting it is crucial to consider statistics pertinent to the tournament, with driving distance, accuracy and greens in regulation playing significant roles. Because Augusta National prioritizes accuracy and precise approach shots, bettors may want to focus on golfers with strong iron play and a history of performing well there.



---


# Advantages Of Prop Bets

Sporting News makes three arguments for prop bets: their lines move more slowly than other bet types, they offer greater variety, and they are usually very easy to understand. Every bet has positives and negatives, and props are no different — but these three are the positives.

The slow-moving lines create a timing edge. Prop bet odds are developed from game lines and totals at sportsbooks, yet prop lines tend to adjust more slowly. If you are watching New York Jets vs. Buffalo Bills and see the total shift because of an incoming winter storm, many bettors will scramble to get on the "under" before the main line moves too far; the better move is to scope out the prop bets for individual players, because most betting sites do not have the personnel to keep tabs on every possible player, so there may be value in an "under" on a quarterback's passing yards while those lines have not caught up.

The variety argument rests on what the main markets lack. Moneylines, point spreads and totals are constant in every major sport but do not offer much variety; props do, and they can add interest to a game that seems one-sided in the major markets. Larger sporting events, especially the Super Bowl, offer a massive variety of bets ranging from the typical to the exotic and everything in between.

The comprehensibility argument is that props tend to ask a question of the bettor — will a specific player hit a home run, will Team X have over/under 3.5 field goals in a game, will Team Y give up a powerplay goal — and whatever the question, props are fairly easy for a newcomer to understand.



---


# Betting The Other Majors And Team Golf Events

The US Open, PGA Championship and British Open — often referred to as The Open Championship — are among the four major championships in professional golf alongside the Masters, and each has unique course challenges and attributes that create many betting opportunities. The most popular markets for these events are to win; top 5, 10, 20 and so on; head-to-head matchups; nationality; first round leader; hole-in-one props; and top amateur.

Team golf events such as the Ryder Cup and the Presidents Cup offer a thrilling twist to tournament viewing. Bettors can choose from betting on the winning team, on outcomes of individual matches, or on prop bets such as which team scores highest in a round, who makes more birdies, or even the best-dressed team captain.

When placing bets on these events, evaluating each team's strengths and weaknesses is vital, and the factors to consider include recent player form, their history on the event's course, and any potential impacts such as injuries.

qid: Which AI-powered chatbot, developed by OpenAI and featured in TechCrunch articles, can assist with tasks ranging from debugging code to composing music, and also generates text based on user prompts?
context:
# ChatGPT's Task Capabilities And Measured Productivity Effects

ChatGPT's skills extend beyond conversation, another likely reason for its staying power. It can complete and debug code, compose music and essays, answer test questions, generate business ideas, write poetry and song lyrics, translate and summarize text, and even emulate a computer running Linux.

The measured effect comes from one study with a specific task set: an MIT study showed that, for tasks like writing cover letters, "delicate" emails and cost-benefit analyses, ChatGPT decreased the amount of time it took workers to complete the tasks by 40% while increasing output quality by 18%, as measured by third-party evaluators.

Ruoxi Shang attributes the breadth to a shift in how such systems are built: "Because [the AI models powering OpenAI] have been trained extensively on vast amounts of data, they [have] shifted focus from training specialized chatbots for specific domains to creating more general-purpose systems that can handle a variety of topics easily through prompting with instructions … [Chatbots like ChatGPT] don't require users to learn any new form of language, as long as they provide a task and some desired output just like how a manager would communicate to an intern."



---


# GPTs: OpenAI's Custom Chatbots And The Dev Day Announcements

GPTs are OpenAI's tool for building custom conversational, action-taking AI systems powered by OpenAI's models, including the models underpinning ChatGPT. They were announced at OpenAI's first-ever developer conference, held Monday, November 6, 2023, where the Microsoft-backed AI startup announced a host of new products — the more notable being tools to create custom "GPTs" (that is, domain-specific chatbots), new text-to-speech models, an API for the text-to-image model DALL-E 3, and an improved version of OpenAI's flagship model GPT-4, called GPT-4 Turbo.

What distinguishes a GPT from a prompt is that the knowledge is built in. With GPTs, a user can train a model on a cookbook collection, for example, so that it can answer questions about ingredients for a specific recipe; or they can give a model their company's proprietary codebases so that developers can check their style or generate code in line with best practices. Some of the initial GPTs, all created by OpenAI, include a Gen Z meme translator, a coloring book and sticker creator, a data visualizer, a board game explainer and a creative writing coach. ChatGPT can accomplish these tasks given carefully engineered prompts and foreknowledge, but purpose-built GPTs drastically simplify things — and might just kill the cottage industry that emerged around creating and editing prompts to feed to ChatGPT.

The consequence TechCrunch draws for ChatGPT itself is a change of role: with GPTs, ChatGPT could become more a gateway to a broader ecosystem of AI-powered chatbots than the end-all-be-all. GPTs introduce a level of personalization far beyond that ChatGPT offers today, and — once OpenAI sorts out its capacity issues — TechCrunch expects an explosion of creativity there. Will ChatGPT be as visible as it once was after GPTs flood the marketplace? Perhaps not; but it will not go away, it will simply adapt and evolve, no doubt in ways not even its creators can anticipate.



---


# ChatGPT FAQ: Basics And Definitions

ChatGPT is a general-purpose chatbot developed by tech startup OpenAI that uses artificial intelligence to generate text after a user enters a prompt; it runs on GPT-4, a large language model that uses deep learning to produce human-like text. GPT stands for Generative Pre-Trained Transformer.

The boundary against the wider category matters: a chatbot can be any software or system that holds dialogue with a person and does not necessarily have to be AI-powered — there are rules-based chatbots that give canned responses to questions — whereas ChatGPT is AI-powered and uses LLM technology to generate text after a prompt. ChatGPT was released for public use on November 30, 2022. Both the free version of ChatGPT and the paid ChatGPT Plus are regularly updated with new GPT models, and the most recent model is GPT-4; the free version requires only a sign-in. There is a free ChatGPT app, at launch limited to U.S. iOS users, with OpenAI saying an Android version is "coming soon," and there is an API, released March 1, 2023.

Anyone can use ChatGPT, and more and more tech companies and search engines are using the chatbot to automate text or quickly answer user questions and concerns. Multiple enterprises use it, although others limit use of the tool. Microsoft announced at its 2023 Build conference that it is integrating its ChatGPT-based Bing experience into Windows 11; the Brooklyn-based 3D display startup Looking Glass uses ChatGPT to produce holograms you can communicate with; and the nonprofit organization Solana integrated the chatbot into its network with a ChatGPT plug-in geared toward end users to help onboard into the web3 space.



---


# ChatGPT Overview And Significance

ChatGPT is OpenAI's text-generating AI chatbot, and it has taken the world by storm: what started as a tool to hyper-charge productivity through writing essays and code from short text prompts has evolved into a behemoth used by more than 92% of Fortune 500 companies for far more wide-ranging needs.

That growth propelled OpenAI itself into becoming one of the most-hyped companies in recent memory, even though CEO and co-founder Sam Altman's firing and swift return raised concerns about the company's direction and opened the door for competitors. The fallout was still settling, but it might empower competitors such as Meta and its LLaMA family of large language models, or help other AI startups get attention and funding as the industry watched OpenAI implode and put itself back together. Whatever the nefarious side of ChatGPT, it was clear that AI tools were not going away anytime soon: since its initial launch nearly a year earlier, ChatGPT had hit 100 million weekly active users, and OpenAI was investing heavily in it.

The capability boundary at the time was defined by model access and modality. GPT-4, which can write more naturally and fluently than previous models, remained largely exclusive to paying ChatGPT users, although it could be accessed for free through Microsoft's Bing Chat in the Microsoft Edge, Google Chrome and Safari web browsers. Beyond GPT-4 and the OpenAI DevDay announcements, OpenAI had recently connected ChatGPT to the internet for all users, and with the integration of DALL-E 3, users could generate both text and images right inside ChatGPT.



---


# ChatGPT FAQ: Capabilities And Limits

ChatGPT can write essays, and its everyday uses include programming, scripts, email replies, listicles, blog ideas and summarization, while advanced uses include debugging code, programming languages, scientific concepts and complex problem solving.

Its coding ability has a stated boundary: how good it is depends on the nature of the program. ChatGPT can write workable Python code but cannot necessarily program an entire app's worth of code, because it lacks context awareness — the generated code is not always appropriate for the specific context in which it is being used. On length, no character limit is documented anywhere, but users have noted some character limitations after around 500 words.

On workflow and detection: OpenAI allows users to save chats in the ChatGPT interface, stored in the sidebar of the screen, with no built-in sharing features yet. Several marketplaces host and provide ChatGPT prompts, either free or for a nominal fee — PromptBase is one, ChatX another, and more launch every day. ChatGPT output can be detected only poorly: several tools claim to detect ChatGPT-generated text, but in TechCrunch's tests they are inconsistent at best.



---


# ChatGPT Custom Instructions And File Analysis

OpenAI launched custom instructions for ChatGPT so users do not have to write the same instruction prompts to the chatbot every time they interact with it, and later extended the feature to all users, including those on the free tier.

The company said the feature lets a user "share anything you'd like ChatGPT to consider in its response." For example, a teacher can say they are teaching fourth-grade math, or a developer can specify the code language they prefer when asking for suggestions; a person can also specify their family size so the text-generating AI can give responses about meals, grocery and vacation planning accordingly. The extension to the free tier allows all users to add various preferences and requirements they want the chatbot to consider when responding.

Separately, ChatGPT began testing file upload and analysis. Subscribers to ChatGPT's Enterprise Plan reported new beta features including the ability to upload PDFs to analyze and ask questions about them directly. The same rollout also means users no longer have to manually select a mode such as DALL-E or browsing when using ChatGPT — instead they are automatically switched to models based on the prompt.

qid: Was there inconsistency in the TechCrunch report on Epic Games' antitrust battle with Google published on November 6, 2023, or in the TechCrunch report on the news publisher's class action antitrust suit against Google published on December 15, 2023, regarding Google's engagement in anticompetitive behavior?
context:
# Google's Parallel Antitrust Proceedings In Late 2023

As of mid-November 2023, Google was fighting antitrust on more than one front at once. The Epic Games case was not its only antitrust case in trial: Google had settled a separate antitrust lawsuit with dating site Match Group the week before November 13, and on November 6 it went to trial with Fortnite maker Epic Games, which hoped to prove that Google engages in anticompetitive behavior with regard to its Android app store, Google Play, and its commission structure. Separately, Google was involved in an antitrust lawsuit with the Department of Justice over its alleged search monopoly.

The Epic case had shed co-plaintiffs on its way to trial. Epic's lawsuit originally involved Match and several U.S. attorneys general, but Google reached a settlement with the attorneys general in October 2023 and with Match the week before November 6, so Epic fought the antitrust battle on its own. The lawsuit, held in the U.S. District Court in California's Northern District, would include testimony from a number of Google and Android execs, including CEO Sundar Pichai, and Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, as well as from Apple, Netflix and other Android developers. Epic, meanwhile, had lost its antitrust battle with Apple and was asking the Supreme Court to weigh in.



---


# The Settlements That Left Epic Standing Alone

Other plaintiffs brought app store antitrust claims against Google and then all settled: all 50 state attorneys general and a number of consumers have tentatively settled, though it is not clear what the deal might include, and Match Group — the company behind Tinder, Match.com, OkCupid and other dating apps — just reached a surprise last-minute settlement too, one that makes it sound like Match effectively gave up. Epic stands alone.

Epic seems to have no interest in settling as long as the "Google tax" exists, and the company has repeatedly said it is not interested in cash. So far it has been willing to push these cases all the way through multiple appeals, cost be damned. It is not clear what Google could proactively offer that would satisfy Epic, since CEO Tim Sweeney has also publicly suggested that Google would simply circumvent any settlement it offers. If you want to see a vision of a future Epic would accept, look to the letter it sent to state attorneys general, laying out a settlement that would basically prohibit Google from doing the anticompetitive things Epic claims it did. Google would not tell The Verge whether it has offered Epic any kind of settlement.



---


# Epic Games v. Google Goes To Trial On November 6, 2023

Epic Games, the maker of Fortnite, went to trial with Google on November 6, 2023, hoping to convince a jury that Google engages in anticompetitive behavior with regard to its Android app store, Google Play, and its commission structure. Match had settled its own antitrust lawsuit with Google the week before, but Epic's case proceeded.

This case differs slightly from Epic's battle with Apple on the same topic, because this time Epic cannot allege there is no other way to load apps onto Android devices, as it could with Apple: Android does allow for sideloading apps. Epic will suggest Google makes that process cumbersome, but the bulk of its arguments will center on what it believes are anticompetitive agreements between Google and device manufacturers and developers.

The precedent Epic's case relies on is a Microsoft case in which courts found Microsoft to have a monopoly over the operating system and to be abusing it, making it hard for users to download alternative browsers, like Netscape, on Windows devices. To make its case, Epic plans to bring claims under Sections 1 and 2 of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act, as well as California's anticompetitive laws, the Cartwright Act and the Unfair Competition Law. It will attempt to argue that Google restrains competition within two separate markets: the distribution of apps to Android users, and the market for payment processing solutions for content inside Android apps.



---


# The U.S. Justice Department's Parallel Antitrust Suits Against Google

The Helena World Chronicle class action arrives alongside the filing of the U.S. Justice Department's lawsuit against Google for monopolizing digital ad technologies, and the complaint also references the Justice Department's 2020 civil antitrust suit over search and search advertising.

The two government cases concern different markets: search and search advertising in the 2020 suit are distinct from the digital ad technologies at issue in the more recent one.



---


# Epic v. Google: What The Trial Is

Epic v. Google is the antitrust case in which Fortnite publisher Epic Games drags a tech giant into court alleging that its mobile app store is an illegal monopoly — and although Epic's parallel claims against Apple already got their day in court, the similar lawsuit against Google never did, which is why the case goes to trial on November 6th, a mere 1,180 days after Epic originally sued.

The déjà vu is the point of confusion the piece sets out to clear up: Epic already went to trial with Apple, resulting in a ruling where Apple mostly won, and its Llamacorn legal gambit failed to #FreeFortnite years ago. The distinction is that the Apple claims were heard and the Google ones were not.

An update dated December 15th, 2023 notes that the case is basically over by then.



---


# Helena World Chronicle's Class Action Antitrust Suit Against Google

A class action lawsuit filed in the week of 15 December 2023 in the U.S. District Court in D.C. accuses Google and parent company Alphabet of anticompetitive behavior in violation of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act and others, on behalf of news publishers. The case was filed by Arkansas-based publisher Helena World Chronicle, which argues that Google "siphons off" news publishers' content, their readers and their ad revenue through anticompetitive means, and it specifically cites new AI technologies such as Google's Search Generative Experience (SGE) and the Bard AI chatbot as worsening the problem.

Helena World Chronicle owns and publishes two weekly newspapers in Arkansas. In the complaint it argues that Google is "starving the free press" by sharing publishers' content on Google, losing them "billions of dollars."

Beyond damages, the suit asks for an injunction that would require Google to obtain consent from publishers before using their website data to train its general artificial intelligence products, including Google's own and those of rivals. It also asks that publishers who opt out of SGE still be allowed to show up in Google search results, among other things.

The law firm handling the case is Hausfeld, whose announcement states that "the anticompetitive effects of Google's scheme cause profound harm to competition, to consumers, to labor, and to a democratic free press," and that "Plaintiff Helena World Chronicle, LLC invokes the Sherman Act and Clayton Act to seek class-wide monetary and injunctive relief to restore and ensure competition for digital news and reference publishing and set up guardrails to preserve a free marketplace of ideas in the new era of artificial intelligence."



---


# Sweeney And Pichai's Settlement Talks

Asked about his settlement talks with Google CEO Sundar Pichai, Tim Sweeney said he could not discuss their content, but that the two met for an hour and had a professional discussion in which they did not reach a settlement — they were, in his words, "rather far apart."

He explained the gap in terms of what Epic was asking for: free and fair competition for everybody, removal of the payments tie, and removal of the anticompetitive measures, which he said obviously leads to far better deals for consumers and developers. What Epic does not want is a special deal just for itself. Sweeney characterised Google's strategy so far, as visible from all these deals, as taking out potential competitors one at a time while they are still weak and small, before they build up or unite into a formidable force — and said Epic is not going to go along with something like that.



---


# Google's News Content Payment Deal With Canada

In November 2023, the month before the Helena World Chronicle suit was filed, Google reached an agreement with the Canadian government under which the search giant would pay Canadian media for use of their content. Under the terms of the deal, Google will provide $73.5 million (100 million Canadian dollars) every year to news organizations in the country, with funds distributed based on the news outlets' headcount.

Negotiations with Meta over the same Canadian law were still unresolved as of mid-December 2023. Meta had begun blocking news in Canada in August, in light of the pressure to pay for content under the new Canadian law.



---


# Epic's Jury Verdict Against Google, December 2023

On Monday, a federal jury sided with Fortnite maker Epic Games in its fight to break Google's control over Android apps, surprising the world. The nine-person jury decided that Google has an illegal monopoly over Android app distribution and in-app payment systems, and that Google illegally tied its Google Play billing system to its app store.

The outcome was striking because "walled garden" rival Apple almost entirely won a similar case two years earlier. For Tim Sweeney, this was, at last, a win.

qid: Did The Roar | Sports Writers Blog report on the Queensland Rugby Union's stance on Rugby Australia's funding to Super Rugby franchises on October 11, 2023, and again on Rugby Australia's efforts to centralize high-performance programs and the potential hiring of Joe Schmidt as the Wallabies coach on December 11, 2023, resulting in a lack of consistency in the support expressed by Super Rugby franchises towards Rugby Australia's decisions?
context:
# The NSW Waratahs' Licence Handover To Rugby Australia

The New South Wales Rugby Union was in the latter stages of handing over its licence to Rugby Australia, The Roar revealed in the week before Oct. 10, 2023 — a move by which the NSW Waratahs, who were on the brink of insolvency, handed over their commercial and high-performance property.

The practical effect is that all male and female Waratahs players, including coaches and high-performance staff, as well as all commercial and operations staff, will run out of RA's office. NSW Waratahs chief executive Paul Doorn informed stakeholders of the decision the previous week.

RA is cognisant that not every Super Rugby franchise will follow suit immediately, but the governing body is hopeful that now one of the two biggest states has agreed to hand over the keys, others will follow swiftly, with the Melbourne Rebels expected to be next. RA chief executive Phil Waugh says building trust back between the governing body and the states is essential to their plans.



---


# The Case For Schmidt Bringing Rugby Smarts To The Wallabies

Several sources told The Roar in December 2023 that Joe Schmidt is exactly the type of person the Wallabies need: the claim is that the highly detailed Schmidt would bring rugby smarts to the Australian program, and the warrant is that the Wallabies' detail and nous were clearly absent on the field over the previous year, which is precisely what his coaching supplies.

The evidence offered for that capability is what his Ireland teams demonstrably did: the manipulation and ability to play both sides of the ruck was clearly visible during his Irish tenure.

The argument also carries a political ground about acceptance within Australian rugby: should Rugby Australia move on him, Schmidt's backing would be largely supported by the Super Rugby franchises.



---


# The QRU's Position On High-Performance Centralisation

In the wake of the Wallabies' 2023 World Cup flop, the Queensland Rugby Union reaffirmed on Oct. 10, 2023 that it is committed to moving to a centralised high-performance model — but will not follow the NSW Waratahs in handing over the keys to Rugby Australia.

The QRU's stated commitment reads: "The QRU is committed to working with Rugby Australia to lead reform of our game at a high-performance level, and help Rugby Australia develop an improved game through high-performance centralisation." The letter defined the scope of that centralisation: it "would include a national player-contracting model, and alignment of key high-performance staff, such as coaching, strength and conditioning, and medical to operate as one national system." The letter, an open letter to members published on Wednesday morning by QRU chief executive David Hanham and chairman Brett Clark, also pointed to RA's involvement in Les Kiss' appointment as Reds coach — the former State of Origin winger turned coach, who has spent the best part of two decades coaching in Ireland and England, replacing Brad Thorn — as an example of the model in practice.

The QRU also expressed strong support for Rugby Australia to conduct a "fully independent and transparent top-to-bottom review of the Wallabies program and how it can be improved" in light of the historic first World Cup pool exit, adding: "It should also provide a clear view of what is needed in a leadership and governance framework to ensure we put the right people, in the right roles, in the right system." The Roar noted the boundary of the consensus: while all five Australian Super Rugby sides are fundamentally on board with moving to a centralised high-performance program, some states, including the ACT Brumbies as well as the QRU, don't want to give up their commercial assets.



---


# Rugby Australia's Debt And Funding Position In 2023

Rugby Australia was forced to take out a $40m loan from Ares to keep the game afloat, and as of Oct. 10, 2023 had around another $15m left to spend from it while looking to borrow up to another $60m.

The purpose of the additional borrowing is to be in the strongest possible position to capitalise on two major money-making events — the 2025 British and Irish Lions series and a home men's World Cup — and succeed. RA is also in the early stages of looking to renew its next broadcast deal, hoping to at least double its current arrangement with Nine Entertainment/Stan Sport, which pays $29m per year until the end of 2025.

The states have their own claims on that money. The QRU expressed its desire for Rugby Australia to reinstate the annual $1.7 million in funding to each of the Super Rugby franchises that was withdrawn following the Covid pandemic to help keep the game afloat, and expressed satisfaction that RA was willing to discuss reinstating it. Meanwhile, The Roar understands the ACT Brumbies sent RA confirmation of solvency for the next 12 months.



---


# Peter Horne's Appointment As Rugby Australia High-Performance Director

Rugby Australia was moving closer to naming World Rugby's director of high-performance Peter Horne as its new director of high-performance, a move The Roar reported on 11 December 2023 could also help land highly-regarded coach Joe Schmidt for the vacant Wallabies job.

The Roar had reported the previous week that Horne emerged as the leading candidate, and it is believed he edged out former Sydney University, Australian Sevens and Harlequins director of rugby Billy Millard for the role. The finer points of the negotiations were being worked out, with an announcement likely over the following week once Horne wrapped up a crucial series of meetings with World Rugby — he was leading World Rugby meetings with tier-two nations that week in Sydney, with former Fiji coach Simon Raiwalui in attendance before officially joining World Rugby. His appointment reflects Rugby Australia's desire to go down an administrative path rather than choose a former coach of any standing, as Millard would have offered, and Horne will sit at the top of the high-performance tree with the next Wallabies coach reporting into him.

His background is given in some detail. Horne joined World Rugby in 2015 as a general manager of high-performance before moving into his current role, and during that tenure the Sydneysider played an important role in setting up competitions, high-performance structures and pathways across developing countries. He also played a role in helping Super Rugby integrate Fiji Drua and Moana Pasifika into the competition. Those successes played out at the recent Rugby World Cup, with Chile, Fiji, Georgia and Portugal delivering encouraging performances that positively reflected World Rugby's desire to spread and build the game. He briefly worked at Saracens as a general manager.



---


# Joe Schmidt's Wallabies Candidacy And The Rival Candidates

The Roar reported on 11 December 2023 that Joe Schmidt — the 2018 World Rugby coach of the year, former Ireland coach and All Blacks assistant — is interested in the vacant Wallabies coaching job, with Dan McKellar, Stephen Larkham, Andy Friend and Ian Foster also remaining interested in the role.

The link the report draws is personal. Peter Horne's close relationship with Schmidt could be one of the keys to landing him: after leaving his Irish post following the 2019 World Cup, ending six years in the job, Schmidt worked alongside Horne at World Rugby, and it is believed the duo have a strong working relationship.



---


# Rugby Australia's Consultancy Approach To David Nucifora

Rugby Australia was trying to get Ireland's long-time director of high-performance David Nucifora on board as a consultant once he wraps up with Ireland, The Roar reported on 11 December 2023, while making clear he was never in the running for the director of high-performance role itself.

The report links that approach to the Schmidt pursuit: should Rugby Australia go down the path of bringing Joe Schmidt into the fold, Schmidt's own relationship with Nucifora could see the Australian reconsider his position with the governing body. In the meantime, Rugby Australia have been making moves to try and twist Nucifora's arm.



---


# The Rugby Australia High-Performance Director Role And Its Remit

The Rugby Australia director of high-performance is the position at the top of the governing body's high-performance structure, described by chief executive Phil Waugh in December 2023 as the biggest job on his leadership team in terms of its impact on the general sentiment around the game in Australia.

Three duties define the role as described. First, the director oversees all of Australia's men's and women's high-performance programs. Second, the holder is tasked with "integrating" those programs, as Rugby Australia tries to centralise all of Super Rugby's high-performance programs. Third — and perhaps most pressing at the time — the director must build a list of coaching candidates to take over from Eddie Jones, with Rugby Australia wanting the new Wallabies coach set in stone by the start of Super Rugby.

The scope conditions attached are timing and seniority. Rugby Australia always said it wanted the role filled by Christmas, and Waugh's framing sets the standard for the appointment: "It's a big job. It's the biggest job on my leadership team in terms of the impact it has on the general sentiment around the game."

qid: After the Sporting News report on December 12, 2023, detailing Manchester United's exit from European competitions, and The Roar | Sports Writers Blog report on December 23, 2023, discussing Manchester United's performance in the English Premier League, was the news regarding Manchester United's performance consistent?
context:
# Manchester United's Defeat To West Ham In December 2023

Goals from West Ham's Jarrod Bowen and Mohammed Kudus beat Manchester United on 23 December 2023, extending United's miserable run in the English Premier League, as reported by The Roar that day.

Bowen bundled home at the second attempt in the 72nd minute for his 11th league goal of the season, breaking the deadlock, and Kudus struck his fourth goal in as many games to settle matters, finishing after a defensive howler from Manchester United — a goal Kobbie Mainoo would not want to see back, and one created by an assist from Lucas Paquetá.

The result is recorded as another worrying setback for manager Erik ten Hag: United had now suffered a 13th defeat in 26 games in all competitions.



---


# Manchester United's European Decline Since Ferguson

The Independent argued on 12 December 2023 that Manchester United's 1-0 defeat to Bayern Munich should have been a landmark low but instead felt grimly routine, because group-stage elimination has become the club's normal European outcome in the post-Ferguson era rather than an aberration.

The grounds are frequency and pattern. Manchester United, one of the grandest and richest names in this competition, have again gone out of the Champions League at the group stage; it is the third time it has happened since Sir Alex Ferguson, meaning it is their most common round of exit in that period. The night is presented as one more entry in a decade of disappointment in a competition in which this club rose to its most emotional heights — a low, but just part of that longer run.

The warrant is the gap between the occasion and the performance. These are not the sounds we are used to hearing after that Champions League theme; something does stir when the anthem is played at Old Trafford amid the lights — well, for most, that is, except the players. United should not be performing like this on what is supposed to be the classic European night at Old Trafford, and the display was a reminder that all they are going to have for some time are their memories. Having been involved in so many ludicrously chaotic matches, the biggest of all ended up being a non-event: this game never threatened to stir anything, and United never threatened at all. That, the argument runs, can now be talked about definitively, since it has been decisively ended.



---


# Manchester United's 2023-24 Champions League Group-Stage Record

Manchester United finished bottom of their 2023-24 Champions League group with four points, in fourth place, eliminated from European competition altogether rather than dropping into the Europa League, The Independent reported on 12 December 2023.

The decisive results came from outside the Bayern fixture. It was not Bayern who eliminated them: it was Galatasaray, who won at Old Trafford and scored six goals over 180 minutes against United, and FC Copenhagen, who qualified instead of them — Rasmus Hojlund's former club will be in the last 16 while his current one will not, making Copenhagen the anomalies in the draw, the outsiders with the spot that had seemed reserved for United. The second place United aimed for went instead to Copenhagen, a club with a fraction of United's budget, and that is where the damage was done. On the final night the Danish side's victory over Galatasaray ensured any United win would be irrelevant, leaving only a slim hope beforehand.

The campaign produced records of the wrong kind. When Coman scored, United became the first Premier League side to concede 15 goals in a Champions League group stage. United won a lone game in the competition, and even that required a penalty save to deny FC Copenhagen a draw. Two months earlier Raphael Varane had said United could win the Champions League; the quadruple Champions League winner may need a rethink. There was no hint of a repeat of their most famous comeback against Bayern, nor even the sense of heroic failure that accompanied their 2010 quarter-final exit to the same club — just crushing failure. When Maguire hobbled off holding his groin and Evans came on, United had a man who played in their 2007-08 Champions League-winning campaign dragooned into service 16 years later.



---


# Preview Of Chelsea's December 2023 Visit To Old Trafford

Manchester United would love a repeat of the previous season's 4-1 home win over Chelsea when the Blues visited Old Trafford that Wednesday, per Sporting News on Dec. 5, 2023.

The pressure on United had grown again following their lacklustre 1-0 defeat at Newcastle on the Saturday, and another setback against a Chelsea side — who beat Brighton & Hove Albion 3-2 the following day — would worsen the misery around Old Trafford.

Sporting News framed the meeting as one between two heavyweights of world football: United and Chelsea are two of only seven teams to have won the modern Premier League, and are only behind Liverpool when it comes to English success with European trophies. Chelsea's recent record against United was poor, but they had won the Premier League twice since United last did so in the 2012/13 season and could exploit the poor form of Ten Hag's side. The article set out to look at a rivalry that stretches back decades and had been sharply in focus over recent years.



---


# Manchester United's 2023/24 Champions League Elimination

Manchester United were out of Europe altogether after a limp display against Bayern at Old Trafford, where Kingsley Coman sealed a 1-0 win for Thomas Tuchel's side on the final day of Champions League group-stage play, per Sporting News on Dec. 12 and Dec. 13, 2023.

The Red Devils finished bottom of their four-team group, leaving them eliminated from Europe in their worst performance in the competition since 2005. On top of that, they set the record for most goals against in a Champions League group stage by an English club, with 15 conceded in their six games.

Their defensive record had collapsed as the season went on: from a Premier League standpoint they sat eighth in the English top flight, but their -5 goal differential was the worst of any club in the top 10.



---


# Tottenham's Premier League Record Of Failing To Win After Leading

OptaJoe recorded on 7 December 2023 that Tottenham had become the first side in Premier League history to fail to win five consecutive games despite going 1-0 up in each match, and the first to lose three consecutive home games despite going 1-0 up in each — a run the post summed up as "Spursy."

The Roar's report places that record in the table. Spurs had rebounded from three consecutive defeats with a stirring 3-3 draw at Manchester City over the weekend, but after this result they sat outside the Champions League qualification spots in fifth place, level with Manchester United.



---


# Erik Ten Hag Under Pressure In December 2023

Erik ten Hag faced a demanding week in early December 2023 amid reports indicating disunity within his team, and by mid-December the pressure around the Dutch boss continued to get more palpable as Manchester United's season continued to slip away.

On Dec. 6, 2023, Sporting News reported that the United manager had faced a demanding week amid reports indicating disunity within his team, and that his players did exceptionally well to block out the noise and focus on footballing matters. # The U.S. Justice Department's Parallel Antitrust Suits Against Google

The Helena World Chronicle class action arrives alongside the filing of the U.S. Justice Department's lawsuit against Google for monopolizing digital ad technologies, and the complaint also references the Justice Department's 2020 civil antitrust suit over search and search advertising.

The two government cases concern different markets: search and search advertising in the 2020 suit are distinct from the digital ad technologies at issue in the more recent one.



---


# Helena World Chronicle's Class Action Antitrust Suit Against Google

A class action lawsuit filed in the week of 15 December 2023 in the U.S. District Court in D.C. accuses Google and parent company Alphabet of anticompetitive behavior in violation of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act and others, on behalf of news publishers. The case was filed by Arkansas-based publisher Helena World Chronicle, which argues that Google "siphons off" news publishers' content, their readers and their ad revenue through anticompetitive means, and it specifically cites new AI technologies such as Google's Search Generative Experience (SGE) and the Bard AI chatbot as worsening the problem.

Helena World Chronicle owns and publishes two weekly newspapers in Arkansas. In the complaint it argues that Google is "starving the free press" by sharing publishers' content on Google, losing them "billions of dollars."

Beyond damages, the suit asks for an injunction that would require Google to obtain consent from publishers before using their website data to train its general artificial intelligence products, including Google's own and those of rivals. It also asks that publishers who opt out of SGE still be allowed to show up in Google search results, among other things.

The law firm handling the case is Hausfeld, whose announcement states that "the anticompetitive effects of Google's scheme cause profound harm to competition, to consumers, to labor, and to a democratic free press," and that "Plaintiff Helena World Chronicle, LLC invokes the Sherman Act and Clayton Act to seek class-wide monetary and injunctive relief to restore and ensure competition for digital news and reference publishing and set up guardrails to preserve a free marketplace of ideas in the new era of artificial intelligence."



---


# What A Ruling Against Google Would Mean For Big Tech

A ruling against Google would not stop at Google: the remedy would likely resemble the Microsoft settlement and the outcome would ripple through the other pending Big Tech cases, because enforcers are using this trial to demonstrate that antitrust law can still take on the largest and most powerful companies in the world.

The grounds for the first half of that claim are the available remedies. If the judge rules against Google, the outcome could look a lot like the Microsoft deal, in which the computer company was required to change its behavior and share its APIs with third-party developers, and was also banned from making anticompetitive and exclusive deals with computer manufacturers. Google might likewise end up having to turn over all or most of the data it has collected to other search engines so they can improve their products and attract more users — a remedy scaled to the disparity the DOJ has cited, that Google gets 16 times more data than Bing does everyday.

The grounds for the ripple effect are the cases already queued behind this one. The FTC sued Amazon in September for using anticompetitive and unfair strategies to illegally maintain its monopoly power. The DOJ has been investigating Apple for years over the company's policy for third-party apps on its devices and whether it unfairly favors its own products. And there is an ongoing case between the FTC and Facebook, in which the agency calls on Facebook to sell Instagram and WhatsApp.

The warrant joining grounds to claim is enforcers' own stake in the result: they will want to show that antitrust law is still relevant and can successfully take on the biggest, most powerful companies in the world, so a win here sets the template the neighbouring cases are argued against. The scope condition is that nothing was settled as of this report — the case is expected to continue for several weeks, bringing to a head one of the biggest fights in tech antitrust since the U.S. took Microsoft to trial in the 1990s.



---


# Google's Parallel Antitrust Proceedings In Late 2023

As of mid-November 2023, Google was fighting antitrust on more than one front at once. The Epic Games case was not its only antitrust case in trial: Google had settled a separate antitrust lawsuit with dating site Match Group the week before November 13, and on November 6 it went to trial with Fortnite maker Epic Games, which hoped to prove that Google engages in anticompetitive behavior with regard to its Android app store, Google Play, and its commission structure. Separately, Google was involved in an antitrust lawsuit with the Department of Justice over its alleged search monopoly.

The Epic case had shed co-plaintiffs on its way to trial. Epic's lawsuit originally involved Match and several U.S. attorneys general, but Google reached a settlement with the attorneys general in October 2023 and with Match the week before November 6, so Epic fought the antitrust battle on its own. The lawsuit, held in the U.S. District Court in California's Northern District, would include testimony from a number of Google and Android execs, including CEO Sundar Pichai, and Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, as well as from Apple, Netflix and other Android developers. Epic, meanwhile, had lost its antitrust battle with Apple and was asking the Supreme Court to weigh in.

# Class Action

## Definition

A class action, as it appears across this corpus, is a single lawsuit pursued on behalf of a group of similarly affected people rather than filed by each person individually.

The corpus documents several such suits from 2023: FTX customers against crypto promoters including Paradigm, a news publisher against Google, consumers against PayPal, and the Authors Guild against OpenAI.

It also shows the mechanism can be blocked by contract, as with Uber's terms of use barring class actions in sexual-assault cases.

## Context

The corpus shows the mechanism used across very different disputes: FTX customers brought a class-action lawsuit accusing crypto investment firm Paradigm and other promoters of defrauding customers by promoting the exchange, publisher Helena World Chronicle filed a class action antitrust suit against Google and Alphabet under the Sherman Act alleging AI tools like Search Generative Experience and Bard siphon off publishers' content and ad revenue, and consumers represented by law firm Hagens Berman filed a class action against PayPal over anti-steering rules that allegedly stifle competition from cheaper platforms like Stripe and Shopify.

The Authors Guild of America, representing Stephen King, John Grisham and 134 other authors, likewise filed its own class-action suit against OpenAI over unauthorized use of copyrighted books in training data, run in parallel to (but distinct from) comedian Sarah Silverman's separate, non-class suit.

Apple's earlier MacBook Pro keyboard class-action settlement is cited in the corpus as a business driver — the corpus notes the settlement cost probably factored into Apple's decision to redesign the keyboard, a change introduced alongside separate updates like a new camera and the removal of the Touch Bar.

## Key Characteristics

- **Collective standing** — a class action lets one or a few plaintiffs (e.g., Helena World Chronicle, the Authors Guild, unnamed FTX customers) litigate on behalf of an entire group with the same underlying grievance, rather than requiring each affected person to sue separately.
- **Can be contractually blocked** — the corpus shows companies can preempt this mechanism: under Uber's terms of use, class action lawsuits cannot be filed against the company in sexual assault cases, forcing survivors to litigate individually and preventing them from advocating for themselves collectively.
- **Used across dispute types** — the corpus applies the same mechanism to fraud (FTX), antitrust (Helena World Chronicle v. Google, PayPal anti-steering), and copyright (Authors Guild v. OpenAI) claims, showing it is a general procedural tool rather than one tied to a single area of law.
- **Settlement exposure shapes corporate behavior** — Apple's keyboard class-action settlement is presented in the corpus as a concrete cost that influenced a subsequent product redesign decision.
- **Defendants, not just plaintiffs, can be named as a group** — the FTX-related suit accuses Paradigm "and others" collectively of defrauding customers, showing the mechanism can target a class of co-defendants as well as aggregate a class of claimants.

## Background (external)

Cornell Law School's Legal Information Institute (Wex) defines a class action generically as "a procedural device that permits one or more plaintiffs to file and prosecute a lawsuit on behalf of a larger group, or 'class'" (Cornell Law School, Legal Information Institute, Wex: "class action," accessed 2026-09-02, https://www.law.cornell.edu/wex/class_action).

# Plea Agreement

## Definition

In the corpus, a plea agreement is the deal by which a criminal defendant (or, in Binance's case, a company) pleads guilty to specified charges in exchange for concessions, rather than going to trial.
It takes effect only once a judge accepts it, and it can bind the party to concrete obligations — cooperating with prosecutors, accepting a recommended fine, stepping back from a role, or admitting specific facts — beyond the bare admission of guilt.

## Context

The corpus shows plea agreements as the mechanism by which several defendants in overlapping 2023 white-collar and criminal cases resolved their charges outside of a trial.
FTX co-founder Gary Wang and Alameda Research CEO Caroline Ellison both pleaded guilty in December 2022 and agreed to cooperate with prosecutors, becoming key witnesses against Sam Bankman-Fried at his fraud trial (doc_0010, doc_0086).
FTX engineering head Nishad Singh similarly pleaded guilty to six charges (doc_0121).
Binance CEO Changpeng "CZ" Zhao and Binance itself each entered separate plea agreements with the U.S. Department of Justice, resolving anti-money-laundering and sanctions violations as part of a $4.3 billion settlement (doc_0374, doc_0375).
YouTube parenting influencer Ruby Franke's plea agreement, accepted by a judge, both formalized her guilty plea to child-abuse charges and documented detailed admissions about the abuse itself (doc_0269).
The corpus also shows a distinct but related instrument — the cooperation agreement Gary Wang signed, which specifically obligated him to meet with prosecutors and answer truthfully (doc_0226) — and notes that a witness's incentive to plead guilty and cooperate (the hope of sentencing leniency) is something a defense team can attack on cross-examination (doc_0293).

## Key Characteristics

- **Court acceptance is required** — a judge must accept the plea agreement before it takes effect; Ruby Franke's sentencing was scheduled only after Judge John J. Walton accepted her plea agreement (doc_0269).
- **Negotiated concessions, not just an admission** — the document can specify what each side gives up: Zhao agreed to a recommended $150 million CFTC fine and to not contradict his acceptance of responsibility, while Binance's agreement barred Zhao from any future role at the company for three years and required it to maintain an independent compliance monitor (doc_0374).
- **Can include cooperation with prosecutors** — Wang and Ellison's guilty pleas were paired with plans to cooperate with, and testify for, the prosecution (doc_0010); Wang's cooperation obligations were spelled out in a separate signed agreement (doc_0226).
- **Distinct from pleading not guilty** — a defendant who instead maintains innocence, as Bankman-Fried did, pleads not guilty and proceeds to trial rather than entering a plea agreement (doc_0010).
- **Can contain substantive factual admissions** — Franke's plea agreement recorded specific admitted details of the abuse itself, beyond the bare fact of guilt (doc_0269).
- **Creates a cross-examination target** — because cooperating witnesses who pleaded guilty may hope for sentencing leniency, defense counsel can (and, per the corpus, did) argue this gives them an incentive to shape testimony favorably to the prosecution (doc_0293).

## Background (external)

Outside the corpus, the general legal definition is broader than any single case above: a plea bargain (or plea agreement) is an agreement between a defendant and a prosecutor in which the defendant agrees to plead guilty to some or all of the charges, usually in exchange for a concession from the prosecutor, such as a reduced charge or a more lenient sentencing recommendation.

# FTX's Inner Circle: Family And Friends Implicated

The Verge's October 26th, 2023 account of the trial catalogued how everyone who loved Bankman-Fried most in the world was caught up in the case. Adam Yedidia, his college roommate, testified with immunity because he was concerned he may have unknowingly worked on code that contributed to the fraud; "I love you Sam," he had texted at one point, "I'm not going anywhere" — that was before he realized FTX had stolen customer funds, at which point he resigned. Nishad Singh, a longtime family friend, copped to what sounded an awful lot like classic embezzlement, saying he had backdated transactions on FTX to help create doctored balance sheets to show to investors, and pleaded guilty to six charges including wire fraud, money laundering, and conspiracy counts around his political donations. Caroline Ellison, Bankman-Fried's ex-girlfriend, told the court about the seven phony balance sheets she had created and was clear that Alameda took customer funds, that Bankman-Fried knew about it, and that he even invested them against her advice.

His family was drawn in too. Joe Bankman, his father, is among the people included in the "small group chat," the Signal group where the FTX inner circle strategized during the exchange's last days. Barbara Fried's political action committee, Mind the Gap, is among the entities that received FTX customer money as political donations; Fried and Bankman lived together in a Bahamas house purchased for them using FTX investor funds, according to a financial expert called by the prosecution, and in a lawsuit filed by FTX's bankruptcy estate the two are alleged to have been given $10 million of FTX customer funds. Gabe Bankman-Fried's nonprofit, Guarding Against Pandemics, got millions from FTX; he was also in a Signal group chat, Donations Processing, that Singh says was used to coordinate the transfer of FTX and Alameda money to various political causes, and in that chat he can be seen recommending that some donations be made "in the dark" to avoid public relations headaches. Singh also said Gabe had an assistant fly to the Bahamas with a stack of blank checks for Singh to sign.

The consequences outlast the trial. Wang, Singh, and Ellison are now felons; even if they never do time — and they may very well be imprisoned or subjected to house arrest — their lives are irrevocably changed, not least by whatever restitution requirements they face, they are barred from taking certain kinds of jobs, and there is the publicity. Bankman, Fried, and Gabe Bankman-Fried's reputations are tarnished, and in the political arenas where they once operated they are suddenly undesirable. Beyond the courtroom, everyone who had money trapped on the exchange when it collapsed — as a result of Alameda purloining customers' funds — had their lives altered: even if they are made whole by the bankruptcy proceedings, that is still money they should have had access to at any time, which may mean houses that were not purchased, medical procedures left undone, and life savings lost. The reporter's summary: it is a Greek tragedy, precipitated by one man's character flaw, the arrogance of Sam Bankman-Fried.



---


# Prosecution And Defense Arguments On Day Two Of The SBF Trial

On the second day of the trial of Sam Bankman-Fried and FTX, the prosecution argued that Bankman-Fried knowingly committed fraud, and it grounded that claim in motive: he did so, prosecutors said, to achieve great wealth, power and influence.

The defense countered with the opposite reading of the same conduct. Its claim was that the FTX founder acted in good faith, never meant to commit fraud or to steal, and basically got in over his head — an argument whose warrant is that inexperience and overreach, rather than intent, explain what happened. The two sides therefore contest intent rather than the underlying events, and the reporting on this exchange comes from Rebecca and Jacquelyn in TechCrunch's Week in Review of October 7, 2023, covering day two of the trial only.

# The SBF Trial Proceedings

Sam Bankman-Fried is in court for alleged fraud and money laundering while leading crypto exchange FTX and sister company Alameda. TechCrunch's 2023-10-02 preview placed the case in the Manhattan Federal Court, describing the disgraced cryptocurrency entrepreneur as accused of orchestrating "one of the biggest financial frauds in American history": the multibillion-dollar collapse of FTX, the crypto exchange he founded and led. SBF, as he is known, has pleaded not guilty to some seven charges of fraud and conspiracy.

The trial kicked off with jury selection October 3. By TechCrunch's 2023-10-06 update the case was entering its next chapter, with proceedings resuming Thursday: as confirmed during a teleconference Wednesday, SBF would be taking the stand along with a handful of other witnesses, as the onus shifted toward the defense after the prosecution brought its case to its conclusion.

Access to the proceedings is limited: no devices are allowed, so reports are being physically put together within the courtroom, or sent to overflow rooms. The jury's composition ranges from a train conductor to a retired investment banker who attended Stanford University, and TechCrunch pointed readers to a special joint episode of its Equity and Chain Reaction podcasts for a better sense of the vibe between the jurors and the rest of the court.

A second account of the same events was arriving in parallel: "Going Infinite," a book by Michael Lewis chronicling the rise and fall of SBF, was set to debut on the first day of the trial.



---


# The Prosecution's Opening Statement Against Bankman-Fried

Thane Rehn, a prosecutor for the government, opened the case against Sam Bankman-Fried with the line "One year ago, it looked like the defendant was on the top of the world," and then argued that this appearance was false: "all of that, all of it, was built on lies," he declared to the jury, adding "Behind the curtains, he was not what he appeared to be." Rehn described a defendant who, as former CEO of FTX, oversaw a supposedly thriving crypto exchange, jetted between international locales, hobnobbed with celebrities like Tom Brady and Larry David, and repeatedly emphasized to customers that their money was safe and secure.

What followed was a roughly 30-minute story that repeatedly emphasized how Bankman-Fried allegedly stole customer funds to facilitate his jet-setting lifestyle, donate millions to political candidates, and finance risky bets. Rehn also directly contested the media framing of the defendant: he was not a crypto "boy" genius, as so many in the media — Fortune included — have written, but a "man" who "stole billions of dollars from thousands of victims." Rehn closed the characterization with a promise to the jury: "You will see the full picture."



---


# Day Two Of The Bankman-Fried Trial: Jury Selection And The Courtroom Audience

On the second day of Sam Bankman-Fried's fraud trial, the jury was selected on Wednesday morning, after which lawyers for the government and then for Bankman-Fried delivered opening statements that told two very different stories of the former FTX CEO's sudden rise and almost instantaneous fall. The central question framed by the proceedings was who Bankman-Fried, the former CEO of crypto exchange FTX, really is: a liar and a fraud, or someone who acted in good faith and, like many a startup founder, flew too close to the sun. That answer, the account notes, ultimately lies with the jury.

The day featured pointed allegations, a friend from MIT, and an audience replete with big names, including Bankman-Fried's professorial parents and Damian Williams, the U.S. attorney for the Southern District of New York. Bankman-Fried himself spent most of the day in court staring into a laptop while seated between his two attorneys. The prosecution's account of his alleged crimes was described as featuring a study in contrasts.



---


# Sam Bankman-Fried

Sam Bankman-Fried is the former CEO of the bankrupt crypto exchange FTX, whose highly anticipated criminal trial started on the Tuesday before TechCrunch's 2023-10-01 report, to determine whether he is guilty of seven counts of fraud and conspiracy. As one former federal prosecutor put it: "The odds seem to be stacked against him at this point."

He was 31 years old and co-founded FTX in 2019; within a few years the once third-largest crypto exchange's valuation hit $32 billion at its peak, and the company is now trying to claw back any funds to distribute to creditors. Before the fall he was even compared to Warren Buffet, and many called him the white horse of crypto — a description TechCrunch notes it never applied to him.

Bankman-Fried, however, maintained his innocence. At The New York Times' DealBook Summit he appeared virtually from the Bahamas and said, "I didn't ever try to commit fraud on anyone; I was shocked by what happened this month"; in a published DM exchange with a Vox reporter he said he regretted filing for bankruptcy and thought that "regulators make everything worse." In January he pleaded not guilty to all counts, which include wire fraud, conspiracy to commit money laundering and conspiracy to misuse customer funds. He could face up to 115 years in jail if convicted on all charges.

TechCrunch's 2023-10-02 summary of his standing on the eve of trial: SBF has been denied bail; his name is mud (or much worse) among those who have lost money in Alameda or FTX; and those who might not have had positions in these still blame him for other crypto woes, because he set off a ripple effect.



---


# Prosecution Opening Statement By Thane Rehn

Assistant US attorney Thane Rehn opened the government's case by pointing at Bankman-Fried and telling the jury, "This man stole billions of dollars from thousands of people." Delivering the statement in the cadence of a high schooler reciting lines in a student play, Rehn dodged explaining cryptocurrency to the jury and instead punched hard on Bankman-Fried lying and stealing, listing the evidence to come: internal company files, what customers were told, the testimony of his co-conspirators, and his own words.

Rehn's narrative contrasted the lifestyle with its foundation. At this time last year, he said, Bankman-Fried had a luxury lifestyle as CEO of the crypto exchange FTX — he hung out with Tom Brady, was on magazine covers, lived in a $30 million penthouse, and spent time with world politicians. "All of that was built on lies," Rehn said. He also told the jury Bankman-Fried sold stock in FTX and borrowed millions from lenders by lying, and laid out the sequence familiar from the news: in May and June of 2022, Alameda Research — the crypto trading company ostensibly helmed by Caroline Ellison — did not have enough to pay its bills, so it pulled customer money to repay loans; by September the hole in the FTX balance sheet was so big that customers could never be repaid.

The Verge's reporter, writing on October 4th, 2023, recorded the defendant's demeanour as the counterpoint: she had never seen Bankman-Fried so still, with the characteristic leg-jiggling absent and only occasional glances at Rehn. His hair was shorn, the result of a haircut from a fellow prisoner per the Wall Street Journal, and he wore a suit bought at a discount at Macy's, also per the Journal; it hung on him, and he appeared to have lost some weight.



---


# The Defense's Good-Faith Case For Bankman-Fried

Mark Cohen, one of Sam Bankman-Fried's lawyers, attacked the prosecution's central premise that his client was a liar who stole from customers, stating early in his opening statement that "Sam didn't defraud anyone." The defense's counter-picture is of a nerdy startup founder who acted in "good faith," not the prosecution's "cartoon of a villain"; Cohen repeatedly harped on Bankman-Fried's allegedly good-faith actions throughout his address to the jury. Bankman-Fried, whose cheekbones were more prominent after spending about seven weeks in a Brooklyn prison, appeared in court as this argument was made.

Cohen also disputed the specific claim that Alameda Research was a covert conduit. Alameda was not subterranean or shady, he said; it was a successful hedge fund. FTX was no Ponzi scheme but a "very innovative, successful company." The business practices between the two were reasonable, he argued, claiming that Alameda acted legally as an FTX customer, payment processor, and market maker — that is, a financial entity that acts as a trading partner for customers looking to buy and sell cryptocurrencies.

The defense's warrant for reading failure as something other than fraud was an analogy Cohen employed throughout: "working at a startup is like building a plane as you're flying it," and businesses sometimes fail. He specifically pointed the finger at Ellison, the former CEO of Alameda, who he said did not adequately protect her hedge fund from the inherent risk of the crypto markets. And when the walls came closing in and the aforementioned plane approached the "eye of the storm," Cohen argued, Bankman-Fried did not act like someone who was guilty — he was willing to give up his personal wealth to make customers whole. "In the end, Sam started and built two billion-dollar businesses," he concluded. "He didn't steal any money."

# ChatGPT's First Year Overview

Over the course of two months from its debut in November 2022, ChatGPT exploded in popularity, from niche online curio to 100 million monthly active users — the fastest user base growth in the history of the Internet. In less than a year, it has earned the backing of Silicon Valley's biggest firms, and been shoehorned into myriad applications from academia and the arts to marketing, medicine, gaming and government.

In short, ChatGPT is just about everywhere, and few industries have remained untouched by the viral adoption of the generative AI's tools. Engadget published this retrospective on 2023-11-30, the first anniversary of its release.



---


# ChatGPT's Task Capabilities And Measured Productivity Effects

ChatGPT's skills extend beyond conversation, another likely reason for its staying power. It can complete and debug code, compose music and essays, answer test questions, generate business ideas, write poetry and song lyrics, translate and summarize text, and even emulate a computer running Linux.

The measured effect comes from one study with a specific task set: an MIT study showed that, for tasks like writing cover letters, "delicate" emails and cost-benefit analyses, ChatGPT decreased the amount of time it took workers to complete the tasks by 40% while increasing output quality by 18%, as measured by third-party evaluators.

Ruoxi Shang attributes the breadth to a shift in how such systems are built: "Because [the AI models powering OpenAI] have been trained extensively on vast amounts of data, they [have] shifted focus from training specialized chatbots for specific domains to creating more general-purpose systems that can handle a variety of topics easily through prompting with instructions … [Chatbots like ChatGPT] don't require users to learn any new form of language, as long as they provide a task and some desired output just like how a manager would communicate to an intern."



---


# Induced AI's Plain-English Workflow Automation

Sam Altman is among the backers of Induced AI, an AI startup founded by two teenagers that aims to help businesses automate workflows in "previously unexplored" ways.

Manish reported the story in TechCrunch's Week in Review of October 7, 2023. Induced AI was founded that same year, and its product lets businesses type their back-office tasks into it in plain English, converting those instructions into pseudo-code in real time.

# Machine Translation

## Definition

In the corpus, machine translation is the automated language-conversion feature that platforms and general-purpose AI models build in to convert user-generated content, product interfaces, or media at scale. It appears as a product feature — Instagram's automatic bio translation, Spotify's AI-driven podcast translation tool, and Roblox's auto-translation pipeline — as well as a capability that general-purpose AI models like Gemini Pro attempt and can fail at.

## Context

Platforms build machine translation into their infrastructure to remove language as a barrier to reach: Roblox's David Baszucki described translation as one of the "invisible" AI functions — alongside safety, efficiency, and moderation — that Roblox has run for two or three years so that a creator's project is "auto-translated into any language" without extra work. Spotify CEO Daniel Ek pointed to a new AI-driven translation product as a way to scale podcast content into non-English markets without commissioning new shows, and extended the same automated-translation logic to advertising, describing generative AI's promise to translate one ad creative into "1,000 or 10,000 or even 100,000" localized versions using the same voice actor. Instagram's automatic translation of user bios is the same category of feature applied to social content rather than podcasts or ads. Separately, general-purpose generative AI models are also evaluated on translation as a capability: TechCrunch's early tests of Google's Gemini Pro found it struggled with a basic French-language prompt, which the reporter took as evidence of "poor multilingual performance."

## Key Characteristics

- **Deployed for scale, not quality alone** — Spotify and Roblox frame automatic translation as a way to reach more languages/markets without proportional human effort, prioritizing coverage over guaranteed accuracy.
- **Embedded as infrastructure** — on Roblox, translation runs as one of several background AI pipelines (with safety, moderation, and efficiency) that operate without the creator or user noticing.
- **Error-prone in practice** — Instagram's automatic translation of the Arabic phrase "Alhamdulillah" ("Praise be to God") into text calling Palestinians terrorists shows machine translation can silently introduce serious, context-dependent errors rather than merely be imprecise.
- **A benchmarked capability of general AI models** — beyond dedicated translation products, general-purpose models like Gemini Pro are tested on translation prompts as one measure of overall model quality, alongside factual accuracy and coding.

# ChatGPT Overview And Significance

ChatGPT is OpenAI's text-generating AI chatbot, and it has taken the world by storm: what started as a tool to hyper-charge productivity through writing essays and code from short text prompts has evolved into a behemoth used by more than 92% of Fortune 500 companies for far more wide-ranging needs.
