When she acts like that I better not be the one acting all strange."



---


# Travis Kelce's Comments On Relationship Privacy

Travis Kelce broke his silence on Taylor Swift's Chiefs game attendance on his podcast on 27 September 2023, while saying he would not speak much more about the relationship, according to CBS Sports' timeline published 12 October 2023.

On the game itself, Kelce said: "To see the slow-motion chest bumps, to see the high-fives with Mom, to see how Chiefs Kingdom was all excited that she was there -- that s--- was absolutely hysterical. It's definitely a game I'll remember, that's for damn sure."

He then set the limit, noting that he wants "to respect both of our lives," and drew a distinction between his own exposure and Swift's: "Yeah, my personal life -- that's not so personal. I did this to myself Jason, I know this. What's real is that you know it is my personal life. ... She's not in the media as much as I am doing this show every single week."



---


# Taylor Swift And Joe Alwyn's Relationship And Breakup

In April 2023 it was revealed that Taylor Swift and British actor Joe Alwyn had broken up after six years of dating. The former couple were notoriously private: the Conversations with Friends star had previously said he did not want to discuss the relationship because doing so "feeds into a weird part of the culture."

Even so, the relationship generated constant rumours about Swift's personal life — enough that her publicist, Tree Paine, was forced to publicly deny some of them. Swift, arguably more famous now than ever before, said the constant attention and swarms of paparazzi would not stop her from living her life.



---


# Swift And Kelce's Public Appearances Together

Taylor Swift and Travis Kelce appeared together publicly through the autumn of 2023, at his games, at her concerts, and away from both. On 22 October Swift returned to Arrowhead Stadium to watch the Kansas City Chiefs beat the Los Angeles Chargers — her fourth time attending one of Kelce's games amid ongoing reports that they were dating — and the pair seemingly confirmed the relationship there. Afterwards Chariah Gordon, the partner of Kelce's teammate Mecole Hardman Jr, posted an Instagram picture of Swift standing next to Kelce and reaching to kiss his cheek. Kelce also responded warmly when a fan shouted "Let's go Taylor's boyfriend" while he waited for an elevator, smiling slightly and pumping his fist into the air.

The couple were also photographed together away from stadiums, including a date earlier that month in New York City after their surprise appearances on the season 49 premiere of Saturday Night Live. Sources alleged to Entertainment Tonight that during that date Kelce got too close to Swift's security personnel and told her bodyguard to step aside; on his podcast Kelce explained what he had said and denied pushing anyone: "I placed my hand on the gentleman's back to let him know I was behind him. If I would have pushed him, he probably would have turned around and tased me." Kelce reciprocated the support in November by travelling to Buenos Aires, Argentina, for one of her Eras Tour shows, where Swift changed her "Karma" lyrics to "Karma is the guy on the Chiefs, coming straight home to me," laughing as fans screamed; after the show the "Style" singer was seen running into his arms and kissing him before he whisked her backstage.



---


# Travis Kelce and Taylor Swift Dating Rumours in 2023

Speculation that Travis Kelce and Taylor Swift were dating began in July 2023, when Kelce confessed that he had tried and failed to give Swift a friendship bracelet bearing his phone number at one of her Eras Tour concerts; he later invited her on his podcast to one of his games at Arrowhead Stadium, an invitation she famously accepted on 24 September 2023, and she had attended three more of his games by 25 November 2023.

Kelce first told the bracelet story to his brother on their podcast back in July. "I was disappointed that she doesn't talk before or after her shows, because she has to save her voice for the 44 songs that she sings," he explained. "So I was a little butthurt I didn't get to hand her one of the bracelets I made for her. If you're up on Taylor Swift concerts, there are friendship bracelets and I received a bunch of them being there, but I wanted to give Taylor Swift one with my number on it."

The NFL star officially addressed the dating rumours during an episode of The Pat McAfee Show on 21 September 2023, in which he mocked his brother Jason Kelce for joking that he "100 per cent" believed his younger sibling was dating Swift. "It's hilarious how much traction this has actually gotten, right now it's like a game of telephone," Kelce said. "Where everybody's whispering in each other's ears and hearing random stuff. No one actually knows what's going on, especially when you got Jason Kelce on live television telling people just both sides - he doesn't know, it's true, this and that." He also said he remained open to pursuing a relationship with Swift, revealing that he had subtly asked whether she would attend one of his games: "I threw it out there, I threw the ball in her court. I told her, you know, I've seen you rock the stage in Arrowhead [Stadium], you might have to come see me rock the stage in Arrowhead and see which one's a little more lit. So, we'll see what happens in the near future."



---


# The Taylor Swift And Travis Kelce Romance Overview

Rumours that singer Taylor Swift and Chiefs tight end Travis Kelce were dating ran for weeks and only intensified as Swift attended five Chiefs games during the season, according to CBS Sports' timeline of the rumoured romance published 12 October 2023.

The report gives the pattern of appearances. At the first game she attended the previous month, the Eras Tour singer was seen chatting with the tight end's mother, Donna Kelce, and cheering emphatically when No. 87 scored a touchdown. The week before publication she was in attendance to watch the Chiefs defeat the Denver Broncos in Week 6 on "Thursday Night Football." She was once again at Arrowhead Stadium, this time to watch the Chiefs take on another AFC West opponent, the Los Angeles Chargers.



---


# The Swift Effect On NFL Ratings And Kelce Jersey Sales

The NFL's focus on the Taylor Swift and Travis Kelce dating rumours paid off in ratings even as it annoyed some sports fans. Per a Deadline report cited by The Independent on 4 October 2023, NBC accumulated an average of 27m viewers for the broadcast, with a total of 29m tuning in during the second quarter. On the New Heights podcast, Jason Kelce told his younger brother: "That's gotta be an NFL record right there," noting that about two million viewers were estimated to be female and joking, "I think a few of them might have been there for Deadpool and, uh, Taylor."

Merchandise moved as well: jersey sales for the Chiefs tight end reportedly spiked by 400 per cent, according to a report from the NFL's e-commerce partner, Fanatics, since Swift began attending her rumoured boyfriend's games.

qid: Has the description of ChatGPT's capabilities by TechCrunch changed between the article published on September 28 and the subsequent article on November 30?
context:
# GPT Model Lineage And The ChatGPT Launch

GPT (Generative Pre-trained Transformer) is the large language model that ChatGPT runs on, and OpenAI had been developing it since 2016 — unveiling GPT-1 in 2018 and iterating it to GPT-3 by June 2020. With the November 30, 2022 release of GPT-3.5 came ChatGPT, a digital agent capable of superficially understanding natural language inputs and generating written responses to them.

The first iteration's limits were plain: it was rather slow to answer and couldn't speak to questions about anything that happened after September 2021, not to mention its issues answering queries with misinformation during bouts of "hallucinations." Even so, that kludgy first iteration demonstrated capabilities far beyond what other state-of-the-art digital assistants like Siri and Alexa could provide — the discriminating feature that set it apart from what came before.



---


# ChatGPT Web Browsing And Plugins

OpenAI formally launched an internet-browsing feature for ChatGPT, ending the chatbot's confinement to training data up to September 2021 — a launch that came some three weeks after the feature was re-introduced in beta following several months in hiatus.

The path there ran through plugins and a withdrawal. OpenAI first connected ChatGPT to the internet by launching plugins, extending the bot's functionality by granting it access to third-party knowledge sources and databases, including the web; plugins were available in alpha to ChatGPT users and developers on the waitlist, with OpenAI saying it would initially prioritize a small number of developers and premium ChatGPT Plus subscribers before rolling out larger-scale and API access. OpenAI then announced that ChatGPT Plus subscribers could use a feature in the app called Browsing, which allows ChatGPT to search Bing for answers; it is enabled from the New Features section of app settings by selecting "GPT-4" in the model switcher and choosing "Browse with Bing" from the drop-down list, and it is available on both the iOS and Android apps. That web browsing capability for Plus subscribers, offered in July, was taken away after users exploited it to get around paywalls.

OpenAI posted on Twitter/X on September 27, 2023 that "ChatGPT can now browse the internet to provide you with current and authoritative information, complete with direct links to sources. It is no longer limited to data before September 2021."



---


# ChatGPT As A User Experience Breakthrough, Not An AI One

Stella Biderman, an AI researcher at Booz Allen Hamilton and the open research group EleutherAI, told TechCrunch that she does not see ChatGPT as an AI breakthrough per se, but as a bonafide "user experience breakthrough" that took generative AI mainstream. TechCrunch adds a supporting observation: OpenAI, which has released dozens of research papers on its models, tellingly never released one on ChatGPT.

The ground for calling it a UX rather than a technical advance is a change in the skill required of users: "Previously you needed to have some skill, albeit not be an expert, to consistently get usable stuff out of [text-generating models]. Now that that's changed … [ChatGPT has] brought a very large amount of attention to and discussion about the technology."

The warrant, in Biderman's framing, is where the effect landed — on the research and development community's attention rather than on capability: "The primary impact [ChatGPT] has had [is] encouraging people training AIs to try to mimic it, or encouraging people studying AIs to use it as their central object of study."



---


# Associated Press And OpenAI's Licensing Deal

Select news outlets proved far more amenable to OpenAI than the authors suing it. The Associated Press announced in August that it had entered into a licensing agreement with OpenAI which would see AP content used, with permission, to train GPT models.

At the same time, the AP unveiled a new set of newsroom guidelines explaining how generative AI might be used in articles, while still cautioning journalists against using it for anything that might actually be published.



---


# ChatGPT Adoption Milestones And Usage Statistics

Roughly a year after its release, ChatGPT had 100 million weekly active users, and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman also revealed that over two million developers use the platform, including more than 92% of Fortune 500 companies.

Two other markers frame that scale. OpenAI hit the one-year anniversary of ChatGPT: what began as a "low-key research preview" evolved into a powerhouse that changed the AI industry forever, and Altman looked back on the night before its launch in a post on X on November 30, 2023 — "a year ago tonight we were probably just sitting around the office putting the finishing touches on chatgpt before the next morning's launch. what a year it's been…" Meanwhile neither Apple nor Google chose an AI app as its app of the year for 2023, despite the success of ChatGPT's mobile app, which became the fastest-growing consumer application in history before that record was broken by Meta's Threads.

Adoption among the general public is far thinner than the headline numbers suggest. Ongoing polling by Pew Research shows that although ChatGPT is gaining mindshare, only about 18% of Americans have ever actually used it — suggesting the language model is not quite as popular or threatening as some would have you think.



---


# The ChatGPT "Winter Break" Laziness Hypothesis

The "winter break hypothesis" proposes that ChatGPT gets worse in December because the model "learned" to do less work over the holidays — an explanation offered by users for a drop in output quality they began noticing in November 2023.

Starting in November, ChatGPT users noticed that the chatbot felt "lazier" than normal, citing instances of simpler answers and of the model refusing to complete requested tasks. Some users think this plays into the winter break hypothesis; others wonder whether the chatbot is simulating seasonal depression. OpenAI confirmed it was aware of the issue but was not sure why it was happening.

What would bear on the hypothesis is whether the model itself changed. OpenAI's ChatGPT account posted on December 8, 2023: "we've heard all your feedback about GPT4 getting lazier! we haven't updated the model since Nov 11th, and this certainly isn't intentional. model behavior can be unpredictable, and we're looking into fixing it." That the weights were unchanged since November 11 and that the behavior is unintentional are the facts against which any seasonal explanation has to be tested.



---


# ChatGPT Legal And Privacy Controversies

ChatGPT has generated a run of legal and privacy controversies: an Australian mayor publicly announced he may sue OpenAI for defamation over ChatGPT's false claims that he had served time in prison for bribery, which would be the first defamation lawsuit against the text-generating service, and there have been other cases of ChatGPT accusing individuals of false crimes.

The libel exposure follows from how the models work: they do not know or care whether something is true, only that it looks true — a problem when the output is used for homework, and potentially libel when it accuses someone of a crime they did not commit. How troubling statements produced by ChatGPT will be handled was expected to play out over the following months as tech and legal experts tackled the fastest moving target in the industry. As of the article, there were no lawsuits specifically targeting ChatGPT, but OpenAI is involved in at least one lawsuit with implications for AI systems trained on publicly available data, which would touch on ChatGPT. There are also plagiarism issues: text-generating AI models like ChatGPT have a tendency to regurgitate content from their training data. Copyright in output sits with the user — the person who requested the input from ChatGPT is the copyright owner.

On privacy, OpenAI has said that individuals in "certain jurisdictions" such as the EU can object to the processing of their personal information by its AI models by filling out a form — the "OpenAI Personal Data Removal Request" — which includes the ability to request deletion of AI-generated references about them, although OpenAI notes it may not grant every request since it must balance privacy requests against freedom of expression "in accordance with applicable laws." In its privacy policy OpenAI makes a passing acknowledgement of the objection requirements attached to relying on "legitimate interest," pointing users to instructions on how to opt out of use of their information to train its models. ChatGPT chats are not public, but OpenAI disclosed a bug, since fixed, that exposed the titles of some users' conversations to other people on the service.

Other controversies span platforms and schools. Discord integrated OpenAI's technology into its bot Clyde, and two users tricked Clyde into providing instructions for making methamphetamine and napalm. CNET found itself in controversy after Futurism reported the publication was publishing articles under a mysterious byline completely generated by AI, and Red Ventures, the private equity company that owns CNET, was accused of using ChatGPT for SEO farming even where the information was incorrect. Several major school systems and colleges, including New York City Public Schools, have banned ChatGPT from their networks and devices, claiming the AI impedes the learning process by promoting plagiarism and misinformation — a claim not every educator agrees with.

# Testimony At The SBF Trial

Across the first three weeks of the trial, a run of former colleagues, an outside investor and a forensic accounting expert testified that FTX customer money flowed into Alameda Research and out again to other uses, and that FTX's investors were never told about the two firms' special relationship. TechCrunch's running coverage, published 2023-10-06, summarises each week.

In week one, FTX's co-founder and CTO Gary Wang testified Thursday on the extent to which Alameda Research was used for whatever purposes he and SBF saw fit: according to Wang, the crypto trading firm pulled funding directly from FTX customers, whose transactions would be funneled toward Alameda and then directed elsewhere. Thursday also brought testimony from Matt Huang, co-founder and managing partner at crypto investment firm Paradigm, which invested $278 million in FTX across 2021 and 2022 and is part of a class-action lawsuit accusing it and others of defrauding customers by promoting FTX. His testimony centered around being left uninformed about FTX's utilization of customer money to keep Alameda Research afloat — a practice Huang says would have halted his involvement — and covered his relationship with FTX stretching back to 2019.

Week two's standout testimony came from Alameda Research's former CEO Caroline Ellison, who claimed she took $14 billion from customers to repay debts to lenders, using them as a line of credit under the instruction of SBF. Ellison also went into detail about how a $2 billion venture fund, FTX Ventures, was funded by money that had previously been allocated to Alameda from third-party lenders. And though there are no charges of bribery in the case, she also testified to paying Chinese officials $150 million to restore access to $1 billion in frozen trading accounts.

The third week featured a couple of noteworthy moments for the prosecution. FTX's former general counsel Can Sun, like many of SBF's former colleagues, opted to cooperate with authorities and testified that SBF asked him to create a theoretical "legal justification" for the use of billions in consumer funds just days before FTX filed for bankruptcy. Robert Boroujerdi, managing director of the hedge fund Third Point, testified about his experience working with SBF and FTX in a partnership that ultimately resulted in a $60 million investment and a lack of awareness about the special relationship between Alameda Research and FTX; had he known of such a relationship, he testified, Third Point would not have invested in FTX in the first place. And earlier in the week, Peter Easton — a University of Notre Dame professor who helped the government prosecution of Enron and WorldCom — testified about what he uncovered after tracing the flow of billions of dollars between Alameda Research and FTX: much of that funding came from customers, and Easton testified that he found user deposits were used by both FTX and Alameda to purchase real estate, make investments or direct funding toward political causes and charities.



---


# Marc-Antoine Julliard's Testimony As FTX's First Witness-Victim

The prosecution's first witness at Sam Bankman-Fried's trial was not a blockbuster name or a former lieutenant-turned-cooperator like Caroline Ellison but a victim: Marc-Antoine Julliard, a Paris-born cocoa trader who lives in London and whose money got stuck on FTX. Julliard testified that on Nov. 8, 2022, in the crypto exchange's final few days, he tried to pull out almost $100,000 in cash and crypto, and that he was never able to. The withdrawal screenshots shown in court were of attempts to move $20,000 USD and about 4 Bitcoin, worth about $20,000 at the time — roughly $100,000 in total, inaccessible.

Julliard explained why he had chosen FTX in 2021 when he decided to invest in crypto, trading currencies like Bitcoin and Dogecoin there. He trusted FTX because Bankman-Fried came across as a leading figure of the industry; because the sheer volume of users mattered to him, and FTX was at the time among the top three biggest exchanges; and because major VC firms had invested. "They don't commit hundreds of millions without doing due diligence, checking the books, the accountancy of the firm, going through several compliance process[es], so that was a vote of confidence for me," he said. He also noted FTX's glossy ads — featuring Gisele Bündchen, for instance — which suggested a very high budget, and reasoned that it wouldn't make sense to spend that much money unless FTX had very strong financials. He opened an account, transferred in both regular money and cryptocurrency, and used the exchange to execute his plan of buying Bitcoin to sell back in five to ten years at higher prices.

In November 2022 things went bad. Julliard followed Bankman-Fried on Twitter and read aloud in court the "FTX is fine. Assets are fine" tweets, along with "FTX has enough to cover all client holdings. We don't invest client assets" and a few others, which gave him the impression that his money was there and that any problem might be technical — anti-spam measures — or regulatory. By the time he tried to get his money out on November 8th, it was too late. Cross-examining a customer whose money is gone is described as a thankless task, but Mark Cohen tried anyway, noting that Julliard was a licensed commodities broker who was trading in crypto because he didn't have to disclose it, that he knew crypto was new and risky, and that he didn't review the terms of service agreement he had assented to when making his FTX account. The next witness called was Bankman-Fried's former college and FTX roommate, Adam Yedidia.



---


# Gary Wang's Testimony At The FTX Fraud Trial

Gary Wang, the lesser-known co-founder of FTX, told a Manhattan courtroom on Thursday that he had committed financial crimes while working at FTX — including wire and commodities fraud — carried out with the help of Sam Bankman-Fried, FTX ex-engineering head Nishad Singh, and Caroline Ellison, who ran sister hedge fund Alameda Research and had been Bankman-Fried's girlfriend.

Asked by Assistant U.S. Attorney Nicolas Roos, "Did you commit financial crimes while working at FTX?" Wang responded, "Yes." Asked whether he saw any of the people he committed those crimes with in the courtroom, Wang — dressed in an oversized and wrinkled suit with a red tie and glasses — awkwardly stood up, looked around, and answered, "Yes"; asked who, he said, "Sam Bankman-Fried." He was one of two former friends of Bankman-Fried's from MIT who also worked at FTX while living with the founder in the Bahamas and who took the stand that week to testify against their former classmate, confidant and boss, a man who allegedly ran a crypto empire that defrauded thousands of customers out of billions of dollars. The trial, set to last six weeks, was to resume on Tuesday with key testimony expected from Ellison, considered the prosecution's star witness, who had already pleaded guilty to multiple charges. Bankman-Fried faces seven federal charges, including wire fraud, securities fraud and money laundering, that could put him in prison for the rest of his life. Thus far Bankman-Fried, 31, has remained mostly quiet in court, intently listening to witnesses and at times writing notes to his attorneys — but as Wang testified against him, he looked visibly upset, shifting his gaze from his former friend to the ground and at one point putting his head in his hands.



---


# FTX's Spending Served Bankman-Fried's Status, Not Philanthropy

The Verge's reporter argued that at every turn the scams at FTX and Alameda led back to making Bankman-Fried more important — not to giving money away, as his stated Effective Altruism rationale claimed. The grounds are the pattern of what the money bought: Singh testified to more than a billion dollars spent on celebrity endorsements, which made FTX very famous even though the futures platform did not operate in the US; the political donations gave Bankman-Fried influence in the highest echelons of power; and Ellison testified to venture investments that gave him more dominance in the tech world.

The warrant joining the pattern to the conclusion is that spending reveals priorities better than statements do: it is easy to lie with words and harder to lie with money. Bankman-Fried went around telling people he wanted to make a lot of money in order to give it away, an idea of the Effective Altruism movement he affiliated himself with, but the amount he funneled to his Paper Bird vehicle alone was ten times the size of his philanthropic spending as outlined by the prosecution's expert Peter Easton — and all of it was vastly outweighed by his investments, the places where he could prove he was very smart by investing in the right companies early.



---


# John J. Ray III Running The FTX Estate

What's left of FTX is now being led by John J. Ray III — the man who cleaned up Enron, and who has said FTX is worse than Enron.

Just before the trial began, the FTX lawyers filed suit against Bankman-Fried's parents, saying they should give back millions of dollars they got from their kid. Ray has also referred to Bankman-Fried's conduct as "really just old-fashioned embezzlement."

# Day Two Of The Bankman-Fried Trial: Jury Selection And The Courtroom Audience

On the second day of Sam Bankman-Fried's fraud trial, the jury was selected on Wednesday morning, after which lawyers for the government and then for Bankman-Fried delivered opening statements that told two very different stories of the former FTX CEO's sudden rise and almost instantaneous fall. The central question framed by the proceedings was who Bankman-Fried, the former CEO of crypto exchange FTX, really is: a liar and a fraud, or someone who acted in good faith and, like many a startup founder, flew too close to the sun. That answer, the account notes, ultimately lies with the jury.

The day featured pointed allegations, a friend from MIT, and an audience replete with big names, including Bankman-Fried's professorial parents and Damian Williams, the U.S. attorney for the Southern District of New York. Bankman-Fried himself spent most of the day in court staring into a laptop while seated between his two attorneys. The prosecution's account of his alleged crimes was described as featuring a study in contrasts.



---


# Prosecution And Defense Arguments On Day Two Of The SBF Trial

On the second day of the trial of Sam Bankman-Fried and FTX, the prosecution argued that Bankman-Fried knowingly committed fraud, and it grounded that claim in motive: he did so, prosecutors said, to achieve great wealth, power and influence.

The defense countered with the opposite reading of the same conduct. Its claim was that the FTX founder acted in good faith, never meant to commit fraud or to steal, and basically got in over his head — an argument whose warrant is that inexperience and overreach, rather than intent, explain what happened. The two sides therefore contest intent rather than the underlying events, and the reporting on this exchange comes from Rebecca and Jacquelyn in TechCrunch's Week in Review of October 7, 2023, covering day two of the trial only.



---


# The SBF Trial Proceedings

Sam Bankman-Fried is in court for alleged fraud and money laundering while leading crypto exchange FTX and sister company Alameda. TechCrunch's 2023-10-02 preview placed the case in the Manhattan Federal Court, describing the disgraced cryptocurrency entrepreneur as accused of orchestrating "one of the biggest financial frauds in American history": the multibillion-dollar collapse of FTX, the crypto exchange he founded and led. SBF, as he is known, has pleaded not guilty to some seven charges of fraud and conspiracy.

The trial kicked off with jury selection October 3. By TechCrunch's 2023-10-06 update the case was entering its next chapter, with proceedings resuming Thursday: as confirmed during a teleconference Wednesday, SBF would be taking the stand along with a handful of other witnesses, as the onus shifted toward the defense after the prosecution brought its case to its conclusion.

Access to the proceedings is limited: no devices are allowed, so reports are being physically put together within the courtroom, or sent to overflow rooms. The jury's composition ranges from a train conductor to a retired investment banker who attended Stanford University, and TechCrunch pointed readers to a special joint episode of its Equity and Chain Reaction podcasts for a better sense of the vibe between the jurors and the rest of the court.

A second account of the same events was arriving in parallel: "Going Infinite," a book by Michael Lewis chronicling the rise and fall of SBF, was set to debut on the first day of the trial.



---


# The Prosecution's Opening Statement Against Bankman-Fried

Thane Rehn, a prosecutor for the government, opened the case against Sam Bankman-Fried with the line "One year ago, it looked like the defendant was on the top of the world," and then argued that this appearance was false: "all of that, all of it, was built on lies," he declared to the jury, adding "Behind the curtains, he was not what he appeared to be." Rehn described a defendant who, as former CEO of FTX, oversaw a supposedly thriving crypto exchange, jetted between international locales, hobnobbed with celebrities like Tom Brady and Larry David, and repeatedly emphasized to customers that their money was safe and secure.

What followed was a roughly 30-minute story that repeatedly emphasized how Bankman-Fried allegedly stole customer funds to facilitate his jet-setting lifestyle, donate millions to political candidates, and finance risky bets. Rehn also directly contested the media framing of the defendant: he was not a crypto "boy" genius, as so many in the media — Fortune included — have written, but a "man" who "stole billions of dollars from thousands of victims." Rehn closed the characterization with a promise to the jury: "You will see the full picture."



---


# Engoron Summary Judgment That Trump Committed Fraud

A judge ruled on Tuesday 26 September 2023 that Donald Trump committed fraud for years while building the real estate empire that catapulted him to fame and the White House. Judge Arthur Engoron, ruling in a civil lawsuit brought by New York's attorney general, found that the former president and his company deceived banks, insurers and others by massively overvaluing his assets and exaggerating his net worth on paperwork used in making deals and securing financing.

As punishment, Engoron ordered that some of Trump's business licences be rescinded, and said he would continue to have an independent monitor oversee the Trump Organization's operations. A Trump spokesperson did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the ruling, and Trump has long insisted he did nothing wrong.

Fortune described the decision, which came days before the start of a non-jury trial in Attorney General Letitia James' lawsuit, as the strongest repudiation yet of Trump's carefully coiffed image as a wealthy and shrewd real estate mogul turned political powerhouse.



---


# Caroline Ellison's Guilty Plea And First Day Of Testimony

Caroline Ellison, head of the hedge fund Alameda Research during its implosion along with FTX, took the stand on October 10th, 2023 having already pleaded guilty to criminal charges — fraud, conspiracy to commit fraud, and money laundering — and told the jury that Bankman-Fried "directed me to commit these crimes." She quantified the taking: "We ultimately took about $14 billion, some of which we were not able to pay back."

Her long-anticipated first day took the form of walking through a damning spreadsheet she had prepared for her ex and boss, now the defendant in a criminal fraud trial. She entered hunched in on herself, wearing a dusty rose dress with a gray blazer over it, looking less like an executive than like a girl who had borrowed her boyfriend's coat because she was cold. Asked by the prosecution to identify Bankman-Fried, she had trouble finding him and gazed around the courtroom for more than 20 seconds — apparently he was incognito with his new haircut — and when she did spot him she identified him as the one wearing a suit, which got chuckles from the rest of the defense table, also all in suits. She tilted her head down to answer questions and lifted it when she had finished each answer.

The defendant's own reaction registered the shift: Bankman-Fried had been vibrating slightly during Wang's testimony, and during Ellison's his bouncing became more noticeable. By the end of the day, The Verge's reporter wrote, the spreadsheet seemed like a sideshow.



---


# Sam Bankman-Fried

Sam Bankman-Fried is the former CEO of the bankrupt crypto exchange FTX, whose highly anticipated criminal trial started on the Tuesday before TechCrunch's 2023-10-01 report, to determine whether he is guilty of seven counts of fraud and conspiracy. As one former federal prosecutor put it: "The odds seem to be stacked against him at this point."

He was 31 years old and co-founded FTX in 2019; within a few years the once third-largest crypto exchange's valuation hit $32 billion at its peak, and the company is now trying to claw back any funds to distribute to creditors. Before the fall he was even compared to Warren Buffet, and many called him the white horse of crypto — a description TechCrunch notes it never applied to him.

Bankman-Fried, however, maintained his innocence. At The New York Times' DealBook Summit he appeared virtually from the Bahamas and said, "I didn't ever try to commit fraud on anyone; I was shocked by what happened this month"; in a published DM exchange with a Vox reporter he said he regretted filing for bankruptcy and thought that "regulators make everything worse." In January he pleaded not guilty to all counts, which include wire fraud, conspiracy to commit money laundering and conspiracy to misuse customer funds. He could face up to 115 years in jail if convicted on all charges.

TechCrunch's 2023-10-02 summary of his standing on the eve of trial: SBF has been denied bail; his name is mud (or much worse) among those who have lost money in Alameda or FTX; and those who might not have had positions in these still blame him for other crypto woes, because he set off a ripple effect.

# US v. Google: Two Months Into The Search Antitrust Trial

As of TechCrunch's November 13, 2023 roundup, the Justice Department's landmark antitrust case against Google was nearly two months old, and the trial record was still producing fresh revelations. TechCrunch framed it as one of the biggest fights in tech antitrust since the U.S. took Microsoft to trial in the 1990s.

An earlier roundup had already surfaced that Google spent $26.3 billion in 2021 making itself the default search engine across platforms, and that Google tried to have Chrome preinstalled on iPhones. Over the couple of weeks preceding this roundup, more of Google's inner workings came to light, including some of the search engine's most lucrative search queries, the shape of the revenue-share agreements between Google and Android OEMs, and why Expedia has a bone to pick with Google.



---


# Google Paid $26.3 Billion In 2021 For Default Search Placement

Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to multiple browsers, phones and platforms — from companies including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla — to be everyone's default search engine. The figure was revealed by Google's search head Prabhakar Raghavan when he testified in court on October 28, according to The Verge.

About $18 billion of that total went directly to Apple, according to a New York Times report published earlier in October 2023, and Google has had its deal with Apple in place since 2003 — so the payment is the current year of a two-decade arrangement, not a one-off. Questioned on the amount of money Google spends to get first pick of search engines, Pichai said the decision was made with the consumer in mind: Google pays big bucks to be everywhere so that it can take in all the data and be the best search engine across different companies' devices, he said, according to The Verge.

The trial also produced evidence that Google understood the value of defaults very early on. U.S. Justice Department lawyer Meagan Bellshaw showed Pichai a 2007 email from a Google product strategy meeting containing data showing that when people changed their browser homepage to Google, they did 15% more Google searches, and that when they switched away, their Google searches dropped 27%. The email summarizing that meeting, sent to Pichai as well as other Google leaders, read: "Nitin argues that focusing on homepage market share is one of the most effective things we can do to make gains in search market share," according to The Verge.



---


# The U.S. Justice Department's Parallel Antitrust Suits Against Google

The Helena World Chronicle class action arrives alongside the filing of the U.S. Justice Department's lawsuit against Google for monopolizing digital ad technologies, and the complaint also references the Justice Department's 2020 civil antitrust suit over search and search advertising.

The two government cases concern different markets: search and search advertising in the 2020 suit are distinct from the digital ad technologies at issue in the more recent one.



---


# The Google Antitrust Case

The Google antitrust case is the U.S. government's trial over Google's dominance in the online search market, stemming from a 2020 antitrust claim, in which the government argues that Google uses its platforms and its deals with partners to block out competition in search or advertising and thereby to hinder competitors from accessing the data they would need to improve their products.

Its defining features are the conduct at issue and the defence offered against it. Google CEO Sundar Pichai testified Monday in the trial, defending Google's business tactics, including its deal with Apple and other partners to make Google the default search engine. Google's answer is that it is just doing business: everybody wants Google as the default engine because it is the best, and that, the company says, does not make its actions illegal.

The important boundary case is which Google antitrust matter this is. The 2020 search claim is separate from the one filed in January by the Department of Justice, along with eight states including New York, California and Colorado, which aims to "halt Google's anticompetitive scheme, unwind Google's monopolistic grip on the market and restore competition to digital advertising." The search case and the digital-advertising case are distinct proceedings and should not be conflated.

The trial is the venue in which the underlying numbers surface. Monday's hearing revealed plenty of juicy tidbits, including the $26.3 billion Google spent making itself the default search engine across platforms in 2021, and how Google tried to take it further and have Chrome preinstalled on iPhones.



---


# Default Search Engine

## Definition

The default search engine is the search provider a device, browser, or platform is pre-configured to use unless a user actively changes the setting — the search box that runs when a person types a query without first choosing an alternative, such as Google on the iPhone's Safari address bar or Firefox's search bar.

## Context

The term is central to *US v. Google*, the DOJ's antitrust case, because default status is the mechanism through which Google secures the overwhelming share of search queries: the Information Services Agreement (ISA) between Apple and Google, in place since 2002/2003, makes Google the default on all Apple devices, and Google separately pays Samsung, Mozilla, and other partners for the same status.
Apple executive Eddy Cue testified that Apple's iPhone setup flow deliberately omits any search-engine choice screen, arguing that presenting users with unfamiliar alternatives would harm the setup experience, while conceding the ISA does not permit Apple to offer such a choice.
Google spent $26.3 billion in 2021 on default-placement deals across browsers, phones, and platforms — about $18 billion of that to Apple alone — a scale that the DOJ used to argue Google understands the mechanism's value: internal 2007 data showed users who set Google as their homepage searched 15% more, while switching away dropped searches 27%.
The Mozilla/Yahoo episode shows the same mechanism working in reverse: when Firefox switched its default from Google to Yahoo under a 2014 deal, Mozilla's CEO testified that user retention declined, illustrating how disruptive changing the default can be even when a paying competitor is involved.
Outside the antitrust trial, the term also frames ordinary consumer behavior: an investor in e-commerce search startup Deft described users' "natural behavior" as following the path of least resistance and just using the default search engine, meaning challenger search products must offer a high-value proposition to displace that inertia.

## Key Characteristics

- **Set by agreement, not by user choice** — default status on major platforms (Apple's Safari/iOS, Android OEMs, Firefox) is typically established through commercial deals (e.g., the Apple-Google ISA, Yahoo-Mozilla's $375M/year deal) rather than user selection at setup.
- **Backed by large recurring payments** — Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 across partners to hold default placement, with roughly $18 billion of that going to Apple.
- **Technically reversible but rarely changed** — Apple and Google both argued switching is easy, but DuckDuckGo's CEO countered that it takes "too many steps" to switch, and Google's own 2005 complaint about Internet Explorer's defaults argued that "most end users do not change defaults," so default status functions as durable market power.
- **Distinct from pre-installation** — Google's separate push to get Chrome and Search merely pre-installed (not necessarily defaulted) on Android and iPhones shows default status is a stronger, more contested tier than simple presence on a device.
- **Drives user behavior even outside browsers** — the concept extends to any search product; consumers default to "the path of least resistance," which challenger search startups must specifically overcome.

## Corpus References

Corpus notes whose source text references this term (evidence-backed, from `term_links.json`):

- [The Google Antitrust Case](google_antitrust_case.md)
- [The Hypocrisy Argument: Google Became The Monopoly It Denounced](google_default_hypocrisy_argument.md)
- [US v. Google: Two Months Into The Search Antitrust Trial](us_v_google_search_antitrust_trial_overview.md)



---


# The DOJ Theory That Google's Default Deals Foreclose Search Rivals

The Justice Department's case against Google is focused on the deals Google makes — with Apple, but also with Samsung and Mozilla and many others — to ensure it is the default search engine on practically every platform.

The grounds the DOJ pressed through Eddy Cue's testimony were framed as a single question: whether Apple picked Google because it is the most lucrative choice or the best product. That question was a key part of Cue's testimony and, in The Verge's account, a key part of the DOJ's entire case. The warrant is the inference joining the two: if the defaults are bought rather than earned, then the network of default agreements, not product quality, is what keeps Google in place across platforms.



---


# The Apple-Google Information Services Agreement

The Information Services Agreement, or ISA, is the deal that makes Google's search engine the default on Apple's products — and it is the reason Apple was in court in US v. Google at all.

The ISA has been in place since 2002, but Eddy Cue was responsible for negotiating its current iteration with Google CEO Sundar Pichai in 2016. In testimony on the day The Verge reported, the Justice Department grilled Cue about the specifics of the deal.

# Helena World Chronicle's Class Action Antitrust Suit Against Google

A class action lawsuit filed in the week of 15 December 2023 in the U.S. District Court in D.C. accuses Google and parent company Alphabet of anticompetitive behavior in violation of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act and others, on behalf of news publishers. The case was filed by Arkansas-based publisher Helena World Chronicle, which argues that Google "siphons off" news publishers' content, their readers and their ad revenue through anticompetitive means, and it specifically cites new AI technologies such as Google's Search Generative Experience (SGE) and the Bard AI chatbot as worsening the problem.

Helena World Chronicle owns and publishes two weekly newspapers in Arkansas. In the complaint it argues that Google is "starving the free press" by sharing publishers' content on Google, losing them "billions of dollars."

Beyond damages, the suit asks for an injunction that would require Google to obtain consent from publishers before using their website data to train its general artificial intelligence products, including Google's own and those of rivals. It also asks that publishers who opt out of SGE still be allowed to show up in Google search results, among other things.

The law firm handling the case is Hausfeld, whose announcement states that "the anticompetitive effects of Google's scheme cause profound harm to competition, to consumers, to labor, and to a democratic free press," and that "Plaintiff Helena World Chronicle, LLC invokes the Sherman Act and Clayton Act to seek class-wide monetary and injunctive relief to restore and ensure competition for digital news and reference publishing and set up guardrails to preserve a free marketplace of ideas in the new era of artificial intelligence."



---


# OpenAI Corporate Deals And Business Moves

Alongside its product releases, OpenAI made a series of corporate moves in 2023: a news-content partnership with Axel Springer, an indemnity promise to business customers over copyright claims, its first acquisition, a $300 million share sale, and a stalled attempt to trademark "GPT."

OpenAI struck a deal with the Berlin-based news publisher Axel Springer, which owns Business Insider and Politico, to "help provide people with new ways to access quality, real-time news content through our AI tools"; under it OpenAI will train its generative AI models on the publisher's content and add recent Axel Springer-published articles to ChatGPT. Bowing to peer pressure, OpenAI also said it would pay legal costs incurred by customers who face lawsuits over IP claims against work generated by an OpenAI tool, though the protections seemingly do not extend to all OpenAI products, such as the free and Plus tiers of ChatGPT. In its first public acquisition in its seven-year history, OpenAI acquired Global Illumination, a New York-based startup leveraging AI to build creative tools, infrastructure and digital experiences; OpenAI wrote in a brief blog post, "We're very excited for the impact they'll have here at OpenAI. The entire team has joined OpenAI to work on our core products including ChatGPT."

# Class Action

## Definition

A class action, as it appears across this corpus, is a single lawsuit pursued on behalf of a group of similarly affected people rather than filed by each person individually.

The corpus documents several such suits from 2023: FTX customers against crypto promoters including Paradigm, a news publisher against Google, consumers against PayPal, and the Authors Guild against OpenAI.

It also shows the mechanism can be blocked by contract, as with Uber's terms of use barring class actions in sexual-assault cases.

## Context

The corpus shows the mechanism used across very different disputes: FTX customers brought a class-action lawsuit accusing crypto investment firm Paradigm and other promoters of defrauding customers by promoting the exchange, publisher Helena World Chronicle filed a class action antitrust suit against Google and Alphabet under the Sherman Act alleging AI tools like Search Generative Experience and Bard siphon off publishers' content and ad revenue, and consumers represented by law firm Hagens Berman filed a class action against PayPal over anti-steering rules that allegedly stifle competition from cheaper platforms like Stripe and Shopify.

The Authors Guild of America, representing Stephen King, John Grisham and 134 other authors, likewise filed its own class-action suit against OpenAI over unauthorized use of copyrighted books in training data, run in parallel to (but distinct from) comedian Sarah Silverman's separate, non-class suit.

Apple's earlier MacBook Pro keyboard class-action settlement is cited in the corpus as a business driver — the corpus notes the settlement cost probably factored into Apple's decision to redesign the keyboard, a change introduced alongside separate updates like a new camera and the removal of the Touch Bar.

## Key Characteristics

- **Collective standing** — a class action lets one or a few plaintiffs (e.g., Helena World Chronicle, the Authors Guild, unnamed FTX customers) litigate on behalf of an entire group with the same underlying grievance, rather than requiring each affected person to sue separately.
- **Can be contractually blocked** — the corpus shows companies can preempt this mechanism: under Uber's terms of use, class action lawsuits cannot be filed against the company in sexual assault cases, forcing survivors to litigate individually and preventing them from advocating for themselves collectively.
- **Used across dispute types** — the corpus applies the same mechanism to fraud (FTX), antitrust (Helena World Chronicle v. Google, PayPal anti-steering), and copyright (Authors Guild v. OpenAI) claims, showing it is a general procedural tool rather than one tied to a single area of law.
- **Settlement exposure shapes corporate behavior** — Apple's keyboard class-action settlement is presented in the corpus as a concrete cost that influenced a subsequent product redesign decision.
- **Defendants, not just plaintiffs, can be named as a group** — the FTX-related suit accuses Paradigm "and others" collectively of defrauding customers, showing the mechanism can target a class of co-defendants as well as aggregate a class of claimants.

## Background (external)

Cornell Law School's Legal Information Institute (Wex) defines a class action generically as "a procedural device that permits one or more plaintiffs to file and prosecute a lawsuit on behalf of a larger group, or 'class'" (Cornell Law School, Legal Information Institute, Wex: "class action," accessed 2026-09-02, https://www.law.cornell.edu/wex/class_action).

# Proving Intent In The FTX Fraud Case

The government's case proceeds in two parts. The first is pretty simple and a little boring: prosecutors must show that certain transactions took place, using whatever records the Southern District of New York has for them.

The second part is where the drama is likely to come, says Christopher LaVigne, a litigation partner and co-chair of the cryptocurrency practice at the law firm Withers: prosecutors have to connect those transactions to Bankman-Fried, show that he knew what he was doing was wrong, and prove that he lied about it anyway. "What was he saying to his parents and his other advisors about this?" LaVigne asks. "What conversations happened between him and his co-conspirators that are now cooperating against him?" To further establish intent, the government can use Bankman-Fried's own words: the indictment calls his November 2022 tweets "false and misleading." "We had him going out directly to the internet," LaVigne says — if he wrote things on Twitter or said things in interviews that weren't true, that's more fodder for the case: "They can point to that and say, 'This is what he said, this is what actually happened.'" Other evidence may include Signal messages and testimony from co-conspirators who pleaded guilty to their own charges. Alameda Research CEO Caroline Ellison, who was also sometimes Bankman-Fried's girlfriend, may play an important role — Bankman-Fried leaked her diaries to The New York Times and was consequently jailed for witness tampering. # Norway's Historical Absence From Major Tournaments

Norway have only ever qualified for four major tournaments — in 1938, 1994, 1998 and 2000 — and have won a combined three matches in those appearances, as reported by The New York Times on 17 November 2023.

The tactical history given alongside that record is of a traditionally defensive-minded side favouring counter-attacks and long balls: at their peak under Egil Olsen in the mid-1990s they often used a striker out of position on the wing, where he would challenge for long, diagonal balls — Jostein Flo, a giant striker often utilised on the right flank at the 1994 World Cup, being the example the article pictures.

The article's own emphasis, though, is that the more pertinent thing about Norway is that historically they generally haven't been very competitive. It adds that they are similar to Italy in that, at times, they have boasted various high-level strikers whose careers roughly overlapped — John Carew, Ole Gunnar Solskjaer, Tore Andre Flo, Steffen Iversen — and at other points have suffered a complete lack of good centre-forwards.



---


# Haaland's Chase Of Norway's International Goalscoring Record

Erling Haaland was just six goals away from Norway's international goalscoring record, making it surely inevitable that he will soon be his nation's most prolific striker ever, as reported by The New York Times on 17 November 2023.

The report notes the two ways of reading the timing: on one hand it will have happened remarkably quickly, since Haaland only scored his first goals for Norway in 2020; on the other, this has been an incredibly long time coming. At this point Norway appear to have the most prolific striker in Europe, and it's not unreasonable to consider where Haaland might end up in the all-time international goalscoring charts worldwide, never mind just among his compatriots.

His rate is the striking figure, with a caveat attached. Haaland is averaging nearly a goal a game for his country, which will inevitably be difficult for the 23-year-old to sustain over his career, but is impressive even at this early stage: excluding countries who have never qualified for a World Cup, only Jorgen Juve, Gigi Riva, Ferenc Puskas and Poul Nielsen, plus Japan's Kunishige Kamamoto, hold their nation's international goalscoring records while also boasting a rate of 0.75 goals per game or more. Even Cristiano Ronaldo, the most prolific international goalscorer of all time with 127 for Portugal, boasts "only" 0.63 goals per game, a lower rate than Romelu Lukaku, Harry Kane and Aleksandar Mitrovic, which owes to his early days as a winger rather than a central striker. Considering how many hat-tricks Haaland scores for Manchester City, it's not beyond the realms of possibility that he could score six goals during this international break to move level with Juve, particularly given Norway's first fixture is a home friendly against the Faroe Islands that Thursday before a European Championship qualifier against Scotland in Glasgow on Sunday — though the Faroes' defence is less leaky than you might expect, having conceded more than three times in a game only twice in their last 22 outings.



---


# NFL Aggressiveness Versus Traditional Game Management

A longtime NFL executive challenged the analytics-driven push toward aggressive play-calling on 16 October 2023, asking whether coaches have "come too far with coaches wanting to 'win' the game instead of sometimes being more traditional" after the Eagles threw a killer interception on third-and-9 from their own 46-yard line while protecting a 14-12 lead against the Jets with two minutes left in the fourth quarter.

The premise attacked is not that aggression is generally wrong. Most would agree teams have gotten smarter in their handling of fourth-down situations, going for it when it makes sense instead of punting almost out of habit; making the aggressive play to win can absolutely be the smart play regardless of results, and it is progress when teams seriously wrestle with these questions, not just on fourth down but in all aspects of strategy. What the exec disputes is the automatic application of that reasoning to a particular game state: Philadelphia could have run the ball on third-and-9, then punted from around midfield, leaving the Jets with barely more than a minute remaining, no timeouts and Zach Wilson behind center facing a ferocious Eagles pass rush. "Are coaches not willing to go against the slight statistical benefit that WPA (win probability added) provides?" he asked. "Is it no longer OK to let your defense win the game when it clearly has a huge talent/performance advantage? This Eagles game was 14-12, not 37-35."

The inference the counter-argument targets is the neglect of situation-specific factors. In that game the Jets' offense had netted 19 yards on its previous three possessions, producing one field goal on a drive that gained 16 of those yards; the Eagles had already suffered three turnovers, and they knew Wilson would be taking over deep in his territory with very little time remaining. "To me, these are exactly the type of factors that a coach needs to consider when deciding," the exec said. "I think they were ignored here." A veteran coach added an incentive-based explanation — critics attuned to the trend toward aggressiveness pounce when teams pass up chances to go for the kill, coaches know team owners tend to be fans rather than football strategists and listen to those criticisms, which creates an incentive to go down swinging: "Everybody thinks they are playing Brady, Manning or Rodgers in two-minute. If before the game someone offered Philly to put its defense against Zach Wilson on a need-field-goal drive starting inside his own 15 with no timeouts and a minute left, you think they would have taken it?" The base rate is thin: the situation Philly faced was the seventh time since 2000 that a team leading by 1-2 points in the final two minutes faced third down with 7-10 yards to go from the minus-40 yard line to midfield with the opponent holding no timeouts; three of the seven passed, resulting in one first down, one sack and Hurts' interception, and of those three only the Eagles lost the game.



---


# Hayes' Reasons For Leaving Chelsea

Emma Hayes explained her departure from Chelsea in terms of family, timing and succession: "The biggest factors are my son, leaving at the top and giving the club enough time to be able to transition without there being too much disruption," she said in her press conference, as reported by The New York Times on 15 November 2023.

The background the article supplies makes the departure less abrupt than it looked. Questions surrounding Hayes' future had cropped up previously in her tenure: she was linked to several jobs in the men's English Football League in the past and has always been interested in managing Spain's national team, although there was never an official conversation with Spain's federation — so it was a question of when, not if, Hayes would leave. Still, news of her decision came as a shock to her staff and players.

The personal grounds are given weight alongside the professional ones. The relentless nature of managing a club takes its toll, and after what will be 12 years at Chelsea come the end of the season, Hayes — a single parent whose father died the previous month — decided it was the right time for a change, professionally and personally.



---


# Jones Defends Leaving Cooper And Hooper Out Of The World Cup Squad

Against criticism of his squad selection, Eddie Jones said on Tuesday, Oct. 16, 2023 that he had no regrets about leaving experienced players such as Quade Cooper and Michael Hooper out of the side for the 2023 World Cup.

He conceded the critics' right to their view while rejecting its authority over his decision: "Everyone's got their own judgment and they're allowed to have that judgment."

His own reasoning rests on a longer horizon than the tournament just played: "My choice was that I decided to go with youth. And I stand by that because I think we've got a lot of good young players who are really going to benefit from that experience at the World Cup, and going forward to the 2027 World Cup."

qid: Between the Engadget report on the Sony WF-1000XM5 earbuds in October 2023 and the Fortune article discussing the Delta SkyMiles® Gold Business American Express Card cardholders' benefits in December 2023, which promotional offer was reported as a first-time occurrence, the discount on Sony WF-1000XM5 earbuds or the 20% statement credit for Delta SkyMiles® Gold Business American Express Card cardholders?
context:
# The Delta SkyMiles Gold Business American Express Card

The Delta SkyMiles Gold Business American Express Card is an airline-type business credit card aimed at small business owners who fly with Delta regularly: it carries a welcome bonus of up to 75,000 miles and perks such as free checked bags and priority boarding, with a $0 intro annual fee for the first year and $99 thereafter.

For that $99 a year, cardholders receive priority boarding, the first checked bag benefit (including for guests), discounts on in-flight purchases, and baggage insurance — reducing travel costs and upgrading the travel experience. The boundary of the product is equally clear in Fortune's 2023-12-12 assessment. The card does not provide access to Delta Sky Club or Delta's airport lounges, which is listed as a con alongside the $99 annual fee; the pros are the free checked bag on Delta flights, the 75,000-mile welcome bonus, and no foreign transaction fees. The rewards structure is called decent but "nothing to write home about," offering 2x miles on just a handful of categories such as advertising, shipping, and dining. The card is therefore best for business owners who plan to fly with Delta frequently, since many of its perks can be used specifically on Delta flights, and it is a good card to hold long-term for the perks and discounts even if your spending is better put on another business card.



---


# Delta SkyMiles Gold Business Card Rewards Rates

The Delta SkyMiles Gold Business American Express Card earns 2x miles in four categories and 1x mile everywhere else: 2x on purchases made directly with Delta, 2x on U.S. purchases for advertising in select media, 2x on U.S. shipping purchases, 2x on dining at restaurants, and 1x mile on every eligible dollar spent on other purchases.

Fortune's 2023-12-12 framing is that these higher rewards rates apply to select purchases that might be helpful to small business owners. The rates accompany a $0 intro annual fee for the first year, then $99.
