# Delta Gold Business Card Fees And Eligibility

The Delta SkyMiles Gold Business American Express Card charges a $99 annual fee with a $0 intro annual fee for the first year, no foreign transaction fee, and a purchase APR of 20.99%–29.99% variable; to qualify, cardholders should aim for a "good" FICO credit score of 690 or better.

Fortune's verdict on whether the fee is worth it is conditional: the $99 annual fee may be worth it for business owners who frequently travel with Delta, because perks like a free checked bag could easily cover it. Credit score is not the only gate — card issuers look at other factors like income, too. The article carries an explicit currency caveat: card details are accurate as of the publish date of 2023-12-12 but are subject to change at any time at the discretion of the issuer, and readers should contact the card issuer to verify rates, fees, and benefits before applying.



---


# The Delta SkyMiles Gold Business Welcome Bonus

The Delta SkyMiles Gold Business Card's welcome bonus is 75,000 Bonus Miles after you spend $6,000 in purchases on the new Card in your first 6 months of card opening — described by Fortune on 2023-12-12 as a big benefit of the card.

The bonus sits alongside a $0 intro annual fee for the first year (then $99). Its value is amplified by how the miles can be spent: cardholders who use their miles to purchase flights receive a 15% discount when they buy Delta flights with miles on the Fly Delta app or the Delta website.



---


# Delta SkyMiles Gold Business Card Travel Perks

The card's travel perks are a free first checked bag, Main Cabin 1 priority boarding, an annual flight credit, 20% back on in-flight purchases, baggage insurance, and car rental loss and damage insurance — several of which extend to travelling companions.

The free first checked bag covers cardholders and up to nine of their guests; because the standard bag fee is $30, using the perk more than three times saves more in bag fees than the annual fee costs. Main Cabin 1 priority boarding likewise covers cardholders and up to nine guests on the reservation, provided they use their SkyMiles number when booking their Delta flights. The flight credit is conditional on spend: cardholders who make eligible purchases totalling $10,000 or more in a year receive a $100 Delta eCredit usable for Delta flights. The 20% back arrives as a statement credit on eligible pre-purchased meals, in-flight food purchases, alcoholic beverages, and audio headsets on Delta flights. Baggage insurance covers cardholders who purchase plane, train, ship or bus ride tickets with the card, kicking in if baggage is stolen, lost, or damaged. Car Rental Loss and Damage Insurance requires the cardholder to book the rental with the card and decline the collision damage waiver at the agency. Terms apply to American Express benefits and offers, enrollment may be required for select benefits, eligibility and benefit level vary by card, and the insurance is underwritten by Amex Assurance Company.



---


# Sony WF-1000XM5 Wireless Earbuds

Sony's WF-1000XM5 wireless earbuds went on sale for $278 during October Prime Day, down from $300 — a $22 discount and their best price yet — and were still going for that price two days later, after the event officially ended.

Engadget calls them the best wireless earbuds on the market right now: Sony improved upon its already remarkable buds with a more comfortable fit, better sound quality and features like adaptive sound and Speak-to-Chat.

The headphone roundup adds detail and a slightly different framing of the size of the cut: $278 is only about $20 off, but it marks the first discount seen for the top pick in Engadget's wireless earbuds buying guide. The pair scored 87 earlier this year — like Sony's over-ear models it comes with a range of useful features, powerful noise cancellation and a warm yet detailed default sound, and the design is much more agreeable than previous Sony earphones.



---


# Sony Headphone And Earbud Deals During Prime Big Deal Day

Sony's headphones and earbuds were discounted at Best Buy during the anti-Prime Big Deal Day sales, led by the flagship WF-1000XM5 earbuds at $280, down from $300 — 7% off.

The over-ear Sony WH-1000XM4 was $250, down from $350 — 29% off; they can last up to 30 hours on a single charge and provide a comfortable listening experience thanks to their plush ear pads. The WF-1000XM5 earbuds improve upon the previous model with richer sound quality, slightly more powerful ANC, and vastly improved comfort thanks to their reduced size and weight. Sony's LinkBuds, which normally retail for $179.99, were $129.99 at Best Buy; the wireless earbuds work great for making calls and offer a unique "open-style" donut-shaped design that keeps the wearer aware of their environment. The Sony LinkBuds S were also on sale for $129.99, $70 off, at Best Buy; unlike the LinkBuds, these offer active noise cancellation, support for the LDAC lossless audio codec, and a slightly more conventional design. Sony's WH-CH720N were down to $99.99, $50 off, at Best Buy; the over-ear headphones may not offer all the bells and whistles of Sony's premium noise-canceling headphones, but they offer decent ANC and up to 35 hours of battery life.



---


# Redeeming Delta SkyMiles With The Takeoff15 Discount

To capture the Takeoff15 discount, cardholders book flights through the Fly Delta app or their Delta SkyMiles account using their card, which yields a 15% discount on the miles price — but only on Delta and Delta Connection flights.

The scope limit matters because Delta has more than 20 airline partners and cardholders can book through airlines such as Air France and Virgin Atlantic; the 15% discount does not extend to those partner bookings. Cardholders can use their miles and their cash to buy flights. Fortune presents the discount as a reason to hold the card long-term, since a heavy Delta user could save thousands of miles over the course of a year. The best bargains on award flights are found through Delta SkyMiles Award Deals: recent deals from Seattle (SEA) had included Chicago (ORD) for 8,000 miles or Auckland, New Zealand (AKL) for 64,000 one way in economy plus taxes and fees, and because flash sales come and go it is a good idea to keep an eye on the site. Other redemption options include booking travel through Delta Vacations, using miles for upgrades, or even buying champagne at the Delta Sky Club — though the best value will most likely be on award tickets.

qid: What team, which would be under the leadership of its ninth manager since May 2013 if a new appointment occurs, is no longer competing in European competitions after a loss to Bayern at their home ground according to Sporting News reports?
context:
# Manchester United's Managers Since Sir Alex Ferguson

If Manchester United were to appoint a new manager in December 2023, that person would be the ninth coach to take charge of a United team following Sir Alex Ferguson's retirement in May 2013, including caretaker and interim managers Ryan Giggs, Ralf Rangnick and Michael Carrick, per Sporting News on Dec. 13, 2023.

The list of managers, their honours and games in charge ran: David Moyes, Community Shield, 51 games; Ryan Giggs (caretaker), no honours, 4 games; Louis van Gaal, FA Cup, 103 games; Jose Mourinho, Community Shield, Europa League and League Cup, 144 games; Ole Gunnar Solskjaer, no honours, 168 games; Michael Carrick (caretaker), no honours, 3 games; Ralf Rangnick (interim), no honours, 29 games; and Erik ten Hag, League Cup, with his games total open because he was still manager of the club.



---


# Manchester United's European Decline Since Ferguson

The Independent argued on 12 December 2023 that Manchester United's 1-0 defeat to Bayern Munich should have been a landmark low but instead felt grimly routine, because group-stage elimination has become the club's normal European outcome in the post-Ferguson era rather than an aberration.

The grounds are frequency and pattern. Manchester United, one of the grandest and richest names in this competition, have again gone out of the Champions League at the group stage; it is the third time it has happened since Sir Alex Ferguson, meaning it is their most common round of exit in that period. The night is presented as one more entry in a decade of disappointment in a competition in which this club rose to its most emotional heights — a low, but just part of that longer run.

The warrant is the gap between the occasion and the performance. These are not the sounds we are used to hearing after that Champions League theme; something does stir when the anthem is played at Old Trafford amid the lights — well, for most, that is, except the players. United should not be performing like this on what is supposed to be the classic European night at Old Trafford, and the display was a reminder that all they are going to have for some time are their memories. Having been involved in so many ludicrously chaotic matches, the biggest of all ended up being a non-event: this game never threatened to stir anything, and United never threatened at all. That, the argument runs, can now be talked about definitively, since it has been decisively ended.



---


# Criticism Of Germany's October 2023 Trip To North America

The DFB took significant flak from the German press for travelling to North America to play the United States and Mexico, with critics attacking the premise that the trip was a sensible use of the international break.

The Sporting News concedes part of the reaction is unworthy — there's likely some form of superiority complex involved, with those following the German national team surely miffed that a European giant is travelling across the globe to meet CONCACAF sides with far thinner World Cup resumes — but grants that a closer look at the travel schedule does invite questions. Most notably, the Germany squad will return to Europe just a single day prior to Borussia Dortmund's first match out of the break, which sees BVB play Werder Bremen on Friday, October 20; Bayern Munich have their first game back against Mainz on Saturday, as does much of the Bundesliga.

Two prominent voices made the case directly. Bayern Munich manager Thomas Tuchel said before the international break: "I don't know if I'd be interested in playing against Mexico in America before [the Euros hosted] in Germany. I don't know if anyone can explain this in a way that I can understand. I don't know who decided it, but it has been decided. There is a difference between a busy schedule and everything away from home and in different time zones. This is at the end of the endurance. No coach in the world at this level will say otherwise." Former Germany international Lothar Matthaus told Bild in the summer: "I don't understand the trip to the USA — for a variety of reasons. I would have tried to create a good atmosphere in Germany before the Euros. That's why I would be in all 10 European Championship stadiums for the friendly matches and would have shown myself there once as a DFB selection. That can create a mood. But what do we want in the US at this point?"



---


# Julian Nagelsmann's Career And His Bayern Munich Dismissal

At just 36 years old when he took the Germany job, Julian Nagelsmann was a rising star who had spent three successful seasons at Hoffenheim followed by two years at RB Leipzig, which catapulted him to the managerial post at Bayern Munich in 2021.

He steered the Bavarian giants to the Bundesliga title in his first season, but was sacked by the club in March of 2023 amid a furious league title fight. The dismissal came as a shock to much of the European football landscape, as the club had performed exceptionally in the Champions League and was still very much in the title race, sitting just a point behind Dortmund.

Now, with a chance for redemption at the helm of the national team, Nagelsmann would see his time begin with a friendly against the United States.



---


# The USMNT's October 2023 Friendlies Against Germany And Ghana

Gregg Berhalter and the U.S. men's national team scheduled friendlies against Germany and Ghana in October 2023 as they continued preparations for the 2024 Copa America and the 2026 FIFA World Cup. The U.S. first took on Germany in Hartford, Connecticut on October 14.

That match doubled as the debut for Germany's new head coach. The 15th-ranked Germans were under new management, so the USMNT served as the first match for Julian Nagelsmann, the 36-year-old who had been out of a job since departing Bayern Munich back in March. Most European countries were busy with Euro 2024 qualifying at that point, but Germany, as tournament hosts, qualified automatically, which opened their schedule for the friendly.

On October 17 the U.S. traveled to GEODIS Park in Nashville, Tennessee to face Ghana, two nations with a deep history of contentious matchups including three consecutive World Cup tournaments in 2006, 2010 and 2014.



---


# Liverpool's Early-Season Form In 2023-24

By 20 October 2023 Liverpool had surpassed pre-season expectations of a new-look team: three points off the top, three goals scored in every Premier League home game, a 100% record in all competitions at Anfield, cruising through the Europa League group stage, and individuals shining.

The Guardian judged it not unreasonable of Jürgen Klopp, however, to expect much more as the season developed. Klopp framed the demand as intrinsic to his job: "You saw so many teams here growing in the direction we wanted and all became better step by step or the manager had to go," he said. "We will try together to get better step by step and show our real face more often than not."



---


# Newcastle vs Crystal Palace Preview, October 2023

Newcastle hosted Crystal Palace live on talkSPORT 2 at 3pm on 21 October 2023 on an impressive run of form across all competitions, having knocked last year's treble winners Manchester City out of the Carabao Cup and beaten Paris Saint-Germain 4-1 in the Champions League, talkSPORT previewed on 20 October.

The obstacle was the opponent's recent record against them: Crystal Palace proved unbeatable for Newcastle last season, with goalless draws in all three of their meetings across all competitions. Palace had been defensively impressive that term, keeping four clean sheets, and sat ninth in the table, just one place behind Newcastle, so they could vault the Magpies with a win.

On team news, Newcastle were without Joe Willock and Harvey Barnes through injury, but Sandro Tonali was available despite allegations of illegal betting that led to him being sent home from Italy's national team squad, and despite fears that he could be banned.



---


# Germany's Decline And The Appointment Of Julian Nagelsmann

Germany entered their October 2023 friendly against the United States in a transitional phase, with Julian Nagelsmann having taken over as new head coach after Hansi Flick was unable to steer the team to safer waters in Qatar.

Germany are considered one of the preeminent national team programs in the world, but recent years have humbled Die Mannschaft. They had been eliminated in the group stage of two straight World Cup tournaments — an unthinkable slip in stature given they had never been bounced from any World Cup that early in history prior to 2018.

The Sporting News set that decline alongside the United States' own position: with the U.S. set to test themselves against one of Europe's most powerful sides, the opponents were entering a transitional phase as well.

qid: Which individual, featured in articles by The Verge and Fortune, is alleged to have used their position to both persuade a former Jane Street colleague to join his trading and development ventures and to inappropriately utilize customer funds, actions that are now central to fraud allegations discussed in TechCrunch?
context:
# Testimony At The SBF Trial

Across the first three weeks of the trial, a run of former colleagues, an outside investor and a forensic accounting expert testified that FTX customer money flowed into Alameda Research and out again to other uses, and that FTX's investors were never told about the two firms' special relationship. TechCrunch's running coverage, published 2023-10-06, summarises each week.

In week one, FTX's co-founder and CTO Gary Wang testified Thursday on the extent to which Alameda Research was used for whatever purposes he and SBF saw fit: according to Wang, the crypto trading firm pulled funding directly from FTX customers, whose transactions would be funneled toward Alameda and then directed elsewhere. Thursday also brought testimony from Matt Huang, co-founder and managing partner at crypto investment firm Paradigm, which invested $278 million in FTX across 2021 and 2022 and is part of a class-action lawsuit accusing it and others of defrauding customers by promoting FTX. His testimony centered around being left uninformed about FTX's utilization of customer money to keep Alameda Research afloat — a practice Huang says would have halted his involvement — and covered his relationship with FTX stretching back to 2019.

Week two's standout testimony came from Alameda Research's former CEO Caroline Ellison, who claimed she took $14 billion from customers to repay debts to lenders, using them as a line of credit under the instruction of SBF. Ellison also went into detail about how a $2 billion venture fund, FTX Ventures, was funded by money that had previously been allocated to Alameda from third-party lenders. And though there are no charges of bribery in the case, she also testified to paying Chinese officials $150 million to restore access to $1 billion in frozen trading accounts.

The third week featured a couple of noteworthy moments for the prosecution. FTX's former general counsel Can Sun, like many of SBF's former colleagues, opted to cooperate with authorities and testified that SBF asked him to create a theoretical "legal justification" for the use of billions in consumer funds just days before FTX filed for bankruptcy. Robert Boroujerdi, managing director of the hedge fund Third Point, testified about his experience working with SBF and FTX in a partnership that ultimately resulted in a $60 million investment and a lack of awareness about the special relationship between Alameda Research and FTX; had he known of such a relationship, he testified, Third Point would not have invested in FTX in the first place. And earlier in the week, Peter Easton — a University of Notre Dame professor who helped the government prosecution of Enron and WorldCom — testified about what he uncovered after tracing the flow of billions of dollars between Alameda Research and FTX: much of that funding came from customers, and Easton testified that he found user deposits were used by both FTX and Alameda to purchase real estate, make investments or direct funding toward political causes and charities.



---


# Day Two Of The Bankman-Fried Trial: Jury Selection And The Courtroom Audience

On the second day of Sam Bankman-Fried's fraud trial, the jury was selected on Wednesday morning, after which lawyers for the government and then for Bankman-Fried delivered opening statements that told two very different stories of the former FTX CEO's sudden rise and almost instantaneous fall. The central question framed by the proceedings was who Bankman-Fried, the former CEO of crypto exchange FTX, really is: a liar and a fraud, or someone who acted in good faith and, like many a startup founder, flew too close to the sun. That answer, the account notes, ultimately lies with the jury.

The day featured pointed allegations, a friend from MIT, and an audience replete with big names, including Bankman-Fried's professorial parents and Damian Williams, the U.S. attorney for the Southern District of New York. Bankman-Fried himself spent most of the day in court staring into a laptop while seated between his two attorneys. The prosecution's account of his alleged crimes was described as featuring a study in contrasts.



---


# FTX's Inner Circle: Family And Friends Implicated

The Verge's October 26th, 2023 account of the trial catalogued how everyone who loved Bankman-Fried most in the world was caught up in the case. Adam Yedidia, his college roommate, testified with immunity because he was concerned he may have unknowingly worked on code that contributed to the fraud; "I love you Sam," he had texted at one point, "I'm not going anywhere" — that was before he realized FTX had stolen customer funds, at which point he resigned. Nishad Singh, a longtime family friend, copped to what sounded an awful lot like classic embezzlement, saying he had backdated transactions on FTX to help create doctored balance sheets to show to investors, and pleaded guilty to six charges including wire fraud, money laundering, and conspiracy counts around his political donations. Caroline Ellison, Bankman-Fried's ex-girlfriend, told the court about the seven phony balance sheets she had created and was clear that Alameda took customer funds, that Bankman-Fried knew about it, and that he even invested them against her advice.

His family was drawn in too. Joe Bankman, his father, is among the people included in the "small group chat," the Signal group where the FTX inner circle strategized during the exchange's last days. Barbara Fried's political action committee, Mind the Gap, is among the entities that received FTX customer money as political donations; Fried and Bankman lived together in a Bahamas house purchased for them using FTX investor funds, according to a financial expert called by the prosecution, and in a lawsuit filed by FTX's bankruptcy estate the two are alleged to have been given $10 million of FTX customer funds. Gabe Bankman-Fried's nonprofit, Guarding Against Pandemics, got millions from FTX; he was also in a Signal group chat, Donations Processing, that Singh says was used to coordinate the transfer of FTX and Alameda money to various political causes, and in that chat he can be seen recommending that some donations be made "in the dark" to avoid public relations headaches. Singh also said Gabe had an assistant fly to the Bahamas with a stack of blank checks for Singh to sign.

The consequences outlast the trial. Wang, Singh, and Ellison are now felons; even if they never do time — and they may very well be imprisoned or subjected to house arrest — their lives are irrevocably changed, not least by whatever restitution requirements they face, they are barred from taking certain kinds of jobs, and there is the publicity. Bankman, Fried, and Gabe Bankman-Fried's reputations are tarnished, and in the political arenas where they once operated they are suddenly undesirable. Beyond the courtroom, everyone who had money trapped on the exchange when it collapsed — as a result of Alameda purloining customers' funds — had their lives altered: even if they are made whole by the bankruptcy proceedings, that is still money they should have had access to at any time, which may mean houses that were not purchased, medical procedures left undone, and life savings lost. The reporter's summary: it is a Greek tragedy, precipitated by one man's character flaw, the arrogance of Sam Bankman-Fried.



---


# VC And Lender Testimony As Collateral Risk For Crypto

The Verge argued that calling lenders, venture capitalists and customers to testify — necessary to establish the basis for some charges — might create collateral damage for the crypto industry beyond Bankman-Fried himself.

The grounds are the shape of the indictment and who it drags in: prosecutors allege that Bankman-Fried lied to FTX investors, so some of those investors may be called on to testify, which is not the kind of thing VC big shots generally enjoy. The worked example is Sequoia Capital: if Sequoia did due diligence around its investment in FTX, whatever Bankman-Fried told its partners could be important — was FTX already sending Alameda customer funds at that point, did Bankman-Fried know, and did he tell the VCs at the time? If he told them it wasn't happening, that would establish intent. Hermine Wong, the former head of policy at Coinbase and a former SEC regulator, adds that Binance was also an early investor in FTX and that former executives may be called on to testify as well.



---


# FTX Ventures Was Funded By Alameda

Caroline Ellison testified that the money behind FTX Ventures came from Alameda Research, even though Bankman-Fried announced the fund publicly without naming its source: on January 14th, 2022 he tweeted, "We're launching a $2b venture fund: FTX Ventures!" She said he did not want to go public with where the funds came from, telling her he thought Alameda's brand was less good and that he did not want his name associated with it.

The Verge reported the episode on October 10th, 2023 as part of Ellison's testimony, framing it as FTX keeping cozy private ties with Alameda while publicly holding it at arm's length — an echo, the reporter wrote, of Bankman-Fried and Ellison's romantic relationship. The same distancing appears in another transaction: Alameda bought Robinhood shares for Bankman-Fried, who moved them to a vehicle called "Emergent Fidelity Technologies" to avoid association with Alameda.

The government's argument in US v. Google is that Google uses its platforms and its deals with partners to block out any competition in search or advertising, thereby hindering competitors from accessing the data they would need to improve their products. The warrant joining the claim to the remedy is that if the deals are what starve rivals of data, then unwinding the deals and redistributing the data restores competition. On that logic, if Judge Amit Mehta rules against Google, the search giant may have to change its behavior and share its APIs with third-party developers; it may also be banned from making anticompetitive and exclusive deals with smartphone and computer manufacturers and wireless carriers; and Google might end up having to turn over all or most of the data it has collected to other search engines so they can improve their products and attract more users. The DOJ has been investigating Apple for years over the company's policy for third-party apps on its devices and whether it unfairly favors its own products. And there is an ongoing case between the FTC and Facebook, in which the agency calls on Facebook to sell Instagram and WhatsApp.

# Default Search Engine

## Definition

The default search engine is the search provider a device, browser, or platform is pre-configured to use unless a user actively changes the setting — the search box that runs when a person types a query without first choosing an alternative, such as Google on the iPhone's Safari address bar or Firefox's search bar.

## Context

The term is central to *US v. Google*, the DOJ's antitrust case, because default status is the mechanism through which Google secures the overwhelming share of search queries: the Information Services Agreement (ISA) between Apple and Google, in place since 2002/2003, makes Google the default on all Apple devices, and Google separately pays Samsung, Mozilla, and other partners for the same status.
Apple executive Eddy Cue testified that Apple's iPhone setup flow deliberately omits any search-engine choice screen, arguing that presenting users with unfamiliar alternatives would harm the setup experience, while conceding the ISA does not permit Apple to offer such a choice.
Google spent $26.3 billion in 2021 on default-placement deals across browsers, phones, and platforms — about $18 billion of that to Apple alone — a scale that the DOJ used to argue Google understands the mechanism's value: internal 2007 data showed users who set Google as their homepage searched 15% more, while switching away dropped searches 27%.
The Mozilla/Yahoo episode shows the same mechanism working in reverse: when Firefox switched its default from Google to Yahoo under a 2014 deal, Mozilla's CEO testified that user retention declined, illustrating how disruptive changing the default can be even when a paying competitor is involved.
Outside the antitrust trial, the term also frames ordinary consumer behavior: an investor in e-commerce search startup Deft described users' "natural behavior" as following the path of least resistance and just using the default search engine, meaning challenger search products must offer a high-value proposition to displace that inertia.

## Key Characteristics

- **Set by agreement, not by user choice** — default status on major platforms (Apple's Safari/iOS, Android OEMs, Firefox) is typically established through commercial deals (e.g., the Apple-Google ISA, Yahoo-Mozilla's $375M/year deal) rather than user selection at setup.
- **Backed by large recurring payments** — Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 across partners to hold default placement, with roughly $18 billion of that going to Apple.
- **Technically reversible but rarely changed** — Apple and Google both argued switching is easy, but DuckDuckGo's CEO countered that it takes "too many steps" to switch, and Google's own 2005 complaint about Internet Explorer's defaults argued that "most end users do not change defaults," so default status functions as durable market power.
- **Distinct from pre-installation** — Google's separate push to get Chrome and Search merely pre-installed (not necessarily defaulted) on Android and iPhones shows default status is a stronger, more contested tier than simple presence on a device.
- **Drives user behavior even outside browsers** — the concept extends to any search product; consumers default to "the path of least resistance," which challenger search startups must specifically overcome.

The important boundary case is which Google antitrust matter this is. The 2020 search claim is separate from the one filed in January by the Department of Justice, along with eight states including New York, California and Colorado, which aims to "halt Google's anticompetitive scheme, unwind Google's monopolistic grip on the market and restore competition to digital advertising." The search case and the digital-advertising case are distinct proceedings and should not be conflated.

# Consumer Search Startups And Switching Barriers

# Class Action

## Definition

A class action, as it appears across this corpus, is a single lawsuit pursued on behalf of a group of similarly affected people rather than filed by each person individually.

The corpus documents several such suits from 2023: FTX customers against crypto promoters including Paradigm, a news publisher against Google, consumers against PayPal, and the Authors Guild against OpenAI.

It also shows the mechanism can be blocked by contract, as with Uber's terms of use barring class actions in sexual-assault cases.

## Context

The corpus shows the mechanism used across very different disputes: FTX customers brought a class-action lawsuit accusing crypto investment firm Paradigm and other promoters of defrauding customers by promoting the exchange, publisher Helena World Chronicle filed a class action antitrust suit against Google and Alphabet under the Sherman Act alleging AI tools like Search Generative Experience and Bard siphon off publishers' content and ad revenue, and consumers represented by law firm Hagens Berman filed a class action against PayPal over anti-steering rules that allegedly stifle competition from cheaper platforms like Stripe and Shopify.

The Authors Guild of America, representing Stephen King, John Grisham and 134 other authors, likewise filed its own class-action suit against OpenAI over unauthorized use of copyrighted books in training data, run in parallel to (but distinct from) comedian Sarah Silverman's separate, non-class suit.

Apple's earlier MacBook Pro keyboard class-action settlement is cited in the corpus as a business driver — the corpus notes the settlement cost probably factored into Apple's decision to redesign the keyboard, a change introduced alongside separate updates like a new camera and the removal of the Touch Bar.

## Key Characteristics

- **Collective standing** — a class action lets one or a few plaintiffs (e.g., Helena World Chronicle, the Authors Guild, unnamed FTX customers) litigate on behalf of an entire group with the same underlying grievance, rather than requiring each affected person to sue separately.
- **Can be contractually blocked** — the corpus shows companies can preempt this mechanism: under Uber's terms of use, class action lawsuits cannot be filed against the company in sexual assault cases, forcing survivors to litigate individually and preventing them from advocating for themselves collectively.
- **Used across dispute types** — the corpus applies the same mechanism to fraud (FTX), antitrust (Helena World Chronicle v. Google, PayPal anti-steering), and copyright (Authors Guild v. OpenAI) claims, showing it is a general procedural tool rather than one tied to a single area of law.
- **Settlement exposure shapes corporate behavior** — Apple's keyboard class-action settlement is presented in the corpus as a concrete cost that influenced a subsequent product redesign decision.
- **Defendants, not just plaintiffs, can be named as a group** — the FTX-related suit accuses Paradigm "and others" collectively of defrauding customers, showing the mechanism can target a class of co-defendants as well as aggregate a class of claimants.

## Background (external)

Cornell Law School's Legal Information Institute (Wex) defines a class action generically as "a procedural device that permits one or more plaintiffs to file and prosecute a lawsuit on behalf of a larger group, or 'class'" (Cornell Law School, Legal Information Institute, Wex: "class action," accessed 2026-09-02, https://www.law.cornell.edu/wex/class_action).

Thursday also brought testimony from Matt Huang, co-founder and managing partner at crypto investment firm Paradigm, which invested $278 million in FTX across 2021 and 2022 and is part of a class-action lawsuit accusing it and others of defrauding customers by promoting FTX. His testimony centered around being left uninformed about FTX's utilization of customer money to keep Alameda Research afloat — a practice Huang says would have halted his involvement — and covered his relationship with FTX stretching back to 2019.

Week two's standout testimony came from Alameda Research's former CEO Caroline Ellison, who claimed she took $14 billion from customers to repay debts to lenders, using them as a line of credit under the instruction of SBF. Ellison also went into detail about how a $2 billion venture fund, FTX Ventures, was funded by money that had previously been allocated to Alameda from third-party lenders. And though there are no charges of bribery in the case, she also testified to paying Chinese officials $150 million to restore access to $1 billion in frozen trading accounts.

The third week featured a couple of noteworthy moments for the prosecution. FTX's former general counsel Can Sun, like many of SBF's former colleagues, opted to cooperate with authorities and testified that SBF asked him to create a theoretical "legal justification" for the use of billions in consumer funds just days before FTX filed for bankruptcy. Robert Boroujerdi, managing director of the hedge fund Third Point, testified about his experience working with SBF and FTX in a partnership that ultimately resulted in a $60 million investment and a lack of awareness about the special relationship between Alameda Research and FTX; had he known of such a relationship, he testified, Third Point would not have invested in FTX in the first place. And earlier in the week, Peter Easton — a University of Notre Dame professor who helped the government prosecution of Enron and WorldCom — testified about what he uncovered after tracing the flow of billions of dollars between Alameda Research and FTX: much of that funding came from customers, and Easton testified that he found user deposits were used by both FTX and Alameda to purchase real estate, make investments or direct funding toward political causes and charities.



---


# OpenAI's Training Data Copyright Lawsuits

Around this time OpenAI's training methods — which involve scraping the public internet for content and feeding it into massive datasets on which the models are taught — came under fire from copyright holders and marquee authors alike.

Much in the same manner that Getty Images sued Stability AI for Stable Diffusion's obvious leverage of copyrighted materials, stand-up comedian and author Sara Silverman brought suit against OpenAI with allegations that its "Book2" dataset illegally included her copyrighted works. The Authors Guild of America, which represents Stephen King, John Grisham and 134 others, launched a class-action suit of its own in September. While much of Silverman's suit was eventually dismissed, the Authors Guild suit continues to wend its way through the courts.

MLB's winter meetings are the window in which many of the top executives, players and agents all come together at the same spot, which makes them always a prime time for moves to happen, per Sporting News' 2023 tracker published Dec. 3, 2023.

For the other teams, the warrant is opportunity cost — knowing Ohtani is off the board relatively soon into the offseason would allow them to shift to other priorities, like trading for Juan Soto or deciding which free-agent pitchers to pursue with the money that might otherwise have been earmarked for Ohtani.

# The Mariners Reported Out Of The Ohtani Chase

Sporting News found that surprising, because Seattle seemed to check a lot of boxes for Ohtani: they are set up to win for a long time with a bunch of young starting pitchers and a co-superstar in Julio Rodriguez; Ohtani would get to be part of the quest for the franchise's first World Series title; he would wear the same uniform as his baseball hero, Ichiro; and he has lived there in the offseason. # The Toronto Reports And Denials Of Dec. 8, 2023

On Friday, Dec. 8, 2023, a cascade of conflicting reports had Ohtani picking the Blue Jays and flying to Toronto, only for other reporters to place him at his home in Southern California with no decision made.

The sequence began with Dodgers Nation's J.P. Hoornstra reporting that Ohtani had selected the Blue Jays, who had reportedly won the sweepstakes; official details were not reported, though the report indicated the deal would shatter Mike Trout's record 12-year, $426.5 million contract. qid: Does the 'Science News For Students' article suggest that previous hydrogel research extensively explored the relationship between salt content and water absorption, while the 'Advanced Science News' article indicates that the hydrogel used in aqueous zinc iodine batteries has been specifically engineered with functional groups for anode and cathode affinity?
context:
# The Zincophilic and Iodophilic Hydrogel Mechanism

The anode and cathode sides of the hydrogel carry different functional groups that make it zincophilic (with an affinity for zinc) and iodophilic (with an affinity for iodine) respectively, and this asymmetry is what lets one electrolyte fix problems at both electrodes.

On the anode side, the design repels dissolved polyiodides — negatively charged ions composed entirely of iodine atoms — allowing the zinc to be deposited uniformly and protecting the anode from iodine-caused corrosion. Ensuring that zinc accumulates evenly on the anode side is the purpose of the hydrogel modification, Hongjin Fan explained, and it mitigates the diffusion back and forth of polysulfide between anode and cathode, the so-called "shuttle effect," which can cause poor cycling stability and severe anode corrosion in batteries. On the cathode side, the polyiodides are immobilized, and redox reactions — in which iodine is both stripped of electrons (oxidation) and granted electrons (reduction) — are sped up thanks to the synchronized rapid transport of ions and electrons, so the hydrogel electrolyte also accelerates the iodine conversion reaction. Finally, the solid nature of the hydrogel electrolyte limits the growth of dendrites through its mechanical strength, acting as a physical barrier not present in liquid electrolytes.



---


# Hetero-Polyionic Hydrogel Electrolyte Design

A hetero-polyionic hydrogel electrolyte is one in which functional groups carrying either positive or negative charges are deliberately introduced into the hydrogel, so that a single "hetero-hydrogel" can mitigate challenges on both the anode and the cathode sides of a zinc-iodine battery.

"The core concept of our research is that we design the hydrogel electrolytes by introducing functional groups [specific groupings of atoms within molecules that have their own characteristic properties] that carry either positive or negative charges," said Hongjin Fan, a professor at Nanyang Technological University's (NTU) School of Physical and Mathematical Sciences and an author of the new paper in Advanced Materials, in which he and his co-authors examine different electrolytes for aqueous zinc ion batteries that take the form of hydrogels — three-dimensional network structures capable of storing large amounts of water. The stated aim of the research is to improve the stability and safety of alternatives to rechargeable lithium-ion batteries using aqueous zinc and hydrogels. The reference is: Peihua Yang, Hong Jin Fan, et al., "Hetero-Polyionic Hydrogels Enable Dendrites-Free Aqueous Zn-I2 Batteries with Fast Kinetics," Advanced Materials (2023), DOI: 10.1002/adma.202306531.



---


# Barriers to Commercializing Zinc-Iodine Batteries

Against the promising cycling results, Hongjin Fan acknowledged there is much to do before the battery can be brought to the mass market — attacking the premise that laboratory stability is enough to make zinc-iodine batteries a lithium-ion substitute.

"We have to note that in terms of mass or volume energy density, so far, the ZIB is still far from the commercial lithium-ion batteries," Fan conceded. "The hydrogel electrolytes need to be further improved in terms of ion conductivity and stability. In addition, hydrogel electrolytes should be compatible with other battery components, including electrodes and separators." He also pointed out that large-scale and cost-effective production methods for hydrogel electrolytes are a prerequisite before aqueous zinc-iodine batteries are ready for widescale commercial use, which will include optimizing the production process of hydrogels as well as sourcing affordable raw materials and minimizing waste generated during manufacturing. "Ensuring the safety and reliability of hydrogel-based batteries is also necessary," Fan concluded. "Rigorous testing and evaluation of the potential environmental impact of hydrogel electrolytes, from raw material extraction to disposal, are vital to meeting sustainability goals and gaining public trust."



---


# Record Salt Loading Hydrogel Results

The gels soaked up more and more saltwater over time, and the top absorber got about three times saltier than previous hydrogels, caching 20 grams (0.7 ounce) of salt per gram of gel — and it absorbed more moisture than previous gels too.

To test moisture uptake, the researchers dried their gels and placed them in environments with different levels of humidity; even in relatively dry air, such as that found in deserts, the best-performing hydrogel absorbed 15 percent more water than previous hydrogels. The team reported its findings on May 18 in Advanced Materials. "We did this in a very simple and low-cost way, which makes it even more exciting," says Díaz-Marín, whose team still needs to test how to get all that water out of the gels afterward. "I am impressed by their results," says Swee Ching Tan, a materials scientist at the National University of Singapore who works with hydrogels but did not take part in the study. "This could be a new world record." The new work, he says, could help with the water crisis by producing safe drinking water in places that lack it.



---


# Hydrogel Zinc-Iodine Battery Cycling Results

Testing their aqueous hydrogel-modified zinc-iodine battery, the team found the decay rate was ultralow, with energy storage capacity retained to an outstanding level over the course of 18,000 discharge and recharge cycles — outstripping the stability of currently available zinc-iodine batteries.

The test battery also delivered some surprising results. "The adhesion between the polyanionic and polycationic hydrogel components is remarkably robust, effectively mitigating the swelling of the hydrogel even in the absence of a cellulose paper scaffold," Hongjin Fan explained. "The unexpectedly strong iodine adsorption capability of the positively charged hydrogel has led to a striking and rapid color transformation, exceeding our initial expectations."



---


# Salty Hydrogel Atmospheric Water Harvesting

A hydrogel is a mesh of large molecules called polymers; the new hydrogel captures humidity — water vapor — from the air and expands like a sponge in water as it does so, then releases the water it has absorbed when heated by the sun.

Carlos Díaz-Marín, a mechanical engineer at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) in Cambridge, leads a team developing a device to address water shortages that would affordably pull water from air without a need for electricity, and the key ingredient is a new, super-salty gel. The idea is not new: many types of hydrogels have been developed to suck water from air, and previous work showed that adding salts to hydrogels upped how much water they could absorb, because salts attract moisture, including from the air, on account of their chemical properties. What was unknown was how much salt a hydrogel could stash, and how pushing that salt content to the maximum might boost the hydrogel's water-slurping power — the question Díaz-Marín and his team set out to answer.



---


# The Lithium Chloride Hydrogel Soaking Experiment

The researchers made tubes of hydrogel from polyacrylamide, a polymer made of long, threadlike molecules, cut the tubes into thin disks, soaked them in water containing different amounts of lithium chloride — a salt — and weighed the disks each day to see how much of the salty water they had absorbed.

The step that mattered was duration. Such tests had been done before, but for relatively short times, Díaz-Marín says: "Instead of soaking for two days, we did this for up to two months." The extra time made a big difference.



---


# Zinc-Iodine Battery Advantages and the Dendrite Problem

Rechargeable zinc-iodine batteries are one potential substitute for lithium-ion batteries, with the advantages of being safer, costing less, and being more friendly to the environment than lithium alternatives.

They are not perfect, however. Composed of a negative iodine electrode and a positive zinc electrode, these batteries suffer from lower energy output compared with commercial non-aqueous lithium batteries, and from the growth of zinc dendrites on the anodes — projections of material that build on electrodes and short batteries when they cross from one electrode to another — as well as corrosion of the zinc anode, which together result in reduced efficiency and even short-circuiting.



---


# MIT Hydrogel Drinking Water Device

The MIT team is designing a hydrogel-based device that produces drinking water rather than growing food: at night, an open box containing their gel captures water vapor from the air; the next day the sun heats the hydrogel in the box, releasing the moisture; the box also contains a material that can be cooled without using electricity, so that when the water vapor touches that cold surface it condenses into droplets — like morning dew on grass — and the clean water falls into a storage chamber.

The team is working to engineer a device that can extract 2 to 5 liters (0.5 to 1.3 gallons) a day, which should supply someone's average drinking-water needs. As places get drier, new sources of drinking water will be needed, and Díaz-Marín says it is great that hydrogels can make water anywhere; for ultra-dry places with few other options, he says, they could be a lifesaver.

# Spotify's Podcast Business Efficiency Pivot

Spotify reported an operating profit for the first time in a year, sending the stock up nearly 10 percent, with the revenue bump largely due to the streamer's $1 price increase earlier in 2023 — but executives also pointed to the downsizing of the podcast operation, which included hundreds of layoffs and the dissolution of Gimlet and Parcast, as a contributing factor. On the investor call, CFO Paul Vogel said podcasting, after being a real "drag" on profit margins in the past, will soon break even and turn toward profitability, and CEO Daniel Ek echoed him: "We're constantly finding new ways to bring more efficiencies out of the business… We've seen some improvements, but you should expect us to continue to look for more improvements going forward because that's just our modus operandi."

The Verge's October 25th, 2023 analysis argued that the adage "content is king" no longer applies at Spotify, which is increasingly focusing on tools that will scale the business rather than content that will attract listeners. Ek and Vogel hammered the efficiency theme — by the writer's transcript they said the word more than 30 times over the 50-minute call — but what was left unsaid about podcasting spoke louder: in the past they would excitedly tout how many millions of podcasts were on the platform, the latest new celebrity show, and the area's explosive growth, and as investors have run out of patience for the time and money such ambitions required, leadership changed its tune. The writer's summary of the new iteration is leaner, less splash, and more scale; Spotify's contributions to podcasting will not necessarily be insignificant — one audio industry professional told her the translation thing could be a total game-changer for the medium, if it is not a complete dud — but they should not be expected in the form of original content.

The open question she was left with is where Spotify's licensing deals fit. She wished someone on the call had asked Ek about the plan for big-name talent like Joe Rogan, Alex Cooper, and Dax Shepard as their deals come up for renewal: on one hand they have the scale, Rogan especially; on the other, they cost a chunk of cash, Rogan especially. It will be interesting, she wrote, to see how much Spotify and its investors can stomach spending on the biggest names in podcasting.



---


# ASX November 2023 Session and RBA Rate Expectations

In the Australian session reported by The Sydney Morning Herald on 5 November 2023, energy companies were the main drag on the index, down one per cent, with Woodside off 0.8 per cent, Santos down 0.4 per cent and Ampol down 1.2 per cent, alongside coal miners Yancoal (down 1.7 per cent) and Whitehaven (down 2 per cent). Lynas Rare Earths was the biggest large-cap decliner at down 3.1 per cent, while industrials fell 0.2 per cent, including Computershare (down 2.9 per cent), Seven West Holdings (down 1.9 per cent) and Worley (down 1.3 per cent).

TMS Capital portfolio manager Ben Clark said the big news for markets on the Monday was Westpac's trading update, which he said led a resurgence in the banking sector's performance. "Westpac's results were better than expected, especially because it's been a bit of a perennial underperformer in the past few years," he said, adding that it set the tone for results from NAB and ANZ due to report in the following week. Clark also described a reversal of the interest-rate trade of recent weeks: "Long-term bond yields came off quite significantly in the last few days following weaker than expected employment data on Friday, which has seen some investors swivel back into growth stocks." On his account the market had switched from pricing in an 80 per cent chance of a rate rise on the Tuesday to 50-50.

Other commentary framed the risk of a further increase. "Our view is that in the high likelihood there is another cash rate increase on Tuesday, that is going to be the nail in the coffin for consumer confidence," said CreditorWatch chief economist Anneke Thompson, amid warnings from some economists that another rate rise would dampen spending intentions just in time for Christmas. The same wrap noted that the men who built pubs and liquor juggernaut Endeavour Group into the world's largest poker machine operator had triggered a public spat over the future of a business they say has lost its way.



---


# ASX December 2023 Session Movers

On the Australian sharemarket session reported by The Sydney Morning Herald on 5 December 2023, Perpetual was the standout gainer, climbing 6.3 per cent after announcing a strategic review of its three-pronged corporate structure that might see it demerge its corporate trust and wealth management businesses and create a more focused asset manager. Endeavour shares lifted 2.4 per cent after the company forecast that earnings before interest and tax in its hotels division would grow by more than $150 million over the next five years.

Utilities and energy stocks were the weakest performers on the local bourse, rising just 0.6 per cent and 0.8 per cent respectively. Only five large-cap stocks declined outright. Evolution Mining sank a mammoth 13 per cent after raising $525 million by selling new shares to institutional investors at $3.80 a share, although the mining sector as a whole still managed to finish in positive territory. Gold miner Newmont was down 1.25 per cent, Origin Energy fell 0.4 per cent, Mercury NZ declined 0.3 per cent and Argo Investments traded 0.1 per cent lower.

Moomoo market strategist Jessica Amir attributed the local market's outperformance of global equities on the Wednesday session to the National Accounts figures, which pointed to the Reserve Bank potentially hitting pause on lifting interest rates. "We know economic growth is slowing, Australian unemployment is likely to pick up next year and inflation is likely to fall," Amir said, adding that this "trifecta" pointed towards the RBA stopping rate rises and then potentially moving to cut, which was what the market had priced in that day.



---


# Uber's Q3 2023 Headline Results

Uber reported third-quarter earnings on Tuesday, November 7, 2023 that show a profitable ride-hail and delivery company chugging along in spite of slowing growth in some sectors.

The company reported revenue of $9.3 billion, an 11% increase year over year. Investors had expected Uber to report revenues of around $9.5 billion (FactSet, Refinitiv), meaning that despite the company's growth it fell short of estimates. Turning to profitability, Uber reported net income of $221 million in the third quarter, or 10 cents per share, compared with a net loss of $1.2 billion, or 61 cents per share, in the same quarter the prior year — again short of expectations that it would generate 12 cents in per-share profit.

Looking ahead, Uber anticipates gross bookings of $36.5 billion to $37.5 billion, up just 6% at the top end from its Q3 result. After reporting, shares of Uber were up 1.6% in trading, after an up-and-down morning of shares exchange.



---


# Wall Street November 2023 Relief Rally

Wall Street closed a strong week on the Friday before this 5 November 2023 report, with the S&P 500 climbing 40.56 points, or 0.9 per cent, to 4,358.3; the Dow Jones Industrial Average gaining 222.24, or 0.7 per cent, to 34,061.32; and the Nasdaq composite jumping 184.09, or 1.4 per cent, to 13,478.28. Stocks surged through the week on rising hopes that the Federal Reserve is finally done with its market-crunching interest rate hikes aimed at getting inflation under control, with a Friday report underscoring easing inflation pressure by showing employers hired fewer workers in October than economists expected.

The report described this as a stunning turnaround from just a week earlier, when Wall Street was reeling after the S&P 500 had fallen 10 per cent below its high point for the year, sending the index into what investors call a "correction". Since then, strong profit reports helped drive some stocks to towering gains: Generac, a maker of back-up generators, soared nearly 28 per cent for its best week since its stock began trading in 2010, and Expedia Group's stronger-than-forecast report sent its stock nearly 22 per cent higher for its best week since the market was surging out of the coronavirus crash in early 2020. Even so, it was interest rates, yields and inflation that were at the centre of all the wild movements for financial markets around the world.

Excitement about a potentially easier Fed was more than enough to offset a fall for Apple, Wall Street's most influential and most valuable US stock, which fell 0.5 per cent despite reporting stronger profit for the latest quarter than analysts expected; analysts said investors were likely disappointed with Apple's revenue forecast for the last three months of 2023.

qid: Does the TechCrunch article suggest that Sam Bankman-Fried's motivation for alleged fraudulent activities was purely altruistic, while the Fortune article focuses on the jury's role in determining the truthfulness of Sam Bankman-Fried's actions, without attributing a specific motive?
context:
# Day Two Of The Bankman-Fried Trial: Jury Selection And The Courtroom Audience

On the second day of Sam Bankman-Fried's fraud trial, the jury was selected on Wednesday morning, after which lawyers for the government and then for Bankman-Fried delivered opening statements that told two very different stories of the former FTX CEO's sudden rise and almost instantaneous fall. The central question framed by the proceedings was who Bankman-Fried, the former CEO of crypto exchange FTX, really is: a liar and a fraud, or someone who acted in good faith and, like many a startup founder, flew too close to the sun. That answer, the account notes, ultimately lies with the jury.

The day featured pointed allegations, a friend from MIT, and an audience replete with big names, including Bankman-Fried's professorial parents and Damian Williams, the U.S. attorney for the Southern District of New York. Bankman-Fried himself spent most of the day in court staring into a laptop while seated between his two attorneys. The prosecution's account of his alleged crimes was described as featuring a study in contrasts.



---


# The Prosecution's Opening Statement Against Bankman-Fried

Thane Rehn, a prosecutor for the government, opened the case against Sam Bankman-Fried with the line "One year ago, it looked like the defendant was on the top of the world," and then argued that this appearance was false: "all of that, all of it, was built on lies," he declared to the jury, adding "Behind the curtains, he was not what he appeared to be." Rehn described a defendant who, as former CEO of FTX, oversaw a supposedly thriving crypto exchange, jetted between international locales, hobnobbed with celebrities like Tom Brady and Larry David, and repeatedly emphasized to customers that their money was safe and secure.

What followed was a roughly 30-minute story that repeatedly emphasized how Bankman-Fried allegedly stole customer funds to facilitate his jet-setting lifestyle, donate millions to political candidates, and finance risky bets. Rehn also directly contested the media framing of the defendant: he was not a crypto "boy" genius, as so many in the media — Fortune included — have written, but a "man" who "stole billions of dollars from thousands of victims." Rehn closed the characterization with a promise to the jury: "You will see the full picture."



---


# The Defense's Good-Faith Case For Bankman-Fried

Mark Cohen, one of Sam Bankman-Fried's lawyers, attacked the prosecution's central premise that his client was a liar who stole from customers, stating early in his opening statement that "Sam didn't defraud anyone." The defense's counter-picture is of a nerdy startup founder who acted in "good faith," not the prosecution's "cartoon of a villain"; Cohen repeatedly harped on Bankman-Fried's allegedly good-faith actions throughout his address to the jury. Bankman-Fried, whose cheekbones were more prominent after spending about seven weeks in a Brooklyn prison, appeared in court as this argument was made.

Cohen also disputed the specific claim that Alameda Research was a covert conduit. Alameda was not subterranean or shady, he said; it was a successful hedge fund. FTX was no Ponzi scheme but a "very innovative, successful company." The business practices between the two were reasonable, he argued, claiming that Alameda acted legally as an FTX customer, payment processor, and market maker — that is, a financial entity that acts as a trading partner for customers looking to buy and sell cryptocurrencies.

The defense's warrant for reading failure as something other than fraud was an analogy Cohen employed throughout: "working at a startup is like building a plane as you're flying it," and businesses sometimes fail. He specifically pointed the finger at Ellison, the former CEO of Alameda, who he said did not adequately protect her hedge fund from the inherent risk of the crypto markets. And when the walls came closing in and the aforementioned plane approached the "eye of the storm," Cohen argued, Bankman-Fried did not act like someone who was guilty — he was willing to give up his personal wealth to make customers whole. "In the end, Sam started and built two billion-dollar businesses," he concluded. "He didn't steal any money."



---


# Sam Bankman-Fried

Sam Bankman-Fried is the former CEO of the bankrupt crypto exchange FTX, whose highly anticipated criminal trial started on the Tuesday before TechCrunch's 2023-10-01 report, to determine whether he is guilty of seven counts of fraud and conspiracy. As one former federal prosecutor put it: "The odds seem to be stacked against him at this point."

He was 31 years old and co-founded FTX in 2019; within a few years the once third-largest crypto exchange's valuation hit $32 billion at its peak, and the company is now trying to claw back any funds to distribute to creditors. Before the fall he was even compared to Warren Buffet, and many called him the white horse of crypto — a description TechCrunch notes it never applied to him.

Bankman-Fried, however, maintained his innocence. At The New York Times' DealBook Summit he appeared virtually from the Bahamas and said, "I didn't ever try to commit fraud on anyone; I was shocked by what happened this month"; in a published DM exchange with a Vox reporter he said he regretted filing for bankruptcy and thought that "regulators make everything worse." In January he pleaded not guilty to all counts, which include wire fraud, conspiracy to commit money laundering and conspiracy to misuse customer funds. He could face up to 115 years in jail if convicted on all charges.

TechCrunch's 2023-10-02 summary of his standing on the eve of trial: SBF has been denied bail; his name is mud (or much worse) among those who have lost money in Alameda or FTX; and those who might not have had positions in these still blame him for other crypto woes, because he set off a ripple effect.



---


# Prosecution And Defense Arguments On Day Two Of The SBF Trial

On the second day of the trial of Sam Bankman-Fried and FTX, the prosecution argued that Bankman-Fried knowingly committed fraud, and it grounded that claim in motive: he did so, prosecutors said, to achieve great wealth, power and influence.

The defense countered with the opposite reading of the same conduct. Its claim was that the FTX founder acted in good faith, never meant to commit fraud or to steal, and basically got in over his head — an argument whose warrant is that inexperience and overreach, rather than intent, explain what happened. The two sides therefore contest intent rather than the underlying events, and the reporting on this exchange comes from Rebecca and Jacquelyn in TechCrunch's Week in Review of October 7, 2023, covering day two of the trial only.



---


# The FTX Trial's Stakes For The Wider Crypto Industry

The Verge argued that the trial of Sam Bankman-Fried is likely to be more consequential than just whether the man himself is found guilty: depending on what evidence is introduced, it could be rough for the entire crypto industry.

The grounds are the unpredictability of what a trial surfaces, voiced by Yesha Yadav, a law professor at Vanderbilt University: "How much damage can this trial do to the already beaten-down reputation of the industry at this point? This trial is going to be an excruciating moment for the industry because no one knows what kind of evidence might come out." The warrant joining that uncertainty to industry-wide stakes is that the industry's reputation is already beaten down, so evidence introduced against one exchange's founder lands on the whole sector rather than on him alone.



---


# Alameda Research As The Alleged Conduit For FTX Customer Funds

In the prosecution's account offered by Thane Rehn, the key to Sam Bankman-Fried's alleged scheme was Alameda Research, a crypto hedge fund that Bankman-Fried also owned. The structure the government described works as follows: Caroline Ellison — Bankman-Fried's on-again off-again girlfriend and the CEO of Alameda — served as a front for the fund, and through that arrangement Bankman-Fried had "secret access" to customer money, both cash and crypto.

Two further relations complete the alleged mechanism. Bankman-Fried is said to have directed employees to conceal the flow of money into FTX's coffers, and to have forged financial documents distributed to lenders and investors. "The defendant lied to the world," Rehn alleged. These are the government's allegations as presented in its opening statement, not established findings.



---


# Sam Bankman-Fried's Federal Fraud Trial

Sam Bankman-Fried, the founder of bankrupt cryptocurrency exchange FTX, is charged with seven counts of fraud and money laundering following the collapse of his cryptocurrency empire the previous year, and was on trial in New York in October 2023.

Two fixed points anchor the proceeding as CNBC described it on 2023-10-06. A U.S. judge revoked Bankman-Fried's bail at a hearing in a New York courthouse on August 11, 2023. And on Thursday, Oct. 5, 2023, Matt Huang, co-founder of Paradigm Operations LP, arrived at the New York court to appear in the case.

# Google Maps' AI Feature Rollout

Google is rolling out a variety of updates for Maps, incorporating AI technology to enhance user experience, TechCrunch reported on November 3, 2023.

The feature is currently available in France, Germany, Japan, the U.K. and the U.S.

Google has plans for further expansion beyond those five markets.

# LinkedIn's New AI Tools

LinkedIn unveiled a string of new AI features spanning its job hunting, marketing and sales products in the week covered by TechCrunch's October 7, 2023 Week in Review, as reported by Ingrid.

Three of the announced features are named: a big update to LinkedIn's Recruiter talent sourcing platform, with AI assistance built into it throughout; an AI-powered LinkedIn Learning coach; and a new AI-powered tool for marketing campaigns.



---


# Anecdotal Evidence Undercuts Google's Gemini Pro Claims

Against Google's promises for Gemini Pro, TechCrunch's rejoinder on 7 December 2023 was blunt: "the anecdotal evidence suggests otherwise." The counter-argument attacks the evidential basis of the launch claims rather than the model's architecture, setting user experience after release against what Google said the model would do.

The grounds are the reception of the rollout itself. A "lite" version of Gemini, Gemini Pro, began rolling out to Bard the day before the article, and it did not take long before users began voicing their frustrations with it on X, formerly Twitter.



---


# Projected Publisher Traffic Losses From AI Search

Publishers believe they will lose somewhere between 20% and 40% of their website traffic once Google's AI products fully roll out, according to a Wall Street Journal report noted by TechCrunch on 15 December 2023. That report also led with a modelling result from the online magazine The Atlantic: when The Atlantic modelled what would happen if Google integrated AI into search, it found that 75% of the time the AI would answer the user's query without requiring a click-through to its website, losing it traffic.

The stakes are set by how much publisher traffic Google currently supplies. According to data from Similarweb cited in the same coverage, Google today drives nearly 40% of publishers' traffic, so a shift to AI-answered queries could have a major impact on publishers' traffic going forward. The suit filed by Helena World Chronicle takes up precisely this question of how AI will impact publishers' businesses.

Some publishers are trying to get ahead of the problem: Axel Springer inked a deal with OpenAI in the same week to license its news for AI model training.



---


# Open Source

Open source, in the corpus's AI-industry usage, is the label companies apply to AI models, tools, and frameworks whose code or methodology they make available for outside use, positioned as the opposite pole from a "closed" or "proprietary" approach where a single company controls access.
The term is contested rather than binary: TechCrunch's own reporting shows companies claiming the "open source" label while attaching licensing restrictions, so the word functions as a marketing and strategic banner as much as a precise technical category.

## Context

The corpus uses "open source" mainly to describe a strategic fault line in generative AI between companies favoring open distribution of models (Meta, Mistral AI, Hugging Face, Stability AI) and companies favoring proprietary control (OpenAI, Google, Microsoft, Anthropic).
Meta's Yann LeCun and roughly 70 co-signatories published an open letter arguing that "increasing public access and scrutiny makes technology safer, not more dangerous," directly rebutting the argument from OpenAI and Google DeepMind that proprietary AI is safer than open source.
A leaked internal Google memo ("we have no moat, and neither does OpenAI") treated the rise of open source AI models — following a Meta foundation model leak in March 2023 — as an existential threat to proprietary LLM providers, because openness lets a broader community collaborate and experiment in ways closed models cannot match.
Meta went on to co-found the AI Alliance with IBM to promote "open innovation" and "open source AI models and frameworks," while pointed omissions from that alliance's membership (Google, OpenAI, Microsoft, Anthropic, Cohere, Adept) map directly onto the open-versus-closed divide.
The label also shows up outside the Meta/OpenAI rivalry: French startup Mistral AI builds "open source large language models," Giskard builds an "open source testing framework" for LLMs, OpenAI's own Whisper speech-recognition system is described as open source, and Auto-GPT is an open-source app built atop OpenAI's proprietary GPT models — showing open and closed components routinely coexist in the same AI stack.
One VC analysis of the generative AI tech stack expects the foundation-model layer to settle into an oligopoly "with the addition of a strong open source contingency that will drive considerable third-party adoption," treating open source as a distinct, persistent segment of the market rather than a transitional phase.

## Key Characteristics

- **Positioned against "proprietary" / "closed"** — the corpus consistently frames open source as the opposite pole from proprietary, centrally-controlled AI development.
- **Safety argument cuts both ways** — proprietary-AI advocates (OpenAI, Google DeepMind) argue closed control limits catastrophic misuse; open source advocates (LeCun and signatories) argue public scrutiny makes technology safer, not more dangerous.
- **The label is contestable** — Meta calls Llama open source, but TechCrunch reports licensing terms (a ban on using Llama to train other models, and a special-license requirement for apps with over 700 million monthly users) that restrict use for large competitors, so the "open source" claim is disputed even by outlets covering it.
- **Used as coalition-building rhetoric** — the AI Alliance's founding materials cast "open innovation" and "open science" against a vision that would "relegate AI innovation... to a small number of companies with a closed, proprietary vision," turning openness into a membership and marketing signal.
- **Spans models, tools, and frameworks** — the corpus applies "open source" to LLMs (Mistral's models, Llama), a testing framework (Giskard), a speech-recognition system (Whisper), and a task-automation app (Auto-GPT), not just to full foundation models.

## Background (external)

Outside the corpus, "open source" has a formal technical definition: the Open Source Initiative (OSI) specifies that open-source software's distribution terms must satisfy ten criteria — including free redistribution, availability of source code, and permission to create derived works — and that access to source code alone is not sufficient to qualify (Open Source Initiative, "The Open Source Definition," https://opensource.org/osd, accessed 2026-09-02).
That formal criteria-based definition does not appear anywhere in the corpus; the corpus instead uses "open source" informally, as a contested marketing and strategic label rather than a precise technical category (see Definition and Key Characteristics above).
