# Sydney Swans' First AFLW Finals Berth

Sydney, winless in their debut season the previous year, secured eighth spot and their first AFLW finals berth in 2023 by storming home with three unanswered goals against Fremantle, The Age reported on 3 November 2023.

"Any club that's able to go from winless one year to a finals berth, it's incredible," Sydney co-captain Chloe Molloy told Fox Footy after the match. "You can see the emotion on the girls' faces. Coming into the season, the odds were against us. Just to get into the eight, we've managed to do that. We're stoked. It's pretty special for the club." Missing star ruck Ally Morphett to a season-ending wrist injury, Laura Gardiner stood tallest in the midfield — the 20-year-old off-season recruit from Geelong had the ball on a string with a game-high 33 disposals and 18 contested possessions — while Molloy (two goals), Montana Ham, Rebecca Privitelli and Brooke Lochland hit the scoreboard.

The Swans' rise had been signalled earlier in the season by a record-breaking win over the Western Bulldogs, propelled by a Chloe Molloy masterclass: after a five-goal second term that included a four-minute burst of three majors, Sydney had already brought up their largest score in an AFLW game by half-time, and while the Bulldogs held their own in the last quarter the damage was done. The total was also the biggest the Dogs had conceded in their history, topping the 83 Melbourne kicked against them in round three. Molloy, the Swans' star off-season recruit and a former Collingwood ace, was a class above, kicking 3.4 from her 28 possessions and playing a crucial role in setting up numerous other Sydney goals. "She was itching to get in there [in the midfield]," Swans coach Scott Gowans said. "We kept her forward deliberately. It was important Chloe played a good block of time forward so we could have a look at it." That weekend the Blues lost to Greater Western Sydney by two points, 8.1 (49) to 7.5 (47), denying Carlton the chance to leapfrog into the top eight.



---


# Sydney Swans Top The AFLW Attendance Charts

The Sydney Swans sat top of the AFLW attendance charts on 26 October 2023, less than two years after their first match in the women's league, with an average attendance of 4,365 from four games — 124 more than the next best club, Adelaide.

They were due to play their final home match of the regular season that weekend, a marquee pride match against Collingwood at Henson Park on the Sunday, where a crowd in excess of 4,000 was expected. Earlier in the season, 5,474 fans were at North Sydney Oval to watch the Swans' first AFLW victory.

Swans forward Bella Smith said the players were proud of the club's attendance record and grateful for the support: "We get there two hours before the start of the game and the hill [at Henson Park] is bare. When you come out for the first team warm-up, the hill is slowly filling and then by the time the first bounce gets around, it is full. You can hear it, the atmosphere is amazing."



---


# AFLW 2023 Finals Qualification And Week One Fixture

The 2023 AFLW finals eight was not decided until the final game of the regular season, when Sydney downed Fremantle by 22 points to leapfrog St Kilda into the final spot, The Age reported on 3 November 2023.

The Saints had kept themselves in the race with a 20-point win over Carlton earlier in the day, 7.4 (46) to 3.8 (26), and with only 0.4 of a percentage point separating Sydney in ninth and St Kilda in eighth, the Swans' win assured them of retaking eighth spot. Had the Saints qualified, it would have been their maiden finals appearance. Saints goalkicker Jesse Wardlaw had a heavy collision with Carlton's Keeley Sherar late in the final quarter of their clash.

The resulting week-one finals fixture was: on Saturday November 11, the First Qualifying Final, Adelaide v Brisbane Lions, 2.35pm local (3.05pm AEDT) at Norwood Oval, and the First Elimination Final, Gold Coast v Sydney, 6.15pm local (7.15pm AEDT) at Heritage Bank Stadium; on Sunday November 12, the Second Elimination Final, Geelong v Essendon, 1.05pm AEDT at GMHBA Stadium, and the Second Qualifying Final, Melbourne v North Melbourne, 3.05pm AEDT at Ikon Park.



---


# The Swans' Matchday Experience Model For Local Attendance

The Sydney Swans' attendance strategy, described on 26 October 2023 by executive GM of marketing Loretta Johns, has two linked components: target local communities, and make match days compelling for fans on and off the field.

The off-field half is delivered through food, entertainment and promotion. "Our team has put a lot of work into sourcing some wonderful food offerings, entertainment and activities for kids, while we've had a local focus in promoting our games," Johns said. At North Sydney Oval that means quince paste and hand-picked grapes, cheddar cheese and biscuits in a little box with beautiful wrapping — "they've really thought about what they're doing and made it an experience."

The local-community half works through partnership as a promotional channel, not just a supplier relationship. At Henson Park, the Swans' other home ground in Sydney's gentrified inner west, "they've gone to microbreweries in the local area and invited them in, but also promoted through their clientele to come to the football" — the local business both provides the offering and supplies an audience.



---


# The Swans' On-Field Turnaround Under Chloe Molloy

After a winless campaign in 2022, the Sydney Swans — led by ex-Collingwood player Chloe Molloy — were competitive in the 2023 AFLW season, winning their first match in round one and sitting within a game of the top eight with two rounds to play as of 26 October 2023.

The Swans recorded their highest total the previous round in a 14-12-96 to 6-3-39 defeat of the Western Bulldogs, the league's winless bottom side, with Molloy recording 17 score involvements to set a new AFLW mark. The Guardian noted the turnaround mattered because fans of Australian rules football in the Harbour City have a reputation for being fickle.



---


# The 'Matildas Effect' And Its Limited Impact On Domestic Women's Sport

The Guardian argued on 26 October 2023 that the popularity of the Matildas' run to the Women's World Cup semi-finals has had only a limited impact on support for domestic women's sport, because the early spike did not persist.

The grounds come from the A-League Women, which launched that month with a first round highlighted by a crowd of more than 11,000 in Sydney — but more modest attendances in subsequent games, including two sub-2,000 crowds in Perth, follow it. The warrant is that a durable effect would show up beyond the opening round; a large first-round crowd followed by small ones is consistent with novelty rather than converted support.

Nicole Livingstone, the AFL's general manager of women's football, made the same point from the league side, saying the "green and gold fever" associated with the Women's World Cup was a one-off and that the AFL has plans in place for long-term growth: "We'll continue to keep building the base and keep building the foundations and have it not just strong at year seven, season eight, but strong for generations to come."



---


# AFLW Crowds Short Of Season-Extension Targets

Average AFLW attendance in 2023 was a little over 2,500 a match — tracking approximately on par with previous seasons, with a finals uptick likely to come — but crowds were short of the targets that could accelerate the extension of the regular season, which grows from 10 games that year to 12 games by 2025.

The league enjoyed strong attendances in round one, partly attributed to the so-called Matildas effect, but some clubs struggled to attract fans in large numbers across the season: crowds of less than 1,500 were recorded in both traditional markets such as Melbourne and Perth and in areas targeted for growth such as Blacktown and the Gold Coast.

Against that backdrop, Nicole Livingstone, general manager of women's football at the AFL, said the Swans' off-field offering had tapped into something "uniquely Sydney" and helped make matches more attractive.

qid: Does the TechCrunch article suggest the absence of a legislative remedy for AI risks and abuses, while the Music Business Worldwide article indicates that the National Music Publishers Association is advocating for regulations in AI development?
context:
# The US Copyright Office's 2023 Study Of AI And Copyright

The US Copyright Office is spearheading one of the key US efforts to address AI and copyright: in the summer of 2023 it issued a call for submissions on the issue of AI and copyright, with the goal of putting together a study to "help assess whether legislative or regulatory steps in this area are warranted."

The call for submissions came as legislators and regulators around the world grappled with the many issues that had emerged since AI technology "went mainstream" about a year earlier. Numerous businesses involved in AI, and those with substantial copyright holdings, submitted their thoughts on the issue — including Universal Music Group and AI developer Anthropic.



---


# The NMPA Submission Calling Generative AI The Greatest Risk To The Creative Class

The National Music Publishers Association's submission to the US Copyright Office, dated October 30, 2023, argues that generative AI may be the greatest risk to the human creative class that has ever existed — and therefore that the Office should adopt proactive protections for human creators and, where uncertain, err on their side.

The argument is deliberately framed as pro-technology at its base. The submission starts by stressing that the NMPA's membership — US music publishers major and independent — are "not opposed" to AI: "There is widespread belief in the music industry that great benefits could come from generative AI systems that can assist human creators." It then goes for the jugular: "However, the development of the generative AI marketplace is marked by breathtaking speed, size and complexity. Hindsight may well prove that there is no hyperbole in saying that generative AI is the greatest risk to the human creative class that has ever existed." The warrant for urgency is temporal: "Even more alarming is that we do not know how long the window is to act before it is too late. We therefore implore the [US Copyright] Office to support proactive protections for human creators and, where there is uncertainty, to err on the side of protecting human creators." MBW notes the position is not a surprise from an organisation that earlier in 2023 joined the fledgling Human Artistry Campaign, whose goal in broadest terms is to ensure AI does not replace or "erode" human culture — yet the submission is hardly a Luddite diatribe against high tech; it advocates regulations and principles it sees as the right way to keep the interests of musical artists and rights holders from being subjugated in the frenzy to build an AI-powered world.



---


# Sony Music's Generative AI Principles For Congress

Dennis Kooker, Sony Music Entertainment's President of Global Digital Business & US Sales, asked Congress at the November 29, 2023 AI Insight Forum to embrace a set of five principles around generative AI, on the argument that "if copyrights are protected and enforced appropriately, we are at the beginning of a multi-decade marathon that will change the creative and commercial landscape for music."

The framing condition Kooker set is that "Music is a tremendous driver for AI technology, and AI technology presents a tremendous opportunity for the creative development of music. But these opportunities must be grounded by the human creators' vision with the machine assisting, not with the machine replacing the human creator." The principles are: Assure Consent, Compensation, and Credit — "New products and businesses built with music must be developed with the consent of the owner and appropriate compensation and credit. It is essential to understand why the training of AI models is being done, what products will be developed as a result, and what the business model is that will monetize the use of the artist's work. Congress and the agencies should assure that creators' rights are recognized and respected." Confirm That Copying Music to Train AI Models is Not Fair Use — "Even worse are those that argue that copyrighted content should automatically be considered fair use so that protected works are never compensated for usage and creators have no say in the products or business models that are developed around them and their work. Congress should assure and agencies should presume that reproducing music to train AI models, in itself, is not a fair use." Prevent the Cloning of Artists' Voices and Likenesses Without Express Permission — "We cannot allow an artist's voice or likeness to be cloned for use without the express permission of the artist. This is a very personal decision for the artist. Congress should pass into law effective federal protections for name, image, and likeness." Incentivize Accurate Recordkeeping — "Correct attribution will be a critical element to artists being paid fairly and correctly for new works that are created. In addition, rights can only be enforced around the training of AI when there are accurate records about what is being copied. Otherwise, the inability to enforce rights in the AI marketplace equates to a lack of rights at all, producing a dangerous imbalance that prevents a thriving ecosystem. This requires strong and accurate record keeping by the generative AI platforms, a requirement that urgently needs legislative support to ensure incentives are in place so that it happens consistently and correctly." And Assure Transparency for Consumers and Artists — "Transparency is necessary to clearly distinguish human-created works from AI-created works. The public should know, when they are listening to music, whether that music was created by a human being or a machine." MBW summarised the intended effect: "The principles will ensure that intellectual property businesses can succeed in this new world alongside tech partners, further advancing investment and expanding economic opportunities."



---


# The UMG, Concord And ABKCO Lawsuit Against Anthropic Over Song Lyrics

Universal Music Group, Concord Music Group and ABKCO filed a lawsuit against AI developer Anthropic seeking potentially tens of millions of dollars for the alleged "systematic and widespread infringement of their copyrighted song lyrics."

Music Business Worldwide noted on 2023-11-30 that the fair use argument Anthropic had advanced in its submission to the US Copyright Office could yet come into play in the company's legal battle with Universal.



---


# Schumer's AI Insight Forum On Creative Copyright

On Wednesday November 29, 2023, US Senate Majority Leader Chuck Schumer held an Artificial Intelligence (AI) Insight Forum to discuss the importance and role of creative copyright and intellectual property in the development of AI — a sign that senior political figures in Washington are becoming increasingly interested in the impact of AI on the law.

Dennis Kooker, Sony Music Entertainment's President of Global Digital Business & US Sales, delivered a speech at the Forum outlining the major music company's position on AI and copyright law.



---


# Works Created Principally Through AI Should Not Be Copyrightable

The NMPA's first policy demand is that works created principally through AI should not be copyrightable: simply giving a prompt to an AI music generator — "compose a power ballad about falling in love" — should not be enough to create a copyrightable work.

The grounds are incentive-based: "Policies surrounding copyrightability of AI-generated content will either serve to incentivize continued investment and effort into human creativity or to disincentivize it," the submission states. The warrant is stated as a principle about what the law must never allow: "The law should never be such that human creators stand to gain more from repeatedly clicking a button to generate massive amounts of AI-produced materials than from putting their hearts, souls, experiences, skills, talents, and emotions into expressive works of art." The remedy the NMPA proposes is that the law treat a musical work created entirely by AI the same way it treats works in the public domain — not copyrightable, and free for anyone to use as they see fit, whether for commercial or other purposes.



---


# Fair Use, Explained Plainly

"Fair use" is, as it sounds, the argument that there are cases where copyrighted material can be used and even replicated that are fair enough.

Music Business Worldwide's 2023-11-23 piece offers a deliberately clumsy example: I read a great book, then I meet you for breakfast, where I tell you about the story and quote a couple of my favorite passages to you. To suggest that this is copyright infringement would not only be silly — it would mean that copyright protections were getting in the way of the commercial furtherment of the author or rightsholder, since you might go and buy the book on the recommendation.



---


# Sony Music's Absence From "Dream Track"

Dennis Kooker's public statements on AI arrived a week after MBW pointed out a notable lack of endorsement from Sony Music Entertainment, and its artists, of YouTube's experimental AI project "Dream Track," which lets creators clone the vocals of successful musicians.

The initial cohort of stars involved in the project included recording artists signed to Warner Music Group and Universal Music Group — or labels within each of those two majors — but no Sony Music artists. In its earlier report MBW suggested that YouTube parent Google's recent submission to the United States Copyright Office, made in response to a request for written submissions as part of a study around copyright law and policy issues raised by AI systems, may have influenced Sony's absence from Dream Track.

# The Ireland Series Loss Backlash As All Blacks Motivation

The Roar argued on Oct. 26, 2023 that where the Springboks play for their country, the All Blacks were playing for themselves as much as anyone — and for the generation of players and leaders who would call time on their international careers at week's end — which is why the World Cup final was personal for the men in black.

The framing question is how New Zealand could withstand and overcome the hitherto unshakable wave of momentum and spirit the Springboks play with under Rassie Erasmus in that weekend's final. The grounds offered for the All Blacks' personal motivation are the backlash and toxicity that followed their historic home series loss to Ireland, described as a humbling and public reminder of the expectation of being an All Black — All Blacks social media managers were forced to delete a thousand comments an hour following the humbling series loss in Wellington.

The warrant is that the hurt persisted and became fuel: the pain of the days and weeks after that dark July, as well as the bumps and bruises along the way — including as recently as August when they suffered their biggest defeat to the Boks to lose the inaugural and prestigious Qatar Cup — still ran deep.



---


# Cheika's Underdog Framing Before The 2023 Semi-Final

Michael Cheika embraced underdog status before Argentina's 2023 World Cup semi-final while pointedly reminding the All Blacks who the favourites were: "The other team are heavy favourites, everyone is expecting a New Zealand and South Africa final. We just have to focus on what is required."

His grounds are a reading of what New Zealand demand of an opponent: "New Zealand has always been an example in rugby, a benchmark. They make you think of high-level skills in a really open game but there are always threats in the lineout, mauls and rucks. You have to take the moments you are in the game and see them coming at you at different times." Cheika, whose Wallabies lost the 2015 final, was readying for another clash against the All Blacks and a second semi-final.

He also refused to over-read Argentina's 2020 win as evidence: "In the game in 2020 there were things you could pinpoint. You can't say that one game means we can do it as there are a lot of games where we haven't. That moment has to be just a part of it. What we have done since then, all the success and failures [matters in our preparation]." The same week he said he hoped Los Pumas "inspired" Argentina "not by our results but by our ambition".



---


# How England And South Africa Reached The 2023 Semi-Final

England arrived at the 2023 Rugby World Cup semi-final as the only side still competing that had yet to lose a game, while South Africa had already beaten two of the tournament favourites. Dominant wins over Argentina, Japan and Chile sealed England's passage to the last eight, and after being given an almighty scare by Samoa in their final pool match, they overcame a Fijian fightback in Marseille to triumph 30-24 — outscored by three tries to two, but carried by captain Owen Farrell's 20 points at the expense of 2023's breakout stars.

The Springboks had done it tough. Comfortable defeats of Scotland, Romania and Tonga could not mask the disappointment of a 13-8 loss to Ireland, which consigned South Africa to second in Pool B. With Ireland then sent home by the All Blacks in the quarters, the Bokke showed their World Cup mettle to edge hosts France 29-28 at the Stade de France, sneaking past Les Bleus in one of the best games of rugby you're ever likely to see.

Both journeys had twists, turns and bumps in the road but left each side within 80 minutes of a Rugby World Cup final. England would be looking to echo the spirit of 2019, when they beat the All Blacks 19-7 to reach the final, but in South Africa they faced a side who had taken their game to new heights just to reach the semis.



---


# Why The Springboks Were Predicted To Beat England At The Stade De France

Sporting News predicted South Africa would beat England in the 2023 Rugby World Cup semi-final at the Stade de France, because the match required a huge step up in quality from Steve Borthwick's side while South Africa had already shown they could match and beat the world's best.

The grounds are England's record read closely. Their tournament form was perfect at face value — Argentina, Japan and Chile, plus Samoa and Fiji, had all provided highlights, and England beat all of them, with Los Pumas also reaching the semi-finals. But only Japan and Chile were defeated with bonus points, and the narrow wins over Samoa and Fiji in the last two games showed that England were certainly gettable.

The recent head-to-head reinforced the point. The last time the sides met was a tumultuous period for English rugby: South Africa's dominant 27-13 victory at Twickenham proved to be the last game in charge for Eddie Jones, the coach who had taken England to the 2019 World Cup final, and Borthwick was hired in his place — now one game away from repeating that feat.



---


# Erasmus And Nienaber Depart After The Springboks' 2023 Title

The 2023 World Cup final victory was the perfect sign-off for the Springboks' management, with director of rugby Rassie Erasmus set to follow head coach Jacques Nienaber out — a duo The Roar says will go down as the greatest coaching pair in rugby history, having led South Africa to back-to-back World Cup triumphs.

Nienaber framed the win as the endpoint of a long plan and thanked the country: "We came a long way with the players. We always planned for this World Cup, since 2018. Massive credit to our fans. They were special from South Africa, 62 million people, the videos we had to play from them. It was unbelievable."

The departures were not only from the coaching box: veteran back-rower Duane Vermeulen would also call time on his illustrious career.



---


# Peter Horne's Appointment As Rugby Australia High-Performance Director

Rugby Australia was moving closer to naming World Rugby's director of high-performance Peter Horne as its new director of high-performance, a move The Roar reported on 11 December 2023 could also help land highly-regarded coach Joe Schmidt for the vacant Wallabies job.

The Roar had reported the previous week that Horne emerged as the leading candidate, and it is believed he edged out former Sydney University, Australian Sevens and Harlequins director of rugby Billy Millard for the role. The finer points of the negotiations were being worked out, with an announcement likely over the following week once Horne wrapped up a crucial series of meetings with World Rugby — he was leading World Rugby meetings with tier-two nations that week in Sydney, with former Fiji coach Simon Raiwalui in attendance before officially joining World Rugby. His appointment reflects Rugby Australia's desire to go down an administrative path rather than choose a former coach of any standing, as Millard would have offered, and Horne will sit at the top of the high-performance tree with the next Wallabies coach reporting into him.

His background is given in some detail. Horne joined World Rugby in 2015 as a general manager of high-performance before moving into his current role, and during that tenure the Sydneysider played an important role in setting up competitions, high-performance structures and pathways across developing countries. He also played a role in helping Super Rugby integrate Fiji Drua and Moana Pasifika into the competition. Those successes played out at the recent Rugby World Cup, with Chile, Fiji, Georgia and Portugal delivering encouraging performances that positively reflected World Rugby's desire to spread and build the game. He briefly worked at Saracens as a general manager.



---


# Ireland's Rugby World Cup Quarter-Final Curse

Ireland's "quarter-final curse" is the pattern by which the team has never won a Rugby World Cup knockout match: on quarter-final weekend, for the eighth time in 10 Rugby World Cups, Ireland headed home defeated, and the wait for a first-ever knockout win goes on. This time was supposed to be different — this Ireland team were different, are different — but come the end, the result was the same.

The boundary of the pattern is how rarely Ireland have even threatened to break it. Since 1991, when Michael Lynagh's late try handed Australia victory, Ireland had not come close to ending their last-eight hoodoo; never mind winning one, they had not led a World Cup quarter-final since the first half of the 1995 defeat to France, a mammoth 10,353 days earlier.

The 2023 defeat will hurt more than any other, because here they had a legitimate chance to reverse the curse. Multiple times they got within a point of the All Blacks, only for their opponents to agonisingly pull away once more — and then there were those 37 phases, the most painful finish in Irish rugby history.

qid: Who is the individual under 30, formerly associated with FTX and Alameda Research, who was described by 'Fortune' as using a front for secret access to customer funds, by 'The Verge' as overwhelmed by the growth of his company to manage it alongside another, and by 'TechCrunch' as both the richest person in his age group with altruistic spending intentions and as someone accused of committing fraud for personal gain?

# Gary Wang's Ownership Stake And Cooperation Deal

Gary Wang, co-founder and chief technology officer of FTX and co-founder of Alameda Research, owned only 10 percent of Alameda and 17 percent of FTX and drew a $200,000-a-year salary with no performance bonuses — though at times he was a billionaire on paper — while Bankman-Fried owned 90 percent of Alameda and 65 percent of FTX. He returned to the US on November 16th, met with the US government on November 17th without having been arrested or charged, offered to cooperate immediately, and pled guilty to various charges a month later. Wang was clear that he was cooperating because he did not want to go to jail, and said he hoped his assistance would lead a sentencing judge to be lenient.

The Verge's reporter drew from the disparity a puzzle she could not resolve: Wang took bizarre risks for a relatively small share. Bankman-Fried did not code, so none of his fingerprints are on the technical changes that let FTX allegedly defraud its customers and investors, while Wang supervised the code behind a key prosecution claim — that Alameda Research was afforded secret, special privileges with FTX's funds. When FTX went down, Wang left himself with no plausible deniability. Wang, a college roommate of Bankman-Fried's, took the stand after Adam Yedidia and, in the reporter's phrase, sang like a canary about the secret privileges he had created for Alameda in the FTX code.

The delivery was heavy going. On October 6th, 2023 Wang had to explain to the jury the difference between a front end and a back end, explain futures trading, and read a great deal into the record, which took a while; it was a tough day for the jury, and probably for Wang, who spoke quickly, perhaps from nerves.



---


# FTX Ventures Was Funded By Alameda

Caroline Ellison testified that the money behind FTX Ventures came from Alameda Research, even though Bankman-Fried announced the fund publicly without naming its source: on January 14th, 2022 he tweeted, "We're launching a $2b venture fund: FTX Ventures!" She said he did not want to go public with where the funds came from, telling her he thought Alameda's brand was less good and that he did not want his name associated with it.

The Verge reported the episode on October 10th, 2023 as part of Ellison's testimony, framing it as FTX keeping cozy private ties with Alameda while publicly holding it at arm's length — an echo, the reporter wrote, of Bankman-Fried and Ellison's romantic relationship. The same distancing appears in another transaction: Alameda bought Robinhood shares for Bankman-Fried, who moved them to a vehicle called "Emergent Fidelity Technologies" to avoid association with Alameda.



---


# Testimony At The SBF Trial

Across the first three weeks of the trial, a run of former colleagues, an outside investor and a forensic accounting expert testified that FTX customer money flowed into Alameda Research and out again to other uses, and that FTX's investors were never told about the two firms' special relationship. TechCrunch's running coverage, published 2023-10-06, summarises each week.

In week one, FTX's co-founder and CTO Gary Wang testified Thursday on the extent to which Alameda Research was used for whatever purposes he and SBF saw fit: according to Wang, the crypto trading firm pulled funding directly from FTX customers, whose transactions would be funneled toward Alameda and then directed elsewhere. Thursday also brought testimony from Matt Huang, co-founder and managing partner at crypto investment firm Paradigm, which invested $278 million in FTX across 2021 and 2022 and is part of a class-action lawsuit accusing it and others of defrauding customers by promoting FTX. His testimony centered around being left uninformed about FTX's utilization of customer money to keep Alameda Research afloat — a practice Huang says would have halted his involvement — and covered his relationship with FTX stretching back to 2019.

Week two's standout testimony came from Alameda Research's former CEO Caroline Ellison, who claimed she took $14 billion from customers to repay debts to lenders, using them as a line of credit under the instruction of SBF. Ellison also went into detail about how a $2 billion venture fund, FTX Ventures, was funded by money that had previously been allocated to Alameda from third-party lenders. And though there are no charges of bribery in the case, she also testified to paying Chinese officials $150 million to restore access to $1 billion in frozen trading accounts.

The third week featured a couple of noteworthy moments for the prosecution. FTX's former general counsel Can Sun, like many of SBF's former colleagues, opted to cooperate with authorities and testified that SBF asked him to create a theoretical "legal justification" for the use of billions in consumer funds just days before FTX filed for bankruptcy. Robert Boroujerdi, managing director of the hedge fund Third Point, testified about his experience working with SBF and FTX in a partnership that ultimately resulted in a $60 million investment and a lack of awareness about the special relationship between Alameda Research and FTX; had he known of such a relationship, he testified, Third Point would not have invested in FTX in the first place. And earlier in the week, Peter Easton — a University of Notre Dame professor who helped the government prosecution of Enron and WorldCom — testified about what he uncovered after tracing the flow of billions of dollars between Alameda Research and FTX: much of that funding came from customers, and Easton testified that he found user deposits were used by both FTX and Alameda to purchase real estate, make investments or direct funding toward political causes and charities.



---


# Alameda Research As The Alleged Conduit For FTX Customer Funds

In the prosecution's account offered by Thane Rehn, the key to Sam Bankman-Fried's alleged scheme was Alameda Research, a crypto hedge fund that Bankman-Fried also owned. The structure the government described works as follows: Caroline Ellison — Bankman-Fried's on-again off-again girlfriend and the CEO of Alameda — served as a front for the fund, and through that arrangement Bankman-Fried had "secret access" to customer money, both cash and crypto.

Two further relations complete the alleged mechanism. Bankman-Fried is said to have directed employees to conceal the flow of money into FTX's coffers, and to have forged financial documents distributed to lenders and investors. "The defendant lied to the world," Rehn alleged. These are the government's allegations as presented in its opening statement, not established findings.



---


# Gary Wang's Testimony At The FTX Fraud Trial

Gary Wang, the lesser-known co-founder of FTX, told a Manhattan courtroom on Thursday that he had committed financial crimes while working at FTX — including wire and commodities fraud — carried out with the help of Sam Bankman-Fried, FTX ex-engineering head Nishad Singh, and Caroline Ellison, who ran sister hedge fund Alameda Research and had been Bankman-Fried's girlfriend.

Asked by Assistant U.S. Attorney Nicolas Roos, "Did you commit financial crimes while working at FTX?" Wang responded, "Yes." Asked whether he saw any of the people he committed those crimes with in the courtroom, Wang — dressed in an oversized and wrinkled suit with a red tie and glasses — awkwardly stood up, looked around, and answered, "Yes"; asked who, he said, "Sam Bankman-Fried." He was one of two former friends of Bankman-Fried's from MIT who also worked at FTX while living with the founder in the Bahamas and who took the stand that week to testify against their former classmate, confidant and boss, a man who allegedly ran a crypto empire that defrauded thousands of customers out of billions of dollars. The trial, set to last six weeks, was to resume on Tuesday with key testimony expected from Ellison, considered the prosecution's star witness, who had already pleaded guilty to multiple charges. Bankman-Fried faces seven federal charges, including wire fraud, securities fraud and money laundering, that could put him in prison for the rest of his life. Thus far Bankman-Fried, 31, has remained mostly quiet in court, intently listening to witnesses and at times writing notes to his attorneys — but as Wang testified against him, he looked visibly upset, shifting his gaze from his former friend to the ground and at one point putting his head in his hands.



---


# Matt Huang And Paradigm's FTX Investment

Matt Huang, co-founder and managing partner of Paradigm, a crypto venture capital firm that invested over $275 million in FTX — a stake that was wiped out — was the third witness to take the stand, and testified about his firm's due diligence.

Huang told the court that Bankman-Fried assured him funds would be used for FTX and not Alameda, and that he was promised Alameda had no preferential treatment on the FTX platform, even though the hedge fund was one of its top traders. Huang said he was concerned about FTX's lack of a board of directors but eventually invested anyway. During cross-examination he said Paradigm pressed Bankman-Fried on the board issue and was told he did not want investors as directors but did plan on having a board with experts.

# Shaqiri Before Facing Inter Miami: Preparation Unchanged, And Team Messi

Ahead of the Chicago Fire's Oct. 4, 2023 match with Inter Miami, Xherdan Shaqiri said the Fire's preparation would not change regardless of whether Lionel Messi played. Speaking in his pre-match availability on the Monday, and reported 90 minutes before kickoff, Shaqiri said: "The preparation is not going to change, we're going to prepare as normal as always. Everybody is excited to play against Inter Miami. If Messi is injured or not, personally I am not thinking too much about this. Of course Inter Miami is a different team when Messi is playing or not playing, you see that in the last games when Messi is in the team they are better, but we prepare like normal for every game." Shaqiri also framed the stakes of the match itself: "These are the best games to play all the time. As a player, you want these kinds of final games and to play for something. We put ourselves in this position, and we have a chance to do it, so now we have to perform."

Asked "Messi or Ronaldo?", Shaqiri confirmed he was Team Messi: "I'm always a big Messi admirer, if I have to choose now I will go with Messi. He won the WC which was the only thing he missed. So for sure Messi." He also said: "For me it's clear, Messi and Ronaldo are the best players in the world… these guys are among the best athletes in the history of sport, along with Michael Jordan and Tom Brady."

# Messi's Four-Game Injury Absence And His 35-Minute Return

Lionel Messi missed four straight Inter Miami games with injury before returning off the bench for 35 minutes against FC Cincinnati on Oct. 7, 2023. He was left out entirely for the Oct. 4 trip to the Chicago Fire: 35 minutes before kickoff the lineups showed him not part of the squad, with Josef Martinez up front as Leonardo Campana was out with a knock. An hour before kickoff, Michelle Kaufman of the Miami Herald reported Messi "did not arrive with the team" to Soldier Field — a strong indication rather than outright confirmation that he would not play. Two hours out, Sporting News noted Gerardo Martino had played his cards extremely close to his chest each week about Messi's injury: asked about Jordi Alba's return, Martino said a timeline was in place, but asked about Messi's he refused to acknowledge whether one existed, saying "I understand your desire to know the exact timelines, but if I had the exact timelines I would share them. I just don't have them." Sporting News judged his involvement unlikely given recent matches but thought he could be more ready over the weekend against FC Cincinnati. Meanwhile Chicago was still feeling Messi fever, with Messi shirt vendors outside Soldier Field and the Fire media team joking that they had "the GOAT in the building."

Against FC Cincinnati he was available. Two hours before kickoff, well-connected Argentine journalist Gaston Edul had reported the night before that Inter Miami were likely to have Messi back in some capacity — "the idea is for Leo Messi to get minutes when Inter Miami plays FC Cincinnati" — which sounded like bench availability, alongside reporting that Messi was battling "fatigue" and a "scar tissue issue." Lineups 45 minutes out confirmed him on the bench, with a photo of his jersey hanging in his locker taken as a good indication he would return. Thirty minutes out, his availability was called a welcome sight for a club whose backs were against the wall and which had to win to stay alive. He entered in the 55th minute, replacing Tomas Aviles in a very attacking change with around 35 minutes to save Inter Miami's season, alongside Jean Mota for David Ruiz. By the time he stepped on the pitch, Inter Miami's early dominance had come and gone; Messi played a part but was unable to fully change the tide of the game.

Five days later, ahead of Argentina's World Cup qualifier, Sporting News noted Messi had been dealing with fitness concerns for weeks and had missed significant time for his club, but was on the national team roster and expected to play a part. According to a report from Argentina he would not start but was likely to play much or all of the second half. With Inter Miami's playoff run officially over, Argentina could feel better about deploying him for a full 90 minutes despite his recent fitness issues, knowing his club season was nearly over and months of rest lay ahead; he had missed the previous match against Bolivia and four Inter Miami games after that, then returned for a half-hour in the club's final fixture before the international break.



---


# Against Messi's MLS MVP And Newcomer Nominations: The League Minutes Do Not Support Them

Sporting News argued on Oct. 7, 2023 that Lionel Messi's nominations for both 2023 MLS Newcomer of the Year and 2023 MLS MVP were unwarranted, attacking the premise that his impact had come in the league at all. Reported 75 minutes before kickoff, the nominations were called a blatant PR move that "laughable doesn't even begin to describe."

The grounds for the objection are the split between competitions: most of the damage Messi had done for Inter Miami came in Cup competitions, and in actual MLS competition he had one goal and two assists in 247 minutes of play. The conclusion drawn was that Messi had been fun, but that the league should not make a mockery of itself by actually giving him either honor.

# Argentina's Squad And Starting XI Against Paraguay, October 2023

Lionel Scaloni's Argentina started 4-3-3 against Paraguay on Oct. 12, 2023: E. Martinez (GK) — Molina, Romero, Otamendi, Tagliafico — De Paul, Mac Allister, E. Fernandez — J. Alvarez, L. Martinez, N. Gonzalez.

Scaloni had named a bloated 36-man squad for that month's matches against Paraguay and Peru, but Angel Di Maria, Paulo Dybala and Juan Foyth were forced to withdraw through injury, and Lisandro Martinez was also unavailable after undergoing another foot operation. Nicolas Tagliafico, who started both September matches, retained his starting spot even though Marcos Acuna was back with the team following an injury. Lionel Messi's club teammate Facundo Farias was included on the roster, but it would have been surprising had he seen the field.

The absences sharpened a generational shift. Messi was helping usher in a youth movement up front, with Julian Alvarez and Alejandro Garnacho considered the future of the forward line, and with Di Maria not fit for duty that month those two were even more in the spotlight against Paraguay and in the follow-up in Peru.



---


# The Cancelled China Tour And The NYCFC Noche d'Or Replacement

Inter Miami's planned two-match tour of China in early November 2023 was cancelled for "commercial and bureaucratic" reasons, and was replaced by a hastily arranged friendly against NYCFC at DRV PNK Stadium on November 10 dubbed the "Noche d'Or" or "Night of Gold" in honor of Lionel Messi's most recent Ballon d'Or.

The tour existed because of the club's elimination from 2023 MLS playoff contention, which left Messi facing nearly a full month off from competitive fixtures before taking the field for Argentina against Uruguay and Brazil in CONMEBOL World Cup qualifying. Likely with the sole intent of keeping Messi fit in that time off, and the added bonus of raking in significant cash, Inter Miami scheduled the China trip after their regular season concluded, expecting to visit two Chinese Super League sides — Qingdao Hainiu on November 5 and Chengdu Rongcheng three days later.

It was reported on October 30 that the planned tour was off, with Gaston Edu of TyC Sports reporting the visit had been cancelled due to commercial and bureaucratic reasons.



---


# The Newell's Old Boys Friendly And Messi's Rosario Roots

After their Asia trip, Inter Miami will host a friendly at DRV PNK Stadium against Newell's Old Boys — a team from Argentina that holds a special place in the hearts of both Lionel Messi and coach Gerardo Martino.

Both men are from the city of Rosario, where Newell's are based. Messi developed at the club's youth academy, and Martino played more than 400 senior games for the club before becoming head coach in 2012. Messi signed for Barcelona after spending six years as a youth player at Newell's, during which time he reportedly scored 234 goals.

"I am delighted to welcome my beloved Newell's to our home here in Miami. It will be a special match due to everything Newell's Old Boys means to me," said the Inter Miami coach. "It will also be a good opportunity to prepare for what will surely be an exciting season."

# Google's Parallel Antitrust Proceedings In Late 2023

As of mid-November 2023, Google was fighting antitrust on more than one front at once. The Epic Games case was not its only antitrust case in trial: Google had settled a separate antitrust lawsuit with dating site Match Group the week before November 13, and on November 6 it went to trial with Fortnite maker Epic Games, which hoped to prove that Google engages in anticompetitive behavior with regard to its Android app store, Google Play, and its commission structure. Separately, Google was involved in an antitrust lawsuit with the Department of Justice over its alleged search monopoly.

The Epic case had shed co-plaintiffs on its way to trial. Epic's lawsuit originally involved Match and several U.S. attorneys general, but Google reached a settlement with the attorneys general in October 2023 and with Match the week before November 6, so Epic fought the antitrust battle on its own. The lawsuit, held in the U.S. District Court in California's Northern District, would include testimony from a number of Google and Android execs, including CEO Sundar Pichai, and Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, as well as from Apple, Netflix and other Android developers. Epic, meanwhile, had lost its antitrust battle with Apple and was asking the Supreme Court to weigh in.



---


# Epic v. Google: What The Trial Is

Epic v. Google is the antitrust case in which Fortnite publisher Epic Games drags a tech giant into court alleging that its mobile app store is an illegal monopoly — and although Epic's parallel claims against Apple already got their day in court, the similar lawsuit against Google never did, which is why the case goes to trial on November 6th, a mere 1,180 days after Epic originally sued.

The déjà vu is the point of confusion the piece sets out to clear up: Epic already went to trial with Apple, resulting in a ruling where Apple mostly won, and its Llamacorn legal gambit failed to #FreeFortnite years ago. The distinction is that the Apple claims were heard and the Google ones were not.

An update dated December 15th, 2023 notes that the case is basically over by then.

# Patent Litigation

## Definition

In the corpus, patent litigation is the set of formal legal proceedings companies use to fight over patent rights — a patent holder's lawsuit in federal district court and, in parallel, a case before the US International Trade Commission (ITC) — with remedies that can include a monetary verdict or an ITC import ban, and with the accused party able to counter-sue or get the asserted patents ruled invalid or unenforceable.

## Context

The corpus documents two concrete disputes that illustrate the mechanics of patent litigation. Sonos sued Google and won a $32.5 million verdict over patent infringement, but a federal judge later threw out that win after finding Sonos' patents "unenforceable and invalid" — showing that a litigation win is not final until it survives post-trial and appellate review. Separately, Masimo sued Apple in the US District Court for the Central District of California in 2020 for trade-secret theft and infringement of 10 patents related to pulse-oximetry (SpO2) sensing technology, and when that case dragged on, Masimo additionally filed a parallel case with the US International Trade Commission (ITC) in 2021; Apple counter-sued Masimo the following year. The ITC route matters because, unlike a district court, it can issue an import ban that blocks the accused product (the Apple Watch Series 9 and Ultra 2) from entering the US market, and any such ban is then subject to a 60-day presidential review period during which the President or US Trade Representative may veto it.

## Key Characteristics

- **Dual venues** — patent disputes can run in federal district court (damages, injunctions) and, in parallel, before the ITC (import bans), as in the Apple-Masimo dispute where Masimo pursued both.
- **Invalidity/unenforceability as a defense** — a defendant can defeat an infringement verdict after the fact by getting the asserted patents ruled unenforceable and invalid, as happened to Sonos' win against Google.
- **Countersuits** — litigation can escalate into cross-litigation, as when Apple sued Masimo back, alleging Masimo's own watch cloned Apple's design.
- **ITC import-ban remedy plus presidential review** — an ITC finding of infringement can trigger a ban on importing the infringing product, but the ban is not final until a 60-day presidential/USTR review period lapses without a veto.
- **Long timelines** — the Apple-Masimo dispute originated roughly a decade before the resulting Apple Watch import ban took effect, illustrating how a single patent dispute can span years across multiple proceedings.

## Background (external)

Outside the corpus, patent litigation is generally described as the process of enforcing patent rights, and it is decided exclusively by federal (not state) courts in the US.

Remedies available in such litigation typically include a permanent or preliminary injunction ordering the infringing act to stop, and a damages award such as a reasonable royalty.

A defendant can raise defenses including that the patent has expired, that it holds a license, or that the patent is invalid or unenforceable, and disputes may also end in a settlement that includes a licensing agreement.

Source: Wikipedia, "Patent infringement," accessed 2026-09-02, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patent_infringement.

# Epic Games v. Google Goes To Trial On November 6, 2023

Epic Games, the maker of Fortnite, went to trial with Google on November 6, 2023, hoping to convince a jury that Google engages in anticompetitive behavior with regard to its Android app store, Google Play, and its commission structure. Match had settled its own antitrust lawsuit with Google the week before, but Epic's case proceeded.

This case differs slightly from Epic's battle with Apple on the same topic, because this time Epic cannot allege there is no other way to load apps onto Android devices, as it could with Apple: Android does allow for sideloading apps. Epic will suggest Google makes that process cumbersome, but the bulk of its arguments will center on what it believes are anticompetitive agreements between Google and device manufacturers and developers.

The precedent Epic's case relies on is a Microsoft case in which courts found Microsoft to have a monopoly over the operating system and to be abusing it, making it hard for users to download alternative browsers, like Netscape, on Windows devices. To make its case, Epic plans to bring claims under Sections 1 and 2 of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act, as well as California's anticompetitive laws, the Cartwright Act and the Unfair Competition Law. It will attempt to argue that Google restrains competition within two separate markets: the distribution of apps to Android users, and the market for payment processing solutions for content inside Android apps.



---


# Epic's Antitrust Claims Against Google Play

Epic's claim is that the Android operating system's Google Play Store constitutes an unlawful monopoly, and that Google is separately tying its Google Play payments platform to that store, keeping other potential app payment mechanisms from competing.

The grounds Epic offers are the frictions it says Google creates: Google makes it so difficult for developers and users to get around its Android app store, and that app store's standard fees, that it has created an illegal monopoly which unjustly enriches Google while artificially driving up app prices because other stores cannot compete. The warrant joining that to the legal claim is the competitive-harm chain — no viable rival stores means no fee discipline, which means the "Google Tax" is paid either by developers or passed along to consumers. Epic wants to break up Google's alleged monopoly on Android app stores and payment methods so developers are not stuck paying that tax.

Google's answer contests the warrant rather than the fees: it says Epic's demands would damage Android's ability to offer a secure user experience and to compete with Apple's iOS. Both sides agree the future of Google's app store could depend on this trial. Epic sued in 2020 after a fight over in-app purchase fees.

# The Reaction To Francesca Scorsese's Slang Video

Francesca Scorsese's TikTok of her father guessing popular slang terms had been viewed one million times by the time The Independent reported on it on 10 October 2023, days after its Thursday posting. Commenters were shocked both to see the legendary director on their screens and that he managed to guess many of the terms correctly.

"Can't believe we live in a world where I get to watch Martin Scorsese become familiar with the term sneaky link. Blessings," read one comment. "I cannot believe I exist in a timeline where I can watch Martin Scorsese film TikToks," said another. A third wrote: "I can't believe I'm watching one of the greatest filmmakers of our lifetime be quizzed by his daughter about teen slang lol," while someone else said: "Gonna describe sneaky links as personal picadillos from now on." It was not Scorsese's first appearance in one of his daughter's TikToks: in April 2021 Francesca went viral asking him to identify "feminine products" such as an eyelash curler, bobby pins, a hair donut and nipple pasties.



---


# Scorsese's Late Career Refutes Tarantino's Claim That Directors Do Not Get Better

Polygon's 2023-10-26 piece attacks the premise behind Quentin Tarantino's 2021 defense of his intention to make "just" 10 movies and retire: "I know film history, and from here on in, directors do not get better." The counter is that this view of both artistry and film is squarely at odds with Martin Scorsese's historic body of work.

The specific premise under attack is the claim of inevitable late-career decline. Scorsese had already made his 10th feature-length narrative film by 1986; he is now 80 years old, and his 27th, Killers of the Flower Moon, is a strong argument that directors are still capable of groundbreaking greatness late in life — and, in Scorsese's case, of continued exhilarating experimentation and discovery.

Polygon presses the point further: since the year 2000, Scorsese has curated a 23-year career within a career, and the quality and variety of his films have come not in spite of his age and experience but because of it. His movies have never been more relevant than in the past two decades, and with each subsequent release, as his career winds down, critical appreciation for him grows — Scorsese worship being the one remaining form of gerontocracy America is perfectly content with, and with good reason.

The mechanism the piece identifies is autonomy. This century Scorsese has zigged and zagged as always, but because he is following his own varied interests rather than moving from compromise to compromise as he once had to in order to keep working: an artist who spent the first 30 years of his career desperate for autonomy finally got it, and now takes full advantage — telling difficult stories, setting his own mega-budgets, and demanding every minute of run time he feels each picture demands. He has used that autonomy to revisit his work and revise the record, creating great new films and adding crucial addendums to past work while blazing new trails and adding layers to his style. Remarkably, the control that eluded him when he was younger has made his films more consistently collaborative and creative, more fluid and alive than he was often allowed to be before the 2000s, with the earned confidence of an artist who knows he will find something great in post. Polygon concludes that this should give Tarantino cause to reconsider, alongside any artist or critic who thinks the creative spark has an expiration date.



---


# Scorsese's Late-Career Genre Departures

Alongside the films that revisit his old themes, Polygon's 2023-10-26 piece identifies a set of radical departures in Scorsese's late era — films whose relation to his body of work is contrast rather than continuation.

2004's The Aviator is his most conventional movie to date, the most traditional, Oscar-baity, Old Hollywood biography he has made, and is best understood as a director-for-hire palate-cleanser after the odyssey of making the perpetually troubled Gangs of New York. 2010's Shutter Island is horror and suspense, an expert exercise in pure genre, part Hammer Films and part Alfred Hitchcock, and it also contains some of the most inventive, moving, and painterly visuals he has ever committed to film.

2011's Hugo is perhaps the hardest Scorsese film to imagine a younger Scorsese making: a 3D Robert Zemeckis-style family film that is also about the end of life and about immortality in art. He made it as a love letter to Georges Méliès, Harold Lloyd, and his own then-12-year-old daughter Francesca, and it seems designed to remind fathers of all the times they tried to introduce their kids to their favorite old films. Hugo is explicitly about Scorsese's legendary cinephilia in a way his earlier films are not, and it is sentimental in a way his work has never been before or since.



---


# Martin Scorsese's Internet-Slang TikTok Quiz

Martin Scorsese put his knowledge of internet slang to the test in a TikTok challenge posted by his daughter, Francesca Scorsese, on Thursday 5 October 2023. The father-daughter duo appeared on camera together while Francesca explained the format to the 80-year-old director: "I'm going to ask you to guess what specific slang terms mean."

Scorsese restated the rules in his own words, in what The Independent calls classic style: "You're going to tell me the slang word and I have to give you what I think it means."



---


# Scorsese's 21st-Century Filmography

In the 21st century alone, Martin Scorsese has made nine feature-length narrative films: Gangs of New York, The Aviator, The Departed, Shutter Island, Hugo, The Wolf of Wall Street, Silence, The Irishman, and Killers of the Flower Moon. Polygon set this out on 2023-10-26.

Polygon still identifies his stretch from 1976's Taxi Driver through 1990's Goodfellas as his peak run, the films that defined his style and his perspective.

But its claim about the later work is that decades from now, the nine features made since 2000 will not be looked back on as half-baked, indulgent afterthoughts from a diminished artist who lost his fastball — a fate some great auteurs suffer in old age. Instead it is a fertile, vital body of work, virtuosic in entirely new ways, and as important in contextualizing his greatness as all the incredible work that preceded it.



---


# Scorsese and Leonardo DiCaprio's Collaboration

The defining relationship of Scorsese's 21st-century career is his partnership with Leonardo DiCaprio, which began with 2002's Gangs of New York — itself the final product of an interesting but ultimately flawed compromise between Scorsese and producer Harvey Weinstein. Polygon described the partnership on 2023-10-26.

Polygon models it as a symbiotic exchange that elevated both men: the industry outsider who needed a safe box-office bet to finally get his epic, expensive dream projects financed, and the teen heartthrob who needed an auteur with arthouse gravitas to take him seriously so the industry would.

To date the project has been wildly successful, producing six films over 21 years, and the first five — Gangs of New York, The Aviator, The Departed, Shutter Island, and The Wolf of Wall Street — are Scorsese's top five highest-grossing films, with the box office for Killers incoming.

The relationship extends beyond casting. Over the years the team-up has served as a true creative marriage, and the two men now share a manager in Rick Yorn, the man responsible for discovering DiCaprio. Polygon presents this as evidence DiCaprio has not "just" been a muse and a face on the posters: he has had a say in deciding which projects Scorsese takes on and has made significant decisions shaping Scorsese's stories — Scorsese entirely reimagined Killers of the Flower Moon after DiCaprio offered notes on an early draft of the script, including shifting focus to a different main character and moving DiCaprio into that role.



---


# Mehmet Oz's TikTok Campaign

Mehmet Oz, one of the few Republican candidates on TikTok, had the advantage of already having a large social media following when he announced his candidacy, thanks to his popularity as Dr. Oz. TechCrunch reported on 2023-10-02 that this head start did not translate into effective platform-native campaigning.

His TikTok presence consisted of reformatted TV ads, rants attacking his opponent, now-Senator Fetterman, and unrelatable videos that inadvertently portrayed him as wealthy and out of touch.

Sorcerers are the magic-slinging wizards of Sanctuary in Diablo 4, as Polygon describes them in its 2023-10-18 guide to the best Sorcerer builds and skills.

Because each element brings its own unique effect, it can be easy to get overwhelmed when trying to design a Sorcerer build — which is the reason Polygon gathered and simplified the best Sorcerer builds for season 2, linking out to more detailed versions of those builds and to their original creators for readers who need more on item affixes or other complex ideas.

# The Barbarian Class in Diablo 4

Barbarians are a relatively simple class in Diablo 4 — they smash stuff — but, as Polygon notes in its 2023-10-19 guide, Diablo 4 is underscored by math so complex that even the simple act of smashing stuff becomes a dizzying equation.

Barbarians are big, muscular, and powerful. They excel at using Bleed to kill their enemies over time, and their unique weapon-swapping system means they get to have more Legendary powers at their disposal than any other class.

Polygon's guide gathers and simplifies the best Barbarian builds for season 2, linking out to the more detailed versions of those builds and to their original creators for readers who need more on item affixes or other complex ideas.

# Diablo 4 Season of Blood Release Date

All of Diablo 4's season 2 changes, as well as the content for Season of Blood, come to the game on Oct. 17 — just a few weeks before fans expect Blizzard to announce Diablo 4's first expansion at BlizzCon 2023. Polygon reported this on 2023-10-04.

Game director Joe Shely and associate game director Joe Piepiora told Polygon the focus on quality-of-life upgrades was largely due to season 2 being the first season where they and the rest of the Diablo 4 team could really listen to feedback.

The reason is timing: because Season of the Malignant launched just over a month after the release of Diablo 4, that season's content was largely finished before players had really gotten to dive into the action-RPG. With season 2, Blizzard has been able to react more to player feedback and finally create some sweeping, specific changes that players had been requesting.
