# Diablo 4 Season 2 Vampiric Powers

Season 2 of Diablo 4 adds Vampiric Powers, which allow players to slot five additional abilities into their character to gain new effects.

There are 22 total Vampiric Powers.

Each is class agnostic, meaning no power is unique to any one class. Polygon states this identically in both its Sorcerer build guide of 2023-10-18 and its Barbarian build guide of 2023-10-19.



---


# Diablo 4 Barbarian Leveling Build

This Barbarian leveling build, based on Lexyu's Barbarian leveling guide at IcyVeins and published by Polygon on 2023-10-19, is purely for leveling — allocating your 58 skill points between levels 1 and 50. As with most Barbarian leveling guides it uses Hammer of the Ancients as the primary skill, since it deals massive damage while remaining very cheap to cast, plus Frenzy, Death Blow, Rallying Cry, Leap, and Wrath of the Berserker. Readers wanting more on item affixes or other Legendary powers are pointed to the original IcyVeins guide.

Skills must be purchased in a specific order, because some require a number of allocated points in the tree to unlock, so new skills must be unlocked before existing ones are enhanced. The order is: Frenzy / Enhanced Frenzy; Hammer of the Ancients / Enhanced Hammer of the Ancients / Furious Hammer of the Ancients; Combat Frenzy; Rallying Cry / Enhanced Rallying Cry / Tactical Rallying Cry; Hammer of the Ancients (ranks 2-3); Leap / Enhanced Leap / Power Leap; Hammer of the Ancients (ranks 4-5); Death Blow / Enhanced Death Blow / Warrior's Death Blow / Death Blow (rank 2-5); Wrath of the Berserker / Prime Wrath of the Berserker / Supreme Wrath of the Berserker; Pit Fighter (ranks 1-3); Tempered Fury; Furious Impulse (ranks 1-3); Walking Arsenal; Hamstring; No Mercy; Expose Vulnerability (ranks 1-3); No Mercy (ranks 2-3); Swiftness (ranks 1-3); Thick Skin (ranks 1-3); Counteroffensive (ranks 1-3); Defensive Stance (ranks 1-3); Slaying Strike (ranks 1-3); Aggressive Resistance; and Prolific Fury.

Once the Weapon Expertise system unlocks, place the two-handed sword in your Technique slot, which causes all of your Hammer of the Ancients damage to make enemies Bleed.

At the start of a new character, complete three dungeons first to collect their Aspects, then place them on a piece of gear, ideally jewelry when possible — replacing these Legendaries with new versions using the imprint system every few levels. They are: Aspect of Ancestral Force from the Sunken Ruins dungeon in Scosglen, which makes Hammer of the Ancients quake outwards, dealing X% of its damage to enemies; Aspect of the Expectant from the Underroot dungeon in Scosglen, where attacking enemies with a Basic Skill increases the damage of your next Core Skill cast by X% up to X%; and Edgemaster's Aspect from the Oldstones dungeon in Scosglen, where skills deal X% increased damage based on Primary Resource when cast, with the maximum benefit at full Primary Resource.



---


# Diablo 4 Sorcerer Element Build Archetypes

Sorcerers are Diablo 4's pure caster class and use elemental magic to differentiate themselves from the spells of the Druid and Necromancer. The class has six Key Passives but only three elements — Lightning, Fire, and Ice — and those elements are what a build is based around, as Polygon set out on 2023-10-18.

Each element maps to a role and to a choice between two Key Passives. Lightning builds use Lightning skills to deal with large groups of enemies at once, ending up with either the Overflowing Energy Key Passive or the Vyr's Mastery Key Passive depending on whether you are in melee range. Ice builds specialize in slowing enemies down to make their attacks easier to survive, taking either the Avalanche Key Passive or the Shatter Key Passive depending on how much the build relies on crowd control. Fire builds are all about big explosions and burning enemies, typically using the Combustion Key Passive for burning enemies or the Esu's Ferocity Key Passive for chunky critical strikes.

The range over which this holds includes a survivability constraint. When making your own Sorcerer build you will likely stick to one element for your main damage sources, but Polygon says that is not the most important thing to remember: Sorcerers die very, very easily in Diablo 4 and have the weakest defensive stats by far, even though they can deal a massive amount of damage when built correctly. To avoid ending up dead more often than not, invest heavily in defensive skills while making your way toward one of the six Key Passives.



---


# Diablo 4 Season 2 Experience and Leveling Changes

One of the most notable changes in Diablo 4's second season update is an increase in experience gains: Blizzard claims players will be able to reach the level cap of 100 about 40% faster than in Season of the Malignant, which had already increased experience gains compared with Diablo 4's launch. Polygon reported this on 2023-10-04.

The process should also be much smoother, as monsters will now match player levels between 55 and 75.

Game director Joe Shely told the press panel that last season players set a goal for themselves — get to level 100 — but many found they were never able to hit that milestone because XP gains were so slow. The change should allow more players to reach the level cap each season, letting them play with a truly maxed-out build.



---


# Season of Blood's Real Draw Is Quality of Life, Not Vampire Powers

Polygon's claim, published 2023-10-04, is that although Diablo 4's Season of Blood brings some cool new vampire powers into the fold, the real star of the second season is its sweeping quality-of-life changes.

The grounds are what those changes do for ordinary play: players will now have an easier time leveling up, gaining quality loot, and just navigating the open world of Sanctuary.

The warrant is that these improvements touch the activities every player performs constantly, which is why they outweigh a headline feature. The reporting basis is a roundtable interview game director Joe Shely and associate game director Joe Piepiora gave to Polygon and other outlets ahead of Blizzard's Oct. 4 livestream, in which they gave additional context on Nightmare Dungeon changes, Renown, and more.

qid: Does the TechCrunch article suggest a different type of investigation involving Influenceable compared to the Sporting News article's mention of the University of Michigan's involvement in an investigation related to document provision?
context:
# The NCAA Investigation Into Michigan's Scouting Scheme

The NCAA is investigating Michigan's football program amid allegations that the Wolverines used illegal in-person scouting and the recording of signals to steal signs this season, as reported by The New York Times on 3 November 2023.

The conference's involvement is dated. Ahead of the Michigan-Michigan State game on 21 October, the Big Ten approached MSU and said it was made aware of "credible evidence" regarding the sign-stealing allegations, and said it would monitor the NCAA's investigation into Michigan.

The timing problem is spelled out. The NCAA investigation is ongoing, a process that typically moves slowly, which makes it difficult to imagine it will reach a resolution by the time the postseason begins. The Big Ten does have the ability to act under its sportsmanship policy, but that doesn't mean it would want to act quickly or decisively before the NCAA completes its entire investigation and allows Michigan a chance to respond to its findings.



---


# Michigan's Counterclaim That Rivals Shared Its Signs

Michigan's counter to the sign-stealing case is that it is hardly alone in trying to decipher opponents' signals, and it has shared evidence with the Big Ten and the NCAA showing that staff members at Ohio State, Purdue and Rutgers exchanged intelligence on the Wolverines' signals before the previous year's Michigan-Purdue Big Ten Championship Game. The Athletic reported that documents breaking down Michigan's signals for numerous plays were compiled by Purdue staffers ahead of that game based on information provided by Ohio State and Rutgers football personnel. The person who supplied the documents told The Athletic that he spent 10 to 12 hours per week trying to decode signals from game video, and that sharing decoded signals with other schools is a common practice.

The counterclaim does not dispose of the charge, because it attacks the wrong premise. The primary difference, per the same reporting, is that Michigan is accused of using in-person scouting — prohibited under NCAA rules for nearly 30 years — to acquire its information, rather than decoding from video.

Ohio State denied the allegation outright. Asked about the claim that Ohio State had given information about Michigan's signs to Purdue before the 2022 Big Ten championship game, coach Ryan Day said, per the Columbus Dispatch: "I can tell you this right now that nobody here did any of that. We went through and made sure we asked all the questions and got our compliance people involved. None of that came back at all. I can answer very strongly that that did not happen." Separately, Yahoo Sports reported that Day and his family have no connection to the Big Ten and NCAA investigations into Michigan; a weekend report had suggested Day may have had some involvement in the probe into the Buckeyes' arch-rivals, but the NCAA told the Big Ten there are no ties that it knows of between the Ohio State coach and the investigation.



---


# Fotiadis Testimony And Johansson's Lobbying Contacts At The LIBE Hearing

At the LIBE committee hearing the journalist Apostolis Fotiadis testified that documents he and his colleagues obtained showed email threads granting a CSAM-scanning "key stakeholder" privileged access inside Johansson's department, and, under pressure from MEPs, the commissioner read out a list of her meetings with technology companies and child safety organizations. TechCrunch reported the session on 25 October 2023.

Fotiadis, one of the journalists involved in the investigation the committee was examining, had also been invited by the committee to participate in the exchange of views, and he took the opportunity to defend their reporting from direct public attacks by Johansson. In a blog post ahead of the hearing — which deploys a crisis-PR-esque headline claim of "setting the record straight" — she criticized the article as "a series of insinuations looking for a home", claiming it paired an outline of "a selection of meetings I had, of events I attended, or conferences I addressed" with "a conspiratorial tone" in an attempt "to create the impression of financial influence where there is none".

Asked by the LIBE committee about the accusation that the journalists had, essentially, been spreading disinformation — and specifically whether he believed Johansson and the Commission's response to it amounted to a restriction on media freedom — Fotiadis responded by saying he did not think that was the case. He went on to express surprise at how the Commission had reacted to the scrutiny, and at its instinct to deploy "spin-doctor" tactics to try to discredit the article rather than engaging with the substance of the concerns being raised. The Commission risks straying close to making attacks on journalists by using such tactics, Fotiadis warned, adding: "You cannot just dismiss everything by calling fake news" — before also noting that Johansson's office had declined multiple interview requests ahead of publication of the article.

On the substance of the reporting, Fotiadis said documents obtained by the journalists included email threads between Commission officials in Johansson's department, DG-Home, and a "key stakeholder" advocating for the use of technology for CSAM-scanning, which indicated what he described as "privileged access" that "speaks directly to cooperation" and goes "way beyond" mere consultation or exchange of views on the proposal.

He gave the committee the shape of that access. "It's an official chain discussing invitation, how the stakeholder would be able to allocate experts that would speak in workshops — first attended by representatives of the Member States, and then afterwards actually by ministers in the Council in a meeting chaired by commissioner Johansson. So when we say facilitate, it's obvious that the EU officials discuss what kind of experts will be available from this particular stakeholder to attend these meetings and to present the point of view, which seems to be a privileged access," he explained. "Also in the same email thread there's mention of EU officials being allocated to specifically attend the cooperation between the stakeholder and DG-Home on the proposal, which to our understanding is something that goes way beyond the level of consultations or exchange of views or exchange of opinions on the proposal and speaks directly to cooperation."

The committee then pressed Johansson about her contacts with companies and other lobbyists during the drafting of the CSAM proposal, with MEPs saying they wanted clear answers to the allegations of commercial interest and heavy lobbying when the Commission was setting up and drafting the proposal. In the event MEPs got some bare bones detail. Asked for a list of these contacts, the commissioner responded that she had met with Google six times; Microsoft, Meta and TikTok three times each; twice with Twitter (X); and once apiece with Apple and Amazon. She also said she had met with the child safety organizations Thorn (twice) and Brave Movement (twice), and with Tech Alliance and ICANN once apiece.

In wider responses related to concerns about how much commercial interest had influenced the Commission, Johansson highlighted her decision for the CSAM-scanning proposal to be "technology neutral" — meaning the draft regulation does not support any specific tech solution — with the suggestion being that EU lawmakers had resisted lobbying by companies for a law that would explicitly favor their existing tech tools.



---


# Michigan's Ten-Page Letter To The Big Ten

Michigan's 10-page letter to the Big Ten attacked the premise that the conference could properly discipline Harbaugh or the university before the NCAA investigation was complete. Posted in full on X by Yahoo Sports' Dan Wetzel on Nov. 9, 2023, the letter argued that the Big Ten would be acting too hastily in suspending Harbaugh or levying any punishment before a full NCAA investigation had concluded, and warned commissioner Tony Petitti against "premature" disciplinary action.

The due-process objection was procedural. Michigan said it had not had the chance to review all the evidence and respond, which oversteps the due process allowed to the university, and that Petitti should not have unilateral authority to punish violations without first a completed investigation and then a response from the Compliance and Reinstatement Committee, the body that would recommend penalties for rules violations.

The evidentiary objection attacked the factual basis. Michigan said it was aware of nothing supporting a claim that athletics personnel at Michigan committed the alleged violations, and that the rule on electronic recordings of games is limited to field equipment used by the institution for the game it is currently playing. It said it had not seen much evidence but had only heard a summary of second- and third-hand information.

The materiality objection attacked the significance of any conduct that did occur. Given the use of sign decoding by other universities, the letter said, there was little reason to believe Stalions' efforts proved meaningful, and it pointed to the teams' average margin of victory since Stalions was suspended. The information obtained was "at most a reflection of information that teams can and easily do obtain through public and permissible sources," making it "highly dubious" that Stalions' observations would have a "material effect on the integrity of the competition." The letter further alleged that in-person scouting and sign-stealing are commonplace across the NCAA — "The conference should act cautiously when setting precedent given the reality that in-person scouting, collusion among opponents, and other questionable practices may well be far more prevalent than believed" — and, per Yahoo Sports, enclosed "two attached documents of Michigan's offensive and defensive signs allegedly stolen and shared by other Big Ten teams."

Michigan submitted this response to the Big Ten's notice of discipline as a step toward resolution. ESPN reported on Wednesday that no conference ruling was expected until Thursday because the Big Ten planned to "take time to absorb" what Michigan had to say, and ESPN's Adam Rittenberg reported on Nov. 8, 2023 that the school had sent its response and that Petitti now had to decide how to proceed with potential discipline.

qid: Between the TechCrunch report on Sam Bankman-Fried's trial and the subsequent TechCrunch report on the allegations against him, was there a change in the portrayal of his actions related to the FTX situation?
context:
# FTX's Bankruptcy And Leadership

The man who represented FTX before Congress after its failure told lawmakers the exchange had effectively no internal governance at all, and the prosecutor bringing the case called Bankman-Fried's alleged crimes one of the biggest financial frauds in American history. TechCrunch reported both on 2023-10-01.

Ray represented the company during a House Financial Services Committee hearing regarding FTX. Asked whether the firm had significant risk management systems, Ray said at the time that "there were virtually no internal controls and no separateness whatsoever," and added that he did not "trust a single piece of paper" in the exchange's organization. Separately, in a press conference, U.S. Attorney Damian Williams called Bankman-Fried's alleged crimes "one of the biggest financial frauds in American history."



---


# The FTX Trial's Stakes For The Wider Crypto Industry

The Verge argued that the trial of Sam Bankman-Fried is likely to be more consequential than just whether the man himself is found guilty: depending on what evidence is introduced, it could be rough for the entire crypto industry.

The grounds are the unpredictability of what a trial surfaces, voiced by Yesha Yadav, a law professor at Vanderbilt University: "How much damage can this trial do to the already beaten-down reputation of the industry at this point? This trial is going to be an excruciating moment for the industry because no one knows what kind of evidence might come out." The warrant joining that uncertainty to industry-wide stakes is that the industry's reputation is already beaten down, so evidence introduced against one exchange's founder lands on the whole sector rather than on him alone.



---


# Day Two Of The Bankman-Fried Trial: Jury Selection And The Courtroom Audience

On the second day of Sam Bankman-Fried's fraud trial, the jury was selected on Wednesday morning, after which lawyers for the government and then for Bankman-Fried delivered opening statements that told two very different stories of the former FTX CEO's sudden rise and almost instantaneous fall. The central question framed by the proceedings was who Bankman-Fried, the former CEO of crypto exchange FTX, really is: a liar and a fraud, or someone who acted in good faith and, like many a startup founder, flew too close to the sun. That answer, the account notes, ultimately lies with the jury.

The day featured pointed allegations, a friend from MIT, and an audience replete with big names, including Bankman-Fried's professorial parents and Damian Williams, the U.S. attorney for the Southern District of New York. Bankman-Fried himself spent most of the day in court staring into a laptop while seated between his two attorneys. The prosecution's account of his alleged crimes was described as featuring a study in contrasts.



---


# Sam Bankman-Fried

Sam Bankman-Fried is the former CEO of the bankrupt crypto exchange FTX, whose highly anticipated criminal trial started on the Tuesday before TechCrunch's 2023-10-01 report, to determine whether he is guilty of seven counts of fraud and conspiracy. As one former federal prosecutor put it: "The odds seem to be stacked against him at this point."

He was 31 years old and co-founded FTX in 2019; within a few years the once third-largest crypto exchange's valuation hit $32 billion at its peak, and the company is now trying to claw back any funds to distribute to creditors. Before the fall he was even compared to Warren Buffet, and many called him the white horse of crypto — a description TechCrunch notes it never applied to him.

Bankman-Fried, however, maintained his innocence. At The New York Times' DealBook Summit he appeared virtually from the Bahamas and said, "I didn't ever try to commit fraud on anyone; I was shocked by what happened this month"; in a published DM exchange with a Vox reporter he said he regretted filing for bankruptcy and thought that "regulators make everything worse." In January he pleaded not guilty to all counts, which include wire fraud, conspiracy to commit money laundering and conspiracy to misuse customer funds. He could face up to 115 years in jail if convicted on all charges.

TechCrunch's 2023-10-02 summary of his standing on the eve of trial: SBF has been denied bail; his name is mud (or much worse) among those who have lost money in Alameda or FTX; and those who might not have had positions in these still blame him for other crypto woes, because he set off a ripple effect.



---


# FTX Fraud Charges And The SEC's Allegation

Sam Bankman-Fried, the founder of the failed cryptocurrency exchange FTX, faced seven counts of wire fraud and conspiracy — specifically, two counts of wire fraud and five conspiracy charges — and the Securities and Exchange Commission alleged that FTX was a fraud "from the start," with a "multi-billion-dollar deficiency caused by his own misappropriation of customer funds." The Verge repeated this framing at the head of each of its trial dispatches through October 2023, and in its October 28th, 2023 write-up reported that Bankman-Fried had been found guilty on seven counts including charges of wire fraud.

The boundary of the concept is the mix of charge types: the indictment paired substantive wire fraud counts with conspiracy counts rather than resting on a single offence, and the SEC's civil allegation about the exchange's origins ran alongside the criminal case rather than being part of it. The Verge's reporter, writing as the prosecution's case neared its end on October 26th, 2023, added an impression of the people the charges swept in: all the co-conspirators seemed oddly younger than their years, as though they had got stuck in the "math camp forever" environment Bankman-Fried created for them and simply failed to grow up.



---


# FTX's Inner Circle: Family And Friends Implicated

The Verge's October 26th, 2023 account of the trial catalogued how everyone who loved Bankman-Fried most in the world was caught up in the case. Adam Yedidia, his college roommate, testified with immunity because he was concerned he may have unknowingly worked on code that contributed to the fraud; "I love you Sam," he had texted at one point, "I'm not going anywhere" — that was before he realized FTX had stolen customer funds, at which point he resigned. Nishad Singh, a longtime family friend, copped to what sounded an awful lot like classic embezzlement, saying he had backdated transactions on FTX to help create doctored balance sheets to show to investors, and pleaded guilty to six charges including wire fraud, money laundering, and conspiracy counts around his political donations. Caroline Ellison, Bankman-Fried's ex-girlfriend, told the court about the seven phony balance sheets she had created and was clear that Alameda took customer funds, that Bankman-Fried knew about it, and that he even invested them against her advice.

His family was drawn in too. Joe Bankman, his father, is among the people included in the "small group chat," the Signal group where the FTX inner circle strategized during the exchange's last days. Barbara Fried's political action committee, Mind the Gap, is among the entities that received FTX customer money as political donations; Fried and Bankman lived together in a Bahamas house purchased for them using FTX investor funds, according to a financial expert called by the prosecution, and in a lawsuit filed by FTX's bankruptcy estate the two are alleged to have been given $10 million of FTX customer funds. Gabe Bankman-Fried's nonprofit, Guarding Against Pandemics, got millions from FTX; he was also in a Signal group chat, Donations Processing, that Singh says was used to coordinate the transfer of FTX and Alameda money to various political causes, and in that chat he can be seen recommending that some donations be made "in the dark" to avoid public relations headaches. Singh also said Gabe had an assistant fly to the Bahamas with a stack of blank checks for Singh to sign.

The consequences outlast the trial. Wang, Singh, and Ellison are now felons; even if they never do time — and they may very well be imprisoned or subjected to house arrest — their lives are irrevocably changed, not least by whatever restitution requirements they face, they are barred from taking certain kinds of jobs, and there is the publicity. Bankman, Fried, and Gabe Bankman-Fried's reputations are tarnished, and in the political arenas where they once operated they are suddenly undesirable. Beyond the courtroom, everyone who had money trapped on the exchange when it collapsed — as a result of Alameda purloining customers' funds — had their lives altered: even if they are made whole by the bankruptcy proceedings, that is still money they should have had access to at any time, which may mean houses that were not purchased, medical procedures left undone, and life savings lost. The reporter's summary: it is a Greek tragedy, precipitated by one man's character flaw, the arrogance of Sam Bankman-Fried.

# Anthropic's Founding By Former OpenAI Researchers

Dario Amodei, a researcher with ties to the effective altruist community, had been on hand at the Rosewood hotel when OpenAI was born, and was leading the lab's efforts to build a neural network called a large language model that could learn from enormous amounts of digital text: by analysing countless Wikipedia articles, digital books and message boards it could generate text on its own, and it also had the unfortunate habit of making things up. It was called GPT-3 and was released in the summer of 2020, and researchers inside OpenAI, Google and other companies thought this rapidly improving technology could be a path to artificial general intelligence. Amodei was unhappy about the Microsoft deal because he thought it was taking OpenAI in a really commercial direction, and he and other researchers went to the board to try to push Altman out, according to five people familiar with the matter; after they failed, they left, worrying, like DeepMind's founders before them, that their new corporate overlords would favour commercial interests over safety.

In 2021 the group of about 15 engineers and scientists created a new lab called Anthropic, with the plan of building AI the way the effective altruists thought it should be done, with very tight controls. Anthropic disputes the account of the board approach: "There was no attempt to remove Sam Altman from OpenAI by the co-founders of Anthropic," said an Anthropic spokesperson, Sally Aldous. "The co-founders themselves came to the conclusion that they wished to depart OpenAI to start their own company, made this known to OpenAI's leadership, and over several weeks negotiated an exit on mutually agreeable terms." Anthropic accepted a $US4 billion investment from Amazon and another $US2 billion from Google two years later. After OpenAI received another $US2 billion from Microsoft, Altman and another senior executive, Greg Brockman, visited Bill Gates at his sprawling mansion on the shores of Lake Washington, outside Seattle; the Microsoft founder was no longer involved in the company day to day but kept in regular touch with its executives.



---


# ChatGPT Overview And Significance

ChatGPT is OpenAI's text-generating AI chatbot, and it has taken the world by storm: what started as a tool to hyper-charge productivity through writing essays and code from short text prompts has evolved into a behemoth used by more than 92% of Fortune 500 companies for far more wide-ranging needs.

That growth propelled OpenAI itself into becoming one of the most-hyped companies in recent memory, even though CEO and co-founder Sam Altman's firing and swift return raised concerns about the company's direction and opened the door for competitors. The fallout was still settling, but it might empower competitors such as Meta and its LLaMA family of large language models, or help other AI startups get attention and funding as the industry watched OpenAI implode and put itself back together. Whatever the nefarious side of ChatGPT, it was clear that AI tools were not going away anytime soon: since its initial launch nearly a year earlier, ChatGPT had hit 100 million weekly active users, and OpenAI was investing heavily in it.

The capability boundary at the time was defined by model access and modality. GPT-4, which can write more naturally and fluently than previous models, remained largely exclusive to paying ChatGPT users, although it could be accessed for free through Microsoft's Bing Chat in the Microsoft Edge, Google Chrome and Safari web browsers. Beyond GPT-4 and the OpenAI DevDay announcements, OpenAI had recently connected ChatGPT to the internet for all users, and with the integration of DALL-E 3, users could generate both text and images right inside ChatGPT.



---


# ChatGPT Adoption Milestones And Usage Statistics

Roughly a year after its release, ChatGPT had 100 million weekly active users, and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman also revealed that over two million developers use the platform, including more than 92% of Fortune 500 companies.

Two other markers frame that scale. OpenAI hit the one-year anniversary of ChatGPT: what began as a "low-key research preview" evolved into a powerhouse that changed the AI industry forever, and Altman looked back on the night before its launch in a post on X on November 30, 2023 — "a year ago tonight we were probably just sitting around the office putting the finishing touches on chatgpt before the next morning's launch. what a year it's been…" Meanwhile neither Apple nor Google chose an AI app as its app of the year for 2023, despite the success of ChatGPT's mobile app, which became the fastest-growing consumer application in history before that record was broken by Meta's Threads.

Adoption among the general public is far thinner than the headline numbers suggest. Ongoing polling by Pew Research shows that although ChatGPT is gaining mindshare, only about 18% of Americans have ever actually used it — suggesting the language model is not quite as popular or threatening as some would have you think.



---


# The OpenAI Board Ousts Sam Altman, November 2023

As reported on November 18, 2023, the OpenAI board had ejected billionaire and AI evangelist Sam Altman from his CEO role after an apparent vote of no confidence. The board's exact wording in a release issued that afternoon: Altman's "departure follows a deliberative review process by the board, which concluded that he was not consistently candid in his communications with the board, hindering its ability to exercise its responsibilities."

What followed was a whirlwind four days for OpenAI, the generative AI poster child behind the smash hit ChatGPT. The board ousted CEO and co-founder Altman and demoted president and co-founder Greg Brockman, who subsequently resigned, paving the way for what looked like a mutiny by staff insisting the founders be reinstated post-haste. By the time TechCrunch wrote again on November 21, 2023, Microsoft had already hired Altman and Brockman to head up a new internal AI unit — though, as things transpired, nothing had actually been signed yet, with rumors suggesting the ousted leaders might actually return to OpenAI after all, in some capacity at least.

TechCrunch cautioned on November 18 that the full truth would not be known for a long time, as the characters in the drama are likely to be NDA'ed up. Per various whispers and leaks, an all-hands meeting about the situation that afternoon did not produce any revelations beyond banal reassurances that the company is fine and they will get a fresh CEO soon.



---


# OpenAI's AI Chip Ambitions

The company has suggested that it might be entering the AI chip market at some point in the future, in an effort to shore up the speed and performance of its API services.

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman had previously pointed to industry-wide GPU shortages for the service's spotty performance, and producing its own processors might mitigate those supply issues while potentially lowering the current four-cent-per-query cost of operating the chatbot to something more manageable.



---


# AlphaGo As Evidence For AI Risk Concerns

Rationalists, effective altruists and others who worried about the risks of AI claimed the computer's win at Go validated their fears. The evidence cited is the pace of progress rather than the game itself: "This is another indication that AI is progressing faster than even many experts anticipated," wrote Victoria Krakovna, who would soon join DeepMind as an "AI safety" researcher, in a blog post.

The consequences inside DeepMind followed the same worry. Its founders were increasingly concerned about what Google would do with their inventions and in 2017 tried to break away from the company; Google responded by increasing the salaries and stock award packages of the DeepMind founders and their staff, and they stayed put. The ethics board never had a second meeting.



---


# Sam Altman's Rise As The Face Of Generative AI

In the year since Altman catapulted ChatGPT to global fame, he became Silicon Valley's sought-after voice on the promise and potential dangers of artificial intelligence, and his sudden and mostly unexplained exit brought uncertainty to the industry's future. He helped start OpenAI as a nonprofit research laboratory in 2015, but it was ChatGPT's explosion into public consciousness that thrust him into the spotlight as a face of generative AI — technology that can produce novel imagery, passages of text and other media. On a world tour in 2023 he was mobbed by a crowd of adoring fans at an event in London.

He has sat with multiple heads of state to discuss AI's potential and perils. On Thursday, 2023-11-16, he took part in a CEO summit at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation conference in San Francisco, where OpenAI is based. At OpenAI's first developer conference the week before, Altman was the main speaker, showcasing a vision for a future of AI agents that could help people with a variety of tasks; days later he announced the company would have to pause new subscriptions to its premium version of ChatGPT because it had exceeded capacity.

qid: What country, featured in articles from both 'Fortune' and 'Business Today | Latest Stock Market And Economy News India', has recently been involved in issuing a relocation warning in Gaza, controlling the entry of essential supplies there, and experienced a surprise attack due to an intelligence failure?
context:
# Hamas October 7 2023 Surprise Attack on Israel

On 7 October 2023, Hamas carried out what Business Today described as the biggest coordinated attack in Israel, capturing some territory in southern Israel and taking control of some military bases and soldiers.

The reaction the report documents was directed at Israel's famed intelligence agency, Mossad, which is known for its intelligence-gathering capability. For some observers, the belief that Mossad was among the best in the spying world was shattered that day. The report is explicit that it was not the fact of an attack that surprised people, but the scale at which Hamas operated.



---


# Israel-Hamas War Context, October 2023

As of TechCrunch's 2023-10-14 report, Israel is retaliating militarily against the attacks on its people, on its soil, and the hostages subsequently taken by Hamas — the ruling organization in Gaza that kidnapped at least 150 people and took them into Gaza during brutal attacks on Israel last weekend that killed 1,300 people. That strategy has seen Israel pummeling the "Gaza Strip" with bombs to eradicate it of Hamas and to get its hostages back, and over 1,500 people in Palestine so far have been killed as a result.

The tech industry in Israel — the country's biggest export and its biggest single contributor to GDP — is also taking a big knock, but inevitably the impact on the smaller and more fragile ecosystem in Gaza has been significantly more serious, and the physical, economic and societal destruction resulting from that leaves any future for the tech industry there in doubt: quite simply, there is no escaping the consequences of the war for anyone, let alone tech workers. Israel has now amassed soldiers near the north of Gaza ahead of an expected ground offensive into the densely populated enclave, and about 1.1 million people living in northern areas have been told to leave in the next day. The UN has warned of "devastating humanitarian consequences" from these latest moves, and a total blockade on the territory is being enforced with fuel, food and water running out; Israel says it won't lift the restrictions unless Hamas frees all hostages. TechCrunch notes the piece was later edited to include relevant information about the attacks by Hamas.



---


# The Scale Of Israel's Technology Sector In 2022

Technology is, without question, a giant part of Israel's economy: in 2022 it contributed more than 18% of the country's GDP, the most of any single sector, according to the latest annual report from the Israel Innovation Authority at the time of writing in October 2023. A total of 14% of Israeli citizens work in high tech, which in a country of just 9.2 million people works out to about 1.3 million.

The startup base is correspondingly large. The active number of startups in the country is 9,000, third-highest in the world after the Bay Area and NYC, and over the last five years those startups collectively brought $95 billion into the country by way of venture capital. Combining the business development of startups with the larger tech companies operating in Israel — Intel, Microsoft, Nvidia, Google and many others have operations there — they collectively exported $71 billion in the prior year, 48.3% of the total amount exported across all industries.

These figures are the pre-war baseline, and the article's own caveat is that all of them are going to be significantly lower this year, not least because the disruptions of the war are coming directly on the heels of a major protest movement.

The context for that qualification is that the world was still coming to terms with Hamas' deadly attacks on Israelis the previous weekend, and with everything that had unfolded in the aftermath, including the barrage of retaliation strikes on Gaza. TechCrunch was explicit that the ramifications for the technology ecosystem pale in comparison to the human toll the fighting is taking on both sides, and that the industry is worth considering only because it bears on how the wider region will weather the destruction and one day recover. In such a small country, just about everyone knows someone who was directly affected by the attacks, or someone involved in the subsequent defense and retaliation — and often all three.



---


# Commentary That Israeli Intelligence and Defence Failed

The dominant online argument on 7 October 2023, as collected by Business Today, was that the attack represented a massive failure of Israeli intelligence and defence. Its grounds are the gap between Israel's reputation and the outcome.

Journalist Rania Khalek said the strategic planning that must have gone into this against "one of the most high-tech occupation and surveillance systems in the world" will be studied by many, adding: "The Israelis must be totally losing it right now." Tarik Cyril Amar wrote: "And the intel, and the special forces training... both areas where Israel mythology will be very upset indeed." A user posting as Mjoachim said Israel's defence forces have lost their fame, noting that the IDF lost an army base and a general was captured right out of his house: "Invincible 'Merkava MK4 MBT's captured, and destroyed...what is wrong with the Israeli security and defence forces? And (what) MOSSAD did?"

Dr Jaswant Gandhi, a professor of management, drew a lesson for another country: the attack on Israel was a "great Mossad failure", and India had to learn a lot and keep all intelligence agencies duly greased and internecine conflict-proof. "Israel_under_attack Great #Mossad failure. GoI has to learn a lot and keep all Intelligence Agencies duly greased and internecine conflict-proof. BHARAT is not immune to #terrorism and internal enemies," he wrote on X. The warrant common to these comments is that a surveillance and special-forces apparatus of this reputation should have detected preparations on this scale.



---


# Israel-Hamas Conflict: The Limited-Market-Impact Base Case

As of mid-October 2023, the Indian stock market's base case was that the Israel-Hamas hostilities would not escalate, and on that assumption the conflict was expected to have only a limited impact on markets. The grounds are threefold. First, the world can ill-afford another full-fledged war while economies are already battling high inflation and interest rates, an ongoing Russia-Ukraine war and a slowing China, which is precisely why many countries are trying to restrict any escalation; the market movement in the week before 14 October 2023 indicated that non-escalation was the presumed base case. Second, the US treasury secretary stated that the current conflict is not likely to significantly impact the global economic outlook. Third, history supports the same conclusion: a study of past conflicts between Israel and Hamas found that they tend to have limited impact on global financial markets, across crude oil, US 10-year yields, US equities and market volatility.

The warrant joining the evidence to the claim is that market impact tracks escalation, not the mere existence of hostilities: because the incentives of major countries point towards containment and because previous Israel-Hamas episodes transmitted little into the four channels that matter (oil, yields, equities, volatility), the priced-in outcome is a contained conflict. The argument is explicitly conditional on the non-escalation premise holding.



---


# Sderot Police Headquarters Seized During the Attack

Younis Tirawi, who reports on Palestinian affairs, said that Hamas militants had taken over the Sderot police headquarters and armoured vehicles in the town on 7 October 2023.

An analyst posting as OSINTtechnical wrote the same day that some of the images coming out of Sderot over the previous few hours were reaching degrees of horror "that I don't really think I can use words to properly describe. Truly disturbing acts of terror directed at civilians."



---


# Visual Intelligence Versus Human Sources

Technological sophistication and massive investment in intelligence means have greatly increased the IDF's visual intelligence gathering capabilities, according to former IDF Intelligence Directorate head General (ret.) Aharon Ze'evi-Farkash — but visual collection and human sources play different roles, and only the latter supplies interpretation.

"I'm sure it doesn't come at the expense of human sources, but as time goes by, gathering visual intelligence is easier than human sources and they bring better results," Ze'evi-Farkash said. "It's hard to bring in a Palestinian 'Ashraf Marwan,' the agent who passed the information to Israel before the Egyptian attack in 1973. It's a problem because the human source is essential to provide an interpretation of the rest of the information that's received, and to make decisions. Golda knew who Marwan was and expected to hear what he would say about the Egyptian deployment in the south." Two further gaps sit alongside that structural point: according to "The New York Times," a year before the attack the IDF stopped monitoring Hamas's radio communications, and the US had put stock in Israeli intelligence regarding Hamas in recent years and had not monitored it independently.



---


# Egypt's Strategic Value To Europe: Gas And Security

The war "underscores the important role Egypt has always played vis-a-vis security in and around Gaza," said Robert Satloff, executive director at The Washington Institute for Near East Policy — a role that is not lost on European governments.

Those governments woke up to Egypt's importance as a regional gas producer after Vladimir Putin's invasion of Ukraine in 2022. European officials visited to assess Egypt's potential as a gas supplier — with Israel's help — to supplant at least some Russian supplies.

WIRED's only complaints about Sennheiser's HD 660S2 (7/10, WIRED Review) — bass-enriched audiophile headphones — were the high price and stiff clamping force, and at this price it can live with the tighter fit given gloriously clear and richly detailed sound. Sony's headphones and earbuds were discounted at Best Buy during the anti-Prime Big Deal Day sales, led by the flagship WF-1000XM5 earbuds at $280, down from $300 — 7% off.
