---


# Black Friday 2023 Headphone Deals Overview

Black Friday is often a boon for deals on headphones and earbuds, and 2023 was no different, Engadget reported on 2023-11-24: the shopping holiday brought a plethora of deals on all kinds of headphones, including several top picks from its guides to the best wireless headphones, wireless earbuds, budget wireless earbuds and gaming headsets.

Other popular models from the likes of Sony, Beats, Bose and Apple were discounted as well, which Engadget says makes it an ideal time to pick up a new set — whether as a gift for someone on a holiday shopping list or to replace aging cans. The roundup collects the best Black Friday deals on headphones and earbuds it could find for 2023.



---


# Sony LinkBuds Open-Ear Earbuds Deal Listings

Sony's standard LinkBuds appear in The Verge's December roundup at around $138 from Amazon, Walmart, Best Buy, and Sony directly, against a normal $179.99, and in WIRED's Prime Day roundup (8/10, WIRED Recommends).

The Verge calls them a clear departure from conventional earbuds, using an "open-style" donut-shaped design instead of typical silicone ear tips, which allows better spatial awareness and, for some, a more comfortable fit; they provide crisp sound quality and excellent voice call performance, though as a result of that design they aren't very practical in louder environments. Possibly their coolest feature is the controls, which let you tap the side of your head rather than the earbud itself — "certainly very Sony." WIRED likes them for the same open-ear design that lets you hear what's going on around you, calling them a great option if you do a lot of city walking or use earbuds somewhere it's important to be aware of your surroundings, "like while feeding lions at the zoo."

qid: What company, recently discussed in TechCrunch articles, is not only facing criticism for its new generative AI model's architecture compared to GPT-4 but is also under scrutiny for its content practices on YouTube and accused of anticompetitive behavior that harms news publishers' revenue?
context:
# Helena World Chronicle's Class Action Antitrust Suit Against Google

A class action lawsuit filed in the week of 15 December 2023 in the U.S. District Court in D.C. accuses Google and parent company Alphabet of anticompetitive behavior in violation of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act and others, on behalf of news publishers. The case was filed by Arkansas-based publisher Helena World Chronicle, which argues that Google "siphons off" news publishers' content, their readers and their ad revenue through anticompetitive means, and it specifically cites new AI technologies such as Google's Search Generative Experience (SGE) and the Bard AI chatbot as worsening the problem.

Helena World Chronicle owns and publishes two weekly newspapers in Arkansas. In the complaint it argues that Google is "starving the free press" by sharing publishers' content on Google, losing them "billions of dollars."

Beyond damages, the suit asks for an injunction that would require Google to obtain consent from publishers before using their website data to train its general artificial intelligence products, including Google's own and those of rivals. It also asks that publishers who opt out of SGE still be allowed to show up in Google search results, among other things.

The law firm handling the case is Hausfeld, whose announcement states that "the anticompetitive effects of Google's scheme cause profound harm to competition, to consumers, to labor, and to a democratic free press," and that "Plaintiff Helena World Chronicle, LLC invokes the Sherman Act and Clayton Act to seek class-wide monetary and injunctive relief to restore and ensure competition for digital news and reference publishing and set up guardrails to preserve a free marketplace of ideas in the new era of artificial intelligence."



---


# Google's Generative AI Disinformation Measures

In its report to the EU disinformation Code, Google — an early adopter of generative AI in search via its Bard chatbot — discusses "recent progress in large-scale AI models" which it suggests has "sparked additional discussion about the social impacts of AI and raised concerns on topics such as misinformation."

Google summarised its approach: "Google is committed to developing technology responsibly and has published AI Principles to guide our work, including application areas we will not pursue," adding, "We have also established a governance team to put them into action by conducting ethical reviews of new systems, avoiding bias and incorporating privacy, security and safety. Google Search has published guidance on AI-generated content, outlining its approach to maintaining a high standard of information quality and the overall helpfulness of content on Search. To help address misinformation, Google has also announced that it will soon be integrating new innovations in watermarking, metadata, and other techniques into its latest generative models. Google also recently joined other leading AI companies to jointly commit to advancing responsible practices in the development of artificial intelligence which will support efforts by the G7, the OECD, and national governments. Going forward we will continue to report and expand upon Google developed AI tools and are committed to advance bold and responsible AI, to maximise AI's benefits and minimise its risks."

On forward commitments over the next six months, Google's report states it has no additional measures planned for YouTube. With generative image capabilities rolling out internally over the next year, it commits Google Search to leveraging the IPTC Photo Metadata Standard to add metadata tags to images generated by Google AI, and notes: "Creators and publishers will be able to add a similar markup to their own images, so a label can be displayed in Search to indicate the images as AI generated."



---


# Theory: Copyright Liability Over OpenAI's Training Data

The proposition is that the board acted over mounting accusations that OpenAI's product was built on a dataset including thousands or millions of copyrighted works, with the CEO systematically downplaying the potential liability. TechCrunch's reporter notes that Altman told him at OpenAI's Dev Day earlier that month that the company does not want to incur any copyright problems by using datasets of pirated books, but that a lot of research he had been reading contradicts that, as does pretty much every AI data scientist he talks to. It is exceedingly hard to imagine that OpenAI built GPT-3 with the copyrighted books database, as seems to be the case, but not GPT-4 or succeeding models.

The framing of the hypothesis is a question about the board's likely reaction: if you were the board and facing those accusations, and your CEO had systematically downplayed the potential liability, how would you feel? "I'd feel very hurt."

What works against it is again the succession. If copyright liability was the reason, it seems unlikely that the board would promote the CTO; presumably OpenAI's Chief Science Officer Ilya Sutskever would also have been in the know, and he is still on the board.



---


# The Claim That SGE And Bard Appropriate Publisher Content

The Helena World Chronicle lawsuit claims that Google's recent advances in AI-based search were implemented with "the goal of discouraging end-users from visiting the websites of Class members who are part of the digital news and publishing line of commerce." The grounds are that Google's AI products both retain users and consume publisher content without permission.

On the Search Generative Experience, the suit argues that SGE offers web searchers a way to seek information in a conversational mode but ultimately keeps users in Google's "walled garden" as it "plagiarizes" their content. The warrant that turns this into a harm publishers cannot escape is that publishers also cannot block SGE, because it uses the same web crawler as Google's general search service, GoogleBot — so opting out of the AI experience would mean opting out of search itself.

On Bard, the suit says Google's Bard AI was trained on a dataset that included "news, magazine and digital publications," citing both a 2023 report from the News Media Alliance and a Washington Post article about AI training data. The Post, which worked with researchers at the Allen Institute for AI, had found that News and Media sites were the third largest category of AI training data.

The case points to other concerns too, such as changing AdSense rates and evidence of improper spoliation of evidence on Google's part through its destruction of chat messages — an issue raised in the recent Epic Games lawsuit against Google over app store antitrust issues, which Epic won.



---


# Google's Copyright Filing Against YouTube's Music Reassurances

MBW's counter to the idea that YouTube's rightsholder assurances settle the matter is that Google's take on copyright "harvesting" by generative AI models sits in odd contrast to the copyright-related reassurances YouTube was careful to make to the music industry during the pre-development, development, and trial launch of "Dream Track."

The premise attacked is that the platform relationship and the parent company's legal position can be read separately. MBW's sources close to Sony Music were keen to point out that the company's general ongoing relationship with YouTube and YouTube Music is a harmonious one — YouTube is now the second largest commercial partner of the major record companies, with a stated ambition to catch up with Spotify in the years ahead, and says it paid out over USD $6 billion to music rightsholders in the year to end of June 2022, with around $2 billion of that coming just from ads on user-generated content. However, the October US Copyright Office filing from Google has definitely put the cat amongst the pigeons at Sony Music HQ, as MBW is sure it has at the other two major record companies, because of its position that "Any prohibition or limitation on the use of copyrighted materials for purposes of AI training would undermine the purpose of copyright and foreclose the many opportunities that come with this technology." As well as part-explaining Sony Music's refusal to be included in Dream Track thus far, Google's USCO filing also perhaps explains the careful words selected by Robert Kyncl and especially Sir Lucian Grainge in their respective comments endorsing YouTube's AI experiment — Grainge's statement, after all, began: "We have a fundamental responsibility to our artists to ensure the digital ecosystem evolves to protect them and their work against unauthorized exploitation, including by generative AI platforms…"



---


# Prediction: AI-Generated Content Will Overwhelm Search

Daron Babin's proposition is that Google results will soon be even worse, dominated entirely by AI-generated crap designed to please the algorithms, produced and published at volumes far beyond anything humans could create — far beyond anything we had ever seen before.

The mechanism he gives is cost collapse at the bottom of the market: "All the assholes that are out there paying shitty link-building companies to build shitty articles now they can go and use the free version of GPT."

The prediction's strong form is that the volume is unstoppable: "They're not gonna be able to stop the onslaught of it," he said, then laughed and laughed, thinking about how puny and irrelevant Google seemed in comparison to the next generation of automated SEO. "You can't stop it!" What would falsify it is exactly that — Google proving able to stop the onslaught, so that results are not dominated by machine-produced content.



---


# Associated Press And OpenAI's Licensing Deal

Select news outlets proved far more amenable to OpenAI than the authors suing it. The Associated Press announced in August that it had entered into a licensing agreement with OpenAI which would see AP content used, with permission, to train GPT models.

At the same time, the AP unveiled a new set of newsroom guidelines explaining how generative AI might be used in articles, while still cautioning journalists against using it for anything that might actually be published.

qid: Who is the individual associated with FTX and Alameda Research that was reported by The Verge as being overwhelmed by their growth, convinced a former Jane Street trader to join him as per Fortune, and is accused of committing fraud for personal gain according to TechCrunch?
context:
# FTX Ventures Was Funded By Alameda

Caroline Ellison testified that the money behind FTX Ventures came from Alameda Research, even though Bankman-Fried announced the fund publicly without naming its source: on January 14th, 2022 he tweeted, "We're launching a $2b venture fund: FTX Ventures!" She said he did not want to go public with where the funds came from, telling her he thought Alameda's brand was less good and that he did not want his name associated with it.

The Verge reported the episode on October 10th, 2023 as part of Ellison's testimony, framing it as FTX keeping cozy private ties with Alameda while publicly holding it at arm's length — an echo, the reporter wrote, of Bankman-Fried and Ellison's romantic relationship. The same distancing appears in another transaction: Alameda bought Robinhood shares for Bankman-Fried, who moved them to a vehicle called "Emergent Fidelity Technologies" to avoid association with Alameda.



---


# Testimony At The SBF Trial

Across the first three weeks of the trial, a run of former colleagues, an outside investor and a forensic accounting expert testified that FTX customer money flowed into Alameda Research and out again to other uses, and that FTX's investors were never told about the two firms' special relationship. TechCrunch's running coverage, published 2023-10-06, summarises each week.

In week one, FTX's co-founder and CTO Gary Wang testified Thursday on the extent to which Alameda Research was used for whatever purposes he and SBF saw fit: according to Wang, the crypto trading firm pulled funding directly from FTX customers, whose transactions would be funneled toward Alameda and then directed elsewhere. Thursday also brought testimony from Matt Huang, co-founder and managing partner at crypto investment firm Paradigm, which invested $278 million in FTX across 2021 and 2022 and is part of a class-action lawsuit accusing it and others of defrauding customers by promoting FTX. His testimony centered around being left uninformed about FTX's utilization of customer money to keep Alameda Research afloat — a practice Huang says would have halted his involvement — and covered his relationship with FTX stretching back to 2019.

Week two's standout testimony came from Alameda Research's former CEO Caroline Ellison, who claimed she took $14 billion from customers to repay debts to lenders, using them as a line of credit under the instruction of SBF. Ellison also went into detail about how a $2 billion venture fund, FTX Ventures, was funded by money that had previously been allocated to Alameda from third-party lenders. And though there are no charges of bribery in the case, she also testified to paying Chinese officials $150 million to restore access to $1 billion in frozen trading accounts.

The third week featured a couple of noteworthy moments for the prosecution. FTX's former general counsel Can Sun, like many of SBF's former colleagues, opted to cooperate with authorities and testified that SBF asked him to create a theoretical "legal justification" for the use of billions in consumer funds just days before FTX filed for bankruptcy. Robert Boroujerdi, managing director of the hedge fund Third Point, testified about his experience working with SBF and FTX in a partnership that ultimately resulted in a $60 million investment and a lack of awareness about the special relationship between Alameda Research and FTX; had he known of such a relationship, he testified, Third Point would not have invested in FTX in the first place. And earlier in the week, Peter Easton — a University of Notre Dame professor who helped the government prosecution of Enron and WorldCom — testified about what he uncovered after tracing the flow of billions of dollars between Alameda Research and FTX: much of that funding came from customers, and Easton testified that he found user deposits were used by both FTX and Alameda to purchase real estate, make investments or direct funding toward political causes and charities.



---


# Marc-Antoine Julliard's Testimony As FTX's First Witness-Victim

The prosecution's first witness at Sam Bankman-Fried's trial was not a blockbuster name or a former lieutenant-turned-cooperator like Caroline Ellison but a victim: Marc-Antoine Julliard, a Paris-born cocoa trader who lives in London and whose money got stuck on FTX. Julliard testified that on Nov. 8, 2022, in the crypto exchange's final few days, he tried to pull out almost $100,000 in cash and crypto, and that he was never able to. The withdrawal screenshots shown in court were of attempts to move $20,000 USD and about 4 Bitcoin, worth about $20,000 at the time — roughly $100,000 in total, inaccessible.

Julliard explained why he had chosen FTX in 2021 when he decided to invest in crypto, trading currencies like Bitcoin and Dogecoin there. He trusted FTX because Bankman-Fried came across as a leading figure of the industry; because the sheer volume of users mattered to him, and FTX was at the time among the top three biggest exchanges; and because major VC firms had invested. "They don't commit hundreds of millions without doing due diligence, checking the books, the accountancy of the firm, going through several compliance process[es], so that was a vote of confidence for me," he said. He also noted FTX's glossy ads — featuring Gisele Bündchen, for instance — which suggested a very high budget, and reasoned that it wouldn't make sense to spend that much money unless FTX had very strong financials. He opened an account, transferred in both regular money and cryptocurrency, and used the exchange to execute his plan of buying Bitcoin to sell back in five to ten years at higher prices.

In November 2022 things went bad. Julliard followed Bankman-Fried on Twitter and read aloud in court the "FTX is fine. Assets are fine" tweets, along with "FTX has enough to cover all client holdings. We don't invest client assets" and a few others, which gave him the impression that his money was there and that any problem might be technical — anti-spam measures — or regulatory. By the time he tried to get his money out on November 8th, it was too late. Cross-examining a customer whose money is gone is described as a thankless task, but Mark Cohen tried anyway, noting that Julliard was a licensed commodities broker who was trading in crypto because he didn't have to disclose it, that he knew crypto was new and risky, and that he didn't review the terms of service agreement he had assented to when making his FTX account. The next witness called was Bankman-Fried's former college and FTX roommate, Adam Yedidia.



---


# The Escalation Of Alameda's Negative Balance

Alameda Research first ran a negative balance on FTX in late 2019, and the amount it was allowed to go negative crept upward in steps, each one justified after the fact — the model of the fraud that Gary Wang's and Caroline Ellison's testimony described was escalation rather than a single decision. As The Verge's reporter summarised Wang's testimony: first it was okay to dip into FTX's profits, then it was okay to take more, then even more; first it was a little line of credit just to provide liquidity, then a bigger one, then an effectively limitless one.

The steps ran as follows. Because Alameda and FTX shared an open-plan office, Wang heard a trader ask Bankman-Fried whether it was okay to keep withdrawing money from the negative account, and Bankman-Fried said it was okay as long as the amount stayed lower than FTX's total trading revenue; he was CEO of both companies at the time. Around 2019 or 2020, Wang checked the database and found Alameda was negative by about $200 million, more than the $150 million FTX had made in revenue — which had to mean Alameda was taking customer money. Wang was surprised and discussed it with Bankman-Fried, who told him he just needed to take into account the value of FTT, the token the two of them had launched; Wang trusted his judgment and did not pursue it. Later Alameda's balance was more negative than FTT and the trading revenue combined, and Wang had further conversations with Bankman-Fried about it. Wang testified he knew at the time that Alameda was using FTX customers' funds and that he knew it was wrong.

The same gradual accommodation shows in Ellison's account. Choking back tears, she testified: "When I started working at Alameda, I don't think I would have believed you if you told me I would be sending false balance sheets to our lenders or taking customer money, but over time, it was something I became more comfortable with."



---


# FTX's Cooperating Witnesses

FTX co-founder and former CTO Gary Wang and Alameda Research's former CEO Caroline Ellison both pleaded guilty in December 2022 to federal criminal charges in relation to the FTX collapse, and both planned to cooperate with prosecutors. TechCrunch reported on 2023-10-01 that they would be major witnesses in the trial, given their close ties to Bankman-Fried, FTX and Alameda.

The criminal charges were not their only exposure. Alongside them, Wang and Ellison face civil penalties from the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC).

qid: Does the Insidesport article suggest that English players in the IPL may not be available for the playoffs, while The New York Times article discusses the Los Angeles Dodgers' performance in the 2020 expanded playoffs without mentioning any player availability issues?
context:
# IPL 2024 Auction: Overseas Availability Concerns

Overseas players who cannot serve a full IPL season should expect their price to suffer, because availability — not just ability — determines what a franchise is buying. At 10.40 AM the live blog put the case directly: there will be a lot of teams eyeing the English players, but they won't be available for the playoffs, and this could go against them in bagging a big contract.

The same reasoning was applied at 12.17 PM to one of the most talked-about players, Josh Hazlewood, who might not be available till the last leg of the tournament — leaving open the question of whether teams would target him at all.



---


# The Angels' 2023 Offseason: Ohtani And Trout Availability

The Los Angeles Angels faced the impending exit of their star two-way player Shohei Ohtani after a heartbreaking 2023 season, and were also open to trading nine-time Silver Slugger hitter Mike Trout should he request it, as reported by Essentially Sports on 18 November 2023.

The report frames this as a huge miss: a team that couldn't do well even with two of the league's biggest talents on its roster may lose those stars at the same time, leaving open the question of whether they will choose to stay in Los Angeles.

It also sets up the Dodgers angle. The Halos' cross-town rivals, the Los Angeles Dodgers, have been eyeing the dynamic Troutani duo for a long time; however, despite fans' expectations, the Dodgers' Ohtani-Trout conquest might not take place — and for good reasons.



---


# The Angels' Manager Search Hinges On What Shohei Ohtani Decides

The Angels' managerial seat stood vacant after Phil Nevin's 2024 club option was rejected, Essentially Sports reported on 2023-10-30. The sequence: after Joe Maddon was relieved of his managerial duties, Nevin signed up as interim manager for the remaining 106 games of 2022, then signed a one-year contract to manage the Angels in 2023 with the interim tag lifted. The Halos rejected his 2024 option after partial two seasons of 119-149 (.444) play under his supervision, and since this was non-negotiable, the seat stands vacant.

The biggest challenge is that Angels star Shohei Ohtani had yet to reveal which team he would be joining. If the Angels re-sign the two-way phenom, the manager would get to head a roster with the 2021 MVP and Mike Trout — a once in a lifetime opportunity. On the flip side, if they lose Ohtani, the roster would need a solid revamp; the Angels are also infamous for their below-par farm system and a playoff drought spanning 9 seasons. As for options: Ray Montgomery could be one, considering he began his tenure with the Angels; Walt Weiss could potentially be a decent fit, having been part of a successful team in the Atlanta Braves as their bench coach since before the 2018 season; and among other options are Ron Washington and Clayton McCullough. Though these options are open, no solid information had been revealed as to who would fill the position.



---


# Obstacles To Mike Trout Leaving The Angels

Essentially Sports raised the obvious objection to any Dodgers-Trout scenario on 18 November 2023: the counter attacks the premise that Trout would switch to another Los Angeles team at all, since he has been pretty persistent about sticking with the Los Angeles Angels from the very start and does not want to leave, even though the team has been transparent about not stopping him should he choose to play elsewhere.

The article then supplies the pressure that works against that preference. It seems the Angels will have a hard time affording a player like Trout in the foreseeable future, as they have to win a good number of games to stay in the playoffs and keep a steady income of revenue throughout the seasons — and considering their 73-game win record that season, that seems like a pipe dream right now.

The remaining scope condition is age and runway: Trout is 32, which means he has already passed the MLB average retirement age of 30, but he still has a lot left to give to the diamond for approximately six more years. The piece closes by putting the choice — Ohtani, Trout, both or neither — to its readers.



---


# Globe Life Field: Texas Rangers Postseason Atmosphere

Globe Life Field ranked No. 7 among the eight remaining 2023 playoff teams' home-field environments in The New York Times' 8 October 2023 ranking, on the grounds that it is "the great unknown." The park opened in 2020, has a capacity of 40,300 and drew an average attendance of 31,272 in 2023.

There have been 16 postseason games in Globe Life Field history, but the Rangers have never appeared in a playoff game at their new-ish home. The explanation is 2020: it was a weird time, and the Dodgers played in all 16 of those games during the expanded playoffs, sweeping the Padres in the NLDS, going seven games with the Braves in the NLCS and then winning the World Series.

The park opened in a season that had no fans and remained open for losing seasons in 2021 and 2022, so Saturday would be the first look at the place with the home team actually playing meaningful baseball in October — hard to rank it any higher until we know what we're dealing with. The old Rangers ballpark could drum up a Texas-sized atmosphere worthy of Stevie Ray Vaughan and Pat Green, but the new place — at least in the regular season — feels very much like a multi-events space that happens to be hosting a ballgame. The Rangers had not been home since Sept. 24, when they won their last five games in Arlington, the last three of which went a long way toward keeping the Mariners out of the postseason. With a closed roof containing all the noise, Globe Life is sure to get awfully loud, and nothing turns a glorified convention center into a real ballpark quite like a late-inning rally in October.



---


# The Dodgers' Pitching Need Versus Ohtani's 2024 Elbow Injury

Essentially Sports argued on 18 November 2023 that it would not be advisable for the Dodgers to hire Shohei Ohtani until 2025: the claim is that the pitching value that makes him attractive is unavailable in 2024, and the warrant is that the team already has the hitting he would otherwise provide.

The need grounds are real. The Dodgers have been in dire need of pitchers for a few seasons — their current highest strikeout total by a pitcher in a single postseason is 137 by Clayton Kershaw, followed by 119 by Bobby Miller and 117 by Julio Urias — so Ohtani's high strikeout rate of 167 that season would make him an invaluable addition.

The hiccup is availability, and the fallback is redundant. Ohtani will not be available to pitch throughout the 2024 season due to an elbow ligament injury he is recovering from, so given that unavoidable absence the article says it would not be advisable to hire him until 2025. Ohtani does have magnificent hitting form as well, but the team already has hitters like Freddie Freeman and Mookie Betts, who recorded 211 and 179 hits respectively that regular season.



---


# Shohei Ohtani's Postseason Ambition With The Dodgers

Shohei Ohtani has never played a postseason game in his big-league career, and joining the Dodgers gives him the opportunity to add collective hardware to his trophy case, The New York Times noted on 9 December 2023.

His individual brilliance was not enough to lift the Angels into the postseason. The Dodgers, by contrast, have won the National League West in 10 of the past 11 seasons, topped 100 victories in five of the past six full seasons, and won the World Series in 2020.

As the Angels foundered in recent years, Ohtani became more vocal about his desire to play for a winner. Only one stage remains for him, and he now has the chance to make a different kind of history.



---


# The Yankees' Failed 2023 And Their Plan To Reset For 2024

The baseball season for the New York teams did not turn out to be their most successful one, Essentially Sports reported on 2023-10-10: both the New York Mets and the New York Yankees failed to make the playoffs and came under scrutiny as the highest spenders in the league. The level of accounting has been higher for the 27-time winners because of the highest expectations.

The management comprehended the situation and was actively seeking to make changes for the 2024 season — be it trimming the squad and releasing a few players, including superstar Gleyber Torres, they were looking to bring about changes. But given that they are already short on options, the article raises the question of whether the move is justified.

qid: After Seeking Alpha recommended a Hold rating for GitLab Inc. on December 3, 2023, due to valuation concerns, did TechCrunch's report on December 18, 2023, regarding the significant pressure on tech companies' valuations reflect a consistent or inconsistent viewpoint on the valuation pressures faced by tech companies like GitLab Inc.?
context:
# GitLab Q3 Earnings Preview, December 2023

GitLab Inc. (GTLB) was due to post its Q3 results after the market closed on the Monday following Seeking Alpha's December 3, 2023 week-ahead preview, going in with a split verdict: Seeking Alpha's Quant Rating system suggested a Hold on valuation concerns, while Wall Street analysts advocated a Buy.

As of the December 3, 2023 preview, the stock had surged 10% for the year — the specific basis for the Quant system's valuation concern. Consensus estimates ahead of the print were EPS of -$0.01 and revenue of $141.04M. The accompanying Earnings Insight noted that GitLab had beaten both EPS and revenue expectations in eight straight quarters, so the estimate figures should be read against an unbroken recent record of upside surprises.



---


# GitLab Sell-Side Analyst Theses, Late 2023

Two sell-side firms held opposite views on GitLab as of Seeking Alpha's December 3, 2023 week-ahead, while reasoning from overlapping premises: Raymond James had recently rated the stock Market Perform, whereas Cantor Fitzgerald started coverage at Overweight with a $55 price target.

Raymond James's Market Perform call rested on a two-sided ground: it cited potential market exuberance on one hand, and growth potential in fiscal 2025 on the other, with that growth potential attributed to a large total addressable market, healthy customers, and a value proposition favouring consolidation over fragmentation. The warrant joining those grounds to a neutral rating is that a genuinely attractive growth story can still be fully — or excessively — reflected in the price, so strong fundamentals do not by themselves justify a buy recommendation.

Cantor Fitzgerald's initiation ran the consolidation premise the other way. It anticipated that GitLab would benefit from product consolidation and from the generative artificial intelligence wave, and treated those two tailwinds as sufficient to underwrite an Overweight rating and a $55 target. Both descriptions are as of the December 3, 2023 preview; the shared premise is that consolidation favours GitLab, and the firms diverge on whether that advantage is already priced in.



---


# NIO Q3 2023 Earnings Preview

NIO (NIO) was set to release its Q3 earnings before the bell on the Tuesday following Seeking Alpha's December 3, 2023 week-ahead preview, with the Wall Street consensus at Buy and Seeking Alpha's Quant Ratings holding at Hold because of concerns about profitability and valuation.

Consensus estimates going into the print were EPS of -$0.23 and revenue of $2.66B. The Earnings Insight attached to the preview is the important qualifier on those numbers: NIO had missed EPS estimates consistently in the past eight quarters and had missed revenue expectations in 50% of those quarters. The Quant system's two stated objections — profitability and valuation — are what separate it from the sell-side's Buy, and both are as of the December 3, 2023 preview date rather than the reported result.



---


# Stone Fox Capital's NIO Stock Doubling Thesis

Stone Fox Capital, an SA Investing Group leader, argued in early December 2023 that NIO shares — then trading at their 2023 lows, having fallen below $8 — had the potential to double to $16.

The grounds are mixed rather than uniformly bullish. Stone Fox Capital attributed the fall below $8 to fluctuating monthly delivery numbers and inconsistent EV deliveries, and flagged that despite an electric vehicle delivery record in Q3, a recent 10% workforce reduction raises concerns for Q4. The warrant joining those observations to a $16 target is the depressed starting point: the same delivery inconsistency that drove the decline has left the stock at its 2023 lows, which is what makes a doubling the analyst's stated upside case.

The scope conditions matter. This is one Seeking Alpha Investing Group author's view as relayed in a December 3, 2023 preview, the $16 figure is framed as potential rather than a formal price target, and the author's own Q4 concern about the workforce cut sits unresolved inside the thesis.

# Comparing "Renaissance" And "The Eras Tour" As Concert Films

The two 2023 concert films sit at different scales and, in Comscore analyst Paul Dergarabedian's framing, should not be compared too closely: "Renaissance" opened at $21 million against the $92.8 million debut of "Taylor Swift: The Eras Tour" in October, yet both figures dwarf the previous concert-film ceiling, and the tours behind them differ by roughly a factor of three in gross.

The structural relations are these. No one expected "Renaissance" to match "The Eras Tour," which was wrapping up its theatrical run with over $250 million globally; prior to Swift, the biggest concert film debuts — titles held by Miley Cyrus and Justin Bieber for their 2008 and 2011 films — had not surpassed the unadjusted sum of $32 million, so $21 million remains a very good start for a concert film. On the touring side, the 39-city, 56-show "Renaissance" tour kicked off in Stockholm, Sweden in May and ended in Kansas City, Missouri in the fall, making over $500 million and attracting over 2.7 million concertgoers, while Swift's ongoing 151-date "Eras Tour" was expected to gross some $1.4 billion. "To have two concert films topping the chart in a single year is pretty unprecedented," Dergarabedian said. The limit of the comparison is his own: "Taylor Swift was a total outlier and the result of a very specific set of circumstances. These two films are similar in genre only."



---


# Box Office

## Definition

Box office, as used throughout the corpus, is the reported revenue figure for a film's ticket sales, cited either as a single weekend's opening or debut number or as a cumulative running gross toward a domestic or global total.
Beyoncé's "Renaissance" is described as having "topped the box office" with "a $21 million debut" from North American ticket sales on its opening weekend (doc_0173), and "Taylor Swift: The Eras Tour" is tracked the same way, launching with "$100 million" in advance sales (doc_0419) and later "surpass[ing] $250m at the global box office" (doc_0046).

## Context

The corpus reports box office in two recurring ways: as a snapshot of a single weekend's ranking (who "topped the box office" that weekend) and as a running cumulative gross that signals a film's overall commercial success or failure.
Concert films sit alongside conventional theatrical releases in this reporting: "Renaissance" and "The Eras Tour" are both measured in the same box-office terms as scripted films like "The Batman" (doc_0081) or Scorsese's "Killers of the Flower Moon" (doc_0192), and both were distributed through a direct deal with AMC Theatres rather than a traditional studio (doc_0419).
2023 industry-wide box office is also used as a barometer of the theatrical exhibition business: analyst Dergarabedian expected the two concert films to help lift the North American box office "to more than $9 billion in 2023," up from "$7.4 billion" in 2022 (doc_0419), and the "Barbenheimer" pairing of Barbie and Oppenheimer is credited with dominating "the 2023 box office and the cultural discussion" (doc_0094).
The term also appears in retrospective judgments of a film's commercial fate: Scorsese and De Niro's "The King of Comedy" (1983) is described as having been "a flop at the box office" despite positive reviews (doc_0193), while Tobe Hooper's "The Texas Chain Saw Massacre" (1974) "made over $30 million at the box office on a budget of around $140,000" (doc_0563), illustrating the term's use for both underperformance and outsized return relative to cost.

## Key Characteristics

- **Reported as a debut and as a cumulative total** — outlets cite both a single weekend's opening number (e.g., "$21 million debut," doc_0173) and a running gross accumulated over a film's release (e.g., "surpassed $250m," doc_0046).
- **Ranking-based** — weekend box office is reported competitively, with films described as "topping" or "ruling" the box office relative to other new releases that same weekend (doc_0173).
- **Applies to concert films alongside scripted releases** — the corpus tracks Beyoncé's and Taylor Swift's concert films using the same box-office vocabulary and comparisons applied to traditional Hollywood films (doc_0173, doc_0419, doc_0081, doc_0192).
- **Used as both a success and failure signal** — the same term describes a "flop" (doc_0193) and a low-budget film's outsized return (doc_0563), as well as a blockbuster's records (doc_0046, doc_0419).
- **Aggregated into industry-wide totals** — individual films' box office performance feeds into annual North American or global box-office totals used to gauge the health of theatrical exhibition (doc_0419, doc_0094).

## Background (external)

The corpus uses "box office" as industry shorthand for a film's ticket-sales revenue without ever defining the term itself.
Outside the corpus, a "box office" (or "ticket office") is literally a place where tickets are sold to the public for admission to an event; by extension, the term is used, especially in the film industry, as a metonym for the amount of business a production earns, and total movie ticket sales have been termed "box office" since at least 1904 (Wikipedia, *Box office*, accessed 2026-09-02).

# AMC Theatres As Direct Distributor Of Concert Films

Both Beyoncé and Taylor Swift chose to partner with AMC Theatres to distribute their concert films rather than going through a traditional studio, an arrangement in which both are reported to be receiving at least 50% of ticket sales.

The parallels run further: both superstars have been supportive of one another, making splashy appearances at the other's premieres, and both had previously released films on Netflix — "Miss Americana" for Swift and "Homecoming" for Beyoncé. The direct-distribution model also came with premium pricing. Movie tickets to the Beyoncé show were more expensive than average, around $23.32 versus Swift's $20.78, according to data firm EntTelligence.

# The Masters Dispute And The "Taylor's Version" Re-Recordings

When music mogul Scooter Braun acquired Taylor Swift's longtime label, Big Machine Records, in 2019, he also gained the rights to the master recordings of Swift's first six studio albums; in November 2020 Braun sold those masters to an investment fund in a deal believed to be worth over $300 million. Swift responded by re-recording her catalogue, and by the end of 2023 had released four "Taylor's Version" albums: Fearless (Taylor's Version) in April 2021, Red (Taylor's Version) in November 2021, Speak Now (Taylor's Version) in July 2023, and 1989 (Taylor's Version) in October 2023.

The Independent suggests it was that decision to re-record the catalogue that catapulted Swift into her 2023 success. Asked by Time about the success of her tour, Swift traced it back to two ordeals: "It's not lost on me that the two great catalysts for this happening were two horrendous things that happened to me. The first was getting cancelled within an inch of my life and sanity. The second was having my life's work taken away from me by someone who hates me."

# The NBA Rookie Of The Year Futures Market

NBA Rookie of the Year is a futures market: bettors across the country can wager on which player they believe will win the coveted award as part of NBA futures betting.

Like other NBA futures odds, it can be bet on before the start of the NBA regular season and throughout the year, and the best NBA betting apps make placing that wager simple and convenient. Sporting News publishes the latest Rookie of the Year odds as posted at online sportsbooks alongside guidance on how to bet on them.



---


# The Timing Trade-Off In Rookie Of The Year Futures Betting

There is a fixed trade-off in when to bet NBA Rookie of the Year futures: the earlier you bet, the better the odds, but you bet without much information that could be key to an educated decision; conversely, if you wait for the data you need for an informed bet, the odds tighten and you see less of a return.

The mechanism is symmetric between bettor and book. When the lines are first released, the season has not started, so there are no statistics, trends or player news — the pre-season odds are so favorable precisely because even the oddsmakers lack the data to craft more specific lines. Once the season starts and you can see how the rookies are performing, you can gather the relevant data; but sportsbooks are gathering the same information and tighten the Rookie of the Year lines in response. So while you can better guess who will hoist the Wilt Chamberlain Trophy, the odds are tighter and your potential return reduced.

Stated as pros and cons: betting early gives an opportunity to find better value and betting odds that are fresh and unadjusted, but carries much higher risk because a player's performance, health and team dynamic can change through the season, and offers limited information. Waiting gives a lot more information for an informed bet and avoids betting on a player not remotely in contention, but reduces the opportunity to find value and the odds may not be as favorable. The range over which this holds is bounded by the individual: it is always important to take your risk tolerance into consideration while weighing the potential rewards, and no matter when you decide to wager, always gather as much information as possible before risking your money.

A futures bet in any sport is a wager on an event usually weeks or months away, settled at the end of a season or a tournament — and predicting the next NBA MVP is a popular futures option at the best sports betting sites.

Every sports betting site will have NBA futures markets, including the NBA Most Valuable Player award, Rookie of the Year odds, regular-season win total OVER/UNDER bets and more; MVP odds are posted at top online sportsbooks and the MVP is far from the only NBA futures bet available.

---


# Over/Under Totals Bet Definition

A totals bet, commonly known as an over/under bet, is a wager on the combined score of both teams in a game: bookmakers set a predicted total score, and bettors choose whether the actual combined score will surpass it ("over") or fall short of it ("under"). Rather than picking the winner or the winning margin, totals betting asks only about the game's combined score, and it sits alongside point spreads and moneylines as a favorite option in sports betting.

The discriminating feature is that the bettor's only concern is whether the final combined score falls over or under the line set by oddsmakers — the identity of the winner is irrelevant. Sporting News illustrates with an NBA game whose total is set at 210.5 points: those who bet the "over" win if the combined score of the two teams is 211 or more, while those who bet the "under" win if the score totals 210 or less. The 0.5 ensures no chance of a tie, since teams cannot score in half-points.

The category is broader than points. Over/under bets involve wagering on whether a particular number will be over or under the figure the bookmaker set, and that number can be combined points scored in a game, total rounds in a fight, or total games in a tennis match.



---


# NBA In-Game Betting: Wagering While The Game Unfolds

In-game betting, also known as live betting, allows you to bet on a game while it is unfolding, and it has exploded nationwide thanks to the increased popularity of online sports betting apps. The action is fast and the odds are constantly shifting, making for a new way to enjoy the flow of a game while staying engaged as a bettor.

Depending on the sportsbook there is usually a strong variety of live betting opportunities. These include game and player prop bets such as whether the next bucket will be worth one, two or three points; bets on the team leading at the end of the current quarter; bets on whether there will be a comeback victory; and wagers boiled down to the results of the next possession.

The most popular sportsbook apps — DraftKings, FanDuel and BetMGM — offer NBA in-game betting, though each has its own lines and betting opportunities.



---


# Moneyline Odds Examples By Sport

Typical moneyline prices look the same across sports — a minus number on the favorite, a plus number on the underdog — but the shape of the market varies with the sport, most obviously where draws or large fields exist. In an NFL game between the Dallas Cowboys (-130) and the New York Giants (+110), the Cowboys are the favorites: a $130 bet on Dallas returns $100 profit if they win, while a $100 wager on the Giants earns $110 profit on an upset. An NBA game between the Los Angeles Lakers (-150) and the Miami Heat (+130) works the same way, with $150 on the Lakers profiting $100 and $100 on the Heat profiting $130.

Baseball and hockey illustrate slight favorites and even money. For an MLB game with the New York Yankees at -120 and the Boston Red Sox at +100, the Yankees are slight favorites — a $120 bet returns $100 profit — while the Red Sox are at even odds, so a $100 bet also returns $100 profit. For an NHL game with the Toronto Maple Leafs at -140 and the Chicago Blackhawks at +120, $140 on Toronto profits $100 and $100 on Chicago profits $120.

Soccer adds a third selection. In an MLS match between the Seattle Sounders (+110), the Draw (+230) and Atlanta United (+140), neither team is a clear favorite though the Sounders have slightly better odds: $100 on Seattle profits $110, $100 on the draw profits $230 if the match ends tied, and $100 on Atlanta profits $140. In soccer, the possibility of a draw is a common outcome to bet on, which is different from many other major sports.

Combat sports, tennis and golf round out the pattern. A UFC fight between Conor McGregor (-200) and Dustin Poirier (+170) pays $100 profit on a $200 bet on McGregor and $170 profit on a $100 bet on Poirier. A tennis match between Serena Williams (-150) and Maria Sharapova (+130) makes Williams the favorite, with $150 on her profiting $100 and $100 on Sharapova profiting $130. PGA Tour odds price individual golfers to win a tournament — Tiger Woods +500, Rory McIlroy +600 — so a $100 bet profits $500 or $600 respectively; in golf, with usually many players in the field, the odds can be much higher than in head-to-head matchups.

On the second day of Sam Bankman-Fried's fraud trial, the jury was selected on Wednesday morning, after which lawyers for the government and then for Bankman-Fried delivered opening statements that told two very different stories of the former FTX CEO's sudden rise and almost instantaneous fall. Bankman-Fried's defense can itself introduce risks for people who dealt with him, because his lawyers have several simultaneous objectives: first and foremost proving their client not guilty, but also — just in case they don't get the outcome they want — laying the groundwork for appeals and sentencing arguments.

# Helena World Chronicle's Class Action Antitrust Suit Against Google

A class action lawsuit filed in the week of 15 December 2023 in the U.S. District Court in D.C. accuses Google and parent company Alphabet of anticompetitive behavior in violation of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act and others, on behalf of news publishers. The case was filed by Arkansas-based publisher Helena World Chronicle, which argues that Google "siphons off" news publishers' content, their readers and their ad revenue through anticompetitive means, and it specifically cites new AI technologies such as Google's Search Generative Experience (SGE) and the Bard AI chatbot as worsening the problem.

Helena World Chronicle owns and publishes two weekly newspapers in Arkansas. In the complaint it argues that Google is "starving the free press" by sharing publishers' content on Google, losing them "billions of dollars."

Beyond damages, the suit asks for an injunction that would require Google to obtain consent from publishers before using their website data to train its general artificial intelligence products, including Google's own and those of rivals. It also asks that publishers who opt out of SGE still be allowed to show up in Google search results, among other things.

The law firm handling the case is Hausfeld, whose announcement states that "the anticompetitive effects of Google's scheme cause profound harm to competition, to consumers, to labor, and to a democratic free press," and that "Plaintiff Helena World Chronicle, LLC invokes the Sherman Act and Clayton Act to seek class-wide monetary and injunctive relief to restore and ensure competition for digital news and reference publishing and set up guardrails to preserve a free marketplace of ideas in the new era of artificial intelligence."

# Class Action

## Definition

A class action, as it appears across this corpus, is a single lawsuit pursued on behalf of a group of similarly affected people rather than filed by each person individually.

The corpus documents several such suits from 2023: FTX customers against crypto promoters including Paradigm, a news publisher against Google, consumers against PayPal, and the Authors Guild against OpenAI.

It also shows the mechanism can be blocked by contract, as with Uber's terms of use barring class actions in sexual-assault cases.

## Context

The corpus shows the mechanism used across very different disputes: FTX customers brought a class-action lawsuit accusing crypto investment firm Paradigm and other promoters of defrauding customers by promoting the exchange, publisher Helena World Chronicle filed a class action antitrust suit against Google and Alphabet under the Sherman Act alleging AI tools like Search Generative Experience and Bard siphon off publishers' content and ad revenue, and consumers represented by law firm Hagens Berman filed a class action against PayPal over anti-steering rules that allegedly stifle competition from cheaper platforms like Stripe and Shopify.

The Authors Guild of America, representing Stephen King, John Grisham and 134 other authors, likewise filed its own class-action suit against OpenAI over unauthorized use of copyrighted books in training data, run in parallel to (but distinct from) comedian Sarah Silverman's separate, non-class suit.

Apple's earlier MacBook Pro keyboard class-action settlement is cited in the corpus as a business driver — the corpus notes the settlement cost probably factored into Apple's decision to redesign the keyboard, a change introduced alongside separate updates like a new camera and the removal of the Touch Bar.

- **Collective standing** — a class action lets one or a few plaintiffs (e.g., Helena World Chronicle, the Authors Guild, unnamed FTX customers) litigate on behalf of an entire group with the same underlying grievance, rather than requiring each affected person to sue separately.
- **Can be contractually blocked** — the corpus shows companies can preempt this mechanism: under Uber's terms of use, class action lawsuits cannot be filed against the company in sexual assault cases, forcing survivors to litigate individually and preventing them from advocating for themselves collectively.

- **Defendants, not just plaintiffs, can be named as a group** — the FTX-related suit accuses Paradigm "and others" collectively of defrauding customers, showing the mechanism can target a class of co-defendants as well as aggregate a class of claimants.

## Background (external)

The Helena World Chronicle lawsuit claims that Google's recent advances in AI-based search were implemented with "the goal of discouraging end-users from visiting the websites of Class members who are part of the digital news and publishing line of commerce." The grounds are that Google's AI products both retain users and consume publisher content without permission.

On the Search Generative Experience, the suit argues that SGE offers web searchers a way to seek information in a conversational mode but ultimately keeps users in Google's "walled garden" as it "plagiarizes" their content. The warrant that turns this into a harm publishers cannot escape is that publishers also cannot block SGE, because it uses the same web crawler as Google's general search service, GoogleBot — so opting out of the AI experience would mean opting out of search itself.

On Bard, the suit says Google's Bard AI was trained on a dataset that included "news, magazine and digital publications," citing both a 2023 report from the News Media Alliance and a Washington Post article about AI training data. The Post, which worked with researchers at the Allen Institute for AI, had found that News and Media sites were the third largest category of AI training data.

A ruling against Google would not stop at Google: the remedy would likely resemble the Microsoft settlement and the outcome would ripple through the other pending Big Tech cases, because enforcers are using this trial to demonstrate that antitrust law can still take on the largest and most powerful companies in the world.

The grounds for the first half of that claim are the available remedies. If the judge rules against Google, the outcome could look a lot like the Microsoft deal, in which the computer company was required to change its behavior and share its APIs with third-party developers, and was also banned from making anticompetitive and exclusive deals with computer manufacturers. Google might likewise end up having to turn over all or most of the data it has collected to other search engines so they can improve their products and attract more users — a remedy scaled to the disparity the DOJ has cited, that Google gets 16 times more data than Bing does everyday.
