# Reece James' Hamstring Injury And Return Timeline

As of 20 October 2023, the best read on Reece James' status was that he would be back in Chelsea's squad for Saturday's home derby against Arsenal, most likely as a substitute, though not at 100 per cent.

The 23-year-old was not called up by England for the internationals over the preceding window, and the idea was that he would work to be ready for the Arsenal game. Yet there had been stories of an injury setback, even that he might need surgery to get to the root of his hamstring issues. Pochettino bustled his way through those questions on the Friday, saying of the hamstring: "It is much better. He is progressing well, still not at his best, 100%. But maybe to help the team at some point …. maybe, he is close to be there." Malo Gusto was available again after his own suspension.

The Guardian noted it had not been straightforward and seemed to remain that way, and drew two takeaways from Pochettino on James with a common thread: first, that James could be like a coiled spring when he finally returned to action, and second, that Pochettino was in no mood to criticise him for his indiscipline — on the contrary, he was happier to talk up James's passion.



---


# Buffalo Bills Defensive Injuries And The 2023 Outlook

The New York Times argued on 16 October 2023 that this can still be Buffalo's season despite defensive injuries, because the rest of the AFC is the key variable and no other team has taken the conference over.

The grounds are comparative rather than absolute. The Bills are diminished and have imperfections, but Buffalo had already defeated the Dolphins, and the other AFC teams aren't exactly peaking: Kansas City and Cincinnati appear easier to defend that season than in the recent past, and it remains to be seen how well the Dolphins hold up. The warrant is that a contender only needs to be better than the available competition, not to match its own earlier form.

An executive agreed on both halves of the point: "Matt Milano and Tre'Davious White, those are huge injuries for that football team. The Bills are not as dominant as they felt going into it with so many injuries on defense. But the division they are in, they will still be able to slug it out and get to where they need to go. Nobody has really emerged in the AFC to unseat these teams at the top."



---


# Tyler Adams' Hamstring Injury Left The USMNT Without A Recognized No. 6

Captain Tyler Adams was the notable absence from the USMNT's October 2023 camp, sidelined with a frustrating long-term hamstring injury. He was initially injured playing for Leeds United back in March, and although he had finally recovered enough to make his Bournemouth debut in the EFL Cup in late September, he played just 20 minutes off the bench before suffering a setback that sidelined him again for the foreseeable future.

The absence mattered because Adams is the one proven defensive midfielder — a No. 6, in soccer jargon — on the USMNT roster. He had been absent from the national team since injuring his hamstring in the spring, and by the Oct. 14 friendly against Germany it was possible he would need a second surgery to address the issue.

Asked about him after that match, Berhalter told reporters: "Tyler's a great player. It's not nice to talk about guys that aren't here, though. I'd rather talk about the guys that are on the field."



---


# Winning Too Soon And Coaching Regime Expectations

The New York Times argued on 16 October 2023 that a bad team winning right away can be counterproductive, because early success resets expectations for fans and ownership and makes it less practical to take one step backward in the short term for a better shot at taking two steps forward down the line.

The test cases are the New York Giants and Minnesota Vikings, both of which exceeded expectations under first-year head coaches in 2022 and reached the playoffs, and both of which were struggling in their second seasons and facing difficult questions about the future. The grounds are that every head coach and general manager wants to win as much as possible, but the goal is to build for the long term, which can require time to do things with sustainability in mind — so whether early success helps or hurts could depend on how well the football leadership has communicated with ownership.

A veteran coach with experience on a half-dozen teams supplied the warrant from inside the building: "The best first year can be that 7-10 season where you show some promise. The Giants won a bunch of games early, people were heaping praise on the head coach, people get the expectation of what the quarterback can be. But oftentimes, you know different internally because you know the house you are living in. You are inside the walls every single day and you know where the roof leaks, where the foundation is cracked." Buffalo is offered as the managed version of the same situation: the Bills surprisingly reached the playoffs in their first season under Sean McDermott, a euphoric moment after a 17-year playoff drought, went 6-10 the next year, then began a steady rise behind Josh Allen and a top defense — but there isn't a Josh Allen on the Giants or Vikings. Minnesota in particular is in an interesting spot, with Kirk Cousins approaching free agency and playing well enough, most likely, to keep the Vikings from climbing too high in the draft order. "They already gave a contract to (tight end) T.J. Hockenson, and they are going to give one to (receiver) Justin Jefferson," an exec said. "Now, what? Are you going into the rookie pool and taking the fourth-best quarterback in the draft? You can look like Atlanta with (Desmond) Ridder pretty quick."



---


# Giants At Eagles, Christmas Day 2023: Storylines To Watch

New York Giants (5-9) at Philadelphia Eagles (10-4), at 4:30 p.m. ET, was the middle game of the Christmas Day tripleheader, Yardbarker previewed on 2023-12-24. The first question is whether the Eagles defense can shake off the rust: appointing Matt Patricia as defensive play-caller didn't change much, with the defense giving up the third-most points in the NFL over their three-game losing streak, 95. Although the unit had reached its lowest point, there were reasons for optimism — New York ranked 31st among teams in points and yards per game that season and had surrendered a staggering 76 sacks, the third-most in a single season in NFL history, and the annual trip to Philadelphia had essentially been a scheduled loss for the Giants, whose last win at Lincoln Financial Field came in 2013.

The second question is whether quarterback Jalen Hurts and the Eagles offense can finally bounce back. The offense had struggled mightily over the last three games with Hurts' ineffectiveness playing a significant role: after averaging the third-most points in the NFL over the first 11 games at 28.2, the Eagles had scored four offensive touchdowns during the skid, three of which came via the "tush push." They might have difficulty throwing against a solid Giants pass defense but could alleviate some woes by running the ball efficiently, since New York gives up 131.6 rushing yards per game, the fourth-most in the league. The third question is whether Giants quarterback Tommy DeVito has any magic left: the Giants may have a terrible offense, but the unit has operated at its best under DeVito, an undrafted rookie and native of Cedar Grove, New Jersey, who had thrown for 858 yards, seven touchdowns and one interception in five games since being named starter, posting the 13th-highest passer rating in the NFL during that stretch at 97.3.



---


# Reece James Return From Injury Chelsea

Reece James was a constant menace to Blackburn's defence as he started for the first time since the opening day of the season on his return from injury, and Mauricio Pochettino admitted he was delighted to have his captain back, The Guardian reported on Nov. 1, 2023.

"He is one of the best full-backs in the world and to have been without him for so long has been difficult," Pochettino said. "But we need to be careful and little by little he will get back to full fitness."



---


# Jacksonville Jaguars' Contender Readiness, 2023

The New York Times argued on 16 October 2023 that the Jaguars, more than the other AFC contenders, seem early in their life cycle and still finding their way — which makes them a little harder to trust in big spots but also leaves greater space for growth.

The immediate scope condition is Trevor Lawrence's knee injury, the big concern coming out of that Sunday: if he is out, expectations shift dramatically, and the writer hopes the test results come back clear.

An executive gave the positive case, resting on coaching pedigree and experience rather than current form: "I like Jacksonville. Doug (Pederson) has a championship pedigree. This team is relatively young. They are scrappy. The fact that they have been there before gives them a chance. I think the quarterback is growing."

qid: Was there inconsistency in the portrayal of the accusations against Sam Bankman-Fried between the TechCrunch report on Sam Bankman-Fried's trial published on October 1, 2023, and the TechCrunch report on the allegations against Sam Bankman-Fried published on October 7, 2023?
context:
# Going Infinite: Michael Lewis's Account Of SBF's Political Dealings

Michael Lewis's book "Going Infinite" debuted on the first day of Sam Bankman-Fried's trial, and details about Bankman-Fried's political dealings emerging from it include his alleged attempt to buy off Donald Trump to get him not to run again for president.

TechCrunch's team was focused on the Manhattan Federal Court for the trial of Bankman-Fried, the disgraced entrepreneur accused of orchestrating the collapse of the cryptocurrency exchange FTX; the Lewis book is the second channel through which the week's revelations arrived. The reporting is framed as allegation rather than established fact, and it comes from the book rather than from courtroom testimony. The item appeared in TechCrunch's Week in Review of October 7, 2023.



---


# Day Two Of The Bankman-Fried Trial: Jury Selection And The Courtroom Audience

On the second day of Sam Bankman-Fried's fraud trial, the jury was selected on Wednesday morning, after which lawyers for the government and then for Bankman-Fried delivered opening statements that told two very different stories of the former FTX CEO's sudden rise and almost instantaneous fall. The central question framed by the proceedings was who Bankman-Fried, the former CEO of crypto exchange FTX, really is: a liar and a fraud, or someone who acted in good faith and, like many a startup founder, flew too close to the sun. That answer, the account notes, ultimately lies with the jury.

The day featured pointed allegations, a friend from MIT, and an audience replete with big names, including Bankman-Fried's professorial parents and Damian Williams, the U.S. attorney for the Southern District of New York. Bankman-Fried himself spent most of the day in court staring into a laptop while seated between his two attorneys. The prosecution's account of his alleged crimes was described as featuring a study in contrasts.



---


# Sam Bankman-Fried

Sam Bankman-Fried is the former CEO of the bankrupt crypto exchange FTX, whose highly anticipated criminal trial started on the Tuesday before TechCrunch's 2023-10-01 report, to determine whether he is guilty of seven counts of fraud and conspiracy. As one former federal prosecutor put it: "The odds seem to be stacked against him at this point."

He was 31 years old and co-founded FTX in 2019; within a few years the once third-largest crypto exchange's valuation hit $32 billion at its peak, and the company is now trying to claw back any funds to distribute to creditors. Before the fall he was even compared to Warren Buffet, and many called him the white horse of crypto — a description TechCrunch notes it never applied to him.

Bankman-Fried, however, maintained his innocence. At The New York Times' DealBook Summit he appeared virtually from the Bahamas and said, "I didn't ever try to commit fraud on anyone; I was shocked by what happened this month"; in a published DM exchange with a Vox reporter he said he regretted filing for bankruptcy and thought that "regulators make everything worse." In January he pleaded not guilty to all counts, which include wire fraud, conspiracy to commit money laundering and conspiracy to misuse customer funds. He could face up to 115 years in jail if convicted on all charges.

TechCrunch's 2023-10-02 summary of his standing on the eve of trial: SBF has been denied bail; his name is mud (or much worse) among those who have lost money in Alameda or FTX; and those who might not have had positions in these still blame him for other crypto woes, because he set off a ripple effect.



---


# Sam Bankman-Fried's Federal Fraud Trial

Sam Bankman-Fried, the founder of bankrupt cryptocurrency exchange FTX, is charged with seven counts of fraud and money laundering following the collapse of his cryptocurrency empire the previous year, and was on trial in New York in October 2023.

Two fixed points anchor the proceeding as CNBC described it on 2023-10-06. A U.S. judge revoked Bankman-Fried's bail at a hearing in a New York courthouse on August 11, 2023. And on Thursday, Oct. 5, 2023, Matt Huang, co-founder of Paradigm Operations LP, arrived at the New York court to appear in the case.



---


# The FTX Trial's Stakes For The Wider Crypto Industry

The Verge argued that the trial of Sam Bankman-Fried is likely to be more consequential than just whether the man himself is found guilty: depending on what evidence is introduced, it could be rough for the entire crypto industry.

The grounds are the unpredictability of what a trial surfaces, voiced by Yesha Yadav, a law professor at Vanderbilt University: "How much damage can this trial do to the already beaten-down reputation of the industry at this point? This trial is going to be an excruciating moment for the industry because no one knows what kind of evidence might come out." The warrant joining that uncertainty to industry-wide stakes is that the industry's reputation is already beaten down, so evidence introduced against one exchange's founder lands on the whole sector rather than on him alone.



---


# The SBF Trial Proceedings

Sam Bankman-Fried is in court for alleged fraud and money laundering while leading crypto exchange FTX and sister company Alameda. TechCrunch's 2023-10-02 preview placed the case in the Manhattan Federal Court, describing the disgraced cryptocurrency entrepreneur as accused of orchestrating "one of the biggest financial frauds in American history": the multibillion-dollar collapse of FTX, the crypto exchange he founded and led. SBF, as he is known, has pleaded not guilty to some seven charges of fraud and conspiracy.

The trial kicked off with jury selection October 3. By TechCrunch's 2023-10-06 update the case was entering its next chapter, with proceedings resuming Thursday: as confirmed during a teleconference Wednesday, SBF would be taking the stand along with a handful of other witnesses, as the onus shifted toward the defense after the prosecution brought its case to its conclusion.

Access to the proceedings is limited: no devices are allowed, so reports are being physically put together within the courtroom, or sent to overflow rooms. The jury's composition ranges from a train conductor to a retired investment banker who attended Stanford University, and TechCrunch pointed readers to a special joint episode of its Equity and Chain Reaction podcasts for a better sense of the vibe between the jurors and the rest of the court.

A second account of the same events was arriving in parallel: "Going Infinite," a book by Michael Lewis chronicling the rise and fall of SBF, was set to debut on the first day of the trial.



---


# FTX Fraud Charges And The SEC's Allegation

Sam Bankman-Fried, the founder of the failed cryptocurrency exchange FTX, faced seven counts of wire fraud and conspiracy — specifically, two counts of wire fraud and five conspiracy charges — and the Securities and Exchange Commission alleged that FTX was a fraud "from the start," with a "multi-billion-dollar deficiency caused by his own misappropriation of customer funds." The Verge repeated this framing at the head of each of its trial dispatches through October 2023, and in its October 28th, 2023 write-up reported that Bankman-Fried had been found guilty on seven counts including charges of wire fraud.

The boundary of the concept is the mix of charge types: the indictment paired substantive wire fraud counts with conspiracy counts rather than resting on a single offence, and the SEC's civil allegation about the exchange's origins ran alongside the criminal case rather than being part of it. The Verge's reporter, writing as the prosecution's case neared its end on October 26th, 2023, added an impression of the people the charges swept in: all the co-conspirators seemed oddly younger than their years, as though they had got stuck in the "math camp forever" environment Bankman-Fried created for them and simply failed to grow up.



---


# Going Infinite: Michael Lewis On Sam Bankman-Fried

Michael Lewis's October 2023 book is an account of Sam Bankman-Fried, published by Allen Lane at $55 on 3 October, The Sydney Morning Herald listed on 1 October 2023.

Its subject is defined by the arc: Bankman-Fried set up his cryptocurrency exchange, FTX, in 2019 and three years later was rolling in money, but when the crypto world went pear-shaped his business hit an irreversible tailspin, and he now faces multiple charges and was due in court on 3 October.

The reviewer's warrant for reading it is the author: "If anyone can be relied on to tell this story of a financial Icarus with verve and narrative flair, it's Michael Lewis, author of Liar's Poker, Moneyball, and The Big Short." A caveat is attached — "No doubt the updated edition will have the verdict on SBF."

qid: Who, according to articles from Fortune, The Age, and TechCrunch, is the individual associated with a vision for AI's future, was not ousted by co-founders of a related company, and is suspected of not being completely honest with the board?
context:
# AlphaGo As Evidence For AI Risk Concerns

Rationalists, effective altruists and others who worried about the risks of AI claimed the computer's win at Go validated their fears. The evidence cited is the pace of progress rather than the game itself: "This is another indication that AI is progressing faster than even many experts anticipated," wrote Victoria Krakovna, who would soon join DeepMind as an "AI safety" researcher, in a blog post.

The consequences inside DeepMind followed the same worry. Its founders were increasingly concerned about what Google would do with their inventions and in 2017 tried to break away from the company; Google responded by increasing the salaries and stock award packages of the DeepMind founders and their staff, and they stayed put. The ethics board never had a second meeting.



---


# The OpenAI Board Ousts Sam Altman, November 2023

As reported on November 18, 2023, the OpenAI board had ejected billionaire and AI evangelist Sam Altman from his CEO role after an apparent vote of no confidence. The board's exact wording in a release issued that afternoon: Altman's "departure follows a deliberative review process by the board, which concluded that he was not consistently candid in his communications with the board, hindering its ability to exercise its responsibilities."

What followed was a whirlwind four days for OpenAI, the generative AI poster child behind the smash hit ChatGPT. The board ousted CEO and co-founder Altman and demoted president and co-founder Greg Brockman, who subsequently resigned, paving the way for what looked like a mutiny by staff insisting the founders be reinstated post-haste. By the time TechCrunch wrote again on November 21, 2023, Microsoft had already hired Altman and Brockman to head up a new internal AI unit — though, as things transpired, nothing had actually been signed yet, with rumors suggesting the ousted leaders might actually return to OpenAI after all, in some capacity at least.

TechCrunch cautioned on November 18 that the full truth would not be known for a long time, as the characters in the drama are likely to be NDA'ed up. Per various whispers and leaks, an all-hands meeting about the situation that afternoon did not produce any revelations beyond banal reassurances that the company is fine and they will get a fresh CEO soon.



---


# DeepMind's Ethics Board And Its Single Meeting In 2015

When Musk invested in DeepMind he broke his own informal rule that he would not invest in any company he didn't run himself, and the downsides were already apparent when, only a month or so after his birthday spat with Larry Page, he again found himself face to face with his former friend. The occasion was the first meeting of DeepMind's ethics board on 14 August 2015, a board set up at the insistence of the startup's founders to ensure their technology did no harm after the sale. The members convened in a conference room just outside Musk's office at SpaceX, but that is where Musk's control ended: when Google bought DeepMind it bought the whole thing, and Musk was out, financially ahead but unhappy. Three Google executives now firmly in control of DeepMind were there, Page, Sergey Brin, a Google co-founder and Tesla investor, and Eric Schmidt, Google's chair, along with other attendees including Reid Hoffman, another PayPal founder, and Toby Ord, an Australian philosopher studying "existential risk".

The DeepMind founders reported that they were pushing ahead with their work but were aware the technology carried serious risks. Mustafa Suleyman gave a presentation called "The Pitchforkers Are Coming", telling the board that AI could lead to an explosion in disinformation and fretting that as the technology replaced countless jobs in coming years the public would accuse Google of stealing their livelihoods, so Google would need to share its wealth with the millions who could no longer find work and provide a "universal basic income". Musk agreed, but it was pretty clear the Google guests were not prepared to embark on a redistribution of their wealth: Schmidt said he thought the worries were completely overblown, and Page, in his usual whisper, agreed, arguing AI would create more jobs than it took away. Eight months later DeepMind had a breakthrough that stunned the AI community and the world, when a DeepMind machine called AlphaGo beat one of the world's best players at the ancient game of Go, a match streamed over the internet and watched by 200 million people across the globe, though most researchers had assumed AI needed another 10 years to muster the ingenuity to do that; the South Korean professional Lee Se-dol played Go against AlphaGo in March 2016.



---


# The AI Risk Paradox Among Tech Billionaires

At the heart of the competition to build artificial intelligence is a brain-stretching paradox: the people who say they are most worried about AI are among the most determined to create it and enjoy its riches, and they have justified their ambition with their strong belief that they alone can keep AI from endangering Earth. The grounds are the shape of the debate itself. Eight years after an argument between Elon Musk and Larry Page, that argument seems prescient, because the question of whether AI will elevate the world or destroy it, or at least inflict grave damage, has framed an ongoing debate among Silicon Valley founders, chatbot users, academics, legislators and regulators about whether the technology should be controlled or set free.

That debate has pitted some of the world's richest men against one another: Musk, Page, Mark Zuckerberg of Meta, tech investor Peter Thiel, Satya Nadella of Microsoft and Sam Altman of OpenAI, all of whom have fought for a piece of a business that one day could be worth trillions of dollars, and for the power to shape it. The narrative anchor is that Musk and Page stopped speaking soon after the party that summer, and that a few weeks later Musk dined with Altman, who was then running a tech incubator, and several researchers in a private room at the Rosewood hotel in Menlo Park, California, a favoured deal-making spot close to the venture capital offices of Sand Hill Road.



---


# Anthropic's Founding By Former OpenAI Researchers

Dario Amodei, a researcher with ties to the effective altruist community, had been on hand at the Rosewood hotel when OpenAI was born, and was leading the lab's efforts to build a neural network called a large language model that could learn from enormous amounts of digital text: by analysing countless Wikipedia articles, digital books and message boards it could generate text on its own, and it also had the unfortunate habit of making things up. It was called GPT-3 and was released in the summer of 2020, and researchers inside OpenAI, Google and other companies thought this rapidly improving technology could be a path to artificial general intelligence. Amodei was unhappy about the Microsoft deal because he thought it was taking OpenAI in a really commercial direction, and he and other researchers went to the board to try to push Altman out, according to five people familiar with the matter; after they failed, they left, worrying, like DeepMind's founders before them, that their new corporate overlords would favour commercial interests over safety.

In 2021 the group of about 15 engineers and scientists created a new lab called Anthropic, with the plan of building AI the way the effective altruists thought it should be done, with very tight controls. Anthropic disputes the account of the board approach: "There was no attempt to remove Sam Altman from OpenAI by the co-founders of Anthropic," said an Anthropic spokesperson, Sally Aldous. "The co-founders themselves came to the conclusion that they wished to depart OpenAI to start their own company, made this known to OpenAI's leadership, and over several weeks negotiated an exit on mutually agreeable terms." Anthropic accepted a $US4 billion investment from Amazon and another $US2 billion from Google two years later. After OpenAI received another $US2 billion from Microsoft, Altman and another senior executive, Greg Brockman, visited Bill Gates at his sprawling mansion on the shores of Lake Washington, outside Seattle; the Microsoft founder was no longer involved in the company day to day but kept in regular touch with its executives.



---


# OpenAI Board's Merger Approach To Anthropic

During the leadership crisis, OpenAI's board of directors approached Dario Amodei, the co-founder and CEO of rival large-language model developer Anthropic, about a potential merger of the two companies, according to a report by The Information.

The approach was part of an effort by OpenAI to persuade Amodei to replace Altman as CEO. Amodei quickly turned down the CEO offer.



---


# The Analyst View That Altman's Exit Was Not A Business Problem

Forrester analyst Rowan Curran speculated that Altman's departure, "while sudden," did not likely reflect deeper business problems — attacking the inference from a shocking exit to trouble in the company's technology or commercial position.

"This seems to be a case of an executive transition that was about issues with the individual in question, and not with the underlying technology or business," Curran said.

qid: Does the article from Cnbc | World Business News Leader suggest that the U.S. presidential election has a significant influence on Ukraine's future, whereas the article from Engadget implies that Russia's invasion of Ukraine has had a major impact on Globalization and the perception of the twenty-first century, indicating differing primary concerns for Ukraine's situation?
context:
# Ukraine 2024 Mobilisation and Negotiation Prospects

Ukraine's Defence Ministry said in the week before 25 December 2023 that its main goal in 2024 is to boost its domestic defence industry in the face of uncertain future supplies from its Western allies. It has also changed conscription laws, foreseeing the need to bolster its forces, which are dwarfed in size by Russia's but are more highly trained and equipped. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that week that the military had asked for up to 500,000 additional conscripts, but that he needed to hear "more arguments" to support the sensitive and costly proposal.

On talks, CNBC reported that with both Ukraine and Russia investing heavily in the war it is unlikely there will be any negotiations to end the conflict or agree a cease-fire, because defence analysts argue that neither side would want to enter negotiations unless in a position of strength and able to dictate terms.

The condition that could change this is political. "In the case of a Republican winning the presidential election next year, especially if that's Donald Trump, who seems to be the front-runner, and [if] funding is decreased substantially, then there will be increased pressure on Ukraine to negotiate," Mario Bikarski, a Europe and Russia analyst at the Economist Intelligence Unit, told CNBC.



---


# Ukraine War 2024 Stalemate Outlook

Military experts and defence analysts told CNBC, in a report published on 25 December 2023, that a breakthrough in Ukraine in 2024 is unlikely. At the start of 2023 hopes were high that a much-vaunted Ukrainian counteroffensive, expected in the spring, would change the dial in the war against Russia; it did not. The experts predict intense fighting is likely to continue into the next year, but say Kyiv's forces are unlikely to launch any more counteroffensives, while Russia is likely to focus on consolidating the territory it has already seized, particularly in eastern Ukraine.

Away from the battlefield, the analysts said the trajectory the Russia-Ukraine war takes in 2024 will mostly be dictated thousands of miles away in the US, Ukraine's largest military supporter, and by whether aid declines in the run-up to and following the US presidential election.

Retired Army Lt. Gen. Stephen Twitty, former deputy commander of the US European Command, told CNBC: "War is an uncertain endeavor. Russia can win the war, or the Ukrainians can win the war. And, as you're seeing things now, if you really think about it, what has been achieved this year? Very little has been achieved by Russia, and you can say the same thing for the Ukrainians." He set out the condition that would break the deadlock: "We're in this situation now where if there's not a clear winner, there's going to be a stalemate, and there's going to be, perhaps, a future frozen conflict. What can tilt the balance, in my view, is if the Ukrainians are not resupplied and they're not re-funded and they don't get the equipment and people that they need. Then this war could tilt to the Russians."



---


# Argument That a Trump Presidency Would Not Doom Ukraine

Kurt Volker challenges the premise that a Trump election victory would mean abandonment of Ukraine, while conceding that it would make future funding uncertain. "I doubt that even if Trump were elected that he would abandon support for Ukraine overall, because it would be a disaster for U.S. interests, and it would appear to be a failure," he told CNBC. "You'd have these images of Russians overrunning places, and brutality and so forth, so I don't think he wants that."

The attack is on the inference from Trump's past relations with Moscow to a wholesale cut-off, not on the observation that his intentions are unclear: "But it's not clear exactly what he would do to try to end the war." For his part, Trump has said he would be able to resolve the Ukraine war "in one day" if reelected, saying he would convince the leaders of Ukraine and Russia to make a deal.



---


# US Election Risk to Ukraine Military Aid

The model CNBC sets out on 25 December 2023 runs from US politics to Ukraine's battlefield prospects. Another year of war in Europe has undoubtedly drained Western military resources and the political appetite to maintain massive amounts of military aid for Ukraine, and ongoing funding for Ukraine is far from secure in 2024, given that the US presidential election could herald a seismic change in attitude toward and support for Kyiv.

The specific variable is former US President Donald Trump, the Republican front-runner, who cultivated close relations with his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin during his presidency. There are concerns that, given those previous good relations with Moscow and his "America First" policy, aid for Ukraine could be shelved rapidly.

The relation holds because of Ukraine's dependency structure, and it is not offset by Europe. "I think it's important to understand the extent to which Ukraine is reliant on the U.S. right now, because it's quite significantly more reliant on the U.S. than it is on the EU," Sam Cranny-Evans, defence analyst at the Royal United Services Institute, told CNBC. "If the U.S. election goes in a way that is not in Ukraine's favor, coupled with the fact that the EU is not really stepping up to the plate — it's ammunition production is so far off what it should have been by now to give Ukraine a hope of surviving and a hope of victory — it's not a very cheery prediction for 2024."



---


# Three Forces: Climate, Authoritarianism And The Internet

Holly Jean Buck frames the twenty-first century as three overlapping stories — climate change, authoritarianism, and the Internet — whose interaction is the real subject.

The first is the energy transition. Burning hills and glowing red skies, stone-dry riverbeds, expanses of brown water engulfing tiny human rooftops: this is the setting for the twenty-first century, and for many working on climate and energy the plot is about making the energy transition happen — completely transforming both energy and land use in order to avoid the most devastating impacts of climate change, or failing to.

The second is authoritarianism, and it is even more urgent. About four billion people, or 54 percent of the world, in ninety-five countries, live under tyranny in fully authoritarian or competitive authoritarian regimes. In this narration the century began with a wave of crushed democratic uprisings and continued with the election of authoritarian leaders around the world who began to dismantle democratic institutions; any illusion of the success of globalization, or of the century representing a break from the brutal twentieth, was stripped away with Russia's most recent invasion of Ukraine. The plot is less clear given the failure of democracy-building efforts in the twentieth century, leaving only a faintly discernable storyline of general resistance and rebuilding imperfect democracies.

The third is the penetration of the Internet into every sphere of daily, social, and political life. Despite turn-of-the-century talk about the Information Age, we are only beginning to conceptualize what this means; the current plot is about the centralization of discourse on a few corporate platforms, whose rise brings potential to network democratic uprisings as well as to buoy authoritarian leaders through post-truth memes and algorithms optimized to dish out anger and hatred. This is a more challenging story to narrate because the setting is everywhere: it unfolds in our bedrooms while we should be sleeping or waking up, filling the most quotidian moments of waiting in line in the grocery store or while in transit, and the characters are us, even more intimately than with climate change. While we are increasingly aware of the influence that shifting our media and social lives onto big tech platforms has on our democracy, less attention is devoted to the influence this has on our ability to respond to climate change.

Put the three together and the expected combination is optimistic: climate activists using the capabilities of the Internet to further both networked protest and energy democracy — in particular, advocacy for a version of "energy democracy" that looks like wind, water, and solar, decentralized systems, and local community control of energy.



---


# Volker's Case for Continued and Expanded Ukraine Aid

Former US Ambassador to NATO Kurt Volker told CNBC he believes American and EU aid packages for Ukraine will be approved come January, and that this funding would tide Ukraine over for another year militarily. His argument goes further than continuity: he says the packages must include more advanced weaponry, such as F-16 fighter jets, which have been pledged by Norway, Denmark and the Netherlands.

# Going Infinite: Michael Lewis On Sam Bankman-Fried

Michael Lewis's October 2023 book is an account of Sam Bankman-Fried, published by Allen Lane at $55 on 3 October, The Sydney Morning Herald listed on 1 October 2023.

Its subject is defined by the arc: Bankman-Fried set up his cryptocurrency exchange, FTX, in 2019 and three years later was rolling in money, but when the crypto world went pear-shaped his business hit an irreversible tailspin, and he now faces multiple charges and was due in court on 3 October.

The reviewer's warrant for reading it is the author: "If anyone can be relied on to tell this story of a financial Icarus with verve and narrative flair, it's Michael Lewis, author of Liar's Poker, Moneyball, and The Big Short." A caveat is attached — "No doubt the updated edition will have the verdict on SBF."



---


# Going Infinite: Michael Lewis's Account Of SBF's Political Dealings

Michael Lewis's book "Going Infinite" debuted on the first day of Sam Bankman-Fried's trial, and details about Bankman-Fried's political dealings emerging from it include his alleged attempt to buy off Donald Trump to get him not to run again for president.

TechCrunch's team was focused on the Manhattan Federal Court for the trial of Bankman-Fried, the disgraced entrepreneur accused of orchestrating the collapse of the cryptocurrency exchange FTX; the Lewis book is the second channel through which the week's revelations arrived. The reporting is framed as allegation rather than established fact, and it comes from the book rather than from courtroom testimony. The item appeared in TechCrunch's Week in Review of October 7, 2023.



---


# Sam Bankman-Fried

Sam Bankman-Fried is the former CEO of the bankrupt crypto exchange FTX, whose highly anticipated criminal trial started on the Tuesday before TechCrunch's 2023-10-01 report, to determine whether he is guilty of seven counts of fraud and conspiracy. As one former federal prosecutor put it: "The odds seem to be stacked against him at this point."

He was 31 years old and co-founded FTX in 2019; within a few years the once third-largest crypto exchange's valuation hit $32 billion at its peak, and the company is now trying to claw back any funds to distribute to creditors. Before the fall he was even compared to Warren Buffet, and many called him the white horse of crypto — a description TechCrunch notes it never applied to him.

Bankman-Fried, however, maintained his innocence. At The New York Times' DealBook Summit he appeared virtually from the Bahamas and said, "I didn't ever try to commit fraud on anyone; I was shocked by what happened this month"; in a published DM exchange with a Vox reporter he said he regretted filing for bankruptcy and thought that "regulators make everything worse." In January he pleaded not guilty to all counts, which include wire fraud, conspiracy to commit money laundering and conspiracy to misuse customer funds. He could face up to 115 years in jail if convicted on all charges.

TechCrunch's 2023-10-02 summary of his standing on the eve of trial: SBF has been denied bail; his name is mud (or much worse) among those who have lost money in Alameda or FTX; and those who might not have had positions in these still blame him for other crypto woes, because he set off a ripple effect.



---


# Day Two Of The Bankman-Fried Trial: Jury Selection And The Courtroom Audience

On the second day of Sam Bankman-Fried's fraud trial, the jury was selected on Wednesday morning, after which lawyers for the government and then for Bankman-Fried delivered opening statements that told two very different stories of the former FTX CEO's sudden rise and almost instantaneous fall. The central question framed by the proceedings was who Bankman-Fried, the former CEO of crypto exchange FTX, really is: a liar and a fraud, or someone who acted in good faith and, like many a startup founder, flew too close to the sun. That answer, the account notes, ultimately lies with the jury.

The day featured pointed allegations, a friend from MIT, and an audience replete with big names, including Bankman-Fried's professorial parents and Damian Williams, the U.S. attorney for the Southern District of New York. Bankman-Fried himself spent most of the day in court staring into a laptop while seated between his two attorneys. The prosecution's account of his alleged crimes was described as featuring a study in contrasts.



---


# Bankman-Fried's Pre-Collapse Public Image Strategy

Before his fall, Bankman-Fried made himself out to be the Good Boy of crypto — the trustworthy face of a sometimes-shady industry — and he was very interested in publicity, sitting for many interviews both before and after the collapse of FTX.

The Verge attributes FTX's quick rise as an industry force at least in part to that appetite for attention: Bankman-Fried gave interviews freely and quickly rose to public prominence, positioning himself as an important, boyish face for crypto even though FTX hadn't been in the business as long as competing exchanges such as Coinbase, Kraken, or Gemini. At one point he told a colleague at FTX that "I honestly think it's negative EV" — possibly "expected value," as in poker — "for me to cut my hair. I think it's important for people to think I look crazy." Because he was so successful at this kind of public relations, his fall from grace became another mark against an industry already roiled by bankruptcies and scandals; The Verge adds that more trouble for the industry is likely to come from one crucial element of the fraud trial, the part where the government must prove intent.



---


# FTX Fraud Charges And The SEC's Allegation

Sam Bankman-Fried, the founder of the failed cryptocurrency exchange FTX, faced seven counts of wire fraud and conspiracy — specifically, two counts of wire fraud and five conspiracy charges — and the Securities and Exchange Commission alleged that FTX was a fraud "from the start," with a "multi-billion-dollar deficiency caused by his own misappropriation of customer funds." The Verge repeated this framing at the head of each of its trial dispatches through October 2023, and in its October 28th, 2023 write-up reported that Bankman-Fried had been found guilty on seven counts including charges of wire fraud.

The boundary of the concept is the mix of charge types: the indictment paired substantive wire fraud counts with conspiracy counts rather than resting on a single offence, and the SEC's civil allegation about the exchange's origins ran alongside the criminal case rather than being part of it. The Verge's reporter, writing as the prosecution's case neared its end on October 26th, 2023, added an impression of the people the charges swept in: all the co-conspirators seemed oddly younger than their years, as though they had got stuck in the "math camp forever" environment Bankman-Fried created for them and simply failed to grow up.



---


# Bankman-Fried's Conduct On Direct Examination

On October 28th, 2023, before the cross-examination had even begun, Judge Lewis Kaplan had already instructed Sam Bankman-Fried to answer the question he was being asked by his own lawyer — which The Verge's reporter called honestly kind of incredible, a man torpedoing his own credibility on direct testimony. The count of "Objection, narrative!" to Bankman-Fried's answers, followed by "Sustained," stood at three; the main thing clear so far, she wrote, was that he really loves the sound of his own voice, and that sometimes when he says "we," he only means himself.

The scolding was a pattern across two days. The day before, during an evidentiary hearing, Bankman-Fried had been repeatedly scolded by Kaplan for not answering prosecutor Danielle Sassoon's questions on cross-examination; on this day he was scolded for not answering his own counsel Mark Cohen's questions on direct, and he occasionally interrupted Cohen with "yes" and "yup." Much of the morning went on vocabulary — explaining "Amazon Web Services" and "database" was a bit too detail-oriented — and when Bankman-Fried tried to define "market manipulation," Kaplan told the jury that he, the judge, was the final authority on that.

In fairness, the reporter added, he was clearer and much easier to understand than at the evidentiary hearing the day before, with a minimum of word salad; she could not tell whether he was more relaxed or simply more rehearsed, and said she would be watching to see whether he became much less coherent once Sassoon got him on cross. The jury watched all of it intently.



---


# Bankman-Fried's Post-Bankruptcy Media Tour

After FTX declared bankruptcy, Bankman-Fried went on an extensive media tour, doing interviews with The New York Times' Andrew Ross Sorkin and Good Morning America — and he kept giving interviews even under house arrest, including with The New Yorker.

The Verge's reading of his motive: Bankman-Fried seemed to think that if he just explained things, everyone would understand that what he did was a mistake, not a crime.

qid: Does the 'Science News For Students' article suggest that previous hydrogel research did not explore the relationship between salt content and water absorption, while the 'Advanced Science News' article indicates that the hydrogel used in aqueous zinc iodine batteries has been specifically engineered with functional groups for anode and cathode affinity?

# The Zincophilic and Iodophilic Hydrogel Mechanism

The anode and cathode sides of the hydrogel carry different functional groups that make it zincophilic (with an affinity for zinc) and iodophilic (with an affinity for iodine) respectively, and this asymmetry is what lets one electrolyte fix problems at both electrodes.

On the anode side, the design repels dissolved polyiodides — negatively charged ions composed entirely of iodine atoms — allowing the zinc to be deposited uniformly and protecting the anode from iodine-caused corrosion. Ensuring that zinc accumulates evenly on the anode side is the purpose of the hydrogel modification, Hongjin Fan explained, and it mitigates the diffusion back and forth of polysulfide between anode and cathode, the so-called "shuttle effect," which can cause poor cycling stability and severe anode corrosion in batteries. On the cathode side, the polyiodides are immobilized, and redox reactions — in which iodine is both stripped of electrons (oxidation) and granted electrons (reduction) — are sped up thanks to the synchronized rapid transport of ions and electrons, so the hydrogel electrolyte also accelerates the iodine conversion reaction. Finally, the solid nature of the hydrogel electrolyte limits the growth of dendrites through its mechanical strength, acting as a physical barrier not present in liquid electrolytes.



---


# Hetero-Polyionic Hydrogel Electrolyte Design

A hetero-polyionic hydrogel electrolyte is one in which functional groups carrying either positive or negative charges are deliberately introduced into the hydrogel, so that a single "hetero-hydrogel" can mitigate challenges on both the anode and the cathode sides of a zinc-iodine battery.

"The core concept of our research is that we design the hydrogel electrolytes by introducing functional groups [specific groupings of atoms within molecules that have their own characteristic properties] that carry either positive or negative charges," said Hongjin Fan, a professor at Nanyang Technological University's (NTU) School of Physical and Mathematical Sciences and an author of the new paper in Advanced Materials, in which he and his co-authors examine different electrolytes for aqueous zinc ion batteries that take the form of hydrogels — three-dimensional network structures capable of storing large amounts of water. The stated aim of the research is to improve the stability and safety of alternatives to rechargeable lithium-ion batteries using aqueous zinc and hydrogels. The reference is: Peihua Yang, Hong Jin Fan, et al., "Hetero-Polyionic Hydrogels Enable Dendrites-Free Aqueous Zn-I2 Batteries with Fast Kinetics," Advanced Materials (2023), DOI: 10.1002/adma.202306531.



---


# Barriers to Commercializing Zinc-Iodine Batteries

Against the promising cycling results, Hongjin Fan acknowledged there is much to do before the battery can be brought to the mass market — attacking the premise that laboratory stability is enough to make zinc-iodine batteries a lithium-ion substitute.

"We have to note that in terms of mass or volume energy density, so far, the ZIB is still far from the commercial lithium-ion batteries," Fan conceded. "The hydrogel electrolytes need to be further improved in terms of ion conductivity and stability. In addition, hydrogel electrolytes should be compatible with other battery components, including electrodes and separators." He also pointed out that large-scale and cost-effective production methods for hydrogel electrolytes are a prerequisite before aqueous zinc-iodine batteries are ready for widescale commercial use, which will include optimizing the production process of hydrogels as well as sourcing affordable raw materials and minimizing waste generated during manufacturing. "Ensuring the safety and reliability of hydrogel-based batteries is also necessary," Fan concluded. "Rigorous testing and evaluation of the potential environmental impact of hydrogel electrolytes, from raw material extraction to disposal, are vital to meeting sustainability goals and gaining public trust."



---


# Record Salt Loading Hydrogel Results

The gels soaked up more and more saltwater over time, and the top absorber got about three times saltier than previous hydrogels, caching 20 grams (0.7 ounce) of salt per gram of gel — and it absorbed more moisture than previous gels too.

To test moisture uptake, the researchers dried their gels and placed them in environments with different levels of humidity; even in relatively dry air, such as that found in deserts, the best-performing hydrogel absorbed 15 percent more water than previous hydrogels. The team reported its findings on May 18 in Advanced Materials. "We did this in a very simple and low-cost way, which makes it even more exciting," says Díaz-Marín, whose team still needs to test how to get all that water out of the gels afterward. "I am impressed by their results," says Swee Ching Tan, a materials scientist at the National University of Singapore who works with hydrogels but did not take part in the study. "This could be a new world record." The new work, he says, could help with the water crisis by producing safe drinking water in places that lack it.



---


# Salty Hydrogel Atmospheric Water Harvesting

A hydrogel is a mesh of large molecules called polymers; the new hydrogel captures humidity — water vapor — from the air and expands like a sponge in water as it does so, then releases the water it has absorbed when heated by the sun.

Carlos Díaz-Marín, a mechanical engineer at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) in Cambridge, leads a team developing a device to address water shortages that would affordably pull water from air without a need for electricity, and the key ingredient is a new, super-salty gel. The idea is not new: many types of hydrogels have been developed to suck water from air, and previous work showed that adding salts to hydrogels upped how much water they could absorb, because salts attract moisture, including from the air, on account of their chemical properties. What was unknown was how much salt a hydrogel could stash, and how pushing that salt content to the maximum might boost the hydrogel's water-slurping power — the question Díaz-Marín and his team set out to answer.



---


# Hydrogel Zinc-Iodine Battery Cycling Results

Testing their aqueous hydrogel-modified zinc-iodine battery, the team found the decay rate was ultralow, with energy storage capacity retained to an outstanding level over the course of 18,000 discharge and recharge cycles — outstripping the stability of currently available zinc-iodine batteries.

The test battery also delivered some surprising results. "The adhesion between the polyanionic and polycationic hydrogel components is remarkably robust, effectively mitigating the swelling of the hydrogel even in the absence of a cellulose paper scaffold," Hongjin Fan explained. "The unexpectedly strong iodine adsorption capability of the positively charged hydrogel has led to a striking and rapid color transformation, exceeding our initial expectations."



---


# The Lithium Chloride Hydrogel Soaking Experiment

The researchers made tubes of hydrogel from polyacrylamide, a polymer made of long, threadlike molecules, cut the tubes into thin disks, soaked them in water containing different amounts of lithium chloride — a salt — and weighed the disks each day to see how much of the salty water they had absorbed.

The step that mattered was duration. Such tests had been done before, but for relatively short times, Díaz-Marín says: "Instead of soaking for two days, we did this for up to two months." The extra time made a big difference.



---


# Zinc-Iodine Battery Advantages and the Dendrite Problem

Rechargeable zinc-iodine batteries are one potential substitute for lithium-ion batteries, with the advantages of being safer, costing less, and being more friendly to the environment than lithium alternatives.

They are not perfect, however. Composed of a negative iodine electrode and a positive zinc electrode, these batteries suffer from lower energy output compared with commercial non-aqueous lithium batteries, and from the growth of zinc dendrites on the anodes — projections of material that build on electrodes and short batteries when they cross from one electrode to another — as well as corrosion of the zinc anode, which together result in reduced efficiency and even short-circuiting.



---


# MIT Hydrogel Drinking Water Device

The MIT team is designing a hydrogel-based device that produces drinking water rather than growing food: at night, an open box containing their gel captures water vapor from the air; the next day the sun heats the hydrogel in the box, releasing the moisture; the box also contains a material that can be cooled without using electricity, so that when the water vapor touches that cold surface it condenses into droplets — like morning dew on grass — and the clean water falls into a storage chamber.

The team is working to engineer a device that can extract 2 to 5 liters (0.5 to 1.3 gallons) a day, which should supply someone's average drinking-water needs. As places get drier, new sources of drinking water will be needed, and Díaz-Marín says it is great that hydrogels can make water anywhere; for ultra-dry places with few other options, he says, they could be a lifesaver.

Kravata is a Colombia-based, seed-stage platform in Alliance DAO's All11 cohort that provides a fiat-to-crypto on and off-ramp for LatAm, founded by Felipe Montes and Juliana Montes. Alameda Research was the cryptocurrency trading firm Bankman-Fried started in 2017 during a crypto bull run, and it was named for Alameda County in California, where its first office was set up. Michael Lewis's October 2023 book is an account of Sam Bankman-Fried, published by Allen Lane at $55 on 3 October, The Sydney Morning Herald listed on 1 October 2023.

The reviewer's warrant for reading it is the author: "If anyone can be relied on to tell this story of a financial Icarus with verve and narrative flair, it's Michael Lewis, author of Liar's Poker, Moneyball, and The Big Short." A caveat is attached — "No doubt the updated edition will have the verdict on SBF."



---


# Proving Intent In The FTX Fraud Case

The government's case proceeds in two parts. The first is pretty simple and a little boring: prosecutors must show that certain transactions took place, using whatever records the Southern District of New York has for them.

The second part is where the drama is likely to come, says Christopher LaVigne, a litigation partner and co-chair of the cryptocurrency practice at the law firm Withers: prosecutors have to connect those transactions to Bankman-Fried, show that he knew what he was doing was wrong, and prove that he lied about it anyway. "What was he saying to his parents and his other advisors about this?" LaVigne asks. "What conversations happened between him and his co-conspirators that are now cooperating against him?" To further establish intent, the government can use Bankman-Fried's own words: the indictment calls his November 2022 tweets "false and misleading." "We had him going out directly to the internet," LaVigne says — if he wrote things on Twitter or said things in interviews that weren't true, that's more fodder for the case: "They can point to that and say, 'This is what he said, this is what actually happened.'" Other evidence may include Signal messages and testimony from co-conspirators who pleaded guilty to their own charges. Alameda Research CEO Caroline Ellison, who was also sometimes Bankman-Fried's girlfriend, may play an important role — Bankman-Fried leaked her diaries to The New York Times and was consequently jailed for witness tampering. The government has indicated FTX co-founder Gary Wang and engineering head Nishad Singh will also be among the witnesses called to testify about Bankman-Fried.



---


# Kraken's SEC Charges And Staking Settlement

Binance's resolution came less than a day after the SEC charged Kraken, the third largest crypto exchange by trading volume, with allegedly operating as an "unregistered securities exchange, broker, dealer and clearing agency."

That was not Kraken's first SEC matter. Separately, in February, Kraken agreed to end crypto staking services for U.S. clients and settled a past suit with the SEC after agreeing to pay $30 million in charges for "disgorgement, prejudgment interest and civil penalties."

qid: What company is at the center of antitrust discussions due to its default search engine deals with various tech companies, impact on the internet's appearance, potential legal outcomes regarding phones and app stores, and allegations of harming news publishers' revenue as reported by The Verge and TechCrunch?
context:
# US v. Google: Two Months Into The Search Antitrust Trial

As of TechCrunch's November 13, 2023 roundup, the Justice Department's landmark antitrust case against Google was nearly two months old, and the trial record was still producing fresh revelations. TechCrunch framed it as one of the biggest fights in tech antitrust since the U.S. took Microsoft to trial in the 1990s.

An earlier roundup had already surfaced that Google spent $26.3 billion in 2021 making itself the default search engine across platforms, and that Google tried to have Chrome preinstalled on iPhones. Over the couple of weeks preceding this roundup, more of Google's inner workings came to light, including some of the search engine's most lucrative search queries, the shape of the revenue-share agreements between Google and Android OEMs, and why Expedia has a bone to pick with Google.



---


# What A Ruling Against Google Would Mean For Big Tech

A ruling against Google would not stop at Google: the remedy would likely resemble the Microsoft settlement and the outcome would ripple through the other pending Big Tech cases, because enforcers are using this trial to demonstrate that antitrust law can still take on the largest and most powerful companies in the world.

The grounds for the first half of that claim are the available remedies. If the judge rules against Google, the outcome could look a lot like the Microsoft deal, in which the computer company was required to change its behavior and share its APIs with third-party developers, and was also banned from making anticompetitive and exclusive deals with computer manufacturers. Google might likewise end up having to turn over all or most of the data it has collected to other search engines so they can improve their products and attract more users — a remedy scaled to the disparity the DOJ has cited, that Google gets 16 times more data than Bing does everyday.

The grounds for the ripple effect are the cases already queued behind this one. The FTC sued Amazon in September for using anticompetitive and unfair strategies to illegally maintain its monopoly power. The DOJ has been investigating Apple for years over the company's policy for third-party apps on its devices and whether it unfairly favors its own products. And there is an ongoing case between the FTC and Facebook, in which the agency calls on Facebook to sell Instagram and WhatsApp.

The warrant joining grounds to claim is enforcers' own stake in the result: they will want to show that antitrust law is still relevant and can successfully take on the biggest, most powerful companies in the world, so a win here sets the template the neighbouring cases are argued against. The scope condition is that nothing was settled as of this report — the case is expected to continue for several weeks, bringing to a head one of the biggest fights in tech antitrust since the U.S. took Microsoft to trial in the 1990s.



---


# Google Paid $26.3 Billion In 2021 For Default Search Placement

Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to multiple browsers, phones and platforms — from companies including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla — to be everyone's default search engine. The figure was revealed by Google's search head Prabhakar Raghavan when he testified in court on October 28, according to The Verge.

About $18 billion of that total went directly to Apple, according to a New York Times report published earlier in October 2023, and Google has had its deal with Apple in place since 2003 — so the payment is the current year of a two-decade arrangement, not a one-off. Questioned on the amount of money Google spends to get first pick of search engines, Pichai said the decision was made with the consumer in mind: Google pays big bucks to be everywhere so that it can take in all the data and be the best search engine across different companies' devices, he said, according to The Verge.

The trial also produced evidence that Google understood the value of defaults very early on. U.S. Justice Department lawyer Meagan Bellshaw showed Pichai a 2007 email from a Google product strategy meeting containing data showing that when people changed their browser homepage to Google, they did 15% more Google searches, and that when they switched away, their Google searches dropped 27%. The email summarizing that meeting, sent to Pichai as well as other Google leaders, read: "Nitin argues that focusing on homepage market share is one of the most effective things we can do to make gains in search market share," according to The Verge.



---


# The Google Antitrust Case

The Google antitrust case is the U.S. government's trial over Google's dominance in the online search market, stemming from a 2020 antitrust claim, in which the government argues that Google uses its platforms and its deals with partners to block out competition in search or advertising and thereby to hinder competitors from accessing the data they would need to improve their products.

Its defining features are the conduct at issue and the defence offered against it. Google CEO Sundar Pichai testified Monday in the trial, defending Google's business tactics, including its deal with Apple and other partners to make Google the default search engine. Google's answer is that it is just doing business: everybody wants Google as the default engine because it is the best, and that, the company says, does not make its actions illegal.

The important boundary case is which Google antitrust matter this is. The 2020 search claim is separate from the one filed in January by the Department of Justice, along with eight states including New York, California and Colorado, which aims to "halt Google's anticompetitive scheme, unwind Google's monopolistic grip on the market and restore competition to digital advertising." The search case and the digital-advertising case are distinct proceedings and should not be conflated.

The trial is the venue in which the underlying numbers surface. Monday's hearing revealed plenty of juicy tidbits, including the $26.3 billion Google spent making itself the default search engine across platforms in 2021, and how Google tried to take it further and have Chrome preinstalled on iPhones.



---


# The Claim That SGE And Bard Appropriate Publisher Content

The Helena World Chronicle lawsuit claims that Google's recent advances in AI-based search were implemented with "the goal of discouraging end-users from visiting the websites of Class members who are part of the digital news and publishing line of commerce." The grounds are that Google's AI products both retain users and consume publisher content without permission.

On the Search Generative Experience, the suit argues that SGE offers web searchers a way to seek information in a conversational mode but ultimately keeps users in Google's "walled garden" as it "plagiarizes" their content. The warrant that turns this into a harm publishers cannot escape is that publishers also cannot block SGE, because it uses the same web crawler as Google's general search service, GoogleBot — so opting out of the AI experience would mean opting out of search itself.

On Bard, the suit says Google's Bard AI was trained on a dataset that included "news, magazine and digital publications," citing both a 2023 report from the News Media Alliance and a Washington Post article about AI training data. The Post, which worked with researchers at the Allen Institute for AI, had found that News and Media sites were the third largest category of AI training data.

The case points to other concerns too, such as changing AdSense rates and evidence of improper spoliation of evidence on Google's part through its destruction of chat messages — an issue raised in the recent Epic Games lawsuit against Google over app store antitrust issues, which Epic won.



---


# The U.S. Justice Department's Parallel Antitrust Suits Against Google

The Helena World Chronicle class action arrives alongside the filing of the U.S. Justice Department's lawsuit against Google for monopolizing digital ad technologies, and the complaint also references the Justice Department's 2020 civil antitrust suit over search and search advertising.

The two government cases concern different markets: search and search advertising in the 2020 suit are distinct from the digital ad technologies at issue in the more recent one.



---


# Google's Agreement Not To Promote Chrome To Safari Users

As part of its search deal with Apple, Google agreed not to promote Chrome to Safari users, according to Bloomberg — a restraint that mattered because Google would otherwise have been able to do this with banners, pop-ups and other annoying means in its other Google apps. The same agreement also meant that Apple never switched to a Google competitor, and never allowed users to choose their browser when setting up their iPhones.

The observation surfaced in the antitrust trial, where the amount Google spent on homepage market share has been a fixing point. Earlier in October 2023, the CEOs of Microsoft and DuckDuckGo testified that their search engines would have been far more successful, even competitive with Google, had they been able to make similar deals with Apple. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella even said he was willing to spend $15 billion per year to get Bing into Apple's default search, per The Information — a stated willingness to pay, not a deal that happened.

A second, related admission came from Google's side: Pichai admitted to attempting to get Tim Cook to preinstall Google on every iOS device back in 2018, according to The Verge. His aim, as reported, was to make Google's and Apple's services so connected as to be inseparable.

qid: Did the article from The Verge suggest that law enforcement adequately assessed the harassment threat towards Janani Umamaheswar and Alex Sinha, while the article from CBSSports.com considers Otto Wallin a greater threat to Anthony Joshua than Joseph Parker is to Deontay Wilder?
context:
# Otto Wallin Fighter Profile

Otto Wallin, as characterized by CBSSports.com on Dec. 23, 2023, is a 33-year-old native of Sweden considered much more a live dog than Joseph Parker — that is, a genuinely plausible upset threat rather than a safe opponent.

His discriminating features are size and stance: standing only half an inch shorter than Joshua's 6-foot-6 frame, Wallin is a southpaw. His reputation was extremely bolstered in 2019, when he lost a title shot against Tyson Fury despite opening up a cut that required 47 stitches above Fury's eye and coming close to giving Wallin a stoppage win.



---


# The Cyberstalker's Twitter Campaign Against Asian Academics

When Janani Umamaheswar looked up the Twitter account her former colleague had flagged in March 2022, she found thousands of tweets posted under S.'s name — most of them racist, sexual, vulgar, and violent, and little of the ranting coherent. The user tweeted at all hours, sometimes nearly a hundred times a day, and the tweets focused solely on three people: Umamaheswar, her husband Alex Sinha, and the Vassar professor Catherine Tan who had alerted them. The account had started posting in October of 2021 — seven months of tweets before they knew it existed. It featured an image of a white woman's face that Umamaheswar recognized as the student she once taught.

The targeting spread by association rather than contact. Sinha had never met or taught S., had never been employed on the same campus as his wife, and by then they lived over six hours away from her; Tan had likewise never taught or met S. and did not know her personally, but had published papers with Umamaheswar, and the account's author had linked Tan back to her, likely through that academic work and their benign social media interactions. Anyone Umamaheswar collaborated with professionally or even interacted with online had become a potential target. The tweets frequently denigrated all three for being Asian, using racial slurs against Umamaheswar and Sinha, alleging Sinha was abusive to his wife, and including lines such as "Live in hell bitch" and "I have super detailed deaths I like to think about them experiencing."

The threats escalated over time and across accounts. Sinha decided he needed to monitor the account closely, screenshot everything, and head off any potential danger; Umamaheswar did not want to keep looking. The graphic nature and racist sentiments sent a wave of fear and anger through Sinha, coming in a year when a white man had murdered six Asian women in three Atlanta-area spas and anti-Asian hate crimes had increased by over 300 percent. "There was this moment of 'wow, this has been happening all this time?'" Sinha said. "We moved to another state. We've been living our lives. We've been raising our kids." The tweets kept coming almost every week except during periods when S. was suspended by Twitter before restarting under a new account, reaching at least 40,000 tweets and counting by Sinha's estimate. They included racist slurs casting Sinha as a "dirty Indian hacker" and a terrorist; a tweet from April 16th, 2022 calling for someone to "get rid of" him; a post a month later pairing an image of a grisly murder in Game of Thrones with a farewell to Alex; and "I would like for these professors to die." As Sinha put it: "She calls for people to murder us. She says that she wants me raped. She would pay money to watch us bleed to death." Other tweets described wanting the three of them hanging off a cliff so she could step on their hands and watch them fall, and ended: "I want them to suffer." While Sinha captured the images, Umamaheswar began writing letters to her current administration and to Vassar on behalf of Tan, alerting them to her history with S.



---


# Catherine Tan's Public Disclosure And Law Enforcement Gaps

On November 9th, 2022, after S.'s letter reached Vassar and S. began publicly replying to her tweets with insults, Catherine Tan decided to stop letting a platform that had enabled her harassment get away with it and went public. "I have a stalker," she tweeted. "Recently, she contacted my employer in effort to get me fired. She is racist, and has begun contacting ASIAN ACADEMICS connected w/ me on this platform. So, if that is you, there's a chance she will send a similar letter to your employer. If this happens…please contact me immediately and I will put you in touch with my investigator." She added: "This has been going on for almost a year. I have NEVER met this harasser. I have NEVER engaged with this harasser. This is my first time publicly acknowledging this person." The tweet was shared 4,350 times and received more than 15,000 likes, and she received messages from other users and academics with stories about their own stalkers.

Tan refused to be scared off the platform. She still posts regularly — photos from dinners with friends or of her horseback riding, tweets about her syllabus, her outfits, her husband, class prepping and grading ("I did it. 50 papers graded across 13 days") — and told The Verge, "I'm not going to stop tweeting. I'm not going to adjust my life for this. I have my book coming out at the end of this year. I don't want this person to be in the back of my head. And most of the time, she isn't." Now and then she learns of the latest threat, post, or racial slur, and it upsets her again. Being a collateral victim of a cyberstalker who started out obsessed with someone else went from irritating to infuriating, and the racial taunting especially hits a nerve: "I'm Vietnamese. I was born in the US. Growing up in the '90s and early 2000s, at that time, American culture wasn't as welcoming." Some of S.'s comments claimed Tan "wants to be white"; Tan says she does not, but did struggle to embrace her Asian American identity in her younger years, and dealing with such comments repeatedly in adulthood was at times depleting. She also situated the harassment in academia's own dynamics: "When you publish or you become more public, you're always going to encounter haters, people who are ready to discredit you, people who are ready to undermine your legitimacy. That's true for everybody, but especially for scholars of color." The Supreme Court recently struck down race-based admissions on college campuses in cases that used Asian Americans as plaintiffs and pawns, arguing affirmative action discriminated specifically against them; yet some universities, like one where Tan previously worked, enroll a student body made up predominantly of people of color while the faculty is still overwhelmingly white, which can leave professors of color feeling, as Tan put it, that "we only belong here because we were given special admission, some sort of affirmative action." That makes harassment more intimidating to report: "It's definitely hard. And the people who will really ruin you won't be the stalkers. They're going to be your peers."

Law enforcement offered little. By winter, Sinha had submitted a complaint about S. to the FBI via an online portal and also tried calling; he did not hear back. Sinha, Umamaheswar, and Tan filed police reports in their local jurisdictions, but as Sinha explained, "The local police here will take a complaint from us, but they won't go over there to arrest." The Southern Connecticut State University Police Department had previously arrested S., who was later released, and the harassment did not stop. Tan asked the Poughkeepsie Police Department in New York whether it might reach out to the Hamden Police Department in Connecticut, where S. lives, for assistance, but Poughkeepsie declined. Sinha contacted the New York Division of Human Rights as a hate crime resource, and since he and Tan both live or work in New York they wanted help filing hate crime complaints with New York State Police. "We're all in different states," Tan said. "It's not easy to arrest somebody. Unless she tries to physically harm us, there's not much we can do." Every state has different laws, Sinha said: "It depends on where you are and where the perpetrator is." As a lawyer he believes there is no question S. is breaking various laws — defamation, aggravated harassment, disorderly conduct, stalking, hate crime motivations — some of which could rise to the level of felonies, yet even with all his knowledge, efforts, documentation, and research he has been stonewalled: "If I can't get some traction here, I don't know who could." It is extraordinary how indifferent police have been, he added: "It's a real struggle. You just need commitment from the law enforcement side, and you need a very clear and easy-to-prove violation." For Tan the open question is danger: "There's the uncertainty of what's gonna happen next because we know that she is confrontational. We know that she's not afraid to take action. It's not just a Twitter diary. Is she capable of violence?"

# Commentary That Israeli Intelligence and Defence Failed

The dominant online argument on 7 October 2023, as collected by Business Today, was that the attack represented a massive failure of Israeli intelligence and defence. Its grounds are the gap between Israel's reputation and the outcome.

Journalist Rania Khalek said the strategic planning that must have gone into this against "one of the most high-tech occupation and surveillance systems in the world" will be studied by many, adding: "The Israelis must be totally losing it right now." Tarik Cyril Amar wrote: "And the intel, and the special forces training... both areas where Israel mythology will be very upset indeed." "Israel_under_attack Great #Mossad failure. GoI has to learn a lot and keep all Intelligence Agencies duly greased and internecine conflict-proof. BHARAT is not immune to #terrorism and internal enemies," he wrote on X. The warrant common to these comments is that a surveillance and special-forces apparatus of this reputation should have detected preparations on this scale.

# Hamas October 7 2023 Surprise Attack on Israel

On 7 October 2023, Hamas carried out what Business Today described as the biggest coordinated attack in Israel, capturing some territory in southern Israel and taking control of some military bases and soldiers.

The reaction the report documents was directed at Israel's famed intelligence agency, Mossad, which is known for its intelligence-gathering capability. For some observers, the belief that Mossad was among the best in the spying world was shattered that day. The report is explicit that it was not the fact of an attack that surprised people, but the scale at which Hamas operated.
