# AI21 Labs' Tel Aviv Office Lease

Less than a month before the war, Globes reported a huge deal in which Amnon Shashua's unicorn AI21 Labs announced it was leasing 7,000 square meters for NIS 15 million annually in Tel Aviv's Da Vinci project.

Writing on 3 December 2023, Globes notes that it will now be interesting to see when the next such big office-space deal is signed in Tel Aviv following the impact of the Israel-Hamas war. Sources in the income-producing property sector in Israel say that over the past few weeks there has been some interest in the sector, although mainly for smaller deals involving hundreds of square meters each.



---


# Israeli Economy in the First Week of the Gaza War

As the first week of fighting in the war in Israel's south drew to a close, the main index on the Tel Aviv Stock Exchange, the Tel Aviv 35, had fallen 6.4% over the week, with financial markets trying to gauge the damage the Israeli economy would sustain. Globes reported on 12 October 2023 that this was clearly a very significant event, but that the fog of war made it hard to estimate its full consequences.

The assessment came from Prof. Leo Leiderman, chief economic adviser at Bank Hapoalim and a professor of economics at Tel Aviv University, who set out for Globes his proposals for rehabilitating the economy and repairing the damage the war would cause. Asked what had been going through his mind in those first days, Leiderman said: "What most preoccupies me is not the economy but concern for the families of the soldiers, the wounded, and the captives, and solidarity with them. I have four relatives from Kibbutz Nir Oz who are still missing, and we have no information about them. I find it hard to understand how a war like this landed on us in a country as powerful as Israel. But we have no choice but to win."



---


# Sderot Police Headquarters Seized During the Attack

Younis Tirawi, who reports on Palestinian affairs, said that Hamas militants had taken over the Sderot police headquarters and armoured vehicles in the town on 7 October 2023.

An analyst posting as OSINTtechnical wrote the same day that some of the images coming out of Sderot over the previous few hours were reaching degrees of horror "that I don't really think I can use words to properly describe. Truly disturbing acts of terror directed at civilians."



---


# Azrieli Group's Office Portfolio In Q3 2023

Azrieli Group (TASE: AZRG) is one of the biggest companies in Israel's income-producing property sector, with 15 office buildings comprising 632,000 square meters of space and 97% occupancy.

In the week before 3 December 2023 Azrieli published its financial results for the third quarter of 2023, saying the company had not been impacted by the war. The company added a caveat: due to the uncertainty about the length of the war and its development, it could not assess the future impact of the war on business activities in Israel in general and on the company in particular.



---


# Bank of Israel Thirty Billion Dollar FX Intervention

On the Monday of the week in which this 12 October 2023 interview was published, the Bank of Israel announced a dramatic plan to sell $30 billion of its foreign currency reserves to stabilise the shekel. By the time of the report the shekel had in fact recovered slightly and was trading at around NIS 3.96/$.

Leo Leiderman endorsed the move: "It's important to welcome the Bank of Israel's decision to intervene, as necessary, in the foreign exchange market, in order to ensure the market's regular operation." He also treated leadership continuity as stabilising, citing the decision to extend the term of Amir Yaron as governor at least for the duration of the war, and in his hope beyond it. He added that the banking system is stable with enough liquidity in the system, and that the behaviour of the investment community in Israel, including the financial institutions, indicates high confidence in the economy's resilience and financial strength — an "asset" he said a level-headed, correct economic policy must preserve.



---


# The Surge In Terror Financing Reports After October 7

Before October 7, IMPA received about 100 reports a day dealing with terror financing; that number jumped to about 1,000 — a 900% increase.

"Overnight, we started receiving hundreds of reports about unusual activity by customers of financial institutions in the State of Israel," Ostrovitch-Levi says. "There is a 900% increase in reports on terror financing, and we don't waste time, everything happens very, very quickly. As we receive the information, we simultaneously pass it on to the operational professionals who locate the money pipelines, and block them. Some information will not necessarily lead to terror financing, but we don't have time to waste. Bank CEOs call and draw our attention to the information they convey to us that warrants special attention." Asked whether information from banks and financial institutions has led to blocking a money pipeline for terrorism, she said: "There was very high-quality intelligence that we passed on to the security agencies. We don't always know the results."



---


# Visual Intelligence Versus Human Sources

Technological sophistication and massive investment in intelligence means have greatly increased the IDF's visual intelligence gathering capabilities, according to former IDF Intelligence Directorate head General (ret.) Aharon Ze'evi-Farkash — but visual collection and human sources play different roles, and only the latter supplies interpretation.

"I'm sure it doesn't come at the expense of human sources, but as time goes by, gathering visual intelligence is easier than human sources and they bring better results," Ze'evi-Farkash said. "It's hard to bring in a Palestinian 'Ashraf Marwan,' the agent who passed the information to Israel before the Egyptian attack in 1973. It's a problem because the human source is essential to provide an interpretation of the rest of the information that's received, and to make decisions. Golda knew who Marwan was and expected to hear what he would say about the Egyptian deployment in the south." Two further gaps sit alongside that structural point: according to "The New York Times," a year before the attack the IDF stopped monitoring Hamas's radio communications, and the US had put stock in Israeli intelligence regarding Hamas in recent years and had not monitored it independently.



---


# Google Maps And Waze Halt Israel-Gaza Traffic Data

Google Maps and Waze stopped live traffic updates in Israel and the Gaza Strip at the request of the Israel Defense Forces, TechCrunch reported on 2023-10-30. A Google spokesperson said the ability to see live traffic conditions and business information was halted temporarily out of "consideration for the safety of local communities."

There is precedent: Google did something similar in 2022 amid the Russian invasion of Ukraine, because the apps were being used to track military movements.

# General MLB Betting Rules At Online Sportsbooks

Every sportsbook has terms and conditions for all bets, MLB included, and while those rules may be specific to each book, some general rules should apply everywhere. # MLB Live In-Game Betting

qid: Does the 'Fortune' article suggest that the foundation of FTX's success is the same as the 'TechCrunch' articles' implication that Sam Bankman-Fried's actions were based on fraudulent intentions?
context:
# John J. Ray III Running The FTX Estate

What's left of FTX is now being led by John J. Ray III — the man who cleaned up Enron, and who has said FTX is worse than Enron.

Just before the trial began, the FTX lawyers filed suit against Bankman-Fried's parents, saying they should give back millions of dollars they got from their kid. Ray has also referred to Bankman-Fried's conduct as "really just old-fashioned embezzlement."



---


# Bankman-Fried's Pre-Collapse Public Image Strategy

Before his fall, Bankman-Fried made himself out to be the Good Boy of crypto — the trustworthy face of a sometimes-shady industry — and he was very interested in publicity, sitting for many interviews both before and after the collapse of FTX.

The Verge attributes FTX's quick rise as an industry force at least in part to that appetite for attention: Bankman-Fried gave interviews freely and quickly rose to public prominence, positioning himself as an important, boyish face for crypto even though FTX hadn't been in the business as long as competing exchanges such as Coinbase, Kraken, or Gemini. At one point he told a colleague at FTX that "I honestly think it's negative EV" — possibly "expected value," as in poker — "for me to cut my hair. I think it's important for people to think I look crazy." Because he was so successful at this kind of public relations, his fall from grace became another mark against an industry already roiled by bankruptcies and scandals; The Verge adds that more trouble for the industry is likely to come from one crucial element of the fraud trial, the part where the government must prove intent.



---


# Prosecution And Defense Arguments On Day Two Of The SBF Trial

On the second day of the trial of Sam Bankman-Fried and FTX, the prosecution argued that Bankman-Fried knowingly committed fraud, and it grounded that claim in motive: he did so, prosecutors said, to achieve great wealth, power and influence.

The defense countered with the opposite reading of the same conduct. Its claim was that the FTX founder acted in good faith, never meant to commit fraud or to steal, and basically got in over his head — an argument whose warrant is that inexperience and overreach, rather than intent, explain what happened. The two sides therefore contest intent rather than the underlying events, and the reporting on this exchange comes from Rebecca and Jacquelyn in TechCrunch's Week in Review of October 7, 2023, covering day two of the trial only.



---


# FTX's Inner Circle: Family And Friends Implicated

The Verge's October 26th, 2023 account of the trial catalogued how everyone who loved Bankman-Fried most in the world was caught up in the case. Adam Yedidia, his college roommate, testified with immunity because he was concerned he may have unknowingly worked on code that contributed to the fraud; "I love you Sam," he had texted at one point, "I'm not going anywhere" — that was before he realized FTX had stolen customer funds, at which point he resigned. Nishad Singh, a longtime family friend, copped to what sounded an awful lot like classic embezzlement, saying he had backdated transactions on FTX to help create doctored balance sheets to show to investors, and pleaded guilty to six charges including wire fraud, money laundering, and conspiracy counts around his political donations. Caroline Ellison, Bankman-Fried's ex-girlfriend, told the court about the seven phony balance sheets she had created and was clear that Alameda took customer funds, that Bankman-Fried knew about it, and that he even invested them against her advice.

His family was drawn in too. Joe Bankman, his father, is among the people included in the "small group chat," the Signal group where the FTX inner circle strategized during the exchange's last days. Barbara Fried's political action committee, Mind the Gap, is among the entities that received FTX customer money as political donations; Fried and Bankman lived together in a Bahamas house purchased for them using FTX investor funds, according to a financial expert called by the prosecution, and in a lawsuit filed by FTX's bankruptcy estate the two are alleged to have been given $10 million of FTX customer funds. Gabe Bankman-Fried's nonprofit, Guarding Against Pandemics, got millions from FTX; he was also in a Signal group chat, Donations Processing, that Singh says was used to coordinate the transfer of FTX and Alameda money to various political causes, and in that chat he can be seen recommending that some donations be made "in the dark" to avoid public relations headaches. Singh also said Gabe had an assistant fly to the Bahamas with a stack of blank checks for Singh to sign.

The consequences outlast the trial. Wang, Singh, and Ellison are now felons; even if they never do time — and they may very well be imprisoned or subjected to house arrest — their lives are irrevocably changed, not least by whatever restitution requirements they face, they are barred from taking certain kinds of jobs, and there is the publicity. Bankman, Fried, and Gabe Bankman-Fried's reputations are tarnished, and in the political arenas where they once operated they are suddenly undesirable. Beyond the courtroom, everyone who had money trapped on the exchange when it collapsed — as a result of Alameda purloining customers' funds — had their lives altered: even if they are made whole by the bankruptcy proceedings, that is still money they should have had access to at any time, which may mean houses that were not purchased, medical procedures left undone, and life savings lost. The reporter's summary: it is a Greek tragedy, precipitated by one man's character flaw, the arrogance of Sam Bankman-Fried.



---


# The Prosecution's Opening Statement Against Bankman-Fried

Thane Rehn, a prosecutor for the government, opened the case against Sam Bankman-Fried with the line "One year ago, it looked like the defendant was on the top of the world," and then argued that this appearance was false: "all of that, all of it, was built on lies," he declared to the jury, adding "Behind the curtains, he was not what he appeared to be." Rehn described a defendant who, as former CEO of FTX, oversaw a supposedly thriving crypto exchange, jetted between international locales, hobnobbed with celebrities like Tom Brady and Larry David, and repeatedly emphasized to customers that their money was safe and secure.

What followed was a roughly 30-minute story that repeatedly emphasized how Bankman-Fried allegedly stole customer funds to facilitate his jet-setting lifestyle, donate millions to political candidates, and finance risky bets. Rehn also directly contested the media framing of the defendant: he was not a crypto "boy" genius, as so many in the media — Fortune included — have written, but a "man" who "stole billions of dollars from thousands of victims." Rehn closed the characterization with a promise to the jury: "You will see the full picture."



---


# Sam Bankman-Fried

Sam Bankman-Fried is the former CEO of the bankrupt crypto exchange FTX, whose highly anticipated criminal trial started on the Tuesday before TechCrunch's 2023-10-01 report, to determine whether he is guilty of seven counts of fraud and conspiracy. As one former federal prosecutor put it: "The odds seem to be stacked against him at this point."

He was 31 years old and co-founded FTX in 2019; within a few years the once third-largest crypto exchange's valuation hit $32 billion at its peak, and the company is now trying to claw back any funds to distribute to creditors. Before the fall he was even compared to Warren Buffet, and many called him the white horse of crypto — a description TechCrunch notes it never applied to him.

Bankman-Fried, however, maintained his innocence. At The New York Times' DealBook Summit he appeared virtually from the Bahamas and said, "I didn't ever try to commit fraud on anyone; I was shocked by what happened this month"; in a published DM exchange with a Vox reporter he said he regretted filing for bankruptcy and thought that "regulators make everything worse." In January he pleaded not guilty to all counts, which include wire fraud, conspiracy to commit money laundering and conspiracy to misuse customer funds. He could face up to 115 years in jail if convicted on all charges.

TechCrunch's 2023-10-02 summary of his standing on the eve of trial: SBF has been denied bail; his name is mud (or much worse) among those who have lost money in Alameda or FTX; and those who might not have had positions in these still blame him for other crypto woes, because he set off a ripple effect.



---


# Bankman-Fried's Post-Bankruptcy Media Tour

After FTX declared bankruptcy, Bankman-Fried went on an extensive media tour, doing interviews with The New York Times' Andrew Ross Sorkin and Good Morning America — and he kept giving interviews even under house arrest, including with The New Yorker.

The Verge's reading of his motive: Bankman-Fried seemed to think that if he just explained things, everyone would understand that what he did was a mistake, not a crime.

qid: Does 'The Guardian' article on the Sydney Swans' game day experience focus on different aspects of fan engagement compared to 'The Guardian' article discussing Mikel Arteta's comments on the importance of enduring challenging moments in a game?
context:
# The Swans' Matchday Experience Model For Local Attendance

The Sydney Swans' attendance strategy, described on 26 October 2023 by executive GM of marketing Loretta Johns, has two linked components: target local communities, and make match days compelling for fans on and off the field.

The off-field half is delivered through food, entertainment and promotion. "Our team has put a lot of work into sourcing some wonderful food offerings, entertainment and activities for kids, while we've had a local focus in promoting our games," Johns said. At North Sydney Oval that means quince paste and hand-picked grapes, cheddar cheese and biscuits in a little box with beautiful wrapping — "they've really thought about what they're doing and made it an experience."

The local-community half works through partnership as a promotional channel, not just a supplier relationship. At Henson Park, the Swans' other home ground in Sydney's gentrified inner west, "they've gone to microbreweries in the local area and invited them in, but also promoted through their clientele to come to the football" — the local business both provides the offering and supplies an audience.



---


# Sydney Swans Top The AFLW Attendance Charts

The Sydney Swans sat top of the AFLW attendance charts on 26 October 2023, less than two years after their first match in the women's league, with an average attendance of 4,365 from four games — 124 more than the next best club, Adelaide.

They were due to play their final home match of the regular season that weekend, a marquee pride match against Collingwood at Henson Park on the Sunday, where a crowd in excess of 4,000 was expected. Earlier in the season, 5,474 fans were at North Sydney Oval to watch the Swans' first AFLW victory.

Swans forward Bella Smith said the players were proud of the club's attendance record and grateful for the support: "We get there two hours before the start of the game and the hill [at Henson Park] is bare. When you come out for the first team warm-up, the hill is slowly filling and then by the time the first bounce gets around, it is full. You can hear it, the atmosphere is amazing."



---


# AFLW Crowds Short Of Season-Extension Targets

Average AFLW attendance in 2023 was a little over 2,500 a match — tracking approximately on par with previous seasons, with a finals uptick likely to come — but crowds were short of the targets that could accelerate the extension of the regular season, which grows from 10 games that year to 12 games by 2025.

The league enjoyed strong attendances in round one, partly attributed to the so-called Matildas effect, but some clubs struggled to attract fans in large numbers across the season: crowds of less than 1,500 were recorded in both traditional markets such as Melbourne and Perth and in areas targeted for growth such as Blacktown and the Gold Coast.

Against that backdrop, Nicole Livingstone, general manager of women's football at the AFL, said the Swans' off-field offering had tapped into something "uniquely Sydney" and helped make matches more attractive.



---


# The Swans' On-Field Turnaround Under Chloe Molloy

After a winless campaign in 2022, the Sydney Swans — led by ex-Collingwood player Chloe Molloy — were competitive in the 2023 AFLW season, winning their first match in round one and sitting within a game of the top eight with two rounds to play as of 26 October 2023.

The Swans recorded their highest total the previous round in a 14-12-96 to 6-3-39 defeat of the Western Bulldogs, the league's winless bottom side, with Molloy recording 17 score involvements to set a new AFLW mark. The Guardian noted the turnaround mattered because fans of Australian rules football in the Harbour City have a reputation for being fickle.



---


# The 'Matildas Effect' And Its Limited Impact On Domestic Women's Sport

The Guardian argued on 26 October 2023 that the popularity of the Matildas' run to the Women's World Cup semi-finals has had only a limited impact on support for domestic women's sport, because the early spike did not persist.

The grounds come from the A-League Women, which launched that month with a first round highlighted by a crowd of more than 11,000 in Sydney — but more modest attendances in subsequent games, including two sub-2,000 crowds in Perth, follow it. The warrant is that a durable effect would show up beyond the opening round; a large first-round crowd followed by small ones is consistent with novelty rather than converted support.

Nicole Livingstone, the AFL's general manager of women's football, made the same point from the league side, saying the "green and gold fever" associated with the Women's World Cup was a one-off and that the AFL has plans in place for long-term growth: "We'll continue to keep building the base and keep building the foundations and have it not just strong at year seven, season eight, but strong for generations to come."



---


# AFLW Longer Quarters And Interchange Cap Rule Changes

In a bid to improve the spectacle of the AFLW, the league introduced longer quarters and an interchange cap in 2023 to help increase scoring, and according to Nicole Livingstone the effect has been positive.

"We've increased game time by eight minutes per match, on average, and we've had record scores across the rounds," she said on 26 October 2023. "Whereas leading into the season we hadn't scored more than 100 goals in a round, we've regularly been scoring over 100 goals in a round."

Livingstone also said the AFL was happy with the level of competition: "Our ladder, from position five to 13 — there's only a game separating it. It just shows that this is a really competitive competition."



---


# Sydney Swans' First AFLW Finals Berth

Sydney, winless in their debut season the previous year, secured eighth spot and their first AFLW finals berth in 2023 by storming home with three unanswered goals against Fremantle, The Age reported on 3 November 2023.

"Any club that's able to go from winless one year to a finals berth, it's incredible," Sydney co-captain Chloe Molloy told Fox Footy after the match. "You can see the emotion on the girls' faces. Coming into the season, the odds were against us. Just to get into the eight, we've managed to do that. We're stoked. It's pretty special for the club." Missing star ruck Ally Morphett to a season-ending wrist injury, Laura Gardiner stood tallest in the midfield — the 20-year-old off-season recruit from Geelong had the ball on a string with a game-high 33 disposals and 18 contested possessions — while Molloy (two goals), Montana Ham, Rebecca Privitelli and Brooke Lochland hit the scoreboard.

The Swans' rise had been signalled earlier in the season by a record-breaking win over the Western Bulldogs, propelled by a Chloe Molloy masterclass: after a five-goal second term that included a four-minute burst of three majors, Sydney had already brought up their largest score in an AFLW game by half-time, and while the Bulldogs held their own in the last quarter the damage was done. The total was also the biggest the Dogs had conceded in their history, topping the 83 Melbourne kicked against them in round three. Molloy, the Swans' star off-season recruit and a former Collingwood ace, was a class above, kicking 3.4 from her 28 possessions and playing a crucial role in setting up numerous other Sydney goals. "She was itching to get in there [in the midfield]," Swans coach Scott Gowans said. "We kept her forward deliberately. It was important Chloe played a good block of time forward so we could have a look at it." That weekend the Blues lost to Greater Western Sydney by two points, 8.1 (49) to 7.5 (47), denying Carlton the chance to leapfrog into the top eight.



---


# UK Support Organisations For Older Adults

The Guardian's 10 October 2023 piece lists five organisations older adults and their families can turn to, each defined by a distinct function.

Age UK has a database of social activities and groups for older folk. The Walking Football Association keeps keen amateur footballers playing long into their 50s and 60s. Action for Elders offers social and exercise programmes.

The Centre for Ageing Better provides information on working and living as an older person, and u3a, a charity collective, provides local opportunities for people no longer in work to acquire new skills and knowledge.



---


# Multivitamins And Cognition In Older Adults

A recent Columbia University study involving 2,200 adults aged 60 and over found that an inexpensive multivitamin formulated specifically for older people improved cognition, memory and focus, The Guardian reported on 10 October 2023.

The results were so marked that the researchers said the supplement could slow age-related memory decline by three years.

The article frames this as an option even where parents do not require intensive "parenting": a simple supplement could help.

qid: Did President Ferdinand Marcos, Jr. express no concern about the Philippines' debt-to-GDP ratio in Business World on October 8, 2023, and did the implications of rising national debt on private investment discussed in Business World on November 5, 2023, contradict his views?
context:
# Philippine 2024 Budget Deficit and Debt Trajectory

The Philippine national budget for 2024 is P5.768 trillion, 9.5% higher than the 2023 budget of P5.268 trillion — an increase of P499.6 billion — and observers note that this first budget fully prepared by the current administration accounts for 21.7% of gross domestic product. Supported mainly by P3.5 trillion in tax revenues, based on 2023 tax revenue projections, it implies a budget deficit of some P2.268 trillion to be funded by additional borrowings, which could increase government debt from P14.24 trillion as of July to P16+ trillion by the end of 2024.

At the Congressional budget hearing, Finance Secretary Benjamin Diokno optimistically provided updates on the government's fiscal and revenue collection performances and presented sources of funding for the national budget. He told the Philippine News Agency on 10 August that tax revenue is projected to increase from P3.5 trillion in 2023 to P6.5 trillion in 2028, while non-tax revenues are expected to decline from P191 billion in 2023 to P184 billion in 2028. Diokno said the Finance department aims to gradually reduce net financing, or new debt, from P1.42 trillion in 2022 to P1.22 trillion in 2024, which will help bring the country's debt-to-GDP ratio to almost below 60% by 2025.

Against that optimism, President Ferdinand Marcos, Jr. told members of the US-ASEAN Business Council who visited Malacañang, in remarks reported by ABS-CBN on 9 August 2023: "We worry about our debt-to-GDP ratio in the Philippines, as it stands at about 63% and that's a little high for us and it is not ideal."



---


# Philippine Inflation In 2023 And The Government Response

In his second State of the Nation Address, President Ferdinand Marcos, Jr. singled out inflation as the country's most pressing problem. In the first nine months of 2023, inflation averaged 6.6%, far above the upper end of the 2-4% target range set by the BSP. If left unchecked, inflation could undermine growth: it not only increases costs to organizations but sets in motion second-round effects as workers start demanding higher wages, consequently increasing business costs and discouraging investments.

Inflation is partly driven by supply-side issues, and the government is allocating more resources to the agriculture sector to boost production. Marcos mentioned that the National Government had distributed 28,000 new tools and machinery to farmers, and that an additional 600 km of farm-to-market roads were laid down to support the 14 million hectares of farmland, enhancing farmer access to markets. He also signed Executive Order No. 28 in May, forming the Inter-Agency Committee on Inflation and Market Outlook, tasked with keeping inflation within government targets and boosting the economy.



---


# Human Capital, Institutions And Infrastructure In The Philippine Plan

The ability of people to take advantage of market opportunities arising from investment rests on human capital, which is why the first goal of the Philippine Development Plan is social transformation, including among other things sustained expenditure on social services, mainly education, health, and social protection. The plan's three goals map onto the policy objectives: the first two goals help attain the developmental objectives of efficiency and equity, which rest on the pillars of sustainability and resilience, while the third fosters societal resilience through an enabling environment encompassing institutions, macroeconomic stability, and the physical and natural environment.

Institutions are vital to economic acceleration, which is why the government's steps to enhance the ease of doing business are welcome, and infrastructure development enables an economy to sustain higher levels of growth, which in turn catalyzes yet more investment. The Public-Private Partnership Act is up for the signature of President Marcos and, if approved, is expected to further enhance the business atmosphere in mobilizing private resources for infrastructure development. The quantities that bound the plan are given together: the government aims to sustain its infrastructure program at 5-6% of GDP through 2028 amid a six-year medium-term fiscal framework that gradually narrows the deficit to 3% of GDP by 2028, down from 7.3% in 2022, so that the debt-to-GDP ratio is reduced from nearly 61% in 2022 to a more sustainable level of at most 53% by 2028.



---


# The Private Sector's Role In Philippine Sustainable Development

Coming off the pandemic and given the current global economic climate, it is opportune for the government to proactively drive actionable policies and programs that focus on building the resiliency of the economy through sustainable development, with greater emphasis on addressing climate change. That is the article's conclusion about timing, and the accompanying claim is that navigating external and domestic economic headwinds will not be an easy feat for the administration.

The warrant for optimism is the private sector's role as an important catalyst for sustainable development: with the private sector sharing industry knowledge and resources and potentially even leading certain socio-economic programs and projects of the National Government, the hope is that AmBisyon Natin 2040, of long and healthy lives for Filipinos that are strongly rooted, comfortable and secure, will be achieved.



---


# Philippine Development Plan 2023-2028 Targets

The Philippine Development Plan 2023-2028 aims for a deep economic and social transformation to reinvigorate job creation and accelerate poverty reduction by steering the economy back to a high-growth path, and two main performance indicators are identified and will be monitored by the National Government.

The first is for the country to graduate into upper middle-income class status within the term of the current administration, for which the economy must grow its per capita income above the threshold set by the World Bank, a gross national income per capita of at least $4,466; in 2022 the Philippines achieved a GNI per capita of $3,950. The second is to lower the poverty level from 18.1% in 2021 to single digits by 2028, the end of the term of the current administration. Both indicators require high growth rates, and for the next year through 2028 the government pencils the growth rate between 6.5% and 8%.



---


# Philippine Debt And The Case For Fiscal Consolidation

The argument for fiscal consolidation is that although the current 61% debt-to-GDP ratio may be manageable for an emerging economy like the Philippines for some time, the country may not have the fiscal space to respond to another potential domestic or external shock. The grounds are historical: the National Government's debt was less than 40% before the pandemic struck, and it expended much of its fiscal space combatting the pandemic, incurring debt and large budget deficits. The warrant is a crowding-out mechanism: if the debt continues to rise more than the economy, risks will increase and the government may crowd out private investment as it competes with the private sector for funds to service its debt.

The planned consolidation entails harmonizing revenue needs with the promotion of investment through the structure and administration of the reformed incentive system. The National Government plans to raise more revenue to finance the country's socio-economic needs, largely through a progressive and simplified tax system and more efficient and effective tax collection measures through digitalization, and to some extent from policy measures such as value-added tax on digital service providers and excise tax on sweetened beverages and junk food. The conclusion is stated as a conditional pair: achieving fiscal stability presupposes the sustainability of fiscal policy, and fiscal stability helps crowd in private investment.



---


# Balanced Versus Deficit Budget in Philippine Fiscal Practice

The DBM calls a budget balanced when revenues match expenditures or disbursements. When expenditures exceed revenues, the government incurs a deficit, which may lead to three situations: the government borrows money either from foreign sources or from the domestic capital market, which increases the debt stock of the National Government and its debt servicing requirements; the government borrows money from the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas; or the government withdraws funds from its cash balances in the Treasury.

The historical case is one of persistent deficits. National Government expenditures have always exceeded total revenues, resulting in annual budget deficits, the DBM declared, and "the National Government had to resort to borrowing to cover said deficits which resulted in the ballooning of foreign and domestic debts," the budget office admitted.

The boundary case is 1994: "in 1994, the government broke the deficit trend by posting a budget surplus of P16 billion through an aggressive privatization and revenue generation program and a prudent expenditure program. Since then, the government has been exerting efforts to maintain the surplus budget policy. The surplus budget policy is important to encourage economic growth," the DBM said.



---


# Powell's Rejection Of Monetary-Fiscal Coordination

Fed Chair Jerome Powell, sitting to Christine Lagarde's right at the panel discussion, signaled he wasn't ready to rely on the kind of cooperation between monetary and fiscal policy she described as sometimes helpful.

His stated ground rejects the premise that the central bank's mandate is contingent on what fiscal authorities do: "Our assignment is to deliver price stability kind of regardless of the stance of fiscal policy."

qid: What is the name of the leading AI development company that is not only the creator behind ChatGPT and is planning to release GPT-4 with vision alongside GPT-4 Turbo API, but is also anticipated to champion an "app store for AI" as a key platform for AI tools and toys, as reported by TechCrunch?
context:
# GPT Model Releases From GPT-3.5 To GPT-4

ChatGPT first launched to the public as OpenAI quietly released GPT-3.5: the model broke cover with ChatGPT, a fine-tuned version of GPT-3.5 that is essentially a general-purpose chatbot able to engage with a range of topics including programming, TV scripts and scientific concepts.

Writers everywhere rolled their eyes at the new technology, much as artists did with OpenAI's DALL-E model, but the chat-style iteration seemingly broadened its appeal and audience. GPT-4 followed on March 14: a powerful image- and text-understanding AI model, released to paying ChatGPT Plus users and through a public API, with developers able to sign up on a waitlist to access the API.



---


# GPTs: OpenAI's Custom Chatbots And The Dev Day Announcements

GPTs are OpenAI's tool for building custom conversational, action-taking AI systems powered by OpenAI's models, including the models underpinning ChatGPT. They were announced at OpenAI's first-ever developer conference, held Monday, November 6, 2023, where the Microsoft-backed AI startup announced a host of new products — the more notable being tools to create custom "GPTs" (that is, domain-specific chatbots), new text-to-speech models, an API for the text-to-image model DALL-E 3, and an improved version of OpenAI's flagship model GPT-4, called GPT-4 Turbo.

What distinguishes a GPT from a prompt is that the knowledge is built in. With GPTs, a user can train a model on a cookbook collection, for example, so that it can answer questions about ingredients for a specific recipe; or they can give a model their company's proprietary codebases so that developers can check their style or generate code in line with best practices. Some of the initial GPTs, all created by OpenAI, include a Gen Z meme translator, a coloring book and sticker creator, a data visualizer, a board game explainer and a creative writing coach. ChatGPT can accomplish these tasks given carefully engineered prompts and foreknowledge, but purpose-built GPTs drastically simplify things — and might just kill the cottage industry that emerged around creating and editing prompts to feed to ChatGPT.

The consequence TechCrunch draws for ChatGPT itself is a change of role: with GPTs, ChatGPT could become more a gateway to a broader ecosystem of AI-powered chatbots than the end-all-be-all. GPTs introduce a level of personalization far beyond that ChatGPT offers today, and — once OpenAI sorts out its capacity issues — TechCrunch expects an explosion of creativity there. Will ChatGPT be as visible as it once was after GPTs flood the marketplace? Perhaps not; but it will not go away, it will simply adapt and evolve, no doubt in ways not even its creators can anticipate.



---


# OpenAI DevDay 2023 Announcements

On November 6, 2023 — prior to the leadership chaos — OpenAI held its first developer conference, OpenAI DevDay, and announced a slew of updates to GPT, including GPT-4 Turbo, a multimodal API, and a GPT store where users can create and monetize their own custom versions of GPT.

GPT-4 Turbo, unveiled at the conference, is a super-charged version of GPT-4, OpenAI's latest language-writing model, and comes in two versions: one that is strictly text-analyzing and another that understands the context of both text and images. The GPT Store was announced alongside it: users and developers would soon be able to make their own GPT with no coding experience required, list it on OpenAI's marketplace, and monetize it in the future. OpenAI also announced the Assistants API to help developers build "agent-like experiences" within their apps, with use cases ranging from a natural language-based data analysis app to a coding assistant or even an AI-powered vacation planner.

The GPT store slipped. According to a memo seen by Axios, OpenAI planned to delay the launch of its highly anticipated GPT store to early 2024; custom GPTs and the accompanying store had been a major DevDay announcement, with the store expected to open the previous month.



---


# ChatGPT FAQ: Basics And Definitions

ChatGPT is a general-purpose chatbot developed by tech startup OpenAI that uses artificial intelligence to generate text after a user enters a prompt; it runs on GPT-4, a large language model that uses deep learning to produce human-like text. GPT stands for Generative Pre-Trained Transformer.

The boundary against the wider category matters: a chatbot can be any software or system that holds dialogue with a person and does not necessarily have to be AI-powered — there are rules-based chatbots that give canned responses to questions — whereas ChatGPT is AI-powered and uses LLM technology to generate text after a prompt. ChatGPT was released for public use on November 30, 2022. Both the free version of ChatGPT and the paid ChatGPT Plus are regularly updated with new GPT models, and the most recent model is GPT-4; the free version requires only a sign-in. There is a free ChatGPT app, at launch limited to U.S. iOS users, with OpenAI saying an Android version is "coming soon," and there is an API, released March 1, 2023.

Anyone can use ChatGPT, and more and more tech companies and search engines are using the chatbot to automate text or quickly answer user questions and concerns. Multiple enterprises use it, although others limit use of the tool. Microsoft announced at its 2023 Build conference that it is integrating its ChatGPT-based Bing experience into Windows 11; the Brooklyn-based 3D display startup Looking Glass uses ChatGPT to produce holograms you can communicate with; and the nonprofit organization Solana integrated the chatbot into its network with a ChatGPT plug-in geared toward end users to help onboard into the web3 space.



---


# ChatGPT Third-Party Integrations And Ecosystem

ChatGPT spread rapidly into other companies' products: Microsoft built GPT-4 into Bing, and OkCupid, Kaito, Snapchat and Discord also implemented ChatGPT, putting pressure on Big Tech's AI initiatives such as Google's.

Microsoft was the anchor integrator. At a press event in Redmond, Washington, Microsoft announced its long-rumored integration of OpenAI's GPT-4 model into Bing, providing a ChatGPT-like experience within the search engine; the announcement spurred a 10x increase in new downloads for Bing globally, indicating sizable consumer demand for new AI experiences. ChatGPT also became generally available through the Azure OpenAI Service, Microsoft's fully managed, corporate-focused offering, where customers must already be "Microsoft managed customers and partners" to apply for special access.

Beyond Microsoft, the integrations spanned browsers, cars and apps. The AI browser assistant Aria, powered by ChatGPT, launched on Opera in May to give users an easier way to search, ask questions and write code, and Opera later brought Aria to Opera GX, the gamer-focused version of its flagship browser, letting users interact directly with a browser AI to find the latest gaming news and tips. Mercedes added ChatGPT to its MBUX infotainment system, with U.S. owners able to opt into a beta programme starting June 16 by telling the car "Hey Mercedes, I want to join the beta program," augmenting the car's conversation skills. SuperChat, from the company behind the iPhone customization app Brass and sticker maker StickerHub, lets iOS users chat with virtual characters — historical and fictional — powered by ChatGPT, with the characters being what distinguishes it from generic AI chat apps. A week after ChatGPT's release, developers Steven Tey and Dom Eccleston made a Chrome extension called ShareGPT to make it easier to capture and share the AI's answers. Auto-GPT, an open-source app created by game developer Toran Bruce Richards, uses GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 to interact with software and services online so it can "autonomously" perform tasks; depending on the objective it is given it can behave in unexpected ways — one Reddit user claims that, given a budget of $100 to spend within a server instance, Auto-GPT made a wiki page on cats, exploited a flaw in the instance to gain admin-level access, took over the Python environment it was running in, and then "killed" itself.

A startup layer formed on top. YC Demo Day's Winter 2023 batch featured no fewer than four startups claiming to be building "ChatGPT for X," all chasing a customer service software market that Acumen Research optimistically predicted would be worth $58.1 billion by 2023: Yuma, serving primarily Shopify merchants with ChatGPT-like AI systems that integrate with help desk software and suggest draft replies to customer tickets; Baselit, using one of OpenAI's text-understanding models to let businesses embed chatbot-style analytics for their customers; Lasso, which takes customer descriptions or videos of processes to automate and combines a ChatGPT-like interface with robotic process automation and a Chrome extension to build the automations; and BerriAI, whose platform helps developers spin up ChatGPT apps over their organization's data through various data connectors.

# Shai Hope's Anchor Innings In The T20 Decider

Shai Hope's 43 off 43 balls steered West Indies to their target in the deciding T20I, an exemplary anchoring innings that the live blog identified as the wicket England really needed.

At 16 overs West Indies were 112-4 with Hope on 29, and he opened the face to steer Rehan Ahmed for his first boundary; Rehan had struggled as the series progressed, and later in the over Powell muscled him over long-on for six, leaving West Indies 21 runs from a hat-trick of T20 series wins that year — South Africa away, India and England at home. In the 17th over, with West Indies 114-5, Hope was quietly guiding his side towards the finish line. The Guardian's report noted West Indies were 62 for three halfway through their innings, and if England had had 15 more runs at the same point they had also made a complete hash of the rest of it — a trap West Indies avoided thanks to Hope's 43-ball 43 as he again steered his side to their target. The batting display may have lacked their usual flamboyance, but until the final ball it was entirely appropriate for the occasion.



---


# West Indies Win The 2023 T20I Series 3-2

West Indies beat England by four wickets in the fifth and deciding T20 international on Dec. 21, 2023, taking the series 3-2 when Shai Hope pinged Chris Woakes over extra cover for six at 19.2 overs, with West Indies 133-6.

It was the 120th six of the series, and Hope played a gem of an innings, calmly anchoring West Indies in an increasingly nervous chase with a run-a-ball 43; England fought admirably to defend a below-par total and, but for Hope, would probably have done it. Cricket on TNT Sports posted that the win claimed the series 3-2 and a white-ball clean sweep. The Guardian's report framed the finish as the sequel to a very different match: Tuesday's ludicrous, record-smashing, high-scoring entertainment had been followed on the same surface by thrilling low-scoring entertainment and a different result claimed in very different style, eventually won with four balls to spare and in the most unfitting of ways — with a massive six — by Hope, again proving himself the right man for a run chase. A series marked by stunning power hitting, roaring run rates and an unexpected midway transformation in England's performances and prospects concluded with a 3-2 triumph for West Indies, who extended their supremacy over England at home to four series in three formats across nearly five years.



---


# Andre Russell's Comeback In The First T20I

Andre Russell was named Player of the Match in the first T20I against England, taking 3-29 and smashing 29 not out off just 14 deliveries in his first T20I in over two years.

He seemed very pleased to be back in maroon, saying: "Life is so funny. Since when I got selected for the West Indies two weeks ago I've been dreaming of being man of the match." His bowling figures at the end of England's innings were 3-19, which the live blog described as balancing the attack perfectly on his comeback. As Tim Wigmore put it, Russell at his best adds so much to the West Indies side — with him at seven, and Holder, Shepherd and Hosein to follow, West Indies bat incredibly deep.



---


# West Indies' Middle Overs In The T20 Decider Chase

Adil Rashid took two wickets through the middle overs of the decider chase — Johnson Charles for 27 and Sherfane Rutherford for 30 — but West Indies still moved to 95-4 with the run rate under control.

In the seventh over Rehan Ahmed's first over disappeared for 12: four singles and a two off the first five balls, then a no-nonsense straight six from Charles, taking West Indies to 51-2. Rashid struck straight away in the eighth, accidentally bowling a very wide, dipping full toss that Charles clunked low to Buttler at short extra cover, 54-3. Moeen replaced Rehan in the ninth and rushed through four singles. In the tenth, West Indies knew how dangerous Rashid was and were content to sit on him — the live blog thought that had been Charles' plan too before he saw a low full toss and his brain went rogue — and at drinks West Indies needed 71 from 60. England reviewed an LBW appeal against Rutherford off a Rashid legbreak that had hit him on the pad in front of middle and leg, but it was comfortably missing leg stump and England lost the review. In the eleventh, after 23 balls without a West Indian boundary, Rutherford lifted Moeen handsomely over extra cover for four. In the twelfth England appealed unsuccessfully for caught behind when Rutherford missed a swipe at Rashid and decided not to risk their last review — a good job, as there was nothing on UltraEdge — before Rutherford launched a full ball down the ground for six. In the thirteenth Rehan returned, perhaps hoping to tempt Rutherford into one big shot too many, but Hope, happily playing the anchor role, faced five of the six deliveries as England ran out of time. In the fourteenth Rutherford hooked new bowler Sam Curran for six more in an over worth 11, with Rutherford on 30 from 23 balls and Hope 19 from 28, both playing their roles to perfection. Buttler then brought Rashid back for his final over knowing it was now or never, and got an immediate reward as Rutherford smashed a drive towards short extra where Curran dived to his left for a superb catch, 95-4.



---


# The Final Overs Of The T20 Series Clinch

England took two late wickets and pushed the decider into its final over, but West Indies got home with nine needed from six balls after Shai Hope had kept the requirement below a run a ball.

Reece Topley had Rovman Powell caught for 8 at short third man by Rashid, a smart low catch to his left, leaving West Indies 113-5 and needing 20 from 21 balls, with the live blog noting England had not given this up. In the 18th over Buttler gambled by continuing with the relatively expensive Rehan Ahmed and it did not come off: Hope skimmed a back cut between short third and backward point for four to move the requirement back below a run a ball, making it very hard to see how England could win. Sam Curran then conceded only one run from the first four balls of a superb penultimate over — with a short break while England called for a dry towel as the ball got very wet — leaving 10 needed from eight balls; Andre Russell then slugged a low full toss straight down the throat of Livingstone at long-on for 3, and England, behind the game throughout the innings, were again dreaming of an improbable victory with West Indies needing 10 from 7. Jason Holder was almost run out first ball of the 19th over, taking a very dodgy single to mid-off and finishing well short when Curran just failed to gather Rashid's throw, leaving nine to win from six balls with Chris Woakes to bowl; Holder then inside-edged Woakes wide of leg stump for three, which would have been four but for an outstanding stop from Rehan Ahmed, putting West Indies 127-6. The Guardian's report judged the outcome had seemed inevitable from the start: with such a meagre target West Indies needed little more than to keep their heads, and though both Topley and Curran conceded only two with their final overs to push the contest into its final over, that never looked in doubt.



---


# The Rain Delay And DLS Position In The First T20I

Rain stopped play in the first T20I with West Indies on 108-4 after 12.4 overs and requiring 64 runs off 44 balls — crucially, six runs ahead of the Duckworth Lewis Stern rate, so that if the rain did not abate the home side would take the spoils.

The heavens cracked out of nowhere and the players scurried off as the covers were hauled on, with Hope on 27 and Powell on 6. The rain then began tailing off and a rope was dragged around the outfield to take off excess water. The Guardian's man in Barbados, Simon Burnton, reported a 9.35 p.m. restart with no overs lost, putting play about eight minutes away; the live blog understood 10.10 p.m. local time — 2.10 a.m. in London — to be the cut off for the match.

# Bankman-Fried's Defense Strategy And Appeal Groundwork

Bankman-Fried's defense can itself introduce risks for people who dealt with him, because his lawyers have several simultaneous objectives: first and foremost proving their client not guilty, but also — just in case they don't get the outcome they want — laying the groundwork for appeals and sentencing arguments.

The consequence is procedural: any piece of evidence they want to introduce for those two purposes has to come into play during the trial. Christopher LaVigne notes that Bankman-Fried's lawyers are already marking arguments that his constitutional rights are being violated by his pretrial incarceration because, among other things, his internet connection wasn't good enough for him to plan his defense — which could be grounds for an appeal.



---


# Day Two Of The Bankman-Fried Trial: Jury Selection And The Courtroom Audience

On the second day of Sam Bankman-Fried's fraud trial, the jury was selected on Wednesday morning, after which lawyers for the government and then for Bankman-Fried delivered opening statements that told two very different stories of the former FTX CEO's sudden rise and almost instantaneous fall. The central question framed by the proceedings was who Bankman-Fried, the former CEO of crypto exchange FTX, really is: a liar and a fraud, or someone who acted in good faith and, like many a startup founder, flew too close to the sun. That answer, the account notes, ultimately lies with the jury.

The day featured pointed allegations, a friend from MIT, and an audience replete with big names, including Bankman-Fried's professorial parents and Damian Williams, the U.S. attorney for the Southern District of New York. Bankman-Fried himself spent most of the day in court staring into a laptop while seated between his two attorneys. The prosecution's account of his alleged crimes was described as featuring a study in contrasts.



---


# FTX Fraud Charges And The SEC's Allegation

Sam Bankman-Fried, the founder of the failed cryptocurrency exchange FTX, faced seven counts of wire fraud and conspiracy — specifically, two counts of wire fraud and five conspiracy charges — and the Securities and Exchange Commission alleged that FTX was a fraud "from the start," with a "multi-billion-dollar deficiency caused by his own misappropriation of customer funds." The Verge repeated this framing at the head of each of its trial dispatches through October 2023, and in its October 28th, 2023 write-up reported that Bankman-Fried had been found guilty on seven counts including charges of wire fraud.

The boundary of the concept is the mix of charge types: the indictment paired substantive wire fraud counts with conspiracy counts rather than resting on a single offence, and the SEC's civil allegation about the exchange's origins ran alongside the criminal case rather than being part of it. The Verge's reporter, writing as the prosecution's case neared its end on October 26th, 2023, added an impression of the people the charges swept in: all the co-conspirators seemed oddly younger than their years, as though they had got stuck in the "math camp forever" environment Bankman-Fried created for them and simply failed to grow up.



---


# The FTX Trial's Stakes For The Wider Crypto Industry

The Verge argued that the trial of Sam Bankman-Fried is likely to be more consequential than just whether the man himself is found guilty: depending on what evidence is introduced, it could be rough for the entire crypto industry.

The grounds are the unpredictability of what a trial surfaces, voiced by Yesha Yadav, a law professor at Vanderbilt University: "How much damage can this trial do to the already beaten-down reputation of the industry at this point? This trial is going to be an excruciating moment for the industry because no one knows what kind of evidence might come out." The warrant joining that uncertainty to industry-wide stakes is that the industry's reputation is already beaten down, so evidence introduced against one exchange's founder lands on the whole sector rather than on him alone.



---


# Prosecution And Defense Arguments On Day Two Of The SBF Trial

On the second day of the trial of Sam Bankman-Fried and FTX, the prosecution argued that Bankman-Fried knowingly committed fraud, and it grounded that claim in motive: he did so, prosecutors said, to achieve great wealth, power and influence.

The defense countered with the opposite reading of the same conduct. Its claim was that the FTX founder acted in good faith, never meant to commit fraud or to steal, and basically got in over his head — an argument whose warrant is that inexperience and overreach, rather than intent, explain what happened. The two sides therefore contest intent rather than the underlying events, and the reporting on this exchange comes from Rebecca and Jacquelyn in TechCrunch's Week in Review of October 7, 2023, covering day two of the trial only.



---


# The SBF Trial Proceedings

Sam Bankman-Fried is in court for alleged fraud and money laundering while leading crypto exchange FTX and sister company Alameda. TechCrunch's 2023-10-02 preview placed the case in the Manhattan Federal Court, describing the disgraced cryptocurrency entrepreneur as accused of orchestrating "one of the biggest financial frauds in American history": the multibillion-dollar collapse of FTX, the crypto exchange he founded and led. SBF, as he is known, has pleaded not guilty to some seven charges of fraud and conspiracy.

The trial kicked off with jury selection October 3. By TechCrunch's 2023-10-06 update the case was entering its next chapter, with proceedings resuming Thursday: as confirmed during a teleconference Wednesday, SBF would be taking the stand along with a handful of other witnesses, as the onus shifted toward the defense after the prosecution brought its case to its conclusion.

Access to the proceedings is limited: no devices are allowed, so reports are being physically put together within the courtroom, or sent to overflow rooms. The jury's composition ranges from a train conductor to a retired investment banker who attended Stanford University, and TechCrunch pointed readers to a special joint episode of its Equity and Chain Reaction podcasts for a better sense of the vibe between the jurors and the rest of the court.

A second account of the same events was arriving in parallel: "Going Infinite," a book by Michael Lewis chronicling the rise and fall of SBF, was set to debut on the first day of the trial.



---


# The Prosecution's Opening Statement Against Bankman-Fried

Thane Rehn, a prosecutor for the government, opened the case against Sam Bankman-Fried with the line "One year ago, it looked like the defendant was on the top of the world," and then argued that this appearance was false: "all of that, all of it, was built on lies," he declared to the jury, adding "Behind the curtains, he was not what he appeared to be." Rehn described a defendant who, as former CEO of FTX, oversaw a supposedly thriving crypto exchange, jetted between international locales, hobnobbed with celebrities like Tom Brady and Larry David, and repeatedly emphasized to customers that their money was safe and secure.

What followed was a roughly 30-minute story that repeatedly emphasized how Bankman-Fried allegedly stole customer funds to facilitate his jet-setting lifestyle, donate millions to political candidates, and finance risky bets. Rehn also directly contested the media framing of the defendant: he was not a crypto "boy" genius, as so many in the media — Fortune included — have written, but a "man" who "stole billions of dollars from thousands of victims." Rehn closed the characterization with a promise to the jury: "You will see the full picture."



---


# Sam Bankman-Fried

Sam Bankman-Fried is the former CEO of the bankrupt crypto exchange FTX, whose highly anticipated criminal trial started on the Tuesday before TechCrunch's 2023-10-01 report, to determine whether he is guilty of seven counts of fraud and conspiracy. As one former federal prosecutor put it: "The odds seem to be stacked against him at this point."

He was 31 years old and co-founded FTX in 2019; within a few years the once third-largest crypto exchange's valuation hit $32 billion at its peak, and the company is now trying to claw back any funds to distribute to creditors. Before the fall he was even compared to Warren Buffet, and many called him the white horse of crypto — a description TechCrunch notes it never applied to him.

Bankman-Fried, however, maintained his innocence. At The New York Times' DealBook Summit he appeared virtually from the Bahamas and said, "I didn't ever try to commit fraud on anyone; I was shocked by what happened this month"; in a published DM exchange with a Vox reporter he said he regretted filing for bankruptcy and thought that "regulators make everything worse." In January he pleaded not guilty to all counts, which include wire fraud, conspiracy to commit money laundering and conspiracy to misuse customer funds. He could face up to 115 years in jail if convicted on all charges.

TechCrunch's 2023-10-02 summary of his standing on the eve of trial: SBF has been denied bail; his name is mud (or much worse) among those who have lost money in Alameda or FTX; and those who might not have had positions in these still blame him for other crypto woes, because he set off a ripple effect.

# Going Infinite: Michael Lewis's Account Of SBF's Political Dealings

Michael Lewis's book "Going Infinite" debuted on the first day of Sam Bankman-Fried's trial, and details about Bankman-Fried's political dealings emerging from it include his alleged attempt to buy off Donald Trump to get him not to run again for president.

TechCrunch's team was focused on the Manhattan Federal Court for the trial of Bankman-Fried, the disgraced entrepreneur accused of orchestrating the collapse of the cryptocurrency exchange FTX; the Lewis book is the second channel through which the week's revelations arrived. # Alameda Research As The Alleged Conduit For FTX Customer Funds

In the prosecution's account offered by Thane Rehn, the key to Sam Bankman-Fried's alleged scheme was Alameda Research, a crypto hedge fund that Bankman-Fried also owned. The structure the government described works as follows: Caroline Ellison — Bankman-Fried's on-again off-again girlfriend and the CEO of Alameda — served as a front for the fund, and through that arrangement Bankman-Fried had "secret access" to customer money, both cash and crypto.

Two further relations complete the alleged mechanism. Bankman-Fried is said to have directed employees to conceal the flow of money into FTX's coffers, and to have forged financial documents distributed to lenders and investors. "The defendant lied to the world," Rehn alleged. These are the government's allegations as presented in its opening statement, not established findings.

# The Prosecution's Opening Statement Against Bankman-Fried

Thane Rehn, a prosecutor for the government, opened the case against Sam Bankman-Fried with the line "One year ago, it looked like the defendant was on the top of the world," and then argued that this appearance was false: "all of that, all of it, was built on lies," he declared to the jury, adding "Behind the curtains, he was not what he appeared to be." # Ellison's Risk Spreadsheet For Venture Investments

Caroline Ellison testified that she prepared a spreadsheet at Bankman-Fried's request in the fall of 2021 and shared it with him, analysing the risk to Alameda of repaying its loans if they were abruptly recalled by its lender Genesis. Bankman-Fried wanted to use $3 billion for venture investments, so Ellison ballparked what that would do to Alameda's risk: in the as-is scenario she put the chance they would not be able to meet the loan recalls at 30 percent, and if Bankman-Fried spent $3 billion on investments, the chance rose to 100 percent — even with FTX customer funds.

What made this the worst of her testimony, in The Verge's account of the October 10th, 2023 proceedings, was not the math, which seemed pretty arbitrary, but the assumption underneath it: Ellison's calculations assumed Alameda could borrow $1.8 billion in normal dollars and $1.5 billion in crypto from FTX, and the spreadsheet made this explicit with a row labeled "FTX borrows," which Ellison said were customer funds. The background condition was that Alameda was also getting loans from outside lenders such as Genesis, because when FTX started there were not a lot of customer funds to borrow.

The day ended with a document shared between Ellison and Bankman-Fried, his comments appearing in bubbles along the main text. Ellison had written that she was worried about "both actual leverage and presenting on our balance sheet." Bankman-Fried responded with a note: "Yup, and could also get worse."

# Sam Bankman-Fried's Federal Fraud Trial

Sam Bankman-Fried, the founder of bankrupt cryptocurrency exchange FTX, is charged with seven counts of fraud and money laundering following the collapse of his cryptocurrency empire the previous year, and was on trial in New York in October 2023.

Two fixed points anchor the proceeding as CNBC described it on 2023-10-06. A U.S. judge revoked Bankman-Fried's bail at a hearing in a New York courthouse on August 11, 2023. And on Thursday, Oct. 5, 2023, Matt Huang, co-founder of Paradigm Operations LP, arrived at the New York court to appear in the case.
