# US v. Google: Two Months Into The Search Antitrust Trial

As of TechCrunch's November 13, 2023 roundup, the Justice Department's landmark antitrust case against Google was nearly two months old, and the trial record was still producing fresh revelations. TechCrunch framed it as one of the biggest fights in tech antitrust since the U.S. took Microsoft to trial in the 1990s.

An earlier roundup had already surfaced that Google spent $26.3 billion in 2021 making itself the default search engine across platforms, and that Google tried to have Chrome preinstalled on iPhones. Over the couple of weeks preceding this roundup, more of Google's inner workings came to light, including some of the search engine's most lucrative search queries, the shape of the revenue-share agreements between Google and Android OEMs, and why Expedia has a bone to pick with Google.



---


# The Claim That SGE And Bard Appropriate Publisher Content

The Helena World Chronicle lawsuit claims that Google's recent advances in AI-based search were implemented with "the goal of discouraging end-users from visiting the websites of Class members who are part of the digital news and publishing line of commerce." The grounds are that Google's AI products both retain users and consume publisher content without permission.

On the Search Generative Experience, the suit argues that SGE offers web searchers a way to seek information in a conversational mode but ultimately keeps users in Google's "walled garden" as it "plagiarizes" their content. The warrant that turns this into a harm publishers cannot escape is that publishers also cannot block SGE, because it uses the same web crawler as Google's general search service, GoogleBot — so opting out of the AI experience would mean opting out of search itself.

On Bard, the suit says Google's Bard AI was trained on a dataset that included "news, magazine and digital publications," citing both a 2023 report from the News Media Alliance and a Washington Post article about AI training data. The Post, which worked with researchers at the Allen Institute for AI, had found that News and Media sites were the third largest category of AI training data.

The case points to other concerns too, such as changing AdSense rates and evidence of improper spoliation of evidence on Google's part through its destruction of chat messages — an issue raised in the recent Epic Games lawsuit against Google over app store antitrust issues, which Epic won.



---


# Google Paid $26.3 Billion In 2021 For Default Search Placement

Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to multiple browsers, phones and platforms — from companies including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla — to be everyone's default search engine. The figure was revealed by Google's search head Prabhakar Raghavan when he testified in court on October 28, according to The Verge.

About $18 billion of that total went directly to Apple, according to a New York Times report published earlier in October 2023, and Google has had its deal with Apple in place since 2003 — so the payment is the current year of a two-decade arrangement, not a one-off. Questioned on the amount of money Google spends to get first pick of search engines, Pichai said the decision was made with the consumer in mind: Google pays big bucks to be everywhere so that it can take in all the data and be the best search engine across different companies' devices, he said, according to The Verge.

The trial also produced evidence that Google understood the value of defaults very early on. U.S. Justice Department lawyer Meagan Bellshaw showed Pichai a 2007 email from a Google product strategy meeting containing data showing that when people changed their browser homepage to Google, they did 15% more Google searches, and that when they switched away, their Google searches dropped 27%. The email summarizing that meeting, sent to Pichai as well as other Google leaders, read: "Nitin argues that focusing on homepage market share is one of the most effective things we can do to make gains in search market share," according to The Verge.



---


# Deft's Competitive Landscape: Search Incumbents

Given that it is building a search solution for e-commerce, Deft already faces challenges from Amazon and Google, both of which have shipped comparable features.

In September 2023, Amazon updated its visual search feature that lets users snap a photo of a product and search for similar items on the platform. Google released its multi-search feature in 2022, letting users fuse images and text — the same combination Deft offers.

Separately, Deft will also face competition from other startups like Objective, a Matrix Partners-backed startup building an API platform for multimodal search.



---


# Danny Sullivan, From Journalist To Google Liaison

After Cutts left, Google replaced him with a handful of people, none of whom could quite fill his shoes: "Those personalities sometimes were standoffish," Forrester said. "Some of them were superior. Some of them were a bit too wallflower."

One of the people Google brought in was Danny Sullivan, a former journalist who started Search Engine Land — the industry publication where Schwartz works — back in the 2000s. In 2009 Sullivan was described as "the closest approximation to an umpire in the search world," so when he published "A deep look at Google's biggest-ever search quality crisis" in 2017 and then took a job as Google's public liaison for Search only a few months later, it felt to some SEOs as though a congressperson working on gun safety legislation had quit to become an NRA lobbyist.

Forrester reports the suspicion without endorsing it. "There is a thread across the industry of people who believe that Google just made Danny an offer he couldn't say no to, and it was designed essentially to take his voice out of the conversation," he said. "I don't believe that's the case," he went on, but compared to Cutts, "I think that Danny specifically stays out of a lot of public conversations because he is in those private conversations with businesses."



---


# Consumer Search Startups And Switching Barriers

The premise attacked is that a better search product wins users. The cautionary case is Neeva, founded by former Google execs, which tried to convince people to switch to paid and private search with additional features; earlier in 2023 the startup shut down its consumer efforts and eventually got acquired by Snowflake.

Adii Pienaar, an investor in Deft, said that Deft has to give compelling reasons to users to switch to its service. His grounds are behavioral rather than technical: "Users' natural behavior for search is to follow the path of least resistance, i.e. most people just pick up their phone and just use the default search engine."

The conclusion he draws sets the bar Deft must clear: "For Deft to change that behavior, they will need to create a high-value proposition."



---


# Projected Publisher Traffic Losses From AI Search

Publishers believe they will lose somewhere between 20% and 40% of their website traffic once Google's AI products fully roll out, according to a Wall Street Journal report noted by TechCrunch on 15 December 2023. That report also led with a modelling result from the online magazine The Atlantic: when The Atlantic modelled what would happen if Google integrated AI into search, it found that 75% of the time the AI would answer the user's query without requiring a click-through to its website, losing it traffic.

The stakes are set by how much publisher traffic Google currently supplies. According to data from Similarweb cited in the same coverage, Google today drives nearly 40% of publishers' traffic, so a shift to AI-answered queries could have a major impact on publishers' traffic going forward. The suit filed by Helena World Chronicle takes up precisely this question of how AI will impact publishers' businesses.

Some publishers are trying to get ahead of the problem: Axel Springer inked a deal with OpenAI in the same week to license its news for AI model training.



---


# Investor Views On Deft's Differentiation

Two of Deft's investors argue it is differentiated, but locate the edge in different places. Caroline Casson, a partner at Vitalize Venture Capital and an investor in Deft, believes the startup has an edge because of its knowledge graph for products. Her grounds are the difficulty of the backend work: "Building a robust e-commerce search engine is incredibly complex on the backend. The extensive knowledge graph that Deft has built combined with AI search capabilities makes for a high-quality user experience. We were excited about early iterations of the product when we invested and we continue to be impressed with each product enhancement," Casson told TechCrunch over email. The warrant is that complexity that is hard to replicate is what makes the quality durable.

Adii Pienaar, another investor and co-founder of WooCommerce, which was acquired by Automattic, told TechCrunch over a call that he sees Deft as solving user experience problems rather than technical ones.

His ground is a change in consumer behavior rather than in technology: "Over the last couple of years, consumers have been trying out new ways to interact with and purchase products. I see Deft as creating a new kind of UX for purchasing."

qid: Did the approach to presenting prop bets to bettors by Sporting News change between the report on NBA prop bets published on October 2, 2023, and the report on NCAAF bowl season prop bets published later?
context:
# Prop Bet Examples By Sport

Every major sport with odds at the best sports betting apps will have prop bets, and the shape of those props follows each sport's statistics. The NBA offers a wide range, varying from player to team bets and leaning heavily on the statistical side of the game: how many points a player will score, the number of assists or three-pointers a player will have, which player will score the first basket. Team props are also available, such as whether a team will lead at the end of a certain quarter, or an over/under on the total number of points a team will score.

The NFL is the king of sports betting, and NFL betting sites have no qualms about showcasing every possible bet type. Bettors find many prop opportunities, especially for the Super Bowl; during the regular season one of the most popular options is the "anytime touchdown scorer" bet, where you wager on a player to score a touchdown at any point in the game, and other props focus on one team or both teams.

Baseball, hockey and soccer follow the same logic on their own stat lines. MLB props focus primarily on individual players and statistical achievements such as home runs, RBI and strikeouts — an over/under for a starting pitcher's strikeouts, or the number of bases a hitter will reach. NHL sites carry the props you would expect from a major North American league, such as player assists or a certain player scoring a goal, plus shots on goal, team goals in a game, and which team will score first. In Major League Soccer, where demand has increased as the sport's popularity grows nationwide, props often focus on individual accomplishments such as scoring a goal or collecting an assist, and also include how many cards the two teams will combine to draw or a team's total number of corner kicks.



---


# The Prop Bet

A prop bet is a "side bet" with a sportsbook on a specific event or statistical accomplishment within a game, and these rarely have anything to do with the outcome of the game itself. Examples include betting on LeBron James scoring over 20 points in a single game, or the Dallas Cowboys gaining over 300 receiving yards in a game.

Props are easy to understand and add a twist to most sporting events, because you can bet on in-game events not tied to the outcome. They are popular throughout the year and are posted for every major sport, but the pinnacle for prop betting is the Super Bowl — the most popular day of the year for prop bets, which range from the typical to the exotic. Sporting News notes that you do not have to wait for the Super Bowl to get involved.



---


# NBA Prop Bets: Definition And Common Markets

A prop bet — short for proposition bet — is a side wager on an aspect of a game that usually doesn't tie directly to the result, and in the NBA prop bets deal with both players and teams.

Their discriminating features, as the Sporting News describes them, are that they are easy to understand, numerous, and cover both player props and team props to give plenty of variety, which is why they are an easy way to jump into basketball betting in what is one of the most popular sports to bet on in the US.

Typical NBA player props include how many points a player will score, the number of rebounds a player will have, how many assists a player will get, rebounds and assists combined, points, rebounds and assists combined, how many steals a player will get, and the number of three-pointers made. Typical NBA team props include which team will reach 10 points first, which team will have the highest-scoring period, which team will score first, which team will win the first half, which team will win the second half, and whether there will be a fourth-quarter comeback victory. All of the best sports betting sites have their own selection of prop bets for each NBA game, so shopping around to find the sportsbooks that best suit your needs matters.



---


# Why Moneyline Odds Change

Lines at sports betting apps change quickly for two primary reasons — public betting and new information — and sportsbooks adjust moneyline odds to stay profitable, balance their book and reflect the most current information about an event. Before setting odds oddsmakers gather extensive data, then release the finalized odds to the public; from that point a bettor can bet immediately or wait for shifts, though predicting those shifts is challenging.

The time dimension shows how an opening price drifts. Odds for the next Super Bowl champion released shortly after the previous Super Bowl are based mostly on the recently concluded season; as the new season approaches and teams make changes, the odds adjust to perceived championship chances, and as games progress the lines keep evolving with team performances.

The mechanism has five named drivers. Public betting patterns move a line because, when a significant amount of money lands on one team or participant, sportsbooks adjust the odds to balance their liability — making the price less favorable for the heavily-bet side and more favorable for the less-bet side to encourage even betting and reduce financial risk. New information matters because changes in player injuries, player substitutions or weather conditions alter the perceived outcome, and books adjust once such information becomes public. Professional bettors move lines because large wagers from sharp bettors often reflect insights or information that can influence the odds. Initial miscalculation is a fourth driver: sometimes the opening odds are perceived as offering value, and heavy betting on one side signals that the initial price was potentially "off," prompting an adjustment. Event dynamics is the fifth, applying to live betting placed while the event is in progress, where the evolving dynamics of the match lead to frequent changes.



---


# Advantages Of Prop Bets

Sporting News makes three arguments for prop bets: their lines move more slowly than other bet types, they offer greater variety, and they are usually very easy to understand. Every bet has positives and negatives, and props are no different — but these three are the positives.

The slow-moving lines create a timing edge. Prop bet odds are developed from game lines and totals at sportsbooks, yet prop lines tend to adjust more slowly. If you are watching New York Jets vs. Buffalo Bills and see the total shift because of an incoming winter storm, many bettors will scramble to get on the "under" before the main line moves too far; the better move is to scope out the prop bets for individual players, because most betting sites do not have the personnel to keep tabs on every possible player, so there may be value in an "under" on a quarterback's passing yards while those lines have not caught up.

The variety argument rests on what the main markets lack. Moneylines, point spreads and totals are constant in every major sport but do not offer much variety; props do, and they can add interest to a game that seems one-sided in the major markets. Larger sporting events, especially the Super Bowl, offer a massive variety of bets ranging from the typical to the exotic and everything in between.

The comprehensibility argument is that props tend to ask a question of the bettor — will a specific player hit a home run, will Team X have over/under 3.5 field goals in a game, will Team Y give up a powerplay goal — and whatever the question, props are fairly easy for a newcomer to understand.



---


# FanDuel Sportsbook: MLB And NBA Markets, Props And Same-Game Parlays

FanDuel is a top destination for MLB bettors looking to bet daily and a name that resonates strongly within the NBA betting community, with popularity and success akin to its counterpart DraftKings. For baseball it offers the staple bets — run lines, where you bet on the margin of victory, and totals, predicting the combined score of both teams — plus dozens of player props allowing bettors to focus on individual performances such as hits, home runs or strikeouts, and an array of game props and futures bets for longer-term outcomes like division champions or MVP candidates.

For basketball, alongside the standard NBA odds, FanDuel stands out with an expansive selection of NBA player and game props, and a unique feature allowing users to create same-game parlays that combine NBA moneylines, totals and props into a personalized bet.

Newcomers to FanDuel's online sportsbook can typically claim $150 in bonus bets, and the book may offer three months of NBA League Pass to sweeten the deal. Claiming the promotion is straightforward and needs no special promo code: prospective bettors must sign up, deposit and place a $5 bet to be eligible.



---


# Why Basketball Odds Fluctuate More Than Other Sports

Basketball odds are known to fluctuate more than those of other sports, and the factors driving those shifts range from having only a few impact players per team to the sheer frequency of games.

That structure creates an exploitable relationship for the bettor. By following a single team you can track its momentum swings, which players tend to get on hot or cold streaks, and how well the team plays at home versus on the road, then use that information to your advantage for both pre-game and live wagers. Similar categories of moneylines, spreads, totals and NBA prop bets should appear across both formats.

The NBA is also special because of the number of bets available for every game, ranging from pre-game to live betting and parlays: adding up the standard bets, game props, player props, in-game betting and more, there is a staggering volume of bets for every NBA game at online sportsbooks.

qid: What company, recently reported by TechCrunch to have made significant profitability in the third quarter, has also faced criticism for not adequately preventing incidents and streamlining driver sign-ups, despite being aware of safety concerns since 2014 and introducing new app features to address them?
context:
# In-Car Camera Proposal

Uber's in-app safety features cannot work for the riders who need them most, so survivors are asking for in-vehicle surveillance and more extensive background checks instead — the argument attorney Rachel Abrams put to TechCrunch on 2023-10-13. Abrams argues that Uber's safety features are insufficient because they're all app-based and only potentially useful if a rider has access to their own phone.

The grounds are the circumstances in which the assaults she has handled actually occurred. "The majority of clients I represent and the women I've spoken to who have been sexually assaulted have experienced: (A) someone else ordered the ride for them; (B) their phone is dead or they can't locate their phone to use the safety shield; or (C) if they could use their phone, they're incapacitated," said Abrams. She says she has interviewed upward of 5,000 survivors over the course of several years and has seen no difference in the number of attacks before or after implementation of these in-app features.

The demands go beyond cameras. Aside from in-vehicle surveillance and more extensive background checks, the survivors are asking Uber to implement driver training on interactions with passengers, a zero-tolerance policy for drivers, sexual harassment education and training, and a more adequate system to encourage customer reporting and monitor customer complaints. On screening, Uber has lobbied against additional background requirements for drivers, which has given the company authority to conduct its own background checks with little or no oversight, unlike most taxi operators. Uber and Lyft say smudged fingerprints can lead to inaccurate results and that fingerprint checks reference historical arrest records, which can have discriminatory effects on some minority communities that face disproportionately high arrest rates; an Uber spokesperson told CNN arrest records are incomplete and often lack information about whether a person has been convicted of a crime.

The evidentiary record available to test the claim is partial. Uber hasn't released safety data for 2021 and 2022, and won't say when it plans to do so, though older data backs up some of Abrams' claims. Uber has published two safety reports — one containing data from 2017 to 2018 and another with data from 2019 to 2020 — and the ride-hail company claims that the rate of sexual assault reported on the app decreased 38% between its first and second reports.



---


# Uber Assault Litigation

Hundreds of women have filed lawsuits against Uber claiming the company hasn't done enough to prevent instances of sexual assault by drivers, and a panel of judges has ruled that more than 80 cases can be consolidated into federal court, TechCrunch reported on 2023-10-13. The stakes are high for both parties, with implications extending to future Uber riders and drivers: the outcome of the case could result in sweeping changes to Uber's platform, which plaintiffs argue will reduce sexual assault and also raise new concerns over privacy. As TechCrunch put it, "Technology lies at the center of this very human story."

Uber has attempted to address sexual assaults by drivers — which the lawsuits claim Uber has known about since 2014 — through new safety features in its app, like a 911 button and the ability to share location with a friend. The additions arrived on a five-year timeline: the 911 button and location-sharing feature were both introduced in 2018; in 2021, Uber introduced a feature that allows riders and drivers to record audio during a trip; and the following year, Uber launched a pilot to provide passengers with live help from an ADT safety agent, as well as PIN verifications to ensure passengers are connected to the correct driver.

Survivors and their attorneys say that response has been inadequate, and they're calling for better technological solutions like in-vehicle surveillance cameras. Rachel Abrams — a sexual assault attorney and partner at law firm Peiffer Wolf Carr Kane Conway & Wise, one of the law firms working on the multidistrict litigation, who filed the petition to consolidate the various actions in federal court — argues the app-based solutions are half-measures that haven't quelled instances of sexual violence against passengers on the platform. Mandatory in-vehicle cameras in Uber cars is "essential for safety," she says, citing data from studies of taxis equipped with in-vehicle cameras, which she says has drastically reduced instances of sexual assaults against passengers, as well as assault of passengers against drivers.

Uber told TechCrunch it cannot comment on pending litigation but said it remains committed to the safety of all users on its platform.



---


# Cruise's Nationwide Driverless Pause

Two days after California suspended its permits, Cruise decided to pause driverless operations in every market where it had started to charge for its robotaxi service, including Austin, Houston and Phoenix. TechCrunch's reporter, writing on 2023-10-30, found the decision surprising given how sources had described an all-hands meeting earlier that week led by co-founder and CEO Kyle Vogt: in that meeting, which came the day after the DMV suspended Cruise's permit, Vogt and other leaders told staff the company had not paused operations elsewhere besides California and gave no indication that it was planning to. Instead, Vogt told employees the company was re-evaluating how it discloses information to regulators to ensure it is clearly communicated, according to an account from sources who heard the call.

Cruise had even quietly launched driverless operations in Miami with just a few vehicles, a move that suggested the company was moving ahead despite its significant problems in California. As for what changed, TechCrunch offers two possibilities: perhaps Cruise execs were pressured by GM, or they looked around and realized that they were losing support from other states. Either way, Cruise said it's now going to examine "processes, systems, and tools and reflect on how we can better operate in a way that will earn public trust."



---


# Uber's Recording Features And Driver Screening

Recording inside an Uber is currently something drivers opt into and control, not something the platform mandates, and driver screening is run by third-party vendors rather than by fingerprint check — the two procedures survivors are asking Uber to change, per TechCrunch on 2023-10-13. Many drivers install their own dash cams to record trips, usually as backup evidence for insurance claims or to defend themselves against unfair deactivations from Uber's platform. Uber is also piloting a new video recording feature for drivers that allows them to record video on their smartphones — but in those cases, the driver decides what and when to record, and when to share that data.

The case for making cameras mandatory is deterrence: "These are predatory, opportunistic drivers taking advantage of vulnerable women, so if they're on film, they likely wouldn't commit the crime," attorney Rachel Abrams told TechCrunch. Uber didn't respond to TechCrunch's request for more information about why it hasn't mandated the use of cameras in ride-hail vehicles, but as with any surveillance, there are privacy issues, and the legality of mandating cameras also varies across local and state laws — so the procedure cannot simply be imposed uniformly. Abrams has her own theory as to why Uber has been slow to implement security cameras: "Cost isn't the issue. It's that it would deter drivers because a lot of drivers don't want cameras. And so if they don't have drivers, they don't make money."

Screening runs through outside vendors. Uber uses third-party companies like Checkr and Appriss to do background checks, which Sergio Avedian, senior contributor at The Rideshare Guy, says "are at best watered down and not guaranteed of bad apples from falling through the cracks." The survivors in the joined lawsuit allege that Uber's "fast and shallow background checks" are substandard and designed to make it as easy as possible for drivers to sign up quickly.

The change the lawsuit asks for is an added screening step: it calls on Uber to also include fingerprinting, which would run prospective drivers through FBI databases. Kevin Conway, managing partner at Peiffer Wolf Carr Kane Conway & Wise, frames the current arrangement as chosen rather than inherited: "This is a very intentional and deliberate decision as evidenced by Uber's active lobbying and resistance against municipalities and regulatory bodies implementing any kind of biometric fingerprinting requirements for drivers."



---


# Discord's Shop, Remix And Client Improvements

Separately from its safety work, Discord announced a slew of new features and enhancements slated to arrive either in the near future or down the line. The platform's in-app shop, which Discord began testing last month with Nitro subscribers, will soon be available to all users; the marketplace features digital items people can use to decorate their avatars and profiles, and Discord will offer store discounts to Nitro members as part of a new perk for signing up.

This week the company will also start a broad roll-out of a feature called Remix, which lets users edit an image directly within Discord's mobile app and share it with their friends and servers.

On the client side, the company spent much of the last year improving its Android and iOS apps, with one recent update improving app launch times on both platforms. In the near future Discord says people can expect a new "Midnight" dark mode that the company claims reduces battery consumption on devices with OLED screens, more functional notification tabs, and a new search feature for the settings menu to make it easier to find the exact option you are looking to tweak.



---


# NHTSA Investigation Of Cruise Pedestrian Incidents

The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) has opened an investigation into GM subsidiary Cruise's AV system following several incidents involving pedestrians in San Francisco, TechCrunch reported on 2023-10-22.

The most recent of those incidents left a woman stuck under a Cruise robotaxi after being hit by a human-driven vehicle.

qid: Between the TalkSport report on Manchester United's future plans published on October 16, 2023, and the Sporting News report on Manchester United's performance in European competitions published on December 12, 2023, was there no change in the narrative regarding Manchester United's success and planning?
context:
# The INEOS Plan For Manchester United's Football Operations

Sir Jim Ratcliffe is demanding an executive role and overall control of Manchester United's day-to-day football matters, and plans to appoint his own sporting director, with former Tottenham and Southampton transfer guru Paul Mitchell one of the main names in the frame, talkSPORT reported on 18 October 2023.

The plan reaches across the club's football leadership. Ratcliffe's arrival raises doubts over the future of current sporting director John Murtough and chief executive Richard Arnold, although manager Erik ten Hag is believed to be on a solid footing despite United's poor start to the season. Sir Dave Brailsford — the mastermind behind Team GB's cycling success at the London 2012 Olympics and director of sport for Ratcliffe's company INEOS — is expected to have a prominent role in any reshuffle. Ratcliffe also has ambitious plans to upgrade Old Trafford and turn it into a 90,000-seat stadium. He wants the deal ratified in time for the January transfer window, though because of FFP concerns there is no guarantee United will be able to spend big. Despite turning 71 the day before the board meeting, his plans appear to centre on long-term stability and success rather than a short-term turnaround in United's fortunes.

The ownership rationale is that Ratcliffe would take charge of footballing matters, something the Glazers have been accused of having little to no interest in. He is already a top-tier European owner through OGC Nice — and also owns Lausanne in Switzerland — where there has been some success but nothing compared to Nice's French riviera neighbours, the club to which Ratcliffe appears set to look for inspiration.



---


# Paul Mitchell's Blueprint For A Manchester United Rebuild

Paul Mitchell argues that Manchester United must define an identity and a five-year blueprint and then hold to it, because consistency of decision-making over that period is what produces sustainable success — a blueprint he laid out while still at Monaco, reported by talkSPORT on 16 October 2023.

His grounds begin with context and end with comparison. "I think context is important to measure what Manchester United's current situation is, but I think they do need to get to the point of really putting down what Manchester United needs to be in the modern game," he explained. "We are a long time from the Sir Alex Ferguson era. Erik ten Hag is a top coach from Ajax but they need a top blueprint not only for now but for the next five years, and work towards that, and sometimes on that journey there are hard moments when you don't get the right results, even though you're doing the right things." The warrant is that results in the short run are a noisy signal: "You have to know that, over that period, the consistency of the decision-making will yield a good end result. I think we've seen that both Manchester City and Liverpool, that when you adopt that long-term strategy you can get real consistency and sustainable success."

The content of the blueprint is an identity statement spanning the whole club: "putting down their identity of what they want to be today, but most crucially what they want to be in five years' time, and where they want to be, and what they want to look like; from everything from young players, to the style of play, to the whole culture peace in Manchester United." There is a counter-consideration attached — almost certain to consult Ralf Rangnick before any approach from Ratcliffe, Mitchell may be warned off a club where long-term thinking has not existed — but should Ratcliffe get his man it could signal exactly the change in fortunes he and every supporter has been hoping for.



---


# Manchester United's European Decline Since Ferguson

The Independent argued on 12 December 2023 that Manchester United's 1-0 defeat to Bayern Munich should have been a landmark low but instead felt grimly routine, because group-stage elimination has become the club's normal European outcome in the post-Ferguson era rather than an aberration.

The grounds are frequency and pattern. Manchester United, one of the grandest and richest names in this competition, have again gone out of the Champions League at the group stage; it is the third time it has happened since Sir Alex Ferguson, meaning it is their most common round of exit in that period. The night is presented as one more entry in a decade of disappointment in a competition in which this club rose to its most emotional heights — a low, but just part of that longer run.

The warrant is the gap between the occasion and the performance. These are not the sounds we are used to hearing after that Champions League theme; something does stir when the anthem is played at Old Trafford amid the lights — well, for most, that is, except the players. United should not be performing like this on what is supposed to be the classic European night at Old Trafford, and the display was a reminder that all they are going to have for some time are their memories. Having been involved in so many ludicrously chaotic matches, the biggest of all ended up being a non-event: this game never threatened to stir anything, and United never threatened at all. That, the argument runs, can now be talked about definitively, since it has been decisively ended.



---


# Preview Of Chelsea's December 2023 Visit To Old Trafford

Manchester United would love a repeat of the previous season's 4-1 home win over Chelsea when the Blues visited Old Trafford that Wednesday, per Sporting News on Dec. 5, 2023.

The pressure on United had grown again following their lacklustre 1-0 defeat at Newcastle on the Saturday, and another setback against a Chelsea side — who beat Brighton & Hove Albion 3-2 the following day — would worsen the misery around Old Trafford.

Sporting News framed the meeting as one between two heavyweights of world football: United and Chelsea are two of only seven teams to have won the modern Premier League, and are only behind Liverpool when it comes to English success with European trophies. Chelsea's recent record against United was poor, but they had won the Premier League twice since United last did so in the 2012/13 season and could exploit the poor form of Ten Hag's side. The article set out to look at a rivalry that stretches back decades and had been sharply in focus over recent years.



---


# The Manchester United Takeover Bidding Process, 2022-2023

The sale process for Manchester United ran for roughly eleven months from November 2022, when the Glazer family announced they were open to offers, to mid-October 2023, when the withdrawal of Qatari bidder Sheikh Jassim bin Al Thani left Sir Jim Ratcliffe clear to complete a partial takeover, as reported by talkSPORT on 18 October 2023.

It was in November 2022, while Qatar was hosting the controversial 2022 World Cup, that the deeply unpopular Glazers revealed they were looking to cash in all or at least some of their shares, a decision that had United fans rejoicing. The move was mainly influenced by the fact that Raine had brokered a deal with Todd Boehly to commit £4.5bn to take control of Chelsea, which gave the Glazers grand ideas that they could rake in as much as double that for a global sporting institution like United. After several rounds of bidding the race narrowed to a straight shootout between Oldham-born Ratcliffe, who had previously offered £4bn to buy Chelsea, and Sheikh Jassim bin Al Thani, who professed to being a lifelong Red Devils fan and set up the "'92 Foundation" in tribute to the famous class of '92 of David Beckham and company.

It had initially been hoped the process would conclude in time for the summer transfer window, but the longer it dragged on — prompting several large-scale protests from United fans — the more apparent it became that Joel and Avram were reluctant sellers, as talkSPORT revealed in March. Sheikh Jassim's public statement promising to restore United "to former glories" was also seen as a thinly veiled swipe at the Glazers, which did not help his negotiating hand. The Qatari banker's patience finally snapped, and his withdrawal at the end of the preceding week left the pathway clear for Ratcliffe to complete what he has always viewed as his dream purchase. At times the saga resembled an X-Factor style judges' houses audition.



---


# Sheffield United vs Manchester United Preview, October 2023

Sheffield United, rock bottom of the Premier League with just one point on the board, hosted Manchester United at 8:00pm on 21 October 2023 live on talkSPORT, with talkSPORT noting the previous day that their hopes could be looking up given Erik ten Hag's men's disappointing season.

Sheffield United's season could not be going much worse. Manchester United sat tenth in the table, having won four and lost four of their opening eight games. # The 2023 Calendar-Year Top Goalscorer Race

Al Nassr striker Cristiano Ronaldo looked set to be the top scorer in the 2023 calendar year after his Boxing Day double against Al Ittihad. He was not the only star in great form, with players across Europe banging them in for fun.

context:
# Jai Opetaia's First-Round Knockout Of Ellis Zorro

Jai Opetaia knocked out Ellis Zorro in the first round in Saudi Arabia early on Sunday morning AEDT, as reported by The Roar on 23 December 2023, moving the unbeaten Australian to 24-0 with 19 stoppages and retaining his Ring Magazine belt.

The finish came with four seconds remaining in the first round, a huge left hand obliterating Zorro; the punch sent the dazed Englishman into the ropes and on to the canvas, and the outclassed Zorro was eventually able to offer a sheepish smile in what was his first loss in 18 professional fights. The bout was reportedly worth $680,000 to the Australian, who was forced to vacate his IBF world title belt to take his place on the mega-card in Riyadh, capping a week of drama in which he was stripped of his IBF status in controversial circumstances.

Opetaia, a former Olympian, said afterwards: "I train for 12 rounds, was prepared for 12 and if the knockout comes, it comes. He was a bit too hesitant and he got clipped, that's the way it goes." Commentator Sergio Mora described the one-punch knockout as "devastating and scary" while fellow pundit Mike Costello added: "At any weight, at any level that's as clinical as it gets in this sport," and "He dismissed Zorro with the minimum of fuss and the maximum of power."



---


# Opetaia's Vacated IBF Cruiserweight Title And Avoided Opponents

Jai Opetaia broke his jaw twice on the way to upsetting Mairis Briedis to win the IBF and Ring belts the previous year, then endured a frustrating wait of 14 months to defend them, as reported by The Roar on 23 December 2023.

Two obstacles are recorded. Multiple opponents have dodged the 28-year-old; and the IBF demanded he fight Briedis next despite the injured Latvian being happy to delay their bout until he is fit early the following year.

Asked whether he had vented his frustrations in the ring, Opetaia acknowledged the frustration but set it aside: "I did, but look at this place, beautiful, I'm happy to be here. I'm pumped; first round knockout, I'm ready for the next fight. The last 18 months is just part of the journey. I'm here in the ring now and that's all that matters. These dudes (promoters) put the people in front of me and I just knock them out."



---


# Eddie Hearn On Opetaia Emulating Usyk And Unifying Cruiserweight

Promoter Eddie Hearn argued in December 2023 that Jai Opetaia has the potential to replicate Oleksandr Usyk's career — unifying the cruiserweight division before moving up to the heavyweights: the claim is that Opetaia will do the exact same thing as Usyk, and the warrant is that he is a pound-for-pound talent whom every fight man already recognises as the No. 1 cruiserweight in the world.

"Every fight man knows," Hearn said of Opetaia, adding: "I believe Jai's going to do the exact same thing (as Usyk) … we're talking about a pound-for-pound talent."

The report attaches a near-term scheduling detail to that path: Opetaia's next fight could be on the Tyson Fury-Oleksandr Usyk card in Riyadh on 17 February.

# Elijah Garcia Stops Armando Resendiz In The Eighth To Open The Canelo-Charlo PPV

Elijah Garcia stopped Armando Resendiz in the eighth round to open the Canelo-Charlo pay-per-view, Sporting News reported in its live coverage of 2023-09-30. The card kicked off at 8:13 p.m. ET with the undefeated Elijah Garcia (15-0, 12 KOs) taking on Armando Resendiz (14-1, 10 KOs) in middleweight action. By 8:39 p.m. ET, through six rounds, Garcia had looked excellent — winning the combination exchanges and landing the heavier shots — while Resendiz was very game and trying to build momentum off his upset win over Jarrett Hurd, but the 20-year-old Garcia was proving to be too much for him.

At 8:56 p.m. ET Garcia finished the job in style. Although Resendiz was in the fight, Garcia's power punches were having more of an effect on him in the later rounds; Garcia dropped Resendiz with a body shot and a hook to the head in the eighth, then took his time picking his spots until a huge combination forced the hand of referee Tony Weeks at the 1:26 mark, giving Garcia his 16th victory. The coverage added that the middleweight division could use some new blood and that Garcia might be the future of the division.



---


# Corrales TKO 10 Castillo: The 2005 Lightweight Classic

Diego Corrales stopped Jose Luis Castillo in the tenth round on May 7, 2005 at the Mandalay Bay Events Centre in Las Vegas, with the WBC, WBO and Ring Magazine lightweight titles at stake, in what Sporting News calls one of the greatest fights in history.

Both men arrived rebuilt after losses to Floyd Mayweather. Corrales had reestablished his image after being outclassed by Mayweather in 2001: he fell short against the excellent Joel Casamayor, then avenged that defeat to pick up the vacant WBO super featherweight crown, and on moving up to lightweight came from behind to stop WBO champion Acelino Frietas. Castillo also had history with Mayweather — many fans believe the Mexican star deserved the decision in April 2002 — but after Mayweather won the rematch decisively, Castillo rebuilt with excellent wins over Juan Lazcano, Casamayor and Julio Diaz, the Lazcano triumph giving him the vacant WBC title.

Despite functional height and reach advantages, Corrales elected to meet Castillo on the inside and the action was incredible. In the 10th, Castillo decked his man with a sharp left hook and then put him over again with another left; after both knockdowns "Chico" spat out his mouthpiece, drawing a point deduction. Battered and woozy with his left eye almost closed, Corrales needed a miracle and found it: when the bout resumed he nailed his man with a hard right and an even harder left, Castillo wilted, and he was stopped seconds later by a savage, head-snapping assault. There's been nothing like it since.



---


# Vazquez SD 12 Marquez III: The Best Of The Most Exciting Modern Trilogy

Israel Vazquez beat Rafael Marquez by split decision over 12 rounds on March 1, 2008 at the Home Depot Centre in Carson, California, retaining the WBC and Ring Magazine super bantamweight titles in the third and best fight of their series. It won Fight of the Year for 2008.

Sporting News argues the two Mexicans turned in the most consistently exciting trilogy in modern boxing history, criminally overlooked; there was an ill-advised part four, won by Marquez, but this was and always will be a trilogy. Where Ali-Frazier II, Gatti-Ward II and Barrera-Morales II did not live up to acts I and III of those fistic plays, Vazquez and Marquez produced three back-to-back classics that will stand the test of time. The only reason the first encounter, won by Marquez, was not awarded Fight of the Year 2007 was that it was beaten by the rematch, won by Vazquez, in the same year.

As in fights one and three, the ebb and flow was incredible, with both men trading hellacious combinations and Vazquez hitting the canvas in round four. Marquez's superior speed and timing was carrying the day, but Vazquez slowly battled back and was aided further when his rival was deducted a point for a low blow in round 10. The 12th and final round took the fight into the stratosphere: desperate for a big finish, Vazquez nailed his countryman in the closing seconds and only the ropes held Marquez up. Ruled a knockdown, that crucial moment gave Vazquez the split decision and his championships.



---


# Adolpho Washington vs Virgil Hill, 1993: The Camera Stoppage

Adolpho Washington's 175lb world title challenge against Virgil Hill in 1993 ended when he went to sit down in his corner at the end of round 11 and his swollen eye hit an intrusive ringside TV camera, opening a cut, talkSPORT recalled on 15 November 2023.

The gash was so bad that the fight was called off, Hill was declared a technical decision winner, and Washington was denied the chance to go all-out in round 12.

It may not have changed the end result — chances are Hill was winning anyway — but stoppage via aggressive TV camera is surely unique in boxing history, and Washington can forever hold a grudge against ringside cameras.

qid: Does the TechCrunch article suggest that Amazon's large language model (LLM) is not trained on kids' responses, while The Age article raises concerns about TikTok's pixel collecting data without consent?
context:
# Alexa Kids Data Handling And The Echo Pop Kids Launch

Amazon says it is not training its LLM on kids' answers, and that "Explore with Alexa" and any future LLM-backed features will continue to follow the same data handling policies as "classic Alexa" — the non-AI Alexa. In practice that means the Alexa app will include a list of the questions asked by kids in the household, for those with a kids' profile, along with the response Alexa provided; that history can be stored or deleted either manually or automatically, depending on the account's settings. These statements were made by the company to TechCrunch and reported on 25 October 2023, alongside the launch of the feature.

The launch also brought hardware. The new Echo Pop Kids speakers became available for purchase at the same time, starting at $49.99 in the U.S., in two new designs — Marvel's Avengers and Disney Princess — that feature corresponding character themes, letting kids hear a greeting, fun fact or joke about an Avenger or Disney Princess in keeping with the theme. Both include six months of access to the Amazon Kids+ subscription service, which, beyond "Explore with Alexa," also offers a range of kid-friendly games, apps, books, videos and more, including custom Alexa themes. Buying a Kids device is not a precondition for the feature, however: "Explore with Alexa" works on any device set to kids mode, or any communal family device, if parents have set up their kids' voice ID.

Two scope limits attach to the launch as described. The experience is available in English only at first, with internationalization further down the road. And the offline arrangement is framed as a stage rather than an endpoint — Amazon eventually wants the generative AI experience integrated at runtime for both kids and adults, while knowing it needs to proceed carefully, especially with kids: "We do want to integrate an LLM in runtime in a more protected way than we would integrate it for adults…However, this approach lets us iterate and figure out the right ways to get both safe and delightful content outputted from the LLM for kids," says Venkataswamy. On the adult side, he says Amazon was preparing to launch an AI-powered "Let's Chat" Alexa experience later that same year.



---


# TikTok Pixel Pre-Consent Data Collection Test

Testing by The Age found that personal information typed into Australian websites was sent back to TikTok often before the user clicked "I consent" to the website's privacy policy.

The test was run by installing a browser extension and then visiting websites such as Sportsbet, Kmart, Beyond Blue and many others. On each site the testers went to sign up for an account, entering personal information including their full name, email address and phone number. Using Omnibug, they could see in real time that information being sent back to TikTok — and, crucially, that this often happened before consent to the site's privacy policy had been given.

The mechanism named in the report is a TikTok tool called "automatic advanced matching," which sees when a user enters text into a form field or a search box and, if it looks like an email address or phone number, scrapes that data.



---


# Amazon's Offline Guardrail Pipeline For Alexa Kids Generative AI

Amazon does not hook kids up to a large language model at runtime; instead it runs the LLM offline to generate content in bulk, puts that content through a review process using both humans and AI, and only then loads the reviewed material into the "Explore with Alexa" experience. "We want to go slow and be intentional and be measured with how we're introducing this new tech, as well as any new tech for kids, which is why we're not just hooking the experience up to an LLM at runtime and kind of letting kids go at it," explains Arjun Venkataswamy, senior product manager for Alexa Kids, in an interview with TechCrunch. "The way that we've integrated an LLM here is we use it to generate content at scale offline, and then go through a review process that includes both humans, as well as AI, and then take that reviewed content and then put it into our experience," he says.

The preconditions that motivate the pipeline are the two failure modes of the technology and the audience: generative AI can be led astray or "hallucinate" answers, while kids could ask inappropriate questions. Amazon's answer is a sequence of constraints applied before any child hears an answer. First, the Alexa Kids science team narrowed the new experience, which leverages Alexa's LLM technology, to include only kid-friendly fun facts and trivia questions. Second, the source material is restricted: initially, the content comes from just two partners, the World Wildlife Fund and A-Z animals. Third, the LLM generates content at scale offline rather than on the device in real time. Fourth, that generated content goes through review by humans and by AI — AI is enlisted here because the model can generate tens of thousands of potential responses, so not every answer can be reviewed by a human before being added to the experience. Fifth, only the reviewed content is put into the experience, so kids are not using generative AI on the fly when conversing with Alexa, and what they hear is pre-reviewed and drawn from a small dataset of just animal facts and sources.

The procedure is scoped to the current, offline arrangement and explicitly does not yet extend to runtime generation for kids. Amazon has no date for that step: "I can't give you a timeline, because we don't have a concrete answer for what exactly we're going to be doing yet, although we do have plans and experiments we're planning to look into," Venkataswamy says. The gating criterion is external validation rather than an internal milestone — "I will say that in terms of our criteria for when we're going to get there, we're working closely with the Family Trust team at Amazon that's connected to a variety of research institutions in the U.S…we want to be able to get some confidence from external partners that our approach is right," he adds. The narrow content scope is likewise provisional: in time the team would like to expand the AI to include other areas of interest to kids, like space, music, video games and sports.



---


# China's Data Laws And Government TikTok Device Bans

China's treatment of data as a state resource, backed by national intelligence laws that let the ruling Communist Party pull data on request from companies based in the country, is the reason a string of governments — Australia among them — have banned TikTok from official devices.

The concept has a documented policy history. In 2016 China designated big data a "fundamental strategic resource," and four years later its government designated data as the fifth "factor of production," joining land, labour, capital and technology. China's National Intelligence Law of 2017 requires all organisations and citizens to "support, assist and co-operate with the state intelligence work," which is the legal basis on which the Party can compel disclosure from domestically based companies.

The device bans are the practical consequence: the Australian government this year banned TikTok on government devices over security concerns related to China's intelligence laws, and governments from Britain, Canada, France and New Zealand have also banned the app from official devices. TikTok's own framing of the disputed tool sits alongside this: "Pixel usage, which is voluntary for our advertising clients to adopt, is an industry-wide tool used to improve the effectiveness of advertising services. Our use of this tool is compliant with all current Australian privacy laws and regulations, and we dismiss any suggestion otherwise."



---


# TikTok's Denial And The OAIC's Monitoring Of The Pixel Claims

TikTok denies that its tracking pixel breaches Australia's privacy laws, attacking not the test results but the credibility and motives of the agency that raised them: "We strongly reject the suggestions outlined by Civic Data and are disappointed that a company would deliberately try to mislead or scare companies without regard to current law or the information available," a TikTok spokeswoman said.

The regulator has not endorsed either side. A spokesman for the Office of the Australian Information Commissioner said the agency was monitoring issues relating to TikTok's handling of personal information, particularly in light of the findings made by the British Information Commissioner's Office in an investigation into the company.

The OAIC's stated position stops short of opening an investigation: "The OAIC will give consideration to the information raised which alleges data scraping in regard to TikTok's practices," the spokesman said.



---


# Meta's Under-13 Policy Versus Its Internal Growth Goals

An internal presentation called "2017 Teens Strategic Focus" appears to specifically target kids under 13, noting that children use tablets as early as 3 or 4, and that "Social identity is an Unmet need Ages 5-11." One stated goal, according to the lawsuit, was specifically to "grow [Monthly Active People], [Daily Active People] and time spent among U13 kids" — a growth objective aimed at the age group Meta's own account rules exclude.

TechCrunch flags an important boundary on what this does and does not show. While Meta does not permit accounts to be run by people under 13, there are plenty of ways it can lawfully and safely engage with that demographic: some kids just want to watch videos from SpongeBob Official, and that is fine. What the law requires is that Meta must verify parental consent, and the ways it can collect and use their data are limited. So targeting under-13s as an audience is not by itself unlawful; the legal question is consent and data use.

qid: Which company, covered by both The Verge and TechCrunch, has influenced internet navigation and local search ranking, while also spending billions to be the default search engine and facing antitrust allegations for affecting news publishers' revenues?
context:
# Google Paid $26.3 Billion In 2021 For Default Search Placement

Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to multiple browsers, phones and platforms — from companies including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla — to be everyone's default search engine. The figure was revealed by Google's search head Prabhakar Raghavan when he testified in court on October 28, according to The Verge.

About $18 billion of that total went directly to Apple, according to a New York Times report published earlier in October 2023, and Google has had its deal with Apple in place since 2003 — so the payment is the current year of a two-decade arrangement, not a one-off. Questioned on the amount of money Google spends to get first pick of search engines, Pichai said the decision was made with the consumer in mind: Google pays big bucks to be everywhere so that it can take in all the data and be the best search engine across different companies' devices, he said, according to The Verge.

The trial also produced evidence that Google understood the value of defaults very early on. U.S. Justice Department lawyer Meagan Bellshaw showed Pichai a 2007 email from a Google product strategy meeting containing data showing that when people changed their browser homepage to Google, they did 15% more Google searches, and that when they switched away, their Google searches dropped 27%. The email summarizing that meeting, sent to Pichai as well as other Google leaders, read: "Nitin argues that focusing on homepage market share is one of the most effective things we can do to make gains in search market share," according to The Verge.



---


# Google's Link-Based Ranking And The Market It Created

Google revolutionized search by evaluating websites based on links from other websites, seeing each link as a vote of relevance and trustworthiness — a structure that made the ranking of any page a function of what other pages pointed to it. The founders pledged to be a neutral navigation system with no ads: just a clean white screen with a search box that would bring people off the Google landing page and out to a helpful website as seamlessly as possible. Users quickly decided this link-based sorting methodology was superior to the existing search engines, and by the end of 1999 Google was handling the majority of online queries.

The model arrived in response to a documented problem. In 1997 an Italian professor published a journal article about what he called Search Engines Persuasion: "Finding the right information on the World Wide Web is becoming a fundamental problem," he wrote, and "a vast number of new companies was born just to make customer Web pages as visible as possible," which "has led to a bad performance degradation of search engines."

The relation between votes and rank held only as long as links were scarce and organic, and it did not. Mapstead, like many early practitioners of SEO, figured out how to adapt: almost as soon as Google took over, a secondary market emerged for links. For a few hundred bucks, a firm in India or the Philippines could provide thousands of links from blog networks built entirely for that purpose. It was easy — buy links that led to your site and watch your ranking in Google's results rise.



---


# US v. Google: Two Months Into The Search Antitrust Trial

As of TechCrunch's November 13, 2023 roundup, the Justice Department's landmark antitrust case against Google was nearly two months old, and the trial record was still producing fresh revelations. TechCrunch framed it as one of the biggest fights in tech antitrust since the U.S. took Microsoft to trial in the 1990s.

An earlier roundup had already surfaced that Google spent $26.3 billion in 2021 making itself the default search engine across platforms, and that Google tried to have Chrome preinstalled on iPhones. Over the couple of weeks preceding this roundup, more of Google's inner workings came to light, including some of the search engine's most lucrative search queries, the shape of the revenue-share agreements between Google and Android OEMs, and why Expedia has a bone to pick with Google.



---


# Default Search Engine

## Definition

The default search engine is the search provider a device, browser, or platform is pre-configured to use unless a user actively changes the setting — the search box that runs when a person types a query without first choosing an alternative, such as Google on the iPhone's Safari address bar or Firefox's search bar.

## Context

The term is central to *US v. Google*, the DOJ's antitrust case, because default status is the mechanism through which Google secures the overwhelming share of search queries: the Information Services Agreement (ISA) between Apple and Google, in place since 2002/2003, makes Google the default on all Apple devices, and Google separately pays Samsung, Mozilla, and other partners for the same status.
Apple executive Eddy Cue testified that Apple's iPhone setup flow deliberately omits any search-engine choice screen, arguing that presenting users with unfamiliar alternatives would harm the setup experience, while conceding the ISA does not permit Apple to offer such a choice.
Google spent $26.3 billion in 2021 on default-placement deals across browsers, phones, and platforms — about $18 billion of that to Apple alone — a scale that the DOJ used to argue Google understands the mechanism's value: internal 2007 data showed users who set Google as their homepage searched 15% more, while switching away dropped searches 27%.
The Mozilla/Yahoo episode shows the same mechanism working in reverse: when Firefox switched its default from Google to Yahoo under a 2014 deal, Mozilla's CEO testified that user retention declined, illustrating how disruptive changing the default can be even when a paying competitor is involved.
Outside the antitrust trial, the term also frames ordinary consumer behavior: an investor in e-commerce search startup Deft described users' "natural behavior" as following the path of least resistance and just using the default search engine, meaning challenger search products must offer a high-value proposition to displace that inertia.

## Key Characteristics

- **Set by agreement, not by user choice** — default status on major platforms (Apple's Safari/iOS, Android OEMs, Firefox) is typically established through commercial deals (e.g., the Apple-Google ISA, Yahoo-Mozilla's $375M/year deal) rather than user selection at setup.
- **Backed by large recurring payments** — Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 across partners to hold default placement, with roughly $18 billion of that going to Apple.
- **Technically reversible but rarely changed** — Apple and Google both argued switching is easy, but DuckDuckGo's CEO countered that it takes "too many steps" to switch, and Google's own 2005 complaint about Internet Explorer's defaults argued that "most end users do not change defaults," so default status functions as durable market power.
- **Distinct from pre-installation** — Google's separate push to get Chrome and Search merely pre-installed (not necessarily defaulted) on Android and iPhones shows default status is a stronger, more contested tier than simple presence on a device.
- **Drives user behavior even outside browsers** — the concept extends to any search product; consumers default to "the path of least resistance," which challenger search startups must specifically overcome.

## Corpus References

Corpus notes whose source text references this term (evidence-backed, from `term_links.json`):

- [The Google Antitrust Case](google_antitrust_case.md)
- [The Hypocrisy Argument: Google Became The Monopoly It Denounced](google_default_hypocrisy_argument.md)
- [US v. Google: Two Months Into The Search Antitrust Trial](us_v_google_search_antitrust_trial_overview.md)



---


# Consumer Search Startups And Switching Barriers

The premise attacked is that a better search product wins users. The cautionary case is Neeva, founded by former Google execs, which tried to convince people to switch to paid and private search with additional features; earlier in 2023 the startup shut down its consumer efforts and eventually got acquired by Snowflake.

Adii Pienaar, an investor in Deft, said that Deft has to give compelling reasons to users to switch to its service. His grounds are behavioral rather than technical: "Users' natural behavior for search is to follow the path of least resistance, i.e. most people just pick up their phone and just use the default search engine."

The conclusion he draws sets the bar Deft must clear: "For Deft to change that behavior, they will need to create a high-value proposition."



---


# Deft's Competitive Landscape: Search Incumbents

Given that it is building a search solution for e-commerce, Deft already faces challenges from Amazon and Google, both of which have shipped comparable features.

In September 2023, Amazon updated its visual search feature that lets users snap a photo of a product and search for similar items on the platform. Google released its multi-search feature in 2022, letting users fuse images and text — the same combination Deft offers.

Separately, Deft will also face competition from other startups like Objective, a Matrix Partners-backed startup building an API platform for multimodal search.

qid: Who is the individual that, before the FTX collapse, was portrayed as a reliable figure in the cryptocurrency sector, and is now facing allegations of directing a multi-billion dollar misappropriation of customer funds and committing fraud for personal gain, with these accusations being discussed in courtroom updates and analyses by both TechCrunch and The Verge?
context:
# FTX Fraud Charges And The SEC's Allegation

Sam Bankman-Fried, the founder of the failed cryptocurrency exchange FTX, faced seven counts of wire fraud and conspiracy — specifically, two counts of wire fraud and five conspiracy charges — and the Securities and Exchange Commission alleged that FTX was a fraud "from the start," with a "multi-billion-dollar deficiency caused by his own misappropriation of customer funds." The Verge repeated this framing at the head of each of its trial dispatches through October 2023, and in its October 28th, 2023 write-up reported that Bankman-Fried had been found guilty on seven counts including charges of wire fraud.

The boundary of the concept is the mix of charge types: the indictment paired substantive wire fraud counts with conspiracy counts rather than resting on a single offence, and the SEC's civil allegation about the exchange's origins ran alongside the criminal case rather than being part of it. The Verge's reporter, writing as the prosecution's case neared its end on October 26th, 2023, added an impression of the people the charges swept in: all the co-conspirators seemed oddly younger than their years, as though they had got stuck in the "math camp forever" environment Bankman-Fried created for them and simply failed to grow up.



---


# Sam Bankman-Fried's Charges And The Collapse Of FTX

Sam Bankman-Fried, the founder of FTX and Alameda Research, is facing seven counts of criminal charges: two counts of wire fraud and five counts of conspiracy charges.

FTX was a failed cryptocurrency exchange founded in 2019. According to a now-deleted profile from FTX investors Sequoia Capital, FTX was founded because of Bankman-Fried's frustration with other exchanges while he was running Alameda Research, his crypto trading firm. According to the SEC, FTX was a fraud "from the start," diverting customers' funds to Alameda, with a "multi-billion-dollar deficiency caused by his own misappropriation of customer funds."



---


# Sam Bankman-Fried

Sam Bankman-Fried is the former CEO of the bankrupt crypto exchange FTX, whose highly anticipated criminal trial started on the Tuesday before TechCrunch's 2023-10-01 report, to determine whether he is guilty of seven counts of fraud and conspiracy. As one former federal prosecutor put it: "The odds seem to be stacked against him at this point."

He was 31 years old and co-founded FTX in 2019; within a few years the once third-largest crypto exchange's valuation hit $32 billion at its peak, and the company is now trying to claw back any funds to distribute to creditors. Before the fall he was even compared to Warren Buffet, and many called him the white horse of crypto — a description TechCrunch notes it never applied to him.

Bankman-Fried, however, maintained his innocence. At The New York Times' DealBook Summit he appeared virtually from the Bahamas and said, "I didn't ever try to commit fraud on anyone; I was shocked by what happened this month"; in a published DM exchange with a Vox reporter he said he regretted filing for bankruptcy and thought that "regulators make everything worse." In January he pleaded not guilty to all counts, which include wire fraud, conspiracy to commit money laundering and conspiracy to misuse customer funds. He could face up to 115 years in jail if convicted on all charges.

TechCrunch's 2023-10-02 summary of his standing on the eve of trial: SBF has been denied bail; his name is mud (or much worse) among those who have lost money in Alameda or FTX; and those who might not have had positions in these still blame him for other crypto woes, because he set off a ripple effect.



---


# John J. Ray III Running The FTX Estate

What's left of FTX is now being led by John J. Ray III — the man who cleaned up Enron, and who has said FTX is worse than Enron.

Just before the trial began, the FTX lawyers filed suit against Bankman-Fried's parents, saying they should give back millions of dollars they got from their kid. Ray has also referred to Bankman-Fried's conduct as "really just old-fashioned embezzlement."



---


# The Prosecution's Opening Statement Against Bankman-Fried

Thane Rehn, a prosecutor for the government, opened the case against Sam Bankman-Fried with the line "One year ago, it looked like the defendant was on the top of the world," and then argued that this appearance was false: "all of that, all of it, was built on lies," he declared to the jury, adding "Behind the curtains, he was not what he appeared to be." Rehn described a defendant who, as former CEO of FTX, oversaw a supposedly thriving crypto exchange, jetted between international locales, hobnobbed with celebrities like Tom Brady and Larry David, and repeatedly emphasized to customers that their money was safe and secure.

What followed was a roughly 30-minute story that repeatedly emphasized how Bankman-Fried allegedly stole customer funds to facilitate his jet-setting lifestyle, donate millions to political candidates, and finance risky bets. Rehn also directly contested the media framing of the defendant: he was not a crypto "boy" genius, as so many in the media — Fortune included — have written, but a "man" who "stole billions of dollars from thousands of victims." Rehn closed the characterization with a promise to the jury: "You will see the full picture."



---


# FTX's Inner Circle: Family And Friends Implicated

The Verge's October 26th, 2023 account of the trial catalogued how everyone who loved Bankman-Fried most in the world was caught up in the case. Adam Yedidia, his college roommate, testified with immunity because he was concerned he may have unknowingly worked on code that contributed to the fraud; "I love you Sam," he had texted at one point, "I'm not going anywhere" — that was before he realized FTX had stolen customer funds, at which point he resigned. Nishad Singh, a longtime family friend, copped to what sounded an awful lot like classic embezzlement, saying he had backdated transactions on FTX to help create doctored balance sheets to show to investors, and pleaded guilty to six charges including wire fraud, money laundering, and conspiracy counts around his political donations. Caroline Ellison, Bankman-Fried's ex-girlfriend, told the court about the seven phony balance sheets she had created and was clear that Alameda took customer funds, that Bankman-Fried knew about it, and that he even invested them against her advice.

His family was drawn in too. Joe Bankman, his father, is among the people included in the "small group chat," the Signal group where the FTX inner circle strategized during the exchange's last days. Barbara Fried's political action committee, Mind the Gap, is among the entities that received FTX customer money as political donations; Fried and Bankman lived together in a Bahamas house purchased for them using FTX investor funds, according to a financial expert called by the prosecution, and in a lawsuit filed by FTX's bankruptcy estate the two are alleged to have been given $10 million of FTX customer funds. Gabe Bankman-Fried's nonprofit, Guarding Against Pandemics, got millions from FTX; he was also in a Signal group chat, Donations Processing, that Singh says was used to coordinate the transfer of FTX and Alameda money to various political causes, and in that chat he can be seen recommending that some donations be made "in the dark" to avoid public relations headaches. Singh also said Gabe had an assistant fly to the Bahamas with a stack of blank checks for Singh to sign.

The consequences outlast the trial. Wang, Singh, and Ellison are now felons; even if they never do time — and they may very well be imprisoned or subjected to house arrest — their lives are irrevocably changed, not least by whatever restitution requirements they face, they are barred from taking certain kinds of jobs, and there is the publicity. Bankman, Fried, and Gabe Bankman-Fried's reputations are tarnished, and in the political arenas where they once operated they are suddenly undesirable. Beyond the courtroom, everyone who had money trapped on the exchange when it collapsed — as a result of Alameda purloining customers' funds — had their lives altered: even if they are made whole by the bankruptcy proceedings, that is still money they should have had access to at any time, which may mean houses that were not purchased, medical procedures left undone, and life savings lost. The reporter's summary: it is a Greek tragedy, precipitated by one man's character flaw, the arrogance of Sam Bankman-Fried.



---


# FTX's Cooperating Witnesses

FTX co-founder and former CTO Gary Wang and Alameda Research's former CEO Caroline Ellison both pleaded guilty in December 2022 to federal criminal charges in relation to the FTX collapse, and both planned to cooperate with prosecutors. TechCrunch reported on 2023-10-01 that they would be major witnesses in the trial, given their close ties to Bankman-Fried, FTX and Alameda.

The criminal charges were not their only exposure. Alongside them, Wang and Ellison face civil penalties from the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC).

qid: Does the TechCrunch article on Meta's GDPR compliance concerns suggest the same legal issue as the TechCrunch article on Meta's responsibility for teen social media monitoring, and does it also differ from the TechCrunch article on Meta's moderation bias affecting Palestinian voices?
context:
# Meta Moderation Bias

TechCrunch's claim, published 19 October 2023, is that Meta has a moderation bias problem rather than a "bug": the suppression of Palestinian voices is the latest in a lengthy history of incidents on Meta platforms that reflect an inherent bias against Palestinian users in its processes, documented by years of complaints from both inside and outside the company. The argument's careful qualifier is that intent is not asserted — the company may not intentionally suppress specific communities, but its moderation practices often disproportionately affect Palestinian users.

The first ground is Meta's own commissioned evidence. During the last violent outbreak between Hamas and Israel in 2021, a report commissioned by Meta and conducted by a third party concluded that the company's actions had an "adverse human rights impact" on Palestinian users' right to freedom of expression and political participation.

The second ground is the pattern of disproportionate scrutiny during that outbreak. Amid the violence following the May 2021 court ruling to evict Palestinian families from Sheikh Jarrah, a neighborhood in occupied East Jerusalem, users across Facebook and Instagram accused Meta of taking down posts and suspending accounts that voiced support for Palestinians. The digital rights nonprofit Electronic Frontier Foundation described Meta's actions in 2021 as "systemic censorship of Palestinian voices," and in its 2022 report on Palestinian digital rights, 7amleh said Meta is "still the most restricting company" compared with other social media giants in the extent of its moderation of the Palestinian digital space.

The third ground is internal. That same month, a group of Facebook employees filed internal complaints accusing the company of bias against Arab and Muslim users; in internal posts obtained by BuzzFeed News, an employee attributed the bias to "years and years of implementing policies that just don't scale globally."

The fourth ground is the measured asymmetry between languages. At the recommendation of its Oversight Board, Meta conducted a third-party due diligence report about the platform's moderation during the May 2021 conflict. The report found that Arabic content was flagged as potentially violating at significantly higher rates than Hebrew content was, and was more likely to be erroneously removed. It noted that Meta's moderation system may not be as precise for Arabic content as for Hebrew, because the latter is a "more standardized language," and suggested that reviewers may lack the linguistic and cultural competence to understand less common Arabic dialects like Palestinian Arabic.

The warrant joining grounds to claim is duration and convergence.
