qid: Does the TechCrunch article suggest that Sam Bankman-Fried's use of wealth was primarily for altruistic purposes, while The Verge article focuses on the ethicality of his financial practices, and does the second TechCrunch article imply that his actions were driven by fraudulent intentions?
context:
# The Risk That Bankman-Fried Implicates The Whole Crypto Industry

The Verge argued that Bankman-Fried's own defense could damage crypto's public perception far beyond his case, because his post-collapse behavior suggests he's something of a wild card.

The grounds are the defenses available to him: he may suggest he was acting on the advice of his lawyers, but he may also introduce other evidence that could be troublesome — implying that he was engaged in standard industry behavior, or that everything that happened was Binance's fault. That may be risky, but "we already know that Bankman-Fried loves risk." Hermine Wong frames the danger as a question: "Is he going to throw the entire industry under the bus? An idea like, 'Everyone was doing this, it's not fair I'm the only one who was charged?'" That may not fly in a court of law, but it could absolutely damage public perception of crypto at large. The precedent is his own conduct: just before he was arrested, Bankman-Fried brought forward messages from a crypto group chat in testimony he planned to give before Congress, in which he primarily blames Binance and his lawyers at the firm Sullivan & Cromwell. Other group chat messages may be brought into evidence during the trial, which Wong says could be embarrassing for the whole industry: "You can imagine some of these founders, CEOs, people of that echelon talk to each other somewhat informally about what's going on. If it seems like his peer group supported him, or worse, fawned over him, that's a real problem for the industry's reputation."



---


# Prosecution And Defense Arguments On Day Two Of The SBF Trial

On the second day of the trial of Sam Bankman-Fried and FTX, the prosecution argued that Bankman-Fried knowingly committed fraud, and it grounded that claim in motive: he did so, prosecutors said, to achieve great wealth, power and influence.

The defense countered with the opposite reading of the same conduct. Its claim was that the FTX founder acted in good faith, never meant to commit fraud or to steal, and basically got in over his head — an argument whose warrant is that inexperience and overreach, rather than intent, explain what happened. The two sides therefore contest intent rather than the underlying events, and the reporting on this exchange comes from Rebecca and Jacquelyn in TechCrunch's Week in Review of October 7, 2023, covering day two of the trial only.



---


# Going Infinite: Michael Lewis's Account Of SBF's Political Dealings

Michael Lewis's book "Going Infinite" debuted on the first day of Sam Bankman-Fried's trial, and details about Bankman-Fried's political dealings emerging from it include his alleged attempt to buy off Donald Trump to get him not to run again for president.

TechCrunch's team was focused on the Manhattan Federal Court for the trial of Bankman-Fried, the disgraced entrepreneur accused of orchestrating the collapse of the cryptocurrency exchange FTX; the Lewis book is the second channel through which the week's revelations arrived. The reporting is framed as allegation rather than established fact, and it comes from the book rather than from courtroom testimony. The item appeared in TechCrunch's Week in Review of October 7, 2023.



---


# Bankman-Fried's Pre-Collapse Public Image Strategy

Before his fall, Bankman-Fried made himself out to be the Good Boy of crypto — the trustworthy face of a sometimes-shady industry — and he was very interested in publicity, sitting for many interviews both before and after the collapse of FTX.

The Verge attributes FTX's quick rise as an industry force at least in part to that appetite for attention: Bankman-Fried gave interviews freely and quickly rose to public prominence, positioning himself as an important, boyish face for crypto even though FTX hadn't been in the business as long as competing exchanges such as Coinbase, Kraken, or Gemini. At one point he told a colleague at FTX that "I honestly think it's negative EV" — possibly "expected value," as in poker — "for me to cut my hair. I think it's important for people to think I look crazy." Because he was so successful at this kind of public relations, his fall from grace became another mark against an industry already roiled by bankruptcies and scandals; The Verge adds that more trouble for the industry is likely to come from one crucial element of the fraud trial, the part where the government must prove intent.



---


# The Defense's Good-Faith Case For Bankman-Fried

Mark Cohen, one of Sam Bankman-Fried's lawyers, attacked the prosecution's central premise that his client was a liar who stole from customers, stating early in his opening statement that "Sam didn't defraud anyone." The defense's counter-picture is of a nerdy startup founder who acted in "good faith," not the prosecution's "cartoon of a villain"; Cohen repeatedly harped on Bankman-Fried's allegedly good-faith actions throughout his address to the jury. Bankman-Fried, whose cheekbones were more prominent after spending about seven weeks in a Brooklyn prison, appeared in court as this argument was made.

Cohen also disputed the specific claim that Alameda Research was a covert conduit. Alameda was not subterranean or shady, he said; it was a successful hedge fund. FTX was no Ponzi scheme but a "very innovative, successful company." The business practices between the two were reasonable, he argued, claiming that Alameda acted legally as an FTX customer, payment processor, and market maker — that is, a financial entity that acts as a trading partner for customers looking to buy and sell cryptocurrencies.

The defense's warrant for reading failure as something other than fraud was an analogy Cohen employed throughout: "working at a startup is like building a plane as you're flying it," and businesses sometimes fail. He specifically pointed the finger at Ellison, the former CEO of Alameda, who he said did not adequately protect her hedge fund from the inherent risk of the crypto markets. And when the walls came closing in and the aforementioned plane approached the "eye of the storm," Cohen argued, Bankman-Fried did not act like someone who was guilty — he was willing to give up his personal wealth to make customers whole. "In the end, Sam started and built two billion-dollar businesses," he concluded. "He didn't steal any money."



---


# Proving Intent In The FTX Fraud Case

The government's case proceeds in two parts. The first is pretty simple and a little boring: prosecutors must show that certain transactions took place, using whatever records the Southern District of New York has for them.

The second part is where the drama is likely to come, says Christopher LaVigne, a litigation partner and co-chair of the cryptocurrency practice at the law firm Withers: prosecutors have to connect those transactions to Bankman-Fried, show that he knew what he was doing was wrong, and prove that he lied about it anyway. "What was he saying to his parents and his other advisors about this?" LaVigne asks. "What conversations happened between him and his co-conspirators that are now cooperating against him?" To further establish intent, the government can use Bankman-Fried's own words: the indictment calls his November 2022 tweets "false and misleading." "We had him going out directly to the internet," LaVigne says — if he wrote things on Twitter or said things in interviews that weren't true, that's more fodder for the case: "They can point to that and say, 'This is what he said, this is what actually happened.'" Other evidence may include Signal messages and testimony from co-conspirators who pleaded guilty to their own charges. Alameda Research CEO Caroline Ellison, who was also sometimes Bankman-Fried's girlfriend, may play an important role — Bankman-Fried leaked her diaries to The New York Times and was consequently jailed for witness tampering. The government has indicated FTX co-founder Gary Wang and engineering head Nishad Singh will also be among the witnesses called to testify about Bankman-Fried.



---


# Bankman-Fried's Defense Strategy And Appeal Groundwork

Bankman-Fried's defense can itself introduce risks for people who dealt with him, because his lawyers have several simultaneous objectives: first and foremost proving their client not guilty, but also — just in case they don't get the outcome they want — laying the groundwork for appeals and sentencing arguments.

The consequence is procedural: any piece of evidence they want to introduce for those two purposes has to come into play during the trial. Christopher LaVigne notes that Bankman-Fried's lawyers are already marking arguments that his constitutional rights are being violated by his pretrial incarceration because, among other things, his internet connection wasn't good enough for him to plan his defense — which could be grounds for an appeal.



---


# John J. Ray III Running The FTX Estate

What's left of FTX is now being led by John J. Ray III — the man who cleaned up Enron, and who has said FTX is worse than Enron.

Just before the trial began, the FTX lawyers filed suit against Bankman-Fried's parents, saying they should give back millions of dollars they got from their kid. Ray has also referred to Bankman-Fried's conduct as "really just old-fashioned embezzlement."

# Google Paid $26.3 Billion In 2021 For Default Search Placement

Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to multiple browsers, phones and platforms — from companies including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla — to be everyone's default search engine. The figure was revealed by Google's search head Prabhakar Raghavan when he testified in court on October 28, according to The Verge.

About $18 billion of that total went directly to Apple, according to a New York Times report published earlier in October 2023, and Google has had its deal with Apple in place since 2003 — so the payment is the current year of a two-decade arrangement, not a one-off. Questioned on the amount of money Google spends to get first pick of search engines, Pichai said the decision was made with the consumer in mind: Google pays big bucks to be everywhere so that it can take in all the data and be the best search engine across different companies' devices, he said, according to The Verge.

The trial also produced evidence that Google understood the value of defaults very early on. U.S. Justice Department lawyer Meagan Bellshaw showed Pichai a 2007 email from a Google product strategy meeting containing data showing that when people changed their browser homepage to Google, they did 15% more Google searches, and that when they switched away, their Google searches dropped 27%. The email summarizing that meeting, sent to Pichai as well as other Google leaders, read: "Nitin argues that focusing on homepage market share is one of the most effective things we can do to make gains in search market share," according to The Verge.

# Default Search Engine

## Definition

The default search engine is the search provider a device, browser, or platform is pre-configured to use unless a user actively changes the setting — the search box that runs when a person types a query without first choosing an alternative, such as Google on the iPhone's Safari address bar or Firefox's search bar.

## Context

The term is central to *US v. Google*, the DOJ's antitrust case, because default status is the mechanism through which Google secures the overwhelming share of search queries: the Information Services Agreement (ISA) between Apple and Google, in place since 2002/2003, makes Google the default on all Apple devices, and Google separately pays Samsung, Mozilla, and other partners for the same status.
Apple executive Eddy Cue testified that Apple's iPhone setup flow deliberately omits any search-engine choice screen, arguing that presenting users with unfamiliar alternatives would harm the setup experience, while conceding the ISA does not permit Apple to offer such a choice.
Google spent $26.3 billion in 2021 on default-placement deals across browsers, phones, and platforms — about $18 billion of that to Apple alone — a scale that the DOJ used to argue Google understands the mechanism's value: internal 2007 data showed users who set Google as their homepage searched 15% more, while switching away dropped searches 27%.
The Mozilla/Yahoo episode shows the same mechanism working in reverse: when Firefox switched its default from Google to Yahoo under a 2014 deal, Mozilla's CEO testified that user retention declined, illustrating how disruptive changing the default can be even when a paying competitor is involved.
Outside the antitrust trial, the term also frames ordinary consumer behavior: an investor in e-commerce search startup Deft described users' "natural behavior" as following the path of least resistance and just using the default search engine, meaning challenger search products must offer a high-value proposition to displace that inertia.

## Key Characteristics

- **Set by agreement, not by user choice** — default status on major platforms (Apple's Safari/iOS, Android OEMs, Firefox) is typically established through commercial deals (e.g., the Apple-Google ISA, Yahoo-Mozilla's $375M/year deal) rather than user selection at setup.
- **Backed by large recurring payments** — Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 across partners to hold default placement, with roughly $18 billion of that going to Apple.
- **Technically reversible but rarely changed** — Apple and Google both argued switching is easy, but DuckDuckGo's CEO countered that it takes "too many steps" to switch, and Google's own 2005 complaint about Internet Explorer's defaults argued that "most end users do not change defaults," so default status functions as durable market power.
- **Distinct from pre-installation** — Google's separate push to get Chrome and Search merely pre-installed (not necessarily defaulted) on Android and iPhones shows default status is a stronger, more contested tier than simple presence on a device.
- **Drives user behavior even outside browsers** — the concept extends to any search product; consumers default to "the path of least resistance," which challenger search startups must specifically overcome.

# Helena World Chronicle's Class Action Antitrust Suit Against Google

A class action lawsuit filed in the week of 15 December 2023 in the U.S. District Court in D.C. accuses Google and parent company Alphabet of anticompetitive behavior in violation of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act and others, on behalf of news publishers. The case was filed by Arkansas-based publisher Helena World Chronicle, which argues that Google "siphons off" news publishers' content, their readers and their ad revenue through anticompetitive means, and it specifically cites new AI technologies such as Google's Search Generative Experience (SGE) and the Bard AI chatbot as worsening the problem.

Helena World Chronicle owns and publishes two weekly newspapers in Arkansas. In the complaint it argues that Google is "starving the free press" by sharing publishers' content on Google, losing them "billions of dollars."

Beyond damages, the suit asks for an injunction that would require Google to obtain consent from publishers before using their website data to train its general artificial intelligence products, including Google's own and those of rivals. It also asks that publishers who opt out of SGE still be allowed to show up in Google search results, among other things.

The law firm handling the case is Hausfeld, whose announcement states that "the anticompetitive effects of Google's scheme cause profound harm to competition, to consumers, to labor, and to a democratic free press," and that "Plaintiff Helena World Chronicle, LLC invokes the Sherman Act and Clayton Act to seek class-wide monetary and injunctive relief to restore and ensure competition for digital news and reference publishing and set up guardrails to preserve a free marketplace of ideas in the new era of artificial intelligence."



---


# The Hypocrisy Argument: Google Became The Monopoly It Denounced

The DOJ's argument, pressed in cross-examination by Bellshaw, is that Google has become the monopoly it denounced years ago — that the company objected to a rival's search default when it was the one being shut out, and now defends the same arrangement when it is the beneficiary.

The grounds are Google's own 2005 letter. Cast your memories back to 2005, when Microsoft's Internet Explorer became the default search engine: Google's legal chief David Drummond sent Microsoft an angry letter saying that making Internet Explorer the search default was anticompetitive. After establishing that Google understands the inherent value of defaults, Bellshaw brought up Drummond's letter precisely to establish the hypocrisy of Google today. The letter declared that problems with a default setting are made worse by how changes to defaults are handled, and that most end users "do not change defaults."

The warrant is that the letter's reasoning has not changed hands with the market position. These are exactly the arguments that other search engine companies, like DuckDuckGo, Brave or Microsoft's Bing, make when they accuse Google of being anticompetitive by making deals with Apple and others — so if Drummond's reasoning was sound in 2005, it convicts Google now. The DOJ doubled down on this in the trial.

The same cross-examination pressed a second consistency question, on the litigation hold. Pichai said that he took action against the history-off default for chat in February to comply with the DOJ's litigation hold, according to CNBC. Bellshaw then pulled up a message exchange in 2021 where Pichai asked for history to be turned off in a group chat. Pichai responded that he wanted to discuss a personnel matter and that the subject had nothing to do with the litigation hold, which he said he takes great care to comply with.



---


# Deft's Competitive Landscape: Search Incumbents

Given that it is building a search solution for e-commerce, Deft already faces challenges from Amazon and Google, both of which have shipped comparable features.

In September 2023, Amazon updated its visual search feature that lets users snap a photo of a product and search for similar items on the platform. Google released its multi-search feature in 2022, letting users fuse images and text — the same combination Deft offers.

Separately, Deft will also face competition from other startups like Objective, a Matrix Partners-backed startup building an API platform for multimodal search.

# Scott McTominay's Advanced Role And Goal Threat

Under Ten Hag, Scott McTominay functions as a marauding midfield engine and late-running goal threat with a licence to create overloads wherever he finds them — the job United once paid Paul Pogba to do.

The structure of the role differs from his previous, more conventional midfield positions. Against low blocks and structured defences — and, the piece notes, nobody is remotely accusing Chelsea of possessing one of those — he provides the extra body in a tightly marked penalty area; but he also pops up in the channels and on the wing, either supporting the man in possession or offering himself for the quick switch of play. The relation between that role and his output shows in the numbers: against Chelsea he scored his fifth and sixth goals of the season, having previously never got more than seven. The piece attributes this partly to opponents still not quite cottoning on to his goal threat — those late runs to the far post, the blur on the edge of the 18-yard box you do not spot until it is too late — and partly to how Ten Hag is using him. The range over which the relation holds is the current team: for all the undoubted leadership qualities of Bruno Fernandes and Harry Maguire, tactically it is McTominay running the show right now, a development with numerous interesting consequences. The Pogba comparison is drawn with the caveat that McTominay is a different kind of player with a different kind of skillset; Pogba's United career never quite worked out, largely — if you believe his most vehement critics — on account of his hair.



---


# The Three Concurrent Roles Of A Manchester United Manager

Barney Ronay models the Manchester United job as three concurrent roles — managing the past, managing the dysfunction of the present, and managing the everyday metrics on which the manager is judged.

First you must manage the past, which is constantly in the room and which skews every act, achievement and expectation. Second you must manage the dysfunction of the present, which expresses itself in every detail from a leaking stadium roof to the deep ills of a playing squad peopled with squatters and long-term missteps. Finally you get to manage the everyday metrics — team, results, style, energy, messaging: win things, improve players, create a coherent and happy internal culture, but do it during an unceasing takeover circus while star players sulk and brief against you, and while the ghost of Hamlet's father still skulks in the eaves. The three hold together only under those conditions; as of the December 2023 Champions League exit, Ronay judged, this felt like the end of one thing, perhaps even the beginning of the end of something else.

# Ten Hag's Attacking Gamble And The Gaps It Leaves

The Guardian argues that Ten Hag is enacting a high-wire act — a daring gamble that United will gain more going forward than they lose going back — and that the Chelsea win is not yet evidence the gamble works.

The grounds are structural: if you commit a midfielder to McTominay's advanced role, you leave gaps elsewhere. One reason Chelsea found it so easy to play through United was that, with the forwards pushed high and McTominay as the secret sauce in the final third, there were open spaces every time they played through the press; Chelsea's goal was a case in point, two simple vertical passes straight through the centre via Mykhailo Mudryk to Cole Palmer, passes McTominay could see coming but could do precious little to stop. The warrant is that the result depended on finishing quality United cannot count on: on another night Chelsea score from one of these counterattacks, and in another game United face a better finisher than Nicolas Jackson, who for all his talent looks like a man playing football in a hall of mirrors. The bet is that lawless abandon will begin to resemble a sustainable attacking blueprint once Lisandro Martínez and Raphaël Varane come back, once Ten Hag brings the defensive line up 10 yards, once Rasmus Højlund hits some form and once Mason Mount gets up to speed — that he can shout down the noise in the short term while building something in the long term. In the raptured afterglow of a big win it felt like a gamble being won, but the writer's own caveat is to come back and check in a few days.

# Barr Moses Recommends "Dare To Lead"

Barr Moses recommends "Dare to Lead: Brave Work. Tough Conversations. Whole Hearts," by Brené Brown, saying that reading a Brené Brown book is like tackling the Sunday crossword puzzle — equal parts challenging and rejuvenating — and that Dare to Lead is no different. Moses is the CEO and co-founder of Monte Carlo, a data observability startup, and co-wrote a technical book on the topic, O'Reilly's "Data Quality Fundamentals: A Practitioner's Guide to Building Trustworthy Data Pipelines," sharing advice on achieving reliable data at scale.

Her grounds are the book's research base and its practical output. Dare to Lead pulls on Brown's decades of research, interviews and experience as a professor at the University of Houston speaking with CEOs, founders and other executives to understand what great leadership looks like and how to achieve it, and she distils four key skill sets great leaders possess while highlighting ways to empower employees to be courageous in the face of adversity and change.

Moses also draws a link to the present AI moment: published in 2018 before the Gen AI wave hit, Dare to Lead addresses what human leaders have to bring to the table that AI and ML currently do not — empathy and connection. As a bonus, the book provides helpful resources to assess leadership strengths and growth opportunities that can make for a fun and informative team building activity.



---


# Bruno Fernandes' Role Against Top Teams

Erik ten Hag argued on 28 October 2023 that Bruno Fernandes' contribution has to change against top opposition: he is at his best with a lot of the ball, so in games where United have less of it his job becomes taking whatever attacking moments arise and otherwise working hard for the team.

"If he does [score] again, I'll be happy," the manager said. "Bruno is an [effective] player when we have a lot of the ball. Then he is at his best. And there are games against top teams when you have less of the ball. So then it is about taking benefit from [any attacking] moments and for the rest you have to work hard for the team. And to get a result because that is the most important, that the team is winning." The warrant is that winning outranks individual effectiveness, so the role adapts to possession rather than the other way round. The Guardian illustrated the point with Fernandes volleying home against Burnley — one of two goals he had scored for the club that season.

# The Manchester United Crisis News Cycle Under Ten Hag

The Guardian's argument is that results at Manchester United no longer settle anything, because the club's crisis news cycle consumes wins as quickly as defeats: a stirring recovery against Chelsea bought Erik ten Hag only a few days' grace.

The grounds are the pattern of the week itself — rancour, rumour and recrimination, barbs in the press and barbs at the press, defeat at Newcastle followed by the Chelsea win and the startling realisation that United were three points behind Manchester City, all before Thursday. The warrant is a claim about the institution rather than the team: such is the way of things at football's most reliable content provider, and this beast must always eat, so the warm flume of goodwill would last only as long as it took for Dominic Solanke to run through on goal for Bournemouth on the Saturday afternoon, returning United to the grip of crisis and the now-familiar lexicon of surly unsourced stories about dressing room discontent. A second, related argument is that assessing any United manager requires filters: Ten Hag would of course take the blame for the early Champions League exit, and plenty of mistakes had been made, not least in the players the manager had been allowed to sign — but to be United manager is to undertake three concurrent roles.



---


# Ratcliffe's Bid For A Manchester United Stake

As of 28 October 2023, Sir Jim Ratcliffe's bid to buy 25% of Manchester United for an inflated £1.3bn in return for control of football policy was expected to go through imminently, marking a new phase in the protracted sale of the club.

Erik ten Hag had overseen his squad through those recent weeks and, despite any implications the deal might have for the futures of his players, did not think the matter was a distraction. "Of course, they are committed to the club but especially they are committed to this team," Ten Hag said. "They want to be successful and are therefore aware you need [to focus on] the team, your teammates. That is how the players are thinking and they are not thinking about strategic reviews or structures or whatever."

The first half in Leuven on 31 October 2023 finished 2-2: Laura De Neve curled Belgium ahead in the ninth minute, Lucy Bronze and Fran Kirby put England in front late in the half, and Tessa Wullaert levelled in first-half injury time, Sport Grill reported.

Having battled to a narrow home win the previous Friday, 27 October, England began on the front foot with a fourth-minute free-kick cleared by Belgium's Nicky Evrard. Belgium drew first blood in this Halloween encounter after Chloe Kelly was penalised for handball just outside the box, allowing De Neve to curl her ninth-minute free-kick straight into the near-top right corner beyond the reach of an outstretched Mary Earps. England struggled to mount a response as Belgium continued to soak up their pressure and hit them on the counter attack, until Alex Greenwood and Jassina Blom banged heads in the 18th minute as they tried to meet an aerial pass, halting play.

That lengthy delay reignited England's intensity, which paid off as Bronze drew a 36th-minute foul from Marie Detruyer and headed in from Kelly's subsequent free-kick two minutes later to restore parity. Kelly then fired wide in the 41st minute as Belgium were forced to substitute De Neve due to injury, which unsettled their defence; while Belgium's defence adjusted, Bronze's header a minute later from Keira Walsh's cross was fired wide on the rebound by Alessia Russo. England continued to press and got their reward in the 44th minute as Lauren Hemp was unleashed up the left flank by Walsh and found Kirby on the pullback to rifle in beyond Evrard and turn the tie around. England's lead lasted only seven minutes into 14 minutes of first-half injury time, as Wullaert was played through on the counter-attack by Janice Cayman to slot into the far left corner and pull Belgium level at the break.

# Europa Conference League Round-Up: Villa And Klaksvik

The Guardian's Europa Conference League round-up of 26 October 2023 led on Aston Villa's statement 4-1 win at AZ Alkmaar, KI Klaksvik becoming the first Faroe Islands club to win in the group stages of a European competition, and Aberdeen throwing away a two-goal lead at home to PAOK Salonika.

Rebecca Welch became the first female referee to take charge of an English Premier League match on 23 December 2023, officiating Fulham's home game against Burnley, as reported by The Roar that day.

# OpenAI's Nonprofit Governance And Capped-Profit Structure

OpenAI's for-profit subsidiary, OpenAI Global, LLC, is fully controlled by OpenAI's nonprofit: the subsidiary is permitted to commercialize its technology, but it is subject to the nonprofit's mission of attaining artificial general intelligence (AGI), which OpenAI defines as AI that can "outperform humans at most economically valuable work."

The discriminating feature of this structure is where the power over AGI sits. The nonprofit OpenAI's board has the power both to determine when the company has achieved AGI and to exclude that AGI from IP licenses and other commercial terms — including terms with Microsoft, one of OpenAI's biggest investors and a steadfast integrator of OpenAI's technologies. OpenAI was founded as a nonprofit in 2015 but restructured in 2019 as a "capped-profit" company in order to raise capital, an acknowledgement of the huge costs associated with training cutting-edge AI systems. Altman underlined the point in an interview with the Financial Times in the week of his firing, saying he "hoped" Microsoft would increase its investment to help pay for "huge" imminent model training costs.



---


# Sam Altman's Rise As The Face Of Generative AI

In the year since Altman catapulted ChatGPT to global fame, he became Silicon Valley's sought-after voice on the promise and potential dangers of artificial intelligence, and his sudden and mostly unexplained exit brought uncertainty to the industry's future. He helped start OpenAI as a nonprofit research laboratory in 2015, but it was ChatGPT's explosion into public consciousness that thrust him into the spotlight as a face of generative AI — technology that can produce novel imagery, passages of text and other media. On a world tour in 2023 he was mobbed by a crowd of adoring fans at an event in London.

He has sat with multiple heads of state to discuss AI's potential and perils. On Thursday, 2023-11-16, he took part in a CEO summit at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation conference in San Francisco, where OpenAI is based. At OpenAI's first developer conference the week before, Altman was the main speaker, showcasing a vision for a future of AI agents that could help people with a variety of tasks; days later he announced the company would have to pause new subscriptions to its premium version of ChatGPT because it had exceeded capacity.



---


# The OpenAI Board's Firing Of Sam Altman

ChatGPT-maker OpenAI said on Friday, 2023-11-17, that it had pushed out its co-founder and CEO Sam Altman after a review found he was "not consistently candid in his communications" with the board of directors. "The board no longer has confidence in his ability to continue leading OpenAI," the artificial intelligence company said in a statement. Mira Murati, OpenAI's chief technology officer, would take over as interim CEO effective immediately while the company searched for a permanent replacement.

OpenAI declined to answer questions on what Altman's alleged lack of candor was about; the statement said only that his behavior was hindering the board's ability to exercise its responsibilities. Altman posted on X that Friday: "i loved my time at openai. it was transformative for me personally, and hopefully the world a little bit. most of all i loved working with such talented people. will have more to say about what's next later."



---


# Sam Altman Fired As OpenAI CEO In November 2023

Sam Altman was fired as CEO of OpenAI late on Friday, November 17, 2023, by the board of directors of OpenAI, Inc. — the 501(c)(3) nonprofit that acts as the governing body for OpenAI, the startup behind ChatGPT, GPT-4 and DALL-E 3. He both left the company's board of directors and stepped down as CEO, with chief technology officer Mira Murati stepping in as interim CEO.

OpenAI announced the shake-up in a post on its official blog; the company's management team was made aware shortly after. The blog post said Altman's departure followed a "deliberative review process by the board" which concluded that Altman "wasn't consistently candid in his communications" with other board members, "hindering its ability to exercise its responsibilities," and that the board "no longer has confidence in [Altman's] ability to continue leading OpenAI." In a joint statement the board wrote that "OpenAI was deliberately structured to advance our mission: to ensure that artificial general intelligence benefits all humanity," said it remained "fully committed to serving this mission," thanked Altman for "his many contributions to the founding and growth of OpenAI," and said that "we believe new leadership is necessary as we move forward" and that Mira, "as the leader of the company's research, product, and safety functions," was "exceptionally qualified" as interim CEO. OpenAI said it would begin a formal search for a permanent CEO immediately.

Altman responded on X: "i loved my time at openai. it was transformative for me personally, and hopefully the world a little bit. most of all i loved working with such talented people. will have more to say about what's next later." The removal came unexpectedly. OpenAI had just hosted its first developer conference, OpenAI DevDay, the week before with Altman emceeing; Altman had spoken at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation conference and at an Oakland, California event on the Thursday. According to The Verge and The New York Times, citing multiple internal sources, OpenAI employees learned of Altman's firing when it was announced publicly. The same change also saw co-founder Greg Brockman step down as chairman of the board while remaining OpenAI's president, reporting to Murati.



---


# OpenAI's Partnerships With Microsoft And The Associated Press

OpenAI's key business partner is Microsoft, which has invested billions of dollars into the startup and helped provide the computing power to run its AI systems. Microsoft said the leadership transition would not affect its relationship: "We have a long-term partnership with OpenAI and Microsoft remains committed to Mira and their team as we bring this next era of AI to our customers," an emailed Microsoft statement said.

A second, narrower arrangement is with a news organization: The Associated Press and OpenAI have a licensing and technology agreement allowing OpenAI access to part of the AP's text archives.



---


# OpenAI's AI Chip Ambitions

The company has suggested that it might be entering the AI chip market at some point in the future, in an effort to shore up the speed and performance of its API services.

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman had previously pointed to industry-wide GPU shortages for the service's spotty performance, and producing its own processors might mitigate those supply issues while potentially lowering the current four-cent-per-query cost of operating the chatbot to something more manageable.



---


# OpenAI's Board Composition In November 2023

The OpenAI board that fired Sam Altman consisted, the company said, of OpenAI's chief scientist Ilya Sutskever plus three non-employees.

Those three were Quora CEO Adam D'Angelo, tech entrepreneur Tasha McCauley, and Helen Toner of the Georgetown Center for Security and Emerging Technology.



---


# OpenAI Share Sale And Valuation Risk After The Firing

The planned sale of OpenAI employee shares that would have valued the startup at about $86 billion was put in jeopardy by Altman's firing.

The Information, speaking to three sources formerly with the company, reported that they no longer expected the sale — led by Thrive Capital — to happen, or, if it did happen, expected it to come with a lesser valuation because of the recent turn of events. Money was also implicated in the causes as well as the consequences: at the time of the firing it was unclear what missteps Altman might have made helming OpenAI, but they evidently related to his relationship with OpenAI's unusual board makeup and corporate governance structure — and perhaps to OpenAI's active talks to raise substantial new capital.



---


# OpenAI's Trust And Safety Departure And FTC Probe

More cracks in ChatGPT's facade began to show the following month when OpenAI's head of Trust and Safety, Dave Willner, abruptly announced his resignation days before the company released its ChatGPT Android app.

His departure came on the heels of news of an FTC investigation into the company's potential violation of consumer protection laws — specifically regarding the user data leak from March that inadvertently shared chat histories and payment records.



---


# Analyst Assessment Of Altman's Departure Impact

Gartner analyst Arun Chandrasekaran argued that Altman's exit "is indeed shocking as he has been the face of" generative AI technology — the ground for the shock being his public role rather than any operational gap.

Chandrasekaran qualified the consequence for the company itself: OpenAI still has a "deep bench of technical leaders," but its next executives will have to steer it through the challenges of scaling the business and meeting the expectations of regulators and society.

# FTX Fraud Charges And The SEC's Allegation

Sam Bankman-Fried, the founder of the failed cryptocurrency exchange FTX, faced seven counts of wire fraud and conspiracy — specifically, two counts of wire fraud and five conspiracy charges — and the Securities and Exchange Commission alleged that FTX was a fraud "from the start," with a "multi-billion-dollar deficiency caused by his own misappropriation of customer funds." The Verge repeated this framing at the head of each of its trial dispatches through October 2023, and in its October 28th, 2023 write-up reported that Bankman-Fried had been found guilty on seven counts including charges of wire fraud.

The boundary of the concept is the mix of charge types: the indictment paired substantive wire fraud counts with conspiracy counts rather than resting on a single offence, and the SEC's civil allegation about the exchange's origins ran alongside the criminal case rather than being part of it. The Verge's reporter, writing as the prosecution's case neared its end on October 26th, 2023, added an impression of the people the charges swept in: all the co-conspirators seemed oddly younger than their years, as though they had got stuck in the "math camp forever" environment Bankman-Fried created for them and simply failed to grow up.



---


# FTX's Inner Circle: Family And Friends Implicated

The Verge's October 26th, 2023 account of the trial catalogued how everyone who loved Bankman-Fried most in the world was caught up in the case. Adam Yedidia, his college roommate, testified with immunity because he was concerned he may have unknowingly worked on code that contributed to the fraud; "I love you Sam," he had texted at one point, "I'm not going anywhere" — that was before he realized FTX had stolen customer funds, at which point he resigned. Nishad Singh, a longtime family friend, copped to what sounded an awful lot like classic embezzlement, saying he had backdated transactions on FTX to help create doctored balance sheets to show to investors, and pleaded guilty to six charges including wire fraud, money laundering, and conspiracy counts around his political donations. Caroline Ellison, Bankman-Fried's ex-girlfriend, told the court about the seven phony balance sheets she had created and was clear that Alameda took customer funds, that Bankman-Fried knew about it, and that he even invested them against her advice.

His family was drawn in too. Joe Bankman, his father, is among the people included in the "small group chat," the Signal group where the FTX inner circle strategized during the exchange's last days. Barbara Fried's political action committee, Mind the Gap, is among the entities that received FTX customer money as political donations; Fried and Bankman lived together in a Bahamas house purchased for them using FTX investor funds, according to a financial expert called by the prosecution, and in a lawsuit filed by FTX's bankruptcy estate the two are alleged to have been given $10 million of FTX customer funds. Gabe Bankman-Fried's nonprofit, Guarding Against Pandemics, got millions from FTX; he was also in a Signal group chat, Donations Processing, that Singh says was used to coordinate the transfer of FTX and Alameda money to various political causes, and in that chat he can be seen recommending that some donations be made "in the dark" to avoid public relations headaches. Singh also said Gabe had an assistant fly to the Bahamas with a stack of blank checks for Singh to sign.

The consequences outlast the trial. Wang, Singh, and Ellison are now felons; even if they never do time — and they may very well be imprisoned or subjected to house arrest — their lives are irrevocably changed, not least by whatever restitution requirements they face, they are barred from taking certain kinds of jobs, and there is the publicity. Bankman, Fried, and Gabe Bankman-Fried's reputations are tarnished, and in the political arenas where they once operated they are suddenly undesirable. Beyond the courtroom, everyone who had money trapped on the exchange when it collapsed — as a result of Alameda purloining customers' funds — had their lives altered: even if they are made whole by the bankruptcy proceedings, that is still money they should have had access to at any time, which may mean houses that were not purchased, medical procedures left undone, and life savings lost. The reporter's summary: it is a Greek tragedy, precipitated by one man's character flaw, the arrogance of Sam Bankman-Fried.



---


# Sam Bankman-Fried's Charges And The Collapse Of FTX

Sam Bankman-Fried, the founder of FTX and Alameda Research, is facing seven counts of criminal charges: two counts of wire fraud and five counts of conspiracy charges.

FTX was a failed cryptocurrency exchange founded in 2019. According to a now-deleted profile from FTX investors Sequoia Capital, FTX was founded because of Bankman-Fried's frustration with other exchanges while he was running Alameda Research, his crypto trading firm. According to the SEC, FTX was a fraud "from the start," diverting customers' funds to Alameda, with a "multi-billion-dollar deficiency caused by his own misappropriation of customer funds."



---


# Prosecution Allegations In The FTX Superseding Indictment

In a superseding indictment filed August 14th, prosecutors argued that Bankman-Fried lied about consumer protection: that his statements that FTX was "avoiding or managing conflicts of interest" and that "as a general principle FTX segregates customer assets from its own assets across our platforms" were lies.

The indictment also says there were special features in FTX's code that "permitted Alameda to spend and withdraw unlimited amounts of money from FTX," created at Bankman-Fried's direction, effectively exempting Alameda from the kinds of risk management other customers faced — while, the government alleges, "Bankman-Fried publicly and repeatedly asserted that Alameda did not have privileged access to FTX." Bankman-Fried is accused of using "billions of dollars in misappropriated FTX customer deposits" to help buy more than $200 million of real estate for himself, make billions of dollars of investments for his own interest, and repay Alameda's lenders. He allegedly used more than $100 million of customer funds to make political contributions; prosecutors can show evidence of those contributions in this trial even though they aren't part of the charges brought. A second trial is scheduled for March 2024, with additional charges.



---


# Testimony At The SBF Trial

Across the first three weeks of the trial, a run of former colleagues, an outside investor and a forensic accounting expert testified that FTX customer money flowed into Alameda Research and out again to other uses, and that FTX's investors were never told about the two firms' special relationship. TechCrunch's running coverage, published 2023-10-06, summarises each week.

In week one, FTX's co-founder and CTO Gary Wang testified Thursday on the extent to which Alameda Research was used for whatever purposes he and SBF saw fit: according to Wang, the crypto trading firm pulled funding directly from FTX customers, whose transactions would be funneled toward Alameda and then directed elsewhere. Thursday also brought testimony from Matt Huang, co-founder and managing partner at crypto investment firm Paradigm, which invested $278 million in FTX across 2021 and 2022 and is part of a class-action lawsuit accusing it and others of defrauding customers by promoting FTX. His testimony centered around being left uninformed about FTX's utilization of customer money to keep Alameda Research afloat — a practice Huang says would have halted his involvement — and covered his relationship with FTX stretching back to 2019.

Week two's standout testimony came from Alameda Research's former CEO Caroline Ellison, who claimed she took $14 billion from customers to repay debts to lenders, using them as a line of credit under the instruction of SBF. Ellison also went into detail about how a $2 billion venture fund, FTX Ventures, was funded by money that had previously been allocated to Alameda from third-party lenders. And though there are no charges of bribery in the case, she also testified to paying Chinese officials $150 million to restore access to $1 billion in frozen trading accounts.

The third week featured a couple of noteworthy moments for the prosecution. FTX's former general counsel Can Sun, like many of SBF's former colleagues, opted to cooperate with authorities and testified that SBF asked him to create a theoretical "legal justification" for the use of billions in consumer funds just days before FTX filed for bankruptcy. Robert Boroujerdi, managing director of the hedge fund Third Point, testified about his experience working with SBF and FTX in a partnership that ultimately resulted in a $60 million investment and a lack of awareness about the special relationship between Alameda Research and FTX; had he known of such a relationship, he testified, Third Point would not have invested in FTX in the first place. And earlier in the week, Peter Easton — a University of Notre Dame professor who helped the government prosecution of Enron and WorldCom — testified about what he uncovered after tracing the flow of billions of dollars between Alameda Research and FTX: much of that funding came from customers, and Easton testified that he found user deposits were used by both FTX and Alameda to purchase real estate, make investments or direct funding toward political causes and charities.

qid: After the report by Fortune on October 13th stating that "Israel's blockade of Gaza means that a region the size of Philadelphia faces a real risk of starvation, says Peace Studies scholar," and the subsequent report by TechCrunch on October 19th claiming that "Israel's retaliatory airstrikes and total blockade have devastated Gaza by cutting access to electricity, water, and vital supplies," is the portrayal of the impact of the blockade on Gaza by the international aid groups as reported by these two news sources consistent or inconsistent?

# The October 2023 Cutoff Of Supplies To Gaza

Israel stopped allowing deliveries of food, fuel and other supplies to Gaza's 2.3 million residents on Oct. 10, 2023, and was reportedly preparing for a ground invasion; on Oct. 12, 2023 it warned 1.1 million Gaza residents in the northern section of the enclave to leave for the southern region in advance of that potential invasion. International aid groups warned that they could not deliver food and other basic services to people in the Gaza Strip and that a "dire" humanitarian crisis was set to worsen. Those groups provide food and other means of support to about 63% of people in Gaza.

What changed in October is the scope of the restriction rather than its existence. International aid groups now face the same problem in Gaza that local businesses and residents have encountered for about 16 years: a blockade that prevents civilians and items, like medicine, from easily moving into or out of the enclosed area, roughly 25 miles long. That 16-year blockade did not apply to the food and fuel that groups brought into Gaza. Now it does.



---


# How The Blockade Produces Food Insecurity And Import Dependence In Gaza

About 64% of people in Gaza are considered food insecure, meaning they do not have reliable access to sufficient amounts of food — one of the several practical effects the blockade has for the average Gazan. The dependence has deepened over time: food as a percentage of Gaza's total imports has skyrocketed by 50% since 2005, when Israel first imposed a temporary blockade, while the amount of food the West Bank and Gaza actually produce has tumbled by 30% since then.

The mechanism suppressing local production is partly infrastructural damage. It is hard for Gaza to produce food within its own borders; one factor is that Israeli airstrikes hit Gaza's only power generation plant and main sewage treatment plant in 2008 and again in 2018. Those attacks resulted in the spread of sewage waste on land and in the water, destroying farmlands and food crops and threatening fish stocks in the ocean as well.



---


# The Israeli Blockade Of Gaza Since 2007

The Israeli blockade of Gaza is a set of permanent air, land and sea blockades that Israel set up around the enclave in 2007, one year after Hamas rose to political power. Its discriminating features are physical control of movement and of goods: Israel controls two physical checkpoints along Gaza which monitor both the entry and exit of people and trucks, limits the kind and quantity of materials that pass into Gaza, and generally prohibits Gazans who do not have work permits or special clearance — for medical purposes, for example — from entering Israel. Egypt, which borders Gaza on its southern end, also oversees one checkpoint that specifically limits people coming and going.

The blockade is not total, and its boundary cases matter. Israel has granted permits to about 17,000 Gaza residents to enter and work in Israel, and while trade continues, the food, fuel and medical supplies that people in Gaza use all first pass through Israel. Gaza is about the size of Philadelphia and requires trade with different businesses and countries in order to maintain and grow its economy, but it is heavily dependent on foreign aid — partially as a result of this blockade regime. Israel's restrictions intensified after Hamas' surprise attack on 20 Israeli towns and several military bases on Oct. 7, 2023, when Israel announced a broad blockade of imports into Gaza that stopped all food, fuel and medical supplies from entering the region.



---


# The Gaza Conflict's Information Environment, Late 2023

Israel has retaliated against Hamas' October 7 attack with unprecedented force against the Palestinian territory, claiming over 9,000 Palestinian lives according to Gaza Health Ministry numbers reported by the Associated Press, as of November 3, 2023.

Reporting capacity in the territory has been degraded on two fronts. The Committee to Protect Journalists reports that at least 30 journalists have been killed since Israel's bombardment and total blockade of the region began, and journalists in Gaza say that without consistent access to food, water and power it is becoming "impossible" to continue reporting.

At the same time, misinformation about the escalating violence is rampant on social media — so the shortfall in professional reporting coincides with an unreliable information supply.



---


# Egypt's Role In The Israel-Hamas War And The Leverage It Creates

The war between Israel and Hamas has turned the spotlight on Egypt's role as a regional powerbroker, potentially winning it Western support as it tries to escape a grinding economic crisis. The structure linking the two is that Egypt's two assets in this conflict — long-held ties to Israel and a border with Gaza — make its stance decisive for outcomes the West wants.

Specifically, Egypt's position is shaping up as key to the fate of any refugees and to a sustained flow of aid for the besieged territory's 2 million residents, after Israel cut off crucial supplies in response to Hamas's deadly Oct. 7 assault. That dependence is what converts Egypt's geography and relationships into potential leverage over Western backing for its economy, as of the reporting date of 2023-10-22.



---


# Displacement And Casualties In Gaza As Of October 12, 2023

The number of people in Gaza displaced from their homes rose quickly over the days preceding Oct. 12, 2023, totaling over 330,000 on that date, with over two-thirds of them staying in UNRWA schools.

Since the war between Israel and Hamas began on Oct. 8, 2023, more than 1,500 Gazans had been killed and more than 5,300 injured, while Hamas attacks had killed more than 1,300 people in Israel and injured about 3,200 others. These are the figures as reported on 2023-10-13.



---


# Meta Response To Suppression Claims

Meta's rebuttal attacks the premise that any pattern of reduced reach for Palestine-related content shows deliberate suppression: the company says the reduced reach came from globally scoped technical bugs and from errors in good-faith enforcement, not from the subject matter of the posts. As reported by TechCrunch on 19 October 2023, Meta said it is closely monitoring its platforms for violations and may inadvertently flag certain content, but that it never intends to "suppress a particular community or point of view."

The scope condition Meta sets around the whole dispute is its terrorist-organization rule: content praising or supporting Hamas — which governs Gaza and is designated as a terrorist organization by the United States and the European Union — is expressly forbidden on Meta's platforms. This is stated in the aftermath of Hamas' attack on Israelis and Israel's retaliatory airstrikes and total blockade cutting access to electricity, water and vital supplies, which have devastated Gaza.

Meta communications director Andy Stone declined to comment on the record and pointed TechCrunch to Meta's newsroom post about the conflict, updated on Oct. 18 with a statement addressing the shadowbanning claims. "Our policies are designed to keep people safe on our apps while giving everyone a voice," it said. "We apply these policies equally around the world and there is no truth to the suggestion that we are deliberately suppressing voice … We can make errors and that is why there is an appeals process for people to tell us when they think we have made the wrong decision, so we can look into it."

The specific counter-explanations are two bugs, each claimed to be global and therefore content-neutral. Meta blamed technical errors for the removal of posts about Palestine during the 2021 conflict, and on the recent shadowbanning claims a company representative pointed TechCrunch to a Threads post by Stone: "We identified a bug impacting all Stories that re-shared Reels and Feed posts, meaning they weren't showing up properly in people's Stories tray, leading to significantly reduced reach. This bug affected accounts equally around the globe and had nothing to do with the subject matter of the content — and we fixed it as quickly as possible." Stone separately directed TechCrunch to the updated newsroom post, which said Meta identified and fixed a "bug" that prevented users from going live: "This was also a global issue that was fixed within a few hours. We understand people rely on these tools and we're sorry to anyone who felt the impact of these issues."

The rebuttal's reach is limited in ways the reporting records. It is unclear whether the bug affected accounts posting content unrelated to Gaza, while Instagram users have posted screenshots showing Stories about Palestine receiving significantly fewer views than other Stories posted the same day, and allege their view counts recovered when they posted content unrelated to the conflict. Meta's representative did not address the other accusations of censorship beyond Story visibility and did not respond to TechCrunch's follow-up questions; Meta initially did not respond to follow-up requests for comment. Asked about comments containing the Palestinian flag, Stone again pointed to the updated newsroom post, which did not directly address the issue, and he declined to comment on allegations of Meta disproportionately flagging Arabic news content, directing TechCrunch to the same post, which did not directly address those allegations either.

# Prosecution And Defense Arguments On Day Two Of The SBF Trial

On the second day of the trial of Sam Bankman-Fried and FTX, the prosecution argued that Bankman-Fried knowingly committed fraud, and it grounded that claim in motive: he did so, prosecutors said, to achieve great wealth, power and influence.

The defense countered with the opposite reading of the same conduct. # The SBF Trial Proceedings

Sam Bankman-Fried is in court for alleged fraud and money laundering while leading crypto exchange FTX and sister company Alameda. TechCrunch's 2023-10-02 preview placed the case in the Manhattan Federal Court, describing the disgraced cryptocurrency entrepreneur as accused of orchestrating "one of the biggest financial frauds in American history": the multibillion-dollar collapse of FTX, the crypto exchange he founded and led. # Meta Moderation Bias

TechCrunch's claim, published 19 October 2023, is that Meta has a moderation bias problem rather than a "bug": the suppression of Palestinian voices is the latest in a lengthy history of incidents on Meta platforms that reflect an inherent bias against Palestinian users in its processes, documented by years of complaints from both inside and outside the company. The argument's careful qualifier is that intent is not asserted — the company may not intentionally suppress specific communities, but its moderation practices often disproportionately affect Palestinian users.

The first ground is Meta's own commissioned evidence. During the last violent outbreak between Hamas and Israel in 2021, a report commissioned by Meta and conducted by a third party concluded that the company's actions had an "adverse human rights impact" on Palestinian users' right to freedom of expression and political participation.

The second ground is the pattern of disproportionate scrutiny during that outbreak. Amid the violence following the May 2021 court ruling to evict Palestinian families from Sheikh Jarrah, a neighborhood in occupied East Jerusalem, users across Facebook and Instagram accused Meta of taking down posts and suspending accounts that voiced support for Palestinians. The digital rights nonprofit Electronic Frontier Foundation described Meta's actions in 2021 as "systemic censorship of Palestinian voices," and in its 2022 report on Palestinian digital rights, 7amleh said Meta is "still the most restricting company" compared with other social media giants in the extent of its moderation of the Palestinian digital space.

The third ground is internal. That same month, a group of Facebook employees filed internal complaints accusing the company of bias against Arab and Muslim users; in internal posts obtained by BuzzFeed News, an employee attributed the bias to "years and years of implementing policies that just don't scale globally."

The fourth ground is the measured asymmetry between languages. At the recommendation of its Oversight Board, Meta conducted a third-party due diligence report about the platform's moderation during the May 2021 conflict. The report found that Arabic content was flagged as potentially violating at significantly higher rates than Hebrew content was, and was more likely to be erroneously removed. It noted that Meta's moderation system may not be as precise for Arabic content as for Hebrew, because the latter is a "more standardized language," and suggested that reviewers may lack the linguistic and cultural competence to understand less common Arabic dialects like Palestinian Arabic.

The warrant joining grounds to claim is duration and convergence. Because the disparity is recurrent across separate escalations, is corroborated from inside the company as well as by outside nonprofits and by Meta's own commissioned reviewers, and is traceable to standing properties of the moderation system rather than to a one-off failure, it is better described as bias inherent in the processes than as an isolated technical error.



---


# Irish DPC's Assessment Of Meta's Consent Model

Meta's lead regulator in the EU for the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), Ireland's Data Protection Commission (DPC), told TechCrunch: "Meta notified the DPC on July 27 of its intention to implement an alternative, consent-based model in which users would be given a choice between ads-funded versions of its platforms, and subscription versions in which, in return for payment of monthly fee, it is said that users will not receive targeted advertising."

The regulator also set out the timing and its cause: "While February 2024 was initially identified by Meta as the earliest date by which its consent model would be operational, it agreed to bring forward that date to November 2023 at the direction of the DPC, the DPC having been concerned to ensure that changes would be implemented to the platforms as soon as practicable in light of earlier findings to the effect that Meta had failed to demonstrate its entitlement to rely on the legal bases on which it was then relying when processing users' data for behavioural advertising purposes. These included findings made by the Court of Justice of the European Union when delivering judgment on July 4, 2023 in a case in which the Court examined the legal bases on which Meta's processing of users' data for behavioural advertising purposes is grounded." On the review itself: "Acting in consultation with its fellow European supervisory authorities, the DPC has been engaged in a detailed regulatory assessment of the consent-based model since it was first proposed by Meta in July. That exercise is being led by the DPC, reflecting its position as Lead Supervisory Authority for Facebook and Instagram in Europe. The exercise has not yet concluded, and no findings have been made to date. It is due to be completed shortly, at which point the DPC will notify Meta if it considers that the manner in which its new user offerings are to be implemented is compatible with Meta's obligations under GDPR." So Meta's move hasn't been signed off by data protection authorities as yet, and further regulatory interventions could follow — Norway's DPA, which has a local ban order on Meta's tracking ads, told TechCrunch it's concerned about the subscription plan, saying it has doubts as to whether it would constitute valid consent.



---


# DSA And DMA Oversight Of Meta's Ad Tracking

Meta's subscription plan faces three overlapping regimes, not one. As well as needing to comply with the GDPR, which delineates the qualities necessary for consent to be legal — such as that it is specific, informed and freely given — Meta is now also subject to the pan-EU Digital Services Act (DSA), which also sets conditions on larger platforms when it comes to tracking and profiling people for ads; so it won't just be data protection authorities making a call on whether Meta's subscription-or-tracking offer flies, since the European Commission is responsible for oversight of very large online platforms' DSA compliance.

Meta has also been designated as a so-called gatekeeper under the DSA's sister regulation, the Digital Markets Act (DMA), which also puts some limits on use of people's data for ads, and the Commission is the sole enforcer of the DMA. Meta is already in the Commission's sights over its approach to the DSA — the EU's executive has in recent days requested more information from the tech giant about its approach to content threats flowing from the Israel-Hamas war and about election security issues — but it remains to be seen whether the EU will apply the same close scrutiny to Meta's ad tracking offer.



---


# BEUC's Consumer-Law Case Against Meta's Pay-Or-Consent Model

BEUC's summary of the issues identified with Meta's model under consumer protection law rests on four grounds, each attached to a distinct provision of consumer law.

First, aggression: Meta is partially blocking the use of Facebook and Instagram until users have selected one option or the other, which constitutes an aggressive practice under European consumer law; through persistence and by creating a sense of urgency, Meta pushes consumers into making a choice they might not want to take. Second, a mistaken belief about what the paid tier buys: many consumers likely think that by opting for the paid subscription as it is presented they get a privacy-friendly option involving less tracking and profiling, when in fact users are likely to continue to have their personal data collected and used, but for purposes other than ads.

Third, misleading framing: Meta provides misleading and incomplete information to consumers which does not allow them to make an informed choice, and is misleading them by presenting the choice as between a paying and a "free" option, while the latter option is not "free" because consumers pay Meta through the provision of their data, as past court rulings have already declared. Fourth, and the warrant tying the rest together, the absence of a real choice: given the market power of Meta's Facebook and Instagram services in the EU and the very strong network effects of social media platforms — since all your friends are on Facebook and Instagram — consumers do not have a real choice, because if they quit the services they would lose all their contacts and interactions built over the years; the very high subscription fee for "ad-free" services is also a deterrent, which likewise means consumers do not have a real choice.



---


# The GDPR Track Running Alongside The Consumer Complaint

As of November 30, 2023 the data protection question about Meta's pay-or-consent offer was unresolved and running on a separate track from the consumer complaint. "The company's approach also raises concerns regarding the GDPR," BEUC's Ursula Pachl noted, and a spokesman for BEUC told TechCrunch it might, at a later stage, file a complaint about Meta's data protection compliance with the relevant privacy authority once it has completed its own assessment of the issues — though he emphasized it was too early to say whether or not it would take that step.

Meta's lead data protection authority in the EU, Ireland's Data Protection Commission (DPC), had for several months been assessing its pay-or-consent offer but had yet to communicate a conclusion. In the meanwhile, Meta maintains that the model it has devised for obtaining users' consent to its ads processing complies with the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) — although, TechCrunch notes, the adtech giant also said that when it was claiming performance of a contract and then legitimate interests for the processing, both of which were subsequently found to be incompatible with the GDPR.

TechCrunch's reading of the incentive: Meta is likely banking on another multi-year round of GDPR complaints, legal challenges and finally a referral to the CJEU, followed by another long wait before a ruling gets handed down, buying it several more years to run with its new legal basis fix and keep feeding its profits by doing what it likes with Europeans' data.

# Alameda Research As The Alleged Conduit For FTX Customer Funds

In the prosecution's account offered by Thane Rehn, the key to Sam Bankman-Fried's alleged scheme was Alameda Research, a crypto hedge fund that Bankman-Fried also owned. The structure the government described works as follows: Caroline Ellison — Bankman-Fried's on-again off-again girlfriend and the CEO of Alameda — served as a front for the fund, and through that arrangement Bankman-Fried had "secret access" to customer money, both cash and crypto.

Two further relations complete the alleged mechanism. Bankman-Fried is said to have directed employees to conceal the flow of money into FTX's coffers, and to have forged financial documents distributed to lenders and investors. "The defendant lied to the world," Rehn alleged. These are the government's allegations as presented in its opening statement, not established findings.

# The Defense's Good-Faith Case For Bankman-Fried

Mark Cohen, one of Sam Bankman-Fried's lawyers, attacked the prosecution's central premise that his client was a liar who stole from customers, stating early in his opening statement that "Sam didn't defraud anyone." The defense's counter-picture is of a nerdy startup founder who acted in "good faith," not the prosecution's "cartoon of a villain"; Cohen repeatedly harped on Bankman-Fried's allegedly good-faith actions throughout his address to the jury. Bankman-Fried, whose cheekbones were more prominent after spending about seven weeks in a Brooklyn prison, appeared in court as this argument was made.

Cohen also disputed the specific claim that Alameda Research was a covert conduit. Alameda was not subterranean or shady, he said; it was a successful hedge fund. The background condition was that Alameda was also getting loans from outside lenders such as Genesis, because when FTX started there were not a lot of customer funds to borrow.

The day ended with a document shared between Ellison and Bankman-Fried, his comments appearing in bubbles along the main text. # FTX Fraud Charges And The SEC's Allegation

Sam Bankman-Fried, the founder of the failed cryptocurrency exchange FTX, faced seven counts of wire fraud and conspiracy — specifically, two counts of wire fraud and five conspiracy charges — and the Securities and Exchange Commission alleged that FTX was a fraud "from the start," with a "multi-billion-dollar deficiency caused by his own misappropriation of customer funds." The Verge repeated this framing at the head of each of its trial dispatches through October 2023, and in its October 28th, 2023 write-up reported that Bankman-Fried had been found guilty on seven counts including charges of wire fraud.

The boundary of the concept is the mix of charge types: the indictment paired substantive wire fraud counts with conspiracy counts rather than resting on a single offence, and the SEC's civil allegation about the exchange's origins ran alongside the criminal case rather than being part of it. The Verge's reporter, writing as the prosecution's case neared its end on October 26th, 2023, added an impression of the people the charges swept in: all the co-conspirators seemed oddly younger than their years, as though they had got stuck in the "math camp forever" environment Bankman-Fried created for them and simply failed to grow up.

# Sam Bankman-Fried

Sam Bankman-Fried is the former CEO of the bankrupt crypto exchange FTX, whose highly anticipated criminal trial started on the Tuesday before TechCrunch's 2023-10-01 report, to determine whether he is guilty of seven counts of fraud and conspiracy. As one former federal prosecutor put it: "The odds seem to be stacked against him at this point."

He was 31 years old and co-founded FTX in 2019; within a few years the once third-largest crypto exchange's valuation hit $32 billion at its peak, and the company is now trying to claw back any funds to distribute to creditors. Before the fall he was even compared to Warren Buffet, and many called him the white horse of crypto — a description TechCrunch notes it never applied to him.

Bankman-Fried, however, maintained his innocence. At The New York Times' DealBook Summit he appeared virtually from the Bahamas and said, "I didn't ever try to commit fraud on anyone; I was shocked by what happened this month"; in a published DM exchange with a Vox reporter he said he regretted filing for bankruptcy and thought that "regulators make everything worse." In January he pleaded not guilty to all counts, which include wire fraud, conspiracy to commit money laundering and conspiracy to misuse customer funds. He could face up to 115 years in jail if convicted on all charges.

# The SBF Trial Proceedings

Sam Bankman-Fried is in court for alleged fraud and money laundering while leading crypto exchange FTX and sister company Alameda. TechCrunch's 2023-10-02 preview placed the case in the Manhattan Federal Court, describing the disgraced cryptocurrency entrepreneur as accused of orchestrating "one of the biggest financial frauds in American history": the multibillion-dollar collapse of FTX, the crypto exchange he founded and led. SBF, as he is known, has pleaded not guilty to some seven charges of fraud and conspiracy.

The trial kicked off with jury selection October 3. By TechCrunch's 2023-10-06 update the case was entering its next chapter, with proceedings resuming Thursday: as confirmed during a teleconference Wednesday, SBF would be taking the stand along with a handful of other witnesses, as the onus shifted toward the defense after the prosecution brought its case to its conclusion.

Access to the proceedings is limited: no devices are allowed, so reports are being physically put together within the courtroom, or sent to overflow rooms. The jury's composition ranges from a train conductor to a retired investment banker who attended Stanford University, and TechCrunch pointed readers to a special joint episode of its Equity and Chain Reaction podcasts for a better sense of the vibe between the jurors and the rest of the court.

The Verge's trial reporter argued that Bankman-Fried's choice to take the stand was a net loss for his defense: like Theranos' Elizabeth Holmes before him, he got on the stand to speak directly to his state of mind in a way no other witness can, but telling your side of the story opens you to a great many questions you might not want to answer on cross-examination — and, having watched a lot of crosses, she called Sassoon's the nastiest she had ever seen.

The warrant is what the charges turn on. The case hinged on conspiracy and intentional deceit: just losing $8 billion is not a crime, though it is very embarrassing, but if Bankman-Fried lied to customers and lenders about what he was doing and how safe FTX was, that is a crime. Because state of mind was the contested issue, his own testimony became the evidence, and it did not hold: Sassoon had established the day before that he has a long history of dishonesty, and on October 31st, through a set of questions about what he did and did not do, she established that the story he told on direct examination was absurd. The direct examination had already supplied grounds. Beyond the two obvious lies the reporter counted him telling on the stand — about Alameda Research's name and about "allow_negative" — she was struck by how little he seemed to know about his own companies: apparently Singh, Wang, and Ellison were out there just doing whatever their little hearts desired, because Bankman-Fried was a CEO, but definitely not the kind that pays any attention to money at his crypto trading firm and futures exchange.



---


# The Prosecution's Opening Statement Against Bankman-Fried

Thane Rehn, a prosecutor for the government, opened the case against Sam Bankman-Fried with the line "One year ago, it looked like the defendant was on the top of the world," and then argued that this appearance was false: "all of that, all of it, was built on lies," he declared to the jury, adding "Behind the curtains, he was not what he appeared to be." Rehn described a defendant who, as former CEO of FTX, oversaw a supposedly thriving crypto exchange, jetted between international locales, hobnobbed with celebrities like Tom Brady and Larry David, and repeatedly emphasized to customers that their money was safe and secure.

What followed was a roughly 30-minute story that repeatedly emphasized how Bankman-Fried allegedly stole customer funds to facilitate his jet-setting lifestyle, donate millions to political candidates, and finance risky bets. Rehn also directly contested the media framing of the defendant: he was not a crypto "boy" genius, as so many in the media — Fortune included — have written, but a "man" who "stole billions of dollars from thousands of victims." Rehn closed the characterization with a promise to the jury: "You will see the full picture."



---


# FTX's Bankruptcy And Leadership

The man who represented FTX before Congress after its failure told lawmakers the exchange had effectively no internal governance at all, and the prosecutor bringing the case called Bankman-Fried's alleged crimes one of the biggest financial frauds in American history. TechCrunch reported both on 2023-10-01.

Ray represented the company during a House Financial Services Committee hearing regarding FTX. Asked whether the firm had significant risk management systems, Ray said at the time that "there were virtually no internal controls and no separateness whatsoever," and added that he did not "trust a single piece of paper" in the exchange's organization. Separately, in a press conference, U.S. Attorney Damian Williams called Bankman-Fried's alleged crimes "one of the biggest financial frauds in American history."
