# Trump Tower Fifth Avenue Penthouse Valuation Dispute

Among the allegations in the New York case was that Trump claimed his Trump Tower apartment in Manhattan — a three-storey penthouse replete with gold-plated fixtures — was nearly three times its actual size, and valued the property at $327 million; no apartment in New York City has ever sold for close to that amount, Attorney General Letitia James said. The Age's comparison in November 2023 listed Trump's 2021 valuation at $US131.3 million and Bloomberg's 2023 valuation at $US40 million, with no current New York estimate available.

The size inflation is documented over a specific window: between 2011 and 2016, Trump valued the apartment on the basis of it being 30,000 square feet (2,787 square metres), almost triple its actual measurement of 10,996 square feet, and because of this New York State arrived at a valuation about a third of Trump's in those years. Space inflation was not the only issue: between 2014 and 2015 Trump increased the apartment's value to $US327 million from $US200 million, which the prosecution argues was to mask a drop in the value of another of his properties. "A discrepancy of this order of magnitude, by a real estate developer sizing up his own living space of decades, can only be considered fraud," Judge Arthur Engoron wrote in his September ruling.

Bloomberg values the property using recent Trump Tower sales and those of comparable Manhattan penthouses. While some splashy residences in much newer Billionaires Row buildings have listed for well in excess of $US100 million, they typically boast higher ceilings, more up-to-date finishes, contemporary layouts, outdoor space and better views. A better comparison, the report says, would be a 9,450-square-foot penthouse in Olympic Tower, five blocks south on Fifth Avenue, on and off the market for $US35 million since 2016; or Carl Icahn's 14,000-square-foot penthouse at Museum Tower on West 53rd Street, listed for $US35 million in 2019 before he attempted to split and sell it as two apartments, both eventually delisted.



---


# Trump Net Worth Valuation Dispute at Trial

Thousands of pages of exhibits detailing the performance of Donald Trump's assets, made available during the New York fraud trial, have provided a deeper look into his fortune. His 2021 statement of financial condition, filed as part of the lawsuit, pegged his net worth at $US4.5 billion. Bloomberg's calculation has consistently been below Trump's figures; at the same time, Bloomberg measured the value of some Trump properties higher than what New York state claims.

Trump took the stand and testified that the properties whose values he is accused of inflating were actually undervalued, based on the premium his "brand" adds. He also said that banks did not rely on his statements of financial condition when weighing loans: "They just weren't a very important element in banks' decision-making process," Trump told the court. "And we'll explain that as this trial goes along."

The Age's 7 November 2023 report set out New York state's valuation of four high-profile Trump properties where the prosecution alleges fraud occurred, alongside Bloomberg's own approach to assessing the assets.



---


# Mar-a-Lago Valuation Dispute

Mar-a-Lago is the sharpest of the valuation disputes: Trump valued the Palm Beach estate as high as $739 million — more than 10 times a more reasonable estimate of its worth, Fortune reported in September 2023 — on the idea that the property could be developed for residential use, when deed terms prohibit that, Attorney General Letitia James said. The Age's November 2023 comparison put Trump's 2021 valuation at $US612.1 million, Bloomberg's 2023 valuation at $US240 million, and New York's 2021 valuation at $US27.6 million.

The gap turns on how the property may be used. Trump made a series of agreements with Palm Beach County and the National Trust for Historic Preservation for Mar-a-Lago to be used only as a club, giving up development rights, so Palm Beach values the property as a business on its tax rolls and in 2021 assessed it at $US27.6 million, lower than comparable residential properties; New York State argues this is the appraisal Trump should have been using. Historically Mar-a-Lago never made much money for the Trump Organisation, but it took in about $US41 million in revenue in 2022 according to Trump's most recent ethics disclosure, compared with $US21 million in 2019. Bloomberg values it at $US240 million based on a combination of comparable residential property sales in the area and its value as a business, reflecting uncertainty around its future status — uncertainty not shared by everyone: if the city and county allowed it, "there is no reason why it wouldn't be able to converted to a full-time private residence," said Eli Beracha, director of the Hollo School of Real Estate at Florida International University. Trump Park Avenue, the residential condo tower on Manhattan's Upper East Side formerly known as the Hotel Delmonico, is not one of Trump's best-known buildings, but according to the prosecution it has been the source of some significant asset inflations. A judge ruled on Tuesday 26 September 2023 that Donald Trump committed fraud for years while building the real estate empire that catapulted him to fame and the White House. # X's Valuation Decline In 2023

X has marked its value at $19 billion, according to internal documents, marking a 56% decrease in value since Elon Musk's purchase in 2022.

That is bad for shareholders and Musk.

But it is potentially good for executives and employees, Amanda explains.

# Google Paid $26.3 Billion In 2021 For Default Search Placement

Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to multiple browsers, phones and platforms — from companies including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla — to be everyone's default search engine. The figure was revealed by Google's search head Prabhakar Raghavan when he testified in court on October 28, according to The Verge.

About $18 billion of that total went directly to Apple, according to a New York Times report published earlier in October 2023, and Google has had its deal with Apple in place since 2003 — so the payment is the current year of a two-decade arrangement, not a one-off. Questioned on the amount of money Google spends to get first pick of search engines, Pichai said the decision was made with the consumer in mind: Google pays big bucks to be everywhere so that it can take in all the data and be the best search engine across different companies' devices, he said, according to The Verge.

The trial also produced evidence that Google understood the value of defaults very early on. U.S. Justice Department lawyer Meagan Bellshaw showed Pichai a 2007 email from a Google product strategy meeting containing data showing that when people changed their browser homepage to Google, they did 15% more Google searches, and that when they switched away, their Google searches dropped 27%. The email summarizing that meeting, sent to Pichai as well as other Google leaders, read: "Nitin argues that focusing on homepage market share is one of the most effective things we can do to make gains in search market share," according to The Verge.



---


# Default Search Engine

## Definition

The default search engine is the search provider a device, browser, or platform is pre-configured to use unless a user actively changes the setting — the search box that runs when a person types a query without first choosing an alternative, such as Google on the iPhone's Safari address bar or Firefox's search bar.

## Context

The term is central to *US v. Google*, the DOJ's antitrust case, because default status is the mechanism through which Google secures the overwhelming share of search queries: the Information Services Agreement (ISA) between Apple and Google, in place since 2002/2003, makes Google the default on all Apple devices, and Google separately pays Samsung, Mozilla, and other partners for the same status.
Apple executive Eddy Cue testified that Apple's iPhone setup flow deliberately omits any search-engine choice screen, arguing that presenting users with unfamiliar alternatives would harm the setup experience, while conceding the ISA does not permit Apple to offer such a choice.
Google spent $26.3 billion in 2021 on default-placement deals across browsers, phones, and platforms — about $18 billion of that to Apple alone — a scale that the DOJ used to argue Google understands the mechanism's value: internal 2007 data showed users who set Google as their homepage searched 15% more, while switching away dropped searches 27%.
The Mozilla/Yahoo episode shows the same mechanism working in reverse: when Firefox switched its default from Google to Yahoo under a 2014 deal, Mozilla's CEO testified that user retention declined, illustrating how disruptive changing the default can be even when a paying competitor is involved.
Outside the antitrust trial, the term also frames ordinary consumer behavior: an investor in e-commerce search startup Deft described users' "natural behavior" as following the path of least resistance and just using the default search engine, meaning challenger search products must offer a high-value proposition to displace that inertia.

## Key Characteristics

- **Set by agreement, not by user choice** — default status on major platforms (Apple's Safari/iOS, Android OEMs, Firefox) is typically established through commercial deals (e.g., the Apple-Google ISA, Yahoo-Mozilla's $375M/year deal) rather than user selection at setup.
- **Backed by large recurring payments** — Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 across partners to hold default placement, with roughly $18 billion of that going to Apple.
- **Technically reversible but rarely changed** — Apple and Google both argued switching is easy, but DuckDuckGo's CEO countered that it takes "too many steps" to switch, and Google's own 2005 complaint about Internet Explorer's defaults argued that "most end users do not change defaults," so default status functions as durable market power.
- **Distinct from pre-installation** — Google's separate push to get Chrome and Search merely pre-installed (not necessarily defaulted) on Android and iPhones shows default status is a stronger, more contested tier than simple presence on a device.
- **Drives user behavior even outside browsers** — the concept extends to any search product; consumers default to "the path of least resistance," which challenger search startups must specifically overcome.

## Corpus References

Corpus notes whose source text references this term (evidence-backed, from `term_links.json`):

- [The Google Antitrust Case](google_antitrust_case.md)
- [The Hypocrisy Argument: Google Became The Monopoly It Denounced](google_default_hypocrisy_argument.md)
- [US v. Google: Two Months Into The Search Antitrust Trial](us_v_google_search_antitrust_trial_overview.md)

# The Google Antitrust Case

The Google antitrust case is the U.S. government's trial over Google's dominance in the online search market, stemming from a 2020 antitrust claim, in which the government argues that Google uses its platforms and its deals with partners to block out competition in search or advertising and thereby to hinder competitors from accessing the data they would need to improve their products.

Its defining features are the conduct at issue and the defence offered against it. Google CEO Sundar Pichai testified Monday in the trial, defending Google's business tactics, including its deal with Apple and other partners to make Google the default search engine. Google's answer is that it is just doing business: everybody wants Google as the default engine because it is the best, and that, the company says, does not make its actions illegal.

The important boundary case is which Google antitrust matter this is. The 2020 search claim is separate from the one filed in January by the Department of Justice, along with eight states including New York, California and Colorado, which aims to "halt Google's anticompetitive scheme, unwind Google's monopolistic grip on the market and restore competition to digital advertising." The search case and the digital-advertising case are distinct proceedings and should not be conflated.

The trial is the venue in which the underlying numbers surface. Monday's hearing revealed plenty of juicy tidbits, including the $26.3 billion Google spent making itself the default search engine across platforms in 2021, and how Google tried to take it further and have Chrome preinstalled on iPhones.



---


# Helena World Chronicle's Class Action Antitrust Suit Against Google

A class action lawsuit filed in the week of 15 December 2023 in the U.S. District Court in D.C. accuses Google and parent company Alphabet of anticompetitive behavior in violation of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act and others, on behalf of news publishers. The case was filed by Arkansas-based publisher Helena World Chronicle, which argues that Google "siphons off" news publishers' content, their readers and their ad revenue through anticompetitive means, and it specifically cites new AI technologies such as Google's Search Generative Experience (SGE) and the Bard AI chatbot as worsening the problem.

Helena World Chronicle owns and publishes two weekly newspapers in Arkansas. In the complaint it argues that Google is "starving the free press" by sharing publishers' content on Google, losing them "billions of dollars."

Beyond damages, the suit asks for an injunction that would require Google to obtain consent from publishers before using their website data to train its general artificial intelligence products, including Google's own and those of rivals. It also asks that publishers who opt out of SGE still be allowed to show up in Google search results, among other things.

The law firm handling the case is Hausfeld, whose announcement states that "the anticompetitive effects of Google's scheme cause profound harm to competition, to consumers, to labor, and to a democratic free press," and that "Plaintiff Helena World Chronicle, LLC invokes the Sherman Act and Clayton Act to seek class-wide monetary and injunctive relief to restore and ensure competition for digital news and reference publishing and set up guardrails to preserve a free marketplace of ideas in the new era of artificial intelligence."



---


# US v. Google: Two Months Into The Search Antitrust Trial

As of TechCrunch's November 13, 2023 roundup, the Justice Department's landmark antitrust case against Google was nearly two months old, and the trial record was still producing fresh revelations. TechCrunch framed it as one of the biggest fights in tech antitrust since the U.S. took Microsoft to trial in the 1990s.

Over the couple of weeks preceding this roundup, more of Google's inner workings came to light, including some of the search engine's most lucrative search queries, the shape of the revenue-share agreements between Google and Android OEMs, and why Expedia has a bone to pick with Google.

# Consumer Search Startups And Switching Barriers

The premise attacked is that a better search product wins users. The cautionary case is Neeva, founded by former Google execs, which tried to convince people to switch to paid and private search with additional features; earlier in 2023 the startup shut down its consumer efforts and eventually got acquired by Snowflake.

Adii Pienaar, an investor in Deft, said that Deft has to give compelling reasons to users to switch to its service. His grounds are behavioral rather than technical: "Users' natural behavior for search is to follow the path of least resistance, i.e. most people just pick up their phone and just use the default search engine."

The conclusion he draws sets the bar Deft must clear: "For Deft to change that behavior, they will need to create a high-value proposition."

# Rugby Australia's Debt And Funding Position In 2023

Rugby Australia was forced to take out a $40m loan from Ares to keep the game afloat, and as of Oct. 10, 2023 had around another $15m left to spend from it while looking to borrow up to another $60m.

The purpose of the additional borrowing is to be in the strongest possible position to capitalise on two major money-making events — the 2025 British and Irish Lions series and a home men's World Cup — and succeed. RA is also in the early stages of looking to renew its next broadcast deal, hoping to at least double its current arrangement with Nine Entertainment/Stan Sport, which pays $29m per year until the end of 2025.

The states have their own claims on that money. The QRU expressed its desire for Rugby Australia to reinstate the annual $1.7 million in funding to each of the Super Rugby franchises that was withdrawn following the Covid pandemic to help keep the game afloat, and expressed satisfaction that RA was willing to discuss reinstating it. Meanwhile, The Roar understands the ACT Brumbies sent RA confirmation of solvency for the next 12 months.



---


# The NSW Waratahs' Licence Handover To Rugby Australia

The New South Wales Rugby Union was in the latter stages of handing over its licence to Rugby Australia, The Roar revealed in the week before Oct. 10, 2023 — a move by which the NSW Waratahs, who were on the brink of insolvency, handed over their commercial and high-performance property.

The practical effect is that all male and female Waratahs players, including coaches and high-performance staff, as well as all commercial and operations staff, will run out of RA's office. NSW Waratahs chief executive Paul Doorn informed stakeholders of the decision the previous week.

RA is cognisant that not every Super Rugby franchise will follow suit immediately, but the governing body is hopeful that now one of the two biggest states has agreed to hand over the keys, others will follow swiftly, with the Melbourne Rebels expected to be next. RA chief executive Phil Waugh says building trust back between the governing body and the states is essential to their plans.



---


# The Case For Schmidt Bringing Rugby Smarts To The Wallabies

Several sources told The Roar in December 2023 that Joe Schmidt is exactly the type of person the Wallabies need: the claim is that the highly detailed Schmidt would bring rugby smarts to the Australian program, and the warrant is that the Wallabies' detail and nous were clearly absent on the field over the previous year, which is precisely what his coaching supplies.

The evidence offered for that capability is what his Ireland teams demonstrably did: the manipulation and ability to play both sides of the ruck was clearly visible during his Irish tenure.

The argument also carries a political ground about acceptance within Australian rugby: should Rugby Australia move on him, Schmidt's backing would be largely supported by the Super Rugby franchises.



---


# The QRU Refuses To Centralise Commercial Functions

The Queensland Rugby Union stopped short of wanting to hand over its commercial property, rejecting the step from high-performance centralisation to full centralisation: "While the QRU is very supportive of high-performance alignment, it will not agree to any proposal on centralising commercial or corporate functions."

The premise it attacks is that consolidating commercial operations under Rugby Australia would strengthen the game. The QRU's reason is local expertise: "The very strength of our State unions is the expertise they bring in their own markets. We are open to work on commercial initiatives together but will always retain our independence for the benefit of Queensland Rugby, its members and stakeholders."

It backed the position with its own financial and participation record. The letter cited a sustainable business model built through the elimination of legacy operating debt, four straight operating profits, and work in partnership with governments to deliver $31 million of improvements to Ballymore through the construction of the National Rugby Training Centre, home of the Wallaroos and Queensland Reds. It also pointed to 71,000 players across the state, including more than 16,000 female participants, 257 schools featuring rugby as part of their program, and the Hospital Cup and regional club competitions, as evidence the game was in good health in Queensland.



---


# The QRU's Position On High-Performance Centralisation

In the wake of the Wallabies' 2023 World Cup flop, the Queensland Rugby Union reaffirmed on Oct. 10, 2023 that it is committed to moving to a centralised high-performance model — but will not follow the NSW Waratahs in handing over the keys to Rugby Australia.

The QRU's stated commitment reads: "The QRU is committed to working with Rugby Australia to lead reform of our game at a high-performance level, and help Rugby Australia develop an improved game through high-performance centralisation." The letter defined the scope of that centralisation: it "would include a national player-contracting model, and alignment of key high-performance staff, such as coaching, strength and conditioning, and medical to operate as one national system." The letter, an open letter to members published on Wednesday morning by QRU chief executive David Hanham and chairman Brett Clark, also pointed to RA's involvement in Les Kiss' appointment as Reds coach — the former State of Origin winger turned coach, who has spent the best part of two decades coaching in Ireland and England, replacing Brad Thorn — as an example of the model in practice.

The QRU also expressed strong support for Rugby Australia to conduct a "fully independent and transparent top-to-bottom review of the Wallabies program and how it can be improved" in light of the historic first World Cup pool exit, adding: "It should also provide a clear view of what is needed in a leadership and governance framework to ensure we put the right people, in the right roles, in the right system." The Roar noted the boundary of the consensus: while all five Australian Super Rugby sides are fundamentally on board with moving to a centralised high-performance program, some states, including the ACT Brumbies as well as the QRU, don't want to give up their commercial assets.



---


# The Rugby Australia High-Performance Director Role And Its Remit

The Rugby Australia director of high-performance is the position at the top of the governing body's high-performance structure, described by chief executive Phil Waugh in December 2023 as the biggest job on his leadership team in terms of its impact on the general sentiment around the game in Australia.

Three duties define the role as described. First, the director oversees all of Australia's men's and women's high-performance programs. Second, the holder is tasked with "integrating" those programs, as Rugby Australia tries to centralise all of Super Rugby's high-performance programs. Third — and perhaps most pressing at the time — the director must build a list of coaching candidates to take over from Eddie Jones, with Rugby Australia wanting the new Wallabies coach set in stone by the start of Super Rugby.

The scope conditions attached are timing and seniority. Rugby Australia always said it wanted the role filled by Christmas, and Waugh's framing sets the standard for the appointment: "It's a big job. It's the biggest job on my leadership team in terms of the impact it has on the general sentiment around the game."



---


# Rugby Australia's Consultancy Approach To David Nucifora

Rugby Australia was trying to get Ireland's long-time director of high-performance David Nucifora on board as a consultant once he wraps up with Ireland, The Roar reported on 11 December 2023, while making clear he was never in the running for the director of high-performance role itself.

The report links that approach to the Schmidt pursuit: should Rugby Australia go down the path of bringing Joe Schmidt into the fold, Schmidt's own relationship with Nucifora could see the Australian reconsider his position with the governing body. In the meantime, Rugby Australia have been making moves to try and twist Nucifora's arm.



---


# Joe Schmidt's Coaching Record With Ireland And The All Blacks

Joe Schmidt took Ireland to the top of World Rugby's rankings while his Irish sides bombed out in successive World Cup quarter-finals under his leadership, and he later helped transform an All Blacks team that reached the 2023 World Cup final, as reported by The Roar on 11 December 2023.

His Ireland tenure is credited with more than results: Schmidt played an instrumental role in not just seeing them become one of the world's best teams but helped usher through transformational change off the field, as Ireland moved to a centralised system.

The New Zealander briefly exited the international coaching scene following the 2019 World Cup, citing a desire to move home to New Zealand to be closer to his family. After initially moving back into the coaching fray with the Blues in Super Rugby, he joined the All Blacks ahead of the previous year's Rugby Championship, as New Zealand Rugby shook up the All Blacks coaching team following their historic series loss to Andy Farrell's Irish. His expertise proved telling: he and Jason Ryan transformed the All Blacks and helped Ian Foster's side reach the final of that year's World Cup after stunning wins over Ireland and Argentina in the knockout stages.

qid: Do the 'Business Line' article's claims about central bankers' response to supply disruptions and the 'Fortune' article's claims about Federal Reserve officials' actions to combat inflation both suggest an increase in interest rates?
context:
# Criticism Of QE And Its Narrower Future Role

The premise that quantitative easing is a benign general-purpose tool is contested: bond-buying has been blamed for distorting financial markets, and episodes such as the Silicon Valley Bank blow-up are seen by some as a direct result of central bank reserves creation under QE, along with regulatory and supervision failures.

The economists surveyed expect its role to narrow accordingly. Only 40% predict central banks will use QE the same way as they did before; a quarter expect them to deploy it more sparingly; about 30% see its only role going forward as a tool to address financial-stability concerns; and a small minority doesn't see it being used again at all.



---


# Federal Reserve Rate Path Expectations Late 2023

By early December 2023 traders widely expected the Federal Reserve to hold its key interest rate steady at its meeting the following week before potentially cutting rates in March, according to data from CME Group, and Fed officials had recently hinted that the federal funds rate may already be at its peak, above 5.25 per cent, up from nearly zero early in 2022. Fed Chair Jerome Powell and others nevertheless warned Wall Street against being overzealous in its predictions about how early a cut could happen.

The bond market moved with those expectations. With inflation down from its peak two summers earlier, Wall Street was hopeful the Fed might be done with its market-shaking hikes. Investors were looking for a slowdown in the job market that came through employers cutting back on open positions rather than laying off workers, and the report cited showed employers advertised just 8.7 million jobs on the last day of October, down 617,000 from a month earlier. US Treasury yields continued to sag from the heights reached during late October: the 10-year yield fell to 4.18 per cent from 4.26 per cent late on the Monday, after having been above 5 per cent and at its highest level in more than a decade during October. The two-year Treasury yield, which more closely tracks Fed expectations, fell from 4.61 per cent just before the economic reports to 4.57 per cent, yo-yoed, and then eased back to 4.57 per cent. Lower yields were one reason cryptocurrency prices had been rising, alongside excitement about a possible bitcoin exchange-traded fund that helped send bitcoin above $US43,000 ($65,600); Robinhood Markets reported a roughly 75 per cent jump in crypto trading volumes during November from a month earlier, said customers added about $US1.4 billion in net deposits during the month, and its own stock rose 10.3 per cent.

A month earlier, in early November 2023, the same expectations were forming from a lower base. Before that week, stocks had been struggling under the weight of rapidly rising Treasury yields catching up to the Fed's main interest rate, which was above 5.25 per cent and at its highest level since 2001. Higher rates and yields slow the economy, hurt investment prices and raise the risk of something breaking in the financial system, such as the three high-profile US bank failures that rattled markets during the spring. "It was really fear that the Fed was going to go too far," said Katie Nixon, chief investment officer for Northern Trust Wealth Management. The Fed had applied that pressure intentionally, hoping to starve inflation of its fuel and to cool the job market, particularly pay raises, because it feared too-strong pay gains could create a vicious cycle keeping inflation high. Analysts said the Friday jobs report offered encouraging signals, with average hourly earnings rising less in October from September than expected, though it did not mean the job was done. Treasury yields tumbled immediately after that report, with the 10-year easing to 4.52 per cent from 4.67 per cent late Thursday and from more than five per cent the previous week, when it hit its highest level since 2007. Traders then moved up expectations for the first Fed cut, potentially by the summer, according to CME Group data. Foreign-exchange strategists at Bank of America wrote in a BofA Global Research report that for investors around the world the "Fed matters more than other central banks" and weak US data is "the only game-changer for markets". A separate report that Friday from the Institute for Supply Management said growth in US services industries such as finance and construction was weaker than economists expected and suggested a slight easing in prices.



---


# Central Bankers' Call For Fiscal Restraint And Structural Growth

Central bankers warn that any failure to scale back fiscal spending risks coming at the cost of yet higher interest rates — the price of continued fiscal expansion is paid through monetary policy. They also want elected officials to put in place policies that help deliver sustainable growth.

Agustin Carstens, the former governor of the Bank of Mexico who is now general manager of the BIS, states the conclusion: "A change in mindset needs to happen. Growth needs to depend less on fiscal and monetary policy, it should depend more on structural policies."



---


# The Debate Over Flexibility In Meeting Inflation Targets

Economists covering 16 of the world's most important central banks say policymakers will allow more time to bring inflation back to target if it means less damage to their economies, and a sizable minority in the Bloomberg special survey sees them going further still, accepting price pressures that are either slightly too strong or too weak — as long as expectations remain anchored. The warrant is credibility: so long as people believe prices will get back toward 2%, central bankers have some leeway in deciding how aggressive they need to be in pursuing that goal.

Bloomberg Economics chief economist Tom Orlik frames the timing condition on the wider debate: "A long period of galloping price gains, and fears that the last yards back to target could be most painful for workers, have reignited the debate about whether central banks should aim for a higher rate of inflation. That's a conversation worth having. But for monetary policymakers, the imperative of retaining credibility means the right time for it is after inflation is back at target, not before."

Flexibility may be needed in the other direction when the next big global slowdown comes. Europe's eight-year experiment with negative rates ended with mixed reviews in the summer of 2022 as to whether it was all worth it, and the Bank for International Settlements argues that there's room for greater tolerance for moderate shortfalls even if they're persistent, because "low-inflation regimes, in contrast to high-inflation ones, have self-stabilizing properties."



---


# The Post-Tightening Monetary Policy Autopsy Of 2023

After the most aggressive monetary-tightening campaign in four decades, academics and economic practitioners are running autopsies on what could have prevented the cost-of-living crisis and how to ensure the same mistakes won't be repeated. Markets have scrambled to price in high-for-longer interest rates, with a new war in the Middle East adding yet more risk to an already uncertain outlook confronting central bankers as they gather for their penultimate meetings of a tumultuous year.

The policy navel-gazing centers on three debates: how much flexibility central banks can allow in reaching their inflation targets, the effectiveness of asset purchases in the policy mix, and the merits of monetary and fiscal coordination. Bloomberg surveyed economists from around the world to gather views on those three debates. Their verdict: central banks won't break their economies in a rush to hit inflation targets, QE will be used more sparingly in the future, and fiscal policy risks countering the work of monetary authorities.



---


# Quantitative Tightening And The Balance Sheet Unwind

Policymakers have little experience in unwinding their balance sheets, where small mistakes can trigger big market turbulence — the Fed experienced some of that when it tried to shrink bond holdings between 2017 and 2019. More recent efforts to reduce portfolios have progressed rather smoothly, but partially for a reason that limits how much reassurance to take from it: central banks have amassed so much debt over the years that they're far away from any thresholds that would trigger a squeeze.

The framing of the tool raises a further question about its range. The fact that central banks are treating quantitative tightening as a technical adjustment rather than as part of their efforts to conquer inflation raises questions about the future use of a tool that's only trusted to work one way. The ECB faces an extra legal burden on bond holdings that comes with operating in a currency union of 20 countries: concerns around illegally financing governments and debt mutualization have already landed the central bank in court several times.



---


# The Case For Raising The Inflation Target

Olivier Blanchard, a former IMF chief economist, has long argued in favor of raising the inflation target, and former European Central Bank Vice President Vitor Constancio has also embraced the idea. The case comes with a strict precondition: it is a controversial view and only possible from a position of credibility, which means central banks would likely have to get inflation back to 2% first.

The supporting ground is that the environment itself has changed. Global trends suggest inflation will be stronger than in the past, with former Bank of England Governor Mark Carney among those saying rates won't return to pre-pandemic lows.

qid: Did the TechCrunch article about the class action antitrust suit filed against Google, published before December 15, 2023, fail to maintain the consistency in reporting Google's competitive practices after the report by The Age on October 22, 2023, claiming that Google manipulates Search to maximize ad revenue, and the subsequent report by TechCrunch on October 31, 2023, regarding Google's expenditure to become the default search engine?
context:
# Helena World Chronicle's Class Action Antitrust Suit Against Google

A class action lawsuit filed in the week of 15 December 2023 in the U.S. District Court in D.C. accuses Google and parent company Alphabet of anticompetitive behavior in violation of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act and others, on behalf of news publishers. The case was filed by Arkansas-based publisher Helena World Chronicle, which argues that Google "siphons off" news publishers' content, their readers and their ad revenue through anticompetitive means, and it specifically cites new AI technologies such as Google's Search Generative Experience (SGE) and the Bard AI chatbot as worsening the problem.

Helena World Chronicle owns and publishes two weekly newspapers in Arkansas. In the complaint it argues that Google is "starving the free press" by sharing publishers' content on Google, losing them "billions of dollars."

Beyond damages, the suit asks for an injunction that would require Google to obtain consent from publishers before using their website data to train its general artificial intelligence products, including Google's own and those of rivals. It also asks that publishers who opt out of SGE still be allowed to show up in Google search results, among other things.

The law firm handling the case is Hausfeld, whose announcement states that "the anticompetitive effects of Google's scheme cause profound harm to competition, to consumers, to labor, and to a democratic free press," and that "Plaintiff Helena World Chronicle, LLC invokes the Sherman Act and Clayton Act to seek class-wide monetary and injunctive relief to restore and ensure competition for digital news and reference publishing and set up guardrails to preserve a free marketplace of ideas in the new era of artificial intelligence."



---


# The U.S. Justice Department's Parallel Antitrust Suits Against Google

The Helena World Chronicle class action arrives alongside the filing of the U.S. Justice Department's lawsuit against Google for monopolizing digital ad technologies, and the complaint also references the Justice Department's 2020 civil antitrust suit over search and search advertising.

The two government cases concern different markets: search and search advertising in the 2020 suit are distinct from the digital ad technologies at issue in the more recent one.



---


# Google Paid $26.3 Billion In 2021 For Default Search Placement

Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to multiple browsers, phones and platforms — from companies including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla — to be everyone's default search engine. The figure was revealed by Google's search head Prabhakar Raghavan when he testified in court on October 28, according to The Verge.

About $18 billion of that total went directly to Apple, according to a New York Times report published earlier in October 2023, and Google has had its deal with Apple in place since 2003 — so the payment is the current year of a two-decade arrangement, not a one-off. Questioned on the amount of money Google spends to get first pick of search engines, Pichai said the decision was made with the consumer in mind: Google pays big bucks to be everywhere so that it can take in all the data and be the best search engine across different companies' devices, he said, according to The Verge.

The trial also produced evidence that Google understood the value of defaults very early on. U.S. Justice Department lawyer Meagan Bellshaw showed Pichai a 2007 email from a Google product strategy meeting containing data showing that when people changed their browser homepage to Google, they did 15% more Google searches, and that when they switched away, their Google searches dropped 27%. The email summarizing that meeting, sent to Pichai as well as other Google leaders, read: "Nitin argues that focusing on homepage market share is one of the most effective things we can do to make gains in search market share," according to The Verge.



---


# The Google Antitrust Case

The Google antitrust case is the U.S. government's trial over Google's dominance in the online search market, stemming from a 2020 antitrust claim, in which the government argues that Google uses its platforms and its deals with partners to block out competition in search or advertising and thereby to hinder competitors from accessing the data they would need to improve their products.

Its defining features are the conduct at issue and the defence offered against it. Google CEO Sundar Pichai testified Monday in the trial, defending Google's business tactics, including its deal with Apple and other partners to make Google the default search engine. Google's answer is that it is just doing business: everybody wants Google as the default engine because it is the best, and that, the company says, does not make its actions illegal.

The important boundary case is which Google antitrust matter this is. The 2020 search claim is separate from the one filed in January by the Department of Justice, along with eight states including New York, California and Colorado, which aims to "halt Google's anticompetitive scheme, unwind Google's monopolistic grip on the market and restore competition to digital advertising." The search case and the digital-advertising case are distinct proceedings and should not be conflated.

The trial is the venue in which the underlying numbers surface. Monday's hearing revealed plenty of juicy tidbits, including the $26.3 billion Google spent making itself the default search engine across platforms in 2021, and how Google tried to take it further and have Chrome preinstalled on iPhones.



---


# Wired's Retracted Claim That Google Manipulates Search Queries

In October 2023, Wired posted an opinion article by lawyer and privacy advocate Megan Gray alleging that Google had accidentally revealed during the trial that it manipulates people's search queries for maximum ad revenue — the example given being the replacement of a search for "children's clothing" with "NIKOLAI-brand kidswear" — and Wired subsequently removed the article for not meeting its standards.

Google rejected the claim in very strong terms, saying the piece was misleading and inaccurate and denying that it ever altered search terms. The Age drew a lesson from the episode's reach: the degree to which the article was shared on social media and boosted in write-ups at other outlets shows just how willing people are to accept foul play on Google's part, and a suspicion of privacy invasion and inappropriate data handling follows the company at all times. The article placed the episode in the wider context of the US case — which, having to prove Google somehow broke the law to achieve the status quo, could be an uphill battle for the government, but which offers everyone else a rare opportunity for insight into what the tech giant does with its enormous market share, and whether it is still focused on being the best or uses its ubiquity to squeeze users for money at the expense of product quality.



---


# The Claim That SGE And Bard Appropriate Publisher Content

The Helena World Chronicle lawsuit claims that Google's recent advances in AI-based search were implemented with "the goal of discouraging end-users from visiting the websites of Class members who are part of the digital news and publishing line of commerce." The grounds are that Google's AI products both retain users and consume publisher content without permission.

On the Search Generative Experience, the suit argues that SGE offers web searchers a way to seek information in a conversational mode but ultimately keeps users in Google's "walled garden" as it "plagiarizes" their content. The warrant that turns this into a harm publishers cannot escape is that publishers also cannot block SGE, because it uses the same web crawler as Google's general search service, GoogleBot — so opting out of the AI experience would mean opting out of search itself.

On Bard, the suit says Google's Bard AI was trained on a dataset that included "news, magazine and digital publications," citing both a 2023 report from the News Media Alliance and a Washington Post article about AI training data. The Post, which worked with researchers at the Allen Institute for AI, had found that News and Media sites were the third largest category of AI training data.

The case points to other concerns too, such as changing AdSense rates and evidence of improper spoliation of evidence on Google's part through its destruction of chat messages — an issue raised in the recent Epic Games lawsuit against Google over app store antitrust issues, which Epic won.



---


# US v. Google: Two Months Into The Search Antitrust Trial

As of TechCrunch's November 13, 2023 roundup, the Justice Department's landmark antitrust case against Google was nearly two months old, and the trial record was still producing fresh revelations. TechCrunch framed it as one of the biggest fights in tech antitrust since the U.S. took Microsoft to trial in the 1990s.

An earlier roundup had already surfaced that Google spent $26.3 billion in 2021 making itself the default search engine across platforms, and that Google tried to have Chrome preinstalled on iPhones. Over the couple of weeks preceding this roundup, more of Google's inner workings came to light, including some of the search engine's most lucrative search queries, the shape of the revenue-share agreements between Google and Android OEMs, and why Expedia has a bone to pick with Google.

context:
# Prosecution And Defense Arguments On Day Two Of The SBF Trial

On the second day of the trial of Sam Bankman-Fried and FTX, the prosecution argued that Bankman-Fried knowingly committed fraud, and it grounded that claim in motive: he did so, prosecutors said, to achieve great wealth, power and influence.

The defense countered with the opposite reading of the same conduct. Its claim was that the FTX founder acted in good faith, never meant to commit fraud or to steal, and basically got in over his head — an argument whose warrant is that inexperience and overreach, rather than intent, explain what happened. The two sides therefore contest intent rather than the underlying events, and the reporting on this exchange comes from Rebecca and Jacquelyn in TechCrunch's Week in Review of October 7, 2023, covering day two of the trial only.



---


# The SBF Trial Proceedings

Sam Bankman-Fried is in court for alleged fraud and money laundering while leading crypto exchange FTX and sister company Alameda. TechCrunch's 2023-10-02 preview placed the case in the Manhattan Federal Court, describing the disgraced cryptocurrency entrepreneur as accused of orchestrating "one of the biggest financial frauds in American history": the multibillion-dollar collapse of FTX, the crypto exchange he founded and led. SBF, as he is known, has pleaded not guilty to some seven charges of fraud and conspiracy.

The trial kicked off with jury selection October 3. By TechCrunch's 2023-10-06 update the case was entering its next chapter, with proceedings resuming Thursday: as confirmed during a teleconference Wednesday, SBF would be taking the stand along with a handful of other witnesses, as the onus shifted toward the defense after the prosecution brought its case to its conclusion.

Access to the proceedings is limited: no devices are allowed, so reports are being physically put together within the courtroom, or sent to overflow rooms. The jury's composition ranges from a train conductor to a retired investment banker who attended Stanford University, and TechCrunch pointed readers to a special joint episode of its Equity and Chain Reaction podcasts for a better sense of the vibe between the jurors and the rest of the court.

A second account of the same events was arriving in parallel: "Going Infinite," a book by Michael Lewis chronicling the rise and fall of SBF, was set to debut on the first day of the trial.



---


# Sam Bankman-Fried's Federal Fraud Trial

Sam Bankman-Fried, the founder of bankrupt cryptocurrency exchange FTX, is charged with seven counts of fraud and money laundering following the collapse of his cryptocurrency empire the previous year, and was on trial in New York in October 2023.

Two fixed points anchor the proceeding as CNBC described it on 2023-10-06. A U.S. judge revoked Bankman-Fried's bail at a hearing in a New York courthouse on August 11, 2023. And on Thursday, Oct. 5, 2023, Matt Huang, co-founder of Paradigm Operations LP, arrived at the New York court to appear in the case.



---


# Day Two Of The Bankman-Fried Trial: Jury Selection And The Courtroom Audience

On the second day of Sam Bankman-Fried's fraud trial, the jury was selected on Wednesday morning, after which lawyers for the government and then for Bankman-Fried delivered opening statements that told two very different stories of the former FTX CEO's sudden rise and almost instantaneous fall. The central question framed by the proceedings was who Bankman-Fried, the former CEO of crypto exchange FTX, really is: a liar and a fraud, or someone who acted in good faith and, like many a startup founder, flew too close to the sun. That answer, the account notes, ultimately lies with the jury.

The day featured pointed allegations, a friend from MIT, and an audience replete with big names, including Bankman-Fried's professorial parents and Damian Williams, the U.S. attorney for the Southern District of New York. Bankman-Fried himself spent most of the day in court staring into a laptop while seated between his two attorneys. The prosecution's account of his alleged crimes was described as featuring a study in contrasts.



---


# Caroline Ellison's Guilty Plea And First Day Of Testimony

Caroline Ellison, head of the hedge fund Alameda Research during its implosion along with FTX, took the stand on October 10th, 2023 having already pleaded guilty to criminal charges — fraud, conspiracy to commit fraud, and money laundering — and told the jury that Bankman-Fried "directed me to commit these crimes." She quantified the taking: "We ultimately took about $14 billion, some of which we were not able to pay back."

Her long-anticipated first day took the form of walking through a damning spreadsheet she had prepared for her ex and boss, now the defendant in a criminal fraud trial. She entered hunched in on herself, wearing a dusty rose dress with a gray blazer over it, looking less like an executive than like a girl who had borrowed her boyfriend's coat because she was cold. Asked by the prosecution to identify Bankman-Fried, she had trouble finding him and gazed around the courtroom for more than 20 seconds — apparently he was incognito with his new haircut — and when she did spot him she identified him as the one wearing a suit, which got chuckles from the rest of the defense table, also all in suits. She tilted her head down to answer questions and lifted it when she had finished each answer.

The defendant's own reaction registered the shift: Bankman-Fried had been vibrating slightly during Wang's testimony, and during Ellison's his bouncing became more noticeable. By the end of the day, The Verge's reporter wrote, the spreadsheet seemed like a sideshow.



---


# FTX Fraud Charges And The SEC's Allegation

Sam Bankman-Fried, the founder of the failed cryptocurrency exchange FTX, faced seven counts of wire fraud and conspiracy — specifically, two counts of wire fraud and five conspiracy charges — and the Securities and Exchange Commission alleged that FTX was a fraud "from the start," with a "multi-billion-dollar deficiency caused by his own misappropriation of customer funds." The Verge repeated this framing at the head of each of its trial dispatches through October 2023, and in its October 28th, 2023 write-up reported that Bankman-Fried had been found guilty on seven counts including charges of wire fraud.

The boundary of the concept is the mix of charge types: the indictment paired substantive wire fraud counts with conspiracy counts rather than resting on a single offence, and the SEC's civil allegation about the exchange's origins ran alongside the criminal case rather than being part of it. The Verge's reporter, writing as the prosecution's case neared its end on October 26th, 2023, added an impression of the people the charges swept in: all the co-conspirators seemed oddly younger than their years, as though they had got stuck in the "math camp forever" environment Bankman-Fried created for them and simply failed to grow up.

# The Prosecution's Opening Statement Against Bankman-Fried

# Plea Agreement

## Definition

In the corpus, a plea agreement is the deal by which a criminal defendant (or, in Binance's case, a company) pleads guilty to specified charges in exchange for concessions, rather than going to trial.
It takes effect only once a judge accepts it, and it can bind the party to concrete obligations — cooperating with prosecutors, accepting a recommended fine, stepping back from a role, or admitting specific facts — beyond the bare admission of guilt.

## Context

The corpus shows plea agreements as the mechanism by which several defendants in overlapping 2023 white-collar and criminal cases resolved their charges outside of a trial.
FTX co-founder Gary Wang and Alameda Research CEO Caroline Ellison both pleaded guilty in December 2022 and agreed to cooperate with prosecutors, becoming key witnesses against Sam Bankman-Fried at his fraud trial (doc_0010, doc_0086).
FTX engineering head Nishad Singh similarly pleaded guilty to six charges (doc_0121).
Binance CEO Changpeng "CZ" Zhao and Binance itself each entered separate plea agreements with the U.S. Department of Justice, resolving anti-money-laundering and sanctions violations as part of a $4.3 billion settlement (doc_0374, doc_0375).
YouTube parenting influencer Ruby Franke's plea agreement, accepted by a judge, both formalized her guilty plea to child-abuse charges and documented detailed admissions about the abuse itself (doc_0269).
The corpus also shows a distinct but related instrument — the cooperation agreement Gary Wang signed, which specifically obligated him to meet with prosecutors and answer truthfully (doc_0226) — and notes that a witness's incentive to plead guilty and cooperate (the hope of sentencing leniency) is something a defense team can attack on cross-examination (doc_0293).

- **Court acceptance is required** — a judge must accept the plea agreement before it takes effect; Ruby Franke's sentencing was scheduled only after Judge John J. Walton accepted her plea agreement (doc_0269).
- **Negotiated concessions, not just an admission** — the document can specify what each side gives up: Zhao agreed to a recommended $150 million CFTC fine and to not contradict his acceptance of responsibility, while Binance's agreement barred Zhao from any future role at the company for three years and required it to maintain an independent compliance monitor (doc_0374).
- **Can include cooperation with prosecutors** — Wang and Ellison's guilty pleas were paired with plans to cooperate with, and testify for, the prosecution (doc_0010); Wang's cooperation obligations were spelled out in a separate signed agreement (doc_0226).
- **Distinct from pleading not guilty** — a defendant who instead maintains innocence, as Bankman-Fried did, pleads not guilty and proceeds to trial rather than entering a plea agreement (doc_0010).
- **Can contain substantive factual admissions** — Franke's plea agreement recorded specific admitted details of the abuse itself, beyond the bare fact of guilt (doc_0269).
- **Creates a cross-examination target** — because cooperating witnesses who pleaded guilty may hope for sentencing leniency, defense counsel can (and, per the corpus, did) argue this gives them an incentive to shape testimony favorably to the prosecution (doc_0293).

The prosecution's first witness at Sam Bankman-Fried's trial was not a blockbuster name or a former lieutenant-turned-cooperator like Caroline Ellison but a victim: Marc-Antoine Julliard, a Paris-born cocoa trader who lives in London and whose money got stuck on FTX. Julliard testified that on Nov. 8, 2022, in the crypto exchange's final few days, he tried to pull out almost $100,000 in cash and crypto, and that he was never able to. The withdrawal screenshots shown in court were of attempts to move $20,000 USD and about 4 Bitcoin, worth about $20,000 at the time — roughly $100,000 in total, inaccessible.

Julliard explained why he had chosen FTX in 2021 when he decided to invest in crypto, trading currencies like Bitcoin and Dogecoin there. He trusted FTX because Bankman-Fried came across as a leading figure of the industry; because the sheer volume of users mattered to him, and FTX was at the time among the top three biggest exchanges; and because major VC firms had invested. "They don't commit hundreds of millions without doing due diligence, checking the books, the accountancy of the firm, going through several compliance process[es], so that was a vote of confidence for me," he said. He also noted FTX's glossy ads — featuring Gisele Bündchen, for instance — which suggested a very high budget, and reasoned that it wouldn't make sense to spend that much money unless FTX had very strong financials. He opened an account, transferred in both regular money and cryptocurrency, and used the exchange to execute his plan of buying Bitcoin to sell back in five to ten years at higher prices.

In November 2022 things went bad. Julliard followed Bankman-Fried on Twitter and read aloud in court the "FTX is fine. Assets are fine" tweets, along with "FTX has enough to cover all client holdings. We don't invest client assets" and a few others, which gave him the impression that his money was there and that any problem might be technical — anti-spam measures — or regulatory. By the time he tried to get his money out on November 8th, it was too late. Cross-examining a customer whose money is gone is described as a thankless task, but Mark Cohen tried anyway, noting that Julliard was a licensed commodities broker who was trading in crypto because he didn't have to disclose it, that he knew crypto was new and risky, and that he didn't review the terms of service agreement he had assented to when making his FTX account. The next witness called was Bankman-Fried's former college and FTX roommate, Adam Yedidia.



---


# Day Two Of The Bankman-Fried Trial: Jury Selection And The Courtroom Audience

On the second day of Sam Bankman-Fried's fraud trial, the jury was selected on Wednesday morning, after which lawyers for the government and then for Bankman-Fried delivered opening statements that told two very different stories of the former FTX CEO's sudden rise and almost instantaneous fall. The central question framed by the proceedings was who Bankman-Fried, the former CEO of crypto exchange FTX, really is: a liar and a fraud, or someone who acted in good faith and, like many a startup founder, flew too close to the sun. That answer, the account notes, ultimately lies with the jury.

The day featured pointed allegations, a friend from MIT, and an audience replete with big names, including Bankman-Fried's professorial parents and Damian Williams, the U.S. attorney for the Southern District of New York. Bankman-Fried himself spent most of the day in court staring into a laptop while seated between his two attorneys. The prosecution's account of his alleged crimes was described as featuring a study in contrasts.



---


# The FTX Trial's Stakes For The Wider Crypto Industry

The Verge argued that the trial of Sam Bankman-Fried is likely to be more consequential than just whether the man himself is found guilty: depending on what evidence is introduced, it could be rough for the entire crypto industry.

The grounds are the unpredictability of what a trial surfaces, voiced by Yesha Yadav, a law professor at Vanderbilt University: "How much damage can this trial do to the already beaten-down reputation of the industry at this point? This trial is going to be an excruciating moment for the industry because no one knows what kind of evidence might come out." The warrant joining that uncertainty to industry-wide stakes is that the industry's reputation is already beaten down, so evidence introduced against one exchange's founder lands on the whole sector rather than on him alone.

context:
# BG3 Ranger: The Beginner Ranged Class

Polygon names Ranger the best ranged class for beginners in Baldur's Gate 3. Rangers are agile hunters who focus on Dexterity as their primary Ability and combine melee, stealth, skills, and magic — a mix that also makes the class harder to get the most out of.

Rangers get Light and Medium Armors and some of the more basic weapons. They also make a lot of choices during character creation and levelling that determine how they play: at level 1 you choose a Favored Enemy — a preferred quarry — and a preferred environment that grants some magical spells. At level 3 you choose a Ranger subclass from Beast Master, Gloom Stalker, or Hunter. Beast Masters get a Companion animal that fights alongside you, Gloom Stalkers focus on stealth, and Hunters get to specialize their melee abilities. Hunter is the best subclass for a Ranger, with the supporting reasoning and the skill and feat picks left to Polygon's separate Ranger build guide.



---


# There Is No Single Best Class In Baldur's Gate 3

Polygon argues that there is no single best class in Baldur's Gate 3 — "barrelmancer aside" — so the choice should be settled by how you want to play rather than by any ranking of raw power.

The grounds are twofold. First, the classes in Baldur's Gate 3, and in pen-and-paper D&D for that matter, are all fairly well-balanced. Second, the game gives you as many opportunities for creative problem solving as it does for punching, so a class that looks weak in a straight fight still has routes to succeed. The warrant joining grounds to claim is that when options are balanced and the game rewards more than one kind of solution, "best" collapses into "best for your intended playstyle." A further supporting point removes the risk of a bad commitment: even when playing solo you still manage the rest of your party, so you get to experiment with multiple classes at once rather than being locked into one. Polygon repeats the same argument verbatim in its Warlock build guide of 2023-12-01, so the position is stated across both articles.



---


# Choosing A Class And Subclass In Baldur's Gate 3

Class selection in Baldur's Gate 3 is one of the most consequential decisions a player makes, and the game forces it at the very start with minimal context to work from. A character's class mostly determines how that character will fight, but with 12 classes and 46 subclasses spread across them, the choice is not straightforward.

Familiar shorthand distinctions — caster versus puncher, melee versus ranged — do not map cleanly onto Baldur's Gate 3 or onto D&D more generally, because the classes overlap heavily, especially as characters level up. That overlap is why no class can simply be declared best or even better than another. The workable selection rule is to focus on what you want to do, or how you want to do it, and choose from there. Polygon's own ranking of the classes orders them subjectively by difficulty to play, placing caster classes toward the harder end on the grounds that spells and spell slots are more to manage than punching things.



---


# Ability Scores Link BG3 Classes To Out-Of-Combat Skills

In Baldur's Gate 3, class determines combat behaviour, but the Ability Score the class relies on determines the out-of-combat skills a character is good at — so choosing a class also chooses a social and exploratory profile.

The mechanism runs in a chain: Baldur's Gate 3 assigns Ability Scores automatically at creation (though they can be tweaked in the character creator), so each class's primary ability ends up as that character's highest score, and the highest score in turn drives the skills tied to it. Two worked cases show the range over which the relation holds. Bards and Sorcerers are both Charisma-based, so their high Charisma also makes them good at Persuasion, Deception, and Intimidation; out of combat those classes are better at talking their way out of — and into — trouble, and at lying. Wisdom-based classes such as Clerics and Druids come out more insightful and more perceptive of their surroundings instead.



---


# Astarion, Baldur's Gate 3 Vampire Companion

Astarion is a haughty elf in Baldur's Gate 3 whom you can either play as or recruit to your party very early on — and he is a vampire, with dealing with his vampirism forming a huge part of the game, should that be something you want to do.

Polygon's framing is that if Baldur's Gate 3 was your introduction to the Forgotten Realms of Dungeons & Dragons, you might be shocked to find out about a lot of stuff tucked away in the world's most famous tabletop role-playing game — and the great thing about Baldur's Gate 3 is how it centers all that weird stuff.



---


# Custom Character Versus Origin Character In Baldur's Gate 3

An Origin character in Baldur's Gate 3 is one of the NPCs from your party that you can simply choose and play as right from the start, whereas a custom character is one you build yourself by picking a race and background.

The discriminating feature is the trade between setup effort and narrative freedom. Playing an Origin character is a perfectly fine way to play if you would rather not go through the process of picking a race and background, but you are then limited to that character's predetermined story. A custom character is a bit more work at the beginning, yet gives you far more freedom to experience the entire story of Baldur's Gate 3. Polygon presents this as the decision to settle before moving on to the class rankings themselves.



---


# Baldur's Gate 3

Baldur's Gate 3, developed by Larian Studios for PlayStation 5 and Windows PC, is ranked 2 on Polygon's best video games of 2023 list of 2023-10-31, and Polygon says it hit at the perfect moment.

The timing argument has two parts. Despite the handful of truly great computer role-playing games released since the early 2000s — Larian itself made waves with its Divinity: Original Sin series in 2014 and 2017 — the genre had largely remained a modern niche; but Dungeons & Dragons has undergone something of a renaissance thanks to actual-play series like Critical Role and Dimension 20, and Larian had two years of player feedback with which to build its new masterpiece. That masterpiece launched in August and garnered the kind of attention that catapults a game from niche interests to widespread acclaim: old CRPG fans finally came home, the Mass Effect generation discovered a new kind of RPG, and D&D fans found an exceptional digital version of their beloved tabletop game to play alone or with their party in co-op.

Critic RG writes that like a good DM, the game teases out story beats that feel personal to you, cleverly luring you into experiences that seem like they would not make sense in anyone else's campaign; every act delivers quiet, memorable character moments and anxiety-inducing battles, all feeling organic, letting the game replicate as closely as a video game can D&D's best feature — the intoxicating sense that anything could happen at any moment. The best games that year told their stories in interesting ways, but Baldur's Gate 3 takes experimental storytelling to another level, with every choice and every new direction a simple success, fail, or crit away; one roll of the dice after another can take you all the way from a crashed Nautiloid to the city of Baldur's Gate itself, and it is the spinning whir of its d20 that defined video game storytelling in 2023.



---


# BG3 Warlock: Pact Casting For Beginners

The Warlock is one of the twelve classes in Baldur's Gate 3, and Polygon names it the best magic class for beginners. Warlocks are casters who made a deal with a higher power for their magic — extreme knowledge-seekers willing to form a pact with otherworldly beings to gain ancient secrets that bolster their magical arsenal.

Because dealing with such powerful creatures demands strong mental power — you have to make a deal with the devil and survive — the Warlock's primary ability score is Charisma. They play a lot like Sorcerers but with a slight emphasis on more academic Skills and fewer spells, and they get Light Armor, so they are a little less squishy than Sorcerers. The defining trade is that Warlocks sacrifice the number of spells they know for sheer power: every Warlock spell slot is the same — the highest level available — and slots recharge on a short rest instead of a long rest. They are not as versatile as other caster classes, but what they do, they do well. Polygon's recommendation is that Warlock suits you if you want a dedicated caster without the prep work a class like Wizard requires: you still use a lot of magic, but you do not have to manage a binder full of spells every morning.

# Gary Wang's Testimony At The FTX Fraud Trial

Gary Wang, the lesser-known co-founder of FTX, told a Manhattan courtroom on Thursday that he had committed financial crimes while working at FTX — including wire and commodities fraud — carried out with the help of Sam Bankman-Fried, FTX ex-engineering head Nishad Singh, and Caroline Ellison, who ran sister hedge fund Alameda Research and had been Bankman-Fried's girlfriend.

Asked by Assistant U.S. Attorney Nicolas Roos, "Did you commit financial crimes while working at FTX?" Wang responded, "Yes." Asked whether he saw any of the people he committed those crimes with in the courtroom, Wang — dressed in an oversized and wrinkled suit with a red tie and glasses — awkwardly stood up, looked around, and answered, "Yes"; asked who, he said, "Sam Bankman-Fried." He was one of two former friends of Bankman-Fried's from MIT who also worked at FTX while living with the founder in the Bahamas and who took the stand that week to testify against their former classmate, confidant and boss, a man who allegedly ran a crypto empire that defrauded thousands of customers out of billions of dollars. The trial, set to last six weeks, was to resume on Tuesday with key testimony expected from Ellison, considered the prosecution's star witness, who had already pleaded guilty to multiple charges. Bankman-Fried faces seven federal charges, including wire fraud, securities fraud and money laundering, that could put him in prison for the rest of his life. Thus far Bankman-Fried, 31, has remained mostly quiet in court, intently listening to witnesses and at times writing notes to his attorneys — but as Wang testified against him, he looked visibly upset, shifting his gaze from his former friend to the ground and at one point putting his head in his hands.



---


# Matt Huang And Paradigm's FTX Investment

Matt Huang, co-founder and managing partner of Paradigm, a crypto venture capital firm that invested over $275 million in FTX — a stake that was wiped out — was the third witness to take the stand, and testified about his firm's due diligence.

Huang told the court that Bankman-Fried assured him funds would be used for FTX and not Alameda, and that he was promised Alameda had no preferential treatment on the FTX platform, even though the hedge fund was one of its top traders. Huang said he was concerned about FTX's lack of a board of directors but eventually invested anyway. During cross-examination he said Paradigm pressed Bankman-Fried on the board issue and was told he did not want investors as directors but did plan on having a board with experts.



---


# Sam Bankman-Fried

Sam Bankman-Fried is the former CEO of the bankrupt crypto exchange FTX, whose highly anticipated criminal trial started on the Tuesday before TechCrunch's 2023-10-01 report, to determine whether he is guilty of seven counts of fraud and conspiracy. As one former federal prosecutor put it: "The odds seem to be stacked against him at this point."

He was 31 years old and co-founded FTX in 2019; within a few years the once third-largest crypto exchange's valuation hit $32 billion at its peak, and the company is now trying to claw back any funds to distribute to creditors. Before the fall he was even compared to Warren Buffet, and many called him the white horse of crypto — a description TechCrunch notes it never applied to him.

Bankman-Fried, however, maintained his innocence. At The New York Times' DealBook Summit he appeared virtually from the Bahamas and said, "I didn't ever try to commit fraud on anyone; I was shocked by what happened this month"; in a published DM exchange with a Vox reporter he said he regretted filing for bankruptcy and thought that "regulators make everything worse." In January he pleaded not guilty to all counts, which include wire fraud, conspiracy to commit money laundering and conspiracy to misuse customer funds. He could face up to 115 years in jail if convicted on all charges.

TechCrunch's 2023-10-02 summary of his standing on the eve of trial: SBF has been denied bail; his name is mud (or much worse) among those who have lost money in Alameda or FTX; and those who might not have had positions in these still blame him for other crypto woes, because he set off a ripple effect.



---


# Bankman-Fried's Pre-Collapse Public Image Strategy

Before his fall, Bankman-Fried made himself out to be the Good Boy of crypto — the trustworthy face of a sometimes-shady industry — and he was very interested in publicity, sitting for many interviews both before and after the collapse of FTX.

The Verge attributes FTX's quick rise as an industry force at least in part to that appetite for attention: Bankman-Fried gave interviews freely and quickly rose to public prominence, positioning himself as an important, boyish face for crypto even though FTX hadn't been in the business as long as competing exchanges such as Coinbase, Kraken, or Gemini. At one point he told a colleague at FTX that "I honestly think it's negative EV" — possibly "expected value," as in poker — "for me to cut my hair. I think it's important for people to think I look crazy." Because he was so successful at this kind of public relations, his fall from grace became another mark against an industry already roiled by bankruptcies and scandals; The Verge adds that more trouble for the industry is likely to come from one crucial element of the fraud trial, the part where the government must prove intent.



---


# FTX's Final Days And The Alameda Shortfall, As Wang Described Them

Much of Gary Wang's Friday testimony focused on the final days at FTX before the operation imploded: after media reports detailing Alameda's business practices and its troubling ties to FTX, an emergency meeting was called between Bankman-Fried, Wang and Singh to discuss shutting down Alameda, and they decided against it because he and Bankman-Fried knew Alameda had no way to repay the roughly $14 billion hole in its books.

Wang, 30, was technology chief for FTX, which spiralled into bankruptcy in November; he spoke so fast that U.S. District Judge Lewis Kaplan and the prosecutor both stopped him at points to ask that he slow his pace. Prosecutors took the jury through a series of tweets beginning on Nov. 7 — posts from the company blaming bank hours for slow withdrawals, while Bankman-Fried tweeted from his personal account assuring customers that all was fine. "FTX was not fine and assets were not fine," Wang testified. On Nov. 12, after FTX declared bankruptcy, Bankman-Fried asked Wang to drive with him to the Bahamas Securities Commission for a meeting; on the drive, Bankman-Fried told Wang to transfer assets to Bahamian liquidators because he believed they would allow him to maintain control of the company. Wang said he was not in the meeting with the securities authority, though Bankman-Fried's dad was present.



---


# Alameda Research As The Alleged Conduit For FTX Customer Funds

In the prosecution's account offered by Thane Rehn, the key to Sam Bankman-Fried's alleged scheme was Alameda Research, a crypto hedge fund that Bankman-Fried also owned. The structure the government described works as follows: Caroline Ellison — Bankman-Fried's on-again off-again girlfriend and the CEO of Alameda — served as a front for the fund, and through that arrangement Bankman-Fried had "secret access" to customer money, both cash and crypto.

Two further relations complete the alleged mechanism. Bankman-Fried is said to have directed employees to conceal the flow of money into FTX's coffers, and to have forged financial documents distributed to lenders and investors. "The defendant lied to the world," Rehn alleged. These are the government's allegations as presented in its opening statement, not established findings.



---


# FTX's Bankruptcy And Leadership

The man who represented FTX before Congress after its failure told lawmakers the exchange had effectively no internal governance at all, and the prosecutor bringing the case called Bankman-Fried's alleged crimes one of the biggest financial frauds in American history. TechCrunch reported both on 2023-10-01.

Ray represented the company during a House Financial Services Committee hearing regarding FTX. Asked whether the firm had significant risk management systems, Ray said at the time that "there were virtually no internal controls and no separateness whatsoever," and added that he did not "trust a single piece of paper" in the exchange's organization. Separately, in a press conference, U.S. Attorney Damian Williams called Bankman-Fried's alleged crimes "one of the biggest financial frauds in American history."



---


# Bankman-Fried's Post-Bankruptcy Media Tour

After FTX declared bankruptcy, Bankman-Fried went on an extensive media tour, doing interviews with The New York Times' Andrew Ross Sorkin and Good Morning America — and he kept giving interviews even under house arrest, including with The New Yorker.

The Verge's reading of his motive: Bankman-Fried seemed to think that if he just explained things, everyone would understand that what he did was a mistake, not a crime.

Alongside its product releases, OpenAI made a series of corporate moves in 2023: a news-content partnership with Axel Springer, an indemnity promise to business customers over copyright claims, its first acquisition, a $300 million share sale, and a stalled attempt to trademark "GPT."

The entire team has joined OpenAI to work on our core products including ChatGPT."

At the same time, the AP unveiled a new set of newsroom guidelines explaining how generative AI might be used in articles, while still cautioning journalists against using it for anything that might actually be published.
