# Large Language Model (LLM)

## Definition

A large language model (LLM) is a neural network trained to learn from enormous amounts of digital text — Wikipedia articles, digital books, message boards — so that it can generate text on its own.

## Context

The corpus traces the term to OpenAI's GPT-3, described as the neural network Dario Amodei's team built by analysing "countless Wikipedia articles, digital books and message boards" so it "could generate text on its own," released in the summer of 2020; it also "had the unfortunate habit of making things up." ChatGPT itself runs on GPT, the LLM lineage OpenAI had developed since 2016, iterating from GPT-1 (2018) to GPT-3 (June 2020) before GPT-3.5 powered ChatGPT's November 2022 launch. In the venture-capital view of the AI market, LLMs sit at the base "foundation model" layer of a broader stack — models, pre-training solutions, fine-tuning tools, middle-layer tooling, and end-market applications — with providers such as OpenAI's GPT-4, Google's Bard, and Anthropic's Claude expected to consolidate into an oligopolistic structure resembling the cloud-provider market. OpenAI's GPT-X models are repeatedly described as proprietary LLMs that other companies build businesses on top of, a dependency that became visible when the November 2023 OpenAI board upheaval led customers to contact rival LLM providers (Anthropic, Google, Cohere) out of concern for continuity.

## Key Characteristics

- **Trained on enormous text corpora** — LLMs learn by analysing vast amounts of digital text (Wikipedia, books, message boards) rather than following hand-written rules.
- **Generative** — once trained, an LLM can generate text on its own in response to a prompt.
- **Prone to fabrication and privacy leakage** — GPT-3 had "the unfortunate habit of making things up," and a Google DeepMind-led test found that prompting ChatGPT to repeat a word endlessly caused OpenAI's LLM to surface private, identifiable information (email addresses and similar) from its training data; a separate Microsoft-affiliated study found GPT-4 more easily "jailbroken" into unsafe outputs than other LLMs.
- **Costly to run and usage-priced** — LLM economics are dominated by compute cost (OpenAI was reported to spend roughly $700,000/day on compute), which is why LLM providers commonly bill by token/usage rather than flat SaaS pricing.
- **Anchors a layered AI stack** — LLMs form the "foundation model" layer beneath middle-layer tooling (fine-tuning, prompt engineering, model orchestration, observability) and top-layer applications that startups build against.
- **Split between proprietary and open approaches** — OpenAI's GPT-X models are proprietary LLMs, contrasted in the corpus with Meta's Llama family and other efforts pushing more "open" LLM development, a split that intensified after a leaked internal Google memo argued neither OpenAI nor Google had a durable "moat" against open-source LLMs.

ChatGPT first launched to the public as OpenAI quietly released GPT-3.5: the model broke cover with ChatGPT, a fine-tuned version of GPT-3.5 that is essentially a general-purpose chatbot able to engage with a range of topics including programming, TV scripts and scientific concepts.

# Alameda Research As The Alleged Conduit For FTX Customer Funds

In the prosecution's account offered by Thane Rehn, the key to Sam Bankman-Fried's alleged scheme was Alameda Research, a crypto hedge fund that Bankman-Fried also owned. The structure the government described works as follows: Caroline Ellison — Bankman-Fried's on-again off-again girlfriend and the CEO of Alameda — served as a front for the fund, and through that arrangement Bankman-Fried had "secret access" to customer money, both cash and crypto.

Two further relations complete the alleged mechanism. Bankman-Fried is said to have directed employees to conceal the flow of money into FTX's coffers, and to have forged financial documents distributed to lenders and investors. "The defendant lied to the world," Rehn alleged. These are the government's allegations as presented in its opening statement, not established findings.



---


# Ellison's Risk Spreadsheet For Venture Investments

Caroline Ellison testified that she prepared a spreadsheet at Bankman-Fried's request in the fall of 2021 and shared it with him, analysing the risk to Alameda of repaying its loans if they were abruptly recalled by its lender Genesis. Bankman-Fried wanted to use $3 billion for venture investments, so Ellison ballparked what that would do to Alameda's risk: in the as-is scenario she put the chance they would not be able to meet the loan recalls at 30 percent, and if Bankman-Fried spent $3 billion on investments, the chance rose to 100 percent — even with FTX customer funds.

What made this the worst of her testimony, in The Verge's account of the October 10th, 2023 proceedings, was not the math, which seemed pretty arbitrary, but the assumption underneath it: Ellison's calculations assumed Alameda could borrow $1.8 billion in normal dollars and $1.5 billion in crypto from FTX, and the spreadsheet made this explicit with a row labeled "FTX borrows," which Ellison said were customer funds. The background condition was that Alameda was also getting loans from outside lenders such as Genesis, because when FTX started there were not a lot of customer funds to borrow.

The day ended with a document shared between Ellison and Bankman-Fried, his comments appearing in bubbles along the main text. Ellison had written that she was worried about "both actual leverage and presenting on our balance sheet." Bankman-Fried responded with a note: "Yup, and could also get worse."



---


# Bankman-Fried And Ellison: Relationship And Alameda Leadership

Caroline Ellison testified that she and Bankman-Fried started sleeping together in the fall of 2018, on and off, when she was a trader and he was CEO, and that they later dated twice — first from the summer of 2020 through the summer of 2021, a relationship they agreed to keep secret though some people found out, and again from the fall of 2021 until the spring of 2022, when they lived together. She was named co-CEO of Alameda with Sam Trabucco in 2021 while she and Bankman-Fried were broken up, and CEO in 2022; the goal, Bankman-Fried told her, was to "optically" separate Alameda Research and FTX. "The whole time we were dating, he was my boss at work," she said. They broke up because she wanted more from the relationship and he was distant and not paying enough attention to her. He did not grant her equity even though she asked, telling her it would be too complicated; instead she got a $200,000 salary, even as CEO, and bonuses twice a year ranging from $100,000 to $20 million.

Bankman-Fried gave a different rationale for the handover. In 2021, he testified, FTX was growing to millions of users with $1 billion of revenue, he was working 12 to 22 hours a day and taking one day off every couple of months, and because FTX had grown so much he could no longer run both companies — so he handed Alameda off to Ellison and Trabucco, who immediately after being named co-CEO promptly drifted away to early retirement. Bankman-Fried did remain involved in hedging and risk at Alameda.

Ellison's proximity also gave her an unusual view of his character. She said Alameda was troubled from her earliest time there in 2018: "Shortly after I started, I learned the company was in worse shape than I realized." Alameda had initially been funded with loans "from acquaintances," and those loans were recalled a few weeks after she arrived; when she asked Bankman-Fried why he had not shared the company's shaky circumstances in the job offer, "He hadn't known how to tell me," she said. She described him as "very ambitious," said he told her there was a 5 percent chance he would become president of the United States, and said he told her that if there were a coin flip where tails destroyed the world and heads made the world twice as good, he would flip the coin — which he called being "risk-neutral," and which The Verge's reporter called a fancy way of saying he was a gambling addict. He made her CEO of his sin-eater hedge fund while refusing to give her equity.



---


# Day Two Of The Bankman-Fried Trial: Jury Selection And The Courtroom Audience

On the second day of Sam Bankman-Fried's fraud trial, the jury was selected on Wednesday morning, after which lawyers for the government and then for Bankman-Fried delivered opening statements that told two very different stories of the former FTX CEO's sudden rise and almost instantaneous fall. The central question framed by the proceedings was who Bankman-Fried, the former CEO of crypto exchange FTX, really is: a liar and a fraud, or someone who acted in good faith and, like many a startup founder, flew too close to the sun. That answer, the account notes, ultimately lies with the jury.

The day featured pointed allegations, a friend from MIT, and an audience replete with big names, including Bankman-Fried's professorial parents and Damian Williams, the U.S. attorney for the Southern District of New York. Bankman-Fried himself spent most of the day in court staring into a laptop while seated between his two attorneys. The prosecution's account of his alleged crimes was described as featuring a study in contrasts.



---


# FTX Ventures Was Funded By Alameda

Caroline Ellison testified that the money behind FTX Ventures came from Alameda Research, even though Bankman-Fried announced the fund publicly without naming its source: on January 14th, 2022 he tweeted, "We're launching a $2b venture fund: FTX Ventures!" She said he did not want to go public with where the funds came from, telling her he thought Alameda's brand was less good and that he did not want his name associated with it.

The Verge reported the episode on October 10th, 2023 as part of Ellison's testimony, framing it as FTX keeping cozy private ties with Alameda while publicly holding it at arm's length — an echo, the reporter wrote, of Bankman-Fried and Ellison's romantic relationship. The same distancing appears in another transaction: Alameda bought Robinhood shares for Bankman-Fried, who moved them to a vehicle called "Emergent Fidelity Technologies" to avoid association with Alameda.



---


# Caroline Ellison's Guilty Plea And First Day Of Testimony

Caroline Ellison, head of the hedge fund Alameda Research during its implosion along with FTX, took the stand on October 10th, 2023 having already pleaded guilty to criminal charges — fraud, conspiracy to commit fraud, and money laundering — and told the jury that Bankman-Fried "directed me to commit these crimes." She quantified the taking: "We ultimately took about $14 billion, some of which we were not able to pay back."

Her long-anticipated first day took the form of walking through a damning spreadsheet she had prepared for her ex and boss, now the defendant in a criminal fraud trial. She entered hunched in on herself, wearing a dusty rose dress with a gray blazer over it, looking less like an executive than like a girl who had borrowed her boyfriend's coat because she was cold. Asked by the prosecution to identify Bankman-Fried, she had trouble finding him and gazed around the courtroom for more than 20 seconds — apparently he was incognito with his new haircut — and when she did spot him she identified him as the one wearing a suit, which got chuckles from the rest of the defense table, also all in suits. She tilted her head down to answer questions and lifted it when she had finished each answer.

The defendant's own reaction registered the shift: Bankman-Fried had been vibrating slightly during Wang's testimony, and during Ellison's his bouncing became more noticeable. By the end of the day, The Verge's reporter wrote, the spreadsheet seemed like a sideshow.

qid: Does 'The Verge' article suggest that Alameda Research had special financial privileges at FTX that other accounts did not, while the 'Fortune' article claims that Alameda Research's business practices with FTX were legal, implying no undue advantage?

# Alameda Absorbed FTX's Losses, Including MobileCoin

Alameda Research functioned as FTX's sin-eater: when FTX took a loss, the loss was moved onto Alameda's balance sheet so that FTX would not look bad. Gary Wang testified that in 2021 FTX was facing a "several hundred million dollar" loss from an exploit in MobileCoin — apparently in April 2021, though Wang did not give a month — and Bankman-Fried directed him to have Alameda take it on instead, because FTX's balance sheets were visible to investors and Alameda's were not.

The relation was general, not a one-off. Ellison testified that her tenure as CEO of Alameda Research was an exercise in optics: when FTX took a loss in the hundreds of millions of dollars because a trader had exploited its system, Wang moved that loss onto Alameda's balance sheet, and FTX's "insurance fund," meant to keep traders from getting stuck with other traders' losses, was totally made up, with Alameda simply picking up the tab. The concealment held all the way to investors: Paradigm Capital's Matt Huang showed the court the balance sheets he had received from Bankman-Fried, and they did not include the loss, which should have appeared in the second-quarter numbers he was given — those instead showed $63 million in trading expenses and $63 million in "other expenses" for the quarter, and an estimated profit of $732 million.

Bankman-Fried offered a benign reading of the same arrangement from the stand: he said the MobileCoin loss, the one Wang said Alameda took to keep off FTX's balance sheet, was a totally innocent matter in which he thought it appropriate that Alameda take the position as a backstop liquidity provider.



---


# Alameda's $65 Billion Line Of Credit At FTX

Alameda Research held a line of credit at FTX that ultimately reached $65 billion, an effectively unlimited borrowing facility unmatched by anyone else on the exchange and carrying no requirement to post collateral. Caroline Ellison testified that there was no contract and no written terms, and that the credit line was not visible to FTX's auditors; when she raised that with Bankman-Fried, he told her not to worry about it.

The defining features are its size, its informality, and its exclusivity. Gary Wang, who set the line up, testified that it did not start that big: Bankman-Fried asked him to increase it a few times because Alameda kept running into its limits — first "a few hundred million," then a billion, then even that was not enough. It was not clear how Wang arrived at $65 billion specifically, but he said he had discussed the number with Bankman-Fried, and that other customers did not have the same privileges. Ellison said the credit was drawn in increments of $100,000 to $10 million at a time and was used primarily for trading: the effectively unlimited funds "allowed us to make profitable trades we couldn't have made otherwise."

The boundary case is the source of the capital and Bankman-Fried's disclaimed knowledge of it. Ellison testified that Alameda and FTX were initially "very integrated," run by the same team from the same office, and that when Alameda was scrounging for funds Bankman-Fried told her FTX would be a good source of capital. On the stand, Bankman-Fried denied he knew about the effectively infinite line of credit Alameda received from FTX — an argument The Verge's reporter found peculiar, summarising the take-away as that the CEO of a financial company simply did not pay attention to finances.



---


# Alameda's Special Privileges Written Into FTX's Code

Gary Wang told the court that Alameda received advantages through code baked into FTX's software granting it special access to the exchange — "We gave special privileges on FTX that gave unlimited withdrawals on the platform to Alameda" — privileges that ultimately resulted in Alameda owing FTX $8 billion worth of customer deposits.

The structure had several linked parts. Alameda was allowed to withdraw and transfer funds and had a $65 billion line of credit. "When customers deposited USD, it went to Alameda," Wang said. "It existed in the computer code. Alameda could have negative balances and unlimited withdrawals." That "bug" in the code was written by Nishad Singh, FTX's director of engineering, and reviewed by Wang, with Bankman-Fried calling the shots. Wang also told the court about a $1 million personal loan he received and a $200 million to $300 million loan in his name from Alameda that was never deposited into his account but was used to make investments into other companies on behalf of FTX — all done by Bankman-Fried, he testified. The escalation was visible over time: in early 2020 Wang discovered for the first time that Alameda's negative balance exceeded FTX's revenue, an indication that Alameda was taking customer funds, and he brought this to Bankman-Fried's attention several times; in late 2021 he discovered Alameda had withdrawn $3 billion from its $65 billion line of credit. The ownership and authority around it: Wang owned 10% of Alameda while his boss owned the other 90%, his compensation was a base salary of $200,000 per year plus stock, and he owned roughly 17% of FTX — and even though they were co-founders, "ultimately it was Sam's decision to make" when there were disagreements. Born in China, Wang moved to the U.S. at age 7 and grew up in Minnesota before going to MIT to study math and computer science, worked at Google after college, and first met Bankman-Fried during high school at a summer camp.



---


# Gary Wang's Ownership Stake And Cooperation Deal

Gary Wang, co-founder and chief technology officer of FTX and co-founder of Alameda Research, owned only 10 percent of Alameda and 17 percent of FTX and drew a $200,000-a-year salary with no performance bonuses — though at times he was a billionaire on paper — while Bankman-Fried owned 90 percent of Alameda and 65 percent of FTX. He returned to the US on November 16th, met with the US government on November 17th without having been arrested or charged, offered to cooperate immediately, and pled guilty to various charges a month later. Wang was clear that he was cooperating because he did not want to go to jail, and said he hoped his assistance would lead a sentencing judge to be lenient.

The Verge's reporter drew from the disparity a puzzle she could not resolve: Wang took bizarre risks for a relatively small share. Bankman-Fried did not code, so none of his fingerprints are on the technical changes that let FTX allegedly defraud its customers and investors, while Wang supervised the code behind a key prosecution claim — that Alameda Research was afforded secret, special privileges with FTX's funds. When FTX went down, Wang left himself with no plausible deniability. Wang, a college roommate of Bankman-Fried's, took the stand after Adam Yedidia and, in the reporter's phrase, sang like a canary about the secret privileges he had created for Alameda in the FTX code.

The delivery was heavy going. On October 6th, 2023 Wang had to explain to the jury the difference between a front end and a back end, explain futures trading, and read a great deal into the record, which took a while; it was a tough day for the jury, and probably for Wang, who spoke quickly, perhaps from nerves.



---


# June 2022: Alameda's Reckoning And Lender Repayment

By 2022 Alameda's negative balance on FTX had become a cause for concern for Caroline Ellison, Nishad Singh, and Gary Wang, who built a spreadsheet to work out how negative Alameda actually was; the version shown in court ran to several pages of attempts to reconcile, and Wang figured Alameda owed FTX about $11 billion at a time when FTX's revenue was about $1.5 billion. Ellison, Singh, Wang, and Bankman-Fried then met in the Bahamas office, where Alameda's lenders wanted their money back and Bankman-Fried directed the group to pay the lenders back using FTX customer funds.

Bankman-Fried considered shutting Alameda down and even wrote a long memo about it, but Wang testified that in a now-deleted Signal discussion of that memo he told Bankman-Fried and Singh they could not shut Alameda down because they could not repay its debt. Another empty Signal chat, with its setting to delete messages after a week, was shown to the court; its members were Ellison, Singh, Wang, and Bankman-Fried.

Bankman-Fried's own account from the stand ran differently. He testified that in June 2022 he heard about the account called "fiat@ftx" tracking how much money Alameda owed to FTX, that he did not know what it was and did not bother to find out because he was busy, and that this was when he directed Ellison to repay Alameda's lenders because he thought Alameda was good for it. He also gave BlockFi and Voyager, two crypto lenders, some capital infusions for good measure.

# Day Two Of The Bankman-Fried Trial: Jury Selection And The Courtroom Audience

On the second day of Sam Bankman-Fried's fraud trial, the jury was selected on Wednesday morning, after which lawyers for the government and then for Bankman-Fried delivered opening statements that told two very different stories of the former FTX CEO's sudden rise and almost instantaneous fall. The central question framed by the proceedings was who Bankman-Fried, the former CEO of crypto exchange FTX, really is: a liar and a fraud, or someone who acted in good faith and, like many a startup founder, flew too close to the sun. Bankman-Fried himself spent most of the day in court staring into a laptop while seated between his two attorneys. The prosecution's account of his alleged crimes was described as featuring a study in contrasts.



---


# The Prosecution's Opening Statement Against Bankman-Fried

Thane Rehn, a prosecutor for the government, opened the case against Sam Bankman-Fried with the line "One year ago, it looked like the defendant was on the top of the world," and then argued that this appearance was false: "all of that, all of it, was built on lies," he declared to the jury, adding "Behind the curtains, he was not what he appeared to be." Rehn described a defendant who, as former CEO of FTX, oversaw a supposedly thriving crypto exchange, jetted between international locales, hobnobbed with celebrities like Tom Brady and Larry David, and repeatedly emphasized to customers that their money was safe and secure.

What followed was a roughly 30-minute story that repeatedly emphasized how Bankman-Fried allegedly stole customer funds to facilitate his jet-setting lifestyle, donate millions to political candidates, and finance risky bets. Rehn also directly contested the media framing of the defendant: he was not a crypto "boy" genius, as so many in the media — Fortune included — have written, but a "man" who "stole billions of dollars from thousands of victims." Rehn closed the characterization with a promise to the jury: "You will see the full picture."



---


# Sam Bankman-Fried

Sam Bankman-Fried is the former CEO of the bankrupt crypto exchange FTX, whose highly anticipated criminal trial started on the Tuesday before TechCrunch's 2023-10-01 report, to determine whether he is guilty of seven counts of fraud and conspiracy. As one former federal prosecutor put it: "The odds seem to be stacked against him at this point."

He was 31 years old and co-founded FTX in 2019; within a few years the once third-largest crypto exchange's valuation hit $32 billion at its peak, and the company is now trying to claw back any funds to distribute to creditors. Before the fall he was even compared to Warren Buffet, and many called him the white horse of crypto — a description TechCrunch notes it never applied to him.

Bankman-Fried, however, maintained his innocence. At The New York Times' DealBook Summit he appeared virtually from the Bahamas and said, "I didn't ever try to commit fraud on anyone; I was shocked by what happened this month"; in a published DM exchange with a Vox reporter he said he regretted filing for bankruptcy and thought that "regulators make everything worse." In January he pleaded not guilty to all counts, which include wire fraud, conspiracy to commit money laundering and conspiracy to misuse customer funds. He could face up to 115 years in jail if convicted on all charges.

TechCrunch's 2023-10-02 summary of his standing on the eve of trial: SBF has been denied bail; his name is mud (or much worse) among those who have lost money in Alameda or FTX; and those who might not have had positions in these still blame him for other crypto woes, because he set off a ripple effect.



---


# Gary Wang's Testimony At The FTX Fraud Trial

Gary Wang, the lesser-known co-founder of FTX, told a Manhattan courtroom on Thursday that he had committed financial crimes while working at FTX — including wire and commodities fraud — carried out with the help of Sam Bankman-Fried, FTX ex-engineering head Nishad Singh, and Caroline Ellison, who ran sister hedge fund Alameda Research and had been Bankman-Fried's girlfriend.

Asked by Assistant U.S. Attorney Nicolas Roos, "Did you commit financial crimes while working at FTX?" Wang responded, "Yes." Asked whether he saw any of the people he committed those crimes with in the courtroom, Wang — dressed in an oversized and wrinkled suit with a red tie and glasses — awkwardly stood up, looked around, and answered, "Yes"; asked who, he said, "Sam Bankman-Fried." He was one of two former friends of Bankman-Fried's from MIT who also worked at FTX while living with the founder in the Bahamas and who took the stand that week to testify against their former classmate, confidant and boss, a man who allegedly ran a crypto empire that defrauded thousands of customers out of billions of dollars. The trial, set to last six weeks, was to resume on Tuesday with key testimony expected from Ellison, considered the prosecution's star witness, who had already pleaded guilty to multiple charges. Bankman-Fried faces seven federal charges, including wire fraud, securities fraud and money laundering, that could put him in prison for the rest of his life. Thus far Bankman-Fried, 31, has remained mostly quiet in court, intently listening to witnesses and at times writing notes to his attorneys — but as Wang testified against him, he looked visibly upset, shifting his gaze from his former friend to the ground and at one point putting his head in his hands.



---


# Bankman-Fried's Decision To Testify Backfired

The Verge's trial reporter argued that Bankman-Fried's choice to take the stand was a net loss for his defense: like Theranos' Elizabeth Holmes before him, he got on the stand to speak directly to his state of mind in a way no other witness can, but telling your side of the story opens you to a great many questions you might not want to answer on cross-examination — and, having watched a lot of crosses, she called Sassoon's the nastiest she had ever seen.

The warrant is what the charges turn on. The case hinged on conspiracy and intentional deceit: just losing $8 billion is not a crime, though it is very embarrassing, but if Bankman-Fried lied to customers and lenders about what he was doing and how safe FTX was, that is a crime. Because state of mind was the contested issue, his own testimony became the evidence, and it did not hold: Sassoon had established the day before that he has a long history of dishonesty, and on October 31st, through a set of questions about what he did and did not do, she established that the story he told on direct examination was absurd. After a brief redirect by his own lawyers, resplendent with word salad, Bankman-Fried stepped down and the defense rested.

The direct examination had already supplied grounds. Beyond the two obvious lies the reporter counted him telling on the stand — about Alameda Research's name and about "allow_negative" — she was struck by how little he seemed to know about his own companies: apparently Singh, Wang, and Ellison were out there just doing whatever their little hearts desired, because Bankman-Fried was a CEO, but definitely not the kind that pays any attention to money at his crypto trading firm and futures exchange.



---


# The SBF Trial Proceedings

Sam Bankman-Fried is in court for alleged fraud and money laundering while leading crypto exchange FTX and sister company Alameda. TechCrunch's 2023-10-02 preview placed the case in the Manhattan Federal Court, describing the disgraced cryptocurrency entrepreneur as accused of orchestrating "one of the biggest financial frauds in American history": the multibillion-dollar collapse of FTX, the crypto exchange he founded and led. SBF, as he is known, has pleaded not guilty to some seven charges of fraud and conspiracy.

The trial kicked off with jury selection October 3. By TechCrunch's 2023-10-06 update the case was entering its next chapter, with proceedings resuming Thursday: as confirmed during a teleconference Wednesday, SBF would be taking the stand along with a handful of other witnesses, as the onus shifted toward the defense after the prosecution brought its case to its conclusion.

Access to the proceedings is limited: no devices are allowed, so reports are being physically put together within the courtroom, or sent to overflow rooms. The jury's composition ranges from a train conductor to a retired investment banker who attended Stanford University, and TechCrunch pointed readers to a special joint episode of its Equity and Chain Reaction podcasts for a better sense of the vibe between the jurors and the rest of the court.

A second account of the same events was arriving in parallel: "Going Infinite," a book by Michael Lewis chronicling the rise and fall of SBF, was set to debut on the first day of the trial.

The MacBook Air is Apple's entry-level laptop, best suited for typical productivity work with a comfortable keyboard, an excellent trackpad, and all-day battery life; the 2020 M1 version with its fanless design remains in the lineup as the budget option, and for many people still ticks the right boxes on performance and price, even if it is long enough in the tooth to have been fully dethroned in The Verge's guide to the best laptops.

The 13-inch M2 MacBook Air had also come down. Along with introducing a 15-inch M2 Air, Apple announced at WWDC 2023 that the 13-inch model now starts at $1,099 instead of $1,199; the base model with 256GB of storage and an eight-core GPU was selling for $899 at B&H Photo, $200 off, while Best Buy and B&H Photo offered an equal discount on the upgraded configuration with a 512GB SSD and 10-core GPU at $1,199, $200 off. The M2 Air is a super slim and light laptop with a 1080p webcam that is actually usable and a handy magnetic charger that frees up one of its precious two USB-C ports; its M2 processor did not kick-start a revolution like the M1 generation but is a great performer for any user outside more demanding creatives. Slight downsides include slower storage in the base 256GB configuration and a notch cutout in its otherwise excellent screen — even so, The Verge said there has not been a more travel-friendly Apple laptop since the polarizing 12-inch MacBook, and this one is good enough to be the No. 1 laptop it recommends.

The 15-inch M2 Air is a lot like a blown-up 13-inch Air, and judging from The Verge's glowing review there is nothing wrong with that: it has the same M2 chip, two Thunderbolt 4 / USB-C ports, MagSafe charging, and a base model with a 256GB SSD and 8GB of RAM, but differs with a larger 15.3-inch notched screen at 2880 x 1864 resolution, six speakers instead of four, a 10-core GPU that costs extra on the 13-inch, and a higher starting price of $1,299, with 512GB of larger, faster storage running $1,499. It started receiving discounts even before it shipped, letting early adopters save between $50 and $100; at the time of writing it was $300 off at Amazon or Best Buy, selling for $999, with the expanded 512GB model also $300 off at Best Buy at $1,199.



---


# MacBook Pricing And Discount Landscape

Apple sells MacBooks equipped with its own M-series chips in a wide range of sizes and price points, starting with the 13-inch MacBook Air from 2020 at $999 and going up to the latest 16-inch MacBook Pro starting at $2,499 — and, as The Verge put it on October 26th, 2023, finding a deal on a current Mac with an M1, M2, or even the new M3 chip, as well as the higher-end M3 Pro and M3 Max, is actually not that difficult.

The discriminating feature of Mac discounting is that it is episodic rather than continuous: Macs may not experience perpetual discounts, but it is not uncommon to see various current models discounted by as much as $400. The alternative route to savings is buying refurbished directly from Apple, which avoids waiting for the changing winds of deals; Apple's refurbished store provides a one-year warranty on all products and generally offers discounts of up to 15 to 20 percent off the price of a new unit.

One boundary case is explicitly excluded. The Verge does not recommend buying any older Intel-based Macs: retailers may try to tempt buyers with very low prices on leftover new or refurbished stock, but there is a reason nobody wants them anymore — they are completely outclassed by all the newer models, unless you have some super-niche Windows Boot Camp needs, and even then you should consider which Windows apps you really need and whether they work with Parallels.



---


# Samsung Galaxy Buds 2 Pro Deal Prices

The Samsung Galaxy Buds 2 Pro were $160 for Black Friday 2023 with a free $10 Amazon gift card, and $169.99 — $60 off — in early December, positioned throughout as the pick for Samsung and Android users rather than an outright top choice.

The Verge's 7 December 2023 roundup said Samsung's most high-end pair, launched the previous year, is a good option for an Android user or Samsung devotee who wants premium earbuds, with top-notch sound quality even better than their predecessor; Samsung Galaxy phone owners can also take advantage of higher bit rate audio, while everybody gets good active noise cancellation and relatively robust IPX7 sweat and water resistance. It listed them at $169.99 ($60 off) at Amazon, B&H Photo and Best Buy. Wired's 19 October 2023 deals post called them one of its top earbud picks for Samsung owners (9/10, WIRED Recommends), producing excellent sound quality with a super comfortable fit and IPX7 water resistance, but noted they lack the multi-device connectivity Wired likes on the Pixel Buds A-Series — "if you mainly use your earbuds with a Samsung phone, these are a great fit for you".

Engadget's 24 November 2023 Black Friday list put them at $160 with a free $10 Amazon gift card, "a good way from their all-time low — they very briefly fell to $105 last year — but it's still $30 or so less than their average selling price in recent months". Engadget says they are not a top pick in any of its guides but are worth a look for Galaxy phone users, since they quickly pair with and swap between other Samsung devices including TVs and support a higher-quality audio codec on Samsung handsets; more generally they are one of the better-sounding pairs Engadget has tested, with impressive clarity and well-controlled bass, comfortable and waterproof. The drawbacks: no simultaneous connection to two devices, and poor five-hour battery life. Engadget gave them a review score of 86 the previous year.



---


# 13-Inch MacBook Air M1 Holiday Deal

The MacBook Air with the M1 chip is a couple of years old at this point but is still officially part of Apple's laptop lineup. It dropped to an all-time low of $750 for October's Prime Day at Amazon, and over the 2023 holiday sales Amazon and Best Buy were selling it for the same price.

It is the budget pick in Engadget's guide to MacBooks and the top pick in its guide to budget laptops; Engadget's review from when it first came out praised its quick speeds, excellent screen and good battery life.



---


# Samsung Galaxy Buds 2 Deal Listings

Samsung's Galaxy Buds 2 appear in The Verge's December roundup at a best price of $89.99 ($60 off) at Best Buy — about $10 more from Amazon, Walmart, and Verizon — and in WIRED's October list as another of its picks for Android users (9/10, WIRED Recommends), with that deal limited to the olive green model.

The Verge calls them a good-sounding pair with active noise cancellation, wireless charging, and a subtle design, and says the price isn't bad for Samsung's entry-level buds, which hit above their weight class on noise cancellation and audio quality. WIRED describes them as a slightly more affordable version of the pricier Samsung set, similar in price to the standard AirPods, getting five hours of battery life with active noise canceling on and an impressive 7.5 hours with it off, coming with a charging case and delivering solid bass via a dual-driver array.



---


# Samsung Smart Monitor M8

The Samsung Smart Monitor M8 was down to just $500, which is $200 off its starting price — though it regularly sells for $600 — and the lowest price Engadget had seen thus far.

This 32-inch display has built-in apps and lets you access streaming services just as you would on a smart TV. It can also act as a smart home hub, showing your smart camera feeds and more.

The discounted model is the updated 2023 version of the monitor that launched at CES 2022.



---


# Samsung Galaxy Watch 6

The new Samsung Galaxy Watch 6 went down to $270 for October Prime Day — reported two days later as $269 and still on sale — which is the lowest price Engadget had seen since it came out a few months earlier.

Engadget's verdict: you cannot get a better smartwatch than this one if you have an Android phone, with bonus points if you have a Samsung phone.

It is smaller and lighter than previous versions. Samsung brought back the spinning bezel on the Classic version, which makes the software's UI easier to navigate, and it has improved performance and updated health and fitness tracking tools.

context:
# Denny Hamlin 2023 Season Autosport Snub

Essentially Sports argued on Dec. 21, 2023 that Denny Hamlin's omission from Autosport's Top 50 drivers of 2023 seemed unjustified, given how much he led and how consistently he performed.

The grounds are his season's numbers and their context. Finding a fan of Hamlin in the NASCAR fandom is a tough task — continuously surrounded by controversy, Joe Gibbs Racing's #11 Toyota Camry driver has been subject to a lot of criticism — but his ability as a race car driver has never been in doubt. As the season entered the decisive playoff phase, it seemed 2023 would be the year his championship drought finally ended: the 43-year-old dominated the first round of the playoffs, was the driver to watch out for, won his first playoff race at Bristol and cruised to the next round. Hamlin later revealed that a shoulder injury prevented him from being at his best as the playoffs progressed, and having to depend much on his weaker arm he stayed in contention for the championship four race until the final race in Martinsville. He secured three wins, 14 top-fives and 19 top-10 finishes in 2023 and led a whopping 998 laps, finishing fifth in the final standings as one of the most consistent and best performers of the season. The piece concedes the counterfactual: a championship trophy would surely have put him in the upper echelons of Autosport's Top 50.



---


# Supercars Drivers In 2023 NASCAR Races

Two drivers who featured in both the 2023 NASCAR season and Autosport's Top 50 Drivers list were Supercars racers Shane van Gisbergen and Brodie Kostecki, Essentially Sports reported on Dec. 21, 2023.

While the pair battled for the championship in the Australian racing circuit, they also raced at the Indianapolis road course race earlier that season. Van Gisbergen had earlier created history by winning on his NASCAR debut at the inaugural Chicago Street Race.



---


# The NFL's Own Scandals, From Kaepernick To The CTE Controversy

The NFL has had its fair share of, as Essentially Sports put it on 2023-10-25, "bumps" down the road. The list given runs from Colin Kaepernick taking a knee during the national anthem to protest against racism, to domestic violence by players, to the Deflategate and Bountygate scandals.

There have been bigger crises as well: the Union of Concerned Scientists accused the NFL of trying to intimidate scientists studying the link between CTE and pro football. The article's closing judgment is nonetheless forward-looking — the NFL is already way past other leagues in terms of revenue, and now with the pivotal shift in its strategy, "America's favorite pastime" is on its way to world domination.



---


# Autosport Top 50 Drivers 2023 NASCAR Representation

Autosport's annual Top 50 drivers list is a ranking of the 50 standout performers in motorsports for the year, a tradition the renowned motorsports publishing brand has continued since 2002, whose announcement every year creates some suspense within the racing community — and in 2023, as Essentially Sports reported on Dec. 21, it included only three NASCAR drivers.

William Byron led the list of NASCAR drivers with a 12th-place ranking, with Kyle Larson and 2023 Cup Series champion Ryan Blaney joining him. The scarcity of NASCAR drivers in the rankings raised some eyebrows, since the year produced numerous cases of NASCAR drivers standing out with their consistency and skills behind the steering wheel, which is what prompted the publication's review of the major exclusions. The boundary condition the piece itself acknowledges: motorsports is a vast field with elite competitions taking place the world over, so some fan favorites are bound to be left out.



---


# NASCAR $7.7 Billion Media Rights Deal

The NASCAR media rights deal reported by Essentially Sports on Dec. 1, 2023 is a seven-year agreement worth $7.7 billion, finalized just days earlier with Fox Sports, NBC, Amazon and Warner Bros. Discovery, securing an average annual revenue of $1.1 billion — almost a 40% increase over the sport's existing media rights deal.

There is no denying that the new deal stunned the NASCAR community; with many still trying to digest it, it gave rise to divided opinions, and while the figure sounds lucrative, there seemed to be more to it than meets the eye. It is public knowledge that NASCAR officials invested plenty of time in negotiating the deal, and securing $1.1 billion a year is something, especially when the sport is supposedly on the wane — it looked like the sanctioning body made it count when it mattered most. The boundary case that complicates the headline number is the audience trend: with the Cup Series already facing a 5% drop in viewership that year, Sports Business Journal journalist Adam Stern, appearing on the Dirty Mo Live podcast, discussed how the new deal could affect the ratings.



---


# The NFL's International Games And Its Concussion Initiatives

Amid the media frenzy surrounding the two lovebirds, other issues get thrown out of the window, Essentially Sports observed on 2023-10-25 — Kaepernick, who? Deflategate, what? Two of those overlooked efforts are its international expansion and its player-safety work.

The NFL had scheduled 5 games abroad that season, organized outside American borders with a view to garnering international appeal. It was also addressing the concussion controversies, having recently added both new concussion rules and a new $100 million initiative called "Play Smart, Play Safe" to make the sport safer for players — and, the article concludes, all the effort is showing.



---


# NASCAR 2024 Offseason Preparation Window

The NASCAR offseason, as characterized by CBSSports.com on Dec. 7, 2023, is the wintertime respite from what is otherwise a demanding, year-long grind of racing — welcome but very short, and decisive out of proportion to its length.

What distinguishes it is what gets settled in it: come 2024 the grind would soon begin again, and exactly what it looked like would be based in large part on these months, when driver lineups, crew lineups and rules packages are set. With much activity going on within the confines of race shops across NASCAR, the piece rounded up the major storylines for the week of Dec. 4 as the offseason continued.



---


# The NFL's Statement Defending Its Taylor Swift Coverage

Following criticism that the league was focusing too much on Taylor Swift, the NFL rejected the premise that its coverage had become disproportionate, in an official statement handed to People on 4 October 2023. It first defended the practice as routine: "We frequently change our bios and profile imagery based on what's happening in and around our games, as well as culturally. The Taylor Swift and Travis Kelce news has been a pop cultural moment we've leaned into in real time, as it's an intersection of sport and entertainment, and we've seen an incredible amount of positivity around the sport."

The league then attacked the proportionality claim directly, arguing that the Swift material was a small share of its output: "The vast majority of our content has remained focused on the game, our players and variety of other initiatives, including our Toy Story Funday Football alt-cast, the international games and more."



---


# NASCAR Media Deal Streaming Diversification Rationale

Sports Business Journal's Adam Stern, speaking on the Dirty Mo Live podcast and quoted by Essentially Sports on Dec. 1, 2023, explained the structure behind NASCAR's media rights deal as the interaction of three pressures: the money available from incumbent partners, the decline of cable, and the demand from teams for more revenue.

Stern said the sanctioning body would have loved to stay with Fox Sports and NBC, but since that would most likely have resulted in less money, NASCAR opted to explore other options. He framed media rights revenue as a key role in sports using MLS as the comparison: "You look at MLS. MLS takes a big deal with Apple, almost all of their games behind the Apple TV's paywall. That was the money they could get and they had to deliver for their industry. Their industry is expected to be a growing business and one of the most sporting ways to be a growing business in sports is to have growing media rights revenue." He added a further factor specific to distribution: the cable universe has been declining, with a drop of a couple of percentage points of subscribers every quarter, which is very concerning — one of the reasons NASCAR did not want to gamble solely on cable users, and with Amazon Prime it had the leisure to explore the streaming arena and glimpse how the future could look.

The relation holds jointly, not separately: "So partially, they [NASCAR] did it to spread their eggs in multiple baskets but also part out of it was to get more money and to make sure they get more money in the industry at the time when their teams are saying we need more money, we are not profitable currently." Stern concluded that NASCAR was more or less left with no choice: "NASCAR is in a tough situation because they had to deliver more money as well and clearly if they went this route, that's a good indication that's because they had to go this route to deliver more money for the industry."

qid: Does the 'Fortune' article suggest that Israel's actions are aggressive by mentioning a warning to Gaza residents to relocate due to a potential ground invasion, while the 'Business Today | Latest Stock Market And Economy News India' article implies that Israel was caught off-guard by a Hamas attack, indicating a lack of intelligence support?
context:
# Hamas October 7 2023 Surprise Attack on Israel

On 7 October 2023, Hamas carried out what Business Today described as the biggest coordinated attack in Israel, capturing some territory in southern Israel and taking control of some military bases and soldiers.

The reaction the report documents was directed at Israel's famed intelligence agency, Mossad, which is known for its intelligence-gathering capability. For some observers, the belief that Mossad was among the best in the spying world was shattered that day. The report is explicit that it was not the fact of an attack that surprised people, but the scale at which Hamas operated.



---


# Commentary That Israeli Intelligence and Defence Failed

The dominant online argument on 7 October 2023, as collected by Business Today, was that the attack represented a massive failure of Israeli intelligence and defence. Its grounds are the gap between Israel's reputation and the outcome.

Journalist Rania Khalek said the strategic planning that must have gone into this against "one of the most high-tech occupation and surveillance systems in the world" will be studied by many, adding: "The Israelis must be totally losing it right now." Tarik Cyril Amar wrote: "And the intel, and the special forces training... both areas where Israel mythology will be very upset indeed." A user posting as Mjoachim said Israel's defence forces have lost their fame, noting that the IDF lost an army base and a general was captured right out of his house: "Invincible 'Merkava MK4 MBT's captured, and destroyed...what is wrong with the Israeli security and defence forces? And (what) MOSSAD did?"

Dr Jaswant Gandhi, a professor of management, drew a lesson for another country: the attack on Israel was a "great Mossad failure", and India had to learn a lot and keep all intelligence agencies duly greased and internecine conflict-proof. "Israel_under_attack Great #Mossad failure. GoI has to learn a lot and keep all Intelligence Agencies duly greased and internecine conflict-proof. BHARAT is not immune to #terrorism and internal enemies," he wrote on X. The warrant common to these comments is that a surveillance and special-forces apparatus of this reputation should have detected preparations on this scale.



---


# Israel-Hamas War Context, October 2023

As of TechCrunch's 2023-10-14 report, Israel is retaliating militarily against the attacks on its people, on its soil, and the hostages subsequently taken by Hamas — the ruling organization in Gaza that kidnapped at least 150 people and took them into Gaza during brutal attacks on Israel last weekend that killed 1,300 people. That strategy has seen Israel pummeling the "Gaza Strip" with bombs to eradicate it of Hamas and to get its hostages back, and over 1,500 people in Palestine so far have been killed as a result.

The tech industry in Israel — the country's biggest export and its biggest single contributor to GDP — is also taking a big knock, but inevitably the impact on the smaller and more fragile ecosystem in Gaza has been significantly more serious, and the physical, economic and societal destruction resulting from that leaves any future for the tech industry there in doubt: quite simply, there is no escaping the consequences of the war for anyone, let alone tech workers. Israel has now amassed soldiers near the north of Gaza ahead of an expected ground offensive into the densely populated enclave, and about 1.1 million people living in northern areas have been told to leave in the next day. The UN has warned of "devastating humanitarian consequences" from these latest moves, and a total blockade on the territory is being enforced with fuel, food and water running out; Israel says it won't lift the restrictions unless Hamas frees all hostages. TechCrunch notes the piece was later edited to include relevant information about the attacks by Hamas.



---


# Sderot Police Headquarters Seized During the Attack

Younis Tirawi, who reports on Palestinian affairs, said that Hamas militants had taken over the Sderot police headquarters and armoured vehicles in the town on 7 October 2023.

An analyst posting as OSINTtechnical wrote the same day that some of the images coming out of Sderot over the previous few hours were reaching degrees of horror "that I don't really think I can use words to properly describe. Truly disturbing acts of terror directed at civilians."



---


# Claim That Mossad Foreknew the Hamas Attack

The counter-claim collected by Business Today on 7 October 2023 attacks the premise that the attack was a surprise at all. Some users speculated that Mossad knew what was going to happen but let Hamas make a mistake so that Israel could launch a ferocious attack on it. One wrote: "Mossad was not so ignorant that it did not know about this #attack. Israel wanted to invade Palestine, but they had no excuse, stupid #Hamas gave them the reason. Hamas is an excuse, new lands are wonderful."

Reacting to that, a user posting as timm said that knowing the proficiency of the Mossad he found the idea of a "surprise attack" to be a willing lie. Journalist Ben Muasya framed the same doubt as a question: "Mossad is overrated. How come they never knew Hamas militants planned a sudden attack on Israel? Or was it a trap to get a reason to retaliate heavily? We wait to see how it goes but it will be messy." Another user argued that no one can carry out such a major attack against Israel without intelligence support, asking "Who gave Hamas Intelligence? It was as if the entire Israeli army and the Mossad were asleep."

What these comments share is a refusal of the inference from "Mossad did not stop it" to "Mossad did not know". Where the failure argument treats the outcome as incompetence, this line treats Mossad's reputation for proficiency as evidence that foreknowledge, or deliberate permission, is the more plausible explanation.



---


# Egypt's Role In The Israel-Hamas War And The Leverage It Creates

The war between Israel and Hamas has turned the spotlight on Egypt's role as a regional powerbroker, potentially winning it Western support as it tries to escape a grinding economic crisis. The structure linking the two is that Egypt's two assets in this conflict — long-held ties to Israel and a border with Gaza — make its stance decisive for outcomes the West wants.

Specifically, Egypt's position is shaping up as key to the fate of any refugees and to a sustained flow of aid for the besieged territory's 2 million residents, after Israel cut off crucial supplies in response to Hamas's deadly Oct. 7 assault. That dependence is what converts Egypt's geography and relationships into potential leverage over Western backing for its economy, as of the reporting date of 2023-10-22.



---


# Displacement And Casualties In Gaza As Of October 12, 2023

The number of people in Gaza displaced from their homes rose quickly over the days preceding Oct. 12, 2023, totaling over 330,000 on that date, with over two-thirds of them staying in UNRWA schools.

Since the war between Israel and Hamas began on Oct. 8, 2023, more than 1,500 Gazans had been killed and more than 5,300 injured, while Hamas attacks had killed more than 1,300 people in Israel and injured about 3,200 others. These are the figures as reported on 2023-10-13.



---


# Israel-Hamas Conflict: The Limited-Market-Impact Base Case

As of mid-October 2023, the Indian stock market's base case was that the Israel-Hamas hostilities would not escalate, and on that assumption the conflict was expected to have only a limited impact on markets. The grounds are threefold. First, the world can ill-afford another full-fledged war while economies are already battling high inflation and interest rates, an ongoing Russia-Ukraine war and a slowing China, which is precisely why many countries are trying to restrict any escalation; the market movement in the week before 14 October 2023 indicated that non-escalation was the presumed base case. Second, the US treasury secretary stated that the current conflict is not likely to significantly impact the global economic outlook. Third, history supports the same conclusion: a study of past conflicts between Israel and Hamas found that they tend to have limited impact on global financial markets, across crude oil, US 10-year yields, US equities and market volatility.

The warrant joining the evidence to the claim is that market impact tracks escalation, not the mere existence of hostilities: because the incentives of major countries point towards containment and because previous Israel-Hamas episodes transmitted little into the four channels that matter (oil, yields, equities, volatility), the priced-in outcome is a contained conflict. The argument is explicitly conditional on the non-escalation premise holding.



---


# Gaza Sky Geeks Accelerator

Gaza Sky Geeks is an Alphabet-backed initiative based in Gaza that provides pre-seed investments, training and technology resources to Palestine's Gazan population, and has been a beacon of entrepreneurship in the region.

It is the largest tech hub in Palestine, providing a wide range of tech training at scale: in 2022, 5,000 coders and developers from across the West Bank and Gaza graduated from the program.

qid: Does the article from 'The Independent - Life and Style' about Will Smith and Jada Pinkett Smith's marriage describe a similar acknowledgment of marital challenges as 'FOX News - Entertainment' reports on Garth Brooks' statement about his past marriage?
context:
# The Smiths' 2021 Public Accounts Of Marital Strain

In late 2021 both Will Smith and Jada Pinkett Smith described the difficulty of their marriage in public, first on her show and then in his memoir. In an October 2021 episode of Red Table Talk, Pinkett Smith said it "takes work" to maintain a spark in the bedroom: "It's hard... the thing Will and I talk about a lot is the journey. We started in this [relationship] at a very young age, 22 years old... I think you expect your partner to know — especially when it comes to sex. It's like: 'Well, if you love me, you should know. If you love me, you should read my mind.' That's a huge pitfall."

The following month Will Smith's memoir was released, detailing several problems the couple had had over the years. He wrote that they were "suffering the brutal death of our romantic fantasies, the burning away of the idealistic illusion of the perfect marriage and the perfect family. Neither of us wanted a divorce; we knew we loved each other, and some aspects of our union were magical. But the structure of the life that we had established was strangling both of us."



---


# The Smiths' Denials Of Open-Marriage, Divorce And Infidelity Rumours

Will Smith and Jada Pinkett Smith have each publicly rejected the recurring claims made about their marriage — that it was an open relationship, that they were divorcing, and that either had been unfaithful. Pinkett Smith attacked the open-relationship premise directly on Facebook, after a quiet decade and a half spent making films and raising their children: "Here is how I will change my statement... Will and I BOTH can do WHATEVER we want, because we TRUST each other to do so. This does NOT mean we have an open relationship... this means we have a GROWN one." Her counter is that mutual freedom follows from trust, not from an open-marriage arrangement, so the inference from one to the other does not hold.

Will Smith answered the separation-and-divorce rumours in a mocking Facebook post: "Under normal circumstances, I don't usually respond to foolishness. But, so many people have extended [to] me their 'deepest condolences' that I figured — 'What the hell… I can be foolish, too!' So, in the interest of redundant, repetitious, over and over-again-ness… Jada and I are… NOT GETTING A DIVORCE!!!!!!!!!!!!!" In an interview on CBS Sunday Morning in October 2023 he also denied the infidelity premise outright: "Never. There's never been infidelity in our marriage... And we have never surprised one another with anything ever." He added that he had decided public chatter about his life "can be of a benefit to people," since "chatter is the first stage to having a real conversation and being able to truly explore if some of the things in your heart are loving, or poisonous."



---


# Will Smith's Response To Jada Pinkett Smith's Memoir Worthy

Will Smith broke his silence on his wife's memoir Worthy on 16 October 2023 in an interview with The New York Times, saying the book "kind of woke him up" and that he had come to realise she is more "resilient, clever and compassionate than he'd understood." He added: "When you've been with someone for more than half of your life, a sort of emotional blindness sets in, and you can all too easily lose your sensitivity to their hidden nuances and subtle beauties." The statement was framed as support for his partner and her success.

Before giving that statement he had appeared to mock the publicity storm surrounding the couple in a video titled "Official statement" posted on Instagram. "So, here's the thing. My opinion is... uh…" he said, before sneezing into the crook of his arm; as he sneezed, the video comically zoomed out to show several different landscapes including lakes and mountains.



---


# Why Will Smith And Jada Pinkett Smith Never Signed A Prenup

Jada Pinkett Smith revealed in an interview with Parade, published 13 October 2023 and given while promoting her memoir Worthy, that she and Will Smith deliberately did not sign a prenuptial agreement before their 1997 wedding, because they had already decided divorce was not in the cards for them. The Independent presents the missing prenup as of a piece with their promise not to divorce: the absence of a legal fallback was itself the commitment.

She described the decision as an unromantic, deliberate conversation rather than a wedding-day gesture: "Listen, weddings are beautiful, but they can be very romanticised. I feel that was a very real moment for the two of us to look each other in the eyes, recognise that there would be tough times in this journey and to say to each other: 'No matter what, we're going to figure it out and that's why we don't need a prenup, because I'm making a promise that divorce won't be necessary, that we will figure this out.'" She added that the promise was made "without all of the bridal wedding beauty; it was just sitting on a log in his mother's backyard, and going: 'Hey' — having to really look at the possibility of us not being together."



---


# How Will Smith And Jada Pinkett Smith Met And Married In 1997

Will Smith and Jada Pinkett Smith met when she auditioned for the role of his girlfriend on The Fresh Prince of Bel-Air; she did not get the part, but the two hit it off — even though Smith was married to Sheree Zampino at the time, with whom he shares son Trey. Smith later described the moment of recognition on Pinkett Smith's Red Table Talk in 2018: "I had a realisation I wasn't with the person I was supposed to be with. I was sitting in a [bathroom] stall and I was crying and laughing uncontrollably, and I knew [Jada] was the woman I was supposed to be with."

The pair only began seriously dating in 1995, after Smith finalised his divorce from Zampino. He proposed in November 1997 and they married just one month later, in Baltimore. Pinkett Smith was not initially enthusiastic about marrying at all: she told People in 2019, "I never wanted to get married. But my mother was like: 'You have to get married' — she's so old-school — and Will wanted a family. So I said: 'All right, maybe it's something I should do.'"



---


# Jada Pinkett Smith's "Entanglement" With August Alsina

Jada Pinkett Smith confirmed in 2020 that she had had a relationship with the singer August Alsina during a period when she and Will Smith were separated, describing it on her Facebook Watch series Red Table Talk as an "entanglement." Alsina and Pinkett Smith were introduced in 2015, but it was only in 2020 that he claimed publicly that the two had dated while she was married and that the Smiths' marriage was open at the time. Alsina said Will Smith had given the pair his "blessing," explaining: "I actually sat down with Will and had a conversation due to the transformation from their marriage to life partnership that they've spoken on several times and it not involving romanticism." He added that he "totally gave myself to that relationship for years of my life and I truly and really, really deeply loved and have a ton of love for her."

Pinkett Smith's representatives called the claims "absolutely not true" on the day they surfaced. Less than two weeks later, she and Will Smith appeared together on Red Table Talk, where she confirmed the relationship but placed it inside an amicable separation that had not been disclosed to the press at the time: "We decided that we were going to separate for a period of time and you go figure out how to make yourself happy and I'll figure out how to make myself happy. From there, as time went on, I got into a different kind of entanglement with August... Yes, it was a relationship absolutely." Prompted by her husband, she confirmed it "was a relationship, absolutely." She also rejected Alsina's framing of permission, saying Will had not given it because the only person who could give her permission was herself. The episode is one of the grey areas in the couple's account of the terms of their separation.



---


# Britney Spears' 55-Hour Marriage To Jason Alexander

Jason Alexander was Britney Spears' first husband: the two married at a wedding chapel in Las Vegas in 2004 and annulled the marriage only 55 hours after the ceremony. Alexander returned to the news in 2022 when he tried to attend Spears' wedding to Sam Asghari, and could be heard in a video saying he was going to crash the nuptials. "She's my first wife, my only wife," he reportedly told security. "I'm her first husband, I'm here to crash the wedding."

Alexander was arrested for trespassing, vandalism, and battery over the incident. A security guard later revealed in court that when Alexander crashed the wedding he also tried to enter Spears' bedroom.

qid: Does the TechCrunch article claim that Google's Gemini has superior architecture and capabilities in comparison to other AI models, while the other TechCrunch article accuses Google of anticompetitive behavior towards news publishers, and does The Verge article also depict Google negatively by portraying it as the antagonist in the Epic v. Google trial?
context:
# Google's Gemini Model Family And Its Capability Claims

Gemini is Google's new flagship generative AI model, unveiled in the first week of December 2023 and meant to power a range of products and services including Bard, Google's ChatGPT competitor. In blog posts and press materials, Google touted Gemini's superior architecture and capabilities, claiming that the model meets or exceeds the performance of other leading generative AI models such as OpenAI's GPT-4, and it emphasised Gemini's coding capabilities and multimodal prowess, claiming that the model can understand images, audio and videos just as well as text.

The family has tiers, and only the lower one shipped. Google did not release the full model, Gemini Ultra — which is set to launch sometime in 2024 in Bard and other products — but only a "lite" version called Gemini Pro. Gemini Pro is therefore not the most capable version of Gemini, and Google compared its performance to GPT-4's predecessor, GPT-3.5, a model that was around a year old. Google nevertheless promised improvements in reasoning, planning and understanding with Gemini Pro over the previous model powering Bard, claiming Gemini Pro was better at summarizing content, brainstorming and writing.

The shipped tier is also narrower than the multimodal claims suggest: Gemini Pro is strictly text-in, text-out, and has proven to be mistake-prone. In a worse look for Google, the company was caught faking a Gemini demo by tuning text prompts with still images off camera.



---


# Anecdotal Evidence Undercuts Google's Gemini Pro Claims

Against Google's promises for Gemini Pro, TechCrunch's rejoinder on 7 December 2023 was blunt: "the anecdotal evidence suggests otherwise." The counter-argument attacks the evidential basis of the launch claims rather than the model's architecture, setting user experience after release against what Google said the model would do.

The grounds are the reception of the rollout itself. A "lite" version of Gemini, Gemini Pro, began rolling out to Bard the day before the article, and it did not take long before users began voicing their frustrations with it on X, formerly Twitter.



---


# Helena World Chronicle's Class Action Antitrust Suit Against Google

A class action lawsuit filed in the week of 15 December 2023 in the U.S. District Court in D.C. accuses Google and parent company Alphabet of anticompetitive behavior in violation of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act and others, on behalf of news publishers. The case was filed by Arkansas-based publisher Helena World Chronicle, which argues that Google "siphons off" news publishers' content, their readers and their ad revenue through anticompetitive means, and it specifically cites new AI technologies such as Google's Search Generative Experience (SGE) and the Bard AI chatbot as worsening the problem.

Helena World Chronicle owns and publishes two weekly newspapers in Arkansas. In the complaint it argues that Google is "starving the free press" by sharing publishers' content on Google, losing them "billions of dollars."

Beyond damages, the suit asks for an injunction that would require Google to obtain consent from publishers before using their website data to train its general artificial intelligence products, including Google's own and those of rivals. It also asks that publishers who opt out of SGE still be allowed to show up in Google search results, among other things.

The law firm handling the case is Hausfeld, whose announcement states that "the anticompetitive effects of Google's scheme cause profound harm to competition, to consumers, to labor, and to a democratic free press," and that "Plaintiff Helena World Chronicle, LLC invokes the Sherman Act and Clayton Act to seek class-wide monetary and injunctive relief to restore and ensure competition for digital news and reference publishing and set up guardrails to preserve a free marketplace of ideas in the new era of artificial intelligence."



---


# Gemini Pro's News Summarization Refusals And Stale Answers

Asked to summarise topical news in early December 2023, Gemini Pro often would not do it, despite having Google Search and Google News at its disposal. It seemed loath to comment on potentially controversial news topics, instead telling users to Google it themselves.

The TechCrunch reporter tried the same prompt and got a very similar response. ChatGPT, by contrast, gave a bullet-list summary with citations to news articles.

There was one partial exception, and it exposed a second problem: Gemini Pro did provide a summary of updates on the war in Ukraine when the reporter asked for one, but the information was over a month out of date.



---


# The Claim That SGE And Bard Appropriate Publisher Content

The Helena World Chronicle lawsuit claims that Google's recent advances in AI-based search were implemented with "the goal of discouraging end-users from visiting the websites of Class members who are part of the digital news and publishing line of commerce." The grounds are that Google's AI products both retain users and consume publisher content without permission.

On the Search Generative Experience, the suit argues that SGE offers web searchers a way to seek information in a conversational mode but ultimately keeps users in Google's "walled garden" as it "plagiarizes" their content. The warrant that turns this into a harm publishers cannot escape is that publishers also cannot block SGE, because it uses the same web crawler as Google's general search service, GoogleBot — so opting out of the AI experience would mean opting out of search itself.

On Bard, the suit says Google's Bard AI was trained on a dataset that included "news, magazine and digital publications," citing both a 2023 report from the News Media Alliance and a Washington Post article about AI training data. The Post, which worked with researchers at the Allen Institute for AI, had found that News and Media sites were the third largest category of AI training data.

The case points to other concerns too, such as changing AdSense rates and evidence of improper spoliation of evidence on Google's part through its destruction of chat messages — an issue raised in the recent Epic Games lawsuit against Google over app store antitrust issues, which Epic won.



---


# The Google Antitrust Case

The Google antitrust case is the U.S. government's trial over Google's dominance in the online search market, stemming from a 2020 antitrust claim, in which the government argues that Google uses its platforms and its deals with partners to block out competition in search or advertising and thereby to hinder competitors from accessing the data they would need to improve their products.

Its defining features are the conduct at issue and the defence offered against it. Google CEO Sundar Pichai testified Monday in the trial, defending Google's business tactics, including its deal with Apple and other partners to make Google the default search engine. Google's answer is that it is just doing business: everybody wants Google as the default engine because it is the best, and that, the company says, does not make its actions illegal.

The important boundary case is which Google antitrust matter this is. The 2020 search claim is separate from the one filed in January by the Department of Justice, along with eight states including New York, California and Colorado, which aims to "halt Google's anticompetitive scheme, unwind Google's monopolistic grip on the market and restore competition to digital advertising." The search case and the digital-advertising case are distinct proceedings and should not be conflated.

The trial is the venue in which the underlying numbers surface. Monday's hearing revealed plenty of juicy tidbits, including the $26.3 billion Google spent making itself the default search engine across platforms in 2021, and how Google tried to take it further and have Chrome preinstalled on iPhones.



---


# Google's Parallel Antitrust Proceedings In Late 2023

As of mid-November 2023, Google was fighting antitrust on more than one front at once. The Epic Games case was not its only antitrust case in trial: Google had settled a separate antitrust lawsuit with dating site Match Group the week before November 13, and on November 6 it went to trial with Fortnite maker Epic Games, which hoped to prove that Google engages in anticompetitive behavior with regard to its Android app store, Google Play, and its commission structure. Separately, Google was involved in an antitrust lawsuit with the Department of Justice over its alleged search monopoly.

The Epic case had shed co-plaintiffs on its way to trial. Epic's lawsuit originally involved Match and several U.S. attorneys general, but Google reached a settlement with the attorneys general in October 2023 and with Match the week before November 6, so Epic fought the antitrust battle on its own. The lawsuit, held in the U.S. District Court in California's Northern District, would include testimony from a number of Google and Android execs, including CEO Sundar Pichai, and Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, as well as from Apple, Netflix and other Android developers. Epic, meanwhile, had lost its antitrust battle with Apple and was asking the Supreme Court to weigh in.



---


# Associated Press And OpenAI's Licensing Deal

Select news outlets proved far more amenable to OpenAI than the authors suing it. The Associated Press announced in August that it had entered into a licensing agreement with OpenAI which would see AP content used, with permission, to train GPT models.

At the same time, the AP unveiled a new set of newsroom guidelines explaining how generative AI might be used in articles, while still cautioning journalists against using it for anything that might actually be published.
