# Manchester United's European Decline Since Ferguson

The Independent argued on 12 December 2023 that Manchester United's 1-0 defeat to Bayern Munich should have been a landmark low but instead felt grimly routine, because group-stage elimination has become the club's normal European outcome in the post-Ferguson era rather than an aberration.

The grounds are frequency and pattern. Manchester United, one of the grandest and richest names in this competition, have again gone out of the Champions League at the group stage; it is the third time it has happened since Sir Alex Ferguson, meaning it is their most common round of exit in that period. The night is presented as one more entry in a decade of disappointment in a competition in which this club rose to its most emotional heights — a low, but just part of that longer run.

The warrant is the gap between the occasion and the performance. These are not the sounds we are used to hearing after that Champions League theme; something does stir when the anthem is played at Old Trafford amid the lights — well, for most, that is, except the players. United should not be performing like this on what is supposed to be the classic European night at Old Trafford, and the display was a reminder that all they are going to have for some time are their memories. Having been involved in so many ludicrously chaotic matches, the biggest of all ended up being a non-event: this game never threatened to stir anything, and United never threatened at all. That, the argument runs, can now be talked about definitively, since it has been decisively ended.



---


# The Manchester United Takeover Bidding Process, 2022-2023

The sale process for Manchester United ran for roughly eleven months from November 2022, when the Glazer family announced they were open to offers, to mid-October 2023, when the withdrawal of Qatari bidder Sheikh Jassim bin Al Thani left Sir Jim Ratcliffe clear to complete a partial takeover, as reported by talkSPORT on 18 October 2023.

It was in November 2022, while Qatar was hosting the controversial 2022 World Cup, that the deeply unpopular Glazers revealed they were looking to cash in all or at least some of their shares, a decision that had United fans rejoicing. The move was mainly influenced by the fact that Raine had brokered a deal with Todd Boehly to commit £4.5bn to take control of Chelsea, which gave the Glazers grand ideas that they could rake in as much as double that for a global sporting institution like United. After several rounds of bidding the race narrowed to a straight shootout between Oldham-born Ratcliffe, who had previously offered £4bn to buy Chelsea, and Sheikh Jassim bin Al Thani, who professed to being a lifelong Red Devils fan and set up the "'92 Foundation" in tribute to the famous class of '92 of David Beckham and company.

It had initially been hoped the process would conclude in time for the summer transfer window, but the longer it dragged on — prompting several large-scale protests from United fans — the more apparent it became that Joel and Avram were reluctant sellers, as talkSPORT revealed in March. Sheikh Jassim's public statement promising to restore United "to former glories" was also seen as a thinly veiled swipe at the Glazers, which did not help his negotiating hand. The Qatari banker's patience finally snapped, and his withdrawal at the end of the preceding week left the pathway clear for Ratcliffe to complete what he has always viewed as his dream purchase. At times the saga resembled an X-Factor style judges' houses audition.



---


# Preview Of Chelsea's December 2023 Visit To Old Trafford

Manchester United would love a repeat of the previous season's 4-1 home win over Chelsea when the Blues visited Old Trafford that Wednesday, per Sporting News on Dec. 5, 2023.

The pressure on United had grown again following their lacklustre 1-0 defeat at Newcastle on the Saturday, and another setback against a Chelsea side — who beat Brighton & Hove Albion 3-2 the following day — would worsen the misery around Old Trafford.

Sporting News framed the meeting as one between two heavyweights of world football: United and Chelsea are two of only seven teams to have won the modern Premier League, and are only behind Liverpool when it comes to English success with European trophies. Chelsea's recent record against United was poor, but they had won the Premier League twice since United last did so in the 2012/13 season and could exploit the poor form of Ten Hag's side. The article set out to look at a rivalry that stretches back decades and had been sharply in focus over recent years.



---


# Manchester United's 2023/24 Champions League Elimination

Manchester United were out of Europe altogether after a limp display against Bayern at Old Trafford, where Kingsley Coman sealed a 1-0 win for Thomas Tuchel's side on the final day of Champions League group-stage play, per Sporting News on Dec. 12 and Dec. 13, 2023.

The Red Devils finished bottom of their four-team group, leaving them eliminated from Europe in their worst performance in the competition since 2005. On top of that, they set the record for most goals against in a Champions League group stage by an English club, with 15 conceded in their six games.

Their defensive record had collapsed as the season went on: from a Premier League standpoint they sat eighth in the English top flight, but their -5 goal differential was the worst of any club in the top 10.



---


# Harry Kane, The Striker Manchester United Did Not Sign

Harry Kane, the England captain and the forward Manchester United neglected to bid for in the summer, unlocked United's defence with a lovely flick to set up Bayern Munich's winner on 12 December 2023 — a reminder, The Independent wrote, of what could have been for United.

The comparison the reports draw is with the striker United did buy. Rasmus Hojlund has at least struck in the Champions League, but in domestic competitions he has been outscored 18-0 by Kane. United, cast out of continental competition altogether, became just the fourth English team to prop up a Champions League group when it concluded, and there was something predictable about the manner of their demise.

The Bayern game also showed one reason why Kane is at Germany's biggest club rather than England's: his side are through with ease and among the favourites for the competition, even if they do look lacking in a few areas.



---


# Manchester United Recent Champions League Failures

Thirty years on from Istanbul, United headed to Turkey knowing they had rarely been convincing in the Champions League in recent years, The Guardian reported on Nov. 27, 2023: a 3-1 away win against Paris Saint-Germain in the 2018-19 round of 16, after losing the home leg 2-0, was the last time they won a crunch match.

In 2020-21 they lost their final two group games and were eliminated, while back in 2015-16 Wolfsburg won the deciding group match to knock them out. United had done little learning in recent times, repeating the same failures in Europe's elite competition. It would not be a disgrace to lose against a good Galatasaray team, especially given Erik ten Hag was missing key players, but if the worst happened, everyone would need to come out of the experience stronger — regardless of the result, it should be a night of education about the demands of the Champions League.



---


# Manchester United's 2023-24 Champions League Group-Stage Record

Manchester United finished bottom of their 2023-24 Champions League group with four points, in fourth place, eliminated from European competition altogether rather than dropping into the Europa League, The Independent reported on 12 December 2023.

The decisive results came from outside the Bayern fixture. It was not Bayern who eliminated them: it was Galatasaray, who won at Old Trafford and scored six goals over 180 minutes against United, and FC Copenhagen, who qualified instead of them — Rasmus Hojlund's former club will be in the last 16 while his current one will not, making Copenhagen the anomalies in the draw, the outsiders with the spot that had seemed reserved for United. The second place United aimed for went instead to Copenhagen, a club with a fraction of United's budget, and that is where the damage was done. On the final night the Danish side's victory over Galatasaray ensured any United win would be irrelevant, leaving only a slim hope beforehand.

The campaign produced records of the wrong kind. When Coman scored, United became the first Premier League side to concede 15 goals in a Champions League group stage. United won a lone game in the competition, and even that required a penalty save to deny FC Copenhagen a draw. Two months earlier Raphael Varane had said United could win the Champions League; the quadruple Champions League winner may need a rethink. There was no hint of a repeat of their most famous comeback against Bayern, nor even the sense of heroic failure that accompanied their 2010 quarter-final exit to the same club — just crushing failure. When Maguire hobbled off holding his groin and Evans came on, United had a man who played in their 2007-08 Champions League-winning campaign dragooned into service 16 years later.

qid: Did the article from 'The Age' about Tyler Mitchell suggest that his career has been unsuccessful due to his early photography experiences, while the article from 'The Roar | Sports Writers Blog' about Graham Arnold indicates that his career choices involved staying with the Australian national team despite offers from Europe?
context:
# Graham Arnold Socceroos Coaching Appearance Record

Graham Arnold would prowl the technical area for a 59th time on the Thursday, taking him clear of Frank Farina as the Socceroos' record-holder for matches coached, in a match against Bangladesh as 2026 World Cup qualifying started, The Roar reported on Nov. 13, 2023.

On the Tuesday, Football Australia CEO James Johnson, who had held firm on Arnold 20 months earlier, congratulated the coach on the impending record-breaking match. In a remarkable few weeks the previous year Arnold had gone from on the nose to a man revived; since then he had been linked to club jobs in Europe but opted to stick with the national team. Arnold, in his second stint as national team manager, also represented the Socceroos 56 times as a player and has been involved in national team coaching ranks since 2000, first as an assistant to Farina and then Guus Hiddink, before a brief period as caretaker coach in 2006. "It's certainly a proud moment and an achievement that I'll reflect on when the time is right," Arnold said. "I look at some of the names on that list – Farina, Arok, Thompson, Rasic – guys I played under or assisted in the early part of my coaching career, and it gives you some perspective on what a journey it's been so far."



---


# Tyler Mitchell On His Career Trajectory And Artistic Outlook

Interviewed by The Age ahead of the NGV Triennial and published on 27 November 2023, Mitchell says early success does not unsettle him — "The idea of the road ahead only excites me" — and that he deliberately allows himself space for quiet periods and for work that does not come off.

He traces his choice of medium to impatience: "I was impatient when I got started and just wanted to make visual things now, and I didn't want to wait for permission, or didn't want to wait on equipment, or didn't want to lug large amounts of equipment up flights of stairs. I just wanted to make something that I felt compelled by, immediately." His career has only blossomed in the years since the trip that started him in photography, and where some artists might feel trepidation at so much success so early, he is clear-eyed about the rhythm of a long career: there will be "very quiet, sleepy periods, and frenetic periods, or hyperactive periods", and it is "always refreshing as a young person to see how the career of a much older, more senior artist has really gone" — senior artists we know and love today "had decades where they were out of style, out of fashion, people thought their work was done, their best work was behind them, and yet, often had resurgences".

Crafting a career, he says, means "allowing space for bad and good, allowing space for artists to make and work through complicated and sometimes not-so-favourable ideas. And I try to give myself that same space. It's only about giving yourself grace and space and thinking one day at a time." Asked about a dream project or collaborator, he says there are too many; with one monograph behind him — 2020's I Can Make You Feel Good — he is hungry to make more.



---


# Graham Arnold 2022 World Cup Qualification Crisis

In March 2022 Graham Arnold seemed a dead man walking — the Socceroos' World Cup qualification campaign was lurching towards failure and the manager was being battered from all sides, The Roar recounted on Nov. 13, 2023.

Arnold's team had finished seven points off automatic qualification for Qatar after a shocking run of one win in seven games, leaving them facing an Asian playoff against the United Arab Emirates and then another against Peru to make the finals. While rumours swirled and ex-players and fans bayed for his blood, Football Australia took the pragmatic course and stuck by Arnold — a decision that likely had more to do with the lateness of the hour and financial considerations than any overwhelming faith in Arnie to turn around the fortunes. But he did just that, with qualification and an excellent run at the finals, bowing out to eventual champions Argentina after nearly taking them to extra time. He also got to answer critics like Mark Bosnich and Craig Foster, bluntly rejecting their negativity with a dismissive "who cares?" — which would have tasted sweet.



---


# Graham Arnold Reflections On Coaching Development

Reflecting on his milestone, Graham Arnold said his 2006 caretaker period taught him a great deal about coaching and that, on reflection, he probably was not ready for it — as quoted by The Roar on Nov. 13, 2023.

"I think back to that caretaker period and how much I learnt about coaching; it was a challenging experience and one that on reflection I probably wasn't ready for. I'm grateful for the opportunity I was given and what it was able to teach me ahead of my pathway into club coaching," he said. "I was able to put lessons from that time into practice, develop and eventually return to the Socceroos much more prepared for the role. It's been a privilege to be part of the national team again with the benefit of that experience, and I'm immensely proud of what this group has been able to achieve in the last four years. In my opinion, there's no greater honour than representing your nation on the international stage. I look at the young players coming through the Socceroos system now full of pride in the work they've put in to get where they are, and the journey that's ahead of them. I've always loved being a part of the Socceroos culture and my desire to see Australia fulfil its footballing potential is still driving me to take this group to further success."



---


# James Johnson Tribute To Graham Arnold

Football Australia CEO James Johnson paid tribute to Graham Arnold in a statement marking the coach's milestone, calling him one of the greatest contributors to the Socceroos, as reported by The Roar on Nov. 13, 2023.

"Graham is one of the greatest contributors to the Socceroos," Johnson said. "He's been a constant in the Australian football landscape for more than 30 years as both a player and coach, being a part of some of the Socceroos most memorable moments. Anyone who knows Arnie will tell you he bleeds green and gold. His love for the Socceroos and football in Australia is both infectious and inspiring. That energy and passion is a huge element to the way he's able to lead and inspire our nation's best male footballers in some of our sport's most challenging arenas. On behalf of Football Australia, I'd like to congratulate Arnie on everything he's achieved in reaching this milestone and we look forward to him continuing to build on what is already an exceptional legacy."



---


# Tyler Mitchell's Vogue Covers And NGV Triennial Works

Tyler Mitchell was just 23 when he became the first Black photographer to shoot the cover of American Vogue, photographing Beyoncé, and in November 2023 three of his works were on show in the NGV's Triennial exhibition, The Age reported on 27 November 2023.

His dreamy, delicately hued Beyoncé portraits spoke of a precocious visual talent, and in the five years since he has exhibited around the world, become an Instagram darling with more than 500,000 followers, and shot what became the most controversial vice-presidential portrait in living memory. When his portrait of Kamala Harris dressed in sneakers and casual clothing was chosen for the cover of Vogue for February 2021, the social media backlash was swift: critics questioned why his alternative image — in which Harris looked more vice-presidential — had not been used instead, and the magazine, bowing to outrage over the perceived lack of respect shown to the first woman to reach such high office, later issued a limited edition using the more formal shot. The controversy did little to dent the New York-based photographer's reputation as a rising star of the medium.

Of the three Triennial works, Picnic depicts a family gathering — young men throwing a football, a child lifted on shoulders, wicker baskets and a thermos, and in the background a darkened wood that perhaps hints at the fragility of a moment so peaceful and pure. In the others his figures are arranged across a sandy expanse in idealised depictions of Black American leisure: in Albany, Georgia a football flies through the air, a father in dress shirt and tails twirls a child, and a young boy rides a toy truck; Vastness focuses on a teenage boy standing patiently as his younger siblings stretch his wildly elongated sleeves out beside him, with a dog nearby sitting listening to a violinist. These carefully staged set-ups are evidence of Mitchell's desire to establish a new visual narrative for Black Americans.



---


# Jordan Morgan's Senior Day At Arizona Stadium

Fifth-year senior captain Jordan Morgan, who had missed his opportunity to play in Senior Day the previous season due to injury, said that being able to compete and win in his final game at Arizona Stadium "means so much." The Tucson native was playing at home for the last time in his career.

"I finally got to finish off with a bang like this at home for the last time in my career, so really enjoyed it," Morgan said.

# Swift And Kelce's Public Appearances Together

Taylor Swift and Travis Kelce appeared together publicly through the autumn of 2023, at his games, at her concerts, and away from both. On 22 October Swift returned to Arrowhead Stadium to watch the Kansas City Chiefs beat the Los Angeles Chargers — her fourth time attending one of Kelce's games amid ongoing reports that they were dating — and the pair seemingly confirmed the relationship there. # Travis Kelce's Moustache Remark And New York Visit

qid: Between the report from The Sydney Morning Herald on the Federal Reserve's stance on interest rate decisions published on October 1, 2023, and the report from The Sydney Morning Herald on investors' expectations regarding the Federal Reserve's interest rate policy published on November 5, 2023, was there a change in the sentiment regarding the Federal Reserve's approach to interest rates?
context:
# Federal Reserve Rate Path Expectations Late 2023

By early December 2023 traders widely expected the Federal Reserve to hold its key interest rate steady at its meeting the following week before potentially cutting rates in March, according to data from CME Group, and Fed officials had recently hinted that the federal funds rate may already be at its peak, above 5.25 per cent, up from nearly zero early in 2022. Fed Chair Jerome Powell and others nevertheless warned Wall Street against being overzealous in its predictions about how early a cut could happen.

The bond market moved with those expectations. With inflation down from its peak two summers earlier, Wall Street was hopeful the Fed might be done with its market-shaking hikes. Investors were looking for a slowdown in the job market that came through employers cutting back on open positions rather than laying off workers, and the report cited showed employers advertised just 8.7 million jobs on the last day of October, down 617,000 from a month earlier. US Treasury yields continued to sag from the heights reached during late October: the 10-year yield fell to 4.18 per cent from 4.26 per cent late on the Monday, after having been above 5 per cent and at its highest level in more than a decade during October. The two-year Treasury yield, which more closely tracks Fed expectations, fell from 4.61 per cent just before the economic reports to 4.57 per cent, yo-yoed, and then eased back to 4.57 per cent. Lower yields were one reason cryptocurrency prices had been rising, alongside excitement about a possible bitcoin exchange-traded fund that helped send bitcoin above $US43,000 ($65,600); Robinhood Markets reported a roughly 75 per cent jump in crypto trading volumes during November from a month earlier, said customers added about $US1.4 billion in net deposits during the month, and its own stock rose 10.3 per cent.

A month earlier, in early November 2023, the same expectations were forming from a lower base. Before that week, stocks had been struggling under the weight of rapidly rising Treasury yields catching up to the Fed's main interest rate, which was above 5.25 per cent and at its highest level since 2001. Higher rates and yields slow the economy, hurt investment prices and raise the risk of something breaking in the financial system, such as the three high-profile US bank failures that rattled markets during the spring. "It was really fear that the Fed was going to go too far," said Katie Nixon, chief investment officer for Northern Trust Wealth Management. The Fed had applied that pressure intentionally, hoping to starve inflation of its fuel and to cool the job market, particularly pay raises, because it feared too-strong pay gains could create a vicious cycle keeping inflation high. Analysts said the Friday jobs report offered encouraging signals, with average hourly earnings rising less in October from September than expected, though it did not mean the job was done. Treasury yields tumbled immediately after that report, with the 10-year easing to 4.52 per cent from 4.67 per cent late Thursday and from more than five per cent the previous week, when it hit its highest level since 2007. Traders then moved up expectations for the first Fed cut, potentially by the summer, according to CME Group data. Foreign-exchange strategists at Bank of America wrote in a BofA Global Research report that for investors around the world the "Fed matters more than other central banks" and weak US data is "the only game-changer for markets". A separate report that Friday from the Institute for Supply Management said growth in US services industries such as finance and construction was weaker than economists expected and suggested a slight easing in prices.



---


# How Treasury Yields And "Higher For Longer" Transmit To Equities

Treasury bonds are seen as some of the safest investments possible, and when they pay higher yields, investors are less likely to pay high prices for stocks and other riskier investments — which is a big reason why the S&P 500 dropped 4.9 per cent in September 2023, dragging what had been a big gain for the year down to 11.7 per cent.

The chain running into those yields is the Federal Reserve's stance. Treasury yields have been climbing sharply as Wall Street accepts a new normal in which the Fed is likely to keep interest rates high for longer; the Fed is trying to push still-high inflation down to its target, and its main tool of high interest rates does that by trying to slow the economy and hurting prices for investments. The Fed's main interest rate is at its highest level since 2001, and the central bank indicated the previous week that it may cut interest rates next year by less than it earlier expected. The data cuts both ways within this model. Friday's economic data showed that not only was inflation a touch cooler than expected in August, so was growth in spending by US consumers, which can be a positive for inflation because it means not as many dollars are pouring into purchases and that in turn could give companies less encouragement to raise prices further — but it may also dent what has been a big driver keeping the US economy out of a recession.



---


# US Treasury Yields And Fed Rate Expectations In October 2023

The mechanism linking data to yields to stocks ran in both directions during October 2023. On 4 October, the yield on the 10-year Treasury, the centrepiece of the bond market, pulled back from its highest level since 2007, down to 4.73 per cent from 4.80 per cent late on the Tuesday, with shorter- and longer-term yields also easing to allow more oxygen for the stock market. Yields fell following reports indicating a slowing US economy, the first suggesting that hiring by employers outside the government was much weaker than expected; on Wall Street that is currently good news because a cooling job market could mean less upward pressure on inflation, which in turn could convince the Federal Reserve to take it easier on interest rates. After already raising its main interest rate to the highest level since 2001, the Fed had indicated it may keep its overnight rate higher next year than earlier expected, and Treasury yields had correspondingly snapped higher as traders accept a new normal of high rates for longer; the Fed pays particular attention to the job market because too much strength there could drive wages much higher, which it fears could keep inflation well above its target of 2 per cent.

By 12 October the same mechanism was running the other way. The stock market has largely been taking its cue from the bond market recently, and weak results announced in the afternoon for an auction of 30-year Treasury bonds sent yields of all kinds higher; higher yields can knock down prices for stocks and slow the economy by making borrowing more expensive. Yields had already been rising in the morning after a report showing consumer-level inflation a touch higher than economists expected, raising worries about the Fed keeping its main interest rate high for a long time as it tries to undercut inflation by knocking down investment prices and slowing the economy. The report also had encouraging nuggets: after ignoring prices for food and fuel, which Fed officials see as a better predictor of where inflation is heading, prices consumers paid were in line with expectations and continued to decelerate from earlier months. A second report said slightly fewer US workers than expected applied for unemployment benefits, indicating a job market with few lay-offs and therefore strength for the overall economy, though it could also add fuel to upward pressure on inflation. After the reports the 10-year Treasury yield rose to 4.7 per cent from 4.56 per cent late Wednesday, and the two-year Treasury yield, which more closely tracks expectations for the Fed, climbed to 5.06 per cent from 4.99 per cent, with yields still down slightly for the week after regressing from more-than-decade highs following speeches that investors saw as hints the Fed may not raise its main overnight rate further. The big jump for the 10-year yield since the summer has pulled mortgage rates to their highest levels since the turn of the millennium, and such moves could slow the economy without requiring more Fed hikes; Seema Shah, chief global strategist at Principal Asset Management, said nothing in Thursday's inflation report should sway the Fed one way or the other on what it will do on 1 November, calling the data "reassuringly uneventful".



---


# The Wall Street September 2023 Selloff And Bond Yields

September 2023 brought a loss of 5.2 per cent so far for the S&P 500, putting it on track to be the worst month of the year by far, as the realisation set in that the Federal Reserve would indeed keep interest rates high for a long time. That growing understanding sent yields in the bond market to their highest levels in more than a decade, which in turn undercut prices for stocks and other investments.

Treasury yields rose again on Tuesday, 2023-09-26, following a mixed batch of reports on the economy: the yield on the 10-year Treasury edged up to 4.55 per cent from 4.54 per cent late on Monday and is near its highest level since 2007, up sharply from about 3.5 per cent in May and from 0.5 per cent about three years ago. One economic report that Tuesday showed confidence among consumers was weaker than economists expected — concerning because strong spending by US households has been a bulwark keeping the economy out of a long-predicted recession.

qid: Has the approach of Sportsbooks in adjusting betting lines and odds, as reported by Sporting News before October 4, 2023, and before November 1, 2023, remained consistent?
context:
# Why Moneyline Odds Change

Lines at sports betting apps change quickly for two primary reasons — public betting and new information — and sportsbooks adjust moneyline odds to stay profitable, balance their book and reflect the most current information about an event. Before setting odds oddsmakers gather extensive data, then release the finalized odds to the public; from that point a bettor can bet immediately or wait for shifts, though predicting those shifts is challenging.

The time dimension shows how an opening price drifts. Odds for the next Super Bowl champion released shortly after the previous Super Bowl are based mostly on the recently concluded season; as the new season approaches and teams make changes, the odds adjust to perceived championship chances, and as games progress the lines keep evolving with team performances.

The mechanism has five named drivers. Public betting patterns move a line because, when a significant amount of money lands on one team or participant, sportsbooks adjust the odds to balance their liability — making the price less favorable for the heavily-bet side and more favorable for the less-bet side to encourage even betting and reduce financial risk. New information matters because changes in player injuries, player substitutions or weather conditions alter the perceived outcome, and books adjust once such information becomes public. Professional bettors move lines because large wagers from sharp bettors often reflect insights or information that can influence the odds. Initial miscalculation is a fourth driver: sometimes the opening odds are perceived as offering value, and heavy betting on one side signals that the initial price was potentially "off," prompting an adjustment. Event dynamics is the fifth, applying to live betting placed while the event is in progress, where the evolving dynamics of the match lead to frequent changes.



---


# How Sportsbooks Set And Move Betting Lines

The best sportsbooks employ oddsmakers and oddsmaking services to set their lines and odds, while other sports betting apps simply copy those lines. The oddsmakers and services use computer models and algorithms that consider analytics, statistics, injury and roster news, performance, matchup data and more to develop the lines and odds. Those lines are then subject to change based on the betting public's reaction and any additional information that emerges before the game, and a book will move the line or change the odds if the public bets heavily on one side.

The governing objective is balance rather than prediction. Every sportsbook's goal is to even out the betting on both sides of every bet, because that lets the book earn the small profit built into the odds and lines without worrying about which side wins. Sportsbooks want even betting so much that they will move a line or change the odds specifically to draw more bets to the other side.

The relation that matters to a bettor is that books do not all move together. The betting is rarely the same at every sportsbook: one book may be forced to move a line or change the odds because of the money it has taken while another is not, and the lines and odds may even differ right from the jump. That divergence is what creates the chance to book a bet at improved odds or a more favorable line.

The range over which this holds is narrow and specific. When a line moves for a legitimate reason such as an injury or roster move, every sportsbook jumps on board, and it is difficult to find value; when a line moves because of betting patterns, only the sportsbook that saw that betting makes the change, and that is the opportunity. Line shopping is the tool for spotting the second kind: choose a side, shop around at online sportsbooks, compare the lines and odds, and pounce when you find one offering something different and more favorable to your viewpoint.



---


# Sportsbooks Recommended For Line Shopping

Sporting News names four big brands whose competitive lines in dozens of states make them the books to shop for the best prices. Caesars' odds and lines are consistently among the best in the country, making it a must-see when shopping lines: its point spreads can be a half-point to two points better than the competition's, and the moneyline odds may be more favorable.

The other three each offer a different edge. BetMGM's lines and odds are consistently competitive, and sports betting promos and odds boosts abound, so a better price on many bets can be found there. DraftKings has more open betting markets than most online sportsbooks, with lines and odds that are always competitive. FanDuel is committed to posting competitive odds and runs so many generous promos and odds boosts that it is always worth a look.



---


# Point Spread Odds And Line Movement

Alongside a point spread, sportsbooks attach odds indicating the potential payout relative to the amount wagered, and those odds sit close to even because the spread itself is designed to level the playing field between the two teams. The same payout can be expressed in several formats: American (for example -110 or +110), Decimal (for example 1.91), and Fractional (for example 10/11), each a different way of stating the same potential return.

Point spread odds are not fixed once set; the shifts are commonly called "line movement." Lines move when the point spread or the odds attached to a particular bet change after sportsbooks have initially set them, and Sporting News identifies several drivers. The most common cause is an imbalance in the money being wagered on one side: if a significant majority of bettors back one team to cover, the top sports betting apps adjust the spread to make the other side more appealing and thereby balance the betting action. A second driver is unexpected events — injuries to key players, changes in team strategy, or significant weather events that might affect a game's outcome; for instance, if a star quarterback is announced as injured days before a big game, the spread might shift in favor of the opposing team. A third driver is information and public perception: when a piece of news or a prevailing sentiment about a team's increased chances of winning gains traction, it influences how people bet and leads sportsbooks to adjust their lines accordingly.



---


# When To Place A Futures Bet On The National Championship

Sporting News argues that choosing when to bet on the NCAA football national championship comes down to risk versus reward, with no timing that gives both the best odds and the best information.

The grounds are two opposing effects of waiting. Making your bets when the lines are first released gives you the best odds and potential winnings, but with precious little information — you might back a team that is clearly not going to win by Week 4. The longer you wait, the clearer the picture becomes thanks to data and team performance, but the odds tighten up because sportsbooks are using that same information to make adjustments. The warrant joining them is that sportsbooks price on the same information the bettor gains, so information and price move together: you will have a more educated choice, but the odds will be less favorable and your payout smaller.



---


# Line Movement As A Signal Of Betting Value

Sporting News argues that bettors should monitor line movement before a game starts, because line moves reveal where the value in a bet lies. The claim is stated for both markets it covers: point spread odds can and do change based on a combination of actual betting patterns, unexpected events, and shifts in public perception, and savvy bettors keep a close eye on these line moves, as they can offer insights into where the value lies in a particular bet.

The grounds are how the lines are made and remade. Sportsbooks set game totals considering factors like recent performances, weather, and player status, and as new data emerges and betting trends develop, this line can shift — if many bettors choose the "over," the sportsbook might raise the total to balance the bets. The warrant joining grounds to claim is that line movements often reflect public betting sentiments and therefore offer insights to informed bettors: because a move encodes information the book has absorbed about data and about where the public money is, watching it tells the bettor something they did not otherwise have. Hence bettors must monitor any line changes before the game starts and strategize accordingly to optimize their betting success.

The argument stops short of endorsing either side of a totals bet in the abstract: neither wager holds a universal advantage, and success in over/under betting hinges on a thorough evaluation of both the set line and the competing teams.



---


# How To Line Shop, Including Futures Markets

The easiest way to line-shop is to find a live odds feed that shows the differences between lines and odds for the same bets at many of the top sportsbooks in the country; it is a one-stop shop and takes just seconds. First, look at such a feed for current opportunities. Second, if you want to go further, perform the task manually — it takes longer but lets you check more sportsbooks, or the chosen few you feel consistently offer the best lines and odds. Third, to do that, download and install more than one of the best sports betting apps on your phone. Fourth, tap around among the sportsbooks to compare lines and odds for the bets you plan.

Futures deserve their own pass, and this is where the payoff is largest. People tend to bet futures at their favorite online sportsbook, but shopping for better odds on any futures bet is worth the time: most game lines are similar across sportsbooks, whereas the odds in futures markets can vary significantly.

The precondition for those differences is a book's own exposure, and timing governs whether you capture them. Sportsbooks sometimes carry higher liabilities for specific teams and offer better odds on others to lay that off; get the timing right and you can easily take advantage of changes in different futures markets driven by liability. The limit is that the only way to find these opportunities is to shop lines.

qid: Who, being recognized as a prodigy in Silicon Valley since his early twenties and described as one of the industry's most brilliant and impactful individuals, faced an unexpected event at OpenAI according to 'Fortune' and 'TechCrunch', and is now planning to launch a new venture as reported by 'TechCrunch'?
context:
# Sam Altman's Rise As The Face Of Generative AI

In the year since Altman catapulted ChatGPT to global fame, he became Silicon Valley's sought-after voice on the promise and potential dangers of artificial intelligence, and his sudden and mostly unexplained exit brought uncertainty to the industry's future. He helped start OpenAI as a nonprofit research laboratory in 2015, but it was ChatGPT's explosion into public consciousness that thrust him into the spotlight as a face of generative AI — technology that can produce novel imagery, passages of text and other media. On a world tour in 2023 he was mobbed by a crowd of adoring fans at an event in London.

He has sat with multiple heads of state to discuss AI's potential and perils. On Thursday, 2023-11-16, he took part in a CEO summit at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation conference in San Francisco, where OpenAI is based. At OpenAI's first developer conference the week before, Altman was the main speaker, showcasing a vision for a future of AI agents that could help people with a variety of tasks; days later he announced the company would have to pause new subscriptions to its premium version of ChatGPT because it had exceeded capacity.



---


# Sam Altman's Career Before OpenAI

Sam Altman, 38 as of November 2023, is not trained as an AI engineer, yet has been seen as a Silicon Valley wunderkind since his early 20s. The defining credential of that earlier phase is that he was recruited in 2014 to take the lead of the startup incubator YCombinator.

The reputation attached to him at the time is captured in YCombinator co-founder Paul Graham's 2014 announcement that Altman would become its president: "Sam is one of the smartest people I know, and understands startups better than perhaps anyone I know, including myself." Graham said then that Altman was "one of those rare people who manage to be both fearsomely effective and yet fundamentally benevolent."



---


# Musk's Founding Of OpenAI And His Departure

Convinced that Larry Page's optimistic view of AI was dead wrong, and angry at his loss of DeepMind, Musk built his own lab: OpenAI was founded in late 2015, just a few months after he met with Sam Altman at the Rosewood hotel in Silicon Valley. Musk pumped money into the lab and his former PayPal buddies, Reid Hoffman and Peter Thiel, came along for the ride; the three men and others pledged to put $US1 billion into the project, which Altman, then 30, would help run, and to get started they poached Ilya Sutskever from Google, one of the graduate students Google had "bought" in Hinton's auction. Initially Musk wanted to operate OpenAI as a nonprofit, free from the economic incentives driving Google and other corporations, but by the time Google wowed the tech community with its Go stunt he was changing his mind about how it should be run: he desperately wanted OpenAI to invent something that would capture the world's imagination and close the gap with Google, and it wasn't getting the job done as a nonprofit.

In late 2017 Musk hatched a plan to wrest control of the lab from Altman and the other founders and transform it into a commercial operation that would join forces with Tesla and rely on supercomputers the car company was developing, according to four people familiar with the matter; when Altman and others pushed back, Musk quit and said he would focus on his own AI work at Tesla. In February 2018 he announced his departure to OpenAI's staff on the top floor of the startup's offices in a converted truck factory, three people who attended said; when he said OpenAI needed to move faster, one researcher retorted that Musk was being reckless, and Musk called the researcher a "jackass" and stormed out, taking his deep pockets with him. On the second day of the trial of Sam Bankman-Fried and FTX, the prosecution argued that Bankman-Fried knowingly committed fraud, and it grounded that claim in motive: he did so, prosecutors said, to achieve great wealth, power and influence.

Across the first three weeks of the trial, a run of former colleagues, an outside investor and a forensic accounting expert testified that FTX customer money flowed into Alameda Research and out again to other uses, and that FTX's investors were never told about the two firms' special relationship. TechCrunch's running coverage, published 2023-10-06, summarises each week.

In week one, FTX's co-founder and CTO Gary Wang testified Thursday on the extent to which Alameda Research was used for whatever purposes he and SBF saw fit: according to Wang, the crypto trading firm pulled funding directly from FTX customers, whose transactions would be funneled toward Alameda and then directed elsewhere. Thursday also brought testimony from Matt Huang, co-founder and managing partner at crypto investment firm Paradigm, which invested $278 million in FTX across 2021 and 2022 and is part of a class-action lawsuit accusing it and others of defrauding customers by promoting FTX. Sam Bankman-Fried is in court for alleged fraud and money laundering while leading crypto exchange FTX and sister company Alameda. TechCrunch's 2023-10-02 preview placed the case in the Manhattan Federal Court, describing the disgraced cryptocurrency entrepreneur as accused of orchestrating "one of the biggest financial frauds in American history": the multibillion-dollar collapse of FTX, the crypto exchange he founded and led. SBF, as he is known, has pleaded not guilty to some seven charges of fraud and conspiracy.

The trial kicked off with jury selection October 3. By TechCrunch's 2023-10-06 update the case was entering its next chapter, with proceedings resuming Thursday: as confirmed during a teleconference Wednesday, SBF would be taking the stand along with a handful of other witnesses, as the onus shifted toward the defense after the prosecution brought its case to its conclusion.

Access to the proceedings is limited: no devices are allowed, so reports are being physically put together within the courtroom, or sent to overflow rooms. The jury's composition ranges from a train conductor to a retired investment banker who attended Stanford University, and TechCrunch pointed readers to a special joint episode of its Equity and Chain Reaction podcasts for a better sense of the vibe between the jurors and the rest of the court.

A second account of the same events was arriving in parallel: "Going Infinite," a book by Michael Lewis chronicling the rise and fall of SBF, was set to debut on the first day of the trial.



---


# The Defense's Good-Faith Case For Bankman-Fried

Mark Cohen, one of Sam Bankman-Fried's lawyers, attacked the prosecution's central premise that his client was a liar who stole from customers, stating early in his opening statement that "Sam didn't defraud anyone." The defense's counter-picture is of a nerdy startup founder who acted in "good faith," not the prosecution's "cartoon of a villain"; Cohen repeatedly harped on Bankman-Fried's allegedly good-faith actions throughout his address to the jury. Bankman-Fried, whose cheekbones were more prominent after spending about seven weeks in a Brooklyn prison, appeared in court as this argument was made.

Cohen also disputed the specific claim that Alameda Research was a covert conduit. Alameda was not subterranean or shady, he said; it was a successful hedge fund. FTX was no Ponzi scheme but a "very innovative, successful company." The business practices between the two were reasonable, he argued, claiming that Alameda acted legally as an FTX customer, payment processor, and market maker — that is, a financial entity that acts as a trading partner for customers looking to buy and sell cryptocurrencies.

The defense's warrant for reading failure as something other than fraud was an analogy Cohen employed throughout: "working at a startup is like building a plane as you're flying it," and businesses sometimes fail. He specifically pointed the finger at Ellison, the former CEO of Alameda, who he said did not adequately protect her hedge fund from the inherent risk of the crypto markets. And when the walls came closing in and the aforementioned plane approached the "eye of the storm," Cohen argued, Bankman-Fried did not act like someone who was guilty — he was willing to give up his personal wealth to make customers whole. "In the end, Sam started and built two billion-dollar businesses," he concluded. "He didn't steal any money."



---


# Day Two Of The Bankman-Fried Trial: Jury Selection And The Courtroom Audience

On the second day of Sam Bankman-Fried's fraud trial, the jury was selected on Wednesday morning, after which lawyers for the government and then for Bankman-Fried delivered opening statements that told two very different stories of the former FTX CEO's sudden rise and almost instantaneous fall. The central question framed by the proceedings was who Bankman-Fried, the former CEO of crypto exchange FTX, really is: a liar and a fraud, or someone who acted in good faith and, like many a startup founder, flew too close to the sun. That answer, the account notes, ultimately lies with the jury.

The day featured pointed allegations, a friend from MIT, and an audience replete with big names, including Bankman-Fried's professorial parents and Damian Williams, the U.S. attorney for the Southern District of New York. Bankman-Fried himself spent most of the day in court staring into a laptop while seated between his two attorneys. The prosecution's account of his alleged crimes was described as featuring a study in contrasts.



---


# Matt Huang And Paradigm's FTX Investment

Matt Huang, co-founder and managing partner of Paradigm, a crypto venture capital firm that invested over $275 million in FTX — a stake that was wiped out — was the third witness to take the stand, and testified about his firm's due diligence.

Huang told the court that Bankman-Fried assured him funds would be used for FTX and not Alameda, and that he was promised Alameda had no preferential treatment on the FTX platform, even though the hedge fund was one of its top traders. Huang said he was concerned about FTX's lack of a board of directors but eventually invested anyway. During cross-examination he said Paradigm pressed Bankman-Fried on the board issue and was told he did not want investors as directors but did plan on having a board with experts.

qid: Between the TechCrunch report on Uber's measures to prevent sexual assaults published on October 13, 2023, and the TechCrunch report on Uber's financial performance in Q3 published on November 7, 2023, was there a change in the type of issues being reported about Uber?

# Uber Assault Litigation

Hundreds of women have filed lawsuits against Uber claiming the company hasn't done enough to prevent instances of sexual assault by drivers, and a panel of judges has ruled that more than 80 cases can be consolidated into federal court, TechCrunch reported on 2023-10-13. The stakes are high for both parties, with implications extending to future Uber riders and drivers: the outcome of the case could result in sweeping changes to Uber's platform, which plaintiffs argue will reduce sexual assault and also raise new concerns over privacy. As TechCrunch put it, "Technology lies at the center of this very human story."

Uber has attempted to address sexual assaults by drivers — which the lawsuits claim Uber has known about since 2014 — through new safety features in its app, like a 911 button and the ability to share location with a friend. The additions arrived on a five-year timeline: the 911 button and location-sharing feature were both introduced in 2018; in 2021, Uber introduced a feature that allows riders and drivers to record audio during a trip; and the following year, Uber launched a pilot to provide passengers with live help from an ADT safety agent, as well as PIN verifications to ensure passengers are connected to the correct driver.

Survivors and their attorneys say that response has been inadequate, and they're calling for better technological solutions like in-vehicle surveillance cameras. Rachel Abrams — a sexual assault attorney and partner at law firm Peiffer Wolf Carr Kane Conway & Wise, one of the law firms working on the multidistrict litigation, who filed the petition to consolidate the various actions in federal court — argues the app-based solutions are half-measures that haven't quelled instances of sexual violence against passengers on the platform. Mandatory in-vehicle cameras in Uber cars is "essential for safety," she says, citing data from studies of taxis equipped with in-vehicle cameras, which she says has drastically reduced instances of sexual assaults against passengers, as well as assault of passengers against drivers.

Uber told TechCrunch it cannot comment on pending litigation but said it remains committed to the safety of all users on its platform.



---


# Counterarguments On Uber's Assault Rate And Duty Of Care

Uber's reported decrease in the rate of sexual assault does not establish that the platform got safer, because the denominator moved and several categories moved the wrong way. While the rate decrease is positive, not all the data delivers the same message: over the same period, the total number of sexual assault reports across five categories fell from 5,981 to 3,824, a drop that could be explained by the decrease of trips from 1.4 billion in 2019 to 650 million in 2020.

The category-level breakdown attacks the inference more directly. While the total number of incidents as a percentage of total number of rides does decrease through the years, the number of incidents in certain categories actually increases — nonconsensual kissing, nonconsensual touching and nonconsensual penetration, or rape, all rose between 2017 and 2019. The total number of rape incidents also rose from 2017 to 2019, and while the number of reported rapes dropped in 2020, the rate has remained the same since 2017. In other words, there has not been an improvement in the rate of rapes on the platform. TechCrunch reported this reading on 2023-10-13.

A second contested premise is procedural. Uber has been sued numerous times over the past few years by passengers who claim they were sexually assaulted during a ride, and Lyft has faced similar lawsuits and accusations. Under Uber's terms of use, class action lawsuits can't be filed against the company in cases of sexual assault, so each case has to be heard individually — which has prevented survivors from advocating for themselves collectively. Judge Charles Breyer in the Northern District of California will preside over pretrial hearings, the first time a federal judge is able to make decisions for a large amount of these cases, which will streamline the proceedings; Breyer may preside over the trials depending on whether the parties agree, and if they do not, the cases go back to their home jurisdiction for trial. Another consolidated lawsuit has also been filed against Uber in California, but it only covers survivors in that state.

Uber's own counter goes to duty rather than to data. It has attempted, through several filings for motions to dismiss, to stop the consolidation of these cases, arguing that the company did not owe a duty to the plaintiffs to protect against criminal conduct. Lawyers representing the survivors will therefore have to prove that Uber owed a duty of care to passengers, including the duty of taking reasonable precautions to ensure their safety. The pretrial matters, including witness and expert depositions and document discovery, will be heard by Judge Charles Breyer, and Abrams expects the timeline of the proceedings to last over the next one to two years.



---


# In-Car Camera Proposal

Uber's in-app safety features cannot work for the riders who need them most, so survivors are asking for in-vehicle surveillance and more extensive background checks instead — the argument attorney Rachel Abrams put to TechCrunch on 2023-10-13. Abrams argues that Uber's safety features are insufficient because they're all app-based and only potentially useful if a rider has access to their own phone.

The grounds are the circumstances in which the assaults she has handled actually occurred. "The majority of clients I represent and the women I've spoken to who have been sexually assaulted have experienced: (A) someone else ordered the ride for them; (B) their phone is dead or they can't locate their phone to use the safety shield; or (C) if they could use their phone, they're incapacitated," said Abrams. She says she has interviewed upward of 5,000 survivors over the course of several years and has seen no difference in the number of attacks before or after implementation of these in-app features.

The demands go beyond cameras. Aside from in-vehicle surveillance and more extensive background checks, the survivors are asking Uber to implement driver training on interactions with passengers, a zero-tolerance policy for drivers, sexual harassment education and training, and a more adequate system to encourage customer reporting and monitor customer complaints. On screening, Uber has lobbied against additional background requirements for drivers, which has given the company authority to conduct its own background checks with little or no oversight, unlike most taxi operators. Uber and Lyft say smudged fingerprints can lead to inaccurate results and that fingerprint checks reference historical arrest records, which can have discriminatory effects on some minority communities that face disproportionately high arrest rates; an Uber spokesperson told CNN arrest records are incomplete and often lack information about whether a person has been convicted of a crime.

The evidentiary record available to test the claim is partial. Uber hasn't released safety data for 2021 and 2022, and won't say when it plans to do so, though older data backs up some of Abrams' claims. Uber has published two safety reports — one containing data from 2017 to 2018 and another with data from 2019 to 2020 — and the ride-hail company claims that the rate of sexual assault reported on the app decreased 38% between its first and second reports.



---


# Uber's Q3 2023 Headline Results

Uber reported third-quarter earnings on Tuesday, November 7, 2023 that show a profitable ride-hail and delivery company chugging along in spite of slowing growth in some sectors.

The company reported revenue of $9.3 billion, an 11% increase year over year. Investors had expected Uber to report revenues of around $9.5 billion (FactSet, Refinitiv), meaning that despite the company's growth it fell short of estimates. Turning to profitability, Uber reported net income of $221 million in the third quarter, or 10 cents per share, compared with a net loss of $1.2 billion, or 61 cents per share, in the same quarter the prior year — again short of expectations that it would generate 12 cents in per-share profit.

Looking ahead, Uber anticipates gross bookings of $36.5 billion to $37.5 billion, up just 6% at the top end from its Q3 result. After reporting, shares of Uber were up 1.6% in trading, after an up-and-down morning of shares exchange.



---


# Uber's Results As A Macro Signal For Startups

The claim is that Uber's quarterly results carry information beyond Uber, and that the same numbers support two readings. Against a backdrop of macroeconomic uncertainty, the former startup darling's results can be viewed as an indication that its business model has matured and is now in a stable, profitable and cash-generating position. On the other hand, under-performing demand results from a company as global as Uber could indicate that consumer spend is coming in lighter than anticipated.

The warrant for treating it as a signal at all is Uber's role in its sector: for startups in the transport and on-demand sectors, Uber's earnings are a regular informational zeitgeist, which is why it is worth understanding where Uber's revenue came from in the third quarter and how each of its top-line sources converted — or not — to bottom-line results.

TechCrunch's own reading: the vibe when discussing Uber's results internally was that it is a very profitable and healthy company today, albeit one not growing as fast as the market had hoped. The fact that Uber's share price was up at the time of writing indicates investors are content thus far to excuse the small Q3 misses and keep their eyes more focused on year-over-year improvements and forward guidance — with more to say when Lyft's numbers arrive.

# Cranberry Industry Scale And Urann's Legacy

Marcus Urann turned a hyper-local fruit into an international industry — Ocean Spray reports today that fresh cranberries account for only 5% of the fruit's production — FOX News Lifestyle reported on 23 November 2023.

"Marcus Urann was very influential in expanding the cranberry market," Brian Wick, executive director of Massachusetts Cranberries, told Fox News Digital. "And that influence is still felt today." When Urann bought his first cranberry bog in 1906, cranberries were available only in the autumn and only fresh; the 5% figure is a testament to the exponential explosion of the industry he inspired, with the fruit now sold internationally as sauce and in juice, much as Urann first conceived in 1912.

The United States is easily the world's largest grower of a fruit essential to the flavour of its national holiday dinner table: American farmers grow twice as many cranberries as No. 2 Canada and about 20 times the production of third-place Chile, according to data from the Cranberry Institute in Carver, Massachusetts, next to Plymouth. Wisconsin, meanwhile, surpassed Massachusetts decades ago as the nation's top cranberry grower. Six out of 10 Americans say cranberry sauce has and always will be on their Thanksgiving table, while more than one third say they "can't live without" it on Thanksgiving, according to Ocean Spray.

# Urann's Canned Cranberry Sauce, 1912

Marcus Urann introduced a way to put cranberries in a can in 1912, inventing the commercial canned cranberry jelly central to Thanksgiving celebrations nationwide today, FOX News Lifestyle reported on 23 November 2023.

Urann purchased cranberry farms in Massachusetts early in the 20th century and saw the cranberry differently — "a global industry crawling along the bogs of Massachusetts". "After he set up cooking facilities at a packinghouse in Hanson, Massachusetts, he began to consider ways to extend the short selling season of the berries," Smithsonian Magazine reported in a 2013 history of cranberries. "Canning them, in particular, he knew would make the berry a year-round product." In 1912 Urann began processing gelled cranberries in cans — cranberry sauce.

"As modest as this seems, Urann's maneuver was revolutionary," write Cox and Walker. "For a fruit that had been marketed almost exclusively as a fresh product, it was a radical proposal to cook and to can." Most importantly, cranberries could now be sold to consumers far from where they were grown.



---


# The Cranberry Wet-Harvesting Method

Wet harvesting works because of a physical property of the fruit: each cranberry is filled with four chambers of air, so the berries float easily — which let Marcus Urann replace hand-picking with flooding, as FOX News Lifestyle reported on 23 November 2023.

The relation runs in three steps. Previously the tiny berries were usually plucked from dried vines by migrant workers. Urann realised the bog could be floated, the berries agitated from their vines, and then easily rounded up while floating in the water.

The method is one of several innovations in cranberry farming that Urann pioneered.



---


# Cranberry Flower and Pollination Biology

Cranberry flowers are hermaphroditic, like those of roses, lilies and daffodils, meaning they contain both male and female parts, which allows them to self-pollinate instead of relying on birds, insects or other pollinators.

A cranberry blossom has four petals that peel back when the flower blooms, exposing the anthers, which contain the plant's pollen; the flower's resemblance to the beak of a bird earned the cranberry its original name, the "craneberry." When cranberries do not self-pollinate, they rely on bumblebees and honeybees to transport pollen from flower to flower. They can also be propagated sexually, by planting seeds, or asexually, through rooting vine cuttings: seed-based propagation allows for higher genetic diversity, which can translate to things like increased disease resistance or more pest tolerance, while asexual reproduction is equally important because it allows growers to create clones of varieties that perform very well in their bogs and grow even more of those high-performing types.



---


# The American Cranberry's Native Range And Harvest Window

The American cranberry is one of the few fruits native to the northern United States, growing for millennia amid the sandy soils and short summers of southeastern Massachusetts and Cape Cod, FOX News Lifestyle reported on 23 November 2023.

Its discriminating constraints are seasonal and geographic: it has only a brief autumn harvest, from late September to early November, and a short shelf life.

The boundary condition on availability follows from that: fresh cranberries were known only in a few areas of the nation that possess the right combination of sandy soil, long summer days and long winter dormancy.



---


# The Cranberry Genome and Molecular Breeding

The cranberry is a diploid — each cell contains one set of chromosomes from the maternal parent and one from the paternal parent — with 24 chromosomes and a genome size less than one-tenth that of the human genome, which makes it comparatively simple to breed.

Insights like these help scientists better understand where potentially valuable genes might be located in the cranberry genome, and diploid crops tend to have fewer genes associated with a single trait, which makes breeding them to emphasize that trait much simpler. Researchers have also described the genetics of the cultivated cranberry's wild relative, the "small cranberry" (Vaccinium oxycoccos); comparing the two can help determine where the cultivated cranberry's agronomically valuable traits reside in its genome, and where some of the small cranberry's cold hardiness might come from. Researchers are developing molecular markers — tools to determine where certain genes or sequences of interest reside within a genome — to help determine the best combinations of genes from different varieties of cranberry that can enhance desired traits, for example to make the fruits larger, more firm or redder in colour.



---


# Ocean Spray, The Cranberry Cooperative

Ocean Spray is the farming cooperative Marcus Urann created with fellow cranberry farming leaders John Makepeace and Elizabeth Lee, still headquartered in Massachusetts today and synonymous with cranberry juice and cranberry sauce, FOX News Lifestyle reported on 23 November 2023.

Its defining feature is scale and reach: it is one of the world's most successful farming cooperatives, and it has helped spread cranberry farming around the country and around the world while putting cranberry juices and sauces into international markets.

Its signature product remains cranberry sauce. The company first sold its cranberry sauce nationally in 1941, its ridged cranberry gel a familiar sight on Thanksgiving tables around the United States.



---


# Cranberry Air Pockets and Seed Dispersal

Every cranberry contains four air pockets, which is why the berries float when farmers flood bogs to harvest them — and the pockets serve a biological role: they enable the berries to float down rivers and streams to disperse their seeds.

The air pockets also make raw cranberries bounce when dropped on a hard surface, a good indicator of whether they are fresh. The dispersal route matters because the usual alternative is closed off: many other plants disperse their seeds via animals and birds that eat their fruits and excrete the seeds as they move around, but as anyone who has tasted them raw knows, cranberries are ultra-tart, so they have limited appeal for wildlife.



---


# Cranberries And New England Regional Identity

Cranberry bogs remain a signature of the landscape in the land of the Pilgrims, and Marcus Urann framed his work as service to the region: "I felt I could do something for New England," he told the Associated Press in a story that ran around the nation on Thanksgiving in 1959, as reported by FOX News Lifestyle on 23 November 2023.

"For Massachusetts and for this region, they're so much a part of our history and our culture," said Brian Wick of Massachusetts Cranberries. "They've been part of a fabric of our region from Indigenous people until today."

Urann saw what cranberries could be far beyond the land of the Pilgrims, and closed his 1959 remarks with a creed: "You know, everything in life is what you do for others."



---


# Why Cranberries Belong to Thanksgiving

Cranberries' close association with Thanksgiving was simply a practical matter at first: fresh cranberries are ready to harvest from mid-September through mid-November, so Thanksgiving falls within that perfect window for eating them.

Cranberry sauce was first loosely described in accounts from the American colonies in the 1600s and appeared in a cookbook for the first time in 1796. The berries' tart flavour, which comes from high levels of several types of acids, makes them more than twice as acidic as most other edible fruits, so they add a welcome zing to a meal full of blander foods like turkey and potatoes. In recent decades the cranberry industry has branched out into juices, snacks and other products in pursuit of year-round markets, but for many people Thanksgiving is still the time when they are most likely to see cranberries in some form on the menu.

Rehn closed the characterization with a promise to the jury: "You will see the full picture."

# Day Two Of The Bankman-Fried Trial: Jury Selection And The Courtroom Audience

On the second day of Sam Bankman-Fried's fraud trial, the jury was selected on Wednesday morning, after which lawyers for the government and then for Bankman-Fried delivered opening statements that told two very different stories of the former FTX CEO's sudden rise and almost instantaneous fall. The central question framed by the proceedings was who Bankman-Fried, the former CEO of crypto exchange FTX, really is: a liar and a fraud, or someone who acted in good faith and, like many a startup founder, flew too close to the sun. That answer, the account notes, ultimately lies with the jury.

By the time his trial began, TechCrunch's 2023-10-01 account framed the whole story as one question: how did the once third-largest crypto exchange get here?

Across the first three weeks of the trial, a run of former colleagues, an outside investor and a forensic accounting expert testified that FTX customer money flowed into Alameda Research and out again to other uses, and that FTX's investors were never told about the two firms' special relationship.
