qid: Has the portrayal of the 'vampire cause' in Polygon articles remained consistent between the November 9, 2023, article discussing the undermining of vampires' menacing air and the November 15, 2023, article highlighting vampires as a hidden presence in the best versions of stories?
context:
# The Surprise Vampire Trope

The surprise vampire is a story that is not a vampire story but that turns out to have vampires in it — a device Polygon rates cooler than a vampire story proper.

It is a rich tradition, unfolding across many different media intended for all kinds of audiences. Sometimes the surprise vampire is a prominent part of a story that is made richer for the unexpected presence of a bloodsucker. Sometimes it is subtle, an easily missable detail that rewards only the most observant. In the best version, Polygon says, the vampires are always there, in the background, waiting for you to discover them — just like in real life.



---


# Laurell K. Hamilton: Vampire Verdict

Polygon's verdict on Laurell K. Hamilton, author of the Anita Blake: Vampire Hunter series (1993-present), is: not a vampire.

Her books are described as the final evolution of an undead Pokémon. Where Anne Rice made vampires sexy but still took pains to remind readers they were fundamentally the stuff of nightmares, Hamilton's Anita Blake series is more like the merrily obscene aesthetic of a 1970s grindhouse flick: her characters bash, slaughter, and jump one another's bones, animated or otherwise, but it is all in good fun, so the sexy and violent vampire has reached a Looney Tunes stage of madcap romp that audiences cannot get enough of. That is exactly why Polygon acquits her. Nothing serves the vampire cause less than undermining the air of looming menace vampires have been cultivating since the 15th century — Vlad the Impaler worked for that nickname, and the last thing they need is an airport novel making a stake through the heart look fun. So Hamilton is not among the denizens of the undead; she is the one thing they have come to fear this millennium: a good punchline.



---


# Season of Blood's Real Draw Is Quality of Life, Not Vampire Powers

Polygon's claim, published 2023-10-04, is that although Diablo 4's Season of Blood brings some cool new vampire powers into the fold, the real star of the second season is its sweeping quality-of-life changes.

The grounds are what those changes do for ordinary play: players will now have an easier time leveling up, gaining quality loot, and just navigating the open world of Sanctuary.

The warrant is that these improvements touch the activities every player performs constantly, which is why they outweigh a headline feature. The reporting basis is a roundtable interview game director Joe Shely and associate game director Joe Piepiora gave to Polygon and other outlets ahead of Blizzard's Oct. 4 livestream, in which they gave additional context on Nightmare Dungeon changes, Renown, and more.



---


# Diablo 4 Season 2 Vampiric Powers

Season 2 of Diablo 4 adds Vampiric Powers, which allow players to slot five additional abilities into their character to gain new effects.

There are 22 total Vampiric Powers.

Each is class agnostic, meaning no power is unique to any one class. Polygon states this identically in both its Sorcerer build guide of 2023-10-18 and its Barbarian build guide of 2023-10-19.



---


# The Lineage Of English-Language Vampire Fiction

Vampire fiction has a long and distinguished pedigree in English, dating from the moment Robert Southey introduced the British Isles to the concept of the coffin-sleeping undead at the turn of the 19th century.

Polygon's organising claim about that lineage is that it tracks its readership: from that starting point onward, the authors of vampiric stories have mirrored the changing face of the society that reads them.



---


# Which Vampire Authors Were Vampires?

Polygon's comic premise is that scholars have largely turned a blind eye to one lingering question about vampire fiction: which of these authors were themselves nosferatu? Was night-stalking Lord Byron secretly a daywalker? Could Anne Rice's innate understanding of deathless sexiness itself result from her fellowship in the camp of the undead?

The stated warrant for pursuing the question is that until we understand which writers have been secretly propagandizing for Dracular overlords, our understanding of the place of vampires in anglophone culture will never be fully complete. On that basis — in the interest of bettering the cause of human understanding and the avoidance of unwilling resurrection — the piece presents a field guide to secretly vampiric authors, past and present, delivering a verdict on each.



---


# Taika Waititi: Vampire Verdict

Polygon's verdict on Taika Waititi, best known in this line for What We Do in the Shadows (2014, 2019-present), is the guide's most severe: Dracula.

The piece first waves away two objections — What We Do in the Shadows is not a work of prose fiction and Waititi is not an author — with the shrug that who is to say what constitutes true literature anyway. It then gives the work's significance: co-created with fellow New Zealander Jemaine Clement, with the two writing and directing the original 2014 movie, it is surely the most culturally pervasive piece of vampire-themed fiction to reach mass audiences over the past few years, and it marks the necessary next step in the inexorable movement of vampiric lore from creeping terror to sexy camp to outright comedy with only the faintest twist of terror to remind us of its origins — two centuries after its English-language birth, the vampire genre has at last been metaphorically defanged. The grounds for the verdict are Waititi's public trajectory: a director and writer who started out charmingly likable, beloved by audiences and critics, was happily invited into our homes, rapidly wore out his welcome, and almost before we knew it curdled into an odorous pestilence we could not seem to be rid of — and when you lose the Chris Hemsworth demographic, you know you are in trouble. Yet audiences keep coming back year after year, drawn by a force they are powerless to explain; when it comes to Our Flag Means Death, we are all Renfields. And since nothing could serve the vampire cause better than tricking us into thinking the threat had passed, the conclusion is that we have not just found a vampire but their king.



---


# Bram Stoker: Vampire Verdict

Polygon's verdict on Bram Stoker, author of Dracula (1897), is: vampire.

The context is the novel's importance. The real breakthrough moment for vampires in the English-speaking world came just before the turn of the 20th century with Dracula, whose story of a Transylvanian count taking residence in the U.K. to launch a centuries-old plan of vampiric conquest and enslavement became the source of pastiches, spinoffs, and cliches almost from the moment it arrived — codifying the basic elements of vampire storytelling for the next half-century or more. Those elements: the foreign, undead aristocrat whose cosmopolitan charm and suave allure stood in for English fears and paranoias about the allure of other nations and races; the bloodsucking conversion process, targeted invariably at either women or the more effeminate among the male set, that reads alarmingly like seduction; and the vampire hunters' tricks and traps, from wooden stakes to garlic to sunlight to good old simple beheadings. The grounds for the verdict lie in Stoker's biography, which Polygon calls almost the inverse of his noble-born immortal count yet fittingly enigmatic: born to a middle-class Protestant Irish family in the 1840s, his life grew progressively more bizarre, including a keen interest in the occult studies of the Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn and in the history and practices of the Freemasons. Cultivating a public reputation, or seeking inspiration for a never-materialized new hit story, are offered as innocent readings — but it is just possible, the piece concludes, that somewhere along the way Stoker had acquired a membership to the most elite secret society of all.



---


# Miguel O'Hara, Spider-Man 2099

Miguel O'Hara, the Spider-Man of 2099, is one of Spider-Man: Across the Spider-Verse's big enigmas — and one of the few things the film reveals about him is that he is kind of a vampire.

Comics readers will know plenty about his whole deal, but the movie does not really explain much, except for a brief scene showing he has fangs and an offhand reference to the vampirism. Polygon's aside is that he is a jerk but still kind of cool, which it says is hard not to be when you are a vampire — "that's kind of the whole quandary with vampires as a metaphor."



---


# The Elder Scrolls: Vampires Everywhere

The Elder Scrolls games hide vampires beneath a conventional surface, and in keeping with the open-ended role-playing philosophy the series espouses, you can also become a vampire — which Polygon says kicks ass.

The fantasy of the Elder Scrolls games often presents as very straightforward: with the exception of Morrowind, each game starts out as a pretty up-the-middle fantasy setting with nary a twist of any kind. But a big reason the series has an enduring fan base is that beneath the surface there is always weird stuff to find, vampires included.



---


# The Count On Sesame Street

Polygon's entry on The Count is its shortest: the writer does not really know why there is a vampire on Sesame Street, but loves him anyway.

# Day Two Of The Bankman-Fried Trial: Jury Selection And The Courtroom Audience

On the second day of Sam Bankman-Fried's fraud trial, the jury was selected on Wednesday morning, after which lawyers for the government and then for Bankman-Fried delivered opening statements that told two very different stories of the former FTX CEO's sudden rise and almost instantaneous fall. The central question framed by the proceedings was who Bankman-Fried, the former CEO of crypto exchange FTX, really is: a liar and a fraud, or someone who acted in good faith and, like many a startup founder, flew too close to the sun. That answer, the account notes, ultimately lies with the jury.

# Helena World Chronicle's Class Action Antitrust Suit Against Google

A class action lawsuit filed in the week of 15 December 2023 in the U.S. District Court in D.C. accuses Google and parent company Alphabet of anticompetitive behavior in violation of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act and others, on behalf of news publishers. The case was filed by Arkansas-based publisher Helena World Chronicle, which argues that Google "siphons off" news publishers' content, their readers and their ad revenue through anticompetitive means, and it specifically cites new AI technologies such as Google's Search Generative Experience (SGE) and the Bard AI chatbot as worsening the problem.

Helena World Chronicle owns and publishes two weekly newspapers in Arkansas. In the complaint it argues that Google is "starving the free press" by sharing publishers' content on Google, losing them "billions of dollars."

Beyond damages, the suit asks for an injunction that would require Google to obtain consent from publishers before using their website data to train its general artificial intelligence products, including Google's own and those of rivals. It also asks that publishers who opt out of SGE still be allowed to show up in Google search results, among other things.

The law firm handling the case is Hausfeld, whose announcement states that "the anticompetitive effects of Google's scheme cause profound harm to competition, to consumers, to labor, and to a democratic free press," and that "Plaintiff Helena World Chronicle, LLC invokes the Sherman Act and Clayton Act to seek class-wide monetary and injunctive relief to restore and ensure competition for digital news and reference publishing and set up guardrails to preserve a free marketplace of ideas in the new era of artificial intelligence."



---


# Google's Link-Based Ranking And The Market It Created

Google revolutionized search by evaluating websites based on links from other websites, seeing each link as a vote of relevance and trustworthiness — a structure that made the ranking of any page a function of what other pages pointed to it. The founders pledged to be a neutral navigation system with no ads: just a clean white screen with a search box that would bring people off the Google landing page and out to a helpful website as seamlessly as possible. Users quickly decided this link-based sorting methodology was superior to the existing search engines, and by the end of 1999 Google was handling the majority of online queries.

The model arrived in response to a documented problem. In 1997 an Italian professor published a journal article about what he called Search Engines Persuasion: "Finding the right information on the World Wide Web is becoming a fundamental problem," he wrote, and "a vast number of new companies was born just to make customer Web pages as visible as possible," which "has led to a bad performance degradation of search engines."

The relation between votes and rank held only as long as links were scarce and organic, and it did not. Mapstead, like many early practitioners of SEO, figured out how to adapt: almost as soon as Google took over, a secondary market emerged for links. For a few hundred bucks, a firm in India or the Philippines could provide thousands of links from blog networks built entirely for that purpose. It was easy — buy links that led to your site and watch your ranking in Google's results rise.



---


# Search As Private Infrastructure, Not A Public Library

The claim is that routing nearly all online information through a single private company has left us arguably worse off than before, because information that is controlled by a private business will always be subject to that business's bottom line — which is exactly why most countries around the world have libraries that are public institutions.

The grounds are a comparison with what the internet was supposed to be. In the beginning it was seen as an improvement on the spirit of the public library: an opportunity to transcend the gatekeepers controlling who could publish a book, allowing mankind to fully connect and share knowledge. Instead, nearly all online information runs through a single company, which assumes a veneer of civic utility, of impassive authority, when it is very much not a neutral entity.

Matt Cutts supplies the insider warrant that the veneer is doing work. "There were so many true believers at Google in the early days," he said. "As companies get big, it gets harder to get things done. Inevitably, people start to think about profit or quarterly numbers." He claimed that, at least while he was there, search quality always came before financial goals, but he believes the public underestimates how Google is shaping what they see: "I deeply, deeply, deeply believe search engines are newspaper-like entities, making editorial decisions." He speculated that the company did not want the public to think too hard about how search works because that awareness "encourages regulators and makes people realize, 'Oh, there's a lot of money here.'"

The consequence is epistemic rather than commercial. There has always been advertising and polemics from cranks, scammers, and liars, but now we see this stuff surfacing alongside truth and we cannot tell the difference, so we move through our lives with a greater sense of distrust and fear and insecurity. At the end of the day, it is Google's world, and the SEOs are only living in it.



---


# The Claim That SGE And Bard Appropriate Publisher Content

The Helena World Chronicle lawsuit claims that Google's recent advances in AI-based search were implemented with "the goal of discouraging end-users from visiting the websites of Class members who are part of the digital news and publishing line of commerce." The grounds are that Google's AI products both retain users and consume publisher content without permission.

On the Search Generative Experience, the suit argues that SGE offers web searchers a way to seek information in a conversational mode but ultimately keeps users in Google's "walled garden" as it "plagiarizes" their content. The warrant that turns this into a harm publishers cannot escape is that publishers also cannot block SGE, because it uses the same web crawler as Google's general search service, GoogleBot — so opting out of the AI experience would mean opting out of search itself.

On Bard, the suit says Google's Bard AI was trained on a dataset that included "news, magazine and digital publications," citing both a 2023 report from the News Media Alliance and a Washington Post article about AI training data. The Post, which worked with researchers at the Allen Institute for AI, had found that News and Media sites were the third largest category of AI training data.

The case points to other concerns too, such as changing AdSense rates and evidence of improper spoliation of evidence on Google's part through its destruction of chat messages — an issue raised in the recent Epic Games lawsuit against Google over app store antitrust issues, which Epic won.



---


# Projected Publisher Traffic Losses From AI Search

Publishers believe they will lose somewhere between 20% and 40% of their website traffic once Google's AI products fully roll out, according to a Wall Street Journal report noted by TechCrunch on 15 December 2023. That report also led with a modelling result from the online magazine The Atlantic: when The Atlantic modelled what would happen if Google integrated AI into search, it found that 75% of the time the AI would answer the user's query without requiring a click-through to its website, losing it traffic.

The stakes are set by how much publisher traffic Google currently supplies. According to data from Similarweb cited in the same coverage, Google today drives nearly 40% of publishers' traffic, so a shift to AI-answered queries could have a major impact on publishers' traffic going forward. The suit filed by Helena World Chronicle takes up precisely this question of how AI will impact publishers' businesses.

Some publishers are trying to get ahead of the problem: Axel Springer inked a deal with OpenAI in the same week to license its news for AI model training.



---


# SEOs Also Say Search Results Have Improved

The strongest challenge to the article's premise is that Sullivan was not the only person insisting search results have improved significantly: out of the dozen-plus SEOs the writer spoke with at length, nearly every single one said search results are way better than they used to be — just objectively more accurate, more useful, more difficult to manipulate.

What gives that testimony force is the absence of an incentive to flatter Google. Except for Sullivan, these were not people with a reason to praise the company; if anything, these were folks who lamented how much harder it had become for them to take advantage of Google.

The effect on the writer was disorientation rather than conviction. This was not what she had been noticing, and certainly not what she had been hearing from friends and journalists and friends who are journalists. Were all of us wrong, or engulfed in some kind of Baader-Meinhof frequency bias delusion? Had she been researching a nonexistent problem? Were Google results actually amazing? Truly, she had lost the plot — was the premise of the piece completely off, and was she the asshole who deserved to be attacked by an alligator?



---


# The U.S. Justice Department's Parallel Antitrust Suits Against Google

The Helena World Chronicle class action arrives alongside the filing of the U.S. Justice Department's lawsuit against Google for monopolizing digital ad technologies, and the complaint also references the Justice Department's 2020 civil antitrust suit over search and search advertising.

The two government cases concern different markets: search and search advertising in the 2020 suit are distinct from the digital ad technologies at issue in the more recent one.

As part of its search deal with Apple, Google agreed not to promote Chrome to Safari users, according to Bloomberg — a restraint that mattered because Google would otherwise have been able to do this with banners, pop-ups and other annoying means in its other Google apps. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella even said he was willing to spend $15 billion per year to get Bing into Apple's default search, per The Information — a stated willingness to pay, not a deal that happened.

# Wired's Retracted Claim That Google Manipulates Search Queries

In October 2023, Wired posted an opinion article by lawyer and privacy advocate Megan Gray alleging that Google had accidentally revealed during the trial that it manipulates people's search queries for maximum ad revenue — the example given being the replacement of a search for "children's clothing" with "NIKOLAI-brand kidswear" — and Wired subsequently removed the article for not meeting its standards.

It also asks that publishers who opt out of SGE still be allowed to show up in Google search results, among other things.

The law firm handling the case is Hausfeld, whose announcement states that "the anticompetitive effects of Google's scheme cause profound harm to competition, to consumers, to labor, and to a democratic free press," and that "Plaintiff Helena World Chronicle, LLC invokes the Sherman Act and Clayton Act to seek class-wide monetary and injunctive relief to restore and ensure competition for digital news and reference publishing and set up guardrails to preserve a free marketplace of ideas in the new era of artificial intelligence."



---


# The Google Antitrust Case

The Google antitrust case is the U.S. government's trial over Google's dominance in the online search market, stemming from a 2020 antitrust claim, in which the government argues that Google uses its platforms and its deals with partners to block out competition in search or advertising and thereby to hinder competitors from accessing the data they would need to improve their products.

Its defining features are the conduct at issue and the defence offered against it. Google CEO Sundar Pichai testified Monday in the trial, defending Google's business tactics, including its deal with Apple and other partners to make Google the default search engine. Google's answer is that it is just doing business: everybody wants Google as the default engine because it is the best, and that, the company says, does not make its actions illegal.

The important boundary case is which Google antitrust matter this is. The 2020 search claim is separate from the one filed in January by the Department of Justice, along with eight states including New York, California and Colorado, which aims to "halt Google's anticompetitive scheme, unwind Google's monopolistic grip on the market and restore competition to digital advertising." The search case and the digital-advertising case are distinct proceedings and should not be conflated.

The trial is the venue in which the underlying numbers surface. Monday's hearing revealed plenty of juicy tidbits, including the $26.3 billion Google spent making itself the default search engine across platforms in 2021, and how Google tried to take it further and have Chrome preinstalled on iPhones.



---


# Google Paid $26.3 Billion In 2021 For Default Search Placement

Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to multiple browsers, phones and platforms — from companies including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla — to be everyone's default search engine. The figure was revealed by Google's search head Prabhakar Raghavan when he testified in court on October 28, according to The Verge.

About $18 billion of that total went directly to Apple, according to a New York Times report published earlier in October 2023, and Google has had its deal with Apple in place since 2003 — so the payment is the current year of a two-decade arrangement, not a one-off. Questioned on the amount of money Google spends to get first pick of search engines, Pichai said the decision was made with the consumer in mind: Google pays big bucks to be everywhere so that it can take in all the data and be the best search engine across different companies' devices, he said, according to The Verge.

The trial also produced evidence that Google understood the value of defaults very early on. U.S. Justice Department lawyer Meagan Bellshaw showed Pichai a 2007 email from a Google product strategy meeting containing data showing that when people changed their browser homepage to Google, they did 15% more Google searches, and that when they switched away, their Google searches dropped 27%. The email summarizing that meeting, sent to Pichai as well as other Google leaders, read: "Nitin argues that focusing on homepage market share is one of the most effective things we can do to make gains in search market share," according to The Verge.



---


# US v. Google: Two Months Into The Search Antitrust Trial

As of TechCrunch's November 13, 2023 roundup, the Justice Department's landmark antitrust case against Google was nearly two months old, and the trial record was still producing fresh revelations. TechCrunch framed it as one of the biggest fights in tech antitrust since the U.S. took Microsoft to trial in the 1990s.

An earlier roundup had already surfaced that Google spent $26.3 billion in 2021 making itself the default search engine across platforms, and that Google tried to have Chrome preinstalled on iPhones. Over the couple of weeks preceding this roundup, more of Google's inner workings came to light, including some of the search engine's most lucrative search queries, the shape of the revenue-share agreements between Google and Android OEMs, and why Expedia has a bone to pick with Google.



---


# The Apple-Google Information Services Agreement

The Information Services Agreement, or ISA, is the deal that makes Google's search engine the default on Apple's products — and it is the reason Apple was in court in US v. Google at all.

The ISA has been in place since 2002, but Eddy Cue was responsible for negotiating its current iteration with Google CEO Sundar Pichai in 2016. In testimony on the day The Verge reported, the Justice Department grilled Cue about the specifics of the deal.

# What Makes A Five-Star Ski Holiday

A five-star ski holiday, as The Independent defines it, is one where the skiing is only part of the product: picture indulging in delectable regional dishes from personal chefs, Michelin-star dining and exhaustive pillow menus, or upgrading your après pints to champagne flutes as you peruse high-end Alpine boutiques. From the Swiss slopes of Zermatt to the pistes of Vail in Colorado, it's not just the snow that sparkles.

The distinguishing features are service and access rather than terrain. Bespoke adventure sports, including heliskiing, meet private ski instructors and pre-warmed boots in these prestigious resorts, while chalet board accommodation ensures there's post-slope cake and canapes waiting, with a side of steamy hot tub sessions. The framing case is envy of the privately chauffeured other side of the mountain — if the unbecoming lug of skis back from the slopes has you envious, it is time to join in with your own glamorous winter getaway. The guide then rounds up the world's most exclusive ski resorts and the lavish gondola-hugging chalets to book for unrivalled luxury off-piste.



---


# Vail: North America's Premium Ski Destination

Vail is North America's premium ski destination and the third-largest mountain ski resort in the US. Its iconic peaks, celebrated après and glamorous villages foster an exclusive atmosphere for travellers to share piste stories over Swiss-style fondue, likely in the company of some famous faces; celebrated après and scenic gondola rides dot Colorado's pistes.

With Iglu Ski, sophisticated skiers can spend seven nights at the ski-in, ski-out Arrabelle in Lionshead Village from £1,888.50pp. On-site spa facilities, a rooftop pool and a lavish plaza of boutiques complement the old-world opulence, and the Eagle Bahn gondola is right outside. Departs 2 December 2023. Return flights from London Heathrow to Eagle County Regional Airport start from £868 with United in January.



---


# Zermatt: 360km Of High-Altitude Slopes Beneath The Matterhorn

Zermatt has 360km of high-altitude slopes and is an oasis for advanced skiers to cruise down linked blues and tackle advanced reds at the foot of the Matterhorn. Rustic charm oozes from the Swiss resort's chalet lodgings, and the car-free town is where you'll find glitzy brands — Moncler to Omega — if you fancy a taste of the finer things in life.

Ski Solutions offers a seven-night stay at Ulysse 8, a five-star chalet in Zermatt, for £1,565pp on chalet board, with a ski instructor available from Monday to Friday at no extra cost. Six cosy bedrooms sleep 12 keen skiers in the chalet opposite the charming Winkelmatten chapel, a short walk from the Matterhorn Express gondola, with wellness rooms that guarantee relaxation after a day on the slopes. Departing 13 January 2024. Return flights from London Luton to Zurich Airport start from £107 with easyJet in January.



---


# Megève: 400km Of Slopes And Mont Blanc Views

Megève is a popular French resort for cross-country trails that guarantees great skiing on 400km of slopes while exuding luxury in extravagant chalets between adventures on the pistes. Plenty of French bistros, boutiques and Michelin-starred favourites are within walking distance of traditional five-star hotels, and views of Mont Blanc complement al fresco morning coffees — this exclusive Alpine destination twinkles in front of the mountain.

Oxford Ski has a contemporary catered chalet in the heart of Megève, Chalet Ariana, that sleeps up to 10 adults and four children in six en-suite bedrooms. Standout features include an indoor swimming pool, boot warmers and proximity to the Chamois gondola. A seven-night stay, including daily housekeeping and advice from a resort expert, will set groups back a hefty €14,750 (£12,720), departing 3 December 2023. Return flights from London Luton to Geneva Airport start from £51 with Wizz Air in December.



---


# Ólafsfjörður: Summit-To-Sea Heliskiing On Iceland's Troll Peninsula

Ólafsfjörður, a small fishing village on northern Iceland's Troll Peninsula, is a haven for heliskiing across 4,000km of terrain with over 256 marked landings. Wellness hotels can be found in the rugged landscape, with geothermal pools ideal for decompressing. The season is the defining constraint: intrepid skiers lusting for the ultimate exclusive adventure can fly between March and June, then ski from summit to sea on Ólafsfjörður's bespoke backcountry journeys.

Scandic Guides offers a five-day heli-assisted ski touring package with professional mountain guides from €4,990pp (£4,314.69), including two summit heli drops per day and five nights of accommodation at the luxe Sigló Hotel, with all meals and airport transfers. Return flights from London Gatwick to Akureyri Airport start from £55 with easyJet in November.



---


# Lech: The White Ring Circuit And Almost Guaranteed Snow

Lech, in the Austrian Alps, has almost 305km of pistes that welcome — almost guaranteed — shedloads of snow each season, making it the deluxe spot for seasoned skiers to holiday in lavish hotels and chalets. An extensive lift network, the legendary White Ring circuit, transports skiers not only to well-groomed runs lined with firs but to elegant apres ski haunts above the upmarket Alpine village, where high-end hotels also see plenty of famous faces.

Bramble Ski offers a grand alpine retreat, Chalech M, with rich wooden interiors and just a three-minute walk from the Schlosskopf chairlift. Highlights of the all-inclusive stay include a complimentary ski instructor for the first two days, pre-dinner canapés and champagne, and an in-resort driver service until 1am. The decadent six-bedroom space, complete with a spa, sleeps 10 for a cool €46,790 (£40,444) per week. Return flights from London Gatwick to Innsbruck Airport start from £64 with easyJet in November.



---


# Mont Tremblant: Quebec's Premier Resort With Old Quebec Charm

Tremblant is Quebec's premier ski resort, sitting at the foot of the eponymous mountain, whose pistes cater well to all abilities. Beginners can start at the edge of the village before progressing onto a series of long greens including the Flying Mile; intermediates have a number of blues, especially around Le Soleil and the Lowell Thomas lift; and advanced skiers can enjoy several terrain parks and steep black runs on both the north and south side of the mountain.

Its distinguishing character is the village. The idyllic, purpose-built settlement has been deliberately built in the style of Old Quebec, with plenty of colourful facades and French-Canadian charm, and offers lively apres and nightlife, often bolstered when locals flock in from Montreal. Non-skiing activities include ice skating, ice fishing and long walking trails, plus a village casino.

British Airways Holidays has trips to the Fairmont Tremblant, one of the more grand hotels in the resort, with an excellent ski-in/ski-out location just a few metres from the lifts, plus impressive spa, pool and sauna facilities, a large terrace, restaurant and outdoor hot tub. From £1,329pp, including seven nights' room-only accommodation, return flights from London Heathrow to Montreal and airport transfers, departing 20 January 2024.

# Sunshine Village: Banff Snow Quality And A Season To Late May

Sunshine Village is one of three ski resorts in Banff National Park, lying around 20 minutes from the town of Banff, with over 3,000 acres of ski area famed for its snow quality and reliable coverage — reflected in a long season that typically runs from mid-November to late May. It caters almost equally to every level of skier, starting at the greens on the slopes of Mount Standish; intermediates are at home in the areas served by the Continental Divide lift and the Tee Pee Town Express, while the more advanced should make a beeline for Goats Eye Mountain, and the off-piste at Delirium Dive is also noteworthy.

The trade-off is where you sleep. Banff is the place to stay for livelier evenings and decent accessibility, though because of the town's distance from the ski area there is less of an 'apres' culture on the slopes. Inghams offers a package at the newest hotel in Banff, the four-star Moose Hotel & Suites in the downtown area, with comfortable rooms — balcony or patio areas giving great views of the Rockies — and a spa featuring two heated rooftop pools that remain open in winter; you are a short shuttle from Sunshine Village, or a 40-minute journey to neighbouring Lake Louise. From £1,482pp including seven nights' room-only accommodation, return flights from London Heathrow to Calgary and transfers, departing 27 January 2024.

# Manchester United's European Decline Since Ferguson

The Independent argued on 12 December 2023 that Manchester United's 1-0 defeat to Bayern Munich should have been a landmark low but instead felt grimly routine, because group-stage elimination has become the club's normal European outcome in the post-Ferguson era rather than an aberration.

The grounds are frequency and pattern. Manchester United, one of the grandest and richest names in this competition, have again gone out of the Champions League at the group stage; it is the third time it has happened since Sir Alex Ferguson, meaning it is their most common round of exit in that period. The night is presented as one more entry in a decade of disappointment in a competition in which this club rose to its most emotional heights — a low, but just part of that longer run.

The warrant is the gap between the occasion and the performance. These are not the sounds we are used to hearing after that Champions League theme; something does stir when the anthem is played at Old Trafford amid the lights — well, for most, that is, except the players. United should not be performing like this on what is supposed to be the classic European night at Old Trafford, and the display was a reminder that all they are going to have for some time are their memories. Having been involved in so many ludicrously chaotic matches, the biggest of all ended up being a non-event: this game never threatened to stir anything, and United never threatened at all. That, the argument runs, can now be talked about definitively, since it has been decisively ended.

# Manchester United Recent Champions League Failures

Thirty years on from Istanbul, United headed to Turkey knowing they had rarely been convincing in the Champions League in recent years, The Guardian reported on Nov. 27, 2023: a 3-1 away win against Paris Saint-Germain in the 2018-19 round of 16, after losing the home leg 2-0, was the last time they won a crunch match.

In 2020-21 they lost their final two group games and were eliminated, while back in 2015-16 Wolfsburg won the deciding group match to knock them out. United had done little learning in recent times, repeating the same failures in Europe's elite competition. It would not be a disgrace to lose against a good Galatasaray team, especially given Erik ten Hag was missing key players, but if the worst happened, everyone would need to come out of the experience stronger — regardless of the result, it should be a night of education about the demands of the Champions League.

Manchester United finished bottom of their 2023-24 Champions League group with four points, in fourth place, eliminated from European competition altogether rather than dropping into the Europa League, The Independent reported on 12 December 2023.

# Manchester United's 2023/24 Champions League Elimination

Manchester United were out of Europe altogether after a limp display against Bayern at Old Trafford, where Kingsley Coman sealed a 1-0 win for Thomas Tuchel's side on the final day of Champions League group-stage play, per Sporting News on Dec. 12 and Dec. 13, 2023.

The Red Devils finished bottom of their four-team group, leaving them eliminated from Europe in their worst performance in the competition since 2005. # Manchester United 2023 Galatasaray Group Decider

United's match against Galatasaray on the Wednesday was not a knockout game, but in truth the scenario was not much different, The Guardian reported on Nov. 27, 2023: defeat would again end United's Champions League campaign prematurely, while a win — assuming Copenhagen lost against Bayern Munich — would put qualifying for the latter stages back in their hands.

United would face the same atmosphere as they had 30 years earlier, because the home fans knew victory would turn their subsequent trip to Denmark into a potential shootout for who goes through with Bayern, with the achievement of knocking out a club with the storied history of United only adding to the pleasure. Galatasaray had already beaten United 3-2 at Old Trafford in early October, Mauro Icardi scoring the winner.

# Manchester United's 2023 Champions League Group Stage Exit

Ten Hag's United compiled arguably the worst performance by any English team in a Champions League group stage in 2023, finishing bottom of their group and shipping 15 goals — more than any other English team ever.

The Guardian conceded it was no Blackburn Rovers, but gave extra marks for United's pedigree, for the fact the group really was not much of a group, and for finishing bottom. There were also many moments of farce along the way, a six-part saga of chaos, collapse and laughter in the dark: Onana diving out of the way of the ball in Munich, Onana again diving out of the way of the ball in Istanbul, Casemiro's red card, lost leads in Manchester, and Marcus Rashford unfairly convicted of a venomous stamp in Copenhagen. And yet, with both group games blank at half-time on the final night, United were still just one goal away from going through to the last 16. Bayern, for all their own flaws, were basically a good version of whatever United were attempting to piece together: Kimmich-Goretzka-Musiala an A-grade version of Amrabat-McTominay-Fernandes, Manuel Neuer the thing Onana is trying so earnestly to be, and Bayern actually did go ahead and sign Harry Kane. From there United's season continued to narrow — they could not win the league, the Champions League or the Carabao Cup, leaving the FA Cup and the extended pursuit of fourth or even fifth place, although the state of the coefficient meant the thing that might keep Manchester United out of Europe the next season could be Manchester United being so bad in Europe that season.



---


# Harry Kane, The Striker Manchester United Did Not Sign

Harry Kane, the England captain and the forward Manchester United neglected to bid for in the summer, unlocked United's defence with a lovely flick to set up Bayern Munich's winner on 12 December 2023 — a reminder, The Independent wrote, of what could have been for United.

The comparison the reports draw is with the striker United did buy. Rasmus Hojlund has at least struck in the Champions League, but in domestic competitions he has been outscored 18-0 by Kane. United, cast out of continental competition altogether, became just the fourth English team to prop up a Champions League group when it concluded, and there was something predictable about the manner of their demise.

The Bayern game also showed one reason why Kane is at Germany's biggest club rather than England's: his side are through with ease and among the favourites for the competition, even if they do look lacking in a few areas.



---


# Everton Case Implications For Manchester City And Chelsea

Sean Dyche declined to comment on the implications of Everton's punishment for Manchester City and Chelsea, The Guardian reported on Nov. 24, 2023.

Manchester City had been charged with 115 financial breaches by the Premier League and deny any wrongdoing; Chelsea were also under investigation by the football authorities.

# Sam Altman's Career Before OpenAI

Sam Altman, 38 as of November 2023, is not trained as an AI engineer, yet has been seen as a Silicon Valley wunderkind since his early 20s. The defining credential of that earlier phase is that he was recruited in 2014 to take the lead of the startup incubator YCombinator.

The reputation attached to him at the time is captured in YCombinator co-founder Paul Graham's 2014 announcement that Altman would become its president: "Sam is one of the smartest people I know, and understands startups better than perhaps anyone I know, including myself." Graham said then that Altman was "one of those rare people who manage to be both fearsomely effective and yet fundamentally benevolent."



---


# Sam Altman's Rise As The Face Of Generative AI

In the year since Altman catapulted ChatGPT to global fame, he became Silicon Valley's sought-after voice on the promise and potential dangers of artificial intelligence, and his sudden and mostly unexplained exit brought uncertainty to the industry's future. He helped start OpenAI as a nonprofit research laboratory in 2015, but it was ChatGPT's explosion into public consciousness that thrust him into the spotlight as a face of generative AI — technology that can produce novel imagery, passages of text and other media. On a world tour in 2023 he was mobbed by a crowd of adoring fans at an event in London.

He has sat with multiple heads of state to discuss AI's potential and perils. On Thursday, 2023-11-16, he took part in a CEO summit at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation conference in San Francisco, where OpenAI is based. At OpenAI's first developer conference the week before, Altman was the main speaker, showcasing a vision for a future of AI agents that could help people with a variety of tasks; days later he announced the company would have to pause new subscriptions to its premium version of ChatGPT because it had exceeded capacity.



---


# The AI Risk Paradox Among Tech Billionaires

At the heart of the competition to build artificial intelligence is a brain-stretching paradox: the people who say they are most worried about AI are among the most determined to create it and enjoy its riches, and they have justified their ambition with their strong belief that they alone can keep AI from endangering Earth. The grounds are the shape of the debate itself. Eight years after an argument between Elon Musk and Larry Page, that argument seems prescient, because the question of whether AI will elevate the world or destroy it, or at least inflict grave damage, has framed an ongoing debate among Silicon Valley founders, chatbot users, academics, legislators and regulators about whether the technology should be controlled or set free.

That debate has pitted some of the world's richest men against one another: Musk, Page, Mark Zuckerberg of Meta, tech investor Peter Thiel, Satya Nadella of Microsoft and Sam Altman of OpenAI, all of whom have fought for a piece of a business that one day could be worth trillions of dollars, and for the power to shape it. The narrative anchor is that Musk and Page stopped speaking soon after the party that summer, and that a few weeks later Musk dined with Altman, who was then running a tech incubator, and several researchers in a private room at the Rosewood hotel in Menlo Park, California, a favoured deal-making spot close to the venture capital offices of Sand Hill Road.



---


# DeepMind's Sale To Google And Facebook's AI Lab

Google offered $US650 million for DeepMind. Mark Zuckerberg of Facebook offered a bigger payout to DeepMind's founders but would not agree to the conditions the founders had set, and DeepMind sold to Google.

Zuckerberg was determined to build an AI lab of his own and hired Yann LeCun, a French computer scientist who had also done pioneering AI research, to run it. A year after Hinton's auction, Zuckerberg and LeCun flew to Lake Tahoe for the same AI conference, and while padding around a suite at the Harrah's casino in his socks Zuckerberg personally interviewed top researchers, who were soon offered millions of dollars in salary and stock. AI was once laughed off; now the richest men in Silicon Valley were shelling out billions to keep from being left behind.



---


# Gaza As A Tech Outsourcing Hub

Gaza, despite being one of the most economically challenged regions in the world, has ironically always been a tech hub — not only for Palestine and Palestinians, but also for the world, with international companies having for many years sought out a presence there to collaborate with talented tech freelancers and the startups that gradually emerged from the region. According to sources who helped build those bridges, Nvidia, famed for its role in the new AI boom, has been working with at least 100 engineers from the region for years; tragically, the initiative to employ Palestinians in this outsourcing was that of Mellanox founder Eyal Waldman, whose daughter was brutally murdered in the attacks by Hamas.

The hub's scale marks its boundary. Since at least 2008, TechCrunch has been covering technology companies out of Palestine, some serving their direct audience and some serving the tech world internationally, and Silicon Valley had taken an increasing interest in Palestine as a tech hub — but like the ecosystem itself, that interest is nascent: to date, those working in the region estimate that as much as $10 million has been invested in the Palestinian tech ecosystem. Notably, in 2017, Salesforce founder and CEO Marc Benioff joined Silicon Valley luminaries in backing the first-ever coding academy to be created in Gaza.



---


# Anthropic's Founding By Former OpenAI Researchers

Dario Amodei, a researcher with ties to the effective altruist community, had been on hand at the Rosewood hotel when OpenAI was born, and was leading the lab's efforts to build a neural network called a large language model that could learn from enormous amounts of digital text: by analysing countless Wikipedia articles, digital books and message boards it could generate text on its own, and it also had the unfortunate habit of making things up. It was called GPT-3 and was released in the summer of 2020, and researchers inside OpenAI, Google and other companies thought this rapidly improving technology could be a path to artificial general intelligence. Amodei was unhappy about the Microsoft deal because he thought it was taking OpenAI in a really commercial direction, and he and other researchers went to the board to try to push Altman out, according to five people familiar with the matter; after they failed, they left, worrying, like DeepMind's founders before them, that their new corporate overlords would favour commercial interests over safety.

In 2021 the group of about 15 engineers and scientists created a new lab called Anthropic, with the plan of building AI the way the effective altruists thought it should be done, with very tight controls. Anthropic disputes the account of the board approach: "There was no attempt to remove Sam Altman from OpenAI by the co-founders of Anthropic," said an Anthropic spokesperson, Sally Aldous. "The co-founders themselves came to the conclusion that they wished to depart OpenAI to start their own company, made this known to OpenAI's leadership, and over several weeks negotiated an exit on mutually agreeable terms." Anthropic accepted a $US4 billion investment from Amazon and another $US2 billion from Google two years later. After OpenAI received another $US2 billion from Microsoft, Altman and another senior executive, Greg Brockman, visited Bill Gates at his sprawling mansion on the shores of Lake Washington, outside Seattle; the Microsoft founder was no longer involved in the company day to day but kept in regular touch with its executives.



---


# OpenAI's AI Chip Ambitions

The company has suggested that it might be entering the AI chip market at some point in the future, in an effort to shore up the speed and performance of its API services.

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman had previously pointed to industry-wide GPU shortages for the service's spotty performance, and producing its own processors might mitigate those supply issues while potentially lowering the current four-cent-per-query cost of operating the chatbot to something more manageable.



---


# Neural Networks And DeepMind's Atari Demonstration

A neural network is a complex algorithm created in the image of the human brain, essentially a giant mathematical system that spends days, weeks or even months identifying patterns in large amounts of digital data. First developed in the 1950s, these systems could learn to handle tasks on their own: after analysing names and addresses scribbled on hundreds of envelopes, for instance, they could read handwritten text. Flush with cash, DeepMind hired researchers who specialised in them.

DeepMind took the concept further, building a system that could learn to play classic Atari games such as Space Invaders, Pong and Breakout to illustrate what was possible. This got the attention of another Silicon Valley powerhouse, Google, and specifically Larry Page, who saw a demonstration of DeepMind's machine playing Atari games and wanted in. The boundary of what the field could then show was pushed again in the spring of 2012, when Geoffrey Hinton, a 64-year-old professor at the University of Toronto, and two graduate students published a research paper that showed the world what AI could do by training a neural network to recognise common objects such as flowers, dogs and cars.

qid: Between the TechCrunch report on EU's call for AI safeguards related to deepfake election risks and the subsequent TechCrunch report on a news publisher filing an antitrust suit against Google, citing AI's harm to their bottom line, was there a change in the portrayal of Google's involvement with AI-related issues?

# The Claim That SGE And Bard Appropriate Publisher Content

The Helena World Chronicle lawsuit claims that Google's recent advances in AI-based search were implemented with "the goal of discouraging end-users from visiting the websites of Class members who are part of the digital news and publishing line of commerce." The grounds are that Google's AI products both retain users and consume publisher content without permission.

On the Search Generative Experience, the suit argues that SGE offers web searchers a way to seek information in a conversational mode but ultimately keeps users in Google's "walled garden" as it "plagiarizes" their content. The warrant that turns this into a harm publishers cannot escape is that publishers also cannot block SGE, because it uses the same web crawler as Google's general search service, GoogleBot — so opting out of the AI experience would mean opting out of search itself.

On Bard, the suit says Google's Bard AI was trained on a dataset that included "news, magazine and digital publications," citing both a 2023 report from the News Media Alliance and a Washington Post article about AI training data. The Post, which worked with researchers at the Allen Institute for AI, had found that News and Media sites were the third largest category of AI training data.

The case points to other concerns too, such as changing AdSense rates and evidence of improper spoliation of evidence on Google's part through its destruction of chat messages — an issue raised in the recent Epic Games lawsuit against Google over app store antitrust issues, which Epic won.



---


# Projected Publisher Traffic Losses From AI Search

Publishers believe they will lose somewhere between 20% and 40% of their website traffic once Google's AI products fully roll out, according to a Wall Street Journal report noted by TechCrunch on 15 December 2023. That report also led with a modelling result from the online magazine The Atlantic: when The Atlantic modelled what would happen if Google integrated AI into search, it found that 75% of the time the AI would answer the user's query without requiring a click-through to its website, losing it traffic.

The stakes are set by how much publisher traffic Google currently supplies. According to data from Similarweb cited in the same coverage, Google today drives nearly 40% of publishers' traffic, so a shift to AI-answered queries could have a major impact on publishers' traffic going forward. The suit filed by Helena World Chronicle takes up precisely this question of how AI will impact publishers' businesses.

Some publishers are trying to get ahead of the problem: Axel Springer inked a deal with OpenAI in the same week to license its news for AI model training.



---


# Google's Generative AI Disinformation Measures

In its report to the EU disinformation Code, Google — an early adopter of generative AI in search via its Bard chatbot — discusses "recent progress in large-scale AI models" which it suggests has "sparked additional discussion about the social impacts of AI and raised concerns on topics such as misinformation."

Google summarised its approach: "Google is committed to developing technology responsibly and has published AI Principles to guide our work, including application areas we will not pursue," adding, "We have also established a governance team to put them into action by conducting ethical reviews of new systems, avoiding bias and incorporating privacy, security and safety. Google Search has published guidance on AI-generated content, outlining its approach to maintaining a high standard of information quality and the overall helpfulness of content on Search. To help address misinformation, Google has also announced that it will soon be integrating new innovations in watermarking, metadata, and other techniques into its latest generative models. Google also recently joined other leading AI companies to jointly commit to advancing responsible practices in the development of artificial intelligence which will support efforts by the G7, the OECD, and national governments. Going forward we will continue to report and expand upon Google developed AI tools and are committed to advance bold and responsible AI, to maximise AI's benefits and minimise its risks."

On forward commitments over the next six months, Google's report states it has no additional measures planned for YouTube. With generative image capabilities rolling out internally over the next year, it commits Google Search to leveraging the IPTC Photo Metadata Standard to add metadata tags to images generated by Google AI, and notes: "Creators and publishers will be able to add a similar markup to their own images, so a label can be displayed in Search to indicate the images as AI generated."



---


# EU Warning On Deepfake Election Risks

The European Union warned in September 2023 that more needs to be done to address the risks that widely accessible generative AI tools may pose to free and fair debate in democratic societies, with the bloc's values and transparency commissioner Vera Jourova highlighting AI-generated disinformation as a potential threat to elections ahead of the pan-EU vote to choose a new European Parliament the following year.

Giving an update on the bloc's voluntary Code of Practice on Disinformation in a speech, Jourova welcomed initial efforts by a number of mainstream platforms to address the AI risks by implementing safeguards to inform users about the "synthetic origin of content posted online," as she put it, but said more must be done. "These efforts need to continue and intensify considering the high potential of such realistic AI products for creating and disseminating disinformation. The risks are particularly high in the context of elections," she warned. "I therefore urge platforms to be vigilant and provide efficient safeguards for this in the context of elections."

The commissioner noted she was meeting representatives of ChatGPT maker OpenAI later that day to discuss the issue. The AI giant is not a signatory to the bloc's anti-disinformation Code as yet, so is likely to be facing pressure to get on board with the effort.



---


# Helena World Chronicle's Class Action Antitrust Suit Against Google

A class action lawsuit filed in the week of 15 December 2023 in the U.S. District Court in D.C. accuses Google and parent company Alphabet of anticompetitive behavior in violation of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act and others, on behalf of news publishers. The case was filed by Arkansas-based publisher Helena World Chronicle, which argues that Google "siphons off" news publishers' content, their readers and their ad revenue through anticompetitive means, and it specifically cites new AI technologies such as Google's Search Generative Experience (SGE) and the Bard AI chatbot as worsening the problem.

Helena World Chronicle owns and publishes two weekly newspapers in Arkansas. In the complaint it argues that Google is "starving the free press" by sharing publishers' content on Google, losing them "billions of dollars."

Beyond damages, the suit asks for an injunction that would require Google to obtain consent from publishers before using their website data to train its general artificial intelligence products, including Google's own and those of rivals. It also asks that publishers who opt out of SGE still be allowed to show up in Google search results, among other things.

The law firm handling the case is Hausfeld, whose announcement states that "the anticompetitive effects of Google's scheme cause profound harm to competition, to consumers, to labor, and to a democratic free press," and that "Plaintiff Helena World Chronicle, LLC invokes the Sherman Act and Clayton Act to seek class-wide monetary and injunctive relief to restore and ensure competition for digital news and reference publishing and set up guardrails to preserve a free marketplace of ideas in the new era of artificial intelligence."



---


# The U.S. Justice Department's Parallel Antitrust Suits Against Google

The Helena World Chronicle class action arrives alongside the filing of the U.S. Justice Department's lawsuit against Google for monopolizing digital ad technologies, and the complaint also references the Justice Department's 2020 civil antitrust suit over search and search advertising.

The two government cases concern different markets: search and search advertising in the 2020 suit are distinct from the digital ad technologies at issue in the more recent one.



---


# Google's Knowledge Graph And Featured Snippets

As described in the Helena World Chronicle complaint, Google's Knowledge Graph is a database, launched in May 2012, from which Google draws a summary of content that it displays as a "Knowledge Panel" to the right of search results when a user searches for information on a topic. The complaint characterises it as one of Google's older question-and-answer technologies and treats it as part of the alleged harm to publishers, alongside newer AI technologies.

The complaint states that "Google compiled this massive database by extracting information from Publishers' websites — what Google calls 'materials shared across the web' — and from 'open source and licensed databases.'" By 2020, the Knowledge Graph had grown to 500 billion facts about 5 billion entities, but the complaint alleges that much of the "collective intelligence" Google tapped into was content "misappropriated from Publishers."

Featured Snippets are a distinct Google technology in which Google algorithmically extracts answers from webpages; the complaint cites them too, on the grounds that they shift traffic away from publishers' websites.



---


# The Apple-Google Information Services Agreement

The Information Services Agreement, or ISA, is the deal that makes Google's search engine the default on Apple's products — and it is the reason Apple was in court in US v. Google at all.

The ISA has been in place since 2002, but Eddy Cue was responsible for negotiating its current iteration with Google CEO Sundar Pichai in 2016. In testimony on the day The Verge reported, the Justice Department grilled Cue about the specifics of the deal.

qid: Regarding the role of House Speaker and the involvement of Rep. Patrick McHenry, is the stance of bipartisan groups of lawmakers as reported by 'Fortune' consistent or inconsistent between the article published on 2023-10-18 and the one on 2023-10-20?

# The Proposal To Expand Patrick McHenry's Speaker Pro Tempore Powers

The proposal, floated by a bipartisan group of lawmakers during the October 2023 speakership vacancy, was to give the interim speaker pro tempore, Rep. Patrick McHenry, R-N.C., more power to reopen the immobilized House and temporarily conduct routine business — in one formulation, more powers for the next several months to at least bring the House back into session and conduct crucial business. Its legal basis is that the House had never ousted its speaker before Kevin McCarthy, and McHenry could tap the temporary powers that were created after the Sept. 11, 2001, terror attacks to ensure continuity of government.

Two boundary conditions define the idea's limits. It was swiftly rejected by Jim Jordan's own ultra-conservative allies — a "betrayal," said Rep. Jim Banks, R-Ind. And McHenry himself has brushed off attempts to take the job more permanently after he was appointed to the role following the unprecedented ouster of McCarthy more than two weeks earlier.



---


# Obstacles To Empowering An Interim Speaker

Elevating Patrick McHenry to an expanded speaker's role could be a possible off-ramp for the crisis, but the premise that it is an easy fix does not hold: it would not be as politically simple as it might seem.

The attack is on the assumption that the votes exist by either route. Republicans are loath to partner with the Democrats in a bipartisan way on the arrangement, and it is highly unlikely Republicans could agree to give McHenry more powers on their own, since their hard-liners don't like it.



---


# The House Paralysis Following Kevin McCarthy's Ouster

For more than two weeks after hard-liners ousted Kevin McCarthy at the start of October 2023, the stalemate shut down the U.S. House, leaving a seat of American democracy severely hobbled at a time of challenges at home and abroad. By Wednesday, 2023-10-18, the House had been stuck 15 days without a speaker — a position of power second in line to the presidency — and the vote for House speaker, once a formality in Congress, had devolved into another bitter GOP showdown for the gavel. As Republicans upset and exhausted by the infighting retreated for private conversations, hundreds of protesters, if not more, amassed outside the Capitol over the Israel-Hamas war, a stark reminder of the dangers of having the House adrift.

By Friday, 2023-10-20, the impasse had deepened into a full-blown crisis, with Republicans holding no realistic or workable plan to unite the fractured GOP majority, elect a new speaker and return to the work of Congress. Majority Leader Steve Scalise said they would "come back and start over" on Monday. Angry, frustrated Republicans left the private session blaming one another for the divisions they had created; a closed-door meeting Thursday to regroup had grown heated at times, with factions blaming one another for sending their majority into chaos. Next steps were highly uncertain as lawmakers started offering new ideas for a possible speaker, but it appeared no one at present could win a GOP majority. "We're in a very bad place right now," McCarthy said earlier.

Republicans predicted the House could essentially stay closed for the foreseeable future — perhaps until the mid-November deadline for Congress to approve funding or risk a federal government shutdown. "We're trying to figure out if there's a way we can get back with a Republican-only solution," said veteran legislator Rep. Tom Cole, R-Okla. "That's what normal majorities do. What this majority has done is prove it's not a normal majority."



---


# Gingrich And Boehner Endorse The Interim Speaker Plan

The novel concept of boosting the interim speaker's role was gaining favor with a pair of high-profile Republicans: former GOP speakers Newt Gingrich and John Boehner. Gingrich's ground for backing it is a vote count, not a dislike of the nominee — he said that while he likes Jim Jordan, he has "no faith" the nominee can get much beyond the 200 votes he won in the first vote.

The warrant Gingrich offered is the cost of continued paralysis: "We can't sit around and suck our thumbs and hope the world will wait until the House Republicans get their act together," he told Fox News' Sean Hannity on his show. Boehner reposted Gingrich's views saying, "I agree," on social media. Both men have deep experience with the subject — both were chased to early retirement.



---


# Tom Cole's Nomination Case For Jim Jordan

In nominating Jim Jordan, veteran Republican Rep. Tom Cole of Oklahoma argued that it was time to end the upheaval he had warned against when Kevin McCarthy was suddenly ousted: "We have a chance today to end that chaos, end that uncertainty," Cole said.

The warrant connecting that goal to Jordan specifically was a claim about his temperament and capacity to lead: Cole said Jordan was not a "shrinking violet" but someone who could lead the House.



---


# The House GOP's Narrow-Majority Vote Math

With Republicans in majority control of the House 221-212, any speaker candidate can lose only a few detractors: a clear majority of 217 votes is required to win the gavel. That arithmetic is what made Jim Jordan's position hopeless — he had to pick up most of his GOP foes to win.

The second ballot on Wednesday, 2023-10-18, showed the math failing: 199 Republicans voted for Jordan and 212 for Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York, leaving no candidate with a clear majority because 22 Republicans voted for someone else. By 2023-10-20 the same constraint had generalized beyond Jordan — it appeared there was no Republican at present who could win the 217 votes needed to become speaker.



---


# Hakeem Jeffries' Bipartisan Offer To Reopen The House

Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries argued that his party was "ready, willing and able" to partner with more traditional Republicans on a path to re-open the House. His ground was the pending business Congress could not conduct while paralyzed — particularly as Congress was being asked to consider President Joe Biden's aid package for Israel, Ukraine and other needs.

He framed the Republican side as incapable of resolving it alone: "The Republicans are unable to function right now," Jeffries said late Tuesday, 2023-10-17, adding on Wednesday that "All options are on the table to end the Republican civil war." Democratic Rep. Pete Aguilar of California nominated Jeffries, noting that the Democratic leader continues to win more votes and is the best choice to move the country forward: "The country cannot afford more delays and more chaos," Aguilar said.



---


# Trump's Backing Of Jim Jordan's Speaker Bid

To win over GOP colleagues, Jim Jordan relied on backing from Donald Trump — the party's front-runner in the 2024 election to challenge President Joe Biden — and on groups pressuring rank-and-file lawmakers for the vote. It was not enough, and in fact backfired on some. "Jim Jordan will be a great speaker," Trump had said on Tuesday, 2023-10-17, outside a courthouse in Manhattan where he is facing business fraud charges. "I think he's going to have the votes soon, if not today, over the next day or two."

The alliance behind that endorsement is long-standing. Jordan has been a top Trump ally, particularly during the Jan. 6 Capitol attack by the former president's backers who were trying to overturn the 2020 election he lost to Biden. Days later, Trump awarded Jordan a Medal of Freedom.



---


# Jim Jordan's Second-Ballot Defeat

Republican Rep. Jim Jordan failed again on Wednesday, 2023-10-18, on a crucial second ballot to become House speaker, with the hard-fighting ally of Donald Trump losing even more GOP colleagues who refused to give him the gavel: he was opposed by 22 Republicans, two more than he lost in first-round voting the day before. What was clear was that Jordan's path to become House speaker was almost certainly lost. As the roll call got under way he lost more than he gained, picking up three backers but adding more detractors, and no further votes were scheduled.

Ahead of the morning vote Jordan, the combative Judiciary Committee chairman and a founding member of the hard-right Freedom Caucus, made an unusual plea for party unity, almost daring his colleagues to put forward the alternative proposal for a temporary speaker. "We've been at this two weeks," he said at the Capitol. "American people deserve to have their government functioning." After the vote he vowed to stay in the race: "We'll keep talking to members, keep working on it." One new Jordan opponent, Rep. Vern Buchanan of Florida, explained his vote: "I think it's time to move on."



---


# Powell's Rejection Of Monetary-Fiscal Coordination

Fed Chair Jerome Powell, sitting to Christine Lagarde's right at the panel discussion, signaled he wasn't ready to rely on the kind of cooperation between monetary and fiscal policy she described as sometimes helpful.

His stated ground rejects the premise that the central bank's mandate is contingent on what fiscal authorities do: "Our assignment is to deliver price stability kind of regardless of the stance of fiscal policy."

# Manfred's Rebuttal To Stripping The Astros' 2017 Title

Many thought taking away the World Series win, essentially nullifying 2017, was the best way to move forward; MLB thought otherwise, and Commissioner Robert Manfred's counter-argument attacked the workability of that remedy rather than the wrongdoing itself, per Essentially Sports on 2023-10-22. In his words: "Once you go down that road of changing what happens on the field, I just don't know how you decide where you stop." The premise he denied was that a clean line could be drawn around which on-field results to revise — and so the Commissioner's Trophy was still legitimate in the eyes of, well, the Commissioner.

A second strand of his objection was practical timing: by the time the controversy was uncovered, the Astros were well into establishing a streak of successful years, and Manfred called the process of stripping the Fall Classic title "difficult and impractical." Already unpopular among the masses, he made things worse for himself when he called the trophy a "piece of metal." He apologized later, but the team kept the championship victory.



---


# How Jim Crane And Jeff Luhnow Rebuilt A Losing Astros Front Office

A decade before this 2023-10-22 retrospective, the Houston Astros were struggling to stay afloat, Essentially Sports recounts. Parting ways with the National League after 50 years of play, the team was looking forward to an American League move, hoping their fortunes would be reversed after regularly ranking near the bottom of divisional standings; the Stros applied every method they could think of to win, and they weren't all above board. Jim Crane obtained club ownership on Nov. 17, 2011, and that same year brought in Jeff Luhnow, a former McKinsey & Company management consultant, as General Manager. In 2014 Crane brought in A.J. Hinch as manager after the firing of Bo Porter — and there began the story of the rise and decline of one of baseball's biggest controversies.

Luhnow had always been more about the numbers than people. Wanting to take out the humanity factor from baseball, he was almost an outcast in the sport when Crane hired him, but his radical approach had worked in St. Louis, giving them two championships in six years — why not the Bayou City next? The Astros had not seen a World Series title yet and hadn't even made the playoffs since 2005. Apparently desperate for any measures, they resorted to cheating, and the article notes that perhaps the biggest surprise was that Luhnow didn't consider his methods to be dishonest.



---


# Minute Maid Park: Houston Astros Postseason Atmosphere

Minute Maid Park ranked No. 5 among the eight remaining 2023 playoff teams' home-field environments in The New York Times' 8 October 2023 ranking, held down by the fact that the Astros have not responded to their own crowd. The park opened in 2000, has a capacity of 41,168 and drew an average attendance of 37,683 in 2023.

Its memorable postseason moment, chosen over Albert Pujols off Brad Lidge or Jorge Soler to the moon, is Chris Burke ending what was then the longest game in MLB postseason history in both time (5 hours, 50 minutes) and innings (18) with a walk-off home run with one out in the 18th inning of the 2005 NLDS. Burke did not start the game but pinch-ran for Lance Berkman in the 10th; Roger Clemens came into the game for Houston in the 16th and pitched three scoreless to pick up the win, but it is Burke's homer that will always be remembered.

The case for a higher ranking is strong on volume: one of the writers called it "the loudest stadium I've ever attended, by at least one standard deviation." The Astros sold out the building 23 times that year and drew 3 million fans for the first time since 2007; the park is big and loud, and visiting fans show up fully exhausted from walking in the south Texas sun. But in all those sellouts the Astros went 6-17, and despite the noise they were 39-42 at home. Before their final homestand the team added some green paint to the batter's eye in response to player complaints, and the Astros responded by going 1-5, with three of those losses coming against the Royals. So the ballpark is packed tighter than toes in a cowboy boot and gets louder than a Pantera concert in a concrete basement, but these Astros just haven't responded to it — raising the question of whether a visiting team should really be all that intimidated.

# How The Astros Scheme Was Exposed And What MLB Did About It

The Astros had stolen signs throughout the 2017 season and the beginning of 2018, but the hornet's nest wasn't broken open until the next year, when The Athletic's Ken Rosenthal and Evan Drellich reported on it — after that, all hell broke loose, Essentially Sports recounted on 2023-10-22. The reaction went badly: no one likes being taken for a fool, and what the Astros had done undermined everything the league stood for. Fair play was the holy grail, yet the team had tread on it heartlessly. Fans were livid, although they didn't get to let out their frustration until 2021.

MLB tried to curb the situation as best it could. In two months the league investigated "68 people, including 23 Astros players, and collect more than 76,000 emails," according to The Athletic, and Luhnow's phone showed signs of deleted information. On Jan. 13, 2020, MLB suspended the disgraced general manager and the skipper for the 2020 season — only for Jim Crane to fire both a few hours later. For many, the solution was severely lacking. After the Jan. 13, 2020 declaration not much came from Manfred: other than suspending the front office, MLB fined the Astros $5 million, the maximum amount, and made them forfeit first- and second-round draft picks. For better or for worse, the inquiry is over.



---


# Astros Players Got Immunity While The Staff Took The Punishment

Investigating an entire organization was an arduous process, and its outcome fell unevenly: while the players were undoubtedly the ones who had put the tactics into play, the Astros staff suffered the heaviest consequences, Essentially Sports reported on 2023-10-22. The ballplayers were instead granted full immunity in exchange for cooperating with the investigation — and, the article asks, who would refuse such an offer?

Not everyone had been comfortable with what the Astros were doing behind the scenes, like Mike Fiers. Of that original team, four were still in Houston at the time of writing: Jose Altuve, Alex Bregman, Lance McCullers Jr. and Justin Verlander. What makes fans ponder their extreme methods is how genuinely skilled each is — yet they participated, willingly or unwillingly, in the biggest baseball scandal in recent years.

# Five MLB Teams Were Hunting For A Manager At The End Of 2023

2023 was a topsy-turvy year for many teams, and amid the heavy restructuring that many MLB clubs had seen of late there were, as Essentially Sports put it on 2023-10-30, pentagonal vacancies for managers. Five teams were in dire need of filling the managerial position as the year ended: the New York Mets, the Los Angeles Angels, the Houston Astros, the Cleveland Guardians and the San Diego Padres.
