# Sam Altman's Career Before OpenAI

Sam Altman, 38 as of November 2023, is not trained as an AI engineer, yet has been seen as a Silicon Valley wunderkind since his early 20s. The defining credential of that earlier phase is that he was recruited in 2014 to take the lead of the startup incubator YCombinator.

The reputation attached to him at the time is captured in YCombinator co-founder Paul Graham's 2014 announcement that Altman would become its president: "Sam is one of the smartest people I know, and understands startups better than perhaps anyone I know, including myself." Graham said then that Altman was "one of those rare people who manage to be both fearsomely effective and yet fundamentally benevolent."



---


# Gaza As A Tech Outsourcing Hub

Gaza, despite being one of the most economically challenged regions in the world, has ironically always been a tech hub — not only for Palestine and Palestinians, but also for the world, with international companies having for many years sought out a presence there to collaborate with talented tech freelancers and the startups that gradually emerged from the region. According to sources who helped build those bridges, Nvidia, famed for its role in the new AI boom, has been working with at least 100 engineers from the region for years; tragically, the initiative to employ Palestinians in this outsourcing was that of Mellanox founder Eyal Waldman, whose daughter was brutally murdered in the attacks by Hamas.

The hub's scale marks its boundary. Since at least 2008, TechCrunch has been covering technology companies out of Palestine, some serving their direct audience and some serving the tech world internationally, and Silicon Valley had taken an increasing interest in Palestine as a tech hub — but like the ecosystem itself, that interest is nascent: to date, those working in the region estimate that as much as $10 million has been invested in the Palestinian tech ecosystem. Notably, in 2017, Salesforce founder and CEO Marc Benioff joined Silicon Valley luminaries in backing the first-ever coding academy to be created in Gaza.



---


# The AI Risk Paradox Among Tech Billionaires

At the heart of the competition to build artificial intelligence is a brain-stretching paradox: the people who say they are most worried about AI are among the most determined to create it and enjoy its riches, and they have justified their ambition with their strong belief that they alone can keep AI from endangering Earth. The grounds are the shape of the debate itself. Eight years after an argument between Elon Musk and Larry Page, that argument seems prescient, because the question of whether AI will elevate the world or destroy it, or at least inflict grave damage, has framed an ongoing debate among Silicon Valley founders, chatbot users, academics, legislators and regulators about whether the technology should be controlled or set free.

That debate has pitted some of the world's richest men against one another: Musk, Page, Mark Zuckerberg of Meta, tech investor Peter Thiel, Satya Nadella of Microsoft and Sam Altman of OpenAI, all of whom have fought for a piece of a business that one day could be worth trillions of dollars, and for the power to shape it. The narrative anchor is that Musk and Page stopped speaking soon after the party that summer, and that a few weeks later Musk dined with Altman, who was then running a tech incubator, and several researchers in a private room at the Rosewood hotel in Menlo Park, California, a favoured deal-making spot close to the venture capital offices of Sand Hill Road.



---


# DeepMind's Sale To Google And Facebook's AI Lab

Google offered $US650 million for DeepMind. Mark Zuckerberg of Facebook offered a bigger payout to DeepMind's founders but would not agree to the conditions the founders had set, and DeepMind sold to Google.

Zuckerberg was determined to build an AI lab of his own and hired Yann LeCun, a French computer scientist who had also done pioneering AI research, to run it. A year after Hinton's auction, Zuckerberg and LeCun flew to Lake Tahoe for the same AI conference, and while padding around a suite at the Harrah's casino in his socks Zuckerberg personally interviewed top researchers, who were soon offered millions of dollars in salary and stock. AI was once laughed off; now the richest men in Silicon Valley were shelling out billions to keep from being left behind.



---


# Sam Altman's Rise As The Face Of Generative AI

In the year since Altman catapulted ChatGPT to global fame, he became Silicon Valley's sought-after voice on the promise and potential dangers of artificial intelligence, and his sudden and mostly unexplained exit brought uncertainty to the industry's future. He helped start OpenAI as a nonprofit research laboratory in 2015, but it was ChatGPT's explosion into public consciousness that thrust him into the spotlight as a face of generative AI — technology that can produce novel imagery, passages of text and other media. On a world tour in 2023 he was mobbed by a crowd of adoring fans at an event in London.

He has sat with multiple heads of state to discuss AI's potential and perils. On Thursday, 2023-11-16, he took part in a CEO summit at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation conference in San Francisco, where OpenAI is based. At OpenAI's first developer conference the week before, Altman was the main speaker, showcasing a vision for a future of AI agents that could help people with a variety of tasks; days later he announced the company would have to pause new subscriptions to its premium version of ChatGPT because it had exceeded capacity.



---


# Musk's Founding Of OpenAI And His Departure

Convinced that Larry Page's optimistic view of AI was dead wrong, and angry at his loss of DeepMind, Musk built his own lab: OpenAI was founded in late 2015, just a few months after he met with Sam Altman at the Rosewood hotel in Silicon Valley. Musk pumped money into the lab and his former PayPal buddies, Reid Hoffman and Peter Thiel, came along for the ride; the three men and others pledged to put $US1 billion into the project, which Altman, then 30, would help run, and to get started they poached Ilya Sutskever from Google, one of the graduate students Google had "bought" in Hinton's auction. Initially Musk wanted to operate OpenAI as a nonprofit, free from the economic incentives driving Google and other corporations, but by the time Google wowed the tech community with its Go stunt he was changing his mind about how it should be run: he desperately wanted OpenAI to invent something that would capture the world's imagination and close the gap with Google, and it wasn't getting the job done as a nonprofit.

In late 2017 Musk hatched a plan to wrest control of the lab from Altman and the other founders and transform it into a commercial operation that would join forces with Tesla and rely on supercomputers the car company was developing, according to four people familiar with the matter; when Altman and others pushed back, Musk quit and said he would focus on his own AI work at Tesla. In February 2018 he announced his departure to OpenAI's staff on the top floor of the startup's offices in a converted truck factory, three people who attended said; when he said OpenAI needed to move faster, one researcher retorted that Musk was being reckless, and Musk called the researcher a "jackass" and stormed out, taking his deep pockets with him. OpenAI suddenly needed new financing in a hurry: Altman flew to Sun Valley for a conference and ran into Satya Nadella, Microsoft's CEO, and a tie-up seemed natural, since Altman knew Microsoft's chief technology officer Kevin Scott and Microsoft had bought LinkedIn from Hoffman, an OpenAI board member; Nadella told Scott to get it done. The deal closed in 2019, leaving Altman and OpenAI with a for-profit company formed under the original nonprofit, $US1 billion in fresh capital, and Microsoft with a new way to build AI into its vast cloud computing service. Not everyone inside OpenAI was happy.



---


# Private Sector Volunteers In Terror Finance Tracking

The network blocking terror financing funds includes many entities, including private citizens: IMPA has been approached by many experts from the private sector — people with intelligence experience because they have worked in these organizations, or with high-tech experience — who "have mobilized like crazy."

"The world's financial intelligence authorities are now at the heart of this struggle, and we're working together to thwart the financing channels that we've located," Ostrovitch-Levi said. "Israeli entrepreneurs in Silicon Valley have contacted us; they write code, search for information, and give us lots of information. We aggregate and examine everything."



---


# Sam Altman's Side Ventures: Helion, Retro And Worldcoin

Altman has a number of possible next steps after leaving OpenAI, because even while running the company he placed large bets on several other ambitious projects.

Among them are Helion Energy, for developing fusion reactors that could produce prodigious amounts of energy from the hydrogen in seawater, and Retro Biosciences, which aims to add 10 years to the human lifespan using biotechnology. Altman also co-founded Worldcoin, a biometric and cryptocurrency project that has been scanning people's eyeballs with the goal of creating a vast digital identity and financial network.

# Adam Yedidia's First Testimony And His Immunity Deal

Late in the afternoon of the second day of Sam Bankman-Fried's trial, the government called Adam Yedidia to the stand, and lead prosecutor Danielle Sassoon disclosed that this college friend of Bankman-Fried had legal immunity during his testimony. Asked why he had made such a deal with the government, Yedidia answered: "I was concerned that I had unwittingly written code that contributed to a crime."

Yedidia, described as a fast-talking graduate of MIT, testified that he and Bankman-Fried were close friends in college. After Bankman-Fried left Jane Street — the high-frequency trading firm where the former billionaire got his start in finance after MIT — he persuaded Yedidia to join him, first as a trader at Alameda and then as a developer at FTX.

The testimony was cut short when the clock neared 4:30 p.m. and court adjourned for the day. Yedidia was scheduled to continue his testimony on Thursday, to be followed by Matt Huang, a former partner at the venture capital firm Sequoia Capital, and then by Gary Wang, a key Bankman-Fried lieutenant and one of the government's star witnesses.



---


# The FTX Trial's Stakes For The Wider Crypto Industry

The Verge argued that the trial of Sam Bankman-Fried is likely to be more consequential than just whether the man himself is found guilty: depending on what evidence is introduced, it could be rough for the entire crypto industry.

The grounds are the unpredictability of what a trial surfaces, voiced by Yesha Yadav, a law professor at Vanderbilt University: "How much damage can this trial do to the already beaten-down reputation of the industry at this point? This trial is going to be an excruciating moment for the industry because no one knows what kind of evidence might come out." The warrant joining that uncertainty to industry-wide stakes is that the industry's reputation is already beaten down, so evidence introduced against one exchange's founder lands on the whole sector rather than on him alone.



---


# The Defense's Good-Faith Case For Bankman-Fried

Mark Cohen, one of Sam Bankman-Fried's lawyers, attacked the prosecution's central premise that his client was a liar who stole from customers, stating early in his opening statement that "Sam didn't defraud anyone." The defense's counter-picture is of a nerdy startup founder who acted in "good faith," not the prosecution's "cartoon of a villain"; Cohen repeatedly harped on Bankman-Fried's allegedly good-faith actions throughout his address to the jury. Bankman-Fried, whose cheekbones were more prominent after spending about seven weeks in a Brooklyn prison, appeared in court as this argument was made.

Cohen also disputed the specific claim that Alameda Research was a covert conduit. Alameda was not subterranean or shady, he said; it was a successful hedge fund. FTX was no Ponzi scheme but a "very innovative, successful company." The business practices between the two were reasonable, he argued, claiming that Alameda acted legally as an FTX customer, payment processor, and market maker — that is, a financial entity that acts as a trading partner for customers looking to buy and sell cryptocurrencies.

The defense's warrant for reading failure as something other than fraud was an analogy Cohen employed throughout: "working at a startup is like building a plane as you're flying it," and businesses sometimes fail. He specifically pointed the finger at Ellison, the former CEO of Alameda, who he said did not adequately protect her hedge fund from the inherent risk of the crypto markets. And when the walls came closing in and the aforementioned plane approached the "eye of the storm," Cohen argued, Bankman-Fried did not act like someone who was guilty — he was willing to give up his personal wealth to make customers whole. "In the end, Sam started and built two billion-dollar businesses," he concluded. "He didn't steal any money."



---


# Alameda Research As The Alleged Conduit For FTX Customer Funds

In the prosecution's account offered by Thane Rehn, the key to Sam Bankman-Fried's alleged scheme was Alameda Research, a crypto hedge fund that Bankman-Fried also owned. The structure the government described works as follows: Caroline Ellison — Bankman-Fried's on-again off-again girlfriend and the CEO of Alameda — served as a front for the fund, and through that arrangement Bankman-Fried had "secret access" to customer money, both cash and crypto.

Two further relations complete the alleged mechanism. Bankman-Fried is said to have directed employees to conceal the flow of money into FTX's coffers, and to have forged financial documents distributed to lenders and investors. "The defendant lied to the world," Rehn alleged. These are the government's allegations as presented in its opening statement, not established findings.



---


# Sam Bankman-Fried's Charges And The Collapse Of FTX

Sam Bankman-Fried, the founder of FTX and Alameda Research, is facing seven counts of criminal charges: two counts of wire fraud and five counts of conspiracy charges.

FTX was a failed cryptocurrency exchange founded in 2019. According to a now-deleted profile from FTX investors Sequoia Capital, FTX was founded because of Bankman-Fried's frustration with other exchanges while he was running Alameda Research, his crypto trading firm. According to the SEC, FTX was a fraud "from the start," diverting customers' funds to Alameda, with a "multi-billion-dollar deficiency caused by his own misappropriation of customer funds."



---


# Day Two Of The Bankman-Fried Trial: Jury Selection And The Courtroom Audience

On the second day of Sam Bankman-Fried's fraud trial, the jury was selected on Wednesday morning, after which lawyers for the government and then for Bankman-Fried delivered opening statements that told two very different stories of the former FTX CEO's sudden rise and almost instantaneous fall. The central question framed by the proceedings was who Bankman-Fried, the former CEO of crypto exchange FTX, really is: a liar and a fraud, or someone who acted in good faith and, like many a startup founder, flew too close to the sun. That answer, the account notes, ultimately lies with the jury.

The day featured pointed allegations, a friend from MIT, and an audience replete with big names, including Bankman-Fried's professorial parents and Damian Williams, the U.S. attorney for the Southern District of New York. Bankman-Fried himself spent most of the day in court staring into a laptop while seated between his two attorneys. The prosecution's account of his alleged crimes was described as featuring a study in contrasts.



---


# Adam Yedidia's Testimony And The $8 Billion Bug

Adam Yedidia, the prosecution's second witness, testified that in June 2022 he submitted a report to Bankman-Fried on Signal showing that $8 billion in customer money held in an internal database tracking cash wired to an Alameda account called "fiat at ftx.com" was missing.

Yedidia met Bankman-Fried in college at MIT and the pair remained close friends; assuming a robotic posture on the stand, he said he worked out of FTX's Hong Kong office from January to October of 2021 and then in the Bahamas until the collapse. He referred to a group Signal thread called "People of the House," referring to Bankman-Fried's $35 million penthouse where many employees lived; on who was paying the rent, Yedidia recalled Bankman-Fried saying he "assumed it's just Alameda paying for it in the end." Yedidia said Bankman-Fried had told him, before he began working in the Bahamas in 2019, that he and Ellison had had sex, and asked whether it was a good idea for them to date — Yedidia said no, and Bankman-Fried responded that he was expecting that answer. One of Yedidia's responsibilities was fixing the bug in the code that gave Alameda preferential treatment. He said he and Bankman-Fried spoke about the missing $8 billion at the pickleball court at the resort in Nassau, Bahamas, where he asked his boss if things were OK because it "seemed like a lot of money" from FTX customers was at risk. "Sam said, we were bulletproof last year. We aren't bulletproof this year," Yedidia testified; asked when they would be bulletproof again, Bankman-Fried said he was not sure, but it might be six months to three years. Yedidia said Bankman-Fried appeared "worried or nervous," which was atypical, but that he still trusted Bankman-Fried and Ellison to "handle the situation." On cross-examination, Christian Everdell, Bankman-Fried's attorney, focused on how Yedidia was the one responsible for developing and reviewing the code.

qid: Who is the individual associated with FTX whose alleged fraudulent actions to attain wealth and power are discussed in articles from Fortune, The Verge, and TechCrunch, and is also mentioned as having informed a trader about permissible withdrawals based on the company's trading revenue?
context:
# Marc-Antoine Julliard's Testimony As FTX's First Witness-Victim

The prosecution's first witness at Sam Bankman-Fried's trial was not a blockbuster name or a former lieutenant-turned-cooperator like Caroline Ellison but a victim: Marc-Antoine Julliard, a Paris-born cocoa trader who lives in London and whose money got stuck on FTX. Julliard testified that on Nov. 8, 2022, in the crypto exchange's final few days, he tried to pull out almost $100,000 in cash and crypto, and that he was never able to. The withdrawal screenshots shown in court were of attempts to move $20,000 USD and about 4 Bitcoin, worth about $20,000 at the time — roughly $100,000 in total, inaccessible.

Julliard explained why he had chosen FTX in 2021 when he decided to invest in crypto, trading currencies like Bitcoin and Dogecoin there. He trusted FTX because Bankman-Fried came across as a leading figure of the industry; because the sheer volume of users mattered to him, and FTX was at the time among the top three biggest exchanges; and because major VC firms had invested. "They don't commit hundreds of millions without doing due diligence, checking the books, the accountancy of the firm, going through several compliance process[es], so that was a vote of confidence for me," he said. He also noted FTX's glossy ads — featuring Gisele Bündchen, for instance — which suggested a very high budget, and reasoned that it wouldn't make sense to spend that much money unless FTX had very strong financials. He opened an account, transferred in both regular money and cryptocurrency, and used the exchange to execute his plan of buying Bitcoin to sell back in five to ten years at higher prices.

In November 2022 things went bad. Julliard followed Bankman-Fried on Twitter and read aloud in court the "FTX is fine. Assets are fine" tweets, along with "FTX has enough to cover all client holdings. We don't invest client assets" and a few others, which gave him the impression that his money was there and that any problem might be technical — anti-spam measures — or regulatory. By the time he tried to get his money out on November 8th, it was too late. Cross-examining a customer whose money is gone is described as a thankless task, but Mark Cohen tried anyway, noting that Julliard was a licensed commodities broker who was trading in crypto because he didn't have to disclose it, that he knew crypto was new and risky, and that he didn't review the terms of service agreement he had assented to when making his FTX account. The next witness called was Bankman-Fried's former college and FTX roommate, Adam Yedidia.



---


# The Escalation Of Alameda's Negative Balance

Alameda Research first ran a negative balance on FTX in late 2019, and the amount it was allowed to go negative crept upward in steps, each one justified after the fact — the model of the fraud that Gary Wang's and Caroline Ellison's testimony described was escalation rather than a single decision. As The Verge's reporter summarised Wang's testimony: first it was okay to dip into FTX's profits, then it was okay to take more, then even more; first it was a little line of credit just to provide liquidity, then a bigger one, then an effectively limitless one.

The steps ran as follows. Because Alameda and FTX shared an open-plan office, Wang heard a trader ask Bankman-Fried whether it was okay to keep withdrawing money from the negative account, and Bankman-Fried said it was okay as long as the amount stayed lower than FTX's total trading revenue; he was CEO of both companies at the time. Around 2019 or 2020, Wang checked the database and found Alameda was negative by about $200 million, more than the $150 million FTX had made in revenue — which had to mean Alameda was taking customer money. Wang was surprised and discussed it with Bankman-Fried, who told him he just needed to take into account the value of FTT, the token the two of them had launched; Wang trusted his judgment and did not pursue it. Later Alameda's balance was more negative than FTT and the trading revenue combined, and Wang had further conversations with Bankman-Fried about it. Wang testified he knew at the time that Alameda was using FTX customers' funds and that he knew it was wrong.

The same gradual accommodation shows in Ellison's account. Choking back tears, she testified: "When I started working at Alameda, I don't think I would have believed you if you told me I would be sending false balance sheets to our lenders or taking customer money, but over time, it was something I became more comfortable with."



---


# FTX's Collapse And Bankruptcy, November 2022

FTX went bankrupt on November 11th, 2022, days after Gary Wang and Bankman-Fried had determined that about $8 billion in customer money was gone. On November 7th, Bankman-Fried tweeted "FTX is fine. Assets are fine," and another tweet in the thread said "FTX has enough to cover all client holdings." Wang testified flatly: "FTX was not fine and assets were not fine because FTX did not have enough assets for customer withdrawals."

Prosecutor Thane Rehn placed the trigger in the same month: when CoinDesk published its article in November 2022, people realized FTX was a house of cards, while Bankman-Fried was tweeting "FTX is fine. Assets are fine" and "We don't invest customer assets even in treasuries."

The day after the bankruptcy, on November 12th, Bankman-Fried directed Wang to send customer funds to Bahamian regulators. Customers could not take their funds off the exchange at that point because FTX had run out of money and its servers had been shut down. Bankman-Fried and his father met with lawyers while Wang waited outside with liquidators; the US lawyers wanted the remaining FTX assets transferred to the US, but Wang testified that Bankman-Fried told him to stall the US lawyers and transfer the funds to the Bahamian regulators instead, who were more likely to let him stay in control of the company. The collapse also propagated outward: the government put Zac Prince, the founder and former CEO of crypto lender BlockFi, on the stand just long enough to blame FTX's bankruptcy for BlockFi's subsequent bankruptcy.



---


# Alameda Absorbed FTX's Losses, Including MobileCoin

Alameda Research functioned as FTX's sin-eater: when FTX took a loss, the loss was moved onto Alameda's balance sheet so that FTX would not look bad. Gary Wang testified that in 2021 FTX was facing a "several hundred million dollar" loss from an exploit in MobileCoin — apparently in April 2021, though Wang did not give a month — and Bankman-Fried directed him to have Alameda take it on instead, because FTX's balance sheets were visible to investors and Alameda's were not.

The relation was general, not a one-off. Ellison testified that her tenure as CEO of Alameda Research was an exercise in optics: when FTX took a loss in the hundreds of millions of dollars because a trader had exploited its system, Wang moved that loss onto Alameda's balance sheet, and FTX's "insurance fund," meant to keep traders from getting stuck with other traders' losses, was totally made up, with Alameda simply picking up the tab. The concealment held all the way to investors: Paradigm Capital's Matt Huang showed the court the balance sheets he had received from Bankman-Fried, and they did not include the loss, which should have appeared in the second-quarter numbers he was given — those instead showed $63 million in trading expenses and $63 million in "other expenses" for the quarter, and an estimated profit of $732 million.

Bankman-Fried offered a benign reading of the same arrangement from the stand: he said the MobileCoin loss, the one Wang said Alameda took to keep off FTX's balance sheet, was a totally innocent matter in which he thought it appropriate that Alameda take the position as a backstop liquidity provider.



---


# Matt Huang And Paradigm's FTX Investment

Matt Huang, co-founder and managing partner of Paradigm, a crypto venture capital firm that invested over $275 million in FTX — a stake that was wiped out — was the third witness to take the stand, and testified about his firm's due diligence.

Huang told the court that Bankman-Fried assured him funds would be used for FTX and not Alameda, and that he was promised Alameda had no preferential treatment on the FTX platform, even though the hedge fund was one of its top traders. Huang said he was concerned about FTX's lack of a board of directors but eventually invested anyway. During cross-examination he said Paradigm pressed Bankman-Fried on the board issue and was told he did not want investors as directors but did plan on having a board with experts.

# Eintracht Frankfurt 5-1 Bayern Munich

Eintracht Frankfurt pulverised Bayern Munich 5-1 on Dec. 9, 2023, snapping the champions' unbeaten Bundesliga run that season with a sensational three-goal first-half performance.

In an explosive first half Eintracht completely overran Bayern and exposed their error-prone backline, scoring three times in 24 minutes. Omar Marmoush opened the account in the 12th minute, drilling in the rebound after Fares Chaibi had hit the crossbar following a miskick from Bayern's Noussair Mazraoui; after more slapdash defending Éric Dina Ebimbe doubled the lead in the 31st minute and Hugo Larsson made it 3-0 five minutes later, benefiting from a Joshua Kimmich error. Kimmich made amends just before the break with a powerful shot from 20 yards, but it did not stop the home side: five minutes after the restart Eintracht made it 4-1 with another textbook quick break, Ebimbe beating Manuel Neuer for his second of the afternoon, and Ansgar Knauff slotted in to make it 5-1 on the hour — Frankfurt becoming the first team in 48 years to score five goals in one hour against Bayern in the Bundesliga since their own 6-0 win in 1975. "There is no need for an explanation," said Bayern midfielder Thomas Müller. "We have to congratulate Frankfurt who deserved the win. They took the fight out of us in that first half hour. When you lose 5-1 then a reaction has to follow. We won't lose our heads now. We don't have enough time but we will bounce back." Bayern, who had a game in hand after the previous week's game against Union Berlin was postponed due to snow, remained second on 32 points, with leaders Bayer Leverkusen on 35 travelling to third-placed VfB Stuttgart, who had 30 points, on the Sunday.

# Newcastle's Elimination From The Group Of Death

Newcastle United were ejected from Europe altogether on the final matchday of the 2023-24 Champions League group stage, finishing with one win and five points after a second cruel comeback in as many games, The Independent reported on 13 December 2023.

For some 45 minutes, including half-time, they could savour the sight of a table that showed them in second, permitting them to imagine a date with Real Madrid or Bayern Munich in the knockout stages. And then, in little more than half an hour, they were out. Christian Pulisic's equaliser threatened to condemn them to the Europa League; Samuel Chukwueze's winner instead meant that spot went to AC Milan. The group of death went down to the dying minutes, but Newcastle have perished — they had savoured a return to Europe, but there will be no continental trips for them in the spring of 2024.

The report's assessment is that Newcastle can nevertheless depart the competition with heads held high: one win and five points seem meagre tallies for their contribution to the competition, and they have proof that it can be unforgiving and reasons to return. # Newcastle's Squad-Depth Deficit In Europe

The Independent argued on 13 December 2023 that Newcastle's Champions League exit owed less to effort than to strength in depth and injuries: Eddie Howe had the luxury of one attacking substitute, Alexander Isak, while three replacements combined for AC Milan's decider — Luka Jovic finding Noah Okafor, who picked out Samuel Chukwueze to place a shot past Martin Dubravka.

After Kylian Mbappe's controversial 98th-minute leveller in Paris, Newcastle could rue the loss of another lead, and once again they may feel entitled to believe they should have won, though for different reasons: for much of the night they were rampant and had Milan reeling, yet last season's Champions League semi-finalists hung in the game, scored twice and hit the woodwork twice more. A third consecutive defeat may come with the sense that their injuries came at a cost. Theirs was another colossal effort and a far better performance than at Everton or Tottenham.

The warrant is that at this level effort is not a substitute for resources. Theirs was the right response to the disappointment in Paris, a stirring effort. # Newcastle's Champions League Defeat To AC Milan

Newcastle lost their final 2023-24 Champions League group game to AC Milan after leading through Joelinton, with Christian Pulisic equalising and Samuel Chukwueze scoring the winner, The Independent reported on 13 December 2023; Newcastle had 17 shots and eight on target but beat Mike Maignan only once, while Milan had two shots on target and scored twice past Martin Dubravka.

# Manchester United's 1-0 Defeat To Bayern Munich, December 2023

Manchester United lost 1-0 at home to Bayern Munich on the final Champions League group matchday, reported by The Independent on 12 December 2023, with Kingsley Coman scoring on 71 minutes from a Harry Kane assist to condemn United to a seventh home defeat of the season.

# What A Ruling For Texas And Florida Would Do To Platforms

The counter to the Texas and Florida laws attacks their central premise — that ordering platforms to stop removing content would correct unfair treatment of conservative speech — by arguing that the same order would strip out curation the platforms need, unleash the content nobody wants, and impose an explanation duty that cannot be scaled.

The premise under attack is stated openly by the laws' authors. The two laws — HB 20 in Texas and SB 7072 in Florida — are very similar in their origins and intentions but diverge slightly in how they seek to restrict social media platforms: in Texas, the law told social media companies that they could no longer remove or demonetize content based on the "viewpoint represented in the user's expression"; in Florida, the law would stop social media companies from banning political candidates or removing or restricting their content. The laws have a few other provisions, but the idea is that conservative politicians in those states want to regulate how tech companies interact with political content. "They're in the same ballpark, the sentiment is the same," Barrett said. "Republican lawmakers in each state believe that — and said explicitly in the course of debating and passing these laws — that 'Silicon Valley oligarchs'… are ideological liberals, and they are censoring people in our states who are conservative, and we are hereby ordering them to stop doing that."

The first counter-ground is the consequence for content. If the court finds that social media companies don't have a First Amendment right to curate the kinds of content that they allow, social platforms could look very different, at least in states that are trying to limit their moderation powers; after years of slow progress on misinformation — and worrisome backsliding on platforms like Elon Musk's X — the Supreme Court's decision could upend that process, sowing chaos online. "Thanks to the First Amendment, Florida and Texas cannot force websites or social media apps to host hateful content, misinformation and spam, as their deeply misguided laws would require," Oregon Senator Ron Wyden, who co-authored Section 230, a law that protects social media companies' content moderation decisions, told TechCrunch. "… A ruling in favor of the Texas and Florida laws would create utter chaos, and make many sites worthless to regular users who want to watch a funny video or see family photos." NetChoice President Steve DelBianco also warned that allowing the state laws to go into effect would unleash "a tidal wave of offensive content and hate speech crashing onto users, creators, and advertisers" that would force Americans to wade through "racial epithets, aggressive homophobia, pornographic material, beheadings, or other gruesome content" just to use social apps.

The second counter-ground is operational. Aside from forcing platforms to allow some forms of content that would otherwise be disallowed, these laws also seek to force social media companies to provide users with individualized explanations when their content is removed or restricted — and because that process is largely conducted algorithmically now, generally with light human intervention or oversight, companies might need to reimagine their content moderation systems or hire way more humans to respond to these incidents, adjustments that would likely be costly and difficult to scale. "As you can imagine, that can get kind of onerous when you're taking down millions and millions of pieces of content a day, and much of that activity of the vast majority of it is currently being done automatically," Barrett said. "The idea that a human being would have to go back and explain each time something came down would be quite a challenge."

The scope condition is conditional and geographic: these consequences follow only if the court rules that platforms lack a First Amendment right to curate, and they bite at least in the states trying to limit moderation powers.

# The Supreme Court's Pair Of Social Media Moderation Cases

The Supreme Court's social media cases are a pair of challenges, which the Court decided it would hear in the week before this October 4, 2023 report, over whether two state laws are allowed to reshape the ability of social media companies to control what does — and doesn't — appear on their platforms. The laws at issue were crafted by Republicans as state-specific measures that order platforms to keep their hands off of some social media posts.

The defining feature of the pair is their shared political origin. Since the early days of the Trump administration, Republicans have accused social media companies of deliberately suppressing conservative viewpoints, and conservative lawmakers in Florida and Texas passed laws to restrict how those companies are allowed to moderate content — whether animated by those perceived differences or by the political perks of accusing social platforms of anti-conservative bias.

The boundary case worth keeping is the evidentiary one. Research has not supported the claims of deliberate suppression of conservative viewpoints. What researchers have demonstrated is something adjacent but different: conservative social media users are disproportionately exposed to political misinformation, a phenomenon that could explain anecdotal claims of ideologically lopsided enforcement on social platforms. Exposure to misinformation, and the enforcement that follows it, is not the same finding as viewpoint-based suppression.

To explain the Supreme Court's decision to wade into these issues — and what happens next — TechCrunch spoke to Paul Barrett, NYU adjunct law professor and Deputy Director of NYU Stern's Center for Business and Human Rights.



---


# Editorial Judgment

## Definition

Editorial judgment is the term used in the Texas/Florida social-media Supreme Court case for social media companies' own claimed First Amendment right to decide what user expression does and does not appear on the platforms they own — a right belonging to the companies, not their users (doc_0256).

## Context

The term appears in the corpus as the crux of the First Amendment question the Supreme Court agreed to decide in the consolidated Texas and Florida cases over state laws (Texas's HB 20 and Florida's SB 7072) restricting how social media companies moderate content: "Do social media companies have a First Amendment protected right to exercise what you might call editorial judgment... in sorting out what expression does and does not appear on the platforms that they own?" (doc_0256).
NYU adjunct law professor Paul Barrett, quoted as the case's explainer, treats editorial judgment and content moderation as two names for the same activity — "what you might call editorial judgment — or what you also might call content moderation" — which is why the case is framed as testing whether content moderation itself counts as constitutionally protected speech (doc_0256).
Barrett is explicit that the underlying question is unsettled: "it's just not clear right now what precisely the First Amendment says about that question" (doc_0256).

## Key Characteristics

- **The platform's right, not the user's** — the case is counterintuitively about whether social media companies (not their users) hold a First Amendment right, since it is the companies' own curatorial decisions that the state laws restrict (doc_0256).
- **Equated with content moderation** — Barrett presents editorial judgment and content moderation as interchangeable labels for the same platform activity of "sorting out what expression does and does not appear" (doc_0256).
- **Framed as a subset of a larger question** — content moderation, and by extension editorial judgment, is described as "a really big and important subset" of what social media companies do, within the broader question of how the First Amendment applies to social media companies (doc_0256).
- **Legally unresolved** — as of the case being taken up, whether this judgment is constitutionally protected speech remained an open question rather than settled doctrine (doc_0256).
- **Consequential if rejected** — if courts find no such protected right, states could compel platforms to carry content (including misinformation and hateful content) and to give individualized explanations for removals, reshaping how moderation is practiced at scale (doc_0256).

# Musk's Removal Of Trust Signals And The Turn To Community Notes

Under Elon Musk, X has pushed the use of an existing crowdsourced fact-checking feature, rebranded as Community Notes, which essentially seeks to outsource the issue to an arm's-length process of aggregating views from platform users, some of which may be appended as contextual notes to dubious tweets.

At the same time, Musk set about removing signals Twitter users were previously able to rely on to help assess the quality of information tweets contained — removing state-affiliated media labels from propaganda outlets and replacing legacy account verifications with pay-to-play. # X's Content Moderation Retrenchment Under Musk

TechCrunch's argument is that X under Musk has very evidently been flying the ship in the opposite direction to the responsible governance the DSA intends to encourage — which is why it attracted so many warnings from EU lawmakers even long before the formal probe of 18 December 2023.

Manchester City led the Premier League table on 28 points, with Liverpool going into second on 27, above Arsenal on goal difference, and Tottenham fourth on 26 after successive defeats, The Roar reported on Nov. 12, 2023.

Aston Villa moved to fifth, three points off the top, with a 3-1 win over Fulham at Villa Park, courtesy of an own goal from Antonee Robinson before strikes from John McGinn and Ollie Watkins. Sheffield United clawed their way off the bottom of the table with a 1-1 draw at Brighton, while Tomas Soucek grabbed a late winner as West Ham came from behind at the London Stadium to beat Nottingham Forest 3-2.



---


# FC Cincinnati Won The 2023 Supporters' Shield As Regular Season Champions

FC Cincinnati won the 2023 Supporters' Shield as Major League Soccer's regular season champion, confirmed on the Wednesday before their Oct. 7, 2023 trip to Inter Miami despite suffering a defeat that day. That made them the best team in Major League Soccer through the 2023 regular season.

The distinction mattered for the opponent: as Sporting News put it 90 minutes before kickoff, Inter Miami's predicament — needing a victory to keep their playoff hopes alive — was made harder because it had to come against that team. It had been an exceptional season for the club, and they were not going to stop just because they had nothing tangible left to gain over the final few matches.



---


# PGMOL Apologies From Autumn 2022

Seven incidents between August and November 2022 appear on the PGMOL apology list, per Sporting News on 2023-09-30. Aston Villa 3-1 Manchester United, November 6, 2022: Lucas Digne's free-kick was one of the highlights of Villa's victory, but a post-match review showed he received additional help following a mistake from the referee — the Red Devils' wall was set more than 10 yards behind the ball, allowing Digne more room to find the back of the net. Nottingham Forest 2-2 Brentford, November 5, 2022: Brentford were awarded a penalty after a collision between Dean Henderson and Yoane Wissa, but replays showed Wissa initiated the contact and Brentford were still given the spot-kick, forcing Webb to apologise to Forest after the match. Fulham 3-0 Aston Villa, October 20, 2022: Douglas Luiz was wrongly sent off for Aston Villa just after the hour mark, thought to have instigated a bust-up when the real perpetrator was in fact Aleksandar Mitrovic.

Manchester United 3-1 Arsenal, September 4, 2022: Arsenal's first defeat of the season came at Old Trafford, but a refereeing decision impacted the match early on — Gabriel Martinelli was denied a goal after a VAR check decided Martin Odegaard had fouled Christian Eriksen, and PGMOL later revealed that the goal should have stood. Newcastle 0-0 Crystal Palace, September 3, 2022: Crystal Palace were let off the hook when Tyrick Mitchell's own goal was ruled out after Joe Willock was thought to have impeded Vicente Guaita between the sticks — the wrong decision despite a lengthy check in the VAR hub. Chelsea 2-1 West Ham, September 3, 2022: Maxwell Cornet thought he scored late on to make it 2-2, but the referee disallowed the goal due to a foul on Edouard Mendy by Jarrod Bowen in the build-up, and Webb apologised to David Moyes after the incident. Crystal Palace 3-1 Aston Villa, August 20, 2022: Webb's first apology in his new role came during Villa's defeat at Selhurst Park, when Andy Madley awarded Palace a penalty following a check on the VAR monitor — a decision that went against Digne and was the wrong call.



---


# Carabao Cup 2023/24 Third Round Results

In the third round of the 2023/24 Carabao Cup the eight Premier League clubs involved in European competition joined the 24 teams advancing from the opening round, per Sporting News on Dec. 19, 2023.

Two results stood out. Championship high-flyers Ipswich produced something of an upset to beat Premier League Wolves 3-2 at home, particularly as Town had fallen two goals behind within 15 minutes. In the major upset on the first night of the third round, Premier League strugglers Luton Town lost 1-0 at third-tier Exeter City. The round's field was made up of 17 Premier League clubs, 7 Championship clubs, 4 League One clubs and 4 League Two clubs.

The results were: Tuesday, Sept. 26, Bradford City (L2) 0-2 Middlesbrough (Ch); Exeter City (L1) 1-0 Luton Town (PL); Ipswich Town (Ch) 3-2 Wolves (PL); Mansfield Town (L2) 2-2 Peterborough United (L1), Mansfield advancing 3-1 on penalties; Port Vale (L1) 2-1 Sutton (L2); Salford City (L2) 0-4 Burnley (PL); Manchester United (PL) 3-0 Crystal Palace (PL). Wednesday, Sept. 27: Aston Villa (PL) 1-2 Everton; Blackburn Rovers (Ch) 5-2 Cardiff City (Ch); Bournemouth 2-0 Stoke City (Ch); Brentford (PL) 0-1 Arsenal (PL); Chelsea (PL) 1-0 Brighton & Hove Albion; Fulham (PL) 2-1 Norwich City (Ch); Lincoln City (L1) 0-1 West Ham (PL); Liverpool (PL) 3-1 Leicester City (Ch); Newcastle United (PL) 1-0 Manchester City (PL).



---


# Liverpool-Arsenal Draw At Anfield, December 2023

Liverpool and Arsenal played out a thrilling 1-1 draw at Anfield on Saturday 23 December 2023, a result that ensured the London side would top the English Premier League on Christmas Day, as reported by The Roar that day.

Arsenal led through defender Gabriel's fourth-minute header from Martin Odegaard's free kick — described as the Gunners' fastest ever goal at Anfield in Premier League history, giving them a three-and-a-half-minute lead — before Mohamed Salah beat David Raya at his near post to level in the 29th minute. Liverpool came closest in the second half and hit the woodwork twice, through Trent Alexander-Arnold and substitute Harvey Elliott.

The standings consequence is stated precisely: Mikel Arteta's team go into Christmas a point clear of Liverpool and third-placed Aston Villa.



---


# Manchester United's Form Slump Before The Fulham Trip

Manchester United went into their November 2023 trip to Fulham needing to get back to winning ways after two major defeats, sitting 8th in the Premier League table with 5 wins and 5 defeats. They had been on a 3-match winning run in all competitions when they faced Man City in their previous Premier League match; there was little hope of winning that match considering their form, and the fears came true as they lost 3-0 in the Manchester derby.

They had some hope in their next match, the EFL Cup round of 16 tie against Newcastle United, especially since they had defeated the Magpies the previous term in the final of the EFL Cup. However, the reigning Carabao Cup champions could not defend their title any longer, losing by another 3-0 margin to Newcastle United.

It still seemed that coach Erik Ten Hag had the backing of the management; however, he would still have to pull his team up from the doom as soon as possible. United's Premier League form read L W L W W L, and their form in all competitions read L W W W L L.



---


# Fulham's Form And League Position, November 2023

Fulham were in a worse situation than Manchester United ahead of their November 2023 meeting, sitting 14th in the league table after a mixed set of results: 3 wins, 3 draws and 4 defeats. They were nonetheless unbeaten in their last two games in all competitions.

They won their last match by a 3-1 margin against Ipswich Town in the EFL Cup round of 16, and before that drew 1-1 against Brighton in their previous Premier League match. However, they were expected to have a tough time holding onto the streak in this match. Fulham's Premier League form read W D L W L D, and their form in all competitions read W L W L D W.



---


# Luton Town's Win Over Newcastle After Lockyer's Cardiac Arrest

Andros Townsend headed the winner for Luton Town as they beat Newcastle United on 23 December 2023, as reported by The Roar that day.

The circumstance the report attaches to the result is that this was Luton's first match since captain Tom Lockyer suffered a cardiac arrest against Bournemouth a week earlier.

qid: Who is the individual that Fortune claims used a colleague as a front for improper financial access, whom TechCrunch did not compare to Warren Buffet, and who has faced allegations by the prosecution of committing fraud for personal gain, as reported by TechCrunch?
context:
# Sam Bankman-Fried

Sam Bankman-Fried is the former CEO of the bankrupt crypto exchange FTX, whose highly anticipated criminal trial started on the Tuesday before TechCrunch's 2023-10-01 report, to determine whether he is guilty of seven counts of fraud and conspiracy. As one former federal prosecutor put it: "The odds seem to be stacked against him at this point."

He was 31 years old and co-founded FTX in 2019; within a few years the once third-largest crypto exchange's valuation hit $32 billion at its peak, and the company is now trying to claw back any funds to distribute to creditors. Before the fall he was even compared to Warren Buffet, and many called him the white horse of crypto — a description TechCrunch notes it never applied to him.

Bankman-Fried, however, maintained his innocence. At The New York Times' DealBook Summit he appeared virtually from the Bahamas and said, "I didn't ever try to commit fraud on anyone; I was shocked by what happened this month"; in a published DM exchange with a Vox reporter he said he regretted filing for bankruptcy and thought that "regulators make everything worse." In January he pleaded not guilty to all counts, which include wire fraud, conspiracy to commit money laundering and conspiracy to misuse customer funds. He could face up to 115 years in jail if convicted on all charges.

TechCrunch's 2023-10-02 summary of his standing on the eve of trial: SBF has been denied bail; his name is mud (or much worse) among those who have lost money in Alameda or FTX; and those who might not have had positions in these still blame him for other crypto woes, because he set off a ripple effect.



---


# Engoron Summary Judgment That Trump Committed Fraud

A judge ruled on Tuesday 26 September 2023 that Donald Trump committed fraud for years while building the real estate empire that catapulted him to fame and the White House. Judge Arthur Engoron, ruling in a civil lawsuit brought by New York's attorney general, found that the former president and his company deceived banks, insurers and others by massively overvaluing his assets and exaggerating his net worth on paperwork used in making deals and securing financing.

As punishment, Engoron ordered that some of Trump's business licences be rescinded, and said he would continue to have an independent monitor oversee the Trump Organization's operations. A Trump spokesperson did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the ruling, and Trump has long insisted he did nothing wrong.

Fortune described the decision, which came days before the start of a non-jury trial in Attorney General Letitia James' lawsuit, as the strongest repudiation yet of Trump's carefully coiffed image as a wealthy and shrewd real estate mogul turned political powerhouse.



---


# The Prosecution's Opening Statement Against Bankman-Fried

Thane Rehn, a prosecutor for the government, opened the case against Sam Bankman-Fried with the line "One year ago, it looked like the defendant was on the top of the world," and then argued that this appearance was false: "all of that, all of it, was built on lies," he declared to the jury, adding "Behind the curtains, he was not what he appeared to be." Rehn described a defendant who, as former CEO of FTX, oversaw a supposedly thriving crypto exchange, jetted between international locales, hobnobbed with celebrities like Tom Brady and Larry David, and repeatedly emphasized to customers that their money was safe and secure.

What followed was a roughly 30-minute story that repeatedly emphasized how Bankman-Fried allegedly stole customer funds to facilitate his jet-setting lifestyle, donate millions to political candidates, and finance risky bets. Rehn also directly contested the media framing of the defendant: he was not a crypto "boy" genius, as so many in the media — Fortune included — have written, but a "man" who "stole billions of dollars from thousands of victims." Rehn closed the characterization with a promise to the jury: "You will see the full picture."



---


# Prosecution And Defense Arguments On Day Two Of The SBF Trial

On the second day of the trial of Sam Bankman-Fried and FTX, the prosecution argued that Bankman-Fried knowingly committed fraud, and it grounded that claim in motive: he did so, prosecutors said, to achieve great wealth, power and influence.

The defense countered with the opposite reading of the same conduct. Its claim was that the FTX founder acted in good faith, never meant to commit fraud or to steal, and basically got in over his head — an argument whose warrant is that inexperience and overreach, rather than intent, explain what happened. The two sides therefore contest intent rather than the underlying events, and the reporting on this exchange comes from Rebecca and Jacquelyn in TechCrunch's Week in Review of October 7, 2023, covering day two of the trial only.



---


# Letitia James Asset Inflation Allegations

Letitia James, a Democrat, sued Trump and the Trump Organization a year before this September 2023 ruling, alleging a pattern of duplicity that she dubbed "the art of the steal" — a twist on the title of Trump's 1987 business memoir "The Art of the Deal."

The lawsuit accused Trump and his company of routinely inflating the value of assets like skyscrapers, golf courses and his Mar-a-Lago estate in Florida, padding his bottom line by billions.



---


# Day Two Of The Bankman-Fried Trial: Jury Selection And The Courtroom Audience

On the second day of Sam Bankman-Fried's fraud trial, the jury was selected on Wednesday morning, after which lawyers for the government and then for Bankman-Fried delivered opening statements that told two very different stories of the former FTX CEO's sudden rise and almost instantaneous fall. The central question framed by the proceedings was who Bankman-Fried, the former CEO of crypto exchange FTX, really is: a liar and a fraud, or someone who acted in good faith and, like many a startup founder, flew too close to the sun. That answer, the account notes, ultimately lies with the jury.

The day featured pointed allegations, a friend from MIT, and an audience replete with big names, including Bankman-Fried's professorial parents and Damian Williams, the U.S. attorney for the Southern District of New York. Bankman-Fried himself spent most of the day in court staring into a laptop while seated between his two attorneys. The prosecution's account of his alleged crimes was described as featuring a study in contrasts.



---


# The SBF Trial Proceedings

Sam Bankman-Fried is in court for alleged fraud and money laundering while leading crypto exchange FTX and sister company Alameda. TechCrunch's 2023-10-02 preview placed the case in the Manhattan Federal Court, describing the disgraced cryptocurrency entrepreneur as accused of orchestrating "one of the biggest financial frauds in American history": the multibillion-dollar collapse of FTX, the crypto exchange he founded and led. SBF, as he is known, has pleaded not guilty to some seven charges of fraud and conspiracy.

The trial kicked off with jury selection October 3. By TechCrunch's 2023-10-06 update the case was entering its next chapter, with proceedings resuming Thursday: as confirmed during a teleconference Wednesday, SBF would be taking the stand along with a handful of other witnesses, as the onus shifted toward the defense after the prosecution brought its case to its conclusion.

Access to the proceedings is limited: no devices are allowed, so reports are being physically put together within the courtroom, or sent to overflow rooms. The jury's composition ranges from a train conductor to a retired investment banker who attended Stanford University, and TechCrunch pointed readers to a special joint episode of its Equity and Chain Reaction podcasts for a better sense of the vibe between the jurors and the rest of the court.

A second account of the same events was arriving in parallel: "Going Infinite," a book by Michael Lewis chronicling the rise and fall of SBF, was set to debut on the first day of the trial.



---


# FTX's Bankruptcy And Leadership

The man who represented FTX before Congress after its failure told lawmakers the exchange had effectively no internal governance at all, and the prosecutor bringing the case called Bankman-Fried's alleged crimes one of the biggest financial frauds in American history. TechCrunch reported both on 2023-10-01.

Ray represented the company during a House Financial Services Committee hearing regarding FTX. Asked whether the firm had significant risk management systems, Ray said at the time that "there were virtually no internal controls and no separateness whatsoever," and added that he did not "trust a single piece of paper" in the exchange's organization. Separately, in a press conference, U.S. Attorney Damian Williams called Bankman-Fried's alleged crimes "one of the biggest financial frauds in American history."



---


# Katherine Maher Appointed Web Summit CEO

Former Wikimedia Foundation CEO Katherine Maher has been appointed as the new CEO of Web Summit, TechCrunch reported on November 3, 2023.

The appointment follows the controversial departure of its previous leader, Paddy Cosgrave.

Maher's appointment comes as the tech conference faces a challenge to rebuild relationships and trust within the tech community.

qid: Does 'The Sydney Morning Herald' suggest that the US economy is slowing down to an optimal level to prevent a recession, while also reporting a prediction by Paul Tudor Jones that the United States economy will enter into a recession early next year?
context:
# Wall Street December 2023 Mixed Session

Most US stocks slipped in the overnight Wall Street session reported on 5 December 2023, though the market stayed near its highest level in 20 months after a mixed set of reports that kept alive questions about whether the world's largest economy can pull off a perfect landing in which it kills high inflation but avoids a recession. The S&P 500 edged down 0.1 per cent for its first back-to-back loss since October, the Dow Jones slipped 0.2 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite rose 0.3 per cent.

Stocks fell more sharply in Asia amid worries about the health of China's economy, the world's second largest. US stocks and Treasury yields wavered after reports showed that US employers advertised far fewer jobs at the end of October than expected, while growth for services businesses accelerated more in the prior month than expected.

The underlying hope on Wall Street at the time was that the US economy was slowing from its recent hot pace by just the right amount: too much strength would give inflation more fuel, but too little would mean a recession. The Australian market's gains that day came after this mixed US session.



---


# The Wall Street September 2023 Selloff And Bond Yields

September 2023 brought a loss of 5.2 per cent so far for the S&P 500, putting it on track to be the worst month of the year by far, as the realisation set in that the Federal Reserve would indeed keep interest rates high for a long time. That growing understanding sent yields in the bond market to their highest levels in more than a decade, which in turn undercut prices for stocks and other investments.

Treasury yields rose again on Tuesday, 2023-09-26, following a mixed batch of reports on the economy: the yield on the 10-year Treasury edged up to 4.55 per cent from 4.54 per cent late on Monday and is near its highest level since 2007, up sharply from about 3.5 per cent in May and from 0.5 per cent about three years ago. One economic report that Tuesday showed confidence among consumers was weaker than economists expected — concerning because strong spending by US households has been a bulwark keeping the economy out of a long-predicted recession.



---


# US Jobs And Services Data In Early October 2023

Wednesday's ADP report suggested private employers added 89,000 jobs last month, a much sharper slowdown in hiring than the 140,000 economists expected. The report does not have a perfect track record in predicting what the more comprehensive jobs report from the US government will say, which was due to arrive on the Friday. Mike Loewengart, head of model portfolio construction at Morgan Stanley Global Investment Office, said that "if Friday's report also shows the labour market is cooling, stock investors may worry a little less about indefinitely higher interest rates".

A second report on the economy said growth in US services industries slowed in September by a touch more than economists expected. The figures were reported by The Age on 4 October 2023 alongside a note that oil prices slumped overnight.



---


# US Equity Sector Moves On 10 October 2023

The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 0.4 per cent to 33,739.30, the S&P 500 gained 0.5 per cent and the Nasdaq Composite added 0.6 per cent, with all 11 major S&P 500 sectors advancing — materials and consumer staples led the gains while technology was the slowest gainer, and energy was among the laggards after its more than 3 per cent rally on Monday.

A measure of US-listed Chinese shares added 3 per cent amid reports that the Asian nation is considering new economic stimulus. "Policymakers have begun to acknowledge a lesser need for further policy action given financial conditions have tightened considerably after the recent surge in Treasury yields," said Ben Jeffery at BMO Capital Markets. "This acknowledgment may have reduced angst around the need for additional rate increases." Investors would be watching for any hints in the September Fed meeting minutes, due Wednesday, that would suggest the Fed may not follow through with the last rise indicated in its economic projections, according to Anna Wong at Bloomberg Economics, who noted that two critical coming indicators for the US economy — Thursday's consumer price index and Friday's University of Michigan consumer-sentiment survey — may give a more definitive read.



---


# Federal Reserve Rate Path Expectations Late 2023

By early December 2023 traders widely expected the Federal Reserve to hold its key interest rate steady at its meeting the following week before potentially cutting rates in March, according to data from CME Group, and Fed officials had recently hinted that the federal funds rate may already be at its peak, above 5.25 per cent, up from nearly zero early in 2022. Fed Chair Jerome Powell and others nevertheless warned Wall Street against being overzealous in its predictions about how early a cut could happen.

The bond market moved with those expectations. With inflation down from its peak two summers earlier, Wall Street was hopeful the Fed might be done with its market-shaking hikes. Investors were looking for a slowdown in the job market that came through employers cutting back on open positions rather than laying off workers, and the report cited showed employers advertised just 8.7 million jobs on the last day of October, down 617,000 from a month earlier. US Treasury yields continued to sag from the heights reached during late October: the 10-year yield fell to 4.18 per cent from 4.26 per cent late on the Monday, after having been above 5 per cent and at its highest level in more than a decade during October. The two-year Treasury yield, which more closely tracks Fed expectations, fell from 4.61 per cent just before the economic reports to 4.57 per cent, yo-yoed, and then eased back to 4.57 per cent. Lower yields were one reason cryptocurrency prices had been rising, alongside excitement about a possible bitcoin exchange-traded fund that helped send bitcoin above $US43,000 ($65,600); Robinhood Markets reported a roughly 75 per cent jump in crypto trading volumes during November from a month earlier, said customers added about $US1.4 billion in net deposits during the month, and its own stock rose 10.3 per cent.

A month earlier, in early November 2023, the same expectations were forming from a lower base. Before that week, stocks had been struggling under the weight of rapidly rising Treasury yields catching up to the Fed's main interest rate, which was above 5.25 per cent and at its highest level since 2001. Higher rates and yields slow the economy, hurt investment prices and raise the risk of something breaking in the financial system, such as the three high-profile US bank failures that rattled markets during the spring. "It was really fear that the Fed was going to go too far," said Katie Nixon, chief investment officer for Northern Trust Wealth Management. The Fed had applied that pressure intentionally, hoping to starve inflation of its fuel and to cool the job market, particularly pay raises, because it feared too-strong pay gains could create a vicious cycle keeping inflation high. Analysts said the Friday jobs report offered encouraging signals, with average hourly earnings rising less in October from September than expected, though it did not mean the job was done. Treasury yields tumbled immediately after that report, with the 10-year easing to 4.52 per cent from 4.67 per cent late Thursday and from more than five per cent the previous week, when it hit its highest level since 2007. Traders then moved up expectations for the first Fed cut, potentially by the summer, according to CME Group data. Foreign-exchange strategists at Bank of America wrote in a BofA Global Research report that for investors around the world the "Fed matters more than other central banks" and weak US data is "the only game-changer for markets". A separate report that Friday from the Institute for Supply Management said growth in US services industries such as finance and construction was weaker than economists expected and suggested a slight easing in prices.



---


# Fed Dovish Comments And The Yield Retreat Of October 2023

Wall Street advanced overnight with the S&P 500 and Nasdaq touching three-week highs as dovish comments from Fed officials pushed Treasury yields lower; following remarks from other top Fed officials on Monday, Atlanta Fed President Raphael Bostic said the US central bank did not need to raise interest rates any further, and that he saw no recession ahead.

The 10-year Treasury yield came off its 16-year peak, on track for its steepest single-day drop since May as trading resumed in the US bond market, which had been closed for a holiday on Monday; ten-year yields tumbled as much as 18 basis points to 4.62 per cent. Fed swaps then showed about a 60 per cent chance the Fed would stay on hold in December, compared with 60 per cent odds on another interest rate rise by then just a week earlier. Oil edged lower, with West Texas Intermediate settling below $US86 a barrel following its biggest rally since April, and the Australian dollar was US64.20¢ at the close as the US dollar fell for a fifth straight day, its longest losing streak since July. Investors were nonetheless still closely monitoring developments in the Middle East: "Everybody has one eye on the Middle East conflict and one eye on what's happening with bond yields," said John Praveen, managing director at Paleo Leon.

qid: After the report by The Verge on October 20, 2023, about Ray-Ban Meta smart glasses and the lifestyle of TikTok users, did the Music Business Worldwide report on November 21, 2023, maintain consistency regarding the behavior of TikTok users in relation to music streaming services?
context:
# The 2023 Luminate Study Of TikTok And Music

TikTok's 2023 report was produced by Luminate researchers who studied data from the US, UK, Germany, Brazil and Indonesia, as well as global data, for a 12-month period from July 1, 2022 to June 30, 2023, and found that "compared to average consumers, TikTok users are significantly more likely to be music streamers."

The study drew on three input streams: consumption data from Luminate Connect, audience insight from the Luminate Music 360 Study, and TikTok engagement volumes provided by the platform — across five markets, the US, UK, Brazil, Indonesia and Germany, as well as globally.



---


# 62% Of US TikTok Users Pay For Music Streaming

According to an analysis commissioned by TikTok and carried out by US market monitor Luminate, 62% of US TikTok users pay for a music streaming service, compared to 43% of all consumers.

Music Business Worldwide's 2023-11-21 report puts that figure in context. TikTok counted 150 million users in the United States as of February 2023, which means that, read through the lens of the Luminate analysis, approximately 93 million TikTok users in the US appear to be paying for a subscription to one of the various streaming services available in the United States, including Spotify, Apple Music and others. For comparison, MBW reported in July that as of February, in the United States, Spotify counted 44.4 million paying subscribers, Spotify rival Apple Music had 32.6 million subscribers, and Amazon Music had 29.3 million subscribers. The framing MBW gives is that TikTok is in the process of reinventing itself as both a partner to music companies and a competitor to streaming and distribution services, and the analysis sheds light on why the ByteDance-owned short video platform has focused so intensely on expanding its services in the music world.



---


# TikTok Users' Merch And Live Music Spending

TikTok's impact on music is not limited to streaming services: the Luminate analysis found TikTok users are also larger spenders on music off-platform, and by wide margins more likely to buy merch and attend live shows than the average consumer.

In the US, 45% of TikTok users bought music-related merch over a 12-month period, compared to 35% of overall music listeners, while 38% attended a live music event during the year, compared to 33% of overall music listeners. Overall, US TikTok users spent 22% more on music-related purchases than overall music listeners, and a similar pattern was found in the four other countries the study looked at.



---


# TikTok Users' Streaming Service Penetration

Including both paid and ad-supported streaming services, roughly nine out of 10 TikTok users in each market Luminate studied used at least one music streaming service.

In the US, 89% of TikTok users subscribed to at least one music streaming service, compared to 74% of overall consumers; in the UK, 85% of TikTok users had a streaming service account, compared to 62% of consumers overall. The study also found a correlation with engagement: "In the global and US markets, TikTok user engagement metrics are strongly associated with streaming volumes. In other words, higher TikTok engagement — whether that's likes, views or shares — corresponds with elevated streaming volumes," the Luminate report stated.



---


# TikTok's Expansion Into Music Services

TikTok has built out music-related services to the point that one could be forgiven for thinking the company plans to reinvent itself as part of the music industry — a distribution service, a streaming service, a live event, artist upload deals, an AI music app and a save-to-streaming feature, layered on in about eighteen months.

The pieces, as MBW listed them on 2023-11-21: in 2022 TikTok launched SoundOn, its own music distribution service, which has partnered with Believe-owned distro company TuneCore and Downtown Holdings-owned B2B tech and services company FUGA. In the summer of 2023 it launched TikTok Music, a premium-only streaming service initially available in Brazil and Indonesia featuring the catalogs of all three major global recording companies (Sony Music, Warner Music Group and Universal Music Group), and quickly expanded it to Australia, Mexico and Singapore, though without Universal's catalog. In October 2023 TikTok announced its first-ever live music event, "TikTok In The Mix," and in the same month struck a deal with Distrokid to have indie artists upload their music to TikTok Music and to Capcut, TikTok's video editing software, as well as to TikTok's Commercial Music Library, which offers a catalog of music for brands to use in TikTok ads. Meanwhile parent ByteDance has launched an AI music-making app, and most recently TikTok unveiled "Add to Music App," which enables users to save music they have discovered directly to their Apple Music, Amazon Music (Prime or Unlimited) or Spotify accounts. MBW reads these partnerships as TikTok moving away from what at times appeared to be a trying relationship with the music industry — in one notable incident, TikTok disabled the use of copyrighted music for users in Australia, in what the platform described as an experiment and many observers saw as a hardball tactic in its licensing negotiations with music rights holders.



---


# TikTok As A Driver Of Music "Glocalization"

The Luminate study found that TikTok's platform appears to be a major driver of the glocalization of music — the trend of local artists, performing in local languages, being elevated to a regional or global platform.

The mechanism has two linked components. First, taste: "TikTok users have a stronger preference for international music than the average music listener," the report said. Second, behaviour: "This preference, combined with the high volume of music discovery and sharing activity on TikTok, can be harnessed to grow a fanbase without borders and has helped to launch global artists from genres such as Reggaeton, Afrobeats and K-Pop." The preference also shows up in how these users choose services: "TikTok users' interest in international music is evident in their music streaming preferences. Compared to the average music listener across each market, this audience is more likely to indicate that 'access to music by global artists' is an extremely important factor when selecting a music streaming service."



---


# TikTok Users' Music Discovery And Sharing Rates

The Luminate study found that the TikTok audience can be an effective marketing tool for artists, because TikTok users in particular are considerably more likely to discover and share music than overall social media and short video platform users.

In the UK, TikTok users were 108% more likely to discover and share music than other social media users; in Germany they were 100% more likely; and US TikTok users were 71% more likely. "In doing so, TikTok users help both emerging and established artists to reach new audiences," the Luminate report stated.



---


# TikTok's Claim To Be The Driving Force Behind Music Discovery

TikTok's argument, made by Global Head of Music Ole Obermann on the back of the Luminate findings, is that "TikTok is the driving force behind music discovery in the industry, and that TikTok users are active, engaged and highly valuable drivers of music industry revenues."

The stated motive for commissioning the research was to move beyond the anecdotal: "TikTok is already famous for being the launchpad for creating viral hits and breaking new artists, but we wanted to understand how TikTok and its users impact the music industry more broadly," Obermann said in a statement, adding that "Luminate's findings prove what we had long known." MBW places the study in a pattern: it is part of an ongoing effort by TikTok to highlight its growing role in the development of global music culture, and last year TikTok released a report asserting that 13 out of the 14 songs to reach number one on the US Billboard Hot 100 in 2022 were driven by viral trends on TikTok.



---


# TikTok Bans And ByteDance Data Concerns

# The Gaza Information War And The Hamas Narrative

Eylon Levy argues that the conflict is not only a kinetic war in Gaza but also an information war, in which the Hamas narrative is adopted far more easily than Israel's account is accepted. His first ground is a case of a claim that collapsed: the day after what he calls the bluff about the Al-Ahli hospital, which the Palestinians claimed had been hit by an Israeli missile killing 800 civilians but which in the end turned out to have been caused by a splinter group of Islamic Jihad, with no hospital destroyed and certainly not 800 people killed, he explained on Sky News that Hamas lies and makes up numbers, and the reporter asked him, almost speechless with surprise, whether he doubts Hamas' numbers. "Life partnership" is the term Will Smith and Jada Pinkett Smith use for their relationship in place of a conventional marriage description, and its defining feature is unconditionality rather than cohabitation or romance. # How Will Smith And Jada Pinkett Smith Met And Married In 1997

Will Smith and Jada Pinkett Smith met when she auditioned for the role of his girlfriend on The Fresh Prince of Bel-Air; she did not get the part, but the two hit it off — even though Smith was married to Sheree Zampino at the time, with whom he shares son Trey. # Separation As An Alternative To Divorce: The "LAT" Partnership

New York City-based relationship expert Susan Winter argues that a long separation like Will Smith and Jada Pinkett Smith's is not a failed marriage but a recognised alternative form of one — a "living apart together" partnership — and that it can be the better choice. Speaking to The Independent in October 2023, she drew a sharp line between separation and divorce: divorce, particularly for Hollywood couples, means lengthy legal processes, from dividing financial assets to creating child custody agreements, whereas a separation carries none of that machinery. Although the terms of the Smiths' separation are not public, Winter believes they are showcasing a non-conventional relationship unfamiliar to the public, one whose visible feature is living in separate homes.

Her grounds are that the arrangement's organising purpose is continuity of the partnership rather than its dissolution: "It's an LAT partnership, meaning 'living apart together.' qid: After the Financial Times reported on October 1, 2023, that investors are showing more interest in Japan due to China's economic slowdown, did the investment trend of U.S.-headquartered venture capitalists, as reported by TechCrunch, show agreement or disagreement with this shift in investor interest towards Japan?
