As that title suggests, the main reason to consider this pair over the Sony WF-1000XM5 is its ANC performance, which is the strongest Engadget has tested from a true wireless model, and it also enjoys Bose's spatial audio tech. The drawbacks: the earpieces are on the larger side, the call quality and battery life at six-ish hours are just OK, and there's no support for multi-device pairing.

qid: Did TechCrunch's portrayal of Scott Hurff's perspective on product design remain consistent between the article published on December 1, 2023, which discussed his experience as a product maker and designer, and the article published on December 21, 2023, which emphasized the importance of decision-making in product design?
context:
# Scott Hurff Recommends "Getting Real"

Scott Hurff recommends "Getting Real: The Smarter, Faster, Easier Way to Build a Successful Web Application," by Jason Fried, David Heinemeier Hansson and Matthew Linderman, calling it an absolute treasure from 2006 that is still teaching him things. As a writer, Hurff does not always write about product design, but when he does he is able to share his perspective as someone who is also a product maker and designer — an intersection that nurtured his own book, "Designing Products People Love: How Great Designers Create Successful Products."

His grounds are the book's originality and its voice. It was the first time anyone building in modern tech put together a practical, straightforward, all-encompassing guide for conceiving, building, shipping and marketing web apps, and Fried and Heinemeier Hansson's words are efficient when they need to be, detailed when it matters, and packed full of nuance that is both unique and endearing. Hurff suspects the book feels like it started as an internal series of posts or a handbook to help scale 37signals beyond the core team, recalling that Basecamp launched in 2004 and had quickly found success.

The warrant he leans on is that the method was proven on its authors' own product: whatever the format, what lends "Getting Real" authenticity is the fact that 37signals used these exact techniques to ship Basecamp and find its customer base. To this day he has never read anything like it — one of those books you can finish in an afternoon but that stays with you far longer, morphing into a reference book for the times when you need some extra perspective.



---


# Product Design In The AI And Spatial Computing Era

Product design is in a moment of profound change and redefinition as technologies like artificial intelligence and spatial computing dramatically affect computing experiences. The two technologies act on different layers: AI, especially, may have only minor impacts on interface design but will significantly impact the holistic product or ecosystem experience, whereas spatial computing will change human-computer interactions and unmoor our understanding of what a computer is.

The consequence for practice is that in this innovation cycle, product design requires a wider perspective of platforms and interconnections between technologies, creating a strong need for technologists and designers to be in the process together.



---


# Digital Technology As A Design Material

The model proposed is to think of digital technologies as a material like paint, stone or wood. For artisans to create with materials they must understand the material's ontology and phenomenology — an artist must know the differences between oil, acrylic and watercolor paints, because each has different properties that affect how and what can be created — and by analogy technologists must "find the grain" of a technology.

The relation this sets up is one of intermediation. As experts on a technology or technology stack, technologists can communicate abstract insights or contribute in more conceptual contexts, adding value to the product design process by sharing their expertise on a technology's characteristics; designers then use this information to shape and exploit technologies in the visual and interaction design process. In this way technologists inform new interaction models, interface metaphors and product channels, and their involvement gives confidence and conviction to the promises of design — becoming an intermediary between the abstract nature of design and the pedantic nature of technology.

The range over which the model matters most is specified: this philosophical perspective is especially important when a product is in a growth stage or when using emerging technologies.



---


# The Strategic Role Of Technologists In Product Innovation

Technologists play a strategic role in product innovation and should bring a metaphysical perspective in addition to being punctilious. Their job is to communicate the essence of a technology and think strategically about the application of technologies to problem spaces, and they are most constructive when they translate the technicals of "how to make X do Y" into "these are the types of products and services realizable with technology X."

The author concedes the difficulty: for most technical leads and software developers this is a mode inversion from their traditional tactical and direct interaction with technology, and the context switch from daily build-and-operate is challenging — but it is paramount to developing successful and innovative products, because technologists are uniquely positioned to generate strategic insights translated from dense technical minutiae that drive innovative business cases and product experiences.

The claim is offered without conditions on product stage or technology maturity: regardless of whether a product is growing or in a stable stage, and whether it employs established or emerging technologies, integrating technologists into the product strategy and design process enriches the final outcome. There is a technology perspective extending beyond the operations and mechanics of the code "factory floor" which provokes innovation — sometimes leading to small, impactful moments of innovation, and sometimes to a brilliant revolution.



---


# Product Design As A Decision-Making Process

Product design is a process, not a discipline or a deliverable, and its core is decision-making with an astute instinct for making the best decisions at the most opportune time. So understood, product design helps reduce risk and leads to more effective innovation through quality decision-making, and the process establishes a guide rail throughout any innovation initiative.

The boundary case the definition rules out is the narrow one. It is understandably easy to limit the scope of product design to color choices, content layout and aesthetics, and too often design is minimized to only the act of making user interfaces pretty; but product design is much deeper and broader in scope than visual design assets — it can give direction and focus to a business strategy, a user experience strategy, or technology explorations.



---


# The Experimental Nature Of Product Innovation And The Technology-Product Gap

Product innovation is experimental and should not always be expected to yield productive results: it requires a learning curve and patience, as the outcomes are often ambiguous and unknown.

That indefiniteness — in terms of both results and timelines — is what business leadership struggles with, since it is challenging to translate pure technology innovation into value creation. The consequence is a gap that opens between technology and product teams, in which technology teams strain to articulate the capabilities and value of a technology innovation, leading to unfilled promises and the perception of "technology for the sake of technology," or quips like "a solution looking for a problem."

The current hype cycle in AI serves as a concrete example. For technology or product executives, the challenge is how to do more than check the AI box — it is about how to meaningfully incorporate AI into a product. The remedy proposed is a reversal of direction: instead of forcing a technology onto a product, the design process flows to the technologies, and in this way the technology becomes a natural solution.



---


# Technology Innovation Must Solve A Business Problem

A technology innovation must solve a business problem, such as improving operational efficiency, growing existing revenue streams, or generating new ones. The problem space may be customer-facing — how can we deliver a new feature? — or internal-facing — how can we make a process more efficient? — but either way the problem is the paramount concern, and the specific technologies or innovations used to solve it are often less critical. Losing perspective of the business needs makes the activities too academic, or a paid hobby.

The warrant is illustrated with an ordinary domestic analogy: hanging a picture. The hole size, bracket, or tools used are immaterial as long as the picture is on the wall and straight. The specifics of the process and technologies are only important as they pertain to how well they solve the problem, the costs to do so, and the overall end user experience.



---


# Georgiana Laudi Recommends "Loved"

Georgiana (Gia) Laudi recommends "Loved: How to Rethink Marketing for Tech Products," by Martina Lauchengco, calling it exactly the comprehensive guide the startup scene so desperately needed. Laudi helps SaaS businesses grow through her agency, Forget the Funnel, which is also the title of the book she co-wrote with her co-founder Claire Suellentrop, whose premise is to present readers with "a customer-led approach for driving predictable, recurring revenue."

Her grounds begin with the problem the book addresses: product marketing, particularly in tech, is one of the most foundational and yet somehow wildly misunderstood disciplines. Lauchengco manages to strike the perfect blend of accessible and comprehensive, so that everyone from founders to practitioners understands the critical role product marketing plays in successful companies and what good looks like at every stage of growth.

What Laudi appreciates most is the ordering of priorities: when it comes to marketing and driving product adoption, even though Lauchengco introduces four fundamentals of product marketing, the first and most critical to get right is customer insight — almost unheard of given that the target market for this book is an industry where engineering and scale reign supreme.



---


# James Wise Recommends "The Coming Wave"

James Wise's holiday pick is "The Coming Wave: Technology, Power, and the 21st Century's Greatest Dilemma," by Mustafa Suleyman with Michael Bhaskar. The recommendation is offered on the strength of who is making it rather than an accompanying rationale, which TechCrunch's write-up does not record.

Wise is a partner at VC firm Balderton Capital, and the London-based investor also wrote his first book, "Start-up Century: Why We're All Becoming Entrepreneurs – and How to Make It Work for Everyone," which launched in the U.K. on 23 November 2023 and which TechCrunch suggests should make a great gift for aspiring entrepreneurs.

qid: Which company, known for creating a Prime-themed sale day and introducing invite-only deals for fast-selling items, experienced a stock decline due to an antitrust lawsuit reported by The Sydney Morning Herald and is also considered by sellers as providing a life-changing opportunity, as discussed by Cnbc | World Business News Leader?
context:
# Amazon Sellers Who Welcomed The FTC Case

On Amazon's own forum for merchants, Seller Central, several users cheered on the FTC and said they hoped the case would result in changes to the company's business practices.

Amazon's tense relationship with merchants has been well-chronicled over the years, with sellers expressing grievances over rising fees, an arcane suspensions process, and heightened competition on the marketplace from all sides including the e-commerce giant itself. "I think it's great, Amazon deserves it," one person commented, adding, "More should be coming on the way." Amazon in recent years made the forum anonymous, but users must have a seller account in order to post. Another post included a screenshot of a message Amazon sent to sellers the day after the FTC filed its complaint, which said, "As your partners, we know that this news may generate questions for you and our business together. This lawsuit does not change anything about our relationship with you or how we operate today." One user called it "BS verbiage," adding, "Businesses that sell in their store are indeed customers. And which of us has gotten good customer service?" Another described their last 12 months of selling on Amazon as "being up all night at an effing casino but I'm stuck, the drugs are starting to wear off, but I'm trying to break even on the mortgage payment I'm using to play. That's how it is selling on Amazon right now to me," and called it a "race to the bottom." "It's long overdue," another commenter wrote. "When they close me down, I'm applying for a job with the FTC." Still, others commented that the FTC's complaint is misguided: "Selling on Amazon is a life-changing opportunity and the amount of sellers that throw stones at the platform is astounding," one user wrote.



---


# Amazon's Buy Box Price Parity Enforcement: The Ripple Rug Case

Late in the day on Oct. 27, 2021, seller Fred Ruckel received an automated email telling him that his popular cat toy, the Ripple Rug, would no longer be shown in Amazon's all-important buy box — the area of the listing where shoppers click "Add to Cart" — because Amazon's software had detected the product being sold somewhere else for a cheaper price.

Ruckel is the sole seller of the Ripple Rug on Amazon, so the move all but ensured his product would disappear from the website, costing him thousands of dollars per day. The email, viewed by CNBC, read: "Below is a list of product(s) in your catalog that are not currently eligible to be the Featured Offer because they are not priced competitively compared to prices for those products from retailers outside Amazon." Unbeknownst to him, Chewy was running a discount promotion and had dropped the price of his product by a few dollars to $39.99 — less than the $43 offer on Amazon. The algorithm flagged it as a lower offer even though the item on Chewy cost $48.54 after shipping and taxes. Ruckel had to choose between lowering the price on Amazon or asking Chewy to raise the price of his product; he opted for the latter.



---


# The FTC's Antitrust Lawsuit Against Amazon

The Federal Trade Commission's sweeping 172-page antitrust lawsuit, filed in late September 2023, accuses Amazon of wielding its monopoly power to squeeze merchants and thwart rivals, which the agency alleges has led to artificially inflated prices and a degraded shopping experience for consumers.

The mechanism the FTC describes is an "anti-discounting strategy" backed by a "massive web-crawling apparatus that constantly tracks online prices" to stifle competition: Amazon punishes third-party sellers who offer cheaper products elsewhere by threatening to disqualify them from appearing in the buy box if it detects a lower price, and losing the buy box is an "existential threat" to sellers' businesses, the complaint alleges. The end result, the FTC argues, is elevated prices across the web — the company steadily hikes the fees it charges sellers and prevents them from discounting on other sites, so sellers often inflate their prices off Amazon, creating an "artificial price floor everywhere." The FTC is seeking to hold Amazon liable for allegedly violating anti-monopoly law but has not yet outlined the specific remedies it believes would best resolve its concerns; in antitrust cases, remedies are often determined only after a court finds the defendant liable. Amazon general counsel David Zapolsky responded in a blog post that third-party sellers set their own prices on the marketplace and that the company invests in tools to help sellers offer "competitive prices": "Even with those tools, some of the businesses selling on Amazon might still choose to set prices that aren't competitive. Just like any store owner who wouldn't want to promote a bad deal to their customers, we don't highlight or promote offers that are not competitively priced." Zapolsky argued the lawsuit could force Amazon to stop highlighting low prices, "a perverse result that would be directly opposed to the goals of antitrust law."



---


# The Amazon Invite-Only Deals System

Invite-only deals are a system Amazon introduced during Prime Day in summer 2023 to make it easier for Prime members to access deals expected to sell out quickly, and the company brought it back for Prime Big Deal Days.

Its scope is limited but broad within that limit: the feature is only available on select products, though it has spread across a variety of categories and price points. The mechanics are simple — if a product is part of the system, a "Request Invite" button appears on the right-hand side, and clicking it gives you a chance to buy at the sale price. The important caveat is that there's no guarantee you'll receive the invite. WIRED points readers to its story on How to Shop Like a Pro During Amazon Prime Day for more on how the program works.



---


# Seller Skepticism That The FTC Picked The Right Issues

Even sellers sympathetic to regulating Amazon question the premise that the FTC's highlighted issues are the ones that would make the seller and consumer experience better. Scott Needham, who sells on Amazon and runs a product-finder tool for other Amazon sellers, said he was "surprised by some of the points that the FTC selected."

"I have over the years been very critical of Amazon," Needham told CNBC. "I've lost a lot of sleep because of some of the things that they have done. And the issues that they brought up, while they are interesting, they haven't created me a lot of pain." He was particularly puzzled by the claim that Amazon is coercive in how it encourages sellers to use Fulfillment by Amazon (FBA), saying many sellers "love FBA" for its compelling value in price and two-day shipping; for many, using FBA does not feel like a requirement, but they believe it will make their businesses "easier and more effective." "I think that the power that Amazon wields over sellers is considerable and absolutely worth looking into," Needham said. "But I'm not sure if this would actually change that." Scott Moller, an Amazon seller and co-founder of an agency that helps merchants run their storefronts, said the company has removed some of the challenges of running an online business: with FBA he can ship an item into an Amazon warehouse for $7.49 per package versus about $12 through a traditional carrier. "I don't have to have my own warehouse," said Moller, who sells grilling accessories under the brand Grill Sergeant. "I can use their staff, their storage, and I can instantly also take the data of advertising, so I can target ads." He also disputed the FTC's claim that Amazon has become littered with ads in search results, causing shoppers to wade through potentially less-relevant products of lesser quality: "We can tailor our ads to hit exactly the consumers we want. It's a perfect marriage of a transaction, and that's one of the beauties of what their marketplace offers." Needham's second objection is timing: he would have been more supportive if the case had been filed a few years ago, pre-pandemic — "I would have felt, yes Amazon is a monopoly… But actually after Covid, into 2023, ecommerce has had a lot of big changes. The competition is just not what it was in 2019." Competitors like Shopify and Walmart are increasingly viable alternatives for many categories of sellers, he said, not to mention rapidly growing Chinese e-commerce companies like Temu, and he has seen significant changes from Amazon as a result, among them a greater ability for sellers to communicate with buyers and offer select customers certain promotions — Shopify gives sellers much more control over customer communication, and although Amazon still controls the process, at least there is one. "I wish it was a clear-cut case," Needham said. "I have a vested interest in the marketplace doing really well, as a seller and as a service provider. And… this case, it doesn't make the marketplace better for sellers."



---


# Retailer Sales Competing With Amazon Prime Day

Amazon Prime Day has inspired many imitators, and shoppers will find sales from competitors like Best Buy, Target, and the like.

WIRED's assessment is mixed: some of these sales are great, and it flags them when they are, but others are worth holding off on until Black Friday and Cyber Monday — when, it jokes, WIRED will again be the Internet's only website with deals posts.

# Amazon's Offline Guardrail Pipeline For Alexa Kids Generative AI

Amazon does not hook kids up to a large language model at runtime; instead it runs the LLM offline to generate content in bulk, puts that content through a review process using both humans and AI, and only then loads the reviewed material into the "Explore with Alexa" experience. "We want to go slow and be intentional and be measured with how we're introducing this new tech, as well as any new tech for kids, which is why we're not just hooking the experience up to an LLM at runtime and kind of letting kids go at it," explains Arjun Venkataswamy, senior product manager for Alexa Kids, in an interview with TechCrunch. "The way that we've integrated an LLM here is we use it to generate content at scale offline, and then go through a review process that includes both humans, as well as AI, and then take that reviewed content and then put it into our experience," he says.

The preconditions that motivate the pipeline are the two failure modes of the technology and the audience: generative AI can be led astray or "hallucinate" answers, while kids could ask inappropriate questions. Amazon's answer is a sequence of constraints applied before any child hears an answer. First, the Alexa Kids science team narrowed the new experience, which leverages Alexa's LLM technology, to include only kid-friendly fun facts and trivia questions. Second, the source material is restricted: initially, the content comes from just two partners, the World Wildlife Fund and A-Z animals. Third, the LLM generates content at scale offline rather than on the device in real time. Fourth, that generated content goes through review by humans and by AI — AI is enlisted here because the model can generate tens of thousands of potential responses, so not every answer can be reviewed by a human before being added to the experience. Fifth, only the reviewed content is put into the experience, so kids are not using generative AI on the fly when conversing with Alexa, and what they hear is pre-reviewed and drawn from a small dataset of just animal facts and sources.

The procedure is scoped to the current, offline arrangement and explicitly does not yet extend to runtime generation for kids. Amazon has no date for that step: "I can't give you a timeline, because we don't have a concrete answer for what exactly we're going to be doing yet, although we do have plans and experiments we're planning to look into," Venkataswamy says. The gating criterion is external validation rather than an internal milestone — "I will say that in terms of our criteria for when we're going to get there, we're working closely with the Family Trust team at Amazon that's connected to a variety of research institutions in the U.S…we want to be able to get some confidence from external partners that our approach is right," he adds. The narrow content scope is likewise provisional: in time the team would like to expand the AI to include other areas of interest to kids, like space, music, video games and sports.



---


# Large Language Model (LLM)

## Definition

A large language model (LLM) is a neural network trained to learn from enormous amounts of digital text — Wikipedia articles, digital books, message boards — so that it can generate text on its own.

## Context

The corpus traces the term to OpenAI's GPT-3, described as the neural network Dario Amodei's team built by analysing "countless Wikipedia articles, digital books and message boards" so it "could generate text on its own," released in the summer of 2020; it also "had the unfortunate habit of making things up." ChatGPT itself runs on GPT, the LLM lineage OpenAI had developed since 2016, iterating from GPT-1 (2018) to GPT-3 (June 2020) before GPT-3.5 powered ChatGPT's November 2022 launch. In the venture-capital view of the AI market, LLMs sit at the base "foundation model" layer of a broader stack — models, pre-training solutions, fine-tuning tools, middle-layer tooling, and end-market applications — with providers such as OpenAI's GPT-4, Google's Bard, and Anthropic's Claude expected to consolidate into an oligopolistic structure resembling the cloud-provider market. OpenAI's GPT-X models are repeatedly described as proprietary LLMs that other companies build businesses on top of, a dependency that became visible when the November 2023 OpenAI board upheaval led customers to contact rival LLM providers (Anthropic, Google, Cohere) out of concern for continuity.

## Key Characteristics

- **Trained on enormous text corpora** — LLMs learn by analysing vast amounts of digital text (Wikipedia, books, message boards) rather than following hand-written rules.
- **Generative** — once trained, an LLM can generate text on its own in response to a prompt.
- **Prone to fabrication and privacy leakage** — GPT-3 had "the unfortunate habit of making things up," and a Google DeepMind-led test found that prompting ChatGPT to repeat a word endlessly caused OpenAI's LLM to surface private, identifiable information (email addresses and similar) from its training data; a separate Microsoft-affiliated study found GPT-4 more easily "jailbroken" into unsafe outputs than other LLMs.
- **Costly to run and usage-priced** — LLM economics are dominated by compute cost (OpenAI was reported to spend roughly $700,000/day on compute), which is why LLM providers commonly bill by token/usage rather than flat SaaS pricing.
- **Anchors a layered AI stack** — LLMs form the "foundation model" layer beneath middle-layer tooling (fine-tuning, prompt engineering, model orchestration, observability) and top-layer applications that startups build against.
- **Split between proprietary and open approaches** — OpenAI's GPT-X models are proprietary LLMs, contrasted in the corpus with Meta's Llama family and other efforts pushing more "open" LLM development, a split that intensified after a leaked internal Google memo argued neither OpenAI nor Google had a durable "moat" against open-source LLMs.

# UMG's USCO Filing Rejecting Fair Use For AI Training

Universal Music Group's response to the US Copyright Office rejected the notion that using copyrighted material to train large language models is "fair use" — a position MBW called unsurprising and the starkest possible contrast to Google's assertion that prohibiting or limiting the use of copyrighted materials for AI training would undermine the purpose of copyright and foreclose the opportunities of the technology.

The filing's own example puts the claim bluntly: "The wholesale appropriation of UMG's enormous catalog of copyright-protected sound recordings and musical compositions to build multibillion commercial enterprises [in AI] is anything but fair use."

qid: Does the 'Business Line' article on investment options for high networth investors suggest ignoring historical performance and management team evaluations before making decisions, unlike the 'Business Line' article's recommendations for investors considering Reliance Industries stock?
context:
# Reliance Industries Share Price and Growth Catalysts

The stock of India's most valued company, Reliance Industries (RIL), has trebled over the last six years after a decade-long underperformance from 2007 to 2017. On a three-year basis, however, RIL has delivered 11 per cent CAGR returns including the value of demerged Jio Financial Services, underperforming the Nifty 50's CAGR of a little over 14 per cent over the same period.

Business Line argued on 9 December 2023 that this is nothing to fret about, because the stock has typically tended to underperform whenever the company has been in a heavy investment phase — something it has embarked on in its green energy ventures.

The catalysts behind the six-year outperformance were the launch of Jio's data services in 2016, the maturation of the retail business, and the subsequent stake sales in FY21. Although the markets have already assigned a significant re-rating in valuation to both businesses, the article holds that scope for further outperformance from them remains, given the opportunity ahead.



---


# The Case For Alternatives In HNI Portfolios

Alternative Investment Funds, Portfolio Management Services and Market Linked Debentures genuinely deserve a place in the portfolio of every high-net-worth investor, because their distinct value propositions, unique features, distinctive risk-return profiles and low correlation with traditional asset classes let HNIs improve portfolio performance, generate alpha and grow wealth faster. The grounds are that the growing number of HNIs, together with their desire to diversify portfolios and access opportunities outside traditional avenues such as stocks, mutual funds and fixed deposits, prompted innovation of existing investment products and led to the emergence of a new asset class known as "Alternatives".

The warrant is an asymmetry of access rather than a difference of principle: although the same principles of financial and investment planning apply to all investors, HNIs have an advantage in that they can choose from a broader range of conventional and unconventional investment opportunities, so investing in unconventional avenues is available to them in a way it is not to others. The recommendation carries explicit conditions. Before investing, investors should conduct thorough research to understand how these investment options work; it is important to consider the past track record and the management team before making investment decisions; and consultation with investment advisors knowledgeable in this area can undoubtedly be beneficial.



---


# AIF Sub-Fund Strategies Available To HNIs

Alternative Investment Funds present a family of sub-strategies that are available only to HNIs, each defined by the stage or credit segment it targets. Start-up funds serve angel investors looking to invest in ideas with the potential to grow into full-scale businesses, providing a platform that brings promoters and investors together; these funds handpick start-ups after extensive due diligence and build a portfolio with the potential to multiply capital several times. Mid-stage private equity funds suit investors hesitant to take start-up risk, letting them invest in companies in the middle of their evolution cycle whose business valuations grow exponentially as they mature and enter the late-stage or pre-IPO stage. Late-stage or pre-IPO funds allow investment in mature companies preparing to list, building a portfolio of companies about to go public and planning to exit after their anticipated blockbuster listing, which can magnify returns in a relatively short period; such funds gained immense popularity after the 2020 stock market rally that witnessed the blockbuster listing of some popular B2C IPOs.

The remaining strategies are defined by instrument rather than stage. Hedge funds invest in both publicly traded and unlisted stocks and manage money using long-only and long-short strategies, the latter allowed to use complex derivative techniques to hedge the portfolio; long-short funds try to optimise returns in every market situation and hence tend to rise and fall less than their peers, so investors with stock and mutual fund portfolios can diversify with them to reduce volatility. Performing credit funds lend to operating companies that cannot raise funds from banks and NBFCs due to their size or credit ratings, specialising in credit risk assessment and offering credit at relatively higher rates after thorough due diligence, which produces higher overall returns than AAA/AA-rated bonds and appeals to investors seeking more from their fixed-income portfolio. Infrastructure funds invest in long-term infrastructure assets owned by PSUs or private companies, such as roads, power transmission lines and solar power plants; most such projects provide essential societal services and thus have intrinsic value, and their cashflows come as annuities backed by Central and State governments, which lowers future cash-flow risk significantly, gives the fund a yield characteristic through regular distributions, and can add capital gains when assets are sold to another fund or infrastructure trust at maturity. Venture debt funds serve start-up promoters who want to raise money without selling equity and cannot approach banks and mutual funds, providing credit to start-ups at high rates, with the higher returns and risk management appealing to risk-taking, yield-hungry investors. The list is explicitly not exhaustive: many more options exist, such as special situation funds and real estate yield funds.



---


# Why Investors Can Continue To Accumulate NTPC

Business Line maintained a positive stance on NTPC on 11 November 2023 and advised investors to continue accumulating the stock, on account of growth plans in place along with strong revenue and earnings visibility due to the assured return model, plus a decent dividend yield of around 3 per cent. The grounds are the track record since the previous call and the reasons behind the re-rating. Since the accumulate rating on NTPC in bl.portfolio dated 13 August 2023, the stock has gained around 48 per cent, majorly on account of growth in earnings as well as a re-rating in the stock from a trailing P/E of around 10 times then to 12 times now.

In the year since Altman catapulted ChatGPT to global fame, he became Silicon Valley's sought-after voice on the promise and potential dangers of artificial intelligence, and his sudden and mostly unexplained exit brought uncertainty to the industry's future. He helped start OpenAI as a nonprofit research laboratory in 2015, but it was ChatGPT's explosion into public consciousness that thrust him into the spotlight as a face of generative AI — technology that can produce novel imagery, passages of text and other media. On a world tour in 2023 he was mobbed by a crowd of adoring fans at an event in London.

He has sat with multiple heads of state to discuss AI's potential and perils. On Thursday, 2023-11-16, he took part in a CEO summit at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation conference in San Francisco, where OpenAI is based. # Sam Altman's Career Before OpenAI

Sam Altman, 38 as of November 2023, is not trained as an AI engineer, yet has been seen as a Silicon Valley wunderkind since his early 20s. The defining credential of that earlier phase is that he was recruited in 2014 to take the lead of the startup incubator YCombinator.

The reputation attached to him at the time is captured in YCombinator co-founder Paul Graham's 2014 announcement that Altman would become its president: "Sam is one of the smartest people I know, and understands startups better than perhaps anyone I know, including myself." Graham said then that Altman was "one of those rare people who manage to be both fearsomely effective and yet fundamentally benevolent."

# Musk's Founding Of OpenAI And His Departure

Convinced that Larry Page's optimistic view of AI was dead wrong, and angry at his loss of DeepMind, Musk built his own lab: OpenAI was founded in late 2015, just a few months after he met with Sam Altman at the Rosewood hotel in Silicon Valley. Musk pumped money into the lab and his former PayPal buddies, Reid Hoffman and Peter Thiel, came along for the ride; the three men and others pledged to put $US1 billion into the project, which Altman, then 30, would help run, and to get started they poached Ilya Sutskever from Google, one of the graduate students Google had "bought" in Hinton's auction. Initially Musk wanted to operate OpenAI as a nonprofit, free from the economic incentives driving Google and other corporations, but by the time Google wowed the tech community with its Go stunt he was changing his mind about how it should be run: he desperately wanted OpenAI to invent something that would capture the world's imagination and close the gap with Google, and it wasn't getting the job done as a nonprofit.

In late 2017 Musk hatched a plan to wrest control of the lab from Altman and the other founders and transform it into a commercial operation that would join forces with Tesla and rely on supercomputers the car company was developing, according to four people familiar with the matter; when Altman and others pushed back, Musk quit and said he would focus on his own AI work at Tesla. In February 2018 he announced his departure to OpenAI's staff on the top floor of the startup's offices in a converted truck factory, three people who attended said; when he said OpenAI needed to move faster, one researcher retorted that Musk was being reckless, and Musk called the researcher a "jackass" and stormed out, taking his deep pockets with him. OpenAI suddenly needed new financing in a hurry: Altman flew to Sun Valley for a conference and ran into Satya Nadella, Microsoft's CEO, and a tie-up seemed natural, since Altman knew Microsoft's chief technology officer Kevin Scott and Microsoft had bought LinkedIn from Hoffman, an OpenAI board member; Nadella told Scott to get it done. Across the first three weeks of the trial, a run of former colleagues, an outside investor and a forensic accounting expert testified that FTX customer money flowed into Alameda Research and out again to other uses, and that FTX's investors were never told about the two firms' special relationship. Thursday also brought testimony from Matt Huang, co-founder and managing partner at crypto investment firm Paradigm, which invested $278 million in FTX across 2021 and 2022 and is part of a class-action lawsuit accusing it and others of defrauding customers by promoting FTX. His testimony centered around being left uninformed about FTX's utilization of customer money to keep Alameda Research afloat — a practice Huang says would have halted his involvement — and covered his relationship with FTX stretching back to 2019.

Week two's standout testimony came from Alameda Research's former CEO Caroline Ellison, who claimed she took $14 billion from customers to repay debts to lenders, using them as a line of credit under the instruction of SBF. # Helena World Chronicle's Class Action Antitrust Suit Against Google

A class action lawsuit filed in the week of 15 December 2023 in the U.S. District Court in D.C. accuses Google and parent company Alphabet of anticompetitive behavior in violation of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act and others, on behalf of news publishers. The case was filed by Arkansas-based publisher Helena World Chronicle, which argues that Google "siphons off" news publishers' content, their readers and their ad revenue through anticompetitive means, and it specifically cites new AI technologies such as Google's Search Generative Experience (SGE) and the Bard AI chatbot as worsening the problem.

Helena World Chronicle owns and publishes two weekly newspapers in Arkansas. In the complaint it argues that Google is "starving the free press" by sharing publishers' content on Google, losing them "billions of dollars."

Beyond damages, the suit asks for an injunction that would require Google to obtain consent from publishers before using their website data to train its general artificial intelligence products, including Google's own and those of rivals. It also asks that publishers who opt out of SGE still be allowed to show up in Google search results, among other things.

The law firm handling the case is Hausfeld, whose announcement states that "the anticompetitive effects of Google's scheme cause profound harm to competition, to consumers, to labor, and to a democratic free press," and that "Plaintiff Helena World Chronicle, LLC invokes the Sherman Act and Clayton Act to seek class-wide monetary and injunctive relief to restore and ensure competition for digital news and reference publishing and set up guardrails to preserve a free marketplace of ideas in the new era of artificial intelligence."

# The U.S. Justice Department's Parallel Antitrust Suits Against Google

The Helena World Chronicle class action arrives alongside the filing of the U.S. Justice Department's lawsuit against Google for monopolizing digital ad technologies, and the complaint also references the Justice Department's 2020 civil antitrust suit over search and search advertising.

The two government cases concern different markets: search and search advertising in the 2020 suit are distinct from the digital ad technologies at issue in the more recent one.

# What A Ruling Against Google Would Mean For Big Tech

A ruling against Google would not stop at Google: the remedy would likely resemble the Microsoft settlement and the outcome would ripple through the other pending Big Tech cases, because enforcers are using this trial to demonstrate that antitrust law can still take on the largest and most powerful companies in the world.

The grounds for the first half of that claim are the available remedies. If the judge rules against Google, the outcome could look a lot like the Microsoft deal, in which the computer company was required to change its behavior and share its APIs with third-party developers, and was also banned from making anticompetitive and exclusive deals with computer manufacturers. Google might likewise end up having to turn over all or most of the data it has collected to other search engines so they can improve their products and attract more users — a remedy scaled to the disparity the DOJ has cited, that Google gets 16 times more data than Bing does everyday.

The grounds for the ripple effect are the cases already queued behind this one. The FTC sued Amazon in September for using anticompetitive and unfair strategies to illegally maintain its monopoly power. The DOJ has been investigating Apple for years over the company's policy for third-party apps on its devices and whether it unfairly favors its own products. And there is an ongoing case between the FTC and Facebook, in which the agency calls on Facebook to sell Instagram and WhatsApp.

The warrant joining grounds to claim is enforcers' own stake in the result: they will want to show that antitrust law is still relevant and can successfully take on the biggest, most powerful companies in the world, so a win here sets the template the neighbouring cases are argued against. The scope condition is that nothing was settled as of this report — the case is expected to continue for several weeks, bringing to a head one of the biggest fights in tech antitrust since the U.S. took Microsoft to trial in the 1990s.



---


# The Google Antitrust Case

The Google antitrust case is the U.S. government's trial over Google's dominance in the online search market, stemming from a 2020 antitrust claim, in which the government argues that Google uses its platforms and its deals with partners to block out competition in search or advertising and thereby to hinder competitors from accessing the data they would need to improve their products.

Its defining features are the conduct at issue and the defence offered against it. Google CEO Sundar Pichai testified Monday in the trial, defending Google's business tactics, including its deal with Apple and other partners to make Google the default search engine. Google's answer is that it is just doing business: everybody wants Google as the default engine because it is the best, and that, the company says, does not make its actions illegal.

The important boundary case is which Google antitrust matter this is. The 2020 search claim is separate from the one filed in January by the Department of Justice, along with eight states including New York, California and Colorado, which aims to "halt Google's anticompetitive scheme, unwind Google's monopolistic grip on the market and restore competition to digital advertising." The search case and the digital-advertising case are distinct proceedings and should not be conflated.

The trial is the venue in which the underlying numbers surface. Monday's hearing revealed plenty of juicy tidbits, including the $26.3 billion Google spent making itself the default search engine across platforms in 2021, and how Google tried to take it further and have Chrome preinstalled on iPhones.



---


# The Claim That SGE And Bard Appropriate Publisher Content

The Helena World Chronicle lawsuit claims that Google's recent advances in AI-based search were implemented with "the goal of discouraging end-users from visiting the websites of Class members who are part of the digital news and publishing line of commerce." The grounds are that Google's AI products both retain users and consume publisher content without permission.

On the Search Generative Experience, the suit argues that SGE offers web searchers a way to seek information in a conversational mode but ultimately keeps users in Google's "walled garden" as it "plagiarizes" their content. The warrant that turns this into a harm publishers cannot escape is that publishers also cannot block SGE, because it uses the same web crawler as Google's general search service, GoogleBot — so opting out of the AI experience would mean opting out of search itself.

On Bard, the suit says Google's Bard AI was trained on a dataset that included "news, magazine and digital publications," citing both a 2023 report from the News Media Alliance and a Washington Post article about AI training data. The Post, which worked with researchers at the Allen Institute for AI, had found that News and Media sites were the third largest category of AI training data.

The case points to other concerns too, such as changing AdSense rates and evidence of improper spoliation of evidence on Google's part through its destruction of chat messages — an issue raised in the recent Epic Games lawsuit against Google over app store antitrust issues, which Epic won.



---


# Google Paid $26.3 Billion In 2021 For Default Search Placement

Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to multiple browsers, phones and platforms — from companies including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla — to be everyone's default search engine. The figure was revealed by Google's search head Prabhakar Raghavan when he testified in court on October 28, according to The Verge.

About $18 billion of that total went directly to Apple, according to a New York Times report published earlier in October 2023, and Google has had its deal with Apple in place since 2003 — so the payment is the current year of a two-decade arrangement, not a one-off. Questioned on the amount of money Google spends to get first pick of search engines, Pichai said the decision was made with the consumer in mind: Google pays big bucks to be everywhere so that it can take in all the data and be the best search engine across different companies' devices, he said, according to The Verge.

The trial also produced evidence that Google understood the value of defaults very early on. U.S. Justice Department lawyer Meagan Bellshaw showed Pichai a 2007 email from a Google product strategy meeting containing data showing that when people changed their browser homepage to Google, they did 15% more Google searches, and that when they switched away, their Google searches dropped 27%. The email summarizing that meeting, sent to Pichai as well as other Google leaders, read: "Nitin argues that focusing on homepage market share is one of the most effective things we can do to make gains in search market share," according to The Verge.



---


# The Apple-Google Information Services Agreement

The Information Services Agreement, or ISA, is the deal that makes Google's search engine the default on Apple's products — and it is the reason Apple was in court in US v. Google at all.

The ISA has been in place since 2002, but Eddy Cue was responsible for negotiating its current iteration with Google CEO Sundar Pichai in 2016. In testimony on the day The Verge reported, the Justice Department grilled Cue about the specifics of the deal.

qid: Between the TechCrunch report on Sam Bankman-Fried's trial published on October 6, 2023, and The Verge's coverage of the same topic, was there consistency in the portrayal of Sam Bankman-Fried's actions related to the FTX collapse?
context:
# Sam Bankman-Fried

Sam Bankman-Fried is the former CEO of the bankrupt crypto exchange FTX, whose highly anticipated criminal trial started on the Tuesday before TechCrunch's 2023-10-01 report, to determine whether he is guilty of seven counts of fraud and conspiracy. As one former federal prosecutor put it: "The odds seem to be stacked against him at this point."

He was 31 years old and co-founded FTX in 2019; within a few years the once third-largest crypto exchange's valuation hit $32 billion at its peak, and the company is now trying to claw back any funds to distribute to creditors. Before the fall he was even compared to Warren Buffet, and many called him the white horse of crypto — a description TechCrunch notes it never applied to him.

Bankman-Fried, however, maintained his innocence. At The New York Times' DealBook Summit he appeared virtually from the Bahamas and said, "I didn't ever try to commit fraud on anyone; I was shocked by what happened this month"; in a published DM exchange with a Vox reporter he said he regretted filing for bankruptcy and thought that "regulators make everything worse." In January he pleaded not guilty to all counts, which include wire fraud, conspiracy to commit money laundering and conspiracy to misuse customer funds. He could face up to 115 years in jail if convicted on all charges.

TechCrunch's 2023-10-02 summary of his standing on the eve of trial: SBF has been denied bail; his name is mud (or much worse) among those who have lost money in Alameda or FTX; and those who might not have had positions in these still blame him for other crypto woes, because he set off a ripple effect.



---


# The FTX Trial's Stakes For The Wider Crypto Industry

The Verge argued that the trial of Sam Bankman-Fried is likely to be more consequential than just whether the man himself is found guilty: depending on what evidence is introduced, it could be rough for the entire crypto industry.

The grounds are the unpredictability of what a trial surfaces, voiced by Yesha Yadav, a law professor at Vanderbilt University: "How much damage can this trial do to the already beaten-down reputation of the industry at this point? This trial is going to be an excruciating moment for the industry because no one knows what kind of evidence might come out." The warrant joining that uncertainty to industry-wide stakes is that the industry's reputation is already beaten down, so evidence introduced against one exchange's founder lands on the whole sector rather than on him alone.



---


# FTX's Bankruptcy And Leadership

The man who represented FTX before Congress after its failure told lawmakers the exchange had effectively no internal governance at all, and the prosecutor bringing the case called Bankman-Fried's alleged crimes one of the biggest financial frauds in American history. TechCrunch reported both on 2023-10-01.

Ray represented the company during a House Financial Services Committee hearing regarding FTX. Asked whether the firm had significant risk management systems, Ray said at the time that "there were virtually no internal controls and no separateness whatsoever," and added that he did not "trust a single piece of paper" in the exchange's organization. Separately, in a press conference, U.S. Attorney Damian Williams called Bankman-Fried's alleged crimes "one of the biggest financial frauds in American history."



---


# Sam Bankman-Fried's Charges And The Collapse Of FTX

Sam Bankman-Fried, the founder of FTX and Alameda Research, is facing seven counts of criminal charges: two counts of wire fraud and five counts of conspiracy charges.

FTX was a failed cryptocurrency exchange founded in 2019. According to a now-deleted profile from FTX investors Sequoia Capital, FTX was founded because of Bankman-Fried's frustration with other exchanges while he was running Alameda Research, his crypto trading firm. According to the SEC, FTX was a fraud "from the start," diverting customers' funds to Alameda, with a "multi-billion-dollar deficiency caused by his own misappropriation of customer funds."



---


# Day Two Of The Bankman-Fried Trial: Jury Selection And The Courtroom Audience

On the second day of Sam Bankman-Fried's fraud trial, the jury was selected on Wednesday morning, after which lawyers for the government and then for Bankman-Fried delivered opening statements that told two very different stories of the former FTX CEO's sudden rise and almost instantaneous fall. The central question framed by the proceedings was who Bankman-Fried, the former CEO of crypto exchange FTX, really is: a liar and a fraud, or someone who acted in good faith and, like many a startup founder, flew too close to the sun. That answer, the account notes, ultimately lies with the jury.

The day featured pointed allegations, a friend from MIT, and an audience replete with big names, including Bankman-Fried's professorial parents and Damian Williams, the U.S. attorney for the Southern District of New York. Bankman-Fried himself spent most of the day in court staring into a laptop while seated between his two attorneys. The prosecution's account of his alleged crimes was described as featuring a study in contrasts.



---


# Going Infinite: Michael Lewis's Account Of SBF's Political Dealings

Michael Lewis's book "Going Infinite" debuted on the first day of Sam Bankman-Fried's trial, and details about Bankman-Fried's political dealings emerging from it include his alleged attempt to buy off Donald Trump to get him not to run again for president.

TechCrunch's team was focused on the Manhattan Federal Court for the trial of Bankman-Fried, the disgraced entrepreneur accused of orchestrating the collapse of the cryptocurrency exchange FTX; the Lewis book is the second channel through which the week's revelations arrived. The reporting is framed as allegation rather than established fact, and it comes from the book rather than from courtroom testimony. The item appeared in TechCrunch's Week in Review of October 7, 2023.



---


# Bankman-Fried's Pre-Collapse Public Image Strategy

Before his fall, Bankman-Fried made himself out to be the Good Boy of crypto — the trustworthy face of a sometimes-shady industry — and he was very interested in publicity, sitting for many interviews both before and after the collapse of FTX.

The Verge attributes FTX's quick rise as an industry force at least in part to that appetite for attention: Bankman-Fried gave interviews freely and quickly rose to public prominence, positioning himself as an important, boyish face for crypto even though FTX hadn't been in the business as long as competing exchanges such as Coinbase, Kraken, or Gemini. At one point he told a colleague at FTX that "I honestly think it's negative EV" — possibly "expected value," as in poker — "for me to cut my hair. I think it's important for people to think I look crazy." Because he was so successful at this kind of public relations, his fall from grace became another mark against an industry already roiled by bankruptcies and scandals; The Verge adds that more trouble for the industry is likely to come from one crucial element of the fraud trial, the part where the government must prove intent.



---


# The SBF Trial Proceedings

Sam Bankman-Fried is in court for alleged fraud and money laundering while leading crypto exchange FTX and sister company Alameda. TechCrunch's 2023-10-02 preview placed the case in the Manhattan Federal Court, describing the disgraced cryptocurrency entrepreneur as accused of orchestrating "one of the biggest financial frauds in American history": the multibillion-dollar collapse of FTX, the crypto exchange he founded and led. SBF, as he is known, has pleaded not guilty to some seven charges of fraud and conspiracy.

The trial kicked off with jury selection October 3. By TechCrunch's 2023-10-06 update the case was entering its next chapter, with proceedings resuming Thursday: as confirmed during a teleconference Wednesday, SBF would be taking the stand along with a handful of other witnesses, as the onus shifted toward the defense after the prosecution brought its case to its conclusion.

Access to the proceedings is limited: no devices are allowed, so reports are being physically put together within the courtroom, or sent to overflow rooms. The jury's composition ranges from a train conductor to a retired investment banker who attended Stanford University, and TechCrunch pointed readers to a special joint episode of its Equity and Chain Reaction podcasts for a better sense of the vibe between the jurors and the rest of the court.

A second account of the same events was arriving in parallel: "Going Infinite," a book by Michael Lewis chronicling the rise and fall of SBF, was set to debut on the first day of the trial.



---


# Bankman-Fried's Post-Bankruptcy Media Tour

After FTX declared bankruptcy, Bankman-Fried went on an extensive media tour, doing interviews with The New York Times' Andrew Ross Sorkin and Good Morning America — and he kept giving interviews even under house arrest, including with The New Yorker.

The Verge's reading of his motive: Bankman-Fried seemed to think that if he just explained things, everyone would understand that what he did was a mistake, not a crime.

qid: Does the 'Sporting News' article claim that the England national rugby union team has had a different path to the Rugby World Cup semifinal compared to the path of The Wallabies (Australian national rugby union team) as implied by the 'Wide World Of Sports' article, with England defeating specific teams and The Wallabies' fate depending on a match between other teams?
context:
# The Wallabies' 2023 Rugby World Cup Pool C Elimination Scenario

The Wallabies' 2023 Rugby World Cup fate rested on Fiji versus Portugal in Toulouse: sitting second in Pool C, Australia would be leapfrogged by Fiji and eliminated if Fiji took a single bonus point, Wide World Of Sports reported from Saint-Etienne on 7 October 2023.

The squad planned to gather in their plush Saint-Galmier hotel at 9pm local time (6am Monday AEDT) to watch what would almost certainly be their World Cup execution; the most likely outcome was that Fiji would win easily and the Wallabies would be pushing confirm on their off-season holiday plans. Fiji's win would send them to the quarter-finals in Marseille.

Wallabies centre Samu Kerevi, who was born in Fiji, spoke after an open training session in front of 1000 keen locals at the Andrezieux-Boutheon rugby club on the Saturday. "We've only got ourselves to blame, we put ourselves in this position," he said. "We'll sit down as a team and watch together on Sunday night. I think we understand the situation ... our results and the way we played, we put ourselves in this position. So the team understands that and we have our belief in anything's possible at the World Cup. But also, we understand how strong Fiji is. And we're proud for them as a proud nation. For myself, I'll be proud of it either way it goes. We'll be ready if it comes our way."



---


# Eddie Jones' Case For Reforming The Australian Rugby System

Eddie Jones argued that the Wallabies' problems are systemic rather than confined to the national team, and that it was crucial for Rugby Australia to get alignment in the code from grassroots through to the top team — with Australia, a two-time world champion, then ranked 10th in the world.

His grounds are the gap he saw at the top of the game and the state of the layer beneath it: "You just got to watch the quarterfinals at the weekend. We're not at that level. And we can't pretend to be at that level. But can we be at that level by 2027? Yes, we can. We're definitely off the pace but the opportunity to get better is there." The warrant is that a team declines when the system under it stops supporting it: "This is not an unusual situation. You've got a team that was struggling for a period of time, you've got underneath it a system that's not supporting it and at some stage you bottom out. This is the opportunity now to change the team — as we've started with picking younger players with bright futures — and then we've got to look at the development system underneath as well. It's not a simple equation that the Wallabies are bad. Let's be serious about this. The Wallabies are not where they need to be but underneath that we need to fix the system to go forward. And if we can do that now we've got a rosy future." He also acknowledged the cost of that change and the fans' pain: "We feel all the supporters hurt and really appreciate the great support we had in France and back in Australia for the team… Sometimes the change you have to have is uncomfortable. It is quite difficult. And sometimes you have to go through this to get into a better state and I believe that the problems we've had particularly at the national team will put us in a better state going forward." Jones clearly believes he is the right man to carry Australia on: "I think I've got the foresight to see where we need to go. I've got the experience of being in difficult situations before."

Earlier, on Oct. 10, Jones advocated specifically for Australian rugby to move to a centralised model, believing the nation had fallen behind the rest of the world: "We're a state-based union that's run by the states, the national union wants to assume more responsibility and when things were going well, no one questioned that. But over the last period of time, they haven't been going so well and this tournament's probably been the icing on the cake where it's got to a stage where I think people, most people probably think there's time for change. But it's not going to go easy." He located the payoff in player development: "[It's] one of the key issues. We need to maximize the development of the players. At the end of the day, that's the key to success and alignment of your resources, for a small country. Because Australia, if you look at the history of rugby, when we were amateur, we were probably ahead of the game because we had the influence of rugby league. We had the influence of AFL and our players were more professional than the rest of the world." And: "I know what's going on and we need to get a better system of developing players. We need to develop better players and we need to develop a larger batch of better players and that only comes through changing the whole system."



---


# The QRU's Position On High-Performance Centralisation

In the wake of the Wallabies' 2023 World Cup flop, the Queensland Rugby Union reaffirmed on Oct. 10, 2023 that it is committed to moving to a centralised high-performance model — but will not follow the NSW Waratahs in handing over the keys to Rugby Australia.

The QRU's stated commitment reads: "The QRU is committed to working with Rugby Australia to lead reform of our game at a high-performance level, and help Rugby Australia develop an improved game through high-performance centralisation." The letter defined the scope of that centralisation: it "would include a national player-contracting model, and alignment of key high-performance staff, such as coaching, strength and conditioning, and medical to operate as one national system." The letter, an open letter to members published on Wednesday morning by QRU chief executive David Hanham and chairman Brett Clark, also pointed to RA's involvement in Les Kiss' appointment as Reds coach — the former State of Origin winger turned coach, who has spent the best part of two decades coaching in Ireland and England, replacing Brad Thorn — as an example of the model in practice.

The QRU also expressed strong support for Rugby Australia to conduct a "fully independent and transparent top-to-bottom review of the Wallabies program and how it can be improved" in light of the historic first World Cup pool exit, adding: "It should also provide a clear view of what is needed in a leadership and governance framework to ensure we put the right people, in the right roles, in the right system." The Roar noted the boundary of the consensus: while all five Australian Super Rugby sides are fundamentally on board with moving to a centralised high-performance program, some states, including the ACT Brumbies as well as the QRU, don't want to give up their commercial assets.



---


# The Wallabies' 2023 Pool Exit And The Review That Followed

Eddie Jones' Wallabies became the first Australian side to bow out of a Rugby World Cup in the pool stages in 2023, and Jones accepted that a review would be required into the flop — a statement that, as The Roar put it, puts the ball firmly in Rugby Australia's court as far as his future goes.

Jones was named Wallabies coach at the start of the year as replacement for Dave Rennie, arriving with grand statements that his team could win the Rugby Championship, the Bledisloe Cup and make a smash and grab on the World Cup. None of those targets were achieved, and Jones changed his tune about building for the future when he named a young team for the doomed Cup campaign. He finished the year with a 2-7 win-loss record, the only two victories coming against lowly Georgia and Portugal.

On the review process, Rugby Australia had so far said it intended backing Jones, and he said he believed he had official support, while refusing to answer a question on potential break clauses in his contract. He said the team — including coaches and players — had already completed their own review of the World Cup disaster, and that the next one would be "a formal review to be done by independent consultants" in which he was ready to participate. He also rejected any suggestion the job was a soft landing: "I didn't come back to Australia to have a holiday – sit down at Coogee Beach, eat fish and chips, have a nice flat white. It was always going to be a battle. When you've got a team that hasn't done well for a long period of time, it's always a battle."



---


# The Case For Schmidt Bringing Rugby Smarts To The Wallabies

Several sources told The Roar in December 2023 that Joe Schmidt is exactly the type of person the Wallabies need: the claim is that the highly detailed Schmidt would bring rugby smarts to the Australian program, and the warrant is that the Wallabies' detail and nous were clearly absent on the field over the previous year, which is precisely what his coaching supplies.

The evidence offered for that capability is what his Ireland teams demonstrably did: the manipulation and ability to play both sides of the ruck was clearly visible during his Irish tenure.

The argument also carries a political ground about acceptance within Australian rugby: should Rugby Australia move on him, Schmidt's backing would be largely supported by the Super Rugby franchises.

Questioned on the amount of money Google spends to get first pick of search engines, Pichai said the decision was made with the consumer in mind: Google pays big bucks to be everywhere so that it can take in all the data and be the best search engine across different companies' devices, he said, according to The Verge.

The trial also produced evidence that Google understood the value of defaults very early on. U.S. Justice Department lawyer Meagan Bellshaw showed Pichai a 2007 email from a Google product strategy meeting containing data showing that when people changed their browser homepage to Google, they did 15% more Google searches, and that when they switched away, their Google searches dropped 27%. The email summarizing that meeting, sent to Pichai as well as other Google leaders, read: "Nitin argues that focusing on homepage market share is one of the most effective things we can do to make gains in search market share," according to The Verge.



---


# US v. Google: Two Months Into The Search Antitrust Trial

As of TechCrunch's November 13, 2023 roundup, the Justice Department's landmark antitrust case against Google was nearly two months old, and the trial record was still producing fresh revelations. TechCrunch framed it as one of the biggest fights in tech antitrust since the U.S. took Microsoft to trial in the 1990s.

An earlier roundup had already surfaced that Google spent $26.3 billion in 2021 making itself the default search engine across platforms, and that Google tried to have Chrome preinstalled on iPhones. Over the couple of weeks preceding this roundup, more of Google's inner workings came to light, including some of the search engine's most lucrative search queries, the shape of the revenue-share agreements between Google and Android OEMs, and why Expedia has a bone to pick with Google.

# Default Search Engine

## Definition

The default search engine is the search provider a device, browser, or platform is pre-configured to use unless a user actively changes the setting — the search box that runs when a person types a query without first choosing an alternative, such as Google on the iPhone's Safari address bar or Firefox's search bar.

## Context

The term is central to *US v. Google*, the DOJ's antitrust case, because default status is the mechanism through which Google secures the overwhelming share of search queries: the Information Services Agreement (ISA) between Apple and Google, in place since 2002/2003, makes Google the default on all Apple devices, and Google separately pays Samsung, Mozilla, and other partners for the same status.
Apple executive Eddy Cue testified that Apple's iPhone setup flow deliberately omits any search-engine choice screen, arguing that presenting users with unfamiliar alternatives would harm the setup experience, while conceding the ISA does not permit Apple to offer such a choice.
Google spent $26.3 billion in 2021 on default-placement deals across browsers, phones, and platforms — about $18 billion of that to Apple alone — a scale that the DOJ used to argue Google understands the mechanism's value: internal 2007 data showed users who set Google as their homepage searched 15% more, while switching away dropped searches 27%.
The Mozilla/Yahoo episode shows the same mechanism working in reverse: when Firefox switched its default from Google to Yahoo under a 2014 deal, Mozilla's CEO testified that user retention declined, illustrating how disruptive changing the default can be even when a paying competitor is involved.
Outside the antitrust trial, the term also frames ordinary consumer behavior: an investor in e-commerce search startup Deft described users' "natural behavior" as following the path of least resistance and just using the default search engine, meaning challenger search products must offer a high-value proposition to displace that inertia.

## Key Characteristics

- **Set by agreement, not by user choice** — default status on major platforms (Apple's Safari/iOS, Android OEMs, Firefox) is typically established through commercial deals (e.g., the Apple-Google ISA, Yahoo-Mozilla's $375M/year deal) rather than user selection at setup.
- **Backed by large recurring payments** — Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 across partners to hold default placement, with roughly $18 billion of that going to Apple.
- **Technically reversible but rarely changed** — Apple and Google both argued switching is easy, but DuckDuckGo's CEO countered that it takes "too many steps" to switch, and Google's own 2005 complaint about Internet Explorer's defaults argued that "most end users do not change defaults," so default status functions as durable market power.
- **Distinct from pre-installation** — Google's separate push to get Chrome and Search merely pre-installed (not necessarily defaulted) on Android and iPhones shows default status is a stronger, more contested tier than simple presence on a device.
- **Drives user behavior even outside browsers** — the concept extends to any search product; consumers default to "the path of least resistance," which challenger search startups must specifically overcome.

- [The Google Antitrust Case](google_antitrust_case.md)
- [The Hypocrisy Argument: Google Became The Monopoly It Denounced](google_default_hypocrisy_argument.md)

# The Google Antitrust Case

The Google antitrust case is the U.S. government's trial over Google's dominance in the online search market, stemming from a 2020 antitrust claim, in which the government argues that Google uses its platforms and its deals with partners to block out competition in search or advertising and thereby to hinder competitors from accessing the data they would need to improve their products.

Its defining features are the conduct at issue and the defence offered against it. Google CEO Sundar Pichai testified Monday in the trial, defending Google's business tactics, including its deal with Apple and other partners to make Google the default search engine. Google's answer is that it is just doing business: everybody wants Google as the default engine because it is the best, and that, the company says, does not make its actions illegal.

The important boundary case is which Google antitrust matter this is. The 2020 search claim is separate from the one filed in January by the Department of Justice, along with eight states including New York, California and Colorado, which aims to "halt Google's anticompetitive scheme, unwind Google's monopolistic grip on the market and restore competition to digital advertising." The search case and the digital-advertising case are distinct proceedings and should not be conflated.

The trial is the venue in which the underlying numbers surface. Monday's hearing revealed plenty of juicy tidbits, including the $26.3 billion Google spent making itself the default search engine across platforms in 2021, and how Google tried to take it further and have Chrome preinstalled on iPhones.



---


# Google's Agreement Not To Promote Chrome To Safari Users

As part of its search deal with Apple, Google agreed not to promote Chrome to Safari users, according to Bloomberg — a restraint that mattered because Google would otherwise have been able to do this with banners, pop-ups and other annoying means in its other Google apps. The same agreement also meant that Apple never switched to a Google competitor, and never allowed users to choose their browser when setting up their iPhones.

The observation surfaced in the antitrust trial, where the amount Google spent on homepage market share has been a fixing point. Earlier in October 2023, the CEOs of Microsoft and DuckDuckGo testified that their search engines would have been far more successful, even competitive with Google, had they been able to make similar deals with Apple. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella even said he was willing to spend $15 billion per year to get Bing into Apple's default search, per The Information — a stated willingness to pay, not a deal that happened.

A second, related admission came from Google's side: Pichai admitted to attempting to get Tim Cook to preinstall Google on every iOS device back in 2018, according to The Verge. His aim, as reported, was to make Google's and Apple's services so connected as to be inseparable.



---


# The U.S. Justice Department's Parallel Antitrust Suits Against Google

The Helena World Chronicle class action arrives alongside the filing of the U.S. Justice Department's lawsuit against Google for monopolizing digital ad technologies, and the complaint also references the Justice Department's 2020 civil antitrust suit over search and search advertising.

The two government cases concern different markets: search and search advertising in the 2020 suit are distinct from the digital ad technologies at issue in the more recent one.
