qid: Which platform is at the center of discussions about the ethical use of AI-driven voice replication for artists, the debate over "reaction" content monetization, the investment in AI technology to combat copyright and trademark abuse, and is also the most used app by kids overnight according to a study reported by sources including Music Business Worldwide, Polygon, and FOX News - Health?
context:
# YouTube's AI Music Incubator And Its Rightsholder Pledges

During its period of discussions with the majors, YouTube made a series of announcements aimed at the biggest issue for any rightsholder regarding AI-driven voice replication of artists: their ability to police it.

In August, YouTube and Universal Music Group jointly announced that the video platform was launching an "AI Music Incubator" — a program by which new tools and innovations would be developed at YouTube in close conjunction with artists and the music business; to progress the incubator, YouTube said it was working behind the scenes with a number of UMG-affiliated artists. Also in August, YouTube publicly committed to three principles or pledges behind its development of music-based generative AI tools. These pledges promised "appropriate protections… for music partners who decide to participate" in such tools, and promised "invest[ment] in the AI-powered technology" that, among other things, would help YouTube "protect our community of viewers, creators, artists and songwriters… [from] trademark and copyright abuse" — all of which seemed to hint at a desire to build a "Content ID"-style system on YouTube to control and police content made by cloning artists' voices. Then, earlier in November, YouTube announced it was developing a specific system for music partners allowing them to request the removal of content on its platform that "mimics an artist's unique singing or rapping voice."



---


# Sony Music's Pipeline Of AI Startup Partnerships

Kooker said Sony Music has "roughly 200 active conversations taking place with startups and established players" right now about building new AI-related products and tools, and that some of these conversations "also include potential equity investments which would accelerate the development of these companies."

He framed this as the optimistic counterweight to the harms: despite the negative impacts of AI, including unauthorized clones and low-quality AI music, there are still "many positive and optimistic developments to highlight," and he highlighted legitimate AI startups and established firms "with music ideas that want to partner with the industry." The products under discussion range from tools for "creative or marketing assistance," to tools that "potentially give us the ability to better protect artist content or find it when used in an unauthorized fashion," as well as "brand new products that have never been launched before."



---


# The US Copyright Office's 2023 Study Of AI And Copyright

The US Copyright Office is spearheading one of the key US efforts to address AI and copyright: in the summer of 2023 it issued a call for submissions on the issue of AI and copyright, with the goal of putting together a study to "help assess whether legislative or regulatory steps in this area are warranted."

The call for submissions came as legislators and regulators around the world grappled with the many issues that had emerged since AI technology "went mainstream" about a year earlier. Numerous businesses involved in AI, and those with substantial copyright holdings, submitted their thoughts on the issue — including Universal Music Group and AI developer Anthropic.



---


# Sony Music's Absence From "Dream Track"

Dennis Kooker's public statements on AI arrived a week after MBW pointed out a notable lack of endorsement from Sony Music Entertainment, and its artists, of YouTube's experimental AI project "Dream Track," which lets creators clone the vocals of successful musicians.

The initial cohort of stars involved in the project included recording artists signed to Warner Music Group and Universal Music Group — or labels within each of those two majors — but no Sony Music artists. In its earlier report MBW suggested that YouTube parent Google's recent submission to the United States Copyright Office, made in response to a request for written submissions as part of a study around copyright law and policy issues raised by AI systems, may have influenced Sony's absence from Dream Track.



---


# Deepfakes And Unauthorized Voice Clones Harm Artists

Kooker argued that the "more dire outputs of early generative AI technology are deep fakes and unauthorized voice clones" of artists, and that in the United States artists are not adequately protected from these deepfakes.

The grounds are economic and reputational. "An artist literally makes their livelihood from their voice," he said. "Deep fakes intentionally exploit an artist's talent and reputation to steal that income stream. Every stream of a deep fake takes streams and royalty payments away from the legitimate artist. Deepfakes are also misleading and confusing to consumers and music fans who are not typically interested in supporting fake versions of their favorite artist." He set this against a qualified optimism: while "the music industry sees great potential with various forms of AI technology in this early phase of AI," so far "the available generative AI products are not delivering on the expected promise of new products in creative industries," because some generative AI platforms "are not expanding the business model or enhancing human creativity."



---


# Sony Music's Generative AI Principles For Congress

Dennis Kooker, Sony Music Entertainment's President of Global Digital Business & US Sales, asked Congress at the November 29, 2023 AI Insight Forum to embrace a set of five principles around generative AI, on the argument that "if copyrights are protected and enforced appropriately, we are at the beginning of a multi-decade marathon that will change the creative and commercial landscape for music."

The framing condition Kooker set is that "Music is a tremendous driver for AI technology, and AI technology presents a tremendous opportunity for the creative development of music. But these opportunities must be grounded by the human creators' vision with the machine assisting, not with the machine replacing the human creator." The principles are: Assure Consent, Compensation, and Credit — "New products and businesses built with music must be developed with the consent of the owner and appropriate compensation and credit. It is essential to understand why the training of AI models is being done, what products will be developed as a result, and what the business model is that will monetize the use of the artist's work. Congress and the agencies should assure that creators' rights are recognized and respected." Confirm That Copying Music to Train AI Models is Not Fair Use — "Even worse are those that argue that copyrighted content should automatically be considered fair use so that protected works are never compensated for usage and creators have no say in the products or business models that are developed around them and their work. Congress should assure and agencies should presume that reproducing music to train AI models, in itself, is not a fair use." Prevent the Cloning of Artists' Voices and Likenesses Without Express Permission — "We cannot allow an artist's voice or likeness to be cloned for use without the express permission of the artist. This is a very personal decision for the artist. Congress should pass into law effective federal protections for name, image, and likeness." Incentivize Accurate Recordkeeping — "Correct attribution will be a critical element to artists being paid fairly and correctly for new works that are created. In addition, rights can only be enforced around the training of AI when there are accurate records about what is being copied. Otherwise, the inability to enforce rights in the AI marketplace equates to a lack of rights at all, producing a dangerous imbalance that prevents a thriving ecosystem. This requires strong and accurate record keeping by the generative AI platforms, a requirement that urgently needs legislative support to ensure incentives are in place so that it happens consistently and correctly." And Assure Transparency for Consumers and Artists — "Transparency is necessary to clearly distinguish human-created works from AI-created works. The public should know, when they are listening to music, whether that music was created by a human being or a machine." MBW summarised the intended effect: "The principles will ensure that intellectual property businesses can succeed in this new world alongside tech partners, further advancing investment and expanding economic opportunities."



---


# Schumer's AI Insight Forum On Creative Copyright

On Wednesday November 29, 2023, US Senate Majority Leader Chuck Schumer held an Artificial Intelligence (AI) Insight Forum to discuss the importance and role of creative copyright and intellectual property in the development of AI — a sign that senior political figures in Washington are becoming increasingly interested in the impact of AI on the law.

Dennis Kooker, Sony Music Entertainment's President of Global Digital Business & US Sales, delivered a speech at the Forum outlining the major music company's position on AI and copyright law.



---


# YouTube's "Dream Track" Voice Cloning Experiment

On November 16, 2023 YouTube unveiled "Dream Track," an experiment enabling creators to clone the vocals, via AI tech and with official consent, of well-known stars.

Charlie Puth's voice is on there. John Legend's voice is on there. Demi Lovato's voice is on there. In fact the voices of a number of well-known recording artists signed to Warner Music Group and Universal Music Group — or labels within each major — are on there. Something conspicuous is not: any endorsement whatsoever from the world's second-biggest recording company, Sony Music Entertainment, or its artists.



---


# The UMG, Concord And ABKCO Lawsuit Against Anthropic Over Song Lyrics

Universal Music Group, Concord Music Group and ABKCO filed a lawsuit against AI developer Anthropic seeking potentially tens of millions of dollars for the alleged "systematic and widespread infringement of their copyrighted song lyrics."

Music Business Worldwide noted on 2023-11-30 that the fair use argument Anthropic had advanced in its submission to the US Copyright Office could yet come into play in the company's legal battle with Universal.

# Sam Bankman-Fried

# Default Search Engine

## Definition

The default search engine is the search provider a device, browser, or platform is pre-configured to use unless a user actively changes the setting — the search box that runs when a person types a query without first choosing an alternative, such as Google on the iPhone's Safari address bar or Firefox's search bar.

## Context

The term is central to *US v. Google*, the DOJ's antitrust case, because default status is the mechanism through which Google secures the overwhelming share of search queries: the Information Services Agreement (ISA) between Apple and Google, in place since 2002/2003, makes Google the default on all Apple devices, and Google separately pays Samsung, Mozilla, and other partners for the same status.
Apple executive Eddy Cue testified that Apple's iPhone setup flow deliberately omits any search-engine choice screen, arguing that presenting users with unfamiliar alternatives would harm the setup experience, while conceding the ISA does not permit Apple to offer such a choice.
Google spent $26.3 billion in 2021 on default-placement deals across browsers, phones, and platforms — about $18 billion of that to Apple alone — a scale that the DOJ used to argue Google understands the mechanism's value: internal 2007 data showed users who set Google as their homepage searched 15% more, while switching away dropped searches 27%.
The Mozilla/Yahoo episode shows the same mechanism working in reverse: when Firefox switched its default from Google to Yahoo under a 2014 deal, Mozilla's CEO testified that user retention declined, illustrating how disruptive changing the default can be even when a paying competitor is involved.
Outside the antitrust trial, the term also frames ordinary consumer behavior: an investor in e-commerce search startup Deft described users' "natural behavior" as following the path of least resistance and just using the default search engine, meaning challenger search products must offer a high-value proposition to displace that inertia.

## Key Characteristics

- **Set by agreement, not by user choice** — default status on major platforms (Apple's Safari/iOS, Android OEMs, Firefox) is typically established through commercial deals (e.g., the Apple-Google ISA, Yahoo-Mozilla's $375M/year deal) rather than user selection at setup.
- **Backed by large recurring payments** — Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 across partners to hold default placement, with roughly $18 billion of that going to Apple.
- **Technically reversible but rarely changed** — Apple and Google both argued switching is easy, but DuckDuckGo's CEO countered that it takes "too many steps" to switch, and Google's own 2005 complaint about Internet Explorer's defaults argued that "most end users do not change defaults," so default status functions as durable market power.
- **Distinct from pre-installation** — Google's separate push to get Chrome and Search merely pre-installed (not necessarily defaulted) on Android and iPhones shows default status is a stronger, more contested tier than simple presence on a device.
- **Drives user behavior even outside browsers** — the concept extends to any search product; consumers default to "the path of least resistance," which challenger search startups must specifically overcome.

# Google Paid $26.3 Billion In 2021 For Default Search Placement

Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to multiple browsers, phones and platforms — from companies including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla — to be everyone's default search engine. The figure was revealed by Google's search head Prabhakar Raghavan when he testified in court on October 28, according to The Verge.

About $18 billion of that total went directly to Apple, according to a New York Times report published earlier in October 2023, and Google has had its deal with Apple in place since 2003 — so the payment is the current year of a two-decade arrangement, not a one-off. Questioned on the amount of money Google spends to get first pick of search engines, Pichai said the decision was made with the consumer in mind: Google pays big bucks to be everywhere so that it can take in all the data and be the best search engine across different companies' devices, he said, according to The Verge.

The trial also produced evidence that Google understood the value of defaults very early on. U.S. Justice Department lawyer Meagan Bellshaw showed Pichai a 2007 email from a Google product strategy meeting containing data showing that when people changed their browser homepage to Google, they did 15% more Google searches, and that when they switched away, their Google searches dropped 27%. The email summarizing that meeting, sent to Pichai as well as other Google leaders, read: "Nitin argues that focusing on homepage market share is one of the most effective things we can do to make gains in search market share," according to The Verge.



---


# US v. Google: Two Months Into The Search Antitrust Trial

As of TechCrunch's November 13, 2023 roundup, the Justice Department's landmark antitrust case against Google was nearly two months old, and the trial record was still producing fresh revelations. TechCrunch framed it as one of the biggest fights in tech antitrust since the U.S. took Microsoft to trial in the 1990s.

An earlier roundup had already surfaced that Google spent $26.3 billion in 2021 making itself the default search engine across platforms, and that Google tried to have Chrome preinstalled on iPhones. Over the couple of weeks preceding this roundup, more of Google's inner workings came to light, including some of the search engine's most lucrative search queries, the shape of the revenue-share agreements between Google and Android OEMs, and why Expedia has a bone to pick with Google.



---


# The Google Antitrust Case

The Google antitrust case is the U.S. government's trial over Google's dominance in the online search market, stemming from a 2020 antitrust claim, in which the government argues that Google uses its platforms and its deals with partners to block out competition in search or advertising and thereby to hinder competitors from accessing the data they would need to improve their products.

Its defining features are the conduct at issue and the defence offered against it. Google CEO Sundar Pichai testified Monday in the trial, defending Google's business tactics, including its deal with Apple and other partners to make Google the default search engine. Google's answer is that it is just doing business: everybody wants Google as the default engine because it is the best, and that, the company says, does not make its actions illegal.

The important boundary case is which Google antitrust matter this is. The 2020 search claim is separate from the one filed in January by the Department of Justice, along with eight states including New York, California and Colorado, which aims to "halt Google's anticompetitive scheme, unwind Google's monopolistic grip on the market and restore competition to digital advertising." The search case and the digital-advertising case are distinct proceedings and should not be conflated.

The trial is the venue in which the underlying numbers surface. Monday's hearing revealed plenty of juicy tidbits, including the $26.3 billion Google spent making itself the default search engine across platforms in 2021, and how Google tried to take it further and have Chrome preinstalled on iPhones.



---


# Google's Agreement Not To Promote Chrome To Safari Users

As part of its search deal with Apple, Google agreed not to promote Chrome to Safari users, according to Bloomberg — a restraint that mattered because Google would otherwise have been able to do this with banners, pop-ups and other annoying means in its other Google apps. The same agreement also meant that Apple never switched to a Google competitor, and never allowed users to choose their browser when setting up their iPhones.

The observation surfaced in the antitrust trial, where the amount Google spent on homepage market share has been a fixing point. Earlier in October 2023, the CEOs of Microsoft and DuckDuckGo testified that their search engines would have been far more successful, even competitive with Google, had they been able to make similar deals with Apple. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella even said he was willing to spend $15 billion per year to get Bing into Apple's default search, per The Information — a stated willingness to pay, not a deal that happened.

A second, related admission came from Google's side: Pichai admitted to attempting to get Tim Cook to preinstall Google on every iOS device back in 2018, according to The Verge. His aim, as reported, was to make Google's and Apple's services so connected as to be inseparable.



---


# The U.S. Justice Department's Parallel Antitrust Suits Against Google

The Helena World Chronicle class action arrives alongside the filing of the U.S. Justice Department's lawsuit against Google for monopolizing digital ad technologies, and the complaint also references the Justice Department's 2020 civil antitrust suit over search and search advertising.

The two government cases concern different markets: search and search advertising in the 2020 suit are distinct from the digital ad technologies at issue in the more recent one.

# Epic's Post-Verdict Remedy Strategy And Global Cases

Told that Google has said it will challenge the verdict, Tim Sweeney said Epic is not going to wait: it will do absolutely everything it can as quickly as it can to start changing the world, rather than pausing for the appeal.

His reasoning for the reach of the win is the market Epic established at trial — a market worldwide excluding China — so this is, in his framing, a worldwide verdict, and Epic presumes any remedies would be worldwide too. Beyond the US case, he pointed to the European DMA, to Epic v. Apple and Epic v. Google cases coming up in Australia, and to another in the UK. He also stressed that the push no longer depends on Epic alone: a lot of legislators, a lot of regulators, and other litigation are all pushing in the direction of openness. On whether the Google verdict helps Epic's Apple appeal, Sweeney said there is no linkage between the cases in law and no legal connection between the two, so it would come down only to whether the court is in any way following current events — to the decisions of the humans involved, the justices and support teams considering the appeal.



---


# Epic Games v. Google Goes To Trial On November 6, 2023

Epic Games, the maker of Fortnite, went to trial with Google on November 6, 2023, hoping to convince a jury that Google engages in anticompetitive behavior with regard to its Android app store, Google Play, and its commission structure. Match had settled its own antitrust lawsuit with Google the week before, but Epic's case proceeded.

This case differs slightly from Epic's battle with Apple on the same topic, because this time Epic cannot allege there is no other way to load apps onto Android devices, as it could with Apple: Android does allow for sideloading apps. Epic will suggest Google makes that process cumbersome, but the bulk of its arguments will center on what it believes are anticompetitive agreements between Google and device manufacturers and developers.

The precedent Epic's case relies on is a Microsoft case in which courts found Microsoft to have a monopoly over the operating system and to be abusing it, making it hard for users to download alternative browsers, like Netscape, on Windows devices. To make its case, Epic plans to bring claims under Sections 1 and 2 of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act, as well as California's anticompetitive laws, the Cartwright Act and the Unfair Competition Law. It will attempt to argue that Google restrains competition within two separate markets: the distribution of apps to Android users, and the market for payment processing solutions for content inside Android apps.



---


# The Settlements That Left Epic Standing Alone

Other plaintiffs brought app store antitrust claims against Google and then all settled: all 50 state attorneys general and a number of consumers have tentatively settled, though it is not clear what the deal might include, and Match Group — the company behind Tinder, Match.com, OkCupid and other dating apps — just reached a surprise last-minute settlement too, one that makes it sound like Match effectively gave up. Epic stands alone.

Epic seems to have no interest in settling as long as the "Google tax" exists, and the company has repeatedly said it is not interested in cash. So far it has been willing to push these cases all the way through multiple appeals, cost be damned. It is not clear what Google could proactively offer that would satisfy Epic, since CEO Tim Sweeney has also publicly suggested that Google would simply circumvent any settlement it offers. If you want to see a vision of a future Epic would accept, look to the letter it sent to state attorneys general, laying out a settlement that would basically prohibit Google from doing the anticompetitive things Epic claims it did. Google would not tell The Verge whether it has offered Epic any kind of settlement.



---


# Epic Games Store Growth And Diversification Beyond Games

Asked what changed after a period when Epic seemed interested in expanding outside games with acquisitions like Houseparty and Bandcamp, Tim Sweeney said Epic has gotten so much traction with Fortnite in so many different ways, and with the Epic Games Store, that it is going to continue investing heavily there.

He called the Epic Games Store "the untold success story in the background": since it launched in 2018 it now has 80 million monthly active users, against Steam's 120 million, which he read as catching up fast. He also claimed Fortnite has more concurrent users right now than all Steam games combined, and promised dramatic changes that benefit all developers over the next few years. The Verge appended an editor's note correcting the concurrency claim: Epic spokesperson Natalie Muñoz confirmed Sweeney had misinterpreted a Polygon story about Fortnite hitting 7.6 million players at a time when the entirety of Steam had 10.1 million; these days Steam generally peaks at over 30 million with valleys of 20 million, while Fortnite's valleys are closer to 3.8 million.



---


# Tech Layoffs In September 2023

September 2023's largest tech layoff was Epic Games, which announced on September 28 that the Fortnite maker was laying off 16% of its workforce, amounting to 870 people.

The month's other cuts ran across streaming, edtech, gaming and analytics. Roku announced on September 6 that it planned to lay off approximately 10% of its workforce, representing over 300 employees. Sensor Tower announced on September 8 that it had laid off approximately 40 people out of the 270-plus at the company, including C-suite executives. Divvy Homes announced on September 11 that it was laying off 94 employees. Roblox confirmed to TechCrunch on September 21 that it had let go of 30 employees in its talent acquisition organization, with no other teams impacted. Byju's announced on September 26 that it planned to cut 5,000 jobs due to restructuring efforts, the startup having eliminated more than 10,000 positions in the past two years. An impacted employee confirmed on September 27 that at least 140 people, if not more, were affected by Talkdesk's third round of layoffs in less than 14 months. Naughty Dog was reportedly cutting at least 25 contract developers, two sources familiar with the situation told Kotaku. In a regulatory filing published September 29, the cybersecurity startup IronNet said it had ceased all business activities as it prepared for Chapter 7 bankruptcy and had laid off its remaining staff.



---


# Project Liberty: Epic's Deliberate Payment Bypass

Epic is the studio behind Fortnite, the extraordinarily popular free-to-play game, which makes money by selling in-game items with its virtual currency V-Bucks; until August 13th, 2020, if a player used an Android or iOS device and installed the game through an official app store, buying V-Bucks triggered an in-app payment fee to Google or Apple — fees critics call the "Google tax" or the "Apple tax," and which Epic definitely was not a fan of.

August 13th, 2020 was a very busy day. Epic announced it was bypassing Apple and Google's app store fees, deploying a hotfix update to Fortnite without either company's knowledge that let players buy V-Bucks directly through its own payment processing option at a discount. Apple and Google almost immediately reacted by kicking Fortnite off their app stores for breaking the rules. Then Epic was ready and waiting with two lawsuits and an attack ad depicting a Fortnite hero throwing a unicorn-llama hammer into a giant screen reminiscent of Apple's famous "1984" Macintosh ad. It was a striking publicity blitz followed by a lot of slow-moving court proceedings: the Apple lawsuit went to court in 2021 and a ruling came down that September, mostly decided in Apple's favor, though both parties are waiting for the Supreme Court to potentially weigh in, while the Google one was delayed again and again.

The premeditation is documented, and Google is countersuing over it. At trial Google pointed out how Epic hatched a secret plan called "Project Liberty" to quietly update Fortnite with code to bypass app store fees, get its app kicked off Apple's and Google's app stores, and sue. It showed out-of-context quotes from internal Epic communications — phrases like "How do we not look like the bad guys?", "Just planting the nefarious seed now" and "I mean everything we're attempting is technically a violation of Google's policy, right?" — to suggest Epic knew it was breaking bad at the time. An email from Epic CEO Tim Sweeney reads: "Here is our official plan for communicating with Google about bypassing the Google Play Store: SAY NOTHING TILL IT SHIPS."

Epic did not try to hide it in court. Epic mentioned Project Liberty in its own opening statement, so by the time Google raised it, it had already been an hour since Epic admitted it intentionally broke Google's rules. "Epic decided to stand up because that's what you do to a bully," Bornstein told the jury.



---


# TuSimple Exits The US Market

TuSimple said in a regulatory filing on Monday 4 December 2023 that it is laying off the majority of its U.S. workforce and selling assets in the country as it exits for Asia.

When TuSimple went public in 2021 it was flying high as the leading self-driving trucks developer in the U.S. Its retreat follows a string of internal controversies and the loss of a critical partnership with truck manufacturer Navistar.

# Manchester United's European Decline Since Ferguson

The Independent argued on 12 December 2023 that Manchester United's 1-0 defeat to Bayern Munich should have been a landmark low but instead felt grimly routine, because group-stage elimination has become the club's normal European outcome in the post-Ferguson era rather than an aberration.

The grounds are frequency and pattern. Manchester United, one of the grandest and richest names in this competition, have again gone out of the Champions League at the group stage; it is the third time it has happened since Sir Alex Ferguson, meaning it is their most common round of exit in that period. The night is presented as one more entry in a decade of disappointment in a competition in which this club rose to its most emotional heights — a low, but just part of that longer run.

The warrant is the gap between the occasion and the performance. These are not the sounds we are used to hearing after that Champions League theme; something does stir when the anthem is played at Old Trafford amid the lights — well, for most, that is, except the players. United should not be performing like this on what is supposed to be the classic European night at Old Trafford, and the display was a reminder that all they are going to have for some time are their memories. Having been involved in so many ludicrously chaotic matches, the biggest of all ended up being a non-event: this game never threatened to stir anything, and United never threatened at all. That, the argument runs, can now be talked about definitively, since it has been decisively ended.



---


# Jean-Claude Blanc and the United Chief Executive Challenge

The question The Guardian posed on 25 December 2023 is whether any chief executive can make Manchester United a best-in-class elite club again — and the candidate in frame is Jean-Claude Blanc, billed as the "Lionel Messi of business" by Nice's chief executive, Fabrice Bocquet.

Blanc's credentials are unusually broad for the role. He has an MBA from Harvard, and at 60 years old has been Juventus CEO and president, CEO at Paris Saint-Germain and at French Tennis, and the executive overseeing the Tour de France.

The boundary on those credentials is the club itself. The report argues that once Blanc, or whoever becomes Arnold's successor, is in place, it will dawn rapidly that United are a one-off hydra-headed beast of a club which is treacherously difficult to control. And there is the competitive gap: across town Manchester City have accrued six championships since United's last in 2013, and boast a commercial operation that leaves Ratcliffe's new concern light years behind.



---


# Paul Mitchell's Blueprint For A Manchester United Rebuild

Paul Mitchell argues that Manchester United must define an identity and a five-year blueprint and then hold to it, because consistency of decision-making over that period is what produces sustainable success — a blueprint he laid out while still at Monaco, reported by talkSPORT on 16 October 2023.

His grounds begin with context and end with comparison. "I think context is important to measure what Manchester United's current situation is, but I think they do need to get to the point of really putting down what Manchester United needs to be in the modern game," he explained. "We are a long time from the Sir Alex Ferguson era. Erik ten Hag is a top coach from Ajax but they need a top blueprint not only for now but for the next five years, and work towards that, and sometimes on that journey there are hard moments when you don't get the right results, even though you're doing the right things." The warrant is that results in the short run are a noisy signal: "You have to know that, over that period, the consistency of the decision-making will yield a good end result. I think we've seen that both Manchester City and Liverpool, that when you adopt that long-term strategy you can get real consistency and sustainable success."

The content of the blueprint is an identity statement spanning the whole club: "putting down their identity of what they want to be today, but most crucially what they want to be in five years' time, and where they want to be, and what they want to look like; from everything from young players, to the style of play, to the whole culture peace in Manchester United." There is a counter-consideration attached — almost certain to consult Ralf Rangnick before any approach from Ratcliffe, Mitchell may be warned off a club where long-term thinking has not existed — but should Ratcliffe get his man it could signal exactly the change in fortunes he and every supporter has been hoping for.



---


# The Manchester United Crisis News Cycle Under Ten Hag

The Guardian's argument is that results at Manchester United no longer settle anything, because the club's crisis news cycle consumes wins as quickly as defeats: a stirring recovery against Chelsea bought Erik ten Hag only a few days' grace.

The grounds are the pattern of the week itself — rancour, rumour and recrimination, barbs in the press and barbs at the press, defeat at Newcastle followed by the Chelsea win and the startling realisation that United were three points behind Manchester City, all before Thursday. The warrant is a claim about the institution rather than the team: such is the way of things at football's most reliable content provider, and this beast must always eat, so the warm flume of goodwill would last only as long as it took for Dominic Solanke to run through on goal for Bournemouth on the Saturday afternoon, returning United to the grip of crisis and the now-familiar lexicon of surly unsourced stories about dressing room discontent. A second, related argument is that assessing any United manager requires filters: Ten Hag would of course take the blame for the early Champions League exit, and plenty of mistakes had been made, not least in the players the manager had been allowed to sign — but to be United manager is to undertake three concurrent roles.



---


# Manchester United Recent Champions League Failures

Thirty years on from Istanbul, United headed to Turkey knowing they had rarely been convincing in the Champions League in recent years, The Guardian reported on Nov. 27, 2023: a 3-1 away win against Paris Saint-Germain in the 2018-19 round of 16, after losing the home leg 2-0, was the last time they won a crunch match.

In 2020-21 they lost their final two group games and were eliminated, while back in 2015-16 Wolfsburg won the deciding group match to knock them out. United had done little learning in recent times, repeating the same failures in Europe's elite competition. It would not be a disgrace to lose against a good Galatasaray team, especially given Erik ten Hag was missing key players, but if the worst happened, everyone would need to come out of the experience stronger — regardless of the result, it should be a night of education about the demands of the Champions League.



---


# Erik Ten Hag's Position Under Ratcliffe

Erik ten Hag's team are treading water at precisely the wrong moment, The Guardian reported on 25 December 2023: Sir Jim Ratcliffe is taking charge of Manchester United's sporting department before making sweeping changes to the posts that will directly affect the manager.

Two lines of authority above Ten Hag are in play. Richard Arnold has left, despite officially staying until the end of the year, and into his role may come Jean-Claude Blanc, the CEO of Ratcliffe's Ineos Sport, as the man Ten Hag reports to. Ten Hag's line manager may change too, as Ratcliffe considers whether a new football director is required — a position held by John Murtough.

The report suggested an early tell of Ten Hag's standing in Ratcliffe's new empire: whether he is sounded out for his view on a prime factor in his ability to coach and manage the side to success, namely United's transfer policy.



---


# The INEOS Plan For Manchester United's Football Operations

Sir Jim Ratcliffe is demanding an executive role and overall control of Manchester United's day-to-day football matters, and plans to appoint his own sporting director, with former Tottenham and Southampton transfer guru Paul Mitchell one of the main names in the frame, talkSPORT reported on 18 October 2023.

The plan reaches across the club's football leadership. Ratcliffe's arrival raises doubts over the future of current sporting director John Murtough and chief executive Richard Arnold, although manager Erik ten Hag is believed to be on a solid footing despite United's poor start to the season. Sir Dave Brailsford — the mastermind behind Team GB's cycling success at the London 2012 Olympics and director of sport for Ratcliffe's company INEOS — is expected to have a prominent role in any reshuffle. Ratcliffe also has ambitious plans to upgrade Old Trafford and turn it into a 90,000-seat stadium. He wants the deal ratified in time for the January transfer window, though because of FFP concerns there is no guarantee United will be able to spend big. Despite turning 71 the day before the board meeting, his plans appear to centre on long-term stability and success rather than a short-term turnaround in United's fortunes.

The ownership rationale is that Ratcliffe would take charge of footballing matters, something the Glazers have been accused of having little to no interest in. He is already a top-tier European owner through OGC Nice — and also owns Lausanne in Switzerland — where there has been some success but nothing compared to Nice's French riviera neighbours, the club to which Ratcliffe appears set to look for inspiration.

# Honorable Mentions on Polygon's Best Movies of 2023 List

Polygon published an honorable-mentions section alongside its best-movies-of-2023 list, defined as movies that received votes but did not crack the top 50.

The listed titles were: The Pope's Exorcist, Bottoms, Rye Lane, No Hard Feelings, Hundreds of Beavers, Evil Dead Rise, Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 3, Nimona, The Starling Girl, Thanksgiving, Guy Ritchie's The Covenant, The Eight Mountains, The Roundup: No Way Out, The Royal Hotel, Red, White & Royal Blue, Blue Jean, The Venture Bros.: Radiant Is the Blood of the Baboon Heart, Quiz Lady, Air, Elemental, Extraction 2, Fair Play, Metalocalypse: Army of the Doomstar, A Haunting in Venice, Fast X, You Hurt My Feelings, The Super Mario Bros. Movie, No One Will Save You, Monster, The Pigeon Tunnel, The Caine Mutiny Court-Martial, Ant-Man and the Wasp: Quantumania, American Fiction, Maestro, Saw X, Maaveeran, The Creator, The Blackening, The Marvels, Afire, Kandahar, Crater, Dark Harvest, Ernest & Celestine: A Trip to Gibberitia, and Indiana Jones and the Dial of Destiny.

# The Roland Doe Case and The Exorcist

Perhaps the most famous instance of purported demonic possession connected to Ouija board usage was the case of "Roland Doe", a young teenage boy from Maryland, who underwent numerous major exorcisms in 1949, said Fr. Dan Reehil.

Doe's story was adapted into the 1971 book "The Exorcist" by William Peter Blatty, which was then made into the 1973 movie starring Ellen Burstyn and Linda Blair.



---


# The Exorcist III

The Exorcist III, written and directed by William Peter Blatty — the original screenwriter of The Exorcist and author of the novel it was based on — is, in Polygon's judgment, the sequel that came closest to capturing the same lightning in a bottle as William Friedkin's original, which nearly 50 years after its theatrical release has withstood the test of time as one of the most terrifying and influential horror films in American cinema. It was the Oct. 31 pick in Polygon's 2023-10-10 Halloween Countdown, listed on Prime Video and the Criterion Channel.

When a series of gruesome murders matching the modus operandi of an infamous serial killer begins to terrorize the city of Georgetown, Lt. William F. Kinderman, played by George C. Scott, investigates the psych ward of a local hospital in search of leads. Confronted with a suspect whose appearance matches that of his late friend Father Damien Karras, Kinderman is thrust into a battle for his very soul as he confronts an evil beyond his comprehension.

Polygon's Toussaint Egan calls the production history a tangled mess of false starts, studio interference, and thwarted artistic ambitions: it was originally conceived with Friedkin in mind to return as director, but he left over creative differences with Blatty; John Carpenter was at one time tapped to direct before he too stepped aside to let Blatty take the reins; and financier Morgan Creek Productions demanded Blatty reshoot the final act, which originally ended without an exorcism. Even so, Egan calls it a fascinating and terrifying film in its own right, with a hodgepodge of fascinating creative choices and literary dialogue that makes it feel like a sister piece to Blatty's The Ninth Configuration — maybe not the Exorcist sequel audiences at the time wanted, but still a damn fine picture.



---


# In The Mouth Of Madness: Carpenter's Apocalypse Trilogy Closer

In the Mouth of Madness is among the wildest movies John Carpenter has ever made — and Polygon notes that is saying something. Starring Sam Neill, Julie Carmen and Jurgen Prochnow, and watchable on YouTube, it follows insurance investigator John Trent (Neill), who is hired to find a missing famous horror novelist; things become increasingly unhinged as the plots of the author's books and the various monsters seem to invade the real world.

Neill, a staple of this list, is absolutely fantastic responding to the horrors of hell, slowly becoming exactly as off-kilter as they are: by the third act the door to hell is halfway open and Trent is ready to dive headfirst into the void, which the reviewer says is honestly how every movie's third act should go. Its place in Carpenter's work is specific — this is the third film in his apocalypse trilogy, which also includes two other stone-cold classics, The Thing and Prince of Darkness, which are not on the list but which the reviewer recommends anyway.



---


# Overlord (2018 Nazi Zombie Film)

Overlord is a slept-on genre-mashing gem that places a cast of excellent actors about to do bigger things — Jovan Adepo, Wyatt Russell, John Magaro, Pilou Asbæk, and more — and up-and-coming director Julius Avery, of The Pope's Exorcist, behind Nazi lines during World War II, where the Nazis are up to more than usual: there be zombies in these labs. It was the Oct. 24 pick in Polygon's 2023-10-10 Halloween Countdown, listed on Paramount Plus and Pluto TV.

On the eve of D-Day, a group of Allied paratroopers are sent into Germany on a covert mission. Things go wrong instantly when their plane crashes, and they soon discover twisted Nazi experiments after connecting with the residents. Things get bloody fast, with great action from second unit director Shaun O'Dell, of The Woman King and Brotherhood of the Wolf, and stunt coordinator Jo McLaren of Heart of Stone.

Polygon's Pete Volk calls it a gleeful, intentionally ridiculous Nazi-zombie-bashing time with tight direction and a fantastic group of actors, recommended for anyone who loves the Wolfenstein games, Call of Duty's Zombies mode, or B-movies with A-movie production.



---


# Polygon's Selection Process for the Best Movies of 2023

Polygon builds its best-movies-of-the-year list by having each of the staff's film fans create an individual ballot of their top movies every year, with an option to rank the entries numerically or simply weight them; those ballots are then used to generate a collective list, weighted by strength of opinion so that a much-seen mainstream movie does not gain too much advantage over a terrific but underseen indie. The result is then published, with the top 10 picks on each staffer's list listed in the comments.

The eligibility rule is that any movie released in the US during that calendar year qualifies. A stated limitation follows from the publication timing: because the list is published in early December, some December releases are underrepresented.

Polygon frames the exercise as inherently difficult, likening a collaborative best-movies list to forming a committee to definitively rank apples and oranges — how to account for personal tastes, or for access when a given movie is only available in certain markets at certain times, or for the fact that the entries are so qualitatively different they have little in common. The weighted-ballot procedure exists to accommodate that spread: the staff describes its collective tastes as eclectic, with some hungriest for action, horror, epic fantasy, or challenging science fiction, some preferring complicated drama or dark neo-noir, and others drawn to musicals, comedy, animated adventures, and other lighter fare. The best-of-the-year list is meant to reflect that range.



---


# Five Nights at Freddy's Movie Development and Release

The possessed-animatronics horror video game Five Nights at Freddy's is less than a decade old, but a movie version had been in the works almost since the game launched — a protracted development process Polygon recounted on 2023-10-26.

Warner Bros. bought the movie rights in 2015, and the project moved over to Blumhouse a couple of years later. Game creator Scott Cawthon wrote and rewrote the script, while kid-horror filmmakers including Gil Kenan of Monster House and Chris Columbus of Gremlins and the first Harry Potter and Percy Jackson movies signed on and jumped off the project.

Finally, under director Emma Tammi, the film hit theaters simultaneously with a Peacock streaming debut. Polygon framed its accompanying Q&A as extremely spoiler-light and aimed at people other than the franchise's most hardcore fans, deliberately not digging into the considerable FNAF lore and focusing instead on who the film is for and what to expect.



---


# Shin Kamen Rider (Hideaki Anno)

Shin Kamen Rider is Hideaki Anno's film starring Sosuke Ikematsu, Minami Hamabe, and Tasuku Emoto, which Polygon calls the best superhero movie of 2023 — one that came from neither Marvel nor DC. It ranked 50 on the outlet's best movies of 2023 list of 2023-10-07 and streams on Prime Video under the title Shin Masked Rider.

Polygon's Pete Volk qualifies the praise: the film might not reach the soaring heights of Shin Godzilla.

What it delivers instead is an incredibly fun time bolstered by terrific costume designs, inventive action sequences, and a delightfully bizarre tone, all while looking gorgeous throughout.

qid: Who is the individual facing a criminal trial on fraud and conspiracy charges, whose alleged success with a crypto exchange is claimed to be based on falsehoods, admitted to being informed of a significant financial discrepancy after judicial prompting, and is accused by the prosecution of intentionally committing fraud for personal gain, as reported by TechCrunch, Fortune, The Verge, and again by TechCrunch?
context:
# The SBF Trial Proceedings

Sam Bankman-Fried is in court for alleged fraud and money laundering while leading crypto exchange FTX and sister company Alameda. TechCrunch's 2023-10-02 preview placed the case in the Manhattan Federal Court, describing the disgraced cryptocurrency entrepreneur as accused of orchestrating "one of the biggest financial frauds in American history": the multibillion-dollar collapse of FTX, the crypto exchange he founded and led. SBF, as he is known, has pleaded not guilty to some seven charges of fraud and conspiracy.

The trial kicked off with jury selection October 3. By TechCrunch's 2023-10-06 update the case was entering its next chapter, with proceedings resuming Thursday: as confirmed during a teleconference Wednesday, SBF would be taking the stand along with a handful of other witnesses, as the onus shifted toward the defense after the prosecution brought its case to its conclusion.

Access to the proceedings is limited: no devices are allowed, so reports are being physically put together within the courtroom, or sent to overflow rooms. The jury's composition ranges from a train conductor to a retired investment banker who attended Stanford University, and TechCrunch pointed readers to a special joint episode of its Equity and Chain Reaction podcasts for a better sense of the vibe between the jurors and the rest of the court.

A second account of the same events was arriving in parallel: "Going Infinite," a book by Michael Lewis chronicling the rise and fall of SBF, was set to debut on the first day of the trial.



---


# FTX Fraud Charges And The SEC's Allegation

Sam Bankman-Fried, the founder of the failed cryptocurrency exchange FTX, faced seven counts of wire fraud and conspiracy — specifically, two counts of wire fraud and five conspiracy charges — and the Securities and Exchange Commission alleged that FTX was a fraud "from the start," with a "multi-billion-dollar deficiency caused by his own misappropriation of customer funds." The Verge repeated this framing at the head of each of its trial dispatches through October 2023, and in its October 28th, 2023 write-up reported that Bankman-Fried had been found guilty on seven counts including charges of wire fraud.

The boundary of the concept is the mix of charge types: the indictment paired substantive wire fraud counts with conspiracy counts rather than resting on a single offence, and the SEC's civil allegation about the exchange's origins ran alongside the criminal case rather than being part of it. The Verge's reporter, writing as the prosecution's case neared its end on October 26th, 2023, added an impression of the people the charges swept in: all the co-conspirators seemed oddly younger than their years, as though they had got stuck in the "math camp forever" environment Bankman-Fried created for them and simply failed to grow up.



---


# Prosecution And Defense Arguments On Day Two Of The SBF Trial

On the second day of the trial of Sam Bankman-Fried and FTX, the prosecution argued that Bankman-Fried knowingly committed fraud, and it grounded that claim in motive: he did so, prosecutors said, to achieve great wealth, power and influence.

The defense countered with the opposite reading of the same conduct. Its claim was that the FTX founder acted in good faith, never meant to commit fraud or to steal, and basically got in over his head — an argument whose warrant is that inexperience and overreach, rather than intent, explain what happened. The two sides therefore contest intent rather than the underlying events, and the reporting on this exchange comes from Rebecca and Jacquelyn in TechCrunch's Week in Review of October 7, 2023, covering day two of the trial only.



---


# Sam Bankman-Fried

Sam Bankman-Fried is the former CEO of the bankrupt crypto exchange FTX, whose highly anticipated criminal trial started on the Tuesday before TechCrunch's 2023-10-01 report, to determine whether he is guilty of seven counts of fraud and conspiracy. As one former federal prosecutor put it: "The odds seem to be stacked against him at this point."

He was 31 years old and co-founded FTX in 2019; within a few years the once third-largest crypto exchange's valuation hit $32 billion at its peak, and the company is now trying to claw back any funds to distribute to creditors. Before the fall he was even compared to Warren Buffet, and many called him the white horse of crypto — a description TechCrunch notes it never applied to him.

Bankman-Fried, however, maintained his innocence. At The New York Times' DealBook Summit he appeared virtually from the Bahamas and said, "I didn't ever try to commit fraud on anyone; I was shocked by what happened this month"; in a published DM exchange with a Vox reporter he said he regretted filing for bankruptcy and thought that "regulators make everything worse." In January he pleaded not guilty to all counts, which include wire fraud, conspiracy to commit money laundering and conspiracy to misuse customer funds. He could face up to 115 years in jail if convicted on all charges.

TechCrunch's 2023-10-02 summary of his standing on the eve of trial: SBF has been denied bail; his name is mud (or much worse) among those who have lost money in Alameda or FTX; and those who might not have had positions in these still blame him for other crypto woes, because he set off a ripple effect.



---


# Day Two Of The Bankman-Fried Trial: Jury Selection And The Courtroom Audience

On the second day of Sam Bankman-Fried's fraud trial, the jury was selected on Wednesday morning, after which lawyers for the government and then for Bankman-Fried delivered opening statements that told two very different stories of the former FTX CEO's sudden rise and almost instantaneous fall. The central question framed by the proceedings was who Bankman-Fried, the former CEO of crypto exchange FTX, really is: a liar and a fraud, or someone who acted in good faith and, like many a startup founder, flew too close to the sun. That answer, the account notes, ultimately lies with the jury.

The day featured pointed allegations, a friend from MIT, and an audience replete with big names, including Bankman-Fried's professorial parents and Damian Williams, the U.S. attorney for the Southern District of New York. Bankman-Fried himself spent most of the day in court staring into a laptop while seated between his two attorneys. The prosecution's account of his alleged crimes was described as featuring a study in contrasts.



---


# The Prosecution's Opening Statement Against Bankman-Fried

Thane Rehn, a prosecutor for the government, opened the case against Sam Bankman-Fried with the line "One year ago, it looked like the defendant was on the top of the world," and then argued that this appearance was false: "all of that, all of it, was built on lies," he declared to the jury, adding "Behind the curtains, he was not what he appeared to be." Rehn described a defendant who, as former CEO of FTX, oversaw a supposedly thriving crypto exchange, jetted between international locales, hobnobbed with celebrities like Tom Brady and Larry David, and repeatedly emphasized to customers that their money was safe and secure.

What followed was a roughly 30-minute story that repeatedly emphasized how Bankman-Fried allegedly stole customer funds to facilitate his jet-setting lifestyle, donate millions to political candidates, and finance risky bets. Rehn also directly contested the media framing of the defendant: he was not a crypto "boy" genius, as so many in the media — Fortune included — have written, but a "man" who "stole billions of dollars from thousands of victims." Rehn closed the characterization with a promise to the jury: "You will see the full picture."



---


# Caroline Ellison's Guilty Plea And First Day Of Testimony

Caroline Ellison, head of the hedge fund Alameda Research during its implosion along with FTX, took the stand on October 10th, 2023 having already pleaded guilty to criminal charges — fraud, conspiracy to commit fraud, and money laundering — and told the jury that Bankman-Fried "directed me to commit these crimes." She quantified the taking: "We ultimately took about $14 billion, some of which we were not able to pay back."

Her long-anticipated first day took the form of walking through a damning spreadsheet she had prepared for her ex and boss, now the defendant in a criminal fraud trial. She entered hunched in on herself, wearing a dusty rose dress with a gray blazer over it, looking less like an executive than like a girl who had borrowed her boyfriend's coat because she was cold. Asked by the prosecution to identify Bankman-Fried, she had trouble finding him and gazed around the courtroom for more than 20 seconds — apparently he was incognito with his new haircut — and when she did spot him she identified him as the one wearing a suit, which got chuckles from the rest of the defense table, also all in suits. She tilted her head down to answer questions and lifted it when she had finished each answer.

The defendant's own reaction registered the shift: Bankman-Fried had been vibrating slightly during Wang's testimony, and during Ellison's his bouncing became more noticeable. By the end of the day, The Verge's reporter wrote, the spreadsheet seemed like a sideshow.

qid: After Jerome Powell's aggressive interest rate hikes mentioned by 'Fortune' on October 6th, 2023, did 'Business Line' report on October 14th, 2023, suggest that central bankers' stance on interest rates was consistent or inconsistent with Powell's approach as reported by 'Fortune'?
context:
# Volcker's And Powell's Rate-Hiking Cycles Compared

The consumer price index rose at a peak of around 14% in 1980 before then-Fed Chair Paul Volcker's hawkish policies sent mortgage rates to 18% within a year — cooling inflation but sparking a recession, and causing a serious downturn in housing in which home sales and building levels cratered while national home prices actually remained stable. At the start of Volcker's term as Fed chair in August 1979 the median U.S. home sales price was $64,700, and even after a near doubling of mortgage rates that figure rose to $69,400 by the second quarter of 1981. A second account puts the average 30-year fixed mortgage peaking at about 18% by late 1981, and records that home sales activity plummeted from 1978 to 1982, with existing-home sales dropping 50% over that period according to the Office of Policy Development and Research.

Over the 18 months preceding October 2023, current Fed chair Jerome Powell has been following a very similar game plan, raising interest rates aggressively to quash inflation and setting the tone for the most aggressive global hiking of rates in the modern era. The average 30-year fixed mortgage rate, the most common type in the U.S., soared from 3.8% in March 2022 to over 7.5% by 2023-10-06, and by the week of 2023-10-20 mortgage rates hit 8%, the highest in more than 20 years. This in turn slowed mortgage purchase applications and caused home sales to plummet, just as in the '80s; but home prices, echoing the dynamic of that era, have yet to collapse. While home sales activity levels this low had not been seen since the 2000s, the housing market more closely mimics that of the '80s, according to a report published in the week of 2023-10-20 by Fortune 500 financial services company First American.



---


# Powell's Rejection Of Monetary-Fiscal Coordination

Fed Chair Jerome Powell, sitting to Christine Lagarde's right at the panel discussion, signaled he wasn't ready to rely on the kind of cooperation between monetary and fiscal policy she described as sometimes helpful.

His stated ground rejects the premise that the central bank's mandate is contingent on what fiscal authorities do: "Our assignment is to deliver price stability kind of regardless of the stance of fiscal policy."



---


# Federal Reserve Rate Path Expectations Late 2023

By early December 2023 traders widely expected the Federal Reserve to hold its key interest rate steady at its meeting the following week before potentially cutting rates in March, according to data from CME Group, and Fed officials had recently hinted that the federal funds rate may already be at its peak, above 5.25 per cent, up from nearly zero early in 2022. Fed Chair Jerome Powell and others nevertheless warned Wall Street against being overzealous in its predictions about how early a cut could happen.

The bond market moved with those expectations. With inflation down from its peak two summers earlier, Wall Street was hopeful the Fed might be done with its market-shaking hikes. Investors were looking for a slowdown in the job market that came through employers cutting back on open positions rather than laying off workers, and the report cited showed employers advertised just 8.7 million jobs on the last day of October, down 617,000 from a month earlier. US Treasury yields continued to sag from the heights reached during late October: the 10-year yield fell to 4.18 per cent from 4.26 per cent late on the Monday, after having been above 5 per cent and at its highest level in more than a decade during October. The two-year Treasury yield, which more closely tracks Fed expectations, fell from 4.61 per cent just before the economic reports to 4.57 per cent, yo-yoed, and then eased back to 4.57 per cent. Lower yields were one reason cryptocurrency prices had been rising, alongside excitement about a possible bitcoin exchange-traded fund that helped send bitcoin above $US43,000 ($65,600); Robinhood Markets reported a roughly 75 per cent jump in crypto trading volumes during November from a month earlier, said customers added about $US1.4 billion in net deposits during the month, and its own stock rose 10.3 per cent.

A month earlier, in early November 2023, the same expectations were forming from a lower base. Before that week, stocks had been struggling under the weight of rapidly rising Treasury yields catching up to the Fed's main interest rate, which was above 5.25 per cent and at its highest level since 2001. Higher rates and yields slow the economy, hurt investment prices and raise the risk of something breaking in the financial system, such as the three high-profile US bank failures that rattled markets during the spring. "It was really fear that the Fed was going to go too far," said Katie Nixon, chief investment officer for Northern Trust Wealth Management. The Fed had applied that pressure intentionally, hoping to starve inflation of its fuel and to cool the job market, particularly pay raises, because it feared too-strong pay gains could create a vicious cycle keeping inflation high. Analysts said the Friday jobs report offered encouraging signals, with average hourly earnings rising less in October from September than expected, though it did not mean the job was done. Treasury yields tumbled immediately after that report, with the 10-year easing to 4.52 per cent from 4.67 per cent late Thursday and from more than five per cent the previous week, when it hit its highest level since 2007. Traders then moved up expectations for the first Fed cut, potentially by the summer, according to CME Group data. Foreign-exchange strategists at Bank of America wrote in a BofA Global Research report that for investors around the world the "Fed matters more than other central banks" and weak US data is "the only game-changer for markets". A separate report that Friday from the Institute for Supply Management said growth in US services industries such as finance and construction was weaker than economists expected and suggested a slight easing in prices.



---


# Bank Of America's Warning Of More Housing "Turbulence"

A Bank of America team led by U.S. economist Jeseo Park warned in the week of 2023-10-06 that there is more "turbulence" coming for the housing market because of high mortgage rates: "With rates likely staying higher for longer, we are cautious of potential turbulence ahead," the group wrote. The grounds are the persistence of high rates rather than a repeat of a past crash — the team said they were getting an eerie feeling of "déjà vu," but it was not 2008 that came to mind, it was the 1980s.

The forecast attached to this warning is qualified. Bank of America had previously forecast 0% home price growth and falling home sales for the full year 2023, but it did not offer a new prediction in its latest note. The warrant joining the rate outlook to the housing outlook runs the other way as well: eventually, as inflation fades and leads the Fed to cut interest rates, housing affordability will improve. "At that stage, we should see a more stable and healthy housing market," Park and her team wrote. "Until then, hang tight, it may be a bumpy ride."



---


# The Post-Tightening Monetary Policy Autopsy Of 2023

After the most aggressive monetary-tightening campaign in four decades, academics and economic practitioners are running autopsies on what could have prevented the cost-of-living crisis and how to ensure the same mistakes won't be repeated. Markets have scrambled to price in high-for-longer interest rates, with a new war in the Middle East adding yet more risk to an already uncertain outlook confronting central bankers as they gather for their penultimate meetings of a tumultuous year.

The policy navel-gazing centers on three debates: how much flexibility central banks can allow in reaching their inflation targets, the effectiveness of asset purchases in the policy mix, and the merits of monetary and fiscal coordination. Bloomberg surveyed economists from around the world to gather views on those three debates. Their verdict: central banks won't break their economies in a rush to hit inflation targets, QE will be used more sparingly in the future, and fiscal policy risks countering the work of monetary authorities.



---


# Criticism Of QE And Its Narrower Future Role

The premise that quantitative easing is a benign general-purpose tool is contested: bond-buying has been blamed for distorting financial markets, and episodes such as the Silicon Valley Bank blow-up are seen by some as a direct result of central bank reserves creation under QE, along with regulatory and supervision failures.

The economists surveyed expect its role to narrow accordingly. Only 40% predict central banks will use QE the same way as they did before; a quarter expect them to deploy it more sparingly; about 30% see its only role going forward as a tool to address financial-stability concerns; and a small minority doesn't see it being used again at all.

# US v. Google: Two Months Into The Search Antitrust Trial

As of TechCrunch's November 13, 2023 roundup, the Justice Department's landmark antitrust case against Google was nearly two months old, and the trial record was still producing fresh revelations. TechCrunch framed it as one of the biggest fights in tech antitrust since the U.S. took Microsoft to trial in the 1990s.

An earlier roundup had already surfaced that Google spent $26.3 billion in 2021 making itself the default search engine across platforms, and that Google tried to have Chrome preinstalled on iPhones. Over the couple of weeks preceding this roundup, more of Google's inner workings came to light, including some of the search engine's most lucrative search queries, the shape of the revenue-share agreements between Google and Android OEMs, and why Expedia has a bone to pick with Google.



---


# Google Paid $26.3 Billion In 2021 For Default Search Placement

Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to multiple browsers, phones and platforms — from companies including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla — to be everyone's default search engine. The figure was revealed by Google's search head Prabhakar Raghavan when he testified in court on October 28, according to The Verge.

About $18 billion of that total went directly to Apple, according to a New York Times report published earlier in October 2023, and Google has had its deal with Apple in place since 2003 — so the payment is the current year of a two-decade arrangement, not a one-off. Questioned on the amount of money Google spends to get first pick of search engines, Pichai said the decision was made with the consumer in mind: Google pays big bucks to be everywhere so that it can take in all the data and be the best search engine across different companies' devices, he said, according to The Verge.

The trial also produced evidence that Google understood the value of defaults very early on. U.S. Justice Department lawyer Meagan Bellshaw showed Pichai a 2007 email from a Google product strategy meeting containing data showing that when people changed their browser homepage to Google, they did 15% more Google searches, and that when they switched away, their Google searches dropped 27%. The email summarizing that meeting, sent to Pichai as well as other Google leaders, read: "Nitin argues that focusing on homepage market share is one of the most effective things we can do to make gains in search market share," according to The Verge.



---


# The Google Antitrust Case

The Google antitrust case is the U.S. government's trial over Google's dominance in the online search market, stemming from a 2020 antitrust claim, in which the government argues that Google uses its platforms and its deals with partners to block out competition in search or advertising and thereby to hinder competitors from accessing the data they would need to improve their products.

Its defining features are the conduct at issue and the defence offered against it. Google CEO Sundar Pichai testified Monday in the trial, defending Google's business tactics, including its deal with Apple and other partners to make Google the default search engine. Google's answer is that it is just doing business: everybody wants Google as the default engine because it is the best, and that, the company says, does not make its actions illegal.

The important boundary case is which Google antitrust matter this is. The 2020 search claim is separate from the one filed in January by the Department of Justice, along with eight states including New York, California and Colorado, which aims to "halt Google's anticompetitive scheme, unwind Google's monopolistic grip on the market and restore competition to digital advertising." The search case and the digital-advertising case are distinct proceedings and should not be conflated.

The trial is the venue in which the underlying numbers surface. Monday's hearing revealed plenty of juicy tidbits, including the $26.3 billion Google spent making itself the default search engine across platforms in 2021, and how Google tried to take it further and have Chrome preinstalled on iPhones.



---


# Google's Parallel Antitrust Proceedings In Late 2023

As of mid-November 2023, Google was fighting antitrust on more than one front at once. The Epic Games case was not its only antitrust case in trial: Google had settled a separate antitrust lawsuit with dating site Match Group the week before November 13, and on November 6 it went to trial with Fortnite maker Epic Games, which hoped to prove that Google engages in anticompetitive behavior with regard to its Android app store, Google Play, and its commission structure. Separately, Google was involved in an antitrust lawsuit with the Department of Justice over its alleged search monopoly.

The Epic case had shed co-plaintiffs on its way to trial. Epic's lawsuit originally involved Match and several U.S. attorneys general, but Google reached a settlement with the attorneys general in October 2023 and with Match the week before November 6, so Epic fought the antitrust battle on its own. The lawsuit, held in the U.S. District Court in California's Northern District, would include testimony from a number of Google and Android execs, including CEO Sundar Pichai, and Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, as well as from Apple, Netflix and other Android developers. Epic, meanwhile, had lost its antitrust battle with Apple and was asking the Supreme Court to weigh in.



---


# Apple Versus Google: A Contrast In Antitrust Conduct

Asked to compare the Apple and Google cases, Tim Sweeney summed up the difference as "Apple was ice and Google was fire" — arguing that Apple keeps all of its antitrust trickery internal to the company while Google had to go outside itself, and that the paper trail this produced is why the Google case played out differently.

His grounds are the mechanics of each scheme. Apple uses its own store and its own payments, and forces developers, OEMs and carriers to all have the same terms. Google, to achieve things with Android, went around paying off dozens of game developers not to compete and dozens of carriers and OEMs not to compete — and when many different companies do deals together, lots of people put things in writing, so it is right there for everybody to read. The warrant is evidentiary rather than moral: Sweeney said the Apple case would be no less interesting if Apple's internal thoughts and deliberations could be seen, but Apple was not putting it in writing whereas Google was, and he observed that because Google distributes Android as open source it had to put these deals more out in the open, even though it still wanted to keep them secret. He was careful not to let Apple off: he called Apple's restrictions on competition absolute — "thou shalt not have a competing store on iOS and thou shalt not use a competing payment method" — and said Apple should receive at least as harsh antitrust scrutiny as Google, adding that documents from both companies show them similarly self-serving in their deals.



---


# What A Ruling Against Google Would Mean For Big Tech

A ruling against Google would not stop at Google: the remedy would likely resemble the Microsoft settlement and the outcome would ripple through the other pending Big Tech cases, because enforcers are using this trial to demonstrate that antitrust law can still take on the largest and most powerful companies in the world.

The grounds for the first half of that claim are the available remedies. If the judge rules against Google, the outcome could look a lot like the Microsoft deal, in which the computer company was required to change its behavior and share its APIs with third-party developers, and was also banned from making anticompetitive and exclusive deals with computer manufacturers. Google might likewise end up having to turn over all or most of the data it has collected to other search engines so they can improve their products and attract more users — a remedy scaled to the disparity the DOJ has cited, that Google gets 16 times more data than Bing does everyday.

The grounds for the ripple effect are the cases already queued behind this one. The FTC sued Amazon in September for using anticompetitive and unfair strategies to illegally maintain its monopoly power. The DOJ has been investigating Apple for years over the company's policy for third-party apps on its devices and whether it unfairly favors its own products. And there is an ongoing case between the FTC and Facebook, in which the agency calls on Facebook to sell Instagram and WhatsApp.

The warrant joining grounds to claim is enforcers' own stake in the result: they will want to show that antitrust law is still relevant and can successfully take on the biggest, most powerful companies in the world, so a win here sets the template the neighbouring cases are argued against. The scope condition is that nothing was settled as of this report — the case is expected to continue for several weeks, bringing to a head one of the biggest fights in tech antitrust since the U.S. took Microsoft to trial in the 1990s.



---


# The U.S. Justice Department's Parallel Antitrust Suits Against Google

The Helena World Chronicle class action arrives alongside the filing of the U.S. Justice Department's lawsuit against Google for monopolizing digital ad technologies, and the complaint also references the Justice Department's 2020 civil antitrust suit over search and search advertising.

The two government cases concern different markets: search and search advertising in the 2020 suit are distinct from the digital ad technologies at issue in the more recent one.
