---


# Google Paid $26.3 Billion In 2021 For Default Search Placement

Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to multiple browsers, phones and platforms — from companies including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla — to be everyone's default search engine. The figure was revealed by Google's search head Prabhakar Raghavan when he testified in court on October 28, according to The Verge.

About $18 billion of that total went directly to Apple, according to a New York Times report published earlier in October 2023, and Google has had its deal with Apple in place since 2003 — so the payment is the current year of a two-decade arrangement, not a one-off. Questioned on the amount of money Google spends to get first pick of search engines, Pichai said the decision was made with the consumer in mind: Google pays big bucks to be everywhere so that it can take in all the data and be the best search engine across different companies' devices, he said, according to The Verge.

The trial also produced evidence that Google understood the value of defaults very early on. U.S. Justice Department lawyer Meagan Bellshaw showed Pichai a 2007 email from a Google product strategy meeting containing data showing that when people changed their browser homepage to Google, they did 15% more Google searches, and that when they switched away, their Google searches dropped 27%. The email summarizing that meeting, sent to Pichai as well as other Google leaders, read: "Nitin argues that focusing on homepage market share is one of the most effective things we can do to make gains in search market share," according to The Verge.



---


# The U.S. Justice Department's Parallel Antitrust Suits Against Google

The Helena World Chronicle class action arrives alongside the filing of the U.S. Justice Department's lawsuit against Google for monopolizing digital ad technologies, and the complaint also references the Justice Department's 2020 civil antitrust suit over search and search advertising.

The two government cases concern different markets: search and search advertising in the 2020 suit are distinct from the digital ad technologies at issue in the more recent one.

qid: After TechCrunch reported on Biden's AI Executive Order as broad but lacking depth without corresponding legislation on October 31, 2023, and Music Business Worldwide shared concerns from the National Music Publishers Association about generative AI being a significant risk to the human creative class on November 30, 2023, is the stance of these two news sources on the need for regulatory measures for AI consistent or inconsistent?
context:
# Reaction To Biden's AI Order

Respondents to Biden's AI executive order attacked the premise that an executive order alone is a sufficient regulatory response, arguing that its breadth is real but its depth is not, and that the substantive work still requires Congress. Senator Mark Warner of Virginia said he was "impressed by the breadth" of the order, though, he implies, not the depth: "I am also happy to see a number of sections that closely align with my efforts around AI safety and security and federal government's use of AI," he said in a statement. "At the same time, many of these just scratch the surface – particularly in areas like health care and competition policy. While this is a good step forward, we need additional legislative measures, and I will continue to work diligently…" TechCrunch's own reading is that given the state of the legislature and the fact that an incredibly contentious election period is upcoming, it will be a miracle if any substantive law whatsoever is passed in the near future, let alone a potentially divisive and complex bill like AI rules.

Paul Barrett, deputy director of the NYU Stern Center for Business and Human Rights, acknowledged both sides of the issue and attacked the inference that direction of travel equals capacity to act. "President Biden is sending a valuable message that certain AI systems create immediate risks that demand immediate attention. The administration is moving in the right direction," he wrote. "But today is just the beginning of a regulatory process that will be long and arduous–and ultimately must require that the companies profiting from AI bear the burden of proving that their products are safe and effective, just as the manufacturers of pharmaceuticals or industrial chemicals or airplanes must demonstrate that their products are safe and effective. Without fresh resources provided by Congress, it's not clear that the federal government has the resources to assess the vastly complicated training process or the adequacy of red-teaming and other necessary testing."

A more favorable reading came from Sheila Gulati, co-founder of Tola Capital, who said the EO showed a "clear intention to walk the line of promoting innovation while protecting citizens." "It is most essential that we don't prevent agile innovation by startups. Putting AI explainability at the forefront, taking a risk-based approach with more focus on areas where harm or bias could be at play, and bringing security and privacy to the center of focus are all sensible steps," she told TechCrunch. "With this executive order and the standards implications through NIST, we would anticipate leadership from standards bodies versus legislators in the near term." It is worth mentioning as well that the federal government is a major customer of today's AI and tech products, and any company that intends to keep them as a customer will want to color inside the lines for the immediate future. Bob Cattanach, partner at legal mega-firm Dorsey and Whitney, added that the timing feels slightly off.



---


# Sony Music's Generative AI Principles For Congress

Dennis Kooker, Sony Music Entertainment's President of Global Digital Business & US Sales, asked Congress at the November 29, 2023 AI Insight Forum to embrace a set of five principles around generative AI, on the argument that "if copyrights are protected and enforced appropriately, we are at the beginning of a multi-decade marathon that will change the creative and commercial landscape for music."

The framing condition Kooker set is that "Music is a tremendous driver for AI technology, and AI technology presents a tremendous opportunity for the creative development of music. But these opportunities must be grounded by the human creators' vision with the machine assisting, not with the machine replacing the human creator." The principles are: Assure Consent, Compensation, and Credit — "New products and businesses built with music must be developed with the consent of the owner and appropriate compensation and credit. It is essential to understand why the training of AI models is being done, what products will be developed as a result, and what the business model is that will monetize the use of the artist's work. Congress and the agencies should assure that creators' rights are recognized and respected." Confirm That Copying Music to Train AI Models is Not Fair Use — "Even worse are those that argue that copyrighted content should automatically be considered fair use so that protected works are never compensated for usage and creators have no say in the products or business models that are developed around them and their work. Congress should assure and agencies should presume that reproducing music to train AI models, in itself, is not a fair use." Prevent the Cloning of Artists' Voices and Likenesses Without Express Permission — "We cannot allow an artist's voice or likeness to be cloned for use without the express permission of the artist. This is a very personal decision for the artist. Congress should pass into law effective federal protections for name, image, and likeness." Incentivize Accurate Recordkeeping — "Correct attribution will be a critical element to artists being paid fairly and correctly for new works that are created. In addition, rights can only be enforced around the training of AI when there are accurate records about what is being copied. Otherwise, the inability to enforce rights in the AI marketplace equates to a lack of rights at all, producing a dangerous imbalance that prevents a thriving ecosystem. This requires strong and accurate record keeping by the generative AI platforms, a requirement that urgently needs legislative support to ensure incentives are in place so that it happens consistently and correctly." And Assure Transparency for Consumers and Artists — "Transparency is necessary to clearly distinguish human-created works from AI-created works. The public should know, when they are listening to music, whether that music was created by a human being or a machine." MBW summarised the intended effect: "The principles will ensure that intellectual property businesses can succeed in this new world alongside tech partners, further advancing investment and expanding economic opportunities."



---


# The AI Legislation Gap Behind Biden's Executive Order

Biden's AI executive order can only be a stopgap, because there is no legislative remedy to potential AI risks and abuses outside of those that can be applied to tech companies in general — and many have argued over the years that those general remedies are also inadequate. The order therefore props up the "voluntary" practices many companies are already choosing to implement, and the limits on what a president can do with a wave of their hand mean it amounts to a lot of sharing results, developing best practices and providing clear guidance.

The grounds for that reading are the state of federal action and the state of prospective law. Federal action on social media and de facto monopolies like Amazon and Google has been sporadic, though a hawkish new FTC may change that trend. Meanwhile, a comprehensive law defining and limiting the use of AI seems as far off now as it was years ago: the industry and technology have evolved so quickly that any rule would likely be outdated by the time it was passed, and it is not even really clear what ought to be legislatively limited as opposed to being left to state law or expert agencies.

The warrant joining grounds to claim is that executive authority cannot substitute for the institutional machinery a durable regime would need. Perhaps the wisest approach is to set up a new federal agency dedicated to regulating AI and technology, but this cannot be accomplished by fiat. In the meantime, the EO at least instructs several AI-focused groups, like one in the Department of Health and Human Services dedicated to handling and assessing reports of AI-related harms in healthcare.



---


# Schumer's AI Insight Forum On Creative Copyright

On Wednesday November 29, 2023, US Senate Majority Leader Chuck Schumer held an Artificial Intelligence (AI) Insight Forum to discuss the importance and role of creative copyright and intellectual property in the development of AI — a sign that senior political figures in Washington are becoming increasingly interested in the impact of AI on the law.

Dennis Kooker, Sony Music Entertainment's President of Global Digital Business & US Sales, delivered a speech at the Forum outlining the major music company's position on AI and copyright law.



---


# The NMPA Submission Calling Generative AI The Greatest Risk To The Creative Class

The National Music Publishers Association's submission to the US Copyright Office, dated October 30, 2023, argues that generative AI may be the greatest risk to the human creative class that has ever existed — and therefore that the Office should adopt proactive protections for human creators and, where uncertain, err on their side.

The argument is deliberately framed as pro-technology at its base. The submission starts by stressing that the NMPA's membership — US music publishers major and independent — are "not opposed" to AI: "There is widespread belief in the music industry that great benefits could come from generative AI systems that can assist human creators." It then goes for the jugular: "However, the development of the generative AI marketplace is marked by breathtaking speed, size and complexity. Hindsight may well prove that there is no hyperbole in saying that generative AI is the greatest risk to the human creative class that has ever existed." The warrant for urgency is temporal: "Even more alarming is that we do not know how long the window is to act before it is too late. We therefore implore the [US Copyright] Office to support proactive protections for human creators and, where there is uncertainty, to err on the side of protecting human creators." MBW notes the position is not a surprise from an organisation that earlier in 2023 joined the fledgling Human Artistry Campaign, whose goal in broadest terms is to ensure AI does not replace or "erode" human culture — yet the submission is hardly a Luddite diatribe against high tech; it advocates regulations and principles it sees as the right way to keep the interests of musical artists and rights holders from being subjugated in the frenzy to build an AI-powered world.

qid: Which entity, currently in the process of recruiting a new Chair due to Andrew Sutch's impending departure, is also addressing concerns over financial result delays caused by an updated valuation from Citrin Cooperman, as reported by Music Business Worldwide?
context:
# Hipgnosis Songs Fund's Results Delay, December 2023

On the morning of 19 December 2023, the board of Hipgnosis Songs Fund, now led by Chairman Rob Naylor, issued a statement announcing that HSF would no longer be issuing its latest financial results that day as previously expected; the results, covering the six months to the end of September 2023, were instead expected to be published sometime before the close of 31 December.

The stated reason was a recently-updated company valuation from HSF's official independent valuer, the US-headquartered Citrin Cooperman. The UK-listed company's board said this valuation was "materially higher than the valuation implied by proposed and recent transactions in the sector", and pointed to two transactions or would-be transactions as evidence: the proposed sale earlier that year of assets to Blackstone-backed Hipgnosis Songs Capital for USD $440 million pre-costs, or $417.5 million post-costs, a proposal ultimately rejected by HSF shareholders; and the sale of 20,000 "non-core" songs from HSF's portfolio to an unnamed buyer, possibly Kobalt Music Group, for $23.1 million, announced on 11 December, a price which according to the board represented a 14.2% discount on Citrin Cooperman's valuation of that portfolio as of 30 September.



---


# Hipgnosis Songs Fund Board Changes September 2023

On 28 September 2023, Hipgnosis Songs Fund confirmed that Andrew Sutch, 73, the Chair of its board since 2018, is stepping down both as HSF board Chair and as a director of the company.

HSF said it had begun a process to recruit a new Chair, and that Sutch will leave his post as and when that person is hired, or in any case before HSF's AGM the following year, in Q4 2024. In addition, Andrew Wilkinson, 72, informed the HSF board of his intention to retire as a board director, a departure that will reduce the company's board to five directors.



---


# The Eight-Day Delay In Flagging The Valuation Concern

MBW argues that the HSF board had known about Citrin Cooperman's latest valuation, as of 30 September, for at least the past eight days before telling investors it was unhappy with it. The evidence is the board's own earlier disclosure: on 11 December 2023 HSF announced that the $23.1 million price of an agreed "non-core" asset sale represented a 14.2% discount versus Citrin Cooperman's latest valuation of the portfolio, which means the board had by then seen that latest valuation.

The warrant is that a board cannot quote a discount against a valuation it has not received, so the 11 December announcement fixes the earliest date of knowledge. Yet it took until 19 December for HSF to alert its investors to its dissatisfaction with the valuation.



---


# The Citrin Cooperman Discount Rate Controversy

The mechanism at the centre of the Hipgnosis valuation dispute is the discount rate Citrin Cooperman applies to HSF's portfolio. Citrin Cooperman continues to stick to an 8.5% discount rate in its valuations despite interest rate rises over the past 12-18 months, and has long refused to move that 8.5% figure upwards to, say, 9% or 9.5%.

The relation between the input and the output is direct and inverse: if Citrin Cooperman ever did raise this discount rate, the independent valuation of Hipgnosis Songs Fund's portfolio would in turn instantly fall. MBW reads the board's 19 December 2023 statement as a clear signal that it has understandable concerns over this now-infamous discount rate.



---


# The HSF Board Versus Hipgnosis Song Management

As part of its 19 December 2023 announcement, the HSF board took something of a swipe at its investment adviser, Merck Mercuriadis' Hipgnosis Song Management. HSF said that after seeing Citrin Cooperman's latest valuation and believing it to be too high, it "sought advice from Hipgnosis Song Management… which is majority owned by funds managed and/or advised by Blackstone, on their opinion on the independent valuer's valuation", and added that HSM "eventually provided an opinion, which was heavily caveated, such that the Board has concerns as to the valuation of the Company's assets in its interim results".

Hipgnosis Song Management issued its own statement the same day, saying it "has fulfilled its duties to [HSF] with respect to both the independent valuation and preparation of the interim results in a timely and efficient manner", and that "notwithstanding the Board's decision to delay publication of the interim financial statements, [we] will continue to work in a constructive manner to support the interests of the Company and its shareholders".



---


# The Board Appoints And Oversees Its Own Valuer

The oddest thing about the board's complaint, MBW argues, is that Citrin Cooperman's valuation of Hipgnosis Songs Fund is, according to HSF's own company documentation, appointed and overseen by the HSF board itself. This attacks the implicit premise that the disputed valuation is something imposed on the board from outside, and therefore something whose failings can be laid at another party's door.

The documentary grounds are two recurring lines in HSF filings. Every annual and interim report from HSF so far states: "Portfolio Independent Valuer… Citrin Cooperman Advisors LLC, formerly Massarsky Consulting, Inc., [is] appointed by the Board to independently value the Company's Catalogues within the Portfolio." Various HSF company reports to date also state: "The [HSF] Board is ultimately and solely responsible for overseeing the valuation of the Company's investments in music catalogues and has appointed [Citrin Cooperman] to perform this specialist work."



---


# JP Morgan's Note Against The HSF Board's Handling Of The Valuation

JP Morgan analyst Christopher Brown, one of the closest watchers of Hipgnosis Songs Fund in recent years, issued a damning note on 19 December 2023 attacking the board's attempt to shift responsibility for the valuation. He wrote that the delay "is an early blow to the credibility of the new [Hipgnosis Songs Fund] Board, and casts further doubt over the credibility of the independent valuer, Citrin Cooperman", and concluded that "[it] is up to the [Hipgnosis Songs Fund] Board to satisfy itself that the independent valuer, whom it hires, is up to the job, rather than try and pin the blame on [Hipgnosis Songs Management]", adding that in JP Morgan's view "a breakdown in the relationship between Board and manager would not be optimal for maximising shareholder value".

Brown said he was surprised that a second valuation expert had not been drafted in to value the HSF portfolio for the latest interim results, especially as Kroll had been appointed to consider the "reasonableness" of Citrin Cooperman's assumptions for HSF's previous set of results to the end of March 2023. He suggested that the easiest solution now for the board is to apply an additional discount rate to the Citrin Cooperman valuation to reflect current market uncertainty, on the basis that it is probably too late to employ another valuer, and quantified the effect: a 0.5% rise in the discount rate, from 8.5% to 9.0%, would "reduce the fair value of the [HSF] portfolio by 7.9%, which on a leveraged basis is [approximately a] 10% reduction in NAV [Net Asset Value]". Should the board go down that route he expected the shares to weaken, given that it represents another "unforced error", and he added that JP Morgan would not be surprised to see Citrin Cooperman resign, having been very publicly undermined by the board that day. Despite all this, JP Morgan retained its "overweight" rating against HSF's share price "in spite of yet another [HSF] own goal".



---


# Hipgnosis Songs Fund Continuation Vote

A 'continuation vote' at Hipgnosis Songs Fund (HSF), the UK-listed music rights fund, is a vote of the firm's shareholders on whether to keep the entity going as a closed-ended investment entity — that is, as a publicly-traded bundle of music rights. It takes place at HSF's Annual General Meeting, and the 2023 vote looked likely to be held on Thursday 26 October, according to an announcement from the firm on 28 September 2023.

The 2023 vote was only "likely" rather than definite because it might still get bumped into November, and its outcome was unknown at the time of reporting, with a looming $440 million transaction that could potentially influence it. The vote itself was not a new event: it had been scheduled ever since HSF went public in 2018, five years after the float.

The changes HSF announced on 28 September invited the question of whether they amounted to concessions designed to keep investors happy and confident in long-term prospects — and voting to keep going. One such measure directly extends the mechanism: if shareholders vote at the next AGM to remain a publicly-traded fund, another continuation vote will be put to HSF shareholders at an Extraordinary General Meeting in January 2026, roughly two years later.

qid: Does the 'Sporting News' article stating Lionel Messi returned to play for Inter Miami after an injury align with the 'Sporting News' claim that he is likely to be back for Inter Miami's match, and does the same source suggest a youth movement in Argentina's forward line involving Messi, Alvarez, and Garnacho?
context:
# Messi's Four-Game Injury Absence And His 35-Minute Return

Lionel Messi missed four straight Inter Miami games with injury before returning off the bench for 35 minutes against FC Cincinnati on Oct. 7, 2023. He was left out entirely for the Oct. 4 trip to the Chicago Fire: 35 minutes before kickoff the lineups showed him not part of the squad, with Josef Martinez up front as Leonardo Campana was out with a knock. An hour before kickoff, Michelle Kaufman of the Miami Herald reported Messi "did not arrive with the team" to Soldier Field — a strong indication rather than outright confirmation that he would not play. Two hours out, Sporting News noted Gerardo Martino had played his cards extremely close to his chest each week about Messi's injury: asked about Jordi Alba's return, Martino said a timeline was in place, but asked about Messi's he refused to acknowledge whether one existed, saying "I understand your desire to know the exact timelines, but if I had the exact timelines I would share them. I just don't have them." Sporting News judged his involvement unlikely given recent matches but thought he could be more ready over the weekend against FC Cincinnati. Meanwhile Chicago was still feeling Messi fever, with Messi shirt vendors outside Soldier Field and the Fire media team joking that they had "the GOAT in the building."

Against FC Cincinnati he was available. Two hours before kickoff, well-connected Argentine journalist Gaston Edul had reported the night before that Inter Miami were likely to have Messi back in some capacity — "the idea is for Leo Messi to get minutes when Inter Miami plays FC Cincinnati" — which sounded like bench availability, alongside reporting that Messi was battling "fatigue" and a "scar tissue issue." Lineups 45 minutes out confirmed him on the bench, with a photo of his jersey hanging in his locker taken as a good indication he would return. Thirty minutes out, his availability was called a welcome sight for a club whose backs were against the wall and which had to win to stay alive. He entered in the 55th minute, replacing Tomas Aviles in a very attacking change with around 35 minutes to save Inter Miami's season, alongside Jean Mota for David Ruiz. By the time he stepped on the pitch, Inter Miami's early dominance had come and gone; Messi played a part but was unable to fully change the tide of the game.

Five days later, ahead of Argentina's World Cup qualifier, Sporting News noted Messi had been dealing with fitness concerns for weeks and had missed significant time for his club, but was on the national team roster and expected to play a part. According to a report from Argentina he would not start but was likely to play much or all of the second half. With Inter Miami's playoff run officially over, Argentina could feel better about deploying him for a full 90 minutes despite his recent fitness issues, knowing his club season was nearly over and months of rest lay ahead; he had missed the previous match against Bolivia and four Inter Miami games after that, then returned for a half-hour in the club's final fixture before the international break.



---


# Messi's Fitness And Inter Miami's Offseason, October 2023

Lionel Messi's club Inter Miami were eliminated from MLS playoff contention by a 1-0 loss to FC Cincinnati the weekend before Argentina's Oct. 12, 2023 qualifier against Paraguay — and that elimination changed the calculus around his minutes for Argentina.

Messi had missed the previous four matches, including Argentina's fixture against Bolivia, but returned for the final 30 minutes against Cincinnati and was powerless to turn the tide after Inter Miami missed so many gilt-edged chances in the first half. Had Inter Miami still been in the playoff hunt with a postseason run on the horizon, Argentina might have played it a bit safer with Messi in this international window; with his long offseason break confirmed, he could be more aggressive with his minutes, knowing that after Inter Miami's final two meaningless regular-season matches he would only have international breaks to keep him sharp until February. Reports on the day said Messi would not start but was likely to play much or all of the second half, with Lautaro Martinez and Julian Alvarez both starting a national team match together for the first time — something World Cup hero Mario Kempes was a big fan of. With Messi starting on the bench, reports also indicated Nicolas Otamendi would wear the captain's armband until Messi entered.

A rumour that Messi could head to Barcelona on loan to cover the gap left by Inter Miami's failure to qualify never made much sense and was squashed on numerous fronts. Inter Miami coach Gerardo Martino made light of it in his post-match press conference after the Cincinnati defeat, saying he would only go to Spain "for fun" — "Is he going for fun? Maybe he's going to visit Barcelona. Other than that, I don't know anything else about it" — while Fabrizio Romano shot it down from a journalistic standpoint. There is not enough of a break for Messi to reasonably integrate with Barcelona, and at 36 years old he is sure to welcome the extended time off.



---


# Argentina's Squad And Starting XI Against Paraguay, October 2023

Lionel Scaloni's Argentina started 4-3-3 against Paraguay on Oct. 12, 2023: E. Martinez (GK) — Molina, Romero, Otamendi, Tagliafico — De Paul, Mac Allister, E. Fernandez — J. Alvarez, L. Martinez, N. Gonzalez.

Scaloni had named a bloated 36-man squad for that month's matches against Paraguay and Peru, but Angel Di Maria, Paulo Dybala and Juan Foyth were forced to withdraw through injury, and Lisandro Martinez was also unavailable after undergoing another foot operation. Nicolas Tagliafico, who started both September matches, retained his starting spot even though Marcos Acuna was back with the team following an injury. Lionel Messi's club teammate Facundo Farias was included on the roster, but it would have been surprising had he seen the field.

The absences sharpened a generational shift. Messi was helping usher in a youth movement up front, with Julian Alvarez and Alejandro Garnacho considered the future of the forward line, and with Di Maria not fit for duty that month those two were even more in the spotlight against Paraguay and in the follow-up in Peru.



---


# Shaqiri Before Facing Inter Miami: Preparation Unchanged, And Team Messi

Ahead of the Chicago Fire's Oct. 4, 2023 match with Inter Miami, Xherdan Shaqiri said the Fire's preparation would not change regardless of whether Lionel Messi played. Speaking in his pre-match availability on the Monday, and reported 90 minutes before kickoff, Shaqiri said: "The preparation is not going to change, we're going to prepare as normal as always. Everybody is excited to play against Inter Miami. If Messi is injured or not, personally I am not thinking too much about this. Of course Inter Miami is a different team when Messi is playing or not playing, you see that in the last games when Messi is in the team they are better, but we prepare like normal for every game." Sporting News noted that many teams had indicated their preparation for Inter Miami varied wildly depending on Messi's availability, while Shaqiri played his cards close to his chest.

Shaqiri also framed the stakes of the match itself: "These are the best games to play all the time. As a player, you want these kinds of final games and to play for something. We put ourselves in this position, and we have a chance to do it, so now we have to perform."

Asked "Messi or Ronaldo?", Shaqiri confirmed he was Team Messi: "I'm always a big Messi admirer, if I have to choose now I will go with Messi. He won the WC which was the only thing he missed. So for sure Messi." He also said: "For me it's clear, Messi and Ronaldo are the best players in the world… these guys are among the best athletes in the history of sport, along with Michael Jordan and Tom Brady."



---


# Inter Miami's 2024 Preseason Fixture List

Sporting News compiled on Nov. 30, 2023 all the known Inter Miami preseason matches confirmed by the club directly or widely reported by media ahead of the 2024 season, which begins in February 2024.

The context is a long break: with the 2023 MLS season closing earlier than expected for Inter Miami, eliminated from playoff contention, Lionel Messi would have significant time off before the new campaign. Preseason friendlies exist because players need game time to build their bodies to the point where they can play full 90-minute matches, especially when contesting multiple games a week — and Inter Miami's preseason would be watched with extra observation because Messi draws considerable attention wherever he goes, home or abroad.

Two items headline the list. An anticipated two-match tour of China was cancelled, the trip proving too difficult logistically to arrange, and was replaced by a friendly against fellow MLS side NYCFC to honor Messi's Ballon d'Or. The biggest confirmed match is the meeting between Messi and rival Cristiano Ronaldo, as Inter Miami announced a pair of fixtures in Saudi Arabia including one against Ronaldo's Al Nassr on February 1. Among the unconfirmed but reported fixtures is Inter Miami vs. River Plate at AT&T Stadium in Dallas, Texas on Saturday, Jan. 20, 2024, with a rumored kickoff time still to be determined.

qid: Which company, recently subjected to an antitrust lawsuit that affected its stock value, offers a two-pack of USB-C-to-USB-C cables for purchase, introduced invite-only deals during Prime Day, and provides a platform that sellers describe as life-changing?
context:
# AirPods Pro Second Generation Deal Listings

The second-generation AirPods Pro appear in three 2023 roundups as the best wireless earbuds for iPhone owners, though by The Verge's December listing the deepest Black Friday discounts had disappeared.

The Verge explains why they're the pick: compared with the base AirPods, the Pros offer better sound quality and active noise cancellation plus seamless iOS integration and a MagSafe-compatible charging case. In 2022 Apple launched a version with improved sound quality and better noise cancellation, onboard volume controls, and a new MagSafe charging case that can beep if misplaced thanks to deeper Find My integration, with an extra swappable tip for smaller ears; a year later Apple released the updated model with a USB-C charging case, adding a more robust IP54 rating for water and sweat resistance and, when paired with Apple's Vision Pro headset, support for lossless audio. During Black Friday The Verge saw steep discounts of up to $60 off on both versions, but those deals have since disappeared: the non-USB-C AirPods Pro can be bought for $189.99 in-store at Micro Center, the next best being $229 ($20 off) for the 2022 buds at B&H Photo, while the USB-C version is only $3 off at $237 from Amazon, Walmart, and B&H Photo — though Best Buy's Plus and Total members can save $12.50. WIRED's general Prime Day roundup calls them the best earbuds if you have an iPhone, with the newer USB-C model (8/10, WIRED Recommends) having redesigned audio infrastructure and some of the best noise canceling and microphones it has heard. WIRED's Apple roundup notes the latest version (9/10, WIRED Recommends) was announced only the month before at Apple's hardware event and was already on sale: identical outside to the old pair but internally changed, with slightly improved sound, new Adaptive Audio features, and a new Conversation Awareness mode that turns audio down and lowers background sound so you can hear someone talking to you — the Lightning-port version being out of stock, "but who wants those anyway?"



---


# Apple's USB-C Accessory Transition

Rumors point to Apple unveiling more USB-C accessories as it shifts away from the Lightning port, with Gurman suggesting USB-C versions of the Magic Trackpad, Magic Mouse and Magic Keyboard will appear at the event.

This makes a lot of sense given the rest of the lineup. Apple ditched the Lightning port in all iPhone 15 models, started adopting USB-C on iPads several years back, and recently unveiled an Apple Pencil with a USB-C charging port.

The driver is regulatory: the change was prompted by European Union rules requiring a standard charging port on certain devices. Having the same port on all Apple devices and accessories will mean consumers have fewer types of cables to worry about.



---


# WIRED Black Friday 2023 USB-C Wall Charger And Hub Deals

WIRED's Apple Black Friday guide of 25 November 2023 listed six discounted USB-C charging and connectivity products: Anker's 67-watt Prime GaN charger, a four-port desktop charger, Apple's dual USB-C 35-watt adapter, a folding two-port charger, Satechi's four-port hub with an SSD slot, and Anker's compact 30-watt iPad adapter.

WIRED likes Anker's chargers and notes its Prime range uses GaN technology to shrink their size; the 67-watt model has fold-out prongs, two USB-C ports and one USB-A, supports fast charging for iPhones as well as Pixel and Samsung Galaxy phones, and can also charge a MacBook. The four-port charger has enough power to juice up two MacBook Pro models simultaneously and suits a desk full of devices, with a little stand to prop it up, a short cord to the outlet, and four USB-C ports outputting 100 watts each; this is the lowest price WIRED has tracked. Apple's dual USB-C port power adapter is called an essential accessory for people who forget to pack chargers: its two USB-C ports recharge a MacBook and iPhone simultaneously, and at 35 watts it is powerful enough to recharge an iPhone 15 Pro Max or iPad Pro. The folding charger packs two USB-C ports, one of which outputs 65 watts when used alone, dropping to 45 watts on the top port and 20 watts on the bottom when two devices are plugged in.

Satechi's four-port hub is, in WIRED's view, a little too large for the number of ports it offers, but for a reason: popping off the aluminium cover reveals a slot for an M.2 SATA solid-state drive, giving access to an external SSD alongside two USB-A jacks, one 100-watt USB-C pass-through charging port and a 4K HDMI at the same time. # The FTC's Antitrust Lawsuit Against Amazon

The Federal Trade Commission's sweeping 172-page antitrust lawsuit, filed in late September 2023, accuses Amazon of wielding its monopoly power to squeeze merchants and thwart rivals, which the agency alleges has led to artificially inflated prices and a degraded shopping experience for consumers.

The mechanism the FTC describes is an "anti-discounting strategy" backed by a "massive web-crawling apparatus that constantly tracks online prices" to stifle competition: Amazon punishes third-party sellers who offer cheaper products elsewhere by threatening to disqualify them from appearing in the buy box if it detects a lower price, and losing the buy box is an "existential threat" to sellers' businesses, the complaint alleges. The end result, the FTC argues, is elevated prices across the web — the company steadily hikes the fees it charges sellers and prevents them from discounting on other sites, so sellers often inflate their prices off Amazon, creating an "artificial price floor everywhere." The FTC is seeking to hold Amazon liable for allegedly violating anti-monopoly law but has not yet outlined the specific remedies it believes would best resolve its concerns; in antitrust cases, remedies are often determined only after a court finds the defendant liable. Amazon general counsel David Zapolsky responded in a blog post that third-party sellers set their own prices on the marketplace and that the company invests in tools to help sellers offer "competitive prices": "Even with those tools, some of the businesses selling on Amazon might still choose to set prices that aren't competitive. Just like any store owner who wouldn't want to promote a bad deal to their customers, we don't highlight or promote offers that are not competitively priced." Zapolsky argued the lawsuit could force Amazon to stop highlighting low prices, "a perverse result that would be directly opposed to the goals of antitrust law."

# Anker 321 Travel Power Strip

The Anker 321 Power Strip was $15, down from $26 — 42 percent off at Amazon. It is an all-in-one 20W USB-C power cube with three AC outlets, two USB-A ports, and one USB-C port, and it is deputy features editor Sarah Jeong's pick.

Her case for it starts from a specific failure. Nobody wants to carry a power strip or extension cord on vacation, and it is probably unnecessary in relatively modern buildings and definitely unnecessary while camping — but sometimes you stay in a charming historical hotel or a lovely cabin in the woods and discover at bedtime that the only electrical socket in the bedroom is in the corner farthest from the bed, with two lamps already plugged into it. Older buildings especially suffer from what she calls loose socket syndrome, where those convenient modern boxy socket extenders with five different USB and USB-C charging ports cannot stay in place and fall right out of the wall because they are too heavy. # OpenAI DevDay 2023 Announcements

On November 6, 2023 — prior to the leadership chaos — OpenAI held its first developer conference, OpenAI DevDay, and announced a slew of updates to GPT, including GPT-4 Turbo, a multimodal API, and a GPT store where users can create and monetize their own custom versions of GPT.

GPT-4 Turbo, unveiled at the conference, is a super-charged version of GPT-4, OpenAI's latest language-writing model, and comes in two versions: one that is strictly text-analyzing and another that understands the context of both text and images. The GPT Store was announced alongside it: users and developers would soon be able to make their own GPT with no coding experience required, list it on OpenAI's marketplace, and monetize it in the future. OpenAI also announced the Assistants API to help developers build "agent-like experiences" within their apps, with use cases ranging from a natural language-based data analysis app to a coding assistant or even an AI-powered vacation planner.

The GPT store slipped. According to a memo seen by Axios, OpenAI planned to delay the launch of its highly anticipated GPT store to early 2024; custom GPTs and the accompanying store had been a major DevDay announcement, with the store expected to open the previous month.



---


# GPT Model Releases From GPT-3.5 To GPT-4

ChatGPT first launched to the public as OpenAI quietly released GPT-3.5: the model broke cover with ChatGPT, a fine-tuned version of GPT-3.5 that is essentially a general-purpose chatbot able to engage with a range of topics including programming, TV scripts and scientific concepts.

Writers everywhere rolled their eyes at the new technology, much as artists did with OpenAI's DALL-E model, but the chat-style iteration seemingly broadened its appeal and audience. GPT-4 followed on March 14: a powerful image- and text-understanding AI model, released to paying ChatGPT Plus users and through a public API, with developers able to sign up on a waitlist to access the API.



---


# GPTs: OpenAI's Custom Chatbots And The Dev Day Announcements

GPTs are OpenAI's tool for building custom conversational, action-taking AI systems powered by OpenAI's models, including the models underpinning ChatGPT. They were announced at OpenAI's first-ever developer conference, held Monday, November 6, 2023, where the Microsoft-backed AI startup announced a host of new products — the more notable being tools to create custom "GPTs" (that is, domain-specific chatbots), new text-to-speech models, an API for the text-to-image model DALL-E 3, and an improved version of OpenAI's flagship model GPT-4, called GPT-4 Turbo.

What distinguishes a GPT from a prompt is that the knowledge is built in. With GPTs, a user can train a model on a cookbook collection, for example, so that it can answer questions about ingredients for a specific recipe; or they can give a model their company's proprietary codebases so that developers can check their style or generate code in line with best practices. Some of the initial GPTs, all created by OpenAI, include a Gen Z meme translator, a coloring book and sticker creator, a data visualizer, a board game explainer and a creative writing coach. ChatGPT can accomplish these tasks given carefully engineered prompts and foreknowledge, but purpose-built GPTs drastically simplify things — and might just kill the cottage industry that emerged around creating and editing prompts to feed to ChatGPT.

The consequence TechCrunch draws for ChatGPT itself is a change of role: with GPTs, ChatGPT could become more a gateway to a broader ecosystem of AI-powered chatbots than the end-all-be-all. GPTs introduce a level of personalization far beyond that ChatGPT offers today, and — once OpenAI sorts out its capacity issues — TechCrunch expects an explosion of creativity there. Will ChatGPT be as visible as it once was after GPTs flood the marketplace? Perhaps not; but it will not go away, it will simply adapt and evolve, no doubt in ways not even its creators can anticipate.



---


# GPT Model Lineage And The ChatGPT Launch

GPT (Generative Pre-trained Transformer) is the large language model that ChatGPT runs on, and OpenAI had been developing it since 2016 — unveiling GPT-1 in 2018 and iterating it to GPT-3 by June 2020. With the November 30, 2022 release of GPT-3.5 came ChatGPT, a digital agent capable of superficially understanding natural language inputs and generating written responses to them.

The first iteration's limits were plain: it was rather slow to answer and couldn't speak to questions about anything that happened after September 2021, not to mention its issues answering queries with misinformation during bouts of "hallucinations." Even so, that kludgy first iteration demonstrated capabilities far beyond what other state-of-the-art digital assistants like Siri and Alexa could provide — the discriminating feature that set it apart from what came before.



---


# ChatGPT FAQ: Basics And Definitions

ChatGPT is a general-purpose chatbot developed by tech startup OpenAI that uses artificial intelligence to generate text after a user enters a prompt; it runs on GPT-4, a large language model that uses deep learning to produce human-like text. GPT stands for Generative Pre-Trained Transformer.

The boundary against the wider category matters: a chatbot can be any software or system that holds dialogue with a person and does not necessarily have to be AI-powered — there are rules-based chatbots that give canned responses to questions — whereas ChatGPT is AI-powered and uses LLM technology to generate text after a prompt. ChatGPT was released for public use on November 30, 2022. Both the free version of ChatGPT and the paid ChatGPT Plus are regularly updated with new GPT models, and the most recent model is GPT-4; the free version requires only a sign-in. There is a free ChatGPT app, at launch limited to U.S. iOS users, with OpenAI saying an Android version is "coming soon," and there is an API, released March 1, 2023.

Anyone can use ChatGPT, and more and more tech companies and search engines are using the chatbot to automate text or quickly answer user questions and concerns. Multiple enterprises use it, although others limit use of the tool. Microsoft announced at its 2023 Build conference that it is integrating its ChatGPT-based Bing experience into Windows 11; the Brooklyn-based 3D display startup Looking Glass uses ChatGPT to produce holograms you can communicate with; and the nonprofit organization Solana integrated the chatbot into its network with a ChatGPT plug-in geared toward end users to help onboard into the web3 space.



---


# OpenAI Developer Platform And API Releases

OpenAI progressively opened its models to developers through paid APIs and fine-tuning programmes, beginning with a paid API for ChatGPT — a move toward monetization whose initial customers included Instacart, Snap (Snapchat's parent company) and Quizlet.

Model access followed. OpenAI announced the general availability of GPT-4: starting July 6, all existing OpenAI developers "with a history of successful payments" could access GPT-4, with access planned for new developers by the end of July. OpenAI said it would in future allow developers to fine-tune GPT-4 and GPT-3.5 Turbo — one of the original models powering ChatGPT — with their own data, as had long been possible with several of OpenAI's other text-generating models, and that the capability should arrive later that year. It then brought fine-tuning to GPT-3.5 Turbo: companies using the model through the API can make it better follow specific instructions, such as always responding in a given language, improve its ability to consistently format responses, and hone the "feel" of its output, such as tone, so it better fits a brand or voice; most notably, fine-tuning lets customers shorten text prompts to speed up API calls and cut costs. OpenAI partnered with Scale AI to allow companies to fine-tune GPT-3.5, though it was unclear whether OpenAI was developing an in-house tuning tool to complement platforms like Scale AI or to serve a different purpose. Fine-tuning costs were $0.008 per 1K tokens for training, $0.012 per 1K tokens for usage input and $0.016 per 1K tokens for usage output. A GPT-4 fine-tuning programme followed, but unlike the GPT-3.5 programme it involves more oversight and guidance from OpenAI teams, largely because of technical hurdles.

OpenAI also extended the platform beyond text. DALL-E 3, its text-to-image model, became available via an API after first coming to ChatGPT-4 and Bing Chat, and OpenAI released a text-to-speech API, the Audio API, offering six preset voices and two generative AI model variants.

# Matt Huang And Paradigm's FTX Investment

Matt Huang, co-founder and managing partner of Paradigm, a crypto venture capital firm that invested over $275 million in FTX — a stake that was wiped out — was the third witness to take the stand, and testified about his firm's due diligence.

Huang told the court that Bankman-Fried assured him funds would be used for FTX and not Alameda, and that he was promised Alameda had no preferential treatment on the FTX platform, even though the hedge fund was one of its top traders. Huang said he was concerned about FTX's lack of a board of directors but eventually invested anyway. During cross-examination he said Paradigm pressed Bankman-Fried on the board issue and was told he did not want investors as directors but did plan on having a board with experts.

# Gary Wang's Testimony At The FTX Fraud Trial

Gary Wang, the lesser-known co-founder of FTX, told a Manhattan courtroom on Thursday that he had committed financial crimes while working at FTX — including wire and commodities fraud — carried out with the help of Sam Bankman-Fried, FTX ex-engineering head Nishad Singh, and Caroline Ellison, who ran sister hedge fund Alameda Research and had been Bankman-Fried's girlfriend.

Asked by Assistant U.S. Attorney Nicolas Roos, "Did you commit financial crimes while working at FTX?" Wang responded, "Yes." Asked whether he saw any of the people he committed those crimes with in the courtroom, Wang — dressed in an oversized and wrinkled suit with a red tie and glasses — awkwardly stood up, looked around, and answered, "Yes"; asked who, he said, "Sam Bankman-Fried." He was one of two former friends of Bankman-Fried's from MIT who also worked at FTX while living with the founder in the Bahamas and who took the stand that week to testify against their former classmate, confidant and boss, a man who allegedly ran a crypto empire that defrauded thousands of customers out of billions of dollars. The trial, set to last six weeks, was to resume on Tuesday with key testimony expected from Ellison, considered the prosecution's star witness, who had already pleaded guilty to multiple charges. Bankman-Fried faces seven federal charges, including wire fraud, securities fraud and money laundering, that could put him in prison for the rest of his life. Thus far Bankman-Fried, 31, has remained mostly quiet in court, intently listening to witnesses and at times writing notes to his attorneys — but as Wang testified against him, he looked visibly upset, shifting his gaze from his former friend to the ground and at one point putting his head in his hands.



---


# Testimony At The SBF Trial

Across the first three weeks of the trial, a run of former colleagues, an outside investor and a forensic accounting expert testified that FTX customer money flowed into Alameda Research and out again to other uses, and that FTX's investors were never told about the two firms' special relationship. TechCrunch's running coverage, published 2023-10-06, summarises each week.

In week one, FTX's co-founder and CTO Gary Wang testified Thursday on the extent to which Alameda Research was used for whatever purposes he and SBF saw fit: according to Wang, the crypto trading firm pulled funding directly from FTX customers, whose transactions would be funneled toward Alameda and then directed elsewhere. Thursday also brought testimony from Matt Huang, co-founder and managing partner at crypto investment firm Paradigm, which invested $278 million in FTX across 2021 and 2022 and is part of a class-action lawsuit accusing it and others of defrauding customers by promoting FTX. His testimony centered around being left uninformed about FTX's utilization of customer money to keep Alameda Research afloat — a practice Huang says would have halted his involvement — and covered his relationship with FTX stretching back to 2019.

Week two's standout testimony came from Alameda Research's former CEO Caroline Ellison, who claimed she took $14 billion from customers to repay debts to lenders, using them as a line of credit under the instruction of SBF. Ellison also went into detail about how a $2 billion venture fund, FTX Ventures, was funded by money that had previously been allocated to Alameda from third-party lenders. And though there are no charges of bribery in the case, she also testified to paying Chinese officials $150 million to restore access to $1 billion in frozen trading accounts.

The third week featured a couple of noteworthy moments for the prosecution. FTX's former general counsel Can Sun, like many of SBF's former colleagues, opted to cooperate with authorities and testified that SBF asked him to create a theoretical "legal justification" for the use of billions in consumer funds just days before FTX filed for bankruptcy. Robert Boroujerdi, managing director of the hedge fund Third Point, testified about his experience working with SBF and FTX in a partnership that ultimately resulted in a $60 million investment and a lack of awareness about the special relationship between Alameda Research and FTX; had he known of such a relationship, he testified, Third Point would not have invested in FTX in the first place. And earlier in the week, Peter Easton — a University of Notre Dame professor who helped the government prosecution of Enron and WorldCom — testified about what he uncovered after tracing the flow of billions of dollars between Alameda Research and FTX: much of that funding came from customers, and Easton testified that he found user deposits were used by both FTX and Alameda to purchase real estate, make investments or direct funding toward political causes and charities.



---


# Prosecution And Defense Arguments On Day Two Of The SBF Trial

On the second day of the trial of Sam Bankman-Fried and FTX, the prosecution argued that Bankman-Fried knowingly committed fraud, and it grounded that claim in motive: he did so, prosecutors said, to achieve great wealth, power and influence.

The defense countered with the opposite reading of the same conduct. Its claim was that the FTX founder acted in good faith, never meant to commit fraud or to steal, and basically got in over his head — an argument whose warrant is that inexperience and overreach, rather than intent, explain what happened. The two sides therefore contest intent rather than the underlying events, and the reporting on this exchange comes from Rebecca and Jacquelyn in TechCrunch's Week in Review of October 7, 2023, covering day two of the trial only.



---


# Yedidia's Cross-Examination And Resignation

Yedidia's testimony ended on a fiery note that was later struck from the record: asked why he had lost faith in FTX and resigned, he said, "FTX defrauded all its customers."

On cross-examination, defense attorney Christian Everdell asked about the long hours employees worked and Yedidia's concern about Wang being near burnout, which had led Yedidia to institute a rule not to wake Wang at night for bug fixes because he needed sleep. Everdell also drilled Yedidia on his high level of compensation in less than two years at FTX: his base salary was between $175,000 and $200,000, but he received multiple bonuses of more than $12 million in cash and company equity. Yedidia said he is now teaching math — geometry and algebra — at a high school; he invested most of the millions he earned as bonuses back into FTX, and his equity stake is now worthless. As FTX was failing, Yedidia said, he was by Bankman-Fried's side, and he highlighted a Signal exchange in November 2022 in which he wrote, "I love you Sam. I'm not going anywhere," explaining that he wrote it because so many people had left. Asked what changed, Yedidia said he learned that FTX customer deposits had been used to pay loans to creditors, and that Alameda's actions seemed "flagrantly wrong."



---


# The SBF Trial Proceedings

Sam Bankman-Fried is in court for alleged fraud and money laundering while leading crypto exchange FTX and sister company Alameda. TechCrunch's 2023-10-02 preview placed the case in the Manhattan Federal Court, describing the disgraced cryptocurrency entrepreneur as accused of orchestrating "one of the biggest financial frauds in American history": the multibillion-dollar collapse of FTX, the crypto exchange he founded and led. SBF, as he is known, has pleaded not guilty to some seven charges of fraud and conspiracy.

The trial kicked off with jury selection October 3. By TechCrunch's 2023-10-06 update the case was entering its next chapter, with proceedings resuming Thursday: as confirmed during a teleconference Wednesday, SBF would be taking the stand along with a handful of other witnesses, as the onus shifted toward the defense after the prosecution brought its case to its conclusion.

Access to the proceedings is limited: no devices are allowed, so reports are being physically put together within the courtroom, or sent to overflow rooms. The jury's composition ranges from a train conductor to a retired investment banker who attended Stanford University, and TechCrunch pointed readers to a special joint episode of its Equity and Chain Reaction podcasts for a better sense of the vibe between the jurors and the rest of the court.

A second account of the same events was arriving in parallel: "Going Infinite," a book by Michael Lewis chronicling the rise and fall of SBF, was set to debut on the first day of the trial.

# FTX Ventures Was Funded By Alameda

Caroline Ellison testified that the money behind FTX Ventures came from Alameda Research, even though Bankman-Fried announced the fund publicly without naming its source: on January 14th, 2022 he tweeted, "We're launching a $2b venture fund: FTX Ventures!" She said he did not want to go public with where the funds came from, telling her he thought Alameda's brand was less good and that he did not want his name associated with it.

The Verge reported the episode on October 10th, 2023 as part of Ellison's testimony, framing it as FTX keeping cozy private ties with Alameda while publicly holding it at arm's length — an echo, the reporter wrote, of Bankman-Fried and Ellison's romantic relationship. The same distancing appears in another transaction: Alameda bought Robinhood shares for Bankman-Fried, who moved them to a vehicle called "Emergent Fidelity Technologies" to avoid association with Alameda.

# Sam Bankman-Fried's Charges And The Collapse Of FTX

Sam Bankman-Fried, the founder of FTX and Alameda Research, is facing seven counts of criminal charges: two counts of wire fraud and five counts of conspiracy charges.

FTX was a failed cryptocurrency exchange founded in 2019. According to a now-deleted profile from FTX investors Sequoia Capital, FTX was founded because of Bankman-Fried's frustration with other exchanges while he was running Alameda Research, his crypto trading firm. According to the SEC, FTX was a fraud "from the start," diverting customers' funds to Alameda, with a "multi-billion-dollar deficiency caused by his own misappropriation of customer funds."

# Prosecution Allegations In The FTX Superseding Indictment

In a superseding indictment filed August 14th, prosecutors argued that Bankman-Fried lied about consumer protection: that his statements that FTX was "avoiding or managing conflicts of interest" and that "as a general principle FTX segregates customer assets from its own assets across our platforms" were lies.

The indictment also says there were special features in FTX's code that "permitted Alameda to spend and withdraw unlimited amounts of money from FTX," created at Bankman-Fried's direction, effectively exempting Alameda from the kinds of risk management other customers faced — while, the government alleges, "Bankman-Fried publicly and repeatedly asserted that Alameda did not have privileged access to FTX." Bankman-Fried is accused of using "billions of dollars in misappropriated FTX customer deposits" to help buy more than $200 million of real estate for himself, make billions of dollars of investments for his own interest, and repay Alameda's lenders. He allegedly used more than $100 million of customer funds to make political contributions; prosecutors can show evidence of those contributions in this trial even though they aren't part of the charges brought. A second trial is scheduled for March 2024, with additional charges.

# Alameda Research As The Alleged Conduit For FTX Customer Funds

In the prosecution's account offered by Thane Rehn, the key to Sam Bankman-Fried's alleged scheme was Alameda Research, a crypto hedge fund that Bankman-Fried also owned. The structure the government described works as follows: Caroline Ellison — Bankman-Fried's on-again off-again girlfriend and the CEO of Alameda — served as a front for the fund, and through that arrangement Bankman-Fried had "secret access" to customer money, both cash and crypto.

Two further relations complete the alleged mechanism. Bankman-Fried is said to have directed employees to conceal the flow of money into FTX's coffers, and to have forged financial documents distributed to lenders and investors. "The defendant lied to the world," Rehn alleged. These are the government's allegations as presented in its opening statement, not established findings.

By 2022 Alameda's negative balance on FTX had become a cause for concern for Caroline Ellison, Nishad Singh, and Gary Wang, who built a spreadsheet to work out how negative Alameda actually was; the version shown in court ran to several pages of attempts to reconcile, and Wang figured Alameda owed FTX about $11 billion at a time when FTX's revenue was about $1.5 billion. # DeepMind's Sale To Google And Facebook's AI Lab

Google offered $US650 million for DeepMind. Mark Zuckerberg of Facebook offered a bigger payout to DeepMind's founders but would not agree to the conditions the founders had set, and DeepMind sold to Google.

Zuckerberg was determined to build an AI lab of his own and hired Yann LeCun, a French computer scientist who had also done pioneering AI research, to run it. A year after Hinton's auction, Zuckerberg and LeCun flew to Lake Tahoe for the same AI conference, and while padding around a suite at the Harrah's casino in his socks Zuckerberg personally interviewed top researchers, who were soon offered millions of dollars in salary and stock. AI was once laughed off; now the richest men in Silicon Valley were shelling out billions to keep from being left behind.



---


# The AI Risk Paradox Among Tech Billionaires

At the heart of the competition to build artificial intelligence is a brain-stretching paradox: the people who say they are most worried about AI are among the most determined to create it and enjoy its riches, and they have justified their ambition with their strong belief that they alone can keep AI from endangering Earth. The grounds are the shape of the debate itself. Eight years after an argument between Elon Musk and Larry Page, that argument seems prescient, because the question of whether AI will elevate the world or destroy it, or at least inflict grave damage, has framed an ongoing debate among Silicon Valley founders, chatbot users, academics, legislators and regulators about whether the technology should be controlled or set free.

That debate has pitted some of the world's richest men against one another: Musk, Page, Mark Zuckerberg of Meta, tech investor Peter Thiel, Satya Nadella of Microsoft and Sam Altman of OpenAI, all of whom have fought for a piece of a business that one day could be worth trillions of dollars, and for the power to shape it. The narrative anchor is that Musk and Page stopped speaking soon after the party that summer, and that a few weeks later Musk dined with Altman, who was then running a tech incubator, and several researchers in a private room at the Rosewood hotel in Menlo Park, California, a favoured deal-making spot close to the venture capital offices of Sand Hill Road.



---


# Sam Altman's Career Before OpenAI

Sam Altman, 38 as of November 2023, is not trained as an AI engineer, yet has been seen as a Silicon Valley wunderkind since his early 20s. The defining credential of that earlier phase is that he was recruited in 2014 to take the lead of the startup incubator YCombinator.

The reputation attached to him at the time is captured in YCombinator co-founder Paul Graham's 2014 announcement that Altman would become its president: "Sam is one of the smartest people I know, and understands startups better than perhaps anyone I know, including myself." Graham said then that Altman was "one of those rare people who manage to be both fearsomely effective and yet fundamentally benevolent."



---


# Gaza As A Tech Outsourcing Hub

Gaza, despite being one of the most economically challenged regions in the world, has ironically always been a tech hub — not only for Palestine and Palestinians, but also for the world, with international companies having for many years sought out a presence there to collaborate with talented tech freelancers and the startups that gradually emerged from the region. According to sources who helped build those bridges, Nvidia, famed for its role in the new AI boom, has been working with at least 100 engineers from the region for years; tragically, the initiative to employ Palestinians in this outsourcing was that of Mellanox founder Eyal Waldman, whose daughter was brutally murdered in the attacks by Hamas.

The hub's scale marks its boundary. Since at least 2008, TechCrunch has been covering technology companies out of Palestine, some serving their direct audience and some serving the tech world internationally, and Silicon Valley had taken an increasing interest in Palestine as a tech hub — but like the ecosystem itself, that interest is nascent: to date, those working in the region estimate that as much as $10 million has been invested in the Palestinian tech ecosystem. Notably, in 2017, Salesforce founder and CEO Marc Benioff joined Silicon Valley luminaries in backing the first-ever coding academy to be created in Gaza.



---


# Anthropic's Founding By Former OpenAI Researchers

Dario Amodei, a researcher with ties to the effective altruist community, had been on hand at the Rosewood hotel when OpenAI was born, and was leading the lab's efforts to build a neural network called a large language model that could learn from enormous amounts of digital text: by analysing countless Wikipedia articles, digital books and message boards it could generate text on its own, and it also had the unfortunate habit of making things up. It was called GPT-3 and was released in the summer of 2020, and researchers inside OpenAI, Google and other companies thought this rapidly improving technology could be a path to artificial general intelligence. Amodei was unhappy about the Microsoft deal because he thought it was taking OpenAI in a really commercial direction, and he and other researchers went to the board to try to push Altman out, according to five people familiar with the matter; after they failed, they left, worrying, like DeepMind's founders before them, that their new corporate overlords would favour commercial interests over safety.

In 2021 the group of about 15 engineers and scientists created a new lab called Anthropic, with the plan of building AI the way the effective altruists thought it should be done, with very tight controls. Anthropic disputes the account of the board approach: "There was no attempt to remove Sam Altman from OpenAI by the co-founders of Anthropic," said an Anthropic spokesperson, Sally Aldous. "The co-founders themselves came to the conclusion that they wished to depart OpenAI to start their own company, made this known to OpenAI's leadership, and over several weeks negotiated an exit on mutually agreeable terms." Anthropic accepted a $US4 billion investment from Amazon and another $US2 billion from Google two years later. After OpenAI received another $US2 billion from Microsoft, Altman and another senior executive, Greg Brockman, visited Bill Gates at his sprawling mansion on the shores of Lake Washington, outside Seattle; the Microsoft founder was no longer involved in the company day to day but kept in regular touch with its executives.



---


# Private Sector Volunteers In Terror Finance Tracking

The network blocking terror financing funds includes many entities, including private citizens: IMPA has been approached by many experts from the private sector — people with intelligence experience because they have worked in these organizations, or with high-tech experience — who "have mobilized like crazy."

"The world's financial intelligence authorities are now at the heart of this struggle, and we're working together to thwart the financing channels that we've located," Ostrovitch-Levi said. "Israeli entrepreneurs in Silicon Valley have contacted us; they write code, search for information, and give us lots of information. We aggregate and examine everything."



---


# AlphaGo As Evidence For AI Risk Concerns

Rationalists, effective altruists and others who worried about the risks of AI claimed the computer's win at Go validated their fears. The evidence cited is the pace of progress rather than the game itself: "This is another indication that AI is progressing faster than even many experts anticipated," wrote Victoria Krakovna, who would soon join DeepMind as an "AI safety" researcher, in a blog post.

The consequences inside DeepMind followed the same worry. Its founders were increasingly concerned about what Google would do with their inventions and in 2017 tried to break away from the company; Google responded by increasing the salaries and stock award packages of the DeepMind founders and their staff, and they stayed put. The ethics board never had a second meeting.



---


# Flexport's Board Composition

Flexport's board was made up largely of investors who were betting on the founder — a composition that matters because Clark's first quarterly board meeting as sole CEO was June 1 and his second was Aug. 31, days before he was forced out.

The board included Founders Fund's Trae Stephens, who had helped start defense-tech firm Anduril Industries, and Michael Ronen, who left SoftBank in 2020. Andreessen Horowitz was represented by Bob Swan, an operating partner at the firm and former CEO of Intel.



---


# USD Funds In China Turn To Overseas Deals

On a weekday afternoon at Red Rock Coffee, the café known for spotting venture capitalists in Silicon Valley, one is likely to overhear a few conversations in Mandarin. With China reopening its borders in spring 2023 following three years of COVID-19 restrictions, managers of U.S. funds in the country have been flocking to the Bay Area.

The trips themselves are not new; their purpose is. While these trips were routine before the pandemic, they have now taken on a fresh purpose of discovering deals beyond China.

As China's domestic investment appeal wanes, some investors start to look for opportunities beyond its borders. Rather than a complete departure, they are merely following the footsteps of Chinese talent who have already embarked on global expansion.

# Cole Palmer Stoppage-Time Penalty Vs Manchester City

Cole Palmer, who left Manchester City for Chelsea in a deal worth around $A82 million in September, showed supreme composure to fire past Ederson in the dying stages of the 4-4 draw at Stamford Bridge, scoring from the spot in the 95th minute, The Roar reported on Nov. 12, 2023.

In his post-match interview he said of penalties: "I'm not going to say I work on them, because I don't. I just trust in my natural abilities."



---


# Cole Palmer's Penalty-Taking Role And Record

Cole Palmer has, in effect, anointed himself as the spot-kick taker for Chelsea, the £1bn team, taking the ball at Turf Moor to open his Chelsea account. "It was just an in-game thing, really," he said, with a matter-of-fact stance. "Once I scored at Burnley, I just thought: 'I'll take them'." If penalties have been the English disease, Palmer has no hesitation when asked if he would be willing to come off the bench as a specialist from 12 yards for a shootout: "Yeah, I would be," he said.

He is not daunted by the last penalty he missed, as a substitute in the shootout when City lost the 2019 FA Youth Cup final to Liverpool. He can only remember failing from 12 yards on one other occasion, "when I was dead, dead young versus [Manchester] United," and a willingness to take responsibility is similarly apparent in open play. "I think I am a player who always wants the ball, anywhere, to try and help the team get out of a difficult situation or create a chance," he said.

One such penalty came at Tottenham in November 2023. Palmer stepped up in the 35th minute and Vicario got a touch on the Englishman's penalty, yet could only deflect it onto the right post, from where the ball ricocheted into the bottom-right corner to pull the West London visitors level.
