# Belgium-England: The Second Half And Wullaert's Penalty

Belgium won the game on 31 October 2023 through Tessa Wullaert's 85th-minute penalty, awarded by referee Esther Staubli after Georgia Stanway handballed Yana Daniels' 83rd-minute effort; Wullaert fired it into the bottom-left corner despite Mary Earps diving the correct way, Sport Grill reported.

England had the better of the half without converting. On the restart Fran Kirby quickly drew a foul from Kassandra Missipo, but Alessia Russo fumbled control from Chloe Kelly's free-kick and her shot was blocked; Nicky Evrard then saved Kirby's shot from Lucy Bronze's pullback pass in the 52nd minute as England continued to test the Red Flames' defence. Just past the hour mark England were given an almighty scare as Wullaert pounced on a through ball and side-stepped both Jess Carter and Millie Bright, only for Earps to block her shot with a stunning save.

Belgium were forced to defend for much of the last half-hour as Russo and Stanway saw shots denied, while substitute Rachel Daly nodded wide in the 80th minute from Keira Walsh's deep corner towards the left post. Sarina Wiegman's Lionesses were eventually made to pay for their wasted chances.



---


# Cole Palmer's Goal Against Manchester City In The 4-4 Draw

Cole Palmer marked his goal against Manchester City with a shrug rather than a celebration, out of respect for the club where he spent 15 years. "I spent 15 years at the club," he noted. "I can't really go and celebrate how I would celebrate if I have scored a 95th-minute equaliser because it would have been disrespectful." Perhaps it summed up Palmer's inability to feel intimidated by anything; there was no getting carried away.

The alternative explanation is that Palmer has scored so many major goals in the last few months that this was merely another. He struck in the Community Shield and the European Super Cup for City, and against Arsenal and Tottenham for Chelsea. That big-match temperament may equip him for tournament football in an England shirt — and so, too, may his nerveless penalty-taking.



---


# Romero's Red Card And Palmer's Penalty Equaliser

The defining moment of Tottenham vs. Chelsea on Nov. 6, 2023 came in the 31st minute, when a wild passage of play ended with Moises Caicedo's goal ruled out, Cristian Romero sent off on VAR review, and Cole Palmer converting the resulting penalty to level the scoreline at 1-1.

The sequence began with the ball pinging around the Tottenham penalty area, Spurs unable to clear after blocking multiple efforts, until Caicedo finally buried a long-distance effort with a low finish inside the left post. Despite initially appearing to count, the offside flag was raised extremely late, with the assistant referee determining, after a moment to think, that Nicolas Jackson was interfering with play from an offside position.

That was only the beginning of the saga. With the goal disallowed, a VAR review began for a penalty, as Romero had swung wildly into the shins of Raheem Sterling: while he got the ball with his tackle, he followed through with extreme force straight onto both of Sterling's legs, and referee Michael Oliver was sent to the monitor. After a few looks, Oliver produced a straight red card for Romero's tackle and awarded Chelsea a penalty, which Palmer dispatched. NBC Sports Soccer's account of the passage described Romero's red card as following a challenge on Enzo Fernandez, with Chelsea given a penalty and Tottenham down to 10 men.



---


# Chelsea 2-0 Blackburn Carabao Cup Last 16

Chelsea beat Blackburn 2-0 at Stamford Bridge to secure a Carabao Cup last-eight spot, with goals from Benoît Badiashile and a rejuvenated Raheem Sterling, The Guardian reported on Nov. 1, 2023.

Even 2-0 up and cruising, Mauricio Pochettino was a bundle of nerves throughout what turned out to be a comfortable victory in the end — no wonder he spends most of his time watching Chelsea on the edge of the touchline with his hands clasped tightly in his pockets and a tense expression. Blackburn certainly caused problems even after the hosts made their intentions clear from the kick-off, when Nicolas Jackson forced a corner with a blocked shot. Travis was very lucky not to concede a penalty when he slid in against Sterling after 10 minutes, with no VAR to overrule what looked like a clear and obvious error from referee Tim Robinson. It took a good save from Leopold Wahlstedt to deny James, but Blackburn then enjoyed a good period of possession in their opponents' half; James was inches away midway through the first half but his shot just eluded the far post, before Enzo Fernández forced Wahlstedt to palm away his effort. The Swedish goalkeeper was at fault when Chelsea finally scored, palming Gallagher's cross — after he had combined with Palmer — straight to the feet of Badiashile, who calmly sidefooted home. Blackburn's supporters then felt aggrieved when a Callum Brittain cross struck Gallagher's trailing arm, but once again Robinson waved away strong appeals for a penalty.

The visitors showed no intention of surrendering when Harry Leonard caught Axel Disasi napping and raced onto a long ball at the start of the second half, only to curl his shot wide; not for the first time, Robert Sánchez was then far too casual as the Chelsea goalkeeper's pass was almost intercepted. Almost 15 minutes passed before Fernández had Chelsea's first effort of the second half, and Palmer came closer from a tight angle; having cleared the ensuing corner, Blackburn shot themselves in the foot trying to play out, as Brittain's pass was intercepted by Palmer and Sterling curled home from the edge of the area to give Pochettino welcome breathing space. Jackson should have made it more comfortable but blazed over from close range, before the post denied the outstanding Palmer a deflected goal. Sterling could and probably should have added to his tally after finding space in behind more than once late on. But it was Palmer who was afforded a standing ovation when withdrawn at the end, as Chelsea's supporters celebrated only their fourth home win of the season — three of them in this competition.



---


# Belgium 3-2 England: The Women's Nations League Result, October 2023

Tessa Wullaert's brace fired Belgium to a dramatic 3-2 home win over England in League A1 of the 2023-24 UEFA Women's Nations League, reported by Sport Grill on 31 October 2023.

Wullaert equalised for Belgium in first-half injury time before taking advantage of Georgia Stanway's handball to fire in an 85th-minute winning penalty.

The result put Belgium second in the group, one point ahead of England and two points behind group leaders the Netherlands, with those two rivals set to meet on 1 December in a blockbuster showdown.

qid: Does the article from The Independent - Travel suggest that Dubai has exploration opportunities throughout the year, while the TechCrunch article indicates that Archer Aviation's expansion plans are specific to the United Arab Emirates?
context:
# Fossil Fuel Lobbyist Access At COP28 In Dubai

The UN's decision to hold the summit in the United Arab Emirates, a major oil and gas producer, wound up giving the fossil fuel industry unprecedented access: there were more fossil fuel lobbyists in Dubai than at any climate conference in the 28 years the United Nations has convened it.

Industry representatives for fossil fuels outnumbered the delegations from every country present at the talks except the United Arab Emirates and Brazil. According to an investigation by the BBC and the Centre for Climate Reporting, COP28 president Sultan Ahmed Al Jaber even used his position to lobby for oil and gas deals with other governments.



---


# Dubai As A Year-Round Destination, Season By Season

Dubai is synonymous with all things luxury paired with a rich history and heritage, and has plenty to offer the traveller looking to immerse themselves in culture while also enjoying the finer things in life. The defining claim of The Independent's guide is that it is a year-round destination whose activities and experiences vary depending on the time of your visit.

The seasonal division runs as follows. Over the winter months Dubai enjoys balmy temperatures and pleasant weather throughout the season, making it the ideal time to get outdoors and explore its more active, adventurous side. In early summer, as temperatures climb, it is the perfect spot for a blend of beach breaks and sightseeing. In the hotter months of June and July, its world-famous waterparks come into their own, while air-conditioned cultural activities and evening tourism — sight-seeing after sunset — are other season-perfect options.

November carries a specific draw: Dubai Design Week takes place around the start of the month, the region's largest creative festival, shining a spotlight on pioneering designers and all things creative via exhibitions, installations, talks, workshops and markets.



---


# Archer Aviation's Abu Dhabi Air Taxi Plan

EVTOL company Archer Aviation plans to start air taxi operations in Abu Dhabi in 2026, TechCrunch reported on 2023-10-22. From there, Archer says it will expand across the UAE as part of a memorandum of understanding with the Abu Dhabi Investment Office.



---


# What A British Airways Holidays Dubai Booking Includes

Booking a Dubai trip with British Airways Holidays is presented as a stress-free start to an Arabian adventure, offering great value breaks with the quality and peace of mind expected from British Airways. The package is ATOL-protected, keeping you and your money safe.

Its defining components are financial flexibility and included extras: flexible payment options with deposits from just £75 per person, with no balance due until four weeks before travel for short haul or seven weeks for long haul; the option for customers to use Avios to pay for flights and part-pay holidays; a generous baggage allowance of 23kg per person included, so you won't encounter any add-on costs; and 24/7 support throughout your trip via a dedicated holiday helpline for any issues while you are away. The upshot, per the guide, is that whatever time of year you travel, from the day you book you can put all your focus on planning an unforgettable trip.



---


# June And July In Dubai: Water Parks By Day, Sightseeing By Night

June and July are the sun-packed months, perfect for those who really like the heat and are happy to spend their days cooling off by the water. Dubai has made a name for itself when it comes to water parks: Wild Wadi, the city's first-ever waterpark, is a perennial favourite for adults and kids alike, with an exhilarating range of rides, surfing machines and a wave pool, while Laguna Waterpark is one of the newer parks on the map, located on the coast with an infinity pool and its own beach, as well as thrilling slides and a boat-themed kids pool.

Visiting in hotter months means you can save sightseeing and cultural activities for night-time, giving you an entirely different way to experience the city. Take an evening dinner cruise along Dubai Creek to experience the twinkling city night lights, or head up the iconic Burj Khalifa at sunset for stunning views. Further architectural highlights include the night-time lights of the Burj Al Arab and the Dubai Frame, a 153-metre-high structure built to resemble a massive picture frame, which provides incredible views of Old and New Dubai. Alternatively, make the most of the air-con with indoor concerts and theatre shows at the stunning Dubai Opera.



---


# Rapido's India Cab Market Expansion

Rapido, the eight-year-old Indian bike taxi startup, is expanding into the cab market in the South Asian nation, where Uber and its homegrown competitor Ola dominate, TechCrunch reported on 2023-10-30.



---


# Dubai's Desert Adventures, Best In November And December

November and December are the best months to head for Dubai and get stuck into outdoor activities, if you are the kind of person who would rather spend their days exploring than soaking up the sun on the beach: the temperature, although still hot with clear blue skies, is a lot cooler than the sweltering summer months.

Dubai's desert offers a wealth of heart-pumping Arabian activities, from dune buggies to quad biking and desert safaris. Whizz through the desert on a dune drive, keeping your eyes peeled for local wildlife along the way — the desert is home to hopping gazelles, several species of reptile and the Arabian Oryx, a species that was saved from the brink of extinction. Choosing a desert safari adds traditional activities like henna tattooing and dance shows, and many safaris culminate in an evening BBQ dinner.



---


# The COP28 Fossil Fuel Deal That Slipped Away At The Eleventh Hour

What would have been a historic deal to tackle a planetary crisis slipped out of reach at the eleventh hour at COP28 — even though climate-vulnerable countries and environmental advocates scored some key wins with clean energy after heated negotiations wrapped up in the United Arab Emirates, a top oil- and gas-producing country.

This was the closest yet that countries have come to striking a global deal to phase out the use of coal, oil, and gas. But the summit was arguably still a home game for fossil fuel interests, who threw their weight around the United Nations climate conference — the 28th Conference of the Parties, or COP28 — where tens of thousands of delegates and activists from nearly every nation on Earth gathered over two weeks to wrangle over the future of fossil fuels. The Verge's December 13th piece surveyed the biggest decisions made in Dubai now that the dust had settled, decisions that could determine how the world is powered in future.



---


# Old Dubai In Winter: The Creek, Al Fahidi And Hatta

The winter months are also a great time to explore Dubai's fascinating history. At Dubai Creek in Deira you will find traditional wooden boats, also known as abras, the oldest form of public transport in Dubai; these take you from one side of the river to the other — a short trip, but a nice way to get a feel for local life.

Along the creek sits the historic Al Fahidi Historical neighbourhood, where you can learn what life in Old Dubai was like. The area is dotted with original buildings and preserved infrastructure like traditional wind towers and the Al Fahidi Fort, one of the oldest buildings in Dubai, built back in 1787.

More history and heritage can be found in nearby Hatta, where craggy mountains and lush valleys cradle citadels, towers and forts. For jaw-dropping views over the historical village, hike up the dramatic Hajar mountains, one of the highest ranges in the Arabian peninsula, and stop by Hatta Heritage Village, a reconstruction of a traditional mountain village where you can see how life was lived centuries ago.



---


# Binance's CEO Succession: Richard Teng

Richard Teng, Binance's former global head of regional markets, will be the exchange's new CEO, Zhao shared in a post on X on the afternoon of Tuesday, November 21, 2023. Teng previously was the CEO of the Financial Services Regulatory Authority at Abu Dhabi Global Market, among other executive roles.

In response to stepping down, Zhao said "it is the right thing to do," adding, "I made mistakes, and I must take responsibility."

Zhao will remain a shareholder and said he will be "available to the team to consult as needed."



---


# Mobility And Logistics Funding Rounds, October 2023

TechCrunch listed three mobility and logistics rounds on 2023-10-22. Hayden AI, an AI and geospatial analytics company, raised $53 million in a Series B funding round led by the Drawdown Fund; its tech is being used by government agencies to enforce traffic violations that obstruct transit buses and capture data to help increase ridership and improve traffic efficiency.

Commercial fleet insurance startup Nirvana Insurance raised a $57 million Series B to expand its big data platform, hire new staff and grow its business in the trucking industry, in a round led by Lightspeed Venture Partners with General Catalyst and Valor Equity Partners also participating; the round doubles Nirvana's valuation to more than $350 million post-money. Supply chain logistics company Transfix raised a $40 million Series F, and is backed by New Enterprise Associates, G Squared and Canvas Ventures.

context:
# Kenwright's 19 Seasons As Everton Chairman

Bill Kenwright spent 19 seasons as Everton chairman, having been on the board since 1989 and taking over as chairman at Goodison Park in 2004. Over that tenure he oversaw 12 finishes inside the Premier League top eight, including fourth place in 2005, while the Merseyside club were also FA Cup finalists in 2009.

Everton said he had led the club through "a period of unprecedented change in English football". These figures are as reported by the BBC on 24 October 2023, at the time of his death.



---


# Bill Kenwright Dies Aged 78 After Liver Cancer Surgery

Everton chairman Bill Kenwright, an acclaimed West End theatre and film producer, died at the age of 78, his family announcing on Tuesday that he "passed away peacefully" on Monday night "surrounded by his family and loved ones". The BBC reported the death on 24 October 2023.

The medical context: Kenwright had surgery to remove a cancerous tumour from his liver eight weeks before his death. On 12 October the Premier League club said the tumour had been removed six weeks earlier and that the operation was "completely successful", but complications meant Kenwright required a "prolonged period in an intensive care unit".

Everton said it was "in mourning" following the death of the club's longest-serving chairman for more than a century, adding: "The club has lost a chairman, a leader, a friend, and an inspiration." His family's statement read: "Bill was driven by his passions and devoted his life to them; his deep love of theatre, film, music and his beloved Everton, and the families they created. He impacted the lives of thousands, whether that be through the launching of careers or his unending loyalty, generosity and unfaltering friendship and support." They added: "We will remember him with huge love and admiration - the shows will of course go on, as he would have wished, and his towering legacy will continue."



---


# Everton Fans' No Confidence Vote Against Kenwright's Board

Against the picture of Kenwright as a beloved, long-serving chairman, an Everton fans' group called for him to be sacked and said it had "no confidence" in him as chairman, with the club fighting against relegation last season. The objection targets the premise that his leadership was serving the club well on the pitch, not his personal standing or his record of longevity.

The dispute had practical consequences. Kenwright and the rest of the board of directors were unable to attend home games last season from January, after what the club described as "threatening correspondence" was received before a game against Southampton. Chief executive Denise Barrett-Baxendale, chief finance and strategy officer Grant Ingles and non-executive director Graeme Sharp have all since left their boardroom roles — but Kenwright remained in his post as chairman until his death.



---


# Everton Ten Point Deduction For PSR Breach

An independent commission imposed a 10-point penalty on Everton for breaching Premier League financial rules — the biggest sporting sanction in Premier League history, for a £19.5m overspend in 2021-22 — as reported by The Guardian on Nov. 24, 2023.

Manager Sean Dyche said he was shocked and aggrieved by the decision, describing the deduction as both disproportionate and unjust. He was ill while on holiday in Dubai when informed of the punishment by Everton's director of football, Kevin Thelwell. Dyche said he was confident Everton's season would not be derailed by the penalty, but warned his players that they could not rely on the club's appeal to rescue them from another relegation battle.



---


# Liverpool 3-0 Brentford Salah 200th English Goal

Liverpool beat Brentford 3-0 with Mohamed Salah continuing his remarkable Anfield scoring record with two more goals to bring up his 200th in English football, The Roar reported on Nov. 12, 2023, leaving them second, just a point behind City, with Tottenham fourth and two points adrift.

The Reds broke the deadlock after two earlier efforts were disallowed by VAR. Only Erling Haaland, on 13, had scored more in the Premier League that season than the Egypt international, who took his tally to 10 by scoring for the sixth successive home game to write another entry in the club's history books. Diogo Jota's late strike then put a quick end to questions over Liverpool's mini-stumble after the draw at Luton and the Europa League defeat in Toulouse.



---


# Everton's Win Over Newcastle, December 2023

Everton trounced Newcastle 3-0 on 7 December 2023 to move clear of the relegation zone despite their ten-point penalty for financial irregularities, as reported by The Roar that day.

The Toffees left it late, with goals from Dwight McNeil, Abdoulaye Doucoure and Brazilian striker Beto enough to down the Magpies. McNeil's opener came from a Kieran Trippier mistake that the Everton man made him pay for, and Goodison Park went wild at what the report calls a massive goal.



---


# Ten Hag's Defence Of Manchester United's Performance

Erik ten Hag tried to put a positive spin on the defeat to West Ham on 23 December 2023 by claiming to the BBC that his side were the better team before the first goal: the claim is that the loss came from a single lapse rather than a systemic failure, and the warrant is that United created the better chances and had recently matched the top of the league.

His grounds for the first part are the shape of the match: "I think it was a decent 72 minutes where we didn't take our chances. We should've gone in the lead but we didn't and then it was one moment of switching off."

His grounds for the second part are the previous fixture, which he uses to set the standard he says the team must reproduce: "At this moment we are not top, but we have seen last week against the top of this league we were head-to-head. We didn't score, we had the best opportunities of the game." He added: "There we defended very well for 90 minutes, that has to be always our standard like what we did there. You have to bring that to every game on the pitch."



---


# Everton Under Sean Dyche As A Derby Threat

The Guardian argued on 20 October 2023 that Sean Dyche's Everton posed a genuine threat in the Merseyside derby, because Liverpool's defensive concerns were matched against a visiting side whose overall performance had improved even if its scoring had not.

The grounds run both ways. Liverpool's defensive concerns were heightened by the loss of Andy Robertson for up to three months with a shoulder injury, but were offset by the visitors' troubles in front of goal: a 3-0 defeat of Bournemouth last time out was only the eighth time Everton had scored more than once in a Premier League match in the past 12 months. Against that, the overall improvement in Everton's performance, coupled with three wins in the past four games, raised Dyche's hopes of capitalising on any post-international fatigue in the opposition ranks.

Klopp's compliments towards Dyche and his local rivals were of the back-handed nature, and they supply the warrant — the threat is stylistic, not a matter of form alone. "Everton are in a good moment," he said. "Burnley in their best moments [under Dyche] were a super-difficult team to play against and you can see that again; it's similar with different players. We have to be ready for second ball fights, runs in behind, a compact defence. It will be a tough one. Burnley games were always tough. We have to have football understanding, patience, put a proper shift in and take the fight."



---


# Tributes To Kenwright From Rooney, Carragher, Burnham And McKellen

Following Bill Kenwright's death, tributes came from both football and theatre. Wayne Rooney, the former Everton and England forward, said: "Devastated to hear the sad news about Bill Kenwright. Known Bill since I was young and he's had a huge impact on me as a person and my career. Great man and a big inspiration. Thoughts are with all Bill's family and friends."

Jamie Carragher, the ex-Liverpool and England defender, said: "Really sad news this. A huge Evertonian who served and loved his club to bits. I'll never forget his and Everton's support every year around the Hillsborough memorial. RIP Bill." # FTX's Fabricated Backstop Insurance Fund

Gary Wang testified on October 6th, 2023 that FTX lied about how much money was in its backstop fund, and the court was shown the code that generated the fake number published on FTX's website: it took the daily trading volume on FTX, multiplied it by a random number, divided it by a billion, and added the result to the number already displayed on the site. That figure had nothing to do with the actual amount of money in the insurance fund.

The fund mattered because of what FTX advertised. In many crypto networks, if someone lost enough money the exchanges could stick other traders with the losses too; FTX touted its automated liquidation as the way to avoid this, so that one customer going bankrupt would not affect the others. In the process of liquidating, FTX would try to sell the collateral on the open market, and if it could not finish, backstop liquidity providers would step in — market makers, including Alameda, which could be compensated for the losses they took from the backstop fund. Wang also testified that when there was not enough money in the fund, money was moved there from Alameda's accounts in order to pay the insurance out.

The prosecution's framing was that this was not merely a matter of Alameda holding special, secret privileges: it claimed those privileges were used to obfuscate basic elements of FTX's operations, exposing the exchange's supposed selling points as a lie.



---


# The Mechanism Of FTX's Collapse

FTX came apart in early November 2022 through a chain with four links: a leaked balance sheet revealed that Alameda's largest holding was FTX's own token in a quantity larger than the token's whole market, the disclosure destroyed confidence, the world's largest rival exchange pulled its holdings out, and the resulting bank run forced FTX and Alameda into Chapter 11 within days. TechCrunch's 2023-10-01 account sets out the sequence: in early November 2022, that all changed.

Concerns surrounding FTX's liquidity grew after CoinDesk published a copy of Alameda's balance sheet, showing the firm held $14.6 billion in assets and $8 billion in liabilities as of June 30, 2022. The balance sheet showed that the $5.82 billion in FTT tokens that Alameda owned was 193% higher than the total FTT market cap, which was about $3 billion at the time — meaning Alameda purported to have more FTT tokens on its balance sheet than what existed in the world. Around the same time it was exposed, the world's largest crypto exchange, Binance, started pulling out its remaining $2.1 billion equivalent of cash in BUSD and FTT; Binance had held an equity position in FTX from 2019 to 2021. That withdrawal essentially triggered a bank run on FTX. FTX and Alameda filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in the U.S. mid-November 2022, Bankman-Fried resigned, and John J. Ray III, the Enron turnaround veteran, was appointed the new CEO.

The condition the whole mechanism rests on is the fragility of the underlying valuations. As TechCrunch put it on 2023-10-02, all of that activity came to a crashing end because the value of cryptocurrencies on FTX was not banked to much more than speculation and the promise of higher value — so when those valuations fell, they fell very, very hard. The chain therefore only runs as described where an asset is priced on expectation, held in size by a related party, and exposed to a counterparty large enough that its exit alone starts the run.



---


# FTX's Absence Of A Chief Risk Officer

The Verge's trial reporter argued that FTX's lack of a chief risk officer was either evidence of stupidity or a deliberate choice — and, since stupidity was unlikely, that Bankman-Fried probably chose not to hire one because he was worried about what such an officer might find. The grounds are that FTX ran a business in which risk management is structurally central, and the warrant is that any competent operator of such a business knows this, so the omission has to be explained by intent rather than oversight.

The claim about centrality rests on what FTX was. FTX was named as it was because it was a futures exchange, which, to borrow Bloomberg columnist Matt Levine's phrase, "sits between the winners and losers of bets" — meaning FTX could not pay out what it owed the winners unless the losers paid up. Risk officers exist to identify a business's potential risks, monitor them, and mitigate them, and those risks run from reputational to regulatory to financial, to say nothing of the regulatory risks specific to crypto. As the reporter put it after Bankman-Fried's own testimony, risk is an inherent part of a futures exchange, which is even more like a casino than regular cryptocurrency, so not having a risk team when you are any kind of financial anything is certainly a choice — and especially a choice when you go around telling everyone your crypto exchange is very good and safe.

Two things sharpen the argument. First, the omission was conceded: Bankman-Fried testified that he made a point of "periodically" handling support tickets himself because "I worried if I didn't, I would lose touch with the actual concerns of the customers," while what he did not do was create a risk team — something he now characterises as a "big mistake." Second, the defense raised the subject itself. Defense lawyer Mark Cohen's opening told the jury FTX "didn't have a chief risk officer, which became an issue when the storm hit," and offered a metaphor of FTX as a plane; the reporter's response was that if FTX was a plane, it was a plane flying with a key component missing, and that bringing this up was a tremendous mistake because the prosecution had not mentioned it.

Alameda Research is the crypto-trading firm Sam Bankman-Fried co-founded in 2017, before FTX existed. FTX came two years later, in 2019, and Bankman-Fried co-founded it as a complement to Alameda — to help bring in revenue and liquidity for the trading arm. The founding order is the discriminating fact: the exchange was created to serve the trading firm, not the other way round.

The feature that later set Alameda's balance sheet apart was how much of it consisted of the affiliated exchange's own token. A report showed that Alameda's largest asset was $3.66 billion of "unlocked FTT," alongside $2.16 billion of "FTT collateral." FTT was the token behind FTX. So the trading firm's single biggest asset was the token issued by the exchange founded to support it.

# FTX Ventures Was Funded By Alameda

Caroline Ellison testified that the money behind FTX Ventures came from Alameda Research, even though Bankman-Fried announced the fund publicly without naming its source: on January 14th, 2022 he tweeted, "We're launching a $2b venture fund: FTX Ventures!" She said he did not want to go public with where the funds came from, telling her he thought Alameda's brand was less good and that he did not want his name associated with it.

The Verge reported the episode on October 10th, 2023 as part of Ellison's testimony, framing it as FTX keeping cozy private ties with Alameda while publicly holding it at arm's length — an echo, the reporter wrote, of Bankman-Fried and Ellison's romantic relationship. The same distancing appears in another transaction: Alameda bought Robinhood shares for Bankman-Fried, who moved them to a vehicle called "Emergent Fidelity Technologies" to avoid association with Alameda.

Much of Gary Wang's Friday testimony focused on the final days at FTX before the operation imploded: after media reports detailing Alameda's business practices and its troubling ties to FTX, an emergency meeting was called between Bankman-Fried, Wang and Singh to discuss shutting down Alameda, and they decided against it because he and Bankman-Fried knew Alameda had no way to repay the roughly $14 billion hole in its books.

Wang, 30, was technology chief for FTX, which spiralled into bankruptcy in November; he spoke so fast that U.S. District Judge Lewis Kaplan and the prosecutor both stopped him at points to ask that he slow his pace. Prosecutors took the jury through a series of tweets beginning on Nov. 7 — posts from the company blaming bank hours for slow withdrawals, while Bankman-Fried tweeted from his personal account assuring customers that all was fine. "FTX was not fine and assets were not fine," Wang testified. On Nov. 12, after FTX declared bankruptcy, Bankman-Fried asked Wang to drive with him to the Bahamas Securities Commission for a meeting; on the drive, Bankman-Fried told Wang to transfer assets to Bahamian liquidators because he believed they would allow him to maintain control of the company. Wang said he was not in the meeting with the securities authority, though Bankman-Fried's dad was present.

# Marc-Antoine Julliard's Testimony As FTX's First Witness-Victim

The prosecution's first witness at Sam Bankman-Fried's trial was not a blockbuster name or a former lieutenant-turned-cooperator like Caroline Ellison but a victim: Marc-Antoine Julliard, a Paris-born cocoa trader who lives in London and whose money got stuck on FTX. Julliard testified that on Nov. 8, 2022, in the crypto exchange's final few days, he tried to pull out almost $100,000 in cash and crypto, and that he was never able to. The withdrawal screenshots shown in court were of attempts to move $20,000 USD and about 4 Bitcoin, worth about $20,000 at the time — roughly $100,000 in total, inaccessible.

Julliard explained why he had chosen FTX in 2021 when he decided to invest in crypto, trading currencies like Bitcoin and Dogecoin there. He trusted FTX because Bankman-Fried came across as a leading figure of the industry; because the sheer volume of users mattered to him, and FTX was at the time among the top three biggest exchanges; and because major VC firms had invested. "They don't commit hundreds of millions without doing due diligence, checking the books, the accountancy of the firm, going through several compliance process[es], so that was a vote of confidence for me," he said. He also noted FTX's glossy ads — featuring Gisele Bündchen, for instance — which suggested a very high budget, and reasoned that it wouldn't make sense to spend that much money unless FTX had very strong financials. He opened an account, transferred in both regular money and cryptocurrency, and used the exchange to execute his plan of buying Bitcoin to sell back in five to ten years at higher prices.

In November 2022 things went bad. Julliard followed Bankman-Fried on Twitter and read aloud in court the "FTX is fine. Assets are fine" tweets, along with "FTX has enough to cover all client holdings. We don't invest client assets" and a few others, which gave him the impression that his money was there and that any problem might be technical — anti-spam measures — or regulatory. By the time he tried to get his money out on November 8th, it was too late. Cross-examining a customer whose money is gone is described as a thankless task, but Mark Cohen tried anyway, noting that Julliard was a licensed commodities broker who was trading in crypto because he didn't have to disclose it, that he knew crypto was new and risky, and that he didn't review the terms of service agreement he had assented to when making his FTX account. The next witness called was Bankman-Fried's former college and FTX roommate, Adam Yedidia.

# Testimony At The SBF Trial

Across the first three weeks of the trial, a run of former colleagues, an outside investor and a forensic accounting expert testified that FTX customer money flowed into Alameda Research and out again to other uses, and that FTX's investors were never told about the two firms' special relationship. TechCrunch's running coverage, published 2023-10-06, summarises each week.

In week one, FTX's co-founder and CTO Gary Wang testified Thursday on the extent to which Alameda Research was used for whatever purposes he and SBF saw fit: according to Wang, the crypto trading firm pulled funding directly from FTX customers, whose transactions would be funneled toward Alameda and then directed elsewhere. Thursday also brought testimony from Matt Huang, co-founder and managing partner at crypto investment firm Paradigm, which invested $278 million in FTX across 2021 and 2022 and is part of a class-action lawsuit accusing it and others of defrauding customers by promoting FTX. His testimony centered around being left uninformed about FTX's utilization of customer money to keep Alameda Research afloat — a practice Huang says would have halted his involvement — and covered his relationship with FTX stretching back to 2019.

Week two's standout testimony came from Alameda Research's former CEO Caroline Ellison, who claimed she took $14 billion from customers to repay debts to lenders, using them as a line of credit under the instruction of SBF. Ellison also went into detail about how a $2 billion venture fund, FTX Ventures, was funded by money that had previously been allocated to Alameda from third-party lenders. And though there are no charges of bribery in the case, she also testified to paying Chinese officials $150 million to restore access to $1 billion in frozen trading accounts.

The third week featured a couple of noteworthy moments for the prosecution. FTX's former general counsel Can Sun, like many of SBF's former colleagues, opted to cooperate with authorities and testified that SBF asked him to create a theoretical "legal justification" for the use of billions in consumer funds just days before FTX filed for bankruptcy. Robert Boroujerdi, managing director of the hedge fund Third Point, testified about his experience working with SBF and FTX in a partnership that ultimately resulted in a $60 million investment and a lack of awareness about the special relationship between Alameda Research and FTX; had he known of such a relationship, he testified, Third Point would not have invested in FTX in the first place. Sam Bankman-Fried is in court for alleged fraud and money laundering while leading crypto exchange FTX and sister company Alameda. Sam Bankman-Fried, the founder of bankrupt cryptocurrency exchange FTX, is charged with seven counts of fraud and money laundering following the collapse of his cryptocurrency empire the previous year, and was on trial in New York in October 2023.

Sam Bankman-Fried, the founder of FTX and Alameda Research, is facing seven counts of criminal charges: two counts of wire fraud and five counts of conspiracy charges.

On 5 August, well before the two were rumoured to be dating, Kelce was asked his celebrity crush, and before he could answer the answer was given for him.

On 21 September, speaking on the Pat McAfee show, Kelce discussed the rumours and sounded somehow surprised people were talking about it: "It is hilarious how much traction this has actually got. It's like that old game in school called telephone where everybody is just whispering in each others ear, just hearing some random stuff. Especially when you got Jason Kelce on live television telling people just both sides." He then admitted he had invited Swift to one of his games, joking they would compete to see who put on the bigger show at Arrowhead Stadium: "I threw it out there, I threw the ball in her court and I told her you know, I've seen you rock the stage in Arrowhead you might have to come see me rock the stage in Arrowhead and see which one is a little more lit. We will see what happens in the near future." On 22 September, Kelce was spotted at his nonprofit charity event wearing a bracelet reading "Vigilante Sh--," the name of one of Swift's songs.



---


# CD Unfamiliarity As A Generational Marker

The mothers who filmed three young Swifties failing to open a CD case treated the moment as a measure of how far technology had moved, and online viewers responded overwhelmingly with "I feel old", FOX News Lifestyle reported on 11 November 2023.

"The girls' struggle with the CD was a wake-up call to how times have changed since we 'cut the cord,'" Schmidt commented, and the mothers could not help but laugh as they realised how different things now are thanks to technology. "Watching the girls grapple with the CD case felt like stepping back in time," Jody, one of the moms, told Fox News Digital. "That moment of pure innocence when the girls first attempted to open the CD case was priceless," said Tia, another mom. "I knew then that we had to flip the camera on to capture the rest of their experience with the CD." The hilarious moment brought laughter not only to the three moms but to the scores of viewers who saw the video on TikTok, and the Gen Zers captured the attention of viewers online whose overwhelming response was "I feel old".

It was not the first time a young person went viral for trying to open a CD: in May, Fox News Digital reported on a mom who showed her 10-year-old daughter's struggle as she attempted to pop a "Now That's What I Call Music! 21" CD (2006).



---


# Britney Spears And Charlie Ebersol

Britney Spears and Charlie Ebersol — known as the co-founder of Tempus Ex Machina and The Company — started dating in 2014 and broke up officially in June 2015, after eight months together. Their relationship was fairly low profile.

Spears had previously explained what drew her to Ebersol, telling People at the time: "There was something about him that made me feel really peaceful and at ease. And he was really hot, too. Adorably hot."

qid: Does the article from Fortune suggest that Generation Z experiences distress primarily due to climate change, while the article from Eos: Earth And Space Science News calls for a deeper understanding of sea surface temperature patterns as a significant climate driver?
context:
# Coupled Models Fail to Reproduce Observed Warming Patterns

Coupled climate models seem unable to simulate observed surface warming patterns across some key regions in which surface sensitivity modulates clouds: most importantly, models do not re-create observed cooling in the equatorial and subtropical eastern Pacific and Southern Ocean, and it is concerning that all models have the same sign of error in the trend patterns (Wills et al., 2022).

Coupled climate models simulate a freely evolving ocean surface and hence have their own expression of internal variability — one would not expect a coupled model to simulate El Niño events at the same time as they happened in nature, except by chance — which complicates comparisons between models and observations, especially on decadal timescales and beyond, for which little is known about the spectrum of internal variability in the real world. Even accounting for internal variability, the pattern failure persists, and models strongly disagree about the timescales over which future warming may occur in these regions. Limited knowledge of the drivers of surface warming pattern biases hampers the ability to evaluate them: it is not known whether the models' inability to reproduce observed trends is due to biases in how they represent the spectrum of internal variability, aerosol forcing, ocean-atmosphere interactions, deep and shallow atmospheric convection, Southern Ocean cloud-radiative properties, ocean thermocline depth, and ocean circulation, or something else entirely.



---


# Open Questions on SST Patterns and Earth's Radiation Budget

The article argues that pressing, fundamental questions for climate dynamics concern how surface temperature patterns come about, how Earth's radiation budget depends on the details of those patterns, and the extent to which the two depend on each other.

Three tasks follow from that claim. First, understanding must improve of the drivers of sea surface temperature patterns — decadal coupled variability; the pace and spatial structure of ocean heat uptake; and forcing by aerosols, greenhouse gases, and volcanoes — as well as the relative timing of these drivers, with the goal of explaining historical patterns quantitatively and predicting their likely future evolution. Second, the dependence of local and remote top-of-the-atmosphere radiative fluxes on the magnitude, spatial scale, and sign (positive or negative) of surface temperature changes must be quantified. Third, it must be explained how ocean heat uptake and radiative feedback are connected on various timescales, both globally and regionally.



---


# Equilibrium Climate Sensitivity and Its Uncertainty

Climate sensitivity quantifies how much Earth's surface warms in response to a doubling of carbon dioxide relative to preindustrial levels, and reducing the uncertainty in its estimates is one of the grand challenges in climate science.

The uncertainty is large because climate sensitivity aggregates myriad processes — from microscale aerosol-cloud interactions to planetary-scale atmospheric and ocean circulations — into one number, and clouds, which are notoriously difficult to measure and simulate, are the main driver of that uncertainty. Various lines of evidence are used to estimate climate sensitivity, including climate model simulations of varying complexity, observations over the past century, proxies that measure climate change in the distant past, and theory. The likely range of estimates was stubbornly constant at a distressingly imprecise 1.5-4.5 K for several decades, though the research community's efforts have recently chipped away at this range.



---


# Emerging Tools for Quantifying the Pattern Effect

Promising new tools and observations are beginning to emerge for quantifying the pattern effect: targeted model experiments and intercomparisons, extended global satellite observations of clouds and radiation, Argo floats sampling deep-ocean heat uptake, estimates of radiative imbalances before the year 2000, and new observational constraints on clouds' sensitivity to environmental controlling factors.

These developments encourage an optimistic outlook on the ability to quantify the pattern effect and its implications over the next couple of years. Working to solve these problems at the intersection of different disciplines and with input from different research communities will likely benefit related research into, for example, the sensitivity of tropical cyclones and future rainfall changes in the southwestern United States or in South America to surface warming patterns.



---


# Gen Z Mental Health And Climate Anxiety

Gen Z has the worst reported mental health of any generation: 45% of young people report having "excellent" or "very good" mental health, according to a 2018 report by the American Psychological Association. One of the major sources of that distress is climate change — nearly seven in 10 Gen Zers say they experience anxiety when viewing climate change content on social media, according to a 2021 Pew Research report.

They are not only reading about the effects of human-caused global warming but living through the consequences. The summer of 2023 reached record-breaking temperatures, with July the hottest month the planet has seen in over 100,000 years; Arizona experienced a monthlong heat wave with temperatures at or above 110 degrees every day; deadly fires broke out across the Mediterranean; suffocating smoke from Canadian wildfires blanketed New York City and the Northeast for days; and ice melt in the Arctic accelerated. Extreme heat is likely here to stay — and get worse — unless countries can rapidly reduce their carbon emissions, which is why Gen Z is more concerned with sustainability than any generation before them.

Greta Thunberg is the emblem the article offers: the 20-year-old has become one of the best-known environmental activists, famously speaking at the United Nations in 2019 with scathing words for world leaders. "You have stolen my dreams and my childhood with your empty words. And yet I'm one of the lucky ones," Thunberg said. "People are suffering. People are dying. Entire ecosystems are collapsing. We are in the beginning of a mass extinction, and all you can talk about is money and fairy tales of eternal economic growth. How dare you!"



---


# The US CLIVAR Pattern Effect Workshop, 2022

To foster work on the pattern effect across research communities, 140 scientists from around the world and from different disciplines gathered for a US CLIVAR (U.S. Climate Variability and Predictability Program) workshop in May 2022 in Boulder, Colorado.

The Eos article presents the current consensus that emerged during that workshop and raises questions that its authors say require urgent attention from scientists.



---


# Paleorecords Must Account for the Pattern Effect

Just as the historical evolution of surface warming and the planet's radiation budget informs Earth's future only to a limited extent, analyses of paleorecords for recent and deep time intervals must account for the pattern effect to be applicable to climate projections of the future.

The supporting case is the Last Glacial Maximum (LGM): the cooling pattern during the LGM differed from the warming pattern observed currently, and from those expected for the next couple of decades and in the equilibrium following a doubling of carbon dioxide, not only in sign but also in the spatial distribution of magnitudes. Because the LGM currently provides the best constraint on the upper bound of equilibrium climate sensitivity (Sherwood et al., 2020), the details of the pattern effect matter greatly. Outstanding questions concern how representative pattern changes in the past century, the past millennium, or quasi-equilibrated times millions of years ago are of expected future changes; the paleorecord could further be crucial for understanding the timescales and relative importance of internal variability, forced response, and extratropical forcing to rates of warming or cooling in the equatorial Pacific in nature and in climate models.



---


# "No Place Is Safe": Climate Impacts on Kalmus's Life

Kalmus concluded that "no place was safe" after a 2020 heat wave — considered nearly impossible if not for the influence of climate change — seared the Pacific Northwest for three days, killing hundreds of people, buckling roadways and sending overheated baby birds jumping from their nests to their deaths, in the very region where he had dreamed of making a life he thought might be buffered from the worst of climate change.

"It feels like it's worse than I thought it would be in 2023," Kalmus said, pointing to record-low Antarctic sea ice and record-high sea surface and land temperatures as signs that Earth systems could be shifting more quickly than the scientific community can grasp. In recent years climate change has begun to sting his personal life: in summer 2020 he sickened himself hiking in a California heat wave, then watched a wildfire burn a few miles from his California home, spewing smoke that left his voice raspy and his head aching, while the searing temperatures killed a dogwood tree in his front yard and his productivity slowed so that he could not focus on science. His family relocated to North Carolina for his wife Sharon's work, but the Pacific Northwest experience planted a seed: if he could not stop climate change and could not avoid it, could he at least find a better way to survive it? He knew what would not work — "I very quickly eliminated the idea of being a prepper — you know, hoarding beans and ammunition," he said — but he found himself daydreaming of a simpler life where he could keep bees, grow vegetables and press cider to drink on a Friday night, living closer to the land.

qid: Does 'The Sydney Morning Herald' suggest that the Federal Reserve's future interest rate decisions will be based on the whims of a magic 8-ball, while another article from 'The Sydney Morning Herald' indicates that there is hope the Federal Reserve may soon stop raising interest rates and possibly start reducing them?
context:
# Federal Reserve Rate Path Expectations Late 2023

By early December 2023 traders widely expected the Federal Reserve to hold its key interest rate steady at its meeting the following week before potentially cutting rates in March, according to data from CME Group, and Fed officials had recently hinted that the federal funds rate may already be at its peak, above 5.25 per cent, up from nearly zero early in 2022. Fed Chair Jerome Powell and others nevertheless warned Wall Street against being overzealous in its predictions about how early a cut could happen.

The bond market moved with those expectations. With inflation down from its peak two summers earlier, Wall Street was hopeful the Fed might be done with its market-shaking hikes. Investors were looking for a slowdown in the job market that came through employers cutting back on open positions rather than laying off workers, and the report cited showed employers advertised just 8.7 million jobs on the last day of October, down 617,000 from a month earlier. US Treasury yields continued to sag from the heights reached during late October: the 10-year yield fell to 4.18 per cent from 4.26 per cent late on the Monday, after having been above 5 per cent and at its highest level in more than a decade during October. The two-year Treasury yield, which more closely tracks Fed expectations, fell from 4.61 per cent just before the economic reports to 4.57 per cent, yo-yoed, and then eased back to 4.57 per cent. Lower yields were one reason cryptocurrency prices had been rising, alongside excitement about a possible bitcoin exchange-traded fund that helped send bitcoin above $US43,000 ($65,600); Robinhood Markets reported a roughly 75 per cent jump in crypto trading volumes during November from a month earlier, said customers added about $US1.4 billion in net deposits during the month, and its own stock rose 10.3 per cent.

A month earlier, in early November 2023, the same expectations were forming from a lower base. Before that week, stocks had been struggling under the weight of rapidly rising Treasury yields catching up to the Fed's main interest rate, which was above 5.25 per cent and at its highest level since 2001. Higher rates and yields slow the economy, hurt investment prices and raise the risk of something breaking in the financial system, such as the three high-profile US bank failures that rattled markets during the spring. "It was really fear that the Fed was going to go too far," said Katie Nixon, chief investment officer for Northern Trust Wealth Management. The Fed had applied that pressure intentionally, hoping to starve inflation of its fuel and to cool the job market, particularly pay raises, because it feared too-strong pay gains could create a vicious cycle keeping inflation high. Analysts said the Friday jobs report offered encouraging signals, with average hourly earnings rising less in October from September than expected, though it did not mean the job was done. Treasury yields tumbled immediately after that report, with the 10-year easing to 4.52 per cent from 4.67 per cent late Thursday and from more than five per cent the previous week, when it hit its highest level since 2007. Traders then moved up expectations for the first Fed cut, potentially by the summer, according to CME Group data. Foreign-exchange strategists at Bank of America wrote in a BofA Global Research report that for investors around the world the "Fed matters more than other central banks" and weak US data is "the only game-changer for markets". A separate report that Friday from the Institute for Supply Management said growth in US services industries such as finance and construction was weaker than economists expected and suggested a slight easing in prices.



---


# How Treasury Yields And "Higher For Longer" Transmit To Equities

Treasury bonds are seen as some of the safest investments possible, and when they pay higher yields, investors are less likely to pay high prices for stocks and other riskier investments — which is a big reason why the S&P 500 dropped 4.9 per cent in September 2023, dragging what had been a big gain for the year down to 11.7 per cent.

The chain running into those yields is the Federal Reserve's stance. Treasury yields have been climbing sharply as Wall Street accepts a new normal in which the Fed is likely to keep interest rates high for longer; the Fed is trying to push still-high inflation down to its target, and its main tool of high interest rates does that by trying to slow the economy and hurting prices for investments. The Fed's main interest rate is at its highest level since 2001, and the central bank indicated the previous week that it may cut interest rates next year by less than it earlier expected. The data cuts both ways within this model. Friday's economic data showed that not only was inflation a touch cooler than expected in August, so was growth in spending by US consumers, which can be a positive for inflation because it means not as many dollars are pouring into purchases and that in turn could give companies less encouragement to raise prices further — but it may also dent what has been a big driver keeping the US economy out of a recession.



---


# US Treasury Yields And Fed Rate Expectations In October 2023

The mechanism linking data to yields to stocks ran in both directions during October 2023. On 4 October, the yield on the 10-year Treasury, the centrepiece of the bond market, pulled back from its highest level since 2007, down to 4.73 per cent from 4.80 per cent late on the Tuesday, with shorter- and longer-term yields also easing to allow more oxygen for the stock market. Yields fell following reports indicating a slowing US economy, the first suggesting that hiring by employers outside the government was much weaker than expected; on Wall Street that is currently good news because a cooling job market could mean less upward pressure on inflation, which in turn could convince the Federal Reserve to take it easier on interest rates. After already raising its main interest rate to the highest level since 2001, the Fed had indicated it may keep its overnight rate higher next year than earlier expected, and Treasury yields had correspondingly snapped higher as traders accept a new normal of high rates for longer; the Fed pays particular attention to the job market because too much strength there could drive wages much higher, which it fears could keep inflation well above its target of 2 per cent.

By 12 October the same mechanism was running the other way. The stock market has largely been taking its cue from the bond market recently, and weak results announced in the afternoon for an auction of 30-year Treasury bonds sent yields of all kinds higher; higher yields can knock down prices for stocks and slow the economy by making borrowing more expensive. Yields had already been rising in the morning after a report showing consumer-level inflation a touch higher than economists expected, raising worries about the Fed keeping its main interest rate high for a long time as it tries to undercut inflation by knocking down investment prices and slowing the economy. The report also had encouraging nuggets: after ignoring prices for food and fuel, which Fed officials see as a better predictor of where inflation is heading, prices consumers paid were in line with expectations and continued to decelerate from earlier months. A second report said slightly fewer US workers than expected applied for unemployment benefits, indicating a job market with few lay-offs and therefore strength for the overall economy, though it could also add fuel to upward pressure on inflation. After the reports the 10-year Treasury yield rose to 4.7 per cent from 4.56 per cent late Wednesday, and the two-year Treasury yield, which more closely tracks expectations for the Fed, climbed to 5.06 per cent from 4.99 per cent, with yields still down slightly for the week after regressing from more-than-decade highs following speeches that investors saw as hints the Fed may not raise its main overnight rate further. The big jump for the 10-year yield since the summer has pulled mortgage rates to their highest levels since the turn of the millennium, and such moves could slow the economy without requiring more Fed hikes; Seema Shah, chief global strategist at Principal Asset Management, said nothing in Thursday's inflation report should sway the Fed one way or the other on what it will do on 1 November, calling the data "reassuringly uneventful".



---


# Australian Market Resilience And The Range-Bound Reading

Novus Capital senior client adviser Gary Glover argued that the Australian sharemarket was surprisingly resilient following a negative lead from Wall Street and the latest inflation data, with markets starting to wake up to the fact that interest rates could stay higher for longer. His ground was the mismatch between the overseas move and the local one: "Considering the damage overnight in the US, Australian markets held on pretty well. I thought it would be a bigger down day across the board."

Glover characterised the market as volatile but quite range-bound, drawing an analogy to previous periods of high inflation in the 1940s and 1970s. The Wall Street lead he referred to was severe: Wall Street's ugly September got even worse on Tuesday as a sharp drop for stocks brought them back to where they were in June, with the S&P 500 tumbling 1.5 per cent for its fifth loss in the last six days, the Dow Jones dropping 1.1 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite losing 1.6 per cent.

qid: After The Independent - Life and Style reported on 2023-10-01 that internet sleep tips and tricks are not guaranteed to work, did FOX News - Health suggest on 2023-12-06 that Time-restricted eating, as a specific approach, could improve the quality of sleep, indicating a potential agreement or disagreement with the effectiveness of internet-advised sleep interventions?
context:
# The DIY Sleep Hacks Insomniacs Report Trying

The Independent's October 2023 report on insomniacs catalogues the remedies people actually use: lavender oil, eating kiwis, masturbation — the days of counting sheep long gone. Jennifer Aniston's top tip for battling insomnia is to "sleep with my phone at least five feet away from me," while Martha Stewart recommends focusing on your breathing; in her 1973 feminist novel Fear of Flying, Erica Jong wrote that sometimes the only way to overcome sleeplessness is to pretend you don't care about nodding off, after which "sleep became piqued, like a rejected lover, and crept up to try to seduce you." The article notes that the internet is littered with tips promising sound sleep, that not all of them are effective and none are foolproof, and that kiwis contain serotonin and antioxidants, which is why they are thought to have sleep-promoting benefits.

Two case histories illustrate the trial-and-error. Social media consultant and mother of two Amy Fieldhouse-Downes began suffering from insomnia after the birth of her second son in 2019 and believes it was rooted in anxiety: "If you Google how to go to sleep, I've probably tried everything on there. Going to bed earlier, going to bed later, meditations that would get cut off by an advert, lavender products, sleep cream, eye masks, Sominex sleep tablets. And I even used it as an excuse to have a few glasses of wine." Only specialised earplugs finally let her rest. Long-time insomniac and video producer Preshita has tried "from drinking chamomile tea to counting backwards from 1,000," and found that showering before bed and keeping her bedroom clutter-free were most effective: "Someone recommended masturbating, and that was another thing that worked."



---


# Realigning The Circadian Clock Through Meal Timing

The goal of the restricted eating is to restore the circadian rhythm, the researchers said, which could help counteract the numerous disruptions that Alzheimer's patients face when it comes to sleep and schedule-related confusion.

Feeding timing is the lever on the clock. "Our study emphasizes the power of feeding timing in aligning the circadian clock and its impact on the brain," said senior study author Paula Desplats, PhD, professor in the Department of Neurosciences at UC San Diego School of Medicine, in a statement to Fox News Digital.

The researchers hope that the public recognizes the importance of the circadian clock in regulating many aspects of health. "Sustaining healthy sleep and eating habits that are more synchronized with the natural environment are vital in a society that is constantly exposed to food, light and shift work," said Desplats.



---


# Sleep School's Impartial Position On The Clock Change's Impact

Against the claim that the clock change is a major disruptor of sleep, a spokesperson for Sleep School — a science-based sleep education and therapy service — told The Independent that the organisation is "impartial" on the extent to which the clocks changing impacts sleep.

The premise it declines to grant is that the timing of the shift is what matters: Sleep School argues instead that the important factors are the duration of time asleep and a consistent schedule.



---


# Translating Time-Restricted Eating Into Human Alzheimer's Trials

The researchers hypothesize that time-restricted eating will carry over from mice to people, and they hope that these findings will lead to human trials; the goal is to obtain funding to start a pilot study of patients next year, which is the test that would confirm or disconfirm the proposition.

The reason they expect it to translate is practical rather than mechanistic. "Accessible interventions like this have great translational potential, as they are available and are usually very well-tolerated," Desplats said.

The proposition is stated in conditional terms, and it identifies the population where the payoff would be largest: "This may have special importance for the elderly, as time-restricted eating does not require limitation in calories or change in the diet, but may offer important benefits ranging from metabolic and sleep regulation to potential cognitive improvement."



---


# The Clock Change, Circadian Disruption And Immunity

The health case against the clock change runs through sleep: moving off daylight saving time interferes with the natural circadian rhythm, the 24-hour biological cycle influenced by morning light and evening darkness, and research shows that even a small reduction in sleep affects the immune system — which matters because a good night's sleep during the winter months is essential protection against the seasonal increase in colds and flu.

Giulia Guerrini, lead pharmacist of the digital pharmacy Medino, sets out the grounds and the practical implication. "It's hard to understate the importance of a good night's sleep," she says. "Having too much or too little sleep can have adverse side effects, so you should aim to get between seven and eight hours of sleep as consistently as possible." She names the clock change as a leading disruptor: "One of the biggest disruptors to our sleep is when UK clocks go forward one hour at 1am on the last Sunday in March and go back one hour at 2am on the last Sunday in October, which is rapidly approaching on 30 October." Her advice follows from the premise that consistency matters most: "One of the most important aspects of a healthy sleep schedule is waking up around the same time each morning, so try to limit yourself to a one-hour window if you need to adjust when you get up in the morning and when you go to sleep at night. One hour sounds like an insignificant amount of time, but it can completely throw our circadian rhythm, or more simply known as internal clock, off balance."



---


# The UC San Diego Time-Restricted Feeding Study In Alzheimer's Mice

Participating in intermittent, time-restricted fasting could lead to a reduced risk of cognitive deterioration, a study published in the journal Cell Metabolism suggests: researchers at University of California San Diego School of Medicine adjusted the feeding schedule of certain groups of mice so that they only ate within six-hour windows each day, which the researchers noted would be equivalent to 14 hours of fasting for humans.

The framing question was about timing rather than content -- it has been proven that what people eat can help prevent or slow Alzheimer's disease, but the study asked about when they eat.

Compared to a control group of mice that ate on demand, the fasting mice showed improvements in memory, were less hyperactive in the evenings and had fewer sleep disruptions. They also were shown to have less buildup of amyloid proteins in the brain, which is a hallmark of Alzheimer's disease.

The size of the effect exceeded what the team expected. "We were hopeful to see some improvements in pathology, but did not expect such profound effects in reducing plaques and inflammation and improving memory," a study author said. "The effects of time-restricted feeding on lower amyloid pathology were also measurable in blood using markers found in the clinic, which was another important finding."



---


# Clocks Going Back And The Drop In Heart Attacks

Not everyone is convinced by the case against the autumn clock change. Charlie Morley, author of Wake Up to Sleep, attacks the premise that putting the clocks back is harmful, citing a 2014 study by the College of Cardiology which reported a significant drop in heart attacks in the 24 hours immediately following the change.

"Fascinatingly, each year when the clocks go back for Daylight Saving and 1.6 billion people across 70 countries gain an extra hour in bed, there is a 21 per cent decrease in heart attacks the next day," he says. "There's also a big drop in suicides and car crashes worldwide. That all adds up to tens of thousands of fewer deaths around the world from just one extra hour of sleep." The claim directly contradicts the road-safety and mental-health premises used by abolition campaigners, attributing the benefit to the extra hour of sleep the change delivers.



---


# Insomnia: Definition And Prevalence

Insomnia is a sleep disorder characterised either by difficulty falling asleep or by difficulty staying asleep, to such an extent that it disturbs the sufferer's ability to function during the day — the daytime impairment being the criterion that separates it from ordinary poor sleep. Globally, an estimated 10 per cent of adults meet the criteria for insomnia, and millions struggle with it in the UK alone.

The risk is unevenly distributed by sex: studies have found women are 40 per cent more likely to be affected than men. Sleep therapist Dr Lindsay Browning locates the onset of that gap after puberty: "This sex difference in insomnia emerges after puberty, suggesting that hormonal differences such as menstruation, pregnancy and menopause may be the cause of this increased risk in women." Symptoms are also persistent — a longitudinal study conducted in the UK found that 69 per cent of respondents affected by the disorder at the start of the study still had insomnia 12 months later.



---


# UK Clock Change Dates For 2023 And 2024

The UK clocks went backwards one hour at 2am on Sunday 29 October 2023, giving an extra hour in bed as the country prepared for the colder months when the sun sets earlier and the days get significantly shorter. "Winter is coming," as The Independent put it on 24 October 2023.

The clocks were not due to go forward again until Sunday 31 March 2024.

qid: Was there inconsistency in the TechCrunch report on the Google antitrust case published after November 5, 2023, or in the TechCrunch report on the class action antitrust suit against Google in reporting Google's anticompetitive behavior?
context:
# The U.S. Justice Department's Parallel Antitrust Suits Against Google

The Helena World Chronicle class action arrives alongside the filing of the U.S. Justice Department's lawsuit against Google for monopolizing digital ad technologies, and the complaint also references the Justice Department's 2020 civil antitrust suit over search and search advertising.

The two government cases concern different markets: search and search advertising in the 2020 suit are distinct from the digital ad technologies at issue in the more recent one.



---


# Helena World Chronicle's Class Action Antitrust Suit Against Google

A class action lawsuit filed in the week of 15 December 2023 in the U.S. District Court in D.C. accuses Google and parent company Alphabet of anticompetitive behavior in violation of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act and others, on behalf of news publishers. The case was filed by Arkansas-based publisher Helena World Chronicle, which argues that Google "siphons off" news publishers' content, their readers and their ad revenue through anticompetitive means, and it specifically cites new AI technologies such as Google's Search Generative Experience (SGE) and the Bard AI chatbot as worsening the problem.

Helena World Chronicle owns and publishes two weekly newspapers in Arkansas. In the complaint it argues that Google is "starving the free press" by sharing publishers' content on Google, losing them "billions of dollars."

Beyond damages, the suit asks for an injunction that would require Google to obtain consent from publishers before using their website data to train its general artificial intelligence products, including Google's own and those of rivals. It also asks that publishers who opt out of SGE still be allowed to show up in Google search results, among other things.

The law firm handling the case is Hausfeld, whose announcement states that "the anticompetitive effects of Google's scheme cause profound harm to competition, to consumers, to labor, and to a democratic free press," and that "Plaintiff Helena World Chronicle, LLC invokes the Sherman Act and Clayton Act to seek class-wide monetary and injunctive relief to restore and ensure competition for digital news and reference publishing and set up guardrails to preserve a free marketplace of ideas in the new era of artificial intelligence."



---


# Google's Parallel Antitrust Proceedings In Late 2023

As of mid-November 2023, Google was fighting antitrust on more than one front at once. The Epic Games case was not its only antitrust case in trial: Google had settled a separate antitrust lawsuit with dating site Match Group the week before November 13, and on November 6 it went to trial with Fortnite maker Epic Games, which hoped to prove that Google engages in anticompetitive behavior with regard to its Android app store, Google Play, and its commission structure. Separately, Google was involved in an antitrust lawsuit with the Department of Justice over its alleged search monopoly.

The Epic case had shed co-plaintiffs on its way to trial. Epic's lawsuit originally involved Match and several U.S. attorneys general, but Google reached a settlement with the attorneys general in October 2023 and with Match the week before November 6, so Epic fought the antitrust battle on its own. The lawsuit, held in the U.S. District Court in California's Northern District, would include testimony from a number of Google and Android execs, including CEO Sundar Pichai, and Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, as well as from Apple, Netflix and other Android developers. Epic, meanwhile, had lost its antitrust battle with Apple and was asking the Supreme Court to weigh in.



---


# What A Ruling Against Google Would Mean For Big Tech

A ruling against Google would not stop at Google: the remedy would likely resemble the Microsoft settlement and the outcome would ripple through the other pending Big Tech cases, because enforcers are using this trial to demonstrate that antitrust law can still take on the largest and most powerful companies in the world.

The grounds for the first half of that claim are the available remedies. If the judge rules against Google, the outcome could look a lot like the Microsoft deal, in which the computer company was required to change its behavior and share its APIs with third-party developers, and was also banned from making anticompetitive and exclusive deals with computer manufacturers. Google might likewise end up having to turn over all or most of the data it has collected to other search engines so they can improve their products and attract more users — a remedy scaled to the disparity the DOJ has cited, that Google gets 16 times more data than Bing does everyday.

The grounds for the ripple effect are the cases already queued behind this one. The FTC sued Amazon in September for using anticompetitive and unfair strategies to illegally maintain its monopoly power.
