# Usage-Based Pricing

## Definition

In the corpus, usage-based pricing (also called consumption pricing) is the charging model that VCs discuss as the one whose "trajectory... has organically aligned with the needs of large language models," with OpenAI's per-token API pricing cited as the motivating example, in contrast to conventional periodic SaaS pricing.

## Context

In the corpus the term surfaces in a TechCrunch roundup of venture capitalists discussing how AI startups should charge for AI-powered tooling, prompted directly by "the OpenAI pricing schema based on tokens and usage."
Rick Grinnell of Glasswing Ventures frames usage-based pricing as the model whose "trajectory... has organically aligned with the needs of large language models," because prompt/output sizes and per-user resource consumption vary significantly from one request to the next.
Lisa Calhoun of Valor VC makes the mechanism concrete: companies like OpenAI charge largely "by the token," which she calls "a very different metric than most cloud computing," and notes cost monitoring may be a key aspect of tracking that metric.
The same discussion frames usage-based pricing as one leg of a three-way choice facing AI startups, alongside conventional periodic SaaS pricing and hybrid structures that blend the two.

## Key Characteristics

- **Cost tracks consumption, not time** — charges scale with resource use (e.g., tokens processed) rather than a fixed subscription period.
- **Aligned with LLM cost structure** — the model fits large language models well because compute cost per request varies with prompt/output size and per-user resource utilization; OpenAI itself reportedly spends upward of $700,000 per day on compute, making usage-based allocation a way to recover those variable costs.
- **Unpopular for budgeting** — tying all costs to volume is "generally unpopular with end users," who prefer the predictability of a fixed periodic fee.
- **Not universal across AI products** — applications that don't rely on an LLM as a backbone, and that make no direct token calls to a model provider, tend to gravitate toward conventional periodic SaaS pricing instead.
- **Persists via hybrid structures** — as LLM adoption widens, vendors are expected to combine tiered periodic payments and usage limits for smaller customers with uncapped usage-based tiers for larger enterprises, rather than replacing usage-based pricing outright.
- **Tied to data dependency** — because large language technology remains heavily dependent on continuous data inflow, the source article argues usage-based pricing is unlikely to disappear even as the market matures.

## Background (external)

Outside this corpus, usage-based pricing (also called pay-per-usage) is a general software/SaaS revenue model: charges are calculated from measured consumption — "the number of users, transactions, amount of storage space used, or other metrics" — rather than a flat recurring fee, and Wikipedia notes many buyers favor it because they see themselves as "relatively light users of the software," while it can create revenue uncertainty and added billing overhead for the seller. (Wikipedia, "Software as a service," accessed 2026-09-02: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Software_as_a_service)

# Barbie (Greta Gerwig)

Barbie is Greta Gerwig's film starring Margot Robbie, Ryan Gosling, and Will Ferrell, ranked 9 on Polygon's best movies of 2023 list of 2023-10-07 and available for digital rental/purchase before streaming on Max.

Polygon concedes that any description of the film's big themes — toxic masculinity, how Barbie branding affects young girls, women as playthings, the commodification of girl power — makes it sound preachy and stilted, but says Gerwig and co-writer Noah Baumbach never hold still long enough for viewers to feel they are sitting through a Gender Studies 101 class. They package these ideas into a giddy satire full of bright and winning performances, pointed jokes aimed at Mattel and the corporate world, terrific casting with Issa Rae as President Barbie, Simu Liu as one of many Kens, and Kate McKinnon as Weird Barbie as standouts, and endless cultural gags, plus bright poppy meta-humor musical numbers including Ryan Gosling turning "I'm Just Ken" into 2023's top movie anthem.

Critic Tasha Robinson calls it perky, playful, and deceptively caustic, one of just a few films — like 1995's The Brady Bunch Movie and 2007's Enchanted — that gleefully satirize a cultural staple while also treating it with real affection. Margot Robbie makes a perfect Barbie, whether in perky-and-plastic mode or slowly revealing her underlying humanity as fears of death and dying leak into the endless party of Barbieland. There is so much going on in this patter-filled, joke-a-second comedy that it feels like 2023's Everything Everywhere All at Once, right down to the big life messages smuggled into all the goofery — a high-speed joke-fest that does not take Barbie any more seriously than she deserves but does pay solemn homage to all the ways, positive and negative, that Barbie fandom makes people feel.

# Banking-as-a-Service

## Definition

Banking-as-a-service (BaaS) is the label TechCrunch's coverage applies to platforms — Synapse and QI Tech — that let banks and fintech companies build financial services on top of them, rather than platforms that serve end customers as a bank would.

## Context

The corpus surfaces the term through two TechCrunch items: Synapse, covered in the fintech newsletter The Interchange as a San Francisco–based company whose platform "enables banks and fintech companies to easily develop financial services," and QI Tech, covered in the general Startups Weekly newsletter as a Brazilian "banking-as-a-service platform" that raised a large Series B.

Both appear as fintech infrastructure providers rather than consumer-facing banks — Synapse sits behind other companies' financial products, and QI Tech's raise is framed as backing for the same kind of platform business in Brazil.

## Key Characteristics

- **Platform, not bank** — the BaaS provider "operates a platform enabling banks and fintech companies to easily develop financial services" rather than serving end customers directly.
- **Infrastructure for others' products** — Synapse's role is to let other banks and fintechs build financial services on top of it, positioning it as embedded infrastructure rather than a retail brand.
- **Investor interest despite volatility** — QI Tech's BaaS platform drew a $200 million Series B, the largest Brazilian raise across all sectors that year, around the same time Synapse laid off 86 people, or about 40% of its staff.
- **Exposure to macro conditions** — an earlier round of Synapse layoffs (18% of its workforce, per a June blog post from CEO Sankaet Pathak) was attributed to "the current macroeconomic conditions" affecting its clients and platforms, indicating BaaS providers' fortunes are tied to the health of the banks/fintechs building on top of them.

## Background (external)

Wikipedia's entry on Banking-as-a-Service defines it more generally: BaaS refers to offering banking products — like deposit accounts, loans, and credit cards — to customers through partnerships with non-bank or non-financial third parties, where the bank handles balance-sheet management (capital, liquidity, credit risk) while the partner, often a fintech, engages the customer directly through its own app, typically connecting to the bank's systems via APIs.

# Embedded Finance

## Definition

In the corpus, embedded finance is the practice a software platform adopts when it integrates financial services and payments directly into its own product surface — exemplified by Rainforest, which "works with software companies to help them embed financial services and payments into their platforms."

## Context

In the corpus the term surfaces through Rainforest, an Atlanta-based startup that "works with software companies to help them embed financial services and payments into their platforms," positioning itself against incumbent processors Fiserv and FIS as well as fintech rival Stripe and its Connect product.
The concept is framed against a counter-claim from a16z general partner Angela Strange, who argued in 2019 that every company would eventually become a fintech; Rainforest's CEO Joshua Silver disagreed, arguing that most software companies do not want to become fintechs and absorb the associated regulatory and compliance burden — they simply want to accept payments and capture the associated revenue.
That disagreement marks the boundary of the concept in the corpus: embedded finance is presented as a narrow slice of financial functionality a software platform adopts, not a full transformation of that platform into a financial institution.

## Key Characteristics

- **Embedding, not becoming** — the software platform integrates financial services and payments into its own product surface; it does not itself become a bank or a fintech.
- **Processor-agnostic competitive layer** — providers enabling embedded finance (Rainforest, Stripe Connect) compete against both legacy processors (Fiserv, FIS) and each other for the same underlying volume.
- **Revenue motive over financial-identity motive** — per the corpus's framing, platforms adopt embedded finance to accept payments and generate revenue, not to take on the regulatory and compliance profile of a fintech.
- **Distinct from the platform's core compliance burden** — because the platform is embedding rather than becoming a financial company, it can avoid the "regulatory and compliance issues" Silver describes as the cost of the alternative "everyone is a fintech" path.

## Background (external)

Outside the corpus, embedded finance is a recognized industry term: Plaid defines it as "the integration of financial services, like payments, lending, or banking services, into non-financial offerings," letting users access financial tools within products they already use (Plaid, "What Is Embedded Finance?", https://plaid.com/resources/fintech/what-is-embedded-finance/, accessed 2026-09-02).

Google plans to push back at Epic's claim that it does not have competition in the app store business — the premise on which Epic's monopoly theory rests. It will point out that not only does the Play Store compete with Apple's App Store, which the Ninth Circuit ruling in the Apple case agreed upon too, but Android also supports competitive app stores like Samsung's Galaxy Store and Amazon's Appstore.

Google's defense denies the premise that Android app stores are a market of their own: "You cannot separate the quality of a phone from the quality of the apps in its app store, and that means Google and Apple compete against each other," began Google lead attorney Glenn Pomerantz. Google's second plank is openness relative to Apple. Epic's claim is that the Android operating system's Google Play Store constitutes an unlawful monopoly, and that Google is separately tying its Google Play payments platform to that store, keeping other potential app payment mechanisms from competing.

The warrant joining that to the legal claim is the competitive-harm chain — no viable rival stores means no fee discipline, which means the "Google Tax" is paid either by developers or passed along to consumers. Epic wants to break up Google's alleged monopoly on Android app stores and payment methods so developers are not stuck paying that tax.

# The ChatGPT Integration Wave, Early 2023

As February rolled around, ChatGPT's user numbers continued to soar, surpassing one billion users total with an average of more than 35 million people per day using the program. The first look at the disruptive potential that generative AI offers came when ChatGPT managed to pass a series of law school exams — albeit by the skin of its digital teeth, Engadget notes.

Microsoft — a major investor in OpenAI which has also baked generative AI capabilities into its own search engine — claims in its EU disinformation Code report that it is taking "a cross product whole of company approach to ensure the responsible implementation of AI."

The report flags Microsoft's "Responsible AI Principles," which it says it developed into a Responsible AI standard v.2, and Information Integrity Principles "to help set baseline standards and guidance across product teams." Microsoft continues: "Recognizing that there is an important role for government, academia and civil society to play in the responsible deployment of AI, we also created a roadmap for the governance of AI across the world as well as creating a vision for the responsible advancement of AI, both inside Microsoft and throughout the world, including specifically in Europe," committing to continue building on these efforts by developing new tools — such as Project Providence with Truepic — and inking partnerships, the examples it gives being the Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity (C2PA) to combat the rise of manipulated or AI created media, EFE Verifica to track false narratives spreading in Spain, Latin America and Spanish-speaking populations, and Reporters Sans Frontières to use their Journalism Trust Initiative dataset in Microsoft products. "These partnerships are part of a larger effort to empower Microsoft users to better understand the information they consume across our platforms and products," it suggests, also citing media literacy campaigns and "cyber-skilling" which it says are "not designed to tell individuals what to believe or how to think; rather, they are about equipping people to think critically and make informed decisions about what information they consume."

On Bing Search, where Microsoft was quick to embed generative AI features — leading to some embarrassing early reviews which demonstrated the tool producing dubious content — the report claims a raft of mitigating measures: applying its AI principles during development and consulting with experts; engaging in pre-launch testing and a limited preview period and phased release; the use of classifiers and metaprompting, defensive search interventions, enhanced reporting functionality, and increased operations and incident response; and updating Bing's terms of use to include a Code of Conduct for users. # COP28 Renewable Energy Commitments And The IEA Outlook

The final texts coming out of COP28 included notable new commitments on clean energy, chief among them a call for the tripling of renewable energy capacity globally by 2030 — something more than 100 countries had already pledged to do while negotiations were taking place the week before.

Leading up to the conference, the world's biggest greenhouse gas polluters, the US and China, committed to working toward that goal together when each country's climate envoys met in California in November. The Verge argued the lack of a clear phase-out plan is a blow to climate action but not a zero sum game: solar and wind power are already cheaper alternatives to coal, oil, and gas in most of the world for meeting new electricity demand, and nearly all of the world's new electricity supply over the next few years is expected to come from renewable and nuclear energy, according to the International Energy Agency. The agency — initially founded to safeguard the world's fuel supply after the 1970s oil crisis — called a global transition to clean energy "unstoppable" earlier in 2023 and forecast that demand for coal, oil, and gas would peak this decade. On that basis, getting cleaner sources of energy online looks inevitable at this point.



---


# The COP28 Final Text's Language On Transitioning Away From Fossil Fuels

Draft language explicitly calling for the phaseout of fossil fuels was stricken from the final text of the agreements brokered at COP28; what the world got instead was a weaker call for "transitioning away from fossil fuels in energy systems, in a just, orderly and equitable manner, accelerating action in this critical decade."

More than 100 countries came to the table pushing for an official agreement to "phase out fossil fuels," which would have addressed a glaring omission in the 2015 Paris accord — an international agreement to stop global warming that never actually mentions coal, oil, or natural gas — but bringing that deal to the finish line required nearly 200 countries to agree on the same language. The final text also calls on countries to work toward "accelerating efforts towards the phase-down of unabated coal power." The Verge notes that every word in that phrase is pretty dirty: coal is the most polluting fossil fuel, one reason it's hard to ignore in a climate agreement, but a commitment to phase down its use is decidedly weaker than one to phase it out, and the wording mirrors a recent letter to participating governments from COP28 president Sultan Ahmed Al Jaber, who is also the CEO of the Abu Dhabi National Oil Company. A landmark United Nations-backed climate report in 2018 found that countries need to cut their emissions nearly in half by 2030 to meet the Paris goals. Before the draft was finalized at the closing plenary, Andreas Sieber, associate director of policy and campaigns at 350.org, said: "This text is a step forward on our path towards phasing out fossil fuels, but is not the historic decision we hoped for … given the overwhelming momentum among countries in support of a renewable energy package and a long overdue fossil fuel phase out, we needed a far more ambitious result."

# The "Unabated" Qualifier As A Fossil Fuel Loophole

The Verge argued that COP28's language about phasing down "unabated" coal carves out a huge loophole for fossil fuels — and that the same is true of the word wherever it is applied, to coal, oil, or gas.

The grounds are what the qualifier permits: it means polluters can continue burning fossil fuels as long as they pair that burning with technologies that capture greenhouse gas emissions. The warrant is that those technologies do not yet do the work the qualifier implies — they are emerging, typically do not capture 100 percent of the emissions, and remain unproven at scale — so an "unabated" commitment allows continued combustion rather than requiring its end.

# The Philippine Climate Resilience Strategy

While price stability and fiscal sustainability are important macroeconomic issues, environmental sustainability is increasingly gaining importance: climate change uncertainties and challenges need to be managed, and both the Philippine government and the private sector are hard-pressed to deliver on their commitments. Despite climate change risks, the Philippines has the opportunity to position itself as a prime destination for foreign investments against climate change, or environmental, social and governance investments. The government calls for embedding resilience, sustainability and nature-based solutions in infrastructure planning and investment to enhance climate resilience, and investments in renewable energy are expected not only to enhance energy security but also to reduce greenhouse gas emissions. From an economic vantage point, GHG emissions are economic "bads" and a cause of inefficiency because they get over-produced; their effects go beyond national borders, and while the Philippines contributes minimally to global GHG emissions, the World Risk Index 2022 report identifies the Philippines as the most disaster-prone country in the world.

The government's stated 2028 outcomes are three: that climate and disaster risk resilience of communities and institutions will increase; that ecosystem resilience will be enhanced; and that a low-carbon economy transition is enabled. To ensure these are realized, the government is set to safeguard cross-sectoral convergence and implement a comprehensive risk management approach to address the adverse consequences posed by climate change, and it will also promote a green and blue economy coupled with improved governance to guarantee long-term climate and disaster resilience.

Reliance Industries has committed a whopping ₹75,000 crore investment into building a comprehensive green energy and green material ecosystem, having identified green energy as its next growth opportunity as the world moves away from conventional fossil-based energy sources towards cleaner and sustainable ones.

The balance ₹15,000 crore is being invested in partnerships, future technologies and value chain in order to build an integrated renewable energy ecosystem. Reliance has already made several investments in companies working on green energy technologies, such as battery technologies, solar cells and panels, clean mobility solutions and software tools for solar energy.

The argument is that a five-year delay in the net-zero timeline lands directly on individual companies' revenue plans, not just on national targets. The world, on average, is about 1.2 degrees Celsius hotter than it was before the industrial revolution — the scientific fact underpinning the COP28 negotiations.

# Nobel Prize

## Definition

In the corpus, the Nobel Prize is the award administered by the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences for the physics, chemistry, and economics categories, exemplified by the 2023 chemistry prize given to Moungi Bawendi, Louis Brus, and Alexei Ekimov for the discovery and synthesis of quantum dots.
Winners split a cash award of 11 million Swedish kronor (about $1 million), drawn from a bequest left by the prize's creator, Swedish inventor Alfred Nobel.

## Context

In the corpus the term appears centered on the 2023 chemistry prize, awarded to Moungi Bawendi, Louis Brus, and Alexei Ekimov for the discovery and synthesis of quantum dots, announced by the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences in Stockholm on 2023-10-04.
That announcement sat within a week of prizes: the physics prize went to Anne L'Huillier, Pierre Agostini, and Ferenc Krausz on 2023-10-03, and the medicine prize went to Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman on 2023-10-02 for mRNA vaccine research, with literature, peace, and economics prizes following on subsequent weekdays.
The term also surfaces outside the sciences-announcement context: a financial column refers in passing to "Nobel Laureate" Paul Krugman to lend authority to an economics analogy, showing the label is used in the corpus as a general marker of eminence as well as a specific science-prize designation.

## Key Characteristics

- **Administered by the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences** for the physics, chemistry, and economics categories, with nominations solicited a year in advance from thousands of university professors and scholars worldwide, and nominee deliberations kept confidential for 50 years.
- **Committee-driven selection** — a committee for each prize discusses candidates over a series of meetings before presenting proposals to the full academy for a vote.
- **Cash award** — laureates split a prize of 11 million Swedish kronor (about $1 million), funded by Alfred Nobel's bequest.
- **Multi-category, staggered announcements** — physics, chemistry, medicine, literature, peace, and economics prizes are announced on separate weekdays within the same week.
- **Confidentiality can be broken accidentally** — the 2023 chemistry winners were identified by Swedish media hours before the official announcement, after the academy sent an early press release "for still unknown reasons."
- **Used loosely as an honorific outside its own announcements** — commentary elsewhere in the corpus invokes "Nobel Laureate" status (e.g., of economist Paul Krugman) simply to signal authority in an unrelated argument.

## Background (external)

Outside this corpus, the Nobel Prizes are a set of six international awards — physics, chemistry, physiology or medicine, literature, peace, and economic sciences — managed by the Nobel Foundation and funded from Alfred Nobel's bequest, first awarded in 1901 and given annually (with rare exceptions, such as wartime gaps in 1940-1942); the economics prize was added later, in 1968, by Sweden's central bank in Nobel's memory. (Wikipedia, "Nobel Prize," accessed 2026-09-02: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize)

Corpus notes whose source text references this term (evidence-backed, from `term_links.json`):

# The 2023 Nobel Prizes Across Categories

The 2023 chemistry prize sat in a week of announcements. On Tuesday, 2023-10-03, the physics prize went to French-Swedish physicist Anne L'Huillier, French scientist Pierre Agostini and Hungarian-born Ferenc Krausz for producing the first split-second glimpse into the super-fast world of spinning electrons. On Monday, 2023-10-02, Hungarian-American Katalin Karikó and American Drew Weissman won the Nobel Prize in medicine for discoveries that enabled the creation of mRNA vaccines against COVID-19.

The prizes in literature, peace and economics followed, with one announcement every weekday until Monday. The Nobel Prizes carry a cash award of 11 million Swedish kronor ($1 million) from a bequest left by the prize's creator, Swedish inventor Alfred Nobel.



---


# The 2023 Nobel Prize In Chemistry For Quantum Dots

Three scientists won the Nobel Prize in chemistry on Wednesday, 2023-10-04, for their work on quantum dots — tiny particles just a few nanometers in diameter that can release very bright colored light and whose applications in everyday life include electronics and medical imaging.

The laureates are Moungi Bawendi of MIT, Louis Brus of Columbia University, and Alexei Ekimov of Nanocrystals Technology Inc. They were honored for their work with the tiny particles that "have unique properties and now spread their light from television screens and LED lamps," according to the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences, which announced the award in Stockholm.



---


# How The 2023 Chemistry Nobel Laureates Reacted

Moungi Bawendi told the news conference he was "very surprised, sleepy, shocked, unexpected and very honored," and asked about the leak, said he didn't know he'd been made a Nobel laureate until he was called by the academy. Louis Brus, a professor emeritus at Columbia, said he didn't pick up the phone when the early morning call came from the Swedish academy to notify him: "It was ringing during the night, but I didn't answer it because I'm trying to get some sleep, basically," he told The Associated Press. He finally saw the news online when he got up around 6 a.m. "I certainly was not expecting this," Brus said.

Alexei Ekimov is the former chief scientist at Nanocrystals Technology, a company based in New York where he started working in 1999. The Swedish academy credited him with demonstrating in the early 1980s that the size of copper chloride nanoparticles affected the colors in glass. "It was really nice that we got it after 40 years of work," Ekimov told the AP; his first publication on the topic was in 1981.



---


# Reactions to the Quantum Dot Nobel

Researchers welcomed the award: "They're the ones who built the foundation," said Warren Chan, a biomedical engineer and chemist at the University of Toronto in Canada, calling the prize well-deserved. "I'm really happy that the field is getting credit for really changing the world."

Chan and his colleagues found one of the first uses for quantum dots in the 1990s, using them to tag cells in lab experiments. He notes that the Nobel committee does not just look at past impacts of a discovery but also considers the effects it may have in the future, and quantum dots could have a whole medley of uses not yet explored; his own team is now using quantum dots to detect infections such as flu and HIV. "I was absolutely thrilled to see this," said Judith Giordan, president of the American Chemical Society. "We have three people recognized who brought this technology from a dream, a hope, a theoretical construct … all the way through synthesis and manufacture."

# The 2023 Chemistry Nobel for Quantum Dots

The 2023 Nobel Prize in chemistry honours three scientists who discovered and created quantum dots: Moungi Bawendi, a chemist at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) in Cambridge; Louis Brus, a chemist based at Columbia University in New York City; and Alexei Ekimov, a physicist now working at Nanocrystals Technology, Inc., in Briarcliff Manor, N.Y.

The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences announced the honour on October 4, and the trio will split a prize of 11 million Swedish kronor, or about $1 million. The award recognises a peculiar class of matter: typically, matter made of the same kinds of atoms arranged in the same way has the same properties, but tiny specks called quantum dots can contain the same molecules yet have different colours and other qualities depending on their size. The ability to make a whole rainbow of quantum dots simply by tweaking their size makes them highly useful — they light up TV screens and help doctors see inside the body.

# The Nobel Prize Nomination And Selection Procedure

The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences, which awards the physics, chemistry and economics prizes, follows an ordered procedure. First it asks for nominations a year in advance from thousands of university professors and other scholars around the world. Then a committee for each prize discusses candidates in a series of meetings. Finally that committee presents one or more proposals to the full academy for a vote.

The confidentiality rule bounds the whole process: the deliberations, including the names of nominees other than the winners, are kept confidential for 50 years.

Meagan Bellshaw's privacy line of questioning attacked the premise that Apple chose Google because Google had the best product: if Apple genuinely regards Google as bad on privacy, then something other than product quality must explain why Apple gives Google a central place on its platform.

# FTX's Absence Of A Chief Risk Officer

The Verge's trial reporter argued that FTX's lack of a chief risk officer was either evidence of stupidity or a deliberate choice — and, since stupidity was unlikely, that Bankman-Fried probably chose not to hire one because he was worried about what such an officer might find. The grounds are that FTX ran a business in which risk management is structurally central, and the warrant is that any competent operator of such a business knows this, so the omission has to be explained by intent rather than oversight.

The claim about centrality rests on what FTX was. FTX was named as it was because it was a futures exchange, which, to borrow Bloomberg columnist Matt Levine's phrase, "sits between the winners and losers of bets" — meaning FTX could not pay out what it owed the winners unless the losers paid up. Risk officers exist to identify a business's potential risks, monitor them, and mitigate them, and those risks run from reputational to regulatory to financial, to say nothing of the regulatory risks specific to crypto. As the reporter put it after Bankman-Fried's own testimony, risk is an inherent part of a futures exchange, which is even more like a casino than regular cryptocurrency, so not having a risk team when you are any kind of financial anything is certainly a choice — and especially a choice when you go around telling everyone your crypto exchange is very good and safe.

Two things sharpen the argument. # ASPI's Analysis Of TikTok Pixel Data Aggregation Risk

Researchers at the Australian Strategic Policy Institute argue that the danger of TikTok's tracking pixel lies less in the type of data collected — which resembles what US tech giants gather — than in how that data can be aggregated and in who can ultimately reach it.

Jocelinn Kang, a technical specialist at the institute, said data from a tracking pixel could be aggregated across websites, apps and social media platforms, and that pixel tracking could identify users through their "browser fingerprint," a combination of their IP address, browser and system details. The linking gets sharper as identifiers accumulate: "However, when more identifying data such as email and phone number is associated with a user, their web activity can be better linked," Kang said.

Strategic Policy Institute researcher Samantha Hoffman said the data collected by TikTok's pixel was similar to that of US-based tech giants Google and Meta, but that the difference was "the intent." Advertising data had "incredible propaganda value," she said, and the warrant joining that to the risk is state access: "If you think about that, plus the access that TikTok is required to give the Chinese government, that's the problem." She notes TikTok itself made that access explicit — in November 2022 the company changed its privacy policy to state clearly that user data can be accessed by some employees from across the world, including China. # Creator Economy Sustainability And Creator Venture Capital

Writing in TechCrunch's 2023-10-13 startups roundup, the newsletter's author argues that creators getting together to work out how to make the job sustainable makes sense, but that creators raising venture capital does not.

The grounds are the two events reported that week. Amanda reported that VidCon is still kicking, and that for the first time the conference hosted an industry leadership summit where creator economy experts and creators could hash out their grievances with the state of the business and share ideas to make the job of a creator more sustainable. Lauren reported that a former TikTok employee is building a social app for content creators to network and "spill the tea," so creators can help each other out making better, more engaging content. Both are creators pooling knowledge rather than capital.

The warrant joining grounds to claim is an economics argument about returns: it is, in the author's words, "so eye-wateringly hard to make money as a creator" that he would love to see the pitch that convinces a VC to cut a check to a creator with a realistic expectation of a venture-scale return. Venture capital requires venture-scale outcomes, and individual creator economics are held not to reach that scale — which is why the peer-support route is endorsed and the VC route is not. The claim is scoped to creators raising venture capital as individuals; it is stated as the author's own view in a newsletter, not as a survey finding.

# The 1992 World Cup: White Ball, Coloured Kits And South Africa's Return

The 1992 World Cup, held in Australia and New Zealand, saw a number of landmark moments: it was the first tournament in which teams wore coloured kits, and it also introduced the white ball, changes in fielding rules, day/night matches and the inclusion of South Africa in the event for the first time following the end of the Apartheid regime.

Those innovations arrived together in a single edition, which is why the Sporting News treats 1992 as a turning point in the competition's history rather than one isolated rule change.

# The 1987 ODI World Cup Format Change

The 1987 ODI World Cup brought two prime changes in the way the tournament was organised: a shift of venue from England to the Indian subcontinent, and games being played in 50 overs instead of 60.

# The First ODI Cricket World Cup, 1975

England hosted the inaugural ODI World Cup in 1975 and held the event the following three times too, with the West Indies winning the first tournament.

The playing conditions were unlike the modern game: initially the game was played in cricket whites and with a red ball instead of a white ball. Eight teams took part in that inaugural tournament — India, Pakistan, England, Australia, West Indies, New Zealand and a composite team from East Africa and Sri Lanka. Current cricketing powerhouse South Africa was banned at the time from international sport due to its policy of racial segregation under the Apartheid system, and so did not take part in the first ODI World Cup.

The early honours went to two teams. The West Indies won the first tournament and defended the title in the second World Cup in 1979, while India's first taste of glory came when they clinched the trophy in 1983 by defeating the West Indies by 43 runs in the final.

# Scorsese's Late Career Refutes Tarantino's Claim That Directors Do Not Get Better

Polygon's 2023-10-26 piece attacks the premise behind Quentin Tarantino's 2021 defense of his intention to make "just" 10 movies and retire: "I know film history, and from here on in, directors do not get better." The counter is that this view of both artistry and film is squarely at odds with Martin Scorsese's historic body of work.

The specific premise under attack is the claim of inevitable late-career decline. Scorsese had already made his 10th feature-length narrative film by 1986; he is now 80 years old, and his 27th, Killers of the Flower Moon, is a strong argument that directors are still capable of groundbreaking greatness late in life — and, in Scorsese's case, of continued exhilarating experimentation and discovery.

Polygon presses the point further: since the year 2000, Scorsese has curated a 23-year career within a career, and the quality and variety of his films have come not in spite of his age and experience but because of it. His movies have never been more relevant than in the past two decades, and with each subsequent release, as his career winds down, critical appreciation for him grows — Scorsese worship being the one remaining form of gerontocracy America is perfectly content with, and with good reason.

The mechanism the piece identifies is autonomy. This century Scorsese has zigged and zagged as always, but because he is following his own varied interests rather than moving from compromise to compromise as he once had to in order to keep working: an artist who spent the first 30 years of his career desperate for autonomy finally got it, and now takes full advantage — telling difficult stories, setting his own mega-budgets, and demanding every minute of run time he feels each picture demands. He has used that autonomy to revisit his work and revise the record, creating great new films and adding crucial addendums to past work while blazing new trails and adding layers to his style. Remarkably, the control that eluded him when he was younger has made his films more consistently collaborative and creative, more fluid and alive than he was often allowed to be before the 2000s, with the earned confidence of an artist who knows he will find something great in post. # What SEO Is, And Why People Hate It

Search engine optimization is the practice of telling the algorithm whatever it needs to hear for a site to appear as high up as possible in search results, leveraging Google's supposed objectivity to lure people in and then, usually, show them some kind of advertising — a business model. It is less straightforward than buying the advertising space labeled "Sponsored" above organic search results; it is more like the Wizard of Oz projecting his voice to magnify his authority.

The discriminating feature is that SEO borrows credibility from a system users believe is neutral. Over time SEO techniques have spread and become insidious, such that googling anything can now feel like looking up "sneaker" in the dictionary and finding a definition that sounds both incorrect and suspiciously as though it were written by someone promoting Nike ("footwear that allows you to just do it!"). Perhaps this is why nearly everyone hates SEO and the people who do it for a living: the practice seems to have successfully destroyed the illusion that the internet was ever about anything other than selling stuff.

The reputational context in 2023 is a broad unhappiness with finding information online, which for almost everyone means the quality of Google Search results. Users call the links that come back "absolutely unusable," "garbage," and "a nightmare" because "a lot of the content doesn't feel authentic." Some blame Google itself, asserting that an all-powerful, all-seeing, trillion-dollar corporation with a 90 percent market share for online search is corrupting our access to the truth; others blame the SEO practitioners.

The stereotype of the practitioner is a hustler: a content goblin willing to eschew rules, morals, and good taste in exchange for eyeballs and mountains of cash — a nihilist in it for the thrills, a prankster gleeful about getting away with something. The writer's own admitted starting position was that a bunch of megalomaniacal jerks were degrading our collective sense of reality because they wanted to buy Lamborghinis and prove they could vanquish the almighty algorithm — which, technically, constitutes many algorithms, but we think of as a single force.

# The 2023 Chemistry Nobel for Quantum Dots

The 2023 Nobel Prize in chemistry honours three scientists who discovered and created quantum dots: Moungi Bawendi, a chemist at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) in Cambridge; Louis Brus, a chemist based at Columbia University in New York City; and Alexei Ekimov, a physicist now working at Nanocrystals Technology, Inc., in Briarcliff Manor, N.Y.

The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences announced the honour on October 4, and the trio will split a prize of 11 million Swedish kronor, or about $1 million. The award recognises a peculiar class of matter: typically, matter made of the same kinds of atoms arranged in the same way has the same properties, but tiny specks called quantum dots can contain the same molecules yet have different colours and other qualities depending on their size. The ability to make a whole rainbow of quantum dots simply by tweaking their size makes them highly useful — they light up TV screens and help doctors see inside the body.



---


# Reactions to the Quantum Dot Nobel

Researchers welcomed the award: "They're the ones who built the foundation," said Warren Chan, a biomedical engineer and chemist at the University of Toronto in Canada, calling the prize well-deserved. "I'm really happy that the field is getting credit for really changing the world."

Chan and his colleagues found one of the first uses for quantum dots in the 1990s, using them to tag cells in lab experiments. He notes that the Nobel committee does not just look at past impacts of a discovery but also considers the effects it may have in the future, and quantum dots could have a whole medley of uses not yet explored; his own team is now using quantum dots to detect infections such as flu and HIV. "I was absolutely thrilled to see this," said Judith Giordan, president of the American Chemical Society. "We have three people recognized who brought this technology from a dream, a hope, a theoretical construct … all the way through synthesis and manufacture."



---


# Bawendi's Controlled Quantum Dot Synthesis

A decade after Ekimov and Brus's discoveries, Moungi Bawendi devised a method to stop the growth of tiny crystals in a solution when they reached a desired size: he first injected chemicals into a solution that instantly formed tiny crystals, then tweaked the temperature of the solution to halt the crystals' growth.

The precondition for the method was a research need rather than a product goal. Bawendi started working on quantum dots after meeting Brus, when the two worked at Nokia Bell Labs, headquartered in Murray Hill, N.J., where researchers needed high-quality quantum dots to study the physics of nanoparticles. "It wasn't because I wanted to make the best quantum dots possible for application," Bawendi said. "It was because we needed to make the best possible quantum dots to study them." It took years of trial and error to work out the method. "I'm deeply honored and surprised and shocked by the announcement this morning," Bawendi said on October 4 at an MIT news conference. "I'm especially honored to share this with Lou Brus," he said of his mentor. "I tried to emulate his scholarship and his mentoring style as a professor myself when I came to MIT."

# Rate My Professors Harassment Of Janani Umamaheswar

In the winter of 2019, Janani Umamaheswar, then an assistant professor in sociology at Southern Connecticut State University, began noticing strange remarks on her Rate My Professors profile, where most comments had previously been positive or at least constructive. One review, rated "awful" with a score of one out of five, read: "Textbook only discusses crimes of the poor. I get discriminated against all semester. I felt like I was in Germany in the 1930s with my grandparents." More followed into early 2020, including "This is the worst professor I've ever had," a claim she had been dishonest about going to school in Canada (she completed her bachelor's and master's at the University of Toronto), an allegation that she had a "tyrannical authoritarian ideology" and practised "discrimination against students with prior substance abuse histories," and one reading: "Emailed me a bribe offering a grade boost if I did her a favor of attending a meeting she was hosting. I did not respond because accepting a bribe is illegal." She had never bribed any students; someone was inventing specific defamatory accusations about her behavior.

Because Rate My Professors users post anonymously, there is no surefire way to verify or screen the people who write reviews, and Umamaheswar and her husband Alex Sinha — then a law professor at Quinnipiac University — could not work out who was posting. He suggested she contact the site to remove the comments, and they assumed the company complied, but a short time later comments in the same tone resurfaced under a new class code; she reached out again, weeks passed, and more posts emerged. # Initial Public Offering (IPO)

## Definition

In the corpus, IPO — used interchangeably with "going public" — names the transition several companies undergo or are preparing to undergo onto a public stock exchange: cybersecurity startup IronNet is reported to have "fail[ed] to gain traction after going public in August 2021," and pre-IPO funds are described as investing in "mature companies preparing to list on the stock exchange" ahead of that transition.

## Context

The corpus uses IPO/going-public language across several unrelated stories, which is what makes the term a recurring hinge concept rather than a one-off mention: cybersecurity startup IronNet "fail[ed] to gain traction after going public in August 2021," after which its stock price kept declining from an initial post-IPO spike; Swedish fintech Klarna is described as "taking steps toward an eventual IPO," restructuring into a U.K. holding company as "an important early step in its plans for an initial public offering"; and logistics company Flexport's ousted CEO Dave Clark counted among his goals helping prepare the company for an IPO, with Flexport having discussed an IPO in a two- to three-year window. The term also appears in Indian investing coverage, where late-stage "pre-IPO funds" let investors buy into "mature companies preparing to list on the stock exchange" before their public debut, distinct from "publicly traded equity" that Alternative Investment Funds (AIFs) are said to be uncorrelated with. Once a company is public, its "stock price" becomes a live signal of investor sentiment, as seen in the Rogers family's boardroom conflict driving down Rogers Communications' stock price, and in Coinbase — "the only one that's publicly traded in the U.S." among major crypto exchanges — seeing its shares swing on Binance/FTX-related news.

## Key Characteristics

- **Transition event** — the corpus marks the same before/after line with "going public" and "publicly traded," as with IronNet going "public in August 2021" and Coinbase being "the only one that's publicly traded in the U.S." among major crypto exchanges.
- **Preceded by preparation** — companies undertake preparatory steps beforehand, such as Klarna's legal-entity restructuring into a U.K. holding company, or Flexport's Dave Clark working toward the goal of helping the company get "IPO ready" within a two- to three-year window it had discussed.
- **Followed by market scrutiny** — once public, a company's stock price becomes a running scoreboard, as with IronNet's post-IPO stock decline and Rogers Communications' stock price reacting to boardroom disputes.
- **Investment-fund target** — "pre-IPO" or late-stage private equity funds exist specifically to let investors buy into companies before this transition, aiming to capture value at listing.
- **Not guaranteed to sustain value** — IronNet's case in the corpus shows an initial post-IPO price spike can be followed by a steep, sustained decline.

## Background (external)

Outside this corpus, an IPO is a company's first sale of stock to the public: a privately held company becomes a public company by selling shares to institutional and retail investors, typically with investment banks acting as underwriters who arrange for the shares to be listed on a stock exchange, a process also known as "floating" or "going public." (Wikipedia, "Initial public offering," accessed 2026-09-02: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Initial_public_offering)

# AIF Sub-Fund Strategies Available To HNIs

Alternative Investment Funds present a family of sub-strategies that are available only to HNIs, each defined by the stage or credit segment it targets. Start-up funds serve angel investors looking to invest in ideas with the potential to grow into full-scale businesses, providing a platform that brings promoters and investors together; these funds handpick start-ups after extensive due diligence and build a portfolio with the potential to multiply capital several times. Mid-stage private equity funds suit investors hesitant to take start-up risk, letting them invest in companies in the middle of their evolution cycle whose business valuations grow exponentially as they mature and enter the late-stage or pre-IPO stage. Late-stage or pre-IPO funds allow investment in mature companies preparing to list, building a portfolio of companies about to go public and planning to exit after their anticipated blockbuster listing, which can magnify returns in a relatively short period; such funds gained immense popularity after the 2020 stock market rally that witnessed the blockbuster listing of some popular B2C IPOs.

The remaining strategies are defined by instrument rather than stage. Hedge funds invest in both publicly traded and unlisted stocks and manage money using long-only and long-short strategies, the latter allowed to use complex derivative techniques to hedge the portfolio; long-short funds try to optimise returns in every market situation and hence tend to rise and fall less than their peers, so investors with stock and mutual fund portfolios can diversify with them to reduce volatility. Performing credit funds lend to operating companies that cannot raise funds from banks and NBFCs due to their size or credit ratings, specialising in credit risk assessment and offering credit at relatively higher rates after thorough due diligence, which produces higher overall returns than AAA/AA-rated bonds and appeals to investors seeking more from their fixed-income portfolio. Infrastructure funds invest in long-term infrastructure assets owned by PSUs or private companies, such as roads, power transmission lines and solar power plants; most such projects provide essential societal services and thus have intrinsic value, and their cashflows come as annuities backed by Central and State governments, which lowers future cash-flow risk significantly, gives the fund a yield characteristic through regular distributions, and can add capital gains when assets are sold to another fund or infrastructure trust at maturity. Venture debt funds serve start-up promoters who want to raise money without selling equity and cannot approach banks and mutual funds, providing credit to start-ups at high rates, with the higher returns and risk management appealing to risk-taking, yield-hungry investors. The list is explicitly not exhaustive: many more options exist, such as special situation funds and real estate yield funds.

# Ray-Ban Meta: Design And Discreetness

The Verge's reviewer found the Ray-Ban Meta glasses both good-looking and genuinely inconspicuous — in many ways, she wrote, they feel like they belong in a spy movie, since James Bond always looks good and the gadgets Q gives him are discreet. The reason design matters is blunt: you will never wear a pair of smart glasses if they make you look like a low-rent Warby Parker model, and aside from the original Bose Frames she had never liked the way she looked in smart glasses before. That these are Ray-Bans and come in more styles than typical smart glasses is what changed it — while Wayfarers are considered universally flattering, rounder frames look better on her, and instead of the usual tortoiseshell or black she could pick a round, transparent blue frame with pink lenses, whose colors she wished were more noticeable in darker lighting but which popped in sunlight. She wore them dolled up for a wedding, in functional but hideous running gear, in sweatpants, and with leather jackets: they go with everything.

The discreetness has a specific shape. No one will know you are wearing tech on your face unless you walk around saying "Hey Meta" at the top of your lungs; nobody knew she was listening to EXO's EXIST album on her commute. There is some faint audio leakage at full volume, but full volume is only necessary to block out the squeaky rails of the New York City subway, and fellow commuters likely will not notice because they have AirPods in or the ambient noise is louder. More troubling, no one batted an eye whenever she took photos and videos in public or private areas. The capture button sits on the top of the right arm.

She compared the experience to Eggsy in Kingsman: The Golden Circle, who takes a call through his glasses during an important dinner and appears to everyone else as a dapper gent in snazzy frames while hearing and seeing things they cannot. # SEO Conference Culture And Its Excesses

After years of being friends online, the SEOs were eager to let loose in person, giving off what Forrester described as "that vibe of a lot of young people with access to a lot of money. And it was like, no expenses spared in New York City."

For Forrester it was the start of a long career of keynote presentations and consummate schmoozing — Clay, the father of SEO, described him as "a cruise director" on the SS SEO. The circuit has treated him well: he has attended events in Napa, Hawaii, and Barbados among many others, as well as "an infinite number of private dinners and these types of things in every city you can think of, at the most lavish restaurants," he said. "I've lost track of how many Michelin-starred meals I've had, 'cause it's now in the dozens, from my time in this industry. And I'm not going to say no to the dinner that everyone's going to, that one company is sponsoring because it's a thank you to everybody who contributed to, whatever it was, you know? And you go and everybody has a good time. You talk about the industry, and that's it. And it becomes the stuff of legends."

Over the years he has seen it all, remembering "walking into hotel rooms and it's two o'clock in the morning, there's drugs and alcohol and everything everywhere, and there's a party going on." He marveled at the audacity of his fellow SEOs: "Somebody showed up and brought her Aston Martin to a conference and parked it at the front door. Immediately got a parking ticket." When he suggested she relocate the car before it got towed, she said she would just move it to the next parking spot and get another ticket — "It's cheaper for me to leave the car parked out front and use it as a way to start conversations with potential clients than it is for me to rent a suite at the hotel and get people to go to the suite to have the same conversation." Then she offered him a joyride around Seattle, and obviously he said yes.

Representing a search engine changed the rules. Once he represented Bing, Forrester more or less stopped drinking at conferences, as had long been the case for his counterpart at Google, an engineer named Matt Cutts, who helped build and then ran the company's web spam team before stepping back in 2014 and leaving in 2016.

# The COP28 Final Text's Language On Transitioning Away From Fossil Fuels

Draft language explicitly calling for the phaseout of fossil fuels was stricken from the final text of the agreements brokered at COP28; what the world got instead was a weaker call for "transitioning away from fossil fuels in energy systems, in a just, orderly and equitable manner, accelerating action in this critical decade."

More than 100 countries came to the table pushing for an official agreement to "phase out fossil fuels," which would have addressed a glaring omission in the 2015 Paris accord — an international agreement to stop global warming that never actually mentions coal, oil, or natural gas — but bringing that deal to the finish line required nearly 200 countries to agree on the same language. The final text also calls on countries to work toward "accelerating efforts towards the phase-down of unabated coal power." The Verge notes that every word in that phrase is pretty dirty: coal is the most polluting fossil fuel, one reason it's hard to ignore in a climate agreement, but a commitment to phase down its use is decidedly weaker than one to phase it out, and the wording mirrors a recent letter to participating governments from COP28 president Sultan Ahmed Al Jaber, who is also the CEO of the Abu Dhabi National Oil Company. A landmark United Nations-backed climate report in 2018 found that countries need to cut their emissions nearly in half by 2030 to meet the Paris goals. Before the draft was finalized at the closing plenary, Andreas Sieber, associate director of policy and campaigns at 350.org, said: "This text is a step forward on our path towards phasing out fossil fuels, but is not the historic decision we hoped for … given the overwhelming momentum among countries in support of a renewable energy package and a long overdue fossil fuel phase out, we needed a far more ambitious result."

Given the colossal stakes, which were at least recently taken seriously, the author asks whether that is really asking too much.

Even sellers sympathetic to regulating Amazon question the premise that the FTC's highlighted issues are the ones that would make the seller and consumer experience better. He was particularly puzzled by the claim that Amazon is coercive in how it encourages sellers to use Fulfillment by Amazon (FBA), saying many sellers "love FBA" for its compelling value in price and two-day shipping; for many, using FBA does not feel like a requirement, but they believe it will make their businesses "easier and more effective." # Dave Clark's Hiring And Flexport's IPO Plan

Clark arrived at Flexport in 2022 as the apparently perfect hire for a tech startup trying to disrupt the age-old logistics industry — he had built Amazon's logistics unit into a juggernaut that rivalled carriers like UPS and FedEx — and among his goals was to help Petersen prepare Flexport for an IPO, something the company had discussed doing within a two- to three-year window.

Since 2021 Petersen had been seeking a successor for then-operating chief Sanne Manders, in part to address what several ex-employees described as lingering issues with the company's troubled billing processes; fixing that was Clark's job. Petersen and Clark worked together as co-CEOs for the first six months, and in March Petersen transitioned to executive chairman — an arrangement meant to free Petersen up to do what he loved, "getting beers with customers," in the words of two former Flexport employees, while Clark, a self-described "builder at heart," was at the wheel. "There's a perfect complement of skill sets," Petersen told Forbes in June 2022. "Mine are much more creative, zero-to-one founder time, and Dave is the supreme executor and a legend in the supply chain world." Buying Deliverr was meant to be the first step in turning Flexport into a more full-scale logistics service. Shopify had acquired Deliverr in May 2022 for $2.1 billion, but the e-commerce software company was being hammered by Wall Street as its Covid pandemic pop faded, and by January 2023 CEO Tobias Lutke knew he needed to get rid of it; around that time Lutke first approached Petersen to float a deal, and Petersen told Clark he should engage with Shopify's team. Initial talks fell apart but resumed when Flexport executives learned Shopify was about to execute deep cost cuts and was eager to sell. Clark and Petersen flew to Miami to meet Shopify's leadership, and as a transaction neared, Clark — who had a reputation as a deft negotiator — got Shopify, already an investor in Flexport, to sweeten it with $40 million in cash and the framework for a $260 million convertible note that could help Flexport on its path to an IPO, according to an internal document analyzing the deal. The sale would be announced alongside Shopify's first-quarter earnings report on May 4. "We did not change the terms of a deal or rush it just to have it line up with an earnings call," Shopify said in a statement, adding that with Flexport "we are tightly mission-aligned to ensure the success of our merchants, which is why we chose to deepen our partnership with them earlier this year." The night before the announcement, Petersen appeared at a "Tech Talk" at Flexport's Bellevue, Washington office to pitch the "Flexport vision" to hundreds of people; asked whether Flexport would ever get into last-mile logistics, he paused, glanced at his watch, and said to keep an eye on the morning news, according to an employee who witnessed the exchange and a person told independently. The comment alarmed Clark and Flexport executives, who were concerned Petersen had disclosed material nonpublic information about a publicly traded company. Petersen did not respond to calls or messages from CNBC, the company declined to make him available for an interview, and a Flexport spokesperson did not respond to CNBC's question about whether Petersen was aware of concerns about his statement.

# Flexport Versus Amazon In End-To-End Supply Chain Services

On Sept. 12, almost a week after Clark was fired, Flexport executives convened in Seattle to launch an end-to-end supply chain service allowing sellers to move products from factories to customers' doorsteps through integrations with major online marketplaces — and earlier that same day, just up the street, Amazon had unveiled a strikingly similar service in front of approximately 2,200 attendees at its annual Accelerate seller conference.

The project was spearheaded by Parisa Sadrzadeh, an executive vice president at Flexport whom Clark had poached from Amazon's logistics unit. Flexport had planned a booth at Accelerate but was told it could not be an exhibitor, which some staffers suspected was due to the competing supply chain products; Amazon said Flexport had discussed securing exhibit space months earlier but did not meet all the requirements to participate, and that its launch was not mentioned in those conversations. Flexport's own event was underwhelming: in a conference room about 50 people watched Sadrzadeh debut the service and then introduce Petersen, who spoke for roughly 20 minutes, according to Burak Yolga, co-founder of a digital freight forwarding company who attended. # DSA Enforcement Powers And Penalties

The European Commission is responsible for enforcing the DSA on larger platforms such as X, which was designated a very large online platform (VLOP) under the DSA back in April 2023. Confirmed breaches of the online governance regime can face a range of major sanctions, including fines of up to 6% of global annual turnover.

The Commission's powers are not limited to fines. The EU can also apply interim measures where it believes there is a risk of serious harm for users, and may even seek to have access to infringing services temporarily blocked. Its 18 December 2023 announcement was careful to caveat the development by affirming that no conclusions had yet been reached.

There is also no confirmed timeline for the probe to conclude. But the fact of its being opened means other tools are put within reach of regulators and could be applied if the EU sees the need to act quickly — such as the interim measures above — so the Commission's official scrutiny of X could have real world implications for how the platform operates sooner rather than later.

# Contract Extension

## Definition

A contract extension is a new agreement that lengthens (and typically updates the pay of) an existing player's or coach's deal with their current team before that deal expires, keeping them with the same organization rather than letting them reach free agency.

## Context

The corpus uses the term across coaching and playing contexts on both sides of an expiring-deal decision point: Jim Harbaugh is described as facing a choice between signing a contract extension at Michigan or leaving for the NFL, while Oregon State's Jonathan Smith received a contract extension through February 2029 (raising his salary to $4.85 million) only for Michigan State to hire him away regardless.
NFL coverage frames the extension as a retention tool used on a player nearing the end of his rookie or veteran deal: Chicago is noted as having "traded for and signed Montez Sweat to a lucrative contract extension," and Detroit's Jared Goff is described as "heading toward a likely contract extension" while still under contract with the Lions.
The corpus also surfaces a cautionary counter-case at Michigan State, where Mel Tucker's 2021 breakout season earned him a 10-year, $95 million contract extension shortly before his tenure collapsed amid misconduct allegations and a for-cause firing — illustrating that an extension is a bet on future performance, not a guarantee of it.
A related but distinct surface form in the corpus, "deal worth," reports the monetary value of a transfer or free-agent signing (e.g., Cole Palmer's move to Chelsea "in a deal worth around $A82 million," Casemiro's "four-year deal worth about £350,000 a week," Victor Caratini's "two-year deal worth $12 million") — these describe a new signing or trade, not the retention of an existing player by their current team, and so are adjacent to but not synonymous with a contract extension.

## Key Characteristics

- **Retention before expiry** — an extension is negotiated while the person is still under their current contract, pre-empting free agency (Harbaugh at Michigan, Goff at Detroit).
- **Term and pay change together** — extensions typically both lengthen the deal and raise pay, as with Jonathan Smith's extension through February 2029 at $4.85 million annually, and Tucker's 10-year, $95 million deal.
- **Used as a retention signal amid uncertainty** — Oregon State's athletic director called reaching an extension with Smith the program's "No. 1 priority" once speculation grew that he might leave, and Chicago signed Montez Sweat to a contract extension immediately after trading for him.
- **Not a guarantee of outcome** — an extension can precede departure anyway (Smith left Oregon State for Michigan State despite his extension) or precede collapse (Tucker was fired for cause not long after his extension).
- **Distinct from "deal worth" reporting** — corpus language describing a new signing or trade's dollar value ("deal worth $X") refers to acquiring a player, not extending an existing one.

# Spider-Man 2 and the Canon Events Critique

Polygon's claim on 2023-10-16 is that while Marvel's Spider-Man 2 does not push against established Spider-Man story as hard as the critic wanted, where it does go is still satisfyingly slant — and that this matters, because if we are going to retell a story we ought to retell it anew: canons were made to be broken, and Spider-Man 2 swings in that direction.

The standard the critic sets is high, and named: they were hungry for the game to treat the established story like Angela Carter repurposing "Little Red Riding Hood" to her whims, like Michael Cunningham plumbing "Rumpelstiltskin" for a story about the desire to have a child, or like Helen Oyeyemi and her body of work — or, in mass media terms, like Star Wars: Visions, which gives creative leeway to a variety of animators and storytellers to play with the very basics of what makes Star Wars Star Wars.

The grounds for the qualified verdict are that wrinkles to critical characters and plot points keep even seasoned Spider-fans on their toes, and that the game plays like a dream: smart additions to combat enhance the power fantasy, with each Spider-Man having a full arsenal of special moves and gadgets that complement one another, making even the most basic encounter feel like a choreographed ballet of kicks, thwips, and zaps. It is beautifully rendered, taking full advantage of the newest PlayStation, with textures on each unlockable suit so detailed you would swear they were real and ray-traced window after ray-traced window in a loving rendition of New York — if you can get past the Frankenstein-ification of the boroughs.

The critic also registers what the game gestures at but cannot develop: hints of greater thematic aspirations appear, including questions about mass incarceration, recidivism, and reintegration into society for formerly incarcerated people, and worries about the surveillance state and what we give up when we engage with modern technology. # Wearable Device

## Definition

In this corpus, "wearable device" (or "wearable") is the umbrella term outlets use for a body-worn consumer or health-tech gadget — a smartwatch, fitness ring, fitness band, or medical-sensing device — interchangeably with specific products like the Apple Watch, Google Pixel Watch, Whoop 4, Ultrahuman Ring Air, and Acurable's respiratory monitors.

## Context

The corpus uses "wearable" as the umbrella term spanning consumer smartwatches (Apple Watch, Google Pixel Watch, Samsung Galaxy Watch), fitness rings (Ultrahuman Ring Air), fitness bands (Whoop 4), and specialized medical-sensing gadgets (Acurable's respiratory monitors, the Willow Go wearable breast pump). Some wearables are purely consumer-facing fitness/lifestyle products sold through holiday deals coverage, while others sit at the boundary of consumer electronics and regulated medical devices — the Apple Watch's SpO2 blood-oxygen sensor and EKG feature are the clearest example, since they triggered patent litigation with medical device makers Masimo and AliveCor over the underlying sensing technology. Acurable is described explicitly as "a medical device company that makes patient-friendly wearable devices to diagnose and manage respiratory conditions at home," showing wearables also serving a clinical diagnostic role outside the smartwatch category.

## Key Characteristics

- **Body-worn form factor** — worn on the wrist (Apple Watch, Pixel Watch, Whoop 4, Galaxy Watch), finger (Ultrahuman Ring Air), or elsewhere on the body (Acurable's respiratory monitors, Willow Go breast pump).
- **On-board sensing** — wearables carry sensors such as accelerometers, gyroscopes, optical heart-rate sensors, and SpO2 (blood-oxygen) sensors; the Apple Watch Series 9's double-tap gesture, for instance, is detected from accelerometer, gyroscope, and optical heart-rate data collected at the wrist.
- **Companion-app dependence** — many wearables (Whoop 4, Ultrahuman Ring Air) have no display of their own and instead offload data to a smartphone app for analysis and coaching.
- **Health/medical crossover** — some wearables function as, or overlap with, regulated medical devices: the Apple Watch's SpO2 and EKG features became the subject of ITC patent disputes with medical device makers Masimo and AliveCor, and Acurable markets its wearables as home-use medical devices to diagnose and manage respiratory conditions such as sleep apnea.
- **Rapid feature iteration** — newer models add capabilities like Sleep Profiles, abnormal heart-rate tracking, and gesture controls (double tap), often gated behind newer chips (the Apple Watch Series 9's S9 chip with four neural engines).

## Background (external)

Outside this corpus, the general definition is broader than any single corpus device: wearable technology comprises small electronic and mobile devices, worn on the body or built into clothing or accessories, that commonly detect and transmit information such as vital signs, sometimes with immediate biofeedback to the wearer (Wikipedia, "Wearable technology," accessed 2026-09-02, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wearable_technology).

# Wearable Fitness Tracker

## Definition

A wearable fitness tracker is a wrist-worn device — spanning dedicated fitness bands such as the Fitbit Charge 6 and general-purpose smartwatches such as the Apple Watch and Google Pixel Watch — that uses onboard sensors to track a person's activity and health signals, including heart rate, blood oxygen saturation (SpO2), and wrist-motion data, and displays the results on-device (doc_0222, doc_0241, doc_0491).

## Context

In the corpus, the category shows up almost entirely through product coverage of the two dominant lines: Apple Watch (Series 9, Ultra 2, SE) and Fitbit/Google's Pixel Watch, alongside Samsung's Galaxy Watch and dedicated bands like the Fitbit Charge 6.
Reviewers repeatedly frame the Apple Watch as "an excellent fitness companion, offering comprehensive health and activity data," and describe the Apple Watch SE's "fitness features and tracking data" as "well-rounded" even though it omits pricier sensors like blood oxygen (doc_0104, doc_0091).
The Fitbit Charge 6 is described as a dedicated fitness tracker distinct from a smartwatch, with an AMOLED touchscreen for activity stats, built-in GPS for outdoor workouts, and week-long battery life (doc_0222).
The first-generation Google Pixel Watch is presented as a smartwatch whose fitness-tracking capability comes from native Fitbit integration, including FDA-cleared EKGs; the same article notes the first-gen model omits the Sleep Profiles, abnormal heart-rate tracking, and nightly SpO2 features that arrived with the second-generation Pixel Watch (doc_0069).
A separate corpus thread ties the category's sensor hardware directly to a patent fight: Apple Watch Series 9 and Ultra 2 use an SpO2 (blood oxygen saturation) sensor that Masimo successfully argued infringed its pulse-oximetry patents, leading the ITC to order an import ban on those two watches (doc_0241).
The corpus also documents how newer silicon expands what a wrist-worn tracker can sense and act on: the Apple Watch Series 9's S9 chip adds four neural engines that process wrist accelerometer, gyroscope, and optical heart-rate sensor data to recognize the Double Tap gesture, a feature unavailable on older Apple Watches that lack that chip (doc_0491).

## Key Characteristics

- **Wrist-worn form factor** — the category covers both single-purpose bands (Fitbit Charge 6) and multi-purpose smartwatches (Apple Watch, Pixel Watch, Galaxy Watch) that add fitness tracking to broader smart functionality (doc_0222, doc_0069).
- **Core sensed metrics** — step count, heart rate, and activity/workout data are baseline across models; higher-end devices add blood oxygen (SpO2) sensing and GPS for mapping outdoor workouts (doc_0104, doc_0222).
- **Tiered sensor availability** — cheaper models in a lineup (e.g., Apple Watch SE) drop specialized sensors like the blood oxygen app while keeping core step/activity tracking, distinguishing entry-level from flagship tiers (doc_0091, doc_0104).
- **On-wrist signal processing is noisy** — detecting subtle wrist gestures and vitals requires filtering accelerometer, gyroscope, and optical heart-rate data against motion artifacts from the arm, muscles, and individual differences in wrist size (doc_0491).
- **Sensor IP is contested territory** — the SpO2 sensor at the center of the Apple–Masimo dispute shows that the sensing hardware inside these devices can itself be the subject of patent litigation with real market consequences (an import ban) (doc_0241).
- **Ecosystem integration matters** — fitness data on a smartwatch is often powered by a partner platform (Fitbit integration on the Pixel Watch) rather than being built entirely in-house (doc_0069).

# Mary Jane's Mission Pacing And The Verdict On Spider-Man 2

Essentially Sports argued on 1 November 2023 that the best thing about Mary Jane's quests in Marvel's Spider-Man 2 is that they never try to overpower the ongoing story: the claim is that restraint improves them, and the warrant is that keeping her sequences within limits lets each character shine without her missions overlapping Peter's or Miles' stories.

The grounds are about proportion. The game's narrative remains intact no matter what, and there never occurs a feeling of the developers trying too hard to make her missions stretch beyond their boundaries; although they are designed well this time, the article commends Insomniac's team for keeping a limit on not making MJ's gameplay moments seem forced or going beyond a certain point. # Platform Culture As A Model Of Political Engagement

The model TechCrunch sets out on 2023-10-02 is that to engage with users online, politicians must understand the culture of the platform — the relation between cultural fit and engagement outcome holds regardless of a politician's reach or resources. On the behaviour side, Ocasio-Cortez is a regular gamer herself and is up to date on the most popular games on Twitch: in 2020 it was "Among Us," while in her most recent stream she played the cooperative puzzle game "Pico Park."
