# Mary Jane's Missions In Spider-Man 2 As An Improvement On Their Reception

Essentially Sports argued on 1 November 2023 that Mary Jane's arc in Marvel's Spider-Man 2 received an impressive elevation over the poorly received missions featuring her in the original 2018 game: the claim is that she can now be called the third unofficial superhero in the latest PS5 exclusive, and the warrant is that the developers gave her the means to fight back, which converts her missions from movement exercises into ones players have a reason to be invested in.

The starting point is the reception problem. In the first title, stepping into MJ's shoes was a great concept, but the developers somehow couldn't execute the plan flawlessly, and missions featuring her as a playable character were heavily criticised by most fans, with nothing too special about those quests whatsoever. Insomniac's sequel, by contrast, has witnessed huge appreciation from fans for delivering a memorable sequel, alongside the epic portrayal of Peter Parker and Miles Morales fighting some of the strongest villains.

The grounds for the improvement are mechanical. Being a journalist at The Daily Bugle, her character is bound to go places to investigate mysteries; the first game had such situations, but the sequel improved on them, giving MJ a lot more strength instead of making her someone who always needs rescuing at the last moment. Compared with the lack of interactivity in 2018's Spider-Man, where all she could do was move from one point to another, MJ is now capable of tackling the enemies around her and making pretty good and lethal moves: the developers have given her a little firepower, if not in too much capacity, so she has weapons instead of being clueless in moments of vulnerability against armed enemies. She has no superpowers, but she has other means to help herself out. Because of that involvement, players now have a reason to be more invested in a given MJ mission, and she can handle circumstances in her own manner, breaking free from the linear approach of just trying to hide and escape. # Melissa Lucashenko: Family History, Late-Discovered Ancestry And A Writing Career

Melissa Lucashenko is a novelist preoccupied with survival who knows a lot about it personally. Born to an Aboriginal mother, Cecile, and a Russian-speaking Ukrainian father — Vladimir Lucashenko, known as Wally Lucas, whose family fled the Russian Revolution via China — she and her six older brothers grew up on the outskirts of Logan, south of Brisbane, in circumstances where the chances of becoming an author, let alone a celebrated one, were remote. "My father was a meatworker and a cane cutter … Mum worked at a fish and chip shop and sold plants at the local markets," she says. "Mum left school in about grade three or four. She was a domestic from a very young age, as her mother and grandmother were. At one point as a young mother she was working three jobs. Dad went to high school but I'm not sure how far he got. As a child, he was in an orphanage in Brisbane at one point with his brothers, after his father was violent, and his mother needed to escape."

She did not know she was of Aboriginal descent until she was 15, when someone she knew "picked it" and told her, "You're Aboriginal … go home and ask your parents." Around that time a photo appeared on her mother's dresser of "this very black woman"; when she asked who it was, her mother said, "Oh, that's my grandmother. That's why we've all got olive skin and dark hair." Lucashenko was shocked and felt "momentary disquiet", something she attributes to internalised racism, but says it "instantly made sense". "For the 40 years since then, I've been learning the culture and I've had different teachers from different mobs and I've taught other people what I know." She later learnt that her grandmother Eleanor had defeated an attempt by authorities to remove her as a child in about 1907 or 1908, in Wolvi in Queensland's Gympie region, and that her great-grandmother Christina Copson had worked as a domestic servant from the age of eight: "She was a slave, she had no rights." The family came under extra scrutiny after Copson shot and injured a man who tried to rape her; she was arrested and jailed for a week, told the judge she had acted in self-defence, and was found not guilty, with her perpetrator jailed for six months instead. The would-be rapist was an Aboriginal man — "No way she would have gotten away with shooting a white assailant," Lucashenko says.

# PhilHealth's Earmarked Revenue Model As A Template For PhilEd

PhilHealth's financing model combines member premiums and local government subsidies for enrolled indigents with earmarked national revenues. It receives a share of the "sin taxes" collected from tobacco and sugar-sweetened beverages, justified on the ground that tobacco smokers and sugar-sweetened beverage drinkers impose an additional burden on the healthcare system and so must contribute to health services; in Fiscal Year 2022 this amounted to P74 billion. Under the Universal Health Care Law, PhilHealth also receives 50% of the government share from the income of the Philippine Amusement Gaming Corp. and 40% of the Charity Fund of the Philippine Charity Sweepstakes Office, which in 2022 amounted to P188 billion.

# Philippine Debt And The Case For Fiscal Consolidation

The argument for fiscal consolidation is that although the current 61% debt-to-GDP ratio may be manageable for an emerging economy like the Philippines for some time, the country may not have the fiscal space to respond to another potential domestic or external shock. The grounds are historical: the National Government's debt was less than 40% before the pandemic struck, and it expended much of its fiscal space combatting the pandemic, incurring debt and large budget deficits. The warrant is a crowding-out mechanism: if the debt continues to rise more than the economy, risks will increase and the government may crowd out private investment as it competes with the private sector for funds to service its debt.

The planned consolidation entails harmonizing revenue needs with the promotion of investment through the structure and administration of the reformed incentive system. The National Government plans to raise more revenue to finance the country's socio-economic needs, largely through a progressive and simplified tax system and more efficient and effective tax collection measures through digitalization, and to some extent from policy measures such as value-added tax on digital service providers and excise tax on sweetened beverages and junk food. The conclusion is stated as a conditional pair: achieving fiscal stability presupposes the sustainability of fiscal policy, and fiscal stability helps crowd in private investment.

# Public Health Guidance

## Definition

Public health guidance, in the corpus, is the population-level recommendations and standards that named authorities — the CDC and the WHO — issue on vaccination, disease-eradication targets, dietary/consumer advice, and antibiotic-resistance standards, as distinct from a clinician's advice to an individual patient.

## Context

In the corpus this guidance takes several concrete forms. The CDC recommends that everyone 6 months and older get a flu vaccine every season, an estimate it grounds in a documented burden of nine million illnesses, four million medical visits, 10,000 hospitalizations, and 5,000 deaths in the 2021-2022 season alone.
The WHO similarly issues disease-eradication targets, such as its aim to eradicate Hepatitis C by 2030, and consumer-facing advice, such as advising against sugar substitutes for weight loss or disease prevention.
On antibiotic resistance, the CDC tracks 18 concerning bacteria for rising drug resistance and the WHO defines a "priority" list of bacteria that new antibiotics should target, and both agencies' guidance underpins hospital-level antibiotic stewardship efforts such as auditing prescriptions and requiring special clearance for the broadest-spectrum drugs.

## Key Characteristics

- **Issued by named authorities** — the corpus attributes guidance specifically to the CDC and the WHO, not to unnamed "experts" or generic health advice.
- **Population-level rationale** — guidance is justified by aggregate burden data (illnesses, hospitalizations, deaths, or bacterial deaths worldwide) rather than any single patient's case.
- **Spans prevention and treatment-adjacent domains** — the corpus shows guidance covering vaccination recommendations, dietary/consumer advice, and antibiotic-prescribing standards.
- **Operationalized locally** — guidance translates into concrete institutional practice, such as hospital antibiotic stewardship programs auditing individual prescriptions to lower "overall population-level risk."
- **Distinct from individual clinical advice** — Dr. Gregg Sylvester's public comments urging flu vaccination echo the CDC's population-level recommendation, but they are expert commentary given to the press rather than a treating clinician's advice to a specific patient.

## Background (external)

More broadly (outside this corpus), public health is "the science of protecting and improving the health of people and their communities," concerned with protecting the health of entire populations — from a neighborhood to a country or region — through prevention, policy recommendations, and health communication, distinct from healthcare professionals like doctors and nurses, who "provide care to individuals and meet their individual needs" (CDC Foundation, "What is Public Health?", accessed 2026-09-02, https://www.cdcfoundation.org/what-public-health).

# Balanced Versus Deficit Budget in Philippine Fiscal Practice

The DBM calls a budget balanced when revenues match expenditures or disbursements. When expenditures exceed revenues, the government incurs a deficit, which may lead to three situations: the government borrows money either from foreign sources or from the domestic capital market, which increases the debt stock of the National Government and its debt servicing requirements; the government borrows money from the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas; or the government withdraws funds from its cash balances in the Treasury.

The historical case is one of persistent deficits. National Government expenditures have always exceeded total revenues, resulting in annual budget deficits, the DBM declared, and "the National Government had to resort to borrowing to cover said deficits which resulted in the ballooning of foreign and domestic debts," the budget office admitted.

The boundary case is 1994: "in 1994, the government broke the deficit trend by posting a budget surplus of P16 billion through an aggressive privatization and revenue generation program and a prudent expenditure program. Since then, the government has been exerting efforts to maintain the surplus budget policy. The surplus budget policy is important to encourage economic growth," the DBM said.

# Bankman-Fried's Pre-Collapse Public Image Strategy

Before his fall, Bankman-Fried made himself out to be the Good Boy of crypto — the trustworthy face of a sometimes-shady industry — and he was very interested in publicity, sitting for many interviews both before and after the collapse of FTX.

# Meta Bias Mechanisms

Meta's disproportionate suppression of Palestinian and Arabic content is produced by a stack of interacting mechanisms rather than any single fault: thin Arabic language resources, categorical policies that cannot handle nuance, a blanket prohibition on support for terrorist organizations, government partnerships that shape policy decisions, automated enforcement backed by "minimally trained humans," and an allocation of moderation resources that tracks regulatory pressure rather than need. TechCrunch set out this account on 19 October 2023, drawing chiefly on the Electronic Frontier Foundation.

The linguistic layer comes first. Meta struggles to navigate the cultural and linguistic nuances of Arabic, a language with over 25 dialects, and has been criticized for neglecting to adequately diversify its language resources. On top of that, the company's black-and-white policies often preclude it from effectively moderating any nuanced topic — content that discusses violence without condoning it is the example given.

The policy layer compounds it. Meta forbids support of terrorist organizations, as most U.S.-based social media companies do, but struggles to moderate content around that prohibition, from user discourse to journalistic updates. Combined with the company's partnership with Israel to monitor posts that incite violence, the rule complicates matters for Palestinians living under Hamas' governance: as EFF points out, something as simple as Hamas' flag in the background of an image can result in a strike. Advocacy groups have separately raised concerns that Meta's partnerships with government agencies, such as the Israeli Cyber Unit, politically influence the platform's policy decisions.

The enforcement layer supplies the inconsistency. Jillian York, EFF's director for international freedom of expression, blames automation and decisions made by "minimally trained humans," and says Meta's zero tolerance policy and imprecise enforcement often suppress content from or about conflict zones. The range of the effect is wider than Palestine: the site's moderation issues have negatively affected multiple non-English speaking regions, including Libya, Syria and Ukraine. "These rules can prevent people from sharing documentation of human rights violations, documentation of war crimes, even just news about what's happening on the ground," York said. "And so I think that is what is the most problematic right now about that particular rule, and the way that it's enforced."

The resourcing layer explains why the effect is unevenly distributed across languages. York says Meta has made more contact with regional Palestinian organizations since 2021 but has been slow to implement recommendations from EFF and other advocacy groups, and that it is "very clear" Meta is not putting the same resources behind Arabic and other non-English languages compared with the attention it gives countries that exert the most regulatory pressure. Moderation of English and other European languages tends to be more comprehensive, for example, because the EU enforces the Digital Services Act.

Meta contests the picture. In its response to the report, human rights director Miranda Sissons said the company was "assessing the feasibility" of reviewing Arabic content by dialect and that it has "large and diverse teams" who understand "local cultural context across the region," including in Palestine; responding to the escalating violence earlier that month, Meta said it had established a "special operations center" staffed with fluent Hebrew and Arabic speakers to monitor and respond to violating content. Despite those apparent efforts, Arabic is still disproportionately flagged as violating — as in the case of journalists reporting news in multiple languages.

# Red-Teaming

## Definition

Red-teaming, as it appears in the corpus, is a named testing practice whose adequacy Paul Barrett says the federal government would need additional resources from Congress to actually assess, alongside the complexity of an AI system's training process.
The corpus itself never explains what the practice involves — it treats the term as already familiar to readers.

## Context

In the corpus the term surfaces in reactions to Biden's October 2023 AI executive order, where it is invoked as a benchmark the federal government would need resources to actually evaluate rather than a practice the EO itself defines or mandates in detail.
Paul Barrett, deputy director of the NYU Stern Center for Business and Human Rights, argued that without fresh resources from Congress, "it's not clear that the federal government has the resources to assess the vastly complicated training process or the adequacy of red-teaming and other necessary testing."
That framing ties red-teaming to the broader argument (also captured in the corpus) that an executive order alone cannot supply the institutional capacity — funding, staff, technical expertise — needed to verify that AI developers' safety testing is sufficient.

## Key Characteristics

- **Named but undefined in the corpus** — doc_0098 uses "red-teaming" only inside Barrett's quote, grouped with "other necessary testing," without describing what the practice involves (doc_0098).
- **One of two things Barrett says need assessing** — Barrett names "the adequacy of red-teaming and other necessary testing," alongside "the vastly complicated training process," as the two things the federal government lacks the resources to assess (doc_0098).
- **Resource-dependent oversight** — the corpus frames evaluating red-teaming adequacy as something the federal government currently lacks the resources to do without additional congressional funding, underscoring that red-teaming claims by AI developers are not independently verified by government within the EO's framework (doc_0098).

## Background (external)

The corpus mentions red-teaming only as a term assumed familiar to readers, without defining the practice itself.
Per NIST's AI Risk Management Framework, red-teaming is a structured exercise in which testers deliberately attempt to identify flaws and vulnerabilities in an AI system, such as harmful or discriminatory outputs, security weaknesses, or ways the system's safeguards can be circumvented, typically under adversarial or unusual conditions (NIST, *AI Risk Management Framework*, accessed 2026-09-02).
Biden's October 2023 executive order itself later directed NIST to set guidelines for red-team testing of AI models before public release, which is the broader regulatory backdrop the corpus's commentators are reacting to.

# The EU AI Office And Its Scientific Advisory Panel

The AI Act will be implemented through a new AI Office set up within the EU's executive, which will coordinate with the Member State oversight bodies that will need to enforce the rules on AI firms and will oversee the most advanced AI models, including by contributing to fostering standards and testing practices — with a scientific panel of independent experts appointed to advise it about GPAI models.

Per internal market commissioner Thierry Breton, work to implement the agreement starts immediately with the set up of the AI Office. "We will welcome new colleagues… a lot of them," said Breton. "We will work — starting tomorrow — to get ready." The AI Office will play a key role in setting risk classification thresholds for GPAIs, but the Commission confirmed there is no budget nor headcount defined for the expert body as yet. Asked about resourcing, a Commission official said it will be decided in the future by the EU's executive taking "an appropriate and official decision," adding: "The idea is that we can create a dedicated budget line for the Office and that we will be able also to recruit the national experts from Member States if we wish to on top of contractual agents and on top of permanent staff. And some of these staff will also be deployed within the European Commission."

The scientific advisory panel, which the law will also establish, is meant to help the Office better understand the capabilities of advanced AI models for the purpose of regulating systemic risk. "We have identified an important role for a scientific panel to be set up where the scientific panel can effectively help the Artificial Intelligence Office in understanding whether there are new risks that have not been yet identified," the official noted. "And, for example, also flag some alerts about the models that are not captured by the FLOP threshold that for certain reasons could actually give rise to important risks that governments should should look at."

# Why A Health System Needs A Chief AI Officer

Mayo Clinic's new chief AI officer argues that AI's sweeping impact and fast growth create the need for a dedicated leadership position, because only a dedicated executive can ensure "clear direction and alignment with broader organizational goals" while balancing the technology's risks against its benefits.

The premise is the scale of the change. In an interview with Fox News Digital, Patel described AI as a "transformative force that has the potential to revolutionize health care delivery, research and operations."

The risk half of the argument supplies the warrant for oversight rather than diffuse ownership. "While AI brings forth myriad benefits, it also carries inherent risks," he said. "A CAIO provides the necessary oversight to ensure that the implementation of AI is ethical, responsible and in line with regulatory guidelines." A chief AI officer also "bridges the knowledge gap," he said, helping teams understand and harness the technology's power. The role is also important in terms of maximizing the use of resources, fostering collaboration across departments and keeping up with future health tech trends, Patel added.

He frames the position as more than technical. "Their expertise is critical in ensuring that the organization remains on the cutting edge of technological advancements while safeguarding patient welfare," he said. "In essence, the chief AI officer is not just a technocrat, but a visionary leader, ensuring that the organization navigates the AI-driven paradigm shift in health care with agility, responsibility and a patient-centric approach."

Castro agreed that the importance of this role is evident as AI becomes a pivotal part of health care. "A chief AI officer can oversee the use and development of AI technologies, ensuring that they are leveraged effectively for patient care, data management and other applications," he said.

# ASPI's Analysis Of TikTok Pixel Data Aggregation Risk

Researchers at the Australian Strategic Policy Institute argue that the danger of TikTok's tracking pixel lies less in the type of data collected — which resembles what US tech giants gather — than in how that data can be aggregated and in who can ultimately reach it.

Jocelinn Kang, a technical specialist at the institute, said data from a tracking pixel could be aggregated across websites, apps and social media platforms, and that pixel tracking could identify users through their "browser fingerprint," a combination of their IP address, browser and system details. The linking gets sharper as identifiers accumulate: "However, when more identifying data such as email and phone number is associated with a user, their web activity can be better linked," Kang said.

Strategic Policy Institute researcher Samantha Hoffman said the data collected by TikTok's pixel was similar to that of US-based tech giants Google and Meta, but that the difference was "the intent." Advertising data had "incredible propaganda value," she said, and the warrant joining that to the risk is state access: "If you think about that, plus the access that TikTok is required to give the Chinese government, that's the problem." She notes TikTok itself made that access explicit — in November 2022 the company changed its privacy policy to state clearly that user data can be accessed by some employees from across the world, including China. "They talk about how even data collected overseas can be used by the company and its partners, and would be kept private unless security organisations make demands of it," Hoffman said. China's national intelligence laws allow the government to pull data upon request from companies based there.

# The Clock Change And Road Accident Risk

The Royal Society for the Prevention of Accidents (RoSPA) has called for the abolition of Daylight Saving Time on road-safety grounds, arguing that turning the clocks back increases the risk of road accidents because more people end up driving during the darker winter months. Its proposed remedy is to adopt British Summer Time permanently: "RoSPA is in favour of this proposal, and is calling for the government to adopt British Summer Time (GMT+1) all year. This would mean road users will no longer experience the sudden onset of darkness during their autumn commutes, potentially saving many lives."

The quantitative grounds come from RAC Foundation figures cited in support of abolishing DST: road traffic collisions increase by 19 per cent in the fortnight after the clocks go back one hour from British Summer Time, and reduce by 11 per cent when the clocks go forward.

# Google Local Search Ranking Factors

Google's public documentation says it uses three categories to rank results that are local to a searcher: relevance, distance, and prominence. To improve local ranking, Google encourages businesses to provide a trove of information on their profile — basics like updated hours of operation and accurate location details, but also responding to reviews, adding photos, and even posting individual items in stock to their Google page. The prominence measure in Maps includes data from the web: links to the business, how the business ranks in traditional search, and press coverage, for example. In this way SEO affects how a business appears in local search results, and news articles and links are one way Google tries to determine the relevance of a page — which is why reporters' inboxes are overrun with spammy requests to buy "guest posts" on their sites from marketers.

The model bounds what a keyword-matched business name can do. Asked whether naming a business after a search term works, Danny Sullivan, Google's public liaison for Search, said, "I doubt it": owners doing this might find success, but Google pulls in other data to serve results to users, like location, reviews, or ratings — a "hodgepodge of different things that we have that are out there." Sullivan added, "I've seen these kinds of things over the years, and they kind of make me laugh and have a bit of a chuckle. But I don't think they're really great marketing campaigns," and said Google's advice has always been that businesses should make decisions that serve their customers, not the platform.

The behaviour the names target is real even if the leverage is limited. The term "Thai food near me" is searched, on average, nearly a million times a month in the US, according to Semrush, a company that provides keyword research and other popular SEO tools; Semrush notes you will need referring domains and optimized content to compete for the term and grades it as "difficult" to rank for — competitive, but not even the hardest category. Adding "near me" to a search term is both a learned behavior and encouraged by Google, since "___ near me" is a top autofilled search suggestion on both Search and Maps and has become synonymous with Google, which is why the joke works. One anomaly showed the distance factor being outweighed: a search The Verge's reporter did in Google Maps for "Thai food near me" from Wisconsin surfaced the Manhattan restaurant as a suggestion above any local businesses, making it easier to find from the Midwest than from Brooklyn. Sullivan said this could be due to Google recognizing there is a business with an exact-match name that has some degree of notoriety that people are searching for in different areas, and that while it could encourage others to name businesses this way, he does not see it as an issue that needs addressing.

# Why IMPA Saw No Pre-Attack Funding Spike

Asked where IMPA was before October 7, given the general debate about why the intelligence agencies gave no warning, Ostrovitch-Levi rejects the premise that a financing signal was there to be seen: "We had no possibility of seeing a spike in fundraising towards October 7."

Her grounds are that the money flow is continuous rather than event-driven, and mostly offshore: "Hamas collects lots of money all the time, and the security agencies deter money transfers. There was no sudden increase in the raising of billions, and you must also remember that most of the money is raised globally, not in Israel. The hundreds of millions of dollars that Hamas receives have been accumulating for years."



---


# Israel's Money Laundering And Terror Financing Prohibition Authority

IMPA is an intelligence body that conducts the most complex international economic investigations and fights terror financing routinely; it has been headed by Adv. Ilit Ostrovitch-Levi since May 2022, and since October 7 most of its work has focused on identifying and blocking terror money pipelines.

Ostrovitch-Levi describes the pivot: "Already on that Saturday night, with Israel under heavy rocket fire, we talked about preparing ourselves for the campaign we're now entering, the fight against terror financing channels. Dozens of our staff have been called up to reserve duty, in large part managers working regularly in the fight against terror financing." The working method is deliberately reactive and continuous: "We work very reactively – we see a fundraising campaign, try to deter it, and stop it from happening again. There are no breaks, because they are constantly active. It's a daily struggle. Our analysts have been sitting on the social networks from day two of the war, just manually monitoring visible sources of information on these networks to locate fundraising campaigns for terrorist organizations operating in Gaza." Three days after the war began, IMPA also issued a call to all global regulated entities for increased vigilance towards terrorism financing campaigns in response to the ongoing war and state of emergency, and to report all activities that raise suspicion of terror support and terror financing in an effective and immediate manner.



---


# Iran's State Funding Of Hamas

"The most significant way to finance terrorism is to finance countries, not fundraising campaigns," Ostrovitch-Levi says: campaigns have intensified greatly over the last month, but the core of the budget for Hamas, Hezbollah, the Houthis and Palestinian Islamic Jihad is Iran, in particular the Quds Force, the special forces of the IRGC.

The dependence is presented as decisive: Hamas has all kinds of additional sources of self-financing — businesses, associations, investments, and all kinds of arrangements it has tried to set up over the years — but "They need state funding, and without Iran they have no ability to exist." On scale: "As far as we know, the budget from Iran to Gaza is in the order of $100 million a year. Gaza could do very nice things with this money, make it even more beautiful than Dubai. But from what we know, most of this budget goes to the military wing of Hamas." Qatar is a distinct case: "Qatar transferred suitcases of cash to Gaza through Israel. Everyone knows this. This money allegedly went to pay salaries and civilian needs (education, health, infrastructure), and therefore Israel transferred it, so it's incorrect to say that it all went to fund terrorism." IMPA is charged with rooting out the sources of funding for terrorism, working together with the National Bureau for Counter Terror Financing of Israel (NBCTF) in the Ministry of Defense, which coordinates all activities to thwart terror financing, along with the Shin Bet, Military Intelligence Directorate (AMAN), and all other relevant intelligence and security agencies.



---


# Kishida's Pitch to Global Investors 2023

Japanese prime minister Fumio Kishida was preparing, in the week of 1 October 2023, to make his strongest ever push for a bet on Asia's biggest advanced economy, as BlackRock founder Larry Fink and other heads of global funds gathered in Tokyo for a series of events to attract investment. "I would urge you to evaluate what we are doing in my country, look at the underlying strength of our economy and our plans for the future and then invest in Japan," Kishida said in a recent speech at the Economic Club of New York.

The pitch followed a month of conferences on the same question. Throughout September, in Tokyo, New York, Hong Kong and London, the world's biggest investment banks hosted a series of conferences for the world's biggest investors, all gravitating around the theme of whether Japan is really back. The events were run by JPMorgan, Goldman Sachs, Bank of America, Mizuho, BNP Paribas and Jefferies, and according to both attendees and hosts the answer is now clearer than it has been in a very long time: Japan is back, but global investors may take a little more persuasion that it is truly back for the duration.



---


# IMPA's Blocking Of A Hamas Fundraising Pipeline In Europe

Two weeks into the war, the Israel Money Laundering and Terror Financing Prohibition Authority received secret intelligence from two European countries warning that "A large, well-known organization is raising funds for Hamas through posts on social networks, and fintech company platforms outside Israel, under the guise of donations to Gaza residents" — and in a swift joint international action, at IMPA's request, one of the European countries blocked the organization's money pipeline by immediately freezing its financial activities.

The intelligence included the name of the organization, its fundraising methods, and the identity of the entities behind it, and the concern was that within days the millions of dollars raised would go directly to the military arm of Hamas. "We are talking about a matter of minutes here. From the moment the authorities in Europe received the information, and we requested the money be blocked, with no court orders or delay, they blocked the transfer of millions of dollars to one of the most active organizations, and from it to Hamas. This is a real-time deterrence," IMPA director general Adv. Ilit Ostrovitch-Levi said. "And then there was a domino effect. Following this blocking, more countries began to look around, and blocked funds intended for terror. All this information, which is now shared at an international level, leads to the closing of more and more Hamas funding pipelines, in real time. With worldwide cooperation, Israel's security and enforcement authorities are thwarting the transfer of millions of dollars earmarked for terrorism, every day."



---


# The Surge In Terror Financing Reports After October 7

Before October 7, IMPA received about 100 reports a day dealing with terror financing; that number jumped to about 1,000 — a 900% increase.

"Overnight, we started receiving hundreds of reports about unusual activity by customers of financial institutions in the State of Israel," Ostrovitch-Levi says. "There is a 900% increase in reports on terror financing, and we don't waste time, everything happens very, very quickly. As we receive the information, we simultaneously pass it on to the operational professionals who locate the money pipelines, and block them. Some information will not necessarily lead to terror financing, but we don't have time to waste. Bank CEOs call and draw our attention to the information they convey to us that warrants special attention." Asked whether information from banks and financial institutions has led to blocking a money pipeline for terrorism, she said: "There was very high-quality intelligence that we passed on to the security agencies. We don't always know the results."



---


# The International Terror Finance Task Force

On the third day of the fighting, the veteran heads of the Netherlands and German anti-money-laundering authorities phoned Ostrovitch-Levi to say they wanted to establish an international task force to assist Israel in the fight against the financing of Hezbollah, Islamic Jihad, and all terrorist organizations and their satellites — and with them and the US, "we established a kind of task force, which is not subject to any country or unifying body, countries that are working in coordination, and meet every few days to exchange intelligence, and advance the struggle."

The measurable effect is in intelligence volume: following an appeal by IMPA to its counterparts around the world, "The amount of information doubled in the month of fighting, compared with the monthly average. Before the war, we received about 24 intelligence reports a month from parallel authorities, compared with 50 today." Asked where those countries were before, Ostrovitch-Levi is blunt: "Many countries felt this had nothing to do with them, that it wasn't their struggle. The international and US mobilization, the task force we founded, the fact that the financial sector abroad suddenly wants to accept the Israeli announcements about the terror entities and people involved, receive intelligence from Israel, and cooperate with us is all only because of October 7. Everyone understands that 'The West is next' isn't an empty statement. This event is the one to make the countries of the world understand they must fight effectively against terror financing, that they need to block Iran effectively."

# Venture Capital

## Definition

In the corpus, venture capital (VC) names the money that specialist VC firms — and the individual "venture capitalists" and partners who run them — put into privately held startups, tracked through a sequence of named funding rounds (seed, pre-Series A, Series A through E and beyond) from Thiel's early backing of DeepMind through FTX's $400 million Series C.

## Context

The corpus shows venture capital operating at both ends of the startup lifecycle. Early-stage examples include Thiel's venture capital firm putting £1.4 million into the not-yet-named DeepMind, and Motier Ventures backing Mistral AI's €105 million seed round, Poolside's separate $126 million seed round, and Index Ventures leading (with Iconiq and Motier Ventures also participating in) Adaptive's seed round at a $100 million valuation — all part of "VC firms fighting for the most competitive funding rounds" in the French AI boom. Later-stage venture capital appears in FTX's $400 million Series C round that pushed its valuation to $32 billion, and in Rainforest's Accel-led $8.5 million seed round alongside Bolt's earlier $355 million Series E. The corpus also treats venture capital as an industry with its own geography and macro trends: Sand Hill Road as the physical center of Silicon Valley VC, Sequoia Capital as a "high-powered venture capital firm" whose former partner was among the witnesses lined up to testify in the FTX trial, Israeli startups drawing $95 billion in venture capital over the prior five years even as funding had already fallen 73% year-over-year in the first half of 2023 — a decline reported in July, before the October Hamas attacks further disrupted the sector — and US-headquartered VC investment into China collapsing from $45.4 billion to $14.5 billion between 2021 and 2022 amid Beijing's tech crackdowns and Washington's new restrictions on outbound U.S. investment in Chinese tech.

## Key Characteristics

- **Equity-for-capital exchange with startups** — VCs and VC firms fund privately held companies in return for an ownership stake, as with Thiel's firm taking a position in DeepMind and Accel leading Rainforest's seed round.
- **Staged by named rounds** — investment is tranched into seed, pre-Series A, and Series A/B/C/D rounds that track a company's maturity, illustrated by FTX's Series C, StarNews Mobile's pre-Series A, and Clearco's Series D.
- **Concentrated in identifiable firms and hubs** — a small set of named firms (Sequoia Capital, Accel, Index Ventures, Motier Ventures, Janngo Capital) and physical hubs (Sand Hill Road) recur as the deal-making core of the industry.
- **Sensitive to macro and geopolitical conditions** — VC deployment can swing sharply with regulatory crackdowns and geopolitics, as shown by the drop in US VC activity in China and the 73% year-over-year decline in Israeli startup funding reported in mid-2023, before the October Hamas attacks further disrupted the sector.
- **Distinct from the startups it funds** — the corpus consistently separates the VC firm/investor role (Sequoia, Accel, Janngo Capital, UpWest) from the founder/startup role it capitalizes, even when the same article covers both.

## Background (external)

More broadly, and outside what this corpus documents, venture capital is generally defined as a form of private-equity financing supplied by specialized firms or funds to startup, early-stage, and emerging companies judged to have high growth potential, in exchange for equity or an ownership stake (Wikipedia, "Venture capital," accessed 2026-09-02, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venture_capital).

# The USD Fund Copycat Playbook In China

USD-denominated funds in China have long operated on a benchmark model: draw inspiration from Silicon Valley startups and use them as templates for investment targets back home. They would seek out the equivalents of Facebook, Amazon and Uber on the other side of the Pacific Ocean and hope they become winners in the country's largely untapped internet market.

The range over which that model worked was two decades. Since their entry into China in the late 1990s, American venture capital firms — led by powerhouses like Sequoia Capital, IDG Capital and GGV — have played a major role in funding high-risk, high-reward startups in the country's consumer internet sector.

The relationship now hangs in the balance as changes at home and abroad diminish the pool of investment opportunities for outside financiers. This dealmaking strategy of American funds in China has become less effective in the face of shifting global and domestic landscapes; driven by a confluence of factors, from China's crackdown on the tech industry to escalating U.S.-China tensions, some of these investors are now turning their gaze to opportunities abroad, tracing the footsteps of a new generation of Chinese-founded startups that are expanding overseas.

A major challenge for dementia treatment is the blood-brain barrier, which controls the movement of ions and molecules from the body to the brain and makes it difficult to get drugs into the central nervous system to tackle problems such as amyloid plaques.

# Lecanemab and Donanemab: The Amyloid Drugs

Lecanemab, produced by Japanese pharmaceutical company Eisai, and donanemab, produced by Eli Lilly of the US, are the first medicines to stop amyloid from forming plaques in the brain — though they only slow, and do not ultimately halt, the progression of Alzheimer's disease.

Alzheimer's disease is triggered by the buildup of a protein called amyloid in the brain, although symptoms may not appear for decades after this accretion has started, and scientists have tried for more than 20 years to find ways to stop amyloid from forming these plaques in the hope this would stop the disease's progression. Lecanemab was recently approved in the US and Japan, where treatments using it have already been launched; a second drug, donanemab, is expected to follow soon, and next year it is anticipated that the UK medical authorities will consider both of them for approval in Britain. # Urban Heat Islands and Chronic Heat Health Effects

Urban heat islands — hot zones of a city where asphalt, high building density and infrastructure push temperatures higher than in surrounding areas — house millions of people who cannot escape the effects of relentless summer heat, and chronic exposure to that excess heat affects cardiovascular, respiratory and mental health.

The exposure pathway runs through daily life outdoors. "People who live in urban areas usually walk to do their daily errands. One of the advantages of living in a city is that things are close and you can use public transport, but that also means you have to spend more time outdoors," said Neelima Tummala, a physician and co-director of the Institute for Environmental Health at George Washington University, who was not involved in the study. In neighbourhoods without parks or large trees, where asphalt and buildings absorb and radiate summer heat, residents can find it hard to escape extreme temperatures either indoors or outdoors, and this kind of continuous exposure can be very dangerous because the body becomes unable to cool itself adequately by sweating. "Prolonged exposure to elevated night-time temperatures can affect sleep quality and mental and cardiac health," Tummala said. "You are constantly at an elevated temperature that your body has to deal with."

The proposition is that OpenAI experienced a major, perhaps pervasive, security issue that Altman downplayed. Petersen and Clark worked together as co-CEOs for the first six months, and in March Petersen transitioned to executive chairman — an arrangement meant to free Petersen up to do what he loved, "getting beers with customers," in the words of two former Flexport employees, while Clark, a self-described "builder at heart," was at the wheel. "There's a perfect complement of skill sets," Petersen told Forbes in June 2022. "Mine are much more creative, zero-to-one founder time, and Dave is the supreme executor and a legend in the supply chain world." Buying Deliverr was meant to be the first step in turning Flexport into a more full-scale logistics service. Shopify had acquired Deliverr in May 2022 for $2.1 billion, but the e-commerce software company was being hammered by Wall Street as its Covid pandemic pop faded, and by January 2023 CEO Tobias Lutke knew he needed to get rid of it; around that time Lutke first approached Petersen to float a deal, and Petersen told Clark he should engage with Shopify's team. Initial talks fell apart but resumed when Flexport executives learned Shopify was about to execute deep cost cuts and was eager to sell. Clark and Petersen flew to Miami to meet Shopify's leadership, and as a transaction neared, Clark — who had a reputation as a deft negotiator — got Shopify, already an investor in Flexport, to sweeten it with $40 million in cash and the framework for a $260 million convertible note that could help Flexport on its path to an IPO, according to an internal document analyzing the deal. The sale would be announced alongside Shopify's first-quarter earnings report on May 4. "We did not change the terms of a deal or rush it just to have it line up with an earnings call," Shopify said in a statement, adding that with Flexport "we are tightly mission-aligned to ensure the success of our merchants, which is why we chose to deepen our partnership with them earlier this year." # Cutting Wear Mass May Raise Toxicity

Emissions Analytics' Nick Molden challenges the assumption that reducing tire wear mass is straightforwardly progress: "The reason I'm worried about that is I'm sure you can reduce that wear mass, but if you do that by making the compound more toxic, you could actually make the environmental impact worse."

The premise under attack is that mass of debris is the right measure of environmental harm; the analogy offered is that such a trade could be akin to increasing a car's fuel efficiency by switching to leaded fuel.

Molden's proposed remedy is knowledge rather than a specific target. He believes what is needed is better understanding, and to that end he recently created the Tyre Emissions Research Consortium, a LinkedIn group with about 1,000 members, with the intent of breaking down the silos individual researchers were working in.

# Pew Polling On American EV Purchase Intent

According to Pew Research, 50 percent of US adults say they are unlikely to buy an EV, while 38 percent said they were likely to consider a battery-powered vehicle.

Concerns about charging and range are at the top of the list of reasons. But environmental concerns also rank high, with many people saying they would consider an EV as a way to reduce carbon emissions. The Verge presents these figures as evidence that the concerns among union workers reflect the attitudes of most Americans writ large.
